units.la: Ecclesiam Unćti sui modernam, in terris hisce militantem, reservavit. Nam & ratio, & vis ac potentia Mundi omnis ad eam internecione delendam, abolendúmque omne ejus sub Cœlo nomen conspirare jam diu equidem visa est; at hodie conspirare non sine successibus huic laetis, illi verò quàm maximè tristibus funestísque videtur. Tametsi verò res ita habet; ubi tamen ad augustissimum illud Dei sacrarium animum, cogitationem & obtutum nostrum convertimus, unde fluit natura rerum, & in res omnes administratio unicè funditur; profectò maximè furens istud pelagus mundi, insani illius Ægei fluctus, & quicquid in nos rerum adversarum undique irruit, virtute Dei Patris, qui juxta scita illa Tertulliani, Agonotheta, Jesu Christi, qui Epistates, & Spiritus S. qui Xystarches noster est; superamus gloriosissimè. Quicunque enim Dei gratia veritatis amorem & pacis studium, ὑδίσην συζυγίαν verè conjunxerunt, etiamsi illius causa sese duriter premi, capite & fortunis omnibus, seu per cuniculos & Sinonio artificio, seu aperto Marte oppugnari sentiant, præsentibus certè illi & ingentibus animis sint oportet. Etenim veritas semper magis denique eluxit impugnata: & lauri imagine repræsentatur, quæ eádem imagó est hominum piorum sub Crucis Christi signis merentium, de quibus præclarè vates ille cecinit:
units.tr: He has kept the modern Church of his Anointed, which is still fighting on this earth. For the reason, power and might of the whole world have long seemed to conspire to destroy her utterly and to wipe out every name of hers under heaven. Today that conspiracy seems to succeed, happily for them and most sadly and fatally for her. Even so, when we turn our mind, thought and gaze to that most august sanctuary of God, from which the nature of things flows and to which the whole governance of things is wholly directed, we overcome, most gloriously, that raging sea of the world, the waves of that mad Aegean, and whatever adversity rushes upon us from every side, by the virtue of God the Father, who (in the words of Tertullian) is our Agonothetes, Jesus Christ our Epistates, and the Holy Spirit our Xystarches. For whoever by God's grace has truly joined the love of truth and the zeal for peace in the sweetest union [ἡδίστην συζυγίαν], even if they feel that they are hard pressed for its sake, in their person and all their fortunes, whether they are attacked through tunnels and by the trickery of Sinon or by open war, must surely have minds that are present and great. For truth always shines forth at last all the brighter when it is attacked, and it is represented by the image of the laurel, which is also the image of pious men who earn their merit under the signs of the Cross of Christ, about whom that famous poet sang well:

units.la: Presso sub ingenti cum pondere palma virescit,
units.tr: Under a heavy weight the palm grows green;

units.la: Sub cruce sic florent dedita corda Deo.
units.tr: So under the cross hearts devoted to God flourish.

units.la: Ipsi interea spirituali & interna pace se oblectant unicè; satis esse confidentes merito, quòd pacem, omni captu humano altiorem habent primùm erga Deum, quem sibi in Christo placatum propitiúmque persentiscunt: deinde erga semetipsos, cùm se frui vera illa εὐθυμία intelligunt: denique erga consortes suæ fidei, quorum voluntatem studiorúmque consensionem quantivis faciunt, Confirment se in adversis & calamitatibus suis homines facti ad amussim seculi, à naturæ lege, à necessitate Divina, à rationis luce, ab exemplorum nube, ab usura temporis, aliísque ejusmodi tralatitiis argumentis, quibus se ex immani illo malorum vortice emersuros
units.tr: Meanwhile they take their delight in spiritual and inward peace alone, being confident enough that they possess a peace higher than all human understanding: first towards God, whom they perceive to be placated and propitious to them in Christ; then towards themselves, when they understand that they enjoy that true cheerfulness [εὐθυμία]; and finally towards the companions of their faith, whose will and agreement in their studies they value above any price. Let men moulded to the plumb-line of the age strengthen themselves in their adversities and calamities with arguments of the common sort: from the law of nature, from divine necessity, from the light of reason, from the cloud of examples, from the passing of time, and other such stock arguments, by which they expect to emerge from that monstrous whirlpool of evils

units.tr: DEDICATION.

units.la: incolumes, dum interim alia omnia denso agmine, perrumpentia in adversis rebus consolationum ejusmodi fructum penitus intervertunt; ne quicquam sperant. Optime vero & potentissime ille miserationum Pater; ille Imperator noster Sapientissimus, suis prospexit, Divina quadam παναρτλία eos instruens, & salutarium consolationum suavissima ϑελκτήρια animis eorum infundens, ut in impetuoso hoc pelago destituti naufragæ ventis, remos adhibeant gratiæ, positaque sarcina peccati adversus infestas malorum omnium, quibus impugnantur, acies certa spe victoriæ, ut fortes milites & Calliniei Christi, depugnent. Quarum consolationum efficacissimarum duplex in Scripturis irriguus fons est. Aliæ enim in universum dulcissimis promissionibus, quarum lætissima in iis seges, & intermicantes ubique gemmæ continentur, languentes animos demulcent: aliæ certa contemplatione personarum, temporum, vicissitudinum, periodorum Ecclesiæ modo fluctuantis & luctantis, modo elucantis: lunæ hujus modò deficientis, modò lucis suæ amplitudinem postliminio recipientis, prostratos humi animos potenter erigunt corroborántque. Quo posteriori in consolationum genere utramque paginam prædictiones Divino Spiritu fusæ, & in Ecclesiæ solius ταμεῖῳ repositæ faciunt. Et in Novo quidem Testamento Regni Christi incunabula, incrementa, progressum adversùs Sathanæ, rufi illius Draconis, organorumque ejus in mundo pestilentissimorum, nefaria molimina & impedimenta undequaque objecta, certamina Sanctorum certaminumque illorum admirabilem catastrophen Divi Johannis Theologi Apocalypsis, mysteriis, temporum jam face clarissimè detectis plerisque, refertissima, repræsentat. Quid enim Ecclesiæ Christianæ commodo, quæ funestissimis hisce temporibus à mundo & principe ejus vehementissimè oppugnatur, ordinari, disponi, dari aut doceri ad piorum consolationem confirmationemque securam sapientius potuit, quam ille S. Johannis disertissimæ præsignificationes, plerequejam rebus ipsis & experiundo coghitæ, ac cognoscendæ serie ordineque suo ad gloriosum illum Jesu Christi adventum, veluti de impressionibus Bestiæ unius, de fraude alterius, de conatibus utriusque; De Babylonis exteriore interiorique habitu, de perpessionibus Ecclesiæ, de Epiniciis hostium, de Christi, Agni Hyperaspistæ valentissimi propugnatione, de victoriis ejus, de supplíciis infestarum Christo potestatum, de eventis denique felicissimis ad consummationem usque seculi in tanta malorum acerbitate & perplexitate duraturis? Cúmque nihil reliqui faciant, intentatúmque adeo omittant æmuli Regni Christi, quòd modo facere videri possit ad ruinas & parietinas suas restaurandas, & demoliendum soloque adæquandum penitus Regnum Christi: cum ad Veritatem Evangelicam opprimendam, & simplices, infirmos, mundóque impensiùs æquo addictos per admirabilem efficaciam violentiæ suæ ad deserenda Christi signa, abjiciendámque hastam propellendos, omnem virium suarum contentionem convertant; nos certè, quibus excubias in muris Sionis Cælestis Imperator mandavit, citra manifestæ in causa ejus prævaricationis nefas committere non possumus, ut Ecclesia, & in hac tot afflicti tentatique simpliciores ea consolatione, admonitione & doctrina, quam ipse Dominus Jesus per servum suum Johannem exulceratissimis rebus & temporibus nostris in Apocalysi hac præparavit, destituatur. Fallimur enim profecto vehementer, si adversarium æmulúmque Christi armis potius corporalibus, quàm gladio verbi Dei debellandum profligandúmque putamus. In animis hominum illum vilescere & interire necesse est, ut revivíscat Christus, & glorificetur in Secula. Hic unicus ille βασα-νισμὸς, cruciatus est, quo multari meretricantem in mundo Babylonem vox ex cœlo resonans Apoc. xviii. 17. severè jussit. Hoc ergò instituto studióque percitus Divinissimi Apocalypseos libri pericopam haud sane ignobilem & postremam, quinimò cætera fere omnia sinu suo complexam, non perfunctorie illustrandam,
units.tr: unharmed, while meanwhile all other things, pressing in dense ranks, break in upon them in adversity and wholly rob them of the fruit of such consolations; they hope for nothing. But most excellently and most powerfully that Father of mercies, that most wise Commander of ours, has looked out for his own, furnishing them with a certain divine all-sufficiency [παναρκία] and pouring into their minds the sweetest soothing charms [θελκτήρια] of saving consolation, so that, abandoned in this stormy sea like shipwrecked men exposed to the winds, they may apply the oars of grace, and, having laid down the burden of sin, may fight against the hostile battle lines of all the evils by which they are assailed, with a sure hope of victory, as brave soldiers and noble conquerors of Christ. There is a double and abundant fountain of these most effective consolations in the Scriptures. For some, in general, soothe drooping spirits with the sweetest promises, in which the most joyful harvest and gems glittering everywhere are contained; others, by a certain contemplation of persons, times, vicissitudes and periods of the Church, now tossed and struggling, now shining forth, and of this moon now waning and now recovering the full extent of its light by postliminy, powerfully raise up and strengthen minds lying prostrate on the ground. In this latter kind of consolation, the prophecies poured out by the Divine Spirit, and laid up in the storehouse [ταμείῳ] of the Church alone, make both pages of Scripture. And in the New Testament indeed, the beginnings and growth of Christ's Kingdom, its progress against Satan, that fiery red dragon, and his pestilential instruments in the world, the wicked machinations and obstacles thrown up on every side, the struggles of the saints and the admirable outcome of those struggles, are set forth in the Apocalypse of the divine John the Theologian, a book very full of mysteries, most of which have now been brightly disclosed by the course of time. For what could have been ordained, arranged, given or taught more wisely for the comfort and secure confirmation of the godly than those most eloquent foretellings of John, most of which are now already grasped and to be grasped by experience of the events themselves, in their order and sequence, leading up to that glorious coming of Jesus Christ: concerning the assaults of one Beast, the deceit of the other, the attempts of both; concerning Babylon's outward and inward condition, the sufferings of the Church, the victory songs of its enemies, the powerful defence of Christ, the Lamb, the most mighty Shield-bearer, his victories, the punishments of the powers hostile to Christ, and finally the most happy outcomes that will endure to the consummation of the age amid such bitterness and perplexity of evils? And since the rivals of Christ's Kingdom leave nothing undone and omit no attempt that might seem able to restore their ruins and walls and to tear down the Kingdom of Christ and level it utterly with the ground; since they turn all the effort of their strength to suppressing the Gospel truth and to driving simple, weak people, who are too much given to the world, by the admirable efficacy of their violence, to abandon the standards of Christ and cast down the spear; we, to whom the heavenly Emperor has entrusted the watch on the walls of heavenly Zion, cannot, without committing the sin of manifest betrayal of his cause, allow the Church, and in it so many afflicted and tempted simpler folk, to be deprived of that consolation, admonition and teaching which the Lord Jesus himself prepared through his servant John in this Apocalypse for our most troubled times and circumstances. For we are greatly mistaken if we think that the adversary and rival of Christ is to be vanquished and overthrown by bodily arms rather than by the sword of the Word of God. He must wither and perish in men's minds, so that Christ may revive and be glorified for ever. This alone is the torment [βασανισμός], the cruciatus, with which the voice sounding from heaven, Apoc. xviii. 17., sternly commanded that Babylon, the harlot of the world, be punished. Stirred by this purpose and zeal, I have undertaken to illustrate, not in a perfunctory way, this section of the most divine book of the Apocalypse, which is by no means ignoble and is the last part, and indeed embraces almost all the rest within its bosom,

units.la: DEDICATIO.
units.tr: DEDICATION.

units.la: sed certa & accurata argumentorum apodixi in ampliorem, quàm forte haƈtenus unquam, Ecclesiæ notitiam ulúmque provehendam suscepi, non eo certè animo, ut crabrones, quod ajunt, irritem; sed ut veritatis illius, quæ secundùm pietatem est, amantes cunƈtos à præcipitiis interitúque per Scripturas, & demonstrationum ex iis, pro viribus meis revocem, & adversariam Christi cohortem, sanguine Sanƈtorum pastam saginatámque, vivis Spiritus S. coloribus sic depiƈtam, qui piè in mundo vivere volunt, toto peƈtore cohorrescant omnes. Hoc verò quicquid operis & laboris est, quia post Deum in terris etiam tutelare aliquod adversùs invidiam & malignitatem hujus Seculi, Veritatis Cœlestis impatientem, patrocínium postulare videtur, Augustæ Majestati proximam Celsitudinem Tuam, SERENISSIME ELECTOR, Seculi nostri Heros incomparabilis, Te, inquam, inter omnes in sublimi fastigio constitutos, plebis Dominicæ Nutritios, Principem Maximum, Tutorem Patronúmque enixissimè optat. Sapientissimè equidem à Sapientissimo
units.tr: but I have undertaken to advance, by a sure and careful demonstration of the arguments, a knowledge of the Church wider and fuller than perhaps anyone has done hitherto. I have certainly not done so with the purpose of stirring up hornets, as they say; rather, I wish through the Scriptures, and by demonstrations drawn from them, to recall everyone who loves that truth which is according to godliness from precipices and ruin, as far as my powers allow, and to paint the adversary's band of Christ, fed and fattened on the blood of the saints, in such living colours of the Holy Spirit that all who wish to live piously in the world may shudder with their whole heart. Moreover, whatever this work and labour amounts to, I humbly beg Your Highness, SERENE ELECTOR, the incomparable hero of our age, who stands next to the august Majesty, is the nourisher of the Lord's people, and is above all others set on the lofty summit as the greatest Prince, the Tutor and Patron, to grant protection; since, after God on earth, it seems to demand some guardian against the envy and malice of this age, which cannot bear heavenly truth. Most wisely, indeed, by the Most Wise...

units.la: DEDICATIO.
units.tr: DEDICATION.

units.la: Mortalium Regum Solomone dictum est, Proverb.xxv.2. Gloria Dei est occultare verbum, & gloria Regum scrutari verbum. Regi Cœlorum gloriosum est occultare verbum quo negotium salutis omne panditur, hactenus, ut non sine attentione sedula, scrutatione continua, & spirituali discretione spiritualium intelligatur à quoquam. Est enim verbum Dei thesaurus in agro abscônditus, & margarita bona quolibet pretio redimenda. Meretur ergo laborem, summámque inquisitiam duce & luce Deo scrutandi abscondita, & in lucem apertam proferendi. Hoc Deus, Rex Cœlestis summus ille, sibi amplum gloriosumque ipsemet ducit. Ecquæ vero Regum terrestrium gloria est? Scrutari verbum, inquit Rex ille Terrestrium summus Solomon. Nam scrutatio veritatis & Verbi Dei, atque in eo etiam prædictionum, quibus Ecclesiæ à Principibus piis regendæ fata consignantur, Reges Principésque sapientes reddit & Populo, cui non ad terrenam duntaxat: quam cum animantibus brutis communem ille habet, sed ad Cœlestem inprimis felicitatem, votorum studiorúmque omnium coronidem unicam, ducatum præbere debent. Nihil enim Rege & Principe, veritatis & beatitudinis solidæ ignaro turpius, nocentius nihil effe potest. Potest enim ille nocere, & ubi viribus suis uti debeat, nescit; belluæ haud absimilis, quæ rationis aureo illo fræno destituta, noxam promiscuè infert. In Civitate sunt homines ad Dei imaginem, & propter ejusdem gloriam conditi: quorum præcipue partes sunt, ut Deum invicem celebrent, & vitam per omnem pietatem & honestatem traducant. Reges ergo Principesque oportet illis esse Duces ad veram sapientiam: quæ sine verbi scrutatione nulla obtingit. Præcipuè autem scrutentur illi verbum, ipsaque etiam Spiritus S. prædictiones oportet, ne potestatem suam Babyloni & Bestiæ tradant: quod qui factitârunt, Christianum illi Orbem innumerabilibus malis implicârunt hactenùs. Possem pientissimorum
units.tr: Solomon, the greatest of earthly kings, said it: Proverbs 25:2, It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter. For the King of heaven it is glorious to hide the Word, in which the whole business of salvation is laid open, so that until now it is understood by no one without diligent attention, continual searching and spiritual discernment of spiritual things. For the Word of God is a treasure hidden in a field and a good pearl, to be bought at any price. It therefore deserves labour and the most earnest inquiry, with God as guide and light, to search out what is hidden and bring it forth into the open light. This God, that supreme King of heaven, counts as ample and glorious for himself. But what is the glory of earthly kings? To search out the word, says Solomon, that greatest of earthly kings. For the searching of the truth and the Word of God, and in it also of the predictions by which the fates of the Church to be governed by pious princes are sealed, makes kings and princes wise, and they ought to offer guidance to the people, not only to the earthly happiness which they share with brute animals, but above all to the heavenly happiness, the one crown of all wishes and endeavours. For nothing can be more shameful or more harmful than a king or prince ignorant of truth and of solid blessedness. For he can do harm, and does not know how to use his powers where he ought; he is not unlike a beast, which, destitute of that golden bridle of reason, inflicts harm indiscriminately. In the commonwealth there are men made in the image of God and created for his glory, whose chief part is to celebrate God together and to lead their lives in all godliness and honesty. Kings and princes must therefore be their leaders to true wisdom, which cannot be obtained without searching the Word. Above all let them search the Word, and the predictions of the Holy Spirit themselves, lest they hand over their power to Babylon and the Beast; those who have done so have entangled the Christian world in countless evils until now. I could say more of the most pious

units.la: DEDICATIO.
units.tr: DEDICATION.

units.la: Judæ Regum, & Principum Christianorum, qui Solomonis isthoc saluberrimum monitum in vita omni expresserunt, exempla testatissima ciere. Nostro certè Seculo Gloriosissimus Princeps, JACOBUS I. Britanniæ, Scotiæ & Hyberniæ Rex Inclytus, Scrutationem ejusmodi haud infra Regales curas suas resīdere ratus, doctissimam in Apocalypsin Paraphrasin publico donavit, dignissimam tanto Rege, cui in libri illius intellectu praeter caeteros Mortales alluxisse DEUM sapientiæ suæ fatem, verissime Jacobus Montacutius, Wintoniensis Episcopus, Præfatione in Opera Regia, prædicavit; sapienter insuper observans, Regum Principumque plus interesse intelligere hunc librum, quàm caeteros rum: & rectius ab iis explicari Vaticinia, quorum dextra vere omnia peragantur. Sed quid Hunc Aliosque memoro, quando, SERENISSIME DOMINE, cum Religiosissimis & Pientissimis Principibus quibusque paria Te facientem, & S. Literarum amore ac scrutinio nemini secundum, denique ex Divini præ-scripti regula tot populorum gubernacula sapientissi-mè, felicissimè ac constantissimè moderantem, melior Orbis universus, consonæ vocis præconio edito, suspicit & veneratur unicè ? Prædicabunt Annales inTe speciem Imperio dignam, intemeratam Justitiam, Prudentiam expuisitam, heroicos Spiritus, Fortitudinem incredibilem, Victorias & palmas concatenatas non dolo illas; sed Virtute, & manu Tua forti patra-tas, successus propitio Numine ex animi ferè sententia fluentes: quæ singula vix verbis adæquari possunt, & vel loquaces Fabios lassabunt. Me verò tenet tene-bitque admiratio sinceræ Pietatis, qua incocto imbu-tóque penitus, & toto pacis Religiosæ Cœlitus accenso Zelo æstuante pectore, & jam olim Juvenis, & etiamnum per Dei gratiam, Ecclesiæ hanc felicitatem impertientis liberalissimè, Senex, cum Constantino Magno de Ecclesiasticæ Pacis auspicatò quandoque
units.tr: Let me call up the most attested examples of the kings and Christian princes of Judah who carried out this most wholesome admonition of Solomon throughout their lives. In our own century, the most glorious prince, JAMES I, the renowned King of Britain, Scotland and Ireland, judging that this kind of inquiry should not be beneath his royal concerns, published a most learned paraphrase of the Apocalypse, one worthy of so great a king, to whom God, beyond other mortals, has shed the rays of his wisdom in the understanding of that book. James Montagu, Bishop of Winchester, rightly proclaimed this in his preface to the King's Works, and wisely observed that it matters more to kings and princes than to others to understand this book, and that prophecies are more rightly explained by those whose right hand truly accomplishes all things. But why do I mention him and others, when, MOST SERENE LORD, the whole better part of the world, with one voice raised in praise, looks up to you alone and venerates you? You are equal to the most religious and pious princes of every kind, second to no one in love and study of the Holy Scriptures, and you govern the reins of so many peoples most wisely, most happily and most steadfastly by the rule of the divine precept. The annals will proclaim in you a majesty worthy of empire, unblemished justice, exquisite prudence, heroic spirit, incredible fortitude, and victories and triumphs strung together, achieved not by trickery but by virtue and by your strong hand, and successes flowing, with God's favour, almost according to the wish of your heart. Each of these can scarcely be matched by words, and would weary even the most talkative Fabii. As for me, I am and will remain held by admiration for sincere piety, which has been steeped and imbued through and through, and whose heat burns in my breast with a zeal for the religious peace kindled from heaven; I was once a young man, and I am still, by the grace of God who so generously bestows this happiness on the Church, an old man, and with Constantine the Great, on the propitious occasion of ecclesiastical peace, at some time...

units.tr: You have most steadfastly and most faithfully striven for the repair of the breach, and you never cease to strive. For with what tribute David Blondel, that great scholar, rightly honoured Your Most Serene Highness thirty-three years ago, "fraternal battle lines and javelins threatening javelins" (mindful that the servants of God are by no means given to quarrels), you have always shrunk from, following the example of your forefathers in the family of Christ; and you still shrink from such things, and you hold back, though in vain, the wicked obstinacy of those who oppose your most holy endeavours. You are about to bring the work of the Henoticum to its longed-for end, if the Lord judges our times worthy of so great a blessing. May you live to see it, and may it not be before you, exulting in the Lord, embrace and cherish, in your princely arms, the lasting peace of Zion so long sought with such longing and zeal, and may you enjoy the fruit of the labour so long and so generously spent! units.tr: Mindful of Your Highness, we shall always weary heaven with our prayers, that God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ may arm Your Serene Highness, S. C. T., with every princely virtue, protect you from every evil, lead you into every good, and increase the happiness of your principality, the splendour of your family, and the vigour of your life, to be prolonged to the years of the eagles; may He pour down blessings from heaven upon your sacred person, your whole household, your counsels, endeavours and works, and keep in health and in flourishing condition the commonwealth, the Church, and all good men who, in these most difficult times, amid the heavy masses of troubles and the storms breaking in on every side, after God have their eyes fixed and unwavering upon your counsels for piety, virtue and prudence; and may He cause the kingdom of Christ to be ever more widely extended. May He preserve you for as long as possible! I was writing these words and consecrating this undying vow.

units.la: Ea plane vivimus tempora, quibus familiam suam probante Domino, & fidem multorum pene dormientem, coelesti censura erigente, non tam prolixos libros, quam prolixos fletus & gemitus deberi, quod de suis Augustinus, epist. 122. queritur, profiteri possumus, ea inquam, tempora, quibus illa Am. v. 13. apprime congruere videantur: Ideo prudens in tempore illo tacebit, quia tempus malum est: & quibus fortitudinem nostram reputare debeamus ממה ודמם silentium & spem. Esai. xxx. 15. Et sane silendum, non oblatrandum, quod ille ajebat, ventis; nedum oblatrandum esse justis, sanctisque Dei judiciis, qua nec plane comprehendi, nec juste reprehendi possunt: ultro fatemur omnes. Sic tamen silendum putamus, ne, ut olim Amydas, sic hodie Christianos silentium perdat. Sunt enim hodie, sunt, qui calamitates nostras argumentum conclamata causa nostra interpretantes, insultare non desinant: Ubi Deus vester, ubi Deus, in quo speratis? Qui adipem sacrificiorum vestrorum comedebant, & vinum libaminum vestrorum bibebant, surgant, & opitulentur vobis, protegant illi vos. Deut. xxxii. 37, 38. Illi non causam, sed fortunam nostram trutinantes, triumphum ante victoriam canere, ab eventu facta notare, religionem ex prosperitate candem in mundo profitentium aestimare pridem consueverunt. Mussitemus hac! Atqui silentium nostrum in consensum, molestia in conscientiam ducitur; uti quondam Marius Salustius locutus est. Et mos ille inolitus veritatis hostibus est, Orthodoxorum abuti silentio, patientiaque suum ad decus. Tacere nostrum illis jacere est, & victi convicitque pronunciamur, qui ea parte, qua veram felicitatem nostram metimur, icti non sumus. Accedit fatalis quaedam multorum cheu! nimis, Babylonis oblivio. Cum primum Angelo illo ex coelo descendente & magnam potestatem habente, terra gloria illis collustrari coepit, ingens glisceba zelus omnium, non deferendi duntaxat, sed detestandi etiam communionem tot vitiis enormibus maculisque scatentem, tot stigmatis ab ipso Spiritu Dei compunctam. Antichristum, Babylonem in externa Ecclesia communione stabulari pridem, odio & aversatione dignissimum, ambiguum nomini bono habebatur; publicam in fide apostasiam, in cultu idolomaniam, in regimine tyrannidem reputanti altius. Ex eo tempore id Ecclesiae hostibus unice cure cordique fuit, dedecora sua nova indies mendacia fuco illita, ut tegerent, lucem verbi D. omnem, pradonum nocturnorum more extinguerent: alios vi aperta mendaciloquorum hypocrisi alios expugnarent, & in castra sua, invitos etiam, horrentes, reluctantesque traducerent. Neque desunt tum Galliones, qui religionis curam posteriore loco amandantes, & in simplicita nescio qua fide stupentes, parum pensi habent, quid de Ecclesia, ejusque fatis Scriptura dixerint, praedixerintque: & universam de religione disceptationem a quadam ingeingeniorum scabie, astrorumque positu arcessere nulli dubitant: tum ϑεῖοι, meticulosi, profiteri, quod res est, & scapham appellare scaphàm reverti: tum infirmi, qui profunditates Sathanæ profundius haud scrutantes, & splendore externo capti, apertis & inconniventibus oculis lucem veritatis intueri, non valent: tum denique Dema, qui mundum, & quæ in eo sunt, impensius diligentes, veritatis cœlestis amo- rem ejerârunt. Hæ aliaque causæ cùm veluti scotomate quodam percussos alios in er- rore obfirment, impedíánique, ne veram à falsa Ecclesia, lucem à tenebris discernant, alios, sustinendæ tentationi gravissimæ impares, & à gratia Dei tantisper de- sertos, ad cœlestem veritatem abnegandam, & sacra minimè sacra amplexanda transversos præcipitésque avertant: alios denique ad oblivionem genuini Papatus sic inducant, ut Babylonem, vivósque colores vix amplius pernoscant; illustrem illam, & planè μυηριάδα de Babylone Magna prophetiam, paulò exigusitiùs, & dedità, quod ajunt, operâ indagandi consilium cepi. Hanc verò dum in Hierarchia Rom. argumentorum irrefragabilium magnâ mole animum, calamúmque meum impellente, repræsento, idem mihi animus præsagit indignationis, adversantium aslum, ferventiorem certè illum, quàm quo olim Judæi adversus Stephanum, insimulatum vehementer, quòd βλάσφημα ῥήματα, blasphema verba adversus sanctum illum lo- cum & legem prolocutus sit, ( Act. vi. 13.) exarserunt. Non lapides, non ignes universos contundenda blasphemiæ (hoc enim nomine solidæ, demonstrationes & ju- stissima accusationes nostra venire solent) sufficere clamabunt, qui Sanctitatis, Infallibilitatis, Catholicismi, totque adeò Ecclesia sua ἀλεσιαστικμάτων, sine suffragiis legitimis, sine sine & modo jactatorum typho inflati, ibi esse synagogam, sponsam, columbam Christi, matrem, & magistram Ecclesiarum omnium, veritatis co- lumnam & stabilimentum, sidem Romanorum tantopere à S. Paulo celebratam, somniant, ubi nos Babylonem M. famosam illam abominationum matrem, jam diu fixisse nidum suum ostendimus. Caterum, si ex vero rem illi putabunt, forte consido, ut non tam mihi, tot argumentorum phalange id satagenti, ut à Babylonis M. pecca- tis & plagis immunes futuri, eadem propere, juxta cœlestis vocis districtum illud mandatum, Exite ex ea, Populè mi, saltem nonnulli excedant: adeòque saluti suæ invigilanti, quàm sibi, gravíssimo in errore versantibus præjudiciorum sascino demen- tatis, & mundani imperii, cum quo pridem Ecclesiam illi commutarunt, flagrantis- simo amore occacatis irascantur. Dictorum verò meorum invidiam mitigabit, spero, quòd non tantùm in Opere ipso, in quo accurata Prophetiam inter, & eventum συμβαίνοντος instituitur, exactissimam Babylonem inter, & Hierarchiam Rom. har- moniam, veluti in speculo quodam, intueri dabitur, cùm credibile neutiquam sit, Spiritum S. sic vaticinantem non cogitâsse de iis, quibus verba vaticinii ubique con- veniunt: verùm etiam non primus ego, non primus Lutherus, Calvinus, Bullingerus, reliquíque post Reformationem Theologi nostri, ἐν τοῖς ἑρμηνεῦσι ἐναμί, potentes in Scripturis, quin & Reges, Principesque Maximi, Sapientissimíque, uti vel sola Sereniss. Angliæ Monarcha Iacobi I. in vaticinium de Babylone M. paraphrasis edecumata, quam Lectorum fidis oculis infrà subjicimus: Sed ante omnes hos innumeri, locupletésque ex quavis ætate testes veritatis, Romam, inquam, non civitatem aliam, Prophetia illa de Babylone M. divinitus proclamatam esse, assa voce pronuntiárunt. Hoc ergo in antecessum, rovitatis calumniam discussuri, demonstrábimus, adductis testimoniis præcipuis, ut sicut ex opere ipso sententia veritatem æqui rerum arbitri agnoscent omnes: sic primo cætu ejusdem antiquitas patefecat. Utque calumnientur parcius ei ὑ ἰναῖλιας, Cardinalem Bellarminum ante omnia audire libeat. Is enim Controversia iv. 4.q.6. postquam præmiserat, Meretricem, quæ sedet super montes septem, esse (quorundam judicio) Diabolí civitatem, quæ in Scriptura sæpè Babylon vocatur, & opponitur civitati Dei, id est, Ecclesiæ, quæ dicitur Hierusalem, subjicit: Sed meo judicio melius per Meretricem intelligitur Roma, ut exponunt Tertullianus & Hieronymus. Testes ergo ipse nobis suppeditat Tertullianum & Hieronymum: idque verissimè. Tertullianus enim contra Judæos cap. 9. sic scribit: sic & Babylon apud Johannem nostrum, Romanæ urbis figura est, proinde & magnæ, & Regno superbæ, & Sanctorum debellatricis. Totidem verbis adversus Marc. lib. iii. 14. repetit. Hieronymus ad Algas quæst. ii. paucis ita definit: Secundum Apocalypsin Johannis, in fronte purpuratæ Meretricis scriptum est nomen blasphemiæ, id est, Romæ æternæ. Quibus Græcorum nounullus Aretham inprimis in Apoc. xvii. poterat annumerare: quin & S. Augustinum ipsum, qui de Civit. Dei lib. xviii. 2. diserte Romam secundam Babyloniam vocat. Et cap. 22. distinctius: Condita est, inquit, Roma velut altera Babylon, & velut prioris filia Babylonis. Mox cap. 27. Romani Babylonem Occidentalem vocat. Sed & Ribera consentientes plures, puta Eusebium, Orosium, Oecumenium, Bedam, Victorinum, alios inducit. Sed illi regerunt, de Roma Civili statu, non Ecclesiastico, de Romano Imperio, non de Romana Ecclesia vaticinium interpretantur. Minime equidem mirum hoc videtur. Illorum enim temporibus Ecclesia dissimillima Imperio fuit. Imperium impium, Ecclesia pia: nostris non item. Nam Ecclesiasticus status in Civilem commutatus est: Ecclesia devoravit Imperium, eo nunc Romanus Papatus consistit. Quando igitur Mysterium Babylonis ad Rom. Hierarchiam accommodamus: accommodamus perpetuò, ut Patres olim, ad Civilem statum; si non Ethnici illic constituti Imperii, at Christiani quidem ad Ethnicum degenerantis, adeòque Ethnici agnina specie induti. In illa Civitate conspicamur purpuratam Meretricem, sedentem super aquas multas, ebriam sanguine Sanctorum, & sanguine Martyrum Christi.
units.tr: We live in times in which the Lord is testing his household, and in which the faith of many, nearly asleep, is being roused by heavenly censure. We may profess that what Augustine complains of in Epistle 122, that long weeping and groaning are owed rather than long books, applies to us. These are the times, I say, to which that saying of Amos 5:13 seems especially suited: "Therefore the prudent shall keep silence in that time, for it is an evil time." By it we ought to measure our strength: quietness [ממה ודמם] and hope, Isaiah 30:15. Indeed we should keep silent and not bark, as he said to the winds, much less bark against the just and holy judgments of God, which can neither be fully grasped nor justly blamed. We all freely admit this. Yet we think we must keep silent in such a way that silence does not, as it once did for Amydas, now destroy Christians. For there are still people today who, interpreting our calamities as proof that our cause is lost, do not cease to mock: "Where is your God, the God in whom you trust? Let those who ate the fat of your sacrifices and drank the wine of your drink offerings rise up and help you, let them protect you" (Deut. 32:37, 38). These men, weighing not our cause but our fortune, have long been accustomed to sing triumph before victory, to judge deeds by their outcome, and to esteem the religion of those professing it in the world by its prosperity. Shall we murmur at this? But our silence is taken for consent and our distress for a guilty conscience, as Marius Sallust once said. It is an ingrained habit of the enemies of truth to abuse the silence and patience of the orthodox for their own glory. To be silent is for us to lie prostrate before them, and we are pronounced beaten and convicted, because we are not struck in that respect by which we measure our true happiness. To this is added a certain fatal forgetfulness of Babylon in many, alas, too many. When the angel who descends from heaven and has great power first began to shine upon the earth with his glory, there arose in everyone a great zeal, not only to abandon but even to detest communion with a fellowship teeming with so many enormous vices and stained with so many marks pricked in by the Spirit of God himself. That Antichrist and Babylon had long been housed in the outward communion of the Church, deserving hatred and abhorrence, was regarded as doubtful for a good name by those who thought more deeply about public apostasy in faith, idolatry in worship and tyranny in government. From that time on it has been the sole care and concern of the Church's enemies, day by day, to cover their disgraces with new lies smeared on like paint, so as to hide the whole light of the Lord's Word, quenching it in the manner of nocturnal robbers. Some they attack by open force, others by the hypocrisy of liars, and they drag into their camp even those who are unwilling, trembling and resisting. Nor are there lacking then those Gallios who, thinking the care of religion a secondary matter, and dazed in some kind of simplicity of faith, care little what Scripture has said and foretold about the Church and its fate; they have no hesitation in drawing the whole dispute about religion from a certain itch of wits and the position of the stars. Then there are the timid, who dare not profess what is the case and call a boat a boat. Then there are the weak, who, not searching the depths of Satan too deeply and captivated by outward splendour, are unable to see the light of truth with open and unblinking eyes. Finally there is Demas, who, loving the world and the things in it too eagerly, has cast out the love of heavenly truth. These and other causes, as if by some kind of scotoma striking them, confirm others in error and prevent them from distinguishing true Church from false, light from darkness. Others, unequal to the most grievous temptation and deserted for a time by the grace of God, they turn aside and cast headlong into renouncing heavenly truth and embracing what is not holy as holy. Finally, others they lead into such forgetfulness of genuine Popery that they can scarcely any longer recognise Babylon and its living colours. I have therefore resolved, with somewhat less detail and, as they say, deliberately, to investigate that famous and altogether wondrous prophecy concerning Great Babylon. But when I set this before the reader in the great mass of irrefutable arguments against the Roman Hierarchy, which drives my mind and pen, the same mind forebodes the indignation and hostile rage of opponents, certainly more fervent than that with which the Jews once flared up against Stephen, who was greatly accused of speaking blasphemous words against that holy place and the law (Acts 6:13). They will cry out that stones and fires are not enough to smash such blasphemy (for solid demonstrations and most just accusations are usually called by this name), those who, puffed up with the pride of their boasted Sanctity, Infallibility, Catholicism, and the whole list of their own ecclesiastical titles, without legitimate suffrages, without end and measure, dream that there is the synagogue, the bride, the dove of Christ, the mother and teacher of all Churches, the pillar and ground of truth, the faith of the Romans so greatly praised by St. Paul, where we show that Babylon, that infamous mother of abominations, has long since fixed her nest. Yet if they think the matter is so in truth, I hope that perhaps not only my many arguments, which labour to show that Babylon's sins and plagues are not shared by those who will be free of them, but some of them at least will hasten out of her, my people, in accordance with the stern command of the heavenly voice, "Come out of her." And those who watch over their own salvation more than their own, who are sunk in the deepest error by the enchantment of prejudices and blinded by a most burning love of the worldly empire for which they long ago exchanged the Church, will be angered. My hope is that the ill will towards what I have said will be softened, not only because in the work itself, in which an exact comparison is made between the prophecy and the event that followed, one can see as in a mirror the most precise harmony between Babylon and the Roman Hierarchy, but also because it is by no means credible that the Holy Spirit, prophesying thus, did not think of those to whom the words of the prophecy agree everywhere. Moreover, I am not the first, nor is Luther the first, nor Calvin or Bullinger, nor the other theologians of ours after the Reformation, who were powerful in the Scriptures among the interpreters, nor even kings and princes, the greatest and wisest, as the paraphrase of the prophecy concerning Great Babylon by the most serene Monarch of England, James I, shows, which we set below before the faithful eyes of the reader. But before all of these, innumerable and rich witnesses of the truth from every age have with one voice declared that that prophecy concerning Great Babylon was divinely proclaimed, I say, of Rome and not of any other city. Therefore, in advance, to dispel the calumny against the truth, we shall demonstrate this by adducing the principal testimonies, so that, as all impartial judges of the matter recognise from the work itself the truth of this opinion, so antiquity itself reveals it at the first assembly. And that the calumniators may be less free to attack, it is pleasing to hear Cardinal Bellarmine first of all. For in Controversy 4, Book 4, question 6, after premising that the harlot who sits upon seven mountains is (in the judgment of some) the city of the Devil, which in Scripture is often called Babylon and is opposed to the city of God, that is the Church, which is called Jerusalem, he adds: "But in my judgment the harlot is better understood as Rome, as Tertullian and Jerome expound." So he himself supplies us with Tertullian and Jerome as witnesses, and most truly so. For Tertullian, against the Jews, chapter 9, writes thus: "So also Babylon in our John is a figure of the Roman city, and therefore of the great one, proud in kingdom and destroyer of the saints." He repeats the same words against Marcion, book 3, chapter 14. Jerome in his letter to Algasia, question 2, briefly defines it thus: "According to the Apocalypse of John, on the forehead of the purple harlot is written the name of blasphemy, that is, of eternal Rome." To these one could add among the Greeks chiefly Arethas on Revelation 17. Indeed St. Augustine himself, who in City of God, book 18, chapter 2, plainly calls Rome a second Babylon, and in chapter 22 more distinctly says: "Rome was founded as another Babylon, and as the daughter of the former Babylon." Soon after, in chapter 27, he calls Rome Western Babylon. But Ribera also brings forward several who agree, namely Eusebius, Orosius, Oecumenius, Bede, Victorinus and others. But they reply that they interpret the prophecy of the civil state of Rome, not the ecclesiastical, of the Roman Empire, not of the Roman Church. This indeed seems by no means strange. For in their times the Church was very unlike the Empire: the Empire was impious, the Church pious. With us it is not so. For the ecclesiastical state has been changed into a civil one; the Church has devoured the Empire, and in that form the Roman Papacy now stands. When therefore we apply the mystery of Babylon to the Roman Hierarchy, we apply it continually, as the Fathers did of old to the civil state, if not to an empire there established that was pagan, at least to a Christian one degenerating into the pagan, and thus clothed in the appearance of a pagan. In that city we behold the purple harlot sitting upon many waters, drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Christ.

units.la: Christi, habentem poculum aureum, plenum abominationibus & immunditiâ fortationis suæ. Sanderus, maximus ille Papalis Monarchiæ Promachus, de visib. Monarch. lib. viii. 8. ex Tertulliano demonstrat, ubi est Imperii superbia, ubi magnitudo Regiæ urbis, ubi Christianorum persecutio viget: ibi certè Babylonem esse, ibi Mulierem illam super populos & gentes, & linguas sedere, cum qua Reges terræ fornicantur, & de vino prostitutionis ejus ebrii sunt. Hisce ergo nominibus Roma fuit Babylon (uti ipse explicat) quandiu illi profani Cæsares rerum Civilium summam illic tenerent. Non autem postquam in Paparum manus deveniret. Cæterum Papatus, Imperiíque status inter se conferantur, & Annales Cæsarum, qui ante Papas illic rerum potiti sunt, à Suetonio, Capitolino, Lampridio, Talito, aliis consignati, & Paparum Cæsaribus succedentium juxta historiam, à domesticis Scriptoribus Platina, Onuphrio, Guicciardino, aliis prodita seriem, perpendantur, comparenturque invicem. Nisi compertum fuerit, Papalem statum se Cæsarum Imperio, potestatis magnitudine, dominatus superbia, Christiano rumque persecutione, adæquâsse: nulli recusamus certè, quin ipsud de nobis feratur Judicium; nos Babylonis nomen Romæ Papali tribuentes, à Patribus dissentire. Secus verò si res habeat, Sanderi suffragio, obtinemus illos, parium pari ratione habitâ, Romam Christianam hodiernam cum Ethnica veteri pariâ facientem, Babylonis stigmate æquè aperte imputuros fuisse, si hodièque spirarent. Sed de Hieronymo quid dicent illi? Is enim Præfat, in lib. Didymi de Spir. S. Ecclesiam Rom. apertè Babylonem, & Meretricem purpuratam vocavit. Et Jerem. r. Ollam à facie Aquilonis ardentem, Ecclesiam, non urbem, nuncuparit: quia Babylonis Senatum, hoc est viros Ecclesiasticos, Senatum vocat Pharisæorum & imperitorum, qui adversus ipsam conjuraverant. Conjuraverunt autem Clerici, non Curia Capitolina Cæsaris. Et hanc ipsam factionem vocat Ollam ardentem. Ex Apocalypsis Prophetia alibi idem Hieronymus miserandum Ecclesiæ Rom. interitum imminere ait. Lege, inquit, epist. 47. ad Marcellinum, Apocalypsin Johannis; & quid de muliere purpurata, & scripta in ejus fronte Blasphemia, septem montibus, aquis multis, & Babylonis cantetur exitu, contuere. Exite, inquit Dominus, de illa populus meus: & ne participes fitis delictorum ejus: & de plagis ejus non accipiatis. Fugite de medio Babylonis, & salvate unusquisque animam suam: Cecidit enim, cecidit Babylon magna, & facta est habitatio Dæmonum, & custodia omnis spiritûs immundi. Excipit quidem & separat ibidem Hieronymus sacra à profanis. Nihilominus in ipsis rebus Sacris & Ecclesiasticis jam tunc ibid. videbat aliquid Babylonem redolens. Est quidem; sic epist. 18. loquitur; sancta Ecclesia: sunt trophæa Apostolorum & Martyrum: est Christi vera confessio: est ab Apostolo prædicata fides: & Gentilitate calcata, in sublime se quotidie erigens. origens vocabulum Christianum: sed ipsa ambitio, potentia, magnitudo urbis: videri & videre: salutari & salutare: laudare & detrahere, vel audire, vel proloqui & tantam frequentiam hominum saltem invitam videre, à proposito Monachorum, & quiete, aliena sunt. Indicat, mores inter Christianos quoque & religiosos seculares jam tum invaluisse. Neque negat, eidem Civitati, quantumvis tum Christi confessione & devotione satis celebri, ultimum exitum ex Apocalypsis prophetia imminere: & de illa audiendum esse ait: Cecidit, cecidit Babylon magna: futuramque Daemonum habitationem, indeque lapsu irreparabili caduram vaticinatur. Quamvis imminentes hasce poenas vitare eam posse asserit, si Ninevitarum instar ad poenitentiam confugiat. Maledictionem; sic lib. II. adversus Jovinian. scribit; quam tibi Salvator in Apocalypsi comminatus est, potes effugere per poenitentiam, habens exemplum Ninevitarum. Utinam vero! si Roma adhuc haberet Imperatores; eosque Christianos, quales Hieronymi tempore erant Romani, excidii causam forte Imperatorum & Secularium ejusmodi iniquitatibus tribueremus. His enim Hieronymus etiam excidii futuri causam tribuendam putavit. Cum vero non amplius Imperatoribus vel Secularibus, sed Clero dominanti pareat, quis non videt e sacrario ipso malum erumpere, ipsumque meretricium Roma non in Imperiali, sed in Ecclesiastico regimine exercendum? Paulinus quoque ruinam Romanam in Apocalypsi praedicatam, ex Curia Imperiali & Secularibus oriturum putavit. Sic enim epist. 51, loquitur: Poteras Roma, intentatas tibi in Apocalypsi minas, non timere, si alia semper ederent munera Senatores tui. Qualia videl. Alithius Senator, vir sanctus in operibus suis pius & valde religiosus edebat. Interim ipse quoque Paulinus epist. 10. filiam Babylonis vocat Romam: & eam filiam Sion postponit, quamvis in aliqua parte, hoc est fidelium & bonorum, Romam quisque facit Filiam Sionis. Noverat tamen ex Prophetia illa, tandem totam in Babylonem convertendam, & populum Dei, si quis in ea superarit, a Deo auditurum: Exite, exite, de illa, minasque adeo Apocalypseos perfensuram. Gregorius M. Romanorum Pontificum praestantissimus, Epist. lib. IV. cap. 32. Scribens ad Johannem Jejunatorem, Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum, pro Oecumenico & Universali Episcopo se venditantem, eundem comparat cum Lucifero, Babylonis spiritualis Rege, qui Isef. XIV. 13. dixit in corde suo: Ego in coelum ascendam, supra astra coeli exaltabo solium meum, sedebo in monte congregationis, in lateribus Aquilonis. Ascendam super altitudinem nubium, similis ero Altissimo. Quid enim, sic. arguit ille, fratres tui omnes, universalis Ecclesiae Episcopi, nisi astra coeli sunt: Quorum vitae simul inter peccata errorésque hominum, quasi inter nocfis tenebras latent. Quibus
units.tr: Christi, having a golden cup, full of the abominations and filthiness of her fornication. Sanderus, that great champion of the Papal monarchy, in De visibili monarchia book 8, chapter 8, shows from Tertullian where there is the pride of empire, where the greatness of the royal city, where the persecution of Christians flourishes: there, surely, is Babylon, there is that woman who sits upon peoples and nations and tongues, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication, and who are drunk with the wine of her prostitution. By these marks, then, Rome was Babylon (as he himself explains) so long as those profane Caesars held the supreme civil power there, but not after it came into the hands of the Popes. Let the Papacy and the condition of the empire be compared with each other, and let the annals of the Caesars, who held power there before the Popes, as recorded by Suetonius, Capitolinus, Lampridius, Tacitus and others, be weighed against the sequence of the Popes succeeding the Caesars, as made known by domestic writers such as Platina, Onuphrius, Guicciardini and others, and let them be set side by side. Unless it is established that the Papal state matched the empire of the Caesars in the greatness of its power, the pride of its domination and the persecution of Christians, we by no means refuse that this judgment be passed upon us: we who attribute the name of Babylon to Papal Rome, and dissent from the Fathers. But if the case stands otherwise, then by Sanders' own vote we hold that those men, weighing like with like, would have stamped Christian Rome of today, which equals ancient pagan Rome, with the brand of Babylon just as openly, if they were still alive today. But what will those men say about Jerome? For in his preface to the book of Didymus on the Holy Spirit he openly called the Church of Rome Babylon and the purple harlot. And at Jeremiah 1 he named the pot burning from the face of the north the Church, not the city, because he calls the senate of Babylon, that is, the churchmen, the senate of the Pharisees and the ignorant who had conspired against it. But it was the clergy who conspired, not the Capitoline curia of Caesar. And this very faction he calls the burning pot. Elsewhere, from the prophecy of the Apocalypse, the same Jerome says that a dreadful ruin hangs over the Roman Church. Read, he says, the Apocalypse of John, in his letter 47 to Marcellinus; and consider what is sung about the purple woman, the blasphemy written on her forehead, the seven hills, the many waters, and the fall of Babylon. Come out, says the Lord, my people from her, and do not be partakers of her sins, and do not receive of her plagues. Flee from the midst of Babylon, and save each his own soul. For she has fallen, fallen is great Babylon, and has become the habitation of demons and the prison of every unclean spirit. Jerome indeed there distinguishes and separates the sacred from the profane. Nevertheless, even in the sacred and ecclesiastical matters themselves, he then saw in the same place something that smelled of Babylon. There is indeed, so he speaks in letter 18: the holy Church, the trophies of the Apostles and Martyrs, the true confession of Christ, the faith preached by the Apostle, and trampling on heathendom, lifting itself daily on high, rising in the name Christian. But ambition itself, power, the greatness of the city, to be seen and to see, to greet and be greeted, to praise and to disparage, to hear or to speak out, and even to see so great a crowd of men, though unwilling, are foreign to the purpose and quiet of monks. He indicates that the manners of the secular clergy and of the religious had already taken hold among Christians as well. Nor does he deny that the final ruin, from the prophecy of the Apocalypse, hangs over that same city, however much it was then renowned for its confession and devotion to Christ; and he says that one must listen to that prophecy: Fallen, fallen is great Babylon, and he foretells that it will become a habitation of demons, and will fall from there in an irreparable collapse. Although he asserts that it could avoid these impending punishments, if, like the Ninevites, it fled to repentance. The curse, so he writes in book 2 against Jovinian, which the Savior threatened you with in the Apocalypse, you can escape through repentance, having the example of the Ninevites. Would that it were so! If Rome still had emperors, and such Christians as the Romans were in Jerome's time, we would perhaps attribute the cause of the destruction to the iniquities of emperors and secular men of that kind. For Jerome also thought that the cause of the coming destruction was to be ascribed to these. But since Rome no longer obeys emperors or secular men, but a dominant clergy, who does not see that the evil breaks out from the sanctuary itself, and that the whoredom of Rome is practised not in the imperial but in the ecclesiastical government? Paulinus too thought that the ruin of Rome foretold in the Apocalypse would arise from the imperial court and secular men. For he speaks thus in letter 51: You, Rome, could have had no fear of the threats leveled against you in the Apocalypse, if your senators always gave other gifts; such as, namely, the senator Alithius, a holy man, pious in his works and very religious, used to give. Meanwhile Paulinus himself, in letter 10, calls Rome the daughter of Babylon, and he sets her after the daughter of Zion, although in some part, that is, in the faithful and good, each makes Rome a daughter of Zion. He knew nonetheless from that prophecy that at last the whole city was to be turned into Babylon, and that God would hear the people of God, if any should be found in it: Come out, come out from her, and so the threats of the Apocalypse would be endured. Gregory the Great, the most distinguished of the Roman pontiffs, in book 4, letter 32, writing to John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople, who was boasting of being the Ecumenical and Universal Bishop, compares him with Lucifer, the king of spiritual Babylon, who said in his heart (Isaiah XIV. 13): I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven, I will sit on the mountain of assembly, on the sides of the north. I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High. For what, he argues, are all your brethren, the bishops of the universal Church, but the stars of heaven? Whose lives, mingled with the sins and errors of men, lie hidden as if in the darkness of night. To whom
