units.la: Quibus dum cupis temet ipsum vocabulo elationis præponere, quid aliud dicis? nisi; In cœlum conscendam? Dum vestra fraternitas despiciens sub se premere conatur, quid aliud dicit, nisi hoc, quod ab antiquo hoste dicitur, Ascendam super altitudinem nubium. Quæ cuncta ergò, cùm flens respicio, &c. Si Gregorio Lucifer, Babylonis Rex, fuit Johannes ille Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha, eò quòd ob Imperialis Sedis eminentiam & prærogativam, ipse quoque supra cateras Episcopos, ipsúmque Romanum etiam, eminentiam affectavit: annon idem potiori ratione Bonifacium III. Romanum Pontificem, omnesque vestigiis ejus inhærentes, quin & superba ὑπερoχῆ, elatione, sua quotidie in pejus proficientes, Universalis & Œcumenici Episcopi axioma, nulla licet Politica loci prærogativa favente amplius palam usurpantes & reliquos Patriarchas & Episcopos, haud aliter quàm vasallos & clitellaria mancipia sua despicientes, quin & subinde pedibus calcantes; Luciferi, Babylonii illius Regis nomen & omen implesse, pridem censuisset, si vivens adhuc, spiritúsque oc̈ulis suis talia usurpasset, attribusque percepisset? Censeret sanè hodiéque, si δίκαιον κρίνειν κρίνεσθαι, justum judicium judicare, cura cordíque ei adhuc esset. Vatem certè gessit, cùm parte v. Reg. Epist. 38. ad eundem Constantinopolitanum Præsidem talia verba fecit: Secundum quod veritas prædixit, pestilentia & gladius per mundum sævit: gentes in gentes insurgunt, terræ concutitur orbis cum habitatoribus suis: terræ dehiscentes solvuntur: omnia, quæ prædicta sunt, fiunt. Rex superbiæ propè est, & (quod dici nefas est) Sacerdotum ei præparatur exercitus: quia cervici militante elationis, qui positi fuerant, ut ducatum præberent humilitatis. Sic plane S. Patres melioris, castiorísque ævi adhuc judicàrunt, divinàrúntque. Postquàm in Babylonem jam Sion Dei degeneravit, & urbs fidelis, Meretrix facta est, non defuerunt plorabundi corruptionis incessentis, grassantisque testes, quorum pars sanctam ἀναξιότητα suam impunè tulit: pars ferro, flammáque eandem fortiter, patienterque expiavit. Episcopi Belgici A. DCCCLX. cum Nicolao I. contentionis serram reciprocantes, Epistolam ad eundem acrem, ab Aventino Annal. Bojor. lib. iv. recitatam scripserunt. Inter alia, Spiritus, inquiunt, Sanctus, author est omnium Ecclesiarum, quo longissimè & latissimè terrarum orbis porrigitur. Civitas Dei nostri, cujus municipes sumus ad universos cœli cardines pertinet: major est urbe, quæ Babylonia à sacris Vatibus appellatur, ut quæ Divinitatem usurpet, cœlo se æquet, se æternam fore judicet, perinde ac si esset Deus, immortalísque sapientia: nec unquam errâsse, errareque posse mendaciter gloriétur. Nihil disertius dici poterat. Et paucis Episcopi cuncta, quæ in Opere nostro produćtiora edidimus, complećtuntur. Quàm exulceratà Ecclesiæ facies Decimo & Undecimo Seculo fuerit, è sinu Hierarchicorum testes magni, Baronius, Genebrardus, Platina, Sabellicus, Wernerus, alii nulli dissidifsimulárunt, ea monumentis suis de Rom. Ecclesia consignantes, qua interiora Babylonis manifeste produnt. Wernerus certe in Temporum fasciculo cum novo Seculo Undecimo novum hominum genus exortum, his verbis repraesentat: Tempus effœminatum incepit circa annum Domini millesimum, in quo fides Christiana valde coepit deficere & declinare à pristina virilitate, uti patet in Prophetia Sanctæ Hildegardis, & in multis regionibus Christianitatis nec Sacramenta, nec Ecclesiastici ritus servabantur. Erantque auguriis & maleficiis intendentes: & erat sacerdos sicut populus. Circa ea tempora in Ecclesia Catholica Salvatoris nostri Collegium Apostolicum sub purpurea, cruentáque veste (Babylonis insigni) imitari gloriatos esse Cardinales, Isidorus Mosennius de Majest. milit. Ecclef. lib. i. p. 1. cap. 5. scribit. Et Sacro-Sanctam militantem Ecclesiam tanquam purpureo totam decoratam esse amictu, Leo Papa constit. 8. jactavit: purpuratam illam meretricem Coccineâ insidentem Bestiæ in memoriam nobis revocans. Circa eadem tempora Petrus Waldo, Lugdunensis civis; coetu instituto segregè, cui Waldensium & Leonistarum inter alia nomen fuit, Rom. Ecclesiam esse Meretricem Babylonicam, veluti quendam doctrinam defendit, uti ex antiquo libro MSC. Magdeburgenses Historici Centur. xii. cap. 8. eruerunt. Neque aliter Bernhardus Morlanensis, ex Cluniacensium Ordine Monachus, qui uti in Honor. Dial. ad calcem 2. Tomi Auctarii Bibliothecæ Patrum, edit. Paris. A. 1620. legere est, hoc Romam vamine jam tum perstringere ausus est. Aurea tempora cæstáque pectora præterierant; Tempora pessima, scilicet ultima jam subierunt. Stant modò stantia sicut, superbia, pax sine pace, Fraus, Venus, Ortia, furtáque conscia noctis opacæ, Schismata, prælia, vis, homicidia, traditiones, Ira, protervia, livor, inertia, seditiones. Stat simulatio, corruit actio religionis: Heu! sua propria deputat omnia REX BABYLONIS.
units.tr: Whereas you wish to set yourself above others by the name of exaltation, what else do you say but: "I will ascend into heaven"? While your brotherhood, looking down upon them, tries to press them under itself, what else does it say but what is said by the ancient enemy: "I will ascend above the height of the clouds"? All these things, therefore, when I look back on them with tears, etc. If Lucifer, king of Babylon, was for Gregory that John, patriarch of Constantinople, because on account of the eminence and prerogative of the imperial see he too aspired to a pre-eminence above the other bishops, and even above the Roman himself: would not the same, with still greater reason, have been judged by Boniface III, Roman pontiff, and by all who cling to his footsteps, and who, in their proud excess, grow worse every day, openly claiming the title of Universal and Ecumenical Bishop, though no political favour of place now supports it, and despising the other patriarchs and bishops no differently than their vassals and beasts of burden, even trampling them underfoot from time to time, to have fulfilled the name and omen of that Lucifer, king of Babylon? He would surely have judged so long ago, had he, while still living, seen such things usurped with his own eyes and perceived them in their attributes. He would surely judge so even today, if he still had a care and concern for judging what is just to be judged justly [δίκαιον κρίνειν κρίνεσθαι]. He certainly acted as a prophet when, in part v of the Register, letter 38, he spoke these words to the same Constantinopolitan ruler: "According as the truth foretold, pestilence and sword rage through the world; nations rise against nations, the circle of the earth is shaken with its inhabitants, the earth splits open and dissolves; all things that were foretold come to pass." The king of pride is near, and (what it is wrong to say) an army of priests is being prepared for him, because those who had been placed to lead the way of humility have become soldiers in the service of the neck of pride. Thus plainly the Holy Fathers of a better and purer age judged and prophesied. After Zion of God had already degenerated into Babylon, and the faithful city had become a harlot, there were not wanting witnesses, weeping over the spreading and advancing corruption, some of whom bore their holy unworthiness with impunity, while others atoned for it bravely and patiently with the sword and fire. The Belgian bishops in 860, sawing back and forth in a dispute with Nicholas I, wrote a sharp letter to him, cited by Aventinus, Annals of Bavaria, book iv. Among other things, they say: the Holy Spirit is the author of all churches, by which it extends furthest and widest over the orb of the earth. The city of our God, whose citizens we are, extends to all the quarters of heaven; it is greater than the city which the sacred prophets call Babylon, which usurps divinity, makes itself equal to heaven, judges itself eternal, as though it were God and immortal wisdom, and boasts that it has never erred and cannot err falsely. Nothing could be said more plainly. And in a few words the bishops embrace all that we have brought forth at greater length in our work. How ulcerated the face of the Church was in the tenth and eleventh centuries, the great witnesses from the bosom of the hierarchs, Baronius, Genebrardus, Platina, Sabellicus, Werner, and others, have not concealed, recording these things in their monuments about the Roman Church, which clearly reveal the inner corruption of Babylon. Werner, in his Fasciculus temporum, certainly represents the new race of men that arose with the new eleventh century in these words: "A effeminate age began about the year of the Lord 1000, in which the Christian faith began greatly to fail and to decline from its former manliness, as is clear from the prophecy of St Hildegard, and in many regions of Christendom neither the sacraments nor the ecclesiastical rites were kept; they were devoted to omens and sorceries, and the priest was like the people." At about that time, Isidorus Mosennius, On the Majesty of the Militant Church, book i, part 1, chapter 5, writes that the cardinals gloried in imitating the apostolic college of our Saviour in the Catholic Church by a purple and bloody garment (the badge of Babylon). And Pope Leo, in constitution 8, boasted that the Sacred and Most Holy Militant Church is wholly adorned as with a purple cloak, recalling to us that purple harlot sitting upon the scarlet beast. About the same time Peter Waldo, a citizen of Lyons, founded a separate assembly, which among other names was called that of the Waldenses and Leonists, and defended the doctrine that the Roman Church is the Babylonian harlot, as the Magdeburg historians, Centuria xii, chapter 8, brought to light from an ancient manuscript book. Nor otherwise Bernhard of Morlaix, a monk of the Order of Cluny, who, as may be read in the Honorius Dialogue at the end of the second tome of the Auctarium of the Bibliotheca Patrum, Paris edition of 1620, dared even then to attack Rome with this verse. The golden times and chaste hearts had passed; the worst times, that is, the last, had now come. Now stand the things that stand, pride, peace without peace, fraud, lust, lewdness and thefts conscious of the dark night, schisms, battles, violence, murders, traditions, anger, wantonness, envy, sloth, seditions. Pretence stands, the action of religion falls: alas! the KING OF BABYLON assigns all these things to his own.

units.la: Eodem modo Honorius Augustodunensis Ecclesiæ Presbyter, Trithemii elogio, Vir in Scripturis Sanctis studiosissimus & valdè eruditus, qui A. MCXX. claruit, in Dialogo de Prædestinatione & Libero Arbitrio, sui temporis Babyloniam depingit. Intuere inquit, Principes & Judices: ecce posita in eis est Bestiæ sedes. Omni tempore ad malum sunt intenti, semper negotiis iniquitatis inexplebiliter occupati: flagitia non solùm faciunt, sed & alios facere instruunt. Sanctaviendunt, scelera emunt: totis viribus laborant, ne soli ad tartara veniant. Verte te ad Clerum,
units.tr: In the same way Honorius of Autun, a presbyter of the Church, described by Trithemius as a man most devoted to the Holy Scriptures and very learned, who flourished in 1120, depicts the Babylon of his own time in the Dialogue on Predestination and Free Will. Look, he says, at the princes and judges: behold, the seat of the Beast is set in them. At all times they are intent on evil, always insatiably occupied with the business of iniquity: they not only commit crimes but also teach others to commit them. They sell holy things, they buy crimes; they labour with all their strength lest they alone come to hell. Turn now to the clergy,

units.la: PROLOGUS GALEATUS.
units.tr: THE HELMETED PROLOGUE.

units.la: Clerum, & videbis in eis Bestiæ tentorium: Dei servitium negligunt, terrenis lucris inserviunt, Sacerdotium per immunditiam polluunt, populum per simulationem seducunt, Deum per mala opera abnegant, omnes Scripturas ad salutem pertinentes abdicant, omnibus modis se laqueos & ruinam populo substernunt, quem circumipsi cæci ad interitum præeunt. Contemplare & Monachorum Concilabula & videbis in eis Bestiæ tabernacula. Perfectam professionem Deum irritidentes, iram ejus provocant, normam regularem moribus & vitâ calcant, per habitum secundum fallunt, multos deceptos ipsi decepti decipiunt. Secularibus negotiis impliciti sunt, in Dei servitio desides existunt. Plerique illorum guliæ & illecebris dediti sunt, quidam in immunditiæ sordibus computrescunt. Aspice etiam habitacula Monialium, & cernes in eis Bestiæ præparatum Thalamum. Hæ à tenera ætate impudicitiam discunt, complices sibi plurimos ad cumulum suæ dominationis asciscunt: velo se operire festinant, quò magis srena luxuriæ laxare queant, omnibus fornicariis pejus prosternuntur, & ut insatiabilis charybdis, nunquam stercore immunditiæ replebuntur. Hæ animas juvenum illaqueant: & hæc vult palmam victoriæ, quæ aliis prævalet in scelere. Verte te ad plebem reliquam, & invenies in ea Bestiæ effigiem. Sacerdotes despiciunt, de Deo quicquam audire contemnunt, totum tempus vitæ in vanitate & jactantia ducunt, & ad omne opus bonum reprobi sunt. Vulgus quoque indoctum Bestiæ habet idolum, Deum verum non nôrunt, Deo ventri-tota intentione deserviunt, per varia carnis desideria diffluunt, & per omnia vitam Bestialem ducunt. Ibidem sic Romam Papalem perstringit: Verte te ad cives Babyloniæ, & vide, quales sint, & per quas plateas tendant. Vide, veni huc ad supercilium montis, ut cuncta possis ædificia cernere DAMNATÆ CIVITATIS. Intuere Principes & Judices (Papam & Cardinales) ecce, posita est in eis Bestiæ sedes. Extat in Tomo Conciliorum Coloniæ editorum, Epistola Leodiensis Ecclesiæ contra Paschalem II. qui eam Ecclesiam & Provinciam Roberto Comiti Flandriæ, igni ferroque vastandam objecerat. In ea epistola Romam rotundo ore Babylonem Clerus ille appellat, asseritque Romam à S. Petro sic Prophetico Spiritu vocatam esse, co quòd Romanis & procellis Ecclesia esset perturbanda. Atque eodem tempore pleriqué alii cum privatim, tum publicè pro concione Gregorio maledixerunt, vociferantes palam, cum odio & libidine dominandi præcipitem agi, atque Antichristum esse. Pietatis sub specie, sic Aventino Annal. Bojor. lib. v. referente, loquebantur, debacchatur honestis nominibus, bonum publicum simulat, titulo Christi negotium Antichristi cogitat, in Babylonia, Templo Dei sedet, super omne id, quod colitur, extollitur, quasi Deus sit; se errare non posse gloriatur. Quid Petrum Blefensem, Archidiaconum Bathonensem, Virum,
units.tr: Look at the clergy, and you will see in them the tent of the Beast. They neglect the service of God, serve earthly gain, pollute the priesthood with uncleanness, seduce the people by pretence, deny God by their evil works, reject all the Scriptures that pertain to salvation, and in every way lay snares and ruin before the people, whom they themselves, being blind, lead on to destruction. Consider also the assemblies of the monks, and you will see in them the tabernacles of the Beast. By their profession of perfection they provoke God and stir up his wrath; they trample the rule of their order underfoot in their conduct and life, and deceive by their outward habit alone, deceiving many while they themselves are deceived. They are caught up in worldly business and are idle in the service of God. Most of them are given over to gluttony and allurements, and some rot away in the filth of uncleanness. Look also at the dwellings of the nuns, and you will see in them the bridal chamber prepared for the Beast. From tender age these women learn immodesty, and they enlist many accomplices to swell their dominion. They hasten to cover themselves with the veil, so that they may the more freely loosen the reins of lust; they are cast down worse than all fornicators, and like an insatiable Charybdis they will never be filled with the dung of uncleanness. These women ensnare the souls of young men, and she claims the palm of victory who surpasses the rest in wickedness. Turn to the rest of the common people, and you will find in them the image of the Beast. They despise the priests, scorn to hear anything about God, spend their whole life in vanity and boasting, and are reprobate for every good work. The untaught common folk also have the idol of the Beast: they do not know the true God, they serve their belly with their whole attention, they dissolve in the various desires of the flesh, and in all things they lead a bestial life. In the same place he thus lashes Papal Rome: Turn to the citizens of Babylon, and see what they are like and through what streets they walk. See, come here to the brow of the mountain, that you may be able to behold all the buildings of THE DAMNED CITY. Look at the princes and judges (the Pope and the Cardinals): behold, the seat of the Beast is set in them. There is extant, in the Tome of Councils published at Cologne, a letter of the Church of Liège against Paschal II, who had exposed that Church and Province to be laid waste with fire and sword by Robert, Count of Flanders. In that letter the clergyman calls Rome Babylon with a round mouth Babylon that clergyman calls it, and asserts that Rome was called Babylon by St Peter in prophetic Spirit, because the Church was to be disturbed by the Romans and their storms. And at the same time many others, both privately and publicly from the pulpit, cursed Gregory, openly shouting that he was driven headlong by hatred and lust for domination and was Antichrist. Under the appearance of piety, as Aventinus reports in the Annals of Bavaria, book 5, they spoke thus: he rages under honourable names, feigns the public good, under the title of Christ plots the business of Antichrist, sits in the Temple of God in Babylon, exalts himself above all that is worshipped, as if he were God; he boasts that he cannot err. What of Peter of Blois, Archdeacon of Bath, a man,

units.la: PROLOGUS GALEATUS.
units.tr: The Prologue in Armour

units.la: Virum, sicut Trithemio celebratur, in Divinis Scripturis studiosum & eruditum, ingenio acutum & vehementem, qui vitia Principum & Praelatorum non palpare, sed arguere noverat, propter eruditionem, & vitae honestatem apud Reges, Principes, & Episcopos in pretio habitum, memorem? Ille Epistolam ad Episcopi Officialem scriptam, hortatur, ut quam primum Babylone illa exeat. Quia, inquit, te affectuosissime diligo in visceribus Jesu Christi, propositi, te salutaribus monitionibus adhortari, ut de Ure Chaldaeorum, & de medio Babylonis, tempestive exeas, ut ministerium damnatissimae villicationis omittas. Clerum subinde Syriam, vitulos Bethel, pingues Samariae, Sacerdotes Baal, judices leges iniquas condentes, appellat. Cantantur, inquit, eorum turpitudines in tentoriis Gath, & in compitis Ascalonis, sic factus est Princeps Sodomorum, discipulis post eum in cathedra pestilentiae Sedentibus.
units.tr: A man, as Trithemius celebrates him, learned in the Divine Scriptures, keen and vehement in intellect, who knew how to censure the vices of princes and prelates rather than flatter them, and who was held in high esteem by kings, princes and bishops on account of his learning and uprightness of life, shall I mention him? He writes a letter to the bishop's official, urging him to leave that Babylon as soon as possible. Because, he says, I love you most affectionately in the bowels of Jesus Christ, I exhort you with wholesome warnings, that you should leave in good time the Chaldeans' furnace and the midst of Babylon, so that you may give up the ministry of that most damnable stewardship. From time to time he calls the clergy Syria, the calves of Bethel, the fat ones of Samaria, the priests of Baal, judges who make unjust laws. Their foulness, he says, is sung in the tents of Gath and in the streets of Ascalon; thus the prince of Sodom has been made, with his disciples sitting after him in the chair of pestilence.

units.la: Sequente Seculo Decimo-tertio fortissimi Imperatoris Friderici II. a Gregorio IX. Pontifice exagitati praeter meritum, nomine Eberhardus Salisburgensis Archiepiscopus, orationem Regimoburgi habuit, in qua captum Gregorium ajebat Imperii confusetudine, ut solus regnet, cuncta eum perturbare, & commiscere, cuncta tumultu complere, ut sursum deorsum omnia ferantur. Jam pridem eos qui Babyloniae, hoc est, Romae Templo Dei incubant, Divinitatem affectare, & strenue id dissimulare. Addit paulo post: Paulus armarium Philosophiae Divinae praecipit, subjecti invicem in timore Christi eliptae. Hoc interesse inter Christianorum, & profanorum Principes, coelestis Doctor & Praeceptor noster, summusque atque immortalis Pontifex docuit, quod hi dominantur subditis, illi serviunt. Formam servi suprema Majestatis suscepit, ut discipulis suis serviret, corumque pedes lavaret. Flamines illi Babyloniae soli regnare cupiunt, serve parem non possunt; non desistent, donec omnia pedibus suis conculcaverint, atque in Templo Dei sedeant, extollantque supra omne id, quod colitur. Fames opum, sitis bonorum inexplicabilis est. Haec apud Aventinum Annal. Bojor. lib. VI. recitata summam eorum, quae tota Opere nostro demonstranda suscepimus, continent.
units.tr: In the following thirteenth century, the most valiant Emperor Frederick II, harassed by Pope Gregory IX beyond his deserts, Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, gave an oration at Regensburg, in which he said that Gregory, by the custom of the Empire, wanted to reign alone, that he disturbed and mingled everything, filled everything with tumult, so that all things were carried up and down. Long ago, those who brood over the Temple of God in Babylon, that is, in Rome, aspire to divinity and stoutly conceal it. He adds shortly after: Paul prescribes the storehouse of divine philosophy: submit yourselves one to another in the fear of Christ. That there is a difference between Christian and secular princes, our heavenly Teacher and Master, and our highest and immortal High Priest, taught: these lord it over their subjects, those serve them. The Supreme Majesty took on the form of a servant, that he might serve his disciples and wash their feet. Those priests of Babylon want to reign alone, they cannot serve as equals; they will not stop until they have trodden all things under their feet and sit in the Temple of God, exalting themselves above everything that is worshipped. The hunger for wealth and the thirst for goods are insatiable. These things, recited from Aventinus, Annals of Bavaria, book VI, contain the sum of what we have undertaken to demonstrate in our whole work.

units.la: Atque eo quidem tempore adeo pervulgata multorum in Germania, Italia, Francia, Anglia, opinio fuit, Romam Babylonem & Magnam illam Meretricem esse, ut impostores quidam Apocalypsin abolere conati sint; maxime Cyrillus Carmelita Graecus, qui tam Mosis, quam Johannis exemplo, novam Apocalypsin e coelis circa An. Christi MCXCII. Dei ipsius digito in argenteis tabulis Graece scriptam super futuro Ecclesiae statu se accepisse gloriatus est.
units.tr: And at that time the opinion was so widespread among many people in Germany, Italy, France and England that Rome is Babylon and that great Harlot, that certain impostors tried to abolish the Apocalypse; above all Cyril, the Greek Carmelite, who boasted that, like Moses and John, he had received a new Apocalypse from heaven around the year of Christ 1192, written in Greek on silver tablets by God's own finger, concerning the future state of the Church.

units.la: Floruit iisdem temporibus Joachimus Abbas Florensis Coenobii, Ordinis S. Benedicti, ex Calabria oriundus, Vir: sic idem, qui supra, Trithemius eum laudat, in Divinis Scripturis studiosus & exercitatus, qui, ut Propheta, suo tempore, habitus, etiam futura praedicere conatus est: sed mihi (sic
units.tr: At the same time there flourished Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore of the Order of St Benedict, a native of Calabria, a man who, as the same Trithemius praises him, was studious and practised in the Divine Scriptures, and who, being regarded as a prophet in his own time, also tried to foretell the future; but to me

units.la: e

( sic Tritbemius optimè judicat ) videtur, illum ex conjecturis Scripturarum magis locutum esse, quàm prophetâsse; hic, inquam, Ioachimus, cum alibi, commentario in primum super Ieremiam, Rom. Ecclesiæ corruptionem & interitum prænuntiavit; tum in primis Rogerio Hovedeno referente, & ex eodem Faxo, Anglo in Commentariis rerum in Ecclesia gestarum repetente, in Colloquio cum Richardo, Rege, explicans mysterium septem Regum in Apocalypsi, quorum quinque ceciderunt, &c.
units.tr: (as Trithemius judges very well) it seems that he spoke more from conjectures drawn from Scripture than prophesied. This Joachim, I say, while elsewhere, in his commentary on the first part of Jeremiah, he foretold the corruption and ruin of the Roman Church; then especially, as Roger of Hoveden reports, and as Faxo, the Englishman, repeats from the same in his Commentaries on the things done in the Church, in a conversation with King Richard, he explained the mystery of the seven kings in the Apocalypse, of whom five have fallen, etc.

units.la: Reges septem, inquit, sunt septem persecutores, Herodes, Nero, Constantius, Mahumet, Melsemutus, Saladinus, & Antichristus. De Antichristo, subjiciebat, cum in urbe Romana jam prognatum esse, & in Apostolica sede sublimatum, atque sic impletum iri verba Apostoli: Extollitur & adversatur super omne, quod dicitur Deus. Quid verò de S. Brigitta, fatidica foemina, à Gregorio ix. in Sanctorum numerum relata, dicam? Illa enim vidua sanctissima, sic iterum Tritbemius, Divino colloquio assueta, & intimæ charitatis perfectione Deo unita, Spiritu quoque Prophetico & miraculis celeberrima, peculiari de Prophetiis & Revelationibus Opere scripto, lib. i. cap. 41. Rom. Episcopum Lucifero, in persona Christi compellat. Nunc ergo, inquit, conqueror super te, Caput Ecclesiæ meæ: qui sedes in sede mea, quam Petro & Successoribus ejus tradidi, ad sedendum in ea triplici authoritate & dignitate: primò, ut potestatem haberent ligandi animas & solvendi à peccato: 2. ut aperirent cœlum poenitentibus: 3. ut clauderent cœlum maledictis & condemnatis. Sed tu, qui deberes solvere animas, & ad me praesentare, verè es animarum interfector. Ego enim instituti Petrum Pastorem ovium mearum: tu autem es Dispersor & Lacerator earum. Tu autem pejor es Lucifero. Is enim ad me habebat invidiam, & nullum concupivit occidere, nisi me; ut pro me dominaretur: tu autem tantò deterior es, quòd non solum occidis me, removendo me à te per mala opera tua: sed & animas occidis per malum exemplum tuum. Deinteps eundem contendit cum Pilato, Juda & Judæis, verbis adeò pragnantibus, adeò Papæ infestis, ut evitanda gravioris invidiæ causa, in repetendis superioribus foedere cogar. Unum tamen addo, prædixisse eandem; Sedem Papæ demergendam esse, ut lapidem ponderosum, & assessores ejus arsuros igni inextinguibilis. Episcopos inde, caterosque Sacerdotes reprehendit, quòd eorum culpa doctrina Christi neglecta & fermè abolita sit, Divina sapientia à Clericis in pravam & vanam conversa, addens, leprosos illos esse & mutos, omniaque Dei praecepta communicasse in unicum, Da pecuniam. Denique vidisse se, ait, Virginem dicentem ad Filium, Romam esse feracem agrum. Respondisse verò Christum, est, sed Zizaniæ. Quò magis ad Reformationem approximatum est, hoc plures, clarioréisque hujus veritatis prodiere testes: A. MCCCXLV. Hayabulus, Minorita, Henrico de Erphordia
units.tr: The seven kings, he says, are seven persecutors: Herod, Nero, Constantius, Mahomet, Melsemutus, Saladin and Antichrist. About Antichrist, he added, that he had already been born in the Roman city and raised up to the apostolic see, and that thus the words of the Apostle would be fulfilled: he exalts himself and sets himself against everything that is called God. But what shall I say about St Bridget, the prophetess, whom Gregory IX enrolled among the saints? For that most holy widow, as Trithemius again says, accustomed to divine converse, united to God by the perfection of intimate charity, and most famous for the prophetic Spirit and for miracles, in her special written work on Prophecies and Revelations, book 1, chapter 41, addresses the Roman bishop as Lucifer, in the person of Christ. "Now therefore," she says, "I complain against you, head of my Church, you who sit in my seat, which I handed over to Peter and his successors, to sit in it with a threefold authority and dignity: first, that they should have the power of binding souls and loosing them from sin; second, that they should open heaven to the penitent; third, that they should shut heaven against the accursed and condemned. But you, who ought to loose souls and present them to me, are truly a murderer of souls. For I appointed Peter as minister of my sheep; but you are their scatterer and tearer. And you are worse than Lucifer. For he had envy toward me, and desired to kill none but me, so that he might rule in my place; but you are so much worse, because you not only kill me, removing me from you by your evil works, but also kill souls by your evil example." Next she contends with the same against Pilate, Judas and the Jews, in words so weighty and so hostile to the Pope that, to avoid the cause of greater odium, I am forced to be sparing in repeating what has been said above. I add one thing, however: she foretold that the Papal see is to be sunk like a heavy stone, and its occupants will burn in unquenchable fire. Then she rebukes the bishops and the other priests, because through their fault the doctrine of Christ has been neglected and nearly abolished, and divine wisdom has been turned by the clergy into something perverse and vain, adding that they are lepers and dumb, and that they have reduced all of God's precepts to one: "Give money." Finally, she says, she saw the Virgin saying to the Son that Rome is a fertile field. Christ replied: "It is, but a field of tares." The closer the approach to the Reformation, the more and clearer the witnesses to this truth that came forth: in 1345 Hayabulus, a Minorite, as Henry of Erfurt relates in his Historical Work on memorable deeds,

units.la: {*} ) ⁊ dia in Opere Historiarum de factis memorabilibus narrante, publicis contentionibus affirmavit identidem, se Divinitus jussum palam pronuntiare, quòd Rom. Ecclesia sit Babylonica Meretrix, Papa & Cardinales Antichristi. Atque idipsum non coram vulgi duntaxat face, sed Avenione etiam coram ipso Pontifice Clemente constanter & intrepide cum declamâsset, dirum ab eodem in modum vexatum esse, Author idem commemorat. Volquini cujusdam homilia super Evangelium de interseminata Zizania, ante Luthceri tempora vulgata, & A. MDLV. Basilea impressa extat. Ibi Author inter alia: Proh! dolor & Proh! dolor, hodie Meretrix antiqua, quæ habet poculum aureum in manu sua plenum abominatione, fornicatione & immunditiâ, quâ mirabiliter inebriat Sacerdotes & Clericos. De quâ in Apocalypsi: Vidi mulierem ebriam de sanguine virorum, & de sanguine Martyrum Christi, Mulierem mollem dicit, emollientem luxuriam carnis, ebriam de sanguine suorum scortorum sive scortatorum. Hæc est illa sanguisuga, quæ fugit sanguinem Ministrorum, & Martyrum Dei, qui Martyres Christi esse debuerant, & fiunt Martyres Diaboli, in honorem ejus & obsequium, carnem & sanguinem consumentes. Cùm vidissem, inquit, homines, miratus sum. Quis non miretur, & horreat, & obstupescat Sacerdotem Domini, ministrum Dei, calice epoto sitibundum, & potare fæces de calice Babylonis. Dantes Aligerus, Florentinus, Vir, sic iterum TritheMius, tam in Divinis Scripturis, quàm in saecularibus literis omnium suo tempore studiosissimus, & valde eruditus Philosophus & Poeta nulli sua ætate inferior, ingenio subtilis, & clarus eloquio, disputator omnium acutissimus, Ludovici Bavari Imperatoris partibus addictus, Papam Meretricem Babylonicam esse, non obscurè Concione 32. Purgat. prodidit. Ibi enim Papæ ministris, id est, Episcopi tribus bicornia capita, quatuor verò quibusdam, quibusdam unum cornu: ipsi verò Meretrici inflar cujusdam arcis. Qui eidem Ludovico Imperatori à secretis fuit, Udalricus de Augusta, in Regiis literis summum Pontificem vocavit, Bestiam ortam è mari. Refert ita in Paralipomenis suis Urspergensis Abbas. Ex prælectionibus Joh. Wiclefi in Apocalypsin, nonnulla collegit Johannes Purvus, Anglus, quæ A. MDXXVIII. ex Livonicis & Polonicis similibus submissa, luci publicæ data sunt. Ibi Purvæus Rom. Ecclesiam apertissimis verbis Meretricem Babylonicam, & Papam Antichristum esse, probat eo argumento, quòd neglecto Dei verbo, suas traditiunculas & nugas doceat, Evangelium insuper, piosque Doctores opprimat: quæstûs gratiâ Indulgentias excogitaverit, potentiam, & splendorem Regni sub falso Donationis Constantini M. nomine ad se pertraxerit, ex mandatis Christi Consilia fecerit, aliisque se flagitiis contaminaverit. Plura ιμφαπηχθηειγ ibidem addit. Jungam huic Michaelem Cesennatem, Minoritarum Generalem, qui à partibus stans Ludovici Bavari, Rom. Ecclesiæ Babylonibylonicum meretricium masculè objecit; qui virus cum tremari nequiret, mortuus in osibus suis combustus est. Idem coætaneus Cæsennatis Johannes de Rupe scissa asserere piaculum non duxit. De Petro Johanne Pyrrhaensi, qui A. MCCCXXV. floruit, testes habemus Volaterranum, & Bernhardum Luzelburgensem, quod Rom. Ecclesiam Babylonitam Meretricem haud semel insigniverit. Cumque idipsum circa eadem tempora Gerhardus Sagareli Parmensis, & Dulanus Novarensis sustinuissent, gravissimas persecutiones illos subiisse Historici perhibent. De Francisco Petrarcha, Hetrusco, quid dicam? Is laudante Trithemio, Vir erat in Divinis Scripturis eruditus, & in secularibus literis omnium sui temporis longè doctissimus, Philosophus, Rhetor, & Poëta celeberrimus, qui litteras humanitatis post longa silentia mortuas, ab inferis revocavit ad superos, non minus sanctâ conversatione, quàm scientiâ clarus emicuit: Amore namque Christi & Philosophiæ Salutaris vitam solitariam aggressus est, in qua usque ad mortem meditando, orando, & scribendo perseverans, toto mundo ejus fama ferebatur. Is ergo Vir talis & tantus, in Italicis suis Rhythmis de Roma sic inter alia:
units.tr: In public disputations he repeatedly affirmed that he had been divinely commanded to declare openly that the Roman Church is the Babylonian harlot and that the Pope and cardinals are Antichrist. He did this not only before the common crowd but also at Avignon, before Pope Clement himself, speaking constantly and fearlessly; the same author records that he was harshly treated by him for it. A homily of a certain Volquinus on the Gospel of the tares sown among the wheat, published before Luther's time and printed at Basel in 1555, survives. There the author says, among other things: "Alas! alas! Today the old harlot, who holds in her hand a golden cup full of abomination, fornication and uncleanness, with which she wondrously intoxicates priests and clerics. Concerning her, the Apocalypse says: 'I saw a woman drunk with the blood of men and with the blood of the martyrs of Christ.' She is called soft, softening the luxury of the flesh, drunk with the blood of her harlots or whoremongers. This is that bloodsucker which flees from the blood of the ministers and martyrs of God, who ought to have been martyrs of Christ, and have become martyrs of the Devil, consuming flesh and blood to his honour and service. When I had seen men," he says, "I marvelled. Who would not marvel, and shudder, and be astonished at a priest of the Lord, a minister of God, thirsty, having drained the cup and drinking the dregs from the cup of Babylon?" Dante Alighieri, the Florentine, a man, again, as Trithemius says, most studious of all his time both in the Divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a very learned philosopher and poet, equal to none of his age in intellect, subtle and clear in eloquence, the most acute of disputants, devoted to the party of the Emperor Louis of Bavaria, plainly declared in the 32nd canto of the Purgatorio that the Pope is the Babylonian harlot. For there, to the Pope's ministers, that is, the bishops, he gives three two-horned heads, and to some four, to some one horn; and to the harlot herself, like a kind of fortress. Ulrich of Augsburg, who was secretary to the same Emperor Louis, in royal letters called the supreme Pontiff the beast rising out of the sea. The Abbot of Ursperg reports this in his Paralipomena. From the lectures of John Wycliffe on the Apocalypse, John Purvey, an Englishman, collected some things, which, sent up along with similar Livonian and Polish material, were brought to light in 1528. There Purvey proves, in the plainest words, that the Roman Church is the Babylonian harlot and the Pope is Antichrist, by the argument that, neglecting the Word of God, she teaches her own trifling traditions and fooleries, moreover oppresses the Gospel and pious teachers; that for the sake of gain she devised indulgences, drew to herself power and splendour of kingdom under the false name of the Donation of Constantine the Great, made counsels out of the commands of Christ, and defiled herself with other crimes. He adds more such matters there. Let me add to this Michael of Cesena, General of the Minorites, who, standing on the side of Louis of Bavaria, boldly charged the Roman Church with being the Babylonian harlot; since he could not be made to tremble, he died, burned in his bones. The same John of Rupescissa, a contemporary of Cesena, did not think it a sin to assert the same. Concerning Peter John of Pyrrha, who flourished in 1325, we have witnesses in Volaterranus and Bernard of Luxembourg, that he branded the Roman Church as the Babylonian harlot more than once. And since Gerard Segarelli of Parma and Dulcinus of Novara maintained the same around the same times, the historians report that they underwent the most grievous persecutions. What shall I say of Francis Petrarch, the Tuscan? He, as Trithemius praises him, was a man learned in the Divine Scriptures, and by far the most learned of all his time in secular letters, a most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician and poet, who called back to the living from the dead the humane letters, long buried after a long silence, and shone no less brightly for his holy way of life than for his learning. For out of love for Christ and for saving philosophy he embraced a solitary life, in which, persevering in meditation, prayer and writing until death, his fame was carried through the whole world. This man, so great and of such standing, says among other things in his Italian rhymes about Rome as follows:

units.la: Scola Errori, templo di erefia.
units.tr: School of error, temple of heresy.

units.la: Gia Roma, or Babylonia falsa é rlla.
units.tr: Now Rome, or false Babylon, is that.

units.la: Hoc est, Schola errorum: Templum hæreseon, quondam Roma, nunc Babylon falsa & mala. In eodem Poëmate haud semel eam vocat Babylonem, Matrem errorum & nidum proditionum. In Epistolis verò suis passim sententiam sequitur. Epistola quarta earum, qua sine titulo fuit, sic ad quendam amicum scribit: Nunc me Gallicus Orbis habet, & Occidentalis Babylon (Avinione Papæ tunc temporis) quâ nihil informius sol videt, & ferox Rhodanus æstuanti cocyto vel tartareo similimus Acheronti, ubi piscatorum inops quondam regnat hæreditas, minimum in modum oblita principii. Stupor est, memoriæ illos hos cernere auro onustos & purpurâ, superbos Principum ac gentium spoliis: videre pro iuversis natibus luxuriosa palatia, & mœnibus clausos montes: pro retibus parvis, quibus olim in æstu Galilæo victus vix exiguus quærebatur, quibus in stagno Genesareth tota nocte laborantes, nihil ceperant, mane autem facto, capta est in nomine Jesu multitudo piscium, audire nunc mendaces linguas, spectare membranas vero vacuas, & pendenti plumbulo versas in retia, quibus in nomine eodem, sed in operibus Belial, credula Christianorum turba concludatur, ut mox squamis exuta, curarum flammis & desolatoriis carbonibus, exuratur, javari ventris expletura voraginem: cernere pro sanctâ solitudine frequentiam sceleratam, & circumfusas acies satellitum pessimorum: pro sobriis voluptuosa convivia, pro peregrinationibus piis otium inhumanum & obscoenum: pro nudis pedibus Apostolorum niveos furum volitare cornipedes auro instratos, auro tectos, aurum mandentes, auro denique propediem, nisi Dominus servilem luxum coerceat, calceandos. Quid multa? Persarum aut Parthorum Reges dicas, quos adorari oporteat, quos salutari fine munere nefas sit. &c. Idem in Epist. 12. de Curia Papa: Nulla ibi pietas, nulla charitas, nulla fides, nulla Dei reverentia, &c. omnia ibi virtute, veroque sunt vacua, plena criminibus, plena fallaciis, plena pessimis artibus: ficte & inaniter omnia fiunt non tantum hominibus, sed Deo, &c. Inde nemo unquam exemplo melior factus, pessimi autem innumerabiles redierunt. Epist. 15. tota calamitatem urbis Romae deplorans, inter alia: Vides populum, inquit, non modo Christi adversarium, sed quod est gravius, sub Christi vexillo rebellantem Christo, militantem Sathanae, & Christi sanguine tumidum atque lascivientem: populum, cui non modo proprie convenire dixeris Evangelicum illud, atque Propheticum; Populus hic me labiis honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me: sed illud etiam Judae Iscariotis, qui Dominum suum prodens & exosculans ajebat, Ave Rabbi: & Judaeorum, qui induitur purpura, coronatum spinis, percutientes & conspuentes illusione amarissima a flexis poplitibus adorabant & salutabant: Ave Rex Judaeorum. Quid enim? Quid, oro, aliud assidue geritur hos inter Christi hostes, & nostri temporis Pharisaeos? Nonne etenim Christum ipsum, cujus nomen die ac nocte altissimis laudibus attollunt, quem purpura atque auro vestiunt, quem gemmis onerant, quem salutant & adorant cernui, eundem in terra eiciunt, vendunt, inundinantur, eundem quasi velatis oculis non visurum, & impiarum opum utpribus coronant, & impuritissimi oris sputis inquinant, & vipereis sibilis insectantur, & venatorum acetum cuspide feriunt, & quantum in eis est, illusum, nudum, inopem, flagellatum, iterum atque iterum in Calvariam trahunt, ac nefariis astantibus crucifurisfigunt. Eo o pudor, o dolor, o indignitas, talium hodie Roma est. Epistolam vero 16. qui legerit, dubitare amplius non poterit, quin Petrarcha Papam statuerit ipsissimam Babylonem, & Antichristum. Aliqua ex ea huc referam. Futurae ibi (in aula Papae) vitae species inanis quaedam fabula, & quae de infernis narrantur, fabulosa omnia habentur. Veritas ibi dementia est, abstinentia vero rusticitas, pudicitia probrum ingens: denique peccandi licentia magnanimitas & libertas eximia: quo pollutior, eo clarior vita; quo plus scelerum, eo plus gloriae: bonum nomen coeno vilius, atque ultima mercium fama est. Et infra: Fatuosa dicam, an infamis Meretrix fornicata cum Regibus terrae, illa equidem ipsa es, quam in Spiritu sacer vidit Evangelista. Illa eadem, inquam, es, non alia, sedens super aquas multas, sive ad littora tribus cincta fluminibus sive rerum atque divitiarum turbâ mortalium, quibus lasciviens ac secura insidens, opum immemor æternarum: sive ut idem, qui vidit, expositi, populi, & gentes, & linguæ, aquæ sunt, super quas Meretrix sedet. Recognosce habitum. Mulier circumdata purpurâ & coccino, & inaurata auro, & lapide pretioso, & margaritis, habens poculum aureum in manu sua plenum abominatione, & immunditiâ fornicationis ejus. Nonne scriptum est Babylon? Nisi illud forsan errorem facit, quòd in illius fronte scriptum erat, Babylon Magna: Tu verò Babylon parva es; parva utique morum ambitu, sed vitiis & ambitu animorum, & infinitâ cupidine, cumulóque malorum omnium non magna modò, sed maxima, & immensa es. Et certè, quod sequitur, tibi uni convenit, non alii: Babylon mater fornicationum & abominationum terræ, mater impia patrum pessimorum, quando quicquid usquam terrarum abominabile, quicquid fornicationum ex te prodit: & cum semper parias, semper tumens, ac talium plenus & gravidus tuus uterus est. Si nunc quoque dissimulas, audi reliqua. Et vidi (inquit) mulierem ebriam de sanguine Sanctorum, & de sanguine Martyrum Jesu. Quid siles? Aut aliam hoc sanguine ebriam ostende: aut omnino, si potes, te hanc ebriam negā. Vera enim Evangelistæ & Apostoli visio sit oportet: qui si te in Spiritu videns miratus est admiratione magna, quantâ nos admiratione perfundimur, qui apertè oculis te videmus? Ex omnibus quidem fornicationibus tuis, de quibus biberunt omnes gentes & Reges, & ex omnibus abominationibus quid expectes, nisi quod Johannes idem ait: Cecidit, cecidit Babylon magna, & facta est habitatio Dæmoniorum? Verè jam talis facta es. Quantò enim homo perditus & desperatæ nequitiæ Dæmone melior? Verè habitatio, imò regnum Dæmonum facta es, qui suis artibus, humanâ licèt effigie, in te regnant. Idem Epist. seq. Illos tenebrarum Principes cum suis opibus Deus vivos ac mortuos mali perdat, qui cœlestis Agni sanguine saginati calcitrant & rebellant. Cur Babylone (apud Papam) vivere eligam? ut videam bonos mergi, malos erigi? repere aquilas, asinos volare: vulpes in curribus; corvos in turribus; columbas in lterquilinio? liberos lupos: agnos in vinculis: Christum denique exulem: ANTICHRISTUM Dominum; Beelzebub judicem? Hæc ad spectacula revocor, non audiam: malè mihi cum illis, malè illis mecum convenit. O crudelis & impia secta hominum, nil nisi se ipsos amantium, idque ipsum perversè prorsus ac nefariè! Quis revelabit oppressum orbem? Quis vindicabit afflictam urbem? Quis eversos mores reformabit? quis colliget sparsas oves? quis pastores errones arguet? quis reducet & retraher in sedem suam? nullúsne licentiæ ac scelerum modus erit? &c. Sed infinitum sit Petrarcha doctissimi liberâ candidâque de mente.
units.tr: That is: School of errors, temple of heresies: once Rome, now false and evil Babylon. In the same poem he calls her Babylon more than once, mother of errors and nest of treacheries. In his Letters he follows the same view throughout. The fourth of these, which has no title, writes thus to a certain friend: "Now the French world holds me, and the Western Babylon (Avignon, where the Pope then was), than which the sun sees nothing more shapeless, and the fierce Rhône, most like the seething Cocytus or the Tartarean Acheron, where the once poor inheritance of the fishermen reigns, very much forgetful of its beginning. It is a wonder, remembering those men, to see these men laden with gold and purple, proud with the spoils of kings and nations; to see luxurious palaces in place of rough buttocks, and mountains enclosed by walls; in place of the small nets with which, in the Galilean heat, a meagre living was scarcely sought, with which they had toiled all night in the lake of Gennesaret and caught nothing, but in the morning, at the name of Jesus, a multitude of fish was taken: now to hear lying tongues, to look at empty parchments and leaden weights hanging down to turn into nets, in which, in the same name but in the works of Belial, the credulous crowd of Christians is shut in, so that, soon stripped of their scales, they are burnt in the flames of cares and the desolating coals, to fill the gulf of a greedy belly; to see, in place of holy solitude, a wicked throng and encircling battalions of the worst henchmen; in place of sober fare, voluptuous banquets; in place of pious pilgrimages, inhuman and obscene idleness; in place of the bare feet of the Apostles, the snow-white horses of thieves flitting about, decked with gold, covered with gold, champing gold, and at last, soon, unless the Lord restrains their servile luxury, to be shod with gold. What more? You would call them the kings of the Persians or Parthians, whom it is right to adore, and whom it is wrong to greet without a gift. etc." The same in Letter 12, on the Papal Court: There is no piety there, no charity, no faith, no reverence for God, etc.; everything there is empty of virtue and truth, full of crimes, full of deceits, full of the worst arts; everything is done falsely and vainly, not only toward men but toward God, etc. Hence no one has ever become better by example, while countless worst men have returned. Letter 15, lamenting the whole calamity of the city of Rome, among other things: You see the people, he says, not only an adversary of Christ, but, what is more grievous, rebelling against Christ under Christ's banner, fighting for Satan, and swollen and wanton with Christ's blood: a people to whom you could fittingly apply not only that saying of the Gospel and of the Prophet, "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me," but also that of Judas Iscariot, who, betraying and kissing his Lord, said, "Hail, Rabbi"; and that of the Jews, who, clothing him in purple, crowned with thorns, struck and spat upon him, and with most bitter mockery, with bended knees, adored and saluted him: "Hail, King of the Jews." For what else, I ask, is continually done among these enemies of Christ and Pharisees of our time? Do they not, indeed, cast out, sell and trade in Christ himself, whose name they extol day and night with the highest praises, whom they clothe in purple and gold, load with gems, greet and adore on bended knee, and yet, as if with eyes veiled, they will not see him; they crown him with the spoils of impious wealth, defile him with the spittle of the most impure mouth, hound him with viperous hisses, strike him with the hunters' vinegar and spear, and, as far as in them lies, mock him, strip him, leave him poor, scourge him, drag him again and again to Calvary, and fix him to the cross with wicked bystanders? O shame, O grief, O indignity: such is Rome today. But whoever reads Letter 16 can no longer doubt that Petrarch judged the Papacy to be very Babylon itself, and Antichrist. I will quote some of it here. In the court of the Pope (in aula Papae) the appearance of the life to come is some empty fable, and all that is told about the infernal regions is held to be fabulous. Truth there is madness, abstinence is rusticity, chastity a great disgrace; finally, license to sin is called greatness of soul and outstanding freedom: the more polluted a life, the more distinguished it is; the more crimes, the more glory; a good name is cheaper than mud, and reputation is the lowest of wares. And below: Shall I call you a foolish or infamous harlot who has fornicated with the kings of the earth? Surely you are that very one whom the holy Evangelist saw in the Spirit. It is that same one, I say, and no other, sitting upon many waters, or upon shores girt by three rivers, or upon the crowd of mortals with their things and riches, in which she, wanton and secure, sits, unmindful of eternal wealth; or, as he who saw her explained, the peoples, and nations, and tongues are the waters upon which the harlot sits. Recognise the dress: a woman clothed in purple and scarlet, gilded with gold, and with precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abomination and the filth of her fornication. Is it not written, Babylon? Unless perhaps this makes an error, that on her forehead was written, Babylon the Great: but you, Babylon, are small; small indeed in the compass of your manners, but great, indeed the greatest and immeasurable, in your vices and the compass of minds, in your boundless greed and the heaping up of all evils. And certainly what follows applies to you alone and to no other: Babylon, the mother of fornications and abominations of the earth, the impious mother of the worst fathers, since whatever abominable thing there is anywhere on earth, whatever fornication comes forth from you; and your womb is always bearing, always swollen, and full and heavy with such things. If you still dissemble, hear the rest: And I saw (it says) a woman drunken with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. Why are you silent? Either show another who is drunk with this blood, or, if you can, deny utterly that you are this drunken one. For the vision of the Evangelist and Apostle must be true: and if he, seeing you in the Spirit, was struck with great wonder, with how great a wonder are we overwhelmed, who see you plainly with our eyes? Of all your fornications, of which all nations and kings have drunk, and of all your abominations, what do you expect, except what John himself says: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and has become the habitation of devils"? Truly you have already become such. For how much better is a lost man of desperate wickedness than a devil? Truly you have become the habitation, nay the kingdom, of devils, who, though in human shape, reign in you by their arts. The same in the following letter: May God destroy those princes of darkness, living and dead, with their wealth, who, fattened on the blood of the heavenly Lamb, kick and rebel. Why should I choose to live in Babylon (at the Pope's court)? To see good men sunk and bad men raised up; eagles creeping and asses flying; foxes in chariots, ravens in towers, doves in the dunghill; wolves set free, lambs in chains; Christ at last an exile, ANTICHRIST lord, Beelzebub judge? I am called back to these spectacles, I will not listen: I am ill matched with them, and they ill matched with me. O cruel and impious sect of men, loving only themselves, and that in a utterly perverse and wicked way! Who will reveal the oppressed world? Who will avenge the afflicted city? Who will reform the overturned morals? Who will gather the scattered sheep? Who will reprove the wandering ministers? Who will lead back and restore them to their seat? Will there be no limit to license and crimes? etc. But let it suffice to have said this of the most learned Petrarch, from his free and candid mind."

units.la: Romana Babylone iudicia referre. Qui plura valet, cum alia, tum illum Epistolarum sine titulo librum, ipsius operibus insertum evolvat. Qui Basiliensis Concilii tempore vixit, Gregorius Heimburgensis, ICTus & Orator celebris, Sigismundi Archiducis Austriae magnus hyperaspistes, scripto de Primatu Papae libello, non semel Papae, ejusque Synagogae Babylonis & Babylonicae Meretricis stigma inussit. Ipse Rex Christianissimus Ludovicus XII. Iulio II. Romano Praesuli moribundo, cuius Neapoli aureo numismate cum hac inscriptione, PERDAM BABYLONIS NOMEN, postquam Mediolani Concilium de emendando statu Ecclesiae celebrasset, animum suum luculenter declaravit. His omnibus addam Iohannem Staphnlaum, Dalmatam, Episcopum Sebenicensem, & Auditorem Rota, qui Oratione ad Auditores reliquos Rota, post direptionem Romae die 15. Maii, A. M D XXVIII. habita, causas scrutatus infortunii praesentis, Romam ipsissimam Babylonem esse, maxima cum admiratione asseveravit: Oratio edita proflat cum testimoniis Practici Ferrariensis, quibus Caesarem Majestatem Papali superiorem esse demonstravit. Inter alia sic ille oravit. Sed unde haec quaeso? Quaesve ob causas tot & gravissima incommoda evenere? Nempe quia omnis caro corruperat viam suam. Eramus omnes cives & habitatores non Romae, urbis Sanctae, sed Babylonis, urbis peccatricis. De qua impletum est temporibus nostris verbum Domini in Esaia: Quomodo facta est Meretrix civitas fidelis, plena iudicio & sanctitate? Iustitia prius habitabat in ea nunc sacrilegi & homicidae: prius gens sancta, populus acquisitionis, nunc populus Gomorrhae, semen nequam, filii scelerati, sacerdotes infideles, socii furum, diligentes munera, sequentes retributiones. Post, allegatâ & recitatâ Apocalypseos de Babylone prophetiâ, singula ejus partes Romae sua applicat, subiicitque. Quod si quispiam pertinacius defendere velit, Apostolum loqui specifice de Babylone, huic ego respondeo, quod potius, quam Apostolus Petrus in prima Epistola sub nomine Babylonis figuraliter Romam significat, dum inquit: Salutat vos Ecclesia in Babylone collecta. Qua observatio ingenua profecto simul & ingeniosa est. Addam denique Iesuitarum primipilos, Franciscum Riberam, & Emmanuelem Viegam. Ille enim in cap. xvi i. Ioh. sic scribit: De Roma intelligendum vaticinium, non solum qualis sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus olim fuit, sed etiam qualis in fine seculi futura est. Hic similiter: Omnia, quae in his capp. commemorantur, in Romanam urbem apertissime quadrant. Caeterum, nomen Babylonis ad eam Romam transferendum, quae antequam reciperet fidem Christi, idolis serviebat, & ad eam etiam, quae erit tempore Antichristi. Consentientes his Iesuitas, Leonhardum Lessium, & Cornelium à Lapide, alibi produximus. Haec illa testium Reformatione Ecclesiae longe antiquiorum, quibus suffragia plura addi possent, Nubes assertionis nostra invidiam mollit non parum, efficietque adeo, notam
units.tr: Romana Babylon has rendered judgments. Whoever has more weight should read, besides the others, the book of Epistles without title, inserted among his works. Gregorius Heimburgensis, who lived at the time of the Council of Basel, a jurist and famous orator, the great champion of Archduke Sigismund of Austria, in his little book on the Primacy of the Pope, more than once branded the Pope, his Synagogue, and the Babylonian Harlot. King Louis XII of France himself, when Julius II, the Roman prelate, was dying, made his mind plainly known: at Naples he struck a gold coin bearing this inscription, I WILL DESTROY THE NAME OF BABYLON, and afterwards held a council at Milan on amending the state of the Church. To all these I will add John Staphylaeus, a Dalmatian, Bishop of Sebenico and an auditor of the Rota, who in a speech delivered to the other auditors of the Rota after the sack of Rome on 15 May 1528, examining the causes of the present misfortune, asserted, to great astonishment, that Rome itself is Babylon. The published speech appears together with the testimonies of the Ferrarese Practicus, by which he showed that the Imperial Majesty is superior to the Papal. Among other things he spoke thus: "But whence, I ask, these things? And for what causes have so many and most grievous calamities come upon us? Indeed, because all flesh had corrupted its way. We were all citizens and inhabitants not of Rome, the holy city, but of Babylon, the sinful city. Of which the word of the Lord in Isaiah has been fulfilled in our times: 'How has the faithful city become a harlot, full of judgment and righteousness? Justice once dwelt in her, but now murderers. Once a holy nation, a people of possession, now the people of Gomorrah, a wicked seed, wicked sons, unfaithful priests, companions of thieves, lovers of bribes, pursuers of rewards.'" Afterwards, having cited and recited the prophecy of Babylon in the Apocalypse, he applies and subjoins each of its parts to Rome. But if anyone should defend more stubbornly that the Apostle speaks specifically of Babylon, to him I reply that the Apostle Peter, in his first Epistle, signifies Rome figuratively under the name of Babylon, when he says: "The Church gathered in Babylon salutes you." Truly this observation is both ingenuous and ingenious. Lastly I will add the chief centurions of the Jesuits, Francisco Ribera and Manuel de Vega. For the former, on Apocalypse chapter 17, writes thus: "The prophecy must be understood of Rome, not only as it once was under the heathen emperors, but also as it will be at the end of the age." The latter likewise: "All the things that are mentioned in these chapters fit most plainly the city of Rome." Moreover, the name of Babylon must be transferred to that Rome which served idols before it received the faith of Christ, and also to that which will be in the time of Antichrist." We have brought forward, in an earlier place, the Jesuits Leonhard Lessius and Cornelius a Lapide, who agree with these. These are the testimonies of men who lived long before the Reformation of the Church, and more could be added to them. units.la: tam mihi, non solum rei ipsius evidentia & prophetia ac complementi partium omnium harmonia exactissima, sed etiam tot testimoniorum S. Patrum, Regum, Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum, Abbatum, Theologorum, Religiosorum ICtorum, Philosophorum, Rhetorum, qui jam olim clarissima lumina, in mediis etiam Papatus tenebris radiarunt, munimenta infiflenti, atque insuper tot Regum, Principum, Rerumpubl. Ecclesiarum Protestantium pientissimarum, florentissimarumque communis sententia, Confessionibus etiam nonnullis καταγοαφας expresse, Interpretem agenti, eorum explicatam animi de Hierarchicis notionem repraesentanti, atque invicte argumentorum apodixi suffulcienti, quam sibi tot Divinorum, humanorumque testimoniorum & argumentorum ingenti mole obrutis, clarissimoque soli oculos clausos, ne dicam gladius, ignesque obvertentibus succenseant, & cum nonnulli saltem illorum prius, quam Divinorum judiciorum torrens inundaverit, Divina gratia, εριλιαχδιω aspirante, Babylone, exeant, tum in universum omnes eandem horreant, & qui pie vivere voluit, penitus abhorreant. Qua votorum, laborumque meorum Summa est.
units.tr: This is my firm conviction, resting not only on the plain evidence of the matter itself and the most exact harmony of all its parts with prophecy and fulfilment, but also on the testimony of so many holy Fathers, kings, archbishops, bishops, abbots, theologians, members of religious orders, jurists, philosophers and rhetoricians, who shone as the clearest lights even in the midst of the darkness of Papacy and served as a bulwark against the enemy; and further on the common judgment of so many of the most pious and flourishing kings, princes, commonwealths and Protestant churches, expressly set down in some confessions [καταγραφάς], which acts as interpreter, sets forth their explained notion of the hierarchical, and is supported by the unconquerable force of argument. Those who bury their eyes beneath the vast weight of so many divine and human testimonies and arguments, and shut them against the clearest sun (not to say that they turn sword and fire against it), inflame themselves against this judgment. When some of them, before the torrent of divine judgments overwhelms them, come out of Babylon by the divine grace inspiring them [ἐριλιαχδιῶ], then in general all abhor it, and whoever wishes to live piously utterly shuns it. This is the sum of my prayers and labours.
