Præjudiciis enim falsarum expositionum remotis & discussis ad clariorem mysterii intelligentiam expeditius longè iter erit.
units.tr: XVI. Since, however, that great Babylon bears on her forehead the name Mystery, and so belongs to the class of things which Scripture calls riddles, not those which it calls a clear saying, Hab. 2:6, a considerable effort must certainly be made to unravel that riddle successfully and to apply it, once unravelled, to a spiritual use, which is very great indeed. For the present, we have resolved to recall to the file of a saner hermeneutic the false interpretations of this mystery, or rather the mysterious distortions and twistings, which some devised long ago with a more innocent mind, but which not a few today devise with a far more guilty intent, their hearts throbbing with a guilty conscience, and which they defend with fierce obstinacy. For once the prejudices of false expositions have been removed and dismissed, the way to a clearer understanding of the mystery will be far more direct.

units.la: XVII. Universum mundum, qui in malo jacet, Babylonis hujus magnæ nomine figurari, nequicquam jam olim Ambrosius, Beda, Arethas, Primasius, Haymo, aliique asseruerunt. S. Johannes enim non mundum universum nomine hoc insignit, sed πόλιν civitatem certam, adeóque civitatem Diaboli, quam, inquit S. Augustinus, œdificat amor sui usque ad contemtum Dei, Civitati Dei oppositam, quæ propterea etiam non tantùm πόλις Civitas, sed etiam ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη Civitas illa magna Apoc. xiv. 8. xviii. 10. 16. 18. vocatur; & eam quidem Civitatem, quæ obtinet regnum in Regna terræ, cap. xvii. 2. xviii. 3. 9. & Reges ac mercatores, eam immodicè plangentes. ibid. v. 10. 11. &c. & populi ac turbæ, gentes & linguæ, quibus ceu aquis illa insidere dicitur cap. xvii. 15. & gentes ab illa inebriatæ cap. xviii. 7. 8. &c. septémque etiam montes quibus insidet. v. 9. quæ singula pars sunt mundi impiorum, cui Diabolus præsidet, distinguuntur. Cùmque cap. xviii. 4. jubeantur quidam exire Babylone, utique illa mundus impiorum esse nequit, cùm ex illo exitus non detur nisi per mortem. 1 Cor. v. 10.
units.tr: XVII. That the whole world, which lies in evil, is figured by the name of this great Babylon, Ambrose, Bede, Arethas, Primasius, Haymo and others have long since asserted in vain. For St John does not designate the whole world by this name, but a certain city, namely the city of the Devil, which, says St Augustine, the love of self builds up even to the contempt of God, set against the City of God. For this reason it is called not merely city but also the great city, that great city, Rev. 14:8; 18:10, 16, 18. It is that city which holds dominion over the kings of the earth, Rev. 17:2; 18:3, 9, and over the kings and merchants who lament her excessively, ibid. vv. 10, 11, etc., and the peoples and crowds, nations and tongues, on which she is said to sit as on waters, Rev. 17:15, and the nations drunk from her, Rev. 18:7, 8, etc., and also the seven mountains on which she sits, v. 9. These are distinguished as individual parts of the world of the impious, over which the Devil presides. And since in Rev. 18:4 some are commanded to come out of Babylon, that Babylon cannot be the world of the impious, since no exit from that world is given except by death, 1 Cor. 5:10.

units.la: XVIII. Quas similésque ob causas Veterum, quibus eventum prædictionis nondum cernentibus fax defuit ad solidam interpretationem, illam explicationem recentiores deseruerunt plerique omnes, interpretes puta tum nostri, tum Pontificii etiam, si à paucis non ita recentibus tamen, Thoma Aquinate, Gaynejo, Castro, Malvenda, Stapletono, Sandero discesseris. Nam & Ribera, & Cornelius à Lapide, & Alcasar, & Bellarminus, & Suarezius, & Viegas, aliique in Commentariis suis alibique παραφρασεῖς illam dedita opera refellunt. Et C. Pareus Exercit. Theol. lib. II. p. 237. hoc etiam telo interpretationem illam oppugnat: Ruina Babylonis non est interitus mundi. Ergo nec Babylon mundus. Probatur antecedens, quia ruina Babylonis & judicium meretricis idem. cap. xvij. 1. & xviij. 2. At hoc non est interitus mundi. Ratio, quia Reges, mercatores, nautæ plangent super eam cap. xviij. 9. Ergo hi erunt post judicium. At non erunt post judicium mundi.
units.tr: XVIII. For these and similar reasons, most of the more recent writers have abandoned that interpretation which the ancients held, when the fire of the outcome of the prophecy had not yet been seen and so had not given them a solid interpretation. I mean our own interpreters, and also the Papists, unless you exclude a few who are not so recent, Thomas Aquinas, Gaynejo, Castro, Malvenda, Stapleton and Sander. For Ribera, Cornelius a Lapide, Alcasar, Bellarmine, Suárez, Viegas and others, in their commentaries and elsewhere, expressly refute that paraphrase [παραφρασεῖς]. C. Pareus, Exercitationes Theologicae, book 2, p. 237, attacks that interpretation with this weapon: The ruin of Babylon is not the destruction of the world. Therefore Babylon is not the world. The antecedent is proved, because the ruin of Babylon and the judgment of the harlot are the same, Rev. 17:1; 18:2. But this is not the destruction of the world. The reason is that kings, merchants and sailors will weep over her, Rev. 18:9. Therefore these will be after the judgment. But they will not be after the judgment of the world.

units.la: XIX. Affinis huic expositioni est illa, quæ Joachimo Abbati autori tribuitur; quámque etiam Seraphinus, Ubertinus de Casalis, & Dantes Italus poëta sectantur, quòd Babylon notet non in universum impiorum omnium multitudinem, sed peculiariter eorum cœtum, qui ex Christianis reprobantur, vel certè eorum, qui ex orbe Romano ad Christi fidem conversi impiè vivunt, Deíque & Christi præcepta negligunt. Cæterum hanc quoque expositionem, eadem argumenta, quæ & superiorem convellunt. A Babylone enim distinguuntur Reges & incolæ terræ, qui Christum ore confessi quidem, at scortationum & abominationum poculo inebriati, temulentíque, qua tales, electorum certè numero accenseri nequeunt. Neque etiam putandum est, vel Babylonem illam veram, & sinceram Christi fidem professuram fuisse, cùm scortatio, quæ illi tribuitur, spiritualis haud dubiè, aliud longè suadeat: vel in eorum numero, qui Babylone exire jussi, ab ea digressuri, adeóque cum muliere non amplius scortaturi, sed intemerato potiùs cultui Dei nomina daturi erant, hypocritas, sanctam professionem vitæ profanitate commaculantes, comparituros nullos fuisse. Si igitur Christiani reprobi alii quidem cum Babylone commiscendi, ab ea tamen distincti, alii verò à Babylonis communione segregandi, puriorìque adeò quoad professionem fidei cœtui adjungendi fuerunt, jam palam omnibus erit, Babylonem magnam proprìè non esse cœtum reproborum in Christiano, Romano cumprimis orbe professam veram fidem Christi, fœda labe vitæ impiæ polluentium.
units.tr: XIX. Akin to this exposition is that which is attributed to the Abbot Joachim, and which Seraphinus, Ubertinus de Casale and the Italian poet Dante also follow, namely that Babylon denotes not the whole multitude of the impious but especially that company of Christians who are reprobate, or certainly those who, converted from the Roman world to the faith of Christ, live impiously and neglect the precepts of God and Christ. But this exposition too is overthrown by the same arguments that overthrow the former one. For the kings and inhabitants of the earth are distinguished from Babylon; they have indeed confessed Christ with their mouths, yet they are drunk with the cup of harlotries and abominations and, as such drunkards, cannot be counted among the number of the elect. Nor should we think either that Babylon would have professed the true and sincere faith of Christ, since the harlotry attributed to her clearly, and without doubt spiritual, suggests something very different; or that there would have been no hypocrites in the number of those who were commanded to come out of Babylon, who were to depart from her and therefore no longer commit harlotry with the woman, but rather give their names to the undefiled worship of God, hypocrites who stain a holy profession with a profane life. If therefore some reprobate Christians were to be mingled with Babylon yet distinguished from her, and others were to be separated from the communion of Babylon and joined to a company purer in its profession of faith, it will now be plain to all that Babylon the Great is not properly the company of the reprobate in Christendom, especially in the Roman world, which professes the true faith of Christ, polluting it with the foul stain of an impious life.

units.la: XX. Certè Pontificii etiam Interpretes hodierni, quantum sciam, communiter hanc non minùs, quam priorem illam interpretationem repudiant. Alcasar etiam, Jesuita Hispalensis, diffusissimus Apocalypseos Interpres, Prol. ad cap. xvij. Disp. 1. eam ratione oppugnare conatur, imbelli tamen, si quid judicare possum, ab acoluthia & consequentia Apocalypseos duƈta. In qua, inquit, evidens est, deflagrationi Babylonis succedere mille pacis annos, his bella Gogi & Magogi, quæ sunt Antichristi & ejus præcursorum. Quis ergo non videat, nec impiorum omnium multitudinem, nec reproborum sigillatim Christianorum cœtum ante mille illos ecclesiasticæ pacis annos finiri? Ast verò distinƈtis visionibus rem eandem, vel rei ejusdem circumstantias diversas declarari, nihil prohibet. Estque hypothesis illa Alcasaris, cui nonnulli alii astipulari etiam videntur, ejusmodi, ut turbet mirè Apocalypseos sensus, & plurima obtorto collo ad confervandam acoluthiam illam rapere cogatur. Igitur temporis illius mille annorum parte quadam, & una cum Gogo & Magogo Babylonem extituram, & mysterio suo defunƈturam suisse, nulli nos dubitamus: rejeƈtáque illa Alcasaris ratione argumentis supra allatis, ceu firmioribus longè, & inconcussis inhæremus.
units.tr: XX. Certainly the Papist interpreters of today, as far as I know, commonly reject this interpretation no less than the former one. Alcasar, the Jesuit of Seville, a very copious interpreter of the Apocalypse, in his Prolegomena to chapter 17, Disputation 1, tries to oppose it by argument, though with a feeble argument, if I can judge, drawn from the order and consequence of the Apocalypse. In which, he says, it is plain that the burning of Babylon is followed by a thousand years of peace, and these by the wars of Gog and Magog, which belong to Antichrist and his forerunners. Who then does not see that the multitude of all the impious, and the company of reprobate Christians taken severally, are not ended before those thousand years of ecclesiastical peace? But indeed there is nothing to prevent the same thing being declared in distinct visions, or different circumstances of the same thing being declared. And Alcasar's hypothesis, which some others also seem to support, is of such a kind that it greatly disturbs the sense of the Apocalypse and is forced to drag very many things by the neck in order to preserve that order. Therefore we do not doubt that Babylon will arise in some part of that period of a thousand years, together with Gog and Magog, and will perish in her mystery. Rejecting Alcasar's reasoning, we cling to the arguments adduced above as far firmer and unshaken.

units.la: XXI. Illud quidem haud inviti accipimus, quòd juxta expositionem hanc Joachimi, & consentientium Babylon magna orbi Romano Christiano congruit, ac proin, si fides illis habenda est, in orbe Romano Christiano stabulatur Babylon illa magna mater scortationum & abominationum, quæ Circeo poculo suo Reges & incolas terræ inebriat. Id si verum est, uti Pontificii illi Doƈtores pertendunt, quis non orbis Christiani Romani, Babylonem magnam in gremio suo tolerantis, communionem omnem deferendam, Babylone infami adeò, Deóque invisa exeundum, graviter ad id stimulante ipsomet Angelo Dei, qui rei hujus gratia ex Cœlo ipso descendit, piis omnibus arbitrabitur?
units.tr: XXI. We gladly accept this much: that according to this exposition of Joachim and those who agree with him, Great Babylon fits the Christian Roman world. So, if their view is to be trusted, that Great Babylon, mother of harlotries and abominations, who with her Circean cup makes the kings and inhabitants of the earth drunk, dwells in the Christian Roman world. If this is true, as those Papist teachers maintain, who among pious people will not judge that all communion must be renounced with the Christian Roman world, which harbours Great Babylon in its bosom, and that one must go out from Babylon, so infamous and hateful to God, the very angel of God strongly urging this, who for this very purpose came down from heaven?

units.la: XXII. Qui per Babylonem magnam veterem Babylonem, Chaldeæ metropolim famosam, intelligendam esse pertendant, oppidò pauci sunt, neque se Pontificiis etiam Doctoribus probant. Idem enim, qui supra, Alcasar his ferè argumentis opinionem illam perstringit: Inprimis Apocalypsis ipsa declarat, Babylonis nomen huic urbi, de qua agitur, inditum, mysticè esse sumendum, quemadmodum Ægypti & Sodomæ nomen supra cap. xj. Jerosolymæ impositum est. Secundò constat Babylonem fuisse in magna planitie ædificatam. At Apocalypseos Babylon supra septem montes sita esse perhibetur. Præterquam quod textus ipse postulat, ut Babylon de qua sermo habetur, acerrimo bello Christianam oppugnet Ecclesiam, atque in hoc cæteris orbis terrarum Civitatibus antecellat. Hoc autem de Babylone hactenus verè affirmari non potest: nec aliquem reperio autorem, qui credat Apocalypseos Prophetiam in posterum implendam esse in ea ipsa urbe, cui proprium fuit Babylonis nomen.
units.tr: XXII. Those who insist that by Great Babylon the ancient Babylon, the famous metropolis of Chaldea, is to be understood are very few, and they do not even win the approval of the Papist teachers. Alcasar, who was mentioned above, attacks this opinion with roughly these arguments: First, the Apocalypse itself declares that the name Babylon given to the city of which it speaks is to be taken mystically, just as the name Egypt and Sodom was given to Jerusalem above in chapter 11. Secondly, it is established that Babylon was built on a great plain, but the Babylon of the Apocalypse is said to be set upon seven mountains. Besides, the text itself requires that the Babylon of which it speaks wage the fiercest war against the Christian Church, and in this surpass all the other cities of the world. This, however, cannot truly be affirmed of Babylon so far, nor do I find any author who believes that the prophecy of the Apocalypse is to be fulfilled in future in that very city which was properly named Babylon.

units.la: XXIII. Non contemnenda sanè sunt hæc Alcasaris argumenta. Quibus & alia non minus stringentia accedunt, cujusmodi sunt, quòd Babylon Apocalyptica tempore S. Johannis imperium habuit in Reges terræ Apoc. xvii. 18. Chaldaica verò tum temporis ejusmodi imperium adeò non obtinuit, ut ipsa potiùs serviverit: quòdque Babylon Apocalyptica & fornicatione sua inquinatura omnes gentes terræ, & captivam Ecclesiam, ex illa quandòque exituram, retentura fuit. Atqui tale quid de Babylone Chaldaica inde à tempore S. Johannis ad nostra usque tempora dici nullo modo potest. Néque deinceps in Babylone Chaldaïca tale quid eventurum cogitari potest, cùm ne quidem illa amplius extet, vel deinceps denuo extitura sit, Prophetis ultimam ejus cladem, perpetuásque desolationes Esaj. xiii. xiv. Jerem. l. 13. 26. 37. 42. clarissimè prædicentibus.
units.tr: XXIII. These arguments of Alcasar are certainly not to be despised. To them are added other no less cogent ones, such as this: that the Apocalyptic Babylon had dominion over the kings of the earth at the time of St John (Rev. 17:18), whereas Chaldean Babylon at that time did not hold such dominion at all, but rather was itself in servitude. Also, the Apocalyptic Babylon, by her fornication, is to defile all the nations of the earth and to hold the captive Church, which will at some point come out of her. Yet nothing of this kind can in any way be said of Chaldean Babylon from the time of St John down to our own day. Nor can it be thought that anything of this kind will happen in Chaldean Babylon hereafter, since it no longer even stands, nor is it to stand again in future, the Prophets most clearly foretelling its final ruin and perpetual desolations (Isa. 13, 14; Jer. 50. 13. 26. 37. 42).

units.la: XXIV. Quòd enim hodiernam urbem בגראד Bagdad cum Babylone vetere, situs ratione eandem Geographi nonnulli, ac cum iis etiam Chaleóndylas & Curopalates faciunt, & olim quoque Arabs Interpres Genef. x. 10. pro בכר convertit בגראד Bagdad, manifesto errore factum esse non amplius habetur dubium. Babylon enim ad Euphratem, Bagdad verò ad Tigrim sita est. Hodiéque rudera Babylonis visuntur procul à Bagdad circiter xl milliaribus, vel, ut Texeira definit, testis ἀνὴρ, quantum itineris possit viator expeditus uno die conficere. Fontes erroris vulgati erudité Celeb. Bochartus Phal. lib. j. cap. 8. aperuit: quòd Seleucia, cùm in Babylonis nomen & opes successisset, non solùm Babylonia (ut apud Plinium & alios Δαμασκός, quia non una fuit Seleucia) sed & Babylon appellata sit. In eodem autem, quo Seleucia, solo, vel certè in proximo Bagdad cùm condita fuerit, factum hinc ut affirmarent Geographi, Bagdad ibi sitam, ubi olim Babylon sita erat. Liquet ergo vel uno hoc indicio certissimo Babylonem veterem neutiquam intelligi: utpote quæ nec S. Johannis tempore extitit, indito jam ante nomine Babylonis illi urbi, quæ nunc Bagdad insignitur, nec unquam deinceps existere debuit.
units.tr: XXIV. That the present city Bagdad [בגראד Bagdad] is held by some geographers to be the same as old Babylon, in respect of its site, and that with them Chalcondyles and Curopalates agree, and that long ago the Arabic interpreter also rendered Gen. 10:10 by Bagdad [בגראד Bagdad] in place of Accad [בכר], is no longer regarded as doubtful: it was an obvious error. For Babylon lies on the Euphrates, but Bagdad on the Tigris. Even today the ruins of Babylon are seen about forty miles from Bagdad, or, as Texeira puts it, a distance which an unencumbered traveller could cover in one day. The sources of the common error have been learnedly revealed by the renowned Bochart (Phaleg, book 1, chapter 8): when Seleucia succeeded to the name and wealth of Babylon, it was called not only Babylonia (as Pliny and others call it, in the Greek manner, because there was not one Seleucia) but also Babylon. Since Bagdad was founded on the same site as Seleucia, or certainly very near it, geographers asserted that Bagdad lay where Babylon once lay. Thus this one most certain indication makes it clear that old Babylon is by no means to be understood: it did not exist even in the time of St John, the name Babylon having already been given to the city now called Bagdad, and it ought never to exist again afterwards.

units.la: XXV. Illi autem urbi, cui tempore S. Johannis Babylon nomen fuit, & à cujus Συναγωγή unà electa fideles S. Petrus 1 Ep. v. 13. salutat, quæque Bagdad hodie vulgò appellatur, Saracenico Imperio obnoxia, neutiquam ea conveniunt, quæ Babyloni Apocalypsis tribuit. Nullius enim Babylon illa Seleucienfis alterutram in partem nominis fuit, ut tam non ei Apocalypticæ Babylonis criteria quadrent, quam non quadrata rotundis aptari possunt.
units.tr: XXV. But that city which in the time of St John was called Babylon, and from whose congregation St Peter greets the faithful, chosen together with her (1 Pet. 5:13), and which is commonly called Bagdad today, subject to the Saracen empire, by no means agrees with what the Apocalypse attributes to Babylon. That Seleucian Babylon bore neither sense of the name, so the marks of the Apocalyptic Babylon fit it no more than square things can be fitted to round ones.

units.la: XXVI. Quin potiùs ea, quæ Babyloni Apocalypsis tribuit, ad Chaldaicæ Babylonis veteris famosissimæ, ceu typi spiritualis illius Babylonis novæ, amussim aprimè congruunt, ut ad hanc S. Johannem, non ad Seleucienfem illam, allusisse ambiguum neutiquam sit. Idque analogia utramque inter veterem Chaldaïcam, & mysticam novam Babylonem clarissimè demonstrat.
units.tr: XXVI. Rather, what the Apocalypse attributes to Babylon fits exactly the ancient and most famous Chaldean Babylon, as the spiritual type of that new Babylon. So it is not doubtful that St John alluded to this city and not to that Seleucian one. The analogy between the old Chaldean Babylon and the mystical new Babylon demonstrates this most clearly.

units.la: XXVII. Etenim Babylonis veteris initia, quæ Genef. xi. 1. 2. 3. 4. narrantur, condendæ urbis Babylonis, & turris in ea vastissimæ ac ἐγγυμίχως rationem ejusmodi pandunt, quòd nepotes Noachi constituendi השם nominis, ne multiplicato genere humano dispergerentur, & non manerent עם populus unus v. 6. שפת אחר ודברים אחרים habens labium unum, & loquens sermones eosdem. v. 1. consilium iniverint. Cujus consilii finem tametsi non omnes eundem conjectant, absurdum tamen videri non potest, si quis ex illis ipsis verbis colligat inconditæ illi multitudini constitutum fuisse, Babylone sedem quampiam exstruere, in qua traditio sermonum ταγγονπ custodiretur, unde etiam oracula divina, & eorum sensus posthac ab illis, qui ab invicem digressuri, & se hiuc illuc diffusuri crant, arcessendi essent, quò corporibus divisi, fidei saltem unitatem tali medio retinerent, & vel sic saltem אחר עם unus populus esse pergerent. Hoc certè significare possunt verba נעשה לנו שם faciamus nobis nomen. v. 4. de quo Histor. Patriarch. Tom. 1. Exercit. xxj. §. 10. 11. fusius disputavimus. Atque hæc Babylonis Chaldaicæ initia fuerunt.
units.tr: XXVII. For the beginnings of the ancient Babylon, narrated in Gen. 11:1-4, the founding of the city of Babylon and of its immense tower, reveal this design: Noah's descendants, resolving to make themselves a name (שם), so that, the human race having multiplied, they would not be scattered and would not remain one people (עם) [אחר עם] having one lip and speaking the same words (v. 6; [שפת אחר ודברים אחרים]; v. 1), took counsel. Although not all conjecture the same end for this counsel, it cannot seem absurd if someone infers from those very words that this shapeless multitude had resolved to build some seat in Babylon, in which the tradition of the words would be kept, whence divine oracles and their sense were afterwards to be sought by those who were about to depart from one another and scatter hither and thither. Thus, divided in body, they might at least retain the unity of faith by such a means, and so remain, at least in this way, one people. Certainly the words "let us make ourselves a name" (v. 4; [נעשה לנו שם]) can signify this, which we have discussed at greater length in the Historia Patriarcharum, vol. 1, exercise 21, §§ 10, 11. And these were the beginnings of Chaldean Babylon.

units.la: XXVIII. Ex talibus initiis in immensum Babylon procedente tempore crevit, & ad ἀκρῶν fastigium suum, cum-
units.tr: XXVIII. From such beginnings Babylon, growing immensely as time went on, rose to the peak [ἀκρῶν] of her power, when-

units.la: {y} potentiæ primis Nebucadnezaris tempore, enixa est. Eam igitur Nebucadnezar ipse Dan. iv. 27. רבתא בבל Babelem magnam insignit, & Jerem. l. 12. יולדת mater Chaldæorum; cap. li. 41. תהלת כל הארץ laus universæ terræ. Esaj. xiii. 19. צבי ממלכות תפארת גאון כשדים gloria regnorum, decus superbiæ Chaldæorum vocatur. Propter opulentiam Esaj. xiv. מדהבה aurea, nec non רכה אוצרות locuples thesaurorum. Jerem. li. 13. & propter potentiam Jerem. l. 23. פטיש כל הארץ malleus universæ terræ vocatur. Potestas ei competiit in multos populos, adeò ut & habitare dicatur על מים רבים super aquas multas Jerem. li. 13. & גברת ממלכות domina Regnorum Esaj. xlvii. 5. appelletur.
units.tr: {y} she gave birth at the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar's power. Nebuchadnezzar himself therefore calls her Babylon the great [רבתא בבל] (Dan. 4:27), and Jeremiah calls her the mother [יולדת] of the Chaldeans (Jer. 50:12), and the praise of the whole earth [תהלת כל הארץ] (Jer. 51:41). In Isaiah 13:19 she is called the glory of kingdoms, the splendour of the pride of the Chaldeans [צבי ממלכות תפארת גאון כשדים]. Because of her wealth she is called golden [מדהבה] (Isa. 14:4), and rich in treasures [רכה אוצרות] (Jer. 51:13). And because of her power she is called the hammer of the whole earth [פטיש כל הארץ] (Jer. 50:23). Power over many peoples belonged to her, so that she is said to dwell upon many waters [על מים רבים] (Jer. 51:13), and is called the lady of kingdoms [גברת ממלכות] (Isa. 47:5).

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Jam & scelera ejus atrocissima passim Prophetæ notant. Erat enim רכה ועונגה tenera & voluptuaria Esai. xlvii. 1. & fornicationi spirituali adeò dedita, ut Jerem. l. 38. dicatur ארץ פסילים terra sculptilium, cujus incolæ באימים יתהוללו in simulachris insaniant. Neque tantùm ipsa spiritualiter scortata est, sed ad similem scortationem alios, vi etiam adhibita, inducere conata est, uti vel folios Danielis & sociorum ejus, quibus falsorum Deorum cultum abnuentibus quæsitissima supplicia dictavit, exemplis liquet. Crudelitas ejus tanta fuit, ut inde Jerem. li. 25. dicatur הר המשחית mons corrumpens, eò quòd truculentia sua omnem terram corruperit, & פטיש כל הארץ malleus totius terræ Jerem. l. 23. ab ipsomet Deo dicatur. Cujus quidem truculentiæ specimen in oppugnando, & captivitati durissimæ mancipando, populo Dei edidit, quem etiam ita captivum retinuit violenter, ut renuerit dimittere Jerem. l. 33. donec cadente Babylone exeundi portam ipse Dominus aperuisset. Blasphemiis adversus verum Deum insolescens ita se jactabat אני ואפסי עוד לא Ego & præter me non est ultra. Esaj. XLVII. 8. 10. Superbia ejus tanta fuit ut זרן שלם Superba Jerem. L. 31. imò אל יהוה זרים adversus Deum ipsum se superbissimè efferens ib. v. 29. dicatur. In corde enim suo dicebat: Ego, non est præter me ultra לא אשב אלמנה ולא ארץ שכול non sedebo vidua, & non cognoscam orbitatem. Jam & incantationibus & veneficiis supra modum dedita fuit, adeò ut ei tribuatur עצמת חברים fortitudo incantatorum Esaj. XLVII. 9. ad quem locum sic Hieronymus: Habet Babylon, omnisque Chaldæa, incantatorum, & augurum, & ariolorum, & Gazarenorum studium, quos nos Aruspices vocamus. Denique cùm opulentissima fuerit, Locuples thesaurorum, Jerem. LI. 13. etiam emporiis, mercatura, & nundinationibus adeò famosa fuit, ut Ezech. XVII. 4. ארץ כנען עיר רכלים terra mercatorum, & urbs negotiatorum dicatur.
units.tr: The prophets also note her most atrocious crimes throughout. She was tender and voluptuous (Isa. 47.1, [רכה ועונגה]) and so given over to spiritual fornication that at Jer. 50.38 she is called a land of graven images ([ארץ פסילים]), whose inhabitants rave among the idols ([באימים יתהוללו]). Nor was she only spiritually unchaste herself. She also tried, even by force, to lead others into the same harlotry, as the examples of Daniel and his companions show, for when they refused to worship false gods she devised the most exquisite tortures for them. Cruelty was so great in her that at Jer. 51.25 she is called a corrupting mountain ([הר המשחית]), because her savagery had corrupted the whole earth, and God himself calls her the hammer of the whole earth (Jer. 50.23, [פטיש כל הארץ]). She showed a sample of this savagery in attacking the people of God and binding them to the harshest captivity. She also held them captive by violence, so that at Jer. 50.33 she refused to let them go, until the Lord himself opened the gate of departure when Babylon fell. Growing insolent in blasphemies against the true God, she boasted: I am, and there is none besides me (Isa. 47.8, 10, [אני ואפסי עוד]). Her pride was so great that at Jer. 50.31 she is called proud ([זרן שלם]), and indeed she is said to have raised herself up most arrogantly against God himself (ibid. v. 29, [אל יהוה זרים]). For she said in her heart: I am, and there is none besides me; I shall not sit as a widow, nor shall I know bereavement ([לא אשב אלמנה ולא ארץ שכול]). She was also given over beyond measure to incantations and sorcery, so that the strength of enchanters is attributed to her (Isa. 47.9, [עצמת חברים]). On this passage Jerome says: Babylon, and all Chaldea, has a passion for enchanters, augurs, soothsayers and Gazarenes, whom we call haruspices. Finally, since she was very wealthy, rich in treasures (Jer. 51.13), she was also so notorious for trade markets, commerce and bargaining that at Ezek. 17.4 she is called a land of merchants and a city of traders ([ארץ כנען עיר רכלים]).

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Propter atrocia hæc scelera judicium Dei sinale etiam horrendúmque sancti Vates Babyloni illi denunciarunt, uti ex Psalm. CXXXVII. 8. 9. Esaj. XIII. 1. &c. XLVII. 1. 2. 3. 5. 9. 11. 13. 14. 15. Jerem. XXV. 12. LI. 8. 9. quibus locis à Persis & Medis, Deo ipso efficiente, vastanda, desolandáque prædicitur, liquet. Quæ etiam divina oracula exactissimè impleta esse, historici narrant. Hieronymus in cap. xiij. Esaj. refert inter signa vastitatis & solitudinis istius quondam potentissimæ Civitatis & hoc monstrari, quòd præ multitudine Dæmonum ac bestiarum nullus eam Pastorum, hoc est, Deserti appetitor intret, additque, se à quodam Elamita, finibus illis egresso, didicisse, venationes Regias esse in Babylone, & omnis generis bestias murorum tantum ejus ambitu contineri. Et in cap. xiv. Esaj. descriptâ Babylonis magnificentiâ subjungit: Hoc tantum narravimus, ut ostenderemus, quòd ad iram Dei omnis potentia pulvis sit & favilla, & cineri comparetur. Si liceret introire barbaras nationes, & videre tantæ urbis extrema vestigia, videremus possessionem Hericii, & paludes aquarum, & verè completum esse, quod nunc Esaiæ vocibus canitur: Scopabo eam, in scopa terens. Exceptis enim muris cochlibus, qui propter bestias concludendas, post annos plurimos instaurantur, omne in medio spatium, solitudo est.
units.tr: For these atrocious crimes the holy prophets also announced to that Babylon a final and dreadful judgment of God. That this was to be laid waste and made desolate by the Persians and Medes, God himself bringing it about, is clear from Ps. 137.8, 9; Isa. 13.1 etc.; 47.1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13, 14, 15; Jer. 25.12; 51.8, 9. Historians also relate that these divine oracles were fulfilled most exactly. Jerome, on Isa. ch. 13, reports among the signs of the desolation and solitude of that once most powerful city that this too is shown: because of the multitude of demons and beasts, no shepherd, that is, no seeker of the wilderness, enters it. He adds that he learned from a certain Elamite who had left those regions that there are royal hunting grounds in Babylon, and beasts of every kind are contained only within the circuit of its walls. And on Isa. ch. 14, after describing the magnificence of Babylon, he adds: We have related this only to show that before the wrath of God all power is dust and ashes and is compared to cinders. If it were permitted to enter as barbarian nations and to see the last traces of so great a city, we would see a hedgehog's lair and marshes of water, and it would be seen to be truly fulfilled what is now sung in the words of Isaiah: I will sweep it with the broom of destruction. For except for the walls, which are restored after many years to enclose the beasts, all the space within is solitude.

units.la: XXXI. Sicut igitur Babylon Apocalyptica vetus illa Chaldaïca esse neutiquam potuit, quippe S. Johannis tempore destructa penitus, neque unquam denceps instauranda, ita Chaldæam Apocalypticæ typum fuisse, & hanc ad illam ubique alludere, sole meridiano clarius est. Ædificatores veteris quæsiverunt nomen. Nova Apocalyptica se ipsam vocat ἡ μυστήριον mysterium, & in eo nomine non parum gloriatur. Vetus Veritatis custos & depositaria esse voluit. Nova mysterii nomine insignita, cœlestis veritatis custos, & mysteriorum Dei interpres esse contendit. Vetus fuit Urbs magna, potens. Talis nova etiam describitur. Vetus fuit mater, genetrix Chaldæorum. No-va μήτηρ mater haberi vult omnium, qui dominationi ejus spirituali subsunt, & conceditur ei, quòd mater sit, sed per πυρνεια fornicationum & abominationum terræ. Vetus potentissima, opulentissima fuit. Potentiæ, opulentiæ viribus ei nova non cedit. Vetus fuit voluptuaria, fornicationis & corporalis & spiritualis sceleribus famosa, crudelis, sanguinaria, Ecclesiæ sanctorum infestissima, adversus Deum blasphema, veneficiis dedita, & nundinationibus inclyta. Singula hæc ita novæ Apocalypsis vindicat, ut hæc ex illa exsculpta quodammodo videatur. Vetus Ecclesiam Dei oppugnat am, expugnatámque captivam abduxit, & pertinacissimè captam retinuit. Nova sanctis Dei bellum ἀσεβεῖν indixit, eósque captivos dûrissimè crudelissimèque habuit. Ex vetere Babylone libertas exeundi divinitus tandem populo Dei indulta est. Ex nova exeundi libertatem divina vox: Exite ex ea populé mi, concesit. Vetus sedisse dicitur super aquis multis. Neque aliter nova. Vetus denique Babylon gravissimum Dei judicium, non tantùm confuso in ea labio, sed ad extremum etiam πανταλεθρία & desolatione finali ei inflicta, experta est. Simile judicium novæ quoque Babyloni Apocalypseos oracula decernunt.
units.tr: XXXI. Just as the ancient Chaldean Babylon could by no means be the Babylon of the Apocalypse, since it had been utterly destroyed in the time of St John and was never to be rebuilt, so it is as clear as midday that the Chaldean Babylon was a type of the Apocalyptic one and that the latter alludes to the former everywhere. The builders of the ancient one sought a name. The new Apocalyptic one calls itself the mystery ([μυστήριον]), and glories not a little in that name. The ancient one wished to be the guardian and depository of truth. The new one, marked with the name mystery, claims to be the guardian of heavenly truth and the interpreter of the mysteries of God. The ancient one was a great and powerful city; the new one is described as such as well. The ancient one was mother, the begetter of the Chaldeans. The new one wishes to be regarded as mother ([μήτηρ]) of all who are subject to her spiritual dominion, and she is granted to be a mother, but of the fornications and abominations of the earth ([πορνεία]). The ancient one was most powerful and most wealthy; the new one does not yield to her in power or wealth. The ancient one was voluptuous, notorious for the crimes of both bodily and spiritual fornication, cruel, bloodthirsty, most hostile to the Church of the saints, blasphemous against God, given to sorceries, and famous for its markets. The new Apocalypse claims each of these features so exactly that it seems to have been carved out of the old one. The ancient one attacked the Church of God, and having conquered it led it away captive and held it most stubbornly in captivity. The new one declared war on the saints of God ([ἀσεβεῖν]) and held them captive most harshly and cruelly. From the ancient Babylon, freedom to depart was at last granted to the people of God by divine decree. From the new one, the divine voice Come out of her, my people has granted freedom to depart. The ancient one is said to have sat upon many waters; so too the new one. Finally, the ancient Babylon experienced a most grievous judgment of God, inflicted on her not only by the confusion of her language but at last by total destruction ([πανωλεθρία]) and final desolation. The oracles of the Apocalypse decree a similar judgment on the new Babylon as well.

units.la: XXXII. Quòd verò Forerius Comment. in Esaj. xxxij. aliique à Malvenda citati, pertendunt, Babylonem intelligi, Antichristianorum urbem, eò quòd Babylone, Antichristus prodituras, & in ea urbe Regnum suum inchoaturus sit; siquidem Babylonem Orientalem, quamcunque illam, intelligunt, iisdem, quibus superior de Babylone Chaldaïco, argumentis debellantur. Etenim Antichristi & Antichristianorum urbem esse Babylonem Apocalypticam, inficiamur nulli, & hactenus interpretum illorum consensum nobis gratulamur. At Babylon seu Chaldaïca, seu Orientalis alia quævis, Antichristi & Antichristianorum metropolis néque fuit, néque, quantum quidem ex vaticiniis constat, erit unquam.
units.tr: XXXII. As for the claim of Forerius, Commentary on Isaiah ch. 32, and others cited by Malvenda, that Babylon is to be understood as the city of the Antichristians, because the Antichrist is to come forth from Babylon and begin his kingdom in that city, since they understand the Eastern Babylon, whatever it may be, the same arguments that I have used above against the Chaldean Babylon defeat them. For I deny to no one that the Apocalyptic Babylon is the city of the Antichrist and of the Antichristians, and I congratulate myself that these interpreters agree with us so far. But Babylon, whether Chaldean or any other Eastern one, neither was nor, as far as it appears from the prophecies, will ever be the metropolis of the Antichrist and the Antichristians.

units.la: XXXIII. Frivolum porro est, quòd Babylonem magnam Saracenismum, seu legem Muhammedis, polygamiam & fœda etiam alia permittentis, Aureolus aliique interpretantur. Quibus etiam bestia, cui meretrix illa inequitare dicitur, est Sultanus ille Ægypti, qui à Sultano Turcarum, tum in Persiæ residente, Regno, puta Syria & Ægypto, spoliatus est. Addunt cecidisse Saracenicam illam Babylonem in Syria A. 1100, quando Christiani Saracenis profligatis terram sanctam recuperárunt. Quomodo verò sic Babylonis nomen erit μυστήριον Mysterium? Quomodo decem cornua, seu Reges, & septem capita, seu montes bestiæ, cui mulier insidet, erunt Sultanus ille Ægypti? Cùm cornua illam mulierem arietatura, non mulier cornua contritura dicatur? Qui etiam sunt Reges illi terræ, quos poculo suo inebriatura mulier illa Saracenica, & qui mulierem denique odio habituri desolaturíque feruntur? Denique turpi metamorphosi mulier ac civitas illa magna, quæ judicanda gravissimè prædicitur, in bestiam ipsam transformatur, & casus ac πτωλιϑρία Babylonis cum Saracenismi in terra sancta cessatione, brevique illo gaudio, quod incerta & mutabilis fortuna ex occupata eadem terra attulit, nihil prorsus commune habet.
units.tr: XXXIII. Further, it is frivolous when Aureolus and others interpret the great Babylon as Saracenism, that is, the law of Muhammad, which permits polygamy and other foul practices. For according to them the beast on which that harlot is said to ride is that Sultan of Egypt who was stripped of the kingdom of Syria and Egypt by the Sultan of the Turks, who then resided in Persia. They add that that Saracen Babylon fell in Syria in A.D. 1100, when the Christians, having routed the Saracens, recovered the Holy Land. But how then will the name of Babylon be a mystery? How will the ten horns, that is, the kings, and the seven heads, that is, the mountains, of the beast on which the woman sits, be that Sultan of Egypt? Since it is said that the horns will make war on the woman, not that the woman will break the horns? Who are also those kings of the earth whom that Saracen woman is to make drunk with her cup, and whom she is finally said to hate, make desolate and destroy? Finally, the woman and that great city, which is foretold to be most gravely judged, is transformed by a shameful metamorphosis into the beast itself; and the fall and destruction ([πτωλιθρία]) of Babylon has nothing at all in common with the cessation of Saracenism in the Holy Land, or with that brief joy which uncertain and changeable fortune brought from the occupation of the same land.

units.la: XXXIV. Neque solidior est sententia Aretæ, ac qui eum sequitur, Caponsachii, Babelem magnam in novam Romam, Constantinopolin transformantium, eò quòd Civitas illa & sedeat super aquas multas. Non enim proprie, sed metaphoricè illud de populis & turbis, & gentibus & linguis accipiendum esse, ipsemet Angelus testis omni exceptione major cap. xvii. 15. docet. Allusio verò est non ad Constantinopolin sed ad Babylonem veterem, quæ propter Euphratis fluminis, ad quod exstructa fuit, magnitudinem, super aquas multas sedere, allegoricè dicitur. Constantinopolis certè urbs nullo modo intelligi potest, quæ etiam S. Johannis tempore potestatem habuerit super Reges terræ. Apoc. xvii. 18. Taceo plerăque alia, quæ sine aperta verborum & historiarum vi urbi illi adaptari nequeunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. Nor is the opinion of Areta, and of Caponsacchi who follows him, who transform the great Babel into New Rome, Constantinople, any more solid, on the ground that that city sits upon many waters. For the Angel himself, a witness beyond all exception, teaches at ch. 17.15 that this must be understood not literally but metaphorically, of peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues. The allusion is not to Constantinople but to the ancient Babylon, which is said allegorically to sit upon many waters because of the greatness of the Euphrates river beside which it was built. Constantinople certainly cannot be understood as the city which, even in the time of St John, had power over the kings of the earth (Rev. 17.18). I pass over many other points which cannot be applied to that city without a clear violence to the words and history.

units.la: XXXV. Quòd verò etiam doctissimus Brigtmannus noster Comment. in Apoc. xvj. 19. per Babylonem magnam, cujus ibi mentio est, novam Romam seu Constantinopolin intelligi opinatur, non plane Aretæ & sequacium causam adjuvat. Distinguit enim Babylonem illam, de qua Septimâ effusâ Phialâ, loco citato sermo est, à throno bestiæ, in quem effusa quinta phiala Apoc. xvi. 10. dicitur, adeóque etiam à Babylone illa, cujus cap. xiv. 8. & xvii. xviii. judicium gravissimum narratur, quam Constantinopolin neutiquam esse, ultro ille largitur. Rectius tamen haud dubiè etiam facturus, si omissa tali distinctione, cujus nullum in Apocalypsi fundamentum, & quæ ambiguos lubricósque ei sensus inducit, de eadem Babylone utrobique sermonem esse statuisset. Quæ enim de ruina illius Constantinopoleos futura divinat, forte sunt Ἀχῆς μὰλλον ἢ ἐλπιδᾶ, optanda quàm speranda magis. Repetita etiam casus Babylonis mentio, non geminam Babylonem, sed ejusdem Babylonis casum geminum arguit.
units.tr: XXXV. But the most learned Brightman, our countryman, in his Commentary on Revelation 16:19, holds that the great Babylon mentioned there is the new Rome, or Constantinople. This does not really help Areta and his followers. He distinguishes that Babylon, which is the subject of the seventh vial poured out in the passage cited, from the throne of the beast, onto which the fifth vial is said to be poured out (Rev. 16:10), and therefore also from that Babylon whose most severe judgment is recounted in chapters 14:8 and 17–18. He freely concedes that this is not Constantinople. It would have been more correct, undoubtedly, for him to drop such a distinction, which has no foundation in the Apocalypse and which introduces ambiguous and slippery senses, and to hold that the discourse is about the same Babylon throughout. What he conjectures about the future ruin of that Constantinople is perhaps "more to be feared than hoped" [ἀχῆς μᾶλλον ἢ ἐλπίδος], something to be wished rather than expected. The repetition of the mention of Babylon also points not to two Babylons but to a double fall of the same Babylon.

units.la: XXXVI. Remotis his paucorum ψευδεπιγραφοι, verterum & recentiorum reliquorum, Pontificiorum etiam interpretum unanimis consensus Romam aurigatur, & Babylonem magnam Romam, occidentalem illam Imperii magni metropolin esse, firmissimè statuit. Ex veteribus indicamus paucos. S. Hieronymus Epist. 151. ad Algasium quæst. 11. paucis ita definit: Secundùm Apocalypsin Johannis, in fronte purpuratæ Meretricis scriptum est nomen blasphemiæ, id est: Romæ æternæ. Tertullianus contra Judæos cap. 9. sic & Babylon, inquit, apud Johannem nostrum Romæ urbis figuram portat, proinde & magnæ & regno superbæ, & Sanctorum debellatricis. August. de Civit. Dei libr. xviij. 2. Romam secundam Babyloniam esse asserit. Et cap. 22. Condita est, ait, Roma velut altera Babylon, & velut prioris filia Babylonis. Mox cap. 27. Romam vocat Babylonem Occidentalem. Præter hos Ribera Jesuita διωγμὸς allegat plures, puta Eusebium, Orofium, Oecumenium, Bedam, Victorinum, alios.
units.tr: XXXVI. Setting aside the few pseudepigraphers [ψευδεπίγραφοι], the unanimous agreement of the other ancient and more recent writers, and of the Papist interpreters as well, carries Rome away, and firmly holds that the great Babylon is Rome, that western metropolis of the great Empire. From among the ancients we cite a few. St. Jerome, in Letter 151 to Algasius, Question 11, defines the matter briefly thus: According to the Apocalypse of John, on the forehead of the purple harlot is written a name of blasphemy, that is, of eternal Rome. Tertullian, Against the Jews, chapter 9, says: Babylon too, in our John, carries the image of the city of Rome, and therefore of the one that is great and proud in its kingdom and the conqueror of the saints. Augustine, On the City of God, book 18, chapter 2, asserts that Rome is a second Babylon. And in chapter 22: Rome was founded, he says, like another Babylon, and like the daughter of the earlier Babylon. Soon after, in chapter 27, he calls Rome the Western Babylon. Besides these, Ribera the Jesuit cites several others, namely Eusebius, Orosius, Oecumenius, Bede, Victorinus and others.

units.la: XXXVII. Pontificii Doctores magno consensu id ipsum asserunt. Cornelius à Lapide Comment. in Apoc. xvii. Consentientes inducit Viegam, Riberam, Lindanum, Alcasarem, Bellarminum, Apringium, Gagnejum, Heselium, Thomam, Rizium. Et qui prius aliter Babylonem nem interpretati sunt, veluti Aretas, Forerius, alii, hos veritatis splendentibus radiis convictos mutasse dictum, & de Roma denique interpretatos esse Ribera fatetur. Addit Alcasar, eandem expositionem haberi in rubricis manuscriptis antiqui Codicis in Bibliotheca S. Laurentii. Et eodem inclinantem Propheriam Malachiæ cujusdam, Bernhardi συγχρόνῳ, ex Arnoldo Wione in Chronicis Benedicti, idem, qui supra, Cornelius à Lapide citat.
units.tr: XXXVII. The Papist teachers assert the same thing with great agreement. Cornelius à Lapide, in his Commentary on Revelation 17, brings forward as agreeing with him Viega, Ribera, Lindanus, Alcasar, Bellarmine, Apringius, Gagnaeus, Hesel, Thomas and Rizius. And Ribera admits that those who previously interpreted Babylon otherwise, such as Areta and Forerius and others, were convinced by the shining rays of truth and changed their view, and interpreted it finally of Rome. Alcasar adds that the same exposition is found in the rubrics of an ancient manuscript codex in the Library of St. Laurence. Cornelius à Lapide, the same as above, also cites a prophecy of Malachy, a certain writer inclined to the same view, who was Bernard's contemporary [συγχρόνῳ], taken from Arnold Wion's Chronicles of Benedict.

units.la: XXXVIII. Et sane Romam intelligi argumentis irrefragibilibus iidem confirmant, ex quibus duo potissimum, à Dominio & situ mulieris illius petita, heic repetere, ere erit. Dominium quod attinet. Angelus ipse definit Apoc. xvii. 18. mulierem illam, quam S. Johannes vidit, esse urbem illam magnam, quæ habet Regnum super Reges terræ. Vocat τὴν πόλιν τὴν μεγάλην urbem illam magnam, quasi diceret, illam quæ omnium ore per antonomosiam Urbs dicitur, & aliis omnibus S. Johannis tempore famosior extitit, quippe habens Imperium in Reges terræ, quod soli tum Romæ competiit. De quo Martialis Epigram. 12. 8. Terrarum Dea, Gentiumque Roma, Cui par est nihil, & nihil secundum.
units.tr: XXXVIII. And indeed, the same authors confirm by unanswerable arguments that Rome is meant, of which two chief ones, drawn from the dominion and the situation of that woman, it will be enough to repeat here. As for the dominion: the angel himself defines, in Revelation 17:18, that the woman whom St. John saw is that great city, which has a kingdom over the kings of the earth. He calls her [τὴν πόλιν τὴν μεγάλην] that great city, as if to say that city which by everyone's mouth is called, by antonomasia, the City, and which was more famous than all others in St. John's time, as it possessed dominion over the kings of the earth, which then belonged to Rome alone. Martial, Epigrams 12.8, speaks of it: Goddess of the lands and of the nations, Rome, to whom nothing is equal and nothing second.

units.la: Quæβασιλεύουσα πόλις imperitans urbs Græcis; Rerum caput & Domina Blomdo; Orbis totius Regina Egnatio vocatur; & quam Ammianus Marcellinus libr. xiv. 5. dicit per omnes quotquot sunt, partes terrarum, ut dominam suspici & Reginam. Romæ & Tacitus Hist. ii. 81. 1. tribuit Reges inservientes, ubi accessisse Romanis Antiochum, vetustis opibus ingentem, & inservientium Regum ditissimum, dicit. De eo historiæ Romanorum veterum plenæ sunt. Tum & situs mulieris Romam manifeste prodit. Idem enim Angelus bestiæ, cui mulier insidebat, septem capita facit ὄρη ἑπτὰ, ὅπου ἡ γυνὴ κάθηταί ἐπ' αὐτῶν septem montes, quibus mulier insidet. Apoc. xvii. 9. Sedebat igitur mulier, quam S. Johannes vidit, super septem montibus. Romam indicari, res ipsa clamat. Testatur enim Dionysius Halicarnasseus libr. 4. Servium Tullium, Regum ultimum, Romæ septem colles uno muro complexum esse. Apud Varronem etiam & Plutarchum mentio est Diei & festi Romani Septimontii dicti, ob septimum collem Romæ additum. Septimontiale sacrum Suetonius in Domitiano nuncupat. Apud Sibyllam quoque lib. 11. initiò Roma ἑπτάλοφος septicollis vocatur. Ovidius Tristium 1. 4.
units.tr: Greek writers call it [βασιλεύουσα πόλις], the city that rules; Blondus calls it the head and mistress of things; Egnatius calls it the queen of the whole world; and Ammianus Marcellinus, book 14, chapter 5, says that it is looked up to as mistress and queen throughout all the parts of the earth, however many there are. Tacitus too, Histories 2.81, ascribes to Rome kings serving, where he says that Antiochus, immense in ancient wealth and the richest of the serving kings, came over to the Romans. Of this the histories of the ancient Romans are full. Then too the situation of the woman clearly reveals Rome. For the same angel makes the seven heads of the beast, on which the woman sat, seven mountains [ὄρη ἑπτά], where the woman sits upon them [ὅπου ἡ γυνὴ κάθηταί ἐπ' αὐτῶν], seven mountains on which the woman sits, Rev. 17:9. The woman whom St. John saw therefore sat upon seven mountains. That Rome is meant, the thing itself proclaims. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 4, testifies that Servius Tullius, the last of the kings, enclosed the seven hills of Rome with a single wall. In Varro and also in Plutarch there is mention of a Roman day and festival called the Septimontium, named after the seventh hill added to Rome. Suetonius, in his life of Domitian, calls it the Septimontial sacrifice. Also in the Sibyl, book 11, Rome at the beginning is called [ἑπτάλοφος], seven-hilled, septicollis. Ovid, Tristia 1.4:

units.la: Sed quæ de septem totum circumspicit orbem
units.tr: But she who looks out over the whole world from her seven

units.la: —— Montibus, Imperii Roma, Deumque laus.
units.tr: —— Rome of the seven hills, glory of the Empire and of the gods.

units.la: Longum esset Poëtarum dicta eodem pertinentia plura repetere. Suntque montes illi septem nominatim Capitolinus, Palatinus, Cœlius, Aventinus, Æsquilinus, Viminalis & Quirinalis. Quod verò Romam hodiernam Papæ sedem non in septem illis montibus, sed in Campo Martio sitam esse, nonnulli causantur, imprudentes sua vineta cædunt, prodentes scilicet, hodiernam Romam non eam esse, quam S. Petrus incoluisse, & Cathedra sua, in quam Pontifices sequentes successuri sint nobilitasse creditur: & parum etiam ad rem dicunt. Sufficit enim ibi sitam fuisse Romam S. Johannis tempore, & novam Romam in Veteris jura successisse, ubicunque situm habeat. Præterea Papa quidem animi causa Laterano se ultra Tiberim in Vaticanum transtulit. Ipsa tamen sedes non est translata. In singulis etiam montibus monasteria visuntur.
units.tr: It would be tedious to repeat the many passages of the poets that bear on the same point. The seven hills are named as the Capitoline, Palatine, Caelian, Aventine, Esquiline, Viminal and Quirinal. As for those who complain that present-day Rome, the seat of the Pope, is not situated on these seven hills but in the Campus Martius, they cut their own vines, since they betray that present-day Rome is not the Rome which St Peter is believed to have inhabited and made noble by his chair, which the Popes who follow him were to succeed to. Their point also has little bearing on the matter. It is enough that Rome was situated there in St John's time, and that the new Rome succeeded to the rights of the old, wherever it has its seat. Moreover, the Pope indeed moved from the Lateran across the Tiber to the Vatican for his own convenience, but the see itself was not moved. Monasteries are also to be seen on each of the hills.

units.la: XXXIX. Accedit his ratio firmior etiam potentiorque, prophetiæ nimirum & historiæ seu eventus, prophetiæ illi, quatenus hactenus impleta est, exactè convenientis, harmonica consonantia, quæ vaticiniorum omnium interpretandorum quædam cynosura & Ariadneum filum est. Sicut enim in humanis rebus imaginis & picturæ similitudo pictoris intentionem demonstrat: sic in divinis sermonis Prophetici & seriei historiae similitudo sententiam Spiritus S. patefacit. Sicigitur, quae Babyloni magnae prophetia tribuit, Romae pleráque jam evenisse constiterit, Romam Babylonem esse, nemo prudens vel cordatus dubitare poterit. At evenisse pleráque, & quae nondum impleta sunt, quin Romae itidem quadrent, adeóque ibi eventura credantur, nihil penitus obstare, in loco uberius demonstrabimus. Roma igitur Babylon est.
units.tr: XXXIX. To these is added a firmer and more powerful argument, namely the harmonious agreement of prophecy and history, or of the event: the prophecy, so far as it has so far been fulfilled, corresponds exactly with the event. This agreement is a kind of guiding star and Ariadne's thread for interpreting all the prophecies. For just as in human affairs the likeness of an image or picture shows the painter's intention, so in divine matters the likeness of the prophetic word to the course of history reveals the meaning of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, since it is established that most of what the prophecy assigns to great Babylon has already come to pass at Rome, no wise or sensible person can doubt that Rome is Babylon. That most things have come to pass, and that those things which are not yet fulfilled also fit Rome equally well and are therefore believed to be going to happen there, nothing at all stands in the way of this; we shall demonstrate it more fully in its place. Rome, then, is Babylon.

units.la: XL. Qui vero Romam Babylonem esse nobiscum confitentur Pontificii Doctores, quibus claritudo aliqua est, paene omnes, ne Pontificem suum, vel Ecclesiam Romanam libera ea confessione laedant, soliciti supra modum sunt. Neque tamen inter eos, quam Romam seligant, constrictos mutuis, quibus invicem digladiantur, argumentis convenit, ut vel hic etiam labium eorum, perinde ut architectorum Babylonis veteris, confusum agnoscas, mutuisque vulneribus cadentes liquidè cernas.
units.tr: XL. As for the Papist teachers who confess with us that Rome is Babylon, almost all of them, of some distinction, are excessively anxious not to injure their Pope or the Roman Church by this free confession. Nor do they agree among themselves about which Rome they mean, nor on the arguments by which they tear at one another; so that here too you may recognise their lips confused, just as those of the architects of old Babylon were, and clearly see them falling by each other's wounds.

units.la: XLI. Notat Alcasar in cap. 17. Apoc. disput. 1. trifariam nos posse de Roma loqui. Primò de Roma prout nunc est. Secundò, prout sub Antichristi adventum fore creditur ab iis, qui illam existimant tunc ad antiquum idolorum cultum, & Christiani nominis persecutionem atque odium rediturum. Tertiò de Roma, prout erat sub antiquis Imperatoribus Ethnicis, cùm Christi Ecclesiam persequerentur. Primam expositionem haereticis, quos Evangelicos intelligit: secundam & tertiam Catholicis Doctoribus dissentientibus scilicet tribuit. Quod si secundam & tertiam falsam & fictitiam prorsus, adeóque non nisi ad tegendam turpitudinem comparatam esse ostenderimus: quid de prima sentiendum, & quae interpretatio Catholica, quae haeretica sit, ultro liquebit. At secundam aequè ac tertiam solidissimis argumentis, ex pharetra etiam Cadmæorum fratrum (si enim alibi, hic maximè juxta Poëta illud
units.tr: XLI. Alcasar, in his commentary on Revelation 17, disputation 1, notes that we can speak of Rome in three ways. First, of Rome as it now is. Second, as it is believed it will be at the coming of Antichrist, by those who think that it will then return to the ancient worship of idols and to the persecution and hatred of the Christian name. Third, of Rome as it was under the ancient heathen Emperors, when they persecuted the Church of Christ. He assigns the first interpretation to the heretics, whom he means as the Evangelicals, and the second and third to the Catholic teachers who disagree with them. But if we show that the second and third are wholly false and fictitious, and devised only to cover up shame, then what should be thought of the first, and which interpretation is Catholic and which heretical, will become plain of its own accord. Indeed, to overthrow the second as well as the third with the most solid arguments, drawn from the quiver of the Cadmean brothers (for if anywhere, here most of all, the verse of the poet applies,

units.la: Cadmæi fratres inter se prælia miscent.) Doctorum Pontificiorum, qui jugulum sibi invicem ipsimet petunt, petitis convellere, in proclivi nobis erit.
units.tr: The Cadmean brothers wage war among themselves), by using the weapons of the Papist teachers who seek each other's throats, will be an easy task for us.

units.la: XLII. Babylon igitur magna est Roma vel Ethnica, sub Imperatoribus persecutoribus, vel Antichristiano-Ethnica, sub finem demum mundi & adventum Antichristi ad Ethnicismum relapsa, vel tertia.
units.tr: XLII. Great Babylon, then, is Rome either heathen, under the persecuting Emperors; or Antichristian-heathen, fallen back into heathenism at the very end of the world and at the coming of Antichrist; or a third kind.

units.la: Atqui nec Ethnica vetus, nec Antichristiano-Ethnica ejusmodi nova est. Ergo tertia.
units.tr: But neither the ancient heathen Rome nor such a new Antichristian-heathen Rome is the one meant. Therefore the third.

units.la: XLIII. Ethnicam veterem solam intelligi, severè per- tendit Alcasar ipse.
units.tr: XLIII. That only the ancient heathen Rome is meant is strictly maintained by Alcasar himself.

units.la: Cum eodem pertendunt Bellarminus, Baronius, Pererius, Salmeron, Maldonatus, alii. Eos tamen non minus strenuè oppugnant socii & tribules, Ribera & Cornelius à Lapide, eo potissimùm argumento freti, quod gravissimum & finale judicium Babyloni magnæ denunciatum in Romam veterem Ethnicam minimè omnium competat. Quando enim, inquiunt illi, vetus Roma Ethnica, venientibus unâ horâ plagis, combusta, funditus deleta, & Babylonis Chaldaicæ Veteris instar, extremo excidio affecta est, quod Babyloni magnæ Apocalypsis pathetice adeò denunciavit?
units.tr: Bellarmine, Baronius, Pererius, Salmeron, Maldonatus and others hold the same view. Yet their own allies and kinsmen, Ribera and Cornelius à Lapide, oppose them no less vigorously, relying chiefly on this argument: that the most grievous and final judgment announced against great Babylon least of all fits ancient heathen Rome. For when, they say, ancient heathen Rome, burned with plagues coming in a single hour, was utterly destroyed, and suffered an extreme overthrow like that of old Chaldean Babylon, what is it that the Apocalypse so vehemently announced against great Babylon?

units.la: XLIV. Ictum huncce verè lethalem à jugulo suo depulsurus Alcasar, judicium Babyloni magnæ intentatum, ad literam ridiculè interpretatur eam vindictam, quam Deus de Roma Ethnica, & tot Martyrum interfectrice sumpsit, cum Ethnicismum sub Constantino Magno abolevit.
units.tr: XLIV. Alcasar, about to ward off this truly deadly blow from his own throat, interprets the judgment threatened against great Babylon literally and absurdly, as the vengeance which God took on heathen Rome, the slayer of so many martyrs, when He abolished heathenism under Constantine the Great.

units.la: Tunc enim, inquit, Deus Romam Ethnicam quasi occidit, eámque in Christianam commutavit, igne amoris Christi succensam. Jesuitæ frigidum Commentum hocce, Jesuita alter, Cornelius à Lapide his verbis, Comment. in Apoc. 17. p. m. 258. Solidissimè elidit: Hæc non tantùm mystica, sed & αὐλίκοις sunt. Convertunt enim triste, atrox & funestum Romae excidium & conflagrationem, quod graphicè depingitur cap. xviij. in laetum, pium & omnibus votis optandum fidei, salutis & charitatis incendium.
units.tr: For then, he says, God as it were slew heathen Rome and changed her into a Christian city, kindled with the fire of Christ's love. The Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide, another Jesuit, demolishes this cold fiction very solidly in these words (Commentary on Apocalypse 17, p. 258): These are not only mystical but also courtly. For they turn the sad, savage and deadly destruction and burning of Rome, which is graphically depicted in chapter 18, into a joyful, pious fire of faith, salvation and love, which is to be wished for by all.

units.la: XLV. Et sanè figmento illo Alcafaris nihil à ratione omni alienum magis excogitari potuit. Babylon enim magna judicata est ob scelera gravissima, & in Coelum usque ascendentia. An Roma Ethnica ob eadem scelera ad Christum conversa est? Babylon cadens facta est domicilium daemonum, custodia omnis Spiritus impuri, & avis infaustae. An talis Roma Ethnica ad Christum conversa? Ex Babylone cadente jubetur exire populus Dei, ne plagarum ejus particeps reddatur. An ex Roma conversa populus Dei exire debuit, ne plagarum ejus, hoc est, conversionis ad Christum particeps reddatur? Babyloni jubentur vindices reddere βαπτισμὸν καὶ πῦρ ὁ ὡς cruciatum & luctum. An conversio ad Christum fuit cruciatus & luctus? Babylonem plagae, mors, luctus, fames & incendium, Deo eam judicante, oppressurae dicuntur; An una hora Roma Ethnica ad Christum conversa? An conversio talis plagarum, mortis, luctus, famis, incendii, & judicii divini nomen commeruit? Denique Babylonem eversam & combustam Reges, qui cum ea fcortati sunt, & mercatores terrae flebiliter deplorarunt. An iidem Romam ad fidem Christi conversam deplorarunt?
units.tr: XLV. Indeed, nothing more alien to all reason could have been invented than that fiction of Alcasar's. For Babylon was judged for most grievous sins, which reached up to heaven. Did heathen Rome turn to Christ for the same sins? Fallen Babylon became a dwelling of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit and a hold of every hateful bird. Was heathen Rome such a place when it turned to Christ? The people of God are commanded to come out of fallen Babylon, lest they share in her plagues. Ought the people of God to have come out of converted Rome, lest they share in her plagues, that is, in her conversion to Christ? Babylon's avengers are bidden to repay her [βασανισμὸν καὶ πένθος] with torment and mourning. Was conversion to Christ torment and mourning? Babylon is said to be overwhelmed by plagues, death, mourning, famine and burning, God judging her. Was heathen Rome, converted to Christ in a single hour, such a thing? Does such a conversion deserve the name of plagues, death, mourning, famine, burning and divine judgment? Finally, the kings who committed fornication with Babylon and the merchants of the earth lament her overthrow and burning with weeping. Did the same men lament Rome when she was converted to the faith of Christ?

units.la: XLVI. Absurditatem mysticae interpretationis Alcasaris palpantes alii, ὑπογυμνάζων aliud excogitarunt. Fingunt nempe judicium Dei impletum esse in Roma, quae sub initium quinti seculi cladem ingentem ab Herulis & Gothis passa est. Atqui & illis Jesuita Suarez. lib. 5. cap. 7. num. 11. Opponit rationem firmissimam, quod scil. desolatio Babylonis Apoc. xviii. praedicta sempiterna futura sit: Ideòque Ideóque, inquit, certum videtur oraculum illud in nullo præcedentium excidiorum Romæ impletum fuisse. Et cap. 21. n. 6. subjicit: Prophetia illa nondum impleta est. Nondum enim Roma penitus extincta fuit. Nam licet aliquas graves calamitates & clades non modicas sub Gothis & Vandalis passa sit, per illas tamen non est impleta illa Johannis prophetia, quia per illa excidia factum non est, ut amplius non inveniatur. Cum igitur Babylonis excidium prædictum esse finale debeat, & fatente, & ex Apoc.xviii. 21.22.23. probante Suarezio, Roma verò ex ruinis à Gothis illatis resurrexerit splendidius feré, quàm antehac fuit, excidium Babylonis, clades Romæ à Gothis factæ esse non possunt. Addit Cornelius à Lapide in Apoc. 17. 1. p. 257. Clades illas non à decem, sed à singulis Regibus Romæ esse inflictas, néque Romam tum fuisse Ethnicam, sed Christianam ac consequenter non tam infidelem, superbam & divitem, ut Babylon describitur. Accedit, quod Roma tum passa est calamitates non à populo Dei Babylone egresso, á quo Babylon pati debuit. Apoc. xviii. 4. sed ab illuvione barbarica, Ariana peste infecta: quodque Babylonis excidium piis materiam gaudii, impiis verò luctus præbitura est, cum clades illa à Barbaris Romæ inflicta piis doloris, impiis verò gaudii causa extiterit.
units.tr: XLVI. Others, feeling the absurdity of Alcasar's mystical interpretation, have devised a different and cruder one. They pretend that the judgment of God was fulfilled in Rome, which suffered a great disaster at the beginning of the fifth century from the Heruli and the Goths. But against this the Jesuit Suarez (book 5, chapter 7, number 11) raises a very firm argument: namely, that the desolation of Babylon foretold in Revelation 18 is to be everlasting. Therefore, he says, that oracle seems certainly not to have been fulfilled in any of the earlier destructions of Rome. And in chapter 21, number 6, he adds: That prophecy is not yet fulfilled. For Rome has not yet been utterly extinguished. For although she suffered some grave calamities and no small disasters under the Goths and Vandals, the prophecy of John was not fulfilled by them, because those destructions did not make it so that she should no longer be found. Since, then, the destruction of Babylon must be foretold as final, and Suarez admits this and proves it from Revelation 18:21, 22, 23, while Rome rose again from the ruins caused by the Goths almost more splendidly than before, the destruction of Babylon cannot be the disaster of Rome inflicted by the Goths. Cornelius à Lapide adds (on Apocalypse 17, p. 257) that those disasters were inflicted on Rome not by the ten kings but by single kings, and that Rome was then not heathen but Christian, and consequently not so unbelieving, proud and rich as Babylon is described. Add to this that Rome then suffered calamities not from the people of God coming out of Babylon, by whom Babylon ought to have been punished (Revelation 18:4), but from a barbarian flood, infected with the Arian plague; and that the destruction of Babylon is to furnish matter for joy to the pious and for mourning to the impious, whereas that disaster inflicted on Rome by the barbarians was a cause of sorrow to the pious and of joy to the impious.

units.la: XLVII. Perstat igitur Cornelii à Lapide adversus tribulis sui Alcasaris ψευδολογίαν argumentum inconcussum & immobile prorsus. Néque desunt nobis argumenta subsidiaria, quibus Alcasaris & sociorum Babylonem de Roma Ethnica vetere explicantium opinio, ccu validissimis arietibus ulteriùs quassari & funditus subverti nullo negotio possit.
units.tr: XLVII. So Cornelius à Lapide's argument against his fellow-Jesuit Alcasar's false reasoning stands unshaken and wholly immovable. Nor are we without subsidiary arguments, by which the opinion of Alcasar and his allies, who explain Babylon as ancient pagan Rome, can easily be battered further with the strongest rams and overthrown from its foundations.

units.la: XLVIII. Etenim primò Babylon in fronte scriptum nomen præfert μυστήριον Mysterium Apoc. xvii. 5. Sive autem sensus est, quæ de Babylone dictura erat, fore arcana, na, mystica summáque admiratione dignissima : sive Babylonem mysterii praetextu ad incestum amorem sui, scortationemque invitaturam, alterutrum qui Romae Ethnicae ccmpetere affcrunt, aliquanto absurdius facient, quàm si quis ex Alexandro M. Cybeles Sacerdotem efficere vellet. Quid enim in Roma Ethnica mysticum adeò, absconditum, admiratione dignum fuit? An Romam Ethnicam, idololatricam, sanguinariam, divino judicio ulciscendam quandoque esse, obscurum esse cuiquam potuit, ut in mysteriis id deputandum fuerit? Quorsum tam solicitè, & quidem mysticè, propheticè describi attinebat id, quod in propatulo fidelium omnium fuit? Et numquid mysterii obtentu & scuto quodam potius, quàm militaris potentiae praesidio ad eam potentiam Roma Ethnica surrexit, in qua orbi universo tremenda fuit? At Romam Christianam talem quandoque futuram, qualem S. Johannes vidit, omnem certè captum superavit, ut mysterium id verissimè insigniri potuerit. Eadémque Roma Christiana certo tempore mysterii seu religionis praetextu fucato mundum seduxit, dominationíque suae asflutissimè subjecit. Verbo dicam: Sub Ethnica Roma robur militare mysticae & religiosae larvae multum praevaluit: Cùm contra Papalis ex mysticis, Mercurialibus, & Venereis tota conflata sit.
units.tr: XLVIII. First, Babylon bears on her forehead the written name μυστήριον, "Mystery" [μυστήριον], Apoc. 17.5. Whether the meaning is that what was to be said of Babylon would be hidden, mystical, and most worthy of wonder, or that Babylon, under the pretext of a mystery, would invite to incestuous love of herself and to fornication, those who assert either of these of pagan Rome will make themselves rather more absurd than if someone wished to make a priest of Cybele out of Alexander the Great. For what in pagan Rome was so mystical, so hidden, so worthy of wonder? Could it be obscure to anyone that pagan Rome, idolatrous and bloodthirsty, would one day be punished by divine judgment, so that this should be counted among mysteries? Why was it necessary to describe so anxiously, and indeed mystically and prophetically, what lay open to all the faithful? And did pagan Rome rise to that power, under which she was dreadful to the whole world, by means of a mystery and a kind of shield, rather than by the protection of military strength? But that Christian Rome would one day be such as St John saw, certainly surpassed all understanding, so that she could rightly be marked with the word mystery. And that same Christian Rome, at a certain time, led the world astray under the false pretext of a mystery or religion, and most completely subjected it to her dominion. To put it briefly: under pagan Rome, military strength greatly prevailed over the mask of mystical and religious show; whereas the Papal power was wholly compounded of mystical, Mercurial, and Venereal elements.

units.la: XLIX. Secundò S. Johannes Babylonem, quam describit, vocat meretricem, adulteram, utpote cum Reges terrae scortati sint; neque meretricem simpliciter, sed ejusmodi, quae ad scortandum secum blanditiis & lenociniis suis etiam Reges terrae inducat. Dicitur enim vino scortationis suae incolas terrae inebriare, ut secum scilicet scortentur, cap. xvii. 2. & xviii. 3. Scortatio haud dubiè non corporalis duntaxat intelligitur, sed inprimis spiritualis, idolatria, quae cultum soli vero Deo debitum , & connubii quadam fide obstrictum in creaturas transfert & τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα λατρεύει , Creaturam supra Creatorem colit, Rom. 1. 25. Alioquin Reges terræ cum muliere hac corporaliter scortantes vix reperias. At fieri potuit, ut cum ea scortarentur, hoc est, cultum & amorem soli vero Deo, soli Christo debitum alienarent, & mulieri tali perfidiose impenderent. Fornicari enim cum meretrice, quod aprime hic notandum, non tam ejusdem fornicationis spiritualis seu idololatriæ communionem notat; (futurum alioquin, ut ipsi Reges cum meretrice fornicantes, secum ipsi invicem fornicarentur, utpote fornicationis communione conjuncti) quam commixtionem spiritualem cum meretrice significat. Proin cum meretrice fornicaturi non communione duntaxat sacrorum jungendi, sed meretrici cultum & amorem religiosum soli Deo debitum delaturi intelliguntur.
units.tr: XLIX. Secondly, St John calls the Babylon he describes a harlot and an adulteress, since the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her; and not simply a harlot, but one who, by her flatteries and enticements, also draws the kings of the earth into fornicating with her. For it is said that she makes the inhabitants of the earth drunk with the wine of her fornication, so that they may fornicate with her, Apoc. 17.2 and 18.3. Undoubtedly fornication here is understood not merely as bodily, but above all as spiritual, that is, idolatry, which transfers to creatures the worship owed to the true God alone and the faith bound by a kind of marriage bond, and serves the creature rather than the Creator [τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα λατρεύει], Rom. 1.25: they worship the creature above the Creator. Otherwise you would scarcely find kings committing bodily fornication with this woman. But it could happen that they fornicated with her, that is, that they alienated the worship and love owed to God alone, to Christ alone, and faithlessly devoted them to such a woman. For to fornicate with a harlot, which is especially to be noted here, signifies not so much a sharing in the same spiritual fornication or idolatry (otherwise it would follow that the kings, fornicating with the harlot, would also fornicate with one another, being joined by the common bond of fornication) as a spiritual intermingling with the harlot. Hence those who are going to fornicate with the harlot are understood to be not merely joining in the communion of sacred rites, but about to bring to the harlot the religious worship and love due to God alone.

units.la: L. Hæc certè Romæ Ethnicæ nullo modo congruunt. Neque enim cum ea ita scortati sunt Reges terræ, ut religiosè eam coluerint, & cultum amorémque soli Deo, soli Christo devinctum, in eam transtulerint. Cultum & amorem ejusmodi Roma Ethnica nunquam à Regibus terræ desideravit, flagitavit nunquam, civile obsequium, cultum comem, servitutem vilem, Regum subservientium grande pretium dominationis & victoriarum suarum reputans. Et tantum abest, ut se à Regibus terræ coli religiosè vel concupiverit unquam, ut etiam Regibus victis, vel in fidem receptis, adeóque sibi obnoxiis, religiones & ceremonias Romanas vel blanditiis, & poculo quodam scortationum propinato; vel aperta vi, in ditionibus suis exercendas imposuerit nunquam, adeóque ne communionem quidem sacrorum, nedum cultum sui religiosum, adeoque scortandi secum necessitatem injunxerit. Documento esse possunt Reges Judeæ, quibus subjectis nunquam sacra sua Romani obtruserunt, sed ἀὐλοροπίαι ita permiserunt, ut procuratores illuc missi religiosis controversiis se se immiscere plane detrectaverint.
units.tr: L. These things by no means fit pagan Rome. For the kings of the earth did not so fornicate with her as to worship her religiously and transfer to her the worship and love bound to God alone and to Christ alone. Pagan Rome never demanded or sought such worship and love from the kings of the earth, reckoning civil obedience, courteous homage, base servitude, and the great price of subservient kings as the reward of her dominion and victories. And so far was she from ever desiring to be worshipped religiously by the kings of the earth, that she never imposed her Roman religions and ceremonies on conquered kings, or on those received into alliance and thus made subject to her, to be practised in their dominions, whether by flattery and a cup of fornication offered to them, or by open force. Accordingly she never laid on them the necessity even of communion in sacred rites, let alone of her own religious worship, or of fornicating with her. The kings of Judea can serve as proof: over them the Romans never forced their own sacred rites, but allowed them their own autonomy [αὐτονομίαι], so much so that the procurators sent there utterly refused to meddle in religious disputes.

units.la: LI. Christianum nomen, fateor, persecuti sunt acerrimè Imperatores Ethnici. An vero propterea Reges inebriarunt poculo scortationis? An, & quos Christianos Reges blanda vi ad colendam Romam, vel amplectenda etiam eorum sacra invitarunt? Et si poculo propinato scortationis invitarunt, qui Reges Christianorum poculum à Roma Ethnica propinatum biberunt? Qui epoto poculo inebriati cum Roma Ethnica scortati sunt? Quin Roma Ethnica trucidans potius Erynnis, quàm alliciens scortum fuit, magis aliarum nationum superstitiones bibit, quàm proprias blanda vi aliis bibendas propinavit.
units.tr: LI. The Christian name, I admit, was most fiercely persecuted by the pagan emperors. But were the kings therefore made drunk with the cup of fornication? And which Christian kings did Rome invite by gentle force to worship her, or even to embrace her rites? And if she invited them with a cup of fornication offered to them, which Christian kings drank the cup offered by pagan Rome? Who, having drunk it and been made drunk, fornicated with pagan Rome? Indeed pagan Rome was more a raging Fury than an alluring harlot; she drank in the superstitions of other nations more than she offered her own to be drunk by others through gentle force.

units.la: LII. Distinguit equidem Alcasar Comment. ad Apoc. 17. 2. inter propinatum poculum prostitutionis, & irae fornicationis. De illo Apoc. xvii. 2. de hoc xiv. 8. & xviii. 13. agi: & illo Reges invitatos esse ad luxuriam; hoc vero luxuriam detrectantes ad iram, supplicia pertractos esse asserit. Poculum prostitutionis bibisse Reges terrae, hoc est, Romanos Senatores, qui mundum suo Imperio gubernabant, & illos etiam Reges ac Principes, qui cum Romano Imperio foedus iniverant: alterum vero irae fornicationis bibisse eos, quos scortari cum ea recusantes Romani ad supplicium poposcerint. Subjicit congruentius fortasse esse id ita accipere, quasi Roma eos, qui cum illa ad spiritualem fornicationem copulabantur, suae irae vino ebrios reddat, id est, illos in iram atque furorem adversus Christi nomen agat.
units.tr: LII. Alcasar, in his Commentary on Apoc. 17.2, indeed distinguishes between the cup of prostitution and the cup of the wrath of fornication. He holds that the former, Apoc. 17.2, and the latter, 14.8 and 18.13, are the subject of different passages: by the former the kings were invited to lust; by the latter, those who refused to indulge in lust are said to be driven to punishment. He asserts that the kings of the earth drank the cup of prostitution, that is, the Roman senators, who governed the world by their empire, and also those kings and princes who had entered into alliance with the Roman empire; but that they drank the cup of the wrath of fornication, those whom the Romans, when they refused to fornicate with her, condemned to punishment. He adds that it is perhaps more fitting to take it thus: as if Rome made drunk with the wine of her wrath those who were joined to her in spiritual fornication, that is, drove them into rage and fury against the name of Christ.
