units.la: LIII. Haec vero διεγραμμένα ac distorta, & ad sustinendam utcunque apud domesticos desperatam causam inducta esse, vel caecus aliquis si non viderit, at palpaverit certè. Sanè etiam Cornelius à Lapide ea sugillat ceu ingeniosa quidem at minimè genuina & vera. Enim verò vel prostitutionem à fornicatione, vel poculum fornicationis, à poculo irae fornicationis distinguere hominis fuit ignorantis textum sacrum originalem, qui simpliciter πορνείας vocat, quam Vulgatus interpres prostitutionis & fornicationis nominibus distinxit. Neque aliud poculum est fornicationis, aliud θυμῷ πορνείας; excandescentiae fornicationis. Nam & poculum fornicationis, quo gentes inebriatura dicitur meretrix, est poculum excandescentiae fornicationis, five quia bibentes ex eo iram Dei accendunt, five quia ipsi ignea vi, fervore & excandescentia cramatis quod in poculo est, ad scortandum incenduntur. Talis enim est Philtrorum natura, ut ad furorem & excandescentiam exardescant, quotquot ea bibunt. Ita de Imperatore Cajo Suetonius cap. 50. Creditur potionatus à Caefonia uxore, amatorio quidem medicamento, sed quod in furorem verterit. Et cujus tandem dementiae fuit somniare ipsosmet pios & fideles Christianos persecutiones quaesitissimas fuftinentes, poculo excandescentiae fornicationis inebriatos fuisse? Sic scilicet illi inebriati fuerunt, uti hic ad verum proserendum Alcafar ipse sobrius fuit.
units.tr: LIII. But these are far-fetched and distorted notions, brought in to sustain in some way a cause despaired of even among his own people; even a blind man, if he does not see them, will surely feel them. Indeed Cornelius à Lapide also sneers at them as clever but by no means genuine or true. For to distinguish prostitution from fornication, or the cup of fornication from the cup of the wrath of fornication, was the mark of a man ignorant of the original sacred text, which simply says πορνείας [porneias], which the Vulgate translator rendered by the two words prostitution and fornication. Nor is there one cup of fornication and another of θυμῷ πορνείας [thymō porneias], the wrath or excitement of fornication. For the cup of fornication, from which the harlot is said to make the nations drunk, is the cup of the excitement of fornication, either because those who drink from it kindle God's wrath, or because they are inflamed to fornicate by the fiery force, heat and excitement of the potion. For such is the nature of philtres, that all who drink them flare up into fury and excitement. So Suetonius, of the emperor Gaius, ch. 50: "He is believed to have been given a potion by his wife Caesonia, a love-charm indeed, but one which turned into madness." And what madman could dream that pious and faithful Christians, enduring the most exquisite persecutions, were made drunk with the cup of the excitement of fornication? So drunk, evidently, were they, just as Alcasar himself was sober in bringing this truth to light.

units.la: LIV. De cætero etiam vino fcortationis inebriatos iram & furorem concepturos adversus pios & bonos omnes, qui fcortatione spirituali non delectarentur, sed reos ejus repre- henderent, & ad castiorem mentem demonstratione tur- pitudinis inflectere conarentur, dubitari non potest.
units.tr: LIV. Moreover, there can be no doubt that those who are drunk with the wine of fornication will conceive anger and fury against all the godly and good who do not delight in her spiritual fornication, who rebuke her for her guilt, and who try to turn minds to a purer state by showing up her shamefulness.

units.la: Nam & gentes scortantes ὀργίζηται iratæ dicuntur. Apoc. xi. 18. At præcipuè & Κυρίως verba illa hoc non intendunt, & de eo quicquid fit, fcortatio in iis, qui ita irascentur & excandescent, & quidem cum Roma ipsa præsupponitur.
units.tr: For nations committing fornication are also said to be angry [ὀργίζηται] (Rev. 11:18). But those words, taken properly [Κυρίως], do not refer to this, and whatever the case, the fornication is presupposed in those who will be angry and inflamed in this way, and indeed with Rome herself.

units.la: LV. Sunto igitur inebriati poculo excandescentiae fcortationis meretricis illius illi, qui cum illa ad fpiritualem fornicationem copulati, irae ejus vino ita inebriati sunt, ut in furorem adversus nomen Christi acti fuerint, uti Alcasar pertendit; manet adhuc quaestio, qui fuerint Reges illi, qui poculum illud bibituri, atque ita cum meretrice illa, Roma scilicet Ethnica, scortaturi, & scortatione ea in rabiem adversus nomen Christi exarsuri fuerant? Nam Romani Senatores illi, qui mundum Imperio suo gubernabant, nec Reges terrae fuerunt, sed pars ministra ipsius Romae, Regibus subigendis oppositae: nec cum Roma Ethnica Spiritualiter scortati, ac proinde etiam ex scortatione ejusmodi, ad persequendum Christi nomen excandescere non potuerunt, nec meretricem seu Romam Ethnicam, ut ille vult odio habuerunt, vel vastarunt & cremarunt, quod de Regibus scortatoribus, diserte affirmatur. Et si omnino cum Regibus terrae scortata est spiritualiter Roma Ethnica, Senatores illi non Reges scortatores fuerint, sed impurae meretricis impuri lenones. At qui tum fuerunt Reges, cum Roma Ethnica spiritualiter fornicantes? Hoc expediat nobis Alcasar, vel quisquam emunctiorum narium alius, & magnus Apollo nobis erit.
units.tr: LV. Let those then be made drunk with the cup of the fury of that harlot, those who, joined with her in spiritual fornication, are so intoxicated with her wine of wrath that they are driven into fury against the name of Christ, as Alcasar contends. The question remains: who were those kings who were to drink that cup, and so fornicate with that harlot, that is, heathen Rome, and by that fornication blaze into rage against the name of Christ? For those Roman senators who governed the world by their empire were not kings of the earth, but a servant part of Rome itself, set against the subjugation of kings. Nor could they have fornicated spiritually with heathen Rome, and therefore could not have been inflamed by such fornication to persecute the name of Christ, nor did they hate or lay waste and burn the harlot, that is, heathen Rome, as he wishes, which is expressly affirmed of the fornicating kings. And if heathen Rome had really fornicated spiritually with the kings of the earth, those senators were not the fornicating kings but the foul pimps of a foul harlot. But who were the kings at the time when they were fornicating spiritually with heathen Rome? Let Alcasar explain this to us, or any other man of keener nose, and great Apollo himself will be our reward.

units.la: LVI. Neque nodum, quem ex S. Johanne dicente, quod famosa meretrix illa vino scortationis Reges & incolas terrae inebriatura fit, ut sic inebriati cum ea scortentur, nexuimus, solvit alter in diversum fere nixus Cornelius a Lapide, qui Comment. ad Apoc. xvij. 2. Vinum interpretatur opes, honores, Romanorum, sive spem lucri, voluptatis & dignitatis a Romanis consequendae, qua Reges & incolas terrae ad secum fornicandum, hoc est, idololatrandum, colendosque Deos suos pellectura fuerit.
units.tr: LVI. Nor does Cornelius a Lapide, who in his commentary on Rev. 17:2 leans in almost the opposite direction, untie the knot which we have tied from St John's words, that the notorious harlot will make the kings and inhabitants of the earth drunk with the wine of fornication, so that, being thus intoxicated, they fornicate with her. He interprets the wine as the riches and honours of the Romans, or the hope of gain, pleasure and dignity to be obtained from the Romans, by which he says she would entice the kings and inhabitants of the earth to fornicate with her, that is, to worship idols, and to worship her gods.

units.la: Ubi inducit etiam emblema: Cupido ... fulminans, cum hac apodosi: Omnia vincit amor.
units.tr: There he also introduces an emblem: Cupid ... thundering, with this motto: Love conquers all.

units.la: LVII. Atqui primo forte meretrix non tam ipsa opes, honores, potentiam amasiis suis ostentat & promittit, quàm ab amasiis, Regibus maximè & potentibus mundi dignatur ipsa. Unde enim ad tantam potentiam & opulentiam crevit, nisi à scortatione frequentata cum Regibus & potentibus terræ? Secundò, vinum scortationis haud dubiè mysticum, spirituale quid est, abblandiens, & lenocinans concupiscentiæ & desideriis Regum; sicut ipsa meretrix nomen μυστήριον mysterium præfert. Tale quid esse potuerunt mysteria doctrinæ, secreta fidei, animarum voluptatem & salutem promittentia,per quæ se infatuari Reges passi sunt, ut cum ea scortarentur, hoc est, à vero & vivo Deo deficientes, se ad meretricis amorem, vanitatem & mendacium converterent. Tertiò aliud longè est unà cum alia scortari, seu communem idololatriam exercere, communes Deos colere, quod opibus Romanorum pelletos homines facturos fuisse à Lapide statuit: aliud cum aliqua scortari. Qui illud faciunt communes meretricis Deos amant, coluntque; qui hoc, ipsam meretricem ceu Deum quendam amant, coluntque. Atqui non illud, sed hoc facturos Reges & incolas terræ Apocalypsis vaticinatur. Proin Cornelio à Lapide æquè ac Alcasari incumbit ostendere, Reges terræ illos, qui cum Roma Ethnica hoc modo scortati fuerint. Quartò denique ne priore quidem modo Reges terræ cum Roma Ethnica scortatos esse, supra ostendimus. Notorium enim est, Romam veterem vel Reges victos delevisse, vel sacra consueta iis permisisse, saltem vino scortationis, hoc est lenociniis, blanditiis, opum, potentiæ, illecebris, quas cum Cupidine fulminante, seu amore omnia vincente ille confert, eos, ut communia secum sacra colerent, nunquam inebriâsse, quin potius aperta vi adversus obnoxios sibi pro lubitu semper consuluisse. Quin tantum abest, ut Ceremonias suas aliis Regibus gentibusque Roma vetus obtruserit, ut ipsa potius à devictis gentibus religionem acceperit. Testatur id Leo Papa Serm. 1. de Petro & Paulo, his verbis: Hæc civitas ignoransque proveētionis authorem cùm pæne omnibus dominaretur gentibus, omnium gentium serviebat erroribus. Et magnam sibi videbatur assumsisse religionem, quia nullam respuebat falsitatem. Atque id adeò verum est, ut cùm Romani illi Christiani nominis hostes infensissimos sese gesserint, non defuerint tamen inter eos etiam Imperatores, qui Christum ipsum inter Deos referendum censuerint, honorésque illi divinos tribuerint. Id de Tiberio Tertullianus Apolog. cap. 5. & 21. Hadriano & Alexandro Severo Lampridius Alexand. Sev. cap. 23. 51. testantur, quorum testimonia Doctiff. Huetius Demonstr. Evang. pag. 63. 64. 65. solidissimè vindicat.
units.tr: LVII. But first, perhaps the harlot does not so much display and promise to her lovers riches, honours and power, as she herself courts her lovers, especially the kings and the mighty of the world. For from what else did she grow to such great power and wealth, except from frequent fornication with the kings and the powerful of the earth? Secondly, the wine of fornication is undoubtedly something mystical and spiritual, flattering and coaxing the lusts and desires of kings, just as the harlot herself bears the name μυστήριον [mysterium]. Such things could have been the mysteries of doctrine, the secrets of faith, promising the pleasure and salvation of souls, by which the kings allowed themselves to be infatuated, so that they fornicated with her, that is, falling away from the true and living God, they turned to love of the harlot, to vanity and lies. Thirdly, it is one thing to fornicate together with another, or to practise a common idolatry, to worship common gods, which Lapide holds would have been done by men driven by the riches of the Romans; it is another thing to fornicate with someone. Those who do the former love and worship the common gods of the harlot; those who do the latter love and worship the harlot herself as some god. But the Apocalypse prophesies that the kings and inhabitants of the earth will do not the former but the latter. Therefore Cornelius a Lapide, no less than Alcasar, is bound to show which kings of the earth fornicated with heathen Rome in this way. Fourthly, finally, we have shown above that the kings of the earth did not fornicate with heathen Rome even in the former way. For it is well known that ancient Rome either destroyed her defeated kings or allowed them their customary rites, and at least never made them drunk with the wine of fornication, that is, with the enticements, flatteries, and allurements of riches and power, which that thundering Cupid, or love conquering all, bestows, so that they would worship with her the rites they shared; rather, she always openly and by force took thought for those under her power as she pleased. Indeed, ancient Rome was so far from forcing her ceremonies upon other kings and peoples that she herself rather received religion from the conquered nations. Pope Leo bears witness to this in Sermon 1 on Peter and Paul, in these words: This city, not knowing the author of its advancement, while it ruled over almost all nations, served the errors of all nations, and it seemed to itself to have taken up a great religion, because it rejected no falsehood. And this is so true that, although those Romans were most bitter enemies of the Christian name, there were nevertheless among them emperors who thought that Christ himself should be counted among the gods and paid divine honours. Tertullian testifies to this about Tiberius in Apology chapters 5 and 21, and Lampridius about Hadrian and Alexander Severus in Alexander Severus chapters 23 and 51, whose testimonies the most learned Huet solidly vindicates in Demonstratio Evangelica, pages 63, 64, 65.

units.la: LVIII. Tertiò Babylon magna inducitur sedens in Be- stia eam portante Apoc. xvii. 7. 8. &c.
units.tr: LVIII. Thirdly, great Babylon is introduced sitting on the beast that carries her, Rev. 17:7, 8, etc.

units.la: Bestia illa meretricis jumentum, haud dubiè populos Babyloni subjectos designat: ut qualis Bestia est, talis etiam Babylon censeri debeat. Atqui Bestia neutiquam populum Romanum gentilem, à Roma Ethnica gubernatum significat. Successit enim Draconi, seu Diabolo gentes ad idololatriam crassam seducenti, quod in Roma Ethnica factum esse, manifestum est. Non igitur Bestia illa Roma esse Ethnica potuit, quod infra dedita operâ demonstrandum suscepimus. Proin nec Babylon eam inequitans Roma Ethnica esse potuit.
units.tr: That beast, the harlot's mount, undoubtedly stands for the peoples subject to Babylon, so that Babylon must be judged to be of the same kind as the beast. But the beast by no means signifies the Roman people, the pagan nation ruled by pagan Rome. For it succeeded the dragon, that is the devil, who seduced the nations into gross idolatry, and it is plain that this happened in pagan Rome. That beast therefore cannot have been pagan Rome, as we have deliberately undertaken to show below. Hence the city that rides it cannot have been pagan Rome either.

units.la: LIX. Accedit denique quartò Babylonis magnæ nun- dinatio animarum, quæ Romæ Ethnicæ nullo modo con- venit.
units.tr: LIX. Lastly, fourthly, there is the trade in souls of great Babylon, which in no way fits pagan Rome.

units.la: Testatur enim Apocalypsis Cap. xviii. 11. 12. 13. eversam Babylonem planxisse mercatores, quia nemo amplius emit τὸν γόμον mercimonium ejus, quas inter mercimonii species postremo loco referuntur etiam ψυχὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων animæ hominum. Cujusmodi mercimonium animarum esse potest, si potestatem in animas, conscientias, puta ex plenitudine potestatis ligandas, solvendas, legibus latis pro lubitu obligandas, remunerandas & puniendas; Cœlo vel Orco inferendas sibi quovis modo aliquis acquisiverit, vel rapuerit, atque ea potestate ad commodum lucrumque etiam suum usus fuerit. Spiritualis igitur nundinatio intelligitur, qualis tribuitur Simoni Mago Act. viii. 18. 19. 20. quibusdam. Καπηλεύοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ cauponantibus sermonem Dei. 2 Cor. ii. 15. fideles πλανῶντες λόγοις ἐμπορευόμενοι fictis sermonibus negotiantibus. 2 Petr. ii. 3. denique iis, qui pietatem quæstum putant, 1 Tim. vi. 5. Atqui nundinationem ejusmodi animarum Roma Ethnica nunquam exercuit, neque quomodo exercuerit, quisquam ostendit hactenus.
units.tr: For the Apocalypse, Rev. 18:11–13, says that when Babylon was overthrown the merchants wept, because no one any longer bought her merchandise [τὸν γόμον], and among the kinds of merchandise, listed last of all, are also the souls of men [ψυχὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων]. What kind of trade in souls could this be? It could be one in which someone has acquired or seized for himself, by any means, power over souls and consciences, namely the power to bind and loose them by the fullness of authority, to oblige them by laws enacted at will, to reward and punish them, and to consign them to heaven or hell, and has then used that power for his own convenience and profit. So it is a spiritual trading that is meant, such as is ascribed to Simon Magus, Acts 8:18–20, and to certain others: peddling [καπηλεύοντες] the word of God, 2 Cor. ii. 15; deceiving with words and trading in feigned speech [πλανῶντες λόγοις ἐμπορευόμενοι], 2 Pet. ii. 3; and finally those who think godliness a source of gain, 1 Tim. vi. 5. But Pagan Rome never carried on a trade of this kind, and no one has so far shown how it might have done so.

units.la: LX. Nam quòd Cornelius à Lapide Comment. ad h. l. mercimonium isthoc animarum interpretatur emptionem vitarum hominum, ut cum gladiatoribus, vel cum bestiis in circo depugnent; adeóque mancipiorum morti destinatorum, uti alter Jesuita Ribera explicat, nimis id certè dilutum est. S. Johannes enim distinctè mercimonium τῶν σωμάτων καὶ ψυχῶν corporum & animarum commemorat. Animarum autem à corporibus distinctarum mercimonium ad ἡμεροπαχίαν ejusmodi & piaculares victimas non requirebatur, cùm ad eam corpora, non animæ concurrerint. Quin consultò Spiritus S. constructionem mutavisse videtur, ut discrimen notaret. Non enim animæ memorantur in secundo casu, ut in præcedentibus, & merces equorum, & rhedarum, & corporum, sed inde transitur ad quartum casum, καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων & animas hominum. Quo significatur haud dubiè, distinctam planè esse, diversámque rationem mercimonii corporum & animarum. Si igitur vetus Roma fidelium, vel aliorum etiam mancipiorum ἀργυ-ρίου vitam infestando, & gladiatoribus bestiis objicien-do, do, mortíque devovendo, vitas hominum in commercio habuit (quanquam insolens hæc locutio foret, cùm ejus rei, quæ destruitur nulla sit ἁμαρτία, mercimonium nullum) mercimonium utique fuisset corporum, quæ sola occidi potuerunt, & non animarum perspicuè adeò à corporibus distinctarum, quas homines occidere, destruere non possunt. Matth. x. 28.
units.tr: LX. For Cornelius à Lapide, in his Commentary on this passage, explains this merchandise of souls as the buying of men's lives, so that they might fight in the circus with gladiators or with wild beasts; and so of slaves doomed to death, as the other Jesuit Ribera explains it. That is certainly far too watered-down. For St John mentions distinctly the merchandise of bodies and souls [τῶν σωμάτων καὶ ψυχῶν] / bodies and souls. But the trade in souls, distinct from bodies, was not needed for such man-hunting [ἡμεροπαχίαν] and for such sacrificial victims, since it is bodies, not souls, that come into play there. Indeed the Holy Spirit seems to have deliberately changed the construction to mark the difference. For the souls are not named in the genitive case as in the preceding items, and of horses, and of chariots, and of bodies, but the sentence then passes to the accusative, and souls of men [καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων] / and souls of men. This undoubtedly signifies that the trade in bodies and souls is entirely distinct and of a different kind. If, then, old Rome had dealt in the lives of Christians, or of other slaves, by harassing them for money and by throwing them to gladiators and beasts, and by devoting them to death, the trade would still have been one in bodies, which alone can be killed, and not in souls, which are so clearly distinct from bodies that men cannot kill or destroy them, Matt. x. 28. (Though this way of speaking would be odd, since there is no trade in a thing that is destroyed, when nothing has been sinned in it.)

units.la: LXI. Supparasitatur quidem heic Jesuitis Hugo Grotius, qui ex Ezech. xxvii. 13. ubi Javan, Thubal & Meschech dicuntur רוכליים כנפש אדם negotiari cum ψυχαῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων cum animabus hominum, hoc est, cum hominibus mancipatis in servitutem; pertendit etiam hic ψυχὰς animas, mancipia notare. Ad quod exemplum Græcos posteriores servulos ψυχάρια vocâsse, observante Doctissimo Meursio, addit. Liberi enim homines, inquit, corporis sui domini, servi nil nisi animam possident, nam corpus est domini. Atqui talium mancipiorum sub voce σωμάτων corporum mentionem fieri oportuit, si de mancipiis in hoc textu omnino sermo est. Neque hic locus, in quo animæ à corporibus distinguuntur, cum loco Ezechielis xxvii.13. in quo distinctio ejusmodi nulla occurrit rectè comparatur. Et si animam possident servi, corpus verò eorum domini esse, utique in Romanorum commercio animæ mancipiorum esse non potuerunt. Græcis quidem σώματα corpora, non ψυχαὶ animæ sæpissimè notant servos & famulitium domesticum, uti ex Aristotele Rhet. 1. & Demosthene Philipp. 3. Linguæ illius callentes probant. Ut verò corpus absolutè ponerètur pro homine libero, anima verè pro homine servo, nec Græcis, nec Latinis S. Johannis tempore cumprimis, in usu fuit. Etsi enim ψυχάρια ultimi Græci dixerunt pro servulis, prout & ultimi Latini eos animalia vocárunt, servos tamen ψυχὰς animas antiquitus vocatos esse, non æquè proclive probatu est. ψυχαγωγαὶ quidem plagiarii dicebantur, non quòd ψυχὴ per se sit servus, sed quòd absolutè posita ea vox, & à corpore non distincta persona humanam, sive ingenuæ, sive servilis conditionis sit, significet.
units.tr: LXI. Hugo Grotius, who, as the learned Meursius observes, relies on Ezek. xxvii. 13, where Javan, Tubal and Meshech are said to trade with the souls of men [רוכליים כנפש אדם], that is, with men reduced to slavery, also here souls is taken to mean slaves. He adds that later Greeks called slaves little souls [ψυχάρια] on this model. For free men, he says, are masters of their own bodies, while slaves possess nothing but a soul, since the body belongs to the master. But if slaves were really meant in this text, mention would have had to be made of such slaves under the word bodies [σωμάτων]. Nor is this passage, in which souls are distinguished from bodies, rightly compared with Ezekiel 27:13, where no such distinction occurs. And if slaves possess a soul while their body belongs to the master, then in Roman commerce the souls of slaves could not have been bought and sold. It is true that the Greeks very often used bodies [σώματα], not souls [ψυχαί], to mean slaves and domestic servants, as the most skilled Greek scholars show from Aristotle's Rhetoric 1 and Demosthenes' Philippic 3. But that the word body should stand absolutely for a free man, and soul truly for a slave, was not in use either among the Greeks or among the Latins, especially at the time of St John. For although the latest Greeks used little souls for household slaves, just as the latest Latins called them animals, it is not so easy to prove that slaves were called souls [ψυχὰς] / animas in antiquity. Kidnappers were indeed called soul-leaders [ψυχαγωγαὶ] / plagiarii, not because a soul [ψυχὴ] is in itself a slave, but because that word, used absolutely and not distinguished from the body, signifies a human person, whether of free or of servile condition.

units.la: LXII. Cùm igitur Roma Ethnica vetus judicium Babyloni intentatum subiverit nunquam mysticum, tale scilicet, quale Babyloni tribuit Apocalypsis, habuerit nihil, fcortationis vino Reges & gentes ad scortandum secum nunquam pellexerit; Bestia illa, quam Babylon inequitare dicitur, nunquam extiterit, denique nec animas etiam à corporibus distinctas nundinari sueverit; uti hactenus firmiter, plerisque famosis doctoribus, adversarum partium consentientibus, astruximus: Babylonem magnam, quam Apocalypsis describit, eam non fuisse, liquidò consequitur.
units.tr: LXII. Therefore, since old pagan Rome never incurred the mystical judgement brought against Babylon, of the kind the Apocalypse ascribes to her, and never had the wine of her fornication with which she led kings and nations to fornicate with her; since that beast which Babylon is said to ride never existed; and since Rome never had the habit of trading even in souls distinct from bodies, as we have so far firmly maintained, with most of the famous teachers of the opposite party agreeing: it clearly follows that the great Babylon described by the Apocalypse was not Rome.

units.la: LXIII. Quos verò hactenus consentientes, & à tribulibus suis in alia omnia euntes vidimus, Blasius Viegas, Franciscus Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, Leonhardus Lessius, alii, ne Ecclesia eorum detrimentum aliquod patiatur, aliam quercum excutiendam sibi putârunt. Pertendunt nempe illi, Babylonem magnam notare Romam Antichristiano-Ethnicam, qualis futura sit paulò ante finem mundi, tempore Antichristi, sub quo Roma à fide Christi & obedientia Papæ ad veterem Ethnicismum relapsura sit. Idque permissurum Deum addunt illi, ut urbem ab Ecclesia secernamus, útque Romani, quorum peculiaria vitia erant fastus & protervia, non suis meritis, sed Christi Petrique gratiæ tribuant, quòd sedem Pontificiam, & Ecclesiæ metropolim obtinent.
units.tr: LXIII. But those whom we have so far seen agreeing with one another, and departing from their own kind in everything else, namely Blasius Viegas, Francisco Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, Leonhard Lessius and others, have thought fit to shake out another oak, so that their Church should suffer no loss. They maintain, namely, that the great Babylon denotes Antichristian-pagan Rome, such as it will be shortly before the end of the world, in the time of Antichrist, under whom Rome will fall back from the faith of Christ and obedience to the Pope into ancient paganism. And they add that God will permit this, so that we may separate the city from the Church, and so that the Romans, whose peculiar vices were pride and arrogance, may attribute to the grace of Christ and Peter, and not to their own merits, that they hold the Papal seat and the metropolis of the Church.

units.la: LXIV. Sententiam hanc verbis ipsius Cornelii à Lapide exponere, haud ἀπαγορεύω fuerit. Porro ita ille Comment. in Apoc. xvij. p. 257. scribit. Cùm liber signatus Apocalypsis, sit Prophetia de futuris in fine mundi sub Antichristo, hinc sequitur, hæc intelligenda esse de Roma Urbe, non quæ est, aut quæ fuit, sed quæ erit in fine mundi, ac consequenter Romam Urbem tum redituram ad pristinam suam gloriam, pariter & idololatriam, aliaque vitia, ac talem fore, qualis fuit tempore S. Johannis sub Domitiano, Nerone, Decio &c. nimirum ex Christiana tum rursus fiet Ethnica; Pontificemque Christianum & fideles ei adhærentes ejiciet, persequetur, & occidet, uti dicitur v. 6. Unde vocatur meretrix, quia omnium Deorum cultu, superstitionibus & vitiis imbuta, quasi meretrix prostituta cunctis gentibus, gentiumque Diis sedebit. De hac enim rectè dicitur, quòd sit Babylon magna, mater fornicationum & abominationum terræ; quòd sit ebria de sanguine Sanctorum, & de sanguine Martyrum Jesu, quóidque Deus judicabit & vindicabit in ea cædem Apostolorum. Quia nimirum in fine mundi ipsa rursum Ethnica æmulabitur persecutiones Imperatorum Ethnicorum in Christianos, itaque Deus in ea puniet & propriam & antiquam patrum infidelitatem. Si quis tamen, ita pergit, per persecutionem malit intelligere hæresin, ac dicere, Romam in fine mundi lapsuram in hæresin, aut simile vitium, uti singulis seculis novas videmus oriri hæreses, ideoque persecuturam Orthodoxos, æquè ac olim Ethnici persecuti sunt, itaque imitaturam & impleturam ipsorum peccata ac propter illa pariter ac sua, à Deo puniendam, ac concremandam, non multùm repugnabo, quamvis contextus magis faveat priori sententiæ. Quemadmodum autem Roma ad Ethnicismum relabi possit, deinceps declarare conatur exemplo Hierosolymæ, quæ, inquit, primò fuit pagana sub Chananæis, secundò fidelis sub Judæis, tertiò Christiana sub Apostolis, quartò pagana rursum sub Romanis, quintò Saracenica sub Turcis. Concludit tandem, se hæc eò dixisse, ut ostendat, se cum heterodoxis in fide candidè & liberaliter agere, non fugere difficultates, non tergiversari, nec affectu agi, sed ratione.
units.tr: LXIV. It would not be out of place to set out this opinion in the very words of Cornelius à Lapide. He writes thus in his Commentary on the Apocalypse, chapter 17, p. 257: Since the Apocalypse, the sealed book, is a prophecy of things future at the end of the world under Antichrist, it follows that these things are to be understood of the city of Rome, not as it is or was, but as it will be at the end of the world; and consequently that the city of Rome will then return to its former glory, and likewise to idolatry and other vices, and will be such as it was in the time of St John under Domitian, Nero, Decius, etc.; namely, from Christian it will then again become pagan; and it will expel, persecute and kill the Christian Pontiff and the faithful who cling to him, as is said in v. 6. Hence it is called a harlot, because, steeped in the worship of all gods, superstitions and vices, it will sit as a harlot prostituted to all nations and to the gods of the nations. For of this city it is rightly said that it is great Babylon, the mother of fornications and abominations of the earth; that it is drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus; and that God will judge and avenge in it the slaughter of the apostles. For in the end of the world it will itself, once again pagan, imitate the persecutions of the pagan emperors against Christians, and so God will punish in it both its own and its fathers' ancient unbelief. If, however, someone prefers, he goes on, to understand persecution as heresy, and to say that Rome at the end of the world will fall into heresy or a similar vice, as we see new heresies arising in every age, and so will persecute the orthodox just as the pagans once persecuted them, and will imitate and fulfil their sins and, for those as well as its own, be punished and burned by God, I shall not greatly object, although the context favours the former opinion more. How Rome may relapse into paganism he then tries to explain by the example of Jerusalem, which, he says, was first pagan under the Canaanites, second faithful under the Jews, third Christian under the apostles, fourth pagan again under the Romans, and fifth Saracen under the Turks. He concludes at last that he has said these things so that he may show that he deals with heterodox writers in faith candidly and generously, does not flee difficulties, does not evade, and is moved not by feeling but by reason.

units.la: LXV. Verùm, ut à postremo ordiar, forte deligendæ Ejusdem hujus sententiæ causam non habuit à Lapide candorem & pocritici. ingenuitatem, qualem de se prædicat, sed desperationem potiùs quandam, & quia futura merè contingentia fingendo pro lubitu, si non castiùs, at cautiùs certè mercari, & infamiam omnem à Roma Christiana averruncare se posse speravit. Alioquin à candore & ingenuitate erga nostros reliqua ejus scripta nimium nimiúmque abesse, nemo, nisi Teresia talpa cœcior, non videt, non palpat.
units.tr: LXV. But to begin with the last point: perhaps Lapide had no candour or ingenuousness of the kind he claims for himself when he chose this opinion. It was rather a kind of despair, and he hoped that by inventing future contingent events at will, he could trade more cautiously, if not more honestly, and so ward off all infamy from Christian Rome. Otherwise, no one who is not blinder than Tiresias or a mole can fail to see and feel that the rest of his writings are far removed from candour and ingenuousness toward our people. hypocritical

units.la: LXVI. Merum autem esse expositionem illam κρησφύγιαν, inde liquet, quòd nullum in Scriptura, nullum in Patribus, nullum in Scholasticis prioribus, firmamentum, nulla rationum momenta, denique præter audaces & vanissimas conjecturas præsidii nihil habet. Proin etiam Doctores Pontificii celeberrimi eam rejiciunt, acriterque flagellant. Suarez lib. 5. cap. 7. n. 10. probari eam sententiam posse negat. Alcasar Not. 13. Proœm. fusè eam refellit. Justinianus in 2 Thess. 2. de ea sic loquitur: Quid hoc aliud est, quàm divinare? Malvenda, qui multùm in hac causa sudavit, eam ceu incredibilem detestatur. E' recentioribus etiam Alphonsus Pandolphus de Fine mundi p. 360. hanc opinionem penitus improbandam, & à veritate prorsus alienam judicat. Quamvis, inquit inter alia, Clarissimæ notæ Theologi, Scotus, Bellarminus, Suarez tradant, fieri posse, ut sedes Apostolica omnium suprema in aliam urbem aut Ecclesiam transferatur, & sic supremus Ecclesiæ Monarcha successor Petri amplius non esset, nec vocaretur Romanus Pontifex, sed totius Ecclesiæ Catholicæ universalis Patriarcha; tamen existimo, id nunquam esse eventurum, neque ante mundi finem Romam à fide
units.tr: LXVI. That this exposition is a last-ditch refuge [κρησφύγιον] is clear from the fact that it has no support in Scripture, none in the Fathers, none in the earlier Schoolmen, no weight of argument, and, in short, nothing but bold and very vain conjectures. For this reason the most celebrated Papist teachers also reject it and lash it fiercely. Suarez, lib. 5, cap. 7, n. 10, denies that this opinion can be proved. Alcasar, Not. 13, Proœm., refutes it at length. Justinian, in 2 Thess. 2, speaks of it thus: What is this other than guessing? Malvenda, who sweated greatly over this question, condemns it as incredible. Among more recent writers, Alphonsus Pandolphus, de Fine mundi, p. 360, judges this opinion to be utterly reprobated and wholly alien to the truth. Although, he says among other things, theologians of the highest reputation, Scotus, Bellarmine, Suarez, teach that it may come about that the apostolic see, the supreme of all, is transferred to another city or Church, and so the supreme Monarch of the Church, the successor of Peter, would no longer exist, nor be called the Roman Pontiff, but the universal Patriarch of the whole Catholic Church; yet I think this will never happen, and that Rome will not fall away from the Catholic faith before the end of the world, which the testimonies of Cyprian and Jerome, which we shall soon also produce, chiefly persuade me of.

units.la: {} à fide Catholica defecturam, quod mihi potissimùm persuadent testimonia Cypriani & Hieronymi. quæ mox etiam producemus.
units.tr: from the Catholic faith, which I am chiefly persuaded of by the testimonies of Cyprian and Jerome, which we shall soon also produce.

units.la: LXVII. Authores hi, ita Alcasar loc. cit. expositionis hujus inventores & patronos premit, rem novam, incertam & improbabilem in medium adducunt. Cui enim unquam venit in mentem, rationi consentaneum esse, ut qui ænigma difficillimum æquè & gravissimum extricare aliter nesciam, novum quiddam & inauditum excogitem, quod sublato ipso ænigmate nullam probabilitatis speciem habeat? Quod si ea fuit eorum mens, ut aliquam Apocalypseos interpretationem invenirent, quæ bonis ingeniis satisfaceret, planè ab eo scopo aberrârunt, siquidem nec eorum declaratio doctorum est consensu recepta, neque invento fides habita.
units.tr: LXVII. These authors, as Alcasar, loc. cit., goes on to press against the inventors and patrons of this exposition, bring forward a novel, uncertain and improbable thing. For who ever thought it reasonable that I, who cannot otherwise untie a riddle so very difficult and so weighty, should devise something new and unheard of, which, were the riddle itself removed, would have no appearance of probability at all? But if their intention was to find some interpretation of the Apocalypse that would satisfy good minds, they have clearly strayed from that aim, since their explanation is not received by the consensus of learned men, nor has the discovery been given credit.

units.la: LXVIII. Neque immeritò idem eosdem hoc argumento inter alia pungit: Cùm res sit adeò incerta, miror illos authores non fuisse veritos, ne quam ansam præberent hæreticis (Evangelicis) Romam ejúsque in Divorum imagines religionem detestantibus, in nos cavillandi, atque adeò jactandi, doctos etiam homines inter nos ipsos reperiri, qui affirment, Romæ perversionem & ad idololatriam reditum fuisse in Apocalypsi prædictam. Rectè tale quid tibi, Alcasar, animus præsagivit. Revera enim Evangelici, quos tu Babyloniæ, hæreticorum infami titulo probrosè traducis, non parùm sibi gratulantur, agnoscúntque, non sine provido Numine evenisse, ut jurati cætera hostes veritati testimonium redderent, confiterentúrque adeò Romam Christianam in idololatriam (quæ imaginum quarumcunque, & quoscunque repræsentantium cultu, ut alias species non attingam, committitur) & Antichristianismum ipsum aliquando prolapsurum esse. Vel igitur vacillabit Divinarum promissionum, quibus freti Ecclesiæ Romanæ perpetuitatem & ἀναμαρτησίαν haftenus vindicaftis, fides vel promissiones illæ obtorto collo raptæ fuerunt ad probandum id, quod gregales hi rotundo ore improbant. Sed & magnificis illis, quibus haftenus Roma superbivit, dictis S. Patrum, veluti S. Cypriani Epist. 55. dicentis, Ad Romanam Ecclesiam perfidia non potest habere accessum; nec non S. Hieronymi lib. 3. contra Rusticum scribentis: Romana fides Petri authoritate munita non potest mutari, (quibus consentaneum etiam Benedicti apud S. Gregorium Dial. lib. 1. 15. prophetiam quòd Roma ab infidelibus nunquam evertenda sit, Alcafar addit) per hanc sententiam vel nulla fides constare potest, vel alius omnino sensus abeo, quem haftenus iis affinxerunt, aptandus fuerit. Quicquid sit, ratum est, Romam Christianam potuisse Antichristianam, idololatricam & quidni etiam quadantenus ethnicam; cùm idololatræ omnes ethnicis nihilo meliores sint, evadere. Quod verò Pontificem ipsum ex hoc incendio eripere Ribera & à Lapide conantur, non succedere dolum fatebuntur, quotquot rem ipsam penitius introspexerint. De quo tamen hic dicendi locus non est, ubi falsas duntaxat de Babylone magna interpretationes ad partes vocamus.
units.tr: LXVIII. Nor without reason does the same writer, among other things, prick them with this argument: Since the matter is so uncertain, I marvel that those authors were not afraid lest they provide an occasion for heretics (Evangelicals), who detest Rome and the worship of the images of the saints, to mock us, and indeed to boast that learned men are found among ourselves who affirm that the perversion of Rome and its return to idolatry was predicted in the Apocalypse. Rightly, Alcasar, your mind foresaw something of this sort. For indeed the Evangelicals, whom you shamefully traduce as Babylon with the infamous title of heretics, rejoice not a little, and acknowledge that it has come about, not without a providential divine will, that enemies sworn to everything else should bear witness to the truth, and should confess that Christian Rome will fall into idolatry (which is committed by the worship of any images whatever, and of whomever they represent, not to touch on other forms) and that Antichristianism itself will one day fall. Either, then, the faith in the divine promises, by which you have hitherto claimed for the Roman Church its perpetuity and impeccability [ἀναμαρτησίαν], will waver, or those promises were wrenched by the neck to prove what these common fellows speak against with full voice. But also, through this opinion, the magnificent sayings of the holy Fathers, in which Rome has hitherto prided herself, such as the saying of St. Cyprian, Epist. 55, Perfidy cannot have access to the Roman Church; and also of St. Jerome, writing in lib. 3 contra Rusticum: The Roman faith, fortified by the authority of Peter, cannot be changed (to which Alcasar adds the prophecy of Benedict in St. Gregory, Dial. lib. 1, 15, that Rome is never to be overthrown by unbelievers, which agrees with this) — through this opinion either no faith can stand, or those sayings must be fitted to a sense altogether different from the one they have hitherto been given. Whatever the case, it is certain that Christian Rome could become Antichristian, idolatrous, and why not, to some extent even heathen, since all idolaters are in no way better than heathens. But that Ribera and Lapide attempt to snatch the Pontiff himself from this fire, those who have looked more deeply into the matter will admit that the trick does not succeed. Yet this is not the place to speak of that, where we are calling only false interpretations of Great Babylon before our tribunal.

units.la: LXIX. Unum hoc à sententiæ hujus assertoribus, Cornelio à Lapide maximè, qui ad Apoc. 17. 17. diserte asserit, Romam ab Antichristo per decem Reges evertendam esse, sciscitari libet, anne cùm Roma Christiana sub finem mundi in Antichristianam degenerabit, Antichristi ipsius sedes & ara futura; an potius cum Antichristo alibi, Hierosolymæ scil: (quam illi sedem Bellarminus aliique deputant) sedente & stabulante communionem habitura, & propter ejusmodi communionem Antichristiana duditura sit? Si prius affirmaverint, jam igitur Roma, non Hierosolyma sedes Antichristi erit, repugnante licet, quantum
units.tr: LXIX. Let us ask one thing of the advocates of this opinion, especially Cornelius à Lapide, who in his note on Apoc. 17:17 plainly asserts that Rome is to be overthrown by Antichrist through ten kings: whether, when Christian Rome degenerates into Antichristian Rome near the end of the world, it will be the seat and altar of Antichrist himself; or whether, rather, Antichrist, sitting and dwelling elsewhere, namely at Jerusalem (which Bellarmine and others assign as his seat), will have fellowship with her and, on account of such fellowship, she will become Antichristian? If they answer the former, then Rome, not Jerusalem, will be the seat of Antichrist, however much it may displease Bellarmine and the others. The Apocalypse also does not allow us to doubt this.

units.la: Dilemma adversus eandem. voluerit, Bellarmino, aliisque. De quo etiam Apocalypsis dubitare non finit. Neque enim Antichristus esse poterit extra Babylonem magnam, & Bestiam, cui illa insidet, hoc est, populos omnes terræ, qui Antichristo parent. Atqui & Babylonem magnam & Bestiam ipsam, cujus septem capita, septem Colles sunt Apoc. xvii. 9. Romæ eadem ostendit, in parte puta dominante & parente. Quod si Roma sub finem mundi Antichristi sedes erit; Roma Christiana, non Ethnica, hoc est, nomen Christi penitus abnegans, Antichristi sedes erit, utpote qui sessurus dicitur in Templo Dei, tanquam Deus, ostentans se ipsum quasi Deum 2 Thess. ii. 4. Quomodo Roma merè Ethnica, nomen Christi penitus ejurans, erit Templum Dei? Si posterius pertenderint, mirabuntur merito omnes, eodem tempore extra Babylonem magnam, Romam scil. illam Ethnicam, quæ dicitur sedere super multis aquis, seu populis, cum qua Reges terræ scortabuntur, cujus scortationis vino incolæ terræ & πάντα τὰ ἔθνη omnes gentes inebriabuntur, quæ mater erit scortationum & abominationum terræ, cujus decem cornua pugnabunt cum Agno; quæ sedebit Regina felicitatem inconcussam sibi promittens; extra inquam Babylonem talem, scorsim, sive Hierosolymæ, sive alibi Antichristum locum aliquem habiturum esse, si extra Romam Ethnicam Antichristus aliquis erit, & propter communionem cum illo Roma Antichristiana erit, jam non Babylon magna, seu Roma Ethnica, verùm Antichristus ille, utpote scaturigo malorum omnium & fundi calamitas, erit mater scortationum, & vino scortationis suæ omnes gentes inebriabit. Nisi forte fictitius ille Antichristus erit pater & Roma mater; ille vinum miscebit, hæc propinabit.
units.tr: Dilemma against the same. For Antichrist cannot be outside Great Babylon, and the Beast on which she sits, that is, all the peoples of the earth who obey Antichrist. But Great Babylon and the Beast itself, whose seven heads are the seven hills, Apoc. xvii. 9, point clearly to Rome, in its dominant and parental part. If Rome is to be the seat of Antichrist at the end of the world, then Christian Rome, not heathen Rome, that is, Rome wholly renouncing the name of Christ, will be the seat of Antichrist, since he is said to sit in the Temple of God, as God, displaying himself as if he were God (2 Thess. 2:4). How will Rome, purely heathen and wholly forswearing the name of Christ, be the Temple of God? If they pursue the latter, everyone will rightly marvel: at the same time, outside Great Babylon, namely that heathen Rome which is said to sit upon many waters, or peoples, with whom the kings of the earth commit fornication, with the wine of whose fornication the inhabitants of the earth and all the nations [πάντα τὰ ἔθνη] will be made drunk, which will be the mother of fornications and abominations of the earth, whose ten horns will fight with the Lamb, which will sit as queen, promising itself unshaken happiness; outside such a Babylon, I say, at a separate place, whether at Jerusalem or elsewhere, Antichrist will have some place, if Antichrist will be somewhere outside heathen Rome, and on account of fellowship with him Rome will be Antichristian; then it will not be Great Babylon, or heathen Rome, but that Antichrist, as the fountain of all evils and the dregs of calamity, who will be the mother of fornications and will make all nations drunk with the wine of his fornication. Unless perhaps that fictitious Antichrist will be the father and Rome the mother: he will mix the wine, she will pour it out.

units.la: LXX. Antichristum ante finem mundi regnaturum tres annos & dimidium, hypothesis est, à qua οἱ ἐξ ἐκκλησίας se dimoveri haud patiuntur, de cujus veritate heic nil disputo. Dividatur tempus illud, decernatúrque, an, quæ Antichristo & Babyloni Scriptura tribuit, ejus intervallo evenire omnia potuerint. Primò quidem Antichristus ille Hierosolymæ, si Deo placet, resìdens, & jam arcem Dominationis suæ occupans, inde communionem cum Roma instituet, eámque seducet, & in malitiæ consortium pertrahet? An, qui tum Pontificem Romæ aget, purpuratorum suorum choro stipatus, & tot gentium præsidiis firmatus, tam segniter Antichristo resistet, ut brevi adeò tempore vincat, & ima summis misceat? Mox Roma ipsa non uni alicui populo, sed tot Regibus & populis idololatriam non vi aliqua, sed illecebris & blandimentis suis obtrudet, adeò ut cum Roma scortentur assiduè. Quin ex scortatione illa potentiam immensam comparabit, & mercatores terræ ita liberaliter ungét, ut opulentissimi evadant. Denique ruet Roma, sed nondum corruet, verùm collectis postliminio viribus sedebit iterum ut Regina, & se superbissimè proferet. Tandem impleta peccatorum mensura obruetur, & excidetur subitò. Atque non sic quidem finis erit omnium, nam & Reges superabunt, & mercatores, qui perditæ Babyloni lessum canent & inferias facient solenniter. Hæccine omnia intra angusti illius, quod Antichristo definiunt, temporis cancellos singula eventura putabimus? Et temerè id asserentibus, prophetiam modo ut ἐξηγεῖσθαι exinanire, vel certè obscurare, & à genuino eventu suo, rebúsque experiundo pridem liquidò cognitis ad nova, incerta, incredibilia, ut Alcasar & Malvenda non sine indignatione quadam appellant, abducere possint, fidem nos habebimus?
units.tr: LXX. That Antichrist will reign three years and a half before the end of the world is a hypothesis from which those of the Church [οἱ ἐξ ἐκκλησίας] refuse to be moved; I do not dispute its truth here. Let that period be divided, and let it be decided whether all the things that Scripture ascribes to Antichrist and Babylon could come to pass within its span. First, indeed, will that Antichrist, residing at Jerusalem, if it please God, and already occupying the citadel of his dominion, from there establish fellowship with Rome, and seduce her, and draw her into the partnership of wickedness? Or will he who then rules as Pontiff at Rome, surrounded by his choir of purple-clad men and strengthened by the protection of so many nations, resist Antichrist so sluggishly that he conquers in so brief a time and mixes the lowest with the highest? Soon Rome herself will thrust idolatry upon not one people but so many kings and peoples, not by any violence but by her enticements and blandishments, so that they constantly commit fornication with Rome. Indeed, she will acquire immense power from that fornication, and will anoint the merchants of the earth so liberally that they become exceedingly rich. Finally Rome will fall, but not yet be ruined; and, having gathered her strength again by the right of return, she will sit again as queen and display herself most arrogantly. At last, when the measure of sins is full, she will be overwhelmed and cut off suddenly. And thus indeed it will not be the end of all: for the kings too will be left, and the merchants, who will sing the dirge over lost Babylon and celebrate her funeral rites solemnly. Shall we think that all these things will come to pass one by one within the bounds of that narrow time which they assign to Antichrist? And shall we trust those who rashly assert it, who can, by such a method, empty the prophecy of its explanation [ἐξηγεῖσθαι], or at least obscure it, and lead it away from its genuine fulfilment, and from events long since clearly known by experience, toward things new, uncertain, incredible, as Alcasar and Malvenda call them, not without some indignation?

units.la: LXXI. Ad dedecus Romæ Christianæ pertinet, quòd Ribera callidum inventum suum ea ratione probabile reddere conatur, quòd multi hodiéque sint Romæ, qui & nominibus minibus & stemmatis se ex Veterum Romanorum genere esse comprobent, genúsque suum referant ad eorundem stirpem, quos ad majorum suorum idololatriam & scelera relapsuros ille divinat: quódque illi minimùm eandem civitatem cum veteribus incolentes, unum etiam cum illis corpus censeri possint. Quid de infamia hac nobilibus Romanorum prosapiis inusta censendum sit, viderint ipsi, conscii soli, qualem Ἰουδαῖον ἐν σἀκκω gerant. Illud saltem injuriam sibi ab amicis factam vægrandem Romani illi interpretabuntur, quod asseverat ille, eos eandem Civitatem cum ethnicis veteribus incolentes, unum etiam corpus cum illis censeri posse, atque idcirco ad ethnicismum relapsuros. An non verò Papa etiam & Cardinales eandem civitatem incolunt? Quid de illis igitur Ribera ariolatur? Et si ingenia & pietatem impietatemque locorum situs, vel civilis compages & contexteratio format, quid de ipso Ribera fieri debuit, qui eandem Hispaniam, non aliam puto, inhabitavit, quæ à Mauris seu Saracenis Africanis diu olim insessa fuit?
units.tr: LXXI. It counts against Christian Rome that Ribera tries to make his clever invention plausible by arguing that many people in Rome today can prove by name and by pedigree that they come from the stock of the ancient Romans, and he predicts that these people will relapse into the idolatry and crimes of their forefathers. He also argues that they can be considered one body with those ancient Romans, since they live in the same city. What should be thought of this infamy stamped on the noble families of Rome, they must judge for themselves, knowing their own consciences, what kind of a Jew in sackcloth [Ἰουδαῖον ἐν σάκκῳ] they wear. At least the Romans will take it as a serious wrong done to them by their friends, that he asserts they "live in the same city with the ancient heathens and can also be considered one body with them", and for that reason will relapse into heathenism. But do not the Pope and the Cardinals also live in the same city? Why then does Ribera prophesy such things about them? And if the character of people, and their piety or impiety, is shaped by the situation of places, or by the structure and composition of the state, what ought to be done about Ribera himself, who lived in the same Spain, I think and no other, which was long ago occupied by the Moors or African Saracens?

units.la: LXXII. Neque momenti alicujus est, quam urget à Lapide, ratio, quòd Apocalypsis sit Prophetia de rebus futuris in fine mundi sub Antichristo; cui etiam succollat subsidiaria ratio Riberæ, quod Apoc. xvi. 19. dicitur, Babylonem magnam venire in memoriam ante Deum, & cap. xviii. 5. recordari Deum iniquitatum ejus. unde colligunt illi, demum sub finem mundi impletum iri, quæ de Babylone magna Apocalypsis prænuntiavit, ac tum veterem etiam Romam Ethnicam, unà cum novissima punitum iri. Etenim Apcc. 1. 19. jubetur S. Johannes scribere quæ vidit, ἃ εἰσι, ἃ μέλλει γίνεσθαι μετὰ ταῦτα, & quæ sunt, & quæ posthac (non in fine duntaxat) futura sunt: Distinguendum illi fuerat judicium Babylonis, à judicii causis, & Babylone ipsa. Judicium peremtorium sub finem mundi, seu extrema tempora consummabitur. At Babylon ipsa diu ante judicium & existet, & longo satis temporis tractu judicium mereri, ac thesaurum iræ Divinæ in diem iræ accumulare debuit. Proin Deus jam jam vindictam ultimam de Babylone expetiturus, recordari iniquitatum Babylonis, & Babylon ipsa in memoriam tum venire ante Dominum dicitur, quia scelerum diu, continuéque patratorum, & mysterii iniquitatis à longo tempore operari, & fata Babylonis provocare non cessantis recordatus Deus ad vindictam procedet; non quia peccata Romæ Ethnicæ, tamdiu interrupta, & oblivione veluti obliterata, vel certè æterna damnatione expiari pridem cœpta, occasione scelerum Romæ novissimæ, memoriam demum subitura, & vindictam flagitatura sunt. Certè sce& shy;lera quædam magnæ Babyloni Apocalypsin tribuere, quæ à Roma Ethnica patrata non sunt, ac proinde, ut in ea pu& shy;nirentur, in memoriam Dei venire non poterant, jam su& shy;pra animadvertimus.
units.tr: LXXII. Of no weight either is the argument pressed by à Lapide, that "the Apocalypse is a prophecy of things to come at the end of the world under Antichrist". Ribera's supporting argument also props it up, that Rev. 16:19 says "great Babylon came into remembrance before God", and 18:5 says "God remembered her iniquities". From these they infer that what the Apocalypse foretold about great Babylon will at last be fulfilled only at the end of the world, and that then ancient heathen Rome will be punished together with the last one. For in Rev. 1:19 John is commanded to write "the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter" [ἃ εἰσι, ἃ μέλλει γίνεσθαι μετὰ ταῦτα], and "the things which are, and which shall come to pass hereafter" (not only at the end). He ought to have distinguished the judgment of Babylon from the causes of the judgment and from Babylon herself. The final judgment will be carried out at the end of the world, or in the last times. But Babylon herself will exist long before the judgment, and over a fairly long span of time she ought to deserve judgment and store up wrath against the day of wrath. Therefore God, about to exact his last vengeance on Babylon, is said to "remember" the iniquities of Babylon, and Babylon herself is said then to "come into remembrance before the Lord", because God, who never ceases to remember the crimes long and continually committed and the mystery of iniquity working from of old, and the fate of Babylon provoked, will proceed to vengeance. It is not because the sins of heathen Rome, long interrupted and as it were blotted out by oblivion, or already begun to be expiated by eternal damnation, will at last come into remembrance and demand vengeance on account of the crimes of the last Rome. Certainly some crimes are attributed by the Apocalypse to great Babylon which were not committed by heathen Rome, and therefore could not come into God's remembrance so that she might be punished for them; we have already noted this above.

units.la: LXXIII. Sibyllarum oracula nequicquam iidem solicitant. Quid enim folia earum ad obscurandam veræ pro& shy;phetiæ veritatem? Quanquam ne obscurant quidem, sed confirmant potiùs, ut ex Apocalypsi desumta, hoc qui& shy;dem in argumento, vero haud sit absimile. Non enim aliud lib. 8. Romæ ante finem mundi denuntiant, quàm cœle& shy;stes plagas, combustionem & desolationem extremam. ἴσαι ὃ Ῥώμη ῥύμη. Erit Roma vicus, inquiunt. At futu­ram sub finem mundi denuò Ethnicam, & ejecto Papa ac Cardinalibus, puniendam, neutiquam illæ præsagiunt. Cùm caput illud Orbis occiderit, inquit Lanctantius lib. vij. 25. & ῥύμη esse cœperit, quod Sibyllæ fore ajunt, quis dubitet, venirse tum finem rebus humanis, orbique ter& shy;rarum? LXXIV. Sic ad liquidum perduximus, Babylonem magnam Sibyllarum de Roma extidio vaticinium. Cum Babylon ne ver.
units.tr: LXXIII. The same men try in vain to call on the oracles of the Sibyls. For what do their leaves matter to the obscuring of the truth of true prophecy? Yet they do not even obscure it; rather they confirm it, as taken from the Apocalypse, and in this matter the two are not very unlike. For in lib. 8 they announce nothing about Rome before the end of the world except heavenly blows, burning and final desolation: "Rome will be a lane" [ἴσαι ὃ Ῥώμη ῥύμη], they say. But that Rome will again be heathen at the end of the world, and, with the Pope and Cardinals cast out, will be punished, those oracles by no means foretell. "When that head of the world has fallen," says Lactantius in lib. 7, 25, "and has begun to be a lane, as the Sibyls say it will be, who would doubt that then the end would come to human affairs and the destruction of the earth?" LXXIV. Thus we have clearly brought it to light that the Sibyls' prophecy about the destruction of Rome is not a prophecy of great Babylon. Since Babylon is not... [Rome is not great Babylon]

units.la: magnam non esse etiam Romam sub finem mundi demum Antichristianam & Ethnicam futuram. Cumque omnino Roma sit, consentientibus Doctorum Romanorum plerorúmque omnium calculis, Roma verò nec Ethnica vetus esse potuerit, uti nobiscum famosissimi Jesuitæ, Ribera,à Lapide, Lesslius, Viegas, alii agnoscunt, & argumenta omni exceptione majora convincunt: nec novissima Antichristiano-Eth-nica esse posset, ut nobiscum Jesuitæ alii haud ignobiliores illis, Alcasar, Suarez, Justinianus, Malvenda, alii, confitentur, & argumenta haud minùs stringentia fidem indubiam faciunt, infallibili consecutionis nexu inferimus, Romam tertiam, nec Ethnicam, nec Antichristiano-Ethnicam, proprie scilicet talem, nomen Christi prorsus ejurantem, sub finem mundi extituram intelligi. ὅτι ἰδία ἀληθαι.
units.tr: that Rome also will not be great at the end of the world, and will be Antichristian and heathen. And since Rome certainly exists, with the agreement of the calculations of the Roman doctors and almost all of them, and since Rome could not be the ancient heathen city, as the most notorious Jesuits, Ribera, à Lapide, Lessius, Viegas and others acknowledge with us, and their arguments, greater than any exception, convince; nor could she be the last, Antichristian-heathen city, as other Jesuits, not less distinguished than those, Alcasar, Suárez, Justinian, Malvenda and others, confess with us, and their arguments, no less binding, make the faith indubitable, we infer by an infallible chain of consequence that a third Rome, neither heathen nor Antichristian-heathen (that is, properly such, utterly renouncing the name of Christ), is to be understood as coming into being at the end of the world. [that these things are true in themselves] ὅτι ἰδία ἀληθαι.

units.la: DISSERTATIO SECUNDA QUA
units.tr: DISSERTATIO SECUNDA QUA

units.la: Falsæ de Bestia, meretricem portante, interpretationes refelluntur. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: The false interpretations of the Beast that carries the harlot are refuted. SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Babylonis mysterium, non intellecto Bestiæ mysterio, cognosci nequit. II. Bestiæ descriptio summaria,
units.tr: I. The mystery of Babylon cannot be understood unless the mystery of the Beast is understood. II. A summary description of the Beast,

units.la: III. IV. ratione totius ,
units.tr: III. IV. in respect of the whole,

units.la: V. & partium , puta capitum,
units.tr: V. and of its parts, namely the heads,

units.la: VI. & cornuum.
units.tr: VI. and the horns.

units.la: VII. Definitio Bestiæ.
units.tr: VII. The definition of the Beast.

units.la: VIII. Meretricis & Bestiæ distinctio.
units.tr: VIII. The distinction between the harlot and the Beast.

units.la: IX. Bestia meretricem portans cum Bestia marina convenit.
units.tr: IX. The Beast carrying the harlot agrees with the sea-Beast.

units.la: X. Repugnantibus Ribera , à Lapide , quorum argumenta solvuntur .
units.tr: X. Ribera and à Lapide dissent; their arguments are answered.

units.la: XI. Bestiam dicens S. Johannes Danielis stylo loquitur.
units.tr: XI. In calling it a Beast, St John speaks in the style of Daniel.

units.la: XII. Bestia mulierem portans cum Bestia priore Apoc. xiij. descripta convenit.
units.tr: XII. The Beast carrying the woman agrees with the earlier Beast described in Rev. xiii.

units.la: XIII. Falsæ interpretationes Bestiæ quatuor recensentur.
units.tr: XIII. Four false interpretations of the Beast are reviewed.

units.la: XIV. Prima Ribera , Viegæ , à Lapide , quòd sit Diabolus in mundo dominans , verbis à Lapide exponitur ,
units.tr: XIV. The first, of Ribera, Viega and à Lapide, that it is the Devil ruling in the world, is set out in à Lapide's words,

units.la: XV. & illustratur amplius.
units.tr: XV. and is further illustrated.

units.la: XVI. Refutatur eadem ab Alcasare , cò quòd Apoc. xiij. 1. à Dracone seu Diabolo destinguatur.
units.tr: XVI. The same is refuted by Alcasar, because Rev. xiii. 1 distinguishes the Beast from the Dragon or Devil.

units.la: XVII. Eadem expositio aliis etiam argumentis refellitur, cujusmodi sunt , quòd dici nequit , meretricem seu Romam , uti pertendunt illi , Antichristiano-Ethnicam Diabolo inequitare,
units.tr: XVII. The same exposition is also refuted by other arguments, such as that the harlot, or Rome, cannot, as they contend, be said to ride the Devil, the Antichristian-heathen power,

units.la: XVIII. quod Diabolus dici nequit fuisse & non esse , & ex abysso ascendere ,
units.tr: XVIII. that the Devil cannot be said to have been and not to be, and to ascend out of the abyss,

units.la: XIX. quòd eidem septem capita, montes , Reges ,
units.tr: XIX. that the seven heads, mountains and kings

units.la: XX. & decem cornua seu Reges aptari nequeunt.
units.tr: XX. and the ten horns or kings cannot be applied to him.

units.la: XXI. Imperium aliquod maximum Bestiæ nomine figuratur.
units.tr: XXI. Some very great empire is figured under the name of the Beast.

units.la: XXII. Expositio secunda Bestiæ , quòd Romanum Imperium Ethnicum notet , verbis Alcasaris proponitur ,
units.tr: XXII. The second exposition, that the Beast denotes the heathen Roman Empire, is set forth in Alcasar's words,

units.la: XXIII. refelliturque tum eo , quod meretrix ipsa Roma Ethnica non fuit, proin nec Bestia ejus jumentum esse potuit,
units.tr: XXIII. and is refuted both by the fact that the harlot herself, heathen Rome, was not, and so her Beast could not have been her mount,

units.la: XXIV. tum argumentis aliis, veluti 1. quòd Bestia succeßit Draconi, per Romam Ethnicam imperanti.
units.tr: XXIV. and by other arguments, for instance (1) that the Beast succeeded the Dragon, which ruled through heathen Rome;

units.la: XXV. Alcasaris exceptio, quòd Draco notet Diabolorum Rempublicam, refellitur.
units.tr: XXV. Alcasar's objection, that the Dragon denotes the commonwealth of devils, is refuted.

units.la: XXVI. II. quod Roma Ethnica fuiße, & non esse, & ascensura ex abyßo, & in exitium abitura dici nequit. Alcasaris exceptio elisa.
units.tr: XXVI. (2) That heathen Rome cannot be said to have been and not to be, and to ascend out of the abyss and go to perdition. Alcasar's objection is overturned.

units.la: XXVII. III. quòd Romæ Ethnicæ septem capita non quadrant. Alcasaris exceptio, quòd septem persecutores Romani intelligi posšint, quatuor argumentis refutata.
units.tr: XXVII. (3) That the seven heads do not fit heathen Rome. Alcasar's objection, that seven Roman persecutors may be meant, is refuted by four arguments.

units.la: XXVIII. Ejusdem exceptio, quod indefinita multitudo persecutorum intelligatur, proponitur,
units.tr: XXVIII. His objection that an indefinite multitude of persecutors is meant is put forward,

units.la: XXIX. & discutitur.
units.tr: XXIX. and is examined.

units.la: XXX. IV. quòd decem cornua Bestiæ, seu totidem Reges, Romæ Ethnicæ non congruunt. Alcasaris detorsio cornuum ad Senatores Romanos proponitur,
units.tr: XXX. (4) That the ten horns of the Beast, or as many kings, do not agree with heathen Rome. Alcasar's twisting of the horns to the Roman senators is put forward,

units.la: XXXI. & quatnor argumentis rejicitur.
units.tr: XXXI. and is rejected by four arguments.

units.la: XXXII. Argumenta ex Apoc. xiij. eidem expositioni opposita.
units.tr: XXXII. Arguments from Rev. xiii. opposed to the same exposition.

units.la: XXXIII. Expositio tertia Viterbiensis, quòd Bestia Imperium Turcicum notet, proponitur,
units.tr: XXXIII. The third exposition, that of the Viterbian, that the Beast denotes the Turkish Empire, is put forward,

units.la: XXXIV. & ab Alcasare ipso, solidisque etiam argumentis convellitur.
units.tr: XXXIV. and is overturned by Alcasar himself, and also by solid arguments.

units.la: XXXV. Expositio quarta Hugonis Grotii, quod Bestia Domitiani Imperium figuret, proponitur.
units.tr: XXXV. The fourth exposition, that of Hugo Grotius, that the Beast figures the empire of Domitian, is put forward.

units.la: XXXVI. Ejusdem absurditas in genere demonstratur.
units.tr: XXXVI. Its absurdity in general is demonstrated.

units.la: XXXVII. & quinque argumentis asseritur.
units.tr: XXXVII. and is maintained by five arguments.

units.la: XXXVIII. Romam parentem non vel Ethnicam veterem, vel Antichristiano-Ethnicam novissimam, sed tertiam denotari, concluditur.
units.tr: XXXVIII. It is concluded that the mother Rome is denoted neither the ancient heathen Rome nor the last Antichristian-heathen Rome, but a third.

units.la: I. Babylonis magnæ mysterium non intelleƈto mysterio Bestiæ, cui impura meretrix illa inequitare dicitur, feliciter extricari nequit. Sicut enim relata se mutuò illustrant, ita Babylon & Bestia, quæ ita ad se invicem, ut rectores ad subditos, imperantes ad parentes referuntur, lucem haud dubiè non contemnendam invicem fœnerantur. Ut verò Bestiæ mysterium intelligentiæ nostræ sese promptiùs osserrat, falsas ejusdem interpretationes ante omnia refelli, adeóque nebulas mysterio, ab iis potissimùm, quorum interest, ut æternis tenebris illud involvatur, offusas discuti, operæ pretium fuerit. Impediunt enim præjudicia inveterata non parùm, ne de re cognitu saluberrima sanum judicium ferri possit.
units.tr: I. The mystery of great Babylon cannot be happily unravelled without understanding the mystery of the Beast on which that impure harlot is said to ride. For as related things throw light on one another, so Babylon and the Beast, which refer to each other as rulers to subjects and as governors to the people they govern, lend one another light that is certainly not to be despised. But so that the mystery of the Beast may present itself more readily to our understanding, it will be worth our while first of all to refute its false interpretations, and so to dispel the mists cast over the mystery, mists cast chiefly by those whose interest it is that it be wrapped in eternal darkness. For long-standing prejudices hinder no little from allowing a sound judgement to be passed on a matter most wholesome to know.

units.la: II. Vidit S. Johannes Meretricem impuram sedentem ἐπὶ θηρίον κόκκινον, γέμον ὀνομάτων βλασφημίας, ἔχον κεφαλὰς ἑπτὰ καὶ κέρατα δέκα. super Bestia coccinea, plena nominibus blasphemiæ, habente septem capita & decem cornua. Apoc. xvii. 3. Bestia haud dubiè systema notat Bestiarum, seu multitudinem hominum animalium Spiritu Dei non præditorum, adeóque populum animalem legibus certis consociatum. Quæ coccinea dicitur, sive propter crudelitatem, quia rea est sanguinis Christi &sanctorum, vel propter apparentiam, quia per professionem externam fidei sanguine Christi colorata & purificata videbatur. Quanquam blasphemiæ illam à Sanctis ejusdem cœtus facile discreverunt.
units.tr: II. St John saw the impure harlot sitting upon a scarlet beast, full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns [ἐπὶ θηρίον κόκκινον, γέμον ὀνομάτων βλασφημίας, ἔχον κεφαλὰς ἑπτὰ καὶ κέρατα δέκα]. Upon the scarlet beast, full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns. Rev. xvii. 3. The Beast doubtless denotes a system of beasts, that is, a multitude of men who are animals not endowed with the Spirit of God, and so an animal people joined together under fixed laws. It is called scarlet either on account of its cruelty, because it is guilty of the blood of Christ and of the saints, or on account of its appearance, because through its outward profession of the faith it seemed to be coloured and purified by the blood of Christ. Yet the saints of that same body easily distinguished it from its blasphemies.

units.la: III. Cùm verò S. Johannes μέγα portentum illud magnum sanè stuperet merito, ejus mysterium ipsi Angelus paulò clariùs exposuit, docens scilicet, quid sit Bestia, ratione tum totius. v. 8. tum partium, puta & capitum v. 9. 10. 11. & cornuum, quorum partim ortus. v. 12. partim obsequium, quod Bestiæ præstabunt v. 13. partim clades v. 14. partim odium conceptum adversus meretricem, hostilitatémque v. 16. declaratur.
units.tr: III. But since St John rightly marvelled greatly at that great wonder [μέγα], its mystery was set out to him a little more clearly by an angel, who taught what the Beast is, in respect of the whole (v. 8), and of its parts, namely its heads (vv. 9, 10, 11), and its horns, of which some are declared in respect of their rise (v. 12), some of their service which they will render to the Beast (v. 13), some of their ruin (v. 14), and some of the hatred they conceive against the harlot and their hostility (v. 16).

units.la: IV. Ratione totius ita Angelus Bestiam describit. v. 8. Bestia, quam vidisti, erat, & non est, & ascensura est ex abysso, & in exitium abitura. Et mirabuntur incolæ terræ, videntes Bestiam, quæ suit, et cum sit, et non est, & tamen est. Sensus paradoxi haud dubiè is est, bestiam simile quid ante se habuisse, & eo intereunte, tanquam propaginem quandam in ejus locum ita successisse, ut in eo revivíscere, & vires suas omnes exercere merito credi possit; & denique interituram prorsus, non mutandam, ut prius illud. Ad intelligendum illud sapientiam spiritualem requirit Angelus v. 9. Hîc est mens, habens sapientiam, innuens, mysterium proponi ejusmodi, cujus intelligentia oculos mentis verbo Dei probè illuminatos exigat, nullámque expositionem probandam, quæ sapientiam non respiat. Certè vir brutus non cognoscit, & vir sultus non intelligit hoc. ꝟ. xcii. 7.
units.tr: IV. In respect of the whole, the angel describes the Beast thus (v. 8): The Beast which you saw was, and is not, and is about to ascend out of the abyss, and to go into perdition. And the inhabitants of the earth will marvel, seeing the Beast that was, and is not, and yet is. The sense of this paradox is doubtless this: the Beast once had something similar before it, and when that perished, it succeeded in its place like a kind of offshoot, so that it may fairly be believed to come back to life in it and to exercise all its powers; and finally it will perish altogether, and not change as the former did. To understand this the angel requires spiritual wisdom (v. 9): Here is the mind which has wisdom, indicating that the mystery is put forward in such a way that its understanding requires the eyes of the mind to be well illumined by the Word of God, and that no exposition is to be accepted which does not respect wisdom. Certainly a brutish man does not know, and a foolish man does not understand this (Ps. xcii. 7).

units.la: V. Partes Bestiæ statuuntur capita & cornua, quia scilicet vis potissima in illis residet. Et capita quidem numero septem v. 9. totidem dicuntur esse montes, in quibus mulier sedet. Quibus verbis sedes Bestiæ mulierem portantis ita insinuatur, ut septem montes illi simul typus & monimentum sint totidem Regum v. 10. quibus octavus accedere debuit. v. 11. nec non totidem populorum eidem imperio obnoxiorum. Nam & in aquis multis, seu populis, & turbis, & gentibus & linguis Apoc. xvii. 1. 15. & in montibus illis septem meretrix sedere dicitur.
units.tr: V. The parts of the Beast are set down as heads and horns, because clearly its principal power resides in them. The heads, seven in number (v. 9), are said to be as many mountains on which the woman sits. By these words the seat of the Beast carrying the woman is so indicated that the seven mountains are at once a type and a memorial of as many kings (v. 10), to whom an eighth was to be added (v. 11), and likewise of as many peoples subject to this empire. For the harlot is said to sit both on many waters, that is, peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues (Rev. xvii. 1, 15), and on those seven mountains.

units.la: VI. Cornua numero decem totidem Reges statuuntur, potestatem, ut Reges, unam horam accepturi cum Bestia & eandem in Bestiam unanimiter translaturi. v. 12. 13. Sensus est, fore ut Reges decem certo saltem tempore unâ regnent, & in Bestiam potestatem suam derivent, adeóque ei serviant, obsequantur, vel saltem comiter eam colant. Hic ortus, hoc obsequium Regum est. Clades eorundem v. 14. recensetur, ubi cum Agno pugnaturi & ab eodem vincendi dicuntur, quia Dominus Dominorum est, & Rex Regum, ac qui cum eo sunt electi & fideles. Sed & cornua, seu Reges illi odio habituri meretricem, desertam faciuri, & nudam carnem ejus comesturi, eámque igne combusturi. v. 16. dicuntur. Sensus est, futurum, ut meretricem agnitam detestentur, destituant eo auxilio, quod illi hastenus tulerunt, populorum suorum obedientiam ei subducant, fomenta ei, præsidiáque omnia eripiant, & igni tandem eam vastent.
units.tr: VI. The horns, ten in number, are set down as as many kings, who, as kings, are to receive power for one hour with the Beast, and unanimously to transfer that power to the Beast (vv. 12, 13). The sense is that the ten kings will for some certain time at least reign together, and will transfer their power to the Beast, and so will serve it, obey it, or at least courteously honour it. This is the rise and this the service of the kings. Their ruin is recounted (v. 14), where they are said to fight with the Lamb and to be conquered by him, because he is the Lord of lords, and King of kings, and those who are with him are chosen and faithful. But the horns, or those kings, are also said to hate the harlot, to make her desolate, and to eat her naked flesh, and to burn her with fire (v. 16). The sense is that it will come about that they detest the harlot once recognised, withdraw from her the help which they have hitherto given her, take from her the obedience of their peoples, strip her of all her supports and protections, and at last lay her waste with fire.

units.la: VII. Sic feralis Bestiæ illius, quæ meretricem portat, Definitio ejusmodi definitio exsurgere potest: Bestia est jumentum meretricis Babylonicæ, eam portans, seu populus eidem subditus animalis Spiritu Dei non præditus, populo cuipiam priùs existenti succedens, eúmque prava imitatione exprimens, capitibus septem, seu totidem montibus, ceu typis populorum septem rectoribus, quibus octavus accedere debuit parentium; nec non omnibus decem, seu totidem Regibus potestatem suam quandoque simul Bestiæ conferentibus, sed post meretricem odio habituris, desolaturis & combusturis, constans, tandémque ad interitum etiam vergens.
units.tr: VII. So a definition of that deadly Beast which carries the harlot may take shape as follows: Definition: the beast is the beast of burden of the Babylonian harlot, carrying her, or a people subject to her, an animal not endowed with the Spirit of God, succeeding some people that existed before, and expressing it by a perverse imitation, with seven heads, or as many mountains, as types of the seven rulers of peoples, to whom an eighth, from among those obeying, was to be added; and also with ten horns, or as many kings who at some time together confer their power on the beast, but who will hate the harlot afterwards, will make her desolate and burn her, consisting, and at last tending also to destruction.

units.la: VIII. Duo hinc statim elicimus, quæ æquos rerum arbitros facilè concessuros confido. Prius est, Meretricem & Bestiam distinguendam esse, ut ejusdem Babylonis partem geminam, dominantem, imperitantem unam, parentem, subditam alteram. Meretrix enim in Bestia sedet, adeóque eam regit, subjicit, & ad facienda imperata quovis modo flectit. Bestia contra quamvis populus unus,
units.tr: VIII. From this we can immediately draw two conclusions, which I trust fair judges will readily grant. The first is that the harlot and the beast must be distinguished, so that Babylon itself is twofold: one part ruling and commanding, the other obeying and subject. For the harlot sits upon the beast, and so rules it, subjects it, and bends it in every way to carry out her commands. The beast, on the other hand, although it is one people,

units.la: G multitudo regnum aliquod constituens, meretricem Βαςιλὶ portat, adeoque eidem paret, subjicitur, & imperata ejus religiose facit. Eadem utrobique Babylon est: sed parte imperante & parente discreta.
units.tr: a multitude constituting some kingdom, carries the queen [Βαςιλὶ], and so obeys her, is subject to her, and devoutly performs her commands. In both cases it is the same Babylon, but distinguished by its ruling and obeying part.

units.la: IX. Posterius est, Bestiam hanc, clitellarium meretricis jumentum, eandem numero esse cum Bestia illa priore maritima, seu ex mari ascendente, quæ Apoc. xiii. 111. describitur, & cap. xiv. 9. ii. xv. 2. xvi. 2. 10. 13. xix. 19. 20. xx. 4. 10. etiam indigitatur. Arguunt id multa satis. Utraque enim ascendere ex mari, seu Abysso: utraque septem capitibus & decem cornibus, seu totidem Regibus constitui: utraque potestatem suam habere à Dracone, seu fuisse & non esse, & esse, blasphemiis horrendis turgere: utraque sequaces habere incolas terræ, non electos & fideles, sed reprobos, non scriptos in libro vitæ Agni: utraque pugnare cum sanctis & Agno, & vincere & vinci dicitur, insinuatúrque. Agnoscit id una nobiscum Alcasar Comment. in Apoc. xvij. 3. ubi inter alia sic ille: Pro comperto habeo Belluam, in qua mulier sedet, eandem esse cum maris Bestia, quæ cap. 13. descripta est: Inter alia hoc etiam utitur argumento: Si, inquit, duæ Bestiæ forent, cùm Johannes utramque descripsisset, neutiquam diceret cap. xix. 19. Et vidi Bestiam, & apprehensa est Bestia. Ubi utroque in loco articulum præponit, ac supponit pariter, unam tantùm esse Bestiam, septem capitibus, & decem cornibus constantem. Addit, S. Johannem Apoc. xix. 20. recensentem finem hostium Ecclesiæ, Bestiæ duntaxat & Pseudoprophetæ (quem eundem cum Bestia posteriore seu terræ recte facit) meminisse. Non igitur, inquit, alia superesset Bestia, præter duas, priorem scilicet & posteriorem. Cúmque posterior non sit illa, quæ meretricem portare dicitur, priorem esse, solidè concludit.
units.tr: IX.
