The second is that this beast, the harlot's packhorse, is numerically the same as that former beast from the sea, or rising out of the sea, which is described in Apoc. xiii. 111., and is also pointed out in chapters 14.9, 2.15, 16.2, 10, 13, 19.19, 20, 20.4, 10. Many things sufficiently prove this. Both rise out of the sea, or the abyss; both are constituted with seven heads and ten horns, or as many kings; both have their power from the Dragon, and both swell with horrible blasphemies, "that was, and is not, and yet is"; both have followers, the inhabitants of the earth, not the elect and faithful but the reprobate, not written in the book of life of the Lamb; and both are said to fight against the saints and the Lamb, and to conquer and be conquered. Alcasar agrees with us on this in his Comment. in Apoc. xvij. 3., where among other things he says: I hold it as established that the beast on which the woman sits is the same as the sea beast described in chapter 13. Among other arguments he uses this one: If, he says, there were two beasts, since John had described each, he would never have said in chapter 19.19, "And I saw the beast, and the beast was taken." In both places he places the article and likewise presupposes that there is only one beast, consisting of seven heads and ten horns. He adds that St John, in Apoc. xix. 20, recounting the end of the enemies of the Church, mentions only the beast and the false prophet (whom he rightly makes the same as the later, or earthly, beast). Therefore, he says, there would remain no other beast besides two, namely the former and the latter. And since the latter is not that which is said to carry the harlot, he solidly concludes that it is the former.

units.la: X. In
units.tr: X. In

units.la: X. In diversum nequicquam nituntur Viegas, Ribera, & à Lapide, qui Bestiam meretricem portantem aliam esse à Bestia priore probare satagunt, his scilicet argumentis: quod Johannes alioquin eam cum præposito articulo designasset: quòdque prior Bestia pardo similis, adeòque maculosa, hæc coccinea dicatur. Ad prius rectè respondet Alcasar, Agnum capitis xiv. & xv. evidenter unum eundemque esse, cùm tamen Johannes capite xiv. i. illi articulum non præfigat. Addere potuit, cap. xiii. ii. ubi sine articulo de Agno & Dracone prius visis ἀρνίον δεῖκων memoratur. Contra de meretrice nondum visa cap. xvii. i. cum gemino articulo ἡ πόρνης ἡ μεγάλης meminit, ut adeò crisin illam de articulo prorsus fallacem & lubricam esse constet. Tum S. Johannem cap. xiii. Bestiam utramque maris & terræ expressisse monet. Cùm autem duas descripserit, rectam Grammaticæ rationem non postulâsse, ut ad priorem designandam articulo uteretur. Ex cæteris igitur verbis dijudicandum eum reliquisse, cujusmodi Bestiam ille intellexisset. Ad posterius idem respondet, etiam pardum hominem discerpentem ejus sanguine ita respergi posse, ut qui priùs maculosus, idem postea coccineus appareat. Addo, aliam rationem esse, ob quam coccinea eadem Bestia dicitur. Etenim & varii coloris esse potuit, ob diversas religiones hominum eidem imperio innexorum: & coccinea, sive ob crudelitatem, sive ob apparentiam, ut supra diximus.
units.tr: X. In the opposite direction Viegas, Ribera and à Lapide strive in vain, who try to prove that the beast carrying the harlot is other than the former beast, namely by these arguments: that John would otherwise have designated it with the prefixed article; and that the former beast is like a leopard, and so spotted, while this one is called scarlet. To the first point Alcasar rightly replies that the Lamb in chapters 14 and 15 is clearly one and the same, although John does not prefix the article to it in chapter 14.1. He could have added chapter 13.11, where, without the article, the Lamb and the Dragon, seen earlier, are mentioned: [ἀρνίον δεῖκων]. On the other hand, of the harlot, not yet seen, he speaks in chapter 17.1 with the double article [ἡ πόρνης ἡ μεγάλης], so that the argument from the article is clearly fallacious and slippery. Then he reminds us that St John in chapter 13 described both beasts, of the sea and of the land. Since he described two, correct grammar did not require him to use the article to designate the former. So one must judge from the other words what kind of beast he meant. To the second point the same author replies that even a leopard tearing a man can be so sprinkled with his blood that what was spotted before appears afterwards scarlet. I add that there is another reason why the same beast is called scarlet: it could be of various colours because of the different religions of the men bound to its empire, and scarlet either because of its cruelty or because of its appearance, as we said above.

units.la: XI. Cùm igitur Bestia meretricem portans cum priore Bestia conveniat, dubitari nequit, quin S. Johannes utrobique ϑηρίον Bestiam dicens, loquatur stylo Danielis, qui cap. vii. 3. quatuor bestias describit, quas vidit ascendentes ex mari, cum quibus diverso licet schemate, at sensu non dispare, descriptis, exactiorem harmoniam demonstrare hujus loci non est. Saltem etiam Alcasar Bestaim stiam maritimam ex quatuor bestiis Danielis conflatam esse, nobiscum agnoscit, & comment. in Apoc. xiij. S. 3. pag. 506. crudité probat.
units.tr: XI. Since, therefore, the beast carrying the harlot agrees with the former beast, there can be no doubt that St John, calling it beast [ϑηρίον] in both cases, speaks in the style of Daniel, who in chapter 7.3 describes four beasts which he saw rising from the sea. To demonstrate a more exact harmony with these descriptions, though they differ in figure but not in sense, is not the task of this place. At least Alcasar also agrees with us that the sea beast is compounded of the four beasts of Daniel, and he proves it plainly in Comment. in Apoc. xiij. S. 3. pag. 506.

units.la: XII. Unum addo, sicut Bestia mulierem portans Bestiæ priori, seu maritimæ quadrat, ita mulierem ipsam Bestiæ posteriori, seu terrenæ, quæ etiam Pseudopropheta Apoc. xvi. 13. xix. 20. & xx. 10. vocatur, planè congruere. Id quoque nobiscum Alcasar fatetur. Et unum eundémque Antichristum per utramque bestiam diversa ratione figurari, Bellarminus, & ante ipsum etiam Rupertus statuunt. Arguit autem id harmonia Bestiæ posterioris cum muliere. Etenim mulier imponit prætextu mysterii. Bestia terrena cornuum duorum Agno similium obtentu. Mulier poculo Icortationis inebriat. Bestia terrena seducit habitantes in terra propter signa,, quæ ipsi datum erat facere coram Bestia. Mulier sævit in omnes fcortationem cum ea abnuentes. Bestia terrena omnes non adorantes imaginem Bestiæ persequitur. Mulier nundinatur animas. Bestiæ quoque terrenæ imago dat signaturam omnibus parvis & magnis, divitibus & pauperibus, liberis & fervis, in manu dextra, aut frontibus eorum, ut ne quis possit emere aut vendere signatura destitutus.
units.tr: XII. I add one thing: just as the beast carrying the woman fits the former beast, or sea beast, so the woman herself fits the later beast, or earthly one, which is also called the false prophet in Apoc. xvi. 13, xix. 20 and xx. 10. Alcasar too confesses this with us. And Bellarmine, and before him Rupert also, hold that one and the same Antichrist is figured by both beasts in different ways. The harmony of the later beast with the woman proves this. For the woman imposes under the pretext of mystery; the earthly beast, under the cover of two horns like the Lamb. The woman intoxicates with the cup of fornication; the earthly beast deceives those who dwell on the earth on account of the signs which it was given to perform before the beast. The woman rages against all who refuse fornication with her; the earthly beast persecutes all who do not adore the beast's image. The woman trades in souls. The image of the earthly beast also gives a mark to all, small and great, rich and poor, free and slaves, on the right hand or on their foreheads, so that no one without the mark can buy or sell.

units.la: XIII. Prælibatis hisce ad discutiendas ψολδευδωιας seu falsas de Bestia mulierem portantes interpretationes, accedimus. Quas in universum quatuor reperi, puta Riberæ, qui Diabolum in mundo dominantem; Alcafaris, qui Romam Ethnicam; Viterbienfis, qui Imperium Turcicum; & Grotii, qui Domitianum intelligi, pertendunt. Weigelii blasphemam interpretationem, à Ven. Crocio Antiweigel.p. 1.p. 78. memoratam attingere horreo.
units.tr: XIII. Having premised these things, we come to examine the false interpretations of the beast carrying the harlot. Of these I have found four in general, namely those of Ribera, who holds that the Devil dominating in the world is meant; Alcasar, who holds it is pagan Rome; Viterbiensis, who holds it is the Turkish Empire; and Grotius, who holds that Domitian is meant. I shudder to touch the blasphemous interpretation of Weigel, recorded by the venerable Crocius in Antiweigel p. 1, p. 78.

units.la: XIV. Primò igitur ad incundem nostram revocanda est expositio, qua Bestiam hanc Diabolum & mundum hunc, quatenus est complexio hominum mundanorum & vitiosorum, adeóque Diabolum in mundo, quasi Regno impietatis suæ dominantem esse statuit. Ita pertendunt Ribera, Blasius, Viegas, à Lapide, alii. Mundi hujus, ita Cornelius à Lapide ad Apoc. xvij. 3. scribit, sustentator, & quasi anima eum dirigens, movens & agitans est Diabolus & consequenter Antichristus Diaboli Vicarius, & princeps. Rursum mundus hic non est aliud, quàm cætus mundanorum, id est, hominum fastuosorum & vitiosorum, qui est corpus politicum Diaboli & Antichristi, sicut Respublica est corpus civile Regis & principis. Bestia ergo est mundus, sive mundi regnum, fastus & pompa, in quo inequitat Babylon, Roma Ethnica & impia, mundi impiorumque domina. Hæc enim præsidet regno Diaboli, ideoque super Diabolum, qui impiorum multitudinem sustinet, & quasi animat & vegetat, sedere dicitur, ut ab eo sustentari, regi & agitari videatur. Unde bestia hæc plena nominibus blasphemiæ, quia sua infidelitate & impietate, tam vita, quàm voce blasphemat Deum.
units.tr: XIV. First, then, the exposition by which this Beast is held to be the Devil and this world, insofar as it is a complex of worldly and vicious men, and so the Devil ruling in the world as in a kingdom of his impiety, is to be recalled to our purpose. Thus argue Ribera, Blasius, Viegas, à Lapide and others. Of this world, thus Cornelius à Lapide on Apoc. xvii. 3. writes: the sustainer, and as it were the soul directing, moving and driving it, is the Devil, and consequently Antichrist, the Devil's vicar and prince. Again, this world is nothing other than the assembly of worldly men, that is, of haughty and vicious men, which is the political body of the Devil and Antichrist, just as a commonwealth is the civil body of a king or prince. The beast, therefore, is the world, or the kingdom of the world, of pride and pomp, on which Babylon rides, pagan and impious Rome, the mistress of the world and of the impious. For she presides over the kingdom of the Devil, and therefore is said to sit upon the Devil, who sustains the multitude of the impious and as it were animates and enlivens them, so that she seems to be sustained, ruled and driven by him. Hence this beast, full of names of blasphemy, blasphemes God by its unbelief and impiety, both in life and in voice.

units.la: XV. Addunt illi, Coccineam dici Bestiam, quia mun- dus regio splendore & fastu triumphet.
units.tr: XV. They add that the Beast is called scarlet, because the world triumphs in royal splendour and pomp.

units.la: Coccum enim & purpuram vestem esse Regum & Principum. Fuisse & non esse, & ascensuram esse de Abysso, & in interitum ire bestiam dicunt, quia ante Christum fuit, & in mundo dominatur impietas & Diabolus; Christo autem veniente non est, quia princeps mundi foras eam ejecit Joh. xiii. 31. & sub finem mundi rursus ex abysso ascendet, Romam ad idololatriam seductura, similis hactenus Draconi vel Ceto, qui nunc e mari caput & dorsum attollit, nunc rursum in illud se totum demergit, tertiò iterum emergit & ascendit. Septem capita ajunt esse primò septem montes, quibus Roma inædificata est: secundò septem Reges, sive collectionem tyrannorum, qui septem ætatibus, sive seculis in mundo, regno impietatis & Diaboli regnárunt, fideles-que
units.tr: For scarlet and purple are the clothing of kings and princes. They say the beast was, and is not, and is about to ascend out of the abyss, and goes to destruction, because it existed before Christ, and impiety and the Devil rule in the world; but when Christ came it no longer existed, because "the prince of this world has been cast out" (John 12.31; the text is cited as John 13.31). At the end of the world it will rise again from the abyss to seduce Rome into idolatry. Until then it is like the dragon or whale, which now lifts its head and back from the sea, now plunges wholly back into it, and a third time emerges and rises. They say the seven heads are, first, the seven hills on which Rome was built; second, seven kings, or a collection of tyrants, who reigned in the world through seven ages, or centuries, under the rule of impiety and the Devil, and persecuted the faithful.

units.la: Diabolus in mundo dominans, verbis à Lapide exponitur. que persecuti sunt. Quales fuerint Cain, Nimrod, Reges Sedomæ ac Ægypti, impii Reges Israëlis & Judæ, Reges Chaldæorum, Assiræ & Syriæ; Imperatores Ethnici Romani & Saraceni, denique Antichristus. Decem cornua, seu decem Reges fore illos, qui sub finem mundi, Antichristo veniente, Romæ, & Romano Imperio subjecti erunt, aut certè ex eo prodibunt, & invidentes Romæ tantas opes & gloriam ejus jugum excutient, eámque invadent, vastabunt, conterentque, ariolantur.
units.tr: The Devil ruling in the world is explained in the words of Cornelius a Lapide. Such were Cain, Nimrod, the kings of Sodom and of Egypt, the impious kings of Israel and Judah, the kings of the Chaldeans, Assyria and Syria, the heathen Roman emperors, the Saracens, and finally Antichrist. They conjecture that the ten horns, or ten kings, will be those who, near the end of the world, when Antichrist comes, will be subject to Rome and the Roman Empire, or will at least arise out of it; envying Rome such great wealth and glory, they will cast off her yoke, and will attack, lay waste, and crush her.

units.la: XVI. Non satisfacit isthæc interpretatio Pontificiis aliis, Alcasari cumprimis, qui passim eam rejicit & refutat, hoc inprimis fretus principio, quòd eadem sit Bestia capitis xiii. & xvii. Atqui Bestia capitis xiii. à Dracone Diabolo, diserté distinguitur. Etenim cap. xii. narratur pugna Draconis, qui v. 9. vocatur ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος, ὁ καλούμενος Διάβολος & Σατανᾶς, ὁ πλανῶν τὴν οἰκουμένην, serpens antiquus, nuncupatus Diabolus & Sathanas ille, seducens orbem habitabilem, qui è cœlo in terram dejectus mulierem, quæ masculum peperit, persecutus est, & cum reliquis seminis ejus bellum gessit. Tum demum cap. xiii. 1. 2. vidit S. Johannes Bestiam ascendentem ex mari, cui Draco dedit potentiam & thronum suum, & potestatem magnam, illam ipsam videlicet, quæ cap. xvii. mulierem portare dicitur. Cùm igitur Draco sit Diabolus & Draconi Bestia successerit, ab eodem thronum & potestatem nacta, Bestia utique à Diabolo licet inspirata, mota & agitata, ipse tamen Diabolus non est. Neque potest simul esse Diabolus, simul multitudo hominum malorum eadem Bestia, quæ à Dracone manifestè adeò distinguitur.
units.tr: XVI. This interpretation does not satisfy other Papists, Alcasar above all, who rejects and refutes it everywhere, relying chiefly on the principle that the beast of chapter 13 and that of chapter 17 are the same. Yet the beast of chapter 13 is expressly distinguished from the dragon, the Devil. For in chapter 12 is narrated the battle of the dragon, who in verse 9 is called the ancient serpent, called the Devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world [ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος, ὁ καλούμενος Διάβολος καὶ Σατανᾶς, ὁ πλανῶν τὴν οἰκουμένην], who, cast down from heaven to earth, pursued the woman who bore a male child, and waged war with the rest of her seed. Then at last, in chapter 13 verses 1 and 2, St John saw the beast rising out of the sea, to which the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority, namely that same beast which in chapter 17 is said to carry the woman. Since therefore the dragon is the Devil, and the beast succeeded the dragon, having received throne and power from him, the beast, though inspired, moved and driven by the Devil, is certainly not the Devil himself. Nor can the Devil be at once the Devil and the same beast, which is clearly distinguished from the dragon.

units.la: XVII. Accedunt alia non minùs prægnantia. Enimverò quid absonum magis putabimus, quàm meretricem, hoc est, ut iidem Interpretes explicant, Romam Antichristiano-Ethnicam fingere Diabolo in mundo quasi Regno impietatis suæ dominanti, uti à Lapide loquitur, inequitantem? Scilicet meretrix & Diaboli sibi dominantis exsors erit, & regno impietatis Diaboli ipsa non etiam accensebitur, & de mundo impiorum non erit. Nam meretrix quidem à Bestia manifeste distinguitur: illa insidere, hæc insideПocлe deri: illa portari, hæc portare dicitur. Tum quid attinebat Sathanam, de cujus perpetua & indefessa grassatione in mundo toties Spiritus S. absque figuris, clara & simplici dictione præmonuit, nunc S. Johanni sub obscuro ejusmodi ænigmate, ceu mysterium quoddam repræsentari? Nimis dilutus est hic color veritati obductus.
units.tr: XVII. Other points, no less telling, follow. Indeed, what could we think more absurd than that the harlot, that is, as the same interpreters explain, Antichristian-heathen Rome, should be imagined as riding upon the Devil, who rules in the world as a kingdom of his own impiety, as a Lapide puts it? Evidently the harlot would then be exempt from the Devil's dominion, would not be counted in the kingdom of the Devil's impiety, and would not be of the world of the wicked. For the harlot is plainly distinguished from the beast: the one is said to sit upon it, the beast to bear her; the one is carried, the other carries. Further, why would the Holy Spirit, who so often warned us plainly and simply, without figures, of Satan's constant and tireless ravaging in the world, now have that thing presented to St John under such an obscure enigma, as some mystery? This colour is far too thin to cover the truth.

units.la: XVIII. Præterea Diabolo in mundo quasi Regno impietatis suæ dominanti neutiquam convenit, quod de Bestia dicitur, illam fuisse & non esse, & de abysso ascendere, & in interitum vadere. Quomodo enim de Diabolo dicendi poterit non est cum perpetuò circumeat is, leonis rugientis instar, quærens quem devoret. 1. Pet. v. 8?
units.tr: XVIII. Moreover, what is said of the beast, that it was and is not, and that it ascends out of the abyss and goes to destruction, by no means fits the Devil as ruling in the world as a kingdom of his impiety. For how could is not be said of the Devil, when he goes about constantly, like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour? (1 Pet. 5.8.)

units.la: Neque obstat, quòd devicto à Christo Diabolo, & principe mundi foras ejecto, à Lapide & Ribera excipiunt. Ita enim victus & foras ejectus à Christo est Diabolus, ut adversus fideles, qui per fidem Christo innexi sunt, quoad potentiam spiritualem nihil virium amplius habeat, neque habuerit unquam. At de cætero regnum & dominium ejus, quod in mundum infidelium obtinet, morte Christi abolitum non est. Imò quoad externam & civilem etiam violentiam adversus electos morte Christi non ita perdomitus est, quin S. Johannis etiam & succedentibus temporibus per tyrannos Ecclesiam gravissimè infestaret. Quid enim aliud fi-bi vult Regnum Draconis, & ab eodem thronus ac potentia omnis in Bestiam transfusa? Quid solutio Sathanæ post exactos mille annos? Qui igitur dicere sustincat, Diabolum inde à morte Christi usque ad novissima Antichristi fiatrii tempora non esse, non sævire, non regnare in mundo.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that Lapide and Ribera except the point that the Devil was conquered by Christ and cast out as prince of this world. For the Devil has been so conquered and cast out by Christ that against the faithful, who are joined to Christ by faith, he has no more spiritual power, and never had any. But his kingdom and dominion over the world of unbelievers has not been abolished by the death of Christ. Indeed, even in his external and civil violence against the elect, he was not so subdued by Christ's death that he did not sorely harass the Church through tyrants, both in St John's time and in the times that followed. For what else does the kingdom of the dragon mean, and the throne and all power transferred from him to the beast? What of Satan's release after the thousand years were completed? Who, then, would dare to say that the Devil is not from the death of Christ until the last days of Antichrist's reign, that he does not rage, does not rule in the world,

units.la: 1. Pet. v. 8 do, & electis etiam palam non insidiari, aperta etiam vi cosdem non oppugnare, næ is pudorem omnem decoxisse merito censebitur.
units.tr: (1 Pet. 5.8) and does not openly lay snares even for the elect, nor assail them by open force? Such a person would rightly be judged to have cast off all shame.

units.la: XIX. Quo etiam sensu septem capita seu totidem Reges habuerit Bestia, hoc est Diabolus, certa ratione assertores sententiæ hujus explicare nequeunt. Frivolum enim & ineptum plane est, quòd collectionem tyrannorum, qui septem mundi ætatibus in mundo, Diaboli Regno regnârunt, fidelésque oppugnârunt, adeóque septem quasi Dynastias & principatus mundi intelligi pertendunt. Scilicet ad hos nos remittunt, ut à nido suo nos avocent. Quin potius Reges hosce septem in montibus seu collibus Romæ, qui illorum typus & monimentum constituuntur, adeóque in Romani imperii ditione, in qua iidem authores supra etiam meretricem à Bestia utique ἀχώεισαν collocarunt, ostendere par erat. In his enim sederunt, regnârunt, & meretricem portârunt. Tum utique capita septem, Reges septem Bestia habuit, cùm meretricem portavit. At pleraque illa capita, Reges plerosque, quos authores illi subtiliter numerant, Bestia, quando meretricem portavit, non habuit. Tacco, quòd ætatis septimæ Rex suppositititius est, & ad sex etiam priores proportionem nullam habet. Quem enim tres anni cum dimidio, quos Antichristo tribuunt, cum ætatibus sex superioribus, quarum singulæ secula integra sibi vendicant, commensum habent?
units.tr: XIX. Nor can the advocates of this opinion explain, on any sound principle, in what sense the beast, that is the Devil, has seven heads or as many kings. For it is quite trivial and absurd to contend that by these seven are meant a collection of tyrants who reigned in the world through the seven ages of the world under the kingdom of the Devil, and who persecuted the faithful, and so seven dynasties or principalities of the world. Clearly they are sending us back to these, to call us away from their own nest. Rather, it was necessary to show that these seven kings are represented by the seven hills or mounds of Rome, which are their type and memorial, and so lie within the domain of the Roman Empire, where these same authors, above, placed the harlot carried by the beast. For on these hills the kings sat, reigned, and carried the harlot. Then, surely, the beast had seven heads, seven kings, when it carried the harlot. But that beast did not have most of those heads, most of those kings, which the authors subtly count, when it carried the harlot. I pass over the fact that the king of the seventh age is a substitute, and bears no proportion even to the six before him. For how can the three and a half years they assign to Antichrist be measured against the six earlier ages, each of which claims whole centuries for itself?

units.la: XX. Ejusdem fere commatis est eorundem Authorum commentum de decem cornibus, seu totidem Regibus, quos sub finem mundi Antichristo caput ex inferis prolaturo Romæ, meretrici scilicet parituros, & ejusdem denique jugum excussuros fingunt. Nititur enim fabula ingeniosè composita de Roma Antichristiano-Ethnica novissima, quam supra & argumentis & consensu Doctorum Pontificiorum communi abundè confutavimus. Brevi adeò tempore decem Reges Romæ subjectum iri, & frenum mox admorsuros, Romámque internecino & exitiali odio appetituros esse, eccui mirum non videbitur? Si tamen tale quid continget (uti etiam contigit, ut intra Cælum, terra, & omnes exercitus crearentur) at certò foreut contingat, liquere pernego. Neque enim prophetia obscura, & ænigma intricatum, quod quò volueris cunque non minùs appositè trahi potest, & impletum ante ejusmodi Romæ statum si non certiùs, at probabilius longè asseri potest, rei adeo mirificæ & incredibilis argumentum censeri potest.
units.tr: XX. Almost of the same kind is the invention of the same authors about the ten horns, or as many kings, whom they imagine will arise near the end of the world, when Antichrist is about to bring up his head from hell, and who will be born at Rome, to the harlot, and will finally cast off her yoke. For the tale is ingeniously composed about the last Antichristian-heathen Rome, which above we have amply refuted both by arguments and by the common agreement of the Papist doctors. That ten kings should be subject to Rome in so short a time, and should soon champ the bit and seek Rome with deadly and destructive hatred, who will not find this surprising? If, however, something of this kind should happen (as it indeed happened that the heavens, the earth and all the armies were created), yet that it will certainly come to pass, I flatly deny that it is clear. For an obscure prophecy and an intricate enigma, which can be drawn to whatever meaning one wishes with equal aptness, and which may be asserted, if not more certainly, at least far more plausibly, to have been fulfilled in such a Rome as already existed, cannot be taken as proof of so marvellous and incredible a thing.

units.la: XXI. Non igitur Diaboli & mundi Regnum catholicum, sed Imperium & Regnum aliquod maximum intelligi, reliqui Doctores Pontificii, magno consensu nobiscum pertendunt. Idque etiam argumentis non contemnendis probant, qualia sunt, quòd apud Danielem similibus Bestiarum ænigmatis certæ Monarchiæ repræsententur: quòd Bestia hæc omnibus populis dicatur imperatura, qua ratione certam universalem Monarchiam indigitari observant: quòd denique id ipsum capitum & cornuum distinctio manifestè arguat. XXII. Romanum hoc esse Imperium, Monarchiam Romanam, iidem Doctores nulli omnino dubitant. Cùm verò mctetricem fecerint Romam Ethnicam veterem, abs seimpetrare non potuerunt, quin Bestiam eam portantem etiam in Roma Ethnica veteri & idololatrica nobis ostendent. Significatur Imperium Romanum idololatriæ deditum, sive Romanus Orbis idololatra, quem Roma Ethnica lege & imperio admiuistrabat, inquit Alcasar Comment. in Apoc. xvij. 3. Alibi in Apoc. xiij. rectè probavit idem, Bestiam mulierem portantem eandem esse cum Bestia maris, quæ Apoc. xiii. describitur. Utramque esse Romanum Imperium idololatriæ deditum, quod olim Ecclesiam Christianam insectabatur, ibidem probare satagit. Vbi semel, inquit, statuamus, in meretrice Romana Ethnicam figurari, ilico compertum fit, eam Bestiam esse Romanum Imperium, Diis commentitiis obsequens, quod à Roma Ethnica administrabatur. Sapienter equidem ita judicavit, cùm dorsum portantis bestiæ ab insidentis meretricis corpore ἀδιάκριτον & indivulsum esse, ratio & communis sensus dubitare non patiantur. Quis enim sanus equum ab equite ei insidente separatum dixerit?
units.tr: XXI. Therefore the other Papist doctors, with great agreement, maintain along with us that what is meant is not the Catholic kingdom of the Devil and the world, but some great empire and kingdom. They also prove this by arguments not to be despised. For example, in Daniel, certain monarchies are represented by similar enigmatic beasts. This beast is said to be about to rule over all peoples, and from this they observe that a certain universal monarchy is indicated. Finally, the distinction of heads and horns plainly argues the same. XXII. These doctors have no doubt at all that this is the Roman Empire, the Roman monarchy. But since they have made the harlot ancient pagan Rome, they have not been able to avoid showing us the beast that carries her as also in ancient pagan and idolatrous Rome. "The Roman Empire given over to idolatry is signified, or the Roman world idolatrous, which pagan Rome governed by law and empire," says Alcasar, Comment. in Apoc. xvij. 3. Elsewhere, on Apoc. xiii., the same writer rightly proved that the beast carrying the woman is the same as the beast of the sea described in Apoc. xiii. There he labours to prove that both are the Roman Empire, given over to idolatry, which formerly persecuted the Christian Church. "Once we establish," he says, "that the harlot figures pagan Rome, it immediately becomes clear that the beast is the Roman Empire, obedient to fictitious gods, which was governed by pagan Rome." He judged this wisely indeed, since reason and common sense do not allow us to doubt that the back of the carried beast is inseparable [ἀδιάκριτον] and not torn from the body of the harlot sitting on it. For who of sound mind would say that a horse is separated from the rider sitting upon it?

units.la: XXIII. Eodem igitur freti principio, argumentum invertimus. Babylon magna, seu meretrix Bestiæ insidens non est Roma vetus Ethnica, uti superiori diatriba clarissimè demonstravimus. Ergo bestia meretricem portans non est Romanum Imperium Ethnicum vetus. Quæ sola demonstratio sufficere elidendo errori poterat. Sed in promptu alia etiam argumenta sunt, quibus simul opinionem illam minuamus, simul figmento illi, quòd Roma vetus Ethnica sit meretrix, fidem amplius etiam detrahamus. Si enim Bestia non est Imperium Romanum Ethnicum, meretricem quoque Romam Ethnicam non esse, Alcasar ipse, & qui eum assectantur, confiteri nobiscum, nisi semel recte placitam hypothesin damnare & refigere constituerint, necessum plane habebunt.
units.tr: XXIII. Relying therefore on the same principle, we turn the argument around. Great Babylon, or the harlot sitting on the beast, is not ancient pagan Rome, as we have most clearly shown in the preceding discourse. Therefore the beast carrying the harlot is not the ancient pagan Roman Empire. This demonstration alone could be enough to refute the error. But other arguments are also at hand, by which we may at once diminish that opinion and at the same time further detract credit from that fiction, that ancient pagan Rome is the harlot. For if the beast is not the pagan Roman Empire, then the harlot is not pagan Rome either. Alcasar himself and those who follow him will necessarily have to concede this with us, unless they resolve to condemn and retract the hypothesis they once rightly adopted.

units.la: XXIV. Atqui Romam veterem Ethnicam non esse Bestiam, primò inde liquet, quia Bestia meretricem portans succeßit Draconi. Clarè id testatur S. Johannes Apoc. XIII. 2. Bestiæ dedit Draco suam potentiam, & thronum suum, & potestatem magnam. Manifestum igitur est, priùs regnasse Draconem, ut Draconem; deinde regnásse Diabolum. Quis verò Draco sit, qui Apoc. XII. 4. 5. &c. stetit coram muliere parturiente, paratus absorbere filium ejus, raptum tamen ad Deum & thronum ejus, dubitari vix potest. Quis enim neget, prolem masculam, quam mulier parturiens enixa est, hoc est, quem Ecclesiam post longam expectationem vidit sceptro ferreo recturum gentes, esse Christum; & notari in Apocalypsi primas insidias, quas Christo tetendit & votum interficiendi Christum cum in morte retinendi, atque una cum Diabolo instrumentum violentiæ illius, Imperium Romanum Ethnicum, per Draconem intelligi? Unde consequitur, Regno Bestiæ, quod Draconi succeßit, Imperium Romanum Ethnicum neutiquam figurari.
units.tr: XXIV. But that ancient pagan Rome is not the beast is clear, first, from this: the beast carrying the harlot succeeded the Dragon. St John clearly testifies to this in Apoc. XIII. 2: "The Dragon gave to the beast his power, and his throne, and great authority." It is therefore manifest that the Dragon reigned first, as Dragon, and afterwards the Devil reigned. Who the Dragon is, who (Apoc. XII. 4, 5, etc.) stood before the woman in labour, ready to devour her child, yet was caught up to God and to his throne, can hardly be doubted. For who would deny that the male offspring which the woman in labour brought forth, that is, the one whom the Church, after long expectation, saw about to rule the nations with an iron sceptre, is Christ? And is it not noted in the Apocalypse that the first snares laid for Christ, and the design of killing him or holding him in death, and, together with the Devil, the instrument of that violence, the pagan Roman Empire, are understood through the Dragon? From this it follows that the pagan Roman Empire is by no means figured by the kingdom of the beast which succeeded the Dragon.

units.la: XXV. Nam quòd Alcasar Comment. in Apoc. xij. 3. 4. contendit, Symbolo Draconis Diabolorum Rempublicam universam denotari, si ita intelligatur, ut infausta Respublica illa ab instrumentis ejus, Romano cum primis Imperio gentili, separetur, recipi non potest. Neque enim Diabolus mulierem & filium ejus ἀμέσως immediatè, & sine instrumentis persecutus est. Instrumenta verò, per quæ dira molimina sua exercuit, Romani Ethnici tum fuerunt, quos penes summa rerum, adeòque etiam nocendi lædendique potestas in orbe potissimùm fuit. Vocatur enim Diabolus Draco, non utique à larva aliqua, qualem in Paradiso assumsit, sed quia magnum corpus habuit in mundo, quod regebat, & per quod nocebat hominibus. Solentque magna Imperia Draconum etiam emblemate in scriptura figurari, uti ex Esaj. xxvii. 1. & Ezech. xxix. 3. ubi Rex Ægypti cum התנים הנהר Dracone magno, cubante in medio fluminum, comparatur, colligi potest.
units.tr: XXV. For what Alcasar contends in his Comment. in Apoc. xij. 3, 4, that by the symbol of the Dragon the whole commonwealth of the Devils is denoted, cannot be accepted if it is understood in such a way that that baneful commonwealth is separated from its instruments, above all the pagan Roman Empire. For the Devil did not pursue the woman and her son immediately, without instruments. The instruments through which he carried out his dire schemes were then the pagan Romans, in whose hands lay the supreme power of affairs, and therefore especially in the world the power of harming and injuring. For the Devil is called Dragon not from some mask which he assumed in Paradise, but because he had a great body in the world, which he ruled, and through which he harmed men. And that great empires are commonly figured in Scripture by dragons as an emblem can be gathered from Isa. xxvii. 1 and Ezek. xxix. 3, where the King of Egypt is compared with the great dragon [הַתַּנִּים הַגָּדוֹל] lying in the midst of the rivers.

units.la: XXVI. Secundò character ille Bestiæ, quod fuerit, & non sit, & ascensura sit ex abyßo, & in exitium abitura sit, Romano Imperio Ethnico concinnè aptari non potest. Nam quòd Alcasar eum verbis illis sensum inducere conatur, ut Bestiam seu Romam Ethnicam fuisse, hoc est, fideles persecutam esse, non esse, in præsentiarum non persequi, ex abyßo ascensuram, hoc est, denuo ad persequendum caput suum ex orco prolaturam esse, & in exitium abituram, seu persecutionem illam cessaturam quandoque esse, intelligatur, parum certè coloris interpretatio habet. Persecuta enim ante B. Johannem Roma Ethnica Ecclesiam est: sed tempore Johannis, quo Domitianus rerum potitus est, persequi non desiit; quod vel S. Johannis exemplum commonstrat. An enim fidem ille in Patmo scilicet suo haerens, in quo propter sermonem Dei, & testimonium Jesu Christi exul visiones divinas excepit, habere potuisset Angelo asseveranti, Bestiam, seu Romam Ethnicam non esse, hoc est, Ecclesiam non persequi, tum scilicet, cùm ipsemet persecutione dirissima superata, novam sustinuit? Deinde Bestia illa ascendisse dicitur ex abysso, quò vero nisi in terram? Cum igitur stylo prophetico abyssus seu mare gentes infideles, terra verò Ecclesiam repraesentet, manifestum est, Bestiae illius originem quidem ad infidelem gentem, qualis Roma Ethnica fuit, referri; at de caetero non ita infidelem ipsam indigitari, quin cum vera Ecclesia commixta, & ejusdem externa in nonnullis saltem professione Deo mentita, ipsa quoque in communione externae Ecclesiae censeretur. Quo sensu etiam Antichristus in domo Dei sedens introducitur. Denique Romam Ethnicam dicere eis ἀπώλειαν ὑπάγειν in exitium abire tum, cùm à persecutione cessans ad Christum conversa est, nimis illud certè ἀλήθη est. Perinde ac si eis ἀπώλειαν in exitium vaderet is, qui ab exitio liberatur, vel ad mortem concederet is, qui vitae restituitur. Talibus φλυαρίαις delectari necessum est illos, qui, quò se vertant, nesciunt.
units.tr: XXVI. Secondly, that character of the beast, that it was, and is not, and is about to ascend out of the abyss, and is going into destruction, cannot be aptly fitted to the pagan Roman Empire. For Alcasar's attempt to draw this sense from those words, so that "was" means that the beast, or pagan Rome, persecuted the faithful, "is not" means that it is not persecuting at present, "will ascend out of the abyss" means that it will bring its head again from the pit to persecute, and "is going into destruction" means that this persecution will at some point cease, has very little plausibility. For pagan Rome had persecuted the Church before St John; but in John's time, when Domitian had taken power, it did not cease to persecute, as the example of St John himself shows. For could he, remaining steadfast in his faith on Patmos, where as an exile "for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ" he received divine visions, have believed the angel who asserted that the beast, or pagan Rome, is not, that is, does not persecute the Church, at the very time when he himself, having survived the most dreadful persecution, endured a new one? Next, that beast is said to have ascended out of the abyss; but to where, unless to the earth? Since in prophetic style the abyss or sea represents unbelieving nations, and the earth represents the Church, it is manifest that the origin of that beast is indeed to be traced to an unbelieving nation, such as pagan Rome was. But for the rest, it is not indicated as so unbelieving that it was not mixed with the true Church, and, professing outwardly at least in some respects while lying to God, it too would be counted in communion with the outward Church. In this sense also the Antichrist is introduced sitting in the house of God. Finally, to say that pagan Rome "is going into destruction" [εἰς ἀπώλειαν ὑπάγειν] at the time when, ceasing from persecution, it was converted to Christ, is certainly a most untrue statement. It is just as if one who is freed from destruction were going into destruction, or one who is restored to life were going to death. Only those who do not know where to turn must delight in such trifles [φλυαρίαις].

units.la: XXVII. Tertiò Romae illius Ethnicae septem capita non satis concinnè Alcasar demonstrat. Intelligit nempe Romae Ethnicae persecutores inter Neronem primum & Julianum ultimum interjectos, puta Domitianum, Trajanum , Antoninum, Severum, Decium , Valerianum & Diocletianum , quorum septem persecutorum Ecclesiæ persecutiones totidem atrocissimæ fuerint. Cæterum primò δωρεὰ hic Alcafar loquitur. Sienim Bestiæ hujus Regem principem constituit Domitianus, S. Johannis persecutor, quomodo S. Johannis tempore non extitit Bestia (uti suprà asseruit) cujus tamen caput princeps extitit? Secundò omittit persecutores Maximinum & Aurelianum, quorum famosissimas persecutiones historiæ pœne omnes computant. Neque obstat, quòd persecutiones illorum inter decantatas decem Sulpitius Severus numerat. Nam & Maximinum idem libr. II. 32. nihilominus inter persecutores, utpote qui nonnullarum Ecclesiarum clericos vexaverit, numerat: & duas alias, nimirum Adriani & Aurelii, Antonini filii, substituit. Et de eo quicquid sit, plures certè quam septem persecutores Neronem exceperunt. Tertiò paradoxum eruditis futurum, non immeritò Alcafar suspicatus est, quòd capitum Bestiæ, quæ Romæ Ethnicæ persecutores esse statuit, numero censùque Neronem, furibundum leonem illum, exclusit. Rationem ille quidem hanc in cap. xiij. 1.pag. 503. reddit, quod Neronis mentio facta, sigillatim jam præcesserit cap. xiij. ubi persecutio à Dracone excitata, per Neronem effectui data fit. Quasi verò persecutio vel filii mulieris nati & ad Deum ac throand ejus evecti, quem Draco absorbere parabat, Neroni, & non Tiberio potiùs adscribi mereatur; vel mulieris etiam marem parientis antequam in desertum illa avolaret, foli Neroni accepta referri debeat. Atqui duravit persecutio illa mulieris, donec alis acceptis in desertum aufugit, ibidemque locum à Deo præparatum, in quo nutriretur, reperit, Apoc. xii. 6. 13. 14. quod factum haud dubiè eo tempore est, quo pacem nacti Christiani Reges Christianos nutritios habuerunt. An verò ad pacem usque Christianis ĭ stianis reddidam solus Nero Ecclesiam persecutus est? Quarto explicare nobis Alcasar non potuit, quid posita hac de septem persecutoribus interpretatione sibi velint verba Apoc. xvii. 10. 11. Quinque ceciderunt; unus est, & alius nondum venit, & cùm venerit, oportet ipsum breve tempus manere, & Bestia quæ erat, & non est, & ipse octavus est, & de septem est, & in interitum vadit. Si quinque illi collapsi ex numero septem illorum Regum sunt, recitet ille nobis quinque principes Romanos persecutores, ex eorum, quos designavit, numero, qui tempore S. Johannis ceciderint.
units.tr: XXVII. Thirdly, Alcasar does not demonstrate the seven heads of that pagan Rome very neatly. He understands the persecutors of pagan Rome to be those placed between Nero, the first, and Julian, the last, namely Domitian, Trajan, Antoninus, Severus, Decius, Valerian and Diocletian, whose seven persecutions of the Church were seven most atrocious ones. But first, Alcasar speaks here without warrant [δωρεὰν]. For if Domitian, the persecutor of St John, is established as the prince and king of this beast, how is it that at the time of St John the beast did not exist (as he asserted above), when its head nevertheless existed as prince? Secondly, he omits the persecutors Maximinus and Aurelian, whose very famous persecutions nearly all histories reckon. Nor does it stand in the way that Sulpicius Severus counts their persecutions among the celebrated ten. For the same writer, in Book II, 32, nevertheless counts Maximinus among the persecutors, inasmuch as he harassed the clergy of some churches, and he substitutes two others, namely Hadrian and Aurelius, son of Antoninus. And whatever the case with that, certainly more than seven persecutors followed Nero. Thirdly, Alcasar rightly suspected, as a paradox that will not be unwelcome to the learned, that among the heads of the beast, which he holds to be the persecutors of pagan Rome, he has left out Nero, that raging lion, in both number and reckoning. He gives this reason, at Apoc. xiii. 1, p. 503: "because mention of Nero has already been made separately in chap. xiii., where the persecution stirred up by the Dragon is carried into effect through Nero." As if indeed the persecution of the woman's son, who was born and caught up to God and his throne, whom the Dragon was preparing to devour, deserved to be ascribed to Nero rather than to Tiberius; or as if the persecution of the woman bearing a male child, before she flew away into the wilderness, should be credited to Nero alone. But that persecution of the woman lasted until, with the two wings of an eagle received, she fled into the wilderness and there found a place prepared by God where she might be nourished (Apoc. xii. 6, 13, 14). This certainly happened at the time when Christian kings, having obtained peace, had Christians as their nurslings. But was the Church persecuted by Nero alone until peace was given to Christians? Fourthly, Alcasar could not explain to us what the words of Apoc. xvii. 10, 11 mean for his interpretation of the seven persecutors: "Five have fallen; one is, and the other has not yet come; and when he has come, he must remain a short time; and the beast which was and is not, he also is the eighth, and is of the seven, and goes into perdition." If those five who have fallen are among the number of those seven kings, let him recite for us five Roman princes who were persecutors, from the number he has designated, and who fell at the time of St John.

units.la: XXVIII. Has similêsque difficultates subodoratus Alcasar videtur, cùm statim ad aliam expositionem delapsus in cap. xiv. 18. monet, septem capitum significationem non opus esse ad septenarium persecutionum numerum posse reduci, sed solùm ad multitudinem Imperatorum Ethnicorum, qui Christianam Ecclesiam vexarunt. Etenim, inquit, receptissima in sacris literis phrasis est, certum numerum pro incerto poni, id quod præcipuè in quibusdam numeris locum habet, qui completi appellantur: cujusmodi sunt septenarius, denarius & millenarius. Subjicit, in septem capitum numero, si certus pro incerto sumatur, significari potest, quamvis voluerit Deus persecutorum numerum Ecclesiæ ignotum esse, non tamen temerè & casu id eventuram, sed in numero certo atque persecto, id est, per summam Dei sapientiam ac dispositionem ordinato ad ipsius Ecclesiæ emolumentum.
units.tr: XXVIII. Alcasar seems to have sensed these and similar difficulties, since he quickly turns to another explanation on chap. xiv. 18 and warns that the significance of the seven heads need not be reduced to a set number of persecutions, but refers only to the multitude of heathen emperors who harassed the Christian Church. For, he says, it is a most common expression in the sacred letters to put a fixed number for an indefinite one, which holds especially for certain numbers called complete, such as seven, ten and a thousand. He adds that in the number of the seven heads, if a definite number is taken for an indefinite one, it can be meant that, although God wished the number of persecutors to be unknown to the Church, it did not happen rashly or by chance, but in a fixed and perfect number, that is, ordered by the supreme wisdom and disposition of God for the advantage of the Church itself.

units.la: XXIX. Scilicet ἀρησάυ ejusmodi opus habuit ille, ut se extricaret iis rationum nodis, quos adversus insulsam expositionem suam nečti posse, tam hebes non fuit, quin animadverteret. Si idonea est hæc explicandi ratio, magno labore & se & alios in explicanda Apocalypsi liberaverit ille. Neque inquirendum ampliùs studiose fuerit in numeros reliquos Apocalypticos, puta, septem Candelabra, Sigilla, Tubas, Capita, Montes, aliáque similia. Adeóque nihil inde aliud quàm mysteriorum quædam confusio suborietur. Quod si alibi definiti numeri pro indefinitis ponuntur, at hic poni non potuerunt. Septem enim illi Reges ita distribuuntur, ut ex iis quinque cecidisse, unus esse, & alius nondum venijse dicatur. Neque obstat, quod v. 11. dicitur Bestia, quæ erat, non esse; & ipse octavus esse, & de septem esse. Qua ratione patescere ait Alcasar, septenarium illum numerum indefinitè pro incerto accipiendum esse. Neque enim hoc consequitur, cùm nihil vetet octo, vel ex numero septem esse, non quia unus ex septem sit, sed quia ratione quadam cum septem illis conveniat.
units.tr: XXIX. Evidently he needed such a device to extricate himself from the knots of argument which he could not tie against his own foolish exposition, and he was not so dull as not to notice them. If this method of explanation is sound, he will have freed both himself and others from great labour in explaining the Apocalypse. Nor would it be necessary to inquire carefully into the other numbers of the Apocalypse, such as the seven candlesticks, seals, trumpets, heads, mountains and the like. Nothing would then arise from this but a certain confusion of mysteries. And if in other places definite numbers are put for indefinite ones, yet here they cannot be. For those seven kings are so distributed that of them five are said to have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come. Nor does it stand in the way that at verse 11 it is said: The beast that was, is not, and he is the eighth, and is of the seven. By this reasoning, Alcasar says, it is evident that the number seven must be taken indefinitely for an unknown number. But this does not follow, since nothing prevents the eighth from being of the seven, not because it is one of the seven, but because in some respect it agrees with those seven.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Quartò denique nec decem cornuum seu decem Regum numerus Romæ Ethnicæ congruere ullo modo potest. Alcasar quidem in cap. xiij. 1. ff. 3. p. 507. ad Senatores Romanos detorquere conatur. Illud mihi certum est, inquit ille, decem isthæc cornua esse symbolum multitudinis Senatorum Romanorum. Sicut enim unum cornu in Scriptura designat principem unum, ita cornua plurima polyarchiam innuunt, seu plurimorum principum gubernationem. Ut autem hoc significaretur, aptissimum fuit decem cornuum symbolum; quippe denarius est multiplicationis numerus, & eam ob rem majores omnes numeri in denario tandem claudūtur. Nam ubi ad denarium pervenitur, protinus ad numerorum initium, sive unitatis regressio fit. Cùm autem senatorum numerus certus ac præfinitus non esset, & exprimendus foret numerus aliquis, qui multitudinis esset symbolum, nullus potuit congruentius assumi, quàm denarius. Ita Zachar. viij. 13. decem homines notant plurimos. Præterea ipse Apocalypseos contextus Cap. 17. 12. explicat, per decem capita figurari Polyarchiam, quæ est multitudo principum eodem tempore vigentium. Atqui ejusmodi erant Romani Senatores. Etenim licet non proprie fuerint Reges, eorum tamen potentia & amplitudo Regum instar erat. Quare Cyneas dixit, Romanum Senatum sibi visum fuisse confessum Regum, uti narrant Plutarchus in Pyrrho, Florus lib. 1. Livius lib. 11. Cohærent cum hoc ipsius textus verba. Decem cornua, decem Reges sunt, qui potestatem tanquam Reges una hora accipiunt. Quid enim obsecro est, una hora, nisi uno eodemque tempore principatum tenere? Quòd autem Reges appellentur, & declaretur pariter, non proprie Reges esse, sed Regum habere potestatem & amplitudinem, quis non in hoc Senatorum Romanorum descriptionem agnoscat? Hactenus ille, veritati nebulas summo offundens opere.
units.tr: Fourthly, finally, the number of the ten horns or ten kings can in no way agree with heathen Rome. Alcasar indeed, on chap. xiii. 1, folio 3, page 507, tries to apply them to the Roman senators. This is certain to me, he says, that these ten horns are a symbol of the multitude of the Roman senators. For just as in Scripture one horn designates one ruler, so many horns signify a polyarchy, or the government of many rulers. To signify this, the symbol of ten horns was most suitable; indeed ten is the number of multiplication, and for this reason all the larger numbers are finally closed off in ten. For when one reaches ten, one immediately returns to the beginning of numbers, or to unity. Since the number of senators was not fixed and determined, and some number had to be expressed which would be a symbol of multitude, none could be assumed more fittingly than ten. Thus at Zechariah 8:13 ten men denote a great many. Moreover the very context of the Apocalypse, chap. 17:12, explains that the polyarchy, which is the multitude of rulers reigning at the same time, is figured by the ten heads. But such were the Roman senators. For although they were not properly kings, their power and dignity were like those of kings. Hence Cineas said that the Roman senate seemed to him an assembly of kings, as Plutarch relates in his Pyrrhus, Florus in book 1, and Livy in book 11. The words of the text agree with this: The ten horns are ten kings, who receive power as kings for one hour. For what, I ask you, is "one hour", except to hold rule at one and the same time? But that they are called kings, and it is likewise declared that they are not properly kings, but have the power and dignity of kings, who does not recognise in this a description of the Roman senators? So far he, clouding the truth with a great mass of mists.

units.la: XXXI. Nos autem jam supra nebulas hasce nonnihil dissipavimus, ostendentes scilicet, Senatores Romanos ipsius Romæ dominantis partem fuisse. Reges verò ab eadem Roma, uti scortatores à scorto, & parentes ab imperante distingui. In promptu tamen alia quoque sunt, Φλνακίας hujus, & distortæ interpretationis nervos incisura. Etenim primò cornua decem, & per illa totidem Reges designati diserte numerantur. Senatores autem Romani non decem, sed ducenti fuerunt, ex Romanis & Sabinis à Romulo primùm lecti. Quæ permutandorum numerorum licentia si recipitur, nihil obstabit, quò minus pro duodecim stellis ducentæ, & pro septem candelabris septuaginta numerentur. Cùm verò alibi numeris veluti 666 & 1260 accuratè inhærecamus, quid opus hic est, per decem cornua seu Reges ducentos, vel polyarchiam etiam quamvis intelligere? Secundò de cornibus seu Regibus illis testatur Angelus cap. xvii. 12. quòd Regnum ἔπω ἰλαϚον nondum acceperint. Saltem igitur S. Johannis tempore nondum Reges illi Regnum acceperunt. Quando vero acceperint, nil heic definio. Senatores autem Romanos tempore S. Johannis nondum potestatem suam, quantacunque illa quondam fuit, accepisse, quis asserere ausit? Tertiò, Reges illi Regnum, seu Regiam potestatem accepisse dicuntur. At qui Senatores vel S. Johannis tempore, vel post ejus tempora regnum acceperunt? Quæ tum polyarchia Romæ, quod plurium regimen obtinuit? Næ hospitem esse Alcasarem nimium oportuit in historia Romana, ex qua constat, urbem Romam à principio Reges habuisse: Libertatem & consulatum Q. Brutum instituisse. Dictaturas ad tempus sumtas: neque decemviralem potestatem ultra biennium, neque Tribunorum militum jus consulare diu valuisse. Non Cinnæ, non Sullæ longam dominationem, & Pompeji Crassíque potentiam citò in Cæsarem: Lepidi atque Antonii arma in Augustum cessisse, qui cuncta discordiis civilibus fessa, nomine Principis sub Imperium accepit, uti Tacitus initio Annalium loquitur. Deinceps vis & potestas imperii penes unum fuit, & jam Galbæ ætate Senatus populique Romani nomina obliterata sunt, uti idem Tacitus Hist. 1. 55: 4. loquitur. Neque unquam Romanus Senatus convaluit, nedum eam ad authoritatem postliminio consurrexit, quam Cynex tempestate, qua Regum confessus cluebat, obtinuit. Quartò cornua illa meretricem odio habitura, & desolatura, & combusturu statuuntur. Ubi verò & quando Senatores Romani Romam Ethnicam odio tali appetitam desolârunt, combusserunt?
units.tr: XXXI. But we have already somewhat dispelled these mists above, showing namely that the Roman senators were part of the ruling power of Rome itself. Kings, however, are distinguished from Rome in the same way as harlots from the harlot, and parents from the ruler. Yet there are other things ready to hand, cutting at the sinews of this nonsense [φλυαρίας] and distorted interpretation. For first, ten horns, and through them as many kings, are explicitly counted. But the Roman senators were not ten but two hundred, first chosen from the Romans and Sabines by Romulus. If this licence of changing numbers is admitted, nothing will stop us from counting two hundred for the twelve stars, and seventy for the seven candlesticks. Since elsewhere we cling precisely to numbers such as 666 and 1260, why is there any need here to understand by the ten horns or kings two hundred, or even a polyarchy? Secondly, concerning those horns or kings, the angel testifies at chap. 17:12 that they have not yet [οὔπω ἔλαβον] received a kingdom. So at least in St John's time those kings had not yet received a kingdom. When they did receive it, I here define nothing. But who would dare to assert that the Roman senators in St John's time had not yet received their power, however great it once was? Thirdly, those kings are said to have received a kingdom, or royal power. But did the senators receive a kingdom either in St John's time or after it? What polyarchy was there then at Rome, which maintained the rule of many? Alcasar must truly have been a stranger to Roman history, from which it is clear that the city of Rome had kings from the beginning; Brutus instituted liberty and the consulship; dictatorships were assumed for a time; neither the power of the decemvirs nor the consular right of the military tribunes lasted long; the long domination of Cinna and of Sulla, and the power of Pompey and Crassus, quickly passed to Caesar; the arms of Lepidus and Antony yielded to Augustus, who, when everything was weary of civil discord, received the empire under the name of Prince, as Tacitus speaks at the beginning of the Annals. Thereafter the power and authority of the empire lay with one man, and already in the age of Galba the names of the Senate and the Roman people were erased, as the same Tacitus says in the Histories 1.55. Nor has the Roman senate ever recovered, still less risen again by right of return to that authority which it held in the time of Cineas, when it was renowned as an assembly of kings. Fourthly, those horns are said to be going to hate the harlot, and to make her desolate and burn her with fire. But where and when did the Roman senators make heathen Rome, so hated, desolate and burn her?

units.la: XXXII. Non desunt alia etiam argumenta, quæ ex cap. xiii. ubi Bestia marina describitur, huc revocari possunt. Agnoscit enim nobiscum Alcasar, quod alii negant, Bestiam marinam eandem esse cum Bestia meretricem portante. Id si verum est, uti verum esse supra etiam probare occupavimus: edisserat nobis Alcasar, quemadmodum Romæ Ethnicæ, quòd v. 1. S. Johannes dicitur vidisse Bestiam ex mari ascendentem: quòd v. 5. duratio Bestiæ definitur mensibus quadraginta & duobus, seu diebus propheticis mille ducentis & sexaginta, hoc est, totidem annis: quòd v. 3. potestatem Bestiæ Draco impertitus dicitur: quòd v. 8. omnes habitatores terræ quorum nomina non scripta sunt in libro vitæ, adorâsse feruntur. Hæc aliaque ejusmodi Romæ Ethnicæ neutiquam quadrant, cujus originem S. Johannes non vidit; quæ annos mille ducentos & sexaginta non duravit: quæ potestatem civilem à Deo per quem Reges regnant, non à Dracone, Diabolo accepit; quámque habitatores terræ omnes adorárunt nunquam.
units.tr: XXXII. There are also other arguments, not lacking, which can be brought back here from chapter 13, where the sea beast is described. For Alcasar agrees with us, which others deny, that the sea beast is the same as the beast carrying the harlot. If this is true, as we have also undertaken to prove above, let Alcasar explain to us how heathen Rome fits: that at verse 1 St John is said to have seen the beast rising out of the sea; that at verse 5 the duration of the beast is defined as forty-two months, or prophetic days, one thousand two hundred and sixty, that is, as many years; that at verse 3 the power of the beast is said to have been given to it by the dragon; that at verse 8 all the inhabitants of the earth whose names are not written in the book of life are said to have worshipped it. These and other things of this kind by no means suit heathen Rome, whose origin St John did not see; which did not last one thousand two hundred and sixty years; which received civil power from God, through whom kings reign, not from the dragon, the devil; and which all the inhabitants of the earth never worshipped.

units.la: XXXIII. Tertia sequitur expositio Annii Viterbiensis, qui Bestiæ figurâ Imperium Turcicum adumbrari asserit. Secundas ei faciunt Caponsachius in Apoc. xiij. Lavisinus lib. de Aquila Esdræ sol. 21. & Luisius Legionensis libro de nominibus Christi. Turcis nempe convenire pertendunt illi, quæ Apoc. xiii. 1-11. Bestiæ marinæ tribuuntur. Turcas quippe ortos esse ex mari, hoc est, variorum populorum, Arabum, Saracenorum, Tartarorum &c. colluvie: similes esse pardo, quia Monarchiæ Græcorum, quam pardo assimilavit Daniel, sedem & potentiam ad se rapuerunt: ursi pedes habere, quia fulcra Monarchiæ Persicæ, ab eodem Daniele urso comparatæ, retinet. Leonis os habere, quia exuvias primæ Monarchiæ Assyriorum possidet: nomen blasphemiæ in capite suo habere, quia Deum Israëlis, & Filium Dei blasphemant: terribiles & crudeles esse, utpote quarum invicta tamdiu potentia fuerit; quique tot jam secula cum sanctis Christi cultoribus bellum ἀπροσ̀ἁ gesserint; denique perdurare posse ad tempus usque Bestiæ assignatum, cùm à vero nihil abhorreat, illos menses quadraginta duos adversus Christianum nomen grassaturos.
units.tr: XXXIII. The third exposition follows that of Annius of Viterbo, who asserts that the Beast's figure shadows the Turkish Empire. Caponsachius on Apocalypse 13, Lavisinus in his book on the Eagle of Esdras, p. 21, and Luisius of León in his book on the names of Christ, give it a second hand. They contend that the things which Revelation 13:1-11 attributes to the sea-beast fit the Turks. The Turks, they say, arose out of the sea, that is, out of the mixed rabble of various peoples: Arabs, Saracens, Tartars and so on. They are like a leopard, because they seized for themselves the seat and power of the Greek monarchy, which Daniel compared to a leopard. They have the feet of a bear, because they keep the supports of the Persian monarchy, which Daniel likened to a bear. They have the mouth of a lion, because they possess the spoils of the first monarchy, that of the Assyrians. They bear the name of blasphemy on their head, because they blaspheme the God of Israel and the Son of God. They are terrible and cruel, since their power has long been invincible, and since they have for so many centuries waged war unceasing [ἀπροσ̀ἁ] against the saints who worship Christ. Lastly, they can endure until the time assigned to the Beast, since nothing is far from the truth in their view: they will rage against the Christian name for forty-two months.

units.la: XXXIV. Cæterùm expositionem hanc merito Alcasar ipse quoque improbat, eò quòd in multis rebus violentiam quandam præ se ferat, & cum allusione ad quartam Danielis bestiam parùm conveniat. Certè imperio Turcico neutiquam congruit, quòd Bestia dicitur portare meretricem. Quæ enim meretrix illa notis illis, quibus in Apocalypsi insignitur, compuncta est, quam Turcæ portent? Certè meretricem illam Romæ esse, ex characteribus indubiis, & scintillantibus quibusdam prophetiæ hujus gemmis supra comprobavimus. Atqui partem aliquam sive imperantem, sive parentem Romæ portari à Turcis, atque ita portari, ut cum ea Turcæ dici possint scortari, nimis profectò absurdum est. Supra etiam veritati dedimus, quòd meretricis mysterium Turcarum sive religioni, sive Imperio non conveniat. Proin nec Bestiæ mysterium ei quadrare potest, cùm ἀχώεσις & ἀδιάσασις esse, palam fit. Quæ verò Authores illi ex cap. xiii. Turcis aptare conantur, ejusmodi sunt, ut Romæ applicentur rectius; uti in loco fidem faciemus.
units.tr: XXXIV. Alcasar himself rightly rejects this exposition as well, because it bears a certain violence in many respects, and it agrees poorly with the allusion to the fourth beast of Daniel. Certainly it does not fit the Turkish Empire at all that the Beast is said to carry a harlot. For what harlot, marked with those signs by which she is branded in the Apocalypse, do the Turks carry? We have already shown from the sure marks and shining gems of this prophecy that that harlot is Rome. Yet to say that the Turks carry some part of Rome, whether ruling or subject, and carry it in such a way that the Turks can be said to whore with it, is surely far too absurd. We have also shown above that the mystery of the harlot does not fit the Turks, whether in religion or in empire. Therefore the mystery of the Beast cannot fit them either, since it is plain that they are [ἀχώεσις] without a seat and [ἀδιάσασις] undivided. As for the things which those authors try to apply to the Turks from chapter 13, they are of such a kind that they apply more fittingly to Rome, as we shall show in its place.

units.la: XXXV. Sic excussis Doctorum Pontificiorum sinistris interpretationibus, una superest obiter perstringenda Hugonis Grotii ιππμφονιξδονι@. Is nempe ut in VeteriTestamento Christum occultare sustinuit, ita in Novo Testamento Antichristum temerariis suis glossematis intricandum abstrudendúmque putavit. Meretricem igitur Romam idololatricam interpretatus, Bestiam jumentum ejus facit Domitianum Imperatorem, utpote qui, patre absente, fuerit, hoc est, uti Tacitus loquitur, nomen sedémque Cæsaris obtinuerit, & non fuerit, eo tempore, quo Vespasiano Principe, Ephesi S. Johannes egerat, cum imperio scilicet, redactus quippe in modum privati, modestiam, inprimisque studium Poëticæ simulans, modica quoque & usurpata antea imperii munia amittens, ut ait Suetonius, ascensurus ex abysso, hoc est, ex latebris suis proditurus denuo, & ex obscuro potens evasurus; atque in interitum abiturus, seu morte non qualibet, verum pessima tragicáque è vivis eximendus, quomodo constet Domitianum domesticorum suorum manibus interfectum periisse.
units.tr: XXXV. Having thus shaken off the perverse interpretations of the Papist teachers, there remains one to be touched on briefly: the [ιππμφονιξδονι@] of Hugo Grotius. He undertook to conceal Christ in the Old Testament, and in the New Testament he thought fit to entangle and hide Antichrist in his rash glosses. Accordingly, he interprets the harlot as idolatrous Rome, and makes the Beast her mount the Emperor Domitian, who, with his father absent, was, that is, as Tacitus puts it, held the name and seat of Caesar, and was not, at the time when, under the Prince Vespasian, St John had been at Ephesus, that is, when he had lost the imperial power. For he was reduced to the position of a private man, feigning modesty, and especially a zeal for poetry, and losing even the small duties of empire which he had previously usurped, as Suetonius says. He was about to ascend out of the abyss, that is, to come forth again from his hiding places and to gain power out of obscurity. And he was about to go into perdition, or to be removed from the living not by just any death but by a most wretched and tragic one, just as it is well known that Domitian perished, killed by the hands of his own household.

units.la: XXXVI. Insulsam planè & infelicem esse hanc, viri cætera doctissimi, Bestiæ hujus crisin, quis non intelligit? Etenim Bestiam, quæ meretricem portat, ejusmodi definiri conveniebat, non quæ dominaretur, sed quæ dominanti ipsa pareret subjicere túrque. At Domitianus Romæ imperavit, non paruit. Tum meretrix ipsa cum Roma Ethnica non fuerit, uti supra demonstravimus, neque Bestia Romæ Ethnicæ pars aliqua esse potuit. At Domitianus Romæ Ethnicæ pars potissima fuit. Quæ duo vel sola commentum isthoc abundè convellunt.
units.tr: XXXVI. Who does not see that this crisis of the Beast is utterly silly and unhappy, learned men in all other respects? For the Beast that carries the harlot ought to have been defined as one that is not the ruler but the subject, submitting to the ruling harlot itself. Yet Domitian ruled at Rome; he did not submit to anyone. Moreover, since the harlot herself was not pagan Rome, as we have shown above, no part of the Beast could be pagan Rome. And Domitian was the chief part of pagan Rome. These two points alone thoroughly overturn this fiction.

units.la: XXXVII. Accedunt hisce alia, velut in cumulum. Primò enim obtigit visio Bestiæ S. Johanni post Vespasianum & Titum sub ipso Domitiano, à quo in Infulam Patmos relegatus erat. Atqui Prophetia de Bestia loquitur, quòd fuerit, & non sit. Quomodo fuit, & non est (saltem juxta interpretationem Grotii) qui, eo ipso tempore & fuit, & rerum potitus est? Et si maximè tum rerum potitus non est, uti fingit Grotius, at fuit certè. Secundò quæ causa reddi potest, cur potiùs Domitiano vel Tiberio, sub quo Christus crucifixus est, vel Neroni, vel Vitellio, non minoribus utique portentis θηρίω Bestiæ stigma inurendum fuerit? An forte S. Johannes Domitianum persecutorem suum ultioni mastare voluit? Tertiò quo sensu Domitianus ex mari vel abysso progressus dici potuit? An etiam magis, quàm præcedentes Cæsares, ex abysso ille prodiit? Quartò, qui fuerunt decem illi Reges septicipitis hujus Bestiæ, Domitiani puta, qui meretricem, hoc est, Grotio interprete idololatriam Ethnicam odisse occœperunt, ac desolárunt tandem combusseruntque? Quintò personam singularem, qualis Domitianus fuit Ϙηρίου Bestiam appellari, non satis congruum est stylo scripturæ, in qua uti ex Prophetia Danielis liquet, Bestiæ nomine imperia vasta adumbrari solent.
units.tr: XXXVII. Other points are added to these, as though piled on top. First, the vision of the Beast came to St John after Vespasian and Titus, under Domitian himself, by whom he had been banished to the island of Patmos. Yet the prophecy speaks of the Beast as was, and is not. How was he, and is not (at least according to Grotius's interpretation), when at that very time he both was and held power? And even if at that time he did not hold power, as Grotius imagines, he certainly was. Second, what reason can be given why the mark of the beast [θηρίω] should rather be branded on Domitian, or on Tiberius under whom Christ was crucified, or on Nero, or on Vitellius, who were no less monstrous? Or perhaps St John wanted to hand over Domitian, his persecutor, to vengeance? Third, in what sense could Domitian be said to have come up out of the sea or the abyss? Did he come out of the abyss any more than the earlier Caesars did? Fourth, who were those ten kings of this seven-headed Beast, namely Domitian's, who began to hate the harlot, that is, according to Grotius, pagan idolatry, and at last made her desolate and burned her? Fifth, it is not fitting for the style of Scripture to call a single person, such as Domitian was, the Beast [θηρίον]. As the prophecy of Daniel makes clear, vast empires are usually shadowed under the name of a beast.

units.la: XXXVIII. Bestiam igitur nec Diabolum mundo universo imperitantem, nec Romanum imperium Ethnicum, nec Imperium Saracenicum, nec Domitianum esse indubitabilibus jam argumentis constat. Cúmque omnino Romæ non alibi terrarum quæri debeat; cùm Characteres ejus Romam demonstrent, & meretricem, quam illa portat, Romæ domicilium suum metaturam esse, supra comprobaverimus: in Roma verò-Ethnica vetere, vel novissima etiam Antichristiano Ethnica inveniri nullo pacto posset, in Roma tertia eam unà cum meretrice sua stabulari, lege nexúque consecutionis firmissima concludimus.
units.tr: XXXVIII. It is therefore now established by indubitable arguments that the Beast is neither the Devil ruling over the whole world, nor the pagan Roman Empire, nor the Saracen Empire, nor Domitian. Since it must be sought at Rome and nowhere else on earth, since its marks point to Rome, and since we have shown above that the harlot it carries will make Rome her dwelling, we conclude with the most certain law and chain of consequence that it cannot be found in ancient pagan Rome, nor in the newest Rome that is pagan in an antichristian way; rather, it must be sought in a third Rome, where it stables the harlot together with her.

units.la: DISSERTATIO TERTIA QUA Verborum, quibus mysterium Babylonis Meretricis & Bestiæ circumscribitur, dubiorum inprimis, sensus indefinitus explicatur. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: THE THIRD DISSERTATION, IN WHICH the words by which the mystery of the Harlot Babylon and the Beast are described, chiefly the doubtful ones, are explained in their undefined sense. A SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Instituti continuatio, & explicandorum verborum Prophetiæ continuatio.
units.tr: I. The continuation of the plan, and the continuation of the prophecy whose words are to be explained.

units.la: II. Babylonem definituro ostendenda est ejus analogia quæ-dam cum Babylone Chaldæa veteri.
units.tr: II. Before defining Babylon, a certain analogy between her and ancient Chaldean Babylon must be shown.

units.la: III. Meretrices olim titulum præferebant.
units.tr: III. Harlots formerly bore a title.

units.la: IV. Babyloniæ meretricis titulus est, Mysterium,
units.tr: IV. The title of the Harlot Babylon is "Mystery,"

units.la: V. prodens scilicet professionem ejus, quod Mysteria Di-vina penes se recondita sola habeat.
units.tr: V. that is, declaring her profession, namely that she alone holds the divine mysteries hidden within herself.

units.la: VI. Babylon igitur religionis prætextu imponit.
units.tr: VI. Babylon therefore imposes upon people under the pretext of religion.

units.la: VII. Mysterium, cujus obtentu imponit, est non pietatis, sed impietatis, quia est mater scortationum.
units.tr: VII. The mystery under whose cover she imposes is not of godliness but of ungodliness, because she is the mother of fornications.

units.la: VIII. IX. Mater est scortationis præcipuè spiritualis, defectionis à Deo vero ad creaturas.
units.tr: VIII. IX. She is the mother of fornication, chiefly spiritual, a defection from the true God to creatures.

units.la: X. Proin in externa Ecclesia meritorium propudium aliquod est, Deo & Christo fidem fallens.
units.tr: X. Therefore, in the outward Church there is some deserved shame, deceiving faith toward God and Christ.

units.la: XI. Scortatio Spiritualis meretricis in eo potissimùm consistit, quòd loco veri Dei se ipsam colendam religiosè prostituit.
units.tr: XI. The spiritual fornication of the harlot consists chiefly in this: that, in place of the true God, she prostitutes herself to be worshipped as God.

units.la: XII. Idololatria seu scortatio duplex meretricis probè distinguitur.
units.tr: XII. The idolatry, or double fornication, of the harlot is carefully distinguished.

units.la: XIII. Meretricis convenientia cum Antichristo.
units.tr: XIII. The harlot's agreement with the Antichrist.

units.la: XIV. Meretrix civitas Magna est, non inclusa tamen Romæ mœnibus.
units.tr: XIV. The harlot is the Great City, yet not enclosed within the walls of Rome.

units.la: XV. Civitas apud Græcos & Latinos ab urbe distin-guitur,
units.tr: XV. Among the Greeks and Latins a city is distinguished from a town (urbs).

units.la: XVI. etiam in S. literis.
units.tr: XVI. This is so also in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: XVII. Est igitur civitas, hoc est multitudo per caput aut capita sociata, adeóque civitas imperitans,
units.tr: XVII. A city, therefore, that is, a multitude joined under a head or heads, and so a ruling city,

units.la: XVIII. non politica, sed religiosa,
units.tr: XVIII. is not civil but religious,

units.la: XIX. eáque non Ethnica sed Christiana, adeoque Hie-rarchia quædam Christiana,
units.tr: XIX. and not heathen but Christian, and so a certain Christian hierarchy,

units.la: XX. quod Bestiæ etiam, Meretricem portantis confideratio arguit.
units.tr: XX. which the consideration of the Beast also that carries the Harlot proves.

units.la: XXI. Est enim Bestia multitudo hominum animalium Meretrici servientium.
units.tr: XXI. For the Beast is a multitude of men, animal-like, serving the Harlot.

units.la: XXII. Typus ejus proponitur Roma vetus.
units.tr: XXII. Ancient Rome is set forth as its type.

units.la: XXIII. Bestia est multitudo hominum Meretrici, seu Hierarchiæ dominanti parens, non infidelis simpliciter, sed Christi nomen præseferens,
units.tr: XXIII. The Beast is a multitude of men, obedient to the Harlot, or to the hierarchy that rules, not simply unbelieving but bearing the name of Christ.

units.la: XXIV. quod etiam antithesis Civitatis sanctæ, nec non Bestia posterior Apoc. xiij. 11. &c. arguit.
units.tr: XXIV. This also the antithesis to the holy city proves, as does the second Beast of Rev. 13:11 and following.

units.la: XXV. Magis etiam materia, ex qua Bestia conflata est, puta gentes, quibus exterius atrium Templi datum est, quæque civitatem sanctam calcare. 42. menses debuerunt.
units.tr: XXV. Even more, the material from which the Beast is compounded: the nations to whom the outer court of the Temple was given, and who were to tread down the holy city forty-two months.

units.la: XXVI. Ejus rei typus proponitur Israël carnalis.
units.tr: XXVI. Fleshly Israel is set forth as the type of this thing.

units.la: XXVII. Babylon meretrix & Bestia quæ sit, ex superioribus definitur.
units.tr: XXVII. What the Harlot Babylon and the Beast are is defined from what has gone before.

units.la: XXVIII. Habitus externus Mulieris est purpura, coccium &c.
units.tr: XXVIII. The outward dress of the Woman is purple, scarlet and so on.

units.la: XXIX. quæ tum ad literam, tum mystico sensu exponuntur.
units.tr: XXIX. These are explained both literally and in a mystical sense.

units.la: XXX. Ad eundem Meretricis habitum pertinet poculum aureum, intus abominationibus plenum, quo notatur cortex verborum Dei traditiones, aliaque tegumenta turpitudinis.
units.tr: XXX. To the same dress of the Harlot belongs the golden cup, full of abominations within, by which is signified the bark of the words of God, that is, traditions, and other coverings of filth.

units.la: XXXI. Interior Meretricis habitus sunt flagitia ejus.
units.tr: XXXI. The inner dress of the Harlot is her wickedness.

units.la: XXXII. Bestiæ constitutio propria explicatur. Ejus ortus exprimitur verbis, quod fuerit, non sit, ascensura sit ex abysso, & abitura in interitum, quibus verbis notatur vel exortus à Dracone,
units.tr: XXXII. The proper constitution of the Beast is explained. Its origin is expressed in the words that it was, is not, and is about to ascend out of the abyss and go into perdition; by these words is noted either its rise from the Dragon,

units.la: XXXIII. vel similitudo cum Israële carnali, cujus regiminis formam affectat.
units.tr: XXXIII. or its likeness to fleshly Israel, whose form of government it aims at.

units.la: XXXIV. Capita Bestiæ septem,
units.tr: XXXIV. The Beast's heads are seven,

units.la: XXXV. sunt septem montes
units.tr: XXXV. they are seven mountains,

units.la: XXXVI. typi Dynastiarum septem & totidem rectorum.
units.tr: XXXVI. the types of seven dynasties and as many rulers.

units.la: K
units.tr: K

units.la: XXXVII. Quibus non succedentes sibi septem potestates urbis Romanæ,
units.tr: XXXVII. Not seven powers of the city of Rome succeeding one another,

units.la: XXXVIII. sed totidem provinciæ ditionis Romanæ denotantur.
units.tr: XXXVIII. but as many provinces of the Roman dominion are denoted.

units.la: XXXIX. Cornua Bestiæ decem affigenda sunt non capitibus singulis Bestiæ, sed septimo monti seu Regi, quatenus ei oblavus convenit, & quidem non semper, sed unam horam, qua ij robur suum Meretrici & Bestiæ collaturi erant ad conservandam unitatem fidei.
units.tr: XXXIX. The ten horns of the Beast are not to be attached to the single heads of the Beast, but to the seventh mountain, or king, inasmuch as an hour of royal power fits it; and not always, but for one hour, in which they were to give their strength to the Harlot and the Beast, to preserve the unity of the faith.

units.la: XL. Consectarium ex iis, quæ de Bestia dicta sunt, deductum.
units.tr: XL. A corollary drawn from what has been said about the Beast.

units.la: XLI. Judicium meretricis explicatur.
units.tr: XLI. The judgment of the harlot is explained.

units.la: XLII. Casus Babylonis ab Angelo Apoc. xviij. 1.2. ingeminatus non est finalis,
units.tr: XLII. The fall of Babylon, repeated by the Angel in Rev. 18:1-2, is not the final one,
