units.la: XLIII. & in Meretricis desolatione, fideliumque ab ea separatione consistit.
units.tr: XLIII. but consists in the desolation of the Harlot and the separation of the faithful from her.

units.la: XLIV. Judicii incrementum in plagis Babyloni à populo Dei infligendis consistit.
units.tr: XLIV. The increase of the judgment consists in the plagues to be inflicted on Babylon by the people of God.

units.la: XLV. Peremtorium & finale ejusdem judicium subita ejus deletione,
units.tr: XLV. Her decisive and final judgment is her sudden destruction,

units.la: XLVI. adeóque [Greek] Babylonis absolvitur.
units.tr: XLVI. and so the judgment of Babylon is completed.

units.la: XLVII. Ex superioribus Babylon magna [Greek] definitur, charactéribúsque suis clarissimis circumscribitur.
units.tr: XLVII. From what has gone before, Babylon the Great [Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη] is defined and circumscribed by her clearest marks.

units.la: I. Quid Babylon Magna, meretrix propudiosa, & eandem portans Bestia non sit, ita explicavimus hactenus, ut ad cognoscendum, quid fit utraque illa, nec Oedipo divinatore, nec natatore Delio quicquam amplius indigeamus. Lucem tamen nonnullam fœneraturi argumento, cujus exactior cognitio si quo alio, hoc certè inprimis tempore momentum haud exiguum habet, ejusdem Babylonis definitionem & demonstrationem solidam molimur. Quam quidem prius quàm aggredimur, lubet in antecessum Prophetiæ de Babylone & Bestia verba, difficiliora cumprimis, quoad sensum saltem indefinitum, explicatiora reddere, ut obscuritate sublata,& præjudiciorum discussis nebulis, ipsa deinceps demonstratio felicius expeditiúsque procedat.
units.tr: I. What Babylon the Great, the shameless harlot, and the Beast that carries her are not, we have so far explained, so that for knowing what each of them is we need neither Oedipus as a diviner nor Delian diver any further. Yet, since we are about to lend some light to a subject whose more exact knowledge is of no small importance, especially at this time, we are undertaking a definition and solid demonstration of this Babylon. Before we begin it, it pleases us to make beforehand the words of the prophecy about Babylon and the Beast, especially the more difficult ones, clearer, at least as to their undefined sense, so that, with obscurity removed and the mists of prejudices dispelled, the demonstration itself may proceed more happily and more readily.

units.la: II. Ante omnia Meretrix illa famosissima vocatur Βα· Babylonem Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη Babylon illa magna Apoc. xvii. 5. Alludi autem ad veterem בבל ורבר Babylonem magnam Dan. iv. 30. cui nomen inditum est à confusione, quia logis quaשם בלל יהוה שפת כל הארץ ibi confudit Deus labium universæ terræ, & inde dispersit eos Jehova super universam terram. Gen. xi. 9. abundè liquet. Qui igitur mysterium Babylonis hujus Apocalypticæ explicare contenderit, ei post tempora S. Johannis demonstrandam esse Babylonem quampiam veteri illi Chaldaicæ non planè dissimilem, in qua scilicet ob studium constituendi nominis exstruendæque vastissimæ turris confusum sit labium, ex qua dispersæ sint gentes, quæ sensim magnam ad potentiam pervenerit, quæ sceleribus multifariis piaculare caput alligârit, quæ sanctos persecuta fuerit, Ecclesiámque ipsam captivam redegerit, ex qua Ecclesia exire jussa paruerit, quæ ob impietatem gravissimam judicium Dei provocaverit, extra omnem dubitationis aleam positum est.
units.tr: II. First of all, that most notorious harlot is called "Babylon the Great" [Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη], Rev. 17:5. Now, it is clear that it alludes to the ancient Babel, "Babylon the Great," Dan. 4:30, which got its name from confusion, because "there the LORD confused the language of all the earth," and "from there the LORD scattered them over all the earth," Gen. 11:9. Therefore, whoever tries to explain the mystery of this apocalyptic Babylon must show, after the time of St John, some Babylon not wholly unlike that ancient Chaldean one, in which, namely, from a desire to make a name and to build a vast tower the language was confused, from which the nations were scattered, which by degrees came to great power, which bound a sinful head with manifold crimes, which persecuted the saints and reduced the Church herself to captivity, from which the Church was commanded to come out and obeyed, and which, because of most grave impiety, provoked the judgment of God: this is placed beyond all doubt.

units.la: III. Olim quidem meretrices pudoris prostituti in cellæ, quam depromptuariam Plautus Amphitr. A. i. sc. i. vocat, seu lupanaris foribus præscribere nomina solebant. Seneca Controv. 2. 1. 1. Meretrix vocata es, in communi loco stetisti, superpositus est cellæ tuæ titulus. Tertullianus de Pudicitia: Sub ipsis libidinum januis, sub ipsis libidinum titulis. Juvenalis Satyr. 6. v. 123. Nuda papillis constitit auratis, titulum mentita Lycisca. Aliquando etiam in fronte signari fuerunt, teste Seneca loc. cit. ubi sic ille: Nomen tuum pependit in fronte, pretia stupri accepisti.
units.tr: III. Indeed, harlots of shameless prostitution were formerly accustomed to write their names over the doors of the little cell, which Plautus calls the "storeroom" (Amphitryon, act 1, scene 1), or of the brothel. Seneca, Controversiae 2.1.1: "You were called a harlot; you stood in a public place; over your cell is set your title." Tertullian, On Modesty: "Under the very doors of lusts, under the very titles of lusts." Juvenal, Satire 6, verse 123: "Naked, she stood with gilded breasts, Lycisca pretending a title." Sometimes too they were marked on the forehead, as Seneca says in the place cited, where he speaks thus: "Your name hung on your forehead; you received the wages of defilement."

units.la: Meretrices olim titulum præferebant. cepisti &c. De quo vide sis plura apud Durantium lib. 1. var. cap. 2. Meretrici proin etiam huic mysticæ præfigendus titulus erat, sed in fronte scilicet, non alibi, quia palam profiteri quid esset, nullam quietem dare oculis & aliorum quoque frontibus signaturam imprimere, uti ex Apoc. XIII. 16. constat, debuit. Opponi etiam debuit præscriptio tituli in fronte meretricis non solùm præscriptioni tituli קדש יהוה Sanctitas Jehovæ in frontali Pontificis,sed etiam præscriptioni tituli Sanctorum seu Servorum Agni, nomen Ⴟ πατρὸς Patris Agni in fronte sua scriptum præferentis. Apoc. VII. 3. XIV. 1. XXII. 4.
units.tr: Harlots formerly bore a title, "...you received," and so on. On this see more in Durantius, Book 1, Varia, chapter 2. So a title ought to have been prefixed to this mystical harlot too, but on the forehead, clearly, and nowhere else, since she was to declare openly what she was, to give no rest to the eyes, and to impress her mark on the foreheads of others too, as is plain from Rev. 13:16. The inscription of a title on the forehead of the harlot ought also to be set against not only the inscription "Holiness to the LORD" [קדש יהוה] on the high priest's frontlet, but also against the inscription of the title of the saints, or servants of the Lamb, who bear the name of the Lamb's Father written on their foreheads: Rev. 7:3; 14:1; 22:4.

units.la: IV. Titulus hic fronti meretricis præfixus est: μυστήριον Mysterium Apoc. XVII. 5. Quod nomen Arethas olim, & post illum Mcnochius, Gagneus, Alcafar, à Lapide, Brigthmannus, alii negant vel titulum esse, vel tituli partem, asseruntque, esse rem ab ipso Johanne additam, ut titulum sequentem Babylon magna &c. non proprie, sed mysticè intelligendum esse insinuctur. quasi scilicet diceretur, super frontem ejus scriptum esse nomen illud μυστή-ριων μυστικὸν mysticum, Babylon magna &c. Quam sententiam merito rejicit, utpote parùm convenientem textui, in quo post verbum ὄνομα γεγραμμένον incisionem exemplaria, non parenthesin habent. Scribendum insuper fuisset non μυστήριον mysterium, sed μυστηρικὸν mysticum, scilicet nomen, in fronte scriptum.
units.tr: IV. This title is prefixed to the harlot's forehead: "Mystery" [μυστήριον], Rev. 17:5. Arethas long ago, and after him Menochius, Gagneius, Alcazar, à Lapide, Brightman and others, deny that this word is a title or part of a title, and assert that it is a thing added by John himself, to suggest that the title that follows, "Babylon the Great" and so on, is to be understood not literally but mystically; as if it were said that the name written on her forehead was that mystical name "mystery," "Babylon the Great" and so on. This opinion is rightly rejected, as ill fitting the text, in which after the words "a name written" the copies have a break, not a parenthesis. Moreover, it would have had to be written not "mystery" [μυστήριον] but "mystical" [μυστικόν], namely the name written on the forehead.

units.la: V. Omnino igitur vox illa μυστήριον ad titulum pertinet, & meretricis jactantiam, professionémque ad amorem sui scortatores allicientis significans, ei opponitur, quòd Cap. XIII. 1. de Dracone dicitur, capitibus ejus ὄνομα βλασφημίας inscriptum esse. Sicut autem Pontificis olim titulus frontali ejus inscriptus, erat: Sanctitas Jehovæ; & agni ac sequacium ejus, Pater, uti supra memi nimus: ita Meretrix isthæc quæ sola veteris Sacerdotii Sacerdotalem panopliam ex professo æmulatur, & affectat, imitandum sibi consilium isthoc statuens, titulum sibi quempiam honorificum, quo oculorum humanorum aciem perstringeret, seque amasiis suis efficaciter commendaret, præfigendum putavit, quem ex professione ipsa meretricis Spiritui S. elicere placuit. Cumque mysterium arcanam Dei voluntatem significet, speciosum eum, & instituto suo planè conducibilem titulum selegit, persuasura scilicet hominibus, se veri mysterii esse depositorium & custodem; se in scrinio pectoris sui clausa habere secreta Dei; se religionis, cultus, ceremoniarum divinitus sibi revelatarum verissimam promam condam esse; à se denique non aliunde, arcanam voluntatem Dei, ejusque intelligentiam omnem arcessendam unicè esse. Atque eodem planè sensu Daniel rx. 36. de Antichristo prædicitur ירבר נפלאות Proloquetur admirabilia, mysteria scilicet, quibus nequitiam suam tecturus, incrustaturúsque erat.
units.tr: V. Therefore the word μυστήριον [mysterion] certainly belongs to the title, and signifies the harlot's boasting and her profession, which entices her lovers to love her. It is set against what is said of the Dragon in chapter XIII. 1, that on his heads was written a name of blasphemy [ὄνομα βλασφημίας]. Just as the title of the Pontiff of old, inscribed on his frontal plate, was Holiness to Jehovah [Sanctitas Jehovæ], and that of the Lamb and his followers was Father [Pater], as we noted above, so this harlot, who alone openly imitates and aspires to the priestly panoply of the old priesthood, resolved on this as her plan of imitation. She thought she should prefix to herself some honourable title that would dazzle the eyes of men and commend her effectively to her lovers, and she chose one which she thought she could draw from the Holy Spirit by her own profession. Since mystery signifies the secret will of God, she chose a showy title, altogether suited to her purpose: she would persuade men that she is the depositary and guardian of the true mystery; that she keeps the secrets of God shut up in the chest of her heart; that she is the most true storehouse of religion, worship and ceremonies divinely revealed to her; and finally that the secret will of God and all understanding of it are to be sought from her alone and from nowhere else. And in exactly this sense Daniel xi. 36 predicts of Antichrist that he will speak wonderful things [ירבר נפלאות], he shall speak marvellous things [Proloquetur admirabilia], namely mysteries, by which he was about to cover and gild his wickedness.

units.la: VI. Sequitur hinc, ei, qui Babylonem magnam demonstrare & definire satagit, necessario ostendendam esse ejusmodi Thaidem, quæ mysteria religionis sacratissima jactet, & sub prætextu Mysterii pietatis oculos fascinet plurimorum, qui meram pietatem apud eam regnare, intimam voluntatem Dei in penetralibus ejus latere, atque ab ea perinde atque ab ipso Deo & spiritu ejus omne fas, religionem omnem hauriendam esse putant. Aliud enim significari voce Μυστήριον, dici certè nulla ratione potest. Etenim omnino μυστήριον Mysterium, vox ab Hebræo סתר Miftar, quod secretum notat, derivata, uti erudite Doctiss. Casaubonus Exercit. 16. ad Baronii 43. notat, non aliud, quàm arcanum ad sacra pertinens, seu, uti Chrysostomus exponit τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα ἢ ἱερὰ ἢ ἀγνὰ μυστήρια, quod fine revelatione divina exprimi & cognosci nequit, adeóque Admirabile quodpiam. Unde ipsi etiam gentiles mysterium insigniunt arcanos suos cultus & religiones πλάνης , καὶ ἐπιπνίας, quæ plerunque impuræ & abominandæ erant, velut Eleusinia Sacra.
units.tr: VI. It follows that whoever sets out to demonstrate and define the great Babylon must necessarily show that she is a harlot of this kind, one who boasts of the most sacred mysteries of religion and, under the pretext of the mystery of godliness, bewitches the eyes of many people. These people think that pure godliness reigns in her, that the inmost will of God lies hidden in her innermost sanctuary, and that all right and all religion are to be drawn from her just as they are from God himself and his Spirit. For the word Mysterium [μυστήριον] can certainly not, by any reasoning, mean anything else. The word mysterium is derived from the Hebrew miftar [סתר], which means secret, as the learned and most learned Casaubon notes (Exercitation 16, against Baronius, §43). It signifies nothing other than a secret thing pertaining to sacred matters, or, as Chrysostom explains, unspeakable or holy or pure mysteries [τὰ ἀπόῤῥητα ἢ ἱερὰ ἢ ἀγνὰ μυστήρια], which cannot be expressed or known without divine revelation, and so is some admirable thing. Hence even the Gentiles themselves applied the name of mysteries to their secret cults and religions, which were for the most part impure and abominable, such as the Eleusinian rites, calling them mysteries of error and deceit [πλάνης καὶ ἐπιπνίας].

units.la: VII. Concedit Spiritus S. meretrici nomen ifthoc μυστήριον, ςήμος, quasi diceret: Revera est mysterium, sed μυστήριον non εὐσεβείας pietatis 1. Tim. iii. 16. verum ἀνομίας iniquitatis, & defectionis in hypocrisi operantis 2 Thess. iii. 7. 10. 1 Tim. iv. 2. Neque hoc tantùm, sed jactantiæ etiam meretricis opponit apertam veritatem, quòd videlicet tantum absit, ut fit mysterium pietatis, ut fit potiùs Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη, ἡ μήτηρ τῶν πορνῶν καὶ τῶν βδελυγμάτων Babylon illa magna, illa mater scortationum & abominationum Apoc. xvii. 5. Quæ dicta esse per μυστηρισμὸν seu irrisionem, quia non sit quod jactat, sed id potiùs, cujus contrarium præ se fert, abundè liquet. Quis enim credat ullum cœtum, civitatem ullam, qualis Babylon definitur, se ipsam prælato quasi in fronte nomine, turpitudinis suæ damnaturam, & ea professione quenquam seducturam?
units.tr: VII. The Holy Spirit grants the harlot this name mystery [μυστήριον], as if he were saying: It is indeed a mystery, but not a mystery of godliness [μυστήριον εὐσεβείας] (1 Tim. iii. 16); rather a mystery of iniquity [ἀνομίας], and of apostasy working through hypocrisy (2 Thess. ii. 7, 10; 1 Tim. iv. 2). He does not stop there. He also sets plain truth against the harlot's boasting: far from being a mystery of godliness, she is rather Babylon the great, the mother of harlots and abominations [Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη, ἡ μήτηρ τῶν πορνῶν καὶ τῶν βδελυγμάτων] (Rev. xvii. 5), that great Babylon, that mother of whoredoms and abominations. That these words are spoken by way of irony [μυστηρισμὸν], or mockery, because she is not what she boasts of but rather the opposite of what she displays, is quite plain. For who would believe that any assembly or city whatever, such as Babylon is described as being, would, with its name written as it were across its forehead, condemn its own shame, and by such a profession seduce anyone?

units.la: VIII. Babylon igitur magna secundum rei veritatem Spiritui S. ea nota compungitur, quòd sit, mater scortationum & abominationum. Supra. v.1. πόρνην μεγάλην Meretricem magnam v. 3. γυναῖκα Mulierem, hîc μητέρα Matrem, nuncupat. Sequioris igitur fœminei, non fortioris & masculini sexus Babylonem facit. Quomodo & mulieris Jezabelis Apoc. ii. 20. 21. mentio est: & Salomon in Proverbiis non uno loco אשה זרה mulieris peregrinæ, fatuos ad se invitantis, cui sapientiam opponit, meminit. Notum scilicet est, eum sexum impotentiorem faciliùs deliciis diffluere; & per χρησμολογίας, ὑλεγίας, omnémque ἀπάτην ad casdem potentius insidiosiúsque allicere, flagrantiúsque & impotentius tum amare, tum odisse. Alluditur autem ad veterem Babylonem, quæ Esai. xlvii. 1. בת בבל filia Babelis vocatur. Denique cum veram Ecclesiam Mulieri in desertum profugæ superiùs cap. xii. 1. 2. prophetia comparaverit Babylonem pro æmula ejusdem se gerere, insinuare eadem opera videtur.
units.tr: VIII. Babylon the great is therefore, in the reality of the matter, branded by the Holy Spirit with this mark: that she is the mother of harlots and abominations. Above, in v. 1, she is called the great harlot [πόρνην μεγάλην]; in v. 3 woman [γυναῖκα]; here she is named mother [μητέρα]. He thus makes Babylon of the weaker, feminine sex, not the stronger, masculine one. Likewise mention is made of the woman Jezebel (Rev. ii. 20, 21), and Solomon in the Proverbs more than once speaks of the strange woman [אשה זרה], the woman of the stranger, who invites fools to herself, and sets wisdom against her. It is well known that this weaker sex more easily dissolves into pleasures, and that by oracles, magic and every kind of deceit it attracts men more powerfully and craftily, and loves and hates them more fiercely and intemperately. The allusion, moreover, is to old Babylon, who is called daughter of Babel [בת בבל] in Isaiah xlvii. 1. Finally, since the prophecy has compared the true Church to a woman who fled into the wilderness (chap. xii. 1, 2 above), it seems at the same time to hint that Babylon plays the rival of that same woman.

units.la: IX. Neque qualiscunque hæc mulier est, sed μήτηρ μεγάλη Meretrix magna Apoc. xvii. 1. seu scortum insatiabile, & cui simile non prostat, imò mater scortationum & abominationum terræ, hoc est, ejusmodi, ex qua in Civitate illa scortationes & abominationes omnes proveniunt, quæ est exemplar, fons & origo omnium fornicationum, & abominabilium scelerum, quæ ipsa seminavit, edidit, eduxit, propagavit, & ad quæ patranda multos filios, hæredes, sectatores, protrudit. Ut verè dicatur Meretrix hæc ex genere βαρβαρῶν Barbaritarum, de quibus Epiphanius in Panario, & Oecumenius in Judam, scripsêre. Scortationem intelligi utramque & spiritualem, quæ est conversio amoris & affectus à Deo ad Creaturam, & corporalem, quæ amoris illiciti fœda prostitutio est; nihil vetat, cùm ut plurimum indissolubili nexu utraque jungatur, & Prophetia matrem appellet non πορνείας scortationis simpliciter, sed πορνῶν scortationum & abominationum terræ. Spiritualis autem νοερὸς intelligitur, non corporalis, quia cum Babylone, civitate scilicet Magna, uti infra v. 18. vocatur, Reges terræ scortati, incolæ terræ vino scortationis ejus inebriati dicuntur, quod de corporali scortatione proprie intelligi nequit. Civitates idolorum cultrices solent in sacris meretrices nuncupari, sicut idololatriæ etiam nomen fornicationis tribuitur. Esaj. xxxiv. 15. Jerem. v. 20. & cap. iv. 1. Ezech. xvj. 3. Mich. 1. 7. inquit Alcasar ad Apoc. xvij. 1. Verbo, defectio intelligitur à vero Deo & Christo Creatore & Redemtore, à Lege & Verbo ejus, quo salus promittitur, ad creaturas, tanquam ad summum bonum: conversio amoris à Deo ad mundum; λατρεία τῆς κτίσεως τῷ κτίσαντι cultus creaturæ supra Creatorem Rom. 1. 25. Apostasia à Deo vivo, perfidia & nefaria idololatria.
units.tr: IX. Nor is this just any woman, but the great harlot [μήτηρ μεγάλη] of Rev. xvii. 1, an insatiable whore, and none like her is to be found; indeed she is the mother of harlots and abominations of the earth. That is to say, she is of such a kind that from her in that city all whoredoms and abominations arise: she is the pattern, source and origin of all fornications and abominable crimes, which she herself has sown, produced, brought forth and propagated, and into whose commission she thrusts many sons, heirs and followers. So this harlot may truly be said to belong to the race of barbarian women [βαρβαρῶν], of whom Epiphanius in the Panarion and Oecumenius on Jude have written. Both kinds of fornication may be understood: the spiritual, which is the turning of love and affection from God to the creature, and the bodily, which is the foul prostitution of unlawful love. Nothing forbids this, since for the most part the two are joined in an indissoluble bond, and the prophecy calls her mother not simply of fornication [πορνείας], but of harlots and abominations of the earth [πορνῶν... καὶ βδελυγμάτων τῆς γῆς]. The spiritual fornication is understood as mental [νοερὸς], not bodily, because it is said that with Babylon, that is the great city, as it is called below in v. 18, the kings of the earth committed fornication, and the inhabitants of the earth were made drunk with the wine of her fornication. This cannot properly be understood of bodily fornication. Cities that worship idols are commonly called harlots in their rites, just as the name of fornication is given to idolatry (Isa. xxxiv. 15; Jer. v. 20; Jer. iv. 1; Ezek. xvi. 3; Mic. i. 7), says Alcazar on Rev. xvii. 1. In a word, the defection is understood as a turning away from the true God and Christ the Creator and Redeemer, from his Law and Word, by which salvation is promised, toward creatures as if they were the highest good. It is a turning of love from God to the world; the worship of the creature rather than the Creator [λατρεία τῆς κτίσεως τῷ κτίσαντι] (Rom. i. 25); apostasy from the living God, treachery and wicked idolatry.

units.la: X. Proin Babylonem veram investigaturo & detecturo quærendum est in Ecclesia externa meritorium aliquod propudium, quod Deo, Christóque fidem fregit, ejusque cruci valedicens quæstum in mundo facere occœpit, quòdque insuper poculo fornicationis propinato Reges & incolas terræ inebriatos ad scortandum secum immaniter seducit: ita ut mulier illa se loco Dei, tanquam Deum, gerens Reges illos & incolas terræ ad se loco Dei viventis relicti amandum, colendum, sibique adeò impertienda ea, quæ solius Dei sunt, aucupandi honoris Divini, captandi quæstus, emolumenti commodorúmque terrestrium gratia, pelliciat.
units.tr: X. Therefore, one who would search out and expose the true Babylon must look for some notorious disgrace in the external Church, one that has broken faith with God and Christ, has bidden farewell to his cross, and has begun to make gain in the world. Moreover, having offered the cup of fornication to drink, she seduces the kings and inhabitants of the earth, made drunk, into fornicating with her monstrously. So that woman, acting in the place of God and as though she were God, entices those kings and inhabitants of the earth to love, worship and in every way attribute to her those things which belong to God alone, in place of the living God whom they have left behind. She does this for the sake of catching divine honour, seeking gain, and earthly advantage and profit.

units.la: XI. Manifestum enim est, scortationem spiritualem ejusmodi Meretrici huic competere, qua non tantum à Deo summo & incommutabili bono se perfidiosè avertat, & ad creaturas, ceu supremum quoddam Numen, si non professione aperta amoris, cultus, religiosi obsequii, (quomodo fœdissima quandoque meretrix perfidiam tegit, & operata iniquitatem, os tamen abstergit, & iniquitatem se patrasse negat) at reipsa tamen se convertat, atque sic non in Deo vivo, sed in Dei vivi operibus non tam glorietur, delicietur, quàm lasciviat turpissimè: Sed etiam ipsa se horribili quadam metamorphosi in Deum permutet, & fascino quodam philtróque propinato ad se, vice Dei & Christi amandum, colendum, glorificandum, Reges & incolas terræ, in se scilicet deliciaturos, & appetitum voluptatémque omnem exsatiaturos, invitet, iisque se cupidissimè prostituat.
units.tr: XI. For it is clear that such a spiritual fornication belongs to this harlot, by which she not only treacherously turns herself away from God, the highest and unchanging good, and turns to creatures as to some supreme deity. She does this even if not by an open profession of love, worship and religious obedience (just as the most foul harlot sometimes hides her faithlessness, and, having committed iniquity, wipes her mouth and denies that she has done wrong), but in fact she does turn. Thus she glories and delights not so much in the living God as in the works of the living God, and wantons most shamefully. Indeed she herself, by a certain horrible metamorphosis, transforms herself into God, and by a kind of charm and offered love-potion she invites the kings and inhabitants of the earth, who are to take their delight in her and satisfy every appetite and pleasure, to love, worship and glorify her in place of God and Christ. And she most eagerly prostitutes herself to them.

units.la: XII. Unde consequens est duplicem, probéque distinguendam, idololatriam meretrici huic competere. Prior illa est, qua religiosum cultum ipsa creaturis impertitur. Posterior, eáque præcipua, quæ hîc spectatur, qua se ipsam pro Numine venditans, ad cultum, venerationem sui Reges & incolas terræ invitat, iisque adeó procumbens satietatem cupiditatum, deliciarum, bonorum omnium, temporalis puta & æternæ salutis promittit. Proin non simpliciter πόρνη, meretrix, sed μήτηρ mater omnium scortationum, poculum aureum plenum abominationibus & impuritate scortationis suæ manu gestans, adeóque philtro quodam ad scortandum secum, in se deliciandum luxuriandumque studiosissimè invitans, inducitur. Quis autem dubitet hanc fœdissimam omnium idololatriam esse, qua quis non tam ipsè creaturas colit, quàm ceu Numen quoddam Divinitatis particeps, & Divinitatem quandam creaturis impertiens, promissa quinetiam felicitate temporali & æterna, creaturis se colendum, adorandum, glorificandum liberaliter offert, prostituitque.
units.tr: XII. It follows that two kinds of idolatry, which must be carefully distinguished, belong to this harlot. The first is that by which she herself pays religious worship to creatures. The second, and the principal one, which is the one considered here, is that by which she, offering herself as a god, invites kings and the inhabitants of the earth to worship and venerate her, and, prostrating herself before them, promises them a satisfying of their desires, pleasures and every good, both temporal and eternal salvation. So she is depicted not simply as harlot [πόρνη], but as mother [μήτηρ] of all fornications, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurity of her fornication, and inviting with a kind of charm, most eagerly, to fornicate with her, to take her delight and to revel in her. Who could doubt that this is the most foul of all idolatries, in which a person does not so much worship creatures themselves, as offer and surrender himself freely to be worshipped, adored and glorified by creatures, as if he were some divinity sharing in the godhead and bestowing a certain divinity on creatures, even promising them temporal and eternal happiness?

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: XIII. Sic meretrix convenit plane cum Homine illo peccati, filio perditionis, ἀντικείμενον Adversario Christi scilicet famosissimo, de quo S. Paulus 2 Thess. II. 4. testatur, quod se efferat ὥστε εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὡς θεὸν καθίσαι super omnem, qui Deus aut Numen dicitur; adeò ut in templo Dei tanquam Deus sedeat, præ se ferens se esse Deum. Hoc scilicet proprie est esse matrem scortationum, & poculo scortationis Reges & incolas terræ ad scortandum secum invitare, quod Apostolus dixit efferre se supra omne quod Deus, aut Numen dicitur, in Templo Dei instar Dei sedere & divinitatem præ se ferre, hoc est, non ad Deum vivum, sed ad se loco Dei promittentem cœli thesauros & felicia quæque, colendum, glorificandum, adeóque sagenæ suæ sacrificandum, reti suo adolendum, invitare liberaliter, & pellicere potenter.
units.tr: XIII. So the harlot plainly agrees with that man of sin, son of perdition, adversary [ἀντικείμενον], namely the most notorious opponent of Christ, of whom St Paul testifies (2 Thess. 2:4) that he exalts himself so as to sit in the temple of God as God [ὥστε εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ ὡς θεὸν καθίσαι] above everything that is called God or divinity; so that he sits in the temple of God as if he were God, displaying that he is God. This is properly what it is to be mother of fornications, and with the cup of fornication to invite kings and the inhabitants of the earth to fornicate with her. What the Apostle said was that he raises himself above everything that is called God or divinity, sits in the Temple of God in the manner of God and displays his divinity; that is, he invites people, not to the living God, but to himself, who in place of God promises the treasures of heaven and every happy thing, to worship and glorify him and so to offer themselves as sacrifice to his net, to burn incense to his drag-net; he invites them freely and entices them powerfully.

units.la: XIV. Pòrro Angelus Dei Apoc. xvii. 18. Babylonem illam magnam, matrem scortationum & abominationum definit πόλιν μεγάλην, ἔχουσαι Βασιλέα ἅτινα τῶν Βασιλέων τῆς γῆς Civitatem magnam, habentem regnum super Reges terræ. Sensus duplex esse potest. Prior, quòd ea Civitas, quæ S. Johannis tempore Regnum in Reges terræ habuit, quandoque in magnam meretricem illam degeneratura sit. Posterior, quòd Babylon illa Civitas sit, quæ Regnum in Reges terræ habitura est. Utrque sensus commodus sit licet, πόλις tamen seu Civitas illa, Romana licet, Romæ tamen mœnibus includi non debet. Tametsi enim Apoc. xvii. 9. Septem montes Romam Urbem mœnibus inclusam arguant, eosdem tamen symbolicè septem Reges, seu populos totidem significare, versus 10. & 11. statim sequentes abundè testantur. Certè πόλις Civitas Romana montibus Romæ non fuit alligata, cùm Cives Romani etiam in Provinciis nati fuerint, uti S. Pauli Tharsensis Cilicis licet, Civis tamen Romani exemplum fidem facit. Ad eandem nempe Civitatem pertinent, qui eodem jure utuntur, ubicunque terrarum sint. Bestia quoque ita in septem urbis Romanæ montibus habitat, ut iis tamen includatur minimè, cùm & capita nonnulla, & cornua ejus sese extra urbem Romanam protendant.
units.tr: XIV. Moreover, the angel of God (Rev. 17:18) describes that great Babylon, mother of fornications and abominations, as the great city, having a kingdom over the kings of the earth. The sense can be twofold. The first is that the city which in St John's time held dominion over the kings of the earth would at some time degenerate into that great harlot. The second is that Babylon is the city which is to hold dominion over the kings of the earth. Although either sense may be acceptable, that city, Roman though it be, ought not to be confined within the walls of Rome. For although Rev. 17:9, the seven mountains, indicate the city of Rome enclosed within its walls, the verses 10 and 11 immediately following amply testify that the same mountains symbolically signify seven kings, or as many peoples. Certainly the Roman city [πόλις] was not bound to the mountains of Rome, since Roman citizens were also born in the provinces, as the example of St Paul of Tarsus in Cilicia makes clear: he was a Roman citizen. For those who enjoy the same right, wherever they are on earth, belong to the same city. The beast too so dwells on the seven mountains of the city of Rome that it is in no way confined by them, since both some of its heads and its horns stretch out beyond the city of Rome.

units.la: XV. Hinc adeò & Græci, & Latini Civitatem ab Urbe distinguunt. Græcis enim quandóque non locum mœnibus cinctum, sed πολιτείαν jus ipsum Civium, sive eodem, sive diversis etiam locis habitantium, denotat. Ita Eustathius ad Iliad. ϱ. οἱ δὴ πολλοὶ φασὶ πόλιν μὲν τὴν πολιτείαν ἄεν δὲ τὴ τάχ. Veteres Civitatem vocant πολιτείαν jus civitatis; urbem verò mœnia. Aristoteles Polit. lib. 1. cap. 2. ἡ ἐκ πολλῶν κωμῶν κοινωνία πόλις. Civitas vocatur ex pluribus vicinitatibus, communitas perfecta. Thucydides lib. vii. Ἀνδρῶν γὰρ πόλις, καὶ ἡ τείχη. Viri Civitas sunt, non mœnia. Tacitus de moribus Germanorum, civitates eos habuisse, urbes non habuisse, sed sparsim habitasse scribit. Cæsar de Bello Gallico lib. 1. Omnis Civitas Helvetia in quatuor pagos divisa est. Lib. vi. Parisii senonibus civitatem patrum memoria conjunxerant. Rutilius de Romana urbe:
units.tr: XV. Hence both Greeks and Latins also distinguish the city from the town. For among the Greeks the word city sometimes denotes not a place surrounded by walls, but the right of citizenship itself, whether of those dwelling in the same place or even in different places. So Eustathius on the Iliad 9 says: the ancients call the city [πόλιν] the citizenship [πολιτείαν], but the town [ἄστυ] the walls. Aristotle, Politics book 1 chapter 2: the community formed from many villages is a city [πόλις]; a city is called a perfect community formed from several neighbourhoods. Thucydides, book 7: a city [πόλις] is men, and the walls are not. Tacitus, in his On the Manners of the Germans, writes that they had civitates, but no towns, and lived scattered. Caesar, in his Gallic War, book 1: all the state of the Helvetii is divided into four cantons. Book 6: within living memory the Parisii had joined their civitas to the Senones. Rutilius, on the city of Rome:

units.la: Fecisti patriam diversis gentibus unam,
units.tr: You made one fatherland out of diverse peoples,

units.la: Profuit injustis te dominante capi.
units.tr: It profited the conquered to be ruled by you.

units.la: Dumque offers victis proprii consortia juris
units.tr: And while you offer to the vanquished the fellowship of your own law,

units.la: Urbem fecisti, quod prius Orbis erat.
units.tr: you made a city of what had been the world.

units.la: Unde Civibus loco motis licet, civitatem ipsam non ilico deficere, Politici etiam scisciunt: Ita Athenienses Athenis direptis in naves aufugerunt, eò quòd Oraculum respondisset: Civitatem Atticam fore salvam in muris ligneis. Megalopolitani quoque, Cleomene eos invadente urbem deseruisse, civitatem secum abduxisse dicuntur. Pompejus denique apud Dionysium lib. 41. cùm ducentos senatores & meliorem civium Romanorum partem Roma secedere audivisset, non in parietibus Civitatem esse dixit. Plutarcham in rem convehere desino, cùm res ex iis quæ dicta sunt, clara efficiatur.
units.tr: Hence, when citizens are moved from their place, political writers also hold that the city itself does not immediately cease to exist. Thus the Athenians, when Athens had been plundered, fled to their ships, because the oracle had answered: the Attic city will be safe within wooden walls. The Megalopolitans too are said to have abandoned their town when Cleomenes invaded it, taking the city with them. Finally, Pompey, as Dionysius reports in book 41, when he heard that two hundred senators and the better part of the Roman citizens were withdrawing from Rome, said that the city was not in the walls. I will stop bringing Plutarch into the matter, since the point is clear enough from what has been said.

units.la: XVI. Neque etiam significatus hic in S. literis propheticis hospes & insitatus est Cant. v. 2. Sponsa sic loquens inducitur: surgam nunc & circuibo בעיר per Civitatem, per plateas, & per loca lata quæram quem diligit anima mea. Ubi Civitatem mœnibus Cinctam nemo intelligit, nisi qui Christum sponsum civitati ejusmodi includere velit. Par ratio est loci Cap. v. 7. Invenerunt me Custodes הסובבים בעיר circumeuntes Civitatem. Ita Apoc. xi. 2. Gentes calcaturæ dicuntur ἐπὶ τῆς πλατείας τῆς πόλεως τῆς μεγάλης in platea Civitatis magnæ, quæ spiritualiter nuncupatur Sodoma & Ægyptus, ubi Christus crucifixus est. Insuper Cap. iii, 12. Vincenti nomen inscribendum dicitur Dei, καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τῆς πόλεως τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς καινῆς Ιερουσαλήμ: & nomen Civitatis illius Dei, nova Hierosolyma. Denique Apoc. xx.9. Gogus & Magogus ascendisse dicuntur in planitiem terræ, & cinxisse τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἡγαπημένην Civitatem illam dilectam. Quibus locis nomine πόλεως Civitatis textum quendam, vel ordinem domorum materialium muris circumdatum significari, nemo castus peritúsque Scripturæ interpres affirmaverit.
units.tr: XVI. Nor is this sense foreign and newly grafted into the prophetic books of Scripture. In Song 5:2 the bride is introduced speaking thus: I will rise now and go about the city [בעיר], through the streets and broad places, and seek him whom my soul loves. Here no one understands the city as enclosed by walls, unless he wishes to shut Christ the bridegroom up in such a city. The case is the same in Song 5:7: the watchmen who go about [הסובבים] the city found me. So in Rev. 11:2 the Gentiles are said to tread on the street of the great city [ἐπὶ τῆς πλατείας τῆς πόλεως τῆς μεγάλης], in the street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where Christ was crucified. Further, Rev. 3:12, to the one who conquers it is said that the name of God is to be written upon him, and the name of the city of God, the new Jerusalem: and the name of that city of God, new Jerusalem. Finally, Rev. 20:9 says that Gog and Magog went up onto the breadth of the earth and surrounded the beloved city [τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἡγαπημένην], that beloved city. In these places no competent and honest interpreter of Scripture would affirm that the word city [πόλεως] signifies some fabric or row of material houses surrounded by walls.

units.la: XVII. Sic Babylon erit πόλις Civitas, hoc est, multitudo sociata per caput aut capita, utens potestate imperandi, tanquam jure metropoleos; & ibi ubi est metropolis illius Imperii, & quocunque Imperium illud extenditur. Dominantem enim, seu imperitantem Civitatem intelligi, vel inde apparet; quod Apoc. xvii. 3. Mulier καθημένη sedens super Bestia inducitur. Regit igitur Bestiam haud aliter, quam eques in equo sedens eum regit, subigitque pro lubitu, uti quidem etiam Apoc. vi. 2. 4. 5. 8. Equites in equis sedentes, 'eósque moderantes & ad obsequium flectentes memorantur.
units.tr: XVII. Thus Babylon will be city [πόλις], that is, a multitude united under one head or several heads, exercising power to command, as by the right of a metropolis; and it will be where the metropolis of that empire is, and wherever that empire extends. That a ruling, or commanding, city is meant is apparent from this, that in Rev. 17:3 the woman is introduced sitting [καθημένη] upon the beast. She therefore governs the beast no differently from a horseman sitting on a horse, who guides it and subdues it at will, as Rev. 6:2, 4, 5, 8 also mention horsemen sitting on horses and controlling them and bringing them to obedience.

units.la: XVIII. Neque tamen societas. & multitudo illa dominans intelligitur hominum politicorum vel fecularium, qui civili potestate utuntur, sed religiosa potiùs principum scilicet alterius generis, quales apud Israëlitas שרי קדש Principes sanctitatis, seu Sanctuarii, dicebantur. Vocatur enim Civitas hæc πόρνη meretrix. At potestatem politicam, five parva five magna, five regia, five δεμοκρατικὴ aut popularis fit, per fe meretricem nemo appellaverit. Quamvis imperium civile falsam religionem exercens ex accidenti meretricem vocari posse, non abnuo. Atqui Babylon non simpliciter meretrix appellatur, sed ad scortandum etiam, adeóque religionem falsam exercendam Reges & incolas terræ propinato fcortationis poculo seducere dicitur. Unde colligere est, Civitatem eam sibi jus docendi & præscribendi religionem arrogare. Quod in civitatibus fine Pontificibus, flaminibus, sacrorum antistitibus fieri non solet. Insuper Apoc. xvii. 18. Mulier illa vocatur Civitas illa Magna, quæ habet Regnum in Reges terræ. Genuina igitur ejus proprietas est, imperare Regibus terræ, adeóque sibi Principes politicos subjicere. Civitas verò & Regnum illud, cui Principes Politici subjiciuntur, Regno Politico utique contradiftinguitur, adeóque Ecclesiasticum esse intelligitur.
units.tr: XVIII. Nor, however, is that dominant society and multitude understood to be of political or secular men, who exercise civil power, but rather of a religious kind, namely of princes of another sort, who among the Israelites were called princes of holiness [שרי קדש], or of the sanctuary. For this city is called harlot [πόρνη], harlot. But no one would call political power, whether small or great, whether royal, democratic [δεμοκρατικὴ] or popular, in itself a harlot. Although I do not deny that a civil government practising a false religion may by accident be called a harlot, yet Babylon is not simply called a harlot, but is said to seduce kings and the inhabitants of the earth, by the offered cup of fornication, even to fornicate with her and so to practise false religion. From this it may be gathered that that city claims for itself the right to teach and prescribe religion. This is not usually done in civil states without pontiffs, flamens and chief priests of the sacred rites. Moreover, Rev. 17:18 calls that woman the great city, which has a kingdom over the kings of the earth. Her genuine characteristic, therefore, is to rule over the kings of the earth, and so to subject political princes to herself. But that city and kingdom to which political princes are subjected is certainly distinguished from a political kingdom, and so is understood to be ecclesiastical.

units.la: XIX. Civitas porrò illa, seu multitudo per caput aut capita sociata dominans religiosa, adeóque Hierarchia quædam Romana cùm Ethnica non fit, uti supra demonstravimus, consequens est, ut Christiana; hoc est, nomine Christi, sed in mendacio, non in veritate, utens, adeóque speciosis prætextibus, & splendida quadam apparentia imponens, sic videlicet, ut prætextu Christi, authoritatis & nominis Divini aliam authoritatem & potestatem loquendi, qua homines ad obedientiam obligentur, meretrix introducat, intelligatur. Quod inprimis inde liquet, quòd prophetia Apoc. xi. 7. 9. 11. xiii. 7. xvii. 14. arguit, simul nomen Christi & meretricis, Agni & Bestiæ habentis comua instar Agni, per omnes gentes prædicari debuisse. Quod fieri non potuit, nisi meretrix illa nomine Christi & Agni ad authoritatem & regnum in se derivandum abuteretur.
units.tr: XIX. Furthermore, that city, or multitude, ruling in religious matters under one head or several heads, and so a certain Roman hierarchy, since it is not pagan (as we have shown above), must be Christian. That is, it uses the name of Christ, but in falsehood and not in truth, and so it imposes itself with specious pretexts and a splendid show. In this way the harlot is understood to introduce, under the pretext of Christ, the authority and name of God, another authority and power of teaching by which men are bound to obedience. This is first shown by the prophecy at Rev. 11:7, 9, 11; 13:7; 17:14, which argues that the name of Christ and of the harlot, of the Lamb and of the Beast that has horns like a lamb, must have been proclaimed among all nations. This could not have happened unless the harlot abused the name of Christ and of the Lamb to draw authority and kingdom to herself.

units.la: XX. Atque id magis etiam consideratio Bestiæ meretricem portantis confirmat. De qua falsas interpretationes cùm supra perstrinxerimus abundè, firmisque rationibus rejecerimus, è re nunc fuerit indefinitam quandam ejusdem explicationem aggredi.
units.tr: XX. Consideration of the Beast carrying the harlot confirms this even more. Since we have already touched abundantly on the false interpretations of it above and rejected them on firm grounds, it will now be appropriate to set out an undefined explanation of it.

units.la: XXI. Stylo Prophetico, uti ex Daniel. cap. vii. inprimis colligitur הוה ἡ ϑηρίον Bestia non unum hominem quempiam, sive regnantem, sive obedientem, sed multitudinem hominum regnum aliquod constituentem, & hoc quidem loco parentem, servientem (Mulier enim in Bestia sedens, adeóque eidem dominans, in servitutem eam redligens inducitur) significat. Certè S. Johannes ipse Apoc. xi. 8. Bestiæ πλιν μεγάλω Civitatem magnam tribuit. Quæ quidem Civitas magna, Bestiæ ditio, non unum aliquod pomœriis suis inclusum oppidum (ita enim Geometrarum esset Civitatem indicare, quæ orbe terrarum maximo pomœrio inclusa foret) sed ditionem amplam, & imperium ejusmodi, in cujus omnibus partibus sunt Cives eodem jure, ab uno Capite ac senatu pendentes. Etenim mulier illa sedens in Bestia sedere dicitur Ἐπὶ τ' ὑδάτων πολλῶν super aquis multis Apoc. xvii. 1. quæ mox versu 15. λαοὶ καὶ ὄχλοι, ἢ γλῶσσαι, ἢ ἔθνη populi, & turbæ & linguæ & gentes exponuntur. Unde colligere clarissimè est, eam multitudinem, quæ Bestia dicitur, & in qua Mulier sedet, esse in multis populis, turbis, gentibus & linguis.
units.tr: XXI. In the prophetic style, as is chiefly gathered from Daniel chapter 7, the beast [חיה, θηρίον] signifies not a single man, whether ruling or obeying, but a multitude of men constituting some kingdom, and here, indeed, a ruling and serving one (for the woman is introduced sitting on the beast and so dominating it, and dragging it into servitude). Certainly St John himself at Rev. 11:8 ascribes the great city [πόλιν μεγάλην] to the beast. This great city, the beast's dominion, is not one town enclosed within its own walls (for to indicate a city enclosed by the greatest boundary of the whole earth would be the language of geometers), but a wide dominion and empire of this kind, in all parts of which the citizens, under the same law, depend on one head and senate. For that woman sitting on the beast is said to sit over many waters [ἐπὶ τῶν ὑδάτων πολλῶν] at Rev. 17:1, which are soon explained at verse 15 as peoples and multitudes, or tongues, or nations [λαοὶ καὶ ὄχλοι, ἢ γλῶσσαι, ἢ ἔθνη]. From this it is very clearly gathered that that multitude, which is called the beast and in which the woman sits, exists among many peoples, crowds, nations and tongues.

units.la: XXII. Typum ejus rei præbet Roma vetus, quæ toti ferè Orbi imperitans, in Orbe universo fuit. Neque enim nisi per Romanos Romanorum Imperium teneri potuit. Hinc Præsides, Proconsules, Legati, Imperatores, Legiones, Mercatores, Publicani in omnibus Provinciis erant. Sicut igitur Romanus Senatus cum Principe, populo Romano, Romanus verò Populus gentibus superpositus fuit regendis, subjcendis: ita Mulier populo suo, & populus ejus multis populis ita & interest & præest, ut multi populi gentes & linguæ ipsi serviant.
units.tr: XXII. Ancient Rome provides a type of this thing, which, ruling over almost the whole world, existed throughout the entire world. For the Roman Empire could not be held except through Romans. Hence there were governors, proconsuls, legates, emperors, legions, merchants and tax collectors in all the provinces. Just as the Roman Senate, with the prince, was set over the Roman people, and the Roman people over the nations, to rule and subdue them, so the woman both takes part in and presides over her people, and her people over many peoples, so that many peoples, nations and tongues serve them.

units.la: XXIII. Hanc porro Bestiam, seu multitudinem hominum animalium Meretrici seu Hierarchiæ dominanti obedientem, esse populum non gentilem vel simpliciter infidelem qualemcunque, sed veri Dei & Christi nomen præ se ferentem, adeóque שפתי חלקות כלב ולא labiæ blanditiarum cum corde & corde loquentes Psalm. xii. 3. Apocalypsis ipsa dubitare neutiquam finit. Bestia enim illa Apoc. xiii. 2. successit Draconi, ejúsque potestatem & thronum
units.tr: XXIII. Moreover, that this Beast, that is, the multitude of men obedient to the harlot or to the ruling hierarchy, is a people not simply Gentile or in any way unbelieving, but one that bears the name of the true God and Christ, and so speaks with smooth lips, with heart and heart [שפתי חלקות כלב ולא] (Ps. 12:3), the Apocalypse itself by no means allows us to doubt. For that Beast at Rev. 13:2 succeeded the Dragon, and took over its power and throne.

units.la: Lines marked with side notes in italic type: "Bestia est multitudo hominum Meretrici, seu Hierarchiæ domínanti obedientem" etc. thronum occupavit. Quòd si igitur Draco, uti supra veritati dedimus, est Sathanas populi Romani ipsum palam adorantis viribus & potestate armatus vestitúsque: utique Bestia, cui Draco thronum suum cessit, est multitudo Christiano nomine non in veritate ovans, eandémque potestatem usurpans. Sicut igitur populus Romanus Diabolum palam adorans, falsos Deos nominans, & Christianam religionem oppugnans Draconi septem capitum accenseatur: ita procedente tempore, quando Draco Bestiæ thronum resignavit, populus eidem succedaneus passim Christianum nomen præ se ferens, verba fundamenti loquens, audiens, vel dici permittens, at de cætero ea vel non intelligens, & in Christum fide recta & sincera non credens, sed potius opiniones hominum erroneas sequens, auctoritatémque humanam nominans, adeóque populus Christianus hypocriticus Deo vero & Christo mentiens, Bestia est. Neque enim Christianus est, quisquis Christum nomine profitetur, juxta S. Augustini etiam sententiam, sapienter ita Enchirid. cap. 5. scribentis: Si diligenter, quæ ad Christum pertinent, cogitentur, nomine tenus invenitur Christus apud quoslibet hæreticos, qui se Christianos vocari volunt, re verò ipsa non est apud eos.
units.tr: Marginal note in italic: "The beast is a multitude of men obedient to the harlot, or to the ruling hierarchy," and so on, took over the throne. If, then, the Dragon, as we have granted above to the truth, is Satan himself, armed and clothed with the powers and authority of the Roman people who openly worship him, then certainly the Beast, to which the Dragon yielded its throne, is a multitude boasting in the Christian name but not in truth, and claiming the same power. Therefore, just as the Roman people, who openly worship the devil, call false gods their own, and attack the Christian religion, are counted among the Dragon of seven heads, so, as time went on, when the Dragon gave up its throne to the Beast, a people succeeding it, bearing the Christian name everywhere, speaking, hearing or allowing the words of the foundation to be spoken, but in other respects not understanding them, not believing in Christ with a right and sincere faith, but rather following erroneous opinions of men and invoking human authority, and so a hypocritical Christian people lying to the true God and Christ, is the Beast. For he is not a Christian who professes Christ only in name, as St Augustine also judged, writing wisely in Enchiridion, chap. 5: If the things that pertain to Christ are carefully considered, Christ is found by name only among any heretics who wish to be called Christians, but in reality he is not among them.

units.la: XXIV. Amplius id ipsum antithesis Civitatis sanctæ demonstrat. Veri enim, ἀνώτερον & ἀγίαν Christiani, sive firmi, sive adulti, sive infirmi, seu pueri in fide, constituunt haud dubiè πλὴν ἁγίαν Civitatem illam sanctam, cujus thronus est in cœlis, quæque adeò se soli Christo Domino, Regi & Capiti ad dextram Dei Patris sedenti regendam permittit. Draco verò cum nominibus falsorum Deorum omnique idolorum vetustorum pompa, & χρησμῶν Oraculorum præstigiis abiit, & throno suo cessit. Quid igitur Bestiæ reliquum est nisi populus Christianus ψεῦδος μὲν, thronum habens in terra, potentiam civitatis
units.tr: XXIV. Furthermore, the antithesis of the holy city demonstrates the same thing. For true Christians, whether strong, mature, weak, or children in faith, undoubtedly constitute that holy city [πλὴν ἁγίαν Civitatem], the higher and holy one, whose throne is in heaven, and which therefore allows itself to be ruled by Christ the Lord alone, the King and Head sitting at the right hand of God the Father. The Dragon, however, departed together with the names of false gods and the whole pomp of ancient idols, and the deceits of oracles [χρησμῶν], and gave up its throne. What then remains of the Beast except a Christian people, false [ψεῦδος μὲν], having its throne on earth and the power of the city

units.la: quod etiam antithesis Civitatis sancta, nec non Bestia posterior A- poc. xiij. 11. & argum. tatis Draconis possidens, & per id, quòd nomine Christi gloriatus licet, veram tamen fidem non habet, à civitate fanéta distinctus? Et quomodo non Bestia populum falsò nominatum Christianum significabit, cum posterior Beftia, quæ Apoc. xiii. 11. &c. describitur, coram priore omnem potestatem ejus faciens, Cornua gerere ὅμοια ἀρνίῳ · similia cornibus Agni dicatur? Quod nihil aliud quàm similitudinem Agni in hypocrisi, five usurpationem subdolam eorum, quæ vero Agno competunt; five cornua illa sint duo testamenta, uti Primafius explicat; five potestas aperiendi & claudendi, significare potest.
units.tr: which is also the antithesis of the holy city, and the later Beast of Rev. 13:11 and the following, possessing the power of the Dragon, and distinguished from the holy city through this, that although it boasts in the name of Christ, it does not have the true faith? And how would the Beast not signify a people falsely named Christian, when the later Beast, which is described at Rev. 13:11 and following, making all the power of the former its own, is said to have horns like [ὅμοια ἀρνίῳ] the horns of the Lamb? This signifies nothing other than a likeness of the Lamb in hypocrisy, or a deceitful usurpation of the things that belong truly to the Lamb. Whether those horns are the two testaments, as Primasius explains, or the power of opening and shutting, they can signify this.

units.la: XXV. Quin imò Apoc. xi. 2. non obscurè indigitatur materia, ex qua Bestia hæc conflata est, scilicet ἔθνη τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἀχίαν πατρὶ φ.. dvo, gentes, quibus exterius atrium Templi datum est, calcantes Civitatem fanctam menses quadraginta duos. quod tempus mensium quadraginta duorum idem est cum tempore, quo Apoc. xiii. 5. Bestia prior μινῦω facere, rem suam gerere, proesperare dicitur. Unde gentes atrium exterius possidentes, Bestiæ materiam esse colligitur. Quid autem gentes atrium exterius possidentes, & civitatem sanctam calcantes aliud sunt, quàm Zizania tritico permixta, Christiani λεγόμενοι, Deum verum, Christum ore confitentes, reapse & opere abnegantes? Nam fecundum id, quod revera sunt, vocantur ἔθνη gentes. Quid enim aliud Christiani hypocritæ, homines ψυχικοὶ animales sunt, quàm gentes, veri Dei & Christi abnegatores? Secundùm id verò, quod nominantur, & esse videri volunt, versari ἐν αὐλῇ in atrio Templi, & civitatem sanctam calcare dicuntur. Quod haud dubiè faciunt illi, qui cum fidelibus quoad id, quod hypocritis, & verè fidelibus commune, adeóque externum fere & terrestre tantum est, conjunguntur, nomine Christi, leftione Scripturarum, verbis fundamenti, sacramentis, loco congregationis communi cum fidelibus utuntur, Συνάχθῶσιν unà cum fidelibus epulantur 2 Pet. 11. 13. qui. denique non tantùm ita in atrio exteriore & civitate sancta versantur, sed etiam civitatem sanctam πατῆσιν calcant, hoc est, eandem graviter premunt, & adversus verè fideles infestos sese gerunt. Nunquam enim non qui secundùm carnem est filius, eum qui secundùm spiritum est, persequitur Gal. iv. 29.
units.tr: XXV. Indeed, Rev. 11:2 plainly points out the material from which this Beast has been formed, namely the nations, to whom the outer court of the Temple has been given, [who] will trample the holy city [τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἁγίαν πατήσουσιν] for forty-two months. This period of forty-two months is the same as the time at which the former Beast, at Rev. 13:5, is said to act [ποιῆσαι], to carry on its affairs and to prosper. Hence the nations possessing the outer court are gathered to be the material of the Beast. But what are the nations possessing the outer court and trampling the holy city, other than tares mixed with wheat, those called Christians [λεγόμενοι], who confess the true God and Christ with their mouths, but in reality and in deed deny them? For according to what they really are, they are called nations [ἔθνη]. For what else are hypocritical Christians, men of the soul, animal [ψυχικοὶ], than nations, deniers of the true God and Christ? But according to what they are named and wish to seem to be, they are said to dwell in the court [ἐν αὐλῇ] of the Temple and to tread the holy city. Those who join with the faithful in what is common to hypocrites and truly faithful, and so is almost only external and earthly, certainly do this: they use the name of Christ, the reading of the Scriptures, the words of the foundation, the sacraments, and the place of the common assembly with the faithful, gather together [Συνάχθῶσιν] and feast along with the faithful [epulantur] (2 Pet. 2:13). Finally, they not only dwell in this way in the outer court and the holy city, but also trample [πατῆσιν] the holy city, that is, press it heavily and conduct themselves hostilely against the truly faithful. For he who is born according to the flesh has always persecuted him who is born according to the Spirit (Gal. 4:29).

units.la: XXVI. Typus hujus rei fuit Israël carnalis.
units.tr: XXVI. The carnal Israel was a type of this thing.

units.la: Etenim populo, qui ceu impurus typicè ab altari removebatur, Templi partem eam, in qua altare erat, quæque קדש ἅγιον carnalis Sanctum appellabatur, ingredi nefas erat. Deus enim eum טמא impurum declaravit in oblationibus suis Ezech. xx. 26. Ejus loco sanctificavit filios Levi, futuros sacerdotale genus, qui adoraturi & sacrificaturi Sanctum ingrederentur, cultùmque divinitus præscriptum celebrarent; Pontifice quotannis semel etiam ipsum Sanctum Sanctorum ingrediente, & injunctum sibi munus obeunte. Qui igitur in atrio stabat, populus Dei licet, impurus tamen typicè & legaliter censebatur. Qui verò sanctum ingrediebantur, Sacerdotes altari devoti, sancti & puri typicè & legaliter censebantur. Ad typum huncce alludens Apocalypsis externam Ecclesiæ Christianæ post Draconis imperium communionem Templo Solomonis typico comparatam ita distribuit, ut partem, atrium scilicet foras projiciendum gentibus, hoc est, Christianis hypocritis, non legaliter tantùm, & typicè (neque enim typum & antitypum in omnibus congruere necessum est) sed verè impuris, impiis & merè animalibus in atrio versantibus, adeoque in externo cultu cum verè fidelibus communicantibus: partem verò sanctis, non in atrio duntaxat, sed Sancto ipsò consistentibus adorantibúsque, & cum vero altari Christo, fide haud simulata communicantibus tribuat. Cúmque tempus
units.tr: For the people, who as unclean were typically removed from the altar, were forbidden to enter that part of the Temple where the altar stood, which was called the carnal Sanctum [קדש ἅγιον]. God declared them unclean [טמא] in their offerings, Ezek. 20:26. In their place he consecrated the sons of Levi, who were to become the priestly race, to enter the Sanctum to worship and to sacrifice and to perform the worship prescribed by God. The High Priest, once a year, entered the Holy of Holies itself and discharged the duty laid upon him. So whoever stood in the outer court, though he was God's people, was reckoned typically and legally unclean. Those who entered the Sanctum, the priests devoted to the altar, were reckoned typically and legally holy and clean. Alluding to this type, the Apocalypse so divides the outward fellowship of the Christian Church after the dragon's rule, which it compares with Solomon's typical Temple, that it assigns the part to the outer court, to be cast out to the Gentiles, that is, to Christian hypocrites. These are not merely legally and typically unclean (for type and antitype need not agree in every point) but truly unclean, impious, and purely animal, who remain in the court and so share in the outward worship with those who are truly faithful. It assigns the other part to the saints, who stand and worship not only in the court but in the Sanctum itself, and who share in the true altar, Christ, with unfeigned faith. And when the time...

units.la: {y} Ejus rei typus proponitur Israël carnalis. gentibus civitatemSanctam calcantibus constitutum Apoc. xiii. Bestiae tribuat, adeoque gentes & Bestiam Synonyma Spiritus S. faciat; liquidò inde, Bestiam multitudinem hominum oretenus Christianum nomen confitentium, fidémque in Christum simulantium esse, conficitur.
units.tr: {y} The type of this thing is set forth in the carnal Israel. The Gentiles, who are placed to tread down the holy city, Rev. 13, the Beast is assigned to them, and so he makes the Gentiles and the Beast synonyms of the Holy Spirit. From this it is clearly concluded that the Beast is a multitude of men who profess the Christian name with their lips and feign faith in Christ.

units.la: XXVII. Quae igitur Ἀπ. quoad sensum indefinitum saltem, sit Babylon, seu Meretrix, quae Bestia, abundè jam colliquescit. Babylon scilicet seu Meretrix est Civitas magna dominans, seu Hierarchia Christiano nomine abutens & mysterii religionisque praetextu imperans populo pro Christiano se venditanti, & se illi religiose cum omni sua potentia subjicienti. Bestia verò est multitudo hominum animalium terrestrem potentiam obtinens, nomen Christianum profess, & religionis mysteriique causa se Hierarchiae Dominanti subjiciens, eique religiose obsequens.
units.tr: XXVII. What Babylon, or the Harlot, and what the Beast are in the Apocalypse, at least in an indefinite sense, is now already largely clear. Babylon, or the Harlot, is the great city that rules, that is, the Hierarchy which abuses the Christian name and, under the pretext of mystery and religion, commands the people who present themselves as Christian and submit to it religiously with all their power. The Beast, however, is a multitude of men holding earthly power, professing the Christian name, subjecting themselves for the sake of religion and mystery to the ruling Hierarchy, and obeying it religiously.

units.la: XXVIII. Habitus Mulieris & Bestiae externus à Spiritu S. Apoc. xvii. 3. 4. describitur, ut Mulier πορφυρᾶ μίνη amicta purpurâ & coccino, & inaurata auro ac lapide pretiosò & margaritis. Bestia similiter Coccinea dicitur. Coccinea utraque statuitur, sive quia Mulieris Bestiae insidentis exterior etiam vestitutus coccineus est (revera enim Spiritus S. characteribus ejusmodi perspicuis rem obscuram lectori etiam simplici insinuare voluit) sive quia per professionem externam fidei in Christum videtur Coccineo sanguinis ejus colore tincta, sive quia sanguinis Christi & sanctorum rea est. Neque quidquam obstare videtur, quò minus singula Spiritus S. voce illa figurare intenderit.
units.tr: XXVIII. The outward appearance of the Woman and of the Beast is described by the Holy Spirit, Rev. 17:3–4: the Woman is clothed in purple [πορφυρᾶ μίνη], purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stone and pearls. The Beast is likewise called scarlet. Scarlet is said of both, either because the outer garment of the Woman who sits on the Beast is also scarlet (for the Holy Spirit wished to suggest the hidden matter to even the simple reader by such clear marks), or because through her outward profession of faith in Christ she seems dyed with the scarlet colour of his blood, or because she is guilty of the blood of Christ and of the saints. Nothing seems to stand in the way of the view that the Holy Spirit intended to represent each detail by that word.

units.la: XXIX. Amictus quoque Mulieris tum ad literam, tum mystico sensu accipi poterit. Ad literam, quia Hierarchia illa, vel Reginae dominio pollentis super Regna terrae fastu sese proferens, vel ærnula apparatus Tabernaculi veteris, ad cujus structuram populus contulit והב וכסף והנחשת ואת־הארגמן והתולעת שני aurum, & argentum, & hyacinthum, & purpuram, & vermiculum cocci. Exod. xxv. 4. 5. vel externo splendore fascinatura & pellestura ad amorem sui, purpuram, coccinum, aurum, argentum, pretiosos lapides, annulos sibi circumpositura, & in externo cultu habituque propalam ostentatura erat. Sensu verò mystico, quia cum fuco & fallaciis, omníque ἐναργέια τῆς ἀπάτης Mulier apparere debuit; in cultu externo jactatura & prætextura scilicet nomen Christi, qui in carne venit, & sanguinem purpureum & coccineum pro Ecclesia effudit, quod purpurae & coccini symbolum significat: nomen Spiritús S. cujus divinam assistentiam sibi arrogare debuit, quæ sicut divina omnia, auri symbolo figurari potuit: nomen Sanctorum, justorum Prophetarum, Apostolorum, Martyrùm, Patrum, qui gemmis & margaritis comparari potuerunt, nomen inprimis Petræ, lapidis pretiosi, super quem Ecclesia ædificata sit.
units.tr: XXIX. The Woman's clothing may also be taken both literally and in a mystical sense. Literally, because that Hierarchy, displaying itself with the pride of a queen who rules over the kingdoms of the earth, or with the bright ornament of the old Tabernacle, to whose construction the people contributed gold, and silver, and brass, and blue, and purple, and scarlet, Exod. 25:4–5, was to be bewitching and enticing to love of itself by outward splendour. It was to surround itself with purple, scarlet, gold, silver, precious stones and rings, and openly display them in its outward worship and dress. In a mystical sense, because the Woman ought to appear with paint and deceits, and with every manifest sign of deception [ἐναργέια τῆς ἀπάτης], boasting and pretending in her outward worship the name of Christ, who came in the flesh and poured out his purple and scarlet blood for the Church, which the symbol of purple and scarlet signifies; the name of the Holy Spirit, whose divine assistance she ought to claim for herself, which, like all divine things, could be represented by the symbol of gold; the name of the Saints, the righteous Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs and Fathers, who could be compared to jewels and pearls; and above all the name of the Rock, the precious stone upon which the Church is built.

units.la: XXXX. Ad exteriorem illum habitum Meretricis etiam Ad eundem
units.tr: XXX. Also concerning that outward dress of the Harlot To the same

units.la: XXX. Ad exteriorem illum habitum Meretricis etiam Auratum Poculum, quod in manu habet, intus abominationibus & impuritate scortationis refertum, pertinet. Poculum igitur isthoc quo ceu philtro quodam Meretrix ad libidinem invitat, aliud extus ostentat, intus promittit aliud. Extus aureum cum sit, magnifica quæque præ se fert, qualia esse possunt cortex Verborum Dei, Apostolicæ traditiones, omníque prætextus ex Scriptura arreptus, quo Meretrix sibi authoritatem conciliare nititur; & similia, quibus ceu illecebris & fraudibus suis circumscriptos irretire misere conatur. Accedunt splendidi, quibus Meretrix superbit, tituli, majestas & splendor imperii, opum, honorum, deliciarum. Sed coruscet licet fulgeátque extus mirificè poculum isthoc, cramate tamen interiore tristius nihil mundus vidit. Abundat enim intus & sub tegmine verborum ac rerum speciosissimarum veneno exquisitissimo, meris abominationibus & impuritate scortationis, falsitatibus, mendaciis abominabilibus, corruptelis verbi Dei, quibus prona credulitate receptis adoptatisque à Deo vivo, à regno Dei, à Christo capite, à vera justitia homines ad alia omnia transversos abripit. Planè sicut philtra meretricum externa specie splendentia, intus autem mixta rebus impurissimis, & abominabilibus, puta cineribus ranarum, bufonum, serpentum, aliisque feralibus ejusmodi, improvidos, & externa specie dementatos impuris amoribus ad insaniam usque devincire, & amasiorum corpora, animâsque pessundaret solent.
units.tr: XXX. To that outward dress of the Harlot also belongs the golden cup which she holds in her hand and which is inside full of abominations and the impurity of fornication. So this cup, with which the Harlot invites men to lust as with a kind of love potion, displays one thing outside and promises another within. Since it is golden outside, it presents all manner of magnificent things, such as the outward shell of the words of God, Apostolic traditions, and every pretext drawn from Scripture, by which the Harlot tries to win authority for herself, and similar devices, by which she wretchedly tries to ensnare those whom she has deceived with her allurements and frauds. Added to these are the splendid titles in which the Harlot takes pride, the majesty and splendour of her rule, her wealth, honours and pleasures. But though this cup may glitter and shine wonderfully outside, the world has never seen anything more sad than its inner filth. For inside, and under the covering of fair words and most beautiful things, it abounds with the most exquisite poison: pure abominations and the impurity of fornication, falsehoods, abominable lies, and corruptions of the Word of God. By these, received and embraced with ready credulity, she drags men away from the living God, the kingdom of God, Christ the head, and true righteousness, turning them aside to all other things. Just as love potions of harlots, shining in outward show but mixed within with the foulest and most abominable things, such as ashes of frogs, toads, serpents and other deadly things of that kind, are wont to bind the heedless, who are maddened by the outward show, in impure love until they reach madness, and to destroy the bodies and souls of their lovers.

units.la: XXXI. Interiorem Meretricis habitum & constitutionem produnt flagitia, quæ ei Apocalypsis imputat. De scortatione ejus horrenda supra vidimus. Accedunt crudelitas seu Tyrannis, blasphemandi cacoëthes, superbia, veneficia, & nundinatio, animarum cumprimis, quæ Dissert. 1. ff. 8-11. indigitata, clara adeò sunt, ut explicatione nulla indigeant. Par ratio est qualitatis loci, quem septicollem Romam in Apocalypsi definiri, abundè supra demonstravimus.
units.tr: XXXI. The Harlot's inner dress and character are revealed by the crimes which the Apocalypse imputes to her. Her horrible fornication we have seen above. To these are added cruelty or tyranny, the itch of blasphemy, pride, sorcery, and trafficking, especially in souls, which are pointed out in Dissert. 1, ff. 8–11, and are so clear that they need no explanation. The same reasoning applies to the character of the place, which we have shown above at sufficient length is defined in the Apocalypse as the seven-hilled Rome.

units.la: XXXII. Bestiæ verò constitutio propria explicationem nonnullam meretur, ratione inprimis ortus capitum & cornuum. Ortum quod attinet, de eo dicitur. Apoc. xvii. 8. quòd fuerit, & non sit, & ascensura sit ex abysso, & in perditionem itura. Cùm fuisse dicitur, supponitur præcessisse quippiam, cum quo Bestia similitudinem quandam habuerit. Duo autem præcesserunt, quibuscum Bestia similitudine quadam coaluisse dici potest. Draconis nimirum Imperium quod attinet, constat, Draconem thronum & potestatem suam cessisse Bestiæ Apoc. xiii.
units.tr: XXXII. The particular constitution of the Beast, however, deserves some explanation, chiefly with respect to the origin of its heads and horns. As for its origin, it is said of it, Rev. 17:8, that it was, and is not, and is about to ascend out of the abyss, and go into perdition. When it is said that it was, it is implied that something preceded it with which the Beast had some resemblance. Two things did precede, with which the Beast may be said to have some resemblance in fact. As far as the rule of the dragon is concerned, it is evident that the Dragon yielded his throne and power to the Beast, Rev. 13.

units.la: 2. Eatenus igitur Bestia cum Dracone convenire debuit. Quæ enim
units.tr: 2. So far, then, the Beast was bound to agree with the Dragon. For what...

units.la: Interior Meretricis habitus ... Interiorem Meretricis habitum (marginal notes, left margin, partly illegible) enim in uno tertio conveniunt ; ea quoque inter se conveniunt. Erat igitur in Dracone ratione ejusdem potestatis & throni ; non est , quod Draco fuit, utpote qui gentes ad crassam idololatriam seduxit, cum Bestia externam illam crassamque idololatriam deseruerit, & ex abysso, multitudine gentium exorta fuerit.
units.tr: The inner dress of the Harlot ... For the inner dress of the Harlot [marginal note, partly illegible] agree in one third point; they also agree with each other. The Beast therefore was in the Dragon in respect of the same power and throne; is not what the Dragon was, since the Dragon led the nations into gross idolatry, whereas the Beast has abandoned that outward and gross idolatry, and came up out of the abyss, having arisen from a multitude of nations.

units.la: XXXIII. Sed & cum praecedente carnali Israële Be- stia similitudinem quandam obtinet.
units.tr: XXXIII. But also, along with the preceding carnal Israel, the Beast bears a certain likeness.

units.la: Etenim 1. Respublica Israëlitarum à Deo ipso instituta, & Deo nomenclatore habens appellationem populi Dei, constabat hominibus circumcisis, qui in cultu Divini exercitio subdebantur Pontifici & sacerdotibus, sedentibus in loco, quem Deus elegerat ; quibus obedire necessum habebant ; quique locum habebant in mundo, in quo Deus habitare dicebatur, & in quo sacrificia Deo offerebantur ; qui tamen circumcisi licet, maximam partem Deum, justitiam & foedus ejus vel ignorabant, & cum soli Deo in bona conscientia inservire debuissent, pro timore Dei praecepti humani obedientiam habuerunt, id ipsum Salvatore nostro Matth. xv. 8. 9. ex Esaj. xxix. 23. hypocritis illis serio exprobrante.
units.tr: For, first: the commonwealth of the Israelites was instituted by God himself, and had from God the name of the people of God. It consisted of circumcised men, who in the exercise of divine worship were subject to the high priest and the priests, who sat in the place God had chosen. They had to obey these, and they had their place in the world where God was said to dwell and where sacrifices were offered to God. Yet although they were circumcised, most of them did not know God, his righteousness, or his covenant. When they ought to have served God alone with a good conscience, they gave obedience to human precepts out of fear of God. Our Saviour seriously rebuked those hypocrites for this very thing, Matth. 15:8, 9, citing Isa. 29:13.

units.la: Quis non cum carnali hoc Israële eatenus congruere Bestiam, multitudinem scilicet hominum animalium Christum oretenus profitentium, at de caetero Hierarchiæ certo in loco dominanti, cultum & sacrificia praescribenti, adeoque non tam Deo, quàm hominibus, non Agno & sponso Ecclesiæ, sed Meretrici profligatissimi pudoris sese subjicientium, intelligit? Erat igitur Bestia, hoc est, similem ante se populum, pro Ecclesia Dei se venditantem habuit, cujus tradux & propago veluti est. At non est; jure scilicet non est, quale olim fuit, quia, vetera transierunt, & omnia nunc nova facta sunt. 2. Cor. v. 17. Neque enim is Novo Testamento induci status debuit, qui sub Vetere obtinuit. Neque amplius Ecclesia potest esse ea, ea, quæ certis montibus, uti mox dicetur, certoque loco affixa est, cùm Ecclesia Christiana Caput suum habens in Cœlo ad dextram Dei, in terra ad locum nullum constringi possit. Bestia igitur talis hominum multitudo, non vera Christi Ecclesia est. Καίπερ ἐπὶ, Et tamen est, Bestia, hæc. Quippe præ se fert nomen Christi, & verbum ejus. In medio quoque ejus sunt Sancti, qui propter communionem externam bene de illis sperant. Iccirco vocatur Ecclesia & populus Dei, sed quia non est, jure videlicet, utpote carens divina institutione, cùm Deus ejusmodi Ecclesiam, cujus Caput sit terrestre, cujus Pastores infallibiles, legislatione ac jurisdictione divinitus non approbata utentem, & quæ certam fixámque sedem in mundo à qua authentica interpretatio verbi arcessenda sit, non instituerit, neque etiam errores, quos Bestia veris dictis admiscet, Verbi Divini testimonium habeant, iccirco Spiritus S. Bestiam illam à Deo prodiisse negans, ex abysso potius infaustum caput protulisse, & interituram fortiter asseverat. Utrumque sensus, & prior ille, & posterior hic, verbis Prophetiæ hujus quin conveniat, negari nequit. Si proin vel uterque, vel alteruter sensus in eo populo, quem Bestiam esse in loco definiemus & demonstrabimus, reperire dabitur, satis prophetiæ fiet haud dubiè.
units.tr: Who does not understand that the Beast agrees with this carnal Israel in so far as it is a multitude of human beings who profess Christ with their lips, but who otherwise are ruled by a hierarchy fixed in one place, which prescribes worship and sacrifices, and so submit themselves not so much to God as to men, not to the Lamb and bridegroom of the Church, but to a harlot of most shameless character? Erat therefore the Beast: that is, it had a people like the one before it, and it presented itself as the Church of God. Such a people is, as it were, its offshoot and progeny. But non est, that is, it is not so by right, as it once was, because the old things have passed away, and all things have now become new (2 Cor. 5:17). For the state that held under the Old Testament ought not to be brought back under the New. Nor can the Church any longer be that which, as will be said presently, was fixed on certain mountains and in a certain place, since the Christian Church, having its Head in heaven at the right hand of God, cannot be confined to any place on earth. Such a multitude of men, therefore, is not the true Church of Christ. And yet it is, this Beast; for it bears before it the name of Christ and his word. In its midst are also the saints, who on account of their outward communion are rightly hoped well of. For this reason it is called the Church and people of God; but it is not, namely by right, since it lacks divine institution, because God has not established a Church of this kind, whose Head is earthly, whose ministers are claimed to be infallible, which uses legislation and jurisdiction not approved by God, and which has no fixed and settled seat in the world from which an authentic interpretation of the Word might be sought. Nor do the errors that the Beast mingles with true statements have the testimony of the Word of God. Therefore the Holy Spirit, denying that this Beast came forth from God, asserts instead that it brought forth an unhappy head from the abyss, and that it will surely perish. Neither of these senses, the former or the latter, can be denied to agree with the words of this prophecy. Therefore, if either or both of these senses can be found in that people which we shall define and demonstrate in place to be the Beast, the prophecy will undoubtedly be fulfilled sufficiently.

units.la: XXXIV. Capita Bestiæ quod attinet, ita de iis Pro- phetia habet Apoc. XVII. 9. 10. 11.
units.tr: XXXIV. As for the heads of the Beast, the prophecy speaks of them thus, Rev. 17:9–11.

units.la: Αἱ ἑπτὰ κεφαλαὶ, ὄρη ἑπτά εἰσιν, ὅπου ἡ γυνὴ κάθηται ἐπ' αὐτῶν. Καὶ βασιλεῖς ἑπτά εἰσιν· οἱ πέντε ἔπεσον, ὁ εἷς ἔστιν, ὁ ἄλλος οὔπω ἦλθε· καὶ ὅταν ἔλθῃ, ὀλίγον αὐτὸν δεῖ μεῖναι. Καὶ τὸ θηρίον ὃ ἦν καὶ οὐκ ἔστι, καὶ αὐτὸς ὄγδοός ἐστι, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἑπτά ἐστι, καὶ εἰς ἀπώλειαν ὑπάγει. Septem capita montes septem sunt in quibus Mulier sedet. Et Reges septem sunt: Quinque ceciderunt, & unus est, & alius nondum venit, & cum venerit, paulisper eum oportet manere. Et Bestia quæ erat, & non est,
units.tr: The seven heads are seven mountains, on which the woman sits. And they are seven kings: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain a short time. And the beast that was and is not, he is also the eighth, and he is of the seven, and he goes into perdition. [Αἱ ἑπτὰ κεφαλαὶ, ὄρη ἑπτά εἰσιν, ὅπου ἡ γυνὴ κάθηται ἐπ' αὐτῶν.
