Καὶ βασιλεῖς ἑπτά εἰσιν· οἱ πέντε ἔπεσον, ὁ εἷς ἔστιν, ὁ ἄλλος οὔπω ἦλθε· καὶ ὅταν ἔλθῃ, ὀλίγον αὐτὸν δεῖ μεῖναι. Καὶ τὸ θηρίον ὃ ἦν καὶ οὐκ ἔστι, καὶ αὐτὸς ὄγδοός ἐστι, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἑπτά ἐστι, καὶ εἰς ἀπώλειαν ὑπάγει.]

units.la: cap. ... est, Ɵille octavus est, & ex septem illis est, & in interitum vadit.
units.tr: ... chapter ... He is the eighth, and he is of those seven, and he goes into perdition.

units.la: - XXXV. Capita septem cùm septem montes dicuntur, septem montium symbola seu imagines intelliguntur. Est que septem montium illorum designatio scintillans quaedam gemma, quæ suo fulgore reliquæ textus obscuritati medetur. Nam Romam septimontiam seu septicollem veluti digito ita Angelus demonstrat, ut res tota etiam simplicibus pellucere possit. Qua de re supra abundè diximus.
units.tr: - XXXV. When the heads are said to be seven mountains, the seven mountains are meant as symbols or images. And the designation of those seven mountains is a shining gem, which by its brightness heals the obscurity of the rest of the text. For the Angel points out Rome, the city of seven hills or seven mountains, as it were with a finger, so that the whole matter can shine through even to simple readers. We have spoken of this matter abundantly above.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Iidem tamen septem montes haud dubiè ita septem colles seu montes, quibus Roma superstructa est, significant, ut simul monimentum etiam statuantur septem dynastiarum, seu regionum, universam ditionem Romanam, ceu sedem Bestiæ complectentium. Solet autem Scriptura quandóque per montes totam aridam, quæ exaggerata super mare & fluvios extat, figurare. Quo sensu Jon. 11.7. alveus maris vocatur extrema seu radices montium. Populi quoque in unum colleēti, & gentes linguis discretæ montium similitudinem habent. Unde Imperium Babylonicum Jerem. LI. 25. mons corrumpens vocatur. Ejusdem verò Bestiæ Regiones & Provincias symbola montium Romæ etiam insinuari, argumento est, quòd eadem Bestiæ capita non tantùm septem montes, sed etiam septem Reges figurant. Montes autem à Regibus divelli non possunt. Et montium seu provinciarum Bestiæ rectores, sive politici, sive Ecclesiastici etiam βασιλεῖς Reges dici non incommodè potuerunt.
units.tr: Nevertheless, these same seven mountains undoubtedly signify the seven hills or mountains on which Rome was built, and at the same time they are set up as a monument to the seven dynasties, or regions, which together make up the whole Roman dominion, the seat of the Beast. Scripture sometimes uses mountains to stand for the whole dry land that rises above the sea and the rivers. In this sense, Jon. 2:6 calls the bed of the sea the extremities or roots of the mountains. Peoples gathered into one, and nations divided by tongues, also have a likeness to mountains. Hence the Babylonian empire is called a destroying mountain in Jer. 51:25. That the regions and provinces of this same Beast are also hinted at by the symbols of the mountains of Rome is shown by the fact that the same heads of the Beast represent not only seven mountains but also seven kings. Mountains, however, cannot be separated from their kings. And the rulers of the mountains or provinces of the Beast, whether civil or ecclesiastical, could not unsuitably be called kings (βασιλεῖς).

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Septem Reges totidem urbis Romanæ potestates principatus & Regimina significare, persuasum plerisque reperio. Habuisse enim Urbem Romanam ordine Reges, Consules, Tribunos, Decemviros, Dictatores, Cæsares, Papas, observant. Ceciderse autem quinque, Reges, Consules, Tribunos, Decemviros, Dictatores: Sextum Caesares esse: Siptimum Papas, nondum venisse: Deniqué Regem Octavum eundem esse cum septimo ab eo distinctum licet ob ingenii & morum in pejus corruptorum dissimilitudinem idem animadvertunt.
units.tr: I find that many people are persuaded that the seven kings signify seven powers, principalities and forms of government of the city of Rome. They observe that Rome was governed in order by Kings, Consuls, Tribunes, Decemvirs, Dictators, Caesars and Popes. Five of these have fallen: the Kings, Consuls, Tribunes, Decemvirs and Dictators. The sixth is the Caesars; the seventh, the Popes, has not yet come. Finally, they hold that the eighth king is the same as the seventh, though distinct from him because of the unlikeness of his character and morals, which have been corrupted for the worse.

units.la: XXXVIII. Caeterum cum potestates illae ad Bestiam Draconi quippe succedentem non faciant; & Rex septimus, ac cum eodem conveniens Octavus non tam ad Bestiam, quàm ad meretricem à Bestia portatam pertineant, concinniùs forte eorundem septem montium, seu septem provinciarum Bestiae rectores sive politicos sive Ecclesiasticos intelligi posse, alii existimant, ut simplicissimus sensus hic sit, initiò habituram Bestiam septem grandes orbis terrae partes, in quibus sedeat, septémque adeò gentibus constituram; & iis totidem minimum Reges imperaturos, qui Bestiae in illis montibus seu partibus orbis, capita censeri possint.
units.tr: XXXVIII. However, since those powers do not correspond to the Beast, which succeeds the Dragon, and since the seventh king, and the eighth who agrees with him, pertain not so much to the Beast as to the harlot carried by the Beast, others think it may fit better to understand the rulers of these same seven mountains, or seven provinces of the Beast, whether political or ecclesiastical. The simplest sense, then, is this: at first the Beast will hold seven great parts of the earth, on which it sits, and will thus establish seven peoples. To these, at least as many kings will rule, and they may be counted as the heads of the Beast in those mountains or parts of the world.

units.la: XXXIX. Cornua decem ejusdem Bestiae Apoc. xvii. 12, 13. definiuntur totidem Reges. Et capita quidem ac cornua eatenus distingui, quòd illis amputatis Bestiam interire necessum est; his verò resectis manere eandem nihil prohibet; clarum est. Tum etiam dubitari vix potest, quin cornua illa non singulis Capitibus, sed uni affigenda & adaptanda sint, hunc scilicet in finem, ut capitis ejus robur in tot potentiae fulcimentis denotetur. Affigi verò septimo Capiti, monti seu Regi, quatenus ei Octavus Rex supervenit, congruentissimè possunt, & fortè etiam debent, quia in superioribus apparuisse unquam eventus reclamat. Praeterea cum Rege illo octavo decem Reges non perpetim, sed μίαν ὥραν unam horam, hoc est καὶ μίαν ὥραν simul eodem tempore horam regnaturi, & Bestiae in octavo illo Rege potestatem ac potentiam suam unanimiter ita impertituri erant, ut à Bestia dissentire in rebus fidei nemini liceat, quin dissentientes ab eo adeóque ipse Agnus, & qui cum eò sunt electi & fideles πανηγυρικῶς & unitis viribus oppugnentur tantisper, donec ab Agno victi, odium adversus meretricem insatiabile concepturi sunt. Denique Reges illi seu cornua Bestiæ, concepto adversus meretricem odio eandem desolaturi, nudaturi, devoraturi, & igne combusturi dicuntur.
units.tr: XXXIX. The ten horns of the same Beast (Rev. 17:12, 13) are defined as ten kings. It is clear that the heads and the horns are distinguished in this respect: if the heads are cut off, the Beast must perish, but if the horns are cut off, nothing prevents the Beast from remaining. Nor can it be doubted that those horns are not to be attached to each head separately, but to one head, clearly for this purpose: that the strength of that head is shown in so many supports of power. They can most fittingly be attached, and perhaps even ought to be attached, to the seventh head, the mountain or king, since the eighth king comes upon him; for experience in earlier times protests against any other arrangement. Moreover, the ten kings are to reign with that eighth king not continually, but for μίαν ὥραν, one hour, that is, καὶ μίαν ὥραν, for one hour at the same time. They are to give their power and might to the Beast through that eighth king, with one accord, so that no one may be allowed to dissent from the Beast in matters of faith. Those who dissent from it, and therefore the Lamb himself, and those who are with him, the chosen and faithful, are attacked πανηγυρικῶς, in a general assault with united forces, for a time, until they are conquered by the Lamb and conceive an insatiable hatred against the harlot. Finally, those kings, or horns of the Beast, are said, having conceived hatred against the harlot, to lay her waste, strip her, devour her and burn her with fire.

units.la: XL. Conficitur hinc, ei, qui Babylonis mysterium evolvere velit, demonstrandum esse ejusmodi Bestiam, seu multitudinem Christi nomen oretenus confitentium, at de caetero cum meretrice scortantium, quæ post Romam Ethnicam ad Christum conversam, habeat septem capita, seu totidem Provincias, rectoribus suis sive Politicis sive Ecclesiasticis subditas, adeóque certo loco, sedi certæ adstringi se velit; & sub septimo capite seu octavo Rege cornua decem, seu totidem Reges cum Rege illo octavo conspirantes, & συμφωνοῦσι ad tempus Agnum & qui cum eo sunt, electos & fideles, hoc est, Christianos, non personatos, sed veros & sinceros, oppugnantes, donec ab Agno victi odium internecinum adversus meretricem concipiant, & ejusdem excidio finali illud denique expleant.
units.tr: XL. From this it follows that whoever wishes to unfold the mystery of Babylon must demonstrate that such a Beast, that is, a multitude of those who confess the name of Christ with their lips but otherwise commit fornication with the harlot, exists. After pagan Rome was converted to Christ, this multitude has seven heads, or as many provinces, subject to their rulers, whether political or ecclesiastical, and so wishes to be bound to a certain place and a certain seat. Under the seventh head, or eighth king, there are ten horns, or as many kings conspiring with that eighth king, who συμφωνοῦσι, agree, to attack for a time the Lamb and those who are with him, the chosen and faithful, that is, the Christians who are not masked but true and sincere. This continues until they are conquered by the Lamb, conceive a deadly hatred against the harlot, and at last fulfil it in her final destruction.

units.la: XLI. De judicio Meretricis dicendum nominihil superest. Per gradus illud procedere Apoc. xvii. 16. innuitur. Distinctius vero illud cap. xviii. explicatur. Ibi enim Angelus è Cœlo descendens habens potestatem magnam, & à cujus gloria illustrata terra est, qui haud dubiè est Angelus ille volans per medium cœlum, habens Evangelium æternum, & euangelizans incolis terræ Apoc. xiv. 6. 7. cum rebore & contentione vocis clamat. v. 2. ἔπεσεν ἔπεσεν Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη, ἡ γέγονεν κατοικητήριον δαιμονίων, ἡ φυλακὴ παντὸς πνεύματος ἀκαθάρτου ἡ μεμισημένη. Cecidit, cecidit Babylon illa magna, & facta est habitaculum dæmonum num, & custodia omnis avis immundæ & odiosæ. Allusio est ad Esaj. xxxiv. 11. 13. 14. 15. Mox verò v. 4. alia vox è Cœlo clamat: ἐξέλθατε ἐξ αὐτῆς ὁ λαός μου, ἵνα μὴ συγκοινωνῆτε ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις αὐτῆς, καὶ ἵνα μὴ λάβητε ἐκ τῶν πληγῶν αὐτῆς. Exite ex ea populE mi, ne communicetis cum peccatis ejus, & ne accipiatis de plagis ejus.
units.tr: XLI. Little remains to be said about the judgment of the harlot. Rev. 17:16 indicates that it proceeds by stages, but ch. 18 explains it more distinctly. There an angel comes down from heaven, having great power, and by whose glory the earth is illuminated. He is undoubtedly that angel flying through mid-heaven, having the eternal gospel and preaching to the inhabitants of the earth (Rev. 14:6, 7). He cries out with strength and force of voice (v. 2): "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, which has become a habitation of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit and a hated thing" [ἔπεσεν ἔπεσεν Βαβυλὼν ἡ μεγάλη, ἡ γέγονεν κατοικητήριον δαιμονίων, ἡ φυλακὴ παντὸς πνεύματος ἀκαθάρτου ἡ μεμισημένη]. This is an allusion to Isa. 34:11, 13–15. Soon afterwards (v. 4) another voice from heaven cries: "Come out of her, my people, lest you share in her sins, and lest you receive of her plagues" [ἐξέλθατε ἐξ αὐτῆς ὁ λαός μου, ἵνα μὴ συγκοινωνῆτε ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις αὐτῆς, καὶ ἵνα μὴ λάβητε ἐκ τῶν πληγῶν αὐτῆς].

units.la: XLII. Evidenter satis duo constant. Prius, casum huncce ingeminatum Babylonis non esse finalem & peremptorium, tum quia cadente Babylone relinquuntur tales, qui cum dæmonibus, Spiritu immundo, avi immunda & odiosa comparantur: tum quia talibus adhuc in Babylone assignatur καταικητήριον domicilium & φυλακή custodia; adeòque Babylon deinceps clavim putei abyssi accipit; tum quia post casum illum nihil de typho suo remittit, sed potius v. 7. Reginæ instar sedens se jactare, & v. 21. adhuc citharœdos tibines habere dicitur: tum quia post eum casum v. 4. Babylone exire jubentur fideles: tum denique quia v. 21. Angelus peculiaris à priore illo v. 1. multùm distinctus ad exequendum judicium finale inducitur. Sicut enim priori Angelo attribuitur, quòd ab ejus gloria illuminata sit terra, sic posteriori non splendor talis, sed fortitudo tribuitur.
units.tr: XLII. Two things are fairly clear. First, this repeated fall of Babylon is not final and decisive. This is shown, first, because when Babylon falls, some remain who are compared to demons, unclean spirits and unclean and hated birds. Second, a dwelling place (κατοικητήριον) and a prison (φυλακή) are still assigned to such people in Babylon, and so Babylon afterwards receives the key of the bottomless pit. Third, after that fall she does not give up her pride; rather, she is said (v. 7) to sit as a queen and boast, and (v. 21) to still have harpists and flute players. Fourth, after that fall (v. 4) the faithful are commanded to come out of Babylon. Finally, a special angel, very different from the earlier angel of v. 1, is introduced (v. 21) to carry out the final judgment. For just as the earlier angel is credited with the earth being illuminated by his glory, so the later angel is credited not with such splendour but with strength.

units.la: XLIII. Posterius est, casum huncce primum Babylonis in separatione populi Dei gloria illuminati communione externa cum Meretrice agnita jam & demonstrata, adeòque fidelium ab iis, qui cum Spiritibus & avibus immundis comparantur, discretione consistere. Quæ haud dubiè est denudatio illa cap. xviii. 16. qua Meretrix absterso hypocriseos & speciosorum titulorum fuco ita detegitur, ut palam jam fidelibus & populo Dei ab Angelo Dei illuminato, qui in Babylone hac captivus quodammodo detinebatur, innotescat, non honestam castámque virginem, sed meritorium esse propudium, in posterum ita relinquendum, & relicto ejus habitaculo nova communio, quam Meretrix, Spiritus & Aves immundæ non ingrediantur, instituatur.
units.tr: XLIII. Second, this first fall of Babylon consists in the separation of the people of God, who have been illuminated with glory, and in the recognition and demonstration of their external communion with the harlot. It consists, therefore, in the separation of the faithful from those who are compared with unclean spirits and birds. This is undoubtedly the stripping described in ch. 18:16, by which the harlot is so uncovered, her hypocrisy and the paint of her showy titles wiped away, that it becomes plain to the faithful and the people of God, enlightened by the angel of God, who was in some way held captive in this Babylon. She is not an honest and chaste virgin but a shameless prostitute for hire, and she is to be left so in future. With her dwelling abandoned, a new communion is to be established, which the harlot, the spirits and the unclean birds do not enter.

units.la: XLIV. Judicii illius incrementum consistit in plagis carum illum primum v. 4. 5. &c. consequentibus. Jubentur enim v. 6. ob peccata in cœlum ascendentia fideles Babylo-ni τὰ διπλᾶ καὶ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῆς, ἐνλαλῶν reduplicare duplicia secundum opera ejus, & in poculo quod infudit, duplum ei infundere. Et ne in infligendis plagis agerent remisse & segniter, addit Angelus v. 7. Quantum glorificavit se ipsam, & lascivivit, tantum ei date cruciatum & luctum, quia in corde suo (puta etiam post casum illum primum) dicit: Sedeo Regina & vidua non sum, & luctum non videbo. Scilicet etiam post casum illum primum Meretrix vulnera sua incurata celans grassari, pro Regina se gerere, solitudinem negare, luctum præ se ferre nullum cum insolenter pergeret, jubetur populus Dei ille scilicet, qui Babylone exivit, non parcere Babyloni triplex æs habenti circa pectus, sed potius ruinis ejus instare, cruciare eam strenuè, adeóque lugendi materiam locupletem etiam invitæ obtrudere. Quod quidem judicium, in continuata demonstratione veritatis, qua sola Meretricis Regnum, authoritas & felicitas imminuitur, adeóque sicceffione ab ea perfecta sine spe ulla reconciliationis, non sine causa constituitur. Sic enim Meretrix nudatur sic desolatur, deseritúrque, sic denique odium passivum incurrens susque déque habetur, Regnumque & potestas Regni ejus continué infringitur, labefactatúrque donec ad tempus cessantibus fatis, iisque continuata impietate provocatis, denique ad finale exitium suum approximet.
units.tr: XLIV. The increase of that judgment consists in the plagues that follow the first, from v. 4 and 5 onwards. For the faithful are commanded (v. 6) to repay Babylon for her sins, which have gone up to heaven, "double, according to her works" [τὰ διπλᾶ καὶ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῆς], and to pour out for her a double portion in the cup she has mixed. Lest they be lax and slack in inflicting the plagues, the angel adds (v. 7): "As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her, because she says in her heart (that is, also after that first fall): I sit a queen, and I am no widow, and I shall see no mourning." Clearly, even after that first fall, the harlot, concealing her unhealed wounds, continues to rage, poses as a queen, denies her desolation and shows no sign of mourning as she persists insolently. Therefore that people of God, namely those who came out of Babylon, are commanded not to spare Babylon, who has a triple brass about her breast, but rather to press upon her ruins, torment her vigorously, and force upon her, even against her will, abundant cause for mourning. This judgment, in the continued demonstration of the truth, by which alone the kingdom, authority and happiness of the harlot are diminished, is not without cause established, so that with her succession completed, there is no hope of reconciliation. For in this way the harlot is stripped, in this way desolated and forsaken, in this way, at last incurring a passive hatred, she is held in contempt. The kingdom and the power of her kingdom are continually broken down and weakened, until, when the fates have for a time ceased, and her continued impiety has provoked them, she finally draws near to her final ruin.

units.la: XLV. Peremtorium & finale ejusdem judicium in subita ejus deletione consistit, quæ sic v. 21. explicatur. Et sustulit unus Angelus robustus lapidem, ut molarem magnum,
units.tr: XLV. The final and decisive judgement of that city consists in its sudden destruction, which is explained in v. 21: And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone,

units.la: Judicii ini-crementum: in plagis Babyloni à populo Dei infligendis consistit. gnum, & conjecit in mare, dicens: sic ἐρμῆναν impetu conjicietur Babylon illa magna civitas & non invenietur amplius. Præceps, celerrimus, & irreparabilis ejus interitus & ναυολιθεία, cui analoga est conjectio montis magni igne ardentis in mare Cap. VIII. 8. memorata, innuitur. Magnus lapis sua mole ruit: cum ingenti impetu si projiciatur, longè maximo, si à valido quopiam robustóque projiciatur. Nec spes est rursum fluitandi in summo, cùm eum & suum pondus, & aliena vis in imo fundo defigant. Sic ergo male peribit Babylon, ut emergendi ne minima quidem spes affulgeat amplius. Conveniétque adeo interitus hic Babylonis mysticæ cum interitu Babylonis Chaldaicæ, de quo sic Jerem. LI. 63. 64. prædictum legere est: Et erit cùm completveris legere librum hunc, ligabis super eum lapidem, & projicies eum in medium Euphratem, & dices ככה תשקע בבל sic submergetur Babel, & non consurget à facie mali, quod ego super eam induco.
units.tr: The increment of judgement consists in the plagues to be inflicted on Babylon by the people of God. And cast it into the sea, saying: With such violence [ὁρμῇ] shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more. By this is indicated her headlong, swift and irreparable ruin, and her sinking [ναυολιθεία], to which corresponds the casting of the great mountain burning with fire into the sea, mentioned in ch. VIII. 8. A great stone falls by its own weight, and with a great impetus when it is thrown, far greater if it is thrown by some strong and mighty man. Nor is there any hope of floating up to the surface again, since both its own weight and an outside force fix it at the bottom. So Babylon will perish so completely that not even the slightest hope of rising again will shine upon her. This destruction of mystical Babylon agrees with the destruction of Chaldean Babylon, of which it is read in advance in Jer. LI. 63, 64: And it shall be, when thou hast made an end of reading this book, that thou shalt bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates, and say: Thus shall Babel sink [ככה תשקע בבל], and shall not rise, from the evil that I will bring upon her.

units.la: XLVI. Ut verò manifestius fiat excidii hujus novissimi gravitas, quibus rebus hoc modo etiam privanda fit Babylon, Spiritus S. V. 22. 23. exprimit. Et vox Citharœdorum, & Musicorum & tibicinum, & tubicinum non audietur in te amplius: & artifex ullus ullius artis non invenietur in te amplius, & vox molæ non audietur in te amplius, & lux lucernæ non lucebit in te amplius. Liquet hinc post priorem etiam casum non defuturos Babyloni Citharœdos, Musicos, tibicines, tubicines, artifices, molam, & vocem sponsi & sponsæ, adeóque futurum amplius ut in ejus templis theatralis Musica perstrepat, in foro non desiderentur artifices, qui magnifica opera moliantur, in familiis denique non desint necessaria, tum ad usum quotidianum, puta molendinæ, ad conterenda femina, præparandámque farinam, ex qua panis μεγάλον coquitur: & Lux lucernæ, facem prælatura operibus quibuscunque (etiam in Templis ejus) tum ad propagationem Civium Babylonis, puta sponsus & sponsa, ex quibus soboles legitimè procreari solet. Hæc omnia cum exspiratura Spiritus S. asseverat, παντελεϑεῖαν Babylonis magis etiam amplificat.
units.tr: XLVI. To make the gravity of this final ruin plainer, the Holy Spirit, in vv. 22, 23, sets out the things by which Babylon is to be deprived in this way: And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers and trumpeters shall be heard no more in thee: and no craftsman of any craft shall be found in thee any more, and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more in thee, and the light of a lamp shall shine no more in thee. From this it is clear that, even after the first calamity, Babylon will not lack harpers, musicians, pipers, trumpeters, craftsmen, a millstone, and the voice of a bridegroom and bride; and that it will again come about that theatrical music resounds in her temples, that craftsmen who undertake magnificent works are not wanting in the marketplace, and that in her households there are not lacking the necessities, both for daily use, such as the mill for grinding grain and preparing the flour from which bread is baked, and the light of a lamp, which will bear a torch for whatever works are done (even in her temples), and for the increase of the citizens of Babylon, namely the bridegroom and bride, from whom offspring are usually lawfully begotten. When the Holy Spirit declares all these things to be taken away, he magnifies even further the complete destruction [παντελεθείαν] of Babylon.

units.la: XLVII. Ex omnibus illis, quæ hactenus ad intelligentiam verborum, quibus Babylonem magnam Prophetia describsit, diximus ultra Babylonis magnæ expresli characteres colliguntur. Babylon scilicet Magna hisce notis clarissimis cognoscitur, quòd sit Civitas magna, seu Hierarchia Romana nomen Christi professa, religionis seu mysteriorum fidei obtentu populum certum animalem ditione & imperio suo obnoxium, in septem collibus, totidémque provinciis habitantem, & Regum plurium potentia ac robore suffultum, ita regens, ut simulata religione cultum soli Deo vivo debitum ab illo depaciscens, fe ceu Divinitatis participem religiosè coli, & amorem, officia Deo debita in se transferri patiatur, eadémque ratione horribilis idololatriæ, luxuriæ, crudelitatis erga sanctos externæ communioni suæ permixtos, superbiæ, blasphemiarum, veneficiorum reatum contrahat, donec justo Dei judicio detectis ejus fraudibus à sanctis & fidelibus agnita & deserta, ob continuatum cumulatúmque reatum tandem finale & horribile judicium subeat, & funditus extirpata corruat.
units.tr: XLVII. From all those things which we have so far said toward understanding the words by which the prophecy described Great Babylon, the clear marks of Great Babylon are gathered. Great Babylon is thus recognised by these most evident signs: that she is a great city, that is, the Roman hierarchy, which professes the name of Christ; that under the pretext of religion, or the mysteries of the faith, she holds a certain people, a animal-like people subject to her power and rule, dwelling on seven hills and in as many provinces, and supported by the power and strength of many kings; and that she so rules, that by pretending religion she takes to herself the worship due to the living God alone, and allows herself to be worshipped as a sharer in divinity, and allows love and the duties owed to God to be transferred to herself. By the same means she incurs the guilt of horrible idolatry, lewdness, cruelty towards the saints who are mixed with her external communion, pride, blasphemies and sorceries; until, by the just judgement of God, her frauds are exposed, she is recognised and forsaken by the saints and the faithful, and, because her guilt has continued and grown, she at last undergoes a final and dreadful judgement and falls, utterly uprooted.

units.la: DISSERTATIO QUARTA
units.tr: DISSERTATIO QUARTA

units.la: QUA
units.tr: IN WHICH

units.la: Ecclesia Romana Christiana distinctis periodis, cui ejusdem parti & tempori Babylonis Magnæ mysterium quadret, definitur, simulque totius controversiæ status figitur.
units.tr: The Roman Christian Church is defined by its distinct periods, to which the mystery of Great Babylon corresponds in respect of that part and time, and at the same time the state of the whole controversy is fixed.

units.la: BREVIARIUM
units.tr: SUMMARY

units.la: I. Præcedentium succincta ἀνακεφαλαίωσις.
units.tr: I. A brief recapitulation of what has gone before.

units.la: II. Ecclesia Romana Christiana quolibet tempore Babylonicæ impietatis rea non fuit.
units.tr: II. The Roman Christian Church was never at any time guilty of Babylonian impiety.

units.la: III. Character generalis eorum, qui quovis tempore, non famosæ Babylonis, sed Ecclesiæ & Sponsæ Christi asseclæ fuerunt.
units.tr: III. The general character of those who at any time were followers, not of infamous Babylon, but of the Church and Bride of Christ.

units.la: IV. Quales eo ipso tempore, quo Ecclesia Romana in Babylonem degeneravit, in externa Ecclesiæ Romanæ communione vixerunt, mortuique sunt.
units.tr: IV. What sort of people lived and died in external communion with the Roman Church at the very time when the Roman Church degenerated into Babylon.

units.la: V. Character generalis eorum qui quolibet tempore Babylonis, & Bestiæ asseclæ fuerunt.
units.tr: V. The general character of those who at any time were followers of Babylon and the Beast.

units.la: VI. Personas in Babylonico vel Bestiali statu positas, & in finem vitæ in eo persistentes solus Deus novit.
units.tr: VI. God alone knows the persons who are placed in a Babylonian or bestial state and who persist in it to the end of their lives.

units.la: VII. Cœtus tamen externus, cui characteres Babylonis & Bestiæ competunt, Babylon, & Bestia haud dubiè est.
units.tr: VII. Nevertheless, the external body to which the marks of Babylon and the Beast apply is undoubtedly Babylon and the Beast.

units.la: VIII. Ecclesiæ Romanæ Christianæ ab ejusdem initio, ad nostra usque tempora septem periodi distinguuntur.
units.tr: VIII. The Roman Christian Church, from its beginning down to our own times, is divided into seven periods.

units.la: IX. Prima ejusdem periodo, ab ejus initio ad Constantinum M. Ecclesia Christi, non Babylon fuit.
units.tr: IX. In its first period, from its beginning down to Constantine the Great, the Church was the Church of Christ, not Babylon.

units.la: X. Secunda quoque periodus à Constantino M. ad Phocam, & Bonifacium III. à Babylonica impietate eximitur.
units.tr: X. The second period also, from Constantine the Great to Phocas and Boniface III, is exempt from Babylonian impiety.

units.la: XI. Satanæ stratagema in seducendis piis, ut sæpe alio consilio revera quid instituant, alio instituere sibi videantur.
units.tr: XI. Satan's stratagem in deceiving the godly: often they seem to themselves to pursue one purpose while in fact they pursue another.

units.la: XII. Eodem seducti Episcopi nonnulli Romani in secunda imprimis periodo, opinionem, splendorem, autoritatem æquo majorem affectárunt.
units.tr: XII. Some Roman bishops, deceived by this, aimed above all in the second period at a reputation, splendour and authority beyond what was fitting.

units.la: XIII. Tertia periodus à Bonifacii III. temporibus ad Gregorium VII. usque porrecta, Babyloni infelix initium dedit.
units.tr: XIII. The third period, stretching from the times of Boniface III to Gregory VII, gave Babylon its unhappy beginning.

units.la: XIV. Néque tamen eo adhuc tempore in Meretricem illam, quam Apocalypsis depingit, planè degeneravit.
units.tr: XIV. Yet even at that time the Church had not wholly degenerated into that harlot whom the Apocalypse portrays.

units.la: XV. Quarta demum periodo, inde à Gregorio VII. ad Bonifacium VIII. usque, supremam etiam in temporalibus potestatem affectans, palam in propudium illud Apocalypticum converti cæpit. De Gregorio VII. testimonium Aventini,
units.tr: XV. Lastly, in the fourth period, from Gregory VII to Boniface VIII, aspiring also to supreme power in temporal affairs, it began openly to turn into that Apocalyptic prostitute. Concerning Gregory VII, the testimony of Aventinus,

units.la: XVI. & Onuphrii.
units.tr: XVI. and of Onuphrius.

units.la: XVII. Demum periodo V. à Bonifacii VIII. temporibus, ad Leonem X. usque Ecclesiæ Romanæ Hierarchia dominans ad summæ impietatis Babylonicæ fastigium surrexit.
units.tr: XVII. Finally, in the fifth period, from the times of Boniface VIII to Leo X, the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church rose to the summit of Babylonian impiety.

units.la: XVIII. Sexta periodus à Leone X. ad finem usque Concilii Tridentini judicio Babylonis initium dedit, quæ septima periodo, à fine Concilii Tridentini ad nostra usque tempora ad pristinam potentiam eniti modis omnibus conatur.
units.tr: XVIII. The sixth period, from Leo X to the end of the Council of Trent, gave Babylon its beginning; the seventh period, from the end of the Council of Trent to our own times, strives in every way to regain its former power.

units.la: XIX. Ex periodorum distinctione isthac status quæstionis figitur: Anne Hierarchia Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans nans à temporibus Gregorii VII. maximè, sit Babylon illa, quam Apocalypsis describit?
units.tr: XIX. From this division of the periods the state of the question is fixed thus: is that dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church, chiefly from the times of Gregory VII, the Babylon which the Apocalypse describes?

units.la: XX. Affirmarunt ante Reformationem plures, post eam, quotquot ab ea se separarunt, facto ipso, & plerique etiam professione affirmant.
units.tr: XX. Before the Reformation several affirmed it; since the Reformation, all who have separated from it affirm it, by their very deed, and most of them also by profession.

units.la: XXI. Ecclesiarum Gallicanarum eam in rem confessio & assertio.
units.tr: XXI. The confession and assertion of the Gallican Churches on this matter.

units.la: XXII. Authoris institutum ulterius.
units.tr: XXII. The author's plan going forward.

units.la: I. Omæ stabulari Babylonem Magnam, Matrem illam scortationum, & abominationum terræ, Pontificiorum etiam Doctorum magno consensu supra firmavimus. In Romam porro Ethnicam, sive veterem, sive futuram etiam quampiam prophetiam isthanc neutiquam cadere, adversus eosdem sententiarum divortiis mirè miseréque distractos, fuse etiam comprobavimus. Denique in Ecclesia Romana Christiana, quatenus ea Hierarchiæ quadam forma, mysterii seu religionis prætextu, multitudini hominum animalium, Christi nomen præ se ferentium, ita imperitat, ut à Deo vero, & lege ejusdem deficiens, Divinum sibi & creaturis honorem conferri patiatur; Prophetiæ hujus complementum demonstrandum esse explicatis supra Prophetiæ verbis, fidem minimè dubiam fecimus.
units.tr: I. We have firmly established, with the great agreement even of Papist teachers, that Great Babylon, the mother of harlotries and abominations of the earth, has its seat at Rome. We have also thoroughly shown, against those same men, who are wonderfully and wretchedly torn apart by their disagreements, that this prophecy in no way falls upon pagan Rome, whether ancient or even some future Rome. Finally, we have made it not in the least doubtful that the fulfilment of this prophecy must be shown in the Roman Christian Church, insofar as that Church, in a certain form of hierarchy and under the pretext of a mystery or religion, so rules over the multitude of men, who bear the name of Christ, that, falling away from the true God and his law, it allows divine honour to be paid to itself and to creatures.

units.la: II. Sicut autem Bestiam vocare Ecclesiam, stylo Spiritus S. est mirari Bestiam, & eidem subjici est adorare Bestiam: Ita Ecclesiam veram vocare Babylonem & Bestiam, est sine dubio sanctos, & eos, qui in Cœlo habitant, blasphemare. Palmarium isthoc scelus in se admiserit, quisquis Ecclesiam Romanam Christianam promiscuè, adeoque universam, singulorúmque temporum, hoc est, Christianos quosvis Romæ, inde à principio Ecclesiæ illius ad nostra usque tempora degentes, Babylonis Magnæ convitio aspergere, adeóque maledicere iis, quibus benedicendum fuerat, animum induxerit. Ut igitur δικαίως κρίνειν κρίνειν justum judicium judicare comperiamur, vilè à pretioso, Ecclesiam Romanam verè Christianam à Babylonica, Florem à Flora distinguere, atque tempus ipsum Meretricis hujus orientis, adolescentis, lascivientis, exolescentis, & ruentis discernere; denique eadem opera subjectum Prophetiæ de Babylone certius constituere, totiúfque quæstionis statum accuratiùs figere, constitutum deliberatúmque habemus. Liquebitque sic, Ecclesiæ Romanæ competere id, quod de Hierosolymitana Esaj. 1.21.22. pronuntiatum reperimus, his verbis: Quomodo facta est meretrix civitas olim fidelis, plena judicii, in qua justitia commorabatur, nunc autem homicidæ: Argentum tuum versum est in scorias: Vinum tuum aqua mixtum est.
units.tr: II. Just as to call the Church a Beast is to wonder at the Beast in the style of the Holy Spirit, and to be subject to it is to worship the Beast, so to call the true Church Babylon and the Beast is undoubtedly to blaspheme the saints and those who dwell in heaven. He has committed this supreme crime who has resolved to pelt the Roman Christian Church indiscriminately, and so the whole of it, and each period of it, that is, all Christians who have lived at Rome from the beginning of that Church down to our own times, with the reproach of Great Babylon, and so to curse those whom he ought to have blessed. Therefore, so that we may find that we judge justly [δικαίως κρίνειν], distinguishing the precious from the worthless, the truly Christian Roman Church from the Babylonian, the flower from the harlot's flower, and to discern the very time of this harlot, rising, wanton, growing old and falling; and at the same time to establish more certainly the subject of the prophecy concerning Babylon, and to fix more precisely the whole state of the question, we have determined and resolved to do so. It will thus be clear that what we find pronounced of the Jerusalem of Isaiah 1.21, 22 belongs to the Roman Church, in these words: How is the faithful city become an harlot, that was full of judgment! righteousness lodged in it; but now murderers. Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water.

units.la: III. Et in universum quidem non famosæ Babylonis sed Ecclesiæ & sponsæ Christi, ceu Συμπολίτης τῶν ἁγίων, οἰκεῖοι καὶ θεοῦ Cives sanctorum & domesticos Dei accensemus omnes illos Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ab ejusdem principio ad nostra usque tempora, asseclas, seu illi Ecclesiam eam rexerunt, seu regenti se quocunque modo subjecerunt, qui Christo animarum suarum pastori & sponso fidem illibatam intemeratámque præstiterunt, Verbo Dei scripto se subjecerunt, ejusdem interpretationem sensúmque sanum & genuinum ex ipsis Scripturis sibi demonstratum receperunt, Divinæ non humanæ ulli autoritati fidem suam omnem obstrinxerunt, solum Deum vivum ex verbi ejusdem præscripto coluerunt, nec ideo cultum amoremque Deo debitum vel in se, vel in creaturas alias transtulerunt, non suis, sed solius Christi Salvatoris unici meritis justitiam, salutem, gloriam suam omnem acceptam retulerunt, & veram unicéque salutarem fidem sinceræ erga Deum & proximum charitatis, vitaque Christo Redemtore
units.tr: III. In general, we count among the fellow-citizens of the saints and members of God's household (Συμπολίτης τῶν ἁγίων, οἰκεῖοι καὶ θεοῦ) not the infamous Babylon but the Church, the bride of Christ, all those adherents of the Roman Church from its beginning down to our own day, whether they ruled that Church or submitted to its ruler in some way, who have kept their faith in Christ, the Shepherd and Bridegroom of their souls, pure and unbroken. They submitted to the written Word of God and accepted its interpretation and sound and genuine sense, as shown to them from the Scriptures themselves. They pledged their whole faith to divine authority alone and not to any human authority. They worshipped the one living God as the Word itself prescribes, and did not transfer the worship and love due to God either to themselves or to other creatures. They ascribed their righteousness, salvation and all their glory to the merits of Christ the sole Saviour and not to their own. They adorned themselves with true and the only saving faith, with sincere charity towards God and neighbour, and with a life of holiness worthy of Christ their Redeemer.

units.la: () 2 tore suo dignæ sanctimonia exornârunt. Sicut maledictus est, qui adorat non Deum: ita maledictus est qui talibus veri Dei adoratoribus maledicit, vel Babylonis assEclas eosdem facit.
units.tr: () 2 adorned with holiness worthy of their Redeemer. As cursed is he who worships not God, so cursed is he who curses such worshippers of the true God, or makes them adherents of Babylon.

units.la: IV. Neque adeò dubitamus, quin eo ipso tempore, quo Ecclesia Romana in Babylonem degeneravit, ac sequentium etiam temporum tractu, Romæ vixerint, moriuntur plures, qui in terrestribus licèt & externis rebus cum Ecclesia communicantes, in statu tamen Cœlesti & spirituali cum ea consortium non habuerunt, adeóque uti à peccatorum Babylonis labe immunes se conservârunt, ita plagarum Babyloni decretarum sive in vita, sive in morte participes redditi non sunt, quos à Babylonis etiam communione distinguimus merito. Tales infelice eo tempore fuerunt, qui Scripturam S. pro sufficienti instrumento doctrinæ habuerunt, fundamentum salutis in eo revelatum amplexi sunt, veritatem ejusdem amárunt, Deo soli, Christóque ad salutem confisi sunt, & piè vixerunt, at de cætero erroribus quibusdam, subinde etiam gravibus impliciti fuerunt, vel eosdem saltem tulerunt, quos quocunque demum nomine venerint, veniántque, non tam pro parte vel Babylonis vel Bestiæ, quàm pro sanctis vinctis & captivis habemus. Quales si nulli cum Babylone & Bestia in eadem externa societate conjuncti fuissent, inebriari Meretrix sanguine sanctorum & testium Jesu (Apoc. xvii. 6.) non potuissent.
units.tr: IV. Nor do we doubt that at the very time when the Roman Church degenerated into Babylon, and throughout the course of the following ages, there have lived and still die many people who, although they communicated with the Church in earthly and external matters, nevertheless had no fellowship with it in heavenly and spiritual matters. Thus, preserved from the stain of Babylon's sins, they did not share in the plagues decreed against Babylon, whether in life or in death, and we rightly distinguish them from communion with Babylon. Such people, unhappily, lived in that time: they held Holy Scripture to be a sufficient instrument of doctrine, embraced the foundation of salvation revealed in it, loved its truth, trusted in God alone and in Christ for salvation, and lived piously. Yet they were at other times entangled in certain errors, sometimes even serious ones, or at least tolerated those errors. Whatever name they have borne or will bear, we regard them not so much as part of Babylon or the Beast, but as holy prisoners and captives. If none of them had been joined with Babylon and the Beast in the same external fellowship, the Harlot could not have been drunk with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus (Apoc. xvii. 6).

units.la: V. Ex adverso Ecclesiæ Romanæ omnes, quocunque demum tempore illi vixerunt Episcopi, Presbyteri, Doctores illi, qui Scripturam unicam fidei & vitæ regulam negligentes, fundamentum salutis ignorantes, & veritatem ejusdem non amantes, dixerunt ac putârunt unquam, se fidei arbitros & dominos esse, à se haud secus quàm ab ipso Spiritu S. verbum Dei, ejúsque infallibilem interpretationem repetendam, leges à sede sua præscriptas & approbatas, aut à Concilio suo injunctas justitiæ & salutis causa recipiendas esse, quinque ad dictum Scripturæ quidvis aliud sub anathemate addiderunt, veritatem interim justitiæ Dei & regni Christi non recte docuerunt, se ipsos supra omne Numen extulerunt, amorem & cultum uni solique Deo debitum in se ipsos, aliásque Dei Creaturas transtulerunt, elationis suæ causa, & mysterii religionisque prætextu bella concitárunt, libertatem Christianam suppresserunt, idololatriæ, crudelitatis erga sanctos, luxuriæ, superbiæ, blasphemiarum, veneficiorum nihil reliqui fecerunt; hi inquam, Tros Rutulúsve, & quocúnque demum nomine insigniti fuerint, sintque adhuc; quacunque ætate vixerint, vivántque non Ecclesia Christi, ejúsque germani fidelésque Rectores, sed Babylon, & Babylonii Romani vel fuerunt, vel etiamnum sunt, quod characteres Babylonis supra expositi abundè comprobant. Pari ratione populus ille Imperii Romani potentiâ suffarcinatus, & multorum populorum potentiâ amplificatus, Christianum equidem nomen præferens, cætera veri fundamenti salutis ignarus, nec veritatis amans, atque se dedens in obsequium ejusmodi Episcoporum & Præpositorum, quales jam descripsimus, ex eoque obsequio justitiam & salutem sperans, Bestia, ejúsque membra, & asseclæ singuli Bestiales sunt, uti Characteres Bestiæ supra allati non minùs firmiter comprobant.
units.tr: V. On the other hand, all those bishops, elders and teachers of the Roman Church, at whatever time they lived, who neglected Scripture as the sole rule of faith and life, were ignorant of the foundation of salvation and did not love its truth, and who ever said or thought that they were the arbiters and masters of faith, and that what they prescribed and approved from their see, or enjoined from their council, was to be received for the sake of righteousness and salvation as if it came from the Word of God and its infallible interpretation, and even from the Holy Spirit himself; who added to the words of Scripture anything else at all under anathema; who did not rightly teach the truth of God's righteousness and the kingdom of Christ; who exalted themselves above every divinity; who transferred the love and worship due to the one God alone to themselves and to other creatures; who stirred up wars for the sake of their own pride and under the pretext of mystery and religion; who suppressed Christian liberty; and who left nothing undone in idolatry, cruelty towards the saints, lust, pride, blasphemy and sorcery: these people, I say, whether they are called Trojans or Rutulians or by whatever name, and whether they lived in any age and still live, are not the Church of Christ or its genuine and faithful rulers, but Babylon. Those who were or still are Roman Babylonians are the ones the marks of Babylon set out above amply prove. In the same way, that people burdened with the power of the Roman Empire and enlarged by the power of many nations, though bearing the Christian name, ignorant of the true foundation of salvation in all else, not loving the truth, and surrendering itself to obedience to such bishops and prelates as we have now described, hoping for righteousness and salvation from that obedience, is the Beast, and its members and each of its adherents are bestial, as the marks of the Beast cited above prove no less firmly.

units.la: VI. Firmum est, & inconcussum stat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc, Dominus novit eos, qui sui sunt. 2 Tim. 11. 19. Et homo quidem intuetur faciem, Deus autem intuetur Cor. 1. Sam.xvi. 7. Neque adeò secundùm visionem oculorum is judicat Esai. xi. 3. sed secundùm veritatem judicium profert, ib. Cap. xlii. 3. De personis igitur Babylonis vel Bestiæ asseclis, & ad finem usque in earundem communione perdurantibus, atque ea ratione rigidum Dei judicium promerentibus, judicium nobis arrogamus nulli, sed Deo soli, quid in homine sit, pernoscenti (Joh. 11. 25.) relinquimus; & de pluribus, iis imprimis, qui Satanæ profunditates non nôrunt, bene speramus. Non noverat Elias septem in carnali Israële myriadas hominum, qui Baali genua non flexerunt: at noverat Deus. Neque etiam Abrahamus noverat Sodomæ exiguum adeò justorum numerum hærere, alioquin tam anxiè pro salute urbis illius non intercessurus: at noverat id Deus. Quos igitur ab æterno præcognovit, eos in medio etiam Babylonis & Bestiæ coetu à peccatis & plagis earundem immunes præstitit: oi δ' λοιποὶ ἐτωρώθησαν reliqui vero occalluerunt.
units.tr: VI. The foundation of God stands firm and unshaken, bearing this seal: The Lord knows those who are his. 2 Tim. 11. 19. Man indeed looks on the face, but God looks on the heart, 1 Sam. xvi. 7. Nor does he judge according to the sight of the eyes, Isa. xi. 3, but pronounces judgment according to truth, ibid. ch. xlii. 3. Therefore, concerning the persons who belong to Babylon or the followers of the Beast, who persist in fellowship with them to the end and thereby deserve God's stern judgment, we claim judgment for no one, but leave it to God alone, who knows what is in a man (John 2:25). Concerning many others, above all those who do not know the depths of Satan, we hope well. Elijah did not know that there were seven thousand men in carnal Israel who had not bent the knee to Baal, but God knew it. Nor did Abraham know that so small a number of righteous men dwelt in Sodom, or he would not have interceded so anxiously for the salvation of that city; but God knew it. Those whom he foreknew from eternity, he preserved, even in the midst of the company of Babylon and the Beast, free from their sins and plagues: but the rest were hardened [οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ ἐπωρώθησαν].

units.la: VII. Tametsi verò de personis in Babylonico & Bestiali statu positis, & ad finem usque vitæ perdurantibus, atque post vitam etiam in statu isthoc peractam πυρὸς ἀιωνίου ἀἴδιον æterni ignis judicium Babyloni & Bestiæ decretum sustinentibus, judicium nobis nulli arrogamus, adeóque Deo judici & Domino uni soliique servos suos relinquimus; cœtum tamen illum populúmque Babylonem & Bestiam esse, in quo reperiuntur & dominantur ii, qui characteribus iis, quos Babyloni & Bestiæ Spiritus S. inussit, insigniti compunctique sunt, pronuntiare oraculis ipsius Spiritùs S. & rerum gestarum conformitate freti, neutiquam veremur. Atque cœtum talem in Romana Ecclesia Christiana λειμών, ejúsque populo subdito jam diu extitisse,& hodieque proh dolor! existere; atque fata sua alacriter in dies provocare, intrepidè asserimus.
units.tr: VII. Although we claim judgment for no one concerning those persons who are placed in the Babylonish and bestial state, and persist in it to the end of life, and who, even after life has been spent in that state, undergo the judgment of eternal fire [πυρὸς αἰωνίου] decreed for Babylon and the Beast, and so leave his servants to God, the one Judge and Lord, we nevertheless do not hesitate to declare, relying on the oracles of the Holy Spirit himself and on the agreement of the events, that that company and that people are Babylon and the Beast, in which are found and hold sway those who are marked and branded with the characters which the Holy Spirit has stamped upon Babylon and the Beast. Such a company, we confidently assert, has long existed in the Christian Church of Rome, and its subject people, and even today, to our grief, still exists; and it eagerly hastens its own fate day by day.

units.la: VIII. Septem porro in universum sunt Ecclesiæ Romanæ Christianæ periodi, quas in historia Papatûs fuse deductas, ὡς σὺν λέγομεν heic repetimus, arbitraturi inde, quatemporestate in Babylonem meretriciam degeneraverit, quibusque búsque gradibus ad summam impietatem processerit. Prima Periodus est Ecclesiæ ejus in doctrina & regimine puririoris, ab ejus initio ad Constantini M. tempora usque: Secunda doctrinam puriorem retinentis, & in regimine dominationem affectantis, à Constantino M. ad Phocam & Bonifacium III. usque: Tertia dominationem in spiritualibus indultu Phocæ adipiscentis, & in doctrina ritibúsque degenerantis, à Bonifacio III. ad Gregorium VII. usque: Quarta dominationem etiam in temporalibus affectantis, & in doctrina ritibúsque in pejus indies vergentis à Gregorio VII. ad Bonifacium VIII. usque: Quinta dominationem etiam in temporalibus, adeóque Cæsareo-Papatum adipiscentis, & eundem profligata doctrina puriori omni, flagitiosè exercentis, à Bonifacio VIII. ad Leonem X. usque: Sexta per Reformationem & separationem fidelium potestatis utriúsque cladem gravissimam patientis, à Leone X. ad Concilii Tridentini finem usque: Septima denique per novella fidei & anathematismos diros in errore obstirmatæ, & cum vera Christi Ecclesia fraude & vi continuò decertantis, à Concilii Tridentini fine ad nostra usque tempora.
units.tr: VIII. There are, moreover, seven periods of the Christian Church of Rome in all. We have set them out fully in the history of the Papacy, and as we say briefly [ὡς συντόμως λέγομεν] we repeat them here, so that it may be judged at what time she degenerated into the harlot Babylon, and by what steps she advanced to the height of impiety. (1) The first period is that of her purer doctrine and government, from its beginning to the times of Constantine the Great. (2) The second is that of one who retained the purer doctrine but aspired to domination in government, from Constantine the Great to Phocas and Boniface III. (3) The third is that of one who obtained domination in spiritual matters by the grant of Phocas, and degenerated in doctrine and rites, from Boniface III to Gregory VII. (4) The fourth is that of one who also aimed at domination in temporal matters, and daily tended for the worse in doctrine and rites, from Gregory VII to Boniface VIII. (5) The fifth is that of one who also obtained dominion in temporal matters, and so a Caesaro-Papacy, and who, with all purer doctrine cast aside, exercised it shamelessly, from Boniface VIII to Leo X. (6) The sixth is that of one who suffered the most grievous wound of both powers through the Reformation and the separation of the faithful, from Leo X to the end of the Council of Trent. (7) The seventh and last is that of one who, hardened in error by new doctrines of faith and dire anathemas, and with fraud and force, continually contends with the true Church of Christ, from the end of the Council of Trent to our own times.

units.la: IX. Primam periodum à Babylonis labe & communione immunem penitus fuisse, vel eo argumento liquet, quod ejus tempore necdum Babylon extitit. Primum ejus seculum verè aureum fuit, quo Ecclesia Calicibus contenta ligneis, uti scitè olim Bonifacius Episcopus Moguntinus pronuntiavit, Sacerdotibus aureis fruebatur. Plerique ferè omnes ad Silvestrum usque Episcopi Romani Pastores fuerunt simplices absque mitris, in messe Euangelii ad martyrium usque laborantes, qui stellæ in dextra Christi permanentes merito dici potuerunt. Romæ Christianæ prima, ita in confutatione primatus Papæ Gregorius Heymburgensis loquitur, gloria fuit non purpura, non divitiæ, non equus albus, non fastus, non dominatus: Sed, Ecce nos relinquimus omnia, & secuti sumus te, Domine. Pontifices ipsi Martyrii laureâ contenti, nihil humilitate, modestia, paupertate, rerum terrestrium contemptu prius & antiquius habuêre. Invalescentibus quin etiam post Apostolorum & Apostolicorum virorum αφιξιν decessum, hæresibus, agrum Domini hinc inde impia licentia vastantibus, Ecclesiam Romanam earundémque contagione diu satis liberam, non tam eas in sinum suum recepisse, quàm casdem verbi Divini gladio fortissimè oppugnasse, Histor. Pap. s. vij. viij. abundè demonstravimus. Tametsi verò Episcopi nonnulli Romani in prima hac periodo vergente, Victor inprimis & Stephanus, supra alios, Orientales maximè, cristas erigere visi, uti ibid. s. xj. xij. &c. narravimus, humanitus nonnihil passi sunt, à Babylonico tamen in spiritualibus & temporalibus dominandi pruritu, & meretricia impuritate animos alienissimos gesserunt, & quam Deo soli fidem debuerunt, intemeratam illibatámque servarunt. Homines fuerunt, à quibus humani nihil alienum erat. Quamvis nonnullis eorum nævis Sathanas, nequissimus talium observator exactorque, procedente tempore in perniciem Ecclesiæ abusus est, prout magnorum virorum in utramque partem exempla validissima esse solent.
units.tr: IX. That the first period was wholly free from the stain and fellowship of Babylon is clear from this argument alone: that Babylon did not yet exist in its time. Its first century was truly golden, when the Church, content with wooden chalices, as the Bishop of Mainz, Boniface, once wittily declared, enjoyed golden priests. Almost all the Roman bishops, down to Silvester, were simple ministers without mitres, labouring in the harvest of the Gospel even to martyrdom, and deservedly could be called stars remaining in the right hand of Christ. The first glory of Christian Rome, as Gregory of Heimburg speaks in his refutation of the primacy of the Pope, was not purple, not riches, not a white horse, not pride, not domination, but: "Behold, we have left all things and followed you, Lord." The pontiffs themselves, content with the laurel of martyrdom, held nothing as more important or ancient than humility, modesty, poverty, and contempt for earthly things. Moreover, when heresies grew strong after the death of the Apostles and apostolic men, ravaging the Lord's field on every side with impious licence, we have amply shown in the Histor. Pap. s. vij. viij. that the Roman Church, which was for long fairly free from their contagion, did not receive them into her bosom, but attacked them most bravely with the sword of the Divine Word. Although some Roman bishops in this first period, which was drawing to its close, above all Victor and Stephen, and most of all among the Eastern bishops, seemed to raise their crests, as we related in the same work, s. xj. xij. and following, and suffered somewhat from human weakness, nevertheless they were far removed from the Babylonish itch to dominate in spiritual and temporal matters and from harlot-like impurity of mind, and they preserved intact and unimpaired the faith which they owed to God alone. They were men, and nothing human was alien to them. Yet Satan, the most wicked observer and exactor of such things, in time abused some of their blemishes to the ruin of the Church, as the most powerful examples of great men usually are, in either direction.

units.la: X. Neque etiam Secundam Ecclesiæ Romanæ periodum Babylonica impietas fœdavit. Verissimè equidem Hieronymus in vita Malchi dixit, Christi Ecclesiam, postquam ad Christianos Principes venit, potentia quidem & divitiis majorem, sed virtutibus minorem factam esse. Et postquam Constantini M. aliorúmque profusa liberalitate Ecclesia nimium quantum dotata, & longæ insuper usura pacis potita est, non desunt sanè, qui de longa pacis malis aperte quiritentur. Isidorus Pelusiota Lib. iii. ep. 408. sic Ecclesiæ sui temporis statum deplorat: Pacis quidem nomen ubique est, res autem ipsa nusquam. Verùm Ecclesia fœminæ cuidam, quæ ex antiqua felicitate excidit, ac signa tantùm habet, similis est. Ornamentorum enim suorum thecas & arculas habet, opibus autem spoliata est. Ita etiam Romani Pontifices degenerarunt, ut Socrate Histor. Eccl. vij. 11. teste πεῖα τῆς ἱερωσύνης ἐπὶ ἀρχαϊσμὸν ultra sacerdotii limites & potentiam processerint, & Basilio etiam ἐοφὸς ἀλυπος occidentale illud supercilium non parum displicuerit. Forte etiam Episcopi nonnulli Romani Monarchiam saltem in spiritualibus meditantes, machinantésque, jam tum Babylonico spiritu turgescere coeperunt, quod non paucorum meditamenta Hist. Pap. ff. xvij. &c. narrata astruere videntur. In universum tamen Ecclesiæ Romanæ Hierarchia nondum in propudiosam Meretricem Babylonicam, qualem Apocalypsis describit, degeneravit, tum quia religio & fides, nævis licèt & ψηφιμιλη-μασι laborans, in præcipuis tamen integra & salva constitit, neque qui obrepserunt errores leviores, & successu temporis in alienum & periculosiorem etiam sensum detorti, vel universales, vel Ecclesiæ lege sanciti, vel invito cuiquam obtrusi fuerunt: tum quia ipsi, qui altiorem in Ecclesia dignitatis gradum, insito hominibus cunctis dominandi affectu, quem novissimum cxui scitè ὁ ἀλᾶνα dixit, affectárunt, plerique saltem, cætera non mali fuerunt, neque vel sibi, vel aliis etiam Divinos honores arrogârunt, nedum enormia illa Babylonicæ Archimeretricis peccata in se admiserunt.
units.tr: X. Nor did Babylonish impiety defile the second period of the Church of Rome either. Jerome truly said in the Life of Malchus: that the Church of Christ, after it came to Christian princes, had become greater in power and riches, but smaller in virtues. And after the Church had been endowed beyond measure by the lavish liberality of Constantine the Great and others, and had moreover enjoyed a long interest of peace, there are certainly not lacking those who openly complain of the evils of long peace. Isidore of Pelusium, Lib. iii. ep. 408, laments the state of the Church of his own time in this way: There is everywhere the name of peace, but the thing itself is nowhere. The Church is like a woman who has fallen from her former happiness and has only the outward signs; she has chests and caskets of her ornaments, but she has been stripped of her wealth. So too the Roman pontiffs degenerated, so that, as Socrates testifies in his Ecclesiastical History vii. 11, they advanced beyond the limits of the priesthood [ἐπὶ τὰ ὅρια τῆς ἱερωσύνης] and into power, and Basil was not a little displeased by that Western supercilium [ὀφρύν] which was free from grief. Perhaps also some Roman bishops, meditating and devising a monarchy at least in spiritual matters, began even then to swell with the Babylonish spirit, as the schemes of not a few, related in Hist. Pap. ff. xvij. and following, seem to show. On the whole, however, the hierarchy of the Roman Church had not yet degenerated into the shameless Babylonian harlot such as the Apocalypse describes; first, because the religion and faith, though it laboured under blemishes and decrees [ψηφισμασι], nevertheless remained whole and safe in its chief points, and the lighter errors which crept in, and in time were twisted into a foreign and more dangerous meaning, were not imposed either as universal or sanctioned by church law, or forced on anyone against his will; and second, because those who, from the innate desire to dominate which belongs to all men, aspired to a higher grade of dignity in the Church, were for the most part not bad in other respects, and did not arrogate divine honours to themselves or to others, much less commit those monstrous sins of the Babylonian archharlot. This is what the wit of one who called it the last boaster [ὁ ἀλαζών] described.

units.la: XI. Est hæc sanè inter Sathanæ stratagemata haud prostremum, quòd homines cætera pios ad multa peccata, quæ nil minus quàm peccata esse videntur, impellit. Cùm enim actiones factáque multa ideo solùm tum laudem, tum reprehensionem merentur, quod vel bonum vel malum in finem instituta videantur, multis nefarii illius μυθοποιοῦ astu.
units.tr: XI. Among Satan's stratagems this is no small one: he drives men who are otherwise pious into many sins that seem to be no sins at all. For many actions and deeds earn praise or blame only because they seem to be designed for a good or an evil end, by the cunning of that fable-maker [μυθοποιοῦ].

units.la: P astu usu venit, quod merito mirari omnes possint, ut suâsmet cogitationes sensúsque minime intelligentes, alio consilio revera quid instituant, alio id instituere sibi videantur. Ne longè abeamus, Jacobus & Johannes, Domini discipuli, cum in quodam Samaritanorum vico una cum Christo admissi hospitio non fuissent, propterea quod Hierosolymam iis per causam religionis invisam contenderent, Dominum sic interrogárunt: Visne jubeamus ignem de Cælo descendere, qui eos conficiat, quemadmodum Elias fecit? Quibus sic Dominus respondit: Οὐκ οἴδατε οἵου πνεύματός ἐστε ὑμεῖς. Nescitis cujus spiritus sitis vos. Luc. ix. 52-55. Videbantur sibi discipuli procul dubio Divinæ gloriæ studio, eáque pietate & charitate, qua Dominum prosequebantur, id cogitasse; alioqui nunquam Dominum sic interrogaturi. Cæterùm quod tulerunt responsum, palam ostendit, impossuisse iis Sathanam, & ab offensione ex denegato hospitio accepta, inveteratóque, quod inter duos illos populos flagrabat, odio, nec non ab occulta quadam vindictæ cupiditate, non à solido gloriæ Divinæ, & religionis puritoris studio cogitationem illorum profectam fuisse.
units.tr: And so it happens, as all may rightly wonder, that people who do not understand their own thoughts and feelings in fact pursue one aim while believing they pursue another. Not to go far afield: when James and John, the disciples of the Lord, were not received as guests in a certain village of the Samaritans, because they were travelling to Jerusalem, which those people hated for reasons of religion, they put this question to the Lord: "Do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?" To this the Lord replied: "You do not know what spirit you are of" [Οὐκ οἴδατε οἵου πνεύματός ἐστε ὑμεῖς]. Luke 9:52-55. The disciples no doubt thought that they were acting out of zeal for the glory of God, and out of that piety and love with which they followed the Lord; otherwise they would never have asked the Lord such a thing. But the answer they received plainly shows that Satan had deceived them, and that their thought had arisen not from solid zeal for the glory of God and for a purer religion, but from the offence taken at the denied hospitality, from the long-standing hatred that burned between those two peoples, and from a hidden desire for revenge.

units.la: XII. Planè ita Romanis Pontificibus illis prioribus ante te & post Constantini M. tempora accidit. Quo tempore coeperunt opinionem, authoritatem splendorémque in Ecclesia ambire & adipisci, equidem nunquam crediderim, eos pietatis expertes fuisse (præter fortè paucos quosdam) cùm minimè vulgaris pietatis vestigia in scriptis eorum reperire sit. Igitur cùm illi non tantùm paterentur se honorificentissimè coli, evehi, liberalissiméque donari, sed etiam in acquirenda indies majore authoritate, & in Ecclesias etiam exoticas potestate diligentem operam ponerent, verisimile est, ita visum illis esse, eum splendorem, & affectatam in alias etiam Ecclesias, quas aberrantes fortè consilio & authoritate sua dirigendas putárunt, potestatem Ecclesiæ Dei {*}ixæ Dei fore vehementer utilem ; ut cùm in majore essent apud Ordines omnes veneratione, eorum multò plus ponderis haberent & monitiones, & reprehensiones, & Ecclesiasticæ censuræ, quibus in officio populum continerent. Sed nihilominus ingenita in homine insatiabilis quædam habendi cupido, summáque animi elatio, qua fit, ut quisque sublimi semper loco suam dignitatem authoritatemque, si fieri posset, esse velit, non ferèquicquam aliud, illas Ecclesiæ utilitates eis persuadebat, etsi nil tale animadverterent, & æquè ac discipuli Christi, quo ea in re spiritu ducerentur, ignorarent.
units.tr: XII. Exactly the same happened to those earlier Roman Pontiffs, both before and after the time of Constantine the Great. I could never believe that at that time they were without piety (except perhaps a few), since traces of no common piety are to be found in their writings. So when they not only allowed themselves to be honoured, exalted and generously endowed with the greatest respect, but also laboured diligently to gain greater authority day by day, and power even over churches far away, it is likely that it seemed to them that this splendour and this desired power over other churches, which they thought were perhaps straying and needed to be directed by their counsel and authority, would be greatly useful to the Church of God. Thus, since they were held in greater veneration by all orders, their admonitions, rebukes and ecclesiastical censures would carry much more weight, and would keep the people in their duty. Yet nonetheless an insatiable desire for having, innate in man, and that great elation of spirit by which each person always wishes, if it could be done, to hold a higher place and authority, almost alone persuaded them of those advantages for the Church, although they noticed nothing of the kind, and, like the disciples of Christ, did not know by what spirit they were led in this matter.

units.la: XIII. Tertia demum Ecclesiæ Romanæ periodus, quæ Phocæ tempore, & Bonifacio III. Papæ originem suam debet, Babylonicæ Meretrici initia planè inauspicata dedit. De infaustis iis temporibus sic celebris ille Johannes de Molinis in Speculo Carmelitarum cap. 6. loquitur: Asque tempore Heraclii Imperatoris (Phocæ successoris) usque ad nostra tempora, die vergente ad vesperam Eclipsin passa Ecclesia ad occasum cecidit, imò ferè ad defectionem pervenit. Cujusmodi fuerit infelix illa periodus unà cum consequentibus, non in melius utique, sed in pejus indies vergentibus, Historia Papatus inde à s. xxxviij. exponit. Liceat hic usurpare illa Horatii Lib. iij. Od. 6. Damnosa quid non imminuit dies? Ætas parentum, pejor avis, tulit Hos nequiores, mox daturos Progeniem vitiosiorem.
units.tr: XIII. Lastly, the third period of the Roman Church, which owes its origin to the time of Phocas and Pope Boniface III, gave the Babylonian harlot a thoroughly ill-omened beginning. Concerning those unlucky times the famous Johannes de Molinis speaks thus in his Speculum Carmelitarum, chapter 6: "From the time of the Emperor Heraclius (successor of Phocas) down to our own times, the Church, suffering an eclipse as the day declined towards evening, fell towards its setting, indeed nearly came to its extinction." What sort of unhappy period that was, together with the periods that followed, which tended not to improve but to grow worse day by day, the History of the Papacy sets out from section 38 onwards. Let me here borrow those words of Horace (Odes, book 3, ode 6): "What does the passing day not diminish for the worse? Our fathers' age, worse than the grandfathers', bore us, who were more worthless still, and we are about to bring forth a yet more degenerate offspring."

units.la: XIV. Tametsi verò sub periodi hujus Tertiæ initia meretrix facta est urbs illa fidelis, adeóque se Babylon illa magna prostituere coepit, nondum tamen efficere potuit, ut veneficiis suis gentes omnes seducerentur, & vino Scortationis ejus incolæ terræ inebriarentur. Neque enim, quando nata est illa meretrix, in prima ætatula sua statim ita prævaluit, ut confestim illecebris suis ad se omnia pertraheret. Ne Roma quidem uno die ædificata est, fuadque, uti in Catone Tullius loquitur, cuique parti ætatis tempestivitas danda est. Bestia scilicet illa, quæ meretricem portare debuit, etsi statim, & in ipsis, quod dicitur, incunabulis meretricis spiritu gravissimè tentaretur, eidem tamen non statim prorsus succubuit, ut in propudium, quale Apocalypsis describit, subito degeneraret. Genius enim Imperatorius, sub cujus alis Meretricula delitescebat, ab initio prævalescens, viriliter adhuc prædominabatur, cum Imperatores utut ιτπ Episcopos Romanos plus æquo colerent, Imperii habenas sibi nondum extorqueri paterentur. Marcescente demum Imperii vigore illi רבשם Robusti, de quibus Daniel. viii. 24. loquitur, succumbere cœperunt, & contra Pontificum ac Sacrificulorum per invalescentem superstitionem potestas vehementer amplificata fuit.
units.tr: XIV. Although that faithful city became a harlot at the beginning of this Third period, and the great Babylon began to prostitute herself, she could not yet bring it about that all nations were seduced by her sorceries and the inhabitants of the earth made drunk with the wine of her fornication. For when that harlot was born, she did not at once prevail so strongly in her infancy as to draw everything to herself by her allurements. Rome itself was not built in a single day; and, as Tullius says in Cato, "each part of life must be given its proper season." That beast, of course, which was to carry the harlot, although she was at once and, as they say, in the very cradle of the harlot, sorely tempted by her spirit, did not immediately yield to her so as to sink suddenly into the shameless condition that the Apocalypse describes. For the imperial genius under whose wings the little harlot lay hidden, being at first vigorous, still ruled with manly strength; although the emperors, however much they honoured the Roman bishops more than was right, did not yet allow the reins of empire to be wrested from their hands. At length, when the vigour of the empire began to wither, those Mighty ones, of whom Daniel 8:24 speaks, began to give way; and, by the growing superstition, the power of the Pontiffs and the sacrificing priests was greatly enlarged.

units.la: XV. Quæ igitur in Tertia Periodo lascivæ juvenculæ instar, quam libidinis pruritus vehementer quidem exagitat, quæ tamen adhuc cum pudore ita colluctatur, ut nondum frontem plane perfricuerit, meretriciæ arti operam dare cœpit; Quarta demum periodo pudorem ita excussit, ut subacto subactori suo protervè inequitare, adeóque unà cum spirituali potestate temporalem etiam omnem, suppressa Imperatoria Regiáque quavis, acquirere vehementissimè laboraverit. Pulchre equidem tum Meretricula illa sibi cavit, ne arcana sua propalarentur, uti his ferè verbis Aventinus Annal. Bojo. Lib. v. ubi res Gregorii VII. furialis illius mundi incendiarii, ipsum Acharonta, ut Patratum ad ἀχμὴν suam perduceret, moventis, sub quo quarta Periodus initium sortita est, prosequitur: Qualis felicitas ejus temporis fuerit, vel hinc æstimare licebit, quòd ejus temporis illustris & gravis imprimis author nomen suum prodere non audet. (excommunicationis metu) & admodum scitè acriterque ad factiones, ad fraudes, ad scelera perventum est. Vera scribere periculum, falsa, crimen. Verissimè tamen idem eodem Libro Aventinus rem ita prodidit: Is Hildebrandus, qui & Gregorius VII. primus Imperium Pontificium condidit, quod successores, per annos quadraginta quinque invito mundo, invitis Imperatoribus adeo duxere, ut Inferos, Superos in servitutem redegerint, subque jugum miserint, ut nunc cuncta fulmine perterritent, Quo bruta tellus, & vaga flumina Quo stix & invisa horrida Taenari sedes, Athlantaeusque finis Concutitur: mutant ima cum summis.
units.tr: XV. Therefore, what the Church was in the Third period, like a wanton young girl, whom the itch of lust vehemently stirs but who still struggles with modesty, so that she has not yet quite hardened her forehead, she began to practise the harlot's art; but in the Fourth period she cast off all shame, so that, having subjugated her own subjugator, she shamelessly rode him, and, together with spiritual power, strove most eagerly to acquire all temporal power too, suppressing every imperial and royal authority. The little harlot then took good care that her secrets should not be made public, as Aventinus, in the Annals of Bavaria, book 5, where he follows the deeds of that raging firebrand of the world, Gregory VII, who stirred up Acheron itself [ἀχμὴν] to bring his own peak of power to its height, under whom the fourth period took its beginning, puts it in roughly these words: "How happy that time was may be judged from this alone: that the illustrious and serious author of that time does not dare to put his name to his work (for fear of excommunication), and that things reached such a pitch of factions, frauds and crimes, so cleverly and fiercely pursued. To write the truth is dangerous, to write falsehoods a crime." Yet in the same book Aventinus recounts the matter most truthfully in this way: "That Hildebrand, who is also called Gregory VII, first founded the Papal empire, which his successors for forty-five years, the world unwilling and the emperors unwilling, so managed that they reduced the powers below and above to slavery and put them under the yoke, so that now they terrify everything with thunderbolts. At whose behest the sluggish earth, the wandering rivers, the Styx, the dreaded seat of Taenarus and the far end of Atlas are shaken; the bottom is turned to the top."

units.la: Et paulò post: Jam Imperator Romanus nihil aliud est, quam appellatio sine corpore, sine specie.
units.tr: And a little later: "Now the Roman emperor is nothing but a name without a body, without an appearance."

units.la: XVI. Clariùs rem totam Onuphrius in vita Gregorii VII. sic explicat: Huic uni cùm omnes Latinæ Ecclesiæ tum præcipuè Romana acceptum referre debet, quòd libera sit, & ab Imperatorum manu eruta, quòd tot divitiis, opibus & prophana ditione locupletata, quòd Regibus, Imperatoribus, Christianis Principibus sit præfecta: à quo postremo, ut omnia verbo uno complectar, maximus ille eximiúsque status, in quo Ecclesia Romana est omnium Christianorum Domina, cùm antea tanquam vilis ancilla, non ab Imperatoribus modò, sed à quovis Principe Romani Imperatoris præsidio fulta, premeretur: ab hoc maximae illius, & omni seculo tremendæ, venerandæque Romani Pontificis, & INFINITÆ pene potestatis jus manavit. Nam etsi ante Romani Pontifices, tanquam religionis Christianæ Capita, Christique vicarii & Petri successores colerentur, non tamen eorum authoritas ultra protendebatur, quàm in fidei dogmatis vel asserendis, vel tuendis. Caeterùm Imperatoribus suberant; ad eorum nutum omnia fiebant; ab eis creabantur; de eis judicare, vel quidquam decernere non audebat Papa Romanus. Primus omnium Romanorum Pontificum Gregorius VII. armis Nortmannorum fretus, opibus Comitissæ Mathildis mulieris per Italiam potentissimæ confisus, discordiaque Germanorum Principum bello civili laborantium inflammatus, præter majorum nomen, contempta Imperatoris authoritate & potestate, cùm summum Pontificatum obtinuisset, Cæsarem ipsum (à quo si non electus, saltem confirmatus fuerat) non dico excommunicare, se etiam Regno Imperióque privare ausus est. Res ante ea Secula inaudita. Nam fabulas, quæ de Anastasia, Arcadio & Leone Iconomacho circumferuntur, nihil moror. Hactenus ille, paucis rem totam complexus, & prima illa Romanæ Ecclesiæ adversus Principes hujusmundi molimina ex vero adumbrans.
units.tr: XVI. Onuphrius explains the whole matter more clearly, in the life of Gregory VII, in these words: "To him alone all the Latin Churches, and especially the Roman, must owe it that she is free and snatched from the hand of the emperors; that she is enriched with so many riches, resources and secular dominion; that she has been placed over kings, emperors and Christian princes. From him, to sum up everything in a word, comes that greatest and most outstanding condition in which the Roman Church is the mistress of all Christians, whereas before she was pressed down like a base maidservant, supported not only by the emperors but by any prince, by the protection of the Roman emperor. From this came the right of that greatest Roman Pontiff, dreaded and venerated in every age, and of an almost INFINITE power. For although before this the Roman Pontiffs were honoured as the heads of the Christian religion, as Christ's vicars and successors of Peter, yet their authority did not extend further than to asserting or defending the dogmas of the faith. Otherwise they were subject to the emperors; everything was done at their nod; they were appointed by them; the Roman Pope did not dare to judge them or to decide anything about them. Gregory VII, the first of all the Roman Pontiffs, relying on the arms of the Normans, trusting in the resources of the Countess Matilda, a woman most powerful throughout Italy, and inflamed by the discord of the German princes who were labouring in civil war, once he had obtained the supreme Pontificate, despised the authority and power of the emperor, and dared not only to excommunicate Caesar himself (by whom he had at least been confirmed, if not elected), but also to deprive him of kingdom and empire. This was unheard of in earlier ages. For I pay no heed to the fables that circulate about Anastasius, Arcadius and Leo the Iconoclast. So far he, who summed up the whole matter in a few words and sketched truly the first attempts of the Roman Church against the princes of this world."

units.la: XVII. Conatus ille Divina & humana subjugandi & Deo hominibúsque pro animi ferocientis libidine imperitandi, adeò feliciter processit, ut jam Periodo Quinta, quam Bonifacius VIII. Mortalium nequissimus, auspicatus est, Hierarchiæ Romanæ, Cæsareo-papatum suum adeptæ, omnia parucrint, quod Periodi ejus historia à nobis pertexta abundè comprobat. De ipso Bonifacio illa sic Platina: Moritur hoc modo Bonifacius ille, qui Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus, nationibus, populis terrorem potiùs, quàm religionem injicere conabatur: quique dare Regna, & auferre, pellere homines & reducere pro arbitrio animi conabatur, aurum undiquaque conquisitum, plus quàm dici potest, sitiens. Tum igitur non amplius Meretrix isthæc lascivire, & cum pudere quodam collustari visa est; sed potiùs attriti instar, profligatique pudoris scorti, quod per omnia artium Meretriciarum fla-gitia gitia progressum, pudorem omnem excussit, subacto subactori suo inequitavit palam, & manu sua tenens aureum poculum, abominationibus & impuritate fornicationis scatens, Reges & incolas terræ potavit, & ad consuetudinem suam meretriciam, veluti fascino quodam, pellexit.
units.tr: XVII.
