That attempt to subjugate things divine and human, and to rule over God and men at the pleasure of a fierce spirit, succeeded so well that by the Fifth Period, which Boniface VIII, most wicked of mortals, initiated, all things had yielded to the Roman Hierarchy, which had attained its Caesaro-papacy, as the history of that period which we have traced out amply proves. Of Boniface himself Platina says this: Boniface died in this manner, he who tried to strike terror into emperors, kings, princes, nations and peoples rather than to instil religion; who tried to give and take away kingdoms, to drive men out and bring them back at his pleasure, and who, thirsting for gold gathered from every quarter, wanted more than can be said. Then indeed this harlot no longer seemed to play wantonly and to be looked at with some shame; rather, like a worn-out, shameless whore who had progressed through all the crimes of harlotry and cast off every sense of modesty, she rode openly on her subjugated rider, and holding a golden cup in her hand, teeming with abominations and the impurity of fornication, she gave drink to the kings and inhabitants of the earth, and by her harlot's custom enticed them, as if by some spell.

units.la: XVIII. Per quatuor & quod excurrit, seculorum fluxum, inde à Gregorio VII. ad Leonem X. usque, sub quarta illa & quinta periodo amplissimè, & paucis validè intercedentibus, Meretrix Babylonica regnavit. Sexta demum Periodus, qua Reformationis Ecclesiasticæ beneficio eam Reges, populique plures desertam, res suas fœdiffimas sibi habere jusserunt, quáque etiam Saneti, qui in Babylonica illa captivitate, cum Babyloniis corpore, & quacunque externi cultus communione permixti squalebant, ab eadem separari, & passim segreges cœtus instituere coeperunt, Divini adversus eandem judicii initia protulit. Adversus quæ tamen ita frontem animumque obstirmavit, ut & per anathematismos Tridentinos universam impietatem suam Babylonicam roboraverit, & sub Septima, quam hucusque volvit agitátque periodo eluctari, & per continuas Ecclesiæ à se separatæ violentas fraudulentásque persecutiones ad pristinum potentiæ & libidinis suæ gradum eniti unicè contendat.
units.tr: XVIII. Through four and more centuries, from Gregory VII to Leo X, under that fourth and fifth period, the Babylonian harlot reigned very widely, with few strongly opposing her. At last came the sixth period, in which, by the benefit of the Ecclesiastical Reformation, many kings and peoples deserted her and bade her keep her own most foul affairs; in which also the saints, who had been defiled in that Babylonian captivity, mixed with the Babylonians in body and in every communion of external worship, began to separate from her and to set up separate assemblies everywhere. This brought forth the beginnings of divine judgment against her. Yet against these she so hardened her brow and mind that through the Tridentine anathemas she strengthened all her Babylonian impiety, and under the seventh period, which she still rolls and turns over, she strives to struggle through and, by continual violent and fraudulent persecutions of the Church separated from her, to strain back towards her former degree of power and lust.

units.la: XIX. Ex periodorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ distinctione isthac ... seu quæstionis status liquidò emergit.
units.tr: XIX. From this division of the periods of the Church of Rome ... or the state of the question clearly emerges.

units.la: Quæritur enim: An Hierarchia Romana, seu Papa Romanus per Clerum suum dominans, seu supremum in spiritualibus æquè ac temporalibus dominium sibi arrogans, in de à temporibus Gregorii VII. seu Anni Christi præter propter millesimi septuagesimi tertii, maximè, adeòque etiam hodierna, sit Babylon illa Magna, Meretrix illa Magna, Mater fornicationum, cujus Sedem, habitum, subditos, peccata enormia, & judicium Angelus Apoc. xviij.
units.tr: The question is this: whether the Roman Hierarchy, or the Roman Pope ruling through his clergy and arrogating to himself supreme dominion over spiritual and temporal affairs alike, from the time of Gregory VII, that is, from about the year of Christ 1073, and above all today, is that Great Babylon, that Great Harlot, the Mother of fornications, whose seat, dress, subjects, enormous sins and judgment the angel describes in Revelation 17, 18 and 19?

units.la: xvij. xviij. & xix. describit ? Dico, inde à temporibus Gregorii vii. maximè. Quamvis enim negotium Antichristi, adeóque etiam Babylonis Magnæ, cujus Distinćto emblemate Antichristi Regnum figuratur; in Mysterio,hoc est, clam & occultè peragi debuerit, ut conversionis illius dies & hora indicari non debeat; & ipse Spiritus S. Apoc. xvii. 1. dicens. Veni, ostendam tibi judicium Archimeretricis illius: de qua tamen verbum antehac nullum secerat, eo ipso tacitè indicaverit, Monstrum ifthoc non nisi à posteriori, five ab effectu cognitum iri, quando jam cum Juda proditore scelus suum peregit: quamvis etiam Romana Hierarchia sub tertia jam periodo in Babylonem & Meretricem degeneraverit, quæstionem tamen merito adstrinxisse videor ad illud tempus, quo Romana Hierarchia dominatum non in spiritualibus duntaxat, sed temporalibus etiam valide appetiit obtinuitque, quo imprimis tempore ad virilem suam ætatem, & paulatim etiam ipsam progressa est.
units.tr: I say that it is so from the time of Gregory VII, and above all. For although the business of Antichrist, and therefore of Great Babylon, whose kingdom is figured by the emblem of Antichrist, had to be carried on in a mystery, that is, secretly and covertly, so that the day and hour of that change should not be disclosed, and although the Holy Spirit himself, saying in Revelation 17:1, Come, I will show you the judgment of that great harlot, and yet having said nothing of her before, has tacitly indicated that this monster would be recognised only afterwards, that is, from its effect, when it had already committed its crime along with Judas the traitor; still, although the Roman Hierarchy had already degenerated into Babylon and the Harlot in the third period, I seem rightly to have confined the question to that time when the Roman Hierarchy not only strongly sought and obtained dominion over spiritual affairs, but also over temporal ones, which especially at that time it began to reach in its manhood, and gradually advanced even to that point itself.

units.la: XX. Quæstionem isthanc ante Reformationem ipsam affirmârunt non pauci gravisque authores, Honorius Augustodunensis, Clerus Leodiensis, Everhardus Salisburgensis, Theodoricus à Nyem, Fraticelli, Fr. Petracha, Nicolaus Clemangis, Wiclefus, Huffus, ipse Galliæ Rex Ludovicus XII. quorum singulorum testimonia Historia Papatus prodidit; aliique complures: post Reformationem five facto, five professione, quotquot ab Ecclesia Romana piam justamque secessionem fecerunt, adeóque Babylone illa exiverunt, & ἐπιμένοντες τῇ χάριτι permanentes in benignitate & gratia Dei, hodieque in fidei Divinæ incorruptibilitate perfistunt.
units.tr: XX. Not a few weighty authors affirmed this question even before the Reformation itself: Honorius of Autun, the Clergy of Liège, Eberhard of Salzburg, Theodoric of Niem, the Fraticelli, Francis Petrarch, Nicolas of Clamanges, Wycliffe, Hus, and the King of France himself, Louis XII; the testimonies of each of these the History of the Papacy has set forth, and several others too. After the Reformation, all who, whether in fact or in profession, withdrew from the Church of Rome in a pious and just secession, and so went out of that Babylon, and continuing [ἐπιμένοντες τῇ χάριτι] in the grace and kindness of God, remain to this day in the incorruptibility of the divine faith.

units.la: XXI. Lubet Ecclesiarum nostrarum sententiam explicare verbis Confessionis Ecclesiarum Gallicanarum, quæ articulo de Romano Pontifice sic sonant: Cùm verò Episcopus
units.tr: XXI. I wish to set out the view of our Churches in the words of the Confession of the Gallican Churches, whose article on the Roman Pontiff runs thus: But when the Bishop

units.la: copus scopus Romanus erecta sibi in Orbe Christiano Monarchia, sibi arroget principatum in omnes Ecclesias & pastores, usque adeo inflatus, ut Deum se appellet: velit adorari: ipse sibi tribuat potestatem in Cœlo & in terra: res ecclesiasticas ad libitum componat: condat articulos fidei: authoritatem Scripturæ velit pendere à sua: eámque ad libidinem interpretetur: animarum mercaturam exerceat: liberet astrictos votis & juramentis: novos Dei cultus instituat: &, quod ad civilia attinet, legitimam magistratuum authoritatem conculcet, dans, adimens, & transferens Regna; credimus, & afferimus, eum esse verum illum & germanum Antichristum, filium perditionis prædictum Verbo Dei; Meretricem purpuratam, insidentem Septem montibus: in magna civitate obtinentem Regnum in Reges terræ; & exspectamus donec Deus, prout promisit, & jam cœpit, eum fractum & victum spiritu oris sui, tandem deleat fulgore adventus sui.
units.tr: Bishop of Rome, having set up for himself a monarchy in the Christian world, claims for himself a principality over all churches and ministers, so swollen with pride that he calls himself God, wishes to be worshipped, assigns to himself power in heaven and on earth, arranges ecclesiastical affairs at will, makes articles of faith, wishes the authority of Scripture to depend on his own, and interprets it as he pleases, carries on a trade in souls, frees from vows and oaths those bound by them, institutes new worships of God, and, as far as civil matters go, tramples on the lawful authority of magistrates, giving, taking away and transferring kingdoms; we believe and affirm that he is the true and genuine Antichrist, the son of perdition foretold in the Word of God, the purple-clad Harlot sitting on seven mountains, holding in the great city the kingdom over the kings of the earth; and we wait until God, as he has promised and has already begun, breaks him and overcomes him with the breath of his mouth, and at last destroys him with the brightness of his coming.

units.la: XXII. Non desunt equidem viri doctissimi, qui Ecclesiarum Euangelicarum isthanc de Hierarchia Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominante sententiam, sive in piis eruditisque suis in Apocalypsin commentationibus, sive dedita etiam opera comprobaverint, adeóque perfrictam illam frontem, quæ nullius criminis rea censeri vult, meretriciæ impietatis suæ palàm, tumorem uteri, lac in mammis, corruptos oculos, & alia hujus generis corruptæ pudicitiæ toti mundo, ceu digitis, monstrantes, convicerint. Neque tamen operam lusuri nos videmur, si demonstrationem eandem, hoc in primis tempore, quo nimiûm illa exultat, & fuco multiplici se abscondere conatur, paulò accuratiùs pro gratiæ Divinæ modulo suscepepimus, bonisque adeò omnibus, æternæ salutis desiderio ardentibus, eadem opera persuaserimus, ne cum Meretricis illius Magnæ peccatis commercium communionémve ullam habeant, quò à plagis Q gis eidem proximè imminentibus salvos se immunésque præstent. Quod felix & faustum τὸ τελεσφόρον Numen esse velit jubeátque!
units.tr: XXII. Indeed there are not lacking most learned men who have confirmed this view of the ruling Hierarchy of the Roman Church, either in their pious and learned commentaries on the Apocalypse or even by deliberate labour, and so have convicted that brazen forehead, which wishes to be thought guilty of no crime, by showing to the whole world, as with fingers, its harlot's impiety, the swelling of the womb, the milk in the breasts, the corrupt eyes, and other things of this kind belonging to a corrupt chastity. Nor do we seem to be about to labour in vain if we have undertaken, somewhat more carefully and according to the measure of divine grace, the same demonstration at this time especially, when she exults too much and tries to hide herself under many a disguise, and have thereby persuaded all good men burning with desire for eternal salvation not to have any fellowship or communion with the sins of that Great Harlot, so that they may keep themselves safe and free from the plagues that are soon to hang over her. May the happy and auspicious Power, the accomplisher [τὸ τελεσφόρον], will and command this!

units.la: DISSERTATIO QUINTA
units.tr: Fifth Dissertation

units.la: QUA Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem Magnam Babylonem esse argumento generali demonstratur. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: In which it is demonstrated by a general argument that the hierarchy, or the clergy of the Church of Rome that rules, is the Great Babylon. A SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Transitio ad sententiam affirmantis demonstrationem.
units.tr: I. The transition to the statement of the affirmative proof.

units.la: II. Syllogismus generalis, seu complexio argumentorum, quibus Hierarchiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem esse Babylonem Magnam demonstratur.
units.tr: II. The general syllogism, or the combination of arguments by which it is demonstrated that the ruling hierarchy of the Church of Rome is the Great Babylon.

units.la: III. Propositionis majoris veritas definiti & definitionis nexu nititur.
units.tr: III. The truth of the major premise rests on the definition and on the connection between the definition and the thing defined.

units.la: IV. Probatio specialis propositionis majoris secundùm lemmata singula,
units.tr: IV. The specific proof of the major premise, taken in its separate lemmas,

units.la: V. quòd scilicet Babylon Magna sit cœtus veteri Babyloni Chaldaicæ quadantenus conveniens,
units.tr: V. namely, that the Great Babylon is a body somewhat resembling the old Chaldean Babylon,

units.la: VI. mysteriorum seu religionis Christianæ falsò prætextu ludens.
units.tr: VI. playing falsely with the pretext of the mysteries, or of the Christian religion.

units.la: VII. VIII. IX. Imperium in Civitate Magna, in populum animalem, septem collibus, totidemque Provinciis distinctum, multorúmque Regum potentia suffultum, obtinens,
units.tr: VII, VIII, IX. Exercising dominion in a Great City, over a fleshly people, divided into seven hills and as many provinces, and supported by the power of many kings,

units.la: X. immani fastu habitúque prætumido sese proserens,
units.tr: X. displaying itself with monstrous pride and a haughty bearing,

units.la: XI. se ipsum ceu Numen Divinitatis particeps subjecti sibi populi venerationi exponens; populúmque eundem à vero Dei cultu, ad sui & creaturarum cultum, salsamque religionem modis omnibus seducens.
units.tr: XI. exposing itself, as though a sharer in the Godhead, to the veneration of the people subject to it; and seducing that same people in every way from the true worship of God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to a corrupt religion;

units.la: XII. Sanctos veri Dei cultores atrociter persequens,
units.tr: XII. cruelly persecuting the true worshippers of God,

units.la: XIII. blasphemiis, luxuria, veneficiis, avaritia, & nundinatione spirituali immaniter se polluens,
units.tr: XIII. defiling itself monstrously with blasphemies, luxury, sorceries, avarice, and spiritual trafficking,

units.la: XIV. denique ob impietatem isthanc severissimum Dei judicium provocans.
units.tr: XIV. and finally, by this impiety, provoking the most severe judgment of God.

units.la: XV. Assumptio posita, quòd Hierarchia Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans ejusmodi cœtus sit.
units.tr: XV. The assumption laid down, that the ruling hierarchy of the Church of Rome is such a body.

units.la: I. Cum Babylon MagnaRomæ quæri omnino debeat, eáque nec in veteri Roma Ethnica inveniri potuerit, & in novissima Roma EthnicoAntichristiana, utpote quæ talis, qualem Ribera descripsit, nulla erit, frustra expectetur; in Roma Christiana, Christi nomen mentita indagandam eandem esse, ex prophetiæ ipsius characteribus Dissertatione III. definivimus. Romam porro Christianam, seu Hierarchiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem inde à Gregorii VII. tempore inprimis Babylonem Magnam in prophetia declarari censerique merito, superiori diatriba affirmavimus. Restat ut rem magni momenti, cui ad insaniam usque, apertæ rei licet, reclamant, certis irrefragabilibúsque argumentis rationúmque ponderibus demonstremus, & apertæ veritati demus.
units.tr: I. Since the Great Babylon must certainly be sought at Rome, and since it could not be found in ancient pagan Rome, and in the newest, pagan-antichristian Rome, which is such as Ribera described, it will be sought in vain; we defined in Dissertation III that it is to be looked for in Christian Rome, which pretends to the name of Christ, from the very marks of the prophecy. Further, in the earlier discourse we affirmed that Christian Rome, or the ruling hierarchy of the Church of Rome, is especially from the time of Gregory VII declared in the prophecy and rightly judged to be the Great Babylon. It remains for us to demonstrate by certain and irrefutable arguments and by the weight of reasons a matter of great importance, which they oppose even to madness, though the thing is plainly open, and to give it to the light of open truth.

units.la: II. Ut verò in antecessum arctè universa compingamus, more eorum, qui in magna rerum messe solent, lubet ἀπόδειξιν nostram moliri Syllogismo generali, rerum, quos tractabimus, momenta brevi συνα-θροισμῷ onnium complexuro. Talis autem est:
units.tr: II. In order to bind together the whole matter closely beforehand, in the manner of those who gather in a great harvest, we choose to construct our proof by a general syllogism, which will comprehend in a brief συναθροισμός [synathroismos, gathering together] the weight of the matters we shall treat. It is as follows:

units.la: Quicunque cætus (1) Babyloni veteri Chaldææ quadamtenus conveniens (2) sub mysteriorum seu religionis Christianæ prætextu (3) imperium in Civitate magna, in populum magnum Christi nomen professum licet, Clero dominanti parentem, septem collibus, totidémque provinciis distinctum, multorúmque Regum potentia suffultum, obtinet, séque (4) immani fastu, habitúque prætumido (5) ceu Numen Divinitatis particeps ab eo religiose coli patitur (6) adeóque populum sibi obnoxium à vero Dei cultu, ad sui & creaturarum cultum salsámque religionem modis omnibus seducit, (7) sanctos veri Dei cultores atrociter persequitur, (8) blasphemiis, (9) luxuria, (10) veneficiis, (11) avaritia & nundinatione spirituali se se immaniter polluit; (12) severúmque iccirco Dei judicium provocans, illud aliquatenus jam subivit, & porro subiturus est; is Babylon Magna, Mater scortationum & abominationum terræ est.
units.tr: Whatever body (1) somewhat resembles old Chaldean Babylon, (2) under the pretext of the mysteries or of the Christian religion, (3) holds dominion over a Great City, over a great people which professes the name of Christ though it is a parent to the ruling clergy, divided into seven hills and as many provinces, and supported by the power of many kings; and which (4) with monstrous pride and a haughty bearing, (5) allows itself to be religiously worshipped by that people as a sharer in the Godhead, and so (6) seduces the people subject to it in every way from the true worship of God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to a corrupt religion; (7) cruelly persecutes the true worshippers of God; (8) defiles itself monstrously with blasphemies, (9) luxury, (10) sorceries, (11) avarice, and spiritual trafficking; (12) and, thereby provoking the severe judgment of God, has already in some measure undergone it, and is yet to undergo it: that body is the Great Babylon, the Mother of harlotries and abominations of the earth.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans, inde à Gregorii VII. temporibus maximè, cætus ejusmodi est.
units.tr: But the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Church of Rome, especially from the time of Gregory VII, is such a body.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans, inde à Gregorii VII. temporibus maximè, Babylon Magna, Mater scortationum & abominationum terræ est.
units.tr: Therefore the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Church of Rome, especially from the time of Gregory VII, is the Great Babylon, the Mother of harlotries and abominations of the earth.

units.la: III. Propositionis majoris veritas omni explicatione major est, utpote quæ Babylonis Magnæ definitionem explicatam continet. Inter definitionem autem & definitum nexus
units.tr: III. The truth of the major premise is greater than any explanation, since it contains the explained definition of the Great Babylon. The connection between the definition and the thing defined

units.la: Propositionis majoris veritas defini-tionis & definitionis nexus nititur. nexus adeò necessarius est, ut posita illa hoc non possit non poni, cùm non re ipsa, sed sola ratione, terminisque differant. Accedit quòd omnia prædicata conjunctim posita definitionis ad instar aut nominis proprii subjecta nominum analogorum demonstrant. Cùm igitur propositio isthæc complexio quædam sit prædicatorum omnium, quæ Babyloni M. Apocalypsis attribuit, manifestum est, id, cui complexio illa competit, Babylonem Magnam esse.
units.tr: The truth of the major premise rests on the definition and on the connection between the definition and the thing defined. This connection is so necessary that, once the one is posed, the other cannot but be posed, since they differ not in fact but only in concept and in terms. Moreover, all the predicates taken together in the definition, like a proper name, show the subjects of the analogous names. Since, therefore, this premise is a combination of all the predicates which the Apocalypse attributes to the Great Babylon, it is plain that that to which the combination applies is the Great Babylon.

units.la: IV. Singula verò ut paucis, dissertatione tertia abundè jam demonstrata licet, repetamus Babylon Magna in propositione majori definitur Cœtus. Vocatur enim πόλις μεγάλη Civitas magna Apoc. xvii. 18. non utique locus mœnibus cinctus, sed multitudo quæpiam per caput aut capita sociata, seu communio quæpiam civium certis legibus convenientium, & religiosa quidem, uti Differt. III. 14. 15. 16. 18. comprobavimus.
units.tr: IV. Let us briefly go through the separate points, though they have already been amply demonstrated in the third dissertation. In the major premise the Great Babylon is defined as a body. For it is called πόλις μεγάλη [polis megalē], the Great City, Apoc. 17:18: not indeed a place enclosed by walls, but a certain multitude joined under one head or several heads, or a certain fellowship of citizens gathered under fixed laws, and indeed a religious one, as we showed in Dissert. III, 14, 15, 16, 18.

units.la: V. Cœtum definimus Babyloni veteri Chaldææ quadantenus convenientem. Neque enim Βαβυλὼν μεγάλη Babylon Magna Apoc. xvii. 5. vocari potuisset, nisi similitudo quædam ei cum בבל רבה Babylone Magna, cujus Prophetia Dan. iv. 30. meminit, intercederet, quod ipsum quoque Differt. III. 2. ostendimus. Ita cùm eadem civitas Magna Apoc. xi. 8. vocatur πνευματικῶς Σόδομα καὶ Αἴγυπτος spiritualiter Sodoma & Ægyptus, similitudinem quampiam cum veteri Sodoma & Ægypto indigitari, palam est.
units.tr: V. We define the body as somewhat resembling old Chaldean Babylon. For it could not have been called Βαβυλὼν μεγάλη [Babylōn megalē], Babylon the Great, Apoc. 17:5, unless some likeness to בבל רבה [Bavel rabbah], Great Babylon, of which the prophecy of Daniel 4:30 speaks, lay between them; which we also showed in Dissert. III, 2. So also, since the same Great City is called in Apoc. 11:8 πνευματικῶς Σόδομα καὶ Αἴγυπτος [pneumatikōs Sodoma kai Aigyptos], spiritually Sodom and Egypt, it is plain that some likeness to old Sodom and Egypt is pointed out.

units.la: VI. Addit definitio, Babylonem M. imperare sub mysteriorum, seu religionis Christianæ prætextu. Habet enim Babylon, Meretrix illa magna, titulum fronti suæ præfixum: μυστήριον Mysterium Apoc. xvii. 5. quo illam sub prætextu scilicet mysterii pietatis & religionis, non cujuslibet, sed Christianæ, utpote in scrinio pectoris sui latentis unicè, ad sui amorem incestum scortatores allicere Differt. III. 5. 6. 18. &c. manifestissimum fecimus.
units.tr: VI. The definition adds that the Great Babylon rules under the pretext of the mysteries, or of the Christian religion. For that Babylon, the great Harlot, has written on her forehead the title μυστήριον [mystērion], Mystery, Apoc. 17:5; by which, under the pretext, namely, of a mystery of godliness and of religion, and not of any religion but the Christian one, as though hidden in the bosom's casket alone, she entices her lovers to illicit love of herself. We made this most evident in Dissert. III, 5, 6, 18, etc.

units.la: VII. Coetui eidem propositio tribuit Imperium in Civitate Magna , in populum M. animalem, septem collibus, totidémque provinciis distinctum, multorúmque Regum potentia suffultum. Non enim qualiscunque Coetus Babylon est, sed dominans, imperitans. Inducitur quippe ceu Mulier sedens super Bestiam, seu Rectrix Bestiæ; Apoc. xvii. 3. & Civitas M. habens Regnum super Reges terræ cap. xviii. 18.
units.tr: VII. The proposition ascribes to the same body dominion in a Great City, over a fleshly people, divided into seven hills and as many provinces, and supported by the power of many kings. For the Babylon is not just any body, but one ruling and commanding. She is introduced indeed as a Woman sitting upon the Beast, that is, the ruler of the Beast, Apoc. 17:3; and the Great City having dominion over the kings of the earth, ch. 18:18.

units.la: VIII. Nullum porro Imperium nisi in loco geri potest. Hinc etiam Apocalypsis Babyloni M. Tribuit civitatem Magnam, ibid. eámque sedere super aquas multas, ibid. v. 1. nec non super septem montes, totidémque capita bestiæ. v. 7. 9. asserit, unde civitatis illius amplitudo æstimari potest.
units.tr: VIII. Moreover, no dominion can exist except in a place. Hence the Apocalypse also ascribes to the Great Babylon the Great City, ibid., and says that she sits upon many waters, ibid. v. 1, and also upon seven mountains, which are seven heads of the beast, vv. 7, 9; from which the extent of that city may be estimated.

units.la: IX. Neque etiam Imperium ullum sine subditis constat. Proin etiam Apocalypsis coetui huic religionis Christianæ prætextu dominanti subditos tribuit, puta Bestiam, Babylonem Meretricem portantem v. 7. quæ v. 8. & seq. dicitur fuisse, & non esse, & velle ascendere ex abysso, & vadere in interitum, non sine stupore incolarum terræ, habens septem capita, seu totidem montes, in quibus Mulier sedet; & decem cornua, seu totidem Reges potestatem unà cum bestia accipientes una hora, potestatem suam tradentes bestiæ, & cum Agno bellum gerentes, tandémque etiam Babyloni ipsi agnitæ demum bellum indicentes. Qua periphrasi Populum Magnum animalem, Christi nomen professum licet, Hierarchiæ dominanti parentem, septem collibus, totidemque provinciis distinctum, multorúmque Regum potentia suffultum, circumscribi Differt. III. 20. 21. &c. 32. 33. &c. argumentis clarissimis demonstravimus.
units.tr: IX. Nor does any dominion stand without subjects. Accordingly the Apocalypse also ascribes to this body, ruling under the pretext of the Christian religion, subjects, namely the Beast which carries the Harlot Babylon, v. 7; which, in vv. 8 ff., is said to have been, and not to be, and to be about to ascend out of the abyss, and to go into perdition, to the astonishment of the inhabitants of the earth; having seven heads, that is, as many mountains, on which the Woman sits; and ten horns, that is, as many kings who receive power together with the beast for one hour, who give their power to the beast, and wage war with the Lamb, and at last also declare war on Babylon herself once acknowledged. By this periphrasis we have demonstrated with the clearest arguments, in Dissert. III, 20, 21, etc., 32, 33, etc., that the people, fleshly, professing the name of Christ though it is a parent to the ruling hierarchy, divided into seven hills and as many provinces, and supported by the power of many kings, is described.

units.la: X. Jam & Babyloni M. ceu Mulieri, Meretrici superbissimæ omnium, habitum singularem, eúmque immani fastu turgentem Apocalypsis aperte tribuit. Dicitur enim cap.xvii. 3. 4. Mulier illa τν περιβεβλημένη πορφύρα ἡ κοκ-κίνῳ, ἡ κεχρυσωμένη χρυσῷ, ἡ λίθῳ τιμίῳ. Amicta purpura & coccino, & inaurata auro, ac lapide pretioso, & margaritis. Quod singulari mysterio neutiquam carere Differt. III.28.29. adstruximus. Ad eundem habitum externum Mulieris refertur etiam ποτήριον χρυσοῦν poculum aureum, quod manu sua gestare dicitur, plenum interiùs abominationibus & impuritate scortationis.
units.tr: X. Now the Apocalypse also plainly ascribes to the Great Babylon, as to the Woman, the most proud of harlots, a singular attire, and her swelling with monstrous pride. For in ch. 17:3, 4 it is said that this Woman was περιβεβλημένη πορφύρα ἢ κόκκινον, ἢ κεχρυσωμένη χρυσῷ, ἢ λίθῳ τιμίῳ [peribeblēmenē porphyra ē kokkinon, ē kechrysōmenē chrysō, ē lithō timiō], clothed in purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold, and precious stone, and pearls. We have shown in Dissert. III, 28, 29 that this is by no means without a singular mystery. To the same external attire of the Woman is also referred the ποτήριον χρυσοῦν [potērion chrysoun], the golden cup, which she is said to hold in her hand, full within of abominations and the impurity of harlotry.

units.la: XI. Ad intimam porro Babylonis, Meretricis Magnæ, Numen Divinitatis particeps à subjecto sibi populo religiose coli patitur: tum populum eundem à vero Dei cultu ad sui & creaturarum cultum, falsáque religionem omnibus seducit. Utrumque illud in Prophetia designatur, quòd Babylon vocatur μήτηρ πορνῶν Mater scortationum & abominationum terræ, cum quâ scortati sint Reges terræ. Apoc. xvii. 1.2. 4.5. &c. fusè admodum Differt. III. 8-13. comprobavimus.
units.tr: XI. Further, the Numen of the Deity, shared with the Harlot Babylon, is allowed to be worshipped religiously by the people subject to her, and she seduces that same people from the true worship of God to the worship of herself and of creatures, and to false religion in every way. Both of these are indicated in the Prophecy, in that Babylon is called "the mother of harlots [μήτηρ πορνῶν] and abominations of the earth," with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication. Apoc. 17:1, 2, 4, 5, etc. We have proved this at great length in Dissertation III, 8–13.

units.la: XII. Crudelitatem Babylonis in persequendis atrociter veri Dei cultoribus, passim etiam Apocalypsis Babyloni tribuit. Nam & habitus ejus coccinum & pupura cap. xvii.4. crudelitatis illius symbolum statuitur: & ebria Mulier illa dicitur sanguine sanctorum, & sanguine testium Jesu. v.6. In ea sanguis Prophetarum & Sanctorum, omniúmque in terra massatorum inventus. cap. xviii. 24. dicitur.
units.tr: XII. The Apocalypse everywhere also attributes to Babylon cruelty in savagely persecuting the true worshippers of God. For her scarlet and purple dress (Apoc. 17:4) is set down as a symbol of that cruelty, and that woman is called drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus (v. 6). In her the blood of the prophets and of the saints, and of all who have been slain on the earth, was found (Apoc. 18:24).

units.la: XIII. Sed & blasphemiarum ream eandem quàm maximè facit. Inducit enim eam sedentem super bestia, quæ plena est nominibus blasphemiæ cap. xvii. 3. Luxuriam ipsa ipsa fcortationum & impuritatis omnis improperatio arguit, quódque ei cap. xviii. 3. δύναμις τὴ φήρης [?] potentia luxuriæ tribuitur, qua scilicet, ἰσχνίαση [?] luxuriavit. v. 7. Pertinet eodem, quòd γέμω [?] merces Babylonicæ luxuriæ instrumenta ib. v. 11. commemorantur; & eidem vox citharædorum, Musicorum, tubicinum &c. cap. xix. 22.23. exprobratur. Sed & Φαρμακεία [?] veneficium ei diserte cap. xviii. 23. adscribitur, utpote quo seduxisse omnes gentes ibid. dicitur. Quò etiam Circæum illud abominationum poculum cap.xvii. 4. referre licet. Denique & ἐμπορεία [?] nundinatio quædam clarè admodum eidem tribuitur. Mercatores enim terræ expotentia luxuriæ ejus divites facti; cap. xviii. 3. nec non flentes lugentésque, eò quod merces eorum, puta aurum, argentum, lapidem pretiosum &c. nemo amplius emat. ib. v. 11. 12. &c. inducuntur.
units.tr: XIII. But she also makes her most clearly guilty of blasphemies. For she is depicted as sitting upon a beast which is full of names of blasphemy (Apoc. 17:3). Her own luxury proves her a reproach for all fornications and impurity, and it is said of her (Apoc. 18:3) that the power [δύναμις τῆς τρυφῆς] of luxury is hers, since she lived in luxury (v. 7). It belongs to the same point that the wares [γόμον] of Babylonian luxury, the instruments of it, are mentioned (ib. v. 11), and that the voice of harpers, musicians and trumpeters, etc. (Apoc. 18:22, 23), is cast in her teeth. But sorcery [φαρμακεία] is also expressly ascribed to her (Apoc. 18:23), since by it she is said to have seduced all nations (ibid.). To this we may also refer that Circean cup of abominations (Apoc. 17:4). Finally, a certain trafficking [ἐμπορία] is very clearly attributed to her as well. For the merchants of the earth were made rich by the power of her luxury (Apoc. 18:3), and weeping and mourning, because no one buys their wares any more, namely gold, silver, precious stones, etc., are introduced (ib. vv. 11, 12, etc.).

units.la: XIV. Denique ob fœditatem, fcortationem, abominationes varias & horribilia peccata Babylonem feverissimum judicium, atque illud per gradus certos procedens, donec penitus aboleatur, ut non amplius sit, subituram, filum Apocalypseos secuti Differt. III. 41.42. &c. demonstravimus.
units.tr: XIV. Finally, on account of her foulness, fornication, various abominations and horrible sins, we have shown, following the thread of the Apocalypse (Dissertation III, 41, 42, etc.), that Babylon was to undergo a most severe judgement, proceeding by definite stages until she is utterly destroyed, so that she shall no more exist.

units.la: XV. Sic adamantino veluti nexu Propositionis veritas constat. Superest, ut Assumptionem, in qua cardo rei totius vertitur, pari demonstrationis robore confirmemus, adeóque ad liquidum perducamus. Hierarchiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem inde à Gregorii VII. temporibus maximè, esse cætum talem, qui (1) Babyloni Chaldææ quadanteus convenieus, (2) sub mysteriorum, seu religionis Christianæ prætextu, (3) imperium in civitate Magna in populum Magnum animalem, Christi nomen professum licet, septem collibus, totidémque provinciis distinctum, multorum Regum potentia suffultum, obtinet; séque (4) immani fastu, habitúque prætumido, (5) ceu Numen Divinitatis particeps ab eo religiosè coli patitur (6) adeóque populum sibi obnoxium à vero Dei cultu ad sui & creaturarum cultum falsámque religionem modis omnibus seducit, (7) sanctos veri Dei cultores atrociter persequitur, (8) blasphemiis, (9) luxuria, (10) veneficiis, (11) avaritia & nundinatione spirituali se se immaniter polluit, (12) severúmque iccirco Dei judicium provocans, illud aliquatenus jam subivit, & porro subiturus est. Quæ duodecim demonstrationis capita, ordine & sigillatim persecuturus, Deum veneror, ut consilium laborémque meum Ecclesiæ prosperet, & aperta rerum luce, prædictionum factorúmque harmonia perspecta, Babylonem agnoscant salutariter, properéque deserant, quotquot ejus amore præpostero ad perniciem suam hactenus arserunt.
units.tr: XV. Thus the truth of the Proposition stands firm, as if bound by an adamantine chain. It remains that we confirm the Assumption, on which the whole matter turns, with equal force of demonstration, and so bring it to clarity. That the hierarchy of the Roman Church, dominant chiefly since the times of Gregory VII, is that assembly which (1) resembles the Chaldean Babylon in a certain way, (2) under the pretext of the mysteries, or of the Christian religion, holds sway in the Great City over a great people, a people of the beast, which professes the name of Christ though it may be, a city divided into seven hills and as many provinces, and supported by the power of many kings; and which (4) with monstrous arrogance and a swollen bearing, (5) allows itself to be worshipped religiously by that people as if it shared in the Divine Majesty, (6) and thus in every way seduces the people subject to it from the true worship of God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to false religion, (7) savagely persecutes the holy worshippers of the true God, (8) is monstrously polluted by blasphemies, (9) luxury, (10) sorceries, (11) and avarice and spiritual trafficking, (12) and by thus provoking the severe judgement of God has already in some measure undergone it, and is yet to undergo it. I am about to pursue these twelve heads of demonstration in order and one by one, and I pray God to prosper my counsel and labour for the Church, so that, with the light of things laid open and the harmony of predictions and facts seen, they may recognise Babylon to their salvation, and quickly abandon her, all those who until now have burned with a perverse love for her to their own ruin.

units.la: DISSERTATIO SEXTA
units.tr: DISSERTATIO SEXTA

units.la: S E X T A
units.tr: S E X T A

units.la: QUA
units.tr: IN WHICH

units.la: Hierarchiam seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem Babelem M. esse probatur. Primò, quia cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri quadantenus convenit.
units.tr: It is proved that the dominant hierarchy or clergy of the Roman Church is Babel the Great. First, because it agrees in some respects with ancient Chaldean Babylon.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Babylonis M. character primus est, quòd ea cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri congruit.
units.tr: I. The first mark of Great Babylon is that it agrees with ancient Chaldean Babylon.

units.la: II. Cum eadem etiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ hierarchiam dominantem congruere, syllogismo argumentorum συναθροισικῶ probatur.
units.tr: II. That the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church also agrees with the same is proved by a syllogism of accumulated arguments [συναθροισικῶ].

units.la: III. Babylon vetus ita dicta est, à confusione labii. Hierarchia Papalis similis confusio & divisio in Schismatis ejus, & dissensionibus horribilibus, quibus structura turris ejusdem nunquam non impeditur; in asserendo primatu Papæ, aliisque dogmatis notatur.
units.tr: III. Ancient Babylon was so called from the confusion of lips. The Papal hierarchy shows a similar confusion and division in its schisms and its horrible dissensions, by which the building of its tower is always hindered; it is marked out in its assertion of the primacy of the Pope and in its other dogmas.

units.la: IV. Papalis Regni divisio & confusio ex ipso Bellarmino prodita.
units.tr: IV. The division and confusion of the Papal kingdom, as shown by Bellarmine himself.

units.la: V. Babylon Chaldæa, & turris in eadem ædificari cœpit eo consilio, ut nepotes Noachi sibi constituerent nomen, & ut maneret populus unus, labium unum.
units.tr: V. Chaldean Babylon, and the tower begun in it, were undertaken with the purpose that the descendants of Noah might make a name for themselves, and that the people might remain one, with one language.

units.la: VI. Hierarchia Papalis apud se solam esse nomen, authoritatem, potestatem definiendi fidem, similiter profitetur, uti ex dictalibus Gregorii VII. Bulla Bonifacii VIII. Maximiniani Epistola supposititia probatur.
units.tr: VI. The Papal hierarchy likewise professes that it alone has the name, the authority and the power of defining the faith; this is proved from the Dictates of Gregory VII, the Bull of Boniface VIII, and the spurious Epistle of Maximian.

units.la: VII. Quin & unitatem populi Ecclesiæ suæ notam constituit, & non nisi una lingua Latina, cultum publicum exercet.
units.tr: VII. Indeed it also makes the unity of its people a mark of its Church, and it conducts public worship in one language only, Latin.

units.la: VIII. Neque tamen magis quam Chaldæa vetus, consusionem & dispersionem sui evitare potuit, quod in Orientalium & Occidentalium Schismate inprimis apparuit.
units.tr: VIII. Yet it has been no better able than ancient Chaldea to avoid its own confusion and dispersion, which appeared above all in the Schism of East and West.

units.la: IX. Babylonis Chaldææ conditor fuit Nimrod, rebellis adversus Deum, potens venator coram Deo, qui religionis prætextu homines, civitatesque sibi subjecit. Idem fuit cum Belo seu Baale.
units.tr: IX. The founder of Chaldean Babylon was Nimrod, a rebel against God, a mighty hunter before the Lord, who under the pretext of religion subjected men and cities to himself. He was the same as Bel or Baal.

units.la: X. Hierarchia Papalis suis Nimrodis, religionis prætextu imperia subjugantibus, & venatoribus coram Deo, & piscatoribus non deest uitur.
units.tr: X. The Papal hierarchy is not lacking in its own Nimrods, who subjugate empires under the pretext of religion, and in hunters before the Lord, and in fishermen.

units.la: XI. Babylon Chaldæa fuit ampla, potens, non tam urbs, quam gens.
units.tr: XI. Chaldean Babylon was vast and powerful, not so much a city as a nation.

units.la: XII. Hierarchia papalis similiter amplitudinem & felicitatem temporalem Ecclesiæ suæ notam jactat. Potestatem quinetiam omnem in Cælo & in terra sibi arrogat.
units.tr: XII. The Papal hierarchy likewise boasts of the vastness and temporal prosperity of its Church. Moreover, it claims for itself all power in heaven and on earth.

units.la: XIII. Babylon vetus habuit Principes, consultores, sapientes, divinatores. Hierarchia papalis similibus abundat, quos inter Cardinales Regibus exæquati, Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, veri Divinatores eminent.
units.tr: XIII. Ancient Babylon had princes, counsellors, wise men and diviners. The Papal hierarchy abounds in similar figures, among whom Cardinals, made equal to kings, and Archbishops and Bishops, true diviners, stand out.

units.la: XIV. Babylon Chaldæa scortationi Spirituali, cultui imaginum inprimis dedita maxime fuit. Hierarchia Papalis cultu imaginum insanit.
units.tr: XIV. Chaldean Babylon was given above all to spiritual harlotry and the worship of images. The Papal hierarchy is mad with the worship of images.

units.la: XV. Babylon vetus fuit ταλύῳ, ipsos Reges suos ceu Numina coluit: aliósque etiam ad idololatriam seduxit, etiam vi adhibita. Convenit plane Hierarchia Papalis.
units.tr: XV. Ancient Babylon was polytheistic [ταλύῳ]; it worshipped its own kings as divinities, and it also led others into idolatry, even by the use of force. The Papal hierarchy plainly agrees.

units.la: XVI. Babylon Chaldæa scortationibus & luxuriæ nefandum in modum dedita fuit. Ejusdem ea in re æmulam se Hierarchia Papalis gerit.
units.tr: XVI. Chaldean Babylon was given over to fornications and to lust in an unspeakable manner. In this matter the Papal hierarchy shows itself to be its rival.

units.la: XVII. Babylon Chaldæa diu populum Dei captivum attinuit, & diris modis divexavit. Hierarchia Papalis fideles, Agni sectatores, Christi testes secum commixtos diu captivos detinuit, & pessimè eosdem habuit.
units.tr: XVII. Chaldean Babylon long held the people of God captive and harassed them in dreadful ways. The Papal hierarchy long kept captive, and treated very badly, the faithful, the followers of the Lamb, and the witnesses of Christ who were mingled with them.

units.la: XVIII. Babylon Chaldæa vel invita tandem populum Dei carceribus solutum libertati restituit. Hierarchia Papalis Ecclesiam diu captivam, Reformationis beneficio à se separatam, & libertate etiam pactis firmata, fruentem, dimittere coacta est.
units.tr: XVIII. Chaldean Babylon, though unwillingly, at last released the people of God from their prisons and restored them to liberty. The Papal hierarchy has been forced to let go the Church, which it held captive for long, which by the blessing of the Reformation was separated from it, and which now enjoys liberty confirmed even by treaties.

units.la: XIX. Post exitum populi Dei ex Babylone veteri, eadem facta est habitatio immundorum bestiarum. Simile quid etiam Hierarchiæ papali contigit.
units.tr: XIX. After the departure of the people of God from ancient Babylon, it became a dwelling of unclean beasts. Something similar has also happened to the Papal hierarchy.

units.la: XX. Blasphemiarum contra Deum, & incantationum rea æquè Babylon vetus & Hierarchia papalis est.
units.tr: XX. Ancient Babylon and the Papal hierarchy are equally guilty of blasphemies against God and of enchantments.

units.la: XXI. Babylon vetus mercatura & negotiationibus inclaruit, sæva & crudelis fuit, judicia Dei securè contempsit, malitiæ suæ confisa, de Deo cogitationem abjecit.
units.tr: XXI. Ancient Babylon was famous for merchandise and trade, it was savage and cruel, it contemptuously disregarded the judgments of God, trusting in its own malice, and it cast thought of God away.

units.la: XXII. Similibus Characteribus Hierarchia Papalis infamis est.
units.tr: XXII. The Papal hierarchy is infamous for similar marks.

units.la: XXIII. Sicut olim Babylonii Reges imperium adeuntes nomina mutárunt, ita Pontifices Romani ad Papatum evecti faciunt idem.
units.tr: XXIII. Just as the Babylonian kings of old changed their names on coming to power, so the Roman Pontiffs, raised to the Papacy, do the same.

units.la: XXIV. Babylon Chaldaica propter impietatem gravissimum Dei judicium Divinitus annuntiatum, subiit.
units.tr: XXIV. Chaldean Babylon, on account of its impiety, underwent the most grievous judgment of God, announced by divine revelation.

units.la: XXV. Hierarchia Papalis ruere jam cæpit, at ad extremum penitus corruet.
units.tr: XXV. The Papal hierarchy has already begun to fall, but at last it will collapse entirely.

units.la: XXVI. Objectio, quòd Theologia Symbolica non sit argumentativa, sokvitur, & argumentum concluditur.
units.tr: XXVI. The objection that symbolic theology is not argumentative is answered, and the argument is concluded.

units.la: I. Primus Babylonis Magnæ Characterest, quòd cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri ea quadantenus convenit. Si igitur Hierarchiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri quadantenus convenire demonstraverimus, characterem isthunc Babylonis M. eidem Hierarchiæ competere, extra dubitationis aleam positum fuerit. Fieri enim non potest, quin Babylon Apocalyptica & Romanæ Ecclesiæ Hierarchia, cum veteri illa Chaldæa analogia quadam congruentes, ipsæ quoque inter se conveniant, cùm quæ in uno tertio conveniunt, ea inter se convenire sana ratio dictitet.
units.tr: I. The first mark of Great Babylon is that it agrees in some respects with ancient Chaldean Babylon. If therefore we demonstrate that the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church agrees in some respects with ancient Chaldean Babylon, it will be placed beyond the chance of doubt that this mark of Great Babylon belongs to that same hierarchy. For it cannot be that the Apocalyptic Babylon and the hierarchy of the Roman Church, each agreeing by a certain analogy with that ancient Chaldea, should not also agree with each other, since sound reason declares that things which agree in one third thing agree with one another.

units.la: II. Analogiam inter Babylonem veterem Chaldaicam & novam mysticam, quoad utriusque initia, potentiam, scelera, & judicium Differt. I. 26-32. exposuimus. Analogiam inter Babylonem Chaldaicam veterem, & Ecclesiæ Romanæ Hierarchiam dominantem, quoad Characteres communes eosdem, aliósque paucis constringere nunc etiam juvabit, ὡς ζυλλογισμὸν rem totam sequenti Syllogismo complectimur.
units.tr: II. We have set out in Dissertation I, 26–32, the analogy between ancient Chaldean Babylon and the new mystical one, as regards their beginnings, power, crimes and judgment. It will now also be helpful to set out briefly the analogy between ancient Chaldean Babylon and the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church, as regards the same common marks and others, and to embrace the whole matter in the following syllogism [ὡς συλλογισμὸν].

units.la: Quicquid cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri convenit quoad ejus nomen, seu significatum nominis; quoad consilium, quo urbem, & in ea turrim exstruere moliti sunt; quoad confusionem labii, & dispersionem populorum; rebellionem Nimrodicam adversus Deum; amplitudinem, potentiam, Principes, consultores, Sapientes, Divinatores; cultum imaginum; πολυθεότης; scortationem, luxuriam, crudelitatem in populum Dei captivum, à Deo denique liberatum; corruptionem postea majorem; blasphemandi Deum, incantandi nefas; mercaturam; fiduciam in se; mutationem nominis Regii; judicium Divinum ob peccata illa, interitúmque: illud cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri analogiam habet, adeòque cæteris paribus, Babylon magna est.
units.tr: Whatever agrees with ancient Chaldean Babylon in its name, or the meaning of its name; in the counsel by which they undertook to build a city and a tower in it; in the confusion of lips and the dispersion of peoples; in the Nimrodic rebellion against God; in vastness, power, princes, counsellors, wise men, diviners; in the worship of images; in polytheism; in harlotry, luxury, cruelty towards the people of God held captive and at last freed by God; in the later and greater corruption; in blaspheming God and the unlawful practice of enchantment; in trade; in trust in itself; in the change of the royal name; in the divine judgment upon those sins, and in its ruin: that has an analogy with ancient Chaldean Babylon, and therefore, other things being equal, is Great Babylon.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri convenit quoad nomen &c.
units.tr: But the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church agrees with ancient Chaldean Babylon in its name, etc.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri analogiam habet, adeoque, cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church has an analogy with ancient Chaldean Babylon, and therefore, other things being equal, is Great Babylon.

units.la: Propositio Major extra dubitationis aleam posita est, cùm fieri non posset, ut in plerisque omnibus similia analogiam habeant nullam; æquè ut fieri nequit, ut ovum cum ovo, lac cum lacte, fur cum fure, lupus cum lupo analogicè non conveniant. Insuper Logicorum axioma, quòd quæ in tertio uno, nedum in pluribus conveniunt, inter se conveniant, æternæ veritatis est. Minorem deinceps per singulas partes stabilitum imus.
units.tr: The major premise has been placed beyond the chance of doubt, since it could not be that things which agree in most respects should have no analogy with one another, just as it cannot be that egg should not agree analogically with egg, milk with milk, thief with thief, wolf with wolf. Moreover, the axiom of the logicians, that things which agree in one third thing, let alone in several, agree with one another, is an eternal truth. We shall next establish the minor premise part by part.

units.la: III. Babyloni Chaldaicæ veteri nomen inditum est à confusione. Propterea enim Deus vocavit nomen ejus Babel quia ibi Deus confudit labium totius terræ. Gen. xi. 9. Quod qua ratione successerit, ibidem exponitur. Ædificaturi enim insano stolidóque molimine turrim ἀεγαρμικὴ, Divino judicio
units.tr: III. The name Babel was given to ancient Chaldean Babylon from confusion. For this reason God called its name Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. Gen. xi. 9. How this came about is explained in that place. For those who were about to build a tower in a mad and foolish undertaking [ἀεγαρμικὴ], by the divine judgment

units.la: Babylon vo-tus ita dicta est, à consu-sione labii.
units.tr: Old Babylon was so called from the confusion of the lip.

units.la: dicio ita labiis difcordarunt, ut conatus omnis irritus ceci-derit. Sicut igitur vetustæ Babylonis ædificatio per consufionem linguarum interrupta est: ita Hierarchiæ Romanæ dominationem suam exstruentis exercentisque, linguæ non semel gravitérque confusæ & divisæ sunt, exaudiente Deo preces Ecclesiæ Psalm. LV. 10. בלע אדני פלג לשונם Perde, Domine, divide linguam eorum, quoniam vidi violentiam & contentionem in civitate. Liquet id in horrendis Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Pontificum inprimis, Schismatibus, quorum nonnulla, illud maximè, quod ab Urbani VI. Papatu ad Constantiense Concilium usque protractum, Historia Papatus s. CXXXVIII. &c. prosequitur, pertinacissimè agitata sunt; nec non in gravissimis dissensionibus circa religionis capita complura, palmarium maximè illud de primatu Papæ: quibus dissensionibus qualibet ætate atque nostra etiam, in Gallia cum primis crebrescentibus, impeditum est, ne turris illa attentata ædificari, & Hierarchia illa utcunque in sublime jam producta, toti Christiano orbi unquam imperare potuerit. Urgétque confusio illa hodiéque ita Regnum Pontificum, ut nunquam ferè concordes esse possint, & in mutua etiam sævissimáque bella non raro prorumpant, quibus efficitur, ut suapte Marte Babylonis hujus architecti intercidant. Taceo confusionem linguarum in asserendo Pontificis primatu, quem alii à Scripturæ solius, alii traditionis insuper authoritate arcessunt, alii cum ejusdem infallibilitate omni modo consociant, alii ab eodem divellunt, alii Ecclesiæ seu Concilio subjiciunt, eidem præferunt alii: in fidei cum Protestantibus controversæ articulis, circa quos ante Tridentini Concilii definitiones dissensum liberrimè est; & qui in ipso Concilio Tridentino ita definiti sunt, ut intercedentibus variis cothurnis & oraculis flexiloquis, labia non unita sint, sed confusa & divisa maneant: in quæstionibus gravissimis de Deo & rebus Divinis, circa quas Doctores Scholastici, Thomistæ, Scotistæ, Prædicatores, Franciscani, Jesuitæ adeò pertinaciter dissident, ut si uspiam, in Scholastica certè architectorum Babylonis Theologia, Babylonica confusio clarissimè conspiciatur.
units.tr: ...so disagreed in their speech that every attempt came to nothing. Just as the building of ancient Babylon was interrupted by the confusion of tongues, so the tongues of those who build up and exercise the domination of the Roman hierarchy have more than once and seriously been confused and divided, God hearing the prayers of the Church. Psalm LV. 10. [בלע אדני פלג לשונם] Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongue, for I have seen violence and strife in the city. This is plain in the horrible Schisms of the Roman Church, especially those of the Popes, of which some, above all that which was drawn out from the Papacy of Urban VI to the Council of Constance, which the History of the Papacy, s. CXXXVIII, etc., follows, were carried on most obstinately; and likewise in very grave dissensions about several heads of religion, most notably the chief one about the primacy of the Pope. By these dissensions, at every age and also in our own, especially in France where they have grown most, it has been prevented that that tower, once attempted, should be built, and that that hierarchy, however far raised on high, should ever be able to rule the whole Christian world. That confusion still presses so hard on the Kingdom of the Pontiffs today that they can almost never be of one mind, and not seldom they break out into mutual and most savage wars, by which it comes about that these architects of Babylon perish by their own might. I pass over the confusion of tongues in asserting the primacy of the Pontiff, which some derive from the authority of Scripture alone, others from tradition as well, others join in every way with his infallibility, others separate him from it, others subject him to the Church or to a Council, and others prefer him to them; and in the articles of faith disputed with the Protestants, on which there was the freest disagreement before the definitions of the Council of Trent, and which were defined in that Council in such a way that, with various buskins and ambiguous oracles coming between, their lips were not united but remain confused and divided; and in the most weighty questions about God and divine things, on which the Scholastic Doctors, the Thomists, Scotists, Preachers, Franciscans and Jesuits disagree so obstinately that if anywhere, certainly in the Scholastic theology of these architects of Babylon, the Babylonian confusion is most clearly seen.

units.la: IV. Quid quòd in Papatu Regnum ipsum divisum & confusum cernitur, juxta prædictionem Dan. 11.41: Quòd autem vidisti pedes & digitos partim figuli, & partim ferreos מלכי פליגו Regnum divisum est, & de plantario ferri erit in eo. Quod optimè explicat, & vel imprudens applicat Bellarminus de Clericis cap. 30. ubi sic ille: Civitas est una (in Papatu) materialiter, & duæ formaliter; quia cœtus Laicorum & cœtus Clericorum formaliter duæ civitates dici possunt, quoniam in ipsis etiam temporalibus rebus diversas leges habent, diversa tribunalia. Omnino in uno Regno divisum Regnum est. Clerici enim secundùm omnia subsunt Papæ. Laici subsunt Regibus, & unà cum Regibus suis Papæ, etiam quoad temporalia, saltem indirectè.
units.tr: IV. Indeed, in the Papacy the kingdom itself is seen to be divided and confused, according to the prediction of Dan. 11.41: But whereas you saw the feet and toes, partly of potter's clay and partly of iron [מלכי פליגו]: the kingdom shall be divided, and there shall be in it of the planting of iron. Bellarmine explains this very well, or applies it without realising it, in On Clerics, chapter 30, where he says: The city is one materially (in the Papacy) but two formally, since the assembly of laypeople and the assembly of clergy can formally be called two cities, because even in temporal matters they have different laws and different courts. Clearly the kingdom is divided within a single realm. For the clergy are subject to the Pope in all things. The laity are subject to kings, and along with their kings they are subject to the Pope, even in temporal matters, at least indirectly.

units.la: V. Babylonis Chaldaicæ veteris initia narrantur Gen. XI. 1-4. Nepotes scilicet Noachi consilium iniverunt constituendi השם nominis, ne multiplicato genere humano dispergerentur, & non manerent אחד עם populus unus. v.6. sed ut haberent אחד שפה labium unum, loquentes דברים אחדים sermones eosdem. v. 1. Qualecunque illorum consilium fuit, sive ædificandi magnam urbem, comparandæ apud posteros famæ celebris, & unà habitandi, dispersionemque vitandi gratia, quod Dei præcepto recens lato, prolificandi scilicet, & terram replendi. Gen. ix. 2. adversari, ignorare certè non potuerunt: sive, quod probabilius est, condendi civitatem unam, quæ foret metropolis, in qua summi nominis sedes esset, per quod nomen una religio & traditio ΜΑΤΗΣ in orbe toto conservaretur, ut gens hominum unus maneret populus, unumque labium, cum Hierarchia Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantis similitudinem quandam obtinent.
units.tr: V. The beginnings of the old Chaldean Babylon are related in Gen. 11.1-4. The descendants of Noah, that is, undertook a plan to make themselves a name [השם], lest, with the human race multiplied, they be scattered, and not remain one people [אחד עם] (v. 6), but might have one language [אחד שפה] and use the same words [דברים אחדים] (v. 1). Whatever their plan was, whether to build a great city, to acquire a famous reputation among posterity, and to live together and avoid dispersion, which they could not have failed to know was opposed to God's recent command to be fruitful and fill the earth (Gen. 9.2), or, what is more probable, to found one city which would be the metropolis, where the seat of the great name would be, so that through that name one religion and one tradition would be kept throughout the whole world, and the human race would remain one people, and one language: in any case they bear a certain likeness to the hierarchy of the dominant Roman Church.

units.la: VI. Ecclesia Romana utique simile in conscientias imperium exercens profitetur, apud se esse nomen, auctoritatem, potestatem Divinam jubendi, dictandi quod velit, nomen quod nominandum est omni homini ad salutem, caput & metropolim, cum qua communicare, à qua jus & fas omne repetere, cui subesse & subjacere in solidum, fit de necessitate salutis, quæque etiam fideles omnes quaversum dispersos efficiat populum unum, & labium unum. Repetat, cui lubet, animo famosos illos Gregorii VII. dictatus, quibus inter alia comprehensum est, quòd unicum sit nomen in mundo: quòd solius Papæ nomen in Ecclesiis recitetur: quòd nullus audeat condemnare Episcopos Romam, metropolim scilicet illam, appellantes: quòd Catholicus non habeatur, qui Romanæ Ecclesiæ non concordat, &c. Repetat bullam Extravagantem Bonifacii VIII. Unam sanctam Ecclesiam &c. quæ his verbis clauditur: Porro subesse Romano Pontifici omni humanæ creaturæ declaramus, definimus & pronuntiamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis. Repetat denique sive Maximiniano, Episcopo Constantinopolitano, sive Maximo cuipiam suppositam mera fraude Epistolam, tantopere Baronio, aliisque laudatam, in qua sic inter alia Ecclesiæ Romanæ caput demulcetur: Omnes fines terræ, qui Dominum sincerè receperunt, & ubique terrarum veram fidem confitentes in potestatem Romanorum Pontificum, tanquam in solem respiciunt, & ex ipso lumen Catholicæ & Apostolicæ fidei recipiunt. Et paulò post: Hunc enim de cæteris mortalibus ex toto terrarum orbe, conditor orbis elegit, cui Cathedram magisterii principaliter possidendam tenere perpetuo privilegii jure concesfit, ut quisquis Divinum aliquod aut profundum nôsse desiderat, ad hujus præceptoris oraculum doctrinámque recurrat.
units.tr: VI. The Roman Church certainly claims to exercise a similar power over consciences: that it has in itself the name, the authority and the divine power to command and to dictate what it wills; the name which must be named to every man for salvation; the head and metropolis, with which one must communicate, from which every right and lawful thing must be sought, and to which to be wholly subject and submissive is of necessity for salvation; and which also makes all the faithful, scattered in every direction, one people, and one language. Let anyone who wishes recall the famous Dictates of Gregory VII, in which, among other things, it is laid down: that there is only one name in the world; that the name of the Pope alone is recited in the churches; that no one may dare to condemn bishops who appeal to Rome, that is, that metropolis; that a man is not to be considered Catholic who does not agree with the Roman Church, and so on. Let him recall the Extravagant bull of Boniface VIII, Unam sanctam Ecclesiam, which closes with these words: Moreover we declare, state and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff. Let him finally recall the letter falsely attributed either to Maximinian, bishop of Constantinople, or to some Maximus, a letter praised so highly by Baronius and others, in which the head of the Roman Church is flattered in these words, among others: All the ends of the earth, who have sincerely received the Lord, and everywhere on earth confessing the true faith, look to the power of the Roman Pontiffs as to the sun, and from it receive the light of the Catholic and Apostolic faith. And a little later: For the Creator of the world has chosen him from all other mortals throughout the whole world, and has granted him the chair of teaching to hold as his principal possession by the perpetual right of privilege, so that whoever desires to know anything divine or profound should have recourse to the oracle and doctrine of this teacher.

units.la: VII. Adeò verò Civitatis seu Metropoleos suæ beneficio unitatem illam tum populi, tum labii conservare Romanenses student, ut unitatem ejusmodi, seu unionem membrorum inter se & cum capite Romano Pontifice in Metropoli illa residente, Ecclesiæ suæ notam propriam & genuinam, jam pridem fecerint. Bellarminus de Ecclesia Libr. iv. 10. ita rem definit: Septima nota est unio membrorum inter se & cum capite. Paulò post: Nunc omnes Catholici (Pontificii) totâ orbe dispersi de omnibus dogmatibus fidei sentiunt idem: nec possunt aliter sentire, cùm omnes subjiciant sensum suum sensui unius & ejusdem Summi Pastoris ex Cathedra Petri, cum consilio aliorum Pastorum Ecclesiam dirigentis. Iisdem penè verbis de Ecclesia Romana Franciscus Costerus Enchirid. Controv. cap. de Ecclesia, gloriatur. Catholici omnes, inquit, ubivis terrarum sub uno capite Romano Pontifice, cui omnes parent & Principes & Reges, ut Christi Vicario, eandem fidem constanter retinent, idem dicunt, idem sentiunt, idem credunt per omnia, & ne in minimo quidem religionis articulo discrepant. Quid quòd unitatem labii in eo etiam Ecclesia Romana affectat, quòd sacra officia nonnisi una lingua, Latina scilicet, quam regnantem & dominantem appellare suevit, peragi posse pertendit?
units.tr: VII. So far indeed do the Romanists strive, by the benefit of their city or metropolis, to preserve that unity, both of people and of language, that they have long since made such unity, or the union of the members with one another and with the Roman Pontiff, the head residing in that metropolis, the proper and genuine mark of their Church. Bellarmine, in On the Church, book 4, chapter 10, defines the matter thus: The seventh mark is the union of the members with one another and with the head. A little later: Now all Catholics (Papists), scattered throughout the whole world, think the same about all the doctrines of faith, nor can they think otherwise, since they all subject their own judgment to the judgment of one and the same Supreme Pastor from the Chair of Peter, together with the counsel of the other pastors who govern the Church. Francis Costerus, in his Enchiridion of Controversies, chapter on the Church, boasts of the Roman Church in almost the same words: All Catholics, he says, wherever they are on earth, under one head, the Roman Pontiff, to whom all Princes and Kings obey as to Christ's Vicar, steadfastly keep the same faith, say the same things, think the same things, believe the same in all points, and do not differ even in the smallest article of religion. Moreover, does the Roman Church not also aim at unity of language in this, that it maintains that the sacred offices can be performed in one language only, namely Latin, which it is accustomed to call ruling and dominant?

units.la: VIII. Tametsi verò ita unitatem populi & labii Romanenses crepant, efficere tamen, quò minùs dispergerentur, & confunderetur labium eorum multis modis, neutiquam potuerunt, ut supra jam ff. ÿ. iÿ. dicere occupavimus. Qui eosdem cum vulpibus Samsonis caudis tenus ad nocendum vastandúmque colligatis, at quoad capita solutis dissipatisque comparaverit, næ is, quod res est, dixerit.
units.tr: VIII. Although the Romanists boast of such unity of people and language, they could by no means bring it about, in many ways, that they should not be scattered and that their language should not be confused, as I have already taken care to say above at ff. ÿ. iÿ. Whoever compares them to the foxes of Samson, tied together by their tails for doing harm, but loosed and scattered as to their heads, would, to be sure, speak the truth.

units.la: S
units.tr: S

units.la: Quot formas quæso ipsa Theologia Pontificia diversifimas suscepit? Cogitet, qui velit, Theologiæ Lombardicæ, Scotisticæ, Thomisticæ, Ockamisticæ, Monasticæ, Interimisticæ, Tridentinæ, Jesuiticæ, Methodisticæ, aliorum variantes, totóque cœlo dissidentes formas. Expendat confusi labii, linguarum, quibus Scholastici utuntur, cyclopiam barbariem, sectarum discrepantes idiotismos. Solus Paræus, Theologus gravissimus, bellum Papisticum secundùm præcipua fidei capita ex Bellarmino aliisque Synagogæ Romanæ Scriptoribus in Irenici sui cap. xxv. fuse pertexens, in articulis magni momenti ducentas triginta novem ἀιλφαὸς ob oculos statuit. Et qualis quæso quantáque fuit dispersio illa Orientalium & Occidentalium Ecclesiarum, gravissimo Schismate ita divulsarum, ut aqua citiùs cum igne, quàm Roma cum Orientalibus in fidam gratiam pacémque solidam redituræ sint. Ne de Ecclesiarum Occidentalium dispersione & separatione ab Ecclesia Romana justa multiplicique dicam.
units.tr: What forms, I ask, has Papist theology itself taken on, so very various? Let anyone who wishes consider the Lombard, Scotist, Thomist, Ockhamist, Monastic, Interim, Tridentine, Jesuit, Methodist theologies, and the varying forms of others, utterly at odds with one another. Let him weigh the Cyclopean barbarism of the confused tongue, the languages the Schoolmen use, and the discordant idioms of their sects. Paraeus alone, a most weighty theologian, who in chapter 25 of his Irenicum, treating at length the Papist war against the chief heads of faith drawn from Bellarmine and other writers of the Roman Synagogue, sets before our eyes two hundred and thirty-nine alphabets of disagreement on articles of great moment. And what, I ask, and how great, was that dispersion of the Eastern and Western Churches, torn apart by the most grievous Schism, so that water will sooner be reconciled with fire than Rome with the Easterners, to return to firm faith and solid peace. I say nothing of the just and manifold dispersion and separation of the Western Churches from the Roman Church.

units.la: IX. Qui Babylonem Chaldaicam veterem in terra Sinear condidit נמרוד Nimrodus à מרד rebellando, ita dictus, quòd in superiores æquè ac in pares omnes surrexisset; נבור ציד לפני יהוה potens venator, seu potens venatione coram Jehova fuisse, Gen. x. 9. dicitur. Ille scilicet à vero Deo ejusque cultu deficiens, ad falsum, impiúmque cultum deflexit, hominésque multos in suam potestatem redegit, sub nomine יהוה Jehovæ, hoc est, præxtextu religionis veræ conservandæ nequiter usus. Sed revera contra Dominum, uti illud לפני Jarchius, aliúque interpretantur. Non voluit, ita Munsterus, tantùm venator esse in terra, sed etiam coram Domino. Voluit quoque regnare in religione, erexit novos cultus coram Domino, usurpavit Sacerdotium vi & ferro, persecutor Prophetarum, Sanctorum, populi Dei, lineæque ex qua Christus oriturus erat. Sanè Nimrodum hunc, eundem esse cum Belo, Nini patre, falsi Numinis cultore, vel inde colligitur, quòd sicut Nimrodum Babylonem condidisse, Moses testis est: ita ejusdem Babylonis conditorem Belum Berosus, Sacerdos Babylonius, & Abydenus, quem utrumque historiam suam ex vetustissimis Chaldæorum monumentis & archivis hausisse constat, nec non Eupolemon in historia Judaica, Alexandro Polyhistore referente, aliíque faciunt. Atque eundem esse Nimrodum & Belum, etiam ratio temporum palàm arguit. Et qui Babyloniis erat בBel, idem Phoenicibus & adjacentibus erat בעל Baal, utróque nomine derivato à בעל Dominus, à quo excidente litera ע juxta morem Chaldaicum fit ב Bel, cujus mentio est Esaj. XLVI. 1. Jerem. L. 2. LI. 44. Phoeniciis autem Hebraicè locutis Baal cum ע retinebatur.
units.tr: IX. He who founded old Chaldean Babylon in the land of Shinar, Nimrod [נמרוד], so called from rebelling [מרד], because he rose up against all, both superiors and equals, is said in Gen. 10.9 to have been a mighty hunter [נבור ציד לפני יהוה], or a mighty hunter before Jehovah. He, of course, falling away from the true God and His worship, turned to a false and impious worship, and reduced many men under his power, wickedly using the name of Jehovah [יהוה], that is, using the pretext of preserving true religion. But in truth he was against the Lord, as Jarchi and others interpret that before [לפני]. He did not wish, so Munster says, merely to be a hunter on earth, but also before the Lord. He also wished to rule over religion; he set up new cults before the Lord, usurped the priesthood by force and by the sword, a persecutor of the prophets, the saints, the people of God, and of the line from which Christ was to arise. That this Nimrod is the same as Bel, the father of Ninus, a worshipper of a false deity, is clear from this too: just as Moses bears witness that Nimrod founded Babylon, so Berosus, a Babylonian priest, and Abydenus, who are known to have drawn their histories from the most ancient Chaldean monuments and archives, and also Eupolemus in his Jewish history, as Alexander Polyhistor reports, and others, make Bel the founder of the same Babylon. That Nimrod and Bel are the same is also plainly shown by the chronology of the times. And he who was Bel [ב] to the Babylonians was Baal [בעל] to the Phoenicians and their neighbours, both names derived from Baal [בעל], lord; from which, by the dropping of the letter ע according to Chaldean custom, comes ב, Bel, which is mentioned in Isa. 46.1, Jer. 50.2, 51.44. But among the Phoenicians, who spoke Hebrew, Baal was kept with the ע.

units.la: X. Neque verò etiam Romanæ Babyloni desunt Nimrodi, Beli, & Baales potentes venatores, non ferarum, sed hominum coram Domino, qui præextextu, seu potiùs calumnia, religionis & verborum Domini: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam: Tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum: Pasce oves meas &c. nec non S. Petri: Ecce duo gladii; Babylonem suam extruxerunt, & sub ejusdem potestatem magnam multitudinem hominum, & piscatoracri thyrso percussam, & decreto eo, quòd de necessitate salutis sit, ut humana Creatura omnis Romano Pontifici subsit; dementatam redegerunt. Qui nomen isthoc potentis venatoris coram Domino non carens invidia, in suavius illud Piscatoris hominum commutárunt, atque ejusmodi seu venatione, seu piscatione hominum id tandem effecerunt, ut in Cœlo & terra, Spiritualibus & temporalibus Dominarentur, quod qua ratione successerit, Historia Papatus periodo III. IV. & V. prosequitur. Meritóque adeo Lutherus Lib. de Captivitate Babylonica Papatum definivit, quòd sit robusta venatio Nimrodi. Est enim Monarchia seu tyrannis temporalis, specie religionis, titulóque Ecclesiæ producta ac promota, juxta illud Poëtæ:
units.tr: Nor indeed does Rome-Babylon lack its Nimrods, Bels and Baals: mighty hunters, not of wild beasts but of men, before the Lord. Under the pretext, or rather the pretence, of religion and the words of the Lord, You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; to you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven; feed my sheep, and also St Peter's Behold, here are two swords, they built their Babylon. Under its power they brought a great multitude of men, struck by the fisherman's rod, and by that decree that it is of necessity for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff, they reduced them to a state of madness. Not content with the name mighty hunter before the Lord, they changed it into the milder fishers of men. By such hunting or fishing of men they finally brought it about that they ruled in heaven and on earth, over spiritual and temporal affairs. How this came about, the History of the Papacy traces in periods III, IV and V. Rightly, therefore, Luther in his book On the Babylonian Captivity defined the papacy as a strong hunting of Nimrod. For it is a temporal monarchy or tyranny, put forward and promoted under the guise of religion and under the title of the Church, according to the saying of the poet:

units.la: Quicquid non possidet armis, Relligione tenet.
units.tr: Whatever he does not possess by arms, he holds by religion.

units.la: XI. Fuit Babylon, gloriante ita Nebucadnezare, urbs רבתא magna. Dan. iv. 27. mater Chaldæorum. Jerem. v. 12. laus universæ terræ. cap. li. 41. gloria Regnorum, decus superbiæ Chaldæorum. Esaj. xiii. 19. מרהבה aurea. Esaj. xiv. 4. nec non רבר אוצורות locuples thesaurorum Jerem. li. 13. & propter insignem potentiam malleus universæ terræ Jerem. l. 23. flagellum & instrumentum bellicum ad dissipandas gentes, & perdenda regna. Jerem. li. 20. Aristoteles Polit. iii. 3. eam ἴθνος μάλλον ἢ πόλιος ... gentis potiùs, quàm urbis circumscriptionem habere, scribit. Plura qui de ejus amplitudine, potentia, opulentia scire desiderat, Ctesium, Herodotum, Berosum Abydenum, Curtium, Philostratum, & è recentioribus, quibus ad ea describenda vix verba sufficiunt; Tzezem, consulat licet.
units.tr: XI. Babylon was, as Nebuchadnezzar boasted, a city great [Aramaic rabta] (Dan. 4:27), the mother of the Chaldeans (Jer. 50:12), the praise of the whole earth (Jer. 51:41), the glory of kingdoms and the pride of the Chaldeans (Isa. 13:19), golden [Hebrew madhebah] (Isa. 14:4), and also rich in treasures [Hebrew rabbat otsarot] (Jer. 51:13); and, on account of its outstanding power, the hammer of the whole earth (Jer. 50:23), a scourge and a weapon of war for scattering nations and destroying kingdoms (Jer. 51:20). Aristotle, Politics III.3, writes that it had the extent of a nation rather than of a city [Greek ethnos mallon ē poleōs]. Whoever wishes to learn more about its size, power and wealth may consult Ctesias, Herodotus, Berosus of Abydenus, Curtius, Philostratus, and among more recent writers Tzetzes, though words hardly suffice to describe it.

units.la: XII. Hierarchiæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantis, ceu Civitatis cujuspiam magnæ, amplitudinem, potentiam, opulentiam quis calamo adæquare potis est? Juvabit intueri indicio suo se prodentem soricem Bellarminum. Is enim & amplitudinem, & felicitatem temporalem Ecclesiæ suæ notam palam jactare non erubescit.
units.tr: XII. Who can match with his pen the extent, power and wealth of the ruling hierarchy of the Roman Church, as though it were some great city? It will be a pleasure to look at Bellarmine, the mole who betrays himself by his own evidence. For he is not ashamed to boast openly of the extent and the temporal prosperity of his Church.

units.la: Et de amplitudine quidem Ecclesiæ Romanæ sic ille de Ecclesia Lib. IV. 7. inter alia ampullatur: Nostram Ecclesiam maximam partem orbis occupâsse, & esse verè Catholicam, ita probamus. Nam tempore Apostolorum in toto mundo fructificare cœpit, ut Paulus dicit Coloss. i. Item tempore Irenæi erat sparsa per totum orbem, id est, per omnes provincias tunc cognitas, id quod ipse refert lib. 1. cap. 3. &c. S. Prosper Libro de ingratis ita cecinit: Sedes Roma Petri, quæ Pastoralis honoris Facta caput mundo, quicquid non possidet armis Relligione tenet.
units.tr: And indeed, concerning the extent of the Roman Church, he boasts among other things in On the Church, Book IV, chapter 7: We prove thus that our Church has occupied the greater part of the world and is truly Catholic. For in the time of the apostles it began to bear fruit throughout the whole world, as Paul says, Col. 1. Likewise in the time of Irenaeus it was spread through the whole world, that is, through all the provinces then known, as he himself reports, Book 1, chapter 3, etc. St Prosper, in his book On the Ungrateful, sang thus: Rome, the seat of Peter, which, made head of the world by the honour of a pastor, whatever it does not possess by arms, it holds by religion.

units.la: Tempore Gregorii M. Ecclesiam nostram fuisse in toto orbe terrarum planum est ex Epistolis ipsius Gregorii ad Episcopos Orientis, Africæ &c. Bernhardus disputans coram Rege Siciliæ Rogerio asserebat, Romano Pontifici suo tempore paruisse Orientem & Occidentem totum, item Franciam, Germaniam, Angliam, Iberos, & plurimas barbaras nationes. vide vitam S. Bernhardi Lib. II. 7. Denique nostro tempore Ecclesia Romana præter Italiam & Hispaniam totam, præter Galliam ferè totam, præter Germaniam, Angliam, Poloniam, Bohemiam, Hungariam, Græciam, Syriam, Æthiopiam, Ægyptum, in quibus multi inveniuntur Catholici, in ipso novo Orbe habet Ecclesias sine admissione hæreticorum; ad Orientem in Indiis; ad Occidentem in America; ad Septentrionem, in Japonia; ad Meridiem, in Brasilia, & exteriore parte Africæ.
