En Civitatem Magnam, Matrem nationum, laudem universæ terræ, gloriam Regnorum, decus superbiæ Romanorum! In historia Papatus ss. CLI. vidimus in Lateranensi Concilio Antonium Puccium verba Psalmi LXXII. 11. Omnes Reges terræ adorabunt eum, & servient ei, his verbis Leoni x. applicantem: Omnes Reges terræ sciunt; quænam potestas tibi data sit in Cœlo & in terra. Assa voce in eodem concilio ss. x. Archiepiscopus Stephanus: Tibi data est omnis potestas. Qui omne dicit, nihil excipit. Quantam igitur potentiam, robur quantum existimabimus Civitatis illius, cujus Rex omnem in Cœlo & terra potestatem habet, & in terra tot Reges Principesque obnoxios habet, quíque adeò non corporibus duntaxat, sed animis inprimis & conscientiis hominum dominatur, de quo plura inferius.
units.tr: That in the time of Gregory the Great our Church was spread through the whole world is plain from Gregory's own letters to the bishops of the East, of Africa, etc. Bernard, disputing before Roger, King of Sicily, asserted that in his time the whole East and West, as well as France, Germany, England, Spain and very many barbarian nations, were subject to the Roman Pontiff. See the Life of St Bernard, Book II, chapter 7. Finally, in our own time the Roman Church, apart from almost all of Italy and Spain, apart from almost all of France, apart from Germany, England, Poland, Bohemia, Hungary, Greece, Syria, Ethiopia and Egypt, in which many Catholics are found, has churches in the New World itself without admitting heretics: to the East in the Indies, to the West in America, to the North in Japan, to the South in Brazil and the outer part of Africa. Behold the Great City, the mother of nations, the praise of the whole earth, the glory of kingdoms, the adornment of the pride of the Romans! In the History of the Papacy, p. 151, we saw Antonius Puccius at the Lateran Council applying the words of Psalm 72:11, All kings of the earth shall worship him and serve him, to Leo X in these words: All kings of the earth know what power has been given to you in heaven and on earth. Likewise at the same council, in session 10, Archbishop Stephen, with the same acclamation: All power has been given to you. He who says all excludes nothing. How great, then, shall we reckon the power and strength of that City, whose King has all power in heaven and on earth, who has so many kings and princes in the earth subject to him, and who rules not only bodies but above all the souls and consciences of men? Of this more below.

units.la: XIII. Babylon Chaldaica suos habuit שרים וחכמים Principes & Sapientes חברים Divinatores נבריים fortes, Heroës, currus, equos &c. Jerem. L. 35. 36. 37. 38. Numquid non etiam Principibus, Sapientibus, Divinaculis, heroibus suis Roma Papalis abundat? In qua tot purpurati Patres praefulgent, Cardinales inprimis, in quibus fi Romanae sedis assentatoribus, veluti Isidoro Mosc0n. de Majestate milit. Eccl. lib. 1. part. 1. cap. 5. credimus, Majestas Reipublicae Christianae resident, vicem gerentes Apostolorum; orbis cardines; Ecclesiae capita, columnae, lumina, lucernae ardentes, candelabra lucis, decoris, praestantiae atque splendoris; stellae fixae in Caelo; Patres Conscripti in Diademate Principis, Divi, Venerabiles, Reverendissimi, Religiosissimi, Splendidissimi, Illustres, Superillustres, Illustrissimi, item, Maximi, Potentissimi, Seniores populi, Senatores & Patritii Maximi, Principes, Reges denique, quorum insuper (ita Nicolaus Clemangis Archidiaconus Bajacensis de corrupto Ecclesiae statu eosdem depingit) Papae assidentium Spiritus, verba tumentia, gestus tam insolentes, ut si artifex quisque vellet superbiae simulachrum fingere, nulla congruentius ratione id facere posset, quam Cardinalis effigiem oculis intuentium objectando; qui ex sortis infimae clericatu in hanc elationem cum sedis Apostolicae pompatu pervenerunt: nunc vero phylacteria sua in tantum dilataverunt, ut non modo Episcopos, sed Patriarchas Primates, sed Archi-Praesules velut infra se positos despiciant, imo se jam ab illis supplicibus propemodum adorari sinant, quin & Reges aequiparare contendant. Quos proin proximo gradu contingunt Patriarchae, Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, sapientes scilicet illi, & rerum Divinarum callidi, imo &
units.tr: XIII. Chaldean Babylon had her princes and wise men [Hebrew sarim vechakhamim], diviners [chabarim], mighty men and heroes [gibborim], chariots, horses, etc. (Jer. 50:35-38). Does not Papal Rome likewise abound in princes, wise men, diviners and heroes of her own? In her so many purple-clad Fathers shine forth, Cardinals above all, in whom, if we believe the flatterers of the Roman See, such as Isidore Moscon, On the Majesty of the Militant Church, Book 1, part 1, chapter 5, the majesty of the Christian Commonwealth resides, taking the place of the Apostles; the hinges of the world; the heads, pillars, lights, burning lamps, candlesticks of light, beauty, excellence and splendour; the fixed stars in heaven; the Conscript Fathers, in the diadem of the Prince; Divine, Venerable, Most Reverend, Most Religious, Most Splendid, Illustrious, Most Illustrious, Most Illustrious; likewise Greatest, Most Powerful, Elders of the people, Senators and Chief Patricians, Princes, and finally Kings. Of these (so Nicolas Clemangis, archdeacon of Bayeux, depicts them in his account of the corrupt state of the Church) the attendants of the Pope are, in spirit, of swollen words and gestures so insolent that if any craftsman wished to fashion an image of pride, he could do it in no more fitting way than by setting before the eyes of onlookers the figure of a Cardinal, who from the rank of the lowest clergy have risen to such height with the pomp of the Apostolic See. Now indeed they have so enlarged their phylacteries that they despise not only bishops but patriarchs, primates and archprelates, as though they were placed beneath them; nay, they already allow themselves to be almost adored by their suppliants, and strive even to equal kings. Next in rank to these come the patriarchs, archbishops and bishops, those wise men, clearly, and skilled in divine matters; indeed, and

units.la: Babylon vetus habuit Principes, consultores, sapientes, divinatores. Hierarchia papalis similibus abundat, quos inter Cardinales Regibus exaequati, Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, veri Divinatores emi-nent. imò & הברים μαν̄ης Divinaculi, qui ab idolo suo, Pontifice, oracula repetunt, Monachi, Abbates, qui etiam S. R. Imperii Principes audiunt, denique Sacerdotes quilibet adeò potentes, pollentésque, ut vel minimus eorum Creator Creatoris sui haberi contendat. Qui equos, currus falcatos Romæ Papalis desiderat, cavalcadam, seu Equitatum quempiam Papæ solennem, ministeria Papæ equitanti vel ab ipsis Regibus præstanda, Prælatos ex Ministris, servis Domini, Equites, Chavalieros factos cogitet.
units.tr: Ancient Babylon had princes, counsellors, wise men and diviners. The papal hierarchy abounds in similar men, among whom the Cardinals, made equal to kings, and the archbishops and bishops stand out as true diviners; indeed also the diviners [Hebrew chabarim; Greek manteis], who seek oracles from their idol, the Pontiff; the monks and abbots, who are heard even as princes of the Holy Roman Empire; and finally any priests so powerful and mighty that even the least of them claims to be the Creator of his Creator. Whoever desires horses and scythed chariots for the Papal Rome, a solemn cavalcade or some procession of horsemen for the Pope, services to be rendered to the riding Pope even by kings themselves, and who imagines prelates turned from ministers, servants of the Lord, into knights, Cavalieri, is thinking of such things.

units.la: XIV. Babylon Chaldaica scortationi inprimis Spirituali, cultui imaginum adeò quidem dedita fuit, ut propterea Jerem. l. 38. dicatur: ארץ פסליים terra sculptilium, cujus incolæ באימים יהוולל in simulachais insaniunt. Quid Roma Papalis? An quidquam cultu imaginum in externo cultu suo prius & antiquius habet? Annon in simulachris aperte insanit, eorumque in cultu proram pupimque religionis collocat? Et ne idololatria ejus multiplex innotescat omnibus, secundum Decalogi præceptum vel pravis interpretationis interpolat, vel audacter etiam expungit? De quo plura etiam in loco.
units.tr: XIV. Chaldean Babylon was devoted above all to spiritual whoredom and to the worship of images, so that Jer. 50:38 calls it a land of graven images [Hebrew eretz pesilim), whose inhabitants rave over idols [Hebrew be'eimim yithollelu]. What of Papal Rome? Does anything come before or earlier than the worship of images in her outward worship? Does she not openly rave over images, and place the prow and stern of religion in their worship? And so that her manifold idolatry may not be known to all, does she, according to the precept of the Decalogue, either corrupt it by wicked interpretation or boldly strike it out altogether? Of this more in its place.

units.la: XV. Fuit etiam Babylon vetus Ταυτη. Adoravit suum Belum, Merodachum, Nebonem, Scfach, alios, quin & Reges suos. Quomodo Regni Proceres unanimi decreto sanxisse leguntur, ut quicunque intra triginta dies a quocunque Deo aut homine, nisi a Rege, quicquam petierint, in speluncam leonum projiciantur. Quod Danieli non Regem Darium, sed Deum suum adoranti, accidit; Dan. vi. 7. 8. &c. Neque Ταυτη simpliciter Babylon fuit, sed ad similem idololatriam alios tum propinato aureo poculo eosdem inebrians Jerem. li. 7. tum vi etiam adhibita inducere conata est, uti ejusdem Danielis & sociorum ejus, quibus falsi Numinis in aurea statua erecta imperatum cultum abnuentibus dirum supplicium Babylonii dictavere, exemplo liquet. Roma Papalis, si qua alia gens, vere μλύϑι@ est. Adorat enim Deum Panaceum, Divos, Divásque, & eorundem etiam reliquias seu certas, seu incertas dubiásque; & supra omnes ipsum Regem suum Pontificem, quem sub Vice-Dei & Vice-Christi nomine verissimis honoribus Divinis prosequitur. Habet & aureum poculum suum, quo Reges populósque terræ inebrians, ad idololatriam similem seducit. In eos porro, qui unius soliúsque Dei timore, à Numinum talium religioso cultu religiose abstinent, atque interea cum Daniele & sociis ejus, uni solique Deo Israëlis litant, ubi ei vires suæ satis placent, ferro flammáque modis dirissimis sævit.
units.tr: XV. Ancient Babylon was also called Ταυτη [Tauta]. It worshipped its own Bel, Merodach, Nebo, Sheshach, and others, and even its kings. As we read, the nobles of the kingdom by unanimous decree enacted that whoever within thirty days asked anything of any god or man, except of the king, should be cast into the lions' den. This happened to Daniel, who prayed to his own God and not to King Darius (Dan. vi. 7, 8, &c.). Babylon was not simply Tauta, but tried to lead others into similar idolatry, first by offering them the golden cup to make them drunk (Jer. li. 7), and then by force, as the example of Daniel and his companions shows. When they refused to worship the image of a false god set up in gold, the Babylonians decreed a dreadful punishment for them. Papal Rome is truly a deceiving nation, more than any other. It worships the god Panaceus, the Divi and Divae, and their relics, whether certain or uncertain and doubtful; and above all it honours its own king, the Pontiff, whom under the name of Vicar of God and Vicar of Christ it honours with the highest divine honours. It also has its golden cup, with which it makes the kings and peoples of the earth drunk and leads them into a similar idolatry. Against those who, from the fear of the one and only God, religiously abstain from the religious worship of such deities, and who meanwhile, with Daniel and his companions, sacrifice to the one God of Israel alone, Rome rages with sword and fire in the most dreadful ways, whenever its own power pleases it well enough.

units.la: XVI. Babylon Chaldæa, si qua alia urbs, scortationibus, luxuriæque multiplici dedita fuit. Erat quippe תנאר ככרה tenera & voluptuaria Esaj. xlvii. 1. Adeò certè moribus corrupta erat, ut Cœlio Rhodigino Antiq. Lect. lib. viij. 11. ex pluribus authoribus referente, Babyloniæ mulieres cum hospitibus turpiter commisceri, in conviviis amicula exuere, pudorémque profanare sueverint. Ut mirum non fuerit Alexandri M. exercitum intra triginta & quatuor dies Babylonica luxuria abreptum, penitus enervatum esse. Roma Papalis dum imperat coelibatum, & in gremio suo fovet concubinarios, & concubinas, scortationis etiam corporalis author pridem facta est. Eadem approbans vota Monachatus, iisdémque obstringens incautos, etiamsi forte quandoque scortationis compertos censuræ subjiciat, occasionem tamen secretæ fornicationis præbet, & æstum libidinis in animo legibus suis retinet. Doctrina insuper de peccato veniali, & quòd concupiscentia non sit peccatum, impuritates aperte fovet.
units.tr: XVI. Chaldaean Babylon, like any other city, was given over to fornication and manifold luxury. It was indeed "tender and delicate" [ענוגה ורכה] (Isa. xlvii. 1). Certainly it was so corrupt in morals that, as Caelius Rhodiginus reports from many authors (Antiq. Lect. lib. viii. 11), the women of Babylon were accustomed to mix shamefully with strangers, to take off their clothes at feasts, and to profane their modesty. It is no wonder that Alexander the Great's army, carried away by Babylonian luxury within thirty-four days, was utterly enervated. Papal Rome, while it enjoins celibacy, and while it cherishes concubinaries and concubines in its bosom, has long since become the author of bodily fornication. By approving the vows of monasticism, and binding the unwary by them, even if it sometimes subjects to censure those found guilty of fornication, it nevertheless provides the occasion for secret fornication, and by its laws keeps the heat of lust alive in the mind. Moreover, its doctrine of venial sin, and that concupiscence is not sin, openly fosters impurities.

units.la: XVII. Babylon Chaldaica populum Dei, ejusdem justo judicio captivum diu attinuit, & in eundem captivum crudeliter satis consuluit. Devoravit me, ita Ecclesia captiva Jerem. li. 34. quiritatur, & contrivit me Nebucadnezar Rex Babel, destituit me vas vacuum, absorpsit me ut Draco, implevit ventrem suum deliciis meis; protrufit me. Roma Papalis simili prorsus ratione Ecclesiam veram Dei, electos & fideles, Sanctos Agni sequaces, longa captivitate maceravit. Toto enim tempore quo dominationem suam Papalis Hierarchia impotenter affectavit, impudentérque exercuit, extitit in ipso Ecclesiæ Romanæ sinu, adeóque cum eo in externa communione permixta vera Dei Ecclesia, abominationibus invalescentibus sese opposuit, tyrannidémque in fortunas & conscientias suas immanem subiit. Idque inferius abundè etiam confirmabimus.
units.tr: XVII. Chaldaean Babylon long held captive the people of God, who were held captive by its just judgment, and dealt cruelly enough with that captive people. "He has devoured me," so the captive Church complains (Jer. li. 34), "Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has crushed me, he has made me an empty vessel, he has swallowed me up like a dragon, he has filled his belly with my delicacies, and cast me out." In a quite similar way Papal Rome has long worn down the true Church of God, its elect and faithful, the holy followers of the Lamb. For the whole time that the Papal hierarchy wickedly aspired to its dominion and shamelessly exercised it, the true Church of God existed within the very bosom of the Roman Church, and, mixed with it in outward communion, opposed itself to the growing abominations, and endured a monstrous tyranny over its property and consciences. We will confirm this more fully below.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Adeò pertinaciter populum Dei captivum vetus Babylon detinuit, ut eum dimittere prorsus renuerit. Sed Deus populi fui vindicem fe gessit. Sic dicit Jehova Deus exercituum: injuste vexati sunt filii Israël, & filii Juda unâ, & omnes, qui eos captivos duxerunt, apprehenderunt eos, recusant eos dimittere ... eorum fortis est, Jehova Deus exercituum nomen ejus est. aget causam eorum ad tranquillandam terram & commovendum habitatores Babel Jerem. l. 33. 34. Sic subitò cecidit Babel. Curavimus Babylonem & non est sanata. Relinquite eam, & eamus quisque in terram suam. Jerem. li. 8. 9. Finita septuaginta annorum captivitate libertati suæ vindicata Ecclesia Dei exivit, patriófque lares revisit. Pari ferè ratione Ecclesia Dei sub jugum dominantis Hierarchiæ Papalis missa, diúque peffimè habita, tandem, indulgente, imò & præcipiente & vincula relaxante Domino, claustra perfregit, Hierarchiæ Papalis communionem etiam externam deferuit, & religionis conscientiarúmque libertate, post exantlata infinita discrimina, pactis etiam adversantium firmata, frui coepit, atque adhuc dum Dei omnipotentis & misericordis gratia, passim fruitur.
units.tr: So stubbornly did old Babylon hold the captive people of God that it refused utterly to let them go. But God showed himself the avenger of his people. "Thus says the LORD of hosts: the children of Israel and the children of Judah were wronged together, and all who took them captive hold them fast, they refuse to let them go... Their redeemer is strong, the LORD of hosts is his name; he will plead their cause, to make the land quiet and to disquiet the inhabitants of Babylon" (Jer. l. 33, 34). So "Babylon suddenly fell. We healed Babylon, but she was not cured. Leave her, and let us each go into his own land" (Jer. li. 8, 9). When the seventy years of captivity were finished, the Church of God, vindicated to its liberty, went out and returned to its ancestral home. In much the same way, the Church of God, sent under the yoke of the ruling Papal hierarchy and held there most wretchedly for a long time, at last, with the Lord indulging, even commanding and loosening its chains, broke the bars, abandoned even the external communion of the Papal hierarchy, and began to enjoy liberty of religion and conscience, confirmed by treaties even with its opponents, after enduring countless dangers; and by the grace of the almighty and merciful God it still enjoys this everywhere.

units.la: XIX. Babylon Chaldaea post separationem Ecclesiae facta dicitur habitatio immundarum bestiarum, ululae, fiiarum struthionis, Draconum, aliorúmque animalium silvestrium Jerem. L. 39. LI. 37. Ferè idem Romae Papali post separationem ab ea fidelium & sanctorum, accidit. Remanserunt in ea, veluti in carcere & custodia, homines ut plurimúm ψυχικοὶ animales, ob veras fidei defectum, immundi, quos in carcere illo non Deus, sed impurae eorum cupiditates, ambitio, avaritia, hypocrisis, mollities adamata vitae luxuries, splendor fortunae, similiáque detinent. Haec certè, non aliud quidquam, eos propellunt, ut Regnum illud impietatis, tanquam portum negotiationis suae, tanto conatu, & contra conscientiam suam, defendant.
units.tr: XIX. Chaldaean Babylon, after the separation of the Church from it, is said to have become a dwelling of unclean beasts, owls, ostriches, dragons, and other wild animals (Jer. l. 39; li. 37). Almost the same thing has happened to Papal Rome after the separation from it of the faithful and holy ones. There remain in it, as in a prison and custody, for the most part men who are "psychic, animal" [ψυχικοὶ], unclean because they lack true faith; in that prison it is not God who holds them, but their impure desires, ambition, avarice, hypocrisy, the softness of a life loved in luxury, the splendour of fortune, and similar things. These alone, and nothing else, drive them to defend that kingdom of impiety, as if it were the harbour of their trade, with such great effort and against their own conscience.

units.la: XX. Adeò adversum Deum ipsum Babylon Chaldaea insolescebat, ut blasphemè ita se jactaverit אני ואפסי עוד לא Ego, & non est praeter me ultra. Esaj. XLVII. 8. 10. unde και ἐξοχὴν superbia, imò אל יהוה adversus Deum ipsum se superbissimè efferens. Jerem. L. 29. 31. dicitur. Incantationibus insuper, ac veneficiis ita dedita fuit, ut ei עצמות חברים fortitudo incantatorum Esaj. XLVII. 9. tribuatur. Blasphemandi & ferociendi simile cacoethes, incantationúmque impietatem similem Ecclesiae Romanae dominantem Hierarchiam transversam abripuisse, affirmamus, atque infra etiam liquidò comprobabimus.
units.tr: XX. Chaldaean Babylon so insolently exalted itself against God himself that it boastfully said, "I am, and there is none else beside me any more" [אני ואפסי עוד] (Isa. xlvii. 8, 10). Hence it is called, pre-eminently, proud, and indeed "against the LORD" [אל יהוה], proudly lifting itself up against God himself (Jer. l. 29, 31). It was also so given over to enchantments and sorceries that "the strength of enchanters" [עצמות חברים] is attributed to it (Isa. xlvii. 9). We affirm that a similar itch for blaspheming and boasting, and a similar impiety of enchantments, has carried away the Papal hierarchy that rules the Roman Church into perversity, and we will also prove this clearly below.

units.la: XXI. Taceo plures alios Babylonis Chaldaicae veteris Characteres in S. historia proditos, veluti quòd ea fuit mercatura & emporiis adeò insignis, ut עיר הכלים Civitas negotiatorum Ezech. xvii. 4. Esaj. xlvii. 15. dici meruerit: quòd fuit αἰχμητὴς quæstui turpi dedita, & propterea רבית אוצרות locuples thesaurus Jerem. li. 13. quòd fuit sæva & crudelis הר המשחית mons perdens, qui perdit totam terram. ibid. v. 25. פטיש כל הארץ malleus universæ terræ. Jer. l. 23. quòd summa securitate judicia Dei imminentia contempsit; imperium sibi perenne, & duraturam, atque nunquam interrumpendam felicitatem sibi promisit, identidem secum ita reputans: In æternum ero Domina: Ego sum, & non est præter me ultra: non sedebo vidua, nec cognoscam orbitatem Esaj. xlvii. 7. 8. &c: quòd malitiæ astutiæque fisa, præsentis Numinis cogitationem habuit nullam, palàm & jactans אין ראני non est, qui me videat. ibid. v. 10.
units.tr: XXI. I pass over several other characters of old Chaldaean Babylon recorded in sacred history: for instance, that its trade and markets were so notable that it deserved to be called "the city of merchants" [עיר הכלים] (Ezek. xvii. 4; Isa. xlvii. 15); that it was given over to shameful gain, and therefore "abundant treasures" [רבית אוצרות] (Jer. li. 13); that it was cruel and savage, "the destroying mountain" [הר המשחית], which destroys the whole earth (ibid. v. 25), "the hammer of all the earth" [פטיש כל הארץ] (Jer. l. 23); that with complete confidence it despised the judgments of God hanging over it, promising itself a lasting empire and a happiness that would endure and never be interrupted, repeatedly reasoning thus with itself: "I shall be a lady for ever. I am, and there is none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, nor know bereavement" (Isa. xlvii. 7, 8, &c.); and that, trusting in its malice and cunning, it took no thought of the present God, boasting openly, "none sees me" [אין ראני] (ibid. v. 10).

units.la: XXII. Similes Characteres qui in Roma Papali inve-
units.tr: XXII. Similar characters, which whoever sets out to investigate in Papal Rome

units.la: stigare studuerit, nullo fere negotio eos inveniet. Ibi enim plena omnia sunt mercatoribus & negotiatoribus, qui pietatem quæstui habentes, per avaritiam, fictis sermonibus fidelium animas ψυχὰς in commercio habent, neque mercaturam suam circa res nauci exercent, sed Ducatus, Regna, Satrapias, Cœlum ipsum, & Cœlestia venum exponunt. Et quis plus quàm Regales Romæ ejusdem Papalis opes, malis artibus, & religionis prætextu quæsitas, sub censum revocare potest? Adeò quidem insatiabilis ejus avaritia est, ut sitim illam opum & thesaurorum nec Tagus, nec Hermus, nec Pactolus, nec postremò, si fit aureus, totus Oceanus explere possit; útque, quod Alphonsum Aragonum Regem pronuntiàsse Panormitanus Lib. j. de dictis & factis Alph. apopht. 8. refert, Harpyiæ non jam amplius insulas, ut Poëtæ existimárunt, incolere, sed ex insulis migrâsse in Curiam Romanam, ibique sedem fixisse videantur. Jam & tyrannidem crudelitatémque Romæ Papalis non tam vestę, quàm cruore innocentum purpuratæ, qui cognoscere avet, in rem præsentem eat, & ad animum sibi revocet iliada horrendæ innumerabilium hominum stragis per Europam ob Missam intermissam editæ, tanta sævitia, & supplicium deterrimorum varietate, quanta priscis tyrannis incognita, & inaudita fuit, ut quemadmodum, Polybio lib. j. hist. judice ἀνθρώπῳ μηδὲν ἀμὸ πρὸν ὃσοπὴ ἄπω τῶν ζῴων nullum inveniri animal potest, quod crudelitate homo non superet, sic inter ipsos homines Zelota Pontificius Romanus cunctos alios immani truculentia superet. Sed & supinum judiciorum Divinorum adversus Ecclesiam suam contemtum validissimè arguunt σεσωμένα de perpetua Ecclesiæ Romanæ, particularis licèt, constantia, qua futurum sit, ut nunquam vel in fide, vel quoad externum etiam fulgorem, splendorem, felicitatémque deficiat, vel etiam ab ea cathedra Petri separari, alióque sedes Apostolica transferri possit: uti Bellarm. de Rom. Pont. lib. iv. 4. innuit. Quò pertinent Alcasaris ad Apoc. xvij. Disp. j. verba: Tantum abest, ut Romana Ecclesia opprimenda iterum sit, ut Gregorius M. lib. ij. Dial. cap. 15. affirmet, S. Benedicto fuisse Divinitus præsignificatum Romam nunquam amplius ab infidelibus eversum iri. Denique tanta licentia factio Romana Papalis Deo hominibúsque illudere religionis prætextu non cessat, ut oculum Dei impietatis & improbitatis suæ multijugæ vindicem metuere nequicquam videatur.
units.tr: He will find them with almost no effort. There everything is full of merchants and traders, who treat piety as a source of profit and, through greed, hold the souls [ψυχάς] of the faithful in trade by means of feigned sermons. They do not deal in trifles, but put up for sale dukedoms, kingdoms, satrapies, Heaven itself and the things of Heaven. And who could bring the wealth of that Papal Rome, gathered by wicked arts and under the pretext of religion, back within any assessment that is more than royal? So insatiable is its avarice that neither the Tagus, nor the Hermus, nor the Pactolus, nor, finally, even the whole ocean, were it made of gold, could quench its thirst for riches and treasures. And so, as Panormitanus reports Alfonso, King of Aragon, to have said, Lib. j. de dictis & factis Alph. apopht. 8, the Harpies seem no longer to inhabit islands, as the poets supposed, but to have migrated from the islands to the Roman Curia and to have fixed their seat there. Again, who wishes to know the cruelty and tyranny of Papal Rome, which is dyed purple not so much by its garments as by the blood of the innocent, let him go to the matter itself and call to mind the horrible Iliad of countless human slaughters throughout Europe, carried out for the sake of the abolished Mass, with such savagery and such a variety of the most dreadful punishments as was unknown and unheard of in the ancient tyrannies. So, as Polybius judges in lib. j. hist., ἀνθρώπῳ μηδὲν ἀμὸ πρὸν ὃσοπὴ ἄπω τῶν ζῴων [no animal can be found that man does not surpass in cruelty], so among men themselves the Roman Papist zealot surpasses all others in brutal ferocity. But also the Church's slothful contempt for the Divine judgments is strongly proved by the σεσωμένα [sealed] constancy of the Roman Church, though only in a particular sense, by which it is to happen that it never fails, either in faith or in outward brilliance, splendour and prosperity, nor can be separated from the chair of Peter, and the apostolic see transferred elsewhere, as Bellarmine hints in de Rom. Pont. lib. iv. 4. To this pertain the words of Alcázar, ad Apoc. xvij. Disp. j.: So far is the Roman Church from being about to be crushed again, that Gregory the Great, Dial. lib. ij. cap. 15, affirms that it was revealed to St Benedict by God that Rome would never again be overthrown by unbelievers. Finally, the Roman Papal faction does not cease to mock God and men under the pretext of religion with such licence that it seems in vain to fear the eye of God, the avenger of its manifold impiety and wickedness.

units.la: XXIII. Haud forte ἀπεσεσηκόντως Josephi Scaligeri de Emend. temp. lib. vj. p. 580. observatio fuerit; quòd antiqui Babyloniorum Reges, ad Imperium accedentes nomen mutare soliti fuerint.
units.tr: XXIII. Perhaps it will not be a ill-fitting observation of Joseph Scaliger, de Emend. temp. lib. vj. p. 580, that the ancient kings of the Babylonians were accustomed to change their names when they came to power.

units.la: Ita Bel-adan privatum nomen erat ejus, qui, postquam ad Imperium accessit, Nabonassar vocatus est. Hoc ergo quia usitatum fuit veteribus Babylonis Regibus, imitandum sibi duxerunt Babylonis novæ Reges, Romani Pontifices, ut ita mutatio illa nominis Parum
units.tr: Thus Bel-adan was the private name of the man who, after he came to the throne, was called Nabonassar. Since this was customary among the ancient kings of Babylon, the new kings of Babylon, the Roman Pontiffs, thought they should imitate it, so that the change of name

units.la: Sicut olim Babylonii Reges imperium adeuntes nomina mutarunt, ita Pontifices Romani ad Papatum evecti faciunt idem. parum non ad putidum illud os porci, uti quidam putârunt, sed aliud multò sublimius, Regium scilicet initium referendum sit. Nam …
units.tr: Just as the Babylonian kings once changed their names on taking up their rule, so the Roman Pontiffs, raised to the Papacy, do the same. That change is to be referred not to that foul mouth of a pig, as some have thought, but to something far more lofty, namely a royal beginning. For …

units.la: Magnos magna decent: Papas sic nomina Regum.
units.tr: Great things befit the great: thus the Popes take the names of kings.

units.la: XXIV. Denique propter impietatem extremam, idolatriam, superbiam, tyrannidem, aliáque peccata Babylon Chaldæa judicium Dei gravissimum meruit, sustinuitque, cujus obnuntiationem duobus postremis Jeremiæ Capitibus, quibus Babylonis σανωλογία graphicè describitur, legere est. Non obstitit urbis celebritas, non ingens capacitas, non mœnium firmitas, non Principum & inhabitatorum multitudo, non Sapientum, Consiliariorum callid*/ itas: non Regis potentia: non simulata pietas, & Divorum, Divarúmque veneratio: non equorum & curruum copia, non sexcenta alia, quò minùs impleta impietatis mensura justam commeritamque denique pœnam lueret, quam exactè juxta Divina oracula, fuséque S. Hieronymus ad Esaj. cap. xiij. narrat.
units.tr: XXIV. Finally, on account of its extreme impiety, idolatry, pride, tyranny and other sins, Chaldean Babylon incurred and endured the most severe judgment of God, the announcement of which can be read in the last two chapters of Jeremiah, where the destruction of Babylon is vividly described. The celebrity of the city did not stand in the way, nor its vast size, nor the strength of its walls, nor the multitude of its princes and inhabitants, nor the cunning of its wise men and counsellors, nor the power of its king, nor its feigned piety and veneration of gods and goddesses, nor the abundance of horses and chariots, nor six hundred other things, so that it might not fill up the measure of its impiety and at last pay the just and deserved punishment, as St Jerome relates exactly, according to the divine oracles and at length, ad Esaj. cap. xiij.

units.la: XXV. Etiam Roma Papalis judiciorum Dei adversus se primordia, deficientibus ob compertam hypocrisin, idololatriam, tyrannidem, abejus Imperio tot Regibus, popululisque, odio ejus sancto flagrantibus, jam degustare coepit. Invenient etiam deinceps fata viam, neque quidquam, cùm definitum tempus aderit, Romam liberabit, & Regnum Pontificium à definito Propheticis oraculis interitu vindicabit; non Majestas Papalis, non thesauri, non assleclarum potentia & numerus, non sanctitas simulata, non Litaniæ ad Sanctulos directæ, non Divi, Divæque, quibus hactenus cultum suum impenderunt omnes, non jejunia sponte suscepta, non peregrinationes ad statuas, non idola, flagellationes, Missæ, suffragia, de congruo & condigno merita, & hujus furfuris nugamenta papalia Συντομος. Una hora venient plaga ejus, mors, & luctus.
units.tr: XXV. Papal Rome too has now begun to taste the first beginnings of God's judgments against itself, as its hypocrisy, idolatry and tyranny have been exposed, and so many kings and peoples, burning with holy hatred of it, have turned away from its rule. Fate will also find its way, and nothing will free Rome when the appointed time arrives, nor will it rescue the Papal kingdom from its destruction, which the prophetic oracles have set. Neither papal majesty, nor treasures, nor the power and number of its followers, nor feigned sanctity, nor litanies addressed to the lesser saints, nor the gods and goddesses to whom all have hitherto devoted their worship, nor voluntary fasts, nor pilgrimages to statues, nor idols, flagellations, Masses, suffrages, papal merits of congruity and condignity, and the trifling playthings of this chaff, will avail. Συντομος [briefly]: In one hour her plague shall come, death and mourning.

units.la: Papalis ruere jam cœpit, et ad extremum penitus ruet. luctus & fames, & igni comburetur, quia fortis est Domi‑ nus ille Deus, qui eam judicabit. Apoc. xviii. 9.
units.tr: The Papal edifice has already begun to fall, and at last it will fall utterly. Mourning and famine, and she shall be burned with fire, because strong is the Lord God who shall judge her. Rev. xviii. 9.

units.la: XXVI. Intueatur se nunc Roma Papalis, Hierarchia dominans, si ita libet, in lucidissimo illo Babylonis Chaldaicæ speculo. Vix abs se impetrabit, quin exactissimam fui in ea effigiem oculis videat, manibúsque palpet. Quamvis enim similia per se nihil probent, & quod vulgò dici solet, Theologia Symbolica per se vim argumentandi nullam habeat; Similitudo tamen ab ipso Spiritu S. proposita, ut attendatur & Ϲωιτῶς comparetur, momentum haud dubiè eximium habet. Neque enim Cœtum illum, seu Civitatem, habentem potestatem in Reges mundi, & iisdem aureum poculum suum propinantem, Spiritus S. Babylonis nomine insignivisset, nisi cum Babylone Chaldaica veteri conspicua analogia convenire. Unde ipsi etiam Apocalypseos Interpretes Pontificii, Alcasar, à Lapide, Ribera, alii, Romæ suæ Veteris seu futuræ novissimæ Antichristianæ veterem Chaldaicam Babylonem, typum fecerunt; atque eo argumento, quòd utramque inter illam similitudo intercedat, Romam alterutram Babylonis mysticæ in Apocalypsi nomine venire arguerunt. Veriori potiorique ratione nos Ecclesiæ Romanæ Hierarchiam dominantem, quæ cœteris omnibus paribus, cum Babylone Chaldaica Veteri συναμωνς congruit, Babylonem Magnam in Apocalypsi adumbratam esse, concludimus.
units.tr: XXVI. Let Papal Rome now, the ruling Hierarchy, if you like, look upon itself in that most clear mirror of Chaldean Babylon. Scarcely will it refrain from seeing its own most exact image in it with its eyes and touching it with its hands. For although similitudes in themselves prove nothing, and, as is commonly said, symbolic theology has no power of argument in itself, yet a similitude set forth by the Holy Spirit himself, so that it may be noted and compared with care, undoubtedly has a very considerable weight. For the Holy Spirit would not have marked that assembly, or city, holding power over the kings of the world and offering them its golden cup, with the name of Babylon, unless it had a clear analogy with ancient Chaldean Babylon. Hence the Papist interpreters of the Apocalypse themselves, Alcázar, à Lapide, Ribera and others, have made ancient Chaldean Babylon a type of their Rome, either present or future, the newest Antichristian city; and by the argument that there is a likeness between the two, they have argued that Rome comes under one or the other as the name of mystic Babylon in the Apocalypse. By the truer and more weighty reasoning, we conclude that the ruling Hierarchy of the Roman Church, which, all other things being equal, agrees exactly with ancient Chaldean Babylon, is the Great Babylon foreshadowed in the Apocalypse.

units.la: DISSERTATIO SEPTIMA
units.tr: DISSERTATIO SEPTIMA

units.la: QUA Hierarchiam seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem Babylonem Magnam esse probatur secundò, quia mysterii prætextu dominatur.
units.tr: In which it is proved, secondly, that the dominant Hierarchy or clergy of the Church of Rome is the Great Babylon, because it rules under the pretext of mystery.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Babylonis M. Character secundus est, quòd in fronte sua scriptum habet nomen μυστήριον, Mysterium. II. Duplex Mysterium S. literæ tradunt, unum pietatis, impietatis alterum. III. Pietatis mysterium est, quicquid à Spiritu S. in verbo scripto revelatum ad doctrinam Evangelii de Christo aurigatur. IV. Impietatis contra est ficta voluntas Dei, ex cerebro humano, sine demonstratione ex indubitabili verbo prolato, quæ ad alia omnia, quàm ad doctrinam Evangelii de Christo dirigitur. V. Mysterium pietatis est Deus in carne revelatus: Impietatis caro personata, Spiritum Dei mentiens. VI. Mysterium Babyloni tributum est impietatis. Hierarchiæ Papali illud competere Syllogismo (ωαθοικῶς probatur. VII. Coronæ Pontificis R. olim inscriptum fuit μυστήριον.
units.tr: I. The second mark of the Great Babylon is that she bears on her forehead the name μυστήριον, Mystery. II. Holy Scripture teaches that there are two mysteries, one of piety and the other of impiety. III. The mystery of piety is whatever is revealed by the Holy Spirit in the written Word and drawn out for the doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ. IV. The mystery of impiety, on the other hand, is a feigned will of God, invented by the human brain, without proof from an undoubted word, and directed to everything except the doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ. V. The mystery of piety is God revealed in the flesh; the mystery of impiety is a flesh playing a part, lying about the Spirit of God. VI. The mystery is ascribed to Babylon as a mystery of impiety, and it is proved by syllogism that this belongs to the Papal Hierarchy. VII. The word μυστήριον was once inscribed on the crown of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: VIII. Rem titulo eo significatam Hierarchiæ Papali competere, documentis asseritur.
units.tr: VIII. The thing signified by that title is shown, by evidence, to belong to the Papal Hierarchy.

units.la: IX. 1. Quia se unam solamque omnis mysterii promam condam facit; & fidem ultimò in dictum Papæ resolvit.
units.tr: IX. 1. Because it makes itself the one and only promoter of every mystery, and ultimately resolves faith into the saying of the Pope.

units.la: X. De analysi fidei sententia Pontificiorum ex Gregorio de Valentia proponitur.
units.tr: X. The opinion of the Papists on the analysis of faith is set out from Gregory of Valencia.

units.la: XI. Ex eadem discussa demonstratur, dictum Papæ ad nullam regulam examinatum Pontificiæ fidei principium esse.
units.tr: XI. From the same discussion it is shown that the saying of the Pope, which has been tested by no rule, is the principle of Papist faith.

units.la: XII. Idem ex Methodistarum novorum de analysi fidei placitis probatur.
units.tr: XII. The same is proved from the views on the analysis of faith held by the new Methodists.

units.la: XIII. XIV. Mysterium illud impietatis amplificatur inde, quòd & fidem Divinitatis Scripturæ, librorum canonicorum, & sensus genuini à dicto Papæ suspendunt.
units.tr: XIII. XIV. That mystery of impiety is further enlarged by the fact that they make the divinity of Scripture, the canonical books, and the genuine sense depend on the saying of the Pope.

units.la: XV. Adeóque privato Spiritui Papæ inædificant.
units.tr: XV. And so they build upon the private spirit of the Pope.

units.la: XVI. Veterum & novorum Doctorum P. testimonia, quibus dictum Papæ fidei principium statuitur, producuntur.
units.tr: XVI. The testimonies of the old and new Teachers of the Papists are brought forward, by which the saying of the Pope is established as the principle of faith.

units.la: XVII. Ex convitiis quibus S. Scripturam Doctores P. impetunt, id ipsum asseritur,
units.tr: XVII. From the abuse with which the Fathers assail Holy Scripture, the same point is asserted,

units.la: XVIII. & documentum illud primum præcipuùmque concluditur.
units.tr: XVIII. and this first and chief proof is concluded.

units.la: XIX. 11. Quia præter illa, quæ scripta sunt, alia mysteria, seu secreta non scripta & silenda obtrudit, & in iis mysteriorum, & Ecclesiæ dignitatem collocat.
units.tr: XIX. 11. Because, besides those things that have been written, it thrusts upon us other mysteries, or secrets, unwritten and to be kept silent, and places in them the dignity both of the mysteries and of the Church.

units.la: XX. Absurditas & ἀκρασία dogmatis.
units.tr: XX. The absurdity and the ἀκρασία of the doctrine.

units.la: XXI. Mysteria religionis Christianæ nulla sileri, omnia publicari debent.
units.tr: XXI. The mysteries of the Christian religion ought not to be concealed at all; all of them ought to be made public.

units.la: XXII. Sapientia mysterii, quam inter perfectos S. Paulus locutus est, non fuit secreta sapientia, paucis communicata.
units.tr: XXII. The wisdom of the mystery which St. Paul spoke among the perfect was not a secret wisdom communicated to a few.

units.la: XXIII. Aliud est doctrina mysteriorum, aliud eorum celebratio. Illa publicanda semper est, ad hanc ἀμύνητι non sunt admittendi, licèt spectatores esse possint.
units.tr: XXIII. The teaching of the mysteries is one thing, and their celebration another. The former must always be made public; the latter, the uninitiated [ἀμύητοι] are not to be admitted to, although they may be spectators.

units.la: XXIV. Sanctum non propterea canibus datum est, si Apostoli quælibet religionis secreta scripserunt.
units.tr: XXIV. The holy thing was not therefore given to dogs, even if the Apostles wrote down any secrets of the religion.

units.la: XXV. Ambigua eam in rem veterum nonnullorum dicta explicantur, veluti Dionysii Areopagitæ.
units.tr: XXV. Some ambiguous sayings of certain ancient writers on this point are explained, such as those of Dionysius the Areopagite.

units.la: XXVI. Basilii.
units.tr: XXVI. Of Basil.

units.la: XXVII. Hilárii.
units.tr: XXVII. Of Hilary.

units.la: XXVIII. Clementis Alexandrini.
units.tr: XXVIII. Of Clement of Alexandria.

units.la: XXIX. Crypsis dogmatis totius, & mysterium impietatis panditur.
units.tr: XXIX. The concealing of the whole doctrine, and the mystery of impiety, is laid open.

units.la: XXX. Consensum in eo cum Judæis & Gentilibus, Peresius & Bellarminus non dissimulant.
units.tr: XXX. Peresius and Bellarmine do not conceal their agreement in this with the Jews and the Gentiles.

units.la: XXXI. III. Quia septem Sacramenta, totidem mysteria, ceu summam religionis, & causam salutis, ac justificationis commendat. Sacramenta procedente tempore mysteria dici cœpta.
units.tr: XXXI. III. Because they commend the seven Sacraments, as many mysteries, as the sum of religion and the cause of salvation and justification. As time went on, the Sacraments began to be called mysteries.

units.la: XXXII. Mysteria symbolica seu Sacramenta duo S. litera & pia antiquitas agnoscunt.
units.tr: XXXII. Holy Scripture and pious antiquity recognise two symbolic mysteries, or Sacraments.

units.la: XXXIII. Iis plura superstitio diversis occasionibus addidit.
units.tr: XXXIII. Superstition has added more of them on various occasions.

units.la: XXXIV. Iisdem, ut & veris Sacramentis falsa doctrina incrustatis, vim miram præter Dei verbum tribuit.
units.tr: XXXIV. Having encrusted these, as well as the true Sacraments, with false doctrine, it has attributed to them a wondrous power beyond the Word of God.

units.la: XXXV. De efficacia Sacramentorum variantes sententiæ Scholasticorum.
units.tr: XXXV. The varying opinions of the Schoolmen on the efficacy of the Sacraments.

units.la: XXXVI. De eadem decretum Tridentinæ Synodi, ab operatione Sacramenti fidem & devotionem ejus, qui suscipit, excludentis, & efficaciam ex opere operato stabilientis.
units.tr: XXXVI. On the same point, the decree of the Council of Trent, which excludes faith and devotion of the recipient from the working of the Sacrament, and establishes its efficacy by the work worked (ex opere operato).

units.la: XXXVII. XXXVIII. Mysterium iniquitatis, quod in ea doctrina continetur, ostensum.
units.tr: XXXVII. XXXVIII. The mystery of iniquity contained in that doctrine is shown.

units.la: XXXIX. IV. Quia Christum in Missa, ceu præcipuo Mysterio, sterio, corporaliter simul & secretè ac invisibiliter adesse & sacrificari pertendit. XL. XLI. Quæ doctrina mysterium iniquitatis summam comprehendit. XLII. Accedit Canon Missæ, inter summa mysteria numeratus, & secreti nomine, ob secretam pronuntiationem, insignitus. XLIII. Præsentia Corporis Christi secreta & invisibilis mysterium impietatis est, quia Sacramentum prorsus evertit, XLIV. quod ex Bellarmini & Concilii Tridentini de modo, quo Corpus in Eucharistia sit, explicatione ulterius liquet. XLV. Thomas Aquinas verum Christi Corpus ex Eucharistia tollit. XLVI. A fide mysterii præsentiæ corporalis Christus ipse graviter dehortatur. XLVII. v. Quia dogmata sua occultat, & sacra sua lingua peregrina, etiam clam demurmurando, paragit. XLVIII. Theologi gentiles diviniora, quæ rebantur, dogmata celabant. XLIX. Idem Sacra & Divini cultus Ceremonias plerasque in occulto tenuere.
units.tr: XXXIX. IV. Because it maintains that Christ is present in the Mass, as the chief Mystery, bodily and at once secretly and invisibly, and is sacrificed. XL. XLI. This doctrine comprises the sum of the mystery of iniquity. XLII. To this is added the Canon of the Mass, counted among the highest mysteries and marked with the name of "secret" because of its secret pronunciation. XLIII. The secret and invisible presence of the Body of Christ is a mystery of impiety, because it utterly overthrows the Sacrament, XLIV. as is made clearer still from Bellarmine's and the Council of Trent's explanation of the manner in which the Body is in the Eucharist. XLV. Thomas Aquinas takes the true Body of Christ away from the Eucharist. XLVI. Christ himself earnestly warns against faith in the mystery of the bodily presence. XLVII. v. Because they hide their doctrines, and prepare their sacred language as a foreign tongue, even muttering it secretly. XLVIII. The Gentile theologians concealed the more divine doctrines, as they supposed. XLIX. The same people kept most of the sacred rites and ceremonies of divine worship in secret.

units.la: L. Imitatione gentilium Pontificii dogmata fidei occultant, dum quædam silenda sciscunt, & à lectione Scripturæ plebem arcent,
units.tr: L. Imitating the Gentiles, the Papists conceal the doctrines of faith, while they decree that certain things are to be kept silent and keep the common people away from reading Scripture,

units.la: LI. & desiderium omne sciendi qua metu, quaratione calida in populo extinguunt.
units.tr: LI. and extinguish in the people every desire to know, by fear and by a hot-headed zeal.

units.la: LII. Quò inprimis implicitæ fidei, seu voluntariæ deditionis in obsequium Papæ, commentum pertinet,
units.tr: LII. To this chiefly belongs the invention of implicit faith, or voluntary surrender to the obedience of the Pope,

units.la: LIII. nec non tyrannis ea, qua plebem, ceu merè animalem, à rerum Sacrarum cognitione & discretione depellunt.
units.tr: LIII. and likewise the tyranny by which they drive the common people, as if merely animal, away from the knowledge and discernment of sacred things.

units.la: LIV. Ab externi cultus intelligentia populum iidem arcent.
units.tr: LIV. The same people keep the populace from understanding the external worship.

units.la: LV. Quod linguæ inprimis peregrinæ in Sacris usus demonstrat.
units.tr: LV. Which the use of a foreign tongue above all in sacred matters demonstrates.

units.la: LVI. Mysterium impietatis in occultatione ea dogmatum & ceremoniarum detegitur.
units.tr: LVI. The mystery of impiety is revealed in this concealment of doctrines and ceremonies.

units.la: LVII. vi. Quia profunditates Sathanæ fovet,
units.tr: LVII. vi. Because it fosters the depths of Satan,

units.la: LVIII. dum & notitiam profunditatum Sathanæ sibi solam arrogat,
units.tr: LVIII. while it claims for itself alone the knowledge of the depths of Satan,

units.la: LIX. & profunditates quasdam Sathanæ pro Dei profunditatibus venditat, quòd Theologia eorum scholastica inprimis comprobat.
units.tr: LIX. and puts forward certain depths of Satan as if they were the depths of God, which their scholastic theology chiefly confirms.

units.la: LX. vii. Quia ope mysterii, & titulis spiritualis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ &c. fucatis, terrenum sibi Imperium acquisivit, retinetque. Olim primatus Ecclesiæ Romanæ à solius loci prærogativa & dignitate pendebat.
units.tr: LX. vii. Because by means of the mystery, and by the titles of the spiritual Catholic Church etc., painted over, it has acquired and keeps a worldly dominion for itself. Formerly the primacy of the Church of Rome depended on the prerogative and dignity of its place alone.

units.la: LXI. Ea paulatim expirante, & nova Roma, Constantinopoli ejusdem æmula, ad mysteria Romani confugerunt, & eorum fuco sibi vindicarunt potestatem supremam tum in spiritualibus,
units.tr: LXI. When this gradually waned, and the new Rome, rival of Constantinople, had recourse to the mysteries of the Romans, and by their disguise claimed for themselves the supreme power,

units.la: LXII. tum in temporalibus,
units.tr: LXII. both in spiritual matters

units.la: LXIII. Papæ Imperium, quod erga principes seculares exercet, merè terrenum est, titulis spiritualis Ecclesiæ catholicæ &c. velatum.
units.tr: LXIII. and in temporal. The dominion which the Pope exercises over secular princes is purely earthly, veiled under the titles of the spiritual Catholic Church etc.

units.la: LXIV. viii. Quia in Hierarchia papali est mysterium illud iniquitatis, quod Homini peccati S. Paulus tribuit, quòdque occultè & latenter jam Apostolorum tempore operari cæpit, usque ad revelationem ejus.
units.tr: LXIV. viii. Because in the Papal Hierarchy is that mystery of iniquity which St. Paul attributes to the Man of Sin, and which began to work secretly and covertly already in the time of the Apostles, until its revelation.

units.la: LXV. Modus, quo mysterium illud Apostolorum tempore operari cæpit, & deinceps operari perrexit, ex serie historiæ narratus.
units.tr: LXV. The manner in which that mystery began to work in the time of the Apostles, and went on working afterwards, is related from the sequence of history.

units.la: LXVI. Argumenti ii. Conclusio.
units.tr: LXVI. Second argument. Conclusion.

units.la: I. Babylonis Magnæ characterem Secundum cujusdem, ceu Meretricis Magnæ, titulus, seu nomen, quod in fronte scriptum habet, suppeditat. Habet autem in fronte sua scriptum nomen Μυστήριον Mysterium. Apoc. xvii. 5. Quo sensu ei titulus hic tribuatur, Differt. iij. 4. 5. 6. investigavimus. Paucis ut dicta & probata repetam, Babylon Magna, Thais illa famosissima non alia re magis, quàm mysterio se ostentare, mysteria religionis sacratissima jactare, prætextu mysterii pietatis oculos plurimorum fascinare, intimam & arcanissimam voluntatem Dei in scrinio pectoris sui abscanditam crepare, omne jus & fas à pectorali suo, perinde atque ab ipso Deo & Spiritu ejus promittere, atque ita mysterii & religionis propriæ prætextu dominium in omnes affectare debuit.
units.tr: I. The second character of the Great Babylon is supplied by the title or name of a certain woman, the Great Harlot, which she has written on her forehead. She has written on her forehead the name Mystery [Μυστήριον]. Apoc. xvii. 5. In what sense this title is given to her we have investigated in Dissertation iii. 4, 5, 6. To repeat briefly what has been said and proved: the Great Babylon, that most notorious Thais, has made a display of nothing so much as of mystery, and has boasted of the mysteries of the most sacred religion; under the pretext of the mystery of piety she has bewitched the eyes of very many; she has rattled the innermost and most hidden will of God, shut away in the casket of her breast; she has promised all law and right from her breast, just as if from God himself and his Spirit; and so under the pretext of mystery and of her own religion she has had to aim at dominion over all.

units.la: II. Mysterium arcanum quodvis, ad sacra pertinens, quod inter μύστης & μυστηρίων cognitum, apud alios siletur, notare, superius Differt. iij. 6. dicere occupavimus. Atque illud in universum duplex S. literæ memorant, unum Σωτηρίας pietatis 1 Tim. iii. 16. alterum ἀνομίας improbitatis 2 Thess. ii. 7. Illud Ecclesiæ, hoc Homini peccati, filio perditionis, ἀντικείμενο adversario Christi, & ἀνόμῳ exlegi tribuitur. Vera proin Ecclesia sine mysterio nulla est: neque etiam mysterio Ecclesia falsa Adversarii Christi, adeóque Antichristi destituitur. Differentiam utriusque nôsse, hoc verò opus, hic labor est.
units.tr: II. I have already taken pains to say, in Dissertation iii. 6, that a mystery is any hidden thing pertaining to sacred matters, known between the initiate [μύστης] and the mysteries [μυστηρίων] and kept silent before others. Holy Scripture speaks of this in general as twofold: one of piety [σωτηρίας], 1 Tim. iii. 16, the other of impiety [ἀνομίας], 2 Thess. ii. 7. The first is attributed to the Church, the second to the Man of Sin, the son of perdition, the adversary [ἀντικειμένου] of Christ and the lawless one [ἀνόμου]. Therefore the true Church is never without a mystery, nor is the false Church of the Adversary, and so of Antichrist, destitute of one. To know the difference between the two is the purpose and labour of this work.

units.la: III. Ecclesia vera loquitur σοφίαν ἐν μυστηρίῳ sapientiam in mysterio, abscanditam illam, quam prædefinivit Deus ab æterno ad gloriam nostram; quam nemo Principum hujus seculi novit, quámque nobis revelavit Deus per Spiritum suum. 1 Cor. ii. 7-10. Præco igitur est Ecclesia Sapientiæ in mysterio, adeóque mysterii, non cujuslibet,
units.tr: III. The true Church speaks wisdom in a mystery [σοφίαν ἐν μυστηρίῳ], the hidden wisdom which God predestined from eternity for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew, and which God has revealed to us through his Spirit (1 Cor. ii. 7-10). The Church is therefore the herald of the wisdom in a mystery, and so of the mystery of godliness, not of just any mystery.

units.la: Pietatis mysterium est, quod ab Spiritu S. in verbo scripto revelatum ad doctrinam. bet, non latentis adhuc & absconditi, sed revelati, non à quovis utique, certè non ab homine, & naturali ejusdem ratione, sed à Spiritu S. Cúmque omnis Spiritús S. revelatio in verbo scripto extet, neque αὐθέντια γραφῆς seu revelatio Divinæ voluntatis per Scripturam sit ἰδίας ἑπιλύσεως propria interpretationis, adeóque à libitu, proprióque motu & sapientia hominis cujusvis interpretationem ex suo ingenio cudentis, non ex penetralibus Scripturæ demonstratis, neutiquam pendeat; manifestum est, Ecclesiam Dei non alia mysteria custodire & prædicare, quàm ea quæ in verbo scripto Prophetarum & Apostolorum revelata reperiuntur, quarúmque genuinus sensus ex eodem verbo ad omnem conscientiam demonstratur. Proin etiam כוד ירוד arcanum, mysterium Domini non cuilibet, sed לאין timentibus ipsum (Psalm. xxv. 14.) non ulli hominum placito, sed soli Deo addictis, revelatur. Et quale sit mysterium pietatis illud ὁμολογουμένως μέγα confessione omnium magnum, idem S. Paulus 1 Tim. iii. 16. his verbis definit: Deus manifestatus est in carne, justificatus in Spiritu, visus Angelis, prædicatus gentibus, creditus in mundo, assumtus in gloriam. Quicquid igitur à Spiritu S. in Verbo scripto revelatum, ad doctrinam Euangelii de Christo incarnato, mortuo pro electis, resuscitato ex morte, prædicato per Apostolos, exaltato ad dextram Dei, aurigatur, mysterium pietatis est, Ecclesiæ Dei eximium.
units.tr: The mystery of godliness is that which the Holy Spirit has revealed in the written Word for teaching. It ought not to be something still hidden and concealed, but something revealed, and revealed not by just anyone, certainly not by man and his natural reason, but by the Holy Spirit. Since every revelation of the Holy Spirit stands in the written Word, and since the authority of Scripture [αὐθέντια γραφῆς], that is, the revelation of the divine will through Scripture, is not a matter of private interpretation [ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως] and does not depend in the least on the whim, the private impulse, or the wisdom of any man who fashions an interpretation from his own intellect rather than from the inner meaning of Scripture, it is plain that the Church of God keeps and proclaims no mysteries other than those revealed in the written Word of the Prophets and Apostles, whose genuine sense is shown from that same Word to every conscience. Accordingly, the secret of the Lord [sōd yhwh] is revealed not to anyone at random, but to those who fear him (Ps. xxv. 14), that is, not to any man's pleasure but only to those devoted to God alone. And the Apostle Paul, in 1 Tim. iii. 16, defines what sort of mystery of godliness it is, which is great by the confession of all [ὁμολογουμένως μέγα], in these words: "God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory." Whatever is revealed by the Holy Spirit in the written Word, and leads to the doctrine of the gospel concerning Christ incarnate, dead for the elect, raised from the dead, preached by the Apostles, and exalted to the right hand of God, is the mystery of godliness, the outstanding treasure of the Church of God.

units.la: IV. Mysterium contra impietatis & improbitatis, Antichristo & Babyloni proprium est ficta voluntas Dei, non in verbo scripto revelata, sed ex scrinio pectoris, cerebroque proprio, sine demonstratione ex indubitabili quadam revelatione Dei prolata, & pro voluntate Dei ac Spiritûs S. non sine inhabitantis & assistentis ejusdem jactantia, venditata, quæque ad alia omnia, quàm ad Euangelium de Christo incarnato, mortuo pro electis, suscitato, per Apostolos praedicato, ad dexteram Dei exaltato, aurigatur. Quomodo etiam apud Gentiles μυστήριον notabat arcanos ipsorum cultus idololatricos, πλάσις ἡ ἀπάτη, qui utplurimum impuri & abominandi licet, Deo tamen revelanti accepti ab iisdem referebantur. Quin & ipsum mysterium pietatis, vel verbis duntaxat ostentatum, at re ipsa abnegatum, vel obtentui sumptum malo consilio, & carnali studio, mysterium improbitatis aliena vi evadere potest.
units.tr: IV. By contrast, the mystery of impiety and wickedness belongs to Antichrist and to Babylon: a fictitious will of God, not revealed in the written Word, but brought forth from the coffer of the breast and from one's own brain, without demonstration from any undoubted revelation of God, and paraded as the will of God and of the Holy Spirit, not without boasting of an indwelling and assisting spirit. Such a mystery is drawn toward everything other than the gospel of Christ incarnate, dead for the elect, raised, preached by the Apostles, and exalted to the right hand of God. In the same way, among the Gentiles, the word "mystery" [μυστήριον] marked their secret idolatrous cults, which were fabrications and deceptions [πλάσις ἡ ἀπάτη]; though for the most part impure and abominable, they were nevertheless referred by their devotees to a god who had revealed them. Indeed, even the mystery of godliness itself, displayed only in words but denied in fact, or assumed as a cover with an evil purpose and carnal zeal, can pass as the mystery of wickedness through an alien power.

units.la: V. Sicut mysterium pietatis est Deus in carne manifestatus, & author salutis credentibus in eum: ita mysterium impietatis est caro personata, Spiritum Dei mentita, & fuco mysteriorum <bl>ξυνφισμένων</bl> sibi parens & struens imperium terrenum in populos & terrarum Dominos. Utrobique sunt <bl>βάθη</bl> profunditates & abstrusa quaedam; ibi Dei, habitantis inaccessam lucem; hic Sathanæ, ex tenebrarum abysso hominibus Spiritu Dei vacuis ad eorundem pernicem ciem miserè illudentis.
units.tr: V. Just as the mystery of godliness is God manifested in the flesh, and the author of salvation to those who believe in him, so the mystery of impiety is a flesh that wears a mask, that falsely claims the Spirit of God, and that, by the veil of counterfeit mysteries [ξυνφισμένων], builds for itself an earthly dominion over peoples and lords of the earth. In both there are depths [βάθη] and certain hidden things: in the one, the depths of God, who dwells in unapproachable light; in the other, the depths of Satan, from the abyss of darkness, which cruelly mocks men who lack the Spirit of God, to their ruin and destruction.

units.la: VI. Ac posterius quidem, impietatis scilicet, mysterium sicut Babyloni Magnæ ceu titulus & nomen in fronte scriptum, à Spiritu Dei tribuitur: ita Ecclesiæ Romanæ Hierarchiæ dominanti competere, sequenti Syllogismo ζυαϑεμιχῶ categoricè probamus.
units.tr: VI. Now, that the mystery of impiety, as the title and name written on the forehead of Great Babylon, is attributed by the Spirit of God to the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church, we prove categorically by the following syllogism:

units.la: Quicunque cœtus Religiosus in Principis sui corona inscriptum quondam gestavit titulum μυστήριον Mysterium: atque insuper reapse mysterium, sed impietatis illud, prodit, dum se solum, unicum mysterii omnis promum condum facit, præter illa quæ scripta, solàque vera sunt, alia mysteria ἀγγαφα, eáque indemonstrabilia jactat; septem Sacramenta, totidémque mysteria justificationis & salutis omnis causam commendat; Christum in in Missa, ceu peculiari mysterio, corporaliter simul atque secretò & invisibiliter præsentem facit; dogmata sua occultat, & cultum externum præcipuum secretè peragit; profunditates Sathanæ fovet, ope mysterii & titulis Spiritualis, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ fucatis terrenum imperium acquisivit, & exercet; denique mysterium iniquitatis latenter in Ecclesia operans consummatum suscepit; ei titulus Babylonis Magnæ μυστήριον Mysterium, jure competit, adeóque is, cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Whatever religious body has once borne on the crown of its prince the inscribed title Mystery [μυστήριον], and indeed actually is a mystery, but of impiety, while it makes itself alone, the sole storehouse of every mystery, and, besides those things which are written and alone true, boasts of other unwritten [ἄγραφα] and indemonstrable mysteries; while it commends seven sacraments, as many mysteries, as the cause of all justification and salvation; while in the Mass it makes Christ present, as a peculiar mystery, bodily and at once secretly and invisibly; while it hides its doctrines and secretly carries out its chief external worship; while it fosters the depths of Satan, and by means of mystery and spiritual titles, falsely assumed for the Catholic Church, has acquired and exercises an earthly dominion; and finally, while it has taken up the mystery of iniquity, working secretly in the Church, to its completion, then the title of Great Babylon Mystery [μυστήριον] rightly belongs to it, and therefore, other things being equal, it is Great Babylon.

units.la: Atqui cœtus Religiosus Hierarchiæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantis talis est.
units.tr: But the religious body of the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church is such.

units.la: Ergo cœtui Religioso Hierarchiæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantis titulus Babylonis Magnæ, μυστήριον Mysterium, competit, adeóque is, cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the title of Great Babylon, Mystery [μυστήριον], belongs to the religious body of the dominant hierarchy of the Roman Church, and therefore, other things being equal, it is Great Babylon.

units.la: Propositionis Majoris ἀντιλεγόμενα certa & necessaria est, tum quia non sine Numine & omine titulus μυστήριον Mysterium in coronam Papæ irrepsit: tum quia nullus cœtus indubitabilibus documentis probare potuit, poterítque, ad mysterium pietatis pertinere, si humanus cœtus, vel homo ullus se solum unicúmque mysterii omnis promum condum faciat, atque cætera illa, quæ propositio expressit, designet: tum quia ea, quæ afferimus, mysterii documenta, approbata licèt ab adversariis, at probata nunquam, vel ob solum Babylonis titulum illum suspicione maxima laborant: tum quia mysterium Babylonis alibi ostendi nequit: tum denique, quia illa ipsa ad mysterium impietatis pertinere, clarissimè constat. Solus enim Deus veri mysterii promus condus ita est, ut fides hominum in solo ejus dicto terminetur & acquiescat: mysteria non scripta, indemonstrabilia nulla sunt, quia Scriptura sola hominem perfectum reddit, & non scripta plane ἀδήλα sunt, nullíque conconscientiæ se manifestant: Sacramenta, seu mysteria symbolica septem non sunt, quia duo dùntaxat Christus instituit, nedum causa justificationis sunt, quia Dei gratia nec in iis continetur, nec ab iis efficitur, cùm gratiæ præsentis signa atque sigilla, adeóque ea posteriora sint: Christus in Missa, quæ sacrificii ejus unici clades est, simul corporaliter, & secretò ac invisibiliter sub speciebus hostiæ præsens esse non potest, cùm ejus verum corpus organicum in Cœlo ad dextram Dei sedens, simul sub speciebus panis sine organis secretò existere non possit, atque à fide talis præsentiæ Christus Matth. xxiv. 26. dehortetur: Profunditates Sathanæ, Dei profunditates non sunt: Regnum Ecclesiæ merè spirituale est, & Deus fucum omnem abominatur. Denique Mysterium ἀπορρήτου pietatis mysterium esse nequit. Superest igitur, ut Minorem ἀπαμίρ demonstremus.
units.tr: The major premise is certain and necessary, and its contested points can be answered: first, because the title Mystery [μυστήριον] did not creep into the Pope's crown without the will and sign of God; second, because no religious body has been able to prove, or ever will be able to prove, by undoubted evidence that it belongs to the mystery of godliness, if a human body, or any man, makes himself the sole storehouse of every mystery and designates those other things which the proposition set out; third, because the evidences of mystery which we allege, although approved by our adversaries, have never been proven and labour under the greatest suspicion for this reason alone, that they bear the title of Babylon; fourth, because the mystery of Babylon cannot be shown elsewhere; and finally, because it is quite clear that these very things pertain to the mystery of impiety. For God alone is the true storehouse of mystery, so that men's faith rests and terminates in his word alone. Unwritten and indemonstrable mysteries do not exist, because Scripture alone makes the man of God complete, and unwritten things are plainly unknown [ἄδηλα] and reveal themselves to no conscience. The sacraments, or the seven symbolic mysteries, do not exist, because Christ instituted only two, and they are not even the cause of justification, because the grace of God is neither contained in them nor effected by them, since they are signs and seals of grace already present, and therefore come afterwards. Christ cannot be present in the Mass, which is a daily reenactment of his one sacrifice, at once bodily, secretly and invisibly under the appearances of the victim, since his true organic body, sitting in heaven at the right hand of God, cannot at the same time exist secretly under the appearance of bread without organs; and Christ, in Matt. xxiv. 26, warns against believing in such a presence. The depths of Satan are not the depths of God. The kingdom of the Church is purely spiritual, and God abominates every pretence. Finally, a mystery of the unspeakable [ἀπορρήτου] cannot be the mystery of godliness. It remains, therefore, that we demonstrate the minor premise.

units.la: VII. Non de nihilo quidem est, quod de corona triplici Pontificis R. quæ Regni nomine venit, quámque simplicem adhuc, uti nonnulli referunt, olim Anastasius Dicoros Imperator Orientis Clodovæo Regi Franciæ, hic verò, Sigeberto Semblacensi teste, Romam S. Petro, non capiti Pontificis imponendam, sed in sacrario ejusdem reponendam, misit, authores idonei referunt; inscriptum esse nomen Μυστήριον Mysterium. Ita Brocardus Pontificius ipse in Apoc. xvii.5. testatur. Addit Josephus Scaliger in Notis ad Nov. Test. Memorantium Romæ agentem ab authore fide digno accepisse, verè id vocabuli tiaræ Pontificis insculptum fuisse; sed Julium eam reconcinnari curasse, suumque nomen subst ituisse hoc pacto: Julius Pontifex Maximus, quod de Julio III. intelligendum, cujus tempore Brocardus vixit, & Tridenti etiam sub initium Concilii commoratus est. Cúmque id ipsum etiam Jacobus Magnæ Britanniæ Rex Pontificiis in Expositione Apocalypseos objecisset, Lessius negare non potuit, sed imbelli
units.tr: VII. It is not without reason that reliable authors report that on the triple crown of the Roman Pontiff, which is called the crown of the kingdom, and which, as some relate, was at first a plain circlet, the Emperor Anastasius Dicorus sent to King Clovis of France; and that Sigebert of Gembloux, as witness, reports that it was sent to Rome to be placed not on the head of the Pontiff but stored in his sacristy, and that the name Mystery [Μυστήριον] was inscribed on it. So Brocardus, himself a Papist, testifies on Apoc. xvii. 5. Joseph Scaliger, in his Notes on the New Testament, adds that when he was in Rome he had heard from a trustworthy author that the word had truly been engraved on the Pope's tiara; but that Julius had it refashioned and substituted his own name in this way: "Julius Pontifex Maximus," which must be understood of Julius III, in whose time Brocardus lived and who also stayed at Trent near the beginning of the Council. When James, King of Great Britain, had thrown this very charge at the Papists in his Exposition of the Apocalypse, Lessius could not deny it, but, with a feeble defence, he retorted that it was in vain to seek mystery within mystery. That was surely not in vain, since in this matter a conspicuous memorial of Great Babylon appears.

units.la: {y} corona Pontificis R. olim inscriptum fuit μυστήριον. imbelli defensione defunctus, regessit, frustra in mysterio mysterium requiri. Non frustra certè, cùm ea in re conspicuum μνημόσωον memoriale Babylonis Magnæ appareat.
units.tr: Once the Pope's crown bore the inscription μυστήριον [mystery]. Lessius, having defended the point feebly, retorted: in vain is mystery sought in mystery. Not in vain, surely, since in this matter the conspicuous memorial [μνημόσυνον] of Babylon the Great appears.

units.la: VIII. Res verò ipsa memoriali hoc repræsentata non minùs certè evidens est. Etenim Ecclesiæ Romanæ Hierarchia dominans Primò se solam veri mysterii promam condam facit, dum fidem saltem acceptatam, in suam tesftificationem ultimò resolvi, & Euangelium à se sola authenticè proponi, & non aliter, quàm per propositionem ejusmodi verum, Divinum, salutare cognosci posse, ejusdemque sensum à sua definitione etiam non demonstrata pendere, pertendit. Secundò, præter illa, quæ scripta sunt alia mysteria seu secreta ἀρχαῖα, quæ Apostoli Episcopis in aurem dixerint, at nec prædicaverint vulgò, nec scripserint, obtrudit. Tertiò septem Sacramenta, totidemque mysteria tanquam summam religionis, & causam justificationis, commendat. Quartò Christum in Missa, ceu peculiari mysterio, corporaliter simul atque secretò & invisibiliter adesse & sacrificari Deo asserit. Quintò dogmata sua sacrorum mysteriorum instar, occultat, & sacra sua lingua peregrina etiam clam demurmurando peragit. Sextò βαθὺς ἔχαρια profunditates Satanæ fovet. Septimò ope mysterii, & titulis Spiritualis, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ &c. fucatis, terrenum Imperium & potentiam acquisivit, retinetque. Octavò denique in ea est mysterium iniquitatis illud, quod Homini peccati S. Paulus 2 Thess. 11. tribuit, quòd occultè & latenter Apostolorum tempore operabatur, usque ad revelationem ejusdem.
units.tr: VIII. The thing itself, represented by this memorial, is no less evident. For the dominant Hierarchy of the Roman Church: first, makes itself the sole dispenser of the true mystery, maintaining that faith, even when accepted, is ultimately resolved into its own attestation, that the Gospel can be authentically proposed by it alone, and that it can be known as true, divine and saving only through such a proposal, and that its sense depends on its own definition, which is not demonstrated. Secondly, it foists upon us, besides the things that have been written, other mysteries or secrets [ἀρχαῖα] which the Apostles whispered into the ears of the bishops but neither preached publicly nor wrote down. Thirdly, it commends seven sacraments, and as many mysteries, as the sum of religion and the cause of justification. Fourthly, it asserts that Christ is present in the Mass, as in a peculiar mystery, bodily and at once secretly and invisibly, and is sacrificed to God. Fifthly, it hides its doctrines as if they were sacred mysteries, and performs its rites in a foreign tongue, even muttering them under its breath. Sixthly, it fosters the depths of Satan [βαθέα]. Seventhly, by means of the mystery, and with the titles of Spiritual, Catholic Church and so on, dressed up, it has acquired and keeps earthly empire and power. Eighthly and finally, in it is that mystery of iniquity which St. Paul ascribes to the man of sin, 2 Thess. 11., because it worked secretly and covertly in the time of the Apostles until its revelation.

units.la: IX. Et primò quidem Hierarchiam Papalem se unam solamque mysterii omnis promam condam facere διαξαγωγὴν est. In cordis enim Papæ scrinio omne jus Divinum conditum clausumque esse, neque aliunde id depromi posse, non gnathonum duntaxat, & parasitorum Papæ afsentatione jactatur, sed communi Pontificiorum veri nominis sententia recipitur. Eò enim plané spectat, assertio eorum de regula & analysi fidei, quam omnem, acceptatam saltem, ἐχάτως ultimò in testificationem authenticam Ecclesiæ (non utique colleƈtivæ, sed repræsentativæ, quæ denique in solo Pontifice, ceu Numine quodam terminatur) resolvi pertendunt. Quo utique pacto Hierarchia Papalis, seu verius, solus Papa cordis sui scrinium, mysteriis aliunde non acceptis, non demonstratis (nulla enim extra Scripturam alia revelatio, ex qua mysterium demonstrari possit, occurrit) sed à solo Spiritu suo proprio, eòque ἀδήλῳ & obscuro scaturientibus, refertum est.
units.tr: IX. And first, indeed, to make the Papal Hierarchy alone the sole dispenser of every mystery [διαξαγωγήν] is so. For it is boasted, not merely by the flatterers and parasites who fawn on the Pope, but is received by the common opinion of Papists in the true sense of the word, that all divine right is stored and locked in the Pope's heart, and cannot be drawn from elsewhere. For their assertion about the rule and analysis of faith clearly aims at this: they maintain that all faith, even when accepted, is ultimately [ἐσχάτως] resolved into the authentic attestation of the Church (not indeed of the church collectively, but representatively, which finally terminates in the Pope alone, as in some divinity). In this way the Papal Hierarchy, or rather the Pope alone, is full of mysteries that are not received from elsewhere, not demonstrated (for no other revelation outside Scripture appears from which a mystery could be demonstrated), but welling up solely from his own spirit, and that spirit hidden [ἀδήλῳ] and obscure.

units.la: X. Lubet receptam Hierarchiæ Papalis de analysi fidei sententiam Gregorii de Valentia, qui, edito prolixo de analysi fidei tractatu, plurimùm hac in re desudavit, veris rei totius summam complexis, quæ in Commentariorum Thomæ Tomo iij. Disp. j. quæst. j. punƈt. j. extant, exponere.
units.tr: X. It pleases us to set out the view of the Papal Hierarchy on the analysis of faith as held by Gregory of Valencia, who, having published a lengthy treatise on the analysis of faith, laboured much in this matter, and summed up the whole truth of the matter in what stands in Commentariorum Thomae, Tomo iii., Disp. i., quaest. i., punct. i.

units.la: Si quis, inquit, rogetur, verbi gratia, quare credat, Deum esse unum & trinum? distinguat utrum sermo sit de causa ipsius fidei secundùm se, cur videlicet firmiter & infallibiliter id credat, vel de causa ob quam acceptaverit eam fidem. Si primum, respondeat, quia Deus revelavit. Si rursùm interrogetur, unde cognoscat Deum revelâsse? Respondeat, se quidem non nôsse id clarè, credere tamen eadem fide infallibiliter, & id quidem non ob aliam revelationem, benè tamen ob infallibilem propositionem Ecclesiæ, tanquam ob conditionem ad id credendum requisitam. Si rursus, unde cognoscat propositionem Ecclesiæ esse infallibilem, similiter dicet, se clarè non nôsse, credere tamen fide infallibili ob revelationem Scripturæ testimonium perhibentis Ecclesiæ, tùm revelationi creditnon ob aliam revelationem, sed ob se ipsam, quamvis ad hoc ipsum opus sit Ecclesiæ propositione, ut conditione requisita. Si autem quis rogetur, cum & revelatio Scripturæ, & propositio infallibilis Ecclesiæ sint obscuræ & incidentes, quid ipsum impulerit, ut hunc quasi Labyrinthum rerum obscurissimarum ingressus, ad fidem modo dicto acceptandam, hoc est, credendam revelationem, propter Ecclesiæ propositionem, & hanc propter revelationem: seu, cur animum induxerit, velle credere, cum alioquin ipsa ratione, seu fundamento habitus fidei secundum se non impelleretur, tum respondeat afferendo rationes atque motiva clariora, quibus & ipse inductus fuit, & quibus prudens induci possit ad acceptandam ejusmodi fidem, cujusmodi sunt, antiquitas, perennitas, efficacia & harmonia doctrinæ, consensus insignium virorum & populorum, & cetera argumenta, quæ supra recensuimus.
units.tr: If someone, he says, is asked, for example, why he believes that God is one and three? Let him distinguish whether the question concerns the cause of faith itself, considered in itself, namely why he believes it firmly and infallibly, or the cause for which he has accepted that faith. If the first, let him answer: because God has revealed it. If he is asked again, how he knows that God has revealed it? Let him answer that he indeed does not know this clearly, but believes it with the same infallible faith, and that not on account of another revelation, but on account of the infallible proposal of the Church, as a condition required for believing. If again he is asked how he knows that the proposal of the Church is infallible, he will similarly say that he does not clearly know it, but believes with infallible faith, on account of the revelation of Scripture bearing witness to the Church; and he believes the revelation, not on account of another revelation, but on account of itself, although for this very work the proposal of the Church is needed as a required condition.
