But if someone is asked, since both the revelation of Scripture and the infallible proposal of the Church are obscure and falling upon him, what has moved him to enter, as it were, this labyrinth of most obscure things, to accept the faith in the manner just described, that is, to believe the revelation on account of the proposal of the Church, and this on account of the revelation; or why he has resolved to wish to believe, when otherwise the reason or foundation of the habit of faith in itself would not move him; then let him answer by setting forth the clearer reasons and motives by which he himself was led, and by which a prudent person may be led to accept such a faith, such as antiquity, perpetuity, the efficacy and harmony of doctrine, the consent of distinguished men and peoples, and the other arguments which we have listed above.

units.la: XI. Cautè admodum licet hic processerit Valentia, ex ejus tamen verbis liquet, ultimò fidem in Papatu in arbitrium & dictum Ecclesiæ, seu Papæ resolvi. Etenim primò causa cur aliquis credat, & cur fidem acceptet eodem recidit. Nemo enim credere potest, nisi fidem, seu id quod credendum est acceptet, quomodo Joh. 1:12. λαμβάνειν τὸν λόγον, accipere, acceptare sermonem Christum, idem est quod credere. Quicquid enim creditur, cognitum assentiendo & fidendo recipitur. Et eadem utriusque ratio est, Divina scilicet revelatio, propter quam & credimus, & verbum propositum acceptamus. Si igitur acceptatæ fidei, seu verbi credendi causa est propositio Ecclesiæ, propositio igitur Ecclesiæ, seu potius Papæ, & revelatio erit, & principium seu causa credendi, adeóque in eam fidem ultimò, ceu suum principium resolvetur. Secundò, qui Deum credit esse triunum, ob Ecclesiæ proponentis authoritatem, is utique id credit ob aliam revelationem, & quidem ultimam, scilicet Papæ. Annon enim est multiplicata revelatio ejusdem verbi seu veritatis, nimirum revelatio ad Prophetas & Apostolos (non ad nos, nam si ad nos, quid ultra opus est?) & revelatio ad Ecclesiam seu Papam præsentem, & propositio Ecclesiæ ejusdem, dicentis, hanc esse revelationem? Tertiò, si revelatio quælibet Dei ἀνή-πςω non est, sed propositionem infallibilem & authenticam Papæ requirit, propositio igitur illa revelatione Divina prior notiorque, adeóque principium fidei erit. Illud enim principium cognoscendi est, ex quo immediatè & primò res cognoscitur. Quartò vel revelatio quælibet Dei, vel propositio Ecclesiæ authentica ἀνήπςω digna quæ per se ipsam cognoscatur, & mūms ὑποδοχῆς ἀξιω digna qualibet receptione. Si prius, authentica Ecclesiæ propositio supervacanea est. Nam quod ἀνήπςον, per se fide dignum est, non est fide dignum propter aliud, nec ad fidem aliud, quàm cognitionem seu apprehensionem sui, requirit. Si posterius, Ecclesiæ propositio, ceu Divina quædam revelatio principium fidei erit, atque in eandem fides resolvetur. Quintò Ecclesia proponit revelationem vel simpliciter eam asserendo, vel certis notis & argumentis demonstrando. Si posterius, Ecclesiæ propositio per se non est authentica & infallibilis, sed duntaxat, quatenus revelationem argumentis & necessariis & insitis demonstrando eidem ministrat, quod adversarii pertinaciter abnuunt. Si prius in Ecclesiæ assertionem & dictum simplex ἀδοχίμαςον ἡ ἀξιωπίςου universam fidem ultimò resolvi necessum est.
units.tr: XI. However cautiously Valencia has proceeded here, it is nevertheless clear from his words that in the end faith in Papacy is resolved into the judgment and dictum of the Church, or of the Pope. For first, the cause why someone believes and why he accepts the faith come to the same thing. For no one can believe unless he accepts the faith, or that which is to be believed; just as in John 1:12 to receive [λαμβάνειν] the word, to accept Christ's word, is the same as to believe. For whatever is believed is received by knowing, assenting and trusting. And the reason for both is the same, namely divine revelation, on account of which we both believe and accept the proposed word. If therefore the proposal of the Church is the cause of accepted faith, or of the word to be believed, then the proposal of the Church, or rather of the Pope, will be both the revelation and the principle or cause of believing, and so faith will be ultimately resolved into it as its principle. Secondly, whoever believes God to be triune on account of the authority of the proposing Church, certainly believes it on account of another revelation, and indeed the last one, namely the Pope's. For is not the revelation of the same word or truth multiplied: revelation to the Prophets and Apostles (not to us, for if to us, what more is needed?), and revelation to the present Church or Pope, and the proposal of the same Church saying that this is revelation? Thirdly, if any revelation of God is not self-evident [ἀνέπαφον], but requires the infallible and authentic proposal of the Pope, then that proposal is prior and better known than the divine revelation, and so will be the principle of faith. For that is the principle of knowing from which a thing is known immediately and first. Fourthly, either any revelation of God, or the authentic proposal of the Church, is self-evident [ἀνέπαφον], worthy to be known through itself, and rather worthy of any reception [μᾶλλον ὑποδοχῆς ἀξιον]. If the former, the authentic proposal of the Church is superfluous. For what is in itself self-evident and worthy of belief does not require to be believed on account of anything else, nor for faith anything but the knowledge or apprehension of itself. If the latter, the proposal of the Church, as some divine revelation, will be the principle of faith, and faith will be resolved into it. Fifthly, the Church proposes a revelation either by simply asserting it, or by demonstrating it with certain marks and arguments. If the latter, the proposal of the Church is not in itself authentic and infallible, but only insofar as it supplies the revelation to us by demonstrating it with necessary and innate arguments, which our adversaries obstinately deny. If the former, then in the simple assertion and dictum of the Church, unapproved or unworthy of belief [ἀδόκιμον ἢ ἀξιόπιστον], the whole faith must necessarily be ultimately resolved.

units.la: XII. Atque idem etiam Methodistarum novissimorum, Walenburgiorum inprimis, de Analysi, placita comprobant. In hanc enim ferè sententiam conspirant, quod Ecclesia dicit, id esse verbum Dei; proin credentem Ecclesiæ, credere Dei verbum, atque adeò credere ipsi Deo, quia Deus nihil revelet, nisi per os Ecclesiæ, hoc est Papæ, & quicquid per illum proponitur, Divinam revelationem esse. Hoc autem, Papam esse ultimum, & necessarium, Dei voluntate, medium notificationis, & unicè sufficiens ad fundandam fidem, colligi ex notis Ecclesiæ, quas inter professioni Scripturæ ut regulæ, & observationi eorum, quæ in illa traduntur, partes nullas relinquunt. Quis proin non videt, in his nullam relinqui authoritatem Scripturæ, ut statim & sine alia authoritate ipsi, tanquam verbo Dei credere teneamur vel possimus; adeóque omnia resolvi in dictum Papæ, & assensum eorum, qui Papam sequuntur, iisque infallibilitatem in omnibus attribui? Et ad fucum tegendum, proponi ex ingenio humano, quasi silente Scriptura aut sepòsita, nota Ecclesiæ; quæ eadem opera accipiantur, ut notæ, imò certissima argumenta infallibilitatis Papæ? Denique Papam planè jam exui illo obtentu ac larva, quasi scilicet, uti etiam Valentia prætexuerat, propter Scripturam ipsi credendum esset, & supra verbum Dei ita collocari, ut mysteria universa ex ipsius sinu, non aliunde, certè non à Deo, utpote à quo dictum & sententiam suam pendere nec demonstrat, neque demonstrare suarum partium putat; arcessi debeant?
units.tr: XII. The Methodists of recent times, especially the Walenburgians, also approve the same opinions on the analysis. For they conspire in roughly this sense: that what the Church says is the Word of God; therefore, by believing the Church, we believe the Word of God, and so believe God himself, because God reveals nothing except through the mouth of the Church, that is, of the Pope; and whatever is proposed through him is a divine revelation. Moreover, that the Pope is the last and necessary means of notification, by God's will, and alone sufficient for founding faith, is gathered from the marks of the Church, among which they leave no part to the profession of Scripture as a rule, nor to the observance of those things which are delivered in it. Who therefore does not see that in these views no authority is left to Scripture, so that we are bound or able to believe it immediately and without other authority, as the Word of God; and so that everything is resolved into the dictum of the Pope and the assent of those who follow the Pope, to whom infallibility is attributed in all things? And to cover the deception, it is put forward from human ingenuity, as though Scripture were silent or set aside, that the marks of the Church, which at the same time are taken as marks, indeed most certain arguments, of the Pope's infallibility? Finally, is the Pope not now quite stripped of that pretext and mask, as though, as Valencia also pretended, he were to be believed for the sake of Scripture, and is it not so placed above the Word of God that all mysteries must be drawn from his bosom, and certainly not from elsewhere, not from God, since he neither demonstrates that his dictum and opinion depend on God, nor thinks it his part to demonstrate this?

units.la: XIII. Amplius etiam illud impietatis mysterium inde liquet, quòd etiam fidem Divinitatis Scripturæ, & librorum Scripturæ Canonicorum, & sensus genuini eorundem à propositione infallibili & authentica, sententiáque definitiva Ecclesiæ seu Papæ non demonstrantis, adeóque Divinitati cognoscendæ ministrantis, sed nudè, & velut ex plenitudine quadam potestatis pronuntiantis, definientis, & ad credendum obligantis, & quidem non cujuslibet Ecclesiæ seu Papæ, sed præsentis duntaxat, nulla habita ratione Ecclesiæ præcedentis, adeóque etiam Apostolicæ (uti Bellarminus de sacr. libr. ꝟ. 25. definit) suspendunt, adeóque eminentissimam authoritatem Scripturæ, suo φιλήματι & arbitrio nefariè subjiciunt, atque sic Scripturam in sceptrum dominationis Papæ impiè converterunt.
units.tr: XIII. Furthermore, that mystery of impiety is also clear from this: they make faith in the divinity of Scripture, in the canonical books of Scripture, and in their genuine sense depend on the infallible and authoritative proposal and definitive sentence of the Church or the Pope. That proposal does not demonstrate the truth and so minister to knowing Scripture's divinity. It speaks bare, as if from a certain fullness of power, defining and binding to belief. It is not the sentence of any Church or Pope, but only of the present one, with no regard to the preceding Church, and so not even to the Apostolic Church (as Bellarmine defines in de sacr. libr. chap. 25). Thus they suspend the most eminent authority of Scripture and wickedly subject it to their own kiss [φιλήματι] and will, and so impiously turn Scripture into the sceptre of papal dominion.

units.la: XIV. Tametsi verò ad tegendam impietatem identidem illi clamant, non negare se authoritatem Scripturæ in se, sed tantùm quærere, quomodo authoritatem obtineat quoad nos, apud nos, hoc est, πῶς πεπίστευκα ἀπ' αὐτῆς, quomodo fides nobis fiat, quòd sit divinitùs inspirata (2 Tim. iii. 14. 15.) non amoliuntur tamen à se ilthoc nefas. Cùm enim de authoritate Scripturæ quæritur, non tam quæritur an à Deo sit, quàm unde nobis constet, à Deo esse? Qui non aliunde nobis ita constare, quàm quia Papa ita dicit, & ad credendum sine ulteriori demonstratione obligat, pertendunt, ii S. Scripturam redigunt in ordinem eorum, quæ loquuntur homines, de quibus merito dubitari potest, utrum Deus iis locutus sit, nec ne? Quo in censu sunt verba illorum Prophetarum, de quibus Deus dicit, exspectandum esse, dum eveniant illorum verba Deut. xviii. 22. Quæ gravis injuria est Scripturæ illata, quasi nulla in iis Divinitas radiaret, & conscientiæ hominum, sine Papæ testimonio, insinuaret. Unde non verentur Scripturam à Pontifice non propositam cum Livio, Alcorano, fabulis Æsopi contendere quam blasphemiam apud Bellarminum de Verbo Dei Lib. iv. 4. nec non Bailium in Catech. aliósque reperire est.
units.tr: XIV. Although, to cover their impiety, they repeatedly cry out that they do not deny the authority of Scripture in itself, but only ask how it has authority for us, among us, that is, "how I have believed from it" [πῶς πεπίστευκα ἀπ' αὐτῆς], how faith comes to us that it is divinely inspired (2 Tim. 3:14, 15), they nonetheless do not put that outrage away from themselves. For when the question concerns the authority of Scripture, it is not so much asked whether it comes from God as how it is known to us that it does. Those who maintain that we know this from nothing else than the fact that the Pope says so and binds us to believe without further demonstration reduce Holy Scripture to the rank of human utterances, about which it may rightly be doubted whether God spoke through them or not. In this class are the words of those prophets of whom God says that one must wait until their words come to pass (Deut. 18:22). A grave injury is done to Scripture, as if no divinity shone forth in it and it did not insinuate itself into people's consciences without the testimony of the Pope. Hence they do not hesitate to set Scripture, when not proposed by the Pontiff, alongside Livy, the Koran and Aesop's fables. This blasphemy may be found in Bellarmine, de Verbo Dei book 4, chap. 4, and in Bailius in Catech., and in others.

units.la: XV. Accedit, quòd nobis jactatum infallibile illud testimonium Papæ pensi non habentibus, Spiritum privatum, quo scilicet duce Scripturæ Divinitas, libri Canonici, & sensus Scripturæ à nobis citra Papæ propositionem & determinationem ullam recipiantur, objectare non verentur illi, qui tamen in privatum Spiritum Papæ, ceu ultimum principium, universam fidem, ipsámque adeò de Scri-
units.tr: XV. In addition, those who have no regard for the infallible testimony of the Pope, of which they boast, do not hesitate to object to us the "private spirit." By this spirit, they say, we receive the divinity of Scripture, the canonical books and the sense of Scripture without any proposal or determination of the Pope. Yet they themselves resolve the whole of faith, and faith concerning Scrip-

units.la: Adeóque privato Spiritui Papæ impedient. Scripturæ Divinitate, libris Canonicis, sensu germano Scripturæ fidem resolvunt. Sicut enim Spiritus hominis, qui Scripturæ Divinitatem credit, ob lucem in ea radiantem, & conscientiæ suæ irradiantem, adeóque etiam notas ac proprietates ejusdem Deum authorem propalantes, Spiritu Dei, qui unus idémque omnibus fidelibus datur, sibi attestante, & animo suo eundem comprobante, non errat, nec privato Spiritu, sed eo, qui unam candémque legem fidei cordibus omnium credentium inscribit, adeóque Spiritus Patris, Filii, & eorundem donatione fidelium omnium, qui θεὸς ἐκ πνεύματος ἐν Deus & Spiritus unus est (Gal. iii. 20. 28. 1 Joh. iii. 27.) ducitur: Ita Spiritus Papæ, sive in cathedra, sive extra cam loquentis, qui juxta certam regulam fidei, quæ omnibus tradita est, se Spiritum lucis omni conscientiæ probare non potest, & sibi soli credi ob solum dictum, sine tabulis & ratione ac demonstratione ulla verbi, quod proponit, postulat, haud dubie Spiritus nec Sanctus, nec communis omnium fidelium, sed proprius, privatus, enthusiasticus est, & non aliis quàm impietatis Babylonicæ mysteriis turget.
units.tr: ture, into the private spirit of the Pope, as the ultimate principle. And so they resolve faith in the divinity of Scripture, in the canonical books and in the genuine sense of Scripture into the private spirit of the Pope. For just as the spirit of a man who believes in the divinity of Scripture, because of the light shining in it and illuminating his conscience, and so also because of its marks and properties declaring God to be its author, does not err, since the Spirit of God, who is one and the same and is given to all the faithful, bears witness to him and confirms it in his mind, and he is led not by a private spirit but by the Spirit who writes one and the same law of faith in the hearts of all believers (and so by the Spirit of the Father and of the Son and by the gift of these to all the faithful, "God and Spirit are one" [θεὸς ἐκ πνεύματος ἐν], Gal. 3:20, 28; 1 John 3:27): so the spirit of the Pope, whether he speaks from the chair or outside it, cannot prove to every conscience that he is the Spirit of light according to a certain rule of faith delivered to all. He demands instead that he alone be believed on his bare word, without tablets, reason or any demonstration of the word he proposes. Undoubtedly that spirit is neither holy nor the common spirit of all the faithful, but proper, private and enthusiastic, and it swells with nothing other than the mysteries of Babylonian impiety.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Hinc adeò est, quod Doctores Pontificii fidei suæ principium non aliud quàm Ecclesiæ seu Papæ, mysteriorum unici promi condi, oraculum, & αὐτὸς ἐφα palam, & assa, quod ajunt, voce profitentur. Veterum & recentiorum νυνὶ ἐς δόξας nonnullas ut proferamus, jam olim Andradius lib. j. defensi Trid. dixit: Fidei Papæ nostra continetur, & ex ejus authoritate falsis omnium pendet. Cosferus Enchir. cap. j. audaciter: Christus Ecclesiam suam à chartaceis scriptis pendere, nec membranis mysteria sua committere voluit, sed ipsius est sublimiori charactere, scribens digito in corde Ecclesiæ. Gretserus Defens. j. cap. j. De verbo Dei: Non recipimus pro verbo Dei, nisi quod definivit Papa in Cathedra Petri. Turrecremata de Eccles. lib. v. 203. sic satis crudè: Papa est membrum scientiæ, & regula credendorum. Augustinus de Ancona quæst. 59. art. j. Novum Symbolum condere ad solum Papam spectat, quia est caput fidei Christianæ, cujus authoritate omnia, quæ ad fidem spectant, firmantur, & roborantur. Sicut potest novum Symbolum condere, ita potest novos articulos supra alios multiplicare. Hostiensis super 2. decret. de Jure-jur. Jus Canonicum est jus Divinum, & quicquid juris promulgat Papa, Deus, cujus Vicarius est, promulgare intelligitur. Ferdinandus de Iricisis, apud Petrum Ciezam Tom. v. Institit. Parv. In manu Papæ sunt animæ hominum, & in ejus arbitrio religio consistit. Eóque impudentiæ Bellarminus de Pontif. Libr. iv. 5. delabitur, ut dicat: Si Papa errare posset præcipiendo vitia, & prohibendo errores, teneretur Ecclesia credere, vitia esse bona, & virtutes esse malas, nisi vellet contra conscientiam peccare. Ejusdem Glossa Decretalium Greg. X. tit. 7, est: Papam de nullo posse aliquid facere, & sententiam, quæ nulla est, facere aliquam. Hæc quippe quia in his, quæ vult, est pro ratione voluntas; nec est, quod ei dicatur, cur ita facis? Ipse enim potest supra jus dispensare, item de justitia potest facere injustitiam. Omitto Bozium, Baronium, Becanum, Valerianum M. Walenburgios, alios, omni virium contentione adnitentes, ut Ecclesiam, seu Papam, ceu unicum unicè sufficiens ad fidem principium (ita diserte Walenburgii loquuntur) credulitati simplicium obtrudant.
units.tr: Hence it is that the Papist teachers openly and plainly profess that the principle of their faith is nothing other than the Church or the Pope, the sole oracle for the coining of mysteries, and that he himself said it [αὐτὸς ἔφα], as they put it, both spoken and written. To bring forward some opinions of older and more recent writers: long ago Andradius, in the first book of his Defence of the Council of Trent, said: "Our faith is contained in the faith of the Pope, and the faith of all depends on his authority." Coster, Enchiridion chap. 1, boldly says: "Christ willed that his Church should depend not on written paper, nor entrust his mysteries to parchment, but they are written with a more sublime character, writing with his finger in the heart of the Church." Gretser, Defence I, chap. 1, On the Word of God: "We do not accept as the Word of God anything except what the Pope has defined in the Chair of Peter." Turrecremata, de Eccles. book 5, 203, quite crudely: "The Pope is a member of knowledge and the rule of things to be believed." Augustine of Ancona, question 59, article 1: "To frame a new creed belongs to the Pope alone, because he is the head of the Christian faith, by whose authority all things that pertain to faith are established and strengthened. Just as he can frame a new creed, so he can multiply new articles above the others." Hostiensis, on the second book of Decretals, On Oaths: "Canon law is divine law, and whatever law the Pope promulgates, God, whose Vicar he is, is understood to promulgate." Ferdinand de Iricisis, quoted by Pedro Ciezza, Tom. v. Institit. Parv.: "The souls of men are in the hand of the Pope, and religion consists in his will." And Bellarmine, de Pontif. book 4, chap. 5, sinks into such shamelessness as to say: "If the Pope could err in commanding vices and forbidding errors, the Church would be bound to believe that vices are good and virtues evil, unless it wished to sin against conscience." Of the same author, the Gloss on the Decretals of Gregory X, title 7, reads: "That the Pope can make something out of nothing, and make a sentence which is no sentence. For since in those things he wills, his will is the reason, nor is it to be said to him, why do you do so? For he can dispense above the law, and can make injustice out of justice." I omit Bozius, Baronius, Becanus, Valerian, M. Walenburg and others, who strive with all their might to thrust upon the credulity of simple people the Church, or the Pope, as the one and wholly sufficient principle of faith (so Walenburg expressly speaks).

units.la: XVII. Et quænam alia ratio Pontificios ad tot convicordia Scripturæ facienda, ad tot enormes blasphemias transfersos abripuit? Veluti cùm γυμνῆ κεφαλῇ & consignatis verbis eam blasphemant, ceu imperfectam, obscuram, non necessariam, plebi lectu periculosam, hæresium matrem & se& semen, literam mortuam, voce Pontificis animandam & vivificandam, indigam supplementi Oraculum traditionum, quarum nulla tamen certitudo est, nasum cereum, edificationis Lesbiæ regulam plumbeam, ad causarum auditionem surdam, ad examen stupidam, ad proprie dictam sententiæ dictionem mutam, vicariam Dei judicis perineptam (ita diserte Serarius Proleg. 10. quæst. 2.) per se, sine voce Papæ, fide nulla dignam; commonitorium veritus quam regulam, corruptam, plebi, ne seducatur interdicendam, imo cremandam potius, quam eidem committeudam, & si quæ similia hinc inde apud Scriptores illorum occurrunt, à quibus merito piæ & castæ aures abhorrent. Ex quibus liquidò cognosci potest impia & horrenda æmulatio Papæ, qua ille adversus Scripturam pridem nefariè exarsit, non aliam certè ob causam, quàm ut ea de ponte præcipitata ipse solus ceu alter Apollo Pythius, vel Jupiter sive Dodonæus, sive Hammonius (quid enim hos inter & illum discriminis sit, cùm utrique ex cerebro suo, & fictæ Divinitatis penetrali quopiam mysteria proferant, parum constat) pro libitu, sine convictione ulla conscientiæ ex Scriptura, oracula fundere, & mysteria ex divite penu scrinii sui, Deo scilicet pleni, promere, denique ceu superbus Dictator, fidei dominari, & omnes Pythagorico dicto suo inaudientes, ad orcum relegare possit.
units.tr: XVII. And what other reason has driven the Papists, turned to so many contradictions of Scripture, into such enormous blasphemies? For example, when with bare head [γυμνῆ κεφαλῇ] and with settled words they blaspheme it as imperfect, obscure, unnecessary, dangerous for the common people to read, the mother and seed of heresies, a dead letter to be animated and quickened by the voice of the Pope, in need of supplement, an oracle of traditions of which there is nonetheless no certainty, a waxen nose, a leaden rule of Lesbian building, deaf to hearing causes, stupid in examination, mute in the proper pronouncing of sentence, a foolish vicar of God the judge (so expressly Serarius, Prolegomena 10, question 2), worthy of no faith by itself without the voice of the Pope; a memorandum-book whose rule is corrupt, to be forbidden to the common people lest they be seduced, or rather to be burned than entrusted to them; and whatever similar things turn up here and there among their writers, from which pious and chaste ears rightly shrink. From these things it can clearly be recognised what impious and horrible rivalry the Pope has long nefariously burned with against Scripture, and for no other cause than this: that, having cast Scripture down from the bridge, he alone, like another Pythian Apollo or Jupiter, whether of Dodona or of Ammon (for what difference there is between these and him is hardly clear, since all of them pour forth mysteries from their own brain and from some inner shrine of fictitious divinity), may pour forth oracles at will from Scripture without any conviction of conscience, draw mysteries from the rich store of his own chest, as it were full of God, and finally, like a proud dictator, lord it over faith and banish to the underworld all who do not heed his Pythagorean saying.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Atque hanc præcipuam ob rationem sicut Babylonis Magnæ, ita Hierarchiæ Papalis fronti infamem illum titulum Mysterii impietatis scilicet, Spiritus S. inusșit, ut à prudente & circumspecto quovis, nullo negotio, cujusmodi illa sit, dijudicari possit. Sunt & aliæ rationes, ob quas titulum huncce Babylonis Hierarchiæ eidem competere asserimus.
units.tr: For this principal reason, the Holy Spirit has stamped on the forehead of the Hierarchy of Papacy, as on that of Great Babylon, the infamous title of mystery, namely of impiety, so that any prudent and watchful person can easily judge what sort of mystery it is. There are also other reasons why we assert that this title belongs to the Hierarchy of Babylon.

units.la: XIX. Secundò igitur ea quoque in re Hierarchia Papalis mysterium iniquitatis prodit, quòd praeter illa, quae scripta sunt, alia mysteria seu secreta ἀγγαφα, quae Apostoli Episcopis in aurem dixerint, at nec praedicaverint vulgò, nec scripserint, obtrudit. Atque ea in re tum Ecclesiae Catholicae, tum mysteriorum multorum, quae silentium requirant, dignitatem consistere, sic Bellarminus de verbo Dei non scripto Lib. iv. 8. probat: Accedat Ecclesiae Catholicae dignitas. Nam ut olim Judaei excellebant omnibus rationibus, quia credita illis eloquia Dei erant, ita praestat Ecclesia Christi omnibus fidelibus, quod ipsa sola, quippe qua sponsa Christi est, noverit omnia mysteria, verae religionis, & conscia sit secretorum sponsi, & propterea vocatur columna & firmamentum veritatis. At si omnia essent scripta & apertissimè, ut haeretici docent, nullum esset privilegium Ecclesiae. Nam nihil minus scirent haeretici, & pagani & Judaei de mysteriis fidei nostrae, quàm nos ipsi & antistites nostri sciunt: neque esset verum, quod ait Irenaeus Lib. iv. 3. In solam Ecclesiam, tanquam in depositorium dives, repositam ab Apostolis scientiam rerum Divinarum. Accedat postremò dignitas mysteriorum multorum, quae silentium requirunt, nec decet ut in Scripturis, quae toti mundo leguntur, explicentur. Si enim ad videnda tremenda Missae mysteria non licet admittere ullos non baptizatos, quomodo licebit eisdem scripta tradere? Hinc Dominus seorsim Discipulis interpretabatur parabolas, quas populo locutus erat Luc. 8. Et Apostolus ait 1 Cor. 2. Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Et passim veteres, cùm de Sacramento Eucharistiae loquuntur, dicere solent: Norunt fideles, norunt initiati. Ante Bellarminum id ipsum Martinus Peresius Ayala de Trad. par. ij. assert. 2. p. 15. testimoniis Dionysii Areopagitae, & Basilii fretus afferere conatus est.
units.tr: XIX. Second, therefore, in this matter too the Papal Hierarchy reveals the mystery of iniquity, in that it imposes, besides those things which are written, other mysteries or secrets [ἄγραφα], which the Apostles are said to have whispered in the ears of the bishops, but which they neither preached publicly nor wrote down. In this matter, that the dignity both of the Catholic Church and of many mysteries which require silence consists, Bellarmine proves thus in his book on unwritten Word of God, Book iv, chapter 8: Let the dignity of the Catholic Church be added. For just as the Jews once excelled in every respect because the oracles of God were entrusted to them, so the Church of Christ offers to all the faithful this advantage: that she alone, being the bride of Christ, knows all the mysteries of the true religion, and is privy to the secrets of the bridegroom; and therefore she is called the pillar and ground of the truth. But if everything were written and most openly, as the heretics teach, the Church would have no privilege. For heretics, pagans and Jews would know the mysteries of our faith no less than we ourselves and our prelates know them; nor would what Irenaeus says be true, Book iv, chapter 3: The knowledge of divine things, deposited by the Apostles, is stored in the Church alone, as in a rich storehouse. Lastly, let the dignity of many mysteries which require silence be added; it is not fitting that they be explained in the Scriptures, which are read by the whole world. For if it is not permitted to admit any unbaptized persons to see the awesome mysteries of the Mass, how will it be permitted to hand them down in writing? Hence the Lord explained the parables privately to his disciples, though he had spoken them to the people, Luke 8. And the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 2: We speak wisdom among the perfect. And the ancients, when they speak of the sacrament of the Eucharist, commonly say: The faithful know, the initiated know. Before Bellarmine, Martinus Peresius Ayala, On Tradition, part 2, assertion 2, p. 15, relying on the testimonies of Dionysius the Areopagite and Basil, attempted to assert the same thing.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Quàm verò inepta, absurda, & malè cohærentia hæc effata sunt? Etenim si mysteria quædam ob dignitatem sive suam, sive Ecclesiæ non scribi, sed sileri debuerunt, etiam viva voce prædicari non possunt. Silentium enim non magis vivæ voci, quàm scripto, imo magis illi, quàm huic repugnat; cùm proprie & per se vivæ voci, scripto autem per accidens, quatenus vivæ vocis signum est, opponatur. Cur igitur traditiones suas mysticas viva voce prædicant? Imò verò cur traditiones suas etiam libris, cujusmodi sunt, Ordo Romanus, Missalia, Breviaria, Rationalia, & infinita hujusmodi, commendant? An in iis minùs, vel magis authenticè, quàm in Scriptura S. legi possunt? Ubi vide immanem & stupendam hominum ἀνεξίσεια. Nolunt enim mysteria omnia commendari libris sacris: & eadem tamen patiuntur commendata libris non sacris. Tum autem à Librorum sacrorum lectione plebem severissimè arcent: non sacros autem suos liberalissimè permittunt. Neque enim in Regulis Indicis librorum prohibitorum cavetur de Missalibus, aut Breviariis, aut Ritualibus, ut de Bibliis. Imò si sibi Traditionarii constarent, prohibendum iis potiùs fuerat, ne usquam mysteria hæc sua, nisi in libris sacris scriberentur, utpote quos à plebe legi ob interdictum pridem desitum est. Et cur tandem Christus, quæ in aurem discipulis dixit, eosdem Ἀπὸ τῶν δωμάτων ἐπὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τὸν τέττον, adeóque publicè prædicare jussit? Matth. x. 27. Si quædam silenda, & paucis selectis revelanda iisdem injunxit?
units.tr: But how foolish, absurd, and ill-connected these assertions are! For if certain mysteries ought not to be written down but kept silent, because of their own dignity or that of the Church, then they cannot be preached even by the living voice. For silence is opposed to the living voice no less than to writing, indeed more to the former than to the latter; since silence is properly and in itself opposed to the living voice, but to writing only accidentally, insofar as writing is a sign of the living voice. Why, then, do they proclaim their mystical traditions by the living voice? Indeed, why do they also commend their traditions in books, such as the Ordo Romanus, Missals, Breviaries, Rationales, and countless works of this kind? Or can these be read with less or more authority than Holy Scripture? Here see the huge and astonishing inconsistency [ἀνεξίσεια] of men. For they do not want all mysteries to be commended in holy books, and yet they tolerate those same mysteries being commended in books that are not holy. Then they keep the common people most strictly from reading the holy books, yet they most liberally permit their own non-sacred books. Indeed, the Rules of the Index of Prohibited Books do not warn about Missals, Breviaries, or Rituals as they do about the Bibles. Indeed, if the Traditionists were consistent with themselves, they should rather have been forbidden to put these mysteries of theirs anywhere except in holy books, since those books have long since ceased to be forbidden to the common people. And why, finally, did Christ command those whom he had whispered to in the ear to preach publicly from the housetops [ἀπὸ τῶν δωμάτων], Matt. 10:27, if he had enjoined on them that certain things should be kept silent and revealed only to a few select people?

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Imò nullum omnino in religione Christiana mysterium pietatis est, quod silentium requirat, & non sit publicè potiùs prædicandum tum Christianis, tum gentilibus, ut Christiani fiant: Propterea enim Christus jussit doceri omnes gentes, & proponi publicè, etiam in tectis ædium ea, quæ in aurem dixerat. Matth. x. 27. xxviii. 19.
units.tr: Indeed, there is no mystery of godliness in the Christian religion at all that requires silence and should not rather be preached publicly, both to Christians and to pagans, so that they may become Christians. For this reason Christ commanded that all nations be taught, and that those things which he had told in the ear be proclaimed publicly, even upon the housetops, Matt. 10:27; 28:19.

units.la: Y Propterea S. Paulus Rom. 1. 14. 15. se ὀφειλέτης debitorem profitetur Græcis & barbaris, sapientibus & insipientibus, additque, promtum se iccirco etiam esse Euangelium prædicare iis, qui Romæ sunt. Propterea etiam non tantum Parabolæ, sed etiam earundem interpretationes seorsim discipulis factæ, scripto consignatæ sunt. Adeò mysteria Spiritus S. publicari voluit.
units.tr: Y For this reason St. Paul, Rom. 1:14–15, declares himself a debtor [ὀφειλέτης] to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, and adds that he is therefore ready to preach the Gospel also to those who are at Rome. For this reason, not only the parables but also their explanations, given privately to the disciples, were committed to writing. So much did the Holy Spirit wish the mysteries to be made public.

units.la: XXII. Neque certè S. Paulus 1 Cor. 11. 6. 7. ubi sapientiam in mysterio se loqui inter perfectos scribit, vel per σοφίαν ἐν μυστηρίῳ sapientiam in mysterio, secretam sapientiam quampiam, omnibus non communicandam, aut certè nunquam scribendam; vel per τελείους perfectos, Episcopos duntaxat, Euangelistas, aut ejusmodi ordinem ullum in Ecclesia, intellexit; vel suum illud λαλῶ loqui, scriptioni oppositum.
units.tr: XXII. Nor certainly did St. Paul, 1 Cor. 2:6–7, where he writes that he speaks wisdom among the perfect, mean by "wisdom in a mystery [σοφίαν ἐν μυστηρίῳ]" some secret wisdom not to be shared with everyone, or at least never to be written down; nor by "the perfect [τελείους]" did he mean the bishops only, the evangelists, or any such order in the Church; nor by his word "I speak [λαλῶ]" did he mean speaking as opposed to writing.

units.la: Fœda hæc verborum Spiritus S. σοφίας sapientia quippe, seu Sapientiam appellavit totam Euangelii doctrinam, quantacunque illa est, oppositam Sapientiæ mundi, quam scilicet Deus ab æterno præfinivit in gloriam nostram, nemo principum sæculi hujus cognovit, & solus Spiritus S. revelavit. v. 6. 7. 8. 10. &c. quæ notæ generales sunt non cujusdam duntaxat, sed totius sapientiæ cœlestis. τελείους quoque seu perfectos, non peculiariter hierophantas quosdam, sed fideles quosvis, infidelibus & sapientibus hujus mundi oppositos, provectiores & firmiores inprimis insignivit; τελείους (ita S. Chrysostomus in h.l.) τὰς πεπαιδευμένους· Καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνοι τελείοι οἱ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδότες, ὅτι ζῶσα ἀδικεῖ, ἢ ἐξαιρέσεως τῶν αὐτῶν, ὅτι μηδὲν αὐτῶν ζημιώσει· perfectos vocavit eos, qui crediderunt. Illi enim perfecti sunt, qui videntes humana valde esse infirma, contemnentésque ea persuaserunt sibi, nihil inde ad se utilitatis redire, cujusmodi sunt fideles. Atque inde etiam nullo negotio conficitur, non recte opponi loqui & scribere; quia eandem doctrinam cùm alii, tum Paulus non tantum prædicavit, sed etiam scripsit, nec eam locutus est in angulis, interve pauços, sed publicè & apud quosvis.
units.tr: By this foul misuse of words, the Holy Spirit called the whole doctrine of the Gospel "wisdom", however great it is, opposed to the wisdom of the world, which "none of the rulers of this age knew, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, and which the Spirit alone revealed", vv. 6, 7, 8, 10, etc. These are general marks not of some particular wisdom but of all heavenly wisdom. He also marked the "perfect [τελείους]", not as some peculiar hierophants, but as any faithful persons, opposed to the unbelieving and wise of this world, and chiefly the more advanced and steadfast; Chrysostom, on this passage, says that the "perfect" are those who have been instructed [τὰς πεπαιδευμένους], for those are perfect who know human things to be very weak, who despise them and are persuaded that nothing useful comes back to them from them, and such are the faithful. And from this it follows at once without difficulty that it is wrong to set speaking against writing, since the same doctrine was not only preached but also written by Paul and others, and he did not speak it in corners or among a few, but publicly and before anyone.

units.la: XXIII. Quod verò de Mysteriis Missæ, ad quæ spectanda non liceat admittere non baptizatos, Bellarmi- nus tricatur, nil Mystagogos juvat.
units.tr: XXIII. As for what Bellarmine maintains about the mysteries of the Mass, that the unbaptized may not be admitted to witness them, this does nothing to help the mystagogues.

units.la: Præstaret certè ad ea, ceu vera impietatis mysteria, admitti omninò neminem. Præterea aliud sunt mysteria, seu Mysteriorum doctrina, aliud eorundem celebratio. Mysterium Eucharistiæ verum, seu Mysterii Eucharistici doctrina (nam Missaticum missum facimus) essentialis adeò certè tacenda, præmendanon est, ut publicè potius prædicari & scribi debuerit, quomodo sine piaculo utique Euangelistæ & Apostoli publicè prædicárunt, scripseruntque. Quòd si essentialia mysterii Eucharistiæ publicari possunt, cur accidentalia, adeóque minutiuscula abscondenda putabimus? Perinde enim id foret, ac si quis hominem quidem nudum ostentari posse, at vestitum à spectantium oculis subduci debere, pertenderet. Quòd verò mysterii ejusdem celebrationem attinet, à communione quidem omnino arcendi sunt ἀμύητοι, sive gentiles sive catechumeni. Cæterùm aspectus ejus corporeus indifferens est, neque in alterutram partem de eo morose contendendum statuimus; licet aliter olim quibusdam visum esse, quo jure, quave injuria, nihil hic dicere attinet, satis constet.
units.tr: It would certainly be best for no one at all to be admitted to these, as if they were the true mysteries of impiety. Moreover, the mysteries themselves are one thing, the doctrine of the mysteries another, and their celebration another. The true mystery of the Eucharist, or the doctrine of the Eucharistic mystery (for we set aside the Mass), is so far from needing to be hidden or kept back that it ought rather to be preached and written publicly, as the Evangelists and Apostles certainly preached and wrote it publicly without sin. But if the essentials of the Eucharistic mystery can be made public, why should we think its accidentals, and so its minor details, must be hidden? That would be like someone arguing that a man may be shown naked but must be kept from the spectators' eyes once he is clothed. As for the celebration of the same mystery, the uninitiated [ἀμύητοι], whether pagans or catechumens, must indeed be kept entirely from communion. Its bodily aspect, however, is indifferent, and we decide not to contend stubbornly about it on either side. That it once seemed otherwise to some, and by what right or wrong, need not be discussed here; that much is well established.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Sed verò, ita Melchior Canus, aliíque argutantur, si Apostoli quælibet religionis secreta tradidissent, contra legem Christi sanctum canibus dedissent, & inter porcos margaritas sparsissent. Quid ergo, inquam ego, fecerunt iidem, cùm præcipua religionis Christianæ mysteria, & inprimis sublimia & tremenda, veluti capita illa de Trinitate, incarnatione, passione Christi vicaria; denique illa ὁμολογεμένως μεγάλα μυστήρια confessione omnium magna mysteria, quæ S. Paulus 1 Tim. iii. 16. paucis complexus est, scripto publicarunt? An sic legis Christi prævaricatores sanctum canibus, porcis margaritas objecerunt? An maxima & sublimissima omnium mysteria fine piaculo publicare; at ea, quæ Papistæ in deliciis unicè habent, quadragesimam dico, purgatorium, imagines, aquam lustralem, quæque ipsi tamen scripto tradere, & præ cæteris commendare, prædicare nulli dubitant, fine piaculo publicare non potuerunt? Quod verum certè nos agnoscimus, quia mysteria pietatis vulgare fas piúmque, at mysteria impietatis tradere nefas iidem duxerunt meritò.
units.tr: But Melchior Canus and others argue that if the Apostles had handed down every secret of religion, they would have given what is holy to the dogs against the law of Christ and cast pearls before swine. What then, I ask, did the same Apostles do when they published in writing the chief and especially sublime and awe-inspiring mysteries of the Christian religion, such as the doctrines of the Trinity, the incarnation, and Christ's vicarious passion; and finally those mysteries which St Paul sums up briefly, by universal confession, great is the mystery of godliness [ὁμολογουμένως μέγα ἐστὶ τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον] (1 Tim. 3:16)? Did they, then, transgress the law of Christ by giving what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine? Or is it the case that the greatest and most sublime of all mysteries may be published without sin, while those which the Papists hold above all others, I mean Lent, purgatory, images, and holy water, which they unhesitatingly commit to writing and commend and preach above the rest, could not be made public without sin? We certainly acknowledge the truth of the former, since the mysteries of godliness may rightly be made common, whereas the mysteries of impiety, those men have rightly judged it wrong to hand down.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Frustra hic Babylonii Mystæ ambiguis quibuldam veterum dictis innituntur, five detorquentes ea in alienum sensum, five muscarum in morem ulceribus aliorum fe fe oblectantes. Dionysium Pfeudo-Areopagitam, & Basilium, duo scilicet Ecclesiæ Orientalis lumina, ceu consentientes sibi Perefius Ayala, aliiquelaudant. Dionysii κυρίως ὀξεως, quas ille Hier. Eccles. cap. j. habet, præstare non tenemur, quia non Areopagita ille verus fuit, sed hujus larva indutus, ferò admodum Ecclesiæ imposuit. Prædicat ille quædam γραφῆς ἐκτὸς μυηθίντα, quædam quæ fine scripto discuntur. Nam, exponente Maximo Scholiaste, idem ei est μύησις, quod μαθήσεις, καταχήσεις, φησίμη. Ubi neutiquam ille dogmata scripta cum non scriptis, sed traditionem, quæ fit viva voce, cum ea quæ fit scripto, adeóque μύησιν cum μυήσει comparat, subtiliùs certè quàm veriùs. Nam illam, quæ fit viva voce, quámque propalari, nisi inter sanctos, vetat, αὐλωπρων, magis à materia abstractam, quàm quæ scripto fit, vocat; ineptiffimè fanè, & fi dogmata cum dogmatis comparavit, salsissimè. An enim Trinitatis dogma minùs αὐλωπρον à materia abftractum est, quia non viva duntaxat voce, sed scripto etiam, codicum scilicet materiæ (propter quam ὑλικὰ materiæ concreta ea, quæ scripta sunt ineptè ineptus ille insignit) puta membranæ, papyro, chartæ traditum est? Facessat longè insana ratiocinatio!
units.tr: In vain do these Babylonian mystagogues rest on certain ambiguous sayings of the ancients, either twisting them to a foreign sense or, like flies, delighting in the sores of others. They praise Dionysius the Pseudo-Areopagite and Basil, the two lights of the Eastern Church, as if they agreed with them, and so do Pereira, Ayala and others. We are not bound to vouch for Dionysius's "strictly speaking" (κυρίως) statements, which he makes in Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chap. 1, since he was not the true Areopagite but, wearing that man's mask, imposed on the Church very late. He speaks of certain things initiated outside Scripture [γραφῆς ἐκτὸς μυηθέντα], and certain things which are learned without writing. For, as the scholiast Maximus explains, for him initiation [μύησις] is the same as instruction [μάθησις], catechesis [κατήχησις] and manifestation [φανέρωσις]. Here he by no means compares written doctrines with unwritten ones; rather he sets the tradition that comes by living voice against that which comes in writing, and so compares initiation with initiation, a comparison that is more subtle than it is true. For the tradition that comes by living voice, which he forbids to be divulged except among the holy, he calls more immaterial [ἀΰλοτέρα] than what is set down in writing; this is very foolish indeed, and, since he compared doctrine with doctrine, extremely silly. For is the dogma of the Trinity less immaterial, because it has been handed down not only by living voice but also in writing, that is, in the material of books (on account of which that foolish fellow calls the things written material [ὑλικά]), namely on parchment, papyrus or paper? Let such insane reasoning be far away!

units.la: XXVI. Majori specie illa Basilii de Spiritu S. cap. 27.
units.tr: XXVI. Basil's passage On the Holy Spirit, chap. 27, has a greater show of support.

units.la: Mystagogi crepant. Sic autem ille. οἱ περὶ τὰς ἐκκλησίας ἐξαρχὰς Αλφισμοῦητίνητος ἀπίσολει καὶ παῤῥησίας, ἐν τῷ κεκρυμμένῳ ἀφθογκτῷ τὸ σημεῖον τῆς μυστηρίου ἐφύλαξαν· ἀδὴ γὰρ ἅλως μυστήριον, τὸ εἰς τῷ δημώδη καὶ ἀκαίαν ἀκοὴν ἐκφέρειν· ἀτ ὁ λόγος τῆς τῶν ἀγεαφῶν παραδόσεως, ὡς μὴ καταμελετη-θῆναι τῶν δογμάτων τῷ γνῶσιν, ἀκαταφρονῆσαι τῆς πολλῆς ψυχῆς Αλὰ Ζωὴν θεῶν· Αλλο γὰρ δόγμα, ἡ ἄλλο κήρυγμα· τὰ μὲν γὰρ δόγματα σιωπῶνται, τὰ δὲ κηρύγματα δημοσιεύεται. Qui in primordiis Ecclesiæ certos ritus præscripserunt Apostoli & Patres, in occulto silentióque mysteriis suam servárunt dignitatem. Neque enim omnino mysterium est, quod ad populares & vulgares aures effertur. Hæc est ratio, cur quædam citra scriptum tradita sunt, ne dogmatum cognitio, propter assuetudinem vulgo veniret in contemtum. Aliud est autem dogma, aliud prædicatio. Nam dogmata silentur, prædicationes verò publicantur. Nihil equidem hic dicam de γηοσικῷ libri, quam jam olim Erasmus ob styli diversitatem & ineptias, gravissimo illo Patre indignas, atque nuper etiam Robertus Cocus prægnantes ob rationes in dubium vocarunt. Hoc verò dicere satis erit, S. Basilium dogmata, quæ silenda, hoc est, non promiscuè apud infideles quovis prædicanda, vel scripto etiam divulganda censet, non mysteria, dogmata, seu articulos Christianæ religionis Catholicos appellasse. Loquitur enim de dogmatibus indefinitè omnibus, qualia quoad doctrinam fidei qui scripto tradenda negaverit, & silenda pertenderit, næ is S. Scripturam universam, una cum mysteriis fidei in ea comprehensis obelo configet. Quid ergo? Dogmata illi sunt ritus seu Ceremoniæ Ecclesiasticæ, cujusmodi ipsemet enumerat signum crucis, conversionem ad orientem, invocationis formulam in Eucharistia, benedictionem aquæ baptismatis & olei, trinam immersionem, genuflexionem, stationem, confessionis formulam. Unde statim τὰ δόγματα dogmata appellat τὰ ἀγραφα τῶν ἰδιῶν consuetudines non scriptas, ealdemque τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ, ἢ τὰ κηρύγματα Euangelio & prædicationi opponit. Eandem inter δόγματα & κηρύγματα distinctionem eodem sensu Eulogius, Archiepiscopus Alexandrinus in Bibliotheca Photii Cod. ccxxx. pag. 833. explicat. Mutuatus utrumque vocis illius sensum ex Scriptoribus sacris est, quibus δόγμα ritum, institutum Luc. II. 1. Act. XVI. 4. XVII. 7. Ephes. II. 15. Colos. II. 14. & δογματίζεσθε ritibus onerari Colos. II. 20. significat. Duriusculum vero est, quòd idem author τὰ δόγματα ἢ τὰ κηρύγματα τῆς ἀντιλιγωνίας ἐχθρὰ ἀφ' ἥλιου ἐπὶ τὸ ἀπολλύειν dogmata & prædicationes idem ad pietatem robur habere asserit. quod ἀπαξ ἐξαλλαγῶς dictum ei condonamus, & disputationis fervori imputamus.
units.tr: The mystagogues make a great noise. Basil says: Those who in the early days of the Church, Apostles and Fathers alike, prescribed certain rites, preserved them in silence and secrecy, keeping the dignity of the mysteries. For that is not altogether a mystery which is brought to popular and common ears. This is the reason some things were handed down without writing, lest knowledge of the dogmas should come into contempt through familiarity. One thing is a dogma, another a proclamation. For dogmas are kept silent, but proclamations are made public. I say nothing here about the genuineness of the book, which Erasmus long ago, and recently Robert Cocus as well, rightly called into question on account of the difference of style and the silliness unworthy of that grave Father. It will be enough to say this: St Basil called dogmas those things that ought to be kept silent, that is, not to be proclaimed indiscriminately to unbelievers, or even published in writing; he did not call the mysteries, dogmas, or articles of Catholic Christian religion by that name. For he is speaking of dogmas in general, and whoever would deny that such matters of the doctrine of faith are to be handed down in writing, and would urge that they be kept silent, would pierce all of Holy Scripture, together with the mysteries of faith contained in it, with a spit. What then? The dogmas he means are the rites or ceremonies of the Church, such as he himself lists: the sign of the cross, facing east, the form of invocation in the Eucharist, the blessing of the water of baptism and of the oil, the threefold immersion, kneeling, the station, and the form of confession. Hence he at once calls these dogmas unwritten customs [τὰ ἄγραφα τῶν ἐθῶν], and opposes them to the Gospel [τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ] or to the proclamation [τὰ κηρύγματα]. Eulogius, Archbishop of Alexandria, explains the same distinction between dogmas and proclamations, in the same sense, in Photius's Bibliotheca, Cod. 230, p. 833. He took both senses of the word from the sacred writers, who use dogma for rite, ordinance (Luke 2:1; Acts 16:4; 17:7; Eph. 2:15; Col. 2:14), and to be burdened with rites [δογματίζεσθε] (Col. 2:20). It is rather harsh, however, that the same author asserts that dogmas and proclamations have the same power for piety. This statement, said once in an unusual way, we pardon him, and we attribute it to the heat of the dispute.

units.la: XXVII. Mosen Veteris Testamenti verba in literis condidisse, & separatim quædam ex occultis secretiora mysteria, septuaginta senioribus, qui doctores deinceps manerent, intimâsse, Hilarius ab adversariis idcirco laudatus in Psalm. 2. dixit. Ad quæ verba Erasmus annotavit: Non credo. Et sanè teste nullo de re adeò à seculo suo remota Hilarius locutus est: nisi forte hoc sibi voluit, Mosen quosdam selectos viros familiarius in legis ceremoniarúmque intelligentia instituisse. Sed quid hoc ad traditionum non scriptarum mysteria silentio tegenda? Nam qui in cognitionem Scripturarum altius penetrant, ii non propterea nova mysteria non scripta, eáque silentio involvenda invehunt, sed ex ipsis Scripturis sensum veritatis hauriunt.
units.tr: XXVII. Hilary, who is praised by the adversaries for this reason, says in his commentary On Psalm 2 that Moses wrote the words of the Old Testament in letters, and that he communicated certain more secret mysteries, separately from the public ones, to the seventy elders, who were to remain as teachers afterwards. Erasmus noted on these words: I do not believe it. And indeed Hilary spoke on a matter so remote from his own age, with no witness at all. Unless perhaps he meant that Moses instructed certain chosen men more closely in understanding the law and its ceremonies. But what does this have to do with unwritten mysteries to be veiled in silence? Those who penetrate more deeply into the knowledge of the Scriptures do not therefore bring in new unwritten mysteries to be wrapped in silence, but draw the sense of truth from the Scriptures themselves.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: XXVIII. Par ratio est Clementis Alexandrini, quæ ex septimo ejus Institutionum libro Eusebius Hist. Eccl. ȷ. 1. citat sequentia: Ἰακώϐῳ τῷ δικαίῳ, ἡ Ἰωάνν̈ης καὶ Πέτρος μετὰ τὸν ἀναστάντα παρὰ ἐσθίωνας τὸν γνῶσιν ὁ κύριος
units.tr: XXVIII. Clement of Alexandria takes the same line. In the seventh book of his Institutions, Eusebius quotes him in Church History 1 as follows: "The Lord, after the resurrection, imparted knowledge to James the Just, to John and to Peter; they handed it on to the other apostles, and the other apostles to the seventy, of whom Barnabas was one." [Ἰακώϐῳ τῷ δικαίῳ, ἡ Ἰωάνν̈ης καὶ Πέτρος μετὰ τὸν ἀναστάντα παρὰ ἐσθίωνας τὸν γνῶσιν ὁ κύριος]

units.la: Ἀποστόλοις παρὰ ἐσθίωνας· οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ Ἀπόστολοι τῆς ἐκκλησίας, ὧν ἐκ τῶν Βαρναβᾶς. Jacobo justo, & Johanni & Petro Dominus post resurrectionem cognitionem impertiit. Quod illi cæteris Apostolis, hi verò septuaginta discipulis, quorum unus fuit Barnabas, tradiderunt. Quod enim solis his tribus γνῶσιν cognitionem immediatè à Christo indultam ille asserit, parum constat, nec idoneo teste probatur. Saltem S. Paulus ex revelatione Christi immediata Euangelium etiam recepit, nec cum carne & sanguine contulit. Esto tamen, his solis ἀμέσως impartitus fuerit γνῶσιν cognitionem, non tamen vel quædam duntaxat mysteria, vel tacenda illa, non scribenda, impartitus est, cùm γνῶσιν indefinitè nominans, omnem haud dubiè intelligat. Quòd si, uti nuper Valesius expositi, γνῶσις Clementi fuit donum scientiæ, seu singulare Charisma illud, quod S. Paulus 1 Cor. xii. 8. λόγον γνώσεως sermonem cognitionis vocat, quámque idem Clemens Strom. libr. vj. Φησὶν ἡ καλλιστέρα τῶν ἐντὸς τῇ ἐπιμελείᾳ, ἡ παρακαλοῦσα scientiam & comprehensionem præsentium, præteritorum, & futurorum definit, nihil hoc ad mysteria quædam duntaxat celanda, non scribenda, attinet. Etsi enim ejusmodi γνῶσις cognitio, seu φρόνησις prudentia & eruditio singularis non omnibus fidelibus competit, ratione tamen doctrinæ fidei extra scripturam, utpote quæ σοφίαν πρὸς σωτηρίαν Sapientem ad salutem, imò & perfectum ad omne opus bonum reddere sola potest 2 Tim. iii. 15. 16. non vagatur, neque mysteria quædam ἀδήλα silentii religiosi Supparo involvenda promit.
units.tr: That knowledge [γνῶσιν] was granted immediately by Christ to these three alone is poorly attested, and he proves it by no reliable witness. St Paul at least received the Gospel by immediate revelation from Christ, and did not confer with flesh and blood. Grant, however, that knowledge was imparted immediately to these alone. Even so, it was not imparted only certain mysteries, or mysteries to be kept silent and not written down. When Clement names "knowledge" without qualification, he undoubtedly means all of it. But if, as Valesius recently explained, Clement's gnosis was the gift of knowledge, that is, the special charisma which St Paul calls "the word of knowledge" [λόγον γνώσεως] in 1 Cor. 12:8, and which Clement himself, in Stromateis vi., describes as "the most beautiful of the inner powers by diligence, which exhorts" [Φησὶν ἡ καλλιστέρα τῶν ἐντὸς τῇ ἐπιμελείᾳ, ἡ παρακαλοῦσα], defining it as the knowledge and comprehension of things present, past and future, then this has nothing to do with certain mysteries that are only to be concealed and not written down. For although this kind of knowledge, or phronesis, prudence and special learning, is not given to all the faithful, the doctrine of faith is not thereby left to wander outside Scripture. Scripture alone can make a person "wise unto salvation" [σοφίαν πρὸς σωτηρίαν], and "perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works" (2 Tim. 3:15–16). It does not bring forward hidden mysteries [ἀδήλα] to be wrapped in religious silence.

units.la: Z
units.tr: Z ## XXIX.

units.la: XXIX. Vin ergo crypsin dogmatis de mysteriis quibusdam non scriptis, silendisque explicemus strictim? Merum in eo est mysterium impietatis, Babylonica fronte dignissimum, quod jam olim etiam Irenæus lib. iv. 15. his verbis detexit: Doctrina Apostolorum est firma & manifesta, & nihil subtrahens, neque alia quidem in abscondito, alia verò in manifesto docentium: Hoc enim fictorum, & pravè seducentium, & hypocritarum est molimen. Hoc scilicet, non aliud quicquam illi satagunt, ut prætensa traditione, seu mysteriis non scriptis, quicquid scriptum non est, & præter, imò contra scripturas, Diaboli & Antichristi fraude, successu temporis in Ecclesiam invectum est; adversus cos, à quibus falsa & impia doctrina ex verbo Dei scripto redarguit, defendere possint, útque tum oracula omnia Papæ, tum mysteria ipsa scripturæ, sensu Ecclesiæ Romanæ, seu Romani Apollinis, explicata, sine ulla veri sensus demonstratione, fide implicita recipiantur superstitione cœca, absque intelligentiæ luce; ita ut veræ interpretationis traditio ad omnes penetrare non possit, sed inter paucos mystas detineri in silentio debeat, ipsiúsque adeò scripturæ lucerna ex hypothesi eorum obscurior, sub illo silentii mysteriorum non scriptorum modio occultetur, & porro extinguatur penitus.
units.tr: Shall I then briefly set out the secret of the doctrine concerning certain unwritten mysteries that must be kept silent? The whole of it is a mystery of iniquity [mysterium impietatis], most worthy of Babylon's brow. Irenaeus already exposed it long ago, in Adv. Haer. iv. 15, in these words: "The teaching of the Apostles is firm and manifest, and it withholds nothing. Nor do the teachers teach one thing in secret and another in the open. For that is the device of fabricators, of deceivers who lead people astray, and of hypocrites." This is precisely what these men are busy with: that under the pretext of tradition, or of unwritten mysteries, whatever is not written, and indeed whatever is beyond and even against Scripture, was brought into the Church over time by the fraud of the devil and Antichrist. They want to use it to defend themselves against those who refute their false and impious doctrine from the written Word of God. Thus all the pronouncements of the Pope, and the mysteries of Scripture themselves as explained by the sense of the Church of Rome, or of the Roman Apollo, are received without any demonstration of the true sense, with implicit faith and blind superstition, and without the light of understanding. So the tradition of true interpretation cannot reach everyone. It must be kept in silence among a few initiates. Scripture's own lamp, on their hypothesis, becomes darker, and is hidden under that bushel of silent, unwritten mysteries and finally snuffed out altogether. ## XXX.

units.la: XXX. Commune isthoc impietatis mysterium Papalis Hierarchia cum Judæis veteribus recentioribúsque nec non Gentilibus infidelibus habent. Jam olim certè Judæis etiam Sathanas persuasit, præter legem scriptam etiam orali, sive ad supplendum illius defectum, sive ad interpretationem ejusdem, opus esse. Unde Christus sic Pharisæos Matth. v. 21. alloquitur: Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη τοῖς Ἀρχαίοις Audivistis, quòd dictum sit veteribus. Ubi ἀκοὴ auditus traditionum receptam, & ῥῆσις seu ῥῆμα dictio traditionem ipsam notat. Ita enim in Sanhedrim cap. ÿ. Halac. ÿ. Hebrew sí audiverunt, id est, traditione acceperunt, dicunt iis. Et apud Maimonidem sæpius Hebrew auditione, id est, traditione didicerunt. Sed & Judæi Christo exprobrare ausi sunt, quòd discipuli ejus Greek traditiones seniorum transgrediantur. Matth. xv. 2. quibus Christus v. 3. Greek objicit, quòd propter traditionem suam mandatum Dei transgrediantur ipsi, & plura etiam ejusmodi Marc. vii. 2. 5. 8. exprobrat. Recentiores similiter Judæi veterum Sapientum suorum traditiones nomine Hebrew legis oralis, quam Hebrew legi scriptæ opponunt: nec non Hebrew Kabbalæ, seu legis per traditionem Mosis acceptæ, & Hebrew Greek legis repetitæ venditant. Hanc à Deo in monte Mosi; ab hoc Josua; à Josua senioribus aliis datatim, & remotis arbitris datam scificunt. De Philosophis veteribus similia Peresius Ayala de Tradit. Eccles. par. ÿ. p. 15. laudat his verbis: Nec hoc solùm Patres primos, sed antiquissimos Philosophos, ut Mercurium Trismegistum, Pythagoram, & plures alios sapientes fuisse legimus, qui parùm vel nihil scripserunt, sed orentenus auditores suos instruebant, ne Philosophia vileesceret, & contemptibilis apud vulgus hominum fieret. Poterat idem Aristotelis disciplinas Greek ab Greek distinctas, & illas selectis duntaxat in aurem insusurratas, has publicatas in desperatæ causæ subsidium advocare. Sanè etiam tam Judæorum quàm Gentilium ea in re consensum Bellarminus laudare non erubuit, egregium inde Greek conflans, naturam ipsam quodammodo clamare videri traditiones non scriptas, vel necessarias, vel certè utilissimas esse. Quos foedi adeo consensus non puduit, eos non magis forte, quàm Vespasianum olim, ex urina vectigal accipere puderet.
units.tr: The Papal hierarchy shares this mystery of impiety with the ancient and more recent Jews, and also with unbelieving Gentiles. Long ago Satan persuaded the Jews too that, besides the written law, an oral law was needed, either to supply its lack or to interpret it. Hence Christ addresses the Pharisees in Matt. 5:21 thus: "You have heard that it was said to the ancients" [Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις]. Here "hearing" [ἀκοή] denotes tradition received, and "saying" [ῥῆσις or ῥῆμα] denotes the tradition itself. So in the Sanhedrin, chapter 'Halac', they say, "if they heard," that is, received it by tradition, "they say to them." And in Maimonides they often "learned by hearing," that is, by tradition. The Jews even dared to reproach Christ because his disciples "transgress the tradition of the elders" [τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων] (Matt. 15:2). Christ answered them in v. 3, objecting that they themselves transgress the commandment of God for the sake of their tradition [διὰ τὴν παράδοσιν ὑμῶν], and in Mark 7:2, 5, 8 he rebukes them for many more things of this kind. Likewise the more recent Jews set the traditions of their ancient sages under the name of "oral law," which they oppose to "written law," and they also peddle the "Kabbalah," that is, the law received by tradition from Moses, and the "repeated" [Greek] law. They claim that it was given by God to Moses on the mount, by Moses to Joshua, and by Joshua to other elders in turn, and then handed on to distant recipients. Peresius Ayala, in De Traditionibus Ecclesiasticis, part 5, p. 15, praises similar things about the ancient philosophers in these words: "We read that not only the first Fathers but also the most ancient philosophers, such as Mercurius Trismegistus, Pythagoras and many other wise men, wrote little or nothing, but instructed their hearers by word of mouth, lest philosophy should become cheap and contemptible among the common people." The same man could also invoke, in desperate need, Aristotle's teachings, divided by the Greeks into esoteric and exoteric, the former whispered only into the ears of select men, the latter published. Bellarmine, too, was not ashamed to praise this agreement of Jews and Gentiles, and from it he forged an excellent argument: that nature itself seems to cry out that unwritten traditions are either necessary or at least most useful. People who are not ashamed of so foul an agreement would perhaps be no more ashamed than Vespasian once was to take a tax on urine.

units.la: Z
units.tr: Z ## XXXI.

units.la: XXXI. Tertiò titulus Mysterii Babylonicæ Hierarchiæ Papali quadrat, quia septem Sacramenta, totidémque mysteria, ceu summam religionis, & causam Justificationis unicè commendat. Constat equidem quæ sacra divinæ gratiæ Symbola in S. literis nominibus ΓΝΟΣ, σφραγὶς signi & sigilli veniunt, ea procedente tempore nominibus μυστήρια mysterii & Sacramenti Ecclesiam insignivisse. Nam vocem μυστήριον mysterii Vulgatus interpres ferè Sacramentum transtulit. Ita sacra signa Damascenus Orthod. fid. lib. iv. 14. ἁγια ἢ ἀχραντα μυστήρια sacra & impolluta mysteria; Chrysostomus Homil. xj. ad populum Antioch. θαυμαστὰ admirabilia. & Homil. x. tom. v. alibique frequenter φρικτὰ μυστήρια tremenda mysteria. Dionysius Areopagita de Hierarch. Eccles. cap. ÿ. ss. 8. πλείστα μυστήρια mysteria vim perficiendi habentia, nuncupant. Visum nonnullis est, ad Græcanica sacra, quæ ferè multiplicibus ritibus nescia quid significantibus constabant, S. Patres ita loquentes respexisse. Probabilius tamen & sanctius etiam est, eos signa sacra, ut partem mysteriorum, sive rerum Divinitus traditarum communi vocabulo denotâsse, aut nomen res spirituales, minimèque sensibus subjectas, fideíque propositas potissimùm designans accommodasse symbolis eas significantibus, & earum loco Ecclesiæ traditis. Quæ enim à sensibus nostris remota in verbo docemur, & fide amplectimur, ea in symbolis suo modo tenemus & cernimus. Quomodo etiam Apoc. 1. 20. μυστήριον mysterium septem stellarum, & Apoc. xvii. 7. μυστήριον γοναικὸς ἢ θηρίου mysterium arcanum per signa adumbratum, signo nomen rei significatæ induente, denotat.
units.tr: Thirdly, the title of Babylonian mystery fits the Papal hierarchy, because it commends seven sacraments, and just as many mysteries, as the sum of religion and as the sole cause of justification. It is certain that the sacred signs of divine grace, which in Holy Scripture are called sēmeia [σημεῖα] and sphragides [σφραγῖδες], that is, signs and seals, were in later times marked by the Church with the names mysteria [μυστήρια] and sacramenta. For the Vulgate translator rendered the word mysterion mostly as sacramentum. So Damascene, in De Orthodoxa Fide iv. 14, calls the sacred signs "holy and unpolluted mysteries" [ἅγια ἢ ἄχραντα μυστήρια]; Chrysostom, in Homily 11 to the people of Antioch, calls them "wonderful" [θαυμαστά], and in Homily 10, vol. 5, and often elsewhere, "tremendous mysteries" [φρικτὰ μυστήρια]; and Dionysius the Areopagite, in De Ecclesiastica Hierarchia v. 8, calls them "very many mysteries having the power of perfecting" [πλεῖστα μυστήρια]. Some have thought that the Fathers, speaking thus, had in view the Greek rites, which largely consisted of many ceremonies whose meaning was unknown. It is more probable, and also more sound, that they used the common term to denote the sacred signs as a part of the mysteries, that is, of things divinely delivered. Or they applied the name to signs which signify spiritual things, which are not chiefly perceived by the senses but proposed by faith, and which were handed down to the Church in place of those signs. For we are taught in the Word, and embrace by faith, things remote from our senses, and in the signs we hold and see them in their own way. So also in Rev. 1:20 "the mystery of the seven stars" [μυστήριον τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀστέρων], and in Rev. 17:7 "the mystery of the woman and of the beast" [μυστήριον γυναικὸς καὶ θηρίου], the hidden meaning, adumbrated by signs, denotes the thing signified, with the sign taking on its name.

units.la: XXXII. Sacra Symbola seu Sacramenta N. T. καὶ ἐξοχὰ sic dicta duo Baptismum & S. Cœnam, non plura, Christus instituit. Duo etiam mysteria, seu symbola my- stica,
units.tr: XXXII. Christ instituted only two sacred symbols, or sacraments, of the New Testament, those called par excellence [καὶ ἐξοχήν]: Baptism and the Lord's Supper, and no more. There are also two mysteries, or mystical symbols,

units.la: stica, eadem scilicet καὶ ἐξοχὴν dicta pia antiquitas agnovit. Suffecerit eam in rem unum, idque clarissimum S. Chrysostomi testimonium, quod ad Joh. xix. 34. seu Hom. lxxxv. in Joh. hæc in verba legere est: ἐξῆλθεν ὕδωρ καὶ αἷμα· ὑχ ἁπλῶς, ὡς ὡς ἐτυχεν, ἐξῆλθον αἱ πηγαί· ἀλλ' ἐπὶ δὴ ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ἡ ἐκκλησία συνέστηκε, ἢ ἔσαν οἱ μυσταγωγούμενοι δὲ ὕδατος μὲν ἀναγεννώμενοι, δὲ αἵματος ἡ ἐκ σαρκὸς τρεφόμενοι. Exivit aqua & sanguis. Non casu & simpliciter hi fontes scaturierunt, sed quoniam ex ambobus Ecclesia constituta est. Sciunt hoc initiati per aquam quidem regenerati, sanguine vero & carne nutriti. Proin etiam duo illa apud Ecclesiam constanter permanserunt.
units.tr: the same ones, namely those called par excellence [καὶ ἐξοχήν], which devout antiquity recognised. One clear testimony will suffice for this, that of St Chrysostom on John 19:34, or Homily 85 on John, which reads thus: [ἐξῆλθεν ὕδωρ καὶ αἷμα· οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ὡς ἔτυχεν, ἐξῆλθον αἱ πηγαί· ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ἡ ἐκκλησία συνέστηκε· ἦσαν οἱ μυσταγωγούμενοι, οἱ μὲν ὕδατος ἀναγεννώμενοι, οἱ δὲ αἵματος καὶ σαρκὸς τρεφόμενοι.] Water and blood came out. The springs did not flow forth simply, by chance, but because the Church was constituted from both. Those who are initiated know this: some are regenerated by water, others are nourished by blood and flesh. Therefore those two have remained constantly in the Church.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Duobus hisce mysteriis symbolicis, solis genuinis justitiæ fidei sigillis, plura superstitio, diversis occasionibus, sine Divinæ institutionis tabulis addidit. Et primò quidem quæ per metaphoram aliquam singularem in scripturis dicta sunt, in ceremonias traduci placuit. Hinc Chrismatio seu Confirmatio ortum habuit. Secundò signa adhibita ad patrationem miraculi, cessante instinctu Spiritus ad miraculum, ad spiritualem gratiam significandam retenta sunt. Hinc extrema unctio. Tertiò quæ in præsentatione personæ coram Ecclesia facta, ea ad exaggerandam existimationem & potestatem Ministrorum, in mysterium & Sacramentum convertere libuit. Hinc Sacramenta, quæ χειροτονία, seu impositione manuum peraguntur. Ipsa quoque vox Sacramenti alicubi usurpata, & utilitas non exigua inde in Ecclesiæ Mystas redundans, numerum locupletavit. Hinc matrimonium. Atque ita Diaboli astus multorum mentes corrupit à simplicitate in Christum (2 Cor. xi. 3.) ut tandem etiam Sacramenta numero certo, septenario scilicet definirentur: quod primùm ab Hugone de S. Victore, qui seculo xii. floruit, in suo de Ceremoniis, Sacramentis, Officiis &c. opere lib. j. cap. 12. mox etiam Lombardo lib. iv. sent. dist. 2. factum. Quem numerum Synodali authoritate in decreto super unione Armeniorum, A. M. C. D. XXXIX. confirmavit. Neque dum tamen declaratum erat omnia haec Sacramenta esse vere & proprie dicta Sacramenta novae legis, neque esse plura vel pauciora. Hoc enim demum in Concilio Tridentino Seff. vij. can. 1. sub anathemate definitum est his verbis: Si quis dixerit, Sacramenta nova legis non fuisse omnia a Jesu Christo Domino nostro instituta; aut esse plura vel pauciora, quam septem, aut aliquod horum septem non esse vere & proprie dictum Sacramentum; anathema sit.
units.tr: Superstition, on various occasions and without any warrant from the tables of divine institution, added many more things to these two symbolic mysteries, the only genuine seals of the justifying faith. First, what was said in Scripture by some singular metaphor was thought fit to be turned into ceremonies. Hence chrismation or confirmation arose. Second, signs used for performing a miracle were kept, once the impulse of the Spirit for the miracle had ceased, to signify spiritual grace. Hence extreme unction. Third, what was done in presenting a person before the Church, they chose to convert into a mystery and sacrament, in order to magnify the esteem and power of the ministers. Hence the sacraments which are performed by cheirotonia [χειροτονία], that is, by the laying on of hands. The word sacrament itself, used somewhere, and the no small advantage that flowed from this to the initiates of the Church, also enriched the number. Hence matrimony. And so the wiles of the Devil corrupted the minds of many from simplicity towards Christ (2 Cor. xi. 3.), until at last the sacraments were fixed at a certain number, namely seven. This was first done by Hugh of St Victor, who flourished in the twelfth century, in his work on the Ceremonies, Sacraments, Offices, etc., book 1, chapter 12, and soon afterwards by Lombard, book 4, Sentences, distinction 2. This number was confirmed by synodal authority in the decree on the union with the Armenians, in the year 1439. Yet it had not yet been declared that all these sacraments were truly and properly called sacraments of the new law, nor that there were neither more nor fewer. This was at last defined under anathema in the Council of Trent, session 7, canon 1, in these words: If anyone shall say that the sacraments of the new law were not all instituted by Jesus Christ our Lord, or that there are more or fewer than seven, or that any one of these seven is not truly and properly a sacrament; let him be anathema.

units.la: XXXIV. Neque satis erat, veris & proprie dictis Sacramentis, seu mysteriis symbolicis, Baptismo & S. Domini ni Coena falsa doctrina incrustatis, & hoc in theatralem & histrionicam pompam, & salutis per abnegationem unici sacrificii Jesu Christi venenum praesentissimum conversa, mysteria salutis sine documentis certis & idoneis Divinae institutionis (frustra enim Bellarminum de effectu & numero Sacram. cap. 24. aliósque ea promere conatos esse, abundè milliésque à nostris ostensum est) non aliam ob rationem, quàm quia ita dignitati & potestati Hierarchiae amplificandae conducere visum est; multiplicásse. In iis enim etiam summam totius religionis Christianae ponere, & causam Justificationis, & Sanctificationis etiam ex opere operato, uti barbara doctrina verbis barbaris exponitur, producendae, ea constituere, perinde atque si efficaciam tantum à gratia Dei & merito Christi sibi impressam continerent, non dubitarunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. Nor was it enough that Baptism and the Lord's Supper, the true and properly so-called sacraments or symbolic mysteries, were encrusted with false doctrine and turned into a theatrical and histrionic pomp, and into a most dangerous poison against salvation through the rejection of the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ. They also multiplied the mysteries of salvation without certain and fitting proofs of divine institution. (For it has been shown by our writers, abundantly and a thousand times, that Bellarmine, On the Effect and Number of the Sacraments, chapter 24, and others who tried to produce such proofs, failed.) They did this for no other reason than that it seemed to serve the enlargement of the dignity and power of the hierarchy. In these they did not hesitate to place the sum of the whole Christian religion, and to set up in them the cause both of justification and of sanctification, to be produced ex opere operato, as this barbarous doctrine is expounded in barbarous words, as if they contained an efficacy impressed on them by the grace of God and the merit of Christ.

units.la: XXXV. De efficacia & virtute Sacramentorum magnis equidem, & dissentientibus studiis olim Scholasticos inter disceptatum est. Continere illa gratiam, non significare duntaxat, omnes fere consentiunt. De modo, quo eam contineant, dissentiunt; an videlicet eam contineant, sicut vas aquam, & pyxis medicinam? an, quia gratiam significant, &, nisi sit defectus ex parte suscipientis, eam semper conferunt? Prius Hugo de S. Victore de Sacram. parte 9. cap. 4. posterius Bonaventura in 4. sent. dist. 1. art. 1. q. 3. sustinet. Sed & de virtute instrumentali in Sacramentis causativa gratiæ disputatum jam olim, an per aliquam virtutem creatam insistentem, sive sacramento inhærentem, ut per causam instrumentalem dispositivam suscipienti gratia conferatur? an vero per solam increatam Dei virtutem ordinationi suæ ex pacto assistentem animo suscipientis Sacramentum immediatè ex ipso gratiæ æterno fonte Deo in recto Sacramenti usu gratiam hauriat? Prius Thomæ Aquinati, ejúsque scholæ; posterius Bonaventuræ, Durando, Scoto, Bieli, aliis olim placuit.
units.tr: XXXV. Indeed the efficacy and virtue of the sacraments was once disputed among the Schoolmen with great and conflicting zeal. Almost all agree that the sacraments contain grace, and do not merely signify it. They differ about the manner in which they contain it: whether they contain it as a vessel contains water, or a box contains medicine? Or whether, because they signify grace, they always confer it, unless there is a defect on the part of the recipient? Hugh of St Victor, On the Sacraments, part 9, chapter 4, upholds the former; Bonaventure, In Sentences 4, distinction 1, article 1, question 3, the latter. Also long ago it was disputed about the instrumental virtue in the sacraments that causes grace: whether grace is conferred on the recipient through some created virtue abiding, that is, inhering in the sacrament, as through an instrumental and disposing cause; or whether the recipient, with a right use of the sacrament, draws grace immediately from the eternal fountain of grace, God himself, through the uncreated power of God alone, who assists by his own ordinance and agreement. The former pleased Thomas Aquinas and his school; the latter pleased Bonaventure, Durandus, Scotus, Biel and others.

units.la: XXXVI. De modo eo continendi & efficiendi gratiam in Tridentino etiam Concilio Dominicanos inter, Tho- mæ, & Franciscanos, Scoti asseclas acribus contenden- tium studiis disceptatum est.
units.tr: XXXVI. On the manner of retaining and effecting grace, which was also disputed with keen zeal at the Council of Trent, between the Dominicans, the followers of Thomas, and the Franciscans, the followers of Scotus.

units.la: Et Patrum quidem Concilii illius erat ambigua isthæc litium fata dirimere. Sed prævalidarum partium metu, ad solitos cothurnos conversi Sess. vij. Can. 6. sub anathemate id solum definiverunt, Sacramenta continere gratiam, quam significant, & gratiam non ponentibus obicem conferre. Et Canone octavo anathema intonuere iis, qui per novæ legis Sacramenta ex opere operato non conferri gratiam, sed solam fidem Divinæ promissionis ad gratiam consequendam sufficere statuunt. Ita Concilium ab operatione Sacramenti etiam accipientis fidem & devotionem exclusit. Ita enim verba illa ex opere operato gratiam conferre, ante Concilium Scholastici intellexerunt, nominatim Albertus in cap. 6. Joh. Petrus de Palude in 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 1. aliique. Ita ipsum Concilium intellexisse, historia ejus dubitare non finit:
units.tr: Indeed, it was the task of the Fathers of that Council to settle this uncertain contest. But fearing the strongest party, they returned to their accustomed buskins and, in Session 7, Canon 6, defined under anathema only this: the Sacraments contain the grace they signify, and confer grace on those who do not place an obstacle in the way. And in Canon 8 they thundered anathema against those who maintain that grace is not conferred through the sacraments of the new law by the work worked, but that faith in the divine promise alone suffices to obtain grace. Thus the Council excluded from the operation of the Sacrament even the faith and devotion of the recipient.
