For before the Council the Schoolmen understood the words to confer grace by the work worked in this way; Albert, on chapter 6 of John, Peter of Palude, on the Fourth Book of the Sentences, distinction 1, question 1, and others, name them. That the Council itself understood them so, its history does not allow us to doubt.

units.la: De eadem decretum Tridentinæ Synodi, ab operatione Sacramenti, fidem & devotionem ejus, qui suscipit, excludenuis, & efficacem ex opere operato, habilitatis. finit: Patres enim in eo præsentes inter eas actiones, quibus pietas excitatur, quásque gratiam parere ex opere operantis, hoc est, non ex ipsius operis, sed operantis viribus & devotione docebant, & eas, quæ gratiam ex opere operato, hoc est, ut ipsi, teste Suavi, nec contradicente Pallavicino, explicárunt, non ex operantis, vel opus recipientis devotione, sed operis ipsius virtute, distinxerunt, & posterioris generis esse Sacramenta Christiana, declárárunt. Atque eodem Jesuitarum modernorum de efficacia attritionis, sine ullo amore Dei, solius absolutionis in Sacramento pœnitentiæ vi, justificationis gratiam operantis, doctrina pertinet.
units.tr: The decree of the Synod of Trent on this same matter excludes from the operation of the Sacrament the faith and devotion of the one who receives it, and makes it effective by the work worked. For the Fathers present there distinguished, among the actions by which piety is aroused, those which produce grace by the work of the worker, that is, not by the power of the work itself but by the strength and devotion of the worker, from those which produce grace by the work worked, that is, as they themselves explained it, as Suavius attests and Pallavicini does not contradict, not by the devotion of the worker or of the one receiving the work, but by the virtue of the work itself; and they declared that the Christian Sacraments belong to the latter kind. And the doctrine of the modern Jesuits belongs to the same view: that attrition without any love of God becomes efficacious for obtaining justifying grace solely by the power of absolution in the Sacrament of Penance.

units.la: XXXVII. Atque sic illa Pontificiorum mysteria symbolica, præterquam quòd sine ulla authoritate verbi Divini (si baptismalem ritum, quatenus is ex verbo Dei retinetur, exceperis) introducta sunt, insuper etiam in hodierna inprimis vitæ & morum profanitate, nihil aliud sunt, & habentur, quàm carnalis fiduciæ ὀχύρωμα, impia hominum in peccatis sibi blandientium κρησφύγετα, speluncæ veluti latronum, denique, verbo dicam. Mysteria iniquitatis, quibus Babylonis Magnæ frons, ceu stigmate quopiam, inusta est. Vera enim mysteria symbolica, seu Sacramenta (ne de falsis & spuriis dicam) revera non sunt causæ salutis, justificationis, vel sanctificationis; neque etiam conditiones ejus, sed signa fœderis per gratiam Spiritus S. partim invitantia ad fidem, qua ad Christum confugimus, & eam moraliter operantia ad communionem cum ipso, quatenus una cum verbo sunt apud Ecclesiam & docent, in quo nomine nos salvari oporteat: partim in fide post explorationem sui utentibus, cum verba consolationis ad singulos fideles, quòd in scripturis extat, fiant efficax adminiculum spei, coronam vitæ in Christo expectantis. Quo sensu dicuntur 1 Petr. iii. 21. σώζειν salvare, Mysterium iniquitatis, quod in ea doctrina continetur, ostensum. vare, quia sunt ἐπερωτήματα interrogationes bonæ conscientiæ ad Deum, adeóque stipulationem de salute præbent. Revera igitur ceu σφραγῖδες sigilla justitiæ fidei (Rom. iv. 11.) non aliam efficaciam habent, quàm objectivam & moralem, puta vim spiritualia bona promissa significandi, commemorandi, certiorandi, & propter veritatem Dei, sistendi.
units.tr: XXXVII. And so those Papist symbolic mysteries, apart from the fact that they were introduced without any authority of the divine Word (except the baptismal rite, insofar as it is retained from the Word of God), moreover, especially in the present profanity of life and morals, are nothing other than, and are regarded as nothing other than, a stronghold [ὀχύρωμα] of carnal confidence, a hiding place [κρησφύγετα] of impious men flattering themselves in their sins, as it were dens of robbers; in a word, mysteries of iniquity, with which the forehead of Babylon the Great is branded as with some mark. For true symbolic mysteries, or Sacraments (not to speak of false and spurious ones), are in truth neither causes of salvation, justification, or sanctification, nor conditions of these; but they are signs of the covenant, which through the grace of the Holy Spirit, partly invite to faith, by which we flee to Christ, and morally work toward communion with him, insofar as they are together with the Word among the Church and teach by what name we ought to be saved; partly, to those who use them after testing themselves in faith, since the words of consolation that stand in the Scriptures for each of the faithful become an effective aid to hope, which expects the crown of life in Christ. In this sense they are said to save [σώζειν] (1 Pet. 3:21), because they are questions [ἐπερωτήματα] of a good conscience toward God, and therefore offer a pledge concerning salvation. Truly, then, as seals [σφραγῖδες] of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11), they have no other efficacy than an objective and moral one, namely the power of signifying, recalling, and assuring of the spiritual goods promised, and of holding them fast on account of the truth of God.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Qui igitur illa Dei dona in opus operatum convertunt, & falsa insuper mysteria symbolica fingunt, adeóque etiam Sacramentis qualibuscunque tribuunt virtutem Physicam operandi gratiam (ita enim hodie Romani loqui amant) seu ex opere operato justificationis gratiam producendi; sive putent virtutem creatam iis indi, per quam ceu causam instrumentalem dispositivam gratia conferatur; sive motum imprimi, sive virtutem Divinam assistere, quæ ad prolationem verborum super materia debita effectum operetur; sive etiam ex pacto tanquam conditiones requisitas, aut causas morales (uti Bellarminus pertendit) gratiæ effectum adducere: ii Testamentum Divinum mutant, eíque φαρμακευτικῶς, propria dispositione aliquid adjiciunt, & in Scriptura φαρμακεῖς incantatores, tribuentes signis efficaciam, quam nec à natura, nec à Divina ordinatione habent, audiunt; denique veritissima iniquitatis mysteria, quibus Babylon Magna insignita est, venditant. Illud cùm faciat profiteaturque Hierarchia Papalis, Babylonis M. mysterium in fronte ejus pellucere, quis bonus negare audit?
units.tr: Therefore those who turn those gifts of God into a work worked, and moreover invent false symbolic mysteries, and so also ascribe to any Sacraments whatever a physical power of working grace (for so the Romanists love to speak today), that is, of producing the grace of justification by the work worked; whether they think that a created power is placed in them, through which grace is conferred as an instrumental and disposing cause; or that a motion is impressed, or that a divine power assists, which brings about its effect upon the matter by the pronouncing of the words; or even that by agreement, as requisite conditions or moral causes (as Bellarmine contends), they bring about the effect of grace: these men change the divine Testament and add something to it by their own arrangement, in a pharmaceutical manner [φαρμακευτικῶς], and are heard, in Scripture, as sorcerers [φαρμακεῖς], enchanters, who attribute to signs an efficacy which they have neither from nature nor from divine ordination; and finally they peddle those most true mysteries of iniquity with which Babylon the Great is marked. Since the Papal Hierarchy does this and professes it, who would be so bold as to deny that the mystery of Babylon the Great shines through on its forehead?

units.la: XXXIX. Quarto Babylonis Magnæ titulus frontalis μυστήριον Mysterium, eatenus quoque Hierarchiæ Papali congruit, quòd Christum in Missa, ceu peculiari mysterio corporaliter simul atque secretè & invisibiliter adesse & Deo sacrificari asserit. Et Missam quidem, quatenus in ea substantia panis & vini in corporis & sanguinis Christi sub.
units.tr: XXXIX. Fourthly, the title on the forehead of Babylon the Great, μυστήριον [Mystery], fits the Papal Hierarchy also in this respect, that it asserts that Christ is present in the Mass, as in a special mystery, bodily, at the same time secretly and invisibly, and is sacrificed to God. And the Mass, insofar as in it the substance of bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ

units.la: iv. Quia Christum in Missa, ceu pracipuo Mysterio, corporaliter simul & secreto ac invisibiliter
units.tr: because Christ, as the chief Mystery, is in the Mass bodily, at the same time secretly and invisibly,

units.la: substantiam invisibilem, ope sacriculi, concepta & murmurata verba proferentis, conversa, Christus in hostia incruentè sacrificari realiter pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum, statuitur, mysteriorum omnium apicem, proram & puppim religionis suæ illi faciunt. In Concilio Lateranensi A. 1215. sub Innocentio III. habito, in quo sensus verborum Christi Pontificius, ambiguis licet verbis, primum definitus est. Scoto ipso 4. dist. 9. q. 3. n. 15. non diffitente; Missa perfectio Mysterii unitatis, Christi scilicet & Ecclesiæ, appellatur. Verba sic habent: Ipse Sacerdos & Sacrificium Iesus Christus, cujus Corpus & sanguis in Sacramento altaris sub speciebus panis & vini veraciter continentur, transsubstantiato pane in corpus, & vini in sanguinem, potestate Divina, ut ad perficiendum Mysterium unitatis accipiamus ipsi de suo, quod accepit ipse de nostro.
units.tr: and the invisible substance, by the power of a little priest uttering the words conceived and muttered, is converted, and Christ is sacrificed bloodlessly, in the Host, really, for the sins of the living and the dead, they make this the summit, prow and stern of their religion, as the crown of all mysteries. This was established at the Lateran Council held in 1215 under Innocent III, in which the Papal sense of the words of Christ was first defined, though in ambiguous terms. Scotus himself, in the Fourth Book, distinction 9, question 3, number 15, does not deny it, and the Mass is called the perfection of the mystery of unity, namely of Christ and the Church. The words are these: The Priest himself and the Sacrifice is Jesus Christ, whose Body and Blood are truly contained in the Sacrament of the altar under the species of bread and wine, the bread being transubstantiated into the body and the wine into the blood by divine power, so that to complete the mystery of unity we may receive from him what he himself received from us.

units.la: XL. Si quod aliud dogma, isthoc certè mysteriis impietatis refertum maximè est. In eo enim mysterii singularis prætextu & verus Christus in falsum mutatur (quomodo enim verus Christus ἀναθεματ@ est, qui in tot hostiis quotidie divisus, multiplicatus in unum ubique punctum seu substantiam ἄπμου redigitur, habens corpus à Spiritu non differens, toties, tot in locis ab hominibus, muribus &c. devoratus?) & verum sacrificium in cruce Deo Patri oblatum in falsum convertitur (an enim verum sacrificium reapse propitiatorium, atque illud ipsum numero, quod in cruce Deo Patri oblatum est, esse potest, quod incruentum est, in quo esse Christi naturale non destruitur, quod in terra peragitur, manente corpore Christi in Cœlo ad dextram Dei, eóque gloriose & ἁπαξ τῳ; quod denique offertur demum postquam Christus ἅπαξ σφαγῆς semel duntaxat oblatus Hebr. ix. 28. μία θυσία unico sacrificio pro peccatis oblato ὡς τὸ ἀλυτικὸς in perpetuum ad dextram Dei consedit. Hebr. x. 12. ut innumera taceam?) & remissio peccatorum per sanguinem unici sacrificii Christi parta, impuro sacerdoti nescio quo murmure Christi loco panaceum aliquod Numen repræsentanti, accepta refertur.
units.tr: XL. If any other dogma, this one is surely crammed full of mysteries of impiety. For under the pretext of a singular mystery both the true Christ is changed into a falsehood (for how is the true Christ, who is daily divided into so many hosts, multiplied, reduced to one single point or substance everywhere, having a body not different from a spirit, devoured so many times, in so many places, by men, mice, etc.? [ἀνάθεμα]) and the true sacrifice offered to God the Father on the cross is turned into a falsehood (for can there be a true sacrifice, truly propitiatory, and that very one in number which was offered to God the Father on the cross, which is bloodless, in which the natural being of Christ is not destroyed, which is carried out on earth while the body of Christ remains in heaven at the right hand of God, and thus gloriously and once for all [ἅπαξ]; which is finally offered after Christ, having been offered only once [ἅπαξ] (Heb. 9:28), sat down at the right hand of God for ever [εἰς τὸ διηνεκές] after one sacrifice [μία θυσία] (Heb. 10:12) offered for sins, not to mention countless others?), and the forgiveness of sins, obtained through the blood of the one sacrifice of Christ, is credited to a sacrificing priest's murmur, who represents some panacea deity in place of Christ.

units.la: XLI. Tam impio scilicet mysterio tegendum erat arcanum seu mysterium non minùs impium, cujus gratia illud inducere placuit. Quod enim de Regibus Judæis posterioribus Tacitus Hist. v. 8. 6. pronuntiat, eos honorem sacerdotii, firmamentum potentiæ assumpsisse, id multò magis Pontifici, ejusque succenturiatis sacerdotibus convenit. Eodem certè tempore, quo Monarchiam absolutam in spiritualibus & temporalibus Romani Pontifices flagrantissimè appetierunt, instituto, & in Lateranensi Concilio definito Missæ sacrificio, sacerdotii honorem potentiæ, quam affectabant, summæ firmamentum assumpserunt, & sacerdotes, qui se Creatorem sui creare profitebantur, potestatis suæ peristromata dilatarunt. Quod Gabriel Biel Lect. 2. in Can. Missæ aperte testatur, asserens, non voluisse Dominum aliquem habere potestatem solvendi & ligandi super corpus mysticum, seu Ecclesiam, nisi haberet potestatem super corpus Christi, & Sacerdotes dignores esse Regibus, Angelis, B. Virgine Maria, quia Christum creant, &c. Et Lect. 4. ita exclamat: Quis unquam vidit talia? Qui creavit me (si fas est dicere) dedit mihi creare se, & qui creavit me sine me, creatur mediante me. Quidni creatores Christi ipsius Domini sui summam in terris minimum potestatem promerentur? Tolle igitur Missam, ruent Sacerdotes, ruet Pontifex summus, ruet potestas in spiritualibus & temporalibus summa, Deique summi æmula. Tum etiam Missa talis in Ecclesiæ orchestram producenda fuit, ut plebi sacrificium pretiosissimum omnium obtruderetur, pretio maximo pro expungendis peccatis licitandum. Pro quo proin dogmate, tanquam pro aris & focis, non frustra illi dimicant, exuturi illud novissimum, minimè ignari, si quæstuosum isthoc & juge sacrificium cessaret, fore ut exsiccetur confestim stagnum, in quo ranæ Apocalypticæ liberius adhuc natant, & coaxant clamosius.
units.tr: XLI. Indeed, a secret that is no less impious than the mystery itself, and for the sake of which it was pleasing to introduce it, had to be covered by so impious a mystery. For what Tacitus says of the later Jewish kings (Hist. 5.8), that they assumed the honour of the priesthood as the firm foundation of their power, applies much more to the Pontiff and his subordinate priests. At the very time when the Roman Pontiffs most ardently sought absolute monarchy in spiritual and temporal affairs, they took up as the firm foundation of their supreme power the honour of the priesthood, through the institution and definition of the Mass sacrifice at the Lateran Council, and the priests, who professed that they create their own Creator, extended the cushions of their authority. Gabriel Biel openly bears witness to this in Lecture 2 on the Canon of the Mass, asserting that the Lord did not wish anyone to have the power of loosing and binding over the mystical body, or the Church, unless he had power over the body of Christ, and that priests are more worthy than kings, angels, and the Blessed Virgin Mary, because they create Christ, etc. And in Lecture 4 he cries out thus: Who has ever seen such things? He who created me (if it is right to say so) has given me the power to create him, and he who created me without me is created through me. Why should the creators of Christ himself, their Lord, not earn for themselves the greatest power on earth, the least of which is supreme? Take away the Mass, and the priests will fall, the supreme Pontiff will fall, supreme power in spiritual and temporal affairs will fall, a rival of the Most High God. Then also such a Mass had to be produced on the stage of the Church, so that the most precious sacrifice of all might be thrust upon the common people, to be bid for at the greatest price for the blotting out of sins. For this dogma, as for altars and hearths, they fight not in vain, and they will cling to that last one, not at all unaware that if this profitable and perpetual sacrifice ceased, the pool in which the Apocalyptic frogs swim more freely still, and croak more loudly, would dry up at once.

units.la: XLII. Accedit quòd non tantùm Canonem Missæ, centonem humana industria malè consarcinatum, inter summa religionis humanæ mysteria deputant, adeò ut Innocentius III. de Missæ mysteriis lib. v. 6. jam olim exclamaverit, tantæ profunditatis ejus verba esse, ut intellectus humanus vix ea penetrare valeat. Et Circius Polonus, cum se ex objectis Canoni erroribus extricare non posset, omnésque ejus expositiones ineptas esse assereret, eò confugerit, ut diceret: non esse quærendam interpretationem Canonis, sed quia sit mysterium à Christo & Apostolis traditum, ideo non intelligendum, sed adorandum esse; sed etiam eundem nomine Secretæ, sive quòd hominibus ejus verba occulta sint, & mysterium tantum humanæ rationis acie prorsus sit impenetrabile, sive quòd cum silentio legi, adeóque mussari & halari potiùs, quàm enuntiari debeat. Unde Concilium Tridentinum Seff. xxij. Can. 9. eos, qui dixerint, Ecclesiæ Romanæ ritum quo summissa voce pars Canonis & verba consecrationis offerunt, damnandum esse, anathemate percutit. Cujus secretæ pronuntiationis originem Johannes Beleth, Honorius Augustodunensis, aliisque acceptam referunt fabulosæ narrationi de pastoribus, qui verba consecrationis, hactenus audita, in agro supra panem & vinum protulerunt, & ea repente, si credere fas est, in carnem & sanguinem mutârunt, ipsi verò ob facinus cœlesti igne consumpti sunt. Rudem fabellam & ab incude adhuc calentem, primus Pseudo-Alcuinus, seculo decimo recentior de Divinit. Offic. tit. de celebr. Missæ retulit, addens, consuetudinem inde venisse in Ecclesia, ut tacitè ista obsecratio atque consecratio à Sacerdote deinceps cantetur. Nisi forte id factum est imitatione sive Gentilium, apud quos sacra abstrudi & presso gutture mussari mos erat, sive Magorum etiam, quorum vetus isthoc axioma fuit: Oportet Magiæ operatorem, si fructum inde consequi velit secretum esse. Quam conjecturam Gabriel Biel lect. 4. in Can. Missæ confirmare videtur, ubi creationem Creatoris per Sacrificulum secretè verba consecrationis proferentem factam probat non fieri naturali potestate, vel meritoria operatione, sed assistente virtute: Secundùm quem modum malefici & incantatrices quosdam effectus producere dicuntur, ut extrahere lac vaccarum de sedibus seu manubriis securium, quod fit non naturali virtute maleficorum, neque ex eorum merito sed virtute occulta, sive bona sive mala assistente.
units.tr: XLII. Moreover, they not only count the Canon of the Mass, a patchwork badly stitched together by human industry, among the highest mysteries of the human religion, so that Innocent III already cried out long ago in de Missæ mysteriis lib. v. 6. that the words of it are of such depth that the human intellect can scarcely penetrate them. And Circius the Pole, when he could not extricate himself from the errors charged against the Canon and admitted that all its explanations were foolish, took refuge in saying that the interpretation of the Canon is not to be sought, but because it is a mystery handed down by Christ and the Apostles, it is to be not understood but adored. Nor is it only for this reason that it is called the Secret, whether because its words are hidden from men and the mystery is wholly impenetrable to the keenness of human reason, or because it must be read in silence and so muttered and breathed out rather than spoken aloud. Hence the Council of Trent, Sess. xxij. Can. 9., strikes with anathema those who say that the rite of the Church of Rome, by which part of the Canon and the words of consecration are offered in a lowered voice, is to be condemned. John Beleth, Honorius of Autun and others trace the origin of this secret pronunciation to the fabulous story of the shepherds who, having heard the words of consecration hitherto, uttered them in a field over bread and wine, and who then, if it is right to believe it, suddenly changed them into flesh and blood; but the shepherds themselves were consumed by fire from heaven for their deed. The rough little tale, still hot from the anvil, was first related by the pseudo-Alcuin, a writer later than the tenth century, de Divinit. Offic. tit. de celebr. Missæ, adding that from this came the custom in the Church that this supplication and consecration should henceforth be sung silently by the priest. Unless perhaps it was done in imitation either of the Gentiles, among whom it was the custom to hide sacred rites and mutter them with a constricted throat, or of the Magi, whose old maxim this was: The operator of magic, if he wishes to obtain its fruit, must be secret. Gabriel Biel, lect. 4. on the Canon of the Mass, seems to confirm this conjecture, where, proving that the Creator's creation, effected by the priest secretly uttering the words of consecration, does not come about by natural power or by meritorious operation, but by an assisting virtue, he goes on: In this way witches and sorceresses are said to produce certain effects, such as drawing milk from cows out of the handles of axes; this is done not by the natural virtue of the sorcerers, nor by their merit, but by a hidden virtue, whether good or evil, that assists them.

units.la: XLIII. Mysterii porro Missatici ἀνμή in eo consistit, quòd pertendunt Hierarchæ, Sacrificulum verba certa secretò demurmurantem corpus verum Christi, sed invisibile & indivisibile, adeóque spirituale sub hostiæ speciebus, mox per desitionem τῶ esse Sacramentalis immolandum, repræsentare. Annon enim corpus humanum, quod σὰρξ carne & sanguine constat, invisibile, indivisibile, spirituale, arcanum, & quidem victimæ pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum destinatum, & secretis etiam cubilibus ac cibariis includendum, adorandúmque mysterium ingens est? Est sanè, sed impietatis, non pietatis. Ita enim panis & vinum non in corpus & sanguinem Christi, sed in spectra quædam Spirituum proprietates mentientia convertunt, & qui pro præsentia reali corporis & sanguinis Christi, tanquam pro aris & focis suis, tantopere dimicant, ii ipsi comica quadam licentia ex Eucharistia & signum & rem significatam exterminant, nuda pro pane accidentia supponunt, & sub accidentium illorum larvis, non corpus Christi, sed substantiam quandam indivisibilem & maximè arcanam, Spiritum nempe, id est, Nihilum sub Nihilo ostentant, & adorandum publicè proponunt, denique spectatoribus & communicantibus suis ludicrum illud occinunt: λaβὲ μηδὲν, ἡ νεχρὶ καλῶς. Accipe nihil, & tene bene.
units.tr: XLIII. Moreover, the crux of the Mass-mystery consists in this: the hierarchs maintain that the priest, murmuring certain words in secret, represents under the appearances of the host the true body of Christ, but invisible and indivisible, and therefore spiritual, to be immolated at once by the cessation of its being [τῷ εἶναι] and to become sacramental. For is not the human body, which consists of flesh [σὰρξ] with blood, invisible, indivisible, spiritual, mysterious, and indeed destined as a victim for the sins of the living and the dead, and to be enclosed also in secret beds and food-chests, and a vast mystery to be adored? It is indeed, but of impiety, not of piety. For in this way they change bread and wine not into the body and blood of Christ but into certain phantoms of spirits that feign the properties of bodies; and those who fight so fiercely for the real presence of the body and blood of Christ, as for their altars and hearths, by a certain comic license banish from the Eucharist both the sign and & the thing signified, and they substitute bare accidents for the bread, and under the masks of those accidents they display not the body of Christ but some indivisible and most mysterious substance, namely Spirit, that is, Nothing under Nothing, and publicly propose it for adoration. Finally they chant that ludicrous formula to their spectators and communicants: [λαβὲ μηδέν, ἔχε καλῶς]. Take nothing, and hold it well.

units.la: XLIV. Sic Bellarminus ipse Corpus Christi ex Coena revera tollit. Ita enim de Eucharistia lib. 1. cap. 2. loquitur: Non habet Christus in Eucharistia modum existendi Corporum, sed potius Spirituum, cum sit totus in qualibet parte. At quod in qualibet parte est, id Spiritus est. Pergit: Itaque dicemus, Christum in Eucharistia adesse verè, realiter, substantialiter, ut Concilium Tridentinum loquitur; sed non dicemus, corporaliter, id est, eo modo, quo suapte natura existunt corpora, nec sensibiliter, mobiliter. Quomodo ergo? Spiritualiter, dici posse agnoscit, juxta illud Bernhardi, in hoc Sacramento exhiberi nobis veram corporis substantiam, sed spiritualiter, non carnaliter. Mox tamen addit, non videri sibi nimis frequentandum esse hoc nomen spiritualiter. Quid igitur faciendum? aut quomodo in Sacramento erit Christus, si neque corporaliter, neque spiritualiter eum ibi esse, tutò dici potest? Concilium Tridentinum definit verè quidem, realiter & substantialiter sub specie rerum sensibilium corpus Christi contineri, non tamen juxta modum existendi naturaliter, sed sacramentaliter. Quomodo verò intelligunt illud Sacramentaliter? An planè, ut est in hoc Sacramento? Hoc verò frivolum foret. Quærendum enim semper foret, quomodo sit in hoc Sacramento, & quid illud significet. Æterna sic esset petitio τῶ ἐν ἀρχῆ. Quod si id referendum in genere est ad naturam, formam, & modum reliquorum Sacramentorum ; eo modo erit corpus Christi in Cœna, quo fuit olim in Circumcisione, Paschate, hodie est in Baptismo. Hæc enim reliqua Sacramenta sunt. An verò in iis post consecrationem fit mutatio substantiæ? An in iis corpus Christi præsens est Sacramentaliter, hoc est, secundùm substantiam corporis sui, & per indistantiam loci? Atqui hoc ipsi pernegant. Vel igitur corpus Christi in Eucharistia præsens est per præsentiam Spiritus S. spiritualia bona in Sacramento significata, obsignata & repræsentata fidei vendicantis: vel nullo modo (nam corporaliter & proprie spiritualiter adesse negant) in Eucharistia præsens est. Prius cùm præfractè Adversarii, ne in castra veritatis transeant, negent, posterius illos asserere debere, adeóque, quod grande iniquitatis mysterium est, corpus Christi ex Eucharistia eliminare, nihilum sub nihilo adorare, & ceu victimam pro peccatis suis Deo Patri offerre, manifestè consequitur.
units.tr: XLIV. Thus Bellarmine himself in fact removes the body of Christ from the Supper. For he speaks thus in de Eucharistia lib. 1. cap. 2.: Christ in the Eucharist has not the mode of existing of bodies, but rather of spirits, since he is whole in every part. But what is in every part is spirit. He goes on: Therefore we shall say that Christ is present in the Eucharist truly, really, substantially, as the Council of Trent speaks; but we shall not say corporeally, that is, in the way in which bodies exist by their own nature, nor sensibly, movably. How then? He admits that it can be said spiritually, according to the saying of Bernard, that in this Sacrament there is offered to us the true substance of the body, but spiritually, not carnally. Soon, however, he adds that he does not think this word spiritually should be used too often. What then is to be done? Or how will Christ be in the Sacrament, if it cannot safely be said that he is there either corporeally or spiritually? The Council of Trent defines that the body of Christ is indeed truly, really and substantially contained under the species of sensible things, yet not according to the mode of existing naturally, but sacramentally. But how do they understand the word Sacramentally? Surely as it is in this Sacrament? That would be frivolous. For one would always have to ask how he is in this Sacrament, and what that signifies. Such a petition would be an eternal begging of the question [ἐν ἀρχῇ]. But if this is to be referred in general to the nature, form and mode of the other sacraments, then the body of Christ will be in the Supper in the way it was once in Circumcision and the Passover, and today is in Baptism; for these are the remaining sacraments. But is there a change of substance in them after consecration? Is the body of Christ present in them sacramentally, that is, according to the substance of his body, and by nearness of place? Yet they flatly deny this. Therefore either the body of Christ is present in the Eucharist through the presence of the Holy Spirit, with the spiritual goods signified, sealed and represented in the Sacrament to faith that lays hold of them; or in no way is it present in the Eucharist (for they deny that it is present corporeally and properly spiritually). Since the Adversaries stubbornly deny the former, lest they pass over into the camp of truth, it clearly follows that they must assert the latter, and so, which is a great mystery of iniquity, eliminate the body of Christ from the Eucharist, adore Nothing under Nothing, and offer it to God the Father as a victim for their sins.

units.la: XLV. Accedit quod Thomas Aquinas Sum. Theol. pag. 3. quæst. 67. art. 3. manifestè corpus Christi verum ab Eucharistico, puta arcano, invisibili & indivisibili illo distinguit.
units.tr: XLV. Moreover, Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae p. 3, q. 67, art. 3, clearly distinguishes the true body of Christ from that Eucharistic body, namely the hidden, invisible and indivisible one.

units.la: Quærit nempe: An totus Christus sub qualibet parte speciei rum, panis vel vini sit? Respondet affirmando, ratione adducta; quòd corpus Christi sit in hoc Sacramento eo modo, quo substantia est sub dimensionibus. Objicienti, quòd corpus Christi, cùm sit organicum, habeat partes determinatè distantes, cùm de ratione corporis organici sit determinata distantia singularum partium ab invicem; sicut oculi ab oculo, & auris ab aure, hoc autem esse non posset, si sub qualibet parte speciei esset totus Christus; diserte respondet: Talis distantia partium est quidem in ipso corpore Christi vero, sed non secundùm hanc distantiam comparatur ad hoc Sacramentum.
units.tr: He asks, Is the whole Christ under every part of the species of bread or wine? He answers yes, giving a reason: the body of Christ is in this Sacrament in the way that a substance is under dimensions. To the objection that the body of Christ, being organic, has parts at determinate distances from one another, since it belongs to the nature of an organic body that each part is at a fixed distance from the others, as the eye from the eye and the ear from the ear, and that this could not be so if the whole Christ were under every part of the species, he replies plainly: Such a distance of parts is indeed in the true body of Christ itself, but it is not according to this distance that it is related to this Sacrament.

units.la: Habe-
units.tr: We have-

units.la: Thomas Aquinas vetus Christi Corpus ex Eucharistia tollit. Habemus hic confitentem reum, quòd corpus illud Eucharisticum seu Missaticum, sub speciebus Hostiæ modo arcano, invisibili & indivisibili latens, & determinata distantia singularum partium ab invicem destitutum, non fit verum Christi corpus. Quid igitur est? Spectrum, nihil, verbo, Mysterium Babylonis fronte dignum.
units.tr: Thomas Aquinas removes the old body of Christ from the Eucharist. Here we have the accused confessing that the Eucharistic or Mass body, lying hidden under the species of the Host in a secret, invisible and indivisible manner, and lacking a determinate distance of its parts from one another, is not the true body of Christ. What then is it? A specter, a nothing; in a word, a mystery worthy of Babylon's brazenness.

units.la: XLVI. Mysterium isthoc corporis Christi in Missa sacreti, arcani, mystici, invisibilis, Christus ipse abhorruit, & ab ejus fide dehortatus omnes graviter est. Matth. xxiv. 26. 27. Si dicant vobis, inquit, Ecce in penetralibus est, ne credatis. Nam ut fulgur exit ab oriente, & lucet usque ad occidentem, sic erit præsentia Filii hominis.
units.tr: XLVI. Christ himself abhorred this mystery of the body of Christ in the Mass, which is secret, hidden, mystical and invisible, and he warned everyone very seriously against believing in it. Matt. 24:26-27. If they say to you, he says, Behold, he is in the inner chambers, do not believe it. For as lightning comes out of the east and shines even to the west, so will be the presence of the Son of man.

units.la: Non potuisset certè Christi mysterium impietatis pontificiæ, totiúsque Papalis Monarchiæ oculum impetere directius. Dicunt enim illi, Hic est. Ita Scotus 4. dist. 9. q. 3. scribit: Verum est, quod HOC est corpus meum, & HIC est corpus meum. Neque decantatius quidquam præsentia reali, substantiali sub accidentibus Symbolorum, nec non phrasibus illis, esse, sub accidentibus contineri, poni in altari, asservari in ciborio. Et qui hoc dicunt, se Vicarios Christi, omnem potestatem habentes, Sacerdotes peccata expiantes, Prophetas infallibiles jactant, adeóque hoc dicunt ut ψευδόχριστοι falsi Christi, & ψευδοπροφῆται falsi Prophetæ. Neque tantùm eos Christus perstringit, qui dicunt, Hic est; sed etiam eos, qui dicunt: ἐν ἐρήμῳ, ἐν ταμείοις in Eremo, in Promptuariis, Ciboriis est. In deserto sunt Monasteria Monachorum: in urbibus sunt ταμεῖα penetralia, promptuaria, Templa; utrobique sunt ciboria, loci cancellis septi, conclavia, in quibus hostia in quosvis usus reconditur, asservatur, & ex quibus promitur. Seductionem insuper Pseudo-prophetarum & Pseudo-christorum illorum ad credendam præsentiam Christi in hoc vel illo loco in eremo, promptuariis refutat Salvator ab Ἐπιφανείᾳ conspicabilitate & claritate adventus sui in carne cujuslibet deinceps exspectandi. Comparat enim illum cum fulgure, exeunte ab oriente, & lucente in occidentem. Quæ ratio directè opposita est doctrinæ de præsentia Corporis Christi arcana, secreta, invisibili, Christi in carne. Adventus deinceps Ἐπιφανὴς clarus, conspicuus, nec alius erit. Ergo, sic ipse Salvator arguit, non est quærendus deinceps hic, illic, in deserto, in penetrali, ante conspicuum illum adventum, ultimum scilicet ad judicium. Quo igitur loco habendum sit ingens illud Hierarchiæ papalis de corpore Christi in Missa arcano & invisibili modo præsente & sacrificando mysterium, abunde liquet.
units.tr: Surely the mystery of Christ could not have struck more directly at the eye of papal impiety and of the whole Papal monarchy. For they say, Here he is. Thus Scotus writes (4 dist. 9 q. 3): It is true that THIS is my body, and HERE is my body. Nothing is sung more often than real presence, substantial presence under the accidents of the symbols, and those phrases too: to be contained under the accidents, to be placed on the altar, to be kept in the ciborium. And those who say this boast that they are Christ's vicars, having all power, priests who expiate sins, infallible prophets; and so they speak as false Christs (ψευδόχριστοι) and false prophets (ψευδοπροφῆται). Nor does Christ rebuke only those who say, Here he is, but also those who say in the desert (ἐν ἐρήμῳ) or in the inner chambers (ἐν ταμείοις), that is, in the wilderness, in the storerooms, in the ciboria. In the desert are the monasteries of the monks; in the cities are the storerooms (ταμεῖα), the inner chambers, the temples. In both places there are ciboria, enclosed places with railings, cupboards in which the host is stored away for whatever uses, and from which it is taken out. Moreover, the Saviour refutes the seduction of those false prophets and false Christs who would have us believe Christ present in this or that place, in the wilderness or in the storerooms, by pointing to the manifest (ἐπιφανείᾳ) and conspicuous coming of himself in the flesh, which everyone is henceforth to await. For he compares it to lightning that comes out of the east and shines into the west. This reasoning is directly opposed to the doctrine of a secret, hidden, invisible presence of Christ's body, of Christ in the flesh. His coming hereafter will be manifest (ἐπιφανής), bright, conspicuous, and no other. Therefore, so the Saviour himself argues, he is not to be sought henceforth here or there, in the desert or in the inner chamber, before that conspicuous coming, namely the last one, at judgment. Where, then, the vast mystery of the papal hierarchy, that the body of Christ is present and sacrificed in the Mass in a hidden and invisible manner, ought to be placed is abundantly clear.

units.la: XLVII. Quintò Babylonis Magnæ titulum Hierarchia Papalis meretur, quia dogmata sua, Sacrorum Eleusiniorum instar, occultat, & sacra sua lingua peregrina, etiam clam demurmurando, peragit.
units.tr: XLVII. Fifthly, the papal hierarchy earns the title of Great Babylon because it hides its doctrines, like the Eleusinian rites, and performs its sacred rites in a foreign tongue, even muttering them under its breath.

units.la: XLVIII. Olim quidem Ethnicorum Theologi, diviniora, quæ ita rebantur, dogmata, ne in vulgus publicata vilescerent, sacro quodam silentio involuta tenuere. Orpheus, citante Justino M. Orat. ad gentes, & Clemente Alexandrino Protrept. p. 36. de Deo verba facturus, ita adhortatus est: Φθέγξομαι εἰς ἡμὶς ἐσὶ, ἡμῖν δὲ ἱερὰ βίβλος Πάντες ἡμῶς· σὺ δ' ἀκοὴ Φαεσφόρος ἑχοντι μύσης Μυσῆ, ἐξαιρίω γὰρ ἀληθία. Effabor, queis fas est, aures claude profanæ, Quisquis es, illustri Musæ, sed edite Luna Audi, verba loquor.
units.tr: XLVIII. Indeed, of old the theologians of the Gentiles, thinking their more divine doctrines to be such, kept them wrapped in a certain sacred silence, lest they become cheap by being published among the common people. Orpheus, as Justin Martyr cites in his Exhortation to the Greeks and Clement of Alexandria in the Protrepticus p. 36, when about to speak of God, urged thus: "I will speak to those for whom it is lawful [Φθέγξομαι οἷς θέμις ἐστί]; shut your ears, profane ones, whoever you are; but you, illustrious Muse, bright offspring of the Moon, listen: I speak words."

units.la: Ex quo illud, <bl>Ἡμὲς δὲ Ἱερὰ βίβλοι</bl>, Sacerdotes Ægyptii, quoties Deorum suorum fata recenserent, Luciano Hom. 3. de Sacrif. teste, præmittere soliti sunt. Pythagoras veneranda doctrinarum mysteria ab exactissima mentis expiatione exordiri solitus, sacrum, quem conscripsit sermonem sic exorsus est:
units.tr: Hence the saying "But we are sacred books" [Ἡμεῖς δὲ ἱεραὶ βίβλοι]: the Egyptian priests, whenever they recounted the fates of their gods, were accustomed to begin with it, as Lucian bears witness (Hom. 3, de Sacrificiis). Pythagoras, who was accustomed to begin the venerable mysteries of his doctrines with the most exact purification of the mind, opened the sacred discourse he wrote in this way:

units.la: Ὢ νέοι, ἀλλὰ σιγᾶτε μεθ' ἡσυχίας τὰ ἱερὰ μαθόντες.
units.tr: "O young men, but be silent, having learned the sacred things in quiet." [Ὦ νέοι, ἀλλὰ σιγᾶτε μεθ' ἡσυχίας τὰ ἱερὰ μαθόντες.]

units.la: O Juvenes tacita colite hæc pia sacra quiete.
units.tr: "O young men, cherish these pious sacred things in peaceful silence."

units.la: Pindari quoque illa citat Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. I. μὴ πᾶσι ἁπλῶς ἀναμφίλεκτα ἐξ ἀρχαίων λόγων, ἐὰν ἐν τισὶν ἱεροῖς σιγῆς ἔδοις. Non apud omnes licere veterem aperire orationem, præterquam fidelissimis silentii viis. Plotinus, Platonicæ sectæ Philosophus Ennead. vj. 9. de visione & fruitione Dei loquens, inquit, τὸ δὲ ἕκαστον ἀλλ' ἢ τὰ τῶν μυστηρίων τὴν ἡ Φθέγματα, τὰ μὴ ἐκφέρειν εἰ μὴ μεμυημένοις. Hoc igitur mysteriorum talium institutio indicat, ubi vetat id hominibus nondum initiatis expiatisque patefacere. Ita omnino de talibus in publicum silebant, aut si quæ proloquerentur, iis verborum involucris sensus suos tegebant, ut nisi iisdem dogmatibus jam imbuti, haud ita facile eos intelligerent. Quomodo Pherecydes apud Laërtium scripta sua Thaleti mittens, Ἀσφα δ' ἀν Φιλόγυ φιλοσοφίαν, τὰ ἀλλα χρὴ νοῦν. Ἀπαντα γὰρ αἰνίγματα. Quæcunque ad Deos pertinentia allegoricè sunt intelligenda. Omnia enim scripta sunt ænigmatica. Pertinent huc Chaldæorum & Pythagoræ symbola, & præsertim Ægyptiorum hieroglyphica, quæ integro volumine Pierius Valerianus, & post eum in Oedipo Ægyptiaco Athanasius Kircherus collegit, explicavitque.
units.tr: Clement of Alexandria also cites these words of Pindar (Strom. I): "It is not permitted for everyone simply to open the ancient discourses, except in the most faithful ways of silence" [μὴ πᾶσιν ἁπλῶς ἀναμφίλεκτα ἐξ ἀρχαίων λόγων, ἐὰν ἐν τισὶν ἱεροῖς σιγῆς ἔδοις]. Plotinus, the Platonist philosopher, speaking of the vision and enjoyment of God (Ennead VI.9), says: "Each thing, except the utterances of the mysteries, which are not to be brought forth except to the initiated." So the institution of such mysteries indicates this, where it forbids revealing them to men not yet initiated and purified. Thus in general they kept silent about such things in public, or if they spoke of them, they veiled their meanings in verbal wrappings, so that unless already steeped in the same doctrines, people would not readily understand them. As Pherecydes, sending his writings to Thales, according to Laertius: "Whatever concerns the gods is to be understood allegorically, for all things are written as enigmas." To this belong the symbols of the Chaldeans and of Pythagoras, and especially the hieroglyphics of the Egyptians, which Pierius Valerianus collected and explained in an entire volume, and after him Athanasius Kircher in his Oedipus Aegyptiacus.

units.la: XLIX. Eodem instituto, & ratione instituti eadem ceptum apud Gentiles olim fuit, ut ad ipsa etiam sacra & Divini cultus ceremonias non omnes auditores spectato- resve admitterent.
units.tr: XLIX. By the same method, and for the same reason, it was once the custom among the Gentiles that not all hearers or spectators were admitted even to their sacred rites and the ceremonies of divine worship.

units.la: Ita enim Diagoræ Atheniensi Atheismi crimen impactum esse, quòd non tantum sacrorum Orphei morem & rationem in medium protulerit, sed etiam Eleusiniæ Cereris & Cabirorum mysteria vulgaverit, Athenagoras Orat. pro Christ. memorat. Sacra quoque Isiaca, Bacchi orgia, Sacra Saboziorum, Cybeles Deûm matris, Bonæ Deæ, Corybantia, Veneris Cypriæ, mysteria Alimuntis, aliæque Ceremoniæ, fœditate sua tenebris, & quo curatissimè tegebantur, silentio dignissimæ, ipsa tamen occultatione, silentio & sanctitatis qualibuscúnque irritamentis venerationem adeptæ sunt. Apud Virg. Æneid.vij.
units.tr: Athenagoras, in his Oratio pro Christianis, records that Diagoras of Athens was charged with atheism because he not only made public the custom and rites of the Orphic mysteries but also revealed the mysteries of Eleusinian Ceres and the Cabiri. The Isiac rites, the orgies of Bacchus, the rites of the Sabazii, of Cybele the mother of the gods, of the Good Goddess, the Corybantic rites, the mysteries of Cyprian Venus, the mysteries of Alimus, and other ceremonies, were worthy of silence because of their foulness and because they were hidden with the greatest care in darkness. Yet by this very concealment, by silence and by whatever stimulus of sanctity they had, they won reverence for themselves. In Virgil, Aeneid 7:

units.la: Procul, o procul este profani Conclamat Vates.
units.tr: "Begone, begone, you profane ones!" cries the prophetess.

units.la: Seneca enim teste, sanctiora tantùm sacrorum initiati sciunt. In sacrificiis inprimis jubebatur populus favere linguis sacris pascere linguas; quæ propriæ & usitatæ erant in sacris dicendi formulæ, quibus silentium imperabatur. Atque ad id significandum Harpocratem tanquam silentii Deum, quem Græci Σιγαλίωνα vocarunt, sacris suis Ægyptii adhibuerunt. Quò referendæ silentii Deæ, Angerona silentii Dea, ore obligato atque signato in ara Volupiæ collocata: Tacita, à Numa Pompilio institu-ta, aliæ, Plura eam in rem viri doctissimi, Guilhelmus Stuckius de Sacris & Sacrificiis Gentil. p. 80. 81. nec non Tobias Pfannerus Syst. Theol. Gentilis cap. j. 6. 7. 8. 13. eruerunt.
units.tr: As Seneca bears witness, only the initiated know the more sacred things of the rites. In sacrifices above all, the people were ordered to keep their tongues favourable and feed their tongues, which were the proper and customary formulas of speech in the rites by which silence was enjoined. To signify this, the Egyptians used Harpocrates in their sacred rites as the god of silence, whom the Greeks called Sigalion. To the same purpose belongs Angerona, the goddess of silence, placed on the altar of Volupia with her mouth bound and sealed; the goddess Tacita, instituted by Numa Pompilius, is another. Learned men have brought many more examples to light on this matter: William Stuckius, de Sacris & Sacrificiis Gentilium, pp. 80–81, and also Tobias Pfanner, Systema Theologiae Gentilis, chapters 1, 6, 7, 8 and 13.

units.la: L. Quid verò Papalis Hierarchia, unde etiam hic Babylonis titulo frontem ejus insignitam constet? Jam supra equidem occupavimus dicere, uti dogmata quædam, quæ ob mysterium scribi non potuerint, velut traditiones arcanà ad se devoluta jactet: uti Missæ sacra occultis murmuribus perficiat occultétque. Quis insuper ignorat, quàm studiosè accuratèque populum suum, laicorum probrosò nomine ad infima subsellia detrusum, mysteriorum ad se duntaxat pertinentium praetextu, à lectione Scripturæ, omníque rerum sacrarum distincta cognitione arceat, sibíque adeò mysteria, qualiacunque illa sunt, ut gryphes aurum, & canis Æsopicus fœnum, retineat? Nota in vulgus sunt emblemata Mystarum, veluti Hosii, qui de Verbo Bb 2 Dei
units.tr: L. But what is the Papal hierarchy, and whence does it appear that this forehead bears the title of Babylon? Indeed I have already above undertaken to say that it puts forward certain doctrines, which could not be written down because of their mystery, as hidden traditions handed down to itself, and that it performs and conceals the sacred rite of the Mass with secret mutterings. Moreover, who does not know how carefully and diligently it keeps its people, whom it has thrust down to the lowest benches under the shameful name of laity, away from the reading of Scripture and from all distinct knowledge of sacred things, on the pretext of mysteries that pertain only to itself; and how it keeps those mysteries, whatever they are, for itself, as griffins keep gold and Aesop's dog keeps hay? The emblems of the initiates are well known among the common people, as Hosius, in On the Word of God, Bb 2 ...

units.la: Imitatio gentilium / Pontificii dogmata / quædam occultant / lectione Scripturæ plebem arcent
units.tr: Imitation of the Gentiles. The Papists conceal certain doctrines; they keep the common people away from the reading of Scripture.

units.la: Dei t. j. p. 640. sic scribit: Laicis lectionem scripturæ permittere, est sanctum dare canibus, & margaritas ante porcos projicere. Hardingus quoque contra Juellum art. 15. sect. 9. Minimè, inquit, consentaneum videtur, ut quisque curiosus & putidus idiota Biblia suo sermone perlegat. Addit que putidus ille Sycophanta, certum esse, nonnulla capita & historias V. T. eam materiam continere, quæ malarum cogitationum occasionem præbitura videtur, si mulieres, virgines, adolescentes, ea legere sinantur. Alphonsus Virvesius Phil. 2. contra August. Confess. Lutherum accusat graviter, quòd liberum fecerit sanctarum scripturarum mysteria evulgari, sanctum canibus dari, & margaritas inter porcos spargi. Antonius Legatus Pyranensis suasit, ut hominibus lectione Epistolarum Pauli publicè interdiceretur, eò quòd nimis Lutheranis faverent. Johannes quoque Montolanus Bononiæ ultricibus flammis consumptus fuit, eò quòd S. Pauli ad Romanos Epistolam publicè prælegisset. Constátque hæreticæ pravitatis Inquisitores inter cætera de hoc capite severè quærere, anne Biblia quis legisset? Ea qui legerit, non impetrata ab Episcopo venia, capitalis sceleris reus habetur. Ne igitur etiam legi possint facilè, versionem eorundem in vernaculum idioma prohibere placuit. Taceo calumnias, quibus à lectione eorum miseram plebem absterrent, veluti quòd sint liber obscurus, idiotis periculosissimus, vix doctoribus, qui in legendis iis omnem ætatem contriverunt, intelligibilis, sensuum varietate perplexus, quorum proin intelligentia sit intricata & dissicilis, à laicis abscondita, soli Ecclesiæ seu Hierarchiæ, imò verò Pontifici soli unique obvia & expositæ, & ex unius Romani Apollinis penetralibus arcessenda.
units.tr: LI. Thus indeed one lives in Papacy; thus the people are mocked. By these arts every desire to know is extinguished in them. Thus the Bible, the testament of the Father, is snatched from people's hands as if they were unworthy of its mysteries, and the keys of knowledge are impiously hidden by those new lawyers who do not wish to enter the kingdom of heaven and who shut its door against others. Since man is born with a desire to know, and inquiry proceeds from that desire, which is the only way to the knowledge of truth, and which, if it is strong, cannot be at rest, they have tried to remove this by two means, fear and reason, and to take it out of men's minds. By fear, when they have passed a law ordering that one sole religion, the most detestable and idolatrous, be worshipped, and when they set up the most atrocious punishments against those who dare to murmur against it. But since it is inborn in the human mind to strive after what is forbidden and to desire what is denied, and little is achieved by punishments among those among whom [they tried further]; so that this desire might be extinguished, or at least checked, by reason as well. For since all desire lies in thought, they judged that care must be taken that the people should not think about the truth of religion. And this could be achieved in the following way: they could be persuaded that accurate knowledge of the truth either does not concern them but only certain particular initiates, or is impossible, or is not necessary, since provision has already been abundantly made for religion and for their salvation. Those who have been so instructed and imbued by their teachers easily brought themselves to let go of all care for religion, and to entangle all their faith in the faith of the initiates whom they have chosen as their guides, content to believe whatever those men believe, even though they are ignorant of what they believe.

units.la: LI. Sic planè in Papatu vivitur, sic ludificatur populus, his artibus omne sciendi desiderium in illo extinguitur, sic Biblia testamentum Patris, populi, ceu mysteriorum ejus cognitione indigni, manibus excutiuntur, & à novis illis legis-peritis intrare Regnum Cœlorum non aventibus, & ejusdem aditum aliis præcludentibus κλεὶς γνώσεως Claves cognitionis impiè absconduntur. Cùmque ad sciendi cupiditatem homo natus sit, & à sciendi cupiditate proficiscatur inquisitio, unica ad veritatis cognitionem via, atque ea si intensa sit, quiescere non possit; hanc duplici via, metu & ratione amoliri, & ex animis hominum tollere, conati sunt. Et metu quidem, cùm ejusmodi legem tulerunt, qua unica quæpiam, & maximè detestanda & idololatrica coli jubetur religio, atque adversus eos, qui vel mutire contra ausi fuerint, atrocissima quæque supplicia constituuntur. Cùm verò insitum humano ingenio sit, niti in vetitum, & negata cupere, atque suppliciis non multùm proficiatur apud eos, apud quos ἰσότ... ulterius tentarunt, ut ratione etiam desiderium ifthoc extingueretur, vel saltem sufflaminaretur. Cùm enim omne desiderium in cogitatione situm sit, ne de veritate religionis cogitaret populus, operam dandam censuerunt. Atqui id assequi licuit ea ratione, quòd persuaderi ei potuit, veritatis accuratam cognitionem vel nihil ad se pertinere, sed ad certos duntaxat mystas quospiam, vel impossibilem esse, vel non necessariam, cùm abundè religioni, & saluti suæ jam provisum sit. Qui ita à doctoribus suis instituti imbutique sunt, facilè ab se impetrárunt, ut abjecta religionis cura omni fidem suam in Mystarum, quos sibi duces delegerunt, fide implicarent, contenti credere, quicquid illi credunt, ignari licet eorum, quæ credunt.
units.tr: LI. Thus indeed one lives under the Papacy; thus the people is deceived. By these arts every desire for knowledge is extinguished in it; thus the Bible, the Father's testament, is wrested from people's hands as though they were unworthy of its mysteries, and the keys of knowledge [κλεὶς γνώσεως] are impiously hidden away by those new lawyers who do not wish to enter the kingdom of heaven and who bar the way to it for others. And since man is born with a desire to know, and inquiry proceeds from that desire, which is the only way to the knowledge of truth, and which, if it is intense, cannot rest, they have tried to remove this by a double way, by fear and by reason, and to take it out of men's minds. By fear indeed, when they passed a law ordering that one particular religion, the most detestable and idolatrous, be worshipped, and established the most savage punishments against those who dared to murmur against it. But since it is inborn in the human mind to strive after what is forbidden and to desire what is denied, and since punishments achieve little among those people, they went further, so that this desire might also be extinguished, or at least checked, by reason. For since every desire lies in thought, they judged that care must be taken that the people should not think about the truth of religion. And this they could accomplish in this way: they could persuade the people that accurate knowledge of the truth either has nothing to do with them but belongs only to certain initiates, or is impossible or unnecessary, since provision has already been amply made for religion and for their salvation. Those who have been so taught and steeped in this by their teachers easily brought themselves to cast off all care for religion and to entangle their faith entirely in the faith of the initiates whom they have chosen as their guides, content to believe whatever those men believe, even though they are ignorant of what they believe.

units.la: LII. Qua in re implicitæ fidei, hoc est, Labyrintho implicatæ, & εἰς ἀδηλον Φεροφόρης Carbonariæ, & atro carbone notandæ, commentum mirè equidem simul infelicem credulitatem populi, simul mysterium illud iniquitatis promovit. Carbonarii lepidam historiam lippis & tonsoribus notam Hosius de authoritate Scripturæ sol. 26. narrat. Est autem fides implicita, qua creduntur fidei mysteria non distincte in semetipsis, sed in communi quodam principio Romanensis, cùm non Scripturam, sed Ecclesiam, sive ἀοὶ̈ς ἱ̈φα Pythagoricum Papæ faciant, planum est, illis fidem illam implicitam nihil aliud esse, quàm voluntariam deditionem in obsequium Papæ, sine ullo examine eorum, quæ is præcipit ad normam Scripturæ, seu, ut clariùs loquamur, firmum constansque propositum loquendi faciendique, quod Papa cum devota sibi hominum multitudine loquitur, facitque. Ἀδιαφανῶς ... inexploratam rerum non demonstratarum, & non certarum assensionem S. Theodoretus alicubi appellat. Proin etiam fidem vel cœcam faciunt, vel non nisi fumida & incerta face instruunt, utpote quam per ignorantiam melius, quàm per notitiam describi, Bellarm. de Justif. lib. j. cap. 7. diserte asserit. Hoc videlicet illi satagunt, ut populum ea ratione à veritatis studio avertant, animósque ejus humiles, & cœcæ obedientiæ habiles reddant, quo melius servire, ab ipsis solis pendere, neque ultra quicquam sapere assuescat. Atqui non fides implicita hæc fides & ignorantia, sed ἀπο- ὀσία defectio à vera fide est, secundùm testimonia Sacræ Scripturæ 1 Tim. iv. 1. 2. 3. 2 Thess. ii. 10. 11. 12.
units.tr: LII. In this matter the invention of "implicit faith," that is, faith entangled as in a labyrinth, and carried into the unseen [εἰς ἄδηλον], to be marked with the charcoal-burner's black coal, has wonderfully promoted both a miserable credulity of the people and that mystery of iniquity. Hosius, in On the Authority of Scripture, sol. 26, tells the charming story of the charcoal-burner, known to people with sore eyes and to barbers. Now implicit faith is that by which the mysteries of faith are believed not distinctly in themselves, but in some common principle of the Roman Church. Since they make not Scripture but the Church, or the Pope, the Pythagorean "he himself said it" [αὐτὸς ἔφα], it is plain that for them that implicit faith is nothing other than a voluntary surrender to the obedience of the Pope, without any examination of the things he commands according to the rule of Scripture; or, to speak more clearly, a firm and constant resolve to speak and to act as the Pope speaks and acts, together with his devoted multitude of men. S. Theodoret somewhere calls it [obscurely, ἀδιαφανῶς] an unexamined assent to things not demonstrated and not certain. Accordingly they also make faith either blind, or furnish it only with a smoky and uncertain torch, since Bellarmine, On Justification, book 1, chapter 7, expressly asserts that it is described by ignorance better than by knowledge. This is exactly what they strive for: to turn the people away from the pursuit of truth in this way, and to make their minds humble and fit for blind obedience, so that they may be accustomed to serve better, to depend on them alone, and to think no further. But this implicit faith and ignorance is not faith at all, but a defection [ἀποστασία] from true faith, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, 1 Tim. 4:1–3; 2 Thess. 2:10–12.

units.la: 2 Tim. iv. 3. 4. Apoc. xiii. 16. Et qui suam fidem ea ratione hominibus substringunt filii scortationum insigniri solent.
units.tr: 2 Tim. iv. 3. 4. Apoc. xiii. 16. And those who bind their faith to men in this way are usually marked as sons of harlotry.

units.la: LIII. Quid porro dicam de vægrandi injuria, quam Mystæ illi sub mysteriorum sibi solis cognitorum prætextu faciunt plebi suæ, quam à rerum sacrarum cognitione, discretione & dijudicatione, ita arcent, ut sendentariam iis assen-
units.tr: LIII. What more shall I say of the wrong done to the laity by those initiates, who under the pretext of mysteries known to themselves alone keep their people so far from knowledge, discernment and judgment of sacred things that they leave them only the sedentary necessity of assenting in everything, like mourners sitting on benches, and, as is common to the obedience owed to the Pope.

units.la: obsequium Papæ, communiter pertinet.
units.tr: obedience owed to the Pope commonly pertains.

units.la: nec non tyrannis ea, qua plebem, eos merè animalem, à rerum Saassentiendi in omnibus necessitatem solam, velut in subscelliis plorantium, relinquant. Scilicet homo spiritualis judicat omnia, ipse vero à nemine judicatur. 1 Cor. 11, 15.
units.tr: and likewise the tyranny by which they leave the people, whom they regard as merely animal, with only the necessity of assenting in all things, like mourners on the benches, away from the knowledge of sacred things. Of course, the spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one. 1 Cor. 11, 15.

units.la: Spiritualis autem ille homo, inquiunt, non laici, non Imperatores, Principes, nobiles, plebeji ulli, quantumvis pii & docti, sunt, sed Papa, & quos ille Spiritu suo dominante dignatur. Solus ille judicat omnia, & à nemine judicari potest. Ita Gratianus dist. 40. Si Papa innumerabiles populos catervatim secum ducat primo mancipio gehennæ, ejus culpas redarguere præsumit Mortalium nullus, quia cunctos ipse judicaturus, à nemine judicandus. Quin Bonifacius VIII. ipse Extra. de major. & obed. ita sibi lenocinatur: Si deviat Spiritualis (Papa) à solo Deo, non ab homine potest judicari, testante Apostolo: Spiritualis homo judicat omnia, ipse autem à nemine judicatur. Sic laici utpote Spiritu dominante, judicante omnia Papæ destituti, & servitutis Spiritu solo præditi, animales illi homines erunt. Atque id parum, nisi etiam canes & porci, quibus secretum dare nefas est. Sanè jam Innocentius III. Papa Epist. ad Metenses Decret. Lib. v. tit. 7. plebem, ceu profanum vulgus, scripturarum sublimitate procul arcendum, & si quis simplex vel indoctus, hoc est, laicus præsumpserit aliquid, ex legis, bestiam, quæ montem tetigisset, lapidandam scisscentis præscripto (Exod. xix. 13.) severè, imò plane vindicandum pronunciavit. Hinc adeo judicium discretionis veri à falso eidem abjudicant, & in conciliis ad suffragandum vocari posse, quamvis pios & devotos, pernegant. Sic scilicet non aliter, per calcatam Dominicam familiam ad Divinos honores, Divinam potestatem grassandam fuerat.
units.tr: Yet, they say, this "spiritual man" is not laymen, not emperors, princes, nobles, or any common people, however devout and learned they may be, but the Pope and those whom he, ruling by his Spirit, deigns to honour. He alone judges all things, and he can be judged by no one. So Gratian, dist. 40: "If the Pope should lead countless peoples in droves to the first slavery of hell, no mortal presumes to rebuke his faults, since he himself is to judge all, and is to be judged by no one." Indeed Boniface VIII himself, Extra, de major. et obed., flatters himself in the same way: "If the spiritual man (the Pope) goes astray, he cannot be judged by anyone but God alone, since the Apostle testifies: 'The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.'" So laymen, being without the Spirit who rules and judges all things in the Pope, and endowed only with the spirit of servitude, will be those animal men. And this would be a small matter, unless dogs and swine are also meant, to whom it is wrong to give what is holy. Certainly Pope Innocent III, in his letter to the Metensians (Decretals, bk. v, tit. 7), ruled that the common people, like the profane crowd, must be kept far away from the lofty heights of Scripture, and that if any "simple or unlearned" person, that is, a layman, should presume to do anything, he must be punished severely, indeed plainly, in accordance with the law that ordered the beast that touched the mountain to be stoned (Exod. 19:13). Hence they deny the common people the power to distinguish truth from falsehood, and they flatly refuse that the pious and devout may be called to vote in councils. Thus, it seems, the Lord's family was trampled underfoot so that divine honours and divine power could be seized in no other way.

units.la: LIV. Jam & ipsa quoque sacra ceremoniásque ita Mysta-
units.tr: LIV. Moreover, the Papist mystagogues also conduct the sacred rites and ceremonies

units.la: gogi Pontificii peragunt, ut Gentilibus neutiquam absimiles, non obscurè ab iis laicos ceu profanos arceant. Inde murmura illa, & barbari populo susurri in consecratione Missæ, sacrúmque in scenica actione potissima silentium. Vix certè ovum ovo similius est, quàm exemplum supra ex Beleth aliisque narratum de Pastoribus, quòd verba consecrationis intellecta in agro repetiissent, cœlesti igne consumptis, & illud Tullii Hostilii Romani Regis, quem Plinius Lib. xxxviii. 2. fulmine ictum narrat, eò quòd ex Numæ Pompilii libris eodem, quo ille, sacrificio Jovem Cœlo devocare conatus esset. Quomodo pari ratione Ludovicus Cœlius Rhodiginus Antiq. Lect. lib. xvj. 14. sic sacrificulum consecrantem cum eodem Tullio comparat. Quæstio diu agitata veteribus est, insitne vis aliqua verbis, certa quadam enuntiantis formula? Equidem veritatis Christianæ cultor quis possit inficiari? Quando Princeps ille rerum ac summi Patris Filius, ex vero verus Deus, præfatione Sacerdotis brevissima fevocetur, eliciaturve à Cœlesti sede. Cui simile quiddam & priscorum vana superstitio aut habuit aut credidit, quando & Tullium Hostilium Pisonis tradidere monumenta, ex Numæ libris eodem operatum sacro, Jovem elicere Cœlo, quem & inde Elicium vocabant, quod in Fastis cecinit Poëta nobilis, conatum, &c.
units.tr: in such a way that they are in no way unlike the rites of the Gentiles, and they plainly keep laymen away from them as profane. Hence come those murmurings and the whispers of the barbarous people during the consecration of the Mass, and the silence that is the chief feature of the sacred stage-play. Surely an egg is hardly more like an egg than this is like the example, related above from Beleth and others, of the shepherds who repeated the words of consecration, which they had understood, in a field, and were consumed by heavenly fire; and like that of Tullus Hostilius, the Roman king whom Pliny (bk. xxxviii, 2) reports as struck by lightning because he had tried, by the same sacrifice as in Numa Pompilius's books, to summon Jupiter down from heaven. In the same way Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus (Antiq. Lect., bk. xvi, 14) compares the little sacrificer consecrating with this same Tullus. The question has long been debated among the ancients: does some power lie in words, in a certain fixed formula of the speaker? Indeed, who among the worshippers of Christian truth could deny it? When that Prince of things and the Son of the supreme Father, true God from true God, is summoned and drawn down from the heavenly seat by a very brief preface of the priest. Something similar the vain superstition of the ancients either had or believed, when the records also handed down that Tullus Hostilius, having performed the rite by the books of Numa, drew Jupiter down from heaven, whom they therefore called Elicius, as the noble poet sang in the Fasti, the attempt, etc.

units.la: LV. Inde inprimis est, quòd sacris suis lingua peregrina populo incognita defungi solent. Salutationes scilicet, preces, hymnos, Canonem Missæ, alia, non vernacula, sed Latina duntaxat lingua exequi leges eorum moresque jubent. Ausiqué sunt Tridentini Mystæ Sess. xxij. can. 9. anathemati subjicere eos, qui vulgari duntaxat lingua Missam celebrari debere asserunt. Iidem cap. 8. Etsi, inquiunt, Missa magnam contineat populi fidelis eruditionem, non tamen expedire visum est Patribus, ut vulgari lingua passim celebraretur. Mox tamen mandant Pastoribus, ut frequenter inter Missarum celebrationem vel per se, vel per per alios ex iis, quæ in Missa leguntur, aliquid exponant, atque inter cætera sanctissimi sacrificii hujus mysterium aliquod declarent, diebus præsertim dominicis & festis, addita ratione, ne oves Christi esuriant, neve parvuli panem petant, & non sit qui frangat. Attenti ad rem suam aliquid exponi, & sacrificii hujus mysterium aliquod declarari jubent. Sed væ illis, qui Canonem, consecrationem inprimis, vernaculo idiomate repræsentare fustinuerint. Mysteria scilicet ad Mystas, non ad putidos idiotas, uti supra Hardingus, pertinent. Sacramenta enim, ita Bellarminus tom. 2. de effectu Sacram. lib. v. 31. scribit, requirunt majestatem & reverentiam, ea autem melius conservatur, si utamur lingua non vulgari & communi.
units.tr: Yet although St Paul (1 Cor. xii. 2–23) assails the use of a foreign tongue in sacred things with many weighty arguments, Bellarmine, as if contradicting him to his face, opposes him: There is, he says, no necessity compelling the sacraments to be administered in the vernacular tongue. Why so, when it has plainly been held contrary to the Apostle? The offering of the sacrifice, he says, consists more in the thing than in the words. The words are not directed to instruct the hearers, but first to consecrate the element, etc. The element, however, understands no language. Second, they are directed to God, who understands all languages. To say nothing of the false hypothesis of an external sacrifice, nor of the shameless conflict with the sayings of St Paul, he clearly also quarrels with the Tridentine initiates, being himself an initiate and a Cardinal. For if, as they judged, the Mass contains a great instruction of the faithful people, and therefore something must frequently be explained to the people and some mystery declared, lest there be none to break bread for the one asking, how is it that nothing in the Mass is directed to the hearers, and no necessity requires the vernacular idiom? Indeed, since it has pleased them that the Mass be celebrated with many words, and most of them not so much directed to God as to the faithful communicants, what madness has driven the priests so that they do not at least pronounce those words, prayers, hymns, etc., in the vernacular and intelligible tongue?

units.la: Tametsi vero S. Paulus 1 Cor. xii. 2-23. pluribus prægnantibúsque argumentis peregrinæ in sacris linguæ usum oppugnat, idem tamen Bellarminus velut in os ei contradicens, repugnat: Nulla, inquiens, est necessitas, quae cogat vulgari lingua Sacramenta ministrari. Quid ita vero, cum Apostolo plane contra visum fuerit? Sacrificii, inquit, oblatio magis in re, quàm in verbis consistit. Verba non diriguntur ad auditores instruendos, sed primò ad elementum consecrandum &c. Elementum autem nullam linguam intelligit; Secundò, ad Deum, qui omnes linguas intelligit. Ut nihil de falsa sacrificii externi hypothesi, nec non de pugna effronti cum sancti Pauli effatis dicam, aperte etiam cum Tridentinis Mystagogis Cardinalis, Mystagogus & ipse, pugnat. Si enim, quod illi censuerunt, Missa magnam populi fidelis eruditionem continet, atque ideo frequenter aliquid, mysterium aliquod populo, ne panem petenti desit, qui frangat, declarandum est, quomodo in Missa nihil est, quod ad auditores dirigatur, nulláque necessitas vernaculum idioma postulat? Quinimò cum Missam multis verbis celebrari placuerit, & talibus quidem plerisque, quæ non tam ad Deum, quàm ad fideles communicantes diriguntur, quis furor agitavit sacrisiculos, ut non ea saltem verba, preces hymnos &c. vernacula & intelligibili lingua pronuntiarent?
units.tr: Although St Paul (1 Cor. 12:2–23 [sic]) attacks, with many weighty arguments, the use of a foreign language in the sacred rites, Bellarmine nevertheless, as if contradicting him to his face, opposes him: "There is no necessity," he says, "that compels the sacraments to be administered in the vulgar tongue." Why so, when the matter has clearly been decided against the Apostle? "The offering of the sacrifice," he says, "consists more in the thing than in the words. The words are not addressed to the hearers for their instruction, but first to the element to be consecrated, etc. The element, however, understands no language; secondly, they are addressed to God, who understands all languages." To say nothing of the false hypothesis of an external sacrifice, nor of the brazen clash with the sayings of St Paul, he also plainly disagrees with the Tridentine mystagogues, being himself a mystagogue as a Cardinal. For if, as they judged, "the Mass contains great instruction for the faithful people, and therefore something frequently has to be explained to the people, lest there be none to break bread for those who ask for it, how is it that in the Mass there is nothing addressed to the hearers, and no necessity demands the vernacular idiom?" Indeed, since it has been decided that the Mass be celebrated with many words, and most of them not so much addressed to God as to the faithful who communicate, what madness has driven the little sacrificers not to pronounce at least those words, prayers, hymns, and so on, in the vernacular and an intelligible language?

units.la: LVI. Mysterium igitur impietatis manifeste subest, ut non immeritò jam olim quoque Salomon Prov. vi. 24. 26. לשון נכר רע אשת ונוכריה mulieri malæ, seu meretricis לשון נכר linguam peregrinam tribuerit. Et Deus ipse Esaj. xxviii. 11. 12. 1 Cor. xiv. 21. 22. ceu poenam comminatus fuerit, quòd בלעגי שפתי ובלשון אחרת in sannis labii & linguâ peregrina ad populum locuturus Propheta sit. Mysterii prætextu Ecclesia Romana, Ecclesiarum omnium mater & Magistra (quo elogio ei Tridentini in hoc ipso argumento blandiuntur) abominationes Missæ tegit, ignorantiam populorum & Regum, Papæ vectigalem, ad confervandam, augendámque dominationem ejus aprimè utilem, alit, cæcam obedientiam fovet, denique hoc veluti characterere insignitos mystici Imperii sui subditos populos distinguit. Sicut nempe olim Romani subditis suis, Hispanis & Gallis Latinam; & Hispani Indis subactis Hispanicam linguam, ceu dominationis suæ insigne, & ut cum lingua in religionem & mores eorum transeant, imposuêre: Ita simili inter alia consilio Latinus Jupiter populis sub jugum suum missis, Latinum in sacris minimùm (nam in cæteris id efficere non potuit) idioma frequentandum injunxit. Cujus rei argumentum non contemnendum est, quod una cum invalescente demum Romani Pontificis Seculo duodecimo πκμέαπλα mos universalis Latino, jam usurpari vulgò desito in sacris idiomate utendi invaluit. Primus enim Gregorius VII. Ulatiflao Bohemiæ Principi vulgaris Sclavonicæ in sacris linguæ usu interdixit, non obesse dictitans, quòd ante actis temporibus prohibitum id non fuerit, cùm Ecclesia multa dissimulaverit & toleraverit, quæ post religionem Christianam stabilitam diligenti subtilique examine emendata fuerint.
units.tr: LVI. There lies manifestly beneath this a mystery of impiety, so that Solomon long ago not without reason ascribed a foreign tongue [לשון נכר] to the evil woman, that is, the harlot (Prov. 6:24, 26). And God himself threatened, as a punishment, that the Prophet would speak to the people in mocking lips and in another tongue (Isa. 28:11–12 [בלעגי שפתי ובלשון אחרת]; 1 Cor. 14:21–22). Under the pretext of mystery the Roman Church, mother and teacher of all churches (an honour the Tridentines flatter her with in this very matter), covers over the abominations of the Mass; it feeds the ignorance of peoples and kings, which is most useful to the Pope for tribute, for preserving and increasing his dominion; it fosters blind obedience; and finally it distinguishes the peoples subject to its mystical empire by this kind of mark. For just as the Romans once imposed Latin on their subjects, the Spaniards and Gauls, and the Spaniards imposed Spanish on the Indians they had subdued, as a badge of their dominion, and so that with the language they might pass over into their religion and customs, so by a similar plan, among others, the Latin Jupiter ordered the peoples sent under his yoke to use the Latin idiom in the sacred rites at least (for in other matters he could not bring this about). The evidence for this is not to be despised: together with the rising power of the Roman Pontiff in the twelfth century, the universal custom of using a language not commonly spoken any longer in the sacred rites gained strength. For Gregory VII was the first to forbid Ulatislaus, Prince of Bohemia, the use of the Slavonic language in the sacred rites, insisting that this was no obstacle, "because it was not forbidden in earlier times, since the Church tolerated and overlooked many things which, after the Christian religion was established, were corrected by careful and subtle examination."

units.la: LVII. Mysterii titulum Babylonicum in fronte Hierarchia Papalis gerere comperitur Sextò, quia Βαβυλὼν τῆ Σατα- ταν profunditates Sathanæ fovet. Profunditates certè Sathanæ Apoc. II. 24. Jezabeli mulieri, Pseudoprophetissæ, fornicationum matri Spiritus S. his verbis tribuit: Vobis autem dico, & reliquis, qui sunt Thyatiris, qui non habent doctrinam hanc, & qui non cognoverunt profunditates Sathanæ, ut ajunt. Quæ verba vel eum sensum habent, quòd Thyatirenses non nulli, Jezabelis asseclæ profunditatum Sathanæ notitiam jactaverint, juxta verba ὡς λέγουσι, sicut dicunt. vel, quòd profunditates, mysteria Dei præse tulerint, quæ tamen reapse non βαθη θεου profunditates, mysteria Dei, sed Sathanæ fuerint. Utroque sensu id Papali Hierarchiæ competit, & Mysterii titulum in fronte ejus conspicuum amplius reddit.
units.tr: LVII. The Papal hierarchy is found to bear the Babylonian title of mystery on its forehead, sixthly, because it fosters the depths of Satan [τὰ βαθέα τοῦ Σατανᾶ]. Certainly Apoc. 2:24 ascribes the depths of Satan to the woman Jezebel, the false prophetess and mother of fornications, in these words of the Holy Spirit: "But I say to you, and to the rest who are in Thyatira, who do not have this teaching, and who have not known the depths of Satan, as they say" [ὡς λέγουσι]. These words may have the sense that some Thyatirans, followers of Jezebel, boasted of knowing the depths of Satan, in line with the words "as they say"; or that they put forward depths, mysteries of God [βαθέα τοῦ θεοῦ], which were in fact not mysteries of God but of Satan. In either sense this applies to the Papal hierarchy, and makes the title of mystery, conspicuous on its forehead, all the more fitting.

units.la: LVIII. Dixit de se S. Paulus 2 Cor. II. ii. οὐ γὰρ ἀγνοοῦμεν Non enim ejus, Sathanæ, cogitationes ignoramus, innuens, paucis, iisque in sacra adversus Sathanam militia veteranis datum esse omnes profunditates, abditos recessus & mysteria Sathanæ pernoscere. Hanc vero sublimem notitiam sibi Romani Mystæ præ cæteris arrogant. Illi enim non tantùm arcanos recessus Sathanæ penetrant, sed etiam rationem exorcismis suis invenerunt, quibus ille vinciri, ligari, expelli, & cum omnibus suis profunditatibus confundi valeat. Illi Sathanam subigunt, mysteria, profunditates suas ipsemet extricet, ad interrogata eorum, etiam malè curiosa, respondeat; uti Rituale Romanum, historiæ Exorcistarum, Cotoni inprimis ab Hadrianæ Fraxineæ Spiritu sciscitantis multa, quæ aliunde cognoscere spes non erat comprobant. Atque id agunt, ut orthodoxa religio apud circumstantes ludibrio exponatur, Papistice contra superstitiones Sathanæ testimonio commendentur. Illi obtentu profunditatum & stratagematum Sathanæ, sibi solis exquisitius cognitorum, viam invenerunt, qua ejus machinationibus eatur obviam, veluti cùm promiscuam libidinem, vel saltem meretriciam, vitandi majoris mali gratia, permiserunt. Illi sapiunt soli, reliqui, veri inprimis Pastores Christi, ut umbra, simplices, imperiti, molitionum Sathanæ ignari, volant. Illi dicentes, se habere verbum, mysterium, quod non pervenerit ad omnes, quod à fidelibus judicari, probari non possit, tantùm non ore profitentur & jactant, se id non accepisse à Deo, cùm verbum Dei pervenerit ad omnes, explorari ab omnibus possit; adeóque non Dei illud, sed Sathanæ profunditates spirare.
units.tr: LVIII. St Paul said of himself, 2 Cor. 2:11: "For we are not ignorant of his devices" [οὐ γὰρ ἀγνοοῦμεν τὰ νοήματα], that is, of the thoughts of Satan, implying that only a few, and those veterans in the sacred warfare against Satan, have been granted to know thoroughly all the depths, hidden recesses and mysteries of Satan. The Roman mystics, however, arrogate this lofty knowledge to themselves above all others. For they not only penetrate the secret recesses of Satan, but have also devised a method by which, through their exorcisms, he can be bound, tied up, expelled, and confounded along with all his depths.
