By these means they subdue Satan, so that he must disentangle his own mysteries and depths and answer their questions, even the badly curious ones. The Roman Ritual and the histories of the exorcists prove this, especially the many things which Cotton asked of the spirit of Hadriana Fraxinea, things which there was no hope of learning from elsewhere. And they do this so that the orthodox religion may be exposed to ridicule among the bystanders, while Papistry is commended by the testimony of Satan against superstitions. On the pretext of the depths and stratagems of Satan, known more exactly to them alone, they have found a way of opposing his machinations, as when, to avoid a greater evil, they have permitted promiscuous lust, or at least lust for harlots. They alone are wise; the rest, and above all the true ministers of Christ, fly about like shadows, simple, unskilled, ignorant of the schemes of Satan. They say they possess a word, a mystery, which has not come to all, and which cannot be judged or tested by the faithful. They do not openly profess, but almost boast, that they did not receive it from God, since the word of God has come to all and can be examined by all. Therefore what they breathe is not the depths of God but of Satan.

units.la: LIX. Jam profunditates etiam quasdam, pro Dei profunditatibus venditant, quas non Dei, sed Sathanæ profunditates esse, liquidò constat. Pertinent eò Theologiæ Scholasticæ, verbo Dei è diametro ferè oppositæ, & ex humanis ut plurimùm testimoniis & philosophicis argutiis conflatæ subtilitates, quibus veritas non tam illustratur, quàm quæsititissimis tricis, strophis, & terminorum abditissimorum prodigiis involvitur, obscuratur, & denique evertitur. Etenim quæ difficilia sunt, contortis spinosis quæstionibus & distinctionibus, terminisque difficiliora & doctissimis etiam vel certè δυσνόητα reddit; quæ verò per se facilia & clara sunt, illa tortuosa & confragosa oratione reddit difficilima, & obscuris quæstionum futilium, nullam εἰκοδομῆς χῆρον, ædificationis usum nullum habentium, ad quas extricandas Oedipo aliquo conjectare, qui Sphingi interpres fuit, aut urinatore Delio opus videatur, involucris obducit, ut nodum in scirpo quæri appareat. Qui in ea exercitatos sensus habent, passim ceu Magistri sententiarum (hoc est בעל חדות seu uti Daniel cap. VIII. 23. vocat מבני חירות Intelligentes ænigmatum, sive spohismatum) subtiles, profundi, Angelici, Seraphici, irrefragabiles, fundatissimi, resoluti, valde resolutivi, scientifici, invicti, acutissimi, universales doctores & Magistri cluent. Imò Lutetiæ fuisse hominem, qui se horribilem sophistam cognominaverit, non minùs gloriosam sibi appellationem ratus, quàm Africani aut Asiatici, Ludovicus Vives de Discipl. lib. iij. testis est. Vivis theologiam illam coloribus Cornelius Musus, Episcopus Bitontinus, Pontificius ipse, Comment. ad Rom. 6. sic depinxit. Divinæ Scripturæ olim quanto damno omnium negligebantur? Vigebat spinosa & molesta nescio quæ Theologia de instantibus relationibus, quidd\itatibus, formalitatibus: itémque hæc omnia Syllogismis arctè contortis, & humanis duntaxat argutiis, quæ procul dubio qua authoritate recipiuntur, ea & refelli possunt, pertractabantur. Is sublimis Theologus habebatur, qui majora portenta pro suis traditiunculis effingere sciret, pretiique pars erat gloriola inanis, non intelligi grandia illa verba, quæ alto supercilio inter mulierculas de sacris literis philosophantes trutinabant. Juraverunt universi verbi divini duces in Magistrorum verba. Hinc sexcentæ sectæ. Posthabebantur Euangelia, Epistolæ, Christiana Philosophia delitescebat, à paucissimis tractabatur, sed frigidè, non dicam insincerè. Nicolaus quoque Beroaldus Doctor Sorbonicus ita de Scholasticis Catal. Test. lib. xvj. conqueritur: Sophisticis nugis arcanæ cœlestésque literæ jam diu nimiùm depravatæ sunt, & obrutæ. Non enim studiorum ingenia exacuunt istæ captiunculæ & tricæ spinosæ, sed mentis succum omnem exhauriunt.
units.tr: LIX. Moreover, they also peddle certain depths as the depths of God, which it is clear are not the depths of God but of Satan. To this belong the subtleties of Scholastic theology, almost diametrically opposed to the word of God, and for the most part compounded of human testimonies and philosophical quibbles. By these, truth is not so much illuminated as wrapped up, obscured and finally overturned, in the most far-fetched snares, twists and wonders of most recondite terms. For what is difficult in itself they make even more difficult, with knotty, thorny questions and distinctions and terms, so that to the most learned they are scarcely intelligible. What is easy and clear in itself they render most difficult by a tortuous and tangled manner of speech. And with obscure, trifling questions, having no use for edification [ἐποικοδομῆς], they cover things over, so that to untangle them one would seem to need an Oedipus to guess the riddles, or a Delian diver, and the knot appears to be sought in a bulrush. Those who are practised in this and have sharp wits are everywhere celebrated as Masters of the Sentences (that is, בעל חדות, or, as Daniel 8:23 calls them, מבין חידות, "understanders of riddles") as "subtle, profound, Angelic, Seraphic, irrefutable, most well-founded, resolute, highly resolutive, scientific, invincible, most acute, universal doctors and masters." Indeed, Ludovicus Vives, in De Disciplinis book 3, is a witness that at Paris there was a man who called himself "a dreadful sophist," thinking this title no less glorious for himself than "African" or "Asian." Vives was described in these colours by Cornelius Musus, Bishop of Bitonto, himself a Papist, in his Commentary on Romans 6: "How much damage was once done by the neglect of the divine Scriptures! There flourished some thorny and troublesome theology of I know not what instant relations, quiddities and formalities, and all these were handled in tightly twisted syllogisms and merely human subtleties, which were refuted and defended by the same authority with which they were received. He was considered a lofty theologian who knew how to fashion greater monstrosities out of his own little doctrines, and part of the price was empty glory: that those grand words, which they weighed with lofty brows among the little women who philosophised about the sacred letters, should not be understood. All the leaders of the divine word swore to the words of the Masters. Hence six hundred sects. The Gospels and Epistles were set aside; Christian philosophy lay hidden, handled by very few, and coldly, not to say insincerely." Nicolaus Beroaldus, Doctor of the Sorbonne, likewise complains of the Scholastics in his Catalogue of Testimonies, book 16: "The heavenly and secret letters have long been too much corrupted and buried by sophistical trifles. For these little captious snares and thorny tricks do not sharpen the wits of students, but drain away all the juice of the mind."

units.la: LX. Septimò mysterii titulum Hierarchia Papalis in fronte impressum gestat eo etiam jure, quia ope mysterii, & titulis Spiritualis, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ &c. fucatis terrenum sibi imperium acquisivit, retinétque. Res certè in propatulo est. Olim quidem Ecclesia Romana πρω-tia sua, seu prærogativam, quam supra reliquas Ecclesias obtinebat, non aliunde derivavit, vel derivare etiam potuit, quàm à loco, seu dignitate sedis, quæ Roma erat, urbs Imperatoria, orbis Domina. Qua ratione compulsi Patres Constantinopolitani Concilii Episcopo Constantinopolitano secunda πρωτία assignarunt, quia Constantinopolis æque ac Roma Imperatori, sive Cæsari Imperii sedem daret. Ita enim sanxerunt τὴν ἀξὶ τὴ Κωνσταντινουπόλεως Πρόεδρον ἔχειν τὰ πρεσβεῖα τῆς πρώτης μετὰ τὴν τῆς Ῥώμης Πρόεδρον, λέγ' τὴν εἶναι αὐτῷ τίμα 'Ῥώμῃ. Constantinopolitanæ Civitatis Episcopum prærogativam honoris post Romanum Episcopum habere, eò quòd sit nova Roma. Chalcedonensis quoque Concilii decretum ejusmodi fuit: τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ῥώμης, διὰ τὸ βασιλεύειν τὴν πόλιν ἐκείνην, οἱ πατέρες ἀπέδωκαν τὰ πρεσβεῖα. Sedi senioris Romæ, quòd Urbs illa imperaret, Patres jure privilegia tribuerunt. Ἴσα πρεσβεῖα ἴσα πρεσβεῖα aequa privilegia τῷ αὐτῷ eadem consideratione motos sanctissimæ novæ Romæ Patres eodem tribuisse, additur. Nulla utrobique primatus à jure Divino, nulla ab institutione Christi, nulla à merito Petri, omnis à dignitate loci, quòd Romæ, quòd Novæ Romæ Episcopi essent, & constitutione Patrum ratio arcessitur.
units.tr: LX. Seventhly, the Papal hierarchy bears the title of mystery impressed upon its forehead also by this right: that, by means of mystery, and by the disguised titles of the Catholic Church etc., it has acquired and still keeps a worldly empire. The matter is certainly plain to see. Formerly the Roman Church did not derive, nor indeed could it have derived, its primacy, or the pre-eminence it held above the other churches, from anything other than the place, or dignity of its see, which was Rome, the imperial city, mistress of the world. For this reason the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople assigned the second primacy to the Bishop of Constantinople, because Constantinople, like Rome, was the seat of the Emperor or Caesar. For so they decreed: "The Bishop of Constantinople shall have the prerogatives of honour after the Bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome" [τὸν μέντοι τῆς Κωνσταντινουπόλεως ἐπίσκοπον ἔχειν τὰ πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς μετὰ τὸν τῆς Ῥώμης ἐπίσκοπον, διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτὴν νέαν Ῥώμην]. The decree of the Council of Chalcedon was of this kind: "To the throne of the elder Rome, because that city ruled, the Fathers granted the prerogatives" [τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ῥώμης διὰ τὸ βασιλεύειν τὴν πόλιν ἐκείνην, οἱ πατέρες ἀπέδωκαν τὰ πρεσβεῖα]. It is added that the Fathers granted equal privileges [ἴσα πρεσβεῖα] to the same, moved by the same consideration, to the most holy New Rome. In both places the primacy is derived not from Divine right, not from the institution of Christ, not from the merit of Peter, but entirely from the dignity of the place, because they were the bishops of Rome and of New Rome, and from the constitution of the Fathers.

units.la: LXI. Constantinopolis Episcopus, ceu æmulus dignitatis, Romano verè ἀλγηδὼν τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν sudor in oculis fuit. Cùm igitur sedis dignitas Constantinopolin paulatim migrâsset, & parùm jam ad extendendas potestatis fimbrias ratio à loci dignitate petita conduceret, astuto consilio ad mysteria, jusque Divinum confugere placuit. Duplicem porro potestatem & in Spiritualibus scil. & in temporalibus, supremam utramque (tametsi sub fuco Spiritualis, temporalis potestas nunquam non tecta fuit)
units.tr: LXI. The Bishop of Constantinople, as a rival in dignity, was truly a pain in the eyes of Rome. Therefore, when the dignity of the see had gradually migrated to Constantinople, and it no longer served well to extend the fringes of power by appealing to the dignity of the place, it pleased the Romans, by a crafty plan, to take refuge in mysteries and in divine right. They sought to claim for themselves a double power, both spiritual and temporal, each supreme (although under the mask of the spiritual, temporal power was never not concealed),

units.la: Babylonis illi architecti moliebantur. Et primò quidem spiritualem supremam sibi vindicárunt callido figmento, quòd S. Petrus Romæ per plures annos Episcopus, supremam in Ecclesiam universam potestatem obtinuerit, eandémque successoribus in eadem sede reliquerit. Commodè verò succurrebant verba Christi ad Petrum Matth. xvi. 18. 19. Tu es Petrus, & supra hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam &c. Tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum &c. Tametsi verò super petra, & non super Petro ædificaturum se Ecclesiam ipsamet Petra, Christus, spospondit, non defuêre tamen ingeniosis pictoribus colores, seu potiùs cerussæ, quibus id omne personæ Petri, Romanorúmque Pontificum, illinerent. Jam quidem A. ccccxxxvii. Marcus Papa in Epistola ad Anastasium & Ægypti Episcopos B. Petri Ecclesiæ Romanæ semper immaculatæ opem ferentis meminit. Sed suspecta omnino Epistola est. At Leo I. si ambitionis, quo urebatur stimulum demseris, verè Magnus A. ccccl verba illa; Tu es Petrus in Anniversi. die Assumpt. Serm. 2. 3. primus strenuè inculcavit; & Romanæ Ecclesiæ primatum iisdem inædificavit. Petrus, ita scribit, petra dicitur, dum fundamentum pronuntiatur &c. in sua fede vivit potestas, excellit authoritas. Nunquam nisi per ipsum dedit, quicquid aliis non negavit Christus. Procedente tempore pro stabilienda μυϲαπλαία Pontificis ὁ Ἀχιμάς ἐ Λιγόιθ &c. fuere illa ipsa Christi ad Petrum dicta obtorto collo rapta: Tu es Petrus, super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Dabo tibi claves Regni Cœlorum. Quicquid ligaveris in terra ligatum erit in Cœlo: Quicquid solveris in terra, solutum erit in Cœlo. Ora vi pro Te, Petre, ne deficiat fides tua. Pasce oves meas, agnos meos. Atque sic Petrus in petram; petra in Papam, claves Regni Cœlorum in Coronas, enses, lanceas, sceptra; pascendi munus in dominationem meram, plenámque in maxima regna, denique in animas & corpora potestatem, metamorphosi inaudita, & mysteriis verbi Divini obtentui sumptis, conversa sunt. Verbo dicam, Mysterii prætextu mysticam seu Spiritualem potestatem supremam sibi Papa rapuit. Mysticæ seu Spiritualis potestatis supremæ prætextu & titulo supremum in temporalibus dominium invasit. Atque sic externa specie Rex Mysticus, non terrenus reapse, Rex terrenus non Mysticus evasit.
units.tr: as those Babylonian architects were devising. And first indeed they claimed for themselves the supreme spiritual power by a clever fiction: that St Peter, as bishop at Rome for many years, obtained supreme power over the whole Church, and left the same power to his successors in the same see. The words of Christ to Peter, Matt. 16:18-19, came conveniently to their aid: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church," etc. "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven," etc. Although Christ himself, the rock, promised to build the Church upon the rock and not upon Peter, there were not lacking ingenious painters with colours, or rather whitewash, to smear all this upon the person of Peter and of the Roman Pontiffs. Already in the year 437, Pope Mark, in his letter to Anastasius and the bishops of Egypt, mentions "the Church of Rome, always unstained, bringing help to the blessed Peter." But the letter is wholly suspect. Leo I, however, if you remove the goad of ambition which burned him, was truly Great. In the year 450, in his sermon on the anniversary of his elevation, he first vigorously pressed the words "You are Peter," and built upon them the primacy of the Church of Rome: "Peter, he writes, is called a rock, since he is pronounced the foundation, etc. Power lives in his see, authority excels. Christ never gave anything to anyone which he did not first give through him." As time went on, to establish the mystery of the Pontiff, those same words spoken by Christ to Peter were seized by the scruff of the neck: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. Pray for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail. Feed my sheep, my lambs." And so Peter became the rock, the rock became the Pope, the keys of the kingdom of heaven became crowns, swords, lances and sceptres; the duty of feeding became unmixed domination, and full power over great kingdoms, and finally over souls and bodies, by an unheard-of metamorphosis, and with the mysteries of the divine word taken up as a cover. In a word, by the pretext of mystery the Pope seized for himself supreme mystical or spiritual power. By the pretext and title of supreme mystical or spiritual power he invaded supreme dominion in temporal matters. And so, in outward appearance, he became a mystical king, not really an earthly one, and an earthly king, not a mystical one.

units.la: LXII. Potestatem utramque supremam, adeóque etiam
units.tr: LXII. That both supreme powers, and therefore also

units.la: in temporalibus imperitandi Imperatoribus, Regibus & Principibus pro lubitu, verbi Divini mysteriis in subsidium adhibitis iidem tuentur. Utrumque enim gladium spiritualem & materialem esse in potestate Ecclesiæ, illum Papæ, hunc Regum & militum manu, sed ad nutum & imperium Papæ exercendum, Bonifacius in Extravagante sua inde probavit, quia dicentibus Apostolis: Ecce duo gladii, Christus non dixit, nimis esse, sed satis; & Petro mox idem dixit: Converte gladium tuum in vaginam. Imperatores, Reges, Principesque quosvis deviantes de throno dejici, vitáque ipsa spoliari posse, mysteria Divini verbi docuerunt eosdem; veluti cùm Petro dictum est: Act. x. 13. Petre mactla, & manduca, & Jeremiæ dictum est cap. i. 10. Ecce constitui te hodie super gentes & Regna, ut evellas, & diruas, & disperdas, & demoliaris, & ædifices, & plantes. Quæ verba Pius V. in Bulla fulminante in caput Elisabethæ Angliæ Reginæ, eò torquet. Longum esset commemorare, quemadmodum Papa piis, uti loqui amant, fraudibus, seu potiùs per Impietatis mysterium, tum promissione veniæ remissionis peccatorum, tum excommunicationis fulminibus, & comminatione inferni, quibus olim Reges Francorum, Pipinum inprimis aliósque ludificabatur, excusso & Orientalium & Occidentadenta-
units.tr: These same men defend the Emperors, Kings and Princes in temporal matters, so that they may rule as they please, with the mysteries of the Divine Word brought in as an aid. Boniface, in his Extravagant, proved from this that both swords, the spiritual and the material, are in the power of the Church: the first in the hand of the Pope, the second in the hand of kings and soldiers, but to be wielded at the nod and command of the Pope. For when the Apostles said, Behold, here are two swords, Christ did not say that there were too many, but enough; and soon afterwards he said to Peter, Put your sword back into its sheath. The same men taught that Emperors, Kings and any Princes who go astray may be cast down from the throne and even stripped of their lives. This is shown when Peter was told, Acts 10:13, Rise, Peter, kill and eat, and when Jeremiah was told, ch. 1:10, Behold, I have set you this day over the nations and kingdoms, to root out, to pull down, to destroy, to overthrow, to build and to plant. Pius V twists these words to this end in his thundering Bull against Elizabeth, Queen of England. It would take too long to recount how the Pope, by what they like to call pious frauds, or rather through the mystery of impiety, both by the promise of pardon and remission of sins and by the thunderbolts of excommunication and the threat of hell, with which he once mocked the Kings of the Franks, Pippin above all, and having shaken off the yoke of the Eastern and Western

units.la: tum in temporalibus dentalium Imperatorum jugo, Romæ, Italiæque potioris dominum se fecerit; & paulatim etiam principum secularium dorso inequitaverit.
units.tr: (Continuation of the same sentence: and gradually also rode on the backs of secular princes.)

units.la: LXIII. Constat sanè, Papæ imperium, quo utitur erga Principes Seculares, Ecclesiastici & Spiritualis, nec non Ecclesiæ Catholicæ inani specie & simulachro velatum, & indirecti, directivi imperii fuco illitum, suapte natura merè esse terrenum, ejusdem planè indolis, cujus est imperium ἀυτοκρατωρ Turcæ in obnoxios sibi Principes, aliósque. Non tantum enim locupletatus est Principum liberalitate territorio proprio, in quo perinde ac ipli antehac, se αυτοκρατορα gerit: sed etiam eorundem cœca credulitate & indulgentia, negligentiáque supina auctus est imperio, quod in eorum imperio serviente ita gerit, ut eorum sibi subjiciat mancipétque jurisdictionem, capita, fortunas & negotia, cum summo Imperio res, quæ ad jus & curam Summarum potestatum Secularium pertinent, ordinet, denique alienum imperium in se transferat. Revera enim Imperator Romanus Papa est, cui Germanus Rex, Romani Imperatoris titulo nequicquam se venditans, fidelitatis & obsequii juramentum per Delegatos præstat. Par planè hodie est ratio Regum Christianorum, quæ olim in Romano Imperio Ethnico fuit Ethnicorum Regum Attali, Masiniffæ, Cogiduni. Tam enim Reges Christiani in Papali Imperio precariò regnant, quàm precario olim Reges Ethnici illi regnârunt, Imperatori servientes. Æquè novis his ac veteribus olim Imperatoribus quadrat illud uncialibus literis incidendum Imperii arcanum, quod his verbis Tacitus Agric. 14. 2. expressit: Vetus ac jam pridem recepta populi Romani consuetudo, ut haberet instrumenta servitutis & Reges.
units.tr: LXIII. It is certainly clear that the power the Pope exercises over secular princes, "ecclesiastical and spiritual," and likewise over the "Catholic Church," veiled under an empty appearance and image, and daubed with the paint of an indirect, "directive" power, is by its very nature purely earthly, of exactly the same kind as the autocratic power [αὐτοκρατωρ] of the Turk over the princes subject to him and others. For he has been enriched not only by the generosity of princes, with a territory of his own, in which, just as the Turk did before, he acts as an autocrat [αὐτοκρατορα]; he has also been increased in power by their blind credulity, indulgence and lazy negligence, so that in their serving authority he so conducts himself as to bring under his subjection and into his grasp their jurisdiction, persons, fortunes and business, and to order, along with the highest authority, matters that belong to the right and care of the supreme secular powers, and finally to transfer to himself a foreign authority. Indeed, the Roman Emperor is in fact the Pope, to whom the German king, vainly puffing himself up with the title of Roman Emperor, swears an oath of fidelity and obedience through his delegates. The position of Christian kings today is exactly the same as that of the kings of the pagan Roman empire, the pagan kings Attalus, Masinissa and Cogidunus. For Christian kings reign under the Papal empire by sufferance, just as those pagan kings once reigned by sufferance, serving the Emperor. That secret of empire, which should be carved in capital letters, fits the new emperors just as it did the old ones, and Tacitus expressed it in these words (Agricola 14): "The old and long-established custom of the Roman people, to keep both instruments of slavery and kings."

units.la: LXIV. Impleat Babylonicum. Hierarchiæ Papalis titulum Octavò non postremum tamen, neque leve certè illud, quòd in Hierarchia Papali est mysterium illud ininiquitatis, quod Homini Peccati S. Paulus 2 Thess. ÿ. 7. tribuit, quódque occultè & latenter jam Apostolorum tempore operabatur, & deinceps operari perrexit, usque ad revelationem ejus. Verba S. Pauli sunt: Τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας, μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται. Nam mysterium jam operatur iniquitatis, tantùm qui detinet nunc, donec ex medio fiat. Ubi μυστήριον ἀνομίας prìè arcanum defectionis à lege significans, operari, latenter scilicet & in occulto jam Apostolorum tempore dicitur, quia Spiritus seductionis jam tum in mundo occultè ad ἀνομίαν defectionem à lege disponere incepit, feminàque adeò jecit, unde omnis seges erroris & mendacii deinceps enata est.
units.tr: LXIV. Let us fill in the Babylonian title of the Papal hierarchy. The eighth point, and certainly not the least or slightest, is that in the Papal hierarchy there is that "mystery of iniquity" which St Paul ascribes to the "man of sin" (2 Thess. 2:7), and which was already secretly and covertly at work in the time of the Apostles and went on working until its revelation. The words of St Paul are: "For the mystery of iniquity already works; only he who now restrains will do so until he is taken out of the way" [τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας, μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται]. Here "mystery of iniquity," meaning the secret defection from the law, is said to be at work, secretly and in hiddenness, already in the time of the Apostles, because the spirit of deception had already begun to dispose the world secretly towards lawlessness [ἀνομίαν], that is, defection from the law, and so had cast the seed from which every crop of error and lie has since sprung.

units.la: I.XV. De operatione occulta mysterii illius nullus du- bitabit, qui ea, quæ in historia Papatus, seu Ecclesiæ Ro- manæ historia septem Periodis distincta, diximus, ad ani- mum revocabit sedulò.
units.tr: LXV. Anyone who carefully recalls what we have said in the history of the Papacy, or the history of the Roman Church, divided into seven periods, will not doubt the secret working of that mystery.

units.la: Paucis ut multa complectamur, jam Apostolorum haud dubiè tempore Sathanas cogitationem multorum animis instillavit, de ἀδεία licentia, seu securitate quodam carnali qua quidvis liceret, dummodo Christo nomen darent, baptizarentur, epuli sacri communione fruerentur, & cum Christianis veris verbi audiendi gratia congregarentur; non cogitantes interim de fidei ingenuitate, & ratione verae justitiae Dei. Apostoli certè de ψευδαδελφοις falsis fratribus, & de illis qui Christum non ἀγὰς ἢ ἁπλῶς castè & sincerè praedicabant, quæsti sunt. In iisdem Sathanas effecit, ut vellent, dicerentque, quod plurimos velle & dicere animadverterant: ut intumescerent unus contra alium super alio, dicentes: Ego sum Cephæ, ego Pauli, ego Apollo. 1 Cor. 1. 12. iv. 6. Unde in Ecclesiam Schismata, contentiones, susurri incesserunt: ut essent φιλοσηματόδοξοι, qui se vellent nominari, sectatoresque que pro honore eorum æmulantes haberent: ut multi docerent hæreses pestiferas de persona inprimis & excellentia Christi, eaque occasione οι φιλοπρωτεύοντες occasionem damnandi hæreses dictatoria potestate, imperandique pædagogicè nancisçerentur: ut persuaderentur multi, rectius controversias per præscriptionis & traditionis authoritatem, quàm per demonstrationem ex scripturis definiri; unde prætextu traditionis apud se potiùs quàm alios depositæ, locus datus est sedi uni se se efferendi supra alias: ut doctrina de libero arbitrio, justitia fidei, & unico sacrificio Christi minùs accuratè, cautè, solidè & perspicuè traderetur, illustraretúrque; multíque adeò in primariis illis fidei capitibus hærerent, alii etiam aberrarent planè: ut Philosophi, Rhetores, Causidici conversi ad Christum, adeóque neophyti, præ cæteris loquendi & docendi in Ecclesia facultate pollerent, eáque Christianam fidem defendentes, & idololatriam, stultitiámque gentilem oppugnantes dicerent, scriberéntque incautiùs, quæ qualia essent, & à quo Spiritu proficiscerentur, ipsi nesciverunt, futura suo tempore materies traditionis non scriptæ, & præceptionis humanæ, ut extra scripturam prolata ab antiquitate minimùm robur authoritatémque haberent: ut unus multis præesset Episcopus, & potestate eximia χειροτονίας seu impositionis manuum polleret: ut controversiæ & lites fidelium ad Episcopos tales deferrentur; unde incrementum sumpsit eorum cupiditas, ut potentes esse & jurisdictionem ac territorium habere cuperent, ditatíque adeò in pace magnis opibus sunt, illi maximè, qui cæteris Episcopis in magnis urbibus præsidebant: ut Imperatores desideriis Episcoporum facturi satis iisdem jurisdictionem concederent, prohibeéntque officialibus suis, ne quenquam in judicio Episcopi avellerent: ut Synodica & Cæsarea authoritate cathedrarum Patriarchalium, Romanæ inprimis in Occidente, ceu primæ sedis, πρωτία confirmarentur: ut Romanam sedem sequerentur multi, ea opinione dementati, quasi à Deo præ cæteris electa esset, ut ejus beneficio Ecclesia à corruptione custodiretur, ut Episcopus unus in reliquos omnes dominium, adeóque titulum & potestatem Episcopi universalis & œcumenici affectaret (quod à Constantinopolitano primùm factum) obtinerétque (ṡti Romanus mox à Cæsare Phoca obtinuit) ut ipse ille λεγόμενος Episcopus universalis paulatim ab obedientia Imperatoris deficiens, sui juris se faceret, & denique se se supra τὴν σίβασμα, seu supra dictum Σεβαστὸν, aliàsque ἐξου-σίας ὑπερηχίους potestates eminentes efferret, quod qua ratione, quibusve gradibus processerit, in loco narravimus. Saltem liquidò inde constat mysterium iniquitatis illud, seu defectionis à Lege Dei ἐν μυστηρίῳ in mysterio, hoc est, multis artibus, & per latentia incrementa operans, in Romana denique Ecclesia ita consummatum esse, ut non frustra Spiritus S. titulum μυστήριον Mysterium, ceu perenne quoddam monumentum in fronte ejus nascendum legendúmque à quovis sanæ mentis, exsculpserit.
units.tr: To sum up briefly: already in the time of the Apostles, Satan without doubt instilled into the minds of many a thought of "adeia" [ἀδεία], a licence or a sort of carnal security, by which anything would be allowed, provided they gave their name to Christ, were baptised, shared in the communion of the holy feast, and gathered with true Christians to hear the Word; meanwhile they did not think about the sincerity of faith and the nature of God's true righteousness. The Apostles certainly complained about "false brethren" [ψευδαδελφοις] and about those who did not preach Christ purely [ἀγνῶς] and simply [ἁπλῶς] and sincerely. Satan brought it about among these people that they wished and said what he had noticed that very many wished and said, so that they puffed themselves up one against another, each over one another, saying: "I am of Cephas, I of Paul, I of Apollos" (1 Cor. 1:12; 4:6). Hence schisms, contentions and whisperings crept into the Church; some wanted to be called after men, and had followers who vied with each other for their honour, "lovers of their own glory" [φιλοδοξοι]; many taught pernicious heresies about the person and especially the excellence of Christ; and on that occasion "those who love to be first" [οι φιλοπρωτεύοντες] found an opportunity of condemning heresies with dictatorial power and of ruling in a schoolmasterly way. Many were persuaded that controversies should be settled by the authority of prescription and tradition rather than by demonstration from the Scriptures; hence, under the pretext of a tradition deposited with themselves rather than with others, room was given to one see to raise itself above the rest. The doctrine of free will, the righteousness of faith and the unique sacrifice of Christ was taught and explained less accurately, cautiously, solidly and clearly, and many clung to those main articles of faith, while others went altogether astray. Philosophers, rhetoricians and lawyers, converted to Christ and therefore newly-baptised, excelled others in the power of speaking and teaching in the Church; defending the Christian faith and attacking idolatry and gentile folly, they said and wrote more rashly, and did not know what sort of things they were or from what spirit they came. In due time this became the matter of unwritten tradition and human precept, so that things brought forward from outside Scripture had the least strength and authority from antiquity. One bishop was set over many, and excelled in the remarkable power of "chirotonia" [χειροτονίας], that is, the laying on of hands. The disputes and quarrels of the faithful were referred to such bishops; from this their desire grew, so that they wished to be powerful and to have jurisdiction and territory; and they were enriched with great resources in peace, especially those who presided over the other bishops in the great cities. Emperors, meeting the desires of the bishops, granted them sufficient jurisdiction and forbade their officials to drag anyone away from a bishop's judgment. By synodical and imperial authority the primacy [πρωτία] of the patriarchal sees, especially the Roman see in the West as the first see, was confirmed. Many followed the Roman see, driven mad by the opinion that it had been chosen by God above the rest, so that by its benefit the Church would be guarded from corruption. One bishop aspired to dominion over all the others, and so to the title and power of universal and ecumenical bishop; this was first attempted by the bishop of Constantinople, and the Roman bishop obtained it soon after from the emperor Phocas. This so-called [λεγόμενος] universal bishop, gradually falling away from obedience to the emperor, made himself his own master, and at last raised himself above "the worship" [τὴν σίβασμα, that is, σέβασμα] or the aforesaid "Augustus" [Σεβαστόν], and other "authorities" [ἐξουσίας] that excel [ὑπερηχίους, that is, ὑπερεχούσας] and eminent powers. By what reasoning and by what steps this came about, we have related in its place. At least it is clearly established from this that the mystery of iniquity, or the defection from the law of God, working "in a mystery" [ἐν μυστηρίῳ], that is, by many arts and by hidden growths, has at last been so fully accomplished in the Roman Church that the Holy Spirit did not in vain carve on its forehead the title "Mystery" [μυστήριον] as a perpetual monument, to be read by everyone of sound mind.

units.la: LXVI. Concludimus, Cœtui religioso Hierarchiæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantis, & titulum μυστήριον Mysterium impietatis scilicet illud Babyloni Magnæ tributum, & rem eo titulo significatam, jure, ceu propriam & eximiam tribui, adeóque eum, cæteris paribus Babylonem Magnam, Matrem fornicationum & abominationum terræ quomodo ipse Spiritus S. Apoc. xvii. 5. statim per μυστηριῶν titulum illum explicat haberi judicarique meritò.
units.tr: LXVI. We conclude that the religious body of the dominant Hierarchy of the Church of Rome deserves, rightly and as its own distinctive possession, the title μυστήριον (Mystery) of impiety, which is given to Great Babylon, and the thing signified by that title; and that therefore, other things being equal, it is rightly regarded and judged to be Great Babylon, the Mother of fornications and abominations of the earth, just as the Holy Spirit himself explains in Rev. 17:5, where he calls her by the title of "mysteries" [μυστηρίων].

units.la: Argumenti 11. Conclu. fo.
units.tr: Argument 11. Conclusion, fol.

units.la: DISSERTATIO OCTAVA
units.tr: DISSERTATIO OCTAVA

units.la: QUA Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem Babylonem Magnam esse, probatur Tertiò, quia in Civitate Magna, Religiosa, in populum Magnum, Christi nomen professum licet, Clero dominanti parentem, septem collibus, totidémque provinciis distinctum, multorúmque Regum potentia suffultum, imperium obtinet.
units.tr: In which it is proved, thirdly, that the Hierarchy, or Clergy of the Roman Church, which rules, is the Great Babylon, because it holds dominion in a Great, Religious City, which is a parent to a Great People that professes the name of Christ, a city divided into seven hills and as many provinces, and supported by the power of many kings.

units.la: SECTIONIBUS TRIBUS DISTINCTA.
units.tr: DIVIDED INTO THREE SECTIONS.

units.la: Quarum Prima Civitatis Romanæ Religiosæ dominantis magnitudinem; Secunda, subditos imperio ejusdem parentes; Tertia Imperium ipsum explicat.
units.tr: Of these, the First sets out the greatness of the ruling Religious City of Rome; the Second, the subjects who are the parents of its rule; and the Third explains the empire itself.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA QUA
units.tr: SECTION ONE, IN WHICH

units.la: Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantis, esse Magnam illam Civitatem, Religiosam, Babylonicam asseritur.
units.tr: It is asserted that the Hierarchy, or Clergy of the ruling Roman Church, is that Great Religious City, the Babylonian one.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Character tertius Babylonis Magnæ est, quòd in Civitate vitate Magna, Religiosa, Imperium in populum Magnum gerit.
units.tr: I. The third mark of the Great Babylon is that, in a Great, Religious City, it exercises dominion over a Great People.

units.la: II. Demonstrationis partes.
units.tr: II. The parts of the demonstration.

units.la: III. Civitas non locum munitum, sed civium potestate imperandi praeditorum coetum notat.
units.tr: III. A city denotes not a fortified place but an assembly of citizens endowed with the power of ruling.

units.la: IV. Duplex civitas, Sancta fidelium, & tyrannica conscientiae dominantium.
units.tr: IV. There are two cities: the Holy City of the faithful, and the tyrannical city of those who dominate consciences.

units.la: V. Necnon Imperium duplex, Summum & subalternum, distinguitur.
units.tr: V. Likewise two empires are distinguished, the supreme and the subordinate.

units.la: VI. Babylon Magna Civitas est religionis praetextu dominans, similis Romae veteri, per Summum & subalternos orbi dominanti.
units.tr: VI. Babylon the Great is a city that dominates under the pretext of religion, like ancient Rome, through its supreme head and subordinate officers over the world it rules.

units.la: VII. Talem civitatem esse Hierarchiam Ecclesiae Romanae, Syllogismo generali demonstratur,
units.tr: VII. That such a city is the Hierarchy of the Roman Church is demonstrated by a general syllogism,

units.la: VIII. ejusque propositio asseritur.
units.tr: VIII. and its major premise is asserted.

units.la: IX. Assumtionis diffusa probatio. Concilii Tridentini de Hierarchia Ecclesiae definitio.
units.tr: IX. A lengthy proof of the minor premise. The definition of the Hierarchy of the Church by the Council of Trent.

units.la: X. Veteris & Pontificiae Hierarchiae differentia.
units.tr: X. The difference between the ancient hierarchy and the Papal hierarchy.

units.la: XI. Presbyterorum & Ministrorum Hierarchiae ordines à Concilio Tridentino distincti.
units.tr: XI. The orders of presbyters and ministers in the Hierarchy as distinguished by the Council of Trent.

units.la: XII. Veteris Ecclesiae ordines.
units.tr: XII. The orders of the ancient Church.

units.la: XIII. Eorundem in Hierarchia Pontificia degeneratio turpis.
units.tr: XIII. Their shameful degeneration in the Papal Hierarchy.

units.la: XIV. Hierarchia omnis Verbo Dei repugnat,
units.tr: XIV. Every hierarchy is repugnant to the Word of God,

units.la: XV. & Hominis peccati, Adversarii Christi nota est.
units.tr: XV. and is a mark of the man of sin, the adversary of Christ.

units.la: XVI. Papatus iniqua dominatio.
units.tr: XVI. The iniquitous domination of the Papacy.

units.la: XVII. Hierarchiam non Spiritus Christi, sed genius Romuli peperit,
units.tr: XVII. The Hierarchy was born not of the Spirit of Christ but of the genius of Romulus,

units.la: XVIII. fatentibus non obscurè Petro Messia de Sibilia,
units.tr: XVIII. as Peter Messia of Seville does not obscurely admit,

units.la: XIX. Auberto Miraeo,
units.tr: XIX. and Aubert Miraeus,

units.la: XX. Gregorio VII. P. ipso, & Petro de Marca,
units.tr: XX. and Gregory VII, the Pope himself, and Peter de Marca,

units.la: XXI. Bellarmino,
units.tr: XXI. and Bellarmine,

units.la: XXII. Justo Lipsio,
units.tr: XXII. and Justus Lipsius.

units.la: XXIII. Ex Hierarchiæ speciebus de Civitatis illius magnitudine judicari potest.
units.tr: XXIII. From the kinds of Hierarchy one can judge the greatness of that city.

units.la: XXIV. Clerici ex Possessino in Gubernantes, Ministrantes, Supererogantes, & Adjuvantes divisi.
units.tr: XXIV. The clerics, according to Possevinus, are divided into governing, ministering, supererogatory and assisting.

units.la: XXV. Gubernantium Princeps Papa successor est Imperatorum veteris Romæ.
units.tr: XXV. The Pope, the prince of the governing clergy, is the successor of the emperors of old Rome.

units.la: XXVI. Curiales.
units.tr: XXVI. The curials.

units.la: XXVIII. Collegia & Congregationes variæ.
units.tr: XXVIII. Various colleges and congregations.

units.la: XXIX. Inter Magistratus Papæ Cardinales eminent, qui non proprie, sed æquivocè tales sunt,
units.tr: XXIX. Among the Pope's magistrates the cardinals stand out, who are such not properly but equivocally,

units.la: XXX. sub appellatione Ecclesiastica Seculares Principes, Regum ipsorum emuli.
units.tr: XXX. and under the name of ecclesiastics are secular princes, rivals of the kings themselves.

units.la: XXXI. Episcopis & Archiepiscopis successu temporis prælati, & à Pontifice mirificè elati ditatique.
units.tr: XXXI. Bishops and archbishops, raised over time and wondrously exalted and enriched by the Pope.

units.la: XXXII. Eorum numerus olim ad titulorum Ecclesiarum in Urbe restrictus fuit: Præfecti sunt quinque Ecclesiis Patriarchalibus Urbis Romæ. Crevit eorum numerus, & decrevit pro libitu Pontificum.
units.tr: XXXII. Their number was once restricted to the titles of the churches in the City. Five patriarchal churches of the city of Rome have prefects. Their number grew, and was reduced at the pleasure of the Popes.

units.la: XXXIII. Officia eorum præcipua, ordinaria & extravagantia.
units.tr: XXXIII. Their principal duties, ordinary and extraordinary.

units.la: XXXIV. Patriarchæ Pontificii.
units.tr: XXXIV. The Papal patriarchs.

units.la: XXXV. Archiepiscopi, seu Metropolitani Pontificii Episcopi, etiam titulares, ex Miraeo recensiti.
units.tr: XXXV. The Papal archbishops, or metropolitans, and bishops, including titular ones, listed from Miraeus.

units.la: XXXVI. Episcopi quo jure olim Presbyteris sint prælati, & quo pacto eorundem potestas creverit.
units.tr: XXXVI. By what right bishops were once set over presbyters, and how their power grew.

units.la: XXXVII. Ordo & gradus incrementi potestatis Episcopalis.
units.tr: XXXVII. The order and degrees of the increase of episcopal power.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ordini ab hominibus instituto Deus non benedixit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. God has not blessed an order instituted by men.

units.la: XXXIX. Pontificii Episcopi ex Concilio Tridentino, & Ambrosio Catharino descripti.
units.tr: XXXIX. The Papal bishops described from the Council of Trent and Ambrose Catharinus.

units.la: XL. Eorundem Emblema ex Zach. xiij. 4. 5. eruitur.
units.tr: XL. Their emblem is drawn from Zach. xiij. 4. 5.

units.la: XLI. Mancipia Pontificiæ libidinis eos esse probatur, tum quia se non à Christo, sed Pontifice immediatè institutos profiteri coguntur: XLII. tum quia juramentum Pontifici, ceu vasalli Principi praestant: XLIII. tum quia Archiepiscopi pallium à Pontifice subjectionis suae symbolum redimunt. XLIV. Clerici gubernantes secundi ordinis sunt Praepositi, Archidiaconi, Archipresbyteri, Vicarii & Consiliarii. XLV. Clerici Ministrantes enumerantur Septem ordines, à Concilio Tridentino definiti. XLVI. Non verbi Divini & sanioris antiquitatis praesidio, sed gentilium veterum & Judaeorum aemulatione introducti sunt. XLVII. Sacerdotum munera, XLVIII. nec non Diaconorum, Subdiaconorum &c. quibus nominibus res convenientes nullae subsunt. XLIX. Canonicorum Collegia, L. & distinctio frivola in Regulares & Seculares. LI. Neutri verè Canonici sunt. LII. Clerici Adjuvantes Doctores Theologiae, Juris Canonici, Catechismi, Praedicatores, Scholastici Ecclesiae enumerati. LIII. Clerici supererogantes sunt Monachi. LIV. Monasticae vitae primordia olim fuerunt Coenobitae, Anachoretae & Saraibitae. LV. Pontificiorum Monachorum à veteris Ecclesiae Monachis discrimen ingens panditur. LVI. Cum Monachis veteribus Saraibitis convenire eosdem asseritur; & eorundem vivum emblema ex Apoc. ix. 3. &c. arcessitur. LVII. Monachatum Pontificium non aliud esse, quàm Politicum seu Babylonicum Papae vaframentum, probatur probatur Primò, quia ordinum beneficio populus in obsequio Pontificis continetur: LVIII. cui rei non parùm ordinum exemptio à potestate Episcoporum confert. LIX. Secundò, quia Cœlibatus omnium Clericorum, adeòque etiam Monachorum Regni Pontificii nervus est. LX. Tertiò, quia ex multitudine ordinum non parùm Romana Curia dotatur. LXI. Quartò, quia Monachorum innumerabilis multitudo substinendo Regno Pontificio non parùm conducit. LXII. Monachi Pontificii sunt vel Anachoretæ, vel Cœnobitæ. LXIII. Basis ordinum sunt regulæ quatuor, Basilii, Augustini, Benedicti & Francisci. LXIV. Mendicantium ordinum genera sunt quatuor, Augustinenses, Prædicatores, Carmelitæ & Franciscani, ad quos plerique alii referuntur. Non mendicantes sunt vel Canonici Regulares, vel non Canonici. LXV. Monachis Jesuitæ anne accensendi sint? LXVI. Monachorum & Jesuitarum differentia in pluribus, horumque deplorata malitia. LXVII. Monachorum & Jesuitarum incredibilis multitudo Civitatem magnam Cleri dominantis propalat. LXVIII. Monachatui affines sunt Confraternitates, quarum origo à Roma Ethnica arcessitur. LXIX. Fraternitatum differentia, quas inter RosarioMarianæ excellunt. LXX. Pontificiæ tyrannidis adminicula eas esse, probatur. LXXI. Civitatem Magnam Cleri dominantis claudunt Equites, tum Honorarii, seu Torquati: LXXII. tum Sacri seu Religiosi, partim minùs proprie tales:
units.tr: XLI. They are shown to be the instruments of Papal lust, first because they are compelled to profess that they were instituted immediately by the Pope and not by Christ: XLII. second, because they swear an oath to the Pope as vassals to a prince: XLIII. third, because archbishops buy the pallium from the Pope, a symbol of their subjection. XLIV. The governing clergy of the second order are the provosts, archdeacons, archpresbyters, vicars and counsellors. XLV. The ministering clergy are enumerated as seven orders, defined by the Council of Trent. XLVI. They were introduced not with the support of the Word of God and a sounder antiquity, but through the emulation of the old Gentiles and the Jews. XLVII. The offices of priests, XLVIII. and likewise of deacons, subdeacons, etc., to which names no corresponding realities answer. XLIX. The colleges of canons, L. and the frivolous distinction into regular and secular. LI. Neither are truly canons. LII. The assisting clergy are enumerated as teachers of theology, of canon law, of the catechism, preachers, and scholastics of the Church. LIII. The supererogatory clergy are the monks. LIV. The beginnings of monastic life were once the cenobites, anchorites and Saraibites. LV. The vast difference between the Papal monks and the monks of the ancient Church is laid open. LVI. It is asserted that the same men agree with the old Saraibite monks, and their living emblem is drawn from Rev. ix. 3, etc. LVII. It is proved that Papal monasticism is nothing other than the political, or Babylonian, device of the Pope; first, because by means of the orders the people are held in obedience to the Pope: LVIII. to which end the exemption of the orders from the power of bishops contributes not a little. LIX. Second, because the celibacy of all clerics, and so also of the monks, is the sinew of the Papal kingdom. LX. Third, because the Roman Curia is endowed not a little by the multitude of orders. LXI. Fourth, because the innumerable multitude of monks contributes not a little to sustaining the Papal kingdom. LXII. The Papal monks are either anchorites or cenobites. LXIII. The foundations of the orders are four rules: of Basil, Augustine, Benedict and Francis. LXIV. There are four kinds of mendicant orders: Augustinians, Preachers, Carmelites and Franciscans, to which many others are referred. The non-mendicants are either regular canons or not canons. LXV. Should the Jesuits be counted among the monks? LXVI. The difference between the monks and the Jesuits in many respects, and the deplorable malice of the latter. LXVII. The incredible multitude of monks and Jesuits reveals the Great City of the ruling clergy. LXVIII. Related to monasticism are the confraternities, whose origin is traced to pagan Rome. LXIX. The differences among the fraternities, of which the Rosary and Marian ones excel. LXX. It is proved that these are aids to Papal tyranny. LXXI. The Great City of the ruling clergy is closed off by the knights, both honorary, or torque-bearing, LXXII. and sacred or religious, some of them less properly so called,

units.la: LXXIII. partim proprië tales, dicti Milites Ecclesiæ, iique vel primi, Johannitæ, Teutonici, Templarii, & S. Lazari; vel à primis derivati, qui plerique honorarii facti sunt.
units.tr: LXXIII. and some properly so called, named Knights of the Church, and these are either the first, the Hospitallers, Teutonic Knights, Templars and of St Lazarus, or those derived from the first, most of whom have been made honorary.

units.la: LXXIV. Vigent hodiéque Teutonici, seu Milites Mariani,
units.tr: LXXIV. The Teutonic Knights, or Marian Knights, still flourish today,

units.la: LXXV. & Johannitæ, seu Equites Hierosolymitani, qui Syria & Rhodo pulsi nunc Melitam incolunt.
units.tr: LXXV. and the Hospitallers, or Knights of Jerusalem, who, driven out of Syria and Rhodes, now dwell in Malta.

units.la: LXXVI. Civitatis Cleri Romani dominantis magnitudo, amplitudo & potentia concluditur, atque eandem Babylonem Magnam esse, cæteris paribus, inde evincitur.
units.tr: LXXVI. The magnitude, extent and power of the city of the ruling Roman clergy are concluded, and from this it is proved that, other things being equal, it is the same Great Babylon.

units.la: I. Babylonis Magnæ character eximius Tertius est, quòd in Civitate Magna, Religiosa, imperium in populum Magnum animalem Christi, nomen professum licet, Clero dominanti parentem, septem collibus, totidemque Provinciis distinctum, multorumque Regum potentia suffultum, obtinet. Definiri enim Babylonem, quod sit Civitas Magna, sedens super aquas multas, Bestiam, habentem septem capita, seu totidem montes, & decem cornua, atque eidem dominans, ex Apoc. xvii. 3. 7. 8. &c. 18. constat. Sensum porro definitionis hujus eum esse, quod Babylon sit Civitas Magna, Religiosa, imperium exercens in populum animalem, Christi nomen professum &c. paulò susius Dissert. iij. 14. &c. 18. 20. 21. &c. 32. 33. &c. demonstravimus.
units.tr: I. The distinguishing mark of the Great Babylon is the third: that in a Great, Religious City it holds dominion over a Great People, which professes the name of Christ, a people subject to the ruling clergy, a city divided into seven hills and as many provinces, and supported by the power of many kings. For it is established from Rev. xvii. 3, 7, 8, etc., and 18, that Babylon is defined as the Great City sitting upon many waters, the Beast having seven heads, that is, as many mountains, and ten horns, and ruling over it. Further, we have demonstrated at somewhat greater length in Dissertations iii. 14, etc., 18, 20, 21, etc., 32, 33, etc., that the sense of this definition is that Babylon is a Great, Religious City exercising dominion over a people subject to it, professing the name of Christ, etc.

units.la: II. Atque hunc quoque Characterem Hierarchiæ, seu Clero Ecclesiæ Romanæ quadrare aprime, nunc pariter demonstrandum fuerit. Cùmque in universum tria esse hujus ἀπoδείξεως capita constet; Primum scilicet, quòd Hierarchia Papalis sit Civitas Magna, Religiosa; Secundum, quòd subditos eadem habeat, Bestiam scilicet, à qua ceu Domina & Rectrix portatur; Tertium, quòd imperium in subditos illos summum exerceat; de primo in præsentiarum οὐν ἡμῖν ποληάμη agere constituimus.
units.tr: II. And now it must likewise be demonstrated that this mark also fits the Hierarchy, or Clergy of the Roman Church. Since it is clear that the demonstration [ἀποδείξεως] has three parts in general: the first, namely, that the Papal Hierarchy is a Great, Religious City; the second, that it has subjects, namely the Beast, by which it is carried as mistress and ruler; the third, that it exercises supreme dominion over those subjects. We have decided to treat the first point for the present, [οὐν ἡμῖν ποληάμη].

units.la: III. Civitatem illam Magnam, quæ Regnum gerit in Reges terræ, non tam urbem quampiam mœnibus cinctam (quanquam à tali, ceu acropoli quadam, originem ducere potest) quàm multitudinem sociatam per caput aut capita, utentem potestate imperandi, tanquam jure Metropoleos Dissert. iij. 14-18. ostendimus. Prophetæ Metaphoras & ænigmata amant. Ita Civitas est quasi Civitas, forum, quasi forum. Ita Apoc. xi. 8. Civitas Magna ubi Christus crucifixus est, Romanam ditionem notat. Aristoteles certè Polit. ii. 1. πόλιν seu Civem definit, ὧ ἐξουσία κοινωνῶν ἀρχῆς βουλευτικῆς, ἢ κεφαλῆς cui potestas est capiendi Magistratum vel deliberativum, vel judicialem. Civitas igitur multitudo justa erit eorum, quibus ista committuntur, quod statim etiam Philosophus arguit. Cùm enim in societate certis legibus unita fit ordo duplex, imperantium & parentium, ii, qui potestatem habent imperandi, potiùs Civium nomine veniunt, quàm ii, quibus necessitas parendi incumbit. Unde Apoc. xvii. 18. Civitas illa Magna, quæ Babylon vocatur, à Regibus terræ, quibus imperat, ut imperans à parente diserte distinguitur. Ut omnino civitatem eam, quæ Βασιλεύει regnat, distingui ab iis, qui reguntur, atque eos qui regunt, non itidem qui reguntur, πόλεως Civitatis nomine venire, necesse sit.
units.tr: III. That Great City, which rules over the kings of the earth, is not so much a city surrounded by walls (though it may derive its origin from such a place, as from a kind of citadel) as an assembly of people joined under a head or heads, exercising the power of command, as we showed by the right of a metropolis in Dissertation iii, 14–18. The prophets love metaphors and enigmas. Thus a city is as it were a city, a forum as it were a forum. So Rev. xi. 8, "the Great City where Christ was crucified," denotes the Roman dominion. Aristotle, certainly, in Politics ii. 1, defines a city [πόλιν] or citizen as one who shares in the power of deliberative or judicial office [ὧ ἐξουσία κοινωνῶν ἀρχῆς βουλευτικῆς, ἢ κεφαλῆς]. Therefore a city will be the just assembly of those to whom these powers are committed, which the Philosopher proceeds to argue at once. For when a society united under fixed laws has a twofold order, of those who command and of those who obey, those who have the power to command are more properly called citizens than those upon whom the necessity of obeying lies. Hence in Rev. xvii. 18 that Great City, which is called Babylon, is expressly distinguished from the kings of the earth over whom it rules, as the ruler from the ruled. So it is necessary that the city which reigns [βασιλεύει] be distinguished from those who are governed, and that those who govern, and not likewise those who are governed, be included under the name of city [πόλεως].

units.la: IV. Duplex omnino in S. literis memoratur πόλις Civitas, una est πόλις ἁγία Civitas Sancta, quæ Regem habet filium Regis cujus mentio est Apoc. xi. 2. 8. 13. Hæc aliquando conculcatur à gentibus; aliquando à gentibus recurgata est; aliquando in dispersione est, aliquando in collectione, instar fratrum unà coram Domino sedentium, & tum in emphasi Civitas vocatur, habens domos, portas, muros, custodes murorum. Vocatur etiam πόλις θεῦ Civitas Dei Apoc. iii. 12. xxii. 9. nec non ἡγαπημένη dilecta ibid. cap. xx. 9. Ἱερουσαλὴμ νέα Hierosolyma nova, cap. xxi. 2. Rursus est Civitas, quæ in sacris literis infamatur, neque aliud est, quàm Regnum terrenum homines dominos habens, & per eos fidei & conscientiæ imperans, in quorum nomine ii, qui ad eam pertinent, loquuntur & agunt, parentes ipsorum legibus, & judicia ipsorum reverentes. Ita Psal. lv. 10. 11. mentio est ע״י Civitatis, in qua est vis injusta & contentio, vanitas ac molestia in medio ejus. Hæc illa est Babylon Magna, quæ καὶ ἰσχυρὰ vocatur πόλις μεγάλη Civitas Magna Apoc. xiv. 8. xvi. 9. xvii. 18. xviii. 16. 18. 19. 21. & πόλις ἰσχυρὰ urbs robusta. Apoc. xviii. 10. S. Augustinus de Civit. Dei lib. j. cap. vocat Civitatem terrenam, quam Civitati Dei gloriosissimæ opponit, quæ terrena Civitas, inquit, cùm dominari incipit, etsi populi serviant, ipsa ei dominandi libido dominatur. Atque de hac heic loci, non de illa sermo est.
units.tr: IV. Holy Scripture mentions two kinds of city (πόλις). One is the holy city (πόλις ἁγία), which has the Son of the King as its king; mention of it is made at Rev. 11:2, 8, 13. Sometimes this city is trampled by the Gentiles, sometimes it is recovered from them. Sometimes it is in dispersion and sometimes in gathering, like brothers sitting together before the Lord, and then it is called City in the emphatic sense, having houses, gates, walls and guards of the walls. It is also called the city of God (πόλις θεοῦ), Rev. 3:12, 22:9, and "beloved" (ἠγαπημένη), ibid. ch. 20:9, and "New Jerusalem" (Ἱερουσαλὴμ καινή), ch. 21:2. There is also a city that is defamed in the sacred writings, and it is nothing other than an earthly kingdom that has men as its lords and rules faith and conscience through them. Those who belong to it speak and act in their name, and they revere their rulers' laws and judgments. Thus Psalm 55:10-11 speaks of the city [עִיר] in which there is unjust violence and strife, vanity and trouble in its midst. This is that great Babylon, which is called the "great city" (πόλις μεγάλη), Rev. 14:8, 16:19, 17:18, 18:16, 18, 19, 21, and the "strong city" (πόλις ἰσχυρά), Rev. 18:10. Augustine, in De Civitate Dei, book 1, chapter as printed, calls it the earthly city, which he sets against the most glorious City of God. This earthly city, he says, when it begins to rule, is itself dominated by the lust for dominion, even though the peoples serve it. It is of this city, and not of that other one, that we are speaking here.

units.la: V. Duplex porro etiam est imperium, Summum & Subalternum, seu delegatum. Illud ei, qui summam & ἀνυπόδοτον potestatem habet, cujusque actus alterius juri non subsunt, ita ut alterius voluntatis humanæ arbitrio irriti reddi possint; competit. Estque vel penes unum in Monarchia, vel penes plures, in Aristocratia & Oligarchia, vel penes omnes in Democratia, & Ochlocratia. Hoc verò illi convenit, qui à summa potestate dependens, inserioribus præest & imperat, pro Summæ potestatis lubitu, ita ut actus ejus universi illius juri subsint, & voluntatis ejus arbitrio rati vel irriti censeantur. Ita S. Petrus hortatur 1 Ep. ii. 13. 14. Subjecti estote cuilibet humanæ creaturæ propter Dominum; εἴτε βασιλεῖ ὡς ὑπερέχοντι, εἴτε ἡγεμόσιν, ὡς δι' αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις. Sive Regi, ut supræeminenti, sive Præfectis, ut missis (delegatis) per eum. Ubi Regis imperium statuitur αὐτοκράτωρ Supereminens, seu summum, cui parendum sine exceptione ulla, si contra Deum imperata non militent; Præfectorum vero, ceu Magistratuum inferiorum, subalternum seu Delegatum, utpote quibus parendum non simpliciter & sine exceptione, sed tanquam missis à Rege, & potestatem suam à Rege ducentibus. De hoc imperantium ἀντιαλληλισμῷ celebre illud S. Augustini, C. qui resistit. xj. q. 3. citatum. Ipsos humanarum rerum gradus adverte: Si aliquid jusserit Curator, faciendum: non tamen si contra Proconsul jubeat: aut si Consul aliquid jubeat, & aliud Imperator, non utique contemnis potestatem, sed eligis majori servire. Nec hinc debet minor irasci, si major prælatus est.
units.tr: V. There is also a twofold rule, supreme and subordinate, or delegated. The supreme rule belongs to one who has supreme power, not answerable to any other (ἀνυπόδοτον), whose acts are not subject to another's right and cannot be annulled by the decision of another human will. It lies either with one person in a monarchy, or with several in an aristocracy or oligarchy, or with all in a democracy or mob rule (ochlocracy). The subordinate rule belongs to one who, depending on the supreme power, presides over and rules inferiors at the pleasure of the supreme power, so that all his acts are subject to that right and are counted valid or void by its will. Thus St Peter exhorts, 1 Pet. 2:13-14: "Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme (ὡς ὑπερέχοντι), or to governors as sent (ὡς δι' αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις) by him." Here the king's rule is set down as supreme, as the one who is over all (αὐτοκράτωρ), to be obeyed without any exception, provided his commands do not conflict with God. The rule of the governors, as lesser magistrates, is subordinate or delegated, since they are not to be obeyed simply and without exception, but as men sent by the king, who derive their power from him. On this mutual relation of rulers, the famous passage of Augustine is cited in C. qui resistit, Causa 11, q. 3: "Consider the very grades of human affairs. If a curator orders something, it is to be done; yet not if a proconsul orders something contrary to it; or if a consul orders something and an emperor something else, you do not, of course, despise power, but you choose to serve the greater. Nor ought the lesser to be angry if the greater is set above him."

units.la: VI. Civitas igitur dominans, qualis Babylon, societas est imperantium seu dominantium, quorum alii summam potestatem, alii ὑπαλλήλων subalternam, & à summa delegatam habent. Civitatis ejusmodi exemplum nobile, argumentóque nostro appositum, Respublica Romana Ethnica, cui Papalis Hierarchia successit, suppeditat. Summa ibi potestas & Imperium una cum tempore vicissitudinem habuit, quam his verbis Tacitus Annal. lib. j. cap. j. explicat: Urbem Romam à principio Reges habuēre. Libertatem & Consulatum L. Brutus instituit. Dictaturæ ad tempus sumebantur: neque Decemviralis potestas ultra biennium, neque Tribunorum militum consulare jus diu valuit. Non Cinnæ, non Sullæ longa dominatio: & Pompeji Crassíque potentia citò in Cæsarem; Lepidi atque Antonii arma in Augustum cessere, qui cuncta discordiis civilibus fessa nomine Principis sub imperium accepit. Summa igitur potestas primò penes Reges, dein penes Consules, mox penes Dictatores, post penes Decemviros, Tribunos militum, Cinnam, Sullam, lam, Pompejum, Crassum, tandem penes Cæsares fuit. Potestas inferior, seu Delegatum Imperium inferiorum Magistratuum fuit, qui pro variante Reipublicæ forma ipsi quoque varii fuerunt, prout & ipsorum magistratuum variata ratio est. Fuerunt autem alii in urbe, seu u ba ii: alii extra urbem, seu Provinciales, quorum differ n ias & propria munera diligenter scriptores Romanorum Magiftratuum, Pomponius Lætus, Alexander ab Alexandro, Dominicus Floccus, Wolphgangus Lazius, Onuphrius Panvinius, Johannes Rofinus, aliique pertractárunt. In urbe v. g. fuerunt Præfectus vel Tribunus Celerum, qui Equitibus præfuit: Consules, qui Senatui præerant, varia pro vario Reip. statu potestate: Censores, qui censendis civium bonis, aliisque vacabant: Prætores, seu juris difceptatores jus loco Consulum dicentes: Præfecti urbis, qui cùm reliquis in rebus urbi præerant, tum causas quoque, quibus provocatio competeret, capitalesque omnes, paucis exceptis intra urbem, & centesimum ab urbe lapidem dijudicabant: Dictatores, gerendi cum summa potestate belli, vel comprimendæ seditionis causa, extra ordinem creati: Decemviri leges cum consulari potestate scribentes: Quæstores, puta urbani, vel ærarii, vel parricidii & rerum capitalium: Tribuni militum, plebis, Ædiles Curules, Cereales &c. Extra urbem in Provinciis erant Proconsules, qui constituta Monarchia à Senatu in Provincias eas, quæ populi fuerunt, missi sunt: Prætores Provinciales, & Proprætores, qui Provinciis in prætura præerant: Legati Proconsulum & Proprætorum, Quæstores Provinciales, & Proquæstores; Triumviri, Quinqueviri, Septemviri ac Decemviri coloniæ deducendæ, & fi qui similia munia alii plures in Provinciis obivere runt.
units.tr: VI. A ruling city, such as Babylon, is therefore a society of rulers or lords, some of whom hold supreme power, while others hold subordinate power delegated from the supreme. A noble example of such a city, well suited to our argument, is supplied by the pagan Roman Commonwealth, which was succeeded by the Papal Hierarchy. There supreme power and rule changed hands over time, as Tacitus explains in these words, Annals book 1, chapter 1: "The city of Rome was ruled by kings from the beginning. Lucius Brutus established liberty and the consulship. Dictatorships were assumed for a limited time; the power of the decemvirs did not last beyond two years, nor did the consular authority of the military tribunes endure long. The domination of Cinna and of Sulla was not long; the power of Pompey and Crassus soon passed to Caesar; the arms of Lepidus and Antony yielded to Augustus, who, under the name of Prince, took the nation, worn out by civil discord, under his rule." Supreme power therefore lay first with the kings, then with the consuls, soon with the dictators, afterwards with the decemvirs, military tribunes, Cinna, Sulla, Pompey and Crassus, and finally with the Caesars. The subordinate or delegated power belonged to the lesser magistrates, who varied with the form of the Commonwealth, just as the arrangement of the magistrates themselves varied. Some were in the city, others outside it, in the provinces. Their differences and proper duties have been carefully treated by writers on Roman magistrates: Pomponius Laetus, Alexander ab Alexandro, Dominicus Floccus, Wolfgang Lazius, Onuphrius Panvinius, Johannes Rosinus and others. In the city, for example, there were the Prefect or Tribune of the Knights (Celerum), who commanded the cavalry; the consuls, who presided over the Senate, with varying power according to the state of the Commonwealth; the censors, who assessed citizens' property and attended to other matters; the praetors, judges of law who pronounced law in place of the consuls; the city prefects, who presided over the city in other matters and also judged cases in which appeal lay, and all capital cases, except a few, within the city and up to the hundredth milestone from it; the dictators, created outside the ordinary order to wage war with supreme power or to suppress sedition; the decemvirs, writing laws with consular power; the quaestors, namely urban, treasury, and those for parricide and capital crimes; the military tribunes, tribunes of the plebs, curule aediles, cereal aediles and so on. Outside the city, in the provinces, there were the proconsuls, sent by the Senate into those provinces which had been of the people once a monarchy was established; the provincial praetors and propraetors, who presided over provinces with praetorian rank; the legates of proconsuls and propraetors; the provincial quaestors and proquaestors; the triumvirs, quinqueviri, septemviri and decemviri for leading out colonies; and several other similar offices which many others held in the provinces.

units.la: VII. Similem propemodum Civitatem Magnam, Societa-
units.tr: VII. A Great City, almost similar to that one: a society of rulers under the nod of one Lord, yet religious, at least in its pretext

units.la: cietatem dominantium ad nutum unius Domini, sed Religiosam illam, quoad prætextum saltem, si obtinere in Hierarchia Papali demonstraverimus, Civitatem illam Magnam Babylonicam in ejus gremio cubare, ultro liquebit. At obtinere eam in Papali Hierarchia, sequenti Syllogismo evincimus.
units.tr: If we show that this religious society, almost similar to the Great City, a society of rulers under the nod of one Lord, holds in the Papal Hierarchy, it will readily be clear that the Great Babylonian City lies in its bosom. We prove that it holds in the Papal Hierarchy by the following syllogism.

units.la: Quicunque Cœtus tuetur Hierarchiam quandam, velut divino jure institutam, atque adeò ipse societas est amplissima dominantium veteri Civitati Romanæ in Urbe & Provinciis dominanti haud absimilis, nisi quòd religionis prætextu, secus quàm illa dominium exercet: ille est Civitas illa Magna dominans, Religiosa, adeoque cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna.
units.tr: Whatever assembly upholds some Hierarchy as if instituted by divine right, and is itself a very wide society of rulers, not unlike the ancient Roman state that ruled in the City and the Provinces, except that it exercises dominion under a pretext of religion, unlike that state: that is the Great City, ruling and religious, and so, other things being equal, Great Babylon.

units.la: Atqui Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans tuetur Hierarchiam quandam, velut Divino jure institutam &c.
units.tr: But the Clergy of the Roman Church, which rules, upholds some Hierarchy, as if instituted by divine right, etc.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans est Civitas illa Magna dominans, Religiosa, adeoque cæteris paribus Babylon Magna.
units.tr: Therefore the Hierarchy, or the ruling Clergy of the Roman Church, is that Great City, ruling and religious, and so, other things being equal, Great Babylon.

units.la: VIII. Propositio dubitatione caret, & tantùm non ipsius Sanderi, maximi illius Monarchiæ Papalis patroni, disertis verbis exprimitur. Ille enim de Visib. Monarch. libr. viij. 8. ex Tertulliano sic Babylonem Magnam demonstrat: Ubi est Imperii superbia, ubi magnitudo Regiæ urbis, ubi Christianorum persecutio viget: ibi certè Babylon esse, ibi Civitatem Magnam esse, ibi Mulierem illam super populos, linguas & gentes sedere cum quâ Reges terræ fornicantur, agnoscitur. Tametsi verò vetus etiam Ecclesia fidelis in Concilio Nicæno Hierarchiam quandam servandi in amplo imperio Ecclesiæ domicilio, ordinis gratia probavit, usurpavitque, illam tamen nec ex divino jure arcessivit, nec vel in fidem & conscientias, vel in potestates seculares exercuit, ac proin ad famosam illam Civitatem Babylonicam non pertinuit, licet Sathanas iis initiis occasionibúsque ad structuram Civitatis Babylonicæ abusus fuerit. Habet quoque vera Christi Ecclesia Civitas Sanêta Dei, Hierarchiam quandam, in qua tamen ἀρχὼ ἱερὰν sacrum Principatum & Dominatum non ullus homo, sed solus Dominus ille Cœlestis Jesus Christus, Princeps & Consummator fidei ac vitæ, Rex, Caput & Dominus Ecclesiæ obtinet. Habet ille in Ecclesia suos Ὑπηρέτας, Διακόνους, Οἰκονόμους, Ministros, Diaconos, Oeconomos. Cæterùm cùm τὴν ἐξουσίαν dominationem, adeóque ἀρχὴν principatum omnem severè interdixerit iisdem, non tam ἱεραρχίαν Hierarchiæ, quæ vox propriè principatum religiosum quendam ab Ecclesiæ Ministris alienissimum tinnit, quàm ἱεροδουλίαν, & ἱεροδιακονίαν hierodulię & hierodiaconię, sacræ servitutis & ministerii rationem eorum munus habet, uti sapienter etiam Critici non nulli Tridentinorum decretorum, apud S. Polanum Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. viij. p. 670. animadverterunt, quos frivolis ratiunculis Pallavicinus Hist. Concil. Trid. Lib. xxj. 13. non tam refellit, quàm perstringit, omne disputationis suæ momentum, non in Christi, non in Apostolorum, sed in Hyperbolici illius doctoris Pseudo-Areopagitæ, Bonaventuræ, Scoti, Pighii, & similium Papalis Principatus hyperaspistarum authoritate collocans. Denique tempus etiam fuit, & Deo volente, erit, quo vera Ecclesia Christi floruit, florebitque, adeóque etiam, juxta verba Hieropsalmis Psalm. xviii. 20. educta est, educeturque במרחב in latum. Néque tamen propterea fuit, erítque unquam Ecclesia ita amplificata, vel amplificanda Civitas illa Magna Babylonica, tum quia cætera omnia imparia sunt: tum quia ὑπέρογκ, & typhus ille ἀρχῆς seu Principatus Babylonici, semper ab illa alienissimus fuit, eritque.
units.tr: VIII. The proposition is beyond doubt, and is almost stated in express words by Sanderus himself, that great champion of the Papal monarchy. In De Visibili Monarchia, book 8, chapter 8, he shows from Tertullian that this is Great Babylon: "Where there is the pride of empire, where there is the greatness of a royal city, where the persecution of Christians flourishes, there, surely, Babylon is, there the Great City is recognised, there is that woman sitting over peoples, tongues and nations, with whom the kings of the earth commit fornication." Although the ancient faithful Church, at the Council of Nicaea, approved and adopted a certain hierarchy, for the sake of order, to be kept within the wide household of the Church, it neither drew that hierarchy from divine right, nor exercised it over faith and consciences or over secular powers. Therefore it did not belong to that infamous Babylonian City, although Satan abused those beginnings and occasions to build up the Babylonian City. The true Church of Christ, the holy City of God, also has a certain hierarchy, yet in it no human being holds the sacred dominion and rule [ἀρχὴ ἱερά], but only that heavenly Lord Jesus Christ, the Prince and Perfecter of faith and life, King, Head and Lord of the Church. In the Church he has his own servants, deacons, stewards, ministers [Ὑπηρέτας, Διακόνους, Οἰκονόμους]. But since he has sternly forbidden them all domination [τὴν ἐξουσίαν] and therefore all rule [ἀρχήν], their office is not so much hierarchy [ἱεραρχία], a word which properly sounds like a certain religious principate most alien to the ministers of the Church, as sacred service and sacred ministry [ἱεροδουλία, ἱεροδιακονία], that is, the manner of hierodulia and hierodiaconia. Some critics of the Tridentine decrees have wisely noted this, as recorded by Polanus, Historia Concilii Tridentini, book 8, p. 670. Pallavicini, Historia Concilii Tridentini, book 21, chapter 13, refutes their trifling little arguments not so much as he brushes them aside, locating the whole weight of his argument not in the authority of Christ or of the Apostles, but in that hyperbolical doctor, the Pseudo-Areopagite, and in Bonaventure, Scotus, Pighius and others like them, defenders of the Papal principate. Finally, there was a time, and by God's will there will be a time, when the true Church of Christ flourished and will flourish; and so, according to the words of the Psalm, Psalm 18:20, it has been led out, and will be led out, into a broad place [במרחב]. Yet for all that, the Church has not been, and never will be, enlarged in such a way as to become that Great Babylonian City, both because all other things are unequal, and because that excess and pride of the Babylonian rule has always been, and will always be, most alien to her.

units.la: IX. Neque minùs Assumptio ἀναγκαῖον est, utpote quæ non tam probatione in re confessa & manifesta, quàm explicatione tali, quæ Babylonicam illam Civitatem Magnam in aprico collocet, indiget. Et in universum quidem Papatus ita Hierarchiam crepat, ut Concilii Tridentini Patres anathema in eos, qui Hierarchiam proprie dictam in Ecclesia locum habere negant, vibraverint. Verba Concilii Sess. xxiij. Can. 6. sic sonant: Si quis dixerit, in Ecclesia Catholica non esse Hierarchiam Divina ordinatione institutam, quæ constet ex Episcopis, Presbyteris & Ministris, anathema sit. Paulo superius cap. 4. Hierarchiam illam esse velut castrorum aciem ordinatam definit, & ad ordinem hunc Hierarchicum præter cæteros Ecclesiasticos gradus, etiam Episcopos, utpote qui in Apostolorum locum successerint, pertinere, declarat. In ordinata illa castrorum acie supremus Hierarcha Papa constituitur, tantùm non omnipotens dominus. Ei Patriarchæ, Archiepiscopi seu Primates, Metropolitani, Episcopi; his Presbyteri jure Divino, ex hypothesi, Episcopis minores, & jurisdictione Ecclesiastica destituti; reliquique ordines majores & minores succenturiantur. Revera igitur in Hierarchia sunt Rex, & Principes, Papa Imperator; Cardinales & Episcopi, instrumenta dominationis, tribuni subuno Imperatore.
units.tr: IX. The assumption is no less necessary, since it needs not so much proof of a matter already admitted and plain, as an explanation that sets that Great Babylonian City in the open. Indeed, in general the Papacy so exalts the Hierarchy that the Fathers of the Council of Trent hurled an anathema against those who deny that a Hierarchy, properly so called, has a place in the Church. The words of the Council, Session 23, canon 6, run thus: "If anyone shall say that in the Catholic Church there is no Hierarchy instituted by divine ordinance, consisting of bishops, presbyters and ministers, let him be anathema." A little earlier, in chapter 4, it defines that Hierarchy as like an army set in battle order, and declares that besides the other ecclesiastical grades, bishops also belong to this hierarchical order, as those who have succeeded to the place of the Apostles. In that army set in order, the supreme Hierarch is the Pope, who is almost an omnipotent lord. Under him are the Patriarchs, Archbishops or Primates, Metropolitans, and Bishops; under these are the presbyters, by divine right, on the hypothesis, inferior to bishops and destitute of ecclesiastical jurisdiction; and the remaining greater and lesser orders serve as reserves. Truly, then, in the Hierarchy there are a King and Princes: the Pope is the Emperor; the Cardinals and Bishops are the instruments of domination, tribunes under one Emperor.

units.la: X. Olim quidem Ecclesiasticam quandam Hierarchiam inter Episcopos & Ecclesias jure non Divino, sed humano & merè Ecclesiastico institutam esse, Spalatensis Archiepiscopus, Marcus Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. libr. iij. 2. solidè probavit. Nempe, sicut ad vitanda Schismata & confusionem tollendam singulorum Episcoporum potestas certis sedibus, & Dioecesibus arctata fuit: ita eodem jure & eadem ratione, ut unitas & concordia inter ipsos Episcopos sarta tecta conservaretur, Provinciæ etiam Ecclesiasticæ divisæ & multiplicatæ fuerunt, ut unius Provinciæ Episcopi in rebus quibusdam Ecclesiasticis fticis illi Episcopo subessent, qui in Metropoli Civitate suam sedem haberet. Hinc Metropolitani. Rursus eandem ob rationem Metropolitani plures incertis casibus uni Primati in Regia Civitate residenti subditi sunt. Hinc Primates seu Archiepiscopi. Demum & Primatibus & Metropolitanis & Episcopis unus Patriarcha in tota regione aliqua, in certis similiter praesidebat. Hinc Patriarchae. In hos quoque Romanus Patriarcha mature imperium ambivit, sed exambivit seriùs. Inde jure non Ecclesiastico Christiano, sed Antichristiano & tyrannico Papa seu Pontifex Maximus, Vicarius scilicet Christi, & Oecumenicum Ecclesiae Caput.
units.tr: X. Marcus Antonius de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato, long ago solidly proved, in De Republica Ecclesiastica, book 3, chapter 2, that a certain ecclesiastical hierarchy was instituted among bishops and churches, not by divine right but by human and merely ecclesiastical right. Indeed, just as the power of individual bishops was restricted to fixed sees and dioceses in order to avoid schisms and remove confusion, so by the same right and the same reasoning, in order that unity and concord might be kept intact among the bishops themselves, ecclesiastical provinces were also divided and multiplied, so that the bishops of one province were subject, in certain ecclesiastical matters, to that bishop who had his see in the metropolitan city. Hence Metropolitans. Again, for the same reason, several Metropolitans were made subject, in certain cases, to one Primate residing in the royal city. Hence Primates or Archbishops. Finally, one Patriarch presided over the Primates, Metropolitans and Bishops in some whole region, in a similar way on certain occasions. Hence Patriarchs. The Roman Patriarch also early sought to gain authority over these, and gained it, but more slowly. Thence, by a right not Christian-ecclesiastical but Antichristian and tyrannical, came the Pope, or Pontifex Maximus, that is, the Vicar of Christ and the Ecumenical Head of the Church.

units.la: XI. Presbyterorum & Ministrorum, quos ad Hierarchiam Synodus Tridentina refert, & septem numero, puta Sacerdotes, seu Presbyteros, Diaconos, Subdiaconos, Acoluthos, Exorcistas, Lectores & Ostiarios, par fere ratio est; si Presbyteros, docentes scilicet & Diaconos, institutos à Christo & Apostolis, sed diversissimo instituto, exceperis.
