Paulatim quidem instituti sunt ab Ecclesia ordines non nulli, ceu utiles convenientésque ad varios Ecclesiae usus & Oeconomias, ut majore cum dignitate, gravitate & decentia publicus Dei cultus in Christianis coetibus paulò frequentioribus exerceretur, utque per varios istos ordinum diversorum gradus illi, qui se in Clerum, hoc est, censum & catalogum hominum Ecclesiasticorum dabant, paulatim in disciplina Ecclesiastica informarentur, adeòque ad supremum Episcopatus vel Presbyteratus ordinem & gradum aliquando promoverentur. Ita igitur Ostiarii constituti sunt, ut ab Ecclesiae introitu arcerent ignotos, externos, minimè Christianos, excommunicatos, energumenos, quin & ipsos Catechumenos, Synaxeos tempore. Exorcistae qui primò quidem, vigentibus adhuc donis, solo vocis imperio in Christi nomine, precibus item ac jejuniis dæmonia ejiciebant, postea, dum in Templis sacra peragebantur, extra Ecclesiam ad Energumenos exibant, & præscriptas precum formulas de libro recitabant, quibus subinde, non semper tamen, Deo volente, & ad totius Ecclesiæ intus precantis intercessionem, non vi ulla exorcismorum Energumeni liberati sunt, quibus precibus superstitione invalescente, etiam certæ exorcismorum formulæ adjunctæ sunt: Lectores & Cantores, qui sacris hymnis atque psalmis decantandis, nec non precum formulis, Euangelio & Epistola prælegendis, populo inserviebant; Pastoribus interim, seu Presbyteris Eucharistiæ benedictionem & distributionem sibi solis reservantibus, sacràsque ad populum conciones recitantibus: Acoluthi, qui non ut famuli & vilia quædam mancipia, sed ut Ministri honorabiles Episcopis, jam supra Presbyterorum conditionem evectis, assisterent, honoris causa eos perpetuò assectarentur, variisque in rebus ad officium eorum pertinentibus iis inservirent, testésque adeò essent bonæ & laudabilis eorum conversationis, & consortio eo ipsi quoque ædificarentur: Subdiaconi, qui Ecclesia amplis possessionibus jam locupletata, Diaconis sublevandis adjuncti sunt. Hæc munera pro ratione temporum, locorum & personarum, ac inprimis in majoribus & matricibus Ecclesiis, quas Episcopales, Cathedrales, Metropolitanas, Patriarchales vocabant, in quibus ob maximum populi concursum cultus Dei magna cum celebritate frequentabatur, utilia esse potuerunt, inprimis cùm vel aliæ non fuerint, vel paucæ certè fuerint Christianorum scholæ, quibus S. Ministerii candidati in universa disciplina Ecclesiastica instruerentur.
units.tr: XI. The number of presbyters and ministers which the Council of Trent refers to the Hierarchy is seven: namely, priests, or presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers and doorkeepers. The case is nearly the same, except for the presbyters who teach, and the deacons, which were instituted by Christ and the Apostles, though by a very different institution. Some orders were gradually instituted by the Church, as useful and fitting for its various uses and economies, so that public worship of God might be carried on with greater dignity, gravity and decorum in the assemblies of Christians, which were somewhat more frequent, and so that, through these various grades of the different orders, those who put themselves forward into the clergy, that is, the register and roll of ecclesiastical persons, might be gradually trained in ecclesiastical discipline, and at times be promoted to the supreme order and grade of bishop or presbyter. Thus doorkeepers were appointed, to keep out of the entrance of the Church strangers, outsiders, those who were by no means Christians, the excommunicated, the possessed, and even the catechumens, at the time of the Synaxis. Exorcists were at first, while the gifts still flourished, those who cast out demons by the command of their voice alone in the name of Christ, and likewise by prayers and fasts. Later, while sacred rites were being performed in the temples, they went outside the Church to the possessed and recited prescribed forms of prayer from a book. By these prayers, often though not always, and by God's will, and through the intercession of the whole Church praying within, the possessed were freed, not by any force of exorcisms. As superstition grew strong, certain set formulas of exorcism were also added to these prayers. Readers and cantors served the people by chanting sacred hymns and psalms, and also by reading the prayer formulas, the Gospel and the Epistle, while the pastors, or presbyters, reserved for themselves alone the blessing and distribution of the Eucharist, and recited the sacred sermons to the people. Acolytes attended bishops, who had already been raised above the condition of presbyters, not as servants and some base slaves, but as honourable ministers; they were always in attendance out of respect, served them in various matters pertaining to their office, and were thus witnesses of their good and praiseworthy conduct, and were edified by that very companionship. Subdeacons were added to help the deacons, when the Church had already been enriched by ample possessions. These offices could be useful, according to the circumstances of times, places and persons, and above all in the greater and mother churches, which they called episcopal, cathedral, metropolitan or patriarchal, in which, because of the very large concourse of people, the worship of God was carried on with great solemnity. They could be useful especially since there were either no other schools of Christians, or certainly very few, in which candidates for the sacred ministry might be instructed in the whole of ecclesiastical discipline.

units.la: XII. Cæterùm una cum Papatu, seu Pontificia in spiritualibus & temporalibus dominatione, nec non Missæ sacrificio invalescente, & radices in Ecclesia agente, Hierarchia illa, ordinésque, munera sua amiserunt, & servata nomina diversam plane potestatem acquiferunt. Accidit plane, quod Augusti ævo accidisse Tacitus A. l. 4. 1. memorat, his verbis: Verso civitatis statu nihil usquam prisci & integri moris: omnis exuta æqualitate jussa principis aspectare; quódque apud eundem Hift. l. 37. 5. Otho ad milites suos dixit, Galbam falsis nominibus feveritatem pro sævitia, parsimoniam pro avaritia, fupplicia & contumelias militum disciplinam appellare. Plane sic verso Ecclesiæ statu, & libertate in dominationem, fide in perfidiam degenerante, nihil prisci integrique, qualis nominibus. Hierarchiæ ordinúmque veterum inerat, moris superat, falsisque nominibus dicti adhuc sunt, dicunturque Episcopi, qui non docent, non pascunt, ex Dei verbo; Sacerdotes, qui, sacrificio vero destituti, non facrificant; Diaconi, qui Ecclesiarum fatis jam dotatarum oblationibus non inserviunt; Acoluthi Episcoporum, qui eos, canibus venaticis, equitibus, militibus prætoriis potiús quàm talibus comitatos, non eo modo, quo olim, afsectantur ampliùs; Exorcistæ, qui nec voce humana, nec Divina potestate Dæmones pellunt; Lectores qui ita legunt, ut à populo non intelligantur. Quid ergo? Nominibus illis Hierarchiæ & ordinum mera jam dominatio, adulterina officia, pinguésque præbendæ subsunt.
units.tr: XII. Moreover, as the papal domination over spiritual and temporal affairs grew strong, and the sacrifice of the Mass took root in the Church, that hierarchy and its orders lost their functions. Although they kept their names, they acquired a plainly different power. What happened then is what Tacitus records as happening in the age of Augustus, in these words: When the condition of the city had changed, nothing of the ancient and sound custom remained anywhere; stripped of all equality, everyone looked to the commands of the prince. And what Otho said to his soldiers in the same author, that Galba called severity by false names: cruelty, and thrift avarice, and the punishments and insults of soldiers discipline. In the same way, with the state of the Church turned, liberty degenerating into domination and faith into perfidy, nothing of the ancient and sound character of the hierarchy and orders remains beyond the names. Those names are still used with false meanings. They are called bishops, who neither teach nor feed from the Word of God; priests, who, having lost the true sacrifice, do not sacrifice; deacons, who no longer serve at the offerings of churches already endowed with wealth; acolytes of the bishops, who no longer attend them in the old way, but follow them with hunting dogs, horsemen and praetorian soldiers rather than such companions; exorcists, who drive out demons neither by the human voice nor by divine power; readers, who read in such a way that the people cannot understand them. What then? Beneath those names of hierarchy and orders there now lie sheer domination, adulterous offices and fat prebends.

units.la: XIII. Cùmque olim Patriarcharum, Archiepiscoporum, Metropolitanorum, Episcoporum dignitas ab humana Ecclesiastica institutione Civitatum magnitudinem, Secularémque dignitatem respiciente, arceflita tota fuerit, uti vel inde maximè liquet, quòd in Conciliis omnes circa Hierarchicam fubordinationem illam controversiæ non nisi ex statutis Ecclesiasticis, & Civitatum typis Secularibus terminatæ sunt: Eò tandem audaciæ Papalis factio prorupit, ut Hierarchiam suam, quæ tantùm à vetere illa Hierarchia, quantum mus farina aspersus à domino pistrini distat, ad jus Divinum & successionem Apostolorum reducere, non dubitaverit. Sanderus enim de visib. Monarch. lib. vij. num. 6. dissertè pertendit, Patriarchas, Primates, & Metropolitanos succedere Apostolis in pleniori potestate, non item Episcopos. Bellarminus quoque de Rom. Pontif. libr. iv. in fine asserit, Petrum instituisse Patriarcham Alexandrinum & Antiochenum, qui ab eo authoritate accepta toti ferè Asiæ & Africæ præfuerint, & Archiepiscopos creare potuerint, qui postea Episcopos crearent. Quæ vanissima esse, & scenæ duntaxat inservire, quis non animadvertit? Quomodo enim ad successionem Apostolicam majoris potestatis reducetur Episcopus v. g. ille, qui ex Seculari sola Provinciarum divisione, aut civitatis in Metropolin erectione, aut ex sola Ecclesiastica institutione Extravag. Sol. de Præb. & dign. in om. factus est Metropolita, sede sua Episcopali in Metropolitanam erecta? Qui verò originem ordinis Hierarchici inter Episcopos merè humanam accuratiùs cognoscere lubet, viros doctissimos, Salmasium de Primatu Papæ, M. Antonii de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. lib. iij. 2. Theophilum Banosium de Politia Civitatis Dei, & Hierarch. Rom. cap. 13. 15. adeat licet.
units.tr: XIII. The dignity of patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans and bishops was once fixed by human ecclesiastical institution, with regard to the size of cities and secular rank. This is especially clear from the fact that in the councils all disputes about that hierarchical subordination were settled only by ecclesiastical statutes and the secular models of cities. At last the Papal faction broke out into such audacity that it did not hesitate to trace its hierarchy back to divine right and the succession of the apostles, although it differs from that old hierarchy as much as a mouse sprinkled with flour differs from the miller. For Sanderus, in de visib. Monarch. lib. vij. num. 6, clearly contends that patriarchs, primates and metropolitans succeed the apostles in fuller power, but bishops do not. Bellarmine too, in de Rom. Pontif. libr. iv. near the end, asserts that Peter instituted the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch, who, having received authority from him, presided over almost all of Asia and Africa and could create archbishops, who afterwards created bishops. Who does not see that these claims are most vain and serve only the stage? For how can a bishop, for example one who became metropolitan merely by a secular division of provinces, or by the erection of a city into a metropolis, or merely by ecclesiastical institution Extravag. Sol. de Præb. & dign. in om., with his episcopal see raised to a metropolitan see, be brought back to the apostolic succession of greater power? Whoever wishes to know more accurately the origin of the hierarchical order among bishops, which is purely human, may consult the most learned men: Salmasius de Primatu Papæ, Marcus Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. lib. iij. 2, Theophilus Banosius de Politia Civitatis Dei, and Hierarch. Rom. cap. 13, 15.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Nuspiam certè Christus, nuspiam Apostoli Hierarchiam, nedum Hierarchicum ordinem ullum instituerunt, quin potius Ecclesiæ Ministris principatum, dominationémque quibuslibet interdictis prohibuerunt. S. Paulus 1 Cor. xii. 28. 29. &c. Ecclesiæ ministeria varia recensens, nullam memorat ἰεραρχίαν, nullos ἀρχοντας principes, ποιμένας Legislatores nullos. Nulli ibi loquentes verba inaudita, & sola authoritate controversias fidei determinantes, nulli peccata ex potestate remittentes, nulli Regibus, Principibúsque dominantes, nulli sacerdotes
units.tr: Certainly nowhere did Christ or the apostles institute a hierarchy, much less any hierarchical order. Rather, they forbade the ministers of the Church any principality or domination whatsoever. St. Paul, 1 Cor. xii. 28, 29, etc., listing the various ministries of the Church, mentions no hierarchy [ἱεραρχίαν], no rulers [ἄρχοντας] or princes, and no shepherds [ποιμένας] or legislators. There are no speakers there uttering unheard-of words, no one determining controversies of faith by authority alone, no one remitting sins by his own power, no one lording it over kings and princes, and no priests

units.la: Hierarchia omnis Verbo Dei reparat. proprië dicti conficientes corpus Domini, & illud pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum offerentes quæ in papatu utramque paginam faciunt.
units.tr: Every hierarchy is repaired by the Word of God. Properly so called, they consecrate the body of the Lord and offer it for the sins of the living and the dead, things which in the Papacy make up both sides of the page.

units.la: XV. Quin potiùs idem eum, qui se ἀντιχρίστου, effert supra Deum, & σέβασμα, omne Augustum, Hominem Peccati, & Adversarium Christi 2 Thess. ii. 3. 4. vocat. Neque obscurè etiam genium ingeniúmque Hierarcharum in Pseudapostolis ἐν πλήρει ἀπιστίας in audacia & elatione gloriantibus, depingit 2 Cor. xi. 20. Toleratis enim, si quis vos in servitutem redigit, si quis devorat, si quis accipit, si quis se effert, si quis in faciem vos cædit. Hæc illorum indoles est. Primò καταδουλοῦν in servitutem redigunt legibus suis, statutis, canonibus, placitis, imperiis Ecclesiam subjiciunt. Atqui non in Regno Christi est servus & liber Gal. iii. 28. sed in Regno Antichristi Apoc. xiii. 6. Ibi sunt alii מחקקים Legislatores, ἄρχοντες & καταχυριεύοντες, alii עברים servi, qui δεσποτικῷ Imperio & jurisdictioni hominum subjacent. Tum Hierarchæ καταδυναστεύουσιν devorant. Finis enim διακονίας dominii est πλησμονὴ σαρκὸς expletio carnis. Qui dominari volunt, iidem etiam bona Ecclesiæ, & oblationes matronarum in potestate sua habere volunt, ut ex illis ditentur, & luxurient, dum propter eorum luxum & fastum alii esurire & egere coguntur. Neque tantùm sic oblata devorant, sed etiam λαμβάνουσι accipiunt non oblata, nihil reliqui facientes, ut Ecclesia unctiores reddat, ne ad fastum luxúmque quidquam desit. Præterea etiam ὑπέρογκα, se extollunt præ se ferentes neminem, nullius judicio se subjicientes, exactoremque fidei & vitæ neminem tolerantes, & ne quidem τῆς ἐξουσίας ὑπερεχόντων potestati supereminenti obsequentes, quin potiùs τὰς δόξας βλασφημοῦντες glorias præcellentes convitiis incessentes 2 Pet. ii. 10. & se supra Deum & omne σέβασμα exaltantes 2 Thess. ii. 4. Denique ὡς πεισω- τὰ διϚεν ... in faciem cædunt. Admonitiones increpationes illorum sunt merè ὑβρι..., maximo cum probro conjunctæ, quomodo Græcis ὕβρις summum opprobrium habitum est ... κεφαλὴν τύπτειν cædere maxillam.
units.tr: XV. Rather, the same Scripture calls him who opposes [ἀντικείμενος], exalts himself above God and every object of worship [σέβασμα], everything called august, the man of sin and the adversary of Christ, 2 Thess. ii. 3, 4. Nor does it obscurely depict the nature and disposition of the hierarchs among the false apostles, full of unbelief [ἐν πλήρει ἀπιστίας], boasting in audacity and pride, 2 Cor. xi. 20: For you put up with it if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you on the face. Such is their character. First, they enslave [καταδουλοῦν]: they reduce the Church to servitude by their laws, statutes, canons, decrees and commands. Yet in the kingdom of Christ there is neither slave nor free, Gal. iii. 28, but in the kingdom of Antichrist there are, Apoc. xiii. 6. There are others who are legislators [מחקקים], rulers [ἄρχοντες] and lords [καταχυριεύοντες], and others who are servants [עברים], subject to despotic [δεσποτικῷ] command and the jurisdiction of men. Then the hierarchs devour [καταδυναστεύουσιν]. For the end of ministry [διακονίας] is dominion, and the end of dominion is the satisfying of the flesh [πλησμονὴ σαρκὸς]. Those who wish to rule also wish to hold in their power the goods of the Church and the offerings of matrons, so that they may grow rich and live in luxury, while others are forced to hunger and want on account of their luxury and pride. And they do not merely devour what has been offered, but also take [λαμβάνουσι], and receive what has not been offered, leaving nothing behind, so that the Church is made richer and nothing is lacking to their pride and luxury. Moreover, they are puffed up [ὑπέρογκα], and lift themselves up, showing themselves to no one, submitting to no one's judgment, tolerating no one as a censor of faith and life, and not even yielding to the power of those who are over them [τῆς ἐξουσίας ὑπερεχόντων]; rather, they revile the glories [τὰς δόξας βλασφημοῦντες], assailing those who excel with insults, 2 Pet. ii. 10, and they exalt themselves above God and every object of worship, 2 Thess. ii. 4. Finally, they strike on the face [ὡς πεισω... in faciem cædunt]. Their admonitions and rebukes are sheer insolence [ὑβρις...], joined with the greatest disgrace, just as among the Greeks insolence [ὕβρις] was held to be the highest disgrace, striking the head [κεφαλὴν τύπτειν], that is, to strike the jaw.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Hæc cum Hierarchia, humana potestate conjunctissima esse, facilè Papatum vel per transfennam insipienti liquet. Ibi enim πρῶτον πίστεως primum fidei principium habetur, omnem animam propter salutem æternam subesse debere Papæ, & si non directè, indirectè saltem omnia & bona & corpora fidelium, sive baptizatorum in ipsius potestate esse. Quemadmodum autem ea potestate Papa utatur, in propatulo est. Accipit, devorat homines & excoriat, Reges sibi mancipat, de thronis suis eos deturbat, arbores Libani exscindit, imparentes sibi interficit, bella in eos excitat, aqua & igni iis interdicit, excruciat, collo inequitat omnium, judicat omnes, à nemine judicandus ipse. Atque dominationis hujus Papalis instrumenta se reliqui gerunt omnes juramento, grandíque pretio ad id conducti, auctoratíque.
units.tr: That this hierarchy is most closely bound up with human power is plain enough, even to a fool who has merely glanced at the Papacy. For there they hold as the first principle of faith [πρῶτον πίστεως] that every soul must be subject to the Pope for the sake of eternal salvation, and that all the goods and bodies of the faithful, that is, of the baptized, are in his power, if not directly then at least indirectly. How the Pope uses that power is out in the open. He takes and devours men and flays them, makes kings his slaves, casts them down from their thrones, cuts down the cedars of Lebanon, kills those who will not obey him, stirs up wars against them, forbids them water and fire, tortures them, rides on the necks of all, judges everyone, and is judged by no one. And all the other agents of this Papal domination conduct themselves by oath, hired and enlisted for a large fee.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Hierarchiam talem non Spiritus Christi, vel Apostolorum, sed genius Romuli peperit. Si enim religionis inanem & ficulneum prætextum, parandæ retinendæque dominationi arreptum dempseris, de cætero Hierarchia Romana, seu Civitas illa magna Babylonica, & civitas Romana dominans vetus aprimè conveniunt. Conferat, cui lubet, inter se Papatus & Imperii Veteris statum, Annalésque Cæsarum, qui ante Papas Romæ rerum sunt potiti, à Suetonio, Capitolino, Lampridio, aliis consignatos, & Paparum, qui Cæsaribus successerunt, juxta historias à Platina, Onuphrio, Guicciardino conscriptas perpendat, comperietque facilè Papalem statum se Cæsarum Imperio Civitatis potestatisque magnitudine, & dominationis superbia adæquasse.
units.tr: Such a hierarchy was not begotten by the Spirit of Christ or of the Apostles, but by the genius of Romulus. For if you remove the empty, fig-leaf pretext of religion, seized to acquire and keep domination, the Roman hierarchy agrees very well in all other respects with that great Babylonian city, the ruling Roman state of old. Let anyone who wishes compare the condition of the Papacy with that of the old Empire. Let him weigh the annals of the Caesars, who held power at Rome before the Popes, as recorded by Suetonius, Capitolinus, Lampridius and others, and the Popes who succeeded the Caesars, as described in the histories of Platina, Onofrio and Guicciardini. He will easily discover that the Papal state equalled the empire of the Caesars in the greatness of its city and power, and in the arrogance of its domination.

units.la: XVIII. Sed age αὐτὸς μάρτυρας Domesticos testes, Pontificios scilicet promamus, ex quibus Hierarchiam Romanam ad amussim veteris Romæ dominantis factam, adeóque à genio non Christi, sed Romuli prognatam esse, magnitudinemque Civitatis dominantis religiosæ, veteris Ethnicæ magnitudinem referre, constet. Ex pluribus paucos citare in testimonium juvabit. Primus esto Petrus Messias de Sibilia, Hispanus, qui Silvam variæ Lectionis scripsit, Venetiis editam. Inter alia sic ille: Translata Imperii sede ab Occidente in Orientem, ut Imperator Constantinopoli, sic Papa Romanus Romæ omnium Ecclesiarum Monarcha sedere affectavit, & tandem Regnum sibi & suis constituit. In locum Consulum, qui olim Imperium Romanum administrabant, successerunt Cardinales non duo numero, sed tot, quot Papæ Hierarchiæ Principi visum fuerit. Archiepiscopi Ducibus sunt adæquati; Episcopi in locum Comitum suffecti; vicarii Episcoporum, Præsidum Imperii dignitatem, Præpositi Præfectorum vicem referunt; Archipresbyteri in locum tribunorum militum substituti sunt; Cancellarii Tribunos plebis repræsentant; Archidiaconi munus Prætoris; Decani Centurionis; Subdiaconi locum Duum virum occupant. Idem Phalangem Clericorum Hierarchiæ ministrorum incredibilem commemorat.
units.tr: XVIII. But come, let us bring forward our own domestic witnesses, namely the Papists, from whom it is evident that the Roman hierarchy was fashioned exactly after the pattern of ruling Rome of old, and so is descended from the genius not of Christ but of Romulus, and that the greatness of the ruling religious city reflects the greatness of the old heathen one. It will help to cite a few of the many as witnesses. Let the first be Peter Messias of Seville, a Spaniard, who wrote the Silva of Varied Reading, published at Venice. Among other things he says: When the seat of empire was transferred from the West to the East, so that the Emperor sat at Constantinople, the Roman Pope likewise aspired to sit at Rome as monarch of all churches, and at last set up a kingdom for himself and his own. In place of the consuls, who once administered the Roman empire, there succeeded cardinals, not two in number but as many as the Pope, the prince of the hierarchy, saw fit. Archbishops are equal to dukes; bishops are substituted for counts; vicars of bishops take the dignity of provincial governors; provosts take the place of prefects; archpriests are substituted for military tribunes; chancellors represent the tribunes of the people; archdeacons hold the office of praetor; deans that of centurion; subdeacons occupy the place of the duumvirs. The same writer records an incredible host of clerics, the phalanx of ministers of the hierarchy.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Succedat Aubertus Miraeus Bruxellensis, author Notitiæ Episcopatuum Orbis Christiani. Is Dedicatione ad Guidonem Bentivolum Rhodiorum Archiepiscopum, sic veteris Romæ gentilis & Papalis Hierarchicæ quoad Imperii magnitudinem analogiam explicat: Ecclesiæ politia, qua nihil illustrius aut laudabilius, verè vinculum est & fulcrum, quod orbem Christianum universum, ligat ac sustinet. Unum ea semper habuit caput & Principem, Romanum Pontificem, legitimum Christi in terris vicarium, Petrique Apostolorum antesignani successorem. Huic proximi olim Patriarchæ quatuor primarii, sed longo proximi intervallo. Sequuntur Metropolitani, sive Archiepiscopi, & longa serie Episcopi singulis suæ diœceses, provinciæ, parœciæ sunt attributæ & commissæ. Divisionis hujus typos ac formas Ecclesia à Republica Romana, qua nulla nec major, nec sanctior (superavit ergo etiam sanctitatem Romæ Papalis) nec bonis exemplis ditior fuit, magna ex parte est mutuata, adeò quidem, ut veteres Provinciæ Ecclesiasticæ cum civilibus fere conveniant: quod ante nos & alii observarunt. Sacræ ipsius politiæ fundamenta primis jacta fuêre seculis: cultu deinde Christiano publicè per Imperatores stabilito, facies tota paulatim magis nosci cœpta. Cujus quidem lumen apud extremos hodie Indos, & alio sole calentes Antipodes effulget, quo populi Romani nomen nunquam penetravit. O felix Roma, gentium domina, & fato quodam ad imperium orbis terrarum nata! Mira profectò in te Dei benignitas. Cùm armorum vim eripuit, supremam legum authoritatem attribuit: nimirum aut (juxta verba Leonis Papæ serm. j. de natali S.S. Petri & Pauli) civitas Sacerdotalis, & Regia, per sacram beati Petri sedem, caput Orbis effecta latius præsideret religione Divina, quàm dominatione terrena.
units.tr: Next let Aubertus Miraeus of Brussels follow, author of the Notitia of the Bishoprics of the Christian World. In his dedication to Guido Bentivoglio, Archbishop of Rhodes, he sets out the analogy between ancient gentile Rome and the Papal hierarchy, as regards the greatness of empire: The polity of the Church, than which nothing is more illustrious or praiseworthy, is truly the bond and prop that binds and sustains the whole Christian world. It has always had one head and prince, the Roman Pontiff, the lawful vicar of Christ on earth and successor of Peter, the foremost of the Apostles. Next to him once stood four chief patriarchs, but at a long remove. Then come the metropolitans, or archbishops, and in a long series the bishops, to each of whom their dioceses, provinces and parishes have been assigned and entrusted. The Church has borrowed the types and forms of this division largely from the Roman Republic, than which none was greater or holier (so that even the holiness of Papal Rome surpassed it) nor richer in good examples. Hence the ancient ecclesiastical provinces agree almost exactly with the civil ones, as others before us have also observed. The foundations of this sacred polity were laid in the earliest centuries; then, when Christian worship was publicly established by the emperors, the whole form gradually began to be better known. Its light now shines even among the farthest Indians and the Antipodes warmed by another sun, where the name of the Roman people never reached. O happy Rome, mistress of the nations, born by some fate for the empire of the world! Truly wonderful is God's kindness toward you. When he took away the force of arms, he granted you the supreme authority of laws; indeed, as Pope Leo says (sermon 1 on the birthday of Saints Peter and Paul), the sacerdotal and royal city, made the head of the world through the holy see of blessed Peter, presides more widely in divine religion than in earthly dominion.

units.la: XX. Quòd ab aliis observatum esse, quòd divisionis diœcesium, provinciarum, parœciarum formam Ecclesia à Republica Romana mutuata sit, Miræus notat, verum est. Ipse enim olim etiam Gregorius VII. lib. vij. epist. 35. ad ipsum observavit, & suavi figmento auxit.
units.tr: XX. That others have observed that the Church borrowed the form of division into dioceses, provinces and parishes from the Roman Republic, as Miraeus notes, is true. For Gregory VII himself observed this long ago in his letter to him (book 7, letter 35), and embellished it with a pleasing fiction.

units.la: Provinciæ, inquit, multo ante Christi adventum tempore divisæ sunt, maxima ex parte, & postea ab Apostolis & B. Clemente prædecessore nostro ipsa divisio est renovata: & in capite provinciarum, ubi dudum Primates legis erant secali, ac primò judiciaria potestas ipsis quoque civitatibus, vel locis celebrioribus Patriarchas vel Primates, qui unam formam tenent, licet diversa sint nomina; leges Divinæ & Ecclesiasticæ poni & esse jusserunt: ad quos Episcopi si necesse fuerint, confugerent, eósque appellarent, ut ipsi nomine primatu fruerentur, & non alii. Reliquæ verò Metropolitanæ Civitates, quæ minores judices habebant, licet majorum comitum essent, haberent tamen Metropolitanos suos, qui prædictis juste obedivit Primatibus: sicut & in legibus Seculi olim ordinatum erat, qui non Primatum, sed aut Metropolitanorum aut Episcoporum nomine fruerentur &c. Nuper etiam Petrus de Marca Parisiensis Archiepiscopus de Concordia Sacerdotii & Imperii lib. j. cap. 3, 4. &c. Ecclesiarum divisionem per Provincias ad exemplum Imperii Romani veteris, ab Apostolis ipsis factam, ab Episcopis, qui erant in majoribus urbibus constituti, per incrementa variorum temporum auctam, tandémque ultimam dispositionem consecutam esse, pluribus probare connixus est.
units.tr: Provinces, he says, were divided long before the coming of Christ, for the most part, and afterwards the division itself was renewed by the Apostles and by blessed Clement, our predecessor; and in the head cities of the provinces, where of old the chief men of the secular law were, and first the judicial power, they ordered the divine and ecclesiastical laws to be set up in the more famous cities or places, Patriarchs or Primates, who keep one form although the names differ; to them bishops, if need be, should flee and appeal, so that they alone might enjoy the title of Primate and not others. The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although they belonged to greater counts, nevertheless had their own metropolitans, who justly obeyed the aforesaid Primates, just as it was once ordained also in the laws of the world that they should enjoy not the title of Primate but of metropolitans or bishops, and so on. Recently too Peter de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, in On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire, book 1, chapters 3 and 4, and so on, has laboured to prove by many arguments that the division of the churches into provinces, on the model of the old Roman Empire, was made by the Apostles themselves; that it was increased by the bishops set up in the greater cities through the growth of various times; and that at last the final arrangement followed.

units.la: XXI. Non prætereundus est Bellarminus, qui Præsat. ad libros de membris Ecclesiæ militantis Papam Imperatorem in terris, Episcopos Tribunos militarium, & Presbyteros Centuriones cohortium facit. Licet, inquit, Imperator Ecclesiæ primus & summus Christus ipse sit, tamen quòd non solùm in terris, sed etiam in cœlis & apud inferos magnos exercitus habeat, quodque solis cœlestibus præsentiam suam, ut par est, aspectabilem præbeat, vicarium Imperatorem ac Ducem exercitui, qui est in terris, Apostolum Petrum ejusque successores summo cum Imperio & potestate præfecit. Ergo Romanus Pontifex, hæres Apostolorum Principis castra in terris ducit, Christúmque ipsum nobis mortalibus quodammodo repræsentat. Proximi sunt Episcopi, qui tribunorum militarium locum sortiti, imperant etiam ipsi non totis castris, sed agmini quisque suo. Siquidem in partem solicitudinis, ut nostri loquuntur, vocati sunt, non in plenitudinem potestatis. Sub his Presbyteri quasi quidam Centuriones singulis cohortibus præsunt, Diaconi, Subdiaconi, Lectores atque Administri ceteri, vel signa atque Aquilas gerunt, vel tubis ac tympanis accendunt ad prælium vel huc atque illuc celeriter discurrentes, mandata Imperatoris ac Ducum ad milites perferunt.
units.tr: XXI. Bellarmine must not be passed over, who in the preface to his books on the members of the militant Church makes the Pope the Emperor on earth, the bishops tribunes of the soldiers, and the presbyters centurions of the cohorts. Although, he says, Christ himself is the first and highest Emperor of the Church, yet since he has great armies not only on earth but also in heaven and among the dead, and since he alone shows his presence visibly to the heavenly ones, as is fitting, he has set the Apostle Peter and his successors over the army on earth as vicar emperor and commander, with supreme command and power. Therefore the Roman Pontiff, heir of the Prince of the Apostles, leads the camp on earth, and in a way represents Christ himself to us mortals. Next come the bishops, who, having obtained the place of military tribunes, also command, each not the whole camp but his own division. For they have been called into a share of the care, as our people say, not into the fullness of power. Under these, presbyters as centurions preside over each cohort; deacons, subdeacons, readers and the other attendants either carry the standards and eagles, or sound the battle with trumpets and drums, or, running swiftly hither and thither, carry the orders of the Emperor and the commanders to the soldiers.

units.la: XXII. Unum addam, cum plures possem, Justum Lipsium, qui editis de Magnitudine Romana libris duobus, sic Lectorem affatur: Romanus ille Dictator, ut sic appellem, & Pontifex fulcrum aut vinculum est, quod sustinet, quod ligat labentes aut dissidentes in malè compacto hoc ædificio partes. Abite non impii solum, sed imperiti, qui aliter nobis constat hanc ipsam Romam, & sacrum in ea Imperium fuisse & esse velut Anchoram fluctuanti diu Europæ. Mira Dei benignitas in hanc urbem! cum legionum vim eripuit, legum attribuit, cum armis imperare noluit, sacris indulsit, & sic quoque facit eam decus, tutelam, columen rerum. Atqui senatus ille vetus non est, inquiunt. Non ille, sed alius: & vide mihi in ista purpura ex omni nostro orbe selectos Proceres, moribus prudentia, annis spectandos. Si vetus ille Cyneas redeat, & hunc confessum videat, nihil ambigat vel cum Regibus iterum vel cum Heroibus comparare. Quid tributa? non tam multa, sed magis innoxia & ultronea sunt. Quid legationes gentium? nec ea desunt, & ex noto ignotoque orbe (tanta diffusio majestatis hujus est) concurritur, & jura & leges Sacrorum binc petunt. Ipsi Reges & Principes adeunt & inclinantur & obnoxia capita uni huic capiti submittunt. Quid Principes aut homines loquor? aërei, terreni, inferi Spiritus sive Genii veretur ac trepidant, & Cœlestem illam in terris potestatem vel invití ac reluctantes agnoscunt. Hactenus ille, ita Romam Pontificiam laudibus ferens, ut ejus majestatem amplitudinemque supra veteris illius extollat.
units.tr: XXII. I will add one, though I could add many: Justus Lipsius, who, in his two books on Roman greatness, addresses the reader thus: That Roman dictator, if I may call him so, and pontiff is the prop or bond that sustains the parts that are slipping or disagreeing in this ill-joined building. Begone, you who are not only impious but ignorant; for it is plain to us that this very Rome, and the sacred empire in it, was and is like an anchor to Europe, long tossed by waves. Wonderful is God's kindness to this city! When he took away the power of the legions, he gave it laws; when he would not have it rule by arms, he granted it sacred things, and so also makes it the glory, protection and pillar of the world. Yet, they say, that ancient senate is gone. Not that one, but another; and look at me, in this purple, at the chosen nobles from our whole world, to be admired for their character, prudence and years. If that old Cineas returned and saw this assembly, he would not hesitate to compare it again with kings or with heroes. What of tributes? They are not so many, but milder and voluntary. What of embassies from the nations? Those are not lacking either; from the known and unknown world (so wide is the diffusion of this majesty) men flock together, and seek laws and rights from here. Kings and princes themselves come, bow down, and submit their bowed heads to this one head. Why speak of princes or men? Aerial, earthly and infernal spirits or genii revere and tremble, and acknowledge that heavenly power on earth, even unwillingly and reluctantly. Thus far he; so he praises Papal Rome that he raises its majesty and greatness above that of the old city.

units.la: XXIII. Amplius verò de magnitudine & amplitudine Civitatis hujus Religiosæ dominantis liquebit, si Hierarchiæ species paucis attigerimus. Inde enim constabit, in Amurathis vel Solimani alicujus aula Constantinopolitana vix tot repertos unquam esse ministros, quot sunt in Hierarchia Pontificis Romani Clerici.
units.tr: XXIII. Moreover, the greatness and extent of this dominant religious state will become clearer if we briefly touch on the species of its hierarchy. For from this it will be evident that in the court of Amurath or of any Solyman at Constantinople there were scarcely ever as many ministers as there are clergy in the hierarchy of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: XXIV. Pontificii igitur ad modulum Hierarchiæ Cœlestis, à Pseudo-Areopagita effictæ, Ecclesiasticam suam Hierarchiam composuerunt. Est enim, uti Lælius Zecchius de Rep. Eccl. cap. 129. ex Glossa quadam Canonica citat, militans Ecclesia à triumphante exemplata. Sicut igitur Cœlestis Hierarchia ab Areopagita illo personato in tres species, atque singulæ hæ species in tres iterum ordines tributæ sunt: ita Ecclesiastica ab iis dividitur, subdividitúrque variè, prout vocem Hierarchia, Ecclesiastici, Clerici alii latiùs, angustiùs alii accipiunt. Latiore significatu Antonius Possevinus Biblioth. Sel. lib. iv. 20. Clericos, seu Ecclesiasticos universos in quatuor classes partitur, puta in Gubernantes, quibus Papam, Cardinales, Patriarchas & Primates, Archiepiscopos seu Metropolitanos, Episcopos & Decanos accenset: Ministrantes, quorum in classe Parochos seu Curatos, Sacerdotes, Diaconos, Subdiaconos, Acoluthos, Exorcistas, Lectores, Ostiarios, Canonicos & Oeconomos collocat: Supererogantes, puta religiosos, Monachos & Sanctimoniales: denique Adjuvantes, Doctores Theologiæ, Juris Canonici, Catechismi, Prædicatores, Disputatores, Scholasticos, Ecclesiasticos. Quàm solida hæc sit partitio, nil hic moramur. Ea saltem ad indagandam Civitatis Babylonicæ amplitudinem uti, haud præter rem fuerit.
units.tr: XXIV. The Papists, therefore, modelled their ecclesiastical hierarchy on the pattern of the celestial hierarchy fashioned by the Pseudo-Areopagite. For it is, as Lelio Zecchi cites from a certain canonical gloss in his De Republica Ecclesiastica, chapter 129, the militant Church copied from the triumphant one. Just as the celestial hierarchy was divided by that masked Areopagite into three orders, and each of these orders into three further ranks, so the ecclesiastical hierarchy is divided and subdivided in various ways, according as different writers understand the terms hierarchy, ecclesiastics, clergy more broadly or more narrowly. In the broader sense, Antonio Possevino, Bibliotheca Selecta book 4, chapter 20, divides all clergy, or ecclesiastics, into four classes: the governing, among whom he counts the Pope, cardinals, patriarchs and primates, archbishops or metropolitans, bishops and deans; the ministering, in whose class he places parish priests or curates, priests, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers, doorkeepers, canons and stewards; the supererogating, namely the religious, monks and nuns; and finally the assisting, namely teachers of theology, of canon law, of catechism, preachers, disputants, scholastics and ecclesiastics. How sound this division is, we need not linger over here. It will be enough, at least, to use it for investigating the extent of the Babylonian state, which is not beside the point.

units.la: XXV. De Papa, Pontifice Maximo, supremo Civitatis illius Principe ac Domino in præsentiarum multa dicere nihil attinet. Olim quidem Julius Cæsar summa potestate, quæ penes populum ante fuerat, deiectis Pompeji in Hispania filiis, & reliquiis belli civilis confectis, rapta, Pater Patriæ, Sacro Sanctus Imperator, Dictator perpetuus renuntiatus est.
units.tr: XXV. Concerning the Pope, the Supreme Pontiff, the chief ruler and lord of that state, there is no need to say much at present. Long ago, indeed, Julius Caesar seized the supreme power that had formerly rested with the people, after the sons of Pompey had been overthrown in Spain and the remnants of the civil war had been finished, and was proclaimed Father of the Country, Sacrosanct Emperor, and perpetual dictator.

units.la: Deinceps successores quamprimum ab exercitu proclamati salutatique, & à Senatu comprobati sunt, teste Dione Cassio Lib. LIII. omnia, quæ in populari forma multum valuerunt, cum ipsis nominibus se recipiebant, creati etiam Pontifices Maximi, & legibus insuper omnibus soluti, quo ipso solo omnia agendi licentiam, supremamque totius Reipublicæ potestatem adepti sunt. Horum in locum successit Papa, qui Pontifex Maximus (cum Christus Ἀρχιερεὺς Sacerdos Magnus Pontifex dici satis habuerit) Episcopus Oecumenicus, Optimus, Maximus in terris Deus, Reipublicæ Christianæ Monarcha invictissimus audit.
units.tr: Thereafter his successors were, as soon as possible, acclaimed and saluted by the army and confirmed by the Senate, as Dio Cassius testifies, book 53. They also took over all those powers which had been of great weight under the popular form, together with the very titles themselves; they were created Supreme Pontiffs as well, and were released from all laws, and by this alone they obtained the licence to do everything and the supreme power over the whole commonwealth. In their place succeeded the Pope, who (since Christ was content to be called high priest [ἀρχιερεύς], Great Priest, and Pontiff) is heard as Supreme Pontiff, Ecumenical Bishop, Best and Greatest, God on earth, and most invincible Monarch of the Christian Commonwealth.

units.la: XXVI. Aulam Papa habet amplissimam splendidissi- mamque.
units.tr: XXVI. The Pope has a vast and splendid court.

units.la: In ea visere est colluviem immensam cubiculariorum, atriensium, pedisequorum, equisonum, satellitum, vasallorum, clientulorum, coquorum, hortulanorum, architectorum, pictorum, cantorum, aliorum, qui luxu diffluentes Apicios, Hortensiosque omnes, teste locuplete Apicio, Papali Archimagiro, superant; quibusque visis, quis non cum Bernhardo libr. IV. cap. 2. Consid. ad Eugenium, exclamat: Dæmonum magis quàm ovium pascua hæc sunt. Scilicet sic faciebat Petrus.
units.tr: In it one may see an immense rabble of chamberlains, ushers, attendants, grooms, bodyguards, hangers-on, cooks, gardeners, architects, painters, singers, and others, who, flowing over with luxury, surpass all the Apicii and Hortensii, Apicius being the rich witness, and the Pope's Archimagirus. At the sight of them, who would not cry out with Bernard, book IV, chapter 2, On Consideration, to Eugenius: These are rather the pastures of demons than of sheep. Surely this is not how Peter did it.

units.la: XXVI. Curialium, qui domi forisque rebus Papæ procurandis inserviunt, caterva & multitudo tanta est,
units.tr: XXVI. The crowd of courtiers who serve the Pope at home and abroad in managing his affairs is as great as that of those locusts which covered the whole surface of the land of Egypt.

units.la: quanta locustarum illarum, quæ totius Ægypti terræ superficiem operuerunt. Sequentes idem, qui supra, Lælius Zechius enumerat: Illustrissimi Cardinales, Illustrissimi Legati, Vicarius Domini Papæ, Summus Pœnitentiarius, Vice-Cancellarius, Camerarius, & Clerici Cameræ, Thesaurarius, Præsidens Cameræ Apostolicæ, Advocatus pauperum, Advocatus Fiscalis, Procurator Fisci, Commissarius Cameræ Apostolicæ, Clericus Sacri Senatus, Auditor Cameræ Apostolicæ, Datarius, Secretarius Domini Papæ, Referendarius, Auditores Rotæ, Protonotarius Apostolicus, Gubernator urbis, Senatores urbis, Judex Marcelli & turris Nonæ, Visitatores Carcerum, Advocati Consistoriales, Procuratores Sacri Palatii, Solicitatores Causarum, Notarii, Congregationes Curiæ Romanæ, Judex delegatus, quorum singulorum munera statumque idem Zechius explicat. Addi possunt Inquisitores, Magister sacri Palatii, Sacellanus, Bibliothecarii, alii, qui in solennibus processionibus, coronationibus & funeribus Pontificum comparere, minimumque suum peragere solent.
units.tr: Lælius Zechius, following the same order as above, lists them: the most illustrious Cardinals; the most illustrious Legates; the Vicar of the Lord Pope; the Chief Penitentiary; the Vice-Chancellor; the Chamberlain and the clerks of the Chamber; the Treasurer; the President of the Apostolic Chamber; the Advocate of the poor; the Advocate of the Fisc; the Procurator of the Fisc; the Commissary of the Apostolic Chamber; the Clerk of the Sacred Senate; the Auditor of the Apostolic Chamber; the Datary; the Secretary of the Lord Pope; the Referendary; the Auditors of the Rota; the Apostolic Protonotary; the Governor of the city; the Senators of the city; the Judge of the Marcellus and of the Tower of Nona; the Visitors of the prisons; the Consistorial Advocates; the Procurators of the Sacred Palace; the Solicitors of causes; the Notaries; the Congregations of the Roman Curia; the delegated Judge. Zechius explains the duties and standing of each of these. To them may be added the Inquisitors, the Master of the Sacred Palace, the Sacristan, the Librarians, and others who are accustomed to appear at the solemn processions, coronations and funerals of the Popes and to perform their small part there.

units.la: XXVIII. Functiones, quas ferè Papa ipse ἀμέσως obire solet, καὶ λοιπὸν Christophorus Marcellus, Archiepiscopus Corcyrensis, in Ceremoniali Romano descripsit. Ne vero nimium curis laboribusque distringatur ipse, Collegia, congregationesque varias instituit, in quibus causæ multiplices disceptantur, definiunturque, ea lege ut Papa approbet. Collegia ejusmodi sunt Consistorium, καὶ ἱερὸν ita appellatum, ex Papa & Cardinalibus unà congregatis conflatum, cujus rationem, consultationes, modum, ordinemque Gabriel Palæotus libro de Sacri Consistorii Consultationibus edito edidit: Cancellaria Apostolica à Paulo Barchinonensi in Practica Cancellariæ Apostolicæ descripta. Camera Apostolica, seu rationum thesauri, ærarii Papalis: Pænitentiaria Apostolica, quæ etiam Prætorium appellatur, cujus minister præcipuus est Pœnitentiarius Papæ, & in qua casus conscientiæ reservati inprimis ventilantur, necnon tesseræ veniales, venalésque cuduntur: Curia Papalis, seu forum externum Ecclesiastico-Papale, quod contentiosum seu litigiosum nuncupari suevit, utpote in qua lites & causæ ex toto Orbe Papali Romam delatæ disceptantur. Rota Romana, ubi lites Romanæ urbis & Patrimonii Petri tractantur: Collegia Officialium & Magistratuum tum Romanorum, tum inferiorum, per totam Romaniam, ditionem Avinionensem, & ubicunque Papa territorii jus habet: Officium Inquisitionis fidei, taurus ille Phalaridis decantatissimus: Sacræ Congregationes Cardinalium, quindecim numero, veluti pro sancta inquisitione; pro signatura gratiæ; pro erectione Ecclesiarum & provisionibus Consistorialibus; pro ubertate annonæ; pro sacris ritibus & Ceremoniis; pro classe paranda & conservanda; pro indice librorum; pro interpretatione & executione Concilii Tridentini; pro gravaminibus sublevandis; pro universitate studii Romani; pro consultationibus Regularium; pro consultationibus Episcoporum, & aliorum Prælatorum; pro viis, pontibus, & aquis curandis; pro Typographia Vaticana; pro consultationibus negotiationum status Ecclesiastici; denique Collegium de propaganda fide, per quod, ceu emissitios oculos, quicquid in omnibus Orbis angulis, vel pro, vel contra se agitur, cernere poterit. Quem ipsum etiam in finem tum Romæ Generales Ordinum residentl, quibus omnia memoratu digna Provinciales communicant: tum Cardinales ibidem constituuntur Protectores Nationum, Religionum, domuum piarum, ad quorum indicia vivæ vocis oraculum ex tripode illa reddatur: tum Primates & Archiepiscopi à suffraganeis suis certiores de cunctis reddiți. diti, digniora scitu Monarchæ suo, sive scripto, sive coram referunt: tum denique Legati à Latere, & Nuncii Apostolici quaquaversum amandati, & per omnes Orbis stationes in excubiis dispositi, nihil non in aulis & Comitiis Regum ac Regnorum, in Curiis & Conciliis Dioecesanis Episcoporum, in Comitiis Provincialibus quorumvis Regularium expiscantur, & ad magnum illum Piscatorem Romanum deferunt.
units.tr: XXVIII. The functions which the Pope himself usually discharges immediately [ἀμέσως], and so on [καὶ λοιπὸν], Christophorus Marcellus, Archbishop of Corfu, has described in the Roman Ceremonial. So that he himself may not be too much burdened by cares and labours, he sets up various colleges and congregations, in which manifold matters are debated and decided, on the condition that the Pope approve them. Such colleges are: the Consistory, so called as being sacred [ἱερὸν], made up of the Pope and the Cardinals gathered together, whose nature, consultations, manner and order Gabriel Palaeotus set forth in his book on the consultations of the Sacred Consistory; the Apostolic Chancery, described by Paulus Barchinonensis in his Practice of the Apostolic Chancery; the Apostolic Chamber, or the treasury of accounts, the papal exchequer; the Apostolic Penitentiary, also called the Praetorium, whose chief officer is the Pope's Penitentiary, and in which cases of conscience reserved to the Pope are chiefly weighed, and where pardon tokens are issued and sold; the Papal Court, or the external forum of the ecclesiastical-papal kind, which is customarily called contentious or litigious, since in it suits and causes brought to Rome from the whole papal world are heard; the Roman Rota, where the suits of the city of Rome and of the Patrimony of Peter are tried; the colleges of officials and magistrates, both Roman and lesser, throughout the Romagna, the Avignon territory, and wherever the Pope has right of rule; the Office of the Inquisition of the faith, that much-celebrated bull of Phalaris; the Sacred Congregations of the Cardinals, fifteen in number, as follows: for the holy Inquisition; for the signature of grace; for the erection of churches and consistorial appointments; for the abundance of the grain supply; for sacred rites and ceremonies; for equipping and maintaining the fleet; for the Index of books; for the interpretation and execution of the Council of Trent; for relieving grievances; for the University of Rome; for the consultations of the Regulars; for the consultations of Bishops and other prelates; for the care of roads, bridges and waters; for the Vatican Press; for the consultations on the affairs of the ecclesiastical state; and finally the College for the Propagation of the Faith, through which, as through outstretched eyes, it can see whatever is done in every corner of the world, either for or against the Pope. For the same purpose, Generals of the Orders residing at Rome, to whom the Provincials communicate all things worth mentioning, and Cardinals appointed there as Protectors of nations, religious orders and pious houses, at whose hints the oracle of the living voice is given forth from that tripod; then Primates and Archbishops, who are informed by their suffragans of all matters, and who report to their Monarch whatever is worth knowing, either in writing or in person; and finally the Legates a latere and the Apostolic Nuncios, sent out in every direction and posted on watch at every station of the world, who fish out everything from the courts and assemblies of kings and kingdoms, from the diocesan courts and synods of bishops, and from the provincial assemblies of any Regulars, and carry it to that great Roman Fisherman.

units.la: XXIX. Inter Magistratus Papæ, seu Hierarchas ejusdem gubernantes principem dignitatis locum Cardinales purpureo pileo, abolláque fulgentes, obtinent. De eorum Origine aucta unà cum incrementis Pontificiæ potestatis, potestate, munere & prærogativis in Historia Papatús ss. LXXIV. LXXV. LXXVI. LXXVII. fusiùs egimus. Pauca de iis ut hoc etiam loco dicam, ex prima institutione fuerunt illi Clerus ordinarius Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quorum proin Officium & munus ἴδιον fuit idem cum officio Clericorum, Presbyterorum inprimis, ut scilicet singuli in suis titulis, seu Ecclesiis, quibus præerant, populum ex Verbo Dei erudirent, Sacramenta administrarent, in regimine Ecclesiæ Romano Episcopo inservirent, aliáque munera Ecclesiastica obirent. Cardinalatus proin ab Ecclesiæ titulo & officio separatus, inane & cassum nomen est. Quòd si etiam Conciliabuli illius, quod Romæ sub Silvestro coïit, actis creditur, in Cardinalium institutione veteris Romæ imago per Christianam renovata est hactenus, quòd sicut illa tribunos plebis urbe abesse vetabat; sic hæc Cardinales ejusdem urbis cardine constrictos tenet, cap. 3. 6. 7. Nisi forte Scenicus ille Imperator instituto purpuratorum Patrum hoc Collegio, veteris Romæ Senatum effinxit, interpolavitque. Porro Romanæ urbis ἱερὰ temporalis sicut Ecclesiæ ipsi Romanæ, ejúsque Episcopo, ita etiam Clero ejusdem occasionem se efferendi præbuit. buit. Adeò enim successu temporis à ratione & forma vera Cardinalium deflexerunt, ut jam nullo modo ampliùs sint veri Cardinales, non modò illi, qui propriarum Ecclesiarum sunt Episcopi, sed ne reliqui quidem etiam Romæ residentes, quia omnes illi sunt Ecclesiæ adventitii, & assuti, non proprièincardinati. Titulos quidem ad speciem assumunt, sed in titulis nullum prorsus officium, quod sit proprium Christi ministrorum Cardinalium seu fixorum, exercent. Plurimi quoque tituli sunt privatarum Ecclesiarum, sive Oratoriorum, etiam Monachorum & Regularium, in quibus publica nulla in plebe fideli erudienda, & ecclesiasticis ac spiritualibus officiis fovenda, nutriendáque exercitia vigent, quæ proin Ecclesiæ non sunt nisi æquivocè Cardinales, etsi quæ verè Cardinales sunt, illæ proprios habent parochos substitutos, satis viles abjectósque, revera tamen veros Cardinales, dum titulos alii, nihil minùs quàm Ecclesiasticis in ecclesiis Cardinalibus, muneribus fungentes, possident.
units.tr: XXIX. Among the magistrates of the Pope, or hierarchs governing under him, the Cardinals, glittering in purple hats and scarlet robes, hold the chief place of dignity. We have treated fully of their origin, together with the growth of papal power, its authority, office and prerogatives, in the History of the Papacy, sections 74, 75, 76 and 77. To say a few things about them here too: from their first institution they were the ordinary clergy of the Roman Church, and their proper office and duty was the same as that of the clergy, especially the presbyters, namely that each, in his own titles, or churches, over which he presided, should instruct the people from the Word of God, administer the sacraments, serve the Roman Bishop in the government of the Church, and perform other ecclesiastical duties. Therefore the Cardinalate, separated from the title and office of the Church, is an empty and hollow name. But if the records of that council which is believed to have met at Rome under Sylvester are trustworthy, then in the institution of the Cardinals an image of old Rome has been renewed by the Christian church to this day: just as old Rome forbade the tribunes of the plebs to be absent from the city, so these Cardinals are held bound to the hinge of the same city (chapters 3, 6 and 7). Unless perhaps that stage-playing emperor, by establishing this college of purple-clad fathers, modelled and remodelled the senate of old Rome. Moreover, just as the temporal holy things of the city of Rome, and the Roman Church itself, and its Bishop, so also the clergy have provided an occasion for putting on airs. For over time they have so departed from the true nature and form of the Cardinals that they are now in no way true Cardinals any longer: not only those who are bishops of their own churches, but not even the rest who reside at Rome, since all of them are adventitious and patched on to the church, not properly incardinated. They do indeed assume titles for show, but in those titles they exercise no office at all proper to the Cardinal, that is, the fixed ministers of Christ. Very many of the titles belong to private churches or oratories, even those of monks and regulars, where no public exercises for instructing the faithful people, and for fostering and nourishing ecclesiastical and spiritual duties, are in force; these therefore are Cardinals of the Church only in name, while those who are truly Cardinals hold substitute parish priests, rather mean and abject men, and yet they are true Cardinals, since others, performing duties in no way cardinal in the ecclesiastical churches, hold the titles.

units.la: XXX. Quid ergo? Qui Cardinales sequiore ætate, qua dominatio mera in Ecclesiam incessit, dicti sunt, hodiéque dicuntur, sub appellatione Ecclesiastica Principes Seculares, dominationis Pontificiæ instrumenta præcipua fuerunt, & sunt hodiéque. Mira scilicet pudendáque metamorphosi, conculcato inprimis à Pontifice Imperatore, & sede ejus ad maximum in terris fastigium evecta, Secularem in typhum toti transierunt, æmuli facti Principum, imò ipsi potiùs Reguli, vel summis Regibus de honore & dignitate controversiam facientes, & galerum suum rubrum aureo diademati æquiparantes; adeò ut Bellarminus in Apologia contra serenissimi Angliæ Regis Jacobi Præfationem, & in plena rerum luce eos Regibus adæquare, adductis triobolaribus & propudiosis ratiunculis non nullis, non dubitaverit. Dicuntur Cardinales, ita Isidorus Mosconius de Majestate Ecclesiæ militantis Lib. j. part. j. cap. 6. ampullatur, vicem gerentes Apostolorum, filii, primi gradus amoris, Pontificis filii summæ dilectionis, & fratres, imò pars corporis ipsius, Cardines Ecclesiæ Dei, Patres Spirituales, Consiliarii, coadjutores & Papæ assessores, Reges, Patres Conscripti in diademate Principis, Principes, Senatores & Patritii Maximi, Luminaria Ecclesiæ, Seniores populi, stellæ fixæ in Cælo, Illustrissimi, potentissimi, lucernæ ardentes, Divi, Venerabiles, repræsentantes non solùm Clerum Urbis Romæ, sed & ipsam Ecclesiam, in quibus residet Majestas Reipublicæ Christianæ. En quàm propinquo gradu Majestatem Pontificiam Semiviri illi, radiante galero conspicui, contingunt:
units.tr: XXX. What then? The Cardinals who, from a later age, when pure domination crept into the Church, were called, and are still called, under an ecclesiastical name, Secular Princes, have been and still are the chief instruments of papal domination. By a strange and shameful metamorphosis, after the Pope, trampling underfoot the emperor, had raised their seat to the highest pinnacle on earth, they have wholly turned to secular pride, becoming rivals of princes, indeed rather petty kinglets themselves, contending over honour and dignity even with the highest kings, and equating their red hat with the golden diadem; so much so that Bellarmine, in his Apology against the Preface of the most serene King James of England, did not hesitate, in full daylight of the facts, to make them equal to kings, bringing forward certain trifling and shameful little arguments. The Cardinals are called, thus Isidorus Mosconius in his book on the Majesty of the Militant Church, book 1, part 1, chapter 6, puffs them up: they stand in the place of the Apostles, sons of the first degree of love, sons of the Pontiff of highest affection, brothers, indeed a part of his body itself, hinges of the Church of God, Spiritual Fathers, counsellors, co-workers and assessors of the Pope, kings, Conscript Fathers in the diadem of the Prince, princes, senators and great patricians, lights of the Church, elders of the people, fixed stars in heaven, most illustrious, most powerful, burning lamps, divine, venerable, representing not only the clergy of the city of Rome but the Church itself, in which the majesty of the Christian commonwealth resides. See how closely those half-men, conspicuous in their shining hat, approach the papal majesty!

units.la: XXXI. Cardinalibus igitur præcipuis status sui cole-umnis Papa utitur. Illis solis Pontificem creandi jus deculit, eodem Populo, Principi, Cleróque erepto. Illos ruzbri galeri honore decoravit, concessitque, ut præcederent primò Episcopis, quibus quondam suberant; dein Archiepiscopio, ac tandem etiam Patriarchis. Amplissimos Diœcesium, Provinciárúmque multarum Præsules, & Archiepiscopos, veluti Moguntinum, Trevirensem, Coloniensem, Germaniæ; Toletanum Hispaniæ; Rhemensem & Rhodum Galliæ; Eboracensem & Cantuariensem Angliæ; Lisbonensem Lusitaniæ; Mediolanensem, Ravennatem, Venetum, Italiæ; Strigoniensem Hungariæ; Pragensem Bohemiæ; Cracoviensem Poloniæ, itemque cæteros eximios per universam Christianam Rempublicam Antistites non raro deligit, qui ipsi Presbyteri Cardinales essent, Cardinalésque Diaconi. Imò ita esse, iis ipsis placuit magnopere, eò quòd per Cardinalatum ad Pontificatum ascenderetur. Cúmque disciplinæ communis regula haberet, unum non nisi uno sacerdotio potiri posse, ne ea infringi videretur, decretum est, ut Episcopatibus licet fruerentur, Episcopi tamen vocarentur. Episcopus, si Cardinalis Diaconus crearetur electus Episcopus; si Cardinalis Presbyter administrator perpetuus sui Episcopatus diceretur. Progressa eò audacia est Clementis V. qui Avinione sedem collocavit, tempore, ut nullus ferè Cardinalis creatus sit, quin Episcopatum vel in titulum, vel in commendam, vel in perpetuam administrationem haberet. Quibus artificiis Ecclesiæ multæ Episcopis orbatæ, Romana vicissim Curia opulentis & potentibus Cardinalibus mactata est. Accesserunt reservationes & provisiones, per quas Pontifices, provisuri scilicet, ne Ecclesiis idonei Pastores desint, reservarunt beneficia Ecclesiastica, quoties & quæcunque demum voluerunt, sibi ea conferendi potestatem arrogantes, eáque invadentes, ut iis Cardinalium suorum dignitatem tutarentur. Atque sic paulatim multæ myriades Ecclesiarum desertæ, & ceu greges orbi pastoribus destituti sunt, ut Cardinalium modò status adornaretur. A beneficiorum pluralitate ad Episcopatuum, maximè subinde dissitorum, pluralitatem perventum est, cumulatæque immensum artes ditandi sunt, donec Regalibus divitiis Regio statui exornando affluerent.
units.tr: XXXI. The Pope therefore uses the chief cardinals as the pillars of his state. He alone conferred on them the right to create the Pontiff, a right taken from the people, the prince and the clergy. He honoured them with the red hat and granted that they should take precedence first of bishops, over whom they had once stood, then of archbishops, and at last even of patriarchs. He often chooses as cardinals the most distinguished bishops and archbishops of dioceses and of many provinces, such as those of Mainz, Trier and Cologne in Germany; Toledo in Spain; Reims and Rodez in France; York and Canterbury in England; Lisbon in Portugal; Milan, Ravenna and Venice in Italy; Esztergom in Hungary; Prague in Bohemia; Kraków in Poland; and other eminent prelates throughout the whole Christian commonwealth. Some of them were made cardinal presbyters and others cardinal deacons. Indeed, they themselves were greatly pleased that a way to the papacy lay through the cardinalate. Since the common rule of discipline held that one man could hold only one priesthood, and so that this rule might not seem to be broken, it was decreed that they might enjoy their bishoprics but still be called bishops. A cardinal deacon who was elected was called bishop; a cardinal presbyter was called perpetual administrator of his bishopric. The boldness of Clement V, who fixed the seat at Avignon, went so far that almost no cardinal was created who did not hold a bishopric in title, in commendam, or in perpetual administration. By these devices many churches were stripped of their bishops, while the Roman Curia in turn was enriched by powerful and wealthy cardinals. There were also reservations and provisions, by which the popes, providing (so that the churches would not lack suitable ministers), reserved ecclesiastical benefices whenever and however they wished, arrogating to themselves the power of conferring them and seizing them, so that the dignity of their cardinals might be protected by them. And so gradually many myriads of churches were deserted and left like flocks without shepherds, so that the rank of the cardinals might be adorned. From the pluralism of benefices there came to be pluralism of bishoprics, often widely scattered, and immense arts of enrichment were heaped up until royal riches flowed in to adorn a royal estate.

units.la: XXXII. Numerus Cardinalium olim ad numerum tulorum Ecclesiarum in urbes, quibus ceu Presbyteri aut Diaconi præerant, restrictus est. Typho Seculi in Ecclesiam irrepente, magis magisque Romani Episcopi præcipuas orbis Ecclesias magnitudine & splendore eminentes elegerunt, aut novas etiam ipsi condiderunt, quas Basilicas & Ecclesias Patriarchales, palatia verò ipsis adjuncta insignia, Patriarchia appellarunt. Nimirum tyrannidem, quam in Orientis Patriarchas frustra Papa affectavit, saltem ludicro hoc dramate, orbem urbi includens, tanquam
units.tr: XXXII. The number of cardinals was once restricted to the number of titular churches in the cities over which they presided as cardinal presbyters or deacons. When the pride of the age crept into the Church, the Roman bishops increasingly chose the principal churches of the world that were outstanding in size and splendour, or even founded new ones themselves, which they called basilicas and patriarchal churches, and the palaces attached to them they called patriarchia. Thus, by this stage-play at least, they enclosed the world within the city, as if the tyranny which the Pope had vainly aimed at over the patriarchs of the East were to be displayed on the stage.

units.la: Hh 2 in fce-
units.tr: Hh 2 in the scene-

units.la: Ecclesiarum Urbis numerus. in scena spectandam exhibere placuit. Ecclesias illas Patriarchales quinque his versibus Poëta expreflit: Paulus, Virgo, Petrus, Laurentius, atque Johannes, Hi Patriarchatus nomen in urbe tenent.
units.tr: The number of the churches of the City. It has pleased [the author] to set them before the eye in a stage scene. The poet expressed those five patriarchal churches in these verses: "Paul, Virgin, Peter, Lawrence, and John; these hold the name of Patriarchate in the city."

units.la: Prima nunc Ecclesia Patriarchalis dicitur Johannis, olim dicta Salvatoris & Lateranenfis à loco, Conftantiana ab authore, & aurea ab ornamentis. Huic Gregorius XI. assignavit septem Episcopos ex vicinis oppidis, pura I piscopum Cardinalem Oftienfem, Sylvæ Candidæ, Portuenfem, Sabinum, Prænestinum, Thufculanum, Albanum, qui ordine certo singulis hebdomadis diebus, vice Pontificis, five præfentis, five absentis peragerent, vel Pontifici sacra celebranti adeflent. Reliquis quatuor Ecclefiis Patriarchalibus singulis septem Ministri, dicti Cardinales Presbyteri, assignati sunt, quibus velut in cumulum octodecim Cardinales Diaconi, cùm primò electio Pontificis ad Cardinales remissa est, acceflerunt. Præcipuis his quinque Ecclesiis additæ duæ sunt Callifti & S. Crucis in Jerusalem, ac procedente tempore aliæ etiam, velut Anaftafii ad tres fontes, S. Mariæ Annunciatæ &c. Paulatim enim ad augendum numerum Cardinalium, plures tituli à Pontificibus excogitati sunt. Licet enim Sixtus V. Bulla A. M. D. LXXXVI. edita numerum Cardinalium ad septuaginta restrinxerit, non ita tamen subsecuti Pontifices fe numero illi alligarunt, quò minùs pro Pontificiæ potestatis plenitudine, vel plures crearent, vel paucioribus etiam five ad locupletandum ærarium, five alias ob causas, contenti effent.
units.tr: The first patriarchal church is now called that of John, formerly called that of the Saviour and of the Lateran from its site, Constantinian from its founder, and golden from its ornaments. To this church Gregory XI assigned seven bishops from the neighbouring towns, namely the Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, Silva Candida, Porto, Sabina, Praeneste, Tusculum and Alba, who in a fixed order on single days of the week were to perform the service in place of the Pontiff, whether present or absent, or to attend the Pontiff when he celebrated sacred rites. To each of the remaining four patriarchal churches were assigned seven ministers, called Cardinal Priests, and to these, as a kind of addition, eighteen Cardinal Deacons were joined when the election of the Pontiff was first referred to the Cardinals. To these five principal churches have been added two, Callixtus and Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and in the course of time others too, such as St Anastasius at the Three Fountains, St Mary of the Annunciation, and so on. For gradually, to increase the number of Cardinals, many titles were devised by the Pontiffs. For although Sixtus V, by his Bull issued in the year 1586 (A.M.D. LXXXVI), restricted the number of Cardinals to seventy, the Pontiffs who followed did not bind themselves to that number; relying on the fullness of papal power, they were content either to create more or, to enrich the treasury or for other reasons, fewer.

units.la: XXXIII. Officia Cardinalium omnium ἐλαίρ sunt, creare Papam, assistere eidem creato jugiter, cundémque in regenda Ecclesia universali & Republica Christiana universa consilio atque ope adjuvare, in consistorio unà cum Papa Nuntiorum Apostolicorum, fi ad Provincias regendas, Le-
units.tr: XXXIII. The offices of all cardinals are these: to elect the Pope, to attend constantly on the one elected, and to help him by counsel and labour in governing the universal Church and the whole Christian commonwealth; to fulfil, together with the Pope in consistory, the duties of apostolic nuncios when sent to govern provinces, and of legates a latere when sent with that title to kings and princes.

units.la: Officia Cardinalium praeti- pua, ordina ria & extravagantia. das, Legatorum à Latere, si ad Reges & Principes mittantur, titulo, munera obire. Accedunt munera eorum extravagantia, quæ sive pace sive bello haud infrequenter sustinent. Nam & militiæ nonnulli se præfici haud illibenter passi sunt, quorum in censu recente in memoria sunt Cardinalis la Valette in Gallia, Cardinalis Regius, seu Infans Hispanicus in Belgio Hispanico, Albertus & Andreas Austriaci, Cardinalis Ferrariensis, quem iccirco ludos merito Dam petra apud Thuanum Annal. lib. xxxv. fecit; Galliæ inprimis famosi ocelli novissimi, Richelius & Mazarinus, summis ferè Regni gubernaculis admoti; aliique.
units.tr: The principal and ordinary offices of cardinals, and their extraordinary ones. Their extraordinary duties, which they not infrequently undertake in peace or in war, are also added. For some of them have not unwillingly allowed themselves to be placed in command of troops; of recent memory in this respect are Cardinal La Valette in France, Cardinal Infante, or the Spanish prince, in the Spanish Netherlands, Albert and Andrew of Austria, and the Cardinal of Ferrara, whom Thuanus rightly made the subject of games in his Annals, book 35, and especially the notorious latest eyes of France, Richelieu and Mazarin, who were raised almost to the highest direction of the kingdom; and others.

units.la: XXXIV. Proximum post Cardinales in Hierarchia Pontificia locum Patriarchæ tum Oecumenici titulares, puta Constantinopolitanus, Alexandrinus, Antiochenus & Hierosolymitanus, tum particulares, qui & Primates dicuntur; Archiepiscopi seu Metropolitani & Episcopi tenent. De Patriarchis particularibus sic Zechius de Rep. Eccl. p. 80. scribit: Sex præterea Patriarchæ extant ex privilegio, vel consuetudine: Scilicet Aquilejensis, Gradensis, Bituricensis, Cantuariensis, Toletanus & Pisanus, quorum duo tantum nomen Patriarchæ retinuere, scilicet Aquilejensis & Gradensis, qui est Patriarcha Venetiarum &c. Hi Patriarchæ præpositi sunt maximis imperiis & Regnis, aliis Episcopis & Archiepiscopis in illis regionibus constitutis præpositi, ad quos summa graviorum negotiorum religionis defertur. Dubitatur tamen merito, an Patriarchas seu Primates omnes recensuerit, cum in quolibet Regno seu Regione Archiepiscopis primas aliquis præsit, nisi forte Primas alicubi dicitur, qui Principem inter Archiepiscopos locum tenet.
units.tr: XXXIV. Next after the cardinals in the papal hierarchy come the patriarchs: first the ecumenical titular ones, namely those of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem; then the particular ones, who are also called primates. Archbishops or metropolitans and bishops hold these offices. Concerning the particular patriarchs, Zechius writes thus in de Rep. Eccl. p. 80.: Besides these there are six patriarchs, by privilege or custom: namely those of Aquileia, Grado, Bourges, Canterbury, Toledo and Pisa, of whom only two have kept the name of patriarch, namely Aquileia and Grado, who is the Patriarch of Venice, etc. These patriarchs are set over the greatest empires and kingdoms, placed over the other bishops and archbishops established in those regions, and to them the supreme direction of the more serious affairs of religion is referred. It is nevertheless rightly doubted whether he has listed all the patriarchs or primates, since in every kingdom or region some primate presides over the archbishops, unless perhaps in some place the man who holds the first rank among the archbishops is called primate.

units.la: XXXV. Archiepiscopi, seu Metropolitani sunt Præsules Episcoporum unius Provinciæ, seu Episcopi Metro-
units.tr: XXXV. Archbishops, or metropolitans, are the presidents of the bishops of a single province, or the bishops of the Metro-

units.la: poleon, sive principalium regionum, aut districtuum urbium, quibus eorundem districtuum seu Provinciarum Episcopi reliqui subsunt, exceptis tamen Episcopis exemptis non paucis, qui in Provinciali, seu in Practica Cancellariæ Apostolicæ, & in Oceano juris notantur, in quorum Dioecesi Metropolitanus jurisdictionem non exercet. Sunt autem, fueruntque olim Archiepiscopi plurimi, quos ordine recensebo: In Italiæ ditione Pontificia tres, Ravennas, Bononiensis & Firmanus: In Regno Neapolitano novendecim, puta Neapolitanus, Capuanus, Salernitanus, Amalphitanus, Surrentinus, Compsanus, Acheruntinus, Tarentinus, Brundisinus, Hydruntinus, Barensis, Tranensis, Sipontinus, Theatinus, Loncianensis, Rhegiensis, Consentinus, Rosciionensis, S. Severinæ, & Beneventanus: In Sicilia tres, Panormitanus, Messanensis, & Montis Regalis: In Sardinia duo, Calaritanus & Turritanus: In Insubria unus Mediolanensis: In Pedemontio duo, Taurinensis & Tarantosiensis: In Etruria tres Florentinus, Senensis & Pisanus: In Liguria unus Genuensis: In ditione Urbinensi Urbinas: In Venetorum ditione quatuor, Spalatensis, Jaderensis: In Dalmatia & Illyrico duo, Ragusinus & Dyrrachinus: In Bulgaria & Græcia unus, Acridanus: In Armenia unus Nexivanensis: In Hispania undecim, Toletanus Burgensis, Compostellanus, Hispalensis, Granatensis, Cæsar Augustanus, Tarraconensis, Valentinus, Bracarensis, Olisiponensis & Eborensis: In Gallia tredecim, Lugdunensis, Rotomagensis, Turonensis, Senonensis, Remensis, Bituricensis, Burdigalensis, Auscensis, Narbonensis, Aquensis, Viennensis, Ebrodunensis & Arelatensis: In Comitatu Venuxino unus, Avinionensis: In Belgio seu Germania inferiore tres, Machlinienfis, Cameracensis, & Ultrajectinus: In Germania septem, Moguntinus, Coloniensis, Trevirensis, Magdenburgensis, Salis-
units.tr: poleis, that is, of the principal regions or the chief cities of districts, to whom the remaining bishops of those districts or provinces are subject. Excepted, however, are the not a few exempt bishops, who are noted in the Provinciale, or in the Practica Cancellariae Apostolicae, and in the Oceanus juris, and in whose diocese the metropolitan does not exercise jurisdiction. There are, however, and formerly were, very many archbishops, whom I shall list in order. In the Papal dominion of Italy three: Ravenna, Bologna and Fermo. In the Kingdom of Naples nineteen: Naples, Capua, Salerno, Amalfi, Sorrento, Conza, Acerenza, Taranto, Brindisi, Otranto, Bari, Trani, Siponto, Chieti, Lanciano, Reggio, Cosenza, Rossano, Santa Severina, and Benevento. In Sicily three: Palermo, Messina and Monreale. In Sardinia two: Cagliari and Torres. In Insubria one: Milan. In Piedmont two: Turin and Tarantasia. In Etruria three: Florence, Siena and Pisa. In Liguria one: Genoa. In the dominion of Urbino Urbino. In the dominion of the Venetians four: Split and Zadar. In Dalmatia and Illyria two: Ragusa and Durazzo. In Bulgaria and Greece one: Ochrida. In Armenia one: Nakhchivan. In Spain eleven: Toledo, Burgos, Compostela, Seville, Granada, Zaragoza, Tarragona, Valencia, Braga, Lisbon and Évora. In France thirteen: Lyons, Rouen, Tours, Sens, Reims, Bourges, Bordeaux, Auch, Narbonne, Aix, Vienne, Embrun and Arles. In the County of Venaissin one: Avignon. In Belgium or Lower Germany three: Mechelen, Cambrai and Utrecht. In Germany seven: Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Magdeburg, Salis-

units.la: tani Pontificii Episcopi. etiam titulares, ex Miræo recensiti. Salisburgensis, Bremensis & Biscuntinus: In Bohemia unus, Bragensis: In Hungaria duo Strigeniensis & Colocensis: In Polonia tres, Gnefnensis, Leopoliensis & Rigensis: In Walachia unus, Baccoviensis: In Britannia duo, Cantuariensis & Eboracensis: In Scotia duo, Sanƈtandreanus, seu Andreopolitanus & Glascoensis: In Hibernia quatuor, Armachanus, Dubliniensis, Cassiliensis & Tuamensis: In Dania unus, Londensis: In Norwegia unus, Nidrofiensis: In Suecia unus, Upsaliensis: In India Orientali duo, Goanus & Cranganorensis: In Occidentali quinque, Mexicanus, S. Dominici, Limensis, S. Fidei & Manilanus. In universum igitur Archiepiscopi, qui Pontifici olim paruerunt, & hodieque maximam partem parent, sunt centum & quinque. His Episcoporum maximus numerus subest, quem recensitum videre est ab Auberto Miræo in libello cui titulum fecit: Notitia Episcopatuum Orbis Christiani, in qua Christianæ (Pontificiæ) religionis amplitudo, (en Civitatem magnam!) elucet. Taceo Episcopos titulares, inertes fucos, per ludibrium ipsis etiam Pontificiis dictos portatiles, imaginarios, qui Africanæ vel Asiaticæ cujuspiam Ecclesiæ pridem à Muhammedanis extinctæ titulo à Pontifice ornati, bicornique mitra, & adunco lituo armati, aposcopi Episcopi vices gerunt; ut huic alex, venationi, aliisve turpioribus voluptatibus indulgere liceat, haud absimili meretrici, quæ ut quamprimum venerem repetere possit, recentes partus aliis nutricibus lactandos tradit: nec non Episcopos Orientales, quos omnes jure sibi subesse debere, licet facto secessionem fecerint, Papa pertendit.
units.tr: ...tani, the Papist bishops, also titular ones, as listed by Miraeus: Salzburg, Bremen and Biscuntinus.
