In Bohemia one, Bragensis; in Hungary two, Strigonia and Colocza; in Poland three, Gnesen, Lemberg and Riga; in Wallachia one, Baccovia; in Britain two, Canterbury and York; in Scotland two, St Andrews, or Andropolis, and Glasgow; in Ireland four, Armagh, Dublin, Cashel and Tuam; in Denmark one, London; in Norway one, Nidaros; in Sweden one, Uppsala; in East India two, Goa and Cranganore; in the West five, Mexico, St Dominic, Lima, St Faith and Manila. In all, then, there are one hundred and five archbishops, who once obeyed the Pope and, for the most part, still obey him today. To these is added a very great number of bishops, which can be seen listed by Aubert Miraeus in the little book he entitled Notitia Episcopatuum Orbis Christiani, in qua Christianæ (Papistic) religionis amplitudo (behold, what a great City!) elucet. I say nothing of the titular bishops, idle drones, called in mockery even by the Papists portable, imaginary, who, adorned by the Pope with the title of some African or Asian church long since extinguished by the Muhammadans, and armed with the two-horned mitre and the crooked staff, perform the duties of a bishop, so that they may indulge in hunting, dice, or other baser pleasures, much like a harlot who hands her newborn infants to other nurses to suckle so that she may quickly return to her lust. Nor do I mention the Eastern bishops, whom the Pope insists must all be subject to him by right, even though they have seceded in fact.

units.la: XXXVI. Et Episcopos quidem omnes esse Presbyteris superiores, Concilium Tridentinum Seff. xxiv. Can. 9. definit. Licet quo jure immediato, Divino an Pontificio, superiores sint, ob partium in Concilio ea de re conflictantium
units.tr: XXXVI. The Council of Trent, Sess. 24, Can. 9, declares that all bishops are superior to presbyters. But by what right they are superior, whether immediately by divine right or by papal right, it has not dared to define, because of the fear of the parties in the Council who contended over this matter.

units.la: Episcopi quo jure olim Presbyteris superiores.
units.tr: By what right bishops were once superior to presbyters.

units.la: Presbyteris superiores fini prælati, quo parentio tormentur. tium metum, definire non sustinuit. Neque tamen superioritatem illam & eminentiam Episcoporum illi honorariam duntaxat, nedum imaginariam faciunt, sed in dominatione quapiam & jurisdictione eminente collocant. Olim quidem Ecclesiastico jure sola ordinationis potestate Episcopus Presbyterum superabant. Quid facit Episcopus, ita Hieronymus ad Evagrium quaerit, excepta ordinatione, quod non faciat Presbyter? quod etiam Chrysostomus in 1 Tim. 3. diserte asserit. Sed postea longe ulterius processum est. In Hispalensi enim Concilio can. 7. & Leonis Decretal. 88. ᾱ eorum recensentur longe plura, puta praeter jus ordinandi etiam jus confirmandi, basilicas, altariaque erigendi, consecrandi, manus baptizandis aut conversis ex haeresi imponendi, publice poenitentem conciliandi, firmatos mittendi, prohibitumque Presbyteris praesente Episcopo baptisterium ingredi, infantes tingere, sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Domini conficere, populum docere, benedicere, salutare, aut plebem exhortari, ut per hoc & discretio graduum, & dignitatis fastigium Summi Pontificis demonstretur. Successu temporis amplius aucta Episcopi potestas est, ita ut Canonistae eam hodie constituant in jure leges condendi & promulgandi, causas in foro externo & ipsius conscientiae in Conciliis suffragandi, judicandi, ordinandi, vocandi, puniendi, visitandi, confirmandi, beneficia conferendi, investiendi, Templa, Monasteria Xenodochia erigendi, bona ecclesiastica administrandi, aliisque ejusmodi, in quibus cumulandis vix sibi Canonistae satisfaciunt.
units.tr: Presbyters are superior... (the Council) has not dared to define. Nor do they make that superiority and eminence of bishops merely honorary, let alone imaginary; they place it in a certain lordship and eminent jurisdiction. Formerly, by ecclesiastical law, the bishop surpassed the presbyter only in the power of ordination. What does a bishop do, Jerome asks in his letter to Evagrius, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not? Chrysostom too states this plainly on 1 Tim. 3. But afterwards matters went much further. For in the Council of Seville, can. 7, and in the Decretal of Leo, 88, far more powers are enumerated: besides the right to ordain, also the right to confirm, to erect and consecrate basilicas and altars, to lay hands on the baptised or on those converted from heresy, to reconcile a penitent publicly, to send out the confirmed, and it is forbidden for presbyters to enter the baptistery in the presence of the bishop, to dip infants, to consecrate the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, to teach the people, to bless, to greet, or to exhort the people, so that by this both the distinction of grades and the summit of the dignity of the Supreme Pontiff may be shown. With the passing of time the power of bishops has been enlarged further, so that today the canonists lay down that they have the right to make and promulgate laws, to vote, judge, ordain, summon, punish, visit and confirm in councils, to confer and invest benefices, to erect temples, monasteries and hospices, to administer ecclesiastical goods, and other things of this kind, in heaping up which the canonists can scarcely satisfy themselves.

units.la: XXXVII. Juvat autem cognoscere quo ordine gradu-
units.tr: XXXVII. It is worth knowing by what steps and degrees the coverings of episcopal power were spread out and its fringes widened.

units.la: ve potestatis Episcopalis peristromata extensa, fimbriaeque dilatatae sunt. Et jure quidem Divino Episcopus & Presbyter nil discrepant, uti ex Act. xx. 17. 28. Ephesf. IV. II. iv. ii. Phil. i. i. i Tim. iv. 14. Tit. i. 3. 6. 7. i Pet. v. i. manifestè colligitur. Atque id ipsum olim quoque docuit Hieronymus, imò Michaële Medina lib. j. de Sacram. Orig. cap. 9. ingenuè confitente, etiam Ambrosius, Augustinus, Sedulius, Primasius, Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Oecumenius, Theopgylactus, quorum tamen sententiam in Aërio Waldensibus & Wiclefo ab ecclesia condemnatam fuisse, idem Medina asserit. Ad vitanda porro schismata primò Alexandrini Presbyteri, Hieronymo narrante, unum ex numero suo electum, & in altiori gradu constitutum Episcopum, à Presbyteris scilicet distinctum vocabant, qui in quavis urbe vel loco præsidebat, non ut Princeps inter Consiliarios, sed ut Consul in Senatu. Constitutum est, ut sine eo nihil fieret, ut ex Ignatii ad Trallianos epistola liquet. Ita libertas Ecclesiæ & Presbyterii, accisa est, ut, quod utile videretur, non fieret, intercedente Episcopo. Accessit mox jus ordinationis ei tributum, ne videlicet quisquam docere, nisi ad Episcopi lubitum posset. Sic enim putabant se hæreses excludere posse, cùm tamen eodem medio hæretici Orthodoxos aliquando excluserint. Demum attributa eidem est jurisdictio, atque ita judicium de doctrina & moribus à Presbyterio & ecclesia ablatum, effectúmque est, ut Christianum esse diceretur, placere Episcopo. Quæsita etiam potestas major est in subjectione plurium Presbyteriorum & Chorepiscoporum. Inventa ad roborandam civitatem magnam Metropolitani in cæteros Episcopos jurisdictio; Patriarchæ quoque in Metropolitanos; Episcopi denique Romani in omnes.
units.tr: ...by what steps the coverings of episcopal power were spread out and its fringes widened. By divine right the bishop and the presbyter do not differ at all, as is clearly gathered from Acts 20:17, 28; Eph. iv. 11; Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 4:14; Titus 1:3, 6, 7; 1 Pet. 5:1. This same thing was also taught in former times by Jerome, and indeed Michael Medina, in book 1 of De Sacramentis originalibus, chapter 9, frankly admits that Ambrose, Augustine, Sedulius, Primasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius and Theophylact taught it too. Medina asserts, however, that their opinion was condemned by the Church in Aerius, in the Waldenses and in Wycliffe. Further, to avoid schisms, first the presbyters of Alexandria, as Jerome relates, chose one from their number, set him in a higher rank and called him bishop, that is, distinct from the presbyters. He presided in each city or place, not as a prince among counsellors but as a consul in the senate. It was established that nothing should be done without him, as is clear from Ignatius's letter to the Trallians. Thus the liberty of the Church and of the presbytery was curtailed, so that whatever seemed useful was not done unless the bishop interceded. Soon after, the right of ordination was granted to him, so that no one could teach unless it pleased the bishop. For they thought they could thereby exclude heresies, though heretics had at times excluded the orthodox by this very means. At last jurisdiction was attributed to him as well, and so the judgment of doctrine and morals was taken away from the presbytery and the congregation, with the result that to be called a Christian came to mean to please the bishop. The power sought also grew greater over the subjection of many presbyters and chorepiscopi. To strengthen the great city, a metropolitan's jurisdiction over the other bishops was devised; likewise a patriarch's over the metropolitans; and finally the Roman bishop's over all.

units.la: XXXVIII. Deus certè illi Ordini, cujus in verbo suo author non est, non benedixit. Qui enim Christi Ministri esse, & procul habere dominium imperiúmque omne deburerant, ii paulatim degenerárunt in Diotrephes, Principes &c pes & Dominos meros, qui se se non vites, non oleas vel ficus fructiferas praestiterunt, renuentes quippe pinguedinem, dulcedinem & fructus suos deferre, sed potius Cynosbatos, rubos, & infrugiferas spinas, quæ elatione seu Prælatura sua non pacem & unitatem Ecclesiæ, sed potius mala innumera, ac dissidia generarunt, & tandem per Hierarchicam illam scalam Antichristum in solio suo collocarunt.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Surely God has not blessed that order, whose author is not in his Word. Those who ought to be ministers of Christ, and to keep far away all lordship and dominion, have gradually degenerated into Diotrephes, mere princes and lords, who have not shown themselves to be vines, olives or fruitful fig trees, refusing to yield their richness, sweetness and fruits, but rather briers, brambles and barren thorns. Through their elation, that is, their prelacy, these have produced not peace and unity in the Church but countless evils and dissensions, and at last, by means of that hierarchical ladder, have set Antichrist on his throne.

units.la: XXXIX. Et quales demum sint, fuerintque hucusque Episcopi Pontificii, Pontificis jam dominantis in Ecclesia Ministri, res ipsa certè loquitur, & Concilii Tridentini Patres in aprico collocarunt. Illi enim Sess. xxxiv. cap. 4. & Can. 8. in explicando Episcoporum munere & potestate nullam ministerii verbi & Sacramentorum mentionem facientes, nominata ordinatione & chrismatione, generalem clausulam addunt: Eos alia pleraque peragere posse, hoc est, equos, canes, si non pejora alia, alere, Regiam dominationem exercere, bella gerere, aliàque ejusmodi Episcopalia exercitia peragere posse. Sanè Ambrosius Catharinus, qui & ipse Concilio interfuit, in opere A. M.D.XLVIII. post Concilium Bononiam translatum impressio, de Consid. & Jud. temp. lib. 4. inter alia tradit, malorum in Ecclesiam irrumpentium, hanc maximam causam esse, quòd Episcopi pene omnes facti sint mercenarii, vel lupi; additque, Episcopatum non amplius esse superintendentiam, & curam gregis: perditam esse cum re ipsa vocis significationem. Nunc enim voce Episcopatus non venire nisi honorem & bonorum temporalium proventum, & qui Episcopatum desiderat, non aliud jam illum desiderare. Concludit: Episcopatum non aliud jam esse, quàm predia rustica & urbana, vel decimas ac census: gregis verò curandi rationem nullam haberi.
units.tr: XXXIX. What the Papist bishops really are, and have been until now, as ministers of the Pontiff who now rules in the Church, the matter itself speaks clearly, and the Fathers of the Council of Trent have set it plainly before us. For in Sess. xxxiv. cap. 4. and Can. 8., when explaining the office and power of bishops, they make no mention at all of the ministry of the Word and the Sacraments. Instead, after naming ordination and chrismation, they add a general clause: that bishops can perform many other things, that is, feed horses and dogs, if not other worse things, exercise royal lordship, wage wars, and carry out other such episcopal exercises. Indeed Ambrosius Catharinus, who was himself present at the Council, in his work printed in 1548 after the Council was transferred to Bologna, de Consid. & Jud. temp. lib. 4., among other things teaches that the greatest cause of the evils breaking into the Church is this: that almost all bishops have become hirelings or wolves. He adds that the episcopate is no longer a superintendence and care of the flock: the meaning of the word has been lost along with the thing itself. For now by the word "episcopate" nothing is understood but honour and the income of temporal goods, and whoever desires the episcopate desires nothing else. He concludes: the episcopate is now nothing other than rural and urban estates, or tithes and rents, and no account at all is taken of caring for the flock.

units.la: XL. Quod igitur de novis quibusdam Pseudo-prophetis Zacharias Cap. xiii. 4. 5. idem de personatis his Episcopis enuntiare licet: In die illo pudefient Prophetæ quisque in visione sua. Non induentur אררית שער למען כחש pallio pilosō, ut mentiantur: Et dicet; Non propheta sum, Agricola sum ego, quia homo fecit me emere a pueritia mea. q. d. Pudebit illos visionis propriæ, deponent pallium pilosum abnegandi ergo suscceptum, repudiabunt nomen Prophetarum, dicent se cultores terræ. Priores pseudo-prophetæ proponent aliquid, quod ipsi viderint & observaverint in Scripturis: austera specie vitæ se commendabunt. Hi novi Pseudo-prophetæ contra, non quod singulis ipsis videbitur, proferent, sed antiqua placita & aberrationes colligent; assument speciem magnificam & superbam, abnegabunt officium interpretandi Scripturas, atque illud ad doctores, ad Concilium, ad Papam amandabunt. Profitebuntur se reapse viros agricolas, sive in metaphora, quia malas herbas ex Ecclesia se extirpare præ se ferunt: sive in litera, quia profitebuntur, se hoc jus ad Ecclesiam regendam habere, quod Princeps habet ad regendum populum, cujus Episcopus est agriculturam, & alias artes victui commodas promovere, divitias sibi & populo coacervare, idque quia אדם Homo, Imperator vel Papa, vel utrumque eos ad hoc non sine pretio investiverint. Vivum hoc, & efficax Episcoporum Pontificiorum recentiorum cum vetustioribus comparatorum emblema est.
units.tr: XL. Therefore what Zechariah (13:4–5) says of certain new pseudo-prophets may also be said of these bishops in disguise: In that day the prophets shall be ashamed, every one of his vision. Neither shall they wear a rough garment to deceive [אדרת שער למען כחש] , and they shall say, I am no prophet, I am a husbandman; for man taught me to keep cattle from my youth. That is, they will be ashamed of their own vision; they will lay aside the hairy garment put on for deception, they will renounce the name of prophets, and say that they are tillers of the earth. The earlier pseudo-prophets put forward something that they themselves had seen and observed in the Scriptures, and commended themselves by a severe appearance of life. These new pseudo-prophets, on the contrary, will not bring forward what seems right to each of them, but will gather up old opinions and errors; they will assume a magnificent and proud appearance, will renounce the office of interpreting the Scriptures, and will refer that task to teachers, to the Council, to the Pope. They will in fact profess themselves to be husbandmen, either in metaphor, since they claim to root out bad weeds from the Church, or literally, since they profess that they have the same right to rule the Church that a prince has to rule the people, whose bishop he is, and to promote farming and other arts useful for living, heaping up riches for themselves and the people. They do this because [אדם] man, that is the emperor or the Pope, or both, have invested them in this office, not without a price. This is the living and effective emblem of the Papist bishops of recent times, when compared with the older ones.

units.la: XLI. Interim ita suis commodis Pontificii Episcopi
units.tr: XLI. Meanwhile the Papist bishops so sail with their own advantages

units.la: velificantur, ut toti etiam, quanti quanti sunt, Domini sui Papæ sint, ejusque dominationi promovendæ, dignitatique exornandæ, ceu γνήσιοι ejusdem vasalli, inserviant. Idque duplici argumento clarissimè liquet. Primus est, quòd institutionem, potestatémque suam ἀμέσως non Christo, sed Pontifici Romano acceptam referre cogantur, licet se in titulis suis Dei gratiâ Episcopos mentiantur. In Concilio equidem Tridentino acriter disceptatum inter Episcopos est, unde dignitatem suam potestatémque immediatè habeant, à Christóne, an à Romano Pontifice? Et à Christo eam immediatè habere, acriter quidem Episcopi nonnulli Galli, Hispani & Germani pertenderant. Itali contra, aliique Papæ Domino suo metuentes, à Pontifice eam immediatè pendere, asseverabant fortiter, adeò quidem, ut Jesuitarum Generalis Lainezius asserere non dubitaverit, si statuatur Episcopos potestatem & superioritatem suam immediatè à Christo, adeoque ex jure divino habere, actum fore de Hierarchia, introductúmque iri Oligarchiam, vel Anarchiam, neque ultra Papam futurum Caput Ecclesiæ, & Vicarium Christi. Addebat Segoviensis Episcopus, unicam voculam Juris Divini Papæ fore causam ruinæ. Pallavicinus quoque Hist. Conc. Trid. lib. xviij. xix. xxj. non dissimulat, acri studio Legatorum, tum Crescentii, verba illa Jure Divino expungentis, tum sequentium, temerariam illam expunctionem non minori ardore, quàm si de rerum summa ageretur, propugnantium, conatus contranitentium suffiaminatos esse. Pervicerunt igitur in re tanti momenti Episcopi Itali, aliique Papæ addicti, effecerúntque, ut in decreto Concilii simpliciter definiretur, Episcopos superiores esse Presbyteris, quo verò jure immediato superiores sint, Divino an Pontificio, dissimularetur. Cúmque interpretatio Concilii penes unum deinceps Pontificem fuerit, sitque adhuc, Episcopi suam potestatem se immediatè habere à Pontifice, adeóque non Christi servos, sed Papæ Vasallos esse, vix ampliùs revocare in dubium possunt.
units.tr: that all of them, however many there are, belong wholly to their lord the Pope and serve to advance his lordship and adorn his dignity, like genuine [γνήσιοι] vassals of his. This is made very clear by a twofold argument. The first is that they are compelled to refer their institution and their power, received immediately [ἀμέσως] not from Christ but from the Roman Pontiff, although in their titles they falsely call themselves bishops by the grace of God. At the Council of Trent there was indeed a sharp dispute among the bishops over whether they hold their dignity and power immediately from Christ or from the Roman Pontiff. Some bishops of France, Spain and Germany strongly contended that they hold it immediately from Christ. The Italians, and others who feared their lord the Pope, on the contrary asserted vigorously that it depends immediately on the Pontiff. So much so that the General of the Jesuits, Lainez, did not hesitate to assert that if it were established that bishops hold their power and superiority immediately from Christ, and so by divine right, the Hierarchy would be undone, an Oligarchy or Anarchy would be introduced, and the Pope would no longer be the Head of the Church and Vicar of Christ. The Bishop of Segovia added that the single little word "by divine right" would be the cause of the Pope's ruin. Pallavicini too, in Hist. Conc. Trid. lib. xviij. xix. xxj., does not conceal that the legates, both Crescentius, who struck out the words by divine right, and those who followed him, defended that rash deletion with no less ardour than if the sum of affairs were at stake, and stifled the efforts of those who resisted. Thus in a matter of such weight the Italian bishops and the others devoted to the Pope prevailed, and they brought it about that the decree of the Council simply defined that bishops are superior to presbyters, while it was left vague whether they are superior by immediate right, divine or papal. And since the interpretation of the Council has since rested with one Pontiff alone, and still does, the bishops can scarcely call into question any longer that they hold their power immediately from the Pope, and so are not servants of Christ but vassals of the Pope.

units.la: XLII. Posterius est, quòd iidem solenni juramento ad authoritatem dominationémque Pontificiam tuendam ob- stringuntur. Olim quidem etiam Episcopi juramentum
units.tr: XLII. The second is that the same bishops are bound by a solemn oath to uphold the authority and dominion of the Pope.

units.la: {a} sum quia juramentum Pontifici, ... vasalli præstabant, ut ordinati scilicet suo Consecratori, non ut Vasalli suo Principi, & non nisi pro recta fide, uti habetur in Epistola, quæ Cornelii Papæ nomine scripta circumfertur, non tuenda dominatione Pontificia, quam nondum Pontifices sibi vindicaverant. Jurabant etiam Papæ non Episcopi in universum omnes, sed soli Romanæ Metropolis suffraganei. Cæteri quisque suo Metropolitano, quod inductis exemplis Hinc mari Londunensis Episcopi, & Ivonis, nec non decreto Gregorii IX. M. Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. lib. iv. 5. 46. 47. comprobat. Postquam vero Papa Romanus, acquisita in Ecclesiam dominatione, sibi & Episcopos, & Metropolitanos, aliosque mancipavit, juramentum fidelitatis, adeóque Homagium Episcopis præscripsit, quod Decret. Greg. lib. v. tit. 24. de jure jurando, cap. 4. inconditis verbis à Gregorio VII. Hildebrando conceptum & expressum ita sonat: Ego N. Episcopus ab hac hora in antea fidelis ero S. Petro, Sanctæque Romanæ Ecclesiæ, Dominóque meo Papæ (ejusque successoribus canonicè intrantibus. Non ero neque in consilio neque in facto, ut vitam perdat, aut membrum, vel capiatur mala captione. Consilium quod mihi, aut per se, aut per literas, aut per nuntium manifestabit, ad ejus damnum nulli pandam. Papatum S. R. E. & regulas S. Patrum adjutor ero ad defendendum aut retinendum (salvo ordine meo) contra omnes homines. Vocatus ad Synodum veniam, nisi præpeditus fuero canonica præpeditione. Legatum Apostolicum, sed quem certum esse cognovero, in eundo & redeundo honorificè tractabo, & in suis necessitatibus adjuvabo. Limina Apostolorum singulis annis, aut per me, aut per certum nuntium visitabo: nisi eorum absolvat licentia. Sic me Deus adjuvet, & hæc S. Evangelia. Clarissimum est, juramentum esse Vasalli erga suum Principem & Dominum, non veri Episcopi ordinati erga suum consecratorem pro retinenda fide catholica & purè praedicando Dei verbo, Sacramentisque ritè administrandis, quale solum in sana olim Ecclesia obtinuit. Expressissimè Pius IV. juramentum ab Ecclesiasticis beneficia postulantibus praestandum inter alia his verbis praecepit: Spondeo & juro summo Pontifici veram obedientiam. Quae usurpatis manifestissima est, & dira tyrannis, qua contra omne jus & fas Papa Episcopos universos sibi fecit proprie subditos, & vasallos, & ipse se supra eos temporalem Principem ac Dominum constituit, cum gravi non Episcoporum duntaxat, & Ecclesiae, sed Principum etiam damno & praejudicio, quibus non tantum eorum subditi eripiuntur, sed etiam alieni Principis jurati Vasalli, hostes profecto acerrimi; intra viscera sua ferendi, alendique obtruduntur.
units.tr: {a} ... for the oath they once swore to the Pope was that of vassals, that is, of men ordained by their consecrator, not of vassals to their prince, and it was taken only for the true faith, as is found in the letter circulated under the name of Pope Cornelius, not for defending papal domination, which the Popes had not yet claimed for themselves. Nor did all bishops in general swear, but only the suffragans of the Roman metropolis. The rest swore to their own metropolitan, as M. Antonius de Dominis in On the Commonwealth of the Church, book 4, chapters 5, 46 and 47, confirms by citing examples from Hinemar of Laon and Ivo, and a decree of Gregory IX. But after the Roman Pope, having won dominion over the Church, had made bishops, metropolitans and others his own, he prescribed to the bishops an oath of fidelity and so a homage. It runs as follows, in the crude words conceived and expressed by Gregory VII, Hildebrand, in Decretals of Gregory, book 5, title 24, On the oath, chapter 4: I, N., bishop, from this hour forward will be faithful to St Peter, to the holy Roman Church, and to my lord the Pope (and to his successors who enter canonically). I will not be party, either in counsel or in deed, to his losing his life or limb, or to his being seized by evil capture. Any counsel which he entrusts to me, either by himself, by letter or by messenger, I will reveal to no one to his harm. I will be a helper in defending and retaining the papacy of the holy Roman Church and the rules of the holy Fathers (saving my order) against all men. When summoned to a synod I will come, unless I am prevented by canonical impediment. An apostolic legate, provided I know him to be genuine, I will honour in going and returning and will help in his needs. I will visit the thresholds of the Apostles every year, either in person or by a certain messenger, unless I am released by their permission. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels. It is most clear that this is the oath of a vassal to his prince and lord, and not that of a true bishop ordained to his consecrator, for retaining the Catholic faith and purely preaching the word of God and rightly administering the sacraments, which alone prevailed in the sound Church of old. Pius IV expressly prescribed, among other things, an oath to be taken by ecclesiastics seeking benefices, in these words: I promise and swear true obedience to the supreme Pontiff. This usurpation is most manifest, and a dire tyranny, by which the Pope, against all right and law, has made all bishops his own subjects and vassals, and has himself set himself above them as temporal prince and lord, to the grave harm and prejudice not only of bishops and the Church but also of princes, from whom not only their subjects are snatched away but also their sworn vassals, who are assuredly their most bitter enemies, are thrust in, to be carried and nourished within their own bowels.

units.la: XLIII. Atque huc etiam referenda est ἀρχιερατικὸν, seu Pallium, quod hodie Archiepiscopis Papa, non tam potestatis, quàm subjectionis symbolum, magno auri pondere redimendum concedit. Hoc enim instructis demum Concilia convocare, Chrisma conficere, basilicas dedicare, Episcopos consecrare, Clericos ordinare, Archiepiscoporum nomen assumere integrum est. Fuit autem initio Pallium vestimenti genus quodpiam, quod Imperatores, simile Imperiali ornamento, praecipuis Episcopis, puta Romano, & Constantinopolitano obtulerunt. Si postea cruces additae sunt, ut Ecclesiasticum penitus ornamentum fieret, quod post ad omnes Episcopos Orientis transiit, & commune omnium Episcoporum indumentum sacrum, in rebus sacris peragendis usurpandum evasit. Valentiniani Imp. temporibus Isidorus Pelusiota Epist. lib. j. ep. 36. sic ejus mysterium explicat: τὸ δὲ Ἀπόστολος ὡμοφόριον ἐξ ἱερέως ὤν, ἀλλ' ὁ λόγος, τῷ δὲ ἀποβάτῳ δορὰ ὀπμαίνει, ὅπερ πάλαι ὁ ἀπόστολος ... ὁ γὰρ Ἀρχιερεὺς τῶν οἰκείων ὑμῶν ἀνάλαβεν. 'O γὰρ ἈρχιεἈλλ᾽ ὡς πᾶν ὡν ἔχει τὸ ἐχειν ὀλκῶν πολλῆ ἡ δεικνυσι τῶν ἀλλὰ ἡ ἡμῖν ἄν, ὅπ μιμητὴς ἐστὶ τῶ ἀγαθῶ καὶ μεγάλῳ μι- μητὴς, ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας Φίρειν τὰ ἡμέρα ἀνεθέληλημένα. Id autem amiculum, quod Episcopus humeris gestat, atque ex lana, non ex lino contextum est, ovis illius, quam Dominus aberrantem quaesivit, inventámque humeris suis sustulit, pellem designat. Episcopus enim, qui Christi typum gerit, ipsius munere fungitur, atque ipso etiam habitu illud omnibus offendit, se boni illius ac magni Pastoris imitatorem esse, qui gregis infirmitates sibi ferendas propositit. Unde etiam liquet, fuisse, uti hodieque est, in Ecclesia orientali pallium illud Episcoporum omnium commune, non Patriarchis & Metropolitanis proprium. Quia vero in Occidentali Ecclesia non commune erat omnium, Romanus Pontifex etiam hinc elationis suæ occasionem rapiendam ratus, & se loco Imperatoris pallii diributorem non sine pingui lucro suo fecit, & illud ad solos Archiepiscopos exceptis Episcopis ψιλοῖς paucis, quibus singulari privilegio gestamen isthoc indulget, restrinxit, eósque hac ratione suos nexu mancipioque fecit. Iis enim Papa imposuit (Dist. 100. Quoniam quidam) ut sententiam, potestatem suam nullam esse, nisi prius Pontifex mittat pallium de corpore B. Petri sumptum, in quo est plenitudo Pontificii officii, uti Sacrar. Cerem. Eccl. Rom. lib. 1. sect. 5. dicitur. Primus Hildebrandus, ut ex ejus ad Lanfrancum, Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum rescripto, à Baronio Tom. xi. A. 1070. n. 17. narrato, liquet, introduxit, ut qui Pallium desiderarent, illud non per literas vel nuntios, uti ante hac moris erat, peterent, sed ipsimet Romam venirent, & consequenter munera ferrent, Dominum suum adorarent. Addidit Hildebrandi successor, Paschalis II. ut Archiepiscopi Romæ coram Pallium licitantes, juramento etiam fidelitatis se Pontifici obstringerent,
units.tr: XLIII. To this also must be referred the archiepiscopal [ἀρχιερατικόν], or pallium, which the Pope today grants to archbishops as a symbol not so much of power as of subjection, to be bought back at a heavy weight of gold. For it is by this that men are at last free to convene councils, make chrism, dedicate basilicas, consecrate bishops, ordain clergy and assume the name of archbishop. Originally the pallium was a kind of garment, similar to the imperial ornament, which the emperors offered to the principal bishops, namely the Roman and the Constantinopolitan. Later crosses were added, so that it became a wholly ecclesiastical ornament, which afterwards passed to all the bishops of the East and became the common sacred vestment of all bishops, to be used in performing sacred rites. In the time of the Emperor Valentinian, Isidore of Pelusium, in his Letters, book 1, letter 36, explains its mystery thus: the garment which the bishop carries on his shoulders, woven of wool and not of linen, designates the skin of that sheep which the Lord sought when it had gone astray and, having found it, bore it on his shoulders. For the bishop, who bears the type of Christ, performs his office and by that very dress shows to all that he is an imitator of that good and great Shepherd, who took upon himself the infirmities of the flock. Hence it is also clear that, as it is still today, that pallium was in the Eastern Church common to all bishops, not peculiar to patriarchs and metropolitans. But because in the Western Church it was not common to all, the Roman Pontiff, thinking this an occasion for his own exaltation, and making himself the distributor of the pallium in place of the emperor, not without a fat profit to himself, restricted it to archbishops alone, except for a few simple bishops, to whom he grants that particular privilege of wearing it, and in this way made them bound and enslaved to himself. For the Pope imposed on them (Dist. 100, Quoniam quidam) the opinion that their authority is null unless the Pontiff first sends the pallium taken from the body of St Peter, in which is the fullness of the pontifical office, as is said in Sacred Ceremonies of the Roman Church, book 1, section 5. Hildebrand was the first to introduce this, as is clear from his rescript to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, reported by Baronius in Annals, volume 11, year 1070, number 17: that those who desired the pallium should seek it not by letter or messenger, as had been the custom before, but should come to Rome in person, and consequently bring gifts and worship their lord. Hildebrand's successor, Paschal II, added that archbishops, when receiving the pallium at Rome in person, should also bind themselves to the Pontiff by an oath of fidelity,

units.la: quò sic summi quique Episcopi, aliorum Episcoporum Duces Patrésque in plenam Papæ clientelam transirent, hic Princeps illorum ac Dominus absolutus, illi verò ejusdem subditi cum plena & servili pœne subjectione fierent. quod ex Paschalis illius Decretali Epistola ad Episcopum Panormitanum de Elect. cap. 4. nec non ex ejusdem ad Archiepiscopum Polonorum epistola, quam ex codice Vaticano Baronius Annal. tom. xy. A. 1102. repræsentat, abundè colligitur. Non igitur ulla lege, non jure ullo, ne Ecclesiastico quidem, Pallii redimendi necessitas inducta est, sed donum Imperiale factum Episcopo Romano ex Ecclesiastica consuetudine sola, uti Greg. Dist. 100. cap.2. fatetur, coepit ab aliis quoque ambiri & emixè postulari. Inde verò Pontifices Romani pallii magna mercede contrahendi necessitatem induxerunt, jurisdictionem nemque suam substratis, & in sublime sublatis his basibus, ut idolum abominationis tantò eminentius super illos collocari possfet, stabiliverunt.
units.tr: By this means all the greatest bishops, the leaders and fathers of the other bishops, would pass into the Pope's full clientage. He would be their prince and absolute lord, and they, his subjects, would be brought into full and servile subjection. This is amply gathered from that decretal letter of Paschal to the bishop of Palermo, de Elect. cap. 4., and also from his letter to the archbishop of the Poles, which Baronius presents from the Vatican codex, Annal. tom. xv. A. 1102. Therefore no law, no right, not even an ecclesiastical one, introduced any necessity of buying the pallium. Rather, the imperial gift made to the Roman bishop by ecclesiastical custom alone, as Gregory Dist. 100. cap. 2. admits, began to be sought after by others too and urgently demanded. From there the Roman pontiffs introduced the necessity of obtaining the pallium for a great price, and by setting these foundations beneath their own jurisdiction and raising them aloft, they established it, so that the idol of abomination might be set up over them all the more eminently.

units.la: XLIV. Inter Clericos, seu Ecclesiasticos gubernantes, sed fecundi ordinis, Possevinus Præpositos, Archidiaconos, Archipresbyteros, Vicarios & Consiliarios, refert, de quibus pauca dicere satis erit. Et Præpositi quidem, alicubi etiam Priores nuncupati, præsunt, seu præponuntur vel claustralibus regularibus, veluti cùm ad regimen Monasterii per Abbatem, vel Superiorem deputantur: vel Clericis Regularibus, quo in censu sunt Capita Collegii Canonicorum, vel Ecclesiarum, quas Collegiatas vocant, qui Archidiaconorum etiam & Decanorum nomine veniunt: vel Rectores etiam Ecclesiarum ruralium. Diversis nominibus officia isthæc venire Mosconius de Majest. Eccl. milit. lib. j. cap. 14. docet: Archidiaconi sunt, qui officium Ecclesiasticum habent cum jurisdictione & præeminentia conjunctum. Tales v. g. in Cathedrali Ecclesia sunt Episcoporum Vicarii, Coadjutores, qui oculi Episcoporum vocantur. Officium & dignitas eorum in eo consistunt, quòd Episcopo ministrant; officium Presbyteri Episcopo Missam celebranti assistentis exercent; absente vel impedito Episcopo Archipresbytero & Canonicis omnibus in celebratione Missarum solennium aliisque functionibus Episcopalibus præferuntur; visitant Ecclesias Dioecesēos, quæ aliàque Decretal. lib. j. tit. 23. legere est. Archipresbyteri sunt Presbyterorum Principes, Decanorum etiam nomine insigniti, qui in Civitatibus funguntur officio Vicarii Episcopi in Spiritualibus in foro poenitentiali & celebratione Divinorum officiorum, Rure verò, seu in pago Plebani etiam dicti, vicarios Episcopi se gerunt. Vicarii seu Vice Domini alii dicuntur dati à lege, alii ab homine. A lege dati sunt, qui absque deputatione, officii sui tenore vicarii efficiuntur, quales Archidiaconos & Archipresbyteros esse diximus. Ab homine dati, qui libera hominum deputatione vices gerunt, quales sunt vicarii in Curia Romana, Legati Apostolici, Cardinalium Legatorum, Patriarcharum, Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum, Ecclesiarum Capitularium Ordinum, Provinciaium &c. vicarii. Consiliarii denique olim simpliciter dicti sunt Cardinales Papæ scil. consultores. Hodie Canonici, præsertim Cathedrales, sunt Consiliarii Episcopi: in Monasteriis Officiales, Conventuales. Possent Ecclesiastici gubernantes alii etiam notari non pauci, veluti personatus, plebani, inquisitores, Legati sive Nuntii Apostolici, sive à latere, Protonotarii Apostolici, Examinatores & testes Synodales, Camerarii, Castellani Romanæ Ecclesiæ, aliique plures quorum differentias & munera Pontificiæ dominationi ministrantia recensere supervacaneum foret.
units.tr: XLIV. Among the clergy, or ecclesiastics, who govern but are of the second order, Possevinus lists provosts, archdeacons, archpresbyters, vicars and counsellors, of whom it will be enough to say a few things. Provosts, who in some places are also called priors, preside over or are placed over either regular cloistered clergy, as when they are appointed to govern a monastery by the abbot or superior, or secular clergy, among whom are the heads of a college of canons or of churches which they call collegiate, who also go by the name of archdeacons and deans, or rectors of rural churches. Moscon teaches, de Majest. Eccl. milit. lib. j. cap. 14., that these offices are called by different names. Archdeacons are those who hold an ecclesiastical office joined with jurisdiction and pre-eminence. For example, in a cathedral church such are the bishops' vicars and coadjutors, who are called the eyes of the bishops. Their office and dignity consist in this, that they minister to the bishop; they perform the office of presbyter assisting the bishop when he celebrates Mass; when the bishop is absent or hindered, the archpresbyter and all the canons are preferred to him in the celebration of solemn Masses and other episcopal functions; they visit the churches of the diocese. What else there is may be read in the Decretals, lib. j. tit. 23. Archpresbyters are the princes of the presbyters, also distinguished by the name of deans, who in the cities discharge the office of the bishop's vicar in spiritual matters, in the penitential court and in the celebration of divine offices; but in the countryside, or in the parish, also called plebani, they act as the bishop's vicars. Vicars, or those who stand in the Lord's place, are said by some to be given by law, and by others to be given by man. Given by law are those who, without any appointment, become vicars by the terms of their office, such as we have said archdeacons and archpresbyters are. Given by man are those who act in place of another by free appointment of men; such are the vicars in the Roman Curia, the Apostolic legates, the vicars of cardinal legates, patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, of chapter churches, of the orders, of the provinces, and so on. Finally, counsellors were formerly called simply the Pope's cardinals, that is, advisers. Today the canons, especially of cathedrals, are the bishop's counsellors; in monasteries, the officials and conventual members. Many other governing ecclesiastics could also be noted, such as personates, plebans, inquisitors, Apostolic legates or nuncios, whether a latere or not, Apostolic protonotaries, examiners and synodal witnesses, chamberlains, castellans of the Roman Church, and several others; to list their differences and offices serving the Papal domination would be superfluous.

units.la: XLV. In secundo Cleri Romani Pontificio imperio in- servientis ordine Ecclesiastici Ministrantes, nominatim
units.tr: XLV. In the second order of the Roman clergy, which serves the Pontifical empire, the ministering ecclesiastics, namely

units.la: Parochi, Sacerdotes, Diaconi, Subdiaconi, Acolsuthi, Exorcistæ, Lectores, Ostiarii, Canonici & Oeconomi reponuntur. Canonicis & Oeconomis exceptis, & Parochis Sacerdotibus annumeratis, reliqui septem totidem ordines, totidemque Sacramenta constituuntur. De quo ita Concilii Tridentini decretum Sess. xxiv. cap. 2. sonat: Cum Divina res sit tam Sancti Sacerdotii ministerium, consentaneum suit, quò digniùs & majori cum veneratione exerceri posset, ut in Ecclesiæ ordinatissima dispositione plures & diversi essent ministrorum ordines qui sacerdotio ex officio deservirent, & ita distributi, ut qui jam Clericali tonsura insigniti essent, per minores ad majores ascenderent. Nam non solùm de Sacerdotibus, sed & de Diaconis sacræ literæ apertam mentionem faciunt, & quæ maximè in illarum ordinatione attendenda sunt, gravissimis verbis docent: & ab ipso ecclesiæ initio sequentium ordinum nomina, atque uniuscujusque eorum propria ministeria, subdiaconi scilicet, acoluthi, exorcistæ, lectores & ostiarii in usu fuisse cognoscuntur, quamvis non pari gradu. Nam subdiaconatus ad majores ordines à Patribus & sacris Conciliis refertur. Canone tertio ejusdem Sessionis anathema vibratur in eos, qui dixerint, ordinem seu sacram ordinationem non esse verè & proprie Sacramentum à Christo Domino institutum.
units.tr: Parish priests, priests, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers, doorkeepers, canons and stewards are placed. With canons and stewards set aside, and parish priests counted among the priests, the remaining seven make up seven orders and as many sacraments. The decree of the Council of Trent, Sess. xxiv. cap. 2., says of this: Since the ministry of the Holy Priesthood is a divine thing, it was fitting that it might be exercised more worthily and with greater reverence, so that in the most orderly arrangement of the Church there should be several and different orders of ministers who serve the priesthood by office, and so distributed that those already marked with clerical tonsure should ascend through the lesser to the greater. For the sacred letters make clear mention not only of priests but also of deacons, and they teach with the gravest words what must chiefly be attended to in their ordination. And from the very beginning of the Church the names of the following orders, and the proper ministries of each, are known to have been in use: subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers and doorkeepers, though not at the same rank. For the subdiaconate is referred by the Fathers and holy Councils to the greater orders. In the third canon of the same session, anathema is hurled against those who say that order, or sacred ordination, is not truly and properly a sacrament instituted by Christ the Lord.

units.la: XLVI. Hæc vero sine ullo verbi Divini & sanæ antiquitatis præsidio asserta, non aliò certè collineant, quàm ut Sacerdotii Pontificii dignitas & potestas, summi verò Sacerdotis, seu Pontificis maximi authoritas & veneratio, Sacramenti scilicet sublimi titulo exornata, sacrosancta apud omnes reddatur. Aliàs enim verissimè Cajetanus, expensa opinionum circa ordines diversitate, jam senex pronuntiavit: Si collecta fuerint, quæ Pontificales codices, quæve ratio authoritasque doctrinæ tradidit, incerta valde apde apparebit, Presbyteratu excepto, reliquorum natura ordinum. Quin ex gentilismo petitam esse subdivisionem Sacerdotum, juxta quam alii sunt Sacerdotes simplices, alii Archipresbyteri, alii Chorepiscopi, alii Episcopi, alii Archiepiscopi &c. ipse Gratianus Proœm. distr. 21. & dist. 80. Cap. in illis non diffitetur. Fuerunt nempe Gentilibus sui Flamines, Archiflamines, Protoflamines. Lombardus quin etiam Dist. 24. singulos ordines ex Judaismo arcessit. Et quid tandem illo ἀλίμακι, gradatione illa ab inferioribus ordinibus ad Sacerdotium usque ineptius? Siccine Christus Sacerdos magnus, Apostoli, veteres illi celeberrimi Episcopi, per abjectos illos gradus ad Sacerdotium magnum, Apostolatum, Episcopatum enixi sunt?
units.tr: XLVI. These things, however, asserted without any support from the Divine Word or sound antiquity, certainly aim at nothing other than to make the dignity and power of the Pontifical priesthood, and the authority and veneration of the supreme priest, or Pontiff Maximus, held sacrosanct before all, adorned with the lofty title of sacrament. For otherwise Cajetan, having weighed the diversity of opinions about the orders, already old, pronounced most truly: If there were collected what the pontifical codices, or what reason and authority of doctrine have handed down, the nature of the orders, the presbyterate excepted, will appear very uncertain. Indeed Gratian himself, Proœm. distr. 21. and dist. 80, Cap. in illis, does not deny that the subdivision of priests, by which some are simple priests, others archpresbyters, others chorepiscopi, others bishops, others archbishops, and so on, was borrowed from paganism. The Gentiles had their own flamens, archflamens and protoflamens. Lombard, moreover, in Dist. 24. derives the individual orders from Judaism. And what is more absurd than that ladder [κλίμακι], that gradation from the lower orders up to the priesthood? Did Christ, the great Priest, and the Apostles, and those famous ancient bishops, strive upward through those abject steps to the great priesthood, the apostolate, and the episcopate?

units.la: XLVII. Sacerdotes & Parochi ita differunt, quòd qui parochi sunt, sacerdotes etiam sint, non, qui Sacerdotes, necessariò Parochi.
units.tr: XLVII. Parish priests and priests differ in this way: every parish priest is a priest, but not every priest is necessarily a parish priest.

units.la: Parochus nempe, qui etiam Curator, Curio, Rector Parochiæ dicitur, sacerdos est, sed residens in παροικία parochia sua, ibidemque sacra officia, à superioribus præscripta obeundo, Pontificium cultum peragens. In eo utramque ferè paginam facit, quòd ceu Sacerdos, non utique secundum vel Melchisedeci vel Levi, sed cujusvis alterius, sacrificat, hoc est, mimicá quadam, sed execrabili planè actione, Christum se sub speciebus panis & vini Deo in Sacrificium propitiatorium offerre simulat: quòdque confessiones audit, & ceu precarius quidam prætor seu Ædilis, sine Divinis suffragiis, satisfactionum injunctarum pretio, peccata remittit. Quorum duorum principalium officiorum respectu Sacerdotem quemvis, Angelis, ipsiqué etiam Beatæ Virgini Ἱεροπώ, ne dicam etiam Christo, cujus creatores se profiteri non erubescunt, multis parasangis antecellere, pertendunt.
units.tr: A parish priest (also called curator, curio, rector of a parish) is a priest, but one who resides in his παροικία [parochia], his parish, and there performs the sacred offices prescribed by his superiors, carrying out Papistical worship. In this he does almost the whole of his work. As a priest, not indeed after the order of Melchizedek or of Levi but of some other kind, he offers sacrifice; that is, by a kind of mimicry, though a wholly execrable action, he pretends to offer Christ to God as a propitiatory sacrifice under the appearances of bread and wine. He also hears confessions, and, like a hired praetor or aedile, he remits sins without divine intercession, for a price of imposed satisfactions. With respect to these two principal duties, they maintain that he far surpasses any priest, and even the angels, and the Blessed Virgin herself [ἱεροπώ], not to say Christ himself, whose creators they are not ashamed to profess to be, by many parasangs.

units.la: XLVIII. Diaconorum, Subdiaconorum, Acolutho- rum, Exorcistarum, Lectorum & Ostiariorum officia hi-
units.tr: XLVIII. The offices of deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers and doorkeepers, which

units.la: strionica Durantes in Rationali, aliique passim describunt. Id verò certum est, nominibus & titulis illis res verbo Dei, & piæ antiquitatis praxi congruentes subesse prorsus nullas: imò alia omnia subesse. Uti supra etiam ostendimus. Merito proin inter Reformationis Capita triginta quatuor à Gallis Concilio Tridentino exhibita, etiam hoc capite quarto à Synodo postulatum est, ut Diaconis & aliis sacris ordinibus restituatur debita & antiqua functio, ne amplius nuda & in ceremoniis tantùm posita nomina dicantur. Et illos minores, officia merè manualia, & sacris longè inferiora, quibus Pontificii Theatri ad agenda Quirinalia, Choragium, scenicúsque apparatus expletur, vel sacramentales, vel omnino necessarios nunquam vetus Ecclesia judicavit, uti pluribus etiam argumentis Petrus Arcadius Corcyræus Concord. Eccles. Orient. & Occid. circa Sacram. administr. lib. vj. 9. asseruit.
units.tr: are described theatrically by Durandus in the Rationale and others everywhere. It is certain, however, that these names and titles have no real content that agrees with the Word of God or with the practice of pious antiquity; indeed, they have nothing but other things beneath them. As we have also shown above. Therefore, rightly, among the thirty-four heads of reform presented by the French to the Council of Trent, this synod also demanded in the fourth head that the due and ancient function be restored to the deacons and the other sacred orders, so that the names are no longer spoken as bare names placed only in ceremonies. As for those lesser offices, purely manual and far beneath sacred duties, by which the theatre of the Papists is furnished for conducting the Quirinalia, the choir and the stage equipment, the ancient Church never judged them either sacramental or necessary at all; as Peter Arcadius of Corcyra has asserted with many arguments in Concord. Eccles. Orient. & Occid. circa Sacram. administr. lib. vj. 9.

units.la: XLIX. Inter Ecclesiasticos ministrantes haud postremum locum Canonici, seu Capitulares obtinent. Eorum Collegia, quotquot in Orbe Pontificio sunt, unà cum eorundem origine & fundatoribus, Aubertus Miræus libro de Collegiis Canonicorum edito fusè edidserit. Jam olim Episcopus unà cum suis Presbyteris in gravioribus inprimis negotiis Ecclesiam gubernare solitus est. In præcipuis æquali Episcopus & Presbyteri potestate gaudebant. Sicut verò Episcopi Papæ, ita Presbyteri Episcopo procedente tempore ita subjecti sunt, ut ejus ferè imperio toti subessent. Cæterùm hoc Presbyterorum, imò & aliorum inferiorum Ministrorum, eidem Ecclesiæ necessariorum, eique inservientium Collegium, vocatur Collegium seu Capitulum Canonicorum. Ita ut Canonici Presbyteri sint, qui in officio Presbyteriali ordinarii sunt in illa Ecclesia Ministri: Canonici verò Diaconi, qui in Diaconali Subdiaconi, qui in Subdiaconali. Hi igitur, qui in una Ecclesia titulabantur, seu ad titulum talis Ecclesiæ, ut ipsius proprii Ministri ordinabantur, & titulati in illa Ecclesia & Canonici dicuntur, hoc est, qui juxta Canones seu Regulas Ecclesiasticas, seu pensionem sive annonam, quæ illis solis distribuitur, qui in Collegium Ministrorum cooptantur, sive titulantur (utraque enim & regula, & pensio canonis nomine olim veniebat) cum deputatione ad tale vel tale ministerium, ordinantur. Habéntque hæc Canonicorum Collegia suos Præfectos, qui Præpositi, Decani vel Abbates, juxta Ecclesiarum consuetudinem vocari solent, sub quorum olim munere & officio erat custodia morum & domesticæ disciplinæ, ut canonicos instruerent, & moribus Ecclesiasticis informarent. Totus ille Clerus Canonicus ita in Ecclesia nondum confusa subesse Episcopo debuit, ut ejusdem Cleri opera in universis suæ Diœcesis Ecclesiis ritè regendis & gubernandis uteretur.
units.tr: XLIX. Among the ministers of the Church, the canons or chapter members hold no small place. Aubert Le Mire, in his book de Collegiis Canonicorum, has set out at length the colleges of canons, all of them throughout the Papal world, together with their origin and founders. Long ago the bishop, together with his presbyters, customarily governed the Church, especially in more serious matters. In the principal matters the bishop and the presbyters enjoyed equal authority. But just as bishops came to be subject to the Pope, so in the course of time the presbyters became subject to the bishop, so that they were almost wholly under his command. Moreover, this college of presbyters, and indeed of the other lesser ministers necessary to the same Church and serving it, is called the college or chapter of canons. Thus the canons are presbyters who are the regular ministers of that Church in the presbyteral office, and the canons deacons are those in the diaconal office, and the canons subdeacons those in the subdiaconal office. Those, therefore, who were titled in one church, or ordained to the title of such a church, as its own ministers, are called titulati and Canonici in that church. That is, they are those who, according to the Canones, that is, the ecclesiastical rules, and the allowance or annual pension distributed to those alone who are co-opted or titled into the college of ministers (for both the rule and the pension were formerly called by the name canonis), are ordained with assignment to this or that ministry. These colleges of canons have their own presidents, who are usually called provosts, deans or abbots, according to the custom of the churches. Under their office and duty was formerly the guardianship of morals and domestic discipline, so that they might instruct the canons and form them in ecclesiastical manners. That whole canonical clergy, in the Church not yet confused, was to be subject to the bishop in such a way that he might use the labour of this clergy in ruling and governing all the churches of his diocese duly.

units.la: L. Canonici hodiè in Regulares & Irregulares seu Seculares distinguuntur. Illi Monasticam vitam in claustris degunt, obedientes viro Religioso uni, absque ullo administrandi jure. Hi καὶ ἱερεῖς Canonici dicti sunt Presbyteri, vel Clerici in minoribus ordinibus constituti, qui in Ecclesia Collegiata vel Cathedrali jus Canonis seu præbendæ habent, quorum hodie officium est stallum habere in Choro, ibique horas Canonicas recitare, seu battologicas preculas otiosè demurmurare. Missas conventuales cantare, Officium Mariæ, defunctorum, celebrare, Psalmos pœnitentiales & graduales cantare, suffragium ferre in Capitulo ad Ecclesiam Collegiatam, ejúsque res & bona curanda, Episcopo celebranti assistere, & in Ecclesia Cathedrali unà cum Episcopo diœcesin consulendo regere. Cùm verò totus clerus Ecclesiæ alicujus ei necessarius, eique deputatus, & ab ea nutritus, sustentatúsque sit Canonicus: & Canonici sint omnes Ministri, qui sub regulis Eccle-
units.tr: L. Canons today are divided into Regular and Irregular, or Secular. The former lead a monastic life in cloisters, obedient to one religious superior, with no right of administration at all. The latter, whom the Greeks called καὶ ἱερεῖς (and priests), are presbyters or clerics in minor orders, who hold the right of a canonry or prebend in a collegiate or cathedral church. Their office today is to have a stall in the choir and there recite the canonical hours, or mutter their tedious little prayers without thought; to sing the conventual masses, to celebrate the Office of Mary and of the dead, to sing the penitential and gradual Psalms, to give their vote in the chapter concerning the collegiate church and the care of its affairs and goods, to assist the bishop when he celebrates, and, in the cathedral church, together with the bishop, to govern and consult on the diocese. Yet since every cleric who is necessary to a church, assigned to it, and fed and supported by it, is a canon, and since all ministers who live under the rules of the Church are canons, [...]

units.la: Seculares Ecclesiasticis, Ecclesiæque alimentis vivunt, inanis certè & puerilis illa distinctio Clericorum in Regulares & Irregulares planè est. Canonicus enim idem est quod regularis. Perinde igitur, ac si dicerent: Regularis est vel regularis vel irregularis.
units.tr: Those who live as secular clergy, on the revenues of the Church and its endowments, this empty and childish distinction between regular and irregular clergy is certainly quite absurd. For a canon is the same thing as a regular. It is therefore just as if they said: "A regular is either regular or irregular."

units.la: LI. Sed neutri fortè Regulares & verè Canonici sunt, utpote à Canonicorum vera significatione alienissimi. Canonici enim qui dicuntur Seculares & Irregulares, cùm non amplius vivant sub regulis Ecclesiasticis, neque vitam communem, ut olim, ducant, neque Ministeria Ecclesiastica Presbyteralia, Diaconalia, Subdiaconalia exerceant, sed sola sessione in Choro, dum Divina Officia peraguntur, contenti sint, & ornamenti potiùs externi, ad distributiones lucrandas, quam officii gratia Ecclesiam frequentent, cæterùm à vera vita Clericali & Canonica immane quantum abhorreant, & preculas suas demurmurando, suavitérque cantillando foris Sanctimoniæ Speciem præbentes, domi cuticulam curent, & Bacchanalia vivant, Canonici utique non sunt nisi nomine tenus. Regulares verò qui dicuntur, cùm à subjectione & obedientia Episcopi se subduxerint, & potiùs cum Schismate Ecclesiam contra Ecclesiam erigant, & publicæ Ecclesiæ loci, in quo degunt, nihil sua institutione inserviant, neque Canonici etiam, neque Regulares sunt. Nam si sibi duntaxat & propriæ congregationi, ab Ecclesia illa, in qua habitant, separatæ, sint Regulares, nihil hoc ad illam Ecclesiam facit, atque ita Ecclesiæ nullius Canonici sunt. Quid ergo? Canonici utriusque Ordinis in doctrina officio & moribus degeneres, deformatique non serviunt nisi ornandæ scenæ, & fascinando sub specie religionis, Spiritualis &c. orbi, quò specie tali in devotione Romani Pontificis, à quo solo pendent, constantiùs perfistat: ipsíqueetiam Canonici pinguibus præbendis suis, laxiorique disciplina delibuti, Imperatori illi suo adhæreant fidelius, promtiusque militent.
units.tr: LI. But perhaps neither are truly Regular and truly Canons, being utterly estranged from the true meaning of canon. For those called Secular and Irregular canons, since they no longer live under ecclesiastical rules, nor lead a common life as once they did, nor exercise the presbyteral, diaconal or subdiaconal ministries, but are content with merely sitting in the choir while the divine offices are performed, and attend the church more for the external adornment and for the sake of gaining distributions than for the sake of their office; and who, far from the true clerical and canonical life, mumbling their prayers and singing them sweetly, present an appearance of holiness abroad while at home they tend their own skins and live in Bacchanalian revelry, are assuredly canons only in name. And those called Regular, since they have withdrawn from the subjection and obedience of the bishop, and rather set up a church against the Church with schism, and serve the public church of the place where they dwell not at all by their institution, are neither canons nor regulars. For if they are regular only for themselves and their own congregation, separated from that church in which they dwell, this has nothing to do with that church, and so they are canons of no church. What then? Canons of both orders, degenerate and deformed in teaching, office and morals, serve only to adorn the stage and to bewitch the world under the appearance of religion, spiritual and so on, so that the world may persevere more constantly in devotion to the Roman Pontiff, on whom alone they depend; and the canons themselves, steeped in their fat prebends and looser discipline, cling more faithfully to that emperor of theirs and serve him more readily.

units.la: LII. Ecclesiasticorum adjuvantium ordo subit, & numerati in eodem à Possevino Doctores Theologiæ, Juris Canonici & Catechismi, Prædicatores, Disputatores & Scholastici Ecclesiastici. De Doctoribus Theologiæ, Scholasticæ scilicet & Juris Canonici, quorum illi de hæresi{a} judicant, hi de jure Pontificio disceptant, non infimi inter Mysterii iniquitatis Epoptas, utpote qui cum Divini & Cæsarei juris ac dignitatis defensoribus à Romano lanista, tanquam Retarii cum Myrmillonibus, committuntur, ut scilicet illorum tridente non solum Imperatores per horum latus confodiat, sed etiam verbum ipsum Dei, & Regem Regum Christum de solio deturbet, suisque pedibus subjiciat, dicere nihil attinet. Cum Theologiam ipsam Scholasticam Majestati verbi Divini, & Jus Canonicum Majestati Juris Cæsarei opprimendæ inducta esse, Historia Papatus ss. xcv. xcvj. xcvij. xcviij. probaverit, quid de Doctoribus ejusmodi judicandum sit, ultro liquet. Doctores Catechismi, seu Catechistæ, omnes pastores esse debent, si Tridentini Concilii decretis stare voluerint. Scholastici Ecclesiastici Ludimagistri sunt, qui omnes aut plerique, saltem in pagis, sunt æditui, cantores, celebrationum Missaticarum ministri. Scholastici vero capitulares præsunt scholis capituli; atque olim etiam capitulares Theologiam docere consueverunt. Inter adjuvantes hosce sunt Doctores illi Seraphici, illuminatissimi, veterani, veteratores, Novatorum flagella, hæreticorum scopuli, quia omnia Babylònici Mysterii μυστηρια, & scorti illius ulcera plusquàm Chironia, meretricio purpuriso illinere, ac vel crassissimas insipidissimasque fabulas soporifero Sophisticesucco, velut adspersa papavere & sesamo condire nôrunt.
units.tr: LII. Next comes the order of the assisting clergy, which Possevino lists as Doctores Theologiæ, Juris Canonici & Catechismi, Prædicatores, Disputatores & Scholastici Ecclesiastici. Concerning the teachers of theology, that is, the scholastic theologians, and of canon law, of whom the former judge heresies and the latter dispute about Papal law, they are not the lowest among the initiates of the mystery of iniquity. They are matched, like retiarii against myrmillones, by the Roman gladiator against the defenders of divine and imperial right and dignity, so that with their trident he not only pierces the emperors through the side, but also hurls from the throne the very Word of God and Christ, King of kings, and places him under his feet. There is no need to say more. Since the Papal history at pages 95, 96, 97 and 98 has proved that scholastic theology itself was introduced to oppress the majesty of the divine Word, and canon law to oppress the majesty of imperial law, it is plain of its own accord what should be judged of teachers of this kind. The teachers of the Catechismi, or Catechistæ, ought all to be ministers, if they wish to abide by the decrees of the Council of Trent. The Scholastici Ecclesiastici are schoolmasters, who all or most of them, at least in the villages, are sacristans, cantors, and ministers of the mass celebrations. The Scholastici vero capitulares preside over the chapter schools; and formerly the chapter members were also accustomed to teach theology. Among these assisting persons are those seraphic, most enlightened doctors, veterans, old campaigners, scourges of the innovators, rocks against heretics, who know how to smear all the mysteries of Babylon's mystery and the ulcers of that harlot, more than Chironian, with harlot's purple, and how to season even the thickest and most insipid fables with a soporific sophistic juice, as if sprinkled with poppy and sesame.

units.la: LIII. Supersunt Ecclesiastici supererogantes, seu Monachi, pars non infima Civitatis magnæ Babylonicæ, qui delecta vita solitaria contemplativa, certisque votis ad cœlibatum, hoc est, matrimonii ejurationem, paupertatem, hoc est, proprietatum abdicationem, & obedientiam, hoc est, servitutem religiosam, certo homini cuipiam devotam obstricto, supererogare, hoc est, plus Deo dare atque solvere, quàm lex ejus postulat, vel ipsi dare atque solvere tenentur, se, detestanda, si qua alia est, hypocrisi, simulant. Bellarminus de Monach. cap. 2. Monachatum definit statum hominum ad perfectionem Christianam per paupertatis, continentiæ & obedientiæ vota tendentium. Contra Azorius Instit. Monach. lib. ix. 5. q. 1. eundem definit, statum hominum perfectorum sub certis mandatis & regulis Deo famulantium. Bellarminus igitur eos ad perfectionem tendere, Azorius perfectionem attigisse, innuunt. Ille perfectionem solis Episcopis deputat, Monachis vero conatum assequendæ ejusdem concedit: hic in perfectorum Chorum Monachos cooptat. Perfectionem Euangelicam appellant utrique, quæ dum Euangelium prædicatur in mundo, non Regni Christi proprie, sed mundi & Antichristi perfectio est. Perfectos PseudoClericos, & cum Monachis veteribus comparatos, PseudoMonachos perfectos qui dixit, perfectionem illorum recte definivit.
units.tr: LIII. There remain the supererogating ecclesiastics, or monks, no small part of the great Babylonian city. Having chosen a solitary and contemplative life, and bound by set vows to celibacy (that is, renunciation of marriage), poverty (that is, giving up property), and obedience (that is, religious servitude devoted to a certain man to whom they are bound), they pretend to supererogate, that is, to give and pay God more than his law requires, or more than they are bound to give and pay him, with whatever detestable hypocrisy there is. Bellarmine, de Monach. cap. 2., defines monasticism as a state of men tending to Christian perfection by the vows of poverty, continence and obedience. Against him, Azorius, Instit. Monach. lib. ix. 5. q. 1., defines it as a state of perfect men serving God under certain commands and rules. So Bellarmine suggests that monks tend toward perfection, while Azorius suggests that they have attained it. The former assigns perfection only to bishops and grants monks the effort to reach it; the latter enrolls monks in the choir of the perfect. Both call it evangelical perfection, which, while the Gospel is preached in the world, is not properly the perfection of Christ's kingdom but of the world and of Antichrist. The man who called them pseudo-clerics, perfect, and, compared with the old monks, perfect pseudo-monks, rightly defined their perfection.

units.la: LIV. Et olim quidem institutum Monachorum privato hominum studio, necessitate temporum, privata pietate ac devotione, non ulla publica institutione emersit. Christus ad Monachatum neminem vocavit: Apostoli Monachum nullum fecerunt: Episcopi & Ecclesia vetus Monachalem vitam nemini unquam præscripserunt. Quid ergo? Ex vita Apostolica, qualem Apostoli, Paulus inprimis, & fideles primitivæ Ecclesiæ, magno fervore Spiritus duxerunt, privati homines nonnulli privato studio, & temporum necessitate invitati, non ulla lege, non ullo præcepto, sed liberè, sponte exempla sumpserunt, ut cælibes viverent, possessiones, certosque reditus nullos haberent, vel in usum pauperum eos distribuerent, ipsi verò relictis omnibus, cum Paulo propriis manibus laborantes, victum sibi compararent; atque de cætero pietatis & pœnitentiæ operibus vacantes, privatam in solitudine vitam degerent. Et Cassianus quidem Collát. 18. cap. 4. tria in Ægypto genera Monachorum facit, puta Cœnobitarum, qui in congregatione pariter consistentes, unius senioris judicio gubernabantur: Anachoretarum qui in Cœnobiis priùs instituti, jamque in actuali conversatione perfecti solitudinis secreta elegère: & Sarabaitarum, qui Ægyptiacæ linguæ proprietate ita dicti, non tam Apostolorum & fidelium primitivæ Ecclesiæ, quàm Ananiæ & Saphiræ exemplum secuti, Monasticam vitam simulantes, à Cœnobiis segreges terrenis & propriis necessitatibus inhiabant, & nomine Monachorum se absque ulla pietatis, studiorum, pœnitentiæ æmulatione, venditabant.
units.tr: LIV. Indeed, in former times the institution of monks arose from private zeal of men, from the necessity of the times, and from private piety and devotion, not from any public institution. Christ called no one to monasticism; the Apostles made no monk; bishops and the ancient Church never prescribed the monastic life to anyone. What then? From the apostolic life, such as the Apostles, Paul above all, and the faithful of the primitive Church lived with great fervour of the Spirit, some private men, moved by private zeal and by the necessity of the times, took up examples freely and of their own accord, not by any law or command: they lived unmarried, had no possessions or fixed incomes, or distributed them for the use of the poor; and they themselves, having left everything, supported themselves by working with their own hands, as Paul did; and thereafter, devoted to works of piety and repentance, they lived a private life in solitude. Cassian, Collat. 18. cap. 4., indeed distinguishes three kinds of monks in Egypt: the Cenobites, who lived together in one community and were governed by the judgment of a single elder; the Anchorites, who, having first been trained in the cenobia and now perfected in their way of life, chose the secrecy of solitude; and the Sarabaites, so called from a peculiarity of the Egyptian language, who followed not so much the example of the Apostles and the primitive faithful as that of Ananias and Sapphira. Feigning the monastic life, they separated themselves from the cenobia, coveted earthly and personal necessities, and passed themselves off as monks without any emulation of piety, learning, or repentance.

units.la: LV. Cum veteribus Monachis sanioribus Cœnobitis & Anachoretis nihil Pontificii Monachi, malæ bellux & ventres pigri, commune habent. Illorum enim vita Monastica non erat nisi privata secessio ad pœnitentiam, hominum de cætero laicorum, non tam docentium quàm plangentium, uti Hieronymus adversus Vigilantium loquitur. Hi in ordine ecclesiastico clerico censeri volunt. Illi consummati Monachi censebantur, antequam se ulla professione externa ulli manciparent. Hi sine professione publica & votorum solennitate Monachi non censentur. Illorum ordines neque à Papa, neque à quoquam alio confirmabantur. Horum ordines non confirmati nullius valoris habentur. Illi neque proprias, neque communes facultates, divitias & latí& latifundia possidebant, sed singuli manuum suarum labore victum quaesitabant. Hi bona alieno sudore parata abliguriunt. Illi, S. Augustino teste, a vero Monachismo omnem rigidam exactionem earum rerum, quae in verbo Divino liberè relinquuntur, removebant. Hi in vestitu, victu, aliisque ejusmodi rebus adiaphoris proram puppimque Monachatus locant. Illorum Monachatus, eodem Augustino teste, nihil aliud erat quàm adjumentum ossiciorum pietatis, quae Christianis in universum omnibus commendantur. Hi ab universo Ecclesiae corpore se separantes, diversam salutis viam calcant. Illi vitam Monasticam, quando ita libuit, deserere poterant. Hi sine piaculo deserere non possunt. Illi, quod rei caput est, suam à vita communi secessionem verae & salvificae fidei, & charitati erga proximum inaedificabant. Hi utriusque naufragium pridem fecerunt, religionémque factitiam, Pontificis R. libidini addictam adoptárunt, adeò quidem ut Monasteria doctrinarum usibus, veraeque fidei olim destinata, jam non sint aliud, quàm vulpecularum, ranarum, locustarum latibula, & nidi idololatrici.
units.tr: LV. The Pontifical monks, bad company and lazy bellies, have nothing in common with the sounder monks of old, the Cenobites and Anchorites. For their monastic life was nothing but a private withdrawal for repentance, being otherwise laymen, not so much teaching as lamenting, as Jerome says against Vigilantius. The latter want to be counted in the clerical order; the former were regarded as monks already before they bound themselves by any outward profession. The latter are not counted as monks without public profession and the solemnity of vows; the orders of the former were confirmed neither by the Pope nor by anyone else; the orders of the latter, if unconfirmed, are held to be of no value. The former possessed neither private nor common resources, riches or great estates, but each sought his living by the labour of his own hands; the latter guzzle goods prepared by the sweat of others. The former, as witnessed by Augustine, removed from true monasticism all rigid exaction of those things which are left free in the Divine Word; the latter set the prow and stern of monasticism in clothing, food, and other such indifferent matters. The monasticism of the former, again as Augustine witnesses, was nothing other than a help to the duties of piety, which are commended to all Christians in general; the latter, separating themselves from the whole body of the Church, tread a different way of salvation. The former could abandon the monastic life whenever it pleased them; the latter cannot abandon it without sin. The former, which is the heart of the matter, built their separation from common life upon true and saving faith and charity toward neighbour; the latter have long since made shipwreck of both and have adopted a manufactured religion, given over to the lust of the Roman Pontiff, so much so that the monasteries, once destined for the uses of teaching and of true faith, are now nothing but dens of foxes, frogs, and locusts, and nests of idolatry.

units.la: LVI. Non minus igitur cucullati Pontificii à veteribus illis Monachis tum quoad professionem ipsam, tum quoad fidei & Charitatis exercitia, quàm Simiae ab hominibus differunt. Meritóque Polydorus Vergilius Hist. Angl. lib. vj. scribit, incredibile dictu, quantum à Majoribus suis Monachi hodierni degeneraverint. Nec minore ratione Marcus Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccles. lib. ÿ. 12.77. de Pontificiis Monachis pronuntiat, eos nec cum Coenobitis, nec cum Anachoretis veteribus, sed potius cum iis, quos Sarabaitas Cassianus, aliique vocant, congruere. Si nostri Minorita, inquit, (non quis, sed quid dixerit, expendatur) Dominicani, Carmelita, Servita, Minimita, ac similes, non sunt ipsissimi Sarabaitae (bonos, si quis est inter ipsos verus Cœnobita excipio) quinam erunt, aut jam diu fuerunt. Etiam Benedictinos quisnam non videt fermè plenissimè jam diu in veros Sarabaitas degenerasse? Ubi summa paupertas eorum etiam in communi? Ubi labores manuum? Ubi austeritas victús & amictús? Quid Monachis cum Clericatu? Quid cum tot deliciis? Hi in curribus & equis, Prisci verò in nomine Domini Dei nostri invocarunt. Et lib. ix. 5.72. hodiernos Monachos cum veteribus comparatos vocat Hermophroditos Religiosos Mendicantes, hoc est, neque verè Clericos, neque veros Monachos, sed utrumque imperfectè, ac persectè Pseudo-clericos, & Pseudo-monachos. Quòd si M. A. de Dominis suspecta est authoritas, Bernhardi Claraevallensis, Apolog. ad Guilh. Abb. Monachos Cluniacenses, aliósque vivis coloribus depingentis, & eorundem jam suo tempore institutA, ceremonias & mores perditos à veterum Monachorum institutis moribúsque integris plurimùm disparantis, potior esto. Sed omni exceptione majus Spiritus S. Emblema, Monachos verè Pontificios Apoc. ix. 3. &c. cum locustis ex tartarei putei fumo natis, contendentis valeat. Hæ densissimis agminibus omnia pervolitantes, lucem Euangelii & solis justitiæ obscurantes, non gramen aut herbas lædentes (neque enim fœno Monachi pascuntur) sed hominibus insidiantes, eósque mirificis præstigiis effascinatos miserè torquentes cruciantésque, similes equis ad prælium paratis, coronas in capite gestantes, faciem humanam ostentantes, capillis mulieribus blandientes, dentibus leoninis minantes, loricis ferreis armati, sonitu alarum terrentes, caudis scorpionum insidiantes &c. inducuntur. Quibus typis haud dubiè Monachorum (quorum imaginem etiam in externo corpore, uti ἀντίψυχα demonstrat, locustæ gerunt) alacritas & ferocia ad nocendum; Regnum, quod Monachi in vertice rasi, & in circulum attonsi passim in mundo obtinent; astus & veteratoriæ artes, quibus in rebus gerendis utuntur; ξενηλοχίαι & blanditiarum lenocinia, quibus in animos hominum irrepunt, nec non πανοολογίαι & απροσωπολοίς μύθοι, quibus tanquam Origano falsorum dogmatum putria salsamenta condiunt; ferina in nocendo sævitia, & indomitum robur; hypocriticæ Sanctimoniæ vis, & Romanorum diplomatum, quibus Monachi, tanquam ἱερὰ κρυπτά commendantur, authoritas; invicta pertinacia, potentissimorum Orbis Principum viribus subnixa; diræ & anathematum fulmina, quorum strepitu & fragore multi tantum non exanimantur; superstitiosarum opinionum virus, quod incautis instillant; aliáque ejusmodi adumbrantur.
units.tr: LVI. The Pontifical hooded men therefore differ from those old monks no less than apes differ from men, both in their profession itself and in the exercise of faith and charity. And rightly Polydore Vergil, Hist. Angl. lib. vj., writes that it is incredible to say how far the monks of today have degenerated from their forefathers. With no less reason Marcus Antonius de Dominis, de Rep. Eccles. lib. v. 12, 77, pronounces about the Pontifical monks that they agree neither with the old Cenobites nor with the Anchorites, but rather with those whom Cassian and others call Sarabaites. "If our Minorites," he says (weigh not who but what was said), "Dominicans, Carmelites, Servites, Minims, and the like, are not the very Sarabaites (I except the good ones, if any true Cenobite is among them), who else will they be, or who have they been for a long time? Who does not see that the Benedictines too have for the most part long since degenerated into true Sarabaites? Where is their extreme poverty, even in common? Where their labour of hands? Where the austerity of food and clothing? What have monks to do with the clergy? What with so many delicacies? These men ride in carriages and on horses; the ancients invoked the name of the Lord our God." And in book ix, 5, 72, he calls the monks of today, compared with the old, "religious hermaphrodites, mendicants," that is, neither truly clerics nor true monks, but imperfectly and perfectly pseudo-clerics and pseudo-monks. But if the authority of M. A. de Dominis is suspect, let the authority of Bernard of Clairvaux, Apolog. ad Guilh. Abb., be preferred, who depicts in lively colours the Cluniac monks and others, whose ceremonies and manners in his own time had been lost and differed greatly from the integrity of the institutions and customs of the old monks. But more weighty than any exception is the emblem of the Holy Spirit, Apoc. ix. 3, etc., which holds that the monks truly Pontifical are the locusts born from the smoke of the Tartarean pit. These, swarming in very dense troops over everything, darken the light of the Gospel and the sun of righteousness; they do not harm the grass or herbs (for monks do not feed on hay), but lie in wait for men, miserably tormenting and torturing those bewitched by wonderful illusions. They are depicted as like horses prepared for battle, wearing crowns on their heads, showing human faces, with hair like women's, threatening with lion's teeth, armed with iron breastplates, terrifying with the sound of their wings, and lying in wait with scorpions' tails, and so on. Doubtless these figures shadow forth the eagerness and ferocity of the monks to do harm (the locusts also bear the image of the monks in their outward body, as the antipsychon shows) [ἀντίψυχα]; the kingdom which monks hold throughout the world, shaven at the crown and tonsured in a circle; the cunning and crafty arts they use in carrying out their affairs; their hospitality-seeking [ξενηλοχίαι] and the seductive flattery by which they creep into men's minds; and also their empty talk [πανοολογίαι] and fables without face or character [απροσωπολοίς μύθοι], with which they season the rotten salt-meats of false doctrines as with oregano; their savage cruelty in harming and their untamed strength; the force of hypocritical sanctity and the authority of Roman decrees, by which the monks are commended as sacred secrets [ἱερὰ κρυπτά]; their invincible obstinacy, supported by the might of the most powerful princes of the world; the dire thunderbolts of anathemas, at whose noise and crash many are almost struck dead; the poison of superstitious opinions, which they instil into the unwary; and other such things are foreshadowed.

units.la: LVII.
