Si igitur, quod res est, dicere licet, Monachatus ille Pontificius, seu Sarabaiticus, religionis & pietatis speciem mentitus, non tam religiosum institutum est, quàm vaframentum politicum, seu potiùs Babylonicum, quo Papa Regnum suum potenter tuetur. Etenim primò Ordinum beneficio populum suum in obedientia continet, & αμπαοςία sua securius interea fruitur. Exceptis paucis bonis viris, quos superstitio dementavit, ut animarum suarum saluti ita consuli posse, perperam confidant: plerisque alia omnia quàm religionis cura, Monachos faciunt. Alii enim vi in Monasteria detruduntur, vel sponte etiam ad ea concedunt, ut vel familiarum dignitas conservetur, & patrimonia ac hæreditates inter paucos distributæ lautiores, opimioréfque existant, vel neccessaria ad victum suppetant, vel facultas sit otio liberalius indulgendi, & fucorum ad instar, apum industria quæsitum paratúmque mel absumendi. Imperator Justinianus Novella 133. merito inter alia Monasticam vitam Imperio utilem esse, ad primum scilicet finem illum respiciens, asserit. Alios desperatio ad subeunda Monasteria, ceu asylà quædam compellit, sive scelerum patratorum pœnam justam reveritos, sive obæratos, foro cedere coactos, in matrimoniis infelices, hominibus exosos, honorum, divitiarum, fortunæ spe magnisque ausis fructratos. Qui igitur occasionem tantam non præstat tantum, sed etiam miræ sanctitatis specie exornat, splendidisque insuper promotionis in hoc seculo, exîstimationisque singularis, nec non eminentioris beatitudinis, aureolarúmque nescio quarum in Cœlo, promissionibus mactat, is haud dubiè populum, veræ inprimis masculæque pietatis & virtutis exsortem, favent-em, obsequentémque sortitur. Illi vicissim, quibus commoda hæc aspirant, pro Domini & patroni adeò benigni prospicientisque honore, fortuna, authoritate, adversus quosvis eam abnuentes in tuto collocanda, inaustum, intentatúmque nihil relinquunt. Habet igitur sic Pontifex incredibili multitudine pectora, linguas, calamos, manus, ad tuendam sustinendámque dominationem suam armatos, ausuros quidvis, si occasio ferat, pro suggestu adversus hostes Papæ declamando, in familias subrependo eásque seu eloquentiæ fuco & πσευδολογία singulari, seu sanctitatis admirabili specie in Papatu confirmando; vel ad eundem seducendo, scriptis Pontificiam authoritatem impudentissimè propugnando; ad extremos Indos & Garamantas Proselythorum lucrifaciendorum gratia cursitando; subditos adversus Principes minùs Papæ addictos, vel eidem infensos concitando; eorundémque jugulum nefariè appetendo; Principes Papæ addictos adversus subditos eidem non addictos inflammando; & modò Principes, modò subditos, prout conducere videtur, omni juramentorum fide exsolvendo. Qua in militia omnes equidem Ordines mirum quantum exercitati sunt; præ cæteris tamen Jesuitæ, Mortalium omnium nequissi-mi, & mi, & ad omne genus fraudum, criminúmque instruſtiſsimi, promtiſſimique, uti abundè paſſim Hiſtoria Papatus confirmat.
units.tr: LVII. If, then, it is fair to say what is the case, this Papal monasticism, or Sarabaitic kind, which wears the mask of religion and piety, is not so much a religious institution as a political trick, or rather a Babylonian one, by which the Pope powerfully defends his kingdom. For firstly, by means of the Orders he keeps his people in obedience, and meanwhile enjoys his ampaosia [αμπαοςία] more securely. Apart from a few good men, whom superstition has driven out of their minds so that they wrongly trust their souls' salvation can be secured this way, most make themselves monks for reasons having nothing to do with concern for religion. Some are forced into the monasteries by violence; others go willingly, either so that the dignity of their families may be kept and the patrimonies and inheritances, shared among a few, may stay more splendid and wealthy, or because they need food, or because they wish to indulge in leisure more freely and, like drones, consume the honey that others have gathered and prepared by their industry. The Emperor Justinian, in Novel 133, rightly asserts among other things that monastic life is useful to the empire, looking surely to that first end. Others, driven by despair, go into the monasteries as into a kind of refuge: some fearing the just punishment of crimes committed, some debtors forced to answer in court, the unhappy in marriage, hated by men, disappointed in hopes of honours, wealth and fortune, and in bold enterprises. Therefore whoever not only offers such an opportunity but also adorns it with the appearance of wonderful holiness, and feeds them with promises of splendid advancement in this age, singular esteem, a higher blessedness, and I know not what golden crowns in heaven, will undoubtedly gain a people lacking true and manly piety and virtue, one that is favourable and obsequious. Those in turn to whom these advantages come, out of honour to such a kindly and provident lord and patron, leave nothing untried or unattempted to place him in safety, with wealth, fortune and authority, against anyone who refuses him that. So the Pontiff has hearts, tongues, pens and hands in incredible numbers, armed to defend and sustain his dominion, ready to dare anything if occasion offers: declaiming from the pulpit against the enemies of the Pope; creeping into families and confirming them in Papacy, either by the varnish of eloquence and singular pseudologia [ψευδολογία], or by the admirable appearance of holiness; or seducing them to the same by impudently defending Papal authority in writings; running about to the farthest Indians and Garamantes to win proselytes; stirring up subjects against princes less devoted to the Pope or hostile to him, and wickedly seeking their throats; inflaming princes devoted to the Pope against subjects who are not; and releasing now princes, now subjects, from every bond of oaths, as seems expedient. In this warfare all the Orders have indeed been wonderfully practised, but beyond the rest the Jesuits, the most wicked of all mortals, and most thoroughly trained and ready for every kind of fraud and crime, as the history of the Papacy everywhere amply confirms.

units.la: LVIII. Non parum Monachorum iſthanc servitutem, & ad tuendam Pontificiam dominationem ſtudia, eorundem à potestate Epiſcoporum exemptio auxit.
units.tr: LVIII. The monks' servitude, and their zeal for defending Papal dominion, have been not a little increased by their exemption from the power of the bishops.

units.la: Nam olim quidem eos Episcopis subjectos fuisse ἀνεξαγώνιον est. Ut vero eos dominationis suæ instrumenta liberiora promtioráque Papa haberet, atque ipsi quoque ampliori libertate fruerentur, tantóque plus haberent, quod imputarent Domino suo, eos ab Episcoporum jurisdictione eximere, sibique mancipare totos collibuit. Ita paulatim Episcoporum, rectorum suorum potestate exiverunt, eóque res devenit, ut de tollendis, vel moderandis saltem eorum exemptionibus, & illis si non in solidum, ex parte saltem Episcopis subjiciendis, in Tridentino Concilio deliberatio suscipieretur. Sed Ordinum Generales, & Theologi Monachi plerique consilio huic tumultuantes gravissimè intercesserunt; usi eo prætextu, si Monasteria Ordinariis subjiciantur, fore ut protinus deformentur. Namque ipsos, utpote vitæ Regularis, & severitatis disciplinæ, quo id genus vitæ conservetur, rudes, omnia temerè permisturos. Episcopi regerebant, privilegium semper esse cum detrimento, & prævaricatione legis, revocationem verò esse quidpiam favorabile, quo negotia ad suam naturam revertantur. Ordinum patroni contra disserebant, exemptionem suam adeò antiquam esse, támque firma præscriptione niti, ut non amplius privilegium, sed lex communis appellari posset. Eo tempore, quo Episcopis adhuc subjecti fuerint, disciplinam Ecclesiasticam in ipsis, & eorum Canonicis adeò amussitatam & severam fuisse, ut in omnes inspectio iis merito tributa fuerit. Si igitur antiquitatem restitutam velint, iis quoque ad antiquos mores revertendum esse. Favebant, ita disceptationis ejus testis S. Polanus Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. viij. scribit, Regularibus Oratores, etiam Legati utilitatibus Curiæ R. addicti, quæ egregio instrumento orbata fuisset, nisi ab ea sola (Monachorum Ordines) penderent. Durante per aliquot dies ea contentione, sensim ea remisit, propterea quòd (uti idem narrat) qui eam excitárunt Episcopi, majorem in dies in ea re difficultatem perspiciebant.
units.tr: For formerly it is indisputable [ἀνεξαγώνιον] that they were subject to the bishops. But so that the Pope might have them as freer and readier instruments of his dominion, and so that they themselves might enjoy greater liberty and have so much more to owe their Lord, he chose to take them out of the jurisdiction of the bishops and bind them wholly to himself. Thus by degrees they departed from the power of the bishops, their rulers, and matters came to such a point that at the Council of Trent a deliberation was undertaken on abolishing, or at least moderating, their exemptions, and on subjecting them to the bishops, if not wholly, at least in part. But the Generals of the Orders and most of the monk theologians, stirring up uproar against this plan, intervened most vigorously, using the pretext that if the monasteries were made subject to the ordinaries, they would at once be ruined. For the bishops, they said, being unpractised in the regular life and in the strict discipline by which that kind of life is preserved, would throw everything into confusion. The bishops replied that a privilege is always to the detriment and violation of law, whereas revocation is something favourable, by which affairs return to their own nature. The patrons of the Orders argued on the contrary that their exemption was so ancient and rested on so firm a prescription that it could no longer be called a privilege but common law. At the time when they were still subject to the bishops, ecclesiastical discipline among them and their canons was so exact and severe that inspection was rightly granted them over everyone. If therefore they wish antiquity restored, they too ought to return to the ancient morals. The Regular orators, and even the legates, devoted to the interests of the Roman Court, favoured them, as S. Polanus, in Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. viii, writes, which would have been deprived of an excellent instrument, unless it depended on that alone (the Orders of monks). While this contention lasted for some days, it gradually slackened, because (as the same writer relates) the bishops who had stirred it up saw greater difficulty in the matter day by day.

units.la: LIX. Secundò non parum etiam emolumenti ad Pontificem ex tot Monachorum Cælibatu redundat. Nam in universum quidem Cælibatus Clericorum & Pontificiæ dominationis arcanum in ipso quoque Tridentino Concilio Cardinalis Rodolphus Pius Carpensis apud eundem S. Polanum Lib. v. his verbis detexit: Si connubia Sacerdotibus permittantur, id inde secuturum, ut familiam, uxores & liberos alentes, ad Principis quisque sui obedientiam respiciens, Pontificis obsequium detrectet: ut liberorum Charitas ab officio ad omnem Ecclesiæ fraudem ac præjudicium abducat: ut de Sacerdotiis in familias hereditario jure asciscendis cogitent, ut denique intra breve tempus Sedes Apostolica Romanæ Urbis cancellos non ascendat. Ante institutum Cœlibatum Sedem Romanam nullum ex aliis civitatibus ac regionibus fructum percepisse; per hunc adeptum dominatum omnium Sacerdotiorum, quæ matrimonium exiguo tempore illi eriperet. Saltem inde liquet, Monachorum etiam Cœlibum tot myriadas Pontifici adlubescere, ne uxorum & liberorum charitas ab obedientia Papæ ad Principum Evergetarum obsequia flectat.
units.tr: LIX. Secondly, no small advantage also accrues to the Pontiff from the celibacy of so many monks. For the secret of clerical celibacy and of Papal dominion in general was disclosed, in the Council of Trent itself, by Cardinal Rudolf Pius of Carpi, in the same S. Polanus, lib. v, in these words: If marriages were permitted to priests, the following would result: each, supporting a household, wife and children, would look to the obedience of his own prince and refuse obedience to the Pope; the love of children would draw him from duty into every kind of fraud and harm to the Church; they would think of acquiring priesthoods for their families by hereditary right; and finally, within a short time, the Apostolic See would not rise beyond the walls of the City of Rome. Before celibacy was instituted, the Roman See received no fruit from other cities and regions; through this it obtained dominion over all priesthoods, which marriage would snatch from it in a short time. From this at least it is clear that the celibacy of so many myriads of monks is pleasing to the Pontiff, lest the love of wives and children turn from obedience to the Pope to the service of princes who are benefactors.

units.la: LX. Tertiò ex Monachorum numerosis Ordinibus Romana Curia non parum ditatur. Id quoque arcanum Gallorum post Concilium Tridentinum finitum querela apud eundem Historicum lib. viij. his verbis refert: Hoc perpetuum, petuum petuum, inquiebant illi, Curiæ Romanæ artificium est, bona Secularibus erepta primò ad Clerum, dein etiam Romam pertrahere. Id scilicet primò satagunt, ut prætextu voti paupertatis Monachi exî-stimationem acquirant, quasi nullam rem temporalem intueantur, sed omnia charitatis causa faciant in populi servitutem. Post, existimatione parta, Curia cum ipsis de voto dispensat, unde facilè ditescunt. Cúmque bene opulenta facta sunt Monasteria, demandantur in commendam, & id omne denique in Curiam R. affluit. De quibus commendis, quàs Romana Curia, famelicis ac voracissimis Harpyis referta, fovet, in loco Σ. Θ plura.
units.tr: LX. Thirdly, the Roman Curia is not a little enriched by the numerous Orders of monks. The Frenchmen's complaint after the Council of Trent was finished also reports this secret, in the same historian, lib. viii, in these words: This is the perpetual artifice of the Roman Curia, they said, to draw goods snatched from the laity first to the clergy, and then also to Rome. They take care first that monks, under the pretext of the vow of poverty, acquire esteem, as if they regarded no temporal thing but did everything for the sake of charity, to the enslavement of the people. Afterwards, once esteem is won, the Curia dispenses them from the vow, whereby they easily grow rich. And when the monasteries have become very wealthy, they are handed over in commendam, and all of it at last flows into the Roman Curia. Concerning these commendams, which the Roman Curia, stuffed with famished and most voracious Harpies, cherishes, more in the place Σ. Θ.

units.la: LXI. Quartò denique vel sola Monachorum innumerabilis multitudo Pontifici R. eum usum præstare potest, ut instructissimis eorum exercitibus si necessitas, acre telum, postulet, Regnum suum tueri, & adversus quosvis vindicare valeat. Non obstabunt vota, quorum relaxandorum Papa sibi potestatem vendicat. Non exercitationis militaris defectus, quia, experientia teste, passim in Civilibus bellis religionis causa exortis ipsi primipili fuerunt, strenuámque Pontificiis partibus pugnando, cædendo, operam navárunt; atque insuper & ingenio & sævitia, si Domini sui causam agi cognoverint, plurimum valent. Non locorum, quibus distracti sunt, intervalla, quia Papa Ordinum Generales secum perpetim Romæ habet, atque illi per suos Ordinum Provinciales, hi per Priores & Abbates expeditissimè quidvis perficiunt, neque parùm existimatio sanctitatis, qua apud populum pollent promovendis quibusvis consiliis conducunt. Si vel in sola Italia, ubi plus quàm decem centena millia Monachorum nomine veniunt, delectum eorum, qui bello idonei sunt, agi contingeret, quantum exercitum, sacrum scilicet, conflari intra breve tempus posse, putabimus? Sabellico Ennead. ix. lib. ix. Lib. ix. teste, Magistri Ordinis Minoritarum Pio Pontifici, expeditionem in Turcas paranti, ex sola Minoritarum familia triginta millia bellatorum, qui bellica munia gnaviter obire possint, nihil sacrorum interpellato cultu, pollicitus est.
units.tr: LXI. Fourthly, finally, the innumerable multitude of monks alone can give the Roman Pontiff this advantage: that if necessity calls for a sharp weapon, he may be able to defend his kingdom with their well-equipped armies and avenge himself on anyone. Vows will not stand in the way, since the Pope claims for himself the power to relax them. A lack of military training is no obstacle, since, as experience bears witness, they have everywhere been the front-line men in civil wars arising from religion, and have strenuously served the Papal side by fighting, slaughtering and striving; and moreover, both in cleverness and in savagery, they are very powerful when they perceive their Lord's cause to be at stake. Distance between the places where they are scattered is no obstacle, since the Pope always has the Generals of the Orders with him at Rome, and these, through their Provincials, and the Provincials through the Priors and Abbots, carry out whatever you like most expeditiously; nor does the reputation for holiness which they enjoy among the people count for little in advancing whatever plans. If the levy of those fit for war were carried out in Italy alone, where more than a million monks are counted, how great an army, namely a sacred one, do we think could be assembled in a short time? According to Sabellicus, Ennead. ix, lib. ix, the Master of the Order of Minorites promised Pope Pius, who was preparing an expedition against the Turks, thirty thousand warriors from the Minorite family alone, who could bravely perform military duties, without any interruption of the sacred worship.

units.la: LXII. Ut verò Civitatis, Babylonicæ magnitudo, vel Cænobitæ verò inter se familias instituunt, communitatem alunt, & in locis quidem plerumque commodissimis amoenissimisque, subinde etiam magnificentia cum Regum palatiis certantibus.
units.tr: LXII. As for the greatness of the Babylonian city, the cenobites set up households among themselves and maintain a common life, usually in the most convenient and pleasant places, and sometimes with a magnificence that rivals royal palaces.

units.la: LXIII. Monasticæ vitæ præcipua basis sunt regulæ, quæ in universum fere quatuor sunt, puta Basilii, Augustini, Benedicti, & Francisci. Paucisque hactenus Ordines reperti sunt, Carthusienses puta, Jesuitæ, & nonnulli alii, qui juxta unam harum regularum, tametsi diversissima ratione, vitæ suæ Monasticæ semitam non terant, quod Azorius Instit. Moral. xiv. 11. Bellarminus de Mon. lib. v. 3. Augustinus Barbosa in Collect. Bullarii, aliique non diffentur.
units.tr: LXIII. The chief foundations of monastic life are the rules, of which there are roughly four: those of Basil, Augustine, Benedict and Francis. Few orders have so far been found outside these, such as the Carthusians, the Jesuits and some others, which, though in very different ways, do not tread the path of monastic life according to one of these rules. Azorius (Instit. Moral. xiv. 11), Bellarmine (de Mon. lib. v. 3), Augustinus Barbosa (in Collect. Bullarii) and others do not dispute this.

units.la: LXIV. Ratione modi acquirendi victus in Mendicantes, & Non Mendicantes dispescuntur. Mendicantium quatuor perhibentur genera, Augustinienses, Praedicatores, Carmelitae, & Minoritae, seu Franciscani. Cùm verò juxta Concilii Tridentini decretum Sess xxv. de Regul. cap. 3. omnibus Monasteriis, exceptis Franciscì fratribus Capucinis & Minoribus de observantia, bona immobilia possidere liceat, solos Capucinos & Minores de observantia propriè Mendicantes esse, colligitur. Neque tamen minus quatuor illi ordines Mendicantium nomine, usitata inter illos distinctione pauperta-ris Altissimae, Mediae, & Infimae veniunt. Ad Augustinienfem referuntur Eremitae discalceati S. Augustini, Societates corrigiarum, seu Tertiarii, Congregationes Poenitentiae Jesu Christi, seu Saccitae, item de Britinis, Lombardiae, Illyricianae, S. Salvatoris Carbonaria, Perufina, alias S. Mariae de populo, Genuensis seu S. Mariae de consolatione, Montis Ortoni, Apuliae, seu Dulceti, S. Mariae de Calorito, S. Antonii in monte Vulturno, Servi beatae Mariae, Brigidiani, Jesuati, Canonici S. Gregorii, Montolivetenses, Hieronymitani Eremitae, Scopetini, Johannis Hierosolymitani, seu Ferrieri, Fratres Petri Confessoris de Mogella, Sepulchritae, seu Fratres Dominici sepulchri, Gilbertini, Victoriani, Coronati, Milites D. Jacobi de Spata, quorum aliorumque plurium congregationes Alphonsus Alvares Guerrera, Aubertus Miraeus, Barbosa, aliique referunt. Ad Praedicatores pertinent Fratres de Militia B. Dominici, aliàs Observantici, & Fratres de militia Jesu Christi, ac pœst Fratres & Sorores de Poenitentia B. Dominici, dicti; Ordo Catharinae de Senis, Conventuales, Hetrusci, Quesillae seu Cloppae. Carmelitis accensentur duae congregationes, Italica & Hispanica, singulae sub suo Generali. Denique Minoritae seu Franciscani sub se quinque primarias congregationes habent, puta Conventualium, qui Claustrales etiam, Gaudentes, dicuntur, & quorum fœtus sunt Minoritæ Discalceati, seu Minores Conventuales Reformati; Observantium, ad quos etiam Observantes Reformati, seu Recollecti referuntur; Tertiorum, sive Tertianorum de Pœnitentia, Capucinorum, & S. Claræ, seu Clarissarum, quæ in Observantes, Reformatos, Urbaniff: Dominas pauperes, & Dominos Nobiles seu ditiores dividuntur. Ad Franciscanos eosdem subdivisione quadam Minimi de S. Paulo, Collectanei, Amadeani, Reformati, de Euangelio, Chiocini cum Barba, de Portiuncula, Paulini, Bosiani, de Augustinis cum perforatis calceis, Servientes, seu Servitæ rediguntur. Non Mendicantes Monachi sunt vel Canonici Regulares quorum ordines sunt Servatoris, seu Scopetinorum, Frisonariorum seu Lateranensium, S. Gregorii in Algo, Marci, Canonicorum Regularium Augustini, Præmonstratensium, seu Candidi Ordinis Norbertini, Benedictinorum, Cœlestinorum, seu Ordinis in Montibus à Cœlestino V. sic dicti, Canonicorum Regularium S. Crucis Conimbricensis in Portugallia, & Cruciferorum; vel Non Canonici, ad quos Antoniani, Guilhelmitæ, Bernhardini, aliás Cistercienses seu Clarevallenses, Fratres Vallis Umbrosæ, aliíque referuntur.
units.tr: LXIV. Monks are divided into Mendicant and Non-Mendicant according to the manner of acquiring their sustenance. Four kinds of Mendicants are reckoned: the Augustinians, the Preachers, the Carmelites, and the Minorites or Franciscans. But since, by the decree of the Council of Trent (Sess xxv. de Regul. cap. 3), all monasteries may hold immovable property, except the Franciscan Capuchin brothers and the Minors of the Observance, it follows that only the Capuchins and the Minors of the Observance are properly mendicants. Nevertheless all four orders are called Mendicants, and under the customary distinction they are classed as of the highest, middle and lowest poverty. To the Augustinienfem order are referred the Discalced Hermits of St Augustine, the Societies of the Girdle or Tertiaries, the Congregations of the Penance of Jesus Christ or Sackcloth-wearers, also those of Britinis, Lombardy, Illyria, St Saviour of the Charcoal-burners, Perugia (otherwise St Mary of the People), Genoa (or St Mary of Consolation), Montortone, Apulia (or Dulcetum), St Mary of Calorito, St Anthony on Mount Vulture, the Servants of the Blessed Mary, the Brigittines, the Jesuati, the Canons of St Gregory, the Montolivetans, the Hieronymite Hermits, the Scopetines, the John of Jerusalem (or Ferrier) brothers, the Brothers of Peter the Confessor of Mogella, the Sepulchrines (or Brothers of the Lord's Sepulchre), the Gilbertines, the Victorines, the Coronati, and the Knights of St James of the Sword; the congregations of these and of many others are described by Alphonsus Alvares Guerrera, Aubertus Miraeus, Barbosa and others. To the Preachers belong the Brothers of the Militia of the Blessed Dominic, otherwise the Observantines, and the Brothers of the Militia of Jesus Christ; then the Brothers and Sisters of the Penance of the Blessed Dominic, the Order of Catherine of Siena, the Conventuals, the Tuscans, and the Quesillae or Cloppae. Two congregations, the Italian and the Spanish, each under its own General, are reckoned to the Carmelites. Finally, the Minorites or Franciscans have five principal congregations under them: the Conventuals, who are also called Claustral or Rejoicing, and from whom sprang the Discalced Minorites or Reformed Conventual Minors; the Observants, to whom the Reformed or Recollect Observants are also referred; the Tertiaries, or Tertianies of the Penance; the Capuchins; and the Poor Clares, or Clarisses, who are divided into Observants, Reformed, Urbanists, Poor Ladies, and Noble or wealthier Ladies. Under the Franciscans, by a certain subdivision, are placed the Minims of St Paul, the Collectanei, the Amadeans, the Reformed, the Gospellers, the Bearded Chiocini, the Portiuncula brothers, the Paulines, the Bosians, the Augustinians with perforated shoes, and the Servants or Servites. Non-Mendicant monks are either Canonici Regulares, whose orders are those of the Saviour (or Scopetines), the Frisonarii (or Lateran canons), St Gregory in Algo, St Mark, the Regular Canons of St Augustine, the Premonstratensians (or White Norbertines), the Benedictines, the Celestines (or the Order on the Mountains, so called from Celestine V), the Regular Canons of the Holy Cross of Coimbra in Portugal, and the Crosiers; or Non Canonici, to whom the Antonines, the Guilhelmites, the Bernardines (otherwise Cistercians or Clairvaux monks), the Brothers of Vallombrosa, and others are referred.

units.la: LXV. Monachis se accenseri Jesuita, inde nomen sirum verè adepti, quòd sicut veteris Romæ satellites devictarum à se gentium nomina præferebant, sic à debellato Jesu illi Jesuitarum cognomen meruerunt; Babylonicæ Meretricis seplasiarii & agyrtæ γόητες, & triariorum in exercitu Papæ stationem obtinentes; graviter ferunt equidem, neque immeritò. Nihil enim minùs quàm μοναχοὶ solitarii sunt, solitudinem pertœsi maximè. In mediis urbibus, in foro, vicis, compitis, curiis Senatorum, aulis Regum ac Principum versantur, in castris quoque, & inter armatorum acies circumvolitant, denique in ipsa quoque gyne-
units.tr: LXV. That the Jesuits are counted among the monks, and so have truly won the name for themselves, is because just as the attendants of old Rome bore the names of the nations they had conquered, so those men earned the surname of Jesuits from the defeated Jesus. They are the perfumers and quacks [γόητες] of the Babylonian harlot, and hold the post of the triarii in the Pope's army. They certainly bear it badly, and not without reason, for they are by no means monks [μοναχοὶ], that is solitaries; they are most weary of solitude. They move about in the middle of cities, in the marketplace, in the streets and crossroads, in the courts of senators and the halls of kings and princes; they also serve in camps and flit about among the battle-lines of armed men; and finally they even make their way into the women's quarters

units.la: Monachis Iesuita an ne accenseri di sint? gynecæa penetrant. Neque reliqui ordines Monastici in suo censu æquo eos animo patiuntur, non minus ægrè ferentes, sua iis privilegia communicari, quos etiam similes esse avi cuipiam fluviatili, quæ indicto avium conventu se piscem, indicto piscium conventu se avem profitebatur, dicere solent. Proin eosdem urgent, ut depósita tandem persona se vel Monachis, vel Episcopis adjungant. Illi neutris se adjungunt, sed modò ad hos, modò ad illos divertunt, utrorumque participes. Nam cùm Monachum solitudo & otium juvet, ipsi quoque à populo se segregare, ne curarum terrenarum contagione afficiantur, videri volunt, atque adeò in umbra foli per spatiosos porticus inambulantes, cogitationibus suis indulgent. E diverso cùm Episcopi munus actione contineatur, ipsi quoque animi gratia ad populum declamant, Sacramenta sua fanis, ægris, publicè, privatim dispensant. Quoniam verò languida nimis Monachorum videbatur conditio, si se totos meditationi dederent, aut odiosa, si rerum satagerent; atque contra ærumnosum nimis exercitúmque Episcoporum munus est, iccirco medium quoddam, & ad felicitatem propensius vivendi genus, quod laboris civilioris, & meditationis vicibus temperaretur, arrisit. Itaque id eatenus attingentes, quatenus visum commodum est, libera ad meditationem & otium sibi tempora reservarunt, sicque rem gesserunt, ut inter Episcopos Semi-Monachi, inter Monachos Semi-episcopi, utrisque merito suspecti habeantur. Adde quòd non inertem navant operam pueris erudiendis, & ad suam rationem informandis, atque inter has curas, non pauca alia moliuntur. Unde non immeritò Monachismo praxis adjungitur, hoc est, μοναχαγμοσυνη, cujus cum eo mixtura artem Jesuiticam, medullámque doctrinæ Papæ constituit. Sicut enim medulla alimentum ultimum est, perfectissimè elaboratum, ita ultima hæc Monachorum natio, quam Monarchiæ Soli-ipsorum nomine non malè nuper Lucius Cornelius Europæus descripsit, una reliquarum omnium instar, ejusque doctrina subtilior quidem succus, ex Monachorum antiquiorum regulis delibatus, & expressus est.
units.tr: Whether the Jesuits are to be counted among the monks? They make their way into the women's quarters. Nor do the other monastic orders suffer them calmly to be counted in their number; they are no less vexed that their privileges are shared with these men, who (they are wont to say) resemble a certain river bird which, when a meeting of birds was called, professed itself a fish, and when a meeting of fish was called, professed itself a bird. So the monastic orders press them to drop their pretence at last and join either the monks or the bishops. They join neither, but turn now to these and now to those, sharing in both. For since solitude and leisure help monks, they too want to appear separated from the people, so that they may not be infected by the contagion of earthly cares; and so, walking about in the shade of the soil through spacious colonnades, they indulge their thoughts. On the other hand, since the office of bishop consists in action, they too, for the sake of display, preach to the people, and dispense their sacraments to the sick and the healthy, publicly and privately. But since the condition of monks would seem too languid if they gave themselves wholly to meditation, or hateful if they busied themselves with affairs; and since the office of bishop is too toilsome and burdensome, a certain middle way of life, more inclined to happiness, which might be tempered by alternations of civil labour and meditation, pleased them. So, touching these things only so far as seemed convenient, they reserved free times for meditation and leisure, and they so conducted their affairs that among the bishops they are semi-monks and among the monks semi-bishops, and are rightly suspected by both. Add that they expend no idle effort on teaching boys and shaping them to their own way, and among these cares they undertake not a few other things. Hence not undeservedly the practice is joined to monkery, that is, monachagmosyne [μοναχαγμοσυνη], and with this mixture they constitute the Jesuit art and the marrow of the Papal doctrine. For as marrow is the final nourishment, most perfectly worked out, so this last race of monks, which Lucius Cornelius Europaeus lately described not badly under the name "Monarchy of the Self-Alone", is one, like all the rest, and its more subtle doctrine is a juice drawn and pressed out from the rules of the older monks.

units.la: LXVI. Dicamus tamen breviter, quibus in rebus Jesuitæ à Monachis reliquis differant maximè. Monachos tria vota nuncupare, Continentiæ, paupertatis & obedientiæ, constat. Jesuitæ professi quartum Missionis votum addunt, quo singulari ratione Papæ se mancipant, ejusque imperata omnia, nulla habita ratione pietatis, æquitatis, juris, facturos promittunt; eáque ratione Pontificis R. molossi, & canes venatici, quos robustus ille Nimrod ad indagandos & opprimendos verè fideles emittit, evadunt. Monachis ex testamento suorum, aut ab intestato legati capio nulla erat, ideóque neque querela de inofficioso competebat. Jesuitæ verò id juris sibi reservarunt, ut hæreditates ad se devolutas nomine quisque privato adire, ac præteritione testamenta rumpere possint. Et quamvis dona grandia Monachi à caducis & moribundis hominibus aucuparentur, id ipsum tamen accuratiùs Jesuitæ præstant. Illud tamen interest, quòd non ad recitandas manè & vesperi næönias se obstringunt, neque cadaveribus Divorum delubra funestant, sed quicquid id est, quod donatur, purum putum sibi habere volunt. Reformarunt quinetiam eam Monachorum turpitudinem, qui mantica per vias onusti, stipem & annonam oftiatim mendicabant. In templis verò sicut in foro, vinum, polentas, ova, gratiis mercabantur. At Jesuitæ domi & foris nil nisi nitorem & Sybariticum luxum præ se ferunt. Suppresserunt etiam quasdam mei & tui appellationes, quæ jam inter Monachos glisceba nt, magnámque incommodorum caudam secum trahebant. Simul etiam ac rerum proprietates distinctæ ftinctæ esse cœperunt; deserta causa publica ad suum quisque commodum collimavit. Unde si ab uno collegio in aliud migrandum erat, colligendæ simul erant omnes farcinulæ, alioqui nuda omnia & inania reperturis. Jesuitæ soli reperere modum, quo nihil possidentes omnia possideant. Nam & depositis omnibus impedimentis secum ambulant passim, & quocunque gentium proficiscuntur, omnem suppellectilem & corporis cultum inter suos opportunum nanciscuntur. Præterea informi quodam habitu Monachi incedentes, tetricum quiddam & inhumanum sapiunt, hi nudis pedibus, hi fenestratis calceis, hi turbinato vertice& capucio, hi cucullo vel nigro, vel albo, vel cineritio, aut contortis funibus horrendi. At Jesuitæ formam communem & usitatam tenent, ut se turbis hominum ultro citròque misceant, rumusculos impunè captent, suúmque vigilum & speculatorum, vel potiùs proditorum munus promptè exequantur. Inde est, quòd ad extremas oras nullo penè sumtu abeunt, & gravissimas Papæ jussu legationes obeunt, quæ Cardinalibus antea demandari solebant. Tantum inter Monachos & Jesuitas, quod ad habitus victúsque formam attinet, interest, quantum inter veteres meretrices aulicas & recentiores: illæ pulchritudinem suam in jejuna quadam corporis exilitate constituebant, unde miserè genium suum affligebant: hæ verò veterem illam hæresin damnantes, corpus suum intus & in cute splendidè curandum, neque quidquam in fraudem genii de demenso detrahendum censent. Denique Monachis pudor nonnullus forte superest, cujus scilicet instinctu nonnulli saltem inter illos minus infesti Regibus, minùs Pontificibus addicti, & sanguinariis consiliis innexi, denique minùs mali reperiuntur. Pudoris hujus claucтra ita Jesuitæ perruperunt, ut in illorum societate vix unus existat, qui non furiosa ac tartarea placita societatis mordicus animo teneat, & vel præsentissimo capitis periculo tueri, manuque, sica, vel veneno armata sancire paratissimus sit. Rebus hujus seculi totos se hactenus immerserunt, Papatum efficacius quàm cæteri rexerunt, dominationem Pontificiam ceu Atlantes sustentarunt, potestatem omnis institutionis ad quascunque doctrinæ partes in scholis & extra eas, ad se traxerunt, gubernationem, intimam inspectionem, & ductum quarumcunque præstantiorum & potentiorum familiarum, in testamentis condendis, arte plagiaria exercenda, liberis parentum obedientiæ subducendis, conjugus procurandis, sibi vindicarunt; Principum & Rerum publicarum arcana, inventa etiam forma modóque exactissimæ per Christianum Orbem Correspondentiæ, scrutati exteris prodiderunt, ipsum humanæ societatis vinculum, quod in data fide & pactorum observantia constitit; pervertere docuerunt; sicariis ad parricidia Regum & Principum viam muniverunt, Pelagiana de gratia & libero arbitrio dogmata ad fastigium produxerunt, Theologiam Moralem & Casuisticam fœdis placitis, Epicureismo & Atheismo impleverunt; Idololatriam, Mariolatriam, Papolatriam, Stauro latriam, Artolatriam, Lipsonolatriam ad summum apicem provexerunt; artes denique Merculiales ac technologias, Jesuiticæ prudentiæ medullam, mentisque oculum, cujusmodi sunt mendaciorum, æquivocationum, reservationum mentalium pudenda cum doctrina, tum praxis, adeò quidem, ut jus fasque esset omnibus Jesuiticam sententiam professis, ementito nomine, dissimulata secta, imò etiam simulata ea, quam acerrimè oderunt, religione, Magistratui imponere, pejerare & ambiguis responsionibus interrogationes eludere; librorum nothorum & pseudepigraphorum inventio, scriptorum antiquorum & recentiorum expurgatio, castratio, falsatio; bonorum per subreptiones, obreptiones, blandiloquia generosas scilicet mendicationes ingurgitatio, alia ejusmodi impunè hactenus exercuerunt, & exercere non desinunt, ut dubitari amplius non possit, quin hoc ultimo patientiæ Dei ævo, Pater mendacii hoc hominum genus, tanquam ultimum fœtum suum, ex matre sycophantia, obstetricantibus omnibus inferorum furiis, suscepetum, instaurandis Babylonici Templi parietibus ex orco emiserit.
units.tr: LXVI. Let us nonetheless say briefly in what respects the Jesuits chiefly differ from the other monks. It is agreed that monks take three vows: of continence, of poverty and of obedience. The professed Jesuits add a fourth vow, of mission, by which they bind themselves in a special way to the Pope, promising to carry out all his commands without regard to piety, fairness or law. In this way they become the mastiffs and hunting dogs of the Roman Pontiff, which that sturdy Nimrod sends out to track down and crush the truly faithful. Monks could take nothing by the will of their own people, or by legacy on intestacy, and so there was no ground for a complaint of an undutiful will. The Jesuits, however, have reserved to themselves the right to take up, in their own private name, inheritances that fall to them, and to overturn wills by disinheritance. And although monks used to fish for large gifts from the feeble and the dying, the Jesuits do this even more carefully. There is this difference, however: they do not bind themselves to recite masses morning and evening, nor do they defile the shrines of the saints with corpses; whatever is given to them, they want to hold purely and simply for themselves. They have also reformed that disgraceful practice of monks who, loaded with bags, begged alms and grain from door to door. In churches, as in the marketplace, they bargained for wine, polenta and eggs as a favour. The Jesuits, at home and abroad, show nothing but polish and Sybaritic luxury. They have also suppressed certain expressions of mine and yours, which were already taking hold among the monks and dragged a great tail of troubles behind them. As soon as the ownership of goods began to be divided, each man aimed at his own advantage, the common cause being abandoned. Hence, if one had to move from one college to another, all one's baggage had to be gathered together, or else one would find everything bare and empty. The Jesuits alone have found a way of possessing everything while possessing nothing. For, having laid aside all encumbrances, they walk about freely, and wherever they go among the nations they find, among their own people, whatever clothing and bodily care is needed. Moreover, the monks, walking in their shapeless habits, have something grim and inhuman about them: some go barefoot, some in latched shoes, some with a pointed hood and cowl, some in black, white or ash-coloured cowls, and some frightful in their knotted cords. But the Jesuits keep to the common and customary dress, so that they may mingle with crowds of people freely, pick up gossip with impunity, and promptly perform the duty of spies and watchmen, or rather of informers. Hence it is that they go to the farthest shores at almost no expense, and undertake the most weighty embassies at the Pope's command, which were formerly entrusted to cardinals. The difference between the monks and the Jesuits in the matter of dress and way of life is as great as between the old court courtesans and the newer kind. The former set their beauty in a certain fasting thinness of body, and so miserably wore down their own genius; the latter, condemning that old heresy, judge that the body must be splendidly cared for within and on the skin, and that nothing should be taken from the due allowance to defraud the genius. Finally, perhaps some shame still remains among the monks, by whose prompting at least some of them are found to be less hostile to kings, less devoted to the Pontiffs, not bound up in bloody counsels, and in short less wicked. The Jesuits have so broken through the barriers of this shame that scarcely one exists in their society who does not hold tenaciously the frenzied and hellish opinions of the society, and who is not ready to defend them at the gravest risk to his life, and to uphold them with the hand, dagger or poison. Up to now they have plunged themselves wholly into the affairs of this age; they have governed the Papacy more effectively than the rest; they have supported the Pontifical dominion like Atlases; they have drawn to themselves the power of all instruction, in the schools and beyond them, in every branch of teaching; they have claimed for themselves the direction, the inner oversight and the guidance of any of the more eminent and powerful families, in drawing up wills, in practising the art of plunder, in withdrawing children from obedience to their parents, and in arranging marriages. They have searched out the secrets of princes and commonwealths and, by a form and manner of correspondence most exact throughout the Christian world, which they devised, they have betrayed them to outsiders. They have taught men to pervert the very bond of human society, which consists in good faith given and the keeping of covenants. They have paved the way for assassins to the murder of kings and princes. They have carried the Pelagian doctrines of grace and free will to their height, and filled moral and casuistical theology with foul opinions, Epicureanism and atheism. They have raised idolatry, Mariolatry, Papolatry, Staurolatry, Artolatry and Lipsonolatry to their highest peak. Finally, they have practised, both in doctrine and in practice, the Mercurial arts and technologies, the marrow of Jesuit prudence and the eye of the mind, namely the shameful arts of lies, equivocations and mental reservations, to such an extent that it is right and lawful for all who profess the Jesuit opinion, under an assumed name and a concealed sect, or even under a pretended religion, which they most bitterly hate, to impose upon the magistrate, to perjure themselves, and to evade questions with ambiguous answers. They have, with impunity, practised up to now the invention of spurious and pseudonymous books, the expurgation, castration and falsification of old and recent writings, and the gorging of goods by stealth, by obreption, and by smooth talk, which they call noble begging, and other such things; and they do not cease to practise them. So that it can no longer be doubted that in this last age of God's patience, the Father of lies, as his final offspring, has brought forth this race of men from the mother of sycophancy, with all the Furies of the underworld attending the birth, and has sent them up out of hell to restore the walls of the Babylonian temple.

units.la: - LXVII. Ex Monasteriorum, quæ Monachi & Jesuitæ insident, multitudine, de Civitatis Babylonicæ amplitudine, magnitudine & potentia judicari nullo negotio potest. Sanè qui Monasteriorum inde à tempore Papatus orientis numerum inire constituerit, eum calculi penè deficient. Sabellicus Enneade ix. testis est, sua ætate, hoc est circa M. MCDXC. Augustinensium Eremitanorum Ordinis Cœnobia, quorum quidem iniri ratio potuerit, citer duo millia, virginum autem trecenta: Carmelitarum septem millia & quinquaginta; Prædicatorum quatuor millia, centum & quadraginta tria extitisse: ab anno etiam Domini MCCXI. usque ad MCCCLXXX. adeóque centum & septuaginta novem annorum brevi intervallo per Orbem Christianum pro Franciscanis seu Minoritis extructa mille & quingenta Cœnobia fuisse. Summa igitur Cœnobiorum intra annos solos trecentos in gratiam Mendicantium tantùm Monachorum, Augustinensium puta, Carmelitarum, Prædicatorum & Franciscanorum, ad quindecim millia exsurgit, non computatis iis, quæ pro Monachis reliquorum ordinum non minùs forte numerosa extructa fuerunt. Sanè etiam Scriptor Italus Durus de Pascolo, Johanne Boreel Epistola Dedicatoria, Broughtoni in Danielem Commentario præmissa, citante, jam olim Monasteria per Orbem Christianum viginti duo centena viginti quinque millia & quardraginta quatuor numeravit. Accedunt Jesuitarum incrementa mira, de quibus etiam ipsimet, veluti certo Divinæ virgulæ argumento, gloriari solent, parùm interim meminores, malam herbam citissimè crescere. Petrus Ribadeneira A. MDCVIII. Catalogo in lucem edito, inde à Jesuitarum incunabulis ad eum usque annum, adeóque intra septuaginta circiter annos, domos professas viginti & unam, Collegia ducenta nonaginta tria, Domos probationis separatæ triginta tres, Domos & Residentias nonaginta sex, Socios denique decem mille quingentos octoginta & unum recensuit. Atque in immensum adeò eorum excrevit numerus, ut Generalis eorum Aquaviva jactasse feratur, plures se breviorique spatio milites in castra, quàm Rex quivis Christianus, cogere posse. Quin etiam tempore interdicti Veneti, cùm jam undique grave Papæ periculum imminaret, Paulo V. Pontifici suppetias quadraginta millium promissse leguntur, ea scilicet lege, ut quotquot in præhio obirent, in catalogo Martyrum scriberentur.
units.tr: LXVII. From the number of monasteries which the monks and Jesuits occupy, the size, greatness and power of the Babylonian city can be judged without any difficulty. Indeed, whoever sets out to count the monasteries from the time of the rise of the Papacy will be short of counters. Sabellicus, in the ninth Ennead, is a witness that in his own age, that is about the year 1490, there were some two thousand convents of the Augustinian Hermits' Order, of which the number could be ascertained, and three hundred for virgins; seven thousand and fifty of the Carmelites; four thousand one hundred and forty-three of the Preachers. Also, from the year of the Lord 1211 to 1380, that is within the space of one hundred and seventy-nine years, some fifteen hundred monasteries were built for the Franciscans, or Minorites, across the Christian world in a short span. The total of monasteries built within these three hundred years for the sake of the mendicant monks alone, namely the Augustinians, Carmelites, Preachers and Franciscans, therefore rises to about fifteen thousand, not counting those built for the monks of the other orders, which were perhaps no less numerous. Indeed the Italian writer Durus de Pascolo, as cited by John Boreel in the dedicatory letter prefixed to Broughton's commentary on Daniel, long ago counted up twenty-two thousand one hundred and twenty-five monasteries across the Christian world, and forty-four of them. To these are added the remarkable increases of the Jesuits, of which they themselves are wont to boast, as a sure sign of divine favour, while being little mindful that the weed grows very quickly. Petrus Ribadeneira, in his catalogue published in 1608, recorded that from the cradle of the Jesuits down to that year, that is within some seventy years, there were twenty-one professed houses, two hundred and ninety-three colleges, thirty-three separate houses of probation, ninety-six houses and residences, and finally ten thousand five hundred and eighty-one members. And their number grew so vastly that their General, Aquaviva, is reported to have boasted that he could raise more soldiers for the camp, and in a shorter time, than any Christian king. Moreover, at the time of the interdict against Venice, when danger to the Pope threatened from every side, it is recorded that forty thousand men were promised to Pope Paul V as aid, on the condition, of course, that whoever died in the battle should be written in the catalogue of martyrs.

units.la: LXVIII. Cum Monachis affinitate quadam juncti sunt non nulli nec clerici, nec laici, sed medium quoddam inter utrosque genus, devoti Seculares (sic enim hybridæ illi appellari gaudent) qui meritis Monachorum inhiantes, sed institutis auste rioribus impares, Sodalitia seu Confraternitates, certis quidem, sed laxioribus legibus sub patrocinio titulóque Sancti vel idoli cujusp am adstrictas incunt, atque eo pacto meritorum Monasticorum omnium fiunt participes, præsertim si φεγγιαξινς isti diebus anniversariis in supplicationum pompa incedentes, obvelata facie, renudatas Scapulas flagris converberent, atque hac ἀσπαληξία prisco s Baalis Sacerdotes graviter æmulentur. Quarum quidem fraternitatum ritus undecunque alii derivent, à Roma Ethnica veteri ad novam Babylonicam dimanavit. Namque vix condita urbe illa septicolli, à Romulo mulo instituti fuêre Sodales Titii & fratrum Arvalium Collegium, de quo apud Rofinum Antiq. Rom. lib. iÿ. 6. pluscula legi possunt. Inde apud Suetonium quoque Sodales Augustales; apud Capitolinum Antoniani. Vetusto quoque marmori apud Tybur inscriptum hodiéque reperitur; Sodales Hadrianales. Atque ad hanc Originem Fraternitates istas Pontificias Pontificii quoque non nulli apud Polydorum Vergilium Lib. vÿ. 6. retulerunt.
units.tr: LXVIII. Some people, neither clergy nor laity but a kind of middle class between the two, are linked to the monks by a certain affinity. They like to be called devout secular persons, since these hybrids prefer that name. Coveting the merits of the monks but unequal to their stricter rules, they form fellowships or confraternities bound by certain but looser rules under the patronage and title of some saint or other idol. In this way they become sharers in all the merits of the monasteries, especially when these [φεγγιαξινς, lamp-bearers] on their anniversary days walk in processions of supplication with veiled faces and beat their bared shoulders with whips. In this self-flagellation [ἀσπαληξία] they earnestly imitate the ancient priests of Baal. Wherever other people derive the rites of these brotherhoods, they flowed from pagan Rome of old into the new Babylon. For scarcely had that seven-hilled city been founded when Romulus established the Titian brethren and the college of the Arval brothers, about which more can be read in Rosinus, Antiq. Rom. lib. iv. 6. Later there were the Augustal brethren mentioned by Suetonius, and the Antonine brethren mentioned by Capitolinus. An ancient marble inscription at Tibur, still found today, names the Hadrianic brethren. Some of the Papists too have traced these Papal brotherhoods to this origin, citing Polydore Vergil, Lib. v. 6.

units.la: LXIX. Primus fraternitates ejusmodi instituisse Bonifacius Anglus, Germanorum circa A. C. D. CCLXX. Apoftolus, putatur. Ex eo tempore longè lateque propagatæ sunt. Quod ex fraternitatum speciebus variis abundè liquet. Aliæ enim institutæ sunt in honorem reliquiarum, vel actionum & passionum quarundam, ut & Divorum Chimæricorum: aliæ in honorem Divorum. Prioris generis sunt fraternitates Sacramenti Altaris, Sancti Sudarii, Circumcisionis, seu Præputii Christi, dulcis nominis Jesu, S. Crucis, Catharinæ Rochi, Animarum Purgatorii &c. Posterioris generis sunt fraternitates institutæ in honorem B. Virginis Mariæ, Patriarcharum, Jobi, Josephi, Sponsi B. Virginis, B. Annæ, Petri, Pauli, Antonii, Adriani, Sebastiani, Huberti, Barbarae, Luciæ, Agathæ, Willebrordi, Ittæ, Benedicti & Scholasticæ, aliæque innumeræ. Quò referri etiam potest, quòd referente Camillo Fannucio Opere pie di Roma lib. iv. 13. Confraternitas Catharinæ Senensis privatim primùm, & post etiam publicè in Ecclesia Orationem quadraginta horarum instituit, quam A. M. DXCII. Clemens VIII. sua authoritate sanxit. Inter fraternitates porro istas Marianæ, à Dominico circa Seculi XIII. initium institutæ, & ab Alano de Rupe restauratæ, excellunt facilè, utpote quæ & magno in pretio habentur, & Oceani instar Papatum inundant, annitentibus inprimis post reformationem Jesuitis, ut à Monachorum reliquorum eosdem antehac promoventium veneratione abstractos homines sibi mancipent. Institutarum & propagatarum à societate sua fraternitatum Parthenicorum multitudinem admirandam ipsimet Imag. primi Seculi Jes. lib. iij. 7. insolenter admodum decantant. Fratrum horum Parthenicorum ⟨Greek⟩ est, B. Virginem Mariam religiose colere, peculiari scilicet instituto modoque orandi, quem Beatæ Mariæ Corollam, Coronam & Rosarium appellant, acceptissimum scilicet omnium Beatæ Mariæ, utpote Dominico à Spiritu S. si Bullæ Pii V. credere fas est, dictatum ab ipsa Maria per varias visiones & apparitiones, puta Alano de Rupe, qui ex Psalterio Mariæ Rosarium fabricavit, Sprengéro aliisque factas, tot denique, tantisque miraculis Divinitùs præstitis, & Papali universæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ authoritate, largissimisque indulgentiis, ne dicam ipsius etiam Diaboli confessione & testimonio, à Dominico uti Alphonsus Fernandes Dominicanus Concert. Prædicat. famil. ad A. MCCXII. scribit, extorto, confirmatum. Varias Marianarum harum fraternitatum species apud Coppensteinium, aliosque videre est.
units.tr: LXIX. Boniface the Englishman, apostle of the Germans around the year 770, is thought to have been the first to found brotherhoods of this kind. From that time they spread far and wide, as is abundantly clear from their various kinds. Some were founded in honour of relics or of certain actions and sufferings, and also of imaginary saints; others in honour of saints. Of the first kind are the brotherhoods of the Sacrament of the Altar, of the Holy Shroud, of the Circumcision or Foreskin of Christ, of the sweet name of Jesus, of the Holy Cross, of Catherine, of Roch, of the Souls in Purgatory, and so on. Of the second kind are the brotherhoods founded in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Patriarchs, Job, Joseph the spouse of the Blessed Virgin, St Anne, Peter, Paul, Anthony, Hadrian, Sebastian, Hubert, Barbara, Lucy, Agatha, Willibrord, Itta, Benedict and Scholastica, and countless others. To this class may also be referred what Camillo Fannucci reports in Opere pie di Roma lib. iv. 13.: the Confraternity of Catherine of Siena first founded, privately and then publicly in the church, the Forty Hours' prayer, which Clement VIII confirmed by his authority in 1592. Among these brotherhoods the Marian ones stand out easily. They were founded by Dominic around the beginning of the thirteenth century and restored by Alanus de Rupe. They are held in great esteem and, like an ocean, flood the Papacy, especially since the Reformation, when the Jesuits strove to bind to themselves men drawn away from the veneration of other monks who had promoted these confraternities before. The Jesuits themselves boast very insolently in Imag. primi Seculi Jes. lib. iii. 7. of the amazing multitude of Marian sodalities which their society has founded and spread. The aim of these Marian brothers is to worship the Blessed Virgin Mary devoutly, by a special rule and manner of prayer which they call the Corolla, Crown and Rosary of the Blessed Mary. It is the most acceptable of all Marian devotions, supposedly dictated by Mary herself through various visions and appearances to Dominic, if we may believe the bull of Pius V, as well as to Alanus de Rupe, who made the Rosary from the Psalter of Mary, and to Sprenger and others. It was confirmed by so many and such great miracles divinely wrought, by the papal authority of the whole Roman Church, and by the most generous indulgences, not to mention the confession and testimony of the Devil himself, extracted, as Alphonsus Fernandes the Dominican writes in Concert. Prædicat. famil. ad A. 1212., from Dominic. Various kinds of these Marian brotherhoods may be seen in Coppenstein and others.

units.la: LXX. Qui fraternitates illas, Rosario-Marianas inprimis, Pontificiæ tyrannidis & idololatriæ adminicula & munimenta dixerit, censuerítque, næ is à vero non procul abluserit. Ut ut enim de fraternitatum illarum fructibus, satisfactione pro peccatis, ampliatione cultus Divini & Sanctorum, patrocinio eorundem ampliore, liberatione à periculis, purgatorio, ipsaque inferni evacuatione mira earum hyperaspistæ garriunt, non postremus tamen earum fructus est, tyrannidis Pontificiæ propagatio. Experientia enim comprobatum est, iis, qui tuendæ Pontificiæ potestatis gratia, Rerum publicarum status turbare, adversus supremas potestates conjurationes inire, & proditiones fovere moliti sunt, nihil fraternitatibus ejusmodi offerri opportunius potuisse. Fratres enim Pontifici devotionem suam amplis & magnificis promissis Spiritualium & corporalium bonorum locupletanti arctissima fide, propensa charitate & obsequuis ita addicti sunt, ut in ejus gratiam nihil non velint nolintque, adeóque etiam eorum, quos Pontificiæ tyrannidis, & idololatriæ Pontificiæ adversarios ferre non possunt, incendia præsentissima procurent. Cleri inemendabilis, Jesuitarum inprimis Promachos strenuos se gerunt, & in militia denique sacra Babylonica, id ferè, quod in Turcica Janitzari & Spahi, præstant. Quæ causa est, quòd fratermitarum, Fratrumque augendo in immensum numero studiosissimè Monachi, Jesuitæ inprimis inhiant. Italia sanè Sacerimis sodalibus ejusmodi referta tota est. In utraque India & Japoniainnumeras ferè Marianas Sodalitates; & ab uno Gregorio Ciscero trecentas constitutas esse, Jesuitæ in Imagine primi sui Seculi pag. 420. gloriantur. Per universam Europam cuncta sodalitatibus impleta sunt, quibus Principes, nobiles, Senatores, judices, cujusvis status & ordinis homines adscribuntur. Quid quod, ita iidem pag. 361. scribunt, militum, quid quòd agrestium, quid quòd reorum, damnatorumque ad triremes, & mendicabulorum initæ sunt sub Mariæ nomine Societates? De Ferdinando II. iidem pag. 421. referunt, quòd omnibus Sodalitatibus Marianis per utramque Austriam, per Hungariæ Bohemiæque Regna, per Stiriam, Carinthiam, Carniolam nomen suum dederit, & in singularum tabulis inscriptum legi voluerit: Ferdinandum Secundum, Virgineum Clientem. Nec suarum, inquiunt illi, contentus ditionum tabulis, Provinciis etiam remotissimis supplicavit; Belgio inprimis nostro, cujus ultimis in finibus celeberrima congregatio Duacena Ferdinandi adscripto nomine, etiamnum gloriatur. Quin & pag. 422. Imperatrices, Reginas, Principissas, Antistites Sates Sacrorum, Nuntios Pontificios, Patres Purpuratos in Parthenias suas tabulas relatos, crepant. Ferdinándum inprimis Tertium, qui, uti pag. 362. illi referunt, his verbis Marianæ Sodalitatis albo nomen suum inscripsit: Illius ego Cœtus sub invocatione Tua congregati, Augustissima Maria, Me libens & merito unum profiteor. Tibi ego Me, Mebsque, Conjugem ac Liberos, Tibi Romanum Imperium, cui me Deus præfecit, Tibi Regna à Majoribus accepta, Tibi, tuteláque tua populum & Exercitus meos, Tibi Tubque Filio militantes committo. Tu me in Tuum admitte, qui Filio Tuo, qui Tibi, qui utriúsque honori vivo, regno, pugno. Tuus igitur ero, Maria. Tui erunt; quicunque mei. Tuæ erunt ditiones, & Regna mea, & Imperium. Tui populi & Exercitus. Tu eos protege, Tu eis vince, Tu in eis regna & impera. Ita voveo MDCXL. Tuus & pietate & justitia Ferdinandus.
units.tr: LXX. Whoever called those brotherhoods, the Rosary-Marian ones above all, props and bulwarks of Papal tyranny and idolatry, and judged so, has not strayed far from the truth. However much their defenders chatter about the fruits of those brotherhoods, satisfaction for sins, the increase of divine worship and of the saints, their greater patronage, deliverance from dangers, purgatory, and even the wonderful emptying of hell, the propagation of papal tyranny is not the least of their fruits. Experience has shown that for those who have plotted to disturb the states of commonwealths, to form conspiracies against the supreme powers and to foster treacheries in the cause of defending papal power, nothing could have been offered more opportunely than brotherhoods of this kind. For the brothers are bound to the Pope with the closest faith, with eager love and obedience, as he enriches their devotion with ample and magnificent promises of spiritual and bodily goods, so that for his favour they will refuse nothing and will will nothing he does not will, and so they even bring about imminent fires against those whom they cannot bear as opponents of papal tyranny and Papal idolatry. They act as eager champions of the unreformable clergy, above all of the Jesuits, and finally in the sacred Babylonian militia they perform roughly the function which the Janissaries and Spahis do in the Turkish army. This is why the Monks, and the Jesuits above all, eagerly strive to increase the number of these brotherhoods and brothers without limit. Italy is entirely crowded with such sodalities. The Jesuits boast in their Imago primi saeculi, p. 420, that in both Indies and Japan there are almost countless Marian sodalities, and that three hundred were founded by Gregory Cisero alone. Throughout the whole of Europe everything is filled with sodalities, to which princes, nobles, senators, judges and men of every rank and order are enrolled. What of the fact that, as the same authors write on p. 361, societies have been founded under Mary's name for soldiers, for country folk, for the guilty and condemned to the galleys, and for beggars? The same authors report on p. 421 that Ferdinand II gave his name to all the Marian sodalities throughout both Austrias, the kingdoms of Hungary and Bohemia, Styria, Carinthia and Carniola, and wished it to be written on each of their registers: Ferdinand the Second, the Virgin's client. Not content, they say, with the registers of his own dominions, he also petitioned the most distant provinces, above all our Belgium, at whose furthest borders the famous Douai congregation still boasts of his name enrolled. Indeed, on p. 422 they crow that empresses, queens, princesses, prelates of sacred things, papal nuncios and cardinals are listed in their Marian registers. Above all they cite Ferdinand III, who, as they report on p. 362, inscribed his name in the roll of the Marian sodality with these words: I, who am gathered into this company under your invocation, most august Mary, freely and rightly profess myself one of you. To you I commit myself, my wife and children, to you the Roman Empire over which God has placed me, to you the kingdoms received from my ancestors, to you, and under your protection, my people and my armies, to you and your Son those serving in war. Admit me among yours, I who live, reign and fight for your Son, for you, and for the honour of both. I shall therefore be yours, Mary. Yours will be all who are mine. Yours will be my dominions, my kingdoms and my empire, my peoples and my armies. Protect them, conquer through them, reign and rule over them. So I vow, 1640. Ferdinand, yours in piety and justice.

units.la: LXXI. Supersunt Sacri Milites, & Religiosi Equites, Civitatis Babylonicæ pars non ignobilis.
units.tr: LXXI. There remain the Sacred Soldiers and the Religious Knights, a not inconsiderable part of the Babylonian city.

units.la: Distinguuntur illi à Secularibus, qui iidem etiam Honorarii & Torquati dici solent, cujusmodi sunt Aurei velleris apud Burgundos & Austriacos: Stellæ, Michaëlis, S. Spiritús, Scuti aurei, Hystricis, Lunæ Crescentis, &c. in Gallia: S. Georgii seu Garterii in Anglia: Annuntiationis Angelicæ apud Sabaudos: Bondæ apud Hispanos: Redemtoris Christi apud Mantuanos: S. Stephani in Hetruria: Lilii apud Navarros & Aragonios: S. Marci apud Venetos: S. Andreæ apud Scotos: Elephanti apud Danos: Seraphini apud Suecos: Spothæ apud Cyprios: aliúque, quorum tamen iis saltem in locis, quæ Pontifici adhuc parent, commune cum Militibus sacris munus est, quòd Promachos fe Ecclesiæ, hoc est, Pontificiæ potestatis gerere tenentur.
units.tr: These are distinguished from the secular knights, and are also commonly called Honorary and Torqued knights. Of this kind are the Order of the Golden Fleece among the Burgundians and Austrians; in France the Order of the Star, of St Michael, of the Holy Spirit, of the Golden Shield, of the Porcupine, of the Crescent Moon, and others; in England the Order of St George, or of the Garter; among the Savoyards the Order of the Annunciation of the Angel; among the Spaniards the Order of the Band; among the Mantuans the Order of the Redeemer Christ; in Etruria the Order of St Stephen; among the Navarrese and Aragonese the Order of the Lily; among the Venetians the Order of St Mark; among the Scots the Order of St Andrew; among the Danes the Order of the Elephant; among the Swedes the Order of the Seraph; among the Cypriots the Order of the Spotha; and others. In those places at least which still obey the Pope, these orders share with the sacred soldiers the duty of bearing arms as champions of the Church, that is, of papal power.

units.la: LXXII. Sacri vero seu Religiosi Milites, dum etiam sunt generum. Alii enim tales sunt minus proprie, alii . Prioris generis sunt partim illi, qui à Pontifice constituuntur, quorum alii S. Petri & Pauli commilitones dicti in familia Pontificis degunt; alii Equites aurati, etiam Comites Palatii Lateranensis creantur; alii ex officialibus Curiae Romanae deliguntur, qui omnes in equites S. Petri, S. Pauli, Lauretanos, S. Spiritus, S. Antonii, Julii, Lilii, Christi &c. dividuntur: partim illi, qui sub certa regula & voto cum subjectione Speciali ad exercitium & defensionem Papalis tyrannidis obligati sunt, cujusmodi olim erant Milites Christi, à Dominico ad Albigensium extirpationem instituti; Equites S. Sepulchri in Hierusalem: Crucé signati, instituti ad praesidium Inquisitorum haereticae pravitatis à Pio V. A. M. DLXIX. denuo confirmati: Equites S. Catharinae: Crucigeri, qui cruciatas olim expeditiones suscepepunt.
units.tr: LXXII. The sacred or religious soldiers, however, are of several kinds. Some are so only in a loose sense, others more properly. Of the first kind are, partly, those appointed by the Pope, some of whom, called fellow soldiers of Saints Peter and Paul, live in the Pope's household; others are created as gilded knights, or as Counts of the Lateran Palace; others are chosen from the officials of the Roman Curia. All of these are divided into the knights of St Peter, St Paul, of Loreto, of the Holy Spirit, of St Anthony, of Julius, of the Lily, of Christ, and so on. Partly they are those who, under a fixed rule and vow, with a special subjection, are bound to the exercise and defence of papal tyranny. Of this kind there once were the Knights of Christ, established by Dominic for the extirpation of the Albigenses; the Knights of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, the Signed with the Cross, established by Pius V in the year 1569 to protect the Inquisitors of heretical depravity and confirmed again; the Knights of St Catherine; and the Crusaders, who once undertook the crusading expeditions.

units.la: LXXIII. Sed xuptws & proprie Equites Religiosi & sacri sunt, qui vulgò Milites Ecclesiae nuncupantur, qui que & in defensione Ecclesiae occupantur, & prima Origine sua, proprióque munere militari tenus ab Ecclesia, Sede Romana, Pontifice dependent, eíqne ἀμέσως subsunt, atque eo etiam respectu homines Ecclesiae, seu Papae dici possunt: & Regulares etiam, seu Religiosi, utpote pleriqué certæ & peculiari regulæ atque ordini, utplurimum Benedicti, Augustini, Cistercienium &c. obstricti, votisque Monasticis castitatis (vel absolutæ, vel conjugalis paupertatis & obedientiæ, quantum scilicet arma tractaturis pro fide Christi sat est, uti Mennenius loquitur, alligati cluent. quorum ordines ex recentioribus Aubertus Miraeus Orig. Equestr. Ord. lib. j. & ij. nec non Franciscus Mennenius in Deliciis Equestribus, aliique describunt. Suntque Equites illi vel primi, vel à primis derivati. Primi sunt, qui olim recuperata per Christianos Palæstina Hierosolymæ instituti sunt ut infideles armis vexent ad orbis Christiani securitatem, Christianos peregrinantes, & sepulchrum Christi visitantes deducant, & contra Saracenos defendant, captivos redimant &c. Erántque primitus S. Johannis, Teutonici, Templarii, & S. Lazari. de quorum fundatoribus, progressu, rebus gestis fusè iidem Miræus & Mennenius disserunt. A primis derivati, & cum iisdem quadantenus convenientes sunt varii, puta Gladiferi, seu Ensiferi (qui postea cum Teutonicis in eundem ordinem coaluerunt) Jacobi de Spatha, de Calatrava, Alcantarae, Mariæ de Mercede, Montesiæ, Christi, sive S. Michaëlis, sive de ala, Bandæ, Hospitalarii S. Spiritus, & S. Antonii, B. Mariæ, Sepulchri Christi apud Italos, S. Mariæ apud Sabaudos, Mariæ de monte Carmelo, apud Gallos. Qui tamen Honorarii plerique esse coeperunt, postquam summus eorum Magistratus Principatibus annexus est.
units.tr: LXXIII. But the Religious and sacred Knights properly so called [κυρίως] are those commonly named Knights of the Church, who both are occupied in defending the Church and, from their first origin and by their proper military office, depend upon the Church, the Roman See, the Pope, and are subject to him immediately [ἀμέσως]. In this respect they can also be called men of the Church, or of the Pope. They are also regular, or religious, since most of them are bound to a fixed and particular rule and order, mostly that of Benedict, Augustine, the Cistercians and so on, and are tied by monastic vows of chastity (either absolute, or conjugal), of poverty and of obedience, insofar as this suffices for those who are to take up arms for the faith of Christ, as Mennenius puts it. Their orders are described by the more recent writers: Aubertus Miraeus in Origines of the Equestrian Orders, books 1 and 2, likewise Franciscus Mennenius in Equestrian Delights, and others. These knights are either the first, or derived from the first. The first are those who were once founded, after Palestine was recovered by Christians, to harass the infidels with arms for the security of the Christian world, to escort Christian pilgrims and visitors to the sepulchre of Christ, to defend them against the Saracens, to ransom captives and so on. At first these were the Knights of St John, the Teutonic Knights, the Templars, and of St Lazarus. Miraeus and Mennenius discuss at length their founders, their progress and their deeds. Derived from the first, and somewhat agreeing with them, are various others, namely the Sword-bearers, or Ensiferi (who later merged with the Teutonic Knights into the same order), the orders of St James of the Sword, of Calatrava, of Alcántara, of Mary of Mercy, of Montesa, of Christ, whether of St Michael or of the Wing, of the Band, the Hospitallers of the Holy Spirit and of St Anthony, of the Blessed Mary, of the Sepulchre of Christ among the Italians, of St Mary among the Savoyards, of Mary of Mount Carmel among the French. Most of these, however, began to become honorary once their chief master was attached to princes.

units.la: LXXIV. Hodie igitur Teutonici Johannitæ præcipuè Religionum nomen merentur.
units.tr: LXXIV. Today, therefore, the Teutonic Knights and especially the Knights of St John deserve the name of religious orders.

units.la: Et Teutonici quidem, dicti aliàs à professione & Symbolo Milites Mariani, nec non Milites Domus Hospitalis S. Mariæ in Hierusalem, A. MCXC. Imperante Henrico VI. occasione beneficentiæ à Civibus non nullis urbium Bremensis & Lubeccensis in obsidione Ptolemaidis sauciatis, miseréque afflictis præstitæ, à Friderico Suevriæ & Brabantiæ Duce, Friderici I. Filio, ex Nobilium prosapia electi institutique eum in finem sunt, ut pauperum in terra sancta palantium curam gererent, armis tum terram sanctam, tum alios Christianorum fines tutarentur. Cœlestinus III. eorum ordinem confirmavit, tributis insignibus, in scuto scilicet candido cruce nigra, & albo pallio; dicta etiam ea lege ut uni Magno Magistro nuncupato, subessent, & duo eorundem genera
units.tr: The Teutonic Knights, otherwise called from their profession and emblem the Marian Knights, and also the Knights of the House of the Hospital of St Mary in Jerusalem, were founded in the year 1190, under the emperor Henry VI. On account of the kindness shown to some citizens of Bremen and Lübeck, who had been wounded and wretchedly afflicted during the siege of Ptolemais, they were chosen from the noble stock by Frederick, Duke of Swabia and Brabant, son of Frederick I, and instituted for this purpose: that they should care for the poor wandering in the Holy Land, and defend with arms both the Holy Land and the other borders of Christians. Celestine III confirmed their order, with its insignia, namely a black cross on a white shield, and a white mantle. They were also bound by this law, that they should be subject to one Grand Master, and that two kinds of them should be established: some should preside over sacred matters, to whom it was not permitted to grow a beard; others, free from shaving and sacred ministries, should be occupied with military duties. When Jerusalem was taken by Saladin, the knights withdrew to Ptolemais, and from there, transferred to Germany, they occupied Prussia. For two centuries they flourished there in renown and strength, until Albert of Brandenburg, created Duke of Prussia in 1525 by Sigismund, King of Poland, straightway embraced the Gospel. For then the knights spread into the rest of Germany, where they enjoy very ample revenues, and there they created Albert of Wolfgang as Grand Master. From that time the younger sons of German princes, and others enrolled in the order, have enjoyed the revenues of the Order.

units.la: Vigent bo-ditæque Teutonici, seu Milites Mariani, nera constituerentur, quorum alii sacris praesessent, quibus barbam alere non licebat; alii à rasura & sacris ministeriis immunes militantibus muneribus distringerentur. Capta à Saladino Hierosolyma Equites Ptolomaidem concesserunt, inde in Germaniam translati Borussiam occuparunt, per duo secula ibidem fama viribusque florentes, donec Albertus Brandenburgicus A. MDXXV. à Sigismundo Poloniae Rege Dux Borussiae creatus, Euangelium mox amplexus est. Tum enim Equites in Germaniam reliquam penetrarunt, in qua amplissimis reditibus gaudent, & in ea Magnum Magistrum Albertum de Volfang creârunt, ex quo tempore Principum Teutonicorum juniores filii, aliique ordine illi adscripti, reditibus Ordinis gaudent.
units.tr: Flourishing are the Teutonic Knights, or Marian Knights, [...] and two kinds of them were to be established, of whom some were to preside over sacred matters, for whom it was not permitted to grow a beard; others, exempt from shaving and sacred ministries, were to be occupied with military duties. After Jerusalem was taken by Saladin, the knights withdrew to Ptolemais, and from there, transferred to Germany, they occupied Prussia, flourishing there in renown and strength for two centuries, until Albert of Brandenburg, created Duke of Prussia in 1525 by Sigismund, King of Poland, straightway embraced the Gospel. For then the knights spread into the rest of Germany, where they enjoy very ample revenues, and there they created Albert of Wolfgang as Grand Master. From that time the younger sons of German princes, and others enrolled in the order, have enjoyed the revenues of the Order.

units.la: LXXV. Johannitae, dicti alias Equites Hierosolymitani, Milites, vel Equites S. Johannis in Hierusalem, Equites Hospitalarii S. Johannis Hierosolymitani, Equites, seu Milites Rhodii, ab insula Rhodo, quam amissa Hierosolymâ insederunt, & ultra ducentos annos contra Saracenos tutati sunt; denique Melitenses ab insula Melite, quam post captam à Turcis Rhodum Carolus V. iis attribuit; parvis initiis, post captam consilio & ope eorum non postrema à Bullianeo Hierosolymam, sub Regibus Hierosolymitanis incrementa sumpserunt, solenni voto obstricti, quo se religionis gratia Hierosolymam venientes suscepturos & Christianorum aras & focos adversus infideles protecturos professi sunt. Ordinis censentur S. Augustini, atque Orationem Dominicam certo numero repetitam Horis Canonicis pronuntiant. Vestitus militaris sunt arma, quibus baltheum rubrum militare cum alba cruce superinduunt, exterius vero clamyde atri coloris cum alba cruce octogona parti sinistrae innexa utuntur. Primus ordinis illius Magister A. MCIII. Raymundus de
units.tr: LXXV. The Johannites, otherwise called Knights of Jerusalem, Soldiers, or Knights of St John in Jerusalem, Knights Hospitallers of St John of Jerusalem, Knights, or Soldiers of Rhodes, from the island of Rhodes, which they occupied after losing Jerusalem and defended for more than two hundred years against the Saracens; and finally the Maltese, from the island of Malta, which Charles V assigned to them after Rhodes was taken by the Turks. They began with small beginnings, but after Jerusalem was taken, with the counsel and help of Bouillon, which was no small help, they grew under the Kings of Jerusalem. They were bound by a solemn vow, by which they professed that, coming to Jerusalem for the sake of religion, they would take up and protect the altars and hearths of Christians against the infidels. They are reckoned to belong to the Order of St Augustine, and they recite the Lord's Prayer a fixed number of times at the canonical hours. Their military dress is armour, over which they wear a red military belt with a white cross, and outside they use a black cloak with a white eight-pointed cross attached to the left side. The first Master of this order was Raymond de

units.la: Podio Florentinus lectus est, qui tali voto clientes suos obstrinxit: Ego N. voveo & promitto Deo Omnipotenti, Beatæque Mariæ semper virgini, ac S. Johanni Baptistæ, perpetuò cum Dei auxilio servare veram obedientiam cuicunque superiori, qui à Deo & religione nostra mihi dabitur: amplius vivere sine proprio, & castitatem servare. In tres porrò classes distinctus ordo est, puta Sacerdotes, & Capellanos, qui sacris operantur, & Dominis suis militantibus fausta & felicia quæque legenda, canenda, oranda impetrare conantur: Equites Nobilis prosapiæ omnes, qui Orationem tantùm Dominicam certo numero pronuntiant, & ordini de cætero dominantur, & Servientes, qui Equitum imperata facere tenentur. Trecentos penè annos in Syria cum strenuè militassent A. MCCC. à Cap-capo Damascenorum Præfecto inde pulsi, Rhodum insulam expugnárunt, ibíque juxta octo linguas seu Nationes, puta Gallicam, Arvenicam, Francicam Occidentalem, Italicam, Hispanicam, Arragoniam, Anglicam, Alemanicam, & Hispanicam Castiliensem, totidem Magistros seu Priores uni Principi subjectos, ac præter hos in Christianorum provinciis alios etiam passim, Ordinum commendatoribus in suis Provinciis præfectos, creárunt. Inde A. MDXXIII. inopes auxilii, discordantium Principum pulsi Melitam insulam A. MDXXIX. insederunt, eámque strenuè adhuc dum tuentur, tantò Monachis reliquis, si superstitionem excipias, laudabiliores, quantò fortius non tam, ut illi, in Christi, quàm in barbarorum, & infidelium viscera sævientes, Christianum Orbem universum propugnant. Sed de his plus satis.
units.tr: Puy, of Florence, who was chosen in 1103, and who bound his clients by this vow: I, N., vow and promise to Almighty God, and to the Blessed Mary, ever a virgin, and to St John the Baptist, to keep perpetually, with God's help, true obedience to whichever superior shall be given me by God and our religion; further, to live without property, and to keep chastity.
