units.la: XXI. Næ hospes in orbe fit, qui de Prophetiæ successu multùm hæsitaverit. Signa erexit Agnus, Christus, non semel in vocatis, electis & fidelibus suis, qui pro ipso adversus Babylonem pugnárunt usque ad sanguinem. Id verò factum cumprimis illustri modo per præconium Euangelii à fidis Pastoribus & doctoribus post initium Seculi quinti supra decimum susceptum, detectásque ab iisdem Thaidis Babylonicæ fraudes. Non deseruit Babylonem, Meretricem Romanus populus, succinctus potentia decem cornuum, hoc est, Regum plurium, saltem non pauciorum, quàm decem (hoc enim ad terribilitatem & potentiam Bestiæ amplificandam sufficit) qui viribus Romani populi suas sociárunt, & συμφερτῇ ἀρετῇ suo quisque loco Papatum asseruerunt, Agnum oppugnárunt.
units.tr: XXI. Surely no one in the world will be a stranger who has doubted much about the success of the prophecy. The Lamb, Christ, has raised signs not once, among his called, chosen and faithful, who fought for him against Babylon even to the shedding of blood. This was done most illustriously through the proclamation of the Gospel by faithful ministers and teachers, begun after the start of the sixteenth century, and by the exposure of the frauds of Babylonian Thais by the same men. The Roman people, girded with the power of the ten horns, did not abandon Babylon, the Harlot. That is, the kings were many, at least not fewer than ten (for this is enough to magnify the terror and power of the Beast), and they joined their forces with the Roman people and, each in his own place, united in virtue [συμφερτῇ ἀρετῇ], upheld the Papacy and attacked the Lamb.

units.la: XXII. Quod si calculum ponere, & numerum decem Regum, Bestiæ cornuum, inire luber (quanquam id præcisè necessarium non est, cùm constet, Scripturam numero signato ac certo pro incerto & vago uti) non penitùs id in τῶν ἀδιαφόρων erit. Constat inprimis, agi de Regibus tributariis & vasallis Papæ. Non enim simpliciter βασιλεῖς, sed ὡς βασιλεῖς, tanquam Reges, adeóque precarii, servientes, appellantur. Legat igitur, qui volet, Epistolas Hildebrandi, qui primus aperto Marte temporalem in Reges & Imperáperatores potestatem affectavit. Is feuda sua profitetur Lib. viij.ep.ult. Hispanias, Gallias, Saxoniam, Hungariam; Lib. ij.ep. 13.63.70. Russiam; ibid. ep. 74. Dalmatiam; Lib.vij. ep.4. Corsicam; Lib.v.ep.4. & L.vj.ep.12. utriusque Siciliae Regnum. Imperatorem ipsum a Papa investituram accipere; tralatitium est. Ad nutum Papae Venetos arma movisse, Baronius tom. ix. A. 726. n. 28. docet. Thusciam & Liguriam Mathildis dono Romanae sedi dediisse perhibetur. Majoricam & Minoricam eidem Hildebrandus Lib. i. ep. 378. vindicat. Sardiniam ad jus Papae pertinere Innocentius III. de Praescript. L. si diligenti affirmat. Danorum Regem Hildebrandus. lib. ij. ep. 51. invitat, ut se, Regnumque suum sibi committat. Lusitaniae duces Regium titulum a Papa Alexandro III. habuisse Innocentius III. lib. i. ep. 100. 441. 448. 449. testatur. Angliae Regem Innocentius IV. teste Matthaeo Paris ad A. 12. 13. audacter vasallum, imo mancipium suum vocat. Ex his Reges Bestiae cornua, R. Pontifici addictissimi nullo negotio colligi decem possunt, puta Rex Hispaniarum, Lusitaniae, Angliae, Daniae, Franciae, Germaniae, Hungariae, Poloniae utriusque Siciliae, Principes & Principatus Italiae.
units.tr: XXII. If I were to make a calculation and seek out the number of the ten kings, the horns of the Beast, this would not be altogether a matter of indifference (although it is not strictly necessary, since it is established that Scripture uses a definite number for an indefinite and vague one). First, it is clear that the question concerns kings who are tributaries and vassals of the Pope. For they are not called simply kings [βασιλεῖς], but as kings [ὡς βασιλεῖς], as if kings, and therefore precarious, servile. Let him who wishes read the letters of Hildebrand, who first openly sought temporal power over kings and emperors. He acknowledges as his fiefs Spain, Gaul, Saxony and Hungary (Book 8, last letter); Russia (Book 2, letters 13, 63, 70); Dalmatia (ibid., letter 74); Corsica (Book 7, letter 4); and the kingdom of both Sicilies (Book 5, letter 4, and Book 6, letter 12). That the emperor himself receives investiture from the Pope is commonplace. That the Venetians took up arms at the Pope's nod, Baronius (vol. 9, A.D. 726, n. 28) teaches. Tuscany and Liguria are said to have been given to the Roman see by the gift of Matilda. Hildebrand claims Majorca and Minorca for the same see (Book 1, letter 378). Innocent III, in De Praescriptionibus, law si diligenti, affirms that Sardinia belongs to the right of the Pope. Hildebrand invites the King of the Danes (Book 2, letter 51) to commit himself and his kingdom to him. Innocent III testifies (Book 1, letters 100, 441, 448, 449) that the dukes of Lusitania had received the royal title from Pope Alexander III. Innocent IV, according to Matthew Paris (A.D. 1213), boldly calls the King of England his vassal, indeed his serf. From these, the horns of the Beast, the kings most devoted to the Roman Pontiff, can without any difficulty be gathered into ten: namely the King of the Spains, of Lusitania, of England, of Denmark, of France, of Germany, of Hungary, of Poland, of both Sicilies, and the princes and principalities of Italy.

units.la: XXIII. Quia tamen mentio est Regum, qui μίαν ὥραν una hora, certo tempore potestatem cum Bestia accipientes, belligeraturi cum Agno, & ab eodem vincendi erant, proclive erit etiam censum instituere Regum decem, qui Reformationis tempore opem Bestiae, & per eam Meretricis ipsi sustentandae tulerunt. Uno quippe eodemque tempore potestatem suam Bestiae & imagini ejus dederunt Germania, Hispania, Gallia, Anglia, Scotia, Hibernia, Hungaria, Dania, Suecia, Bohemia. Quantis viribus in Germania Carolus, in Hispania idem Carolus, & mox filius ejus Philippus II. in Gallia Franciscus I. in Anglia & Hibernia Henricus VIII. in Scotia Maria, in Hungaria Ludovicus, eique succedaneus Ferdinandus; in Dania Christiernus; in Suecia Sigismundus; in Bohemia Ferdinandus, alii pro Clero Romanæ Ecclesiæ dominante pugnárunt? In omnibus idem regnabat Spiritus, consilium idem fervebat, nempe ad tranquillitatem status, religionem & pietatem usurpari suetam, auctoritate legibúsque humanis constituendam, neque permittendum cuiquam esse, ut diversum à reliquis sapiat. Cúmque invenirent in mundo Bestiam habentem nomen Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, & in qua hucusque vera Ecclesia Sanctorum cum Ecclesia malignantium, Bestiæ & Agni asseclæ, commixti egerunt, facile animum induxerunt, ut pro ea, quam Ecclesiam Catholicam reputabant, depugnarent, & seducti, assuetíque avitis erroribus, cum ipso Agno, inscii & communi errore abrepti, voluntariáque superstitione fascinati, sacro bell² decernerent.
units.tr: XXIII. Since there is mention of the kings who, one hour [μίαν ὥραν], receiving power with the Beast for a set time, were to make war on the Lamb and be conquered by him, it will be easy to draw up a list of the ten kings who, at the time of the Reformation, brought aid to the Beast and through it to the Harlot whom they were to sustain. For at one and the same time Germany, Spain, France, England, Scotland, Ireland, Hungary, Denmark, Sweden and Bohemia gave their power to the Beast and to its image. With what forces did Germany under Charles, Spain under the same Charles and soon after under his son Philip II, France under Francis I, England and Ireland under Henry VIII, Scotland under Mary, Hungary under Louis and his successor Ferdinand, Denmark under Christian, Sweden under Sigismund, and Bohemia under Ferdinand, fight for the clergy of the Roman Church in power? In all of them the same spirit reigned and the same design burned: that the religion and piety customary in the Church should be retained for the sake of the peace of the state, established by authority and human laws, and that no one should be allowed to think differently from the rest. And when they found in the world a Beast bearing the name of the Catholic Church, in which until now the true Church of the saints has mingled and acted together with the Church of the wicked, the followers of the Beast and of the Lamb, they readily made up their minds to fight for what they regarded as the Catholic Church, and, led astray and accustomed to their ancestral errors, carried off by common error along with the Lamb himself, and charmed by voluntary superstition, they resolved on holy war.

units.la: XXIV. Distingui hic potest conflictus Bestiæ & cor- nuum ejus cum Sanctis, à conflictu eorundem cum Agno.
units.tr: XXIV. Here the conflict of the Beast and its horns with the saints can be distinguished from their conflict with the Lamb.

units.la: Jam pridem enim à Bestia & cornibus ejus oppugnari coeperant Sancti quando videlicet ii errores, superstitiones, peccata in externo Ecclesiæ coetu invalescentia reprehenderunt, iisdemque animosè se opposuerunt. Hac enim de causa illi hæreticos damnati, & multi eorum morte puniti sunt. Interim Imperatores non nulli, & Reges multi Papæ authoritatem Regnúmque concutere & retundere non formidarunt. Ubi verò planè masculum illorum robur evanguit, atque illi seu vitio suo, seu rebus adversis fracti, fasces suos Papæ insolescenti submiserunt, tum demum Agnus ipse directè impeti coepit, & subservitum est Papæ, sicaput Ecclesiæ infallibile jactanti, & hæreticos damnanti eos omnes, qui negare sustinerent, ullius verbum præter quam Christi in Ecclesia audiendum, aut pertimescendum esse. Hoc quidem post Concilium Constantiense apertè fa-ctum
units.tr: For the saints had already begun to be attacked by the Beast and its horns when, that is, they rebuked those errors, superstitions and sins that were gaining strength in the external assembly of the Church, and opposed them courageously. For this reason they were condemned as heretics, and many of them were punished with death. Meanwhile some emperors and many kings did not fear to shake and beat down the authority and rule of the Pope. But when their manly strength had clearly failed, and they, broken either by their own fault or by adverse circumstances, submitted their rods to the Pope, who was growing insolent, then at last the Lamb himself began to be attacked directly, and submission was made to the Pope, who boasted that he was the infallible head of the Church and who condemned as heretics all who dared to deny that the word of anyone but Christ in the Church was to be heard or feared. This was indeed openly done after the Council of Constance.

units.la: Bestia cornuum conflictus Sanctis Agno dimicat ctum est. Licet enim paulò post in Basileensi Concilio definitum esset, Concilium esse supra Papam, facilè tamen Eugenius in Conciliabulo Florentino seorsim instituto, & successores ejus, cumprimis Julius & Leo in Concilio Lateranensi adversus Pisanum, aliquid contra Papam ausum, congregato, definitionis illius fulmen cusa definitione contraria, ne à sententia Papæ ad Concilium appellare fas cuiquam sit, extinxerunt. Cùmque non obstantibus Papalibus ejusmodi ψηφισμασι Lutherus à Leone X. damnatus ad Concilium provocâsset, & Papæ denique authoritatem in controversiam vocâsset, Christumque unum solum Ecclesiæ Caput & Dominum vindicâsset, tum demum Bestia cum cornibus suis Papæ suppetias tulerunt, Leoni Lutherum damnanti strenuè inservierunt, & Lutheranos passim, maximè propter hoc doctrinæ caput, neci dederunt. Quid in Germania passim, Hispania, Gallia, Anglia, Scotia, Portugallia, Hungaria, Bohemia, alibíque factum sit, historiarum monumenta, Martyrúmque fasti, testatum abundè faciunt.
units.tr: For although it was soon afterwards defined at the Council of Basel that the Council is above the Pope, nevertheless Eugenius, in the conciliabulum at Florence which he held separately, and his successors, above all Julius and Leo in the Lateran Council assembled against the Pisan council, which had dared something against the Pope, by a contrary definition extinguished the thunderbolt of that definition, so that it should be lawful for no one to appeal from the sentence of the Pope to a council. And when, notwithstanding such papal decrees, Luther, condemned by Leo X, had appealed to a council, and had finally called the authority of the Pope into question, and had claimed that Christ alone is the one Head and Lord of the Church, then at last the Beast with its horns came to the aid of the Pope, zealously served Leo in condemning Luther, and everywhere put the Lutherans to death, above all on account of this main point of doctrine. What was done in Germany, Spain, France, England, Scotland, Portugal, Hungary, Bohemia and elsewhere, the records of histories and the calendars of martyrs bear abundant witness.

units.la: XXV. Quem verò, inquies, Bestiæ & cornuum ejus conflictus ille cum Agno successum nactus est? Respondeat Angelus ipse v. 14. Et Agnus vincet eos, (decem Reges) quia Dominus Dominorum est, & Rex Regum, & qui cum ipso vocati, & electi & fideles. Neque hoc oraculum eventus destituit. Vicit Sathanum Christus, & cessit iræ gratiæ. Nunquam enim Sancti, vocati, electi, alii præterquam Christo se subjecerunt. Est autem quædam victoria non vinci. Simul etiam quando Christi authoritas à Bestia & cornibus ejus oppugnata est, palmæ instar sub pondere illo surrexit, à jugo Babylonis liberata, ex eadem exivit. Pax enim post conflictationem multiplicem ei data est primò in Imperio Germanico, dein in aliis etiam Regnis, in quibus ipsimet Reges Meretricem agnoscere, & flagrantes, adeóque sancto perfectóque odio odisse coeperunt. In Anglia enim post Eduardum & Johannam Grajam Elisabetha Ecclesiæ se addixit tota. In Scotia Mariæ Jacobus vi. successit, & Regnum à Babylonis tyrannide liberavit. In Suecia in locum Sigismundi persecutoris, qui Poloniæ Rex factus est, Carolus patruus ejus subiit, doctrinæ Euangelicæ addictus. In Dania & Norwegia Christierno Fridericus succesit, Euangelicam veritatem ipse quoque amplexus. Taceo, quod in Gallia quoque, Hungaria, Bohemia, Polonia, Belgio Hispanico Euangelicis pactorum vi religionis libertas concessa est; & apud quosdam effectum est, si non ut veritatem amarent, tamen ut meretricem odio haberent, ejusque carnes comederent: qua de re in loco pluribus agendum fuerit.
units.tr: XXV. But, you will ask, what success did that conflict of the Beast and its horns with the Lamb have? Let the angel himself answer, v. 14: The Lamb will conquer them (the ten kings), because he is Lord of lords, and King of kings, and those who are with him are called, and chosen, and faithful. Nor has this oracle been left unfulfilled by the event. Christ has conquered Satan, and yielded to grace in his wrath. For never have the saints, the called, the chosen, submitted themselves to anyone but Christ. There is, however, a certain victory in not being conquered. At the same time, when the authority of Christ was attacked by the Beast and its horns, it rose like a palm under that weight, and, freed from the yoke of Babylon, came forth from it. For peace was given to it after manifold struggle, first in the German Empire, then also in other kingdoms, in which the kings themselves began to acknowledge the Harlot and to hate her with a burning and therefore holy and perfect hatred. For in England, after Edward and Lady Jane Grey, Elizabeth gave herself wholly to the Church. In Scotland James VI succeeded Mary and freed the kingdom from the tyranny of Babylon. In Sweden, in place of Sigismund the persecutor, who became king of Poland, his uncle Charles succeeded, devoted to the evangelical doctrine. In Denmark and Norway Frederick succeeded Christian, having himself also embraced the evangelical truth. I pass over the fact that in France too, Hungary, Bohemia, Poland and the Spanish Netherlands, freedom of religion was granted by the force of evangelical treaties; and among some it was brought about that, if they did not love the truth, they at least held the Harlot in hatred and ate her flesh. This matter will have to be treated at more length in another place.

units.la: XXVI. Concludimus, Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem, Bestiam septicipitem, septimontiam & διναμεγίνου habere sibi obnoxiam parentémque, adeóque cæteris partibus, Babylonem Magnam esse. "Οπερ εἰδον δἐζαι.
units.tr: XXVI. We conclude that the hierarchy, or the clergy of the Roman Church in power, has the sevenfold-headed Beast, the seven-hilled one, and has the one that is subject to it and is its parent, and therefore in other respects is the Great Babylon. Which I saw [ὅπερ εἶδον].

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS VIII.
units.tr: DISSERTATION VIII.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA,
units.tr: THIRD SECTION,

units.la: QUA
units.tr: IN WHICH

units.la: Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem sibi, Imperii ecclesiastici & spiritualis titulo, summum & merè terrenum in Reges & populos terræ Imperium vendicare asseritur, tertiumque argumentum concluditur.
units.tr: The hierarchy, or the clergy of the Roman Church ruling over itself, is shown to claim for itself, under the title of ecclesiastical and spiritual empire, the supreme and purely earthly empire over the kings and peoples of the earth, and the third argument is concluded.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Hierarchia Papalis ita Regnis mundi præest, ut in ea sibi spiritualis & Ecclesiastici titulo merè terrenum Imperium vindicet, II. quod conspicuum Babylonis M. Criterion est. III. Probatio innexa Syllogismo, cujus propositio est ἀνάγκη, assumtio uberius demonstratur. IV. Tyrannorum differentia. Babylon, Papa Mysterii obtentu, adeòque fraude Imperium quæsivit. V. Regnum Dei in mundo essentiale & Oecumenicum distinguitur: Illud Deus in Civitate mundana per homines administrat. VI. Secularis potestatis radix est immediata Dei institutio, & delegatio quorundam cæteris dominantium. Reges proin & Principes mundi à Deo immediatè dependent. Scholasticorum elenchus.
units.tr: I. The Papal hierarchy presides over the kingdoms of the world in such a way that, under the title of spiritual and ecclesiastical, it claims for itself a purely earthly empire, II. which is the conspicuous criterion of Great Babylon. III. The proof, bound into a syllogism whose major premise is necessity [ἀνάγκη], is demonstrated more fully in the minor premise. IV. The difference between tyrants. Babylon, under the pretext of the mystery, and so by fraud, sought empire. V. The kingdom of God in the world is distinguished into the essential and the oecumenical: God administers the former in the earthly city through men. VI. The root of secular power is the immediate institution of God and the delegation of some to rule over others. Kings and princes of the world therefore depend immediately on God. Refutation of the Scholastics.

units.la: VII. Solis terram illustrantis immediatè, & potestatis Secularis similitudo.
units.tr: VII. The sun illuminating the earth immediately, and the likeness of secular power.

units.la: VIII. Christus Rex temporalis nunquam fuit.
units.tr: VIII. Christ was never a temporal king.

units.la: IX. Proinetiam suis in Ecclesia Ministris Regnum temporale nunquam delegavit.
units.tr: IX. Therefore he never committed a temporal kingdom to his ministers in the Church either.

units.la: X. Regnum Christi œconomicum potestate legislatoria & & judiciali constat. Solus ille Ecclesiæ Caput est.
units.tr: X. The economic kingdom of Christ consists in legislative and judicial power. He alone is the Head of the Church.

units.la: XI. Neque in Cælum digressus potestatem dominantem ulli homini communicavit.
units.tr: XI. Nor, having departed into heaven, did he communicate ruling power to any man.

units.la: XII. Nullus proin homo per modum Capitis, sive interno, sive externo in ecclesiam influxu, eandem regit.
units.tr: XII. No man, therefore, rules the Church by way of head, whether by inward or outward influence.

units.la: XIII. Ecclesia ante, & post Christi in Cælum ascensum eadem, nonsimilis duntaxat, quoad regimen ejus est.
units.tr: XIII. The Church is the same before and after Christ's ascension into heaven; it is only similar as regards its government.

units.la: XIV. Christus ad gloriam evectus homines ministros duntaxat instituit, dominum neminem, & pari potestate omnes.
units.tr: XIV. Christ, raised to glory, appointed only men as ministers, no lord, and all with equal power.

units.la: XV. Quin dominationem quamvis in Ecclesia vetuit.
units.tr: XV. Indeed he forbade domination in the Church.

units.la: XVI. Claves Ecclesiæ dedit Regni Cœlorum, non terrarum.
units.tr: XVI. He gave the keys of the Kingdom of heaven, not of the earth.

units.la: XVII. Ecclesiæ universæ potestas tum spiritualis, tum ministerialis est.
units.tr: XVII. The power of the whole Church is both spiritual and ministerial.

units.la: XVIII. Temporalis potestas ecclesiastica essentialiter nec subjecta, nec subordinata est.
units.tr: XVIII. Ecclesiastical temporal power is essentially neither subject nor subordinate.

units.la: XIX. Potestas, & subjectum potestatem habens distinguitur.
units.tr: XIX. Power and the subject that holds power are distinguished.

units.la: XX. Bellarminus duplicem subordinationem distinguens refellitur.
units.tr: XX. Bellarmine, who distinguishes a twofold subordination, is refuted.

units.la: XXI. Hierarchici in explicanda potestatis secularis subordinatione sibi parum constant.
units.tr: XXI. The hierarchists are poorly consistent in explaining the subordination of secular power.

units.la: XXII. Solis & Lunæ similitudine subordinationem frustra Pontifices ipsi explicare conantur.
units.tr: XXII. The Pontiffs themselves try in vain to explain the subordination by the similitude of the sun and moon.

units.la: XXIII. Frustra etiam Bellarminus similitudine Spiritus & Carnis.
units.tr: XXIII. Bellarmine also tries in vain, by the similitude of spirit and flesh.

units.la: XXIV. Bonifacii viij. pro potestatis ecclesiasticæ in civi-lem imperio imbelles ratiunculæ.
units.tr: XXIV. The feeble little arguments of Boniface VIII for ecclesiastical power over the civil empire.

units.la: XXV. Potestatis utriusque civilis & ecclesiasticæ domi-nantis limites omnes Papa perrupit.
units.tr: XXV. The Pope has broken through all the limits of both civil and ecclesiastical dominant power.

units.la: XXVI. Supremam in Spiritualibus potestatem indulgen-te Phoca, rapuit. Argumenta ex Gregorio M. eidem opposita.
units.tr: XXVI. He seized supreme power in spiritual matters by the indulgence of Phocas. Arguments from Gregory the Great opposed to it.

units.la: XXVII. Baronii figmentum de nomine Episcopi univer-salis à Gregorio oppugnato, elisum.
units.tr: XXVII. Baronius's fiction about the title of universal bishop, opposed by Gregory, is refuted.

units.la: XXVIII. Florentinæ Synodi de potestate summa Papæ in Spiritualibus definitio.
units.tr: XXVIII. The definition of the Council of Florence on the supreme power of the Pope in spiritual matters.

units.la: XXIX. Absolutæ potestatis Christo neutiquam subjectæ plenitudinem Papæ tribui, probatur.
units.tr: XXIX. It is proved that the fullness of absolute power, in no way subject to Christ, is attributed to the Pope.

units.la: XXX. Idem ex supremæ Majestatis indiciis, potestate le-gislatoria,
units.tr: XXX. The same is established from the marks of supreme majesty: the legislative power

units.la: XXXI. XXXII. & judiciali summa Papæ tributa con-ficitur.
units.tr: XXXI. and XXXII. and the judicial power, attributed to the Pope as supreme.

units.la: XXXIII. Extensio potestatis Pontificiæ ad subjectionem creaturæ omnis.
units.tr: XXXIII. The extension of papal power to the subjection of every creature.

units.la: XXXIV. Potestati absolutæ Papæ commentum infalli-bilitatis in quæstionibus juris & facti mirè velifica-tur.
units.tr: XXXIV. The fiction of infallibility is wonderfully added to the absolute power of the Pope in questions of right and of fact.

units.la: XXXV. Distinctionum infallibilitatis Papæ fucus.
units.tr: XXXV. The deceit of the distinctions of papal infallibility.

units.la: XXXVI. Papæ doctoris publici & privati distinguendi criteria nulla suppetunt.
units.tr: XXXVI. There are no criteria left for distinguishing the Pope as public teacher from the Pope as private teacher.

units.la: XXXVII. Prætextu potestatis in spiritualibus supremæ, potestatem supremam etiam in temporalibus Papa sibi rapuit; imò illam propter hanc sibi vendicavit.
units.tr: XXXVII. Under the pretext of supreme power in spiritual matters, the Pope seized supreme power also in temporal ones; indeed he claimed the former on account of the latter.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quadruplex potestas Papæ temporalis distin-guitur. Prima est in patrimonium Petri, seu statum Ecclesiasticum: Secunda in Regna homagio Ecclesiæ ob-stricta: Tertia in omnes reliquos Imperatores, Reges, Principes & populos.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The temporal power of the Pope is distinguished fourfold. The first is over the patrimony of Peter, or the ecclesiastical state; the second over kingdoms bound to the Church by homage; the third over all remaining emperors, kings, princes and peoples.

units.la: XXXIX. De potestate temporali Papæ, directa ea, an indirecta sit, Theologi, Canonistæ & Politici disceptant; Politici utramque inficiantur.
units.tr: XXXIX. Theologians, canonists and politicians dispute whether the temporal power of the Pope is direct or indirect; the politicians deny both.

units.la: XL. Theologi indirectam, ratione potestatis spiritualis temporali dominantis, Canonistæ directam propugnant.
units.tr: XL. Theologians defend an indirect power, by reason of his spiritual power ruling over the temporal; canonists defend a direct one.

units.la: XLI. Theologos Papæ in temporalibus potestatem verbis indirectam, re directam tueri, probatur tum sententia Bellarmini, quæ discutitur:
units.tr: XLI. It is proved that theologians defend an indirect power of the Pope in temporal matters in words, but a direct one in fact, both by the opinion of Bellarmine, which is examined:

units.la: XLII. tum quia potestatem ei supremam & legislatoriam,
units.tr: XLII. and because they claim for him supreme and legislative power,

units.la: XLIII. & judicialem, secundum quam exercere judicia civilia,
units.tr: XLIII. and judicial power, by which he may exercise civil judgments

units.la: XLIV. & personas Regum Principumque judicare possit, vendicant.
units.tr: XLIV. and judge the persons of kings and princes.

units.la: XLV. Theologi nonnulli, directam Papæ in temporalibus potestatem tribuentes, inducuntur.
units.tr: XLV. Some theologians who attribute direct power to the Pope in temporal matters are introduced.

units.la: XLVI. Bellarmini assertiones nonnullæ, ex quibus eum reapse directam Papæ potestatem agnoscere evincitur, erutæ.
units.tr: XLVI. Some assertions of Bellarmine are drawn out, from which it is shown that he in fact acknowledges a direct papal power.

units.la: XLVII. Baronii assertiones similes.
units.tr: XLVII. Similar assertions of Baronius.

units.la: XLVIII. Pontifices ipsos summam & directam in temporalibus potestatem sibi arrogare, probatur, primò, quia gnathones in tantum culmen cathedram suam extollentes æquo animo admittunt. Secundò, quia indirectam sibi potestatem tribuentibus indignantur. Tertiò, quia Canonistas, aliósque gnathones nullis hactenus censuris notant.
units.tr: XLVIII. It is proved that the Pontiffs themselves arrogate to themselves supreme and direct power in temporal matters: first, because they calmly admit flatterers who raise their chair to such a height. Second, because they are indignant at those who grant them only indirect power. Third, because they have so far marked canonists and other flatterers with no censures.

units.la: XLIX. Quartò quia Pontifices etiam rem ipsam definiunt, posthabitis distinctionibus asserentes, suum esse utrumque gladium.
units.tr: XLIX. Fourth, because the Pontiffs also define the matter itself, setting aside distinctions and asserting that both swords are theirs.

units.la: L. Quintò quia absolutam & directam in temporalibus potestatem exercent: uti liquet tum ex historia Bonifacii viij.
units.tr: L. Fifth, because they exercise absolute and direct power in temporal matters, as is clear both from the history of Boniface VIII

units.la: LI. tum ex actibus variis exercitæ erga Reges varios potestatis civilis:
units.tr: LI. and from the various acts of power exercised against various kings in civil matters.

units.la: LII. qui etiam Jurisconsultis Pontificiis, Roussel[i]o inprimis recensentur:
units.tr: LII. These are also recounted among the Papist jurists, Rousselius above all.

units.la: LIII. tum ex imperio, quo hactenus erga Imperatores, Reges & Principes usus est. Et primò quidem in Imperatorum constitutione & coronatione.
units.tr: LIII. and from the command which he has hitherto exercised over emperors, kings and princes. And first indeed in the creation and coronation of emperors.

units.la: LIV. Eo animo Imperatores à Papa coronari, ut sui juris & beneficii eosdem faciat, probatur ex historia Friderici Barbarossæ.
units.tr: LIV. That emperors are crowned by the Pope with the intention of making them subject to his right and benefice is proved from the history of Frederick Barbarossa.

units.la: LV. Ludovici Bavari.
units.tr: LV. of Louis of Bavaria.

units.la: LVI. Ferdinandi I.
units.tr: LVI. of Ferdinand I.

units.la: LVII. nec non ex dogmatis Pontificiis, qualia sunt, quòd authoritate Papali Imperium ab Orientalibus ad Occidentales translatum sit, Electorum Romani Imperii institutio Papam authorem habeat, & vacantis Imperii administratio ad Papam redeat:
units.tr: LVII. and also from Papist dogmas, such as that by papal authority the empire was transferred from the Easterners to the Westerners, that the institution of the electors of the Roman Empire has the Pope as its author, and that the administration of a vacant empire returns to the Pope.

units.la: LVIII. denique ex juramento, quo Imperatores sibi Papa devincit.
units.tr: LVIII. Finally, from the oath by which the Pope binds emperors to himself.

units.la: LIX. Regum etiam constitutionem & coronationem ad se Pontifices traxerunt, ut eorundem sceptra sibi subjicerent.
units.tr: LIX. The Pontiffs have also drawn the creation and coronation of kings to themselves, so that they might subject their sceptres to themselves.

units.la: LX. In Imperatoribus Regibúsque constituendis eodem jure Papa utitur, quo Romani Imperatores Ethnici olim usi sunt, quod Pontificiæ dominationis arcanum meritò habetur.
units.tr: LX. In creating emperors and kings the Pope uses the same right that the pagan Roman emperors once used, which is rightly regarded as the secret of papal domination.

units.la: LXI. Qua in constituendis Imperatoribus & Regibus, eadem in deponendis iisdem potestate Papa, Excommunicationis peregrino fine usurpatæ subsidio, utitur.
units.tr: LXI. In creating emperors and kings, and in deposing them, the Pope uses the same power, employing excommunication, usurped for an alien end, as an aid.

units.la: LXII. Initium factum ab Imperatoribus Orientalibus:
units.tr: LXII. The beginning was made with the Eastern emperors.

units.la: LXIII. promotum Gregorii vij. & succedentium tempore etiam ad Occidentales. Excommunicatorum & depositorum à Papa Imperatorum septem, Regúmque plurium exempla.
units.tr: LXIII. It was advanced in the time of Gregory VII and his successors even to Western ones. Examples of seven emperors excommunicated and deposed by the Pope, and of several kings.

units.la: LXIV. Excommunicatos Reges & Principes quo loco Papa habeat, ex Urbani II. decreto, & Pauli IV. bulla, aliísque ostenditur.
units.tr: LXIV. Where the Pope places excommunicated kings and princes is shown from the decree of Urban II, the bull of Paul IV, and others.

units.la: LXV. In eosdem omnia, quæ in privatos licere, quin occidi etiam eos, si vi Regnum retineant, posse, iidem pertendunt.
units.tr: LXV. They maintain that everything permitted against private persons is permitted against these, and that they may even be killed if they hold the kingdom by force.

units.la: LXVI. Causa abdicandorum ita Principum sola hæresis à Perronio, ab aliis longè plures recensentur.
units.tr: LXVI. Perronius alone cites heresy as the cause for deposing princes; others cite far more.

units.la: LXVII. Quarta Pontificis potestas est in Clerum universum quoad temporalia æquè ac spiritualia. De exemptione à Civili potestate Cleri decreta Bonifacii VIII. Conciliorum Constantiensis & Tridentini.
units.tr: LXVII. The fourth power of the Pope is over the whole clergy, in temporal matters as much as in spiritual. On the exemption of the clergy from civil power, as decreed by Boniface VIII and the Councils of Constance and Trent.

units.la: LXVIII. De eadem sententia Suarezii & Bellarmini propósita, obitérque perstricta.
units.tr: LXVIII. The same opinion of Suárez and Bellarmine is set forth and briefly censured.

units.la: LXIX. Dei verbo exemplis V. & N. T. Imperatorum Christianorum legibus, Reipublicæ utilitati quàm maximè illa adversatur.
units.tr: LXIX. By the word of God, by examples from the Old and New Testament, and by the laws of Christian emperors, this is most adverse to the utility of the commonwealth.

units.la: LXX. Querelæ Pontificum de violatis Ecclesiæ libertatibus iniquitas. Bullæ Cœnæ Domini adversus Imperatores, Reges &c. crudelitas.
units.tr: LXX. The complaints of the Pontiffs about violated liberties of the Church are unjust. The cruelty of the bull In Coena Domini against emperors, kings and others.

units.la: LXXI. Gersonis rationes, quòd ob temporalia nemo excommunicari possit, Pontificiis oppositæ.
units.tr: LXXI. Gerson's reasons, that no one can be excommunicated on account of temporal matters, set against the Papists.

units.la: LXXII. Potestatem, quam Spiritualis, & Ecclesiasticæ jurisdictionis prætextu Papa extra territorium suum usurpat, esse imperium merè terrenum, evidenti argumento, quod Ecclesia jurisdictionem propriè dictam nullam habeat, conficitur,
units.tr: LXXII. That the power which the Pope usurps outside his own territory, under the pretext of spiritual and ecclesiastical jurisdiction, is purely earthly empire, is concluded by the clear argument that the Church has no jurisdiction properly so called.

units.la: LXXIII. & argumentum concluditur,
units.tr: LXXIII. and the argument is concluded,

units.la: LXXIV. atque Papæ Innocentii IV. ipsius consensu amplius firmatur.
units.tr: LXXIV. and it is further confirmed by the consent of Pope Innocent IV himself.

units.la: I. Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiae Romanae dominantem in Civitate Magna praesse populo magno, quem Bestiae nomine. Prophetia insignit, hactenus apertae veritati dedimus. Superest ad argumenti tertii, quo eandem Hierarchiam Babylonem M. esse astruimus, plenam apodixin membrum tertium, quo demonstrandum denceps est, Hierarchiam seu Clerum Ecclesiae Romanae dominantem ita Populo Magno, Imperio Romano Pseudo-Christiano, Regnisque compluribus praesse, ut in ea summum sibi, Spiritualis & Ecclesiastici titulo, merè terrenum imperium, dominiumque vendicet.
units.tr: I. We have set out the truth plainly that the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, presides in the Great City over the great people, which the prophecy marks with the name of the Beast. There remains, for the third argument, by which we assert that the same hierarchy is Great Babylon, a complete proof in its third member, in which it must now be shown that the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, presides over the Great People, the Pseudo-Christian Roman Empire, and many kingdoms, in such a way that in them it claims for itself, under the title of spiritual and ecclesiastical, the supreme and purely earthly empire and dominion.

units.la: II. Etenim Babylonis Magnae conspicuum criterion Prophetia statuit, quòd Regnum in populos, Regna multa, Bestiam Regibus sociatam pluribus, gerit. Propterea enim Mulier illa, magna Meretrix sedere super aquis multis Apoc. xvii. 1, 15. super Bestia coccinea, septicipite; septimontia, & decem cornua, ibid. v. 3. & Bestia portare illam, v. 7. Mulier in septem montibus sedere, v. 9. dicitur. Sedet autem super aquis multis, super Bestia coccinea, ut earum Domina & rectrix. Sicut jumenti insessor ejusdem Dominus & rector est. Hinc adeò Mulier illa jactabunda in corde suo dicit, Apoc. xviii. 7. Sedeo Regina, ut sessione Regiam potestatem significari, dubitari non possit. Vicissim Bestia Mulierem eam portat, ut animal subjugale mutum 2 Pet. ii. 16. adeoque Mulieris Imperio obnoxium. Aperte verò v. 18. Mulier definitur Civitas illa Magna quae Regnum habet in Reges terrae, ubi Civitatis Magnae genuina & formalis proprietas statuitur, imperare Regibus terrae. Cùmque Regnum illud Civitatis Magnæ ita declaretur, ut ei subjiciantur Reges seu Principes politici, adeóque imperio politico illud contradistinguatur, Ecclesiasticam indigitari, hoc est, merè temporale licet, Ecclesiastici tamen & spiritualis prætextu titulóque fucatum, consequitur, quod ipsum etiam Differt. iij. 18. uberiús confirmavimus.
units.tr: II. Indeed, the prophecy sets out a clear mark of Great Babylon: it holds dominion over peoples and many kingdoms, and it carries the Beast joined with many kings. For this reason that woman, the great harlot, is said to sit upon many waters (Rev. 17:1, 15), upon a scarlet beast (ibid. v. 3) with seven heads, seven mountains, and ten horns, and the Beast is said to carry her (v. 7), and the woman sits on seven mountains (v. 9). She sits upon the waters, and upon the scarlet beast, as their lady and ruler, just as the rider of a beast is its master and driver. Hence that boastful woman says in her heart, "I sit a queen" (Rev. 18:7). That sitting signifies royal power, and no one can doubt it. In turn, the Beast carries her as a dumb beast of burden (2 Pet. 2:16), and so is subject to the woman's rule. Moreover, at v. 18 the woman is described as that great city, which has a kingdom over the kings of the earth, where the true and formal property of the Great City is laid down: to rule over the kings of the earth. Since that kingdom of the Great City is declared in such a way that kings or political princes are subject to it, and so it is distinguished from political empire, it follows that an ecclesiastical power is indicated: a power that is merely temporal, yet disguised under the pretext and title of the ecclesiastical and spiritual. We have confirmed this more fully in Differt. iii. 18.

units.la: III. Ejusmodi Imperium sibi Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem in Reges & populos terræ, ipsamque adeò Bestiam sibi subditam arrogare & gerere, sequenti syllogismo conficimus:
units.tr: III. We establish by the following syllogism that such an empire claims for itself, and exercises, a hierarchy or clergy of the Roman Church that dominates over the kings and peoples of the earth, and so subjects the Beast itself to itself:

units.la: Quicunque Cœtus in Principe suo supremam in spiritualibus potestatem sibi arrogat, ejusque prætextu & titulo summum, atque illud merè terrenum & temporale in Reges & populos terræ imperium gerit, ille Ecclesiasticæ & Spiritualis potestatis titulo Regnum in Reges & populos terræ terrenum obtinet, & ceu Regina super aquis multis, ipsaque Bestia sedet; adeoque cæteris paribus, est Babylon Magna.
units.tr: Whatever body claims for itself supreme power in spiritual matters over its prince, and under the pretext and title of that power exercises supreme and purely earthly and temporal empire over the kings and peoples of the earth, that body holds an earthly kingdom over the kings and peoples of the earth by the title of ecclesiastical and spiritual power, and sits as a queen over many waters, and upon the Beast itself; and therefore, other things being equal, it is Great Babylon.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans in Principe suo, Papa, supremam in Spiritualibus sibi potestatem arrogat, ejusque prætextu & titulo summum, atque illud merè terrenum & temporale in Reges & populos terræ imperium gerit.
units.tr: But the Hierarchy, or the Clergy of the Church of Rome, ruling through its prince, the Pope, claims for itself supreme power in spiritual matters, and under the pretext and title of that power it wields a supreme empire over kings and peoples of the earth, one that is purely earthly and temporal.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans in Principe suo, Papa, Ecclesiastica & Spiritualis potestatis titulo Regnum in Reges & populos terræ terrenum obtinet, & ceu Regina super aquis multis ipsaque Bestia sedet, adeoque cæteris paribus, est Babylon Magna.
units.tr: Therefore the Hierarchy, or the Clergy of the Church of Rome, ruling through its prince, the Pope, holds an earthly kingdom over kings and peoples of the earth under the title of ecclesiastical and spiritual power, and sits like a queen over many waters, and on the beast itself; and so, other things being equal, it is Babylon the Great.

units.la: Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ heic non simpliciter, sed in Principe suo Papa, diserte nomine, quia is ceu Monarcha, solus, summæ potestatis in Hierarchia illa subjectum, Hierarchici verò reliqui omnes, quisque suo loco & gradu, dominationis instrumenta, & Papæ Domini sui respectu, subditi & vasalli habentur. Quo sensu intellecta Propositio dubitationem omnino nullam habere poteft, neque de ejus nexu, puto, sanus quisquam ambiget. Neque etiam Assumtio magis revocari in dubium potest, quam supra Differt. vi. 60-64. obiter jam astruximus. Inprælentiarum tamen uberiorem argumento lucem fœneraturi, de Pontificis potestate consentanea ei, quam Prophetia Babyloni tribuit, paulò differendum fuisse fuerit.
units.tr: Here I name the Hierarchy, or the Clergy of the Church of Rome, not simply but expressly in its prince, the Pope, because he alone, as monarch, is the subject of supreme power within that Hierarchy, while all the other members of the Hierarchy, each in his own place and rank, are regarded as instruments of domination and, in relation to the Pope as their lord, as subjects and vassals. Understood in this sense, the proposition cannot admit any doubt at all, and I think no sane person doubts its connection. Nor can the Assumption be called into question any more than we have already briefly established above in Dissertation vi, pp. 60–64. Yet since we are now about to bring a fuller light to the argument, it would have been fitting to say a little more about the power of the Pontiff, which corresponds to that which the prophecy ascribes to Babylon.

units.la: IV. Solent tyranni non tam fraude, quàm aperta vi sibi ad dominationem iniquam gradum munire. Quidam tamen & fraude & vi, arte & Marte, vulpina & leonina indole usi, ad eandem grassantur, uti impostor insignis Muhammed, & Propheram Divinitus missum se mentitus, & aperta vi dominationem rapuit. Babylon Magna, ejusque Princeps Papa Mysterii titulo, fraude potiùs, quàm aperta vi, in populos & Reges terræ imperium affectavit; atque illud fraude & malis artibus quæsitum vi retinet, licet Ecclesiastici, spiritualis Regiminis fuco perpetim illitum. Primò igitur potestatem Spiritualem, ecclesiasticam soli Christo eximiam, invasit, sibique sine juris tabulis vindicavit. Tum potestatis illius prætextu & titulo, non tam Politici, quàm Ecclesiastici Principis axioma præ se ferens, adeóque transmissis inanibus vim imperii intuitus, in Reges & populos, terræ imperium merè terrenum erexit. Id quibus gradibus & modis processerit, Historia Papatus distinctis periodis in aprico statuit. Sicut igitur olim Zopyrus apud Babylonios amicum ementitus, arte perfecit, quod frustrà Marte Darius tentavit: ita Papa mysterii obtentu id assecutus est, quod aperto Marte nemo alius, quantumvis potentia, robore & sapientia præpollens, assequi potuisset unquam.
units.tr: IV. Tyrants usually fortify their path to unjust domination not so much by fraud as by open force. Some, however, using both fraud and force, art and war, with the nature of the fox and of the lion, press on to the same end, as the notorious impostor Muhammed did, who falsely claimed to be a prophet sent by God and seized dominion by open violence. Babylon the Great, and her prince the Pope, under the title of Mystery, aimed at empire over the peoples and kings of the earth by fraud rather than by open force; and having sought it by fraud and wicked arts, she keeps it by force, though always smeared over with the paint of ecclesiastical, spiritual government. First, then, she invaded spiritual and ecclesiastical power, which belongs uniquely to Christ, and claimed it for herself without any title-deeds. Then, under the pretext and title of that power, bearing the maxim of a political rather than an ecclesiastical prince, and so, having passed over empty forms and looking to the reality of power, she raised up an empire over kings and peoples that is purely earthly. By what steps and methods this came about, the history of the Papacy sets out clearly in distinct periods. Thus, just as Zopyrus once, feigning friendship among the Babylonians, accomplished by craft what Darius had vainly attempted by war, so the Pope, under cover of the Mystery, has achieved what no one else, however powerful, strong and wise, could ever have achieved by open war.

units.la: V. Duplex omnino in mundo est potestas dominans, Regnum duplex, unum essentiale Dei Patris, Filii, & Spiritus S. quo is mundum à se creatum potenter, providenter gubernat: alterum, Oeconomicum Christi, quod is secundum οἰκονομίαν gratiæ, singulari modo, qua Ὑπάρχων ... administrat. Illud Deus Triunus in civitate mundana per homines, suos in mundo vicarios & delegatos, liberè, sapientérque ita administrat, ut potestatem eminentem, quà subditos partim sapienti vigilantique directione, partim vi armata in officio contineant, iis conferat. Non tantùm enim natura, quæ hominem progignit ζῷον πολιτικόν animal civile, sociale, & alios quidem virtute dominandi, & supremam etiam puppis partem occupandi; alios propensione ad serviendum in imis etiam quandoque subselliis, instruit, imperandi parendique ordinem in humano genere sancit; sed etiam verbum Dei illum clarissimis verbis confirmat, explicans scilicet, quæ sit illa natura, quæ hominem πολιτικὸν civilem esse voluit, & civitates instituit, adeóque alios imperare, parere alios jussit. Non est potestas, ita S. Paulus Rom. xiii. 1. 2. nisi à Deo. Quæ autem sunt potestates, à Deo ordinatæ sunt. Qui igitur potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Manifestum igitur est, Deum ipsum naturæ humanæ propensionem ad dominandum vel parendum ita implantâsse, ut, ubicunque potestas rectrix & gubernatrix apparet, eam immediatè à Deo non aliunde esse, constet. Qui author est totius naturæ humanæ, idem ordinis adeò necessarii, non alius quisquam author esse potuit. Christus ipse Joh. xix. 11. in potestate Pilati idem innuit, respondens ipsi: Non haberes potestatem adversus me ullam, nisi tibi data esset desuper. Scitè proin S. Augustinus contra Faust. lib. xxÿ. 78. ait, æterna lege juberi, ut ordo naturalis conservetur.
units.tr: V. There are altogether two dominating powers in the world, two kingdoms: one is the essential kingdom of God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, by which he governs powerfully and providently the world created by himself; the other is the economic kingdom of Christ, which he administers in a singular manner according to the dispensation [οἰκονομίαν] of grace, by which he is [Ὑπάρχων ...]. The triune God administers the first in the worldly state, freely and wisely, through men, his vicars and delegates in the world, so that he bestows on them the eminent power by which they keep subjects in duty, partly by wise and watchful direction, partly by armed force. For nature, which begets man as a civil, social animal [ζῷον πολιτικόν], not only equips some with the virtue of ruling and of taking the highest place in the ship, and others with a disposition to serve, even at times on the lowest benches, and has established the order of commanding and obeying in the human race; but the word of God also confirms this most clearly, explaining what that nature is which willed that man be a political [πολιτικὸν], civil being, and founded states, and so ordered some to rule and others to obey. There is no power, so Saint Paul says (Rom. 13:1–2), except from God. The powers that exist are ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God. It is therefore plain that God himself has implanted in human nature such an inclination to rule or to obey that, wherever a governing and directing power appears, it is evident that it is not from anywhere else but immediately from God. He who is the author of all human nature could not be the author of any other, than of this necessary order. Christ himself, in John 19:11, signifies the same concerning the power of Pilate, answering him: You would have no power over me at all, unless it were given you from above. Rightly, therefore, Saint Augustine says against Faustus, book 22, chapter 78, that by eternal law it is commanded that the natural order be preserved.

units.la: Regnum Dei in mundo essentiale Oeconomicum ... dispensatur, Illud Deus in civitate mundana per homines administrat.
units.tr: The essential kingdom of God in the world... is dispensed economically; the former God administers in the worldly state through men.

units.la: VI. Radix igitur & Origo Secularis potestatis universæ est immediata Dei institutio, & delegatio quorundam cœteris dominantium, uti & natura & Dei verbum arguunt. Falsique adeo sunt Theologi Scholastici, aliique, qui Reges & Principes immediatè à Deo pendere negantes, potestatem omnem dominantem, toti equidem Reipublicæ corpori, & communitati à Deo immediatè concessam, at deinceps à communitate, cui illa velit tribui, asserunt; ita ut verum, proximum & immediatum subjectum potestatis secularis sit multitudo, cui immediatè illam Deus communicarit, Principibus tamen tradendam, sive uni, Monarchicè; sive pluribus, Aristocraticè; sive toti multitudini, Democraticè; quod Bellarminus de Laicis cap. 6. sustinet. Atqui potestas hæc non in universum duntaxat consideratā, sed etiam in particulari, prout est in hoc, vel illo statu, immediatè à Deo est. Quicunque enim in quolibet statu eam actu exercet, loco & vice Dei, ceu ab ipso immediatè delegatus, non multitudinis delegantis eam exercet, adeóque proximè & immediatè eam à Deo habet. Multitudo quippe naturaliter regi, non regere debet, próin naturaliter regenda, non rectiva est. Secus si foret, Reges non Divino, sed merè humano jure regnarent, neque verum esset, quod de se Divina Sapientia profitetur Prov. viii. 15. 16. Per me Reges regnant, & Principes justitiam decernunt, per me Principes dominantur, & Principes & omnes judices terræ. Frequentissimi quinetiam casus sunt, quibus multitudo rectori cuipiam juste prorsus, invita & repugnans, subjicitur. Quòd verò aliquando multitudo se ad eam regiminis formam redigit, quæ ei maximè placet, non aliud id arguit, quàm esse in multitudine potestatem deputandi, vel eligendi personam, seu personas, à quibus regatur. Deputatis verò jam & electis Deus immediatè potestatem politicam {a}icam concedit, cujus potestatis verum & immediatum subjectum non est multitudo, sed Rex, Senatus, populus, prout ipsa multitudo uni ex his formis subest.
units.tr: VI. The root and origin, therefore, of all secular power is the immediate institution of God, and the delegation of certain persons to rule over the others, as both nature and the word of God show. Those scholastic theologians, and others, are therefore mistaken, who deny that kings and princes depend immediately on God, and who say that all dominating power is granted immediately by God to the whole body of the commonwealth and community, but thereafter is handed on by the community to whomever it wishes; so that the true, proximate and immediate subject of secular power would be the multitude, to which God has immediately communicated it, yet to be entrusted to princes, whether to one, in monarchy; or to several, in aristocracy; or to the whole multitude, in democracy. Bellarmine maintains this in De laicis, chapter 6. But this power is immediately from God not only when considered in general, but also in particular, as it is in this or that state. For whoever in any state actually exercises it, in the place and stead of God, as one immediately delegated by him, does not exercise it as one delegated by the multitude, and so he holds it proximately and immediately from God. For the multitude, being by nature to be ruled and not to rule, is therefore by nature a thing to be governed, not a governing one. Otherwise, kings would reign not by divine but merely by human right, and it would not be true what Divine Wisdom professes of itself in Prov. 8:15–16: By me kings reign, and princes decree justice; by me princes rule, and the princes and all the judges of the earth. There are indeed very frequent cases in which a multitude is subjected quite justly to some ruler, even unwilling and resisting. But when the multitude at some time reduces itself to that form of government which pleases it most, this proves nothing other than that the multitude has the power of appointing or choosing the person, or persons, by whom it is to be governed. But once they have been appointed and chosen, God immediately grants political power, whose true and immediate subject is not the multitude but the king, the senate, or the people, according as the multitude itself is subject to one of these forms.

units.la: VII. Sicut igitur lumen, quo terra illustratur, merito dicitur immediatè esse à Sole, etiamsi prius, saltem naturā, idem lumen recipiatur in multis inferioribus sphæris & elementis, quæ terram immediatè illuminant, cùm lumen ubicunque est, proximè & immediatè soli Soli acceptum referatur, utpote qui solus lumen efficit, licet aër illud deferat, & terræ applicet: Sic potestas secularis summa, in quocunque demum sit, immediatè à solo Deo est, licet ab hominibus & per homines applicetur, quia ab ipso solo efficitur, est, quod est, & potest. Communitas enim personam eligens, quæ summa potestate utatur, non tam potestatem Divinam, utpote quam ipsa non habet, personis, quàm personas potestati Divinæ applicat, quia non potestas, sed personæ potestatem acceptura determinatio à Deo ei concessa est.
units.tr: VII. Just as the light by which the earth is illuminated is rightly said to come immediately from the Sun, even though it is first received, at least in nature, in many lower spheres and elements that light the earth directly, since wherever light is found it is referred immediately and proximately to the Sun alone, which alone produces light, although the air carries it and applies it to the earth, so supreme secular power, in whatever form it exists, comes immediately from God alone, although it is applied by men and through men, because it is by God alone that it is effected that it is what it is and can do what it can. For the community that elects a person to exercise supreme power does not so much apply the divine power to the persons (since it does not itself possess that power) as apply the persons to the divine power, because it is not the power but the persons who are to receive it that are designated, and the designation is granted to them by God.

units.la: VIII. Regnum temporale Christus, qua Mediator & homo, neque in terris his administravit, neque exaltatus ad dextram Dei administrat. Neque enim recipiendum est dogma, quod Canonistæ & Theologi nonnulli pontificii, quorum argumenta Paulus Comitolus Jesuita, libro contra septem Theologos Venetos edito, colligit, tuentur, statuentes scilicet, Deum Patrem ex singulari privilegio filium Christum, cùm mortalis adhuc in terris degeret, totius mundi Regem & Dominum, etiam in temporalibus, esse voluisse. Quod insulsum dogma distertæ ipsius Christi protestationi repugnat, rigidè negantis, Regnum suum esse οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου ex hoc mundo Joh. xviii. 36. Sicut nempe ipse Christus non erat de hoc mundo Joh. xvii. 14. Sed Dominus de Coelo 1 Cor. xv. 47. ita nec ejus Regnum erat de hoc mundo, neque ipse RegnoCœlesti, spirituali destinatus, occupatúsque totus, temporale vel affectare vel administrare pensi quicquam habuit. Atque id aperta veritate convicti, Jesuitæ alii, Maldonatus & Bellarminus confiteri nobiscum coacti sunt. Quorum ille sic in Matth. cap. 27. scribit: Sunt qui Christum quodammodo invitum facere volunt Regem, hæreticósque eos putent, qui temporalem etiam Regem fuisse negant, cùm ipse in judicio interrogatus palam respónderit: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo; id est, non est mundanum, non est terrenum, non est temporale, sed Cœleste & spirituale. Pluribus deinceps probat, Christi Regnum, Beatorum societatem & fidelium congregationem, seu Ecclesiam, licet in mundo sit, non tamen esse de mundo, quia originem ejus ex Cœlo habet, cùm ejus caput Christus de Cœlo descendérit & fides, quæ Ecclesiæ forma sit, charitas, quæ ejus vinculum, & spes, quæ præmia illa promittat, de Cœlo dentur. Consentanea Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. lib. v. 4. scribit.
units.tr: VIII. Christ, as Mediator and man, neither administered a temporal kingdom in this world nor administers one now that he is exalted at the right hand of God. We must not accept the dogma that some Canonists and Papist theologians hold, whose arguments the Jesuit Paulus Comitolus collects in his book against the seven Venetian theologians, namely that God the Father, by a singular privilege, wished the Son Christ, while he still lived as a mortal on earth, to be King and Lord of the whole world, even in temporal affairs. This foolish dogma conflicts with Christ's own plain declaration, in which he flatly denies that his kingdom is not of this world [οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου] (John 18:36). Just as Christ himself was not of this world (John 17:14), and the Lord is from heaven (1 Cor. 15:47), so his kingdom was not of this world, nor was he himself, destined for the heavenly and spiritual kingdom and wholly occupied with it, ever concerned to aspire to or administer anything temporal. Convinced by this plain truth, other Jesuits, Maldonatus and Bellarmine, were compelled to agree with us. Of these, the former writes thus on Matthew 27: "There are those who wish, in a way, to make Christ King against his will, and they think those heretics who deny that he was even a temporal King, since he himself, when questioned in judgement, openly answered: My kingdom is not of this world; that is, it is not worldly, not earthly, not temporal, but heavenly and spiritual." He then proves at length that Christ's kingdom, the society of the blessed and the congregation of the faithful, or the Church, although it is in the world, is not of the world, because it has its origin from heaven: its head Christ came down from heaven, and the faith that forms the Church, the charity that is its bond, and the hope that promises those rewards, are all given from heaven. Bellarmine writes to the same effect in De Romano Pontifice, book 5, chapter 4.

units.la: IX. Quòd si temporale Regnum Christus, qua Mediator, homo, dominus Ecclesiæ, habuit & administrare vit nunquam: suis etiam in Regno suo merè spirituali, ecclesiastico ministris illud delegare, commendare nunquam voluit, neque illi non delegatum, commendatum in se recipere, citra horrendi raptus crimen potuerunt. Palam proin est, eos, qui se Christi in Regno ejus spirituali, Ecclesiâ, Ministros, quin & vicarios profitentur, atque interea terrenum, temporale Regnum affectant, vel gerunt etiam, non Civitatis Christi, sed Babylonis Magnæ gemuinos affectas esse. Quanquam si maximè Christus, quâ Mediator, Regnum temporale in mundo gessisset, gerétque adhuc, parum in eo præsidii Papa, Ecclesia, quoad temporalia haberet. Etenim Regnum tale Christus administrasset, & administraret adhuc, vel ut Deus, vel ut filius naturalis Dei, vel ut Mediatoris Regio officio præditus, vel tus, vel ut homo super omnia exaltatus, vel ut Redemptor, qui sanguinis sui pretio id acquisiverit. Atqui in his omnibus nec hæredem, nec Proregem ullum in terris instituit. Nam nec Principes nec dominos proprio ipsorum jure spoliavit; & Apostolis non aliud quàm spirituale, in spiritualibus, ministerium commisit.
units.tr: IX. But if Christ, as Mediator, man and Lord of the Church, never had or administered a temporal kingdom, and never wished to delegate or commit it to his ministers in his purely spiritual, ecclesiastical kingdom, then they could not receive it, when it had not been delegated or committed to them, without the horrible crime of usurpation. It is therefore plain that those who profess themselves ministers, and even vicars, of Christ in his spiritual kingdom, the Church, and yet aspire to or even exercise an earthly, temporal kingdom, are not true followers of the City of Christ but genuine aspirants to Babylon the Great. Yet even if Christ, as Mediator, had exercised a temporal kingdom in the world, and still did, the Pope and the Church would have little help from it in temporal matters. For Christ would have administered such a kingdom, and still administers it, either as God, or as the natural Son of God, or as Mediator invested with the royal office, or as man exalted above all things, or as Redeemer, who acquired it at the price of his blood. But in none of these respects has he appointed any heir or vice-king on earth. For he has not despoiled princes or lords of their own right, and to the Apostles he committed nothing but spiritual ministry in spiritual things.

units.la: X. Regnum Christi Oeconomicum, ut ad illud accedam, <bl>οἰκονομία</bl> & <bl>διακονία</bl>, potestate dominante & legislatoria & judiciali absolvitur. In his enim <bl>τὸ κύριον</bl> seu jus Majestatis Christi Regis consistit. Et potestas quidem legislatoria habet <bl>Ϭυσιχώων</bl> gubernationis externum versum; ceu sceptrum quoddam dominationis ejus, & interiorem Spiritus operationem. Verbo externo Christus Rex ac Dominus noster subditis suis fidei ac vitæ præcepta impartitur, quorum repagulis circumseepti in officio continentur. Interna Spiritûs operatione spiritualem motum ac sensum germanis membris, ceu mysticum eorundem caput infundit. Sicut autem caput naturale primum, præcipuum & dominans membrum in corpore humano est, sensus tum internos tum externos genuino vigore instruit, & movendi virtutem spiritúsque in reliqua corporis membra diffundit: sic caput hoc mysticum in Ecclesiæ corpore <bl>ἀναλόγως</bl> eadem præstat. Nam & ordinis dignitate, & persectionum amplitudine, & vegetandi virtute supra omnia membra sua infinitis modis Christum eminere; S. Scriptura perspicuè Psal. viii. 7. 8. Matth. xxviii. 18. Rom. xii. 5. 1 Cor. xii. 6. 27. Ephes. i. 22. 23. iv. 12. 15. 16. Col. i. 18. iii. 11. testatur. Etsi enim partes quasdam officii fui, respectu ministerii externi, cum servis suis, tanquam instrumentis, æquabili inter eos authoritate communicavit, tamen dominii partem ullam, nedum universalem universi sui gubernationem, tam non in plures, nedum in unum quempiam contulit, quàm non ea se ipse abdicavit. Potestas denique judicialis eidem tributa, potestatem coërcendi refractarios, studium ac zelum justitiæ ferventissimum, & sapientiam eximiam, ad cujus normam judicium format, complectitur.
units.tr: X. Christ's economic kingdom, to come to it, which consists in economy [οἰκονομία] and ministry [διακονία], is carried out by dominating, legislative and judicial power. For in these lies the right [τὸ κύριον] of the majesty of Christ the King. The legislative power has an external aspect of government, as a kind of sceptre of his lordship, and an inner operation of the Spirit. By the external word, Christ the King and our Lord imparts to his subjects the precepts of faith and life, by whose barriers they are enclosed and kept in their duty. By the inner operation of the Spirit he infuses spiritual motion and sense into his true members, as their mystical head. For just as the natural head is the first, principal and ruling member in the human body, and furnishes the internal and external senses with genuine vigour and diffuses the power of movement and spirit into the other members of the body, so this mystical head performs the same functions in the body of the Church, analogously [ἀναλόγως]. For Christ excels all his members in infinite ways, in the dignity of his order, in the amplitude of his perfections, and in the power to quicken them, as Holy Scripture clearly attests: Ps. 8:7-8; Matt. 28:18; Rom. 12:5; 1 Cor. 12:6, 27; Eph. 1:22-23; 4:12, 15-16; Col. 1:18; 3:11. For although with respect to the external ministry he has shared certain parts of his office with his servants, as instruments, with equal authority among them, he has conferred no part of lordship on several, much less on any single person, and no part of the universal government of his whole realm, just as he himself did not abdicate it. Lastly, the judicial power attributed to him embraces the power to restrain the refractory, a most fervent zeal and care for justice, and exceptional wisdom, by whose rule he forms his judgements.

units.la: XI. Sicut porro Christus in mundo adhuc degens, adeóque in terris corpore suo superstes, Regnum suum ministerio Apostolorum & discipulorum rexit: ita in sacrarium cœleste digressus idem Apostolorum, Prophetarum, Evangelistarum, Pastorum, & Doctorum ministerio regere pergit. Potestatem dominantem utramque tum legislatoriam, tum judiciariam exercuit in terris solus, neque ulli Ministrorum suorum communicavit, quod ne ipsi quidem Hierarchici ire inficias ausint. Ingressus in Cœlum, neque absens tamen Spiritu & verbo suo, neque corpore mortuus est; sed corpore in throno Regio magnificentiæ confidens, Spiritu & verbo corpori suo conjunctissimus, succedaneum Proregem, venientem in partem dominii, vel vicarium delegata potestate herili & dominica utentem, instituit prorsus nullum. Neutro enim, ceu immortalis & Ecclesiæ præsentissimus indiget. Vivit adhuc & regnat in Ecclesia, & post ejus in Cœlum ascensionem, æquè ac ante eam, multi unum corpus sumus in Christo (non in quoquam capite vel domino alio, puta Petro, Pontifice) singuli (ne Petro quidem excepto) alter alterius membra; non Christi (quanquam verè Christi membra omnes sumus quoad κτῆσιν possessionem) sed alter alterius, quoad usum communem, ut constet planè neminem fidelium aliam ad alios, quàm membri σύσσωμοι corporei, relationem habere, capitis verò prorsus nullum Rom. xii. 5. Quinimò Regnum isthoc & potestas dominans, quoad exercitii saltem vigorem Christo Domino à Patre post ascensionem in Cœlum & glorificationem donatum esse, S. Paulus Ephes. 1. 19-22. ajens, Deum Patrem {·} trem Christum ad dextram suam collocantem, dedisse Ecclesiæ κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ πάντα Caput super omnia, testatur. Quomodo igitur exaltatus ad Dextram Dei successorem habet in Regno, quod tum demum efficacissimè auspicatus est? Sed & Regnum actuale Christum ἀρχιτης per se ipsum sine vicario & successore ullo exercere, idem S. Paulus testatur, dicens: ἡ̂ν αὐτὸς ἐστιν ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ἐκκλησίας, & ipse (non alius) est illud (nota emphasin articuli) caput corporis Ecclesiæ, qui est principium, primogenitus ex mortuis, ut sit in omnibus ipse (non alius, adeoque solus) πρωτεύων Primatum tenens Col. i. 18. Quin & Regimen isthoc totum esse spirituale, corporalis præsentiæ ἀδιάστατον neutiquam indigum, mox v. 19. 20. declarat, ajens: Quia in ipso complacuit omnem plenitudinem (potestatis, spiritus, dominii, principatus, operationum, perfectionum) inhabitare, & per eum reconciliare omnia in ipsum, pace facta per sanguinem crucis ejus per ipsum, sive quæ in terris, sive quæ in Cœlis sunt. Perspicuè idem 1 Cor. xii. 4. 5. 6. &c. asserit: Divisa sunt charismata, τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα Spiritus autem idem (non alius in capite Christo, alius in alio capite, cùm Spiritus idem non sit, nisi in uno capite) Divisiones ministrationum sunt, & idem Dominus. Divisiones operationum sunt, idem autem Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. Etv. 12. Sicut corpus unum est, & membra habet multa: omnia autem membra corporis cum sint multa, unum tamen corpus sunt: ita & Christus. Ubi manifestè Christum aliquid unum facit simul cùm tota ecclesia, ita ut Christus & Ecclesia sint unicum corpus integrum, ex capite unico, & pluribus membris conflatum. Et prosecutus similitudinem, omnibus ministris varia officia, quæ supra διαιρέσεις χαρισμάτων, διακονιῶν, ἐνεργημάτων, divisiones gratiarum, ministeriorum, operationum, vocaverat, ita applicat, ut dominantem potestatem, etiam post ascensionem Christi in Cœlum tribuat nemini. Quod enim eodem capite v. 21: dicit: Caput non potest dicere pedibus, non indigeo vobis, proclive probatu est, non intelligi caput regens, & in membra spiritu suo influens, quale solus Christus est, & quale pedibus ad dominandum & influendum neutiquam indiget, sed membrum corporis, in quo sunt excellentiora charismata, atque caput ejusmodi in corpore Ecclesiæ non unicum illud, sed multiplex.
units.tr: XI. Again, just as Christ, while still living in the world, and so surviving on earth in his body, ruled his kingdom through the ministry of the Apostles and disciples, so, having withdrawn into the heavenly sanctuary, he goes on ruling through the ministry of the same Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Pastors and Teachers. He alone exercised on earth the dominating power, both legislative and judicial, and communicated it to none of his ministers, as not even the Hierarchists themselves dare deny. Having entered heaven, he is neither absent, since he is present by his Spirit and word, nor dead in body, but trusting in his body on the royal throne of majesty, and most closely joined to it by Spirit and word, he has appointed no vice-king as a successor, to come into a share of the lordship, nor any vicar exercising delegated lordly power at all. For he needs neither, being immortal and most present to the Church. He still lives and reigns in the Church, and after his ascension into heaven, just as before it, we, being many, are one body in Christ (not in any other head or lord, such as Peter or the Pontiff), each of us (not even Peter excepted) members one of another. We are members of Christ, though not in the sense of Christ's members, since all of us are truly Christ's members as to possession [κτῆσις]; but we are members one of another as to common use. So it is plain that none of the faithful has any relation to the others except that of members of one bodily body, and no relation of head at all (Rom. 12:5). Moreover, St Paul testifies in Eph. 1:19-22 that this kingdom and dominating power, at least as to the vigour of its exercise, was given to Christ our Lord by the Father after his ascension into heaven and glorification, saying that God the Father, setting Christ at his right hand, gave him to the Church as head over all things [κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ πάντα]. How then, exalted to the right hand of God, can he have a successor in the kingdom, which he most effectively began only then? But the same St Paul also testifies that Christ himself rules the actual kingdom, without any vicar or successor, saying: and he himself is the head of the body of the Church [ἥν αὐτός ἐστιν ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ἐκκλησίας] (note the emphasis of the article), who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he himself (not another, and so alone) may hold the first place [πρωτεύων] (Col. 1:18). Indeed he declares at once in vv. 19-20 that this whole rule is spiritual and in no way needs bodily presence: for it pleased (the Father) that in him all fulness (of power, spirit, dominion, principality, operations, perfections) should dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, through him, whether things on earth or things in heaven. Clearly the same thing is asserted in 1 Cor. 12:4-6 and following: There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit [τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα]; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works all in all. And v. 12: For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though they are many, are one body: so also is Christ. Here he manifestly makes Christ one thing together with the whole Church, so that Christ and the Church are one complete body, made up of one head and many members. Pursuing the comparison, he applies to all the ministers the various offices that above he had called divisions of gifts, ministries, operations [διαιρέσεις χαρισμάτων, διακονιῶν, ἐνεργημάτων], in such a way that he grants dominating power to no one, not even after Christ's ascension into heaven. For what he says in the same chapter, v. 21: The head cannot say to the feet, I have no need of you, is easily shown to refer not to the ruling head that infuses its spirit into the members, such as Christ alone is, and which the feet in no way need for ruling and infusing, but to a member of the body, in which the more excellent gifts are found. Such a head in the body of the Church is not that single one but many.

units.la: XII. Agnoscunt Hieromonarchici, neque Petrum habuisse, neque Papam ullum habere internum gratiæ & dominii influxum, quo præsint Ecclesiæ, eamque regant. Hunc enim soli Christo competere. Ita eorum coryphæus, de Turre-cremata de Eccl. lib. 1. c. 23. ad. 4. Sed præter internum influxum cum Thoma Aquinate statuit alium externum, externæ gubernationis, ei similem, quo caput externis sensibus, præsertim visu, hominem in actibus exterioribus dirigit. Cæterum quàm id dilutum sit, nemo non videt. Præterquam enim quòd potestas quam Papa sibi ceu caput Ecclesiæ & vicarius Christi arrogat, cum oculo corpus dirigente nihil commune habet, neque visus insuper, neque auditus, neque ullus sensus eorum, qui in capita radicantur, dici ipsum caput possunt. Etiam caput, quâ excellentius corporis membrum, ab oculo S. Paulus 1 Cor. xii. 21. distinxit. Oculus scilicet, auris &c. sunt membra, licet in capite, capiti tamen contradistincta, quæque non regunt, dominantur, ut caput, sed à capite reguntur. Caput verò, quâ caput nullum aliud officium habet, quàm ut interno influxu totum corpus regat, missô in nervos & per nervos in membra, ipsúmque etiam oculum spiritu, qui cuilibet membro congruentem motum impertitur.
units.tr: XII. The Hierarchists acknowledge that neither Peter nor any Pope has had an inward influx of grace and dominion by which he presides over the Church and governs it, since this belongs to Christ alone. So their leader, de Turrecremata, de Eccl. lib. 1. c. 23. ad. 4. But besides the inward influx, he holds with Thomas Aquinas that there is another, external influx of external government, similar to it, by which the head directs the man in external acts, chiefly through sight. How weak this is, however, everyone sees. For apart from the fact that the power which the Pope claims for himself, as head of the Church and vicar of Christ, has nothing in common with the eye that directs the body, neither sight, nor hearing, nor any of the senses which are rooted in the head can be called the head itself. St Paul in 1 Cor. 12:21 distinguished the head, as the more excellent member of the body, from the eye. The eye, the ear and so on are members, though they are in the head; yet they are distinct from the head, and they do not rule or dominate as the head does, but are ruled by the head. The head, on the other hand, since it has no other office than to govern the whole body by inward influx, sends spirit into the nerves, and through the nerves into the members, and into the eye itself, which imparts to each member its fitting motion.

units.la: XIII. Sed
units.tr: XIII. But

units.la: XIII. Sed forte Hierarchicorum hypobolimæum in Ecclesia caput obtrudentium πεῶν ψευδο[?] illud est, quòd statuunt, Ecclesiam, seu gubernationem ejus post Christi discessum non esse eandem, quæ fuit primitiva, sed aliam eidem similem, proin etiam non eadem, per unicum caput Christum, sed simili, per Papam, ceu succenturiatum Atlantem gubernandam esse. Quasi scilicet Christi, non mortui utique, sed viventis adhuc, imò δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου potentiam vitæ indissolubilis (Hebr. vii. 16) habentis, corporalis præsentia, vel absentia gubernationem ipsam variet. Non dicam, eosdem corporis Christi in ciboriis, hostia, præsentiam corporalem jactare, & in ea præsentia religionis suæ arcem collocare. At nos in sacrarium ἀχειροποίητον[?] illum receptum, indeque ad finem usque mundi corpore suo non rediturum profitemur. Absentia tamen illa non magis idoneam causam præbet vicario capiti, quàm olim typici Pontificis, in typico Sacrario agentis, aut Mosis in monte cum Domino loquentis, mora, ejusmodi subrogationem ratam, Deóque gratam effecisset. Si Rex terrenus, peregrè prosiciscens is esset, qui nihilominus momento quolibet, secretâ viâ aliquâ, ministris suis animo & consiliis adesse, eósque singulis momentis instruere, & per illos totam Regni gubernationem expedire, perinde ac si corpore præsens foret, posset, nullo utique eo casu Prorege indigeret, sed suum ipsemet Regnum nihilo secius gubernaret, ipsiúsque adeo solâ absentiâ corporalis ne minimam quidem gubernationis varietatem induceret. Par ratio est Christi, corpore suo absentis, at Spiritu, consilio, gratia Ecclesiæ suæ, corpori suo, à quâ non re avelli, sed ratione duntaxat, & καὶ ἀχειροποίητον[?] distingui potest, conjunctissimi, qui proin animo, Spiritu, monitis, consiliis, inspirationibus salutaribus Ecclesiæ militanti perpetuò præsens, unus Pastores, ministri ministros suos, præsentissimus regit, moderatur, ut verus Princeps, quem omnes solum Principem dominúmque suum agnoscunt, & sequuntur.
units.tr: XIII. But perhaps the substitute head which the Hierarchists thrust into the Church is that false figment, the notion that the Church, or its government, after Christ's departure is not the same as it was in the primitive age, but another like it, and therefore not governed through the one head Christ but through a similar head, the Pope, as a substitute Atlas. As if the government itself varied according to the bodily presence or absence of Christ, who is not dead, but still living, and indeed has "the power of an indissoluble life" [δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου] (Heb. 7:16). I will not say that they boast of the bodily presence of the body of Christ in the pyx and the host, and place the stronghold of their religion in that presence. We, however, confess that he was received into the heaven "not made with hands" [ἀχειροποίητον] and that he will not return in his body until the end of the world. Yet that absence gives no better cause for a vicarious head than the delay of the typical High Priest, who acted in the typical sanctuary, or of Moses, who spoke with the Lord on the mountain, would have made such a substitution valid and pleasing to God. Suppose an earthly king were travelling abroad, yet at every moment, by some secret way, were able to be present in mind and counsel with his ministers, and to instruct them at every moment, and through them to conduct the whole government of the kingdom just as if he were present in person. In that case he would certainly have no need of a viceroy, but would govern his own kingdom no less, and his bodily absence alone would not produce the slightest variation in its government. The case of Christ is the same: though absent in body, he is most closely united to his body, from which he cannot be torn away, but only distinguished in reason and in the heaven "not made with hands".
