Therefore, present always to the militant Church in spirit, counsel, admonitions, and salutary inspirations, he alone, as the true Prince whom all acknowledge as their only Prince and Lord, rules and governs his ministers, who are his servants, most present of all, and they follow him.

units.la: XIV. Neque postremum illud est, quòd Christus eos, quos in terris Ecclesiæ suæ præfecit, Ministros omnes, patri potestate serviente, Monarcham, Hierarchiam, Dominum nullum instituit. Etenim Apostolos ipsos universos jussit esse ὑπηρέτας operarios, quales sunt in messe Luc. x. 2. Joh. iv. 34-38. Piscatores hominum Matth. iv. 19. testes resurrectionis Christi Act. i. 22. præcones verbi Matth. xxviii. 19. Marc. xvi. 15. Pastores, doctores Ephes. iv. 11. Legatos 2 Cor. vi. 20. quæ, aliáque ejusmodi, curam, ministerium, œconomiam, non dominium, imperium, significant. Etiam claves Regni cœlorum, non ut Dominis, sed ut servis & œconomis à Deo Apostolis promissæ, datæque sunt, cùm claudere & aperire nisi ex mandato Christi non potuerint, neque aperuerint clauserintque proprium quippiam, & sui peculii sed id, quod alienos thesauros & opes, sicut Christo Domino placitum est, condit, promitque, atque id ipsum non unius cujuspiam ἀπεόεικτμα sit, sed æqua potestate Apostolis cunctis, & eorum in communi munere successoribus competat. Nam Apostolos quidem in omni officio ac munere Apostolico, omnique dignitate & potestate inter se pares, & omnino æquales fuisse abundè constat, cùm & Ecclesia omnibus ex æquo fuerit commendata Matth. xxviii. 19. Joh. xx. 21. & æquè omnes à Christo instructi, edocti, Spiritu S. repleti fuerint. Act. 11.4. & Apostolum nullum aliis præstare, vel majorem esse, diserte Christus Matth. xviii. 1. 2. &c. Marc. ix. 33. Luc. ix. 46. &c. negaverit. Præclarè proin S. Cyprianus de Simplic. Prælat. sic ὁσπη illam Apostolorum: Loquitur Dominus ad Petrum: Ego tibi dico, quia tu es Petrus &c. tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum. Et idem ait post resurrectionem: Pasce oves meas; Et quamvis Apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam parem potestatem tribuat, & dicat: Sicut me misit Pater, & ego mitto vos &c. tamen ut unitatem manifestaret, unitatis ejusdem originem ab uno incipientem, sua authoritate disposuit, Hoc utique erant & cæteri Apostoli, quod erat Petrus, pari consortio præditi & honoris & potestatis, sed exoratum ab unitate proficiscitur, ut Ecclesia una monstretur. Si igitur Apostolorum omnium munus merè ὑπηρε-τικὸν ministeriale & serviens fuit, & æquabilis potestas dignitas & existimatio omnium fuit, multò magis eorum, qui post Apostolorum tempora Ecclesiæ præsunt, munus ministeriale, & potestas dignitásque æqualis censenda fuerit.
units.tr: XIV. Nor is this the least point: Christ did not appoint any monarch, hierarchy or lord over all the ministers whom he set over his Church on earth, the Father's power serving him. For he ordered all the apostles themselves to be "servants" [ὑπηρέτας] and workers, such as are in the harvest (Luke 10:2; John 4:34-38), fishers of men (Matt. 4:19), witnesses of Christ's resurrection (Acts 1:22), heralds of the Word (Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:15), pastors and teachers (Eph. 4:11), ambassadors (2 Cor. 5:20). These and similar words signify care, ministry and stewardship, not lordship or command. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were also promised and given to the apostles by God, not as to masters but as to servants and stewards, since they could not lock or unlock except by Christ's command, and they did not open or shut anything of their own or of their own property, but what Christ the Lord had pleased to store up and bring forth from the treasures and riches of others; and this power belongs not to any one person's private possession, but with equal authority to all the apostles and to their successors in the common office. For it is abundantly clear that the apostles were in every office and ministry, in all dignity and power, equal among themselves and entirely alike, since the Church was committed equally to all (Matt. 28:19; John 20:21), and all were equally instructed and taught by Christ and filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:4). And Christ expressly denied that any apostle excelled the others or was greater (Matt. 18:1-2 etc.; Mark 9:33; Luke 9:46 etc.). Therefore St Cyprian, in de Simplic. Prælat., rightly speaks thus of that saying of the apostles: "The Lord speaks to Peter: 'I say to you, that you are Peter etc. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.' And he says the same after the resurrection: 'Feed my sheep.' And although after his resurrection he gives equal power to all the apostles and says, 'As the Father has sent me, so I send you' etc., yet to show the unity, he arranged by his own authority that the origin of that unity should begin from one. Indeed the other apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership of honour and power, but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church may be shown to be one." If therefore the whole office of all the apostles was purely ministerial [ὑπηρετικὸν] and serving, and the power, dignity and estimation of all was equal, much more must the ministerial office and the equal power and dignity be judged to belong to those who preside over the Church after the time of the apostles.

units.la: XV. Dominationem verò in Ecclesia quibuslibet interd- ictis. Christus vetuit.
units.tr: XV. That Christ forbade every kind of domination in the Church.

units.la: Ad ipsos enim Apostolos sic locutus est Luc. xxii. 25. Reges gentium dominantur iis, & qui potestatem habent super eas, benefici vocantur, εὐεργέται vos autem non sic. Quibus verbis manifestè Christus excludit ab Ecclesia, quâ talis est, omnem dominatum, forensem jurisdictionem & præfecturam ejusmodi, quæ præfecturas seculares quoquo modo imitetur. Neque enim Christus vel de Tyrannis loquitur, utpote qui εὐεργέται beneficii non sunt; vel apud S. Matthæum cap. xx. 25. usus vocabulo καταχυριεύειν injustum duntaxat imperium intelligit. Potius ea voce imperium Regum cum violentia, seu vi coactiva erga refractarios conjunctum describitur, & ab Apostolis removetur. Et quicquid sit, κυριεύειν, & καταχυριεύειν promiscuè ab Euangelistis usurpatur; cùm illa voce Lucas, hac S. Matthæus usus fuerit, & illa etiam κυριότης dominatio, quæ εὐεργεσία beneficentiam comitem habet, adeóque minimè tyrannica Apostolis interdicitur. Fratres quippe, qui Christo interdicti hujus occasionem præpræbuerunt, non utique tyrannidem, sed potestatem duntaxat eminentiorem affectarunt. Et ἡ καθολικὴ apud LXX. Interpretes non semel in poticrem partem accipitur. Veluti Genes. 1. 28. Psalm. LXXII. 8. Psalm. CX. 2. ubi ipsi Christo domino tribuitur. Similiter etiam καθολικῶν annotante Eustathio idem sonat quod κοιναλῶν in Homer. Il. 1. 318. & Odyss. ά. 247.
units.tr: For Christ spoke thus to the Apostles themselves, Luke 22:25: The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors [εὐεργέται], but you shall not be so. By these words Christ plainly excludes from the Church, as such, every domination, every forensic jurisdiction and every prefecture of that kind which would in any way imitate secular governments. Nor is Christ speaking of tyrants, since they are not benefactors [εὐεργέται]; nor, in Matthew 20:25, where he uses the word katakyrieuein [καταχυριεύειν], does he mean merely unjust rule. Rather, by that word the rule of kings joined with violence, that is, coercive force against the refractory, is described and removed from the Apostles. Whatever the case, kyrieuein [κυριεύειν] and katakyrieuein [καταχυριεύειν] are used interchangeably by the Evangelists, Luke having used the one and Matthew the other; and kyriotēs [κυριότης], dominion, which has beneficence [εὐεργεσία] as its companion, is by no means forbidden to the Apostles as tyrannical. For the brothers who gave Christ occasion for this prohibition were not seeking tyranny, but only a more eminent power. And the word katholikē [καθολικὴ] in the Seventy is not once taken in a bad sense: for example Genesis 1:28, Psalm 72:8, and Psalm 110:2, where it is attributed to Christ the Lord himself. Likewise katholikōn, according to Eustathius's note, means the same as koinōn [κοινῶν] in Homer, Iliad 1.318 and Odyssey 1.247.

units.la: XVI. Quid quòd Salvator optimus Apostolis, ceu servis & Oeconomis, totique Ecclesiæ dedit κλεῖδας βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν, claves Regni Cœlorum, non utique Regni terrarum Matth. xvi. 19? In criminibus enim, ita præclarè Bernhardus lib. j. de consid. ad Eugen. cap. 6. Eugenium Papam admonet, non in possessionibus est potestas vestra, quoniam propter illa, & non propter has accepistis claves Regni Cœlorum. Sequitur, quænam tibi major videtur potestas peccata remittendi, an prædia dividendi? Habent hæc terrena & infima judices suos Reges & Principes terræ; quid sines alienos invaditis? quid falcem vestram in alienam messem extenditis? Cur major vis esse Domino, qui interpellatus à quodam dicente: Dic fratri meo, ut dividat hæreditatem, respondit: Quis me constituit judicem inter vos? Scilicet judice S. Paulo 2 Tim. II. 4. οὐδεὶς στρατευόμενος ἐμπλέκεται ταῖς τοῦ βίου πραγματείαις, nemo, qui militat Domino, implicatur Seculi hujus negotiis, curis, imperiis temporalibus.
units.tr: XVI. What more? Did the best of Saviours give the keys of the kingdom of heaven [κλεῖδας βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν] to the Apostles, as servants and stewards, and to the whole Church, the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, and not, surely, of the kingdom of earth (Matthew 16:19)? For Bernard, in book 1 On Consideration, chapter 6, admonishes Pope Eugenius most aptly: Your power lies not in possessions, since you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven for sins, and not for these. Consider: which seems to you the greater power, to remit sins or to divide estates? These earthly and lowly matters have their own judges, the kings and princes of the earth. Why do you invade the boundaries of others? Why do you stretch your sickle into another's harvest? Why should the Lord seem to have had greater power, who, when someone appealed to him, saying, "Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me," answered, "Who made me a judge between you?" Clearly, with St Paul as judge (2 Timothy 2:4), no one who serves as a soldier entangles himself [οὐδεὶς στρατευόμενος ἐμπλέκεται] in the affairs of this life [ταῖς τοῦ βίου πραγματείαις]: no one who fights for the Lord is entangled in the business, cares and temporal commands of this world.

units.la: XVII. Quid verò multis? Ecclesiæ totius, quæ à Christo capite, Rege & Domino unico διαρρήκτως regitur, potestas ab eodem delegata est merè tum Spiritualis tum ministerialis. Spiritualis, tum quia Ecclesiæ finis solus & proprius est, ut fideles, qui ipsa Ecclesia sunt, æternam supernaturalem beatitudinem consequantur: tum quia media salutis, Christi redemtio, remissio peccatorum, justificatio fidei, pœnitentia, prædicatio verbi, Sacramentorum dispensatio, merè Spiritualia sunt, neque cum rebus temporalibus commercii quicquam habent: tum quia ipsius Christi Domini & Regis Ecclesiæ unici, potestas, quam in Ecclesiam ceu corpus suum mysticum exercuit, merè spiritualis fuit, neque de hoc mundo extitit Joh. xviii. 36. tum quia non aliam, quàm animarum curam & ἐπιμελείαν concernit: tum quia omnia Christi præcepta, cujusmodi sunt, Docete, solvite, ligate, remittite, retinete, baptizate, hoc facite, spirituali objecto coërcentur: tum quia obedientia Ecclesiæ præpositis debita, iis in rebus consistit, in quibus à Christo præpositi sunt, præpositi autem sunt in animarum cura, invigilantes scilicet, quasi rationem pro animabus reddituri. Hebr. xiii. 7. 17. tum denique quia pœnæ, quas irrogat Ecclesia, non utique corporales & ἀναγκαστικαὶ coactivæ sunt, sed spirituales, consistentes in denuntiatione mali à Deo infligendi potiùs, quàm malum ipsum ex potestatis plenitudine infligentes, adeoque etiam à vi coactiva remotæ prorsus, cùm vel ipsa excommunicatio, nedum pœnitentiæ præscriptio corporali vi & coactione ab Ecclesia, quâ talis est sucipi nequeat. Sed & Ministerialem esse omnem Ecclesiæ potestatem, abundè jam probavimus, atque ulterius inde liquet, quia omnis potestas Ecclesiæ data Christo in conversione infidelium, justificatione impii, regeneratione & renovatione naturæ corruptæ inservit, neque inservit aliter, quàm verbum gratuitæ reconciliationis cum Deo scriptum conservando, prædicando, interpretando, per sigilla externa gratiæ obsignando, remissionem peccatorum credentibus annuntiando, iram Dei incredulis & impiis quibusvis denuntiando. Quòd si verò Ecclesiæ Ministris verbum gratiæ ita prædicantibus, explicantibus, peccatorum remissionem fidelibus promittentibus, cæteræque demandati ossicii partes obeuntibus, fiat hominum ad Deum vera conversio, fio, non utique Ecclesiæ Ministri effectus ejus causæ principes sunt, sed mera organa, per quæ Deus pro lubitu, dans incrementum plantationi & rigationi hominum operatur 1 Cor. iii. 7. Præclarè sic eam in rem S. Augustinus in Psalm. 35. loquitur: Justitia tua sicut montes Dei. Qui sunt montes Dei? qui dicti sunt nubes, ipsi sunt & montes Dei, magni prædicatores montes Dei. Et quomodo, quando oritur sol, priùs luce montes illustrat, & inde lux ad humillima terrarum descendit: sic quando venit Dominus noster Jesus Christus, priùs radiavit in altitudinem Apostolorum, priùs illustravit montes, & sic descendit lux ejus ad convalles terrarum, & ideo dicit in Psalm. 120. (121) v. 1. Levavi oculos meos in montes, unde veniet auxilium mihi. Quid ergo? Montes tibi dabunt auxilium? Non. Audi sequentia. Auxilium meum à Domino, qui fecit cælum & terram. Hactenus ille.
units.tr: XVII. But why say more? The whole Church, which is governed without interruption [διαρρήκτως] by Christ, its one Head, King and Lord, has received its power from him, and it is purely both spiritual and ministerial. It is spiritual: first, because the sole and proper end of the Church is that the faithful, who are the Church itself, attain eternal, supernatural blessedness; second, because the means of salvation, namely Christ's redemption, the remission of sins, justification by faith, repentance, the preaching of the Word and the dispensing of the sacraments, are purely spiritual and have nothing to do with temporal affairs; third, because the power of Christ himself, the Lord and sole King of the Church, which he exercised over the Church as his mystical body, was purely spiritual and, as John 18:36 says, was not of this world; fourth, because it concerns only the care and oversight [ἐπιμελείαν] of souls; fifth, because all Christ's precepts, such as Teach, loose, bind, forgive, retain, baptize, do this, are confined to a spiritual object; sixth, because the obedience owed by the Church to its rulers consists in those matters in which Christ has set them over it, and they are set over the care of souls, watching over them, that is, as those who must give account for souls (Hebrews 13:7, 17); seventh and finally, because the penalties the Church imposes are not corporal and compulsory [ἀναγκαστικαὶ] or coercive, but spiritual, consisting in the announcement of the evil that God will inflict, rather than in inflicting the evil itself from the fullness of power. They are therefore wholly remote from coercive force, since not even excommunication, much less the prescription of repentance, can be carried out by the Church as such with bodily force and compulsion. But we have already sufficiently proved that all the Church's power is ministerial, and it is further clear that, since all the power given by Christ to the Church serves the conversion of unbelievers, the justification of the ungodly, and the regeneration and renewal of corrupt nature, it serves in no other way than by preserving, preaching and interpreting the written word of free reconciliation with God, by sealing it with the outward signs of grace, by announcing the remission of sins to believers and proclaiming the wrath of God to unbelievers and the impious of every kind. But if the ministers of the Church, preaching and explaining the word of grace, promising the remission of sins to the faithful and discharging the other parts of their commissioned office, bring about a true conversion of men to God, the ministers of the Church are not the chief causes of that effect, but mere instruments through which God works as he pleases, giving the increase to the planting and watering of men (1 Corinthians 3:7). St Augustine speaks admirably to this effect on Psalm 35 (36): Your justice is like the mountains of God. Who are the mountains of God? Those who were called clouds, they are also the mountains of God, the great preachers, the mountains of God. And as, when the sun rises, it first lights the mountains, and from them the light descends to the lowest parts of the earth, so when our Lord Jesus Christ came, he first shone upon the height of the Apostles, first illuminated the mountains, and so his light descended into the valleys of the earth. Therefore he says in Psalm 120 (121):1, "I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me." What then? Will the mountains give you help? No. Hear what follows: "My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." So far Augustine.

units.la: XVIII. Potestas porro temporalis & Ecclesiastica ita comparatæ sunt, ut neutra alteri vel dominetur, vel serviat, nullâque inter eas essentialiter consideratas subjectio, dependentia, colligatio intercedat secus quàm Hieromonarchici, Secularem Ecclesiasticæ subjicientes, pertendunt. Atque id olim etiam Gelasius, quamvis Papa, perspicuè asseruit, utpote qui invectus in Anastasium Imperatorem quòd se ille aliquando in absolutionem Petri Episcopi Alexandrini Ecclesiastica censura icti ingessisset, sic tomo de anath. vinc. potestatem utramque disparavit: Fuerint hæc ante adventum Christi, ut quidam figuraliter, adhuc tamen in carnalibus actionibus constituti, pariter Reges existerent, & pariter Sacerdotes. Quod Sanctum Melchisedec fuisse, sacra prodit historia. Quod in suis Diabolus quoque imitatus est, utpote qui semper, quæ Divino cultui convenirent, sibimet tyrannico Spiritu vendicare contendit, ut pagani, Imperatores iidem, & Maximi Pontifices , dicerentur. Sed cùm ad verum ventum est (Christum) eundem Regem & Pontificem , ultra sibi , nec Imperator Pontificis nomen imposuit , nec Pontifex Regale fastigium vindicavit. Quamvis enim membra ipsius , id est , veri Regis atque Pontificis , secundùm participationem naturæ magnificè utrúmque in sacra generositate sumpsisse dicantur , ut simul Regale genus & Sacerdotale subsistant 1 Pet. ÿ. 6. Attamen Christus memor fragilitatis humanæ , quod suorum saluti congrueret , dispensatione magnifica temperans , sic actionibus propriis , dignitatibus distinctis officia potestatis utriúsque discrevit , volens suos medicinali humilitate salvari , non humana superbia rursus intercipi , ut & Christiani Imperatores pro æterna vita Pontificibus indigerent , & Pontifices pro temporalium cursu rerum , Imperialibus dispositionibus uterentur : quatenus Spiritualis actio à carnalibus distaret incursibus : & idea militans Deo minimè secularibus negotiis se implicaret 2 Tim. ÿ. 2. ac vicissim non ille rebus Divinis præsidere videretur , qui esset negotiis secularibus implicatus : ut & modestia utriusque ordinis curaretur , ne extolleretur utroque suffultus : & competens qualitatibus actionum specialiter professio aptaretur. Totidem ferè verbis , utramque potestatem isthanc Nicolaus I. licet totus Spiritu Monarchiæ tumens , Epist. lib. 1. cap. 8. distinxit. Duo igitur Pontifices illi non temporalem potestatem Ecclesiasticæ subjecerunt , sed utramque personis, dignitatibus, officiis, actibus dispararunt rectissimè , ad testimonium dicendum citati merito adversus ἱεροκαταχωνευτὴν Pontificem alterum , Bonifacium VIII. qui in Extravagante Unam Sanctam , definiens , Spiritualem & materialem gladium esse in potestate Ecclesiæ , hunc pro Ecclesia , illum ab Ecclesia exercendum : illum sacerdotis , hunc manu Regum & militum , sed ad nutum & patientiam Sacerdotis, subjicit: Oportet autem gladium esse subgladio, & temporalem auctoritatem Spirituali subjici potestati.
units.tr: XVIII. Moreover, temporal and ecclesiastical power are so constituted that neither dominates the other or serves it, and no subjection, dependence or subordination exists between them when considered in their essence, except as the Hierocrats maintain, who make the secular subject to the ecclesiastical. Even Gelasius, though a pope, clearly asserted this long ago. When he attacked the Emperor Anastasius, because that emperor had once interfered in the absolution of Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, from ecclesiastical censure, he separated the two powers in these words, in his tome on the anathemas: These things existed before the coming of Christ, so that some, figuratively, though still engaged in carnal actions, were at once kings and priests together. That holy Melchizedek was such is shown by sacred history. The devil too imitated this among his own, since he always strove with tyrannical spirit to claim for himself what belonged to divine worship, so that the same men were called both pagan emperors and chief pontiffs. But when the true one came, Christ, the same King and Priest, neither did the emperor henceforth assume the name of pontiff, nor did the pontiff claim the royal dignity. For although his members, that is, of the true King and Priest, are said by participation in his nature to have taken up both nobly in holy nobility, so that the royal race and the priestly stand together (1 Peter 2:9), yet Christ, mindful of human frailty, and tempering with magnificent dispensation what would serve the salvation of his own, distinguished the duties of each power by distinct actions and dignities, willing that his people be saved by medicinal humility and not again be seized by human pride, so that Christian emperors would need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs would use imperial arrangements for the course of temporal affairs. Thus spiritual action would be kept apart from carnal assaults, and so one who is a soldier of God would not entangle himself in secular business (2 Timothy 2:4), and conversely, he who is entangled in secular business would not seem to preside over divine things. Thus the moderation of each order is preserved, lest either be exalted by being supported by the other, and a profession suited to the qualities of its actions is fitted to each. Nicholas I, though wholly swollen with the spirit of monarchy, distinguished these two powers in almost the same words, in Epistles book 1, chapter 8. Those two pontiffs therefore did not subject the temporal power to the ecclesiastical; they rightly separated the two in persons, dignities, offices and acts. They are rightly cited as witnesses against another pontiff, Boniface VIII, the [ἱεροκαταχωνευτὴν] (desecrator of holy things), who, in the Extravagant Unam Sanctam, defined that the spiritual and the material sword are both in the power of the Church: the one to be wielded by the Church, the other for the Church; the one by the hand of priests, the other by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the nod and sufferance of the priest. He subjects the temporal authority to the spiritual power: For the sword must be under the sword, and temporal authority must be subject to spiritual power.

units.la: XIX. Distincta quidem sunt potestas, & subjectum potestatem habens, ita ut subjectum habens potestatem politicam Ecclesiae, & vicissim habens potestatem Ecclesiasticam secularem subjici possit, debeatque. Sed potestates ipsae ita discretae sunt, ut neutra alteri subjici, neutra in alterius fines involare possit, debeatque. Et frustra omnino subordinationem politicae potestatis Hierarchici fingunt. Dignitas quippe & officium, quod est in subordinato, non potest non esse in subordinante, cum ab eo in subordinatum derivetur. Hinc adeo Princeps se violatum putat, cum ministri ejus subordinati in officiis exequendis impediuntur; & Papa, spreta legati sui authoritate, se ac sedem suam Apostolicam contemni queritur. Atqui res omnes & personae praesupponuntur esse liberae, nisi contrarium probetur.
units.tr: There is a real distinction between a power and the subject who holds it, so that a subject who holds political power may and should be subject to ecclesiastical power, and vice versa. But the powers themselves are so separate that neither may or should be subjected to the other or intrude into the other's territory. The Hierarchists are wholly wrong to invent a subordination of political power. Dignity and office in the subordinate must necessarily be in the one who subordinates, since it is derived from him into the subordinate. Hence a prince thinks himself violated when his subordinate ministers are hindered in carrying out their duties, and the Pope complains that his own authority and the Apostolic See are despised when his legate's authority is scorned. Yet all things and persons are presumed to be free unless the contrary is proved.

units.la: XX. Bellarminus contra Barcl. cap. 2. nequicquam ictum hunc exire conatur, distinguens subordinationem duplicem, quarum altera eo modo intelligatur, ut potestas, quae est in subordinato, derivetur a subordinante, qualis sit potestas vicarii, Legati, judicis sive praesidis, ab eo derivata, cujus aliquis vicarius Legatus, judex est: altera vero ita intelligatur, ut una non derivetur ab altera, sed ob id duntaxat alteri subjiciatur, & subordinetur, quia finis unius subjicitur & subordinatur fini alterius; qualis sit subjectio & subordinatio variarum artium, sculptoriae, oratoria, astronomicae, & similium, ad artem regendi populos, quae Regia & architectonica dicitur. In priori subordinatione potestatem subordinantis includere potestatem subordinati, in posteriore non item: ac potestatem secularem Ecclesiasticae subordinari posteriori, non priori modo, asserit. Quemadmodum, inquit, ars Regia non includit artem Sculptoriam, neque Sculptoria derivatur à Regia, & tamen ars Regia imperat Sculptoriæ, eámque subjectam & subordinatam habet, & potest ac debet Rex sculptori jubere, ut non sculpat statuas obscenas, ne corrumpatur juventus, neque ex auro vel argento, ut ea metalla serventur ad usum magis necessarium; neque statuas suas nimis magno pretio vendat, ad coërcendam avaritiam: sic ars Ecclesiastica regendi animas, quæ est ars artium, & præcipuè residet in Papa, non includit necessariò artem Regiam, neque necesse est, ut omnia Regna deriventur ab Ecclesia, & tamen quia finis ejus est vita æterna, ad quam subordinantur omnes alii fines, subjecta & subordinata est illi ars politica regendi populos, & potest ac debet summus Pontifex Regibus imperare, ut non abutantur potestate Regia. Cæterum apertam sic fallaciam Bellarminus committit, artem cum subjecto habente artem confundens turpiter. Artis equidem cujusque finis subordinari fini artis superioris rectè dicitur, illius scilicet, quæ sit architectonica; sicut finis fræenifactoriæ subordinatur equestri, quæ illi modum fræna faciendi præscribit. At inter artem Regiam gubernandi populos, & artem sculptoriam talis subordinatio nulla est; neque finis artis sculptoriæ, fini artis Regiæ ullo modo inservit. Alioquin ars Regia, tanquam indigens, ut ipsa perfectè exerceatur, arte sculptoria, eidem modum efficiendi statuas, ut commodè artis Regiæ regendi populos fini per statuas ejusmodi consequendo inserviant, præscribere deberet. Non igitur potestati Regiæ ars sculptoria, sed sculptor, seu habens artem sculptoriam subjicitur, quia sculptor, ceu subditus Regis circa usum vel abusum artis suæ Regi parere tenetur, non circa artem ipsam, utpote quam imperio suo præcipiendo, ut tales vel tales statuas efficiat, quibus
units.tr: XX. Bellarmine, against Barclay, chap. 2, tries in vain to escape this blow by distinguishing a twofold subordination. In one sense, the power that belongs to the subordinate is derived from the superior, as the power of a vicar, legate, or judge or president is derived from the one whose vicar, legate, or judge he is. In the other sense, one thing is not derived from another, but is subjected and subordinated to it merely because the end of the one is subjected and subordinated to the end of the other. Such is the subjection and subordination of the various arts (sculpture, oratory, astronomy, and the like) to the art of ruling peoples, which is called royal and architectonic. In the former subordination, the power of the superior includes the power of the subordinate; in the latter it does not. He asserts that secular power is subordinated to ecclesiastical power in the latter way, not the former. As, he says, the royal art does not include the art of sculpture, and sculpture is not derived from the royal art, yet the royal art commands sculpture and holds it subjected and subordinated, and the King can and ought to order the sculptor not to make obscene statues, lest youth be corrupted, nor to make them of gold or silver, so that those metals may be kept for more necessary use, nor to sell his statues at too high a price, to restrain avarice. So the ecclesiastical art of ruling souls, which is the art of arts and resides especially in the Pope, does not necessarily include the royal art, nor is it necessary that all kingdoms be derived from the Church; yet because its end is eternal life, to which all other ends are subordinated, the political art of ruling peoples is subjected and subordinated to it, and the supreme Pontiff can and ought to command kings that they not abuse royal power. But Bellarmine commits an obvious fallacy here, shamefully confusing the art with the subject who possesses the art. Indeed, the end of any art is rightly said to be subordinated to the end of a higher art, namely one that is architectonic; just as the end of the bridle-maker's art is subordinated to the horseman's art, which prescribes for it the manner of making bridles. But between the royal art of governing peoples and the art of sculpture there is no such subordination, nor does the end of the sculptor's art serve the end of the royal art in any way. Otherwise the royal art, needing the art of sculpture in order to be perfectly exercised, would have to prescribe for it the manner of making statues, so that they might conveniently serve the end of the royal art of ruling peoples. Therefore it is not the art of sculpture that is subject to political power, but the sculptor, that is, the one who has the art of sculpture. The sculptor, as the King's subject, is bound to obey the King regarding the use or abuse of his art, not regarding the art itself, which the King does not direct by commanding that he make such and such statues,

units.la: { } quibus Regia ars finem suum consequi possit; vel etiam admissos errores ostendendo arte sua, & corrigendo, non dirigit. Pari igitur ratione potestati ecclesiasticæ subjicitur & fubordinatur is, qui potestatem politicam habet, & vicissim potestati politicæ is, qui Ecclesiasticam habet: sed neutra potestas alteri subjicitur & fubordinatur ullo modo, quin potiùs utraque ex ipsius etiam Gelasii & Innocentii confessione supra posita, dignitate, officio, & actibus prorsus inter fe discretæ sunt.
units.tr: by which the royal art can attain its end; or even by pointing out errors admitted and correcting them by his art. By the same reasoning, he who has political power is subjected and subordinated to ecclesiastical power, and conversely he who has ecclesiastical power is subjected to political power. But neither power is subjected and subordinated to the other in any way; rather, both, by the very confession of Gelasius and Innocent set forth above, are wholly distinct from each other in dignity, office, and acts.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Et sanè ipsimet Hieromonarchici subjectionem illam secularis potestatis explicare nequeunt. Vel enim talis est per derivationem, vel per fubalternationem, vel per subordinationem, vel propter eminentiam dignitatis in spirituali supra fecularem. Non fieri per derivationem ipsimet confitentur. Neque etiam per fubalternationem fieri potest, quia fubalternata potestas omnia principia sua in fubalternante habere deberet. Quis autem dixerit secularem potestatem principia sua, saltem analoga, habere supernaturalia, quæ habet naturalia maximè propria sibique sufficientissima. Sed & subordinationem heic locum habere non posse, supra asseruimus. Frustra certè Contarenus tract. de potestate Pontificis, & Molina tract. 2. disp. 21. de justi. & jure, subordinationem heic fingunt, qualis est inter architectonicam atque eidem famulantes. Sublata enim architectonica, corruunt omnes subordinatæ, sicut sublata arte equestri simul frænifactoria ruit. At sublata Ecclesiastica potestate non ilico seculus tollitur. Imò prior est politia quàm Ecclesia, quia juxta Optatum Lib. v. Ecclesia est in Republica, non Respublica in Ecclesia. Denique nulla hic subjectio locum habet propter eminentiam dignitatis in Spirituali supra secularem, quia quod dignius & excellentius est, non statim imperium & jus habet in id, quod ignobilius & minùs dignum est. In humanis
units.tr: Indeed the Hieromonarchists themselves cannot explain that subjection of secular power. For it is either by derivation, or by subalternation, or by subordination, or because of the eminence of dignity of the spiritual over the secular. They themselves admit that it does not happen by derivation. Nor can it happen by subalternation, since a subalternated power ought to have all its principles in the power above it. But who would say that secular power, at least in its analogous principles, has supernatural principles, when it has natural principles that are most proper to it and wholly sufficient for it? But we have already asserted above that subordination cannot have a place here. Certainly Contarenus, in his treatise on the power of the Pontiff, and Molina, in treatise 2, disputation 21, on justice and right, vainly invent a subordination here of the kind that exists between the architectonic art and the arts serving it. For when the architectonic art is removed, all the subordinate arts fall, just as the bridle-making art falls along with the horseman's art. But when ecclesiastical power is removed, the political power is not at once destroyed. Indeed the state is prior to the Church, since, according to Optatus, Book 5, the Church is in the commonwealth, not the commonwealth in the Church. Finally, there is no subjection here owing to the eminence of dignity of the spiritual over the secular, since what is more worthy and excellent does not immediately have command and right over what is baser and less worthy. In human affairs, nobles can indeed surpass commoners in dignity, yet without any command over them.

units.la: Hierarchici in explicanda potestatis secularis subordinatione sibi parum constant. nis præsertim, ubi nobiles plebejos anteire dignitate, sine ullo tamen in hos imperio, possunt.
units.tr: The Hierarchists are poorly consistent with themselves in explaining the subordination of secular power, especially where nobles can rank above commoners in dignity without any command over them.

units.la: XXII. Frustra igitur planè Romani Pontifices, in propria causa favorabiles sibi ipsis judices, similitudine solis & lunæ subordinationem illam explicare conati sunt. Quos inter sic Innocentius III. Lib. 1. Epist. 401. &c. Solita, de major. & obed. causam expedit. Porrò, inquiens, sicut Luna lumen suum à sole sortitur quâ revera minor est illo, quantitate simul & qualitate, situ pariter & effectu, sic Regalis potestas, ab auctoritate Pontificiali, suæ fortitur dignitatis splendorem, cujus conspectu quanto magis inhæret, tanto minori lumine decoratur: & quò plus ejus elongatur aspectu, eò plus proficit in splendore. Scitè profectò, acutè & eleganter, si res ita haberet, & ambitioni Papali veritas astipularetur. Sed docebunt nos, qui ædilitatem gerunt sine suffragiis, quo pacto Nero, Domitianus, Trajanus, Hadrianus, Antoninus, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, aliique gentiles, veri & legitimi Imperatores utique à Romanis Pontificibus habuerint potestatem, si sicut Luna splendorem à Sole, ita Imperator à Pontifice suam potestatem acciperet? Quòd si Imperatores Ethnici non à Pontificibus, sed immediatè à Deo suam habuerunt potestatem, cur Christiani Principes ab iis eam accipere debuerunt? Unde constat eos vel accepisse, vel accipere debuisse? Atqui solus Deus ille Sol est, à quo immediatè omne potestatis suæ lumen sicut Ecclesia, ita etiam Respublica fœneratur. Illud quoque bellè dictum, Principes politicos, quò sunt Romano Pontifici propiores, eò ad instar Lunæ minori pollere potestate, quò verò remotiores, eò majori. Etenim si de jure hoc Innocentius intellexit, cedò tabulas, commissionem, diplomata! Si de facto, ceu alter Cajaphas, vatem Papa gessit. Verè enim generatio Papæ, ceu summi Monarchæ, fuit corruptio, aut saltem depressio maxima Principum hujus seculi. Ubi enim sunt tot Duces, tot Reguli, Romæ vicini, Beneventanus, Spoletanus, alii? Quò tandem dejectus, & Roma, ipsáque Italia exactus est Romanorum, nomine & voce duntaxat nunc, non re & facto Imperator? Persa & Indus, Hispanus, Gallus, Anglus, alii, quia remotiores adhuc splendent, neque ita, ut viciniores, absorpti extinctique sunt. Sol hic jam verè sol, & solus lucere cupit, & splendore suo omnes utriusque hemispherii stellas, lampadas scilicet tam spirituales, quàm temporales, tam Regum folia, quàm Episcoporum Cathedras non modò præstringere, sed planè extinguere satagit. Nec contentus suo in diem dominio, jam etiam noýti præesse conatur, ac ne Luna vel stellæ splendeant, ipse vim naturæ facit; ipse, tellure interposita, &, ut interjaceat, per vim sedibus suis convulsa, hoc est, terrena potestate per nefas arrepta, perpetuam eis eclipsin minatur.
units.tr: XXII. Therefore the Roman Pontiffs, judges favourable to themselves in their own cause, have tried in vain to explain that subordination by the likeness of the sun and the moon. Among them Innocent III, in Book 1, Letter 401, etc., "Solita," on majority and obedience, settles the matter thus: "Moreover, just as the moon receives its light from the sun, though it is really smaller than the sun in quantity and quality, in position and effect alike, so royal power receives the splendour of its dignity from pontifical authority; the more it clings to the sight of that authority, the less it is adorned with light, and the further it is removed from its gaze, the more it gains in splendour." Certainly this is cleverly and elegantly put, if things were so and truth lent support to Papal ambition. But those who held the aedileship without votes will teach us how Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, and other pagans, true and lawful emperors, could have had power from the Roman Pontiffs, if the emperor received his power from the Pope as the moon receives its splendour from the sun. But if the pagan emperors had their power not from the Pontiffs but immediately from God, why ought Christian princes to have received it from them? Where is it established that they have received it or ought to have received it? Yet God alone is that Sun from whom, immediately, every light of power is borrowed, both by the Church and by the commonwealth. It is also well said that political princes, the nearer they are to the Roman Pontiff, the less they are strong in power, like the moon, and the more remote they are, the greater their power. For if Innocent meant this by right, let him produce the charters, the commission, the diplomas! If in fact, then, like another Caiaphas, the Pope has played the prophet. For indeed the rise of the Papacy, as of a supreme monarch, was the corruption, or at least the greatest depression, of the princes of this age. For where are so many dukes and petty kings, neighbours of Rome, the Beneventan, the Spoletan, and others? To what state has Rome herself, and Italy itself, been reduced, and driven out, so that the Roman emperor now exists only in name and voice, not in reality and deed? The Persian and the Indian, the Spaniard, the Frenchman, the Englishman, and others, since they are more remote, still shine, and have not been swallowed up and extinguished as their nearer neighbours were. This Sun is now truly a sun, and wishes to shine alone, and with its splendour it strives not only to dim but utterly to extinguish all the stars of both hemispheres, that is, the lamps both spiritual and temporal, kings' thrones no less than bishops' chairs. Nor, content with its present dominion from day to day, does it now try to rule even the night; and so that the moon and the stars may not shine, it does violence to nature itself, interposing the earth, and, so that it may lie between, by force tearing them from their seats, that is, having seized earthly power by wickedness, it threatens them with perpetual eclipse.

units.la: XXIII. Neque plus roboris habet potestatis Ecclesiasticæ cum spiritu seu anima, & politicæ cum carne comparatio, quam sic Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. lib. v. cap. 6. 7. urget: Ecclesiastica & Civilis potestas nonnisi unum corpus constituunt unámque societatem, non aliter quàm Spiritus & Caro in homine unam personam faciunt. Sed Ecclesiastica potestas, quæ est tanquam anima & spiritus, est principalis pars, quoniam sibi scopum proponit salutem æternam. Altera potestas est tanquam caro collata ad Spiritum, duntaxat temporalem Reip. pacem pro fine suo habet. Ergo spiritualis potestas est suprema, & potestt civili imperare. Equidem similitudine Spiritus & Carnis Ecclesiasticam & civilem potestatem etiam S. Patres nonnulli, Gregorius Nazianzenus inprimis Orat. 15. ad subditos timore perculsos, usi sunt, eo scilicet sensu, quòd Ecclesiastica dignior sit & præstantior civili, quod ultro largi- Tractatus Bellarminus etiam similitudine Spiritus et Carnis. largimur. Sed eadem turpiter Jesuitæ abutuntur, ut Papæ, spirituali scilicet, Principum carnalium dorso pro libitu inequitanti potestatem vindicent. Quorum proin sensu alienissima comparatio est. An enim sicut Spiritus vitam corpori, & cuilibet ejus parti impartitur: ita spiritualis potestas civili propriam functionem & administrationem præscribit? An, sicut corpus sine anima consistere nequit, temporalis etiam potestas sine Ecclesiastica consistere non potest? An sicut Spiritus & corpus efficiunt unum quid, hominem puta, & hoc illi essentialiter subordinatur: ita etiam Ecclesiastica & civilis potestas unum quid per se efficiunt? & una ad alteram essentialiter refertur? An denique sicut Spiritus in corpus directè agit, ecclesiastica similiter in civilem, eam movendo, regendo, præceptis legibúsque informando, directè agit? Hoc sanè Bellarminus, aliique Papicolæ non pauci, affirmare non sustinent. Si Scripturæ (Eph. iv. 15. 16.) similitudinem admittimus, nos omnes non nisi unum corpus sumus, cujus caput Christus, Spiritu suo unicuique membro idoneam vim largitur.
units.tr: Nor does the comparison of ecclesiastical power with spirit or soul, and civil power with flesh, carry any more force than Bellarmine presses it in De Romano Pontifice, book 5, chapters 6 and 7: Ecclesiastical and civil power together constitute one body and one society, just as spirit and flesh make one person in a man. But ecclesiastical power, which is as it were the soul and spirit, is the principal part, since it sets before itself the goal of eternal salvation. The other power is like flesh joined to the spirit; it has for its end only the temporal peace of the commonwealth. Therefore spiritual power is supreme and can command civil power. Indeed, some of the holy Fathers, above all Gregory Nazianzen in Oration 15, To the Subjects Terrified by Fear, have used the likeness of spirit and flesh for ecclesiastical and civil power, in the sense that the ecclesiastical is worthier and more excellent than the civil, which we readily grant. Bellarmine's treatise also (the likeness of spirit and flesh). But the Jesuits shamefully abuse the same comparison, so as to claim for the Pope, who is spiritual, a power to ride at will upon the backs of carnal princes. Therefore the comparison is wholly alien to their meaning. For does spiritual power prescribe to civil power its proper function and administration, just as the spirit imparts life to the body and to each of its parts? Or, just as the body cannot subsist without the soul, can temporal power also not subsist without ecclesiastical power? Or, just as spirit and body make one thing, a man, and the body is essentially subordinate to him, do ecclesiastical and civil power likewise make one thing by themselves, and is the one essentially related to the other? Or finally, just as the spirit acts directly upon the body, does ecclesiastical power likewise act directly upon civil power, moving it, ruling it and shaping it with precepts and laws? Bellarmine and not a few other Papal partisans do not venture to affirm this. If we admit the likeness of Scripture (Eph. 4:15, 16), we are all only one body, whose head is Christ, who by his Spirit grants to each member its fitting power.

units.la: XXIV. Ficulnea folia Bonifacius VIII. in Extrava- gante Unam Sanctam pro Ecclesiasticæ potestatis in civi- lem imperio affert.
units.tr: XXIV. Boniface VIII, in the Extravagant Unam Sanctam, brings forward withered fig leaves for the empire of ecclesiastical power over civil power.

units.la: Cujusmodi sunt, quòd Christus Petro dixerit Joh. xxj. 15. Pasce oves meas: adeóque non quasdam duntaxat, sed universas pascendi munus injunxerit: quòd Luc. xxij. 38. idem Apostolis dicentibus; Ecce gladii duo, non responderit, nimis esse, sed satis, immuens in Ecclesiæ potestate esse gladios duos spiritualem & temporalem: quòd Matth. xxvj. 52. idem Petro dicens, converte gladium tuum in vaginam, in potestate ejus etiam temporalem gladium esse declaraverit: quod S. Paulus scribens Rom. xiij. 1. Non est potestas, nisi à Deo; quæ autem sunt, à Deo ordinatæ sunt, significaverit ordinem esse inter gladios, adeóque gladium temporalem esse sub gladio spidio spirituali ordinatum, & tanquam inferiorem reduci per alium in suprema: quòd denique (1 Cor. 11. 15.) spiritualis homo dijudicet omnia, adeóque etiam Papa Spiritualis Imperatorem. Ita scilicet Dei omnipotentis verbum obtorto collo rapi oportuit, ut immensæ Pontificis cupiditati, & impotenti desiderio imperandi Regibus serviret. Taceo, quòd S. Petro dicta, Papa auferat non pretio, sed vi. Quis ποιμαίνειν pascere idem esse, quòd imperare Regibus & Principibus mundi, eos pro libitu deponere, habiles, inhabilésve reddere, calcibus ferire, denique πυμβασιλικῶς regnare dixerit? Sunto Reges & Principes oves Pastorum Ecclesiæ in spiritualibus. Ast iidem pastores sunt Regum & Principum etiam oves in temporalibus. Cúmque & discipuli Christi quæsiverint, & Christus respónderit de duobus gladiis non diversi generis, sed materiali utroque; & Petrus gladium ejusmodi materialem tractans, à Christo objurgatus fuerit, extrema utique impudentia, ne dicam impietas est Bonifacii, seu Malifacii hujus, duos inde gladios diversissimi generis, quorum unus alteri dominetur, conflantis, & sibi utrumque vindicantis, quin & eosdem non contra hostes Christi, sed contra Christum ipsum & membra ejus stringentis. Tum & putidissimum est cavillum in voce πλαγιδίου ordinata, quæ non potestatum diversarum vel subordinationem vel connexionem quamcunque, sed eminentis, adeóque supremæ potestatis cujusvis in terris, & temporalis quidem, utpote quæ sola gladio munita est Divinam ordinationem & deputationem notat. Denique nec Papa est πνευματικὸς spiritualis ille homo, cui dijudicandi omnia facultatem Apostolus committit, nec si esset, solus esset, nec ἀνάγκης illa judicium supremum sive in spiritualibus sive in temporalibus, sed discretionem spiritualium, & per Spiritús S. gratiam significat.
units.tr: Such are these: that Christ said to Peter (John 21:15), "Feed my sheep," and so enjoined upon him the duty of feeding not certain sheep only but all; that when the apostles said (Luke 22:38), "Behold, here are two swords," he did not answer that they were too many but enough, thereby indicating that in the power of the Church there are two swords, the spiritual and the temporal; that when he said the same to Peter (Matt. 26:52), "Put your sword back into its sheath," he declared that the temporal sword is also in his power; that when St Paul wrote (Rom. 13:1), "There is no power but of God, and those that are have been ordained by God," he signified that there is an order between the swords, and so the temporal sword is ordered under the spiritual sword and is brought back, as an inferior, to the supreme through another; and finally that (1 Cor. 2:15) the spiritual man judges all things, and therefore the spiritual Pope also judges the Emperor. Thus, evidently, the word of almighty God had to be dragged by the neck so that it would serve the boundless greed of the Pontiff and his powerless desire to command kings. I pass over the fact that the Pope takes what was said to St Peter not by price but by force. Who has said that to feed [ποιμαίνειν] is the same as to rule over the kings and princes of the world, to depose them at will, to make them fit or unfit, to trample them under foot, and finally to reign [βασιλικῶς] royally? Let kings and princes be the sheep of the Church's shepherds in spiritual matters. But the same shepherds are also the sheep of kings and princes in temporal matters. And since the disciples of Christ asked, and Christ answered, about two swords not of different kinds but both of material substance, and since Peter, handling such a material sword, was rebuked by Christ, it is surely the utmost impudence, not to say impiety, of this Boniface, or rather Malefactor, to construct from this two swords of the most diverse kind, one of which rules over the other, to claim both for himself, and to draw them not against the enemies of Christ but against Christ himself and his members. Then too there is a most stinking quibble in the word ordinata [τεταγμέναι], which denotes not any subordination or connection whatever of different powers, but the divine ordination and appointment of an eminent and therefore supreme power of any kind on earth, and indeed of a temporal one, since that alone is armed with the sword. Finally, the Pope is not that spiritual [πνευματικὸς] man to whom the Apostle commits the faculty of judging all things; nor, even if he were, would he be alone; and that word [ἀνακρίνει] does not signify a supreme judgment, whether in spiritual or in temporal matters, but the discernment of spiritual things, and this through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XXV. Ad liquidum haætenus perduximus, duplicem esse in mundo potestatem unam in temporalibus dominantem, quam per vicarios suos, summas in terra potestates Deus exercet, alteram in spiritualibus dominantem, soli Christo, Regi & capiti Ecclesiæ summo eximiam, ministerialem quin etiam, Ecclesiæ commissam: potestatis civilis radicem esse immediatam institutionem & delegationem, Dei, adeóque Reges & Principes à Deo solo, & ἀμέσως immediatè dependere: Christum solum unicumque Ecclesiæ caput & Regem esse: Ecclesiæ post ejusdem in Cœlum ascensum gubernationem eandem esse, quæ fuit primitiva, Christo in terris adhuc degente: potestatem Ministrorum Ecclesiæ quorumvis merè & spiritualem & ministerialem esse, procul omni dominatione & Monarchia, vel hierarchia visibili: Utramque denique & civilem & Ecclesiasticam potestatem ita distinctam esse, ut neutra alteri vel dominetur vel pareat, adeóque temporalis etiam Ecclesiasticæ nullo modo vel subordinetur vel subjiciatur. Quemadmodum verò Hierarchia Papalis repagula, limitésque sacros omnes, supremam sibi in Spiritualibus æquè ac temporalibus potestatem malis artibus quæsitam nefariè exercendo, perrupérit, in propatulo est. XXVI. Et supremam quidem in spiritualibus potestatem Phocæ Imperatoris indultu Bonifacius III. Romanæ sedi primus asseruit: dum se Romanæ sedis Episcopum, Universalem & Oecumenicum Episcopum declaravit. Quem titulum nemo acriùs, nemo frequentiùs, vehementiùsque, quàm post Pelagium II. cujus verba Historia Patuss. 36. repræsentat: ipse Gregorius M. Romanus & ipse Episcopus, paulò ante adversus Constantinopolitanum impugnávit, Deo sine dubio detegente molitionem Sathanæ, & per os ejus, cujus successores huc contenderunt, Antichristianam superbiam damnante. Passim illæ nomen universalis Episcopi, tanquam profanum, superbum, stultum, elationis titulum, acerbè traducit & configit. Operæ pretium est argumentorum arietes, quibus Epist. lib. iv. ep. 32. 34. 36.38. Oecumenici tituli isthoc monstrum validissimè concussit, ὡς συνᾳ̈ξθλω repetere. Pertendit igitur primò, si unus Episcopus vel Patriarcha universalis dicatur, cæteris Episcoporum & Patriarcharum nomen derogari. Quæ ratio manifesta est. Omnis enim Episcopi illa ἀλκοτοιά est, ut secundùm regulam Christi se typum Ecclesiæ exhibeat, reddens rationem & fraternitati & Christo, & cum eadem fratres veros admittat, falsis anathema dicat, denique in commune consulat de iis, quæ ad ἐυπαξίαν pertinent. Si autem unus est universalis Episcopus, erit idem singularis, & reliqui omnes erunt ἀλλοτριοπίσκοποι, denique servi unius. Atqui Christus dedit pastores & doctores. Hoc verò, ita Gregorius, vel de omnibus intelligendum est, vel de uno. Si prius, ille universalis igitur non habet vocationem à Christo. Si posterius, cæteris Episcopis & Pastoribus esse non dabitur, quia plures esse universales, non possunt Secundò, ait, pacem & viscera universalis Ecclesiæ hoc superbo nomine turbari. Ubi proponit Paulum, ad dilaceratiónem corporis dominici, per quam membra illius se aliis quodammodo capitibus sociabant toto animo cohorrefcentem. Quid si enim quis urgeat ἀνωμία & paritatem omnimodam à Christo institutam? Numquid propterea excommunicari poterit? Et qua conscientia id fiet? Necessum hic erit contentiones, schismata suboriri, & turbari cuncta. Tertiò, gratiæ communiter omnibus effusæ contradici, arguit, libertati puta Christianæ, à qua est, ut quivis Christianus sit Libertus Domini, humanæ Cathedræ, vel authoritati nulli in spiritualibus mancipatus. Quartò, Paulus (1. Cor. 1. 12.) ita ille, membra Dominici corporis certis extra Christum quasi capitibus & ipsis Apostolis subjici particulariter evitavit: tu (ita Johannem Constantinopolitanum alloquitur) quid Christo, universalis Ecclesiæ capiti in extremi judicii es dicturus examine, qui cuncta ejus membra tibimet conaris universalis appellatione supponere? Petrus Apostolus primum membrum Sanctæ & universalis Ecclesiæ est. Paulus, Andreas, Johannes quid aliud quàm singularium sunt plebium capita? Et tamen sub uno capite omnes sunt membra Ecclesiæ. Unum igitur caput deseri, si universalis Episcopus agnoscatur, atque hoc amplius Apostolica dignitate, ipsúmque Petrum eam potestatem non accepisse, arguit. Non erant quidem Apostoli certarum plebium Episcopi, sed μέριμναν πασῶν τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν solicitudinem pro omnibus Ecclesiis habebant. 2. Cor. xi. 28. 29. Nemo tamen illorum ad se unum omnia revocavit, imò eorum quivis aliis suum ἀρχιλεον & καινον fundamentum & Canonem integrum inviolatúmque reliquit. Epistola 36. sic loquitur: Ille qui in eleemosynis, orationibus atque jejuniis videbatur occupatus, ex eo in quo sedebat cinere, ex ea, quam praetendebat humilitate, jactantiam sumpsit: ita ut universa sibi tentet adscribere, & omnia, quæ (NB) soli uni capiti cohærent, videlicet Christo, per elationem pompatici sermonis ejusdem Christi sibi studeat membra subjugare. En, judice Gregorio universalis Episcopi titulus, soli uni capiti Christo cohæret, & qui eum sibi arrogat, Christi membra sibi subjugare studet. Quintò, imitationem hanc esse Diaboli, qui omnibus præesse, nemini subesse voluit, adeóque titulum illum totum Luciferianum esse, astruit. Quis, inquit, in tam perverso vocabulo, nisi ille imitandus proponitur, qui despectis Angelorum legionibus, secum socialiter constitutis, ad culmen conatus est singularitatis erumpere: ut & nulli subesse, & solus omnibus præesse videretur? Qui etiam dixit: In Cælum conscendam: supra astra Cæli exaltabo solium meum &c. Agnoscit manifestè in Ecclesia neminem esse oportere, qui solus præesse judicare, à nemine judicari, & cæteros omnes sibi subesse velit. Sextò, elationem illam, characterem Antichristi esse, innuit. Omnia inquit, quæ prædicta sunt, fiunt. Rex superbiæ propè est, & quod dici nefas est, Sacerdotum est præparatus exitus: quia cervici militant elationis, qui ad hoc positi fuerant, ut ducatum præbeant humilitatis. Sed &c Ep. lib. vj. ep. 30. ad Imp. Mauritium, sic animi sui sensa pandit: Ego autem fidenter dico, quia quisquis se universalem Sacerdotem vocat, vel vocari desiderat, in elatione sua Antichristum præcurrit, quia superbiendo se cæteris præponit. Nec dispari superbia ad errorem ducitur, quia sicut perversus ille, Deus videri vult super omnes homines, ita quisquis iste est, qui solus sacerdos appellari appetit, super cæteros sacerdotes se extollit. Et passim elationis nomine utens, manifestè ad Antichristum ὑπερηφανοῦντα, efferentem se supra omne, quod Deus aut venerabile dicitur, alludit. Septimò, titulum illum superbiam meram redolere, & Christi Sanctorumque humilitati repugnare, graphicè passim admonet. Octavò, ex verbis Christi Matth. xxiii. 8. 10. Vos autem nolite appellari Rabbi &c. argumentum depromit. Quid ergo, inquit ad Constantinopolitanum, frater charißime, in illo terribili examine venientis judicis dicturus es, qui non solum pater, sed etiam generalis pater in mundo vocari appetis? Quæ sanè feriens prægnánsque ratio est. Nonò, Scandalum Johanni Gregorius graviter objicit. Ecce, inquit, ex hoc nefando elationis vocabulo Ecclesia scinditur. Fratrum omnium corda ad scandalum provocantur. Numquid mente excidit, quod veritas dicit: Qui scandalizaverit unum de pusillis istis, qui in me credunt, expedit ei, ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus &c. Addit, contra charitatem isthoc militare, utpote quæ quærat quæ sua, cùm ita se supra alios efferens, aliena quærat. Decimò, tandem eo argumento Johannem premit, quod nec Episcopi Romani antehac, nec Sanctorum quisquam hactenus eo vocabulo usus fuerit. Ut cuncta, inquit, brevi cingulo locutionis astringam, Sancti ante legem, Sancti sub lege, sancti sub gratia, omnes hi perficientes corpus Domini, in membris sunt Ecclesiæ constituti, & nemo se unquam universalem vocare voluit. Et Sedis ipsius Romanæ exemplum his verbis urget. Numquid non, sicut vestra sanctitas novit, per venerandum Chalcedonense Concilium hujus Apostolicæ sedis Antistites, cui, Deo disponente, deservio, universales oblato honore vocati sunt? Sed tamen nullus unquam, tali vocabulo appellari voluit: nullus sibi hoc temerarium nomen arripuit, ne, si sibi in Pontificatús gradu gloriam singularitatis arriperet, hanc omnibus fratribus denegâsse videretur. Non tantùm igitur à Constantinopolitana, sed à Romana etiam sede Universalis Episcopi axioma, diserte removet. Tantùm abest, ut decantatum illud: Tu es Petrus &c. Tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum: Pasce oves meas &c. Constantinopolitano Gregorius occinat. Quòd verò de Synodi Chalcedonensis decreto, quo Romano honor tituli Universalis Episcopi oblatus sit, idem Gregorius dixit, aliquid sibi præter veritatem indulsit. Nullum enim Decretum proferri potest, nullum scriptum publicum, adeò ut Baronius ad A. 451. librarii fraudem suspicari cogatur.
units.tr: XXV. Up to this point we have made it clear that there are two powers in the world. One rules in temporal affairs, and God exercises it through his vicars, the supreme powers on earth. The other rules in spiritual affairs, belongs exclusively to Christ, the King and head of the Church, and is committed to the Church as a ministerial power. The root of civil power is the immediate institution and delegation of God, so kings and princes depend immediately on God alone. Christ alone is the one head and King of the Church. After his ascension into heaven, the government of the Church is the same as it was in the primitive Church, while Christ still dwelt on earth. The power of the ministers of the Church, of whatever kind, is purely spiritual and ministerial, far removed from all domination, monarchy or visible hierarchy. Finally, the civil and ecclesiastical powers are so distinct that neither rules over the other or obeys it, and so the temporal power is in no way subordinate or subject to the ecclesiastical. But how the Papal hierarchy has broken through all the sacred barriers and boundaries, wickedly exercising a supreme power over spiritual matters as well as temporal, which it obtained by evil arts, is obvious. XXVI. Boniface III was the first to claim for the Roman see a supreme power in spiritual matters, by the favour of the Emperor Phocas, when he declared himself bishop of the Roman see, universal and ecumenical bishop. No one attacked this title more sharply, more often and more vehemently than Gregory the Great, after Pelagius II, whose words the History of Patus. 36 presents. Gregory, himself Roman and himself a bishop, had a little earlier assailed it against the Constantinopolitan, God undoubtedly revealing the scheme of Satan, and condemning through his mouth the Antichristian pride of those whose successors have pressed on in this direction. Everywhere he bitterly brands and rebukes that name, universal bishop, as profane, proud, foolish, a title of arrogance. It is worth setting out the battering-rams of arguments with which, in Epist. lib. iv. ep. 32, 34, 36, 38, he most powerfully shook this monster of the ecumenical title, repeating them as a fellow-contestant [ὡς συναθλῶν]. He argues, first, that if one bishop or patriarch is called universal, the name of bishop and patriarch is taken away from all the others. The reason is plain. For every bishop's whole office [ἀλκοτοιά] is to show himself, according to Christ's rule, a type of the Church, giving account both to his brethren and to Christ, admitting true brethren with them, condemning false ones as accursed, and finally taking counsel in common about matters that pertain to good order [εὐταξία]. But if there is one universal bishop, he will also be the only one, and all the rest will be bishops of others [ἀλλοτριοπίσκοποι], in short, the servants of one. Yet Christ gave pastors and teachers. Now, says Gregory, this must be understood either of all or of one. If of all, then that universal bishop does not have his calling from Christ. If of one, there will be no room for other bishops and pastors, since several cannot be universal. Secondly, he says, the peace and the very heart of the universal Church are disturbed by this proud name. Here he sets before us Paul, who, wholly aghast at the rending of the Lord's body, through which its members were in some way joining themselves to other heads. What if someone should press the point about anomy [ἀνωμία] and the complete equality instituted by Christ? Will he then be able to be excommunicated? And with what conscience will it be done? Here contentions and schisms will necessarily arise, and everything will be thrown into confusion. Thirdly, he argues that the grace poured out commonly on all is contradicted, namely Christian liberty, from which it follows that every Christian is a freedman of the Lord, subject to no human chair or authority in spiritual matters. Fourthly, Paul (1 Cor. 1:12) avoided in this way the members of the Lord's body being subjected in particular to certain heads outside Christ, and to the apostles themselves: "You," he says, addressing John of Constantinople, "what will you say to Christ, the head of the universal Church, in the examination of the last judgment, you who try to place all his members under yourself by the title of universal? Peter the Apostle is the first member of the holy and universal Church. Paul, Andrew, John, what else are they than heads of particular peoples? And yet all are members of the Church under one head." He argues, therefore, that if a universal bishop is acknowledged, one head is forsaken, and this, moreover, with apostolic dignity, and that Peter himself did not receive that power. The apostles were indeed not bishops of particular peoples, but they had the care of all the churches, "solicitude for all the Churches" (2 Cor. 11:28, 29). Yet none of them drew everything back to himself alone; rather, each of them left to the others their own foundation and rule [ἀρχιλεον & καινον], whole and inviolate. Epistle 36 speaks thus: He who seemed occupied with almsgiving, prayers and fasting, took from the ashes on which he sat, and from the humility he professed, a boastfulness, so that he tries to ascribe the whole to himself, and seeks to subject to himself by the pompous elation of his words the members of Christ, all those things which (note this) cling to the one head alone, namely Christ. Behold, according to Gregory's judgment, the title of universal bishop clings to the one head, Christ alone, and whoever arrogates it to himself seeks to subject the members of Christ to himself. Fifthly, he asserts that this imitation is that of the devil, who wished to rule over all and be subject to no one, and that the whole of that title is Luciferian. "Who," he says, "is set before us in such a perverse term as to be imitated, except him who, having despised the legions of angels joined with him in fellowship, tried to break forth to the height of singularity, so as to seem both subject to no one and alone over all? He also said: 'I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne,' etc." He plainly acknowledges that in the Church there ought to be no one who wishes to rule alone, to judge and be judged by no one, and to have all others subject to him. Sixthly, he hints that such elation is the mark of Antichrist. All, he says, things which have been foretold come to pass. The king of pride is near, and what it is wrong to say, the end is prepared for the priests, because those who were set up to offer the leadership of humility have become soldiers of arrogance. But also in Ep. lib. vj. ep. 30, to the Emperor Maurice, he unfolds the feelings of his mind thus: I say boldly that whoever calls himself, or desires to be called, the universal priest, in his elation runs before Antichrist, because by his pride he sets himself above the others. Nor is it by a different pride that men are led into error, for as that wicked one wishes to be seen as God above all men, so whoever it is that seeks to be called the sole priest raises himself above the other priests. And everywhere, using the word elation, he clearly alludes to Antichrist, exalting himself [ὑπερηφανοῦντα], lifting himself above everything that is called God or venerable. Seventhly, he repeatedly warns, in vivid terms, that this title smells of pure pride and is opposed to the humility of Christ and the saints. Eighthly, he draws an argument from the words of Christ, Matt. 23:8, 10: But you are not to be called Rabbi, etc. "What, then," he says to the Constantinopolitan, "dear brother, will you say in that terrible examination of the coming judge, you who desire to be called not only father, but even general father in the world?" This is surely a striking and weighty argument. Ninthly, Gregory gravely charges John with scandal. "Behold," he says, "from this accursed term of elation the Church is torn apart. The hearts of all the brethren are provoked to scandal. Has it escaped your mind what the truth says: 'Whoever shall offend one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone were hung about his neck,' etc.?" He adds that this title runs counter to charity, since charity seeks not its own, whereas one who thus exalts himself above others seeks what is another's. Tenthly, finally, he presses John with the argument that neither the Roman bishops before this nor any of the saints hitherto have used that term. "To bind everything," he says, "in a short girdle of speech: the saints before the law, the saints under the law, the saints under grace, all these, who make up the body of the Lord, have been placed as members of the Church, and no one ever wished to call himself universal." And he presses the example of the Roman see itself in these words: "Did not the bishops of this apostolic see, to whom by God's disposition I am subject, as your holiness knows, get called universal by the honour offered at the venerable Council of Chalcedon? Yet no one ever wished to be called by such a term; no one seized for himself this rash name, lest, if he seized for himself the glory of singularity in the rank of pontificate, he should seem to have denied it to all his brethren." He therefore removes, plainly, the axiom of universal bishop not only from the Constantinopolitan see but also from the Roman see. So far is it from Gregory singing to the Constantinopolitan that well-known text: "You are Peter, etc. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven: feed my sheep," etc. As for the fact that Gregory also said that the honour of the title universal bishop had been offered to the Roman see by a decree of the Council of Chalcedon, he took a liberty beyond the truth. For no decree can be produced, no public record, so that Baronius, at the year 451, is compelled to suspect a copyist's fraud.

units.la: XXVII. Solemnia plane hic insanit Baronius, qui ad A. 595 .num.36. &c. distinguit significationem nominis universalis & œcumenici Episcopi. Ut primò significet unum solalum singularem Episcopum, præter quem alius nemo sit, & cui Episcopi cœteri omnes subsint ut filii, non ut fratres: Secundò eum denotet, qui cœteris duntaxat supremineat, & curam gerat totius Ecclesiæ, sed generalem ita, ut particulares Episcopos non excludat. Priore sensu intelligendum esse Gregorium, rectéque ita eum id nominis, ut vanum scelestum & sacrilegum execrari. Altero autem sensu nunquam putâsse damnandum. Illo Johannem se pro universali Episcopo venditâsse; hoc verò Romanum Episcopum meritò se universalem nuncupare, non improbante Gregorio. Atque isthoc etiam Bellarmini, aliorúmque χριζζυχαν εst, ridiculum planè & falsum, si quod aliud. Nam & Papa, Episcopus Romanus, se pro Universali & Oecumenico venditat priore sensu, quia licet reliquis Episcoporum nomen nondum ademerit, rem tamen abstulit, dum negat eos esse Episcopos cum plena, propria, primaria, & ab ipso Christo immediatè accepta potestate, adeóque eos pro ministris & vicariis, mancipiisque suis habet, uti supra probavimus: & Gregorius id nominis execratus est in quovis, sive Constantinopolitano, sive Romano Episcopo, posteriore, ac multò magis priore sensu, tum quia id reprehendit, quod sibi Johannes arrogavit; qui nunquam id sibi arrogavit, quòd solus esset in orbe Episcopus, reliquis sibi Patriarcharum, Metropolitanorum Episcoporum titulos constanter retinentibus, uti vel ex solo corpore juris Græco-Romani colligere est, ubi idem ille Constantinopolitanus Episcopus Johannes se πατριάρχην Οικουμενικὸν Patriarcham Universalem, Antistitem verò Deabolis Dyrrachii Metropolitanum, fratrem dilectum συλλειτουργὸν comministrum, & φιλίᾳ Φιλοχρῖστον Episcopum religiosissimum insignit. Quippe sub Constantinopolitani ditione Archiepiscopi, Episcopi fuerunt, æquè ac sub Romani, etiam tum, cùm se Oecumenicum vocabat: tum quia Gregorius in Epistolis supra laudatis Oecumenicum describit eum, qui omnibus dignior appareat, nulli subsit, omnibus prepræsit solus, Imperatori se præponat, & omnia Christi membra sibi subjiciat, qualia utique suo Oecumenico Papæ Romani vendicant: tum denique, quia testibus etiam Pomponio Læto in Phoca, Sabellico Enneadis viij. lib. 6. Blondo Dec. 1. lib. 9. aliisque, hoc utrumque inter Constantinopolitanum & Romanum Episcopum certamen intercessit, non uter solus in orbe Episcopus maneret, sed uter esset caput omnium Ecclesiarum, sive Princeps omnium Pontificum: tum denique quia id ipsum, quod sibi Constantinopolitanus arrogavit, à Phoca Romano tributum fuit, fatente Baronio ad A. 606. ubi sic ille: Quid ergo suo edicto contulit Romanæ Ecclesiæ Phocas? Nihil planè, nisi quod declaravit, sua sententia indebitè usurpari ab Episcopo Constantinopolitano Oecumenici nomen, quod Romanæ duntaxat deberetur Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: XXVII. Baronius here plainly raves in full measure. At A.D. 595, no. 36, and following, he distinguishes the meaning of the names universal and ecumenical bishop. First, that the name signifies one sole bishop, besides whom there is no other, and to whom all other bishops are subject as sons, not as brothers. Secondly, that it denotes one who stands above the rest only and takes charge of the whole Church, yet in a general sense that does not exclude particular bishops. Gregory, he says, is to be understood in the former sense, and rightly execrated the name as a vain, wicked and sacrilegious title when applied to anyone. In the latter sense he never thought it deserved condemnation. In the former sense, John claimed to be a universal bishop; in the latter, the Roman bishop may rightly call himself universal, and Gregory did not object. This distinction of Bellarmine and others is utterly ridiculous and false, if anything is [χριζζυχαν εst]. For the Pope, the Roman bishop, does set himself up as universal and ecumenical in the former sense. Although he has not yet taken the name away from the other bishops, he has taken the reality, since he denies that they are bishops with full, proper, primary power, received immediately from Christ himself. He therefore holds them as ministers, vicars and his own bondsmen, as we have shown above. Gregory execrated this name when it was applied to any bishop, whether of Constantinople or of Rome, and in the latter sense even more so, for two reasons. First, he rebuked what John had claimed for himself, and John never claimed that he alone was bishop in the world, since the other patriarchs, metropolitans and bishops constantly kept their titles. This is clear from the body of Greco-Roman law alone, where the same Constantinopolitan bishop John styles himself ecumenical patriarch [πατριάρχην Οικουμενικὸν] and universal patriarch, but calls the bishop of Dyrrachium a metropolitan, his dear brother and fellow minister [συλλειτουργὸν], and most religious bishop, friend of Christ [φιλίᾳ Φιλοχρῖστον]. Indeed, under the authority of the Constantinopolitan archbishop there were bishops, just as under the Roman one, even at the time when he called himself ecumenical. Second, Gregory, in the epistles cited above, describes the ecumenical bishop as one who appears worthier than all, is subject to no one, presides alone over all, places himself before the emperor, and subjects all the members of Christ to himself, which is exactly what the Roman Pope claims for his ecumenical office. Third, as Pomponius Laetus in his Phocas, Sabellicus in the eighth book of the sixth Ennead, Blondus in Decade 1, book 9, and others testify, a contest arose between the Constantinopolitan and the Roman bishop, not as to which of them would remain the sole bishop in the world, but as to which would be the head of all churches, or the prince of all pontiffs. Lastly, what the Constantinopolitan claimed for himself was granted by Phocas the Roman, as Baronius admits at A.D. 606, where he says: What then did Phocas confer on the Roman Church by his edict? Nothing at all, except that he declared that the title of ecumenical, which was due to the Roman Church alone, was by his judgment wrongly usurped by the bishop of Constantinople.

units.la: XXVIII. Ex Gregorii igitur dictis
units.tr: XXVIII. Ex Gregorii igitur dictis

units.la: XXVIII. Ex Gregorii igitur dictis παλαιολόγος Papatum à Phoca parricida inauspicatò in Ecclesiam introductum, ἀυτοκράτορ & ἐαυτὸν ἀμωρύμορον habemus. Cæterum quàm immensum tyrannidis in Ecclesiam Dei Chaos hoc uno Universalis, seu Oecumenici nomine occultetur, abundè procedente tempore in hunc usque diem patefactum est. Et in Synodo quidem Florentina decretum conditum est in hæc verba, quæ sunt in literis Unionis Eugenii Papæ Sessione ultima: Ο ἐξόμολο τὴν ἁγίαν ἀποστολικὴν καθέδραν, καὶ τὸν Ῥωμαῖον ἀρχιερέα εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην τὸν ποιμένα κατέχειν, αὐτὸν ὁ Ῥωμαῖον ἀρχιερεὺς Διδάσκαλον εἶναι τῆς μακαρίας πίστεως καὶ κορυφαῖος τῶν Ἀποστόλων, καὶ ἀληθῶς παππηρητὴν Χριστοῦ, καὶ πάσης τῆς Ἐκκλησίας κεφαλὴν, καὶ πάντων τῶν Χριστιανῶν παπέρα καὶ διδάσκαλον ὑπάρχειν, καὶ αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ μακαρίᾳ πίστει καὶ ποιμαίνειν, καὶ διδύναι, καὶ κυβερνᾶν τὴν καθολικὴν Ἐκκλησίαν ὑπὸ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ πληρη ἐξουσίαν. Definimus, sanctam Apostolicam sedem, & Romanum Pontificem in universum Orbem terræ tenere primatum: & ipsum Pontificem Romanum successorem esse beati Petri Principis Apostolorum, & verè Christi vicarium, totiusque Ecclesiæ Caput, & omnium Christianorum Patrem & doctorem existere: & ipsi in beato Petro pascendi, regendi & gubernandi universalem Ecclesiam à Domino nostro Iesu Christo plenam potestatem traditam esse. Quod quidem Eugenii in propria causa testis judicisque decretum non ita pridem Valerianus M. Capucinus, jussus Divino aliquo testimonio Pontificium Vicariatum comprobare, nomine sacrarum literarum Spiritu S. moderante consignatarum venditare miser non erubuit.
units.tr: XXVIII. From Gregory's words, therefore, we have the Papacy introduced into the Church unluckily by the parricide Phocas, the autocrat and self-styled [παλαιολόγος; ἀυτοκράτορ; ἐαυτὸν ἀμωρύμορον]. But how immense a chaos of tyranny over the Church of God is hidden under this one word, universal or ecumenical, has been made plain, more than enough, as time went on, down to the present day. Indeed, at the Council of Florence a decree was framed in these words, which are in the letters of union of Pope Eugenius, in the last session: We define that the holy Apostolic See and the Roman Pontiff hold the primacy over the whole world, and that the Roman Pontiff himself is the successor of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and the true vicar of Christ, and the head of the whole Church, and the father and teacher of all Christians; and that to him, in blessed Peter, was delivered by our Lord Jesus Christ the full power of feeding, ruling and governing the universal Church. [Ο ἐξόμολο τὴν ἁγίαν ἀποστολικὴν καθέδραν, καὶ τὸν Ῥωμαῖον ἀρχιερέα εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην τὸν ποιμένα κατέχειν, αὐτὸν ὁ Ῥωμαῖον ἀρχιερεὺς Διδάσκαλον εἶναι τῆς μακαρίας πίστεως καὶ κορυφαῖος τῶν Ἀποστόλων, καὶ ἀληθῶς παππηρητὴν Χριστοῦ, καὶ πάσης τῆς Ἐκκλησίας κεφαλὴν, καὶ πάντων τῶν Χριστιανῶν παπέρα καὶ διδάσκαλον ὑπάρχειν, καὶ αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ μακαρίᾳ πίστει καὶ ποιμαίνειν, καὶ διδύναι, καὶ κυβερνᾶν τὴν καθολικὴν Ἐκκλησίαν ὑπὸ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ πληρη ἐξουσίαν.] This decree, which Eugenius, a witness and judge in his own cause, issued, was lately offered, wretchedly and without blushing, by Valerianus of Capuchin, who had been ordered to vouch for the Papal vicariate by some divine testimony, under the name of the sacred letters, written under the moderating guidance of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XXIX. Sic igitur juxta Hieromonarchicos, Papa est universalis seu Oecumenicus Episcopus, ut sit Christi in terris Vicarius, qui sic vice Christi in Ecclesia fungatur, ut caput etiam ipse dicatur totius militantis Ecclesiæ. Quod etsi fateantur non æquo aut jure, aut gradu cum ipso Christo, quem solum hoc nomine in Scripturis venire non ignorant eum habere, tamen sic amplificant postea, ut facilè appareat, dicis tantùm causa Christum præferri, & αὐτὸν ἐξουσίαν plenam potestatem, uti Eugenius dicebat, seu absolutam plenitudinem potestatis, uti loqui etiam amant, eidem tribui.
