Etenim primò Papam sic αὐτοκράτορα facium, uti nulli proprius potestati, quæcunque illa tandem sit, civilis aut Ecclesiastica obnoxium esse velint, ne tum quidem, cum officio minimè fungitur. Si Papa (ita apud Gratianum dist. 40. legere est) sua & fraternæ salutis negligens deprehenditur, inutilis & remissus in suis operibus, & insuper à bono taciturnus, quod magis officit sibi & omnibus, nihilominus innumerabiles populos cervatim secum ducit primo mancipio gehennæ, cum ipso plagis multis in æternum vapulaturos, hujus culpas isthic redarguere præsumit Mortalium nullus, quòd cunctos ipse judicaturus à nemine est judicandus, nisi deprehendatur à fide devius. Et rursus causa 9. q. 3. Nemo judicabit primam sedem justitiam temperare desiderantem. Neque enim ab Augusto, neque ab omni Clero, neque à Regibus, neque à Populo judex judicabitur. Ex quibus verbis Glossator concludit, tum à Concilio Papam non posse judicari, tum Pontificis sententiæ standum esse, quamvis totus in aliquo contra eum sententiaret. Præterea ne accusari quidem de homicidio vel adulterio eundem posse, idem Glossator ad caput Non nos dist. 49. diserte notat. Et causa 9. q. 3. hic canon habetur: Aliorum hominum causas Deus per homines voluit terminari: sed sedis istius Præsulem suo, sine quæstione reservavit arbitrio. Voluit enim Petri Apostoli successores Cælo tantum debere innocentiam, & subtilissimi discussoris indagini inviolatam habere conscientiam. Licet verò à Concilio saltem eum judicari posse, censeant nonulli, ipse tamen Papa judicium isthoc validè contemnit, vel declinat, & gnathones ejus, veluti Hieronymus Albanus lib. j. de potestate Concilii, Caranza Controv. 4. alii pernegant, ullum reperiri posse criminis casum, in quo universalis Ecclesiæ Pastor judicari ab ullo Episcoporum Concilio possit. Nam etiam quod de hæresi excipit canon Si Papa, supra allatus, hodie nova stropha, asserta scilicet Papæ in jure & facto infallibilitate, redditum inutile est. Adeo in pejus populus quotidie vergit. Secundò Papæ ab omni potestate ita exempti, omnes reliquos absque ulla prorsus exceptione subjiciunt. Sic enim in Extravagante de Majoritate & obedientia, capite Unam sanctam definitam legimus. Si deviat terrena potestas, judicabitur à spirituali potestate. Sed si deviat Spiritualis potestas, minor à suo superiori: si verò suprema, à solo Deo, non ab homine judicari poterit, testante Apostolo: Spiritualis homo judicat omnia, ipse verò à nemine judicatur. Et mox : Subesse Romano Pontifici omnem humanam Creaturam declarãmus, dicimus esse de necessitate salutis. Apud Gratianum causa 9. q. 3. Aliorum sic legere est: Patet Sanctorum voce Pontificum dignitatem sedis hujus factam toto orbe venerabilem, dum illi quicquid fidelium est, ubique submittitur, dum totius corporis caput esse designatur. Neque in Spiritualibus duntaxat, sed in secularibus etiam negotiis Papæ subesse sine discrimine omnes severè iidem sanciunt, uti infra comprobabimus. Tertiò Papæ ψηφίσματα, decreta, sententias ejusmodi esse, ut contra eas ne hiscere quidem cuiquam liceat, iidem pertendunt. Ita enim apud Gratianum Dist. 19. legere est: Sic omnes Apostolicæ sedis sanctiones accipiendæ sunt, tanquam ipsius Divina voce Petri firmatæ: Et Causa 19. q. 4. Nemini de sedis Apostolicæ judicio judicare, aut illius sententiam retractare permissum, videlicet propter Ecclesiæ Romanæ primatum Christi munere in beato Apostolo Petro Divinitus collatum. Quin & jugum molestissimum ab eodem impositum, æquo animo ferendum esse, sic Dist. 19. cap: In memoriam, decernitur: Licet vix ferendum ab illa Sancta sede imponatur jugum, tamen feramus, & pia devotione toleremus. Denique ne quid ad insolentiam reliqui fiat, Glossator in caput Quanto personam, de Translatione Episcopi in Decretalibus, γυμῆ κιφαλὴ intima Papatus scrinia referans, asserit, Papam habere caeleste arbitrium, & ideo naturam rerum mutare, substantialia unius rei applicando alii. Et de nullo posse aliquid facere, & sententiam, quæ nulla est, facere aliquam: in his quæ vult ei esse pro ratione voluntatem, nec esse, qui ei dicat, cur ita facis? Posse enim supra jus dispensare, & de injustitia facere justitiam, corrigendo jura & mutandam demum plenitudinem obtinere potestatis.
units.tr: XXIX. So, according to the hierarchical monarchists, the Pope is the universal or ecumenical bishop, in that he is Christ's vicar on earth, who so acts in place of Christ in the Church that he is himself called the head of the whole militant Church. Although they confess that he holds this not with equal right or rank as Christ himself, whom they know alone comes by this name in the Scriptures, they afterwards so magnify him that it is easily seen that Christ is named only for form's sake, and that full authority, as Eugenius put it, or absolute fullness of power, as they like to say, is granted to the Pope. First, they make the Pope such an autocrat that they wish him to be subject to no proper power, civil or ecclesiastical, whatever it may be, not even when he does not discharge his office at all. If the Pope (as it is read in Gratian, dist. 40) is found negligent of his own salvation and that of his brethren, idle and slack in his works, and moreover silent about the good, which harms himself and all the more, and still leads countless peoples in herds with him to the first servitude of hell, where he will be beaten with many blows forever, no mortal presumes to rebuke his faults there, since he who is to judge everyone is to be judged by no one, unless he is found to have strayed from the faith. And again, causa 9, q. 3: No one shall judge the first See, which desires to temper justice. For a judge shall not be judged by Augustus, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people. From these words the Glossator concludes both that the Pope cannot be judged by a council, and that the Pontiff's sentence must stand even if the whole world judged against him. Moreover, the same Glossator clearly notes, on the chapter Non nos, dist. 49, that he cannot even be accused of murder or adultery. And in causa 9, q. 3 this canon is held: God willed that the causes of other men be settled by men; but the prelate of that See he reserved, beyond question, to his own judgment. For he willed that the successors of the Apostle Peter owe their innocence to heaven alone, and keep their conscience inviolate before the search of the most subtle examiner. But although some think that at least a council can judge him, the Pope himself utterly despises or evades such a judgment, and his flatterers, such as Hieronymus Albanus, book 1, on the power of a council, and Caranza, Controversy 4, and others, flatly deny that any case of crime can be found in which the universal pastor of the Church could be judged by any council of bishops. For even what the canon Si Papa, cited above, excepts concerning heresy has now been made useless by a new trick, namely by the assertion of the Pope's infallibility in law and in fact. So the people daily sink lower. Second, the Popes, freed from every power in this way, make all the rest subject without any exception whatever. Thus in the Extravagant on the majority and obedience, we read the definition in the chapter Unam sanctam: If earthly power goes astray, it shall be judged by spiritual power. But if spiritual power goes astray, the lesser by its superior; but if the highest, it can be judged by God alone, not by man, the Apostle testifying: the spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one. And soon after: We declare, we state, we define, and we pronounce it altogether necessary for salvation, that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff. In Gratian, causa 9, q. 3, Aliorum, it is read thus: It is plain from the voice of the saints that the dignity of this See is made venerable throughout the world, since whatever of the faithful there is, is submitted to it everywhere, while it is designated the head of the whole body. And these same men solemnly decree that all are subject to the Pope without distinction, not only in spiritual matters but in secular affairs too, as we shall prove below. Third, they maintain that the Pope's decrees, ψηφίσματα, decisions and sentences are such that no one may so much as murmur against them. Thus in Gratian, Dist. 19, it is read: All the sanctions of the Apostolic See are to be received as if confirmed by the very voice of Peter himself. And Causa 19, q. 4: It is not permitted for anyone to judge the judgment of the Apostolic See, or to retract its sentence, namely on account of the primacy of the Roman Church, divinely conferred by Christ's office upon the blessed Apostle Peter. Indeed, that a most burdensome yoke laid on by the same See must be borne with an even mind is decreed in Dist. 19, cap. In memoriam: Although a yoke is laid on by that holy See which can hardly be borne, let us bear it nonetheless, and endure it with pious devotion. Finally, lest anything be left out in the way of arrogance, the Glossator, on the chapter Quanto personam, de Translatione Episcopi, in the Decretals, [γυμῆ κιφαλὴ], bringing forth the inner recesses of the Papacy, asserts that the Pope has a heavenly judgment, and so may change the nature of things, applying the substance of one thing to another; and that he can make something out of nothing, and make a sentence, which is nothing, into something; in those things that he wills, his will is the reason, and there is no one who may say to him, why do you do so? For he can dispense above the law, and make justice out of injustice, by correcting laws, and finally obtain a fullness of power that may be changed.

units.la: XXX. Cùm duo feré sint, ex quibus τὸ κύριον Majestas, seu suprema nullùque obnoxia potestas Reipublicæ cujusvis dominantis à Politicis discernitur, puta νομοθετικὴ & δικαστικὴ legislatoria & judicialis potestas summa, quibus etiam Christi in Ecclesiam potestatem dominantem supra ff. x. definivimus, utramque Curiam Romanam Papæ non in orbis partem vel particulam quampiam, uti dominantes hujusmundi solent, sed in universum orbem, saltem Christianum & in spiritualibus minimùm, summam vindicare, adeóque absolutum & ἀνυπεύθυνον Monarcham à Deo ipso supra naturæ vim constitutum eum venditare, in propatulo est. Ad νομοθετικὴν seu legislatoriam illam summam potestatem omnium, quæ salutarem fidem & mores concernunt, infallibilis & suprema constituendi definiendique facultas, de qua abunde supra Diff. vij. 9. 10. &c. egimus; pertinet: imò id, quod dictavit Gregorius VII. absque Papæ autoritate nullum librum, nullúmque Capitulum canonicum haberi: quod Nicolaus I. non dubitavit profiteri, successores verò ejus in ipsum Gratiani decretum receperunt: Vetus & Novum Testamentum non nisi ex Pontificum constitutione à Christianis recipi meruisse. Neque immeritò ad eandem retuleris & illud, quòd Bellarmino aliisque prodentibus, dispensat Pontifex in votis & juramentis, quæ Deus ipse jussit reddi, quorum solutio de jure Divino est: quòd Conciliorum, quamvis Oecumenicorum, decreta omnia à suo nutu Papæ suspendunt; quòd denique secundùm plenitudinem potestatis de jure se posse supra jus dispensare, gloriatus quondam Innocentius III. est. XXXI. Ad δικαιοκρισίαν seu judicialem potestatem Magistratuum constitutio, & judicum atque judiciorum ordo referri solet. Utramque in orbis universi Ecclesia supremam sibi Papa arrogat. Et Magistratuum Ecclesiasticorum constitutionem quod attinet, notissimi sunt Gregoriani dictatus, quòd solus R. Pontifex jure dicatur universalis. Quòd ille solus possit deponere Episcopos, vel reconciliare: Quòd Legatus ejus etiam inferioris gradus omnibus Episcopis praesit in Concilio, & adversus eos sententiam dopositionis dare possit: Quòd illi soli liceat pro temporis necessitate novas leges condere, novas plebes congregare, de Canonia Abbatiam facere, & è contra, divitem Episcopatum dividere, & inopes unire: Quòd illi liceat de sede ad sedem, necessitate cogente, Episcopos transmutare: Quòd absque Synodali conventu possit Episcopos deponere & reconciliare: Quòd de omni Ecclesia, quocunque voluerit, clericos valeat ordinare. Quorum omnium communis haec sententia est, quod omnes Magistratus Ecclesiastici (tales quippe sunt Episcopatus, Canonicatus, Abbatiae) quoad institutionem & administrationem universam sint juris arbitriique Papalis. Quo quidem praetextu, proximis ante Concilium Constantiense & Basileense Seculis, nihil: fere horum non reapse exercuerunt, donec alibi atque alibi frenata aliquantum est intolerabilis illorum licentia, ita tamen, ut quicquid ejus remissum est, Curia Romana, quasi ex gratia concessum beneficium atque privilegium interpretetur. Quid quòd Episcopi in Conciliis etiam nonnisi Magistratuum & consiliariorum vice fungi creduntur. Hinc enim Leo X. in Concilio Lateranensi edixit, solum Romanum Pontificem pro tempore existentem tanquam authoritatem super omnia concilia habentem, Conciliorum indicendorum, transferendorum, ac dissolvendorum plenum jus & potestatem habere. Quam potestatem, quotiescunque potuerunt, strenuè exercuerunt, in Concilio inprimis Tridentino, in cujus statim exordio Papae disertis verbis per Legatos Patribus eandem inculcarunt. Plura de Papae in Episcopos quoivis quovis imperio & jurisdictione Dissert. viij. Sect. j. 40. 41. diximus.
units.tr: XXX. Since there are almost two things by which the sovereignty (τὸ κύριον), that is, the supreme power of any governing commonwealth that answers to no one, is distinguished by the political writers, namely the legislative (νομοθετικὴ) and judicial (δικαστικὴ) supreme power, and since we have defined the dominating power of Christ over the Church in the preceding pages, it is plain that the Roman Curia claims both of these for the Pope, not over a part or some portion of the world, as worldly rulers usually do, but over the whole world, at least the Christian world, and in spiritual matters at the very least, and that it puts him forward as an absolute and unaccountable [ἀνυπεύθυνον] monarch, appointed by God himself above the force of nature. The legislative, or supreme, power over everything that concerns saving faith and morals belongs to the infallible and supreme authority to establish and define, which we have already discussed at length in Dissertation VII, sections 9 and 10 and following. Indeed, that saying of Gregory VII belongs here: that without the Pope's authority no book and no canonical chapter is to be held, which Nicholas I did not hesitate to profess, and which his successors received into Gratian's decree: that the Old and New Testaments deserved to be received by Christians only by the constitution of the Pontiffs. Nor would you be wrong to refer to the same head that, as Bellarmine and others declare, the Pope dispenses from vows and oaths, which God himself commanded to be paid, though their release is by divine law; that he suspends at his nod all the decrees of councils, even ecumenical ones; and finally that Innocent III once boasted that by the fullness of power he could by right dispense above the law. XXXI. The establishment of the magistrates, and the order of judges and courts, is usually referred to the judicial power (δικαιοκρισία) of the magistrates. The Pope claims for himself the supreme authority over both in the whole Church of the world. As for the establishment of ecclesiastical magistrates, the Gregorian dictates are very well known: that the Roman Pontiff alone is rightly called universal; that he alone may depose or reinstate bishops; that his legate, even of lower rank, presides over all bishops in a council and may pronounce a sentence of deposition against them; that he alone may, as the need of the time requires, enact new laws, gather new peoples, make an abbey out of a canonry, and on the other hand divide a wealthy bishopric and unite poor ones; that he may transfer bishops from see to see when necessity compels; that without a synodal assembly he may depose and reinstate bishops; that he may ordain clergy from any church whatever. The common view of all these is that all ecclesiastical magistracies (such as bishoprics, canonries and abbeys) are wholly under the right and discretion of the Papacy, both as to their institution and their whole administration. Under this pretext, in the centuries just before the Councils of Constance and Basel, they scarcely exercised any of these powers in fact, until in various places their intolerable licence was somewhat restrained; yet whatever was relaxed of it, the Roman Curia interprets as a benefit and privilege granted as if of grace. Moreover, bishops are even believed in councils to act only in the place of magistrates and counsellors. For this reason Leo X, in the Lateran Council, decreed that the Roman Pontiff who exists at the time, as one having authority over all councils, has full right and power to call, transfer and dissolve councils. Whenever they could, they vigorously exercised this power, above all in the Council of Trent, at whose very beginning the Popes, through their legates, impressed the same claim upon the Fathers in plain words. We have said more about the Pope's imperial and jurisdictional power over bishops in Dissertation VIII, section 1, paragraphs 40 and 41.

units.la: XXXII. Sed & judicandi potestatem supremam & ἀυτοκέφαλον sibi Papa eximiam facit. Quod isdem dictatus Hildebrandini arguunt, quibus inter alia cautum est, quòd sententia Papæ à nullo debeat retractari, & ipse omnium solus retractare possit: quòd à nemine ipse judicari debeat, quòd nullus audeat condemnare Apostolicam sedem appellantem: quòd majores causæ cujuscunque Ecclesiæ ad eum referri debeant.
units.tr: XXXII. But the Pope also makes for himself a remarkable supreme and autocephalous power of judging. The same Hildebrandine dictates show this, among which it is laid down, that a sentence of the Pope must be retracted by no one, and that he alone can retract all sentences; that he himself ought to be judged by no one; that no one dares to condemn one who appeals to the Apostolic See; that the greater cases of any church ought to be referred to him.

units.la: Igitur etiam jus omne absolvendi à peccatis poenitentes uni sibi ac primò competere Papa gloriatur, eoque nomine partem quidem ejus Presbyteris atque Episcopis, ceu subdelegatis judicibus committit, partem vero, quae videlicet multum vel majestatis vel quaestus habet, soli sibi curiaeque suae exercendam reservat. Atque illud absolvendi, seu clavium jus ita interpretatur, quasi potestas sit quaedam non indicandi & declarandi ex Dei verbo Divinam mentem, sed propria quaedam & principalis authoritas judicandi, adeóque simpliciter vel absolvendi vel condemnandi, & eo quidem effectu, ut in coelo eandem sententiam Deus ipsemet approbare debeat. Similiter animas ex igne purgatorio liberare, arbitrii Papalis est. Quamobrem etiam tam varias, & tam multas per ecreas agni imaguncula, rosaria, grana, medalias, corollas, & id genus infinita alia, indulgentiarum species animarum liberandarum gratia passim terrarum liberali manu Papa constituere solet. Vanus vero hic conatus, vana jactantia fuerit, nisi simul ipsi etiam Angeli & Daemones ad nutum Papae illius imperiis sententiisque obedire cogantur, hactenus scilicet, ut animas jubente Papa, vel Angeli in Coelum sublevent, vel daemones in tartara detrudant. Sic enim etiam quondam Clemens VI. in Bulla Jubilaei diserte Angelis Paradisi imperavit, ut animam illius (quem scilicet ipse à peccatis suis immunem & absolutum pronuntiaverat) à purgatorio prorsus absolutam ad Paradisi gloriam introducant. Licet verò à concepta ejusmodi formula deinceps Papæ abstinuerint, reapse tamen jus isthoc in Angelos & dæmonas, judicii scilicet sui ministros, satellites, lictoresque, suo sacrarum clavium usu, sibi arrogant, atque exercent. Et quidni hoc sibi tribuant, cùm quilibet sacerdos poenitentiarius, si Theophilo Remundo Jesuitæ fides est, cacodæmones pro satellitibus, beatas mentes pro ministris habeat?
units.tr: Therefore the Pope also boasts that the whole right of absolving penitents from sins belongs first and foremost to himself alone, and in this respect he entrusts a part of it to presbyters and bishops, as judges delegated under him, but reserves the part which carries much majesty or profit for himself and his Curia alone to exercise. And he interprets this right of absolving, or of the keys, as if it were not a power of indicating and declaring the divine mind from God's word, but a certain proper and principal authority of judging, and so of simply absolving or condemning, with such effect that God himself must approve the same sentence in heaven. Likewise, to free souls from the purgatorial fire is at the Papal discretion. Wherefore the Pope usually establishes, with a liberal hand throughout the lands, so many and such various kinds of indulgences for the sake of freeing souls, through the little images of the Lamb, rosaries, beads, medals, chaplets, and countless other things of that sort. Yet this effort would be empty and this boasting vain, unless the Angels and the Demons themselves were also compelled to obey the Pope's commands and sentences, to this extent at least, that at the Pope's bidding the Angels raise souls to heaven or the demons thrust them down into hell. For Clement VI once, in the Bull of Jubilee, expressly commanded the Angels of Paradise that they should lead his soul (whom, of course, he himself had pronounced free of his sins and absolved) entirely freed from purgatory into the glory of Paradise. Although the Popes afterwards abstained from using such a formula, they nonetheless claim and exercise for themselves, by the use of their sacred keys, that same right over the Angels and demons, who are the ministers, attendants and lictors of their judgment. And why should they not attribute this to themselves, since, if the Jesuit Theophilus Raynaud is to be believed, every penitentiary priest has evil demons for attendants and blessed minds for ministers?

units.la: XXXIII. Potestati huic in spiritualibus immensæ & principali, & velut Divinæ Majestati vicariali, omnes omnino homines, non tantùm sacris dedicatos, quorum personas & res, sacramentis etiam devinctas, omnique aliorum imperio exemtas soli Pontifici obnoxias esse pertendunt, sed sacrorum eorundem prætextu, quosvis etiam homines, Reges, Principes, ac summas quásque potestates ita subesse, ut absque subjectione hac æternæ & temporalis salutis compos esse nemo mortalium queat, iidem scifcunt. Neque enim Pontifices non nulli, Pontificiæ sedis obedientiam ad æternam salutem consequendam simpliciter necessariam esse, dissimularunt. Jam olim Gregorius VII. dictavit. Quòd Catholicus non habeatur, qui non concordat Romanæ Ecclesiæ, hoc est, Curiæ Papæ. Bonifacii quoque Octavi decantatum illud, subesse Romano Pontifici omnino esse de necessitate salutis, in ipsum jus canonicum receptum est. Sed &, Pio IV. auctore, in publicam, juratámque fidei professionem hæc transierunt: Sanctam Catholicam Apostolicam Romanam Ecclesiam, omnium Ecclesiarum matrem & magistram agnosco: Romanóque Pontifici, B. Petri Apostolorum Principis successori, & Jesu Christi Vicario veram obedientiam spondeo ac juro. Iisdem vestigiis insistens Paulus V. initio hujus seculi, cùm Jacobus Angliæ Rex subditis suis Pontificiis securitatis publicæ causa juramenti formulam proposuisset, qua solùm illud negabatur, ita Regem potestati Pontificiæ esse subjectum, ut per eam Regnum ipsi jure auferri aut subditi juramento fidelitatis solvi possint, Brevi, quod vocant, Apostolico, transmisso pronuntiavit, hujusmodi juramentum salva fide catholica & salute animarum præstari non posse cùm multa contineat, quæ fidei & saluti aperte adversentur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Over this power, immense and principal in spiritual matters, and as it were vicarious of the Divine Majesty, they maintain that absolutely all men are subject to the Pope alone, not only those dedicated to sacred things, whose persons and goods, bound also by the sacraments and exempt from the rule of all others, they claim are answerable to him alone; but also, under the pretext of those same sacred things, that all men whatever, kings, princes and every supreme power, are so subject that no mortal can attain eternal and temporal salvation without this subjection. Nor have some Popes concealed that obedience to the Papal See is simply necessary for attaining eternal salvation. Long ago Gregory VII dictated: that he is not to be held a Catholic who does not agree with the Roman Church, that is, the Curia of the Pope. The much-sung saying of Boniface VIII, that it is entirely necessary for salvation to be subject to the Roman Pontiff, has also been received into the canon law itself. And under the authority of Pius IV these words passed into the public and sworn profession of faith: I acknowledge the holy Catholic, Apostolic, Roman Church as the mother and teacher of all churches; and I promise and swear true obedience to the Roman Pontiff, successor of the blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and Vicar of Jesus Christ. Following the same footsteps, Paul V at the beginning of this century, when James, King of England, had proposed to his Papist subjects, for the sake of public security, a form of oath in which the only thing denied was that the King is so subject to Papal power that by it the kingdom could rightfully be taken from him or the subjects released from their oath of allegiance, issued a so-called Apostolic Brief declaring that such an oath cannot be taken without loss of the Catholic faith and of the salvation of souls, since it contains many things that openly oppose faith and salvation.

units.la: XXXIV. Accedit commentum calidum callidúmque infallibilitatis, quam in potestate utraque tum legislatoria tum judiciali exercenda, Pontifici, ceu summo in terris Numini, post Concilium maximè Tridentinum (nam ante illud, exceptis Curialibus & Canonistis nonnullis, pleríque alii, Ecclesiæ seu Concilio generali ipso etiam Papa superiori, infallibilitas isthanc dotem vindicârunt) cùm alii, tum Jesuitæ, Cœli Pontificii Atlantes, tribuere nulli erubescunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. There is also the warm and crafty fiction of infallibility. After the Council of Trent especially, the Pope, as the supreme deity on earth, is credited with infallibility in exercising both legislative and judicial power. Before that council, apart from some Curialists and Canonists, most writers ascribed this privilege to the Church or to a general council, which they placed above the Pope himself. Yet the Jesuits, the Atlases of the Papal heaven, and others do not blush to grant it to him.

units.la: Postquam enim ad triarios istos res Papæ devenerunt, usque adeò in consensum Pontificia infallibilitas vertit, ut Suarez disp. 5. de fide sect. 8. n. 4. afferere non dubitaverit, docere ita hoc tempore omnes Catholicos.
units.tr: For once the Pope's affairs had come into the hands of these champions, Papal infallibility gained such general acceptance that Suarez, in De fide, disp. 5, sect. 8, n. 4, did not hesitate to assert that all Catholics at this time teach it thus.

units.la: Alii verò oppositum dogma errorem esse hæresi proximum pronuntiant. Olim tamen timidè satis, & suspenso veluti gradu Jesuitæ heic incesserunt. Bellarminus enim de Rom. Pontif. lib. iv. 2. visus est utcunque agnoscere, Primò, posse Pontificem, etiam ut Pontificem, errare in controversiis facti particularibus, quæ ex informatione testimoniisque hominum præcipuè pendeant; Secundò, posse Pontificem, ut privatum Doctorem, errare etiam in controversiis juris universalibus, tam fidei, quàm morum.
units.tr: Others, however, pronounce the opposite doctrine to be an error bordering on heresy. The Jesuits at first advanced here rather timidly and with a hesitant step. Bellarmine, in De Romano Pontifice, book 4, ch. 2, seemed to admit, at least in part, that the Pope, even as Pope, can err in particular controversies of fact, which depend chiefly on the information and testimony of men; and, secondly, that the Pope, as a private teacher, can err even in universal controversies of law, both of faith and of morals.

units.la: Cæterùm, uti errores solent quotidiè in pejus proficere, non passi sunt Papolatræ Jesuitæ his limitibus distinctionum Bellarminionarum, utpote infirmo admodum tibicine nixarum, se constringi. Neque enim tantùm hæreseos accusare audent, quotquot infallibilitatem Papæ in quæstionibus juris in dubium revocant, etsi Bellarminus eorum sententiam proprie hæreticam esse negaverit, cùm adhuc, inquit, videantur tolerari ab Ecclesia, qui illam sequuntur; sed etiam vehementer se opponunt iis, qui cum Melchiore Cano Loc. Comm. lib. v. 6. statuunt, Papam posse errare in quibuslibet quæstionibus facti, cujuscunque momenti illæ sint, veluti in canonizatione Sanctorum, & approbatione certorum ordinum. Quin occasione definitionum Anti Janseniticarum ab Innocentio X. insigni ignorantiæ fratre, cuisarum eò tandem vesaniæ Jesuitæ procesferunt, ut in thesibus die 12. Dec. A. MDCLXI. Lutetiæ in Collegio Claromontano propositis & propugnatis, ausi sint asserere, Christum Ecclesiæ suæ regimen ita Papis commisisse, ut ipsis eandem, quam habebat ipse infallibilitatem, concesserit, quoties ex cathedra loquerentur. Unde hanc conclusionem elicuere: Datur ergo in Ecclesia Romana Controversiarum fidei judex infallibilis, etiam extra Concilium generale, tum in quæstionibus juris, tum facti. Historiam thesium illarum à Jesuitis assertarum, à sanioribus Galliæ Theologis, ipsáque Sorbona & Curia suprema Parisiensi oppugnatarum, fuse Historia Papatus ff. CCLXXVI. CCLXXXVIII. edidit.
units.tr: However, as errors usually grow worse each day, the Jesuit Papolaters did not allow themselves to be bound by these limits of Bellarmine's distinctions, which rest on a very weak prop. They dare to charge with heresy not only all who call the Pope's infallibility in questions of law into doubt, although Bellarmine denied that their opinion was properly heretical, since, he says, those who follow it still seem to be tolerated by the Church; they also strongly oppose those who, with Melchior Cano, Loci communes, book 5, ch. 6, maintain that the Pope can err in any questions of fact, of whatever importance they may be, such as the canonization of saints and the approval of certain orders. Indeed, on the occasion of the anti-Jansenist definitions of Innocent X, a notably ignorant brother, the Jesuits went so far in their madness that, in theses proposed and defended on 12 December 1661 at the Clermont College in Paris, they dared to assert that Christ so committed the government of his Church to the Popes that he granted them the same infallibility he himself had, whenever they spoke ex cathedra. From this they drew the conclusion: There is therefore in the Roman Church an infallible judge of controversies of faith, even apart from a general council, both in questions of law and of fact. The history of those theses, asserted by the Jesuits and opposed by the saner theologians of France, and by the Sorbonne itself and the Supreme Court of Paris, has been set out at length in the Historia Papatus, pp. 276–288.

units.la: XXXV. Paradoxum ifthoc Pontificiæ in quæstionibus juris vel facti, vel utrisque infallibilitatis, frustra distinctionum quarundam sophisticarum pigmento incrustare Papolatræ satagunt, veluti cùm infallibilem esse, quà Pontificem, Doctorem publicum, non quà Doctorem privatum, & particularem personam, asserunt. Siccine ex eodem ore manabit dulce & amarum, calidum & frigidum? Et qua publicus doctor non nisi ex Deo, quà privatus etiam ex Diabolo Papa loqui poterit? Ac duplici etiam corde, ex cujus abundantia modò bonum, modò malum proloquetur, prædituserit? Non malè ipse Bellarminus: Potest quidem Deus ex corde hæretico extorquere veræ fidei confessionem, sicut verba posuit quondam in ore asinæ Bileam: at violentum erit, & non secundum morem Providentiæ Dei, suaviter omnia disponentis. Verùm tum asina sunt, cùm asina Bileami non locuta fuerit præter animi sensum, uti cor hæreticum veræ fidei confessionem edens loqui deberet. Tum confessio ejusmodi extorta quasi fidiculis, cujus nulla forte exempla proferentur, non satis conveniret personæ summi capitis, & Monarchæ ex cathedra, velut tripode quodam pronuntiantis, cùm hîc, si uspiam alibi, ex cordis abundantia os loquatur.
units.tr: XXXV. The Papolaters labour in vain to cover this paradox of Papal infallibility, whether in questions of law or of fact or both, with the paint of certain sophistical distinctions. For example, they assert that the Pope is infallible as Pope, a public teacher, not as a private teacher and particular person. Will sweet and bitter, warm and cold, flow from the same mouth? And how can the Pope speak as a public teacher only from God, and as a private one also from the devil? Or, with a double heart, out of whose abundance he now utters good and now evil, will he be judged a fit man? Bellarmine himself put it well: God can indeed draw from a heretical heart a confession of the true faith, just as he once put words into the mouth of Balaam's ass; but it would be forced, and not in keeping with the manner of God's Providence, which orders all things sweetly. Yet then they are asses, since Balaam's ass did not speak beyond the sense of its mind, whereas a heretical heart, when it makes a confession of the true faith, ought to speak from its own disposition. Moreover, such a confession extracted as if by the rack, for which perhaps no examples can be produced, would hardly suit the person of the supreme head and monarch who pronounces ex cathedra, as if from a tripod, when here, if anywhere else, the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart.

units.la: XXXVI. Quid verò multis? Personæ & Doctoris pu- blici Papæ discernendi criteria nulla Papolatris suppetunt.
units.tr: XXXVI. But why say more? The Papolaters have no criteria for distinguishing the person of the Pope from the Pope as public teacher.

units.la: Nam quòd Papam tum loqui ut publicum doctorem, adeoque Prophetam, cùm ex Cathedra loquitur, pronuntiat & definit, iidem asserunt, neutiquam illi se expediunt. Non dicam parùm constare iis, quid sit ex Cathedra loqui. Etenim ad id, ut ex Cathedra aliquid Pontifex definiat, quidam satis esse credunt, si delectorum Cardinalium sententia fuerit ante explorata: alii Collegium omne Cardinalium advocandum censent: alii neutrum necessarium existimant, dum intelligentes alii in consilium advocati fuerint. Factum inde, ut cùm nuper in causa Jansenitica nonnulla Innocentius X. delectis tantùm Cardinalibus adhibitis definivisset, Jansenitæ rite & ex cathedra definita illa esse, pernegaverint, Jesuitæ contra definitiones illas, ceu sacro-sanctas adoraverint. Hæ omnes sententiæ quando coeperint, quæ earum sit probabilior improbabiliorque, quæ periculo magis minusve vacet; imò quantopere dissidium isthoc Romanum Ecclesiam in varias partes distrahat, heic agitare nihil attinet. Rite expensis singulis cathedra illa, seu potestas definiendi infallibilis erit scrinium pectoris Papæ, adeóque Papa privatus doctor, proprióque motu & voluntate placita Oracula fundens. Cardinales enim sapientesque alii in consilium adhibiti, cùm infallibiles ipsi neutiquam censeantur, decretis Pontificiis infallibilitatem conferre non poterunt. Quid quòd omnes Bullæ Pontificis, etsi meræ bullæ sint, omnes Epistolæ decretales, omnia ejusdem Brevia Apostolica, Monitoria, Definitiones, Rescripta, Literæ Apostolicæ sub annulo Piscatoris expediuntur, ad exercitium potestatis clavium pertinent, & à sede Apostolica manant, adeóque actus Cathedrales sunt? Quòd si igitur ex cathedra infallibiliter agit, infallibilis erit in istis omnibus, nihilque amplius supererit, de cujus infallibilitate dubitari, vel disceptari queat. Præterea quilibet Papa, inde abeo quo, electus, coronatus, consecratus, adoratus est, momento censetur sacram illam Petri sedem, seu Cathedram insidere. Nullum proin temporis momentum excogitari potest, quo extra illam quæri aut concipi possit, adeóque quo aliquid extra Cathedram agat, statuatque. Quantò rectius ipsa Glossa in capite à recta, animadvertente etiam Silvestro Prieria in Summa, voce Ecclesia sect. 3. scribit: Ecclesia, quæ errare non potest, dicitur non Papa, sed congregatio fidelium, quæ scilicet tenet fidem, quam Petrus cum aliis populis docuit. Et hæc dicitur Ecclesia Romana, & fides Ecclesiæ Romanæ, sive sint Romæ sive alibi. Imò ipse Papa Johannes xxii. Extravag. quia quorundam (quam non condidit utique nisi delectis Cardinalibus adhibitis, adeóque non minùs forte quàm nuper bullam suam Innocentius ex cathedra protulit) disertè in hæc verba, adversus Franciscanos nonnullos antecedentium Paparum definitiones in subsidium causæ suæ advocantes, prorupit: Quod autem, quod in prædicta ratione præmittitur (videlicet, quòd illa, quæ per clavim scientiæ in fide ac moribus à Summis Pontificibus semel sunt definita, eorum Successoribus non licet revocare in dubium, nec contrarium affirmare: licet secus sit, sicut dicunt, in iis, quæ per clavim potestatis per Summos Pontifices ordinantur) prorsus sit contrarium veritati, patet ex sequentibus evidenter. Rationes deinceps subjungit, nonnullas, sanè prorsus inanes.
units.tr: For when they state and define that the Pope then speaks as a public teacher, and therefore as a prophet, when he speaks ex cathedra, they by no means extricate themselves. I need not say that it is little agreed among them what it is to speak ex cathedra. Some believe it is enough, for a Pope to define something ex cathedra, if the opinion of selected Cardinals has been tested beforehand; others think the whole college of Cardinals must be summoned; others judge that neither is necessary, provided that some learned men have been called in for counsel. The result is that when Innocent X, in the Jansenist affair, had recently defined certain matters with only selected Cardinals consulted, the Jansenists flatly denied that those definitions had been made duly and ex cathedra, while the Jesuits adored those definitions as sacrosanct. When all these opinions began, which is more or less probable, which is more or less free of danger, and indeed how far this Roman discord divides the Church into various parts, it is pointless to discuss here. Once each point is duly weighed, that cathedra, or the power of infallible definition, will be the casket of the Pope's breast, and so the Pope will be a private teacher, pouring forth oracles pleasing to himself by his own motion and will. For the Cardinals and other wise men called in for counsel, since they are by no means considered infallible themselves, cannot confer infallibility on Papal decrees. What of the fact that all Papal bulls, even if they are mere bulls, all decretal letters, all his Apostolic briefs, monitions, definitions, rescripts, and Apostolic letters issued under the Fisherman's ring, pertain to the exercise of the power of the keys and proceed from the Apostolic See, and are therefore cathedral acts? If, then, he acts infallibly ex cathedra, he will be infallible in all of these, and nothing will remain whose infallibility could be doubted or disputed. Moreover, from the moment any Pope is elected, crowned, consecrated, and adored, he is held to occupy that sacred seat of Peter, or cathedra, at that very moment. Therefore no moment of time can be imagined in which he could be sought or conceived outside it, and so in which he could act or decide anything outside the cathedra. How much more rightly the Gloss itself, on the chapter A recta, and Silvester Prierias too, in the Summa, under the word Ecclesia, section 3, writes: The Church, which cannot err, is called not the Pope but the congregation of the faithful, which indeed holds the faith that Peter taught with the other peoples. And this is called the Roman Church, and the faith of the Roman Church, whether they be at Rome or elsewhere. Indeed Pope John XXII himself, in the Extravagant Quia quorundam (which he certainly did not compose except with selected Cardinals consulted, and so perhaps no less than Innocent recently issued his bull ex cathedra), burst out expressly in these words against certain Franciscans who invoked the definitions of earlier Popes in support of their cause: That, however, which is premised in the said argument (namely, that those things which have once been defined by the Supreme Pontiffs through the key of knowledge in faith and morals may not be called in doubt by their successors, nor may the contrary be affirmed, although it is otherwise, as they say, with those things which are ordained by the Supreme Pontiffs through the key of power) is entirely contrary to the truth, as is clearly evident from what follows. He then adds reasons, some of them altogether empty.

units.la: XXXVII. Hactenus fuit potestas quam in spiritualibus sibi summam & irrefragabilem Papa in quolvis arrogat. Prætextu potestatis illius Papa tectus scilicet ligandi solvendíque specie, peccata remittendi existimatione, titulo clavium Petri, administratione Ecclesiæ universæ, supremam denique in cunctis Ecclesiæ causis potestate, sibi potestatem supremam etiam in temporalibus adscivit, ceu appendicem prioris, sed ita ut facilè appareat, hanc illi esse αὐτόν aut certè περὶ αὐτοῦ τὰ πνεῦμα τῶν ἔργων. Vilis enim admodum foret Papatus Oecumenicus, hoc sive præsidio sive satellitio non communitus, stipatúsque. Neque enim minùs lætabile quicquam iis accideret, quàm si res rediret non dicam ad Petros, Linos, Clementes, Melchiades, Silvestros, quibus nihil tutius fuit speluncis, nil catacumbis certius, sed ad securiores istis elatiorésque Damasos, Julios, Liberios, Leones, qui supra cæteros Episcopos immane quantum elati licet, tamen & Imperatorem adhuc dominum suum agnoscebant, & ex eorundem nutu in temporalibus toti pendebant. Illustrem illam servitutem, sanctitatis nomine decoratam nemini Pontifices posteriores inuiderent. Sic enim Romæ, si uspiam alibi, pietas laudatur & alget. Itaque freti dicto Apostolorum Luc. xxii. 38. Ecce duo gladii, hic, induxère sibi in animum, aliisque persuadère, duas esse potestates, Spiritualem & secularem, atque utramque in Pontifice copulari, immemores scilicet tum illius, quod sapienter olim Synesius monuit: Συνάδειν τὴν βασιλέων τῇ ἱερωσύνῃ, ἵνα ζυγκλαφῆ τὰ δούλ- λωμα. Regnum jungere sacerdotis, est inglomerabilia conglomerare: tum decantatæ etiam gnomæ inclyti illius Pontificis Gelasii, asserentis: ante adventum Christi figuraliter adhuc in carnalibus actibus constitutos pariter Reges & Sacerdotes fuisse. Atque id in suis quoque Diabolum imitatum esse, ut pagani Imperatores iidem & maximi Pontifices dicerentur. Sed cum ad verum ventum est Regem Iesum Christum, eundemque Pontificem, ultra sibi nec Imperatorem Pontificis nomen impossuisse, nec Pontificem Regale fastigium sibi vendicare. Sed deinceps alius Pontificibus fuit ἡμῖς ἐν σήμερον. Quippe jam olim Innocentius III. in publico sermone, quem de coronatione Papali tertium habuit, in hæc verba prorupit: Ecclesia sponsa non nupsit vacua, sed dotem mihi tribuit absque pretio pretiosam, spiritualem plenitudinem, & latitudinem Imperialem, magnitudinem & multitudinem utrorumque. In signum spiritualium contulit mihi Mitram, in signum temporalium dedit mihi coronam; Mitram pro sacerdotio, Coronam pro Regno; illius me constituens in vicarium, qui habet in vestimento & femore suo scriptum: Rex Regum, & Dominus Dominantium. Et Babylonem magnam, quæ Regnum in Reges terræ habet: quæ ceu Rectrix & domina Bestiæ septicipiti & δικαιοσύνης, aquísque seu populis multis insidet.
units.tr: XXXVII. So far we have had the power which the Pope claims for himself in spiritual matters as supreme and irrefragable over everyone. Under cover of that power, the Pope, pretending to bind and loose, believing he forgives sins, under the title of the keys of Peter, by the administration of the whole Church, and finally by supreme power in all Church affairs, has also claimed for himself supreme power even in temporal matters, as an appendage of the former. Yet it is easily apparent that this is αὐτόν, or rather the spirit of its works [περὶ αὐτοῦ τὰ πνεῦμα τῶν ἔργων]. For the Ecumenical Papacy would be a very poor thing if it were not fortified and surrounded by this protection or this bodyguard. Nor would anything be less welcome to them than if affairs returned not, I say, to Peters, Linuses, Clements, Melchiades, and Silvesters, for whom nothing was safer than caves and nothing surer than the catacombs, but to the more secure and more exalted Damasuses, Julians, Liberiuses, and Leos, who, though they were raised immeasurably above the other bishops, still acknowledged the Emperor as their lord and depended wholly on his nod in temporal matters. Later Popes would not begrudge anyone that illustrious servitude, adorned with the name of holiness. For thus at Rome, if anywhere else, piety is praised and freezes. Therefore, relying on the saying of the Apostles, Behold, here are two swords (Luke 22:38), they persuaded themselves and others that there are two powers, spiritual and secular, and that both are joined in the Pope, forgetting, of course, both what Synesius once wisely warned: To join kingship to priesthood is to heap together things that cannot be heaped, for a kingdom to join a priest, is to conglomerate the inconglomerable [Συνάδειν τὴν βασιλέων τῇ ἱερωσύνῃ, ἵνα ζυγκλαφῆ τὰ δούλλωμα]; and also the much-sung maxim of the famous Pope Gelasius, who asserted: Before the coming of Christ, kings and priests alike were still figuratively constituted in carnal acts. And the devil imitated this among his own, so that the pagan emperors were also called the greatest priests. But when the true time came, King Jesus Christ, who is also Priest, neither the Emperor took to himself the name of Pontiff, nor did the Pontiff claim for himself the royal dignity. But for the later Popes it was a matter of "today" [ἡμῖς ἐν σήμερον]. Indeed, long ago Innocent III, in the public sermon he gave third on his papal coronation, burst out in these words: The Church, the bride, did not marry empty-handed, but gave me a dowry, without price and precious: spiritual fullness, and imperial breadth, the greatness and the multitude of both. As a sign of the spiritual, she gave me a mitre; as a sign of the temporal, she gave me a crown; a mitre for the priesthood, a crown for the kingdom; appointing me vicar of him who has written on his vesture and on his thigh: King of kings, and Lord of lords. And he is Babylon the great, which has a kingdom over the kings of the earth; which, as the ruler and mistress of the seven-headed beast, sits upon many waters, that is, peoples.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quadruplex omnino temporalis potestas
units.tr: XXXVIII. Four kinds of temporal power in all

units.la: est, quam sibi Papa non tam pretio, quam vi rapuit. Prima in Provincias eas, quas Patrimonii Petri & Ecclesiastici Status titulo per Legatos Cardinales, aliosque gubernatores ita solus regit, ut nihil in eos juris vel Imperatori, vel Regibus, Principibúsque aliis competat. Secunda in Regna & Principatus, quos feudali nexu obstrictos, vel tenet vel prætendit. Tertia in reliqui Orbis universi Imperatores, Reges & Principes. Quarta denique in obnoxium sibi clerum Ecclesiæ universum. Et Primam quod attinet, Pontifex Cæsaris manubiis ditatus, ejusque jugum{ cervicibus suis excutiens, in medio Italiæ regit urbem Romam, totumque Latium, magnam partem Hetruriæ, Umbriæ, Ducatus Spoletani, Perusiæ, Bononiæ, Ferrariæ, Flaminiæ, Agrum Picenum, & partem Samnii. Quibus accessit Urbini Ducatus, quem Duce Urbinate pulso, Leo X. Laurentio Medicæo cognato suo tradidit. Ravennam, Imolam, Faventiam, Forum Julii, Serviam & Bononiam Julius II. bello recuperavit. Avenionensem Comitatum Clemens VI. à Johanna Neapolitana emptum, ditionis Pontificiæ fecit. Ad Secundam pertinent Regna homagio Ecclesiæ obstricta; & à Pontifice prætensa, cujusmodi in Urbis Romæ Regestris Regnum Neapolitanum, Siciliæ, Arragoniæ, Sardiniæ, Hierosolymæ, Angliæ, Hiberniæ & Hungariæ numerantur. Neapolitanum & Siciliæ Regna ita Pontifici obnoxia sunt, ut Hispaniarum Rex utriusque respectu Pontificis Vasallus, eidem feudalem servitutem in hunc usque diem præstet. Cùmque Hierosolymitanum Regnum olim per Fridericum primum Siciliæ Regem Regno Siciliæ unitum fuerit, eodem Papa jure illud quoque ad se pertinere asserit. Arragoniam sub juris esse pertendit, idem, ea ratione fretus, quòd Petrus II. Aragoniæ Rex Innocentio III. indulgenti, ut posthac Aragoniæ Reges non Romæ, sed in proprio Regno, Archiepiscopo Tarraconensi, seu Pontificio Legato coram Coronom acciperent, censum aliquot auri pondo promiserit. Sardiniæ Regnum suum esse nexu mancipiòque asserit, eò quòd Pontificis quondam ope & consilio Januenses & Pisani insulam illam Saracenis extorserint, atque illa per Calixti II. investituram Pisanis, atque mox
units.tr: The Pope has seized these, not so much by purchase as by force. The first is over those provinces which, under the title of the Patrimony of Peter and the Ecclesiastical State, he alone governs through cardinal legates and other governors, so that neither the Emperor, nor kings, nor other princes have any right over them. The second is over the kingdoms and principalities which he either holds or claims, bound to him by feudal tie. Third is over the emperors, kings and princes of the whole rest of the world. Fourth and last is over the whole clergy of the Church, who are bound to him. As for the first, the Pontiff, enriched with the spoils of Caesar and shaking off that yoke from his neck, rules in the heart of Italy the city of Rome and all Latium, a large part of Etruria, Umbria, the Duchy of Spoleto, Perugia, Bologna, Ferrara, Flaminia, the Picene territory and part of Samnium. To these was added the Duchy of Urbino, which Leo X, after driving out the Duke of Urbino, handed over to his kinsman Lorenzo de' Medici. Ravenna, Imola, Faenza, Forum Julii, Cervia and Bologna Julius II recovered by war. Clement VI made the county of Avignon, which he bought from Joanna of Naples, a part of papal dominion. To the second belong the kingdoms bound to the Church by homage and claimed by the Pope; of this kind the registers of the City of Rome list the kingdoms of Naples, Sicily, Aragon, Sardinia, Jerusalem, England, Ireland and Hungary. The kingdoms of Naples and Sicily are so subject to the Pope that the King of Spain, for both, is the Pope's vassal and to this day renders him feudal service. And since the kingdom of Jerusalem was once united to the kingdom of Sicily by Frederick I, the king of Sicily, the same Pope asserts by that right that it also belongs to him. He claims that Aragon is under his jurisdiction, relying on this reason: that Peter II, King of Aragon, when Innocent III indulged him, promised a yearly tribute of some pounds of gold, on condition that thereafter the kings of Aragon should receive the crown not at Rome but in their own kingdom, from the Archbishop of Tarragona or the papal legate. He claims that the kingdom of Sardinia is his by feudal bond and title, because the Genoese and Pisans wrested that island from the Saracens with the help and counsel of a former Pope, and it then fell, through the investiture of Calixtus II to the Pisans, and soon afterwards to James, King of Aragon, invested by Boniface VIII.

units.la: Jacobo Regi Arragoniæ, Bonifacio VIII. investiente, obtigerit. Sed & Angliæ Hiberniæque Regnum in censu feudorum Papalium habetur, eo quod A. M CCII. Johannes Angliæ Rex excommunicatus à Papa, ut sacrorum communionem recuperaret, Regna sua, S. Petri denarium pollicitus, eidem feudataria fecerit, & homagium Ecclesiæ Romanæ præstiterit. Bullam authenticam Innocentii III. eam in rem in Vaticano haberi gloriantur. Denique & Hungariæ Regnum in albo Pontificiorum seudorum numeratur, eam scilicet ob causam, quòd & Lancellotus, Hungariæ Rex obsequium Papæ solenniter quondam promiserit, & Stephanus Regis Hungariæ nomen à Pontifice impetraverit, & Ludovicus II. ob injuriam Legato Pontificio factam excommunicatus, absolutionem obtinuerit ea lege, ut quotannis centum argenti marcas, servitutis auctoramentum, pensitet. Præterea Hildebrandum olim alia quoque Regna veluti Hispaniam universam, Galliam, Saxoniam, Russiam, Dalmatiam, Corsicam, Majoricam, Minoricam, Daniam, in feudorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ censu collocâsse, superieri diatriba Sr. xxÿ. ex ejusdem epistolis comprobavimus. Taceo, quòd aliorum etiam Regum sceptra Pontifici mancipare, adeóque ipsum Imperium Romanum, cæteráque Regna omnia Papæ feudali nexu devincta esse, ejusdem parasitastri, reclamantibus licet cordatioribus quibusque, asserere non verecundantur. Nota sunt Gregorii VII. Urbani II. cum Henricis, Hadriani IV. & Rolandi, post Alexandri III. dicti, cum Friderico I. Innocentii III. cum Philippo, Honorii III. Gregorii IX. Innocentii IV. cum Friderico II. Bonifacii VIII. cum Alberto Imperatore & Philippo Pulchro Galliæ Rege, certamina haud equidem vulgaria, quibus Pontifices ipsummet Imperium Romanum fui juris & beneficii facere omnibus viribus annixi sunt. Tertia potestas est in omnes reliquos sive Imperatores, sive Reges, sive Principes, quotquot vasallos seu feudatarios suos esse, pronuntiare apertis verbis semper & ubique sustinent. Cum Gregorio quippe VII. Epist. lib. vj. 6. statuunt, Deum B. Petro omnes Principatus & potestates orbis terrarum subjecisse, jusque ligandi & solvendi in Cælo & terra contradidisse: Prætextu enim statu Ecclesiæ, disciplinæ Ecclesiæ in excommunicationis censura, doctrinæ Ecclesiæ de meritis operum Ecclesiæ, authoritatis in remittendis peccatis & officiis cuique suis exponendis, solvendis hominibus religione sacramenti alligatis, & postremò solennitatum Ecclesiæ in coronis Cæsarum capitibus imponendis, gemmas eas Papa collegit, quibus triplicem mundani Regni sui coronam (quam Regnum vocari Platina in Paulo II. Guicciardinus Histor. libr. ix. testantur) exornavit, seque non Principem duntaxat, sed Principum terrarum Principem, Regem Regum, Dominúmque Dominantium constituit.
units.tr: Moreover the kingdom of England and Ireland is counted among the Papal feudal holdings, because in the year 1202 John, King of England, excommunicated by the Pope, wishing to recover communion in the sacraments, promised the penny of St Peter and made his kingdoms feudal to him, and rendered homage to the Roman Church. They boast that the authentic bull of Innocent III to this effect is kept in the Vatican. Finally, the kingdom of Hungary is also listed in the roll of Papal fiefs, for this reason: that Ladislaus, King of Hungary, once solemnly promised obedience to the Pope; that Stephen obtained the title of king of Hungary from the Pope; and that Louis II, excommunicated for an injury done to a papal legate, obtained absolution on condition that he pay each year a hundred marks of silver as the price of his servitude. Besides, I have shown from the letters of Hildebrand in the previous discourse, Sr. xxÿ., that he once also placed other kingdoms, namely all Spain, Gaul, Saxony, Russia, Dalmatia, Corsica, Majorca, Minorca and Denmark, among the census of the fiefs of the Roman Church. I say nothing of the fact that his parasites, though the more sensible among them object, are not ashamed to assert that the sceptres of other kings also are handed over to the Pope, and that the Roman Empire itself and all other kingdoms are bound to the Pope by feudal tie. The struggles of Gregory VII and Urban II with the Henries, of Hadrian IV and of Roland, afterwards called Alexander III, with Frederick I, of Innocent III with Philip, of Honorius III, Gregory IX and Innocent IV with Frederick II, of Boniface VIII with the Emperor Albert and with Philip the Fair, King of France, are well known; these were by no means ordinary quarrels, in which the Pontiffs strove with all their might to make the Roman Empire itself subject to their right and benefit. The third power is over all the others, whether emperors, kings or princes, whomever they hold to be their vassals or feudatories; this they always and everywhere maintain in plain words. For with Gregory VII, Epist. lib. vj. 6, they lay down that God subjected to St Peter all principalities and powers of the world, and handed over to him the right of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth. For under the pretext of the state of the Church, the discipline of the Church in the censure of excommunication, the Church's doctrine of the merits of works, its authority in remitting sins and in assigning duties to each person, in releasing men bound by the religion of a sacrament, and finally the Church's solemn rites in placing crowns on the heads of Caesars, the Pope gathered those jewels with which he adorned the triple crown of his worldly kingdom (which Platina in the life of Paul II and Guicciardini in book ix of his History testify is called a kingdom), and made himself not merely prince but Prince of the princes of the earth, King of kings and Lord of lords.

units.la: XXXIX. Quia verò in dubium revocare Hieronymo narchici non potuerunt, quin temporalis potestas sit etiam in Imperatoribus, Regibus & Principibus, hinc quæri in ipso Papatu cœptum est quomodo sit in Papa, directè an indirectè, seu uti aliis verbis alii exprimunt, per se, an per accidens: tum, in utro major, in Papa, an in Imperatore, Regibus & Principibus? Estque pro variis sententiis variè pronuntiatum, prout alii aliis plus minúsve Papæ vel Regibus addicti, adulatíque sunt. Triplicia autem facta sunt castra, puta Theologorum, Canonistarum, & Politicorum. Et Politici quidem Romanum Pontificem jure Divino, sive Christi institutione ullum habere rerum temporalium dominium, potestatem vel jurisdictionem ullam, sive directè dicas sive indirectè, sive absolutè sive respectivè ad bonum spirituale, vel posse etiam Reges & Principes pes ob quantumvis crimen dominiis suis temporalibus spoliari pernegant, protestati interim severè, se Pontificem Caput Ecclesiæ agnoscere, neque ea in re ejus authoritatem in Ecclesiam imminutam ullo modo velle. Quorum in Castra Clerus Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ nuper Lutetiæ congregatus, uti ff. CCCXLIII. narravimus aperte transiit.
units.tr: XXXIX. Since the hierarchs could not, however, call into doubt that temporal power also exists in emperors, kings and princes, it began to be asked within the papacy itself how it exists in the Pope: directly or indirectly, or, as others say in other words, per se or per accidens; and further, in which of them it is greater, in the Pope or in the emperors, kings and princes? And it has been pronounced variously according to the different opinions, as some were more or less devoted and flattering to the Pope or to the kings. There are three camps: those of the theologians, the canonists and the politicians. The politicians deny absolutely that the Roman Pontiff has by divine right, that is by the institution of Christ, any dominion over temporal things, any power or jurisdiction over them, whether you say directly or indirectly, absolutely or relatively to a spiritual good; and they deny that kings and princes may be stripped of their temporal dominions for any crime whatsoever. At the same time they solemnly declare that they acknowledge the Pope as Head of the Church and that they do not wish in any way his authority over the Church to be diminished. The clergy of the Gallican Church, lately gathered at Paris, openly passed over to this camp, as we related at ff. CCCXLIII.

units.la: XL. Theologi verò & Canonistæ hactenus quidem consentiunt, quòd Papæ authoritas in rebus politicis summa sit, ac proinde longè longéque major, quàm in ullo Imperatore Rege ac Principe. Et potestatem igitur politicam Ecclesiasticæ subjiciunt, & Principes Papæ subesse docent, non tantùm ut ab eo moneri, & poenis Ecclesiasticis coërceri possint, sed etiam, ut poenis temporalibus, instituendo, destituendo, regna transferendo, prout ipse expedire judicaverit, in ordinem redigi valeant. Dissentiunt tamen iidem si non re ipsa, at verborum saltem apicibus. Theologi enim verecundiores paulò, & nominatim Bellarminus, ac indicæ eodem de Rom. Pont. lib. v. i. Hugo de S. Victore, Alexander Alensis, Bonaventura, Durandus, Petrus ab Alliaco, Gabriel Biel, Driedo, Turrecremata, Pighius, Cajetanus, Soter, Sanderus &c. Pontificem quâ Pontificem negant directè & immediatè habere ullam potestatem temporalem, & solam spiritualem directè habere asserunt. Indirectè tamen, & ratione spiritualis potestatis eum habere summam petestatem in temporalibus, iidem dissimulant nulli. Sensum dicti hunc reddunt, quòd Papa quatenus Papa, non sit Rex vel Imperator, neque eadem gerere, quæ Regis sunt vel Imperatoris in eo Regno, eóque Imperio posset: attamen ob spiritualem potestatem, & subjectam eidem, uti supra mentem eorum indicavimus, civilem, possit & Regibus & Imperatoribus, si ita Ecclesiæ & animarum saluti conducere. re judicaverit, pro authoritate sua uti. Quomodo Imperator quidem ipse non est singularum familiarum δεσποτης, eo scilicet ipso, quod Imperator est, cùm non possit pro arbitrio Titii aut Mævii fundos vendere, vel in usum suum convertere, sicut Titius & Mævius, quibus de suo agere licet, quod libet. Attamen si ita sit ex usu & necessitate Reipublicæ, cui præest, non tantum jubebit vendere, sed ipse quoque addicit, non tanquam δεσποτης, sed tanquam Imperator, vi eminentis potestatis, qua pollet. Pari ratione Papam, qua Papa est, de Imperio Germanorum, vel Regno Gallorum non posse pro arbitrio statuere, hoc est, tributa imponere, bella indicere, pacem pangere, quæ Monarcharum ipsorum partes sunt: Si tamen necessitas & usus Ecclesiæ postulet, vi eminentis suæ potestatis jubebit bellum suscipere contra Turcas, Reges vel noxios Ecclesiæ, vel inutiles à culmine suo deturbabit, quin & alios in eorundem locum, probandos à se, vel improbandos etiam substitui mandabit. Contra Atheologi, seu Canonistæ, quos inter Bellarminus loc. cit. Augustinum Triumphum, Alvarum Pelagium, Hostiensem, Panormitanum, Sylvestrum, alios numerat; potestatem jurisdictionis spiritualium & temporalium immediatam à Deo esse in solo Pontifice, secularem verò in Principibus esse obnoxiam, & administram Papæ; tum Papam ut Papam jure Divino obtinere plenissimam potestatem in universum terrarum orbem, quà in temporalibus, quà in spiritualibus: denique Dominium Principum translatum ad Ecclesiam, & rusidere in Summo Pontifice, ut vicario summi & veri Regis Christi, adeóque posse Pontificem Regna liberè dare & eripere quibus velit nolitque afferunt.
units.tr: XL. The theologians and canonists have so far agreed that the authority of the Pope in political matters is supreme, and therefore far, far greater than that of any emperor, king or prince. So they subject political power to ecclesiastical power, and teach that princes are subject to the Pope, not only so that they may be admonished by him and restrained by ecclesiastical penalties, but also so that they may be brought into order by temporal penalties, by appointing, deposing and transferring kingdoms, as he shall judge expedient. Yet these same men differ, if not in substance, at least in the niceties of words. For the theologians, somewhat more modest, and especially Bellarmine in On the Roman Pontiff, book v, chapter 1, and in the same place Hugh of St Victor, Alexander of Hales, Bonaventure, Durandus, Pierre d'Ailly, Gabriel Biel, Driedo, Torquemada, Pighius, Cajetan, Soto, Sanders etc., deny that the Pontiff, as Pontiff, has any temporal power directly and immediately, and assert that he has only spiritual power directly. Yet none of them hides that he has indirectly, and by reason of his spiritual power, the highest power over temporal things. They explain the meaning of this statement thus: the Pope, as Pope, is not a king or emperor, nor can he perform in that kingdom or empire the functions of a king or emperor; but on account of his spiritual power, and the civil power subject to it, as we indicated above in their view, he may use that civil power, for the sake of his authority, against kings and emperors, if he judges that it serves the Church and the salvation of souls. Just as the emperor himself is not the despotes of every family, precisely because he is emperor, since he cannot sell the estates of Titius or Maevius at his own pleasure, or turn them to his own use, as Titius and Maevius, who may do with their own property what they please. Yet if the use and necessity of the Commonwealth, over which he presides, require it, he will not only order them to be sold, but he himself will also adjudge them, not as despotes but as emperor, by the force of the eminent power which he possesses. By the same reasoning, the Pope, as Pope, may not decide at his own pleasure about the Empire of the Germans or the kingdom of the French, that is, impose taxes, declare war, make peace, which are the functions of the monarchs themselves; yet if the necessity and use of the Church demand it, he will by the force of his eminent power order war to be undertaken against the Turks, and will cast down from their height kings who are harmful or useless to the Church, and will even order others to be put in their place, whom he approves or disapproves. Against them the atheologians, or canonists, among whom Bellarmine in the same place counts Augustinus Triumphus, Alvarus Pelagius, Hostiensis, Panormitanus, Sylvester and others, maintain that the power of jurisdiction over spiritual and temporal things is immediately from God and resides in the Supreme Pontiff alone, while secular power in princes is subordinate and serves the Pope; then that the Pope, as Pope, holds by divine right the fullest power over the whole world, both in temporal and in spiritual matters; finally that the dominion of princes has been transferred to the Church and resides in the Supreme Pontiff, as vicar of the supreme and true King, Christ, and therefore that the Pope may freely give and take away kingdoms from whomever he wishes and does not wish.

units.la: XLI. Dixeris, immane quantum sententiam Theolo- gorum à sensu Canonistarum distare. Sed phaleræ sunt ad populum, & fucus merus Theologorum, qui directe & indire-
units.tr: XLI. You may say that the opinion of the theologians differs enormously from the meaning of the Canonists. But these are trappings for the common people, and sheer pretence on the part of the theologians, who wish their arguments to appear separated from the horrid and bold assertions of the Canonists, which are hateful to the whole world, by the distinction between direct and indirect power.

units.la: Theologi
units.tr: Theologians

units.la: Papa in temporali
units.tr: The Pope in temporal

units.la: bus potestas
units.tr: -bus, power

units.la: indirectæ potestatis distinctione rationes suas ab horridis & audacibus, totíque orbi meliori invisis Canonistarum assertionibus disjungere videri volunt. Etenim si ritè rem putemus, amicè cum Canonistis conspirant, & directæ Pontificum potestati Regum, Principiúmque omnium Coronas, & sceptra æque atque illi, mancipiant. Indirectam potestatem Papæ verbo vocant, directam re ipsa faciunt, identidem illud Thomæ Aquinatis 2. dist. 44. inculcantes: In Papa est apex utriusque potestatis. Neque aliam ob causam iidem potestatem temporalem. Ecclesiasticæ subjiciunt, uti quidem ex Bellarmino de R. Pontif. lib. v. 7. aliisque constat, & supra idem à nobis discussum est. Quin Bellarminus idem, Theologus scilicet, ibid. cap. 6. ita indirectam illam potestatem declarat, ut simul tamen rotundè asserat, Papam in ordine ad bonum spirituale summam potestatem habere disponendi de temporalibus rebus omnium Christianorum. Atqui summa potestas ἀναγκαστικὴ seu coactivè (nam sine vi & cogendi jure summa potestas nulla constat) de temporalibus est utique dominium in temporalia directum atque supremum. Et si nulla re nisi in fine aut ordine ad finem potestas Papæ à potestate Regum & Principum temporali differt, utique forma & essentia non differt. Papa igitur quoad essentialem & formalem rationem dominii etiam temporalis, fit orbis Christiani dominus. Quinimo superioris finis, ad quem potestas Papæ collimat, respectus dominium ejusdem non tam minuit, quàm auget, quia quò nobilior finis est, eò firmior potestas, quæ ad illum finem exercenda est, esse debet. Accedit quod temporalia multa ad bonum spirituale dirigere non magis Papa, quàm politicus Princeps potest; mediatè autem ad bonum spirituale dirigere omnia non minus Politicus Princeps potest, debétque, quàm Papa. Nulla igitur differentia apparet, ne quidem in ipso fine. Quinimò Theologi cum Bellarmino summam de rebus Temporalibus potestatem in ordine ad bonum spirituale disponendi Papæ, non ut Imperatori vel Regi, sed ut Principi spirituali & propter subjectionem ad potestatem spiritualem tribuentes, non obscurè Babylonis Magnæ titulum, qui est μυστήριον Mysterium Pontificis fronti inurunt. Faciunt enim eum Imperatorem & Regem mysticum, uti supra etiam fusius comprobavimus.
units.tr: For if we judge the matter rightly, they agree in friendship with the Canonists, and they hand over to the direct power of the Popes the crowns and sceptres of all kings and princes just as the Canonists do. They call the power of the Pope indirect in name, but make it direct in fact, repeatedly pressing that saying of Thomas Aquinas, 2. dist. 44: In the Pope is the apex of both powers. Nor do they subject temporal power to ecclesiastical power for any other reason; this is clear from Bellarmine, de R. Pontif. lib. v. 7, and others, and I have already discussed the same point above. Indeed Bellarmine himself, a theologian, ibid. cap. 6, declares that indirect power in such a way that at the same time he flatly asserts that the Pope, in order to attain spiritual good, has the highest power to dispose of the temporal affairs of all Christians. But supreme power that is compulsive [ἀναγκαστικὴ], or coercive (for without force and the right of compulsion no supreme power exists), over temporal affairs is surely a direct and supreme dominion over temporal things. And if the power of the Pope differs from the temporal power of kings and princes in nothing but the end, or the ordering toward the end, then surely it does not differ in form and essence. Therefore the Pope, as regards the essential and formal nature of dominion, even temporal dominion, becomes lord of the Christian world. Moreover, the respect of the higher end toward which the Pope's power aims does not so much diminish his dominion as increase it, because the nobler the end, the firmer ought to be the power that must be exercised to reach that end. Besides, the Pope can no more direct many temporal matters to spiritual good than a civil prince can; yet a civil prince can and must, no less than the Pope, direct all things mediately to spiritual good. Therefore no difference appears, not even in the end itself. Indeed, the theologians, with Bellarmine, in granting to the Pope the supreme power of disposing of temporal affairs in order to attain spiritual good, not as to an emperor or king but as to a spiritual prince, and on account of his subjection to spiritual power, openly stamp on the brow of the Pope the title of Great Babylon, which is the mystery [μυστήριον] Mystery. For they make him an emperor and king in a mystical sense, as we have also proved at greater length above.

units.la: XLII. Direĉtam reapse esse potestatem, quam de rebus temporalibus in ordine ad bonum spirituale disponendi Papæ Theologi Pontificii tribuunt, liquebit magis etiam, si Papæ potestas spiritualis, quæ indirectè operari dicitur leges Principum temporales, deinde in judiciis rerum temporalium; ac demum circa personas ipsas Regum & Principum consideretur. Quantum ad leges quæ res temporales concernunt, equidem Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. lib. v. 6. fatetur, non posse Papam, ut Papa est, ordinariè condere legem civilem, vel confirmare aut infirmare leges civiles Principum, posse tamen eundem hæc omnia, si lex aliqua civilis sit necessaria ad salutem animarum, & eam Reges nolint condere: aut si alia sit noxia saluti animarum, eámque Reges abrogare graventur. Affert eam in rem Glossæ ad cap. Possessor. in sexto regulam isthanc, ut per legem Pontificiam abrogata, censeatur lex Imperialis, si hæc periculum animarum concernat. Potestatem igitur legislatoriam sibi Papa asserit in casu salutem animarum concernente, quam directam esse liquet, tum quia non pendet in tali casu potestas ejus ab ullo homine: tum quia ad exercitium potestatis ejusmodi potestas civilis eminens requiritur; absque qua est nihil potestas spiritualis, qua talis, sive directè sive indirectè in civilibus operatur: tum quia potestas talis conjunctam habere coactionem, & vim adversus refractarios habere debet: tum quia non dissimilis est potestati Regum in bona subditorum in casu necessitatis, salutis publicæ, ob dominium eminens, quæ merè civilis & directa est: tum quia judicium de tali casu erit penes solum Pontificem, qui casum pro lubitu finget, vel verum etiam casum definiet solus, & tali in casu Imperatorum, Regum & Principum potestatem legislatoriam sibi obnoxiam habebit: tum denique quia leges purè civiles nullo casu ad supernaturalia, sed ad merè civilia & naturalia extenduntur. Quamvis enim contingere posset, ut lex civilis, permissiva imprimis feratur, quæ servata saluti animarum noxia foret, veluti si usuræ injustæ, concubinatus, injusta homicidia, gradus in matrimonio Divino jure prohibiti, aliaque ejusmodi vel præciperentur, vel permitterentur, ejus tamen abrogatio ad salutem animarum subditorum protinus necessaria non foret, quia talis lex etiam non abrogata, homini Christiano observanda non est, qui patienter potius tyrannorum supplicia feret, quàm adversus Deum quidquam committet. Ecclesiæ integrum quidem est leges civiles animarum saluti utiles urgere rationibus, precibus, & eos qui leges impias ferunt, si rogati non abrogaverint, censuris ecclesiasticis plectere. At leges ipsas civiles ejusmodi vel rogare & ferre, vel abrogare vel confirmare, vel irritas pronuntiare, non est nisi illius, qui eminentem, summam, & directam in Civilibus potestatem, nemini mortalium obnoxiam habet. Proin potestas Papæ in ferendis abrogandisque ejusmodi legibus vel omnino nulla, vel merè civilis, summa & directa erit.
units.tr: XLII. That the power which the Pontifical theologians attribute to the Pope to dispose of temporal affairs in order to attain spiritual good is in truth a direct power will become clearer still if we consider the spiritual power of the Pope, which is said to act indirectly upon the temporal laws of princes, then upon the judgments concerning temporal affairs, and finally upon the persons of the kings and princes themselves. As for laws which concern temporal affairs, Bellarmine, de Rom. Pont. lib. v. 6, indeed admits that the Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily enact a civil law, or confirm or invalidate the civil laws of princes; yet he can do all these things if some civil law is necessary for the salvation of souls and the kings are unwilling to enact it, or if another law is harmful to the salvation of souls and the kings are reluctant to abrogate it. In support of this he cites the rule of the Gloss on cap. Possessor, in the Sixth Book: that an Imperial law is deemed abrogated by a Papal law if that law concerns the danger of souls. The Pope therefore claims for himself a legislative power in a case concerning the salvation of souls, and it is clear that this power is direct: first, because his power in such a case depends on no man; second, because for the exercise of such power a supreme civil authority is required, without which spiritual power, as such, is nothing, whether it acts in civil matters directly or indirectly; third, because such a power must have coercion joined to it and must have force against the recalcitrant; fourth, because it is not unlike the power of kings over the goods of subjects in a case of necessity or public safety, on account of eminent dominion, which is purely civil and direct; fifth, because the judgment about such a case will rest with the Pontiff alone, who will feign the case at his pleasure, or he alone will define whether the case is real, and in such a case he will hold the legislative power of emperors, kings and princes in subjection to himself; and finally, because purely civil laws are in no case extended to supernatural matters, but to merely civil and natural ones. For although it could happen that a civil law, especially one that is permissive, should be enacted which, if observed, would be harmful to the salvation of souls, such as laws ordering or permitting unjust usury, concubinage, unjust homicides, degrees of marriage forbidden by divine law, or other such things, nevertheless its abrogation would not be immediately necessary for the salvation of the subjects, because such a law, even if not abrogated, is not to be observed by a Christian, who would rather bear patiently the punishments of tyrants than commit anything against God. It is indeed within the power of the Church to urge civil laws useful to the salvation of souls by reasons and prayers, and to punish with ecclesiastical censures those who enact impious laws if, when asked, they do not repeal them. But to ask for, enact, abrogate, confirm or declare void such civil laws belongs to none but him who holds eminent, supreme and direct power in civil affairs, subject to no mortal. Therefore the power of the Pope in enacting and abrogating such laws will either be altogether nonexistent or purely civil, supreme and direct.

units.la: XLIII. Quoad judicia civilia idem Bellarminus de Rom. Pontif. lib. v. 6. fatetur, non posse Papam ut Papam ordinariè judicare de rebus temporalibus. Attamen pertendit, in casu, quo id animarum saluti necessarium est, posse Pontificem assumere etiam temporalia judicia, quan-do
units.tr: XLIII. As for civil judgments, Bellarmine, de Rom. Pontif. lib. v. 6, admits that the Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily judge temporal affairs. Yet he maintains that in a case where this is necessary for the salvation of souls, the Pontiff can also assume temporal judgments, when

units.la: judicia-lem, secundum quam exercere judicia civilia do nimirum non est ullus, qui judicare possit, ut cum duo Reges supremi contendunt, vel quando qui possunt debent judicare, non volunt sententiam ferre. Allegat eundem in sensum Innocentii III. cap. Per venerabilem, qui filii sint legitimi, sententiam, quòd jurisdictionem temporalem solùm casualiter Pontifex exercere possit. An verò temporalia judicia assumere ob necessitatem salutis animarum, non est directam in temporalia potestatem exercere? Sanè finem potestatis temporalis exercitæ nullam in potestate ipsa differentiam gignere, nisi quoad modum exercitii, prout finis nobilior vel ignobilior est supra evicimus. Ineptum verò planè Bellarminus ejus affert exemplum, afferens, tum temporalia judicia Papam assumere posse, cùm nullus est qui possit judicare, ut cùm duo Reges supremi contendunt &c. Nam etsi discordibus Principibus supremis nullus est, qui ex officio aut authoritate judicare velit aut possit, salus tamen animarum non periclitabitur, quia arbitria locum habere, & periculum omne averruncare possunt. Si igitur Papa in hoc casu judicis partes rapuerit, directam utique, non indirectam in temporalibus potestatem exercebit. Quod turgidus inprimis & Imperativus Pontificum discordes Principes dijudicantium stylus manifestè arguit. Veluti cùm verba illa: Præcipimus, mandamus &c. bullis suis intexere nulli verecundantur. Præterea longè aliud est casualiter, uti ex Innocentio Bellarminus allegavit, temporalia judicia exercere; aliud indirectè.
