Casualiter enim apud Innocentium nihil aliud significat, quàm posse Pontificem non ordinariè terrena judicare, sed extraordinariè, & in certis quibusdam casibus, in quibus tamen directè potestate temporali judicat, non indirectè spirituali. In casibus illis putat Innocentius causas seculares & judicia temporalia ad Papam devolvi. Devolutio autem causarum nihil secum fert indirecti, diređti, sed diređtissimam ejusdem generis potestatem supponit.
units.tr: there is no one who can judge (the rule by which civil judgments are to be exercised), namely, when there is no one who can judge, as when two supreme kings are in dispute, or when those who can and ought to judge are unwilling to pass sentence. To the same effect he cites from Innocent III, cap. Per venerabilem, qui filii sint legitimi, the opinion that the Pope can exercise temporal jurisdiction only occasionally. But is it not to exercise direct power over temporal things to take up temporal judgments for the necessity of the salvation of souls? Surely we have shown above that the end for which temporal power is exercised makes no difference in the power itself, except as to the manner of its exercise, according as the end is nobler or less noble. But Bellarmine's example is plainly absurd, when he says that the Pope may take up temporal judgments when there is no one who can judge, as when two supreme kings dispute, and so on. For even if no one has the office or authority to judge between supreme princes who are at odds, and wishes or is able to do so, the salvation of souls will not be endangered, because arbitration can take place and avert any danger. If therefore the Pope in this case seizes the part of judge, he will certainly exercise direct and not indirect power over temporal things. The swollen and imperious style of the Popes, judging between discordant princes, clearly proves this. Thus they are not ashamed to insert into their bulls such words as: We command, we order, and so on. Moreover, to exercise temporal judgments occasionally, as Bellarmine cited from Innocent, is something quite different from doing so indirectly. For occasionally, in Innocent, means nothing other than that the Pope may not judge earthly matters in the ordinary way, but extraordinarily, and in certain cases, in which he nevertheless judges directly by temporal power, not indirectly by spiritual power. In those cases Innocent thinks that secular causes and temporal judgments devolve upon the Pope. But the devolution of causes implies nothing indirect; it presupposes a most direct power of the same kind.

units.la: XLIV. Denique quoad personas, fatetur iterum Bellarminus, non posse Papam ut Papam ordinarie temporales Principes deponere, etiam justa de causa, eo modo quo deponit Episcopos, tanquam ordinarius judex. Tamen inquit potest mutare Regna, & uni auferre, atque alteri conferre, tanquam summus Princeps spiritualis, si id necessarium sit ad animarum salutem. Quomodo vero mutare Regna, Reges Principesque instituere, exauctorare, de gradu summae potestatis Majestatisque deturbare potest is, qui temporalem potestatem directam in eosdem non habet? Quomodo directam potestatem temporalem Regibus & Principibus conferre & auferre pro animi lubitu, qui eadem destituitur, potest?
units.tr: XLIV. Finally, as regards persons, Bellarmine again concedes that the Pope, as Pope, cannot ordinarily depose temporal princes, even for a just cause, in the way that he deposes bishops, as an ordinary judge. Yet, he says, he can change kingdoms, and take them from one and give them to another, as the supreme spiritual Prince, if this is necessary for the salvation of souls. But how can one who has no direct temporal power over kings and princes change kingdoms, appoint or dismiss kings and princes, and cast them down from the rank of supreme power and majesty? How can one who is destitute of direct temporal power bestow and take away direct temporal power from kings and princes at his own pleasure?

units.la: XLV. Non igitur in dilatandis Pontificiae in temporalibus potestatis periştromatis castiores, sed cautiores nonnihil; imo, si rem pensitemus, crudeliores Theologi Pontificii, quàm Canonistae sunt. Dum enim orbem Christianum lenocinio tali fallere conantur, revera terribilius multo in Pontifice temporalis potestatis telum, spirituali mucrone praepilatum reddunt, adeóque diluta & evanida directae & indirectae potestatis distinctiuncula tanquam tectorio inepto & ὀφ φαρμάκῳ, non tam duriorem Canonistarum sententiam emolliunt, quàm rem ipsam exasperant, dominiúmque totius orbis Papae, tanquam Imperatori Mystico, spiritualium praetextu, gubernacula totius orbis invadenti, asserunt. Neque alii Theologi etiam fuco tali delectantur, potius habentes scapham appellare scapham, & directum Papae dominium non re duntaxat, sed verbo etiam vindicare. Maximos enim Theologos Pontifices contrarium sentire Alexander Correrius de potest. Papae lib. y. demonstrat, & Bellarmini, consentientiumque Theologorum de indirecta duntaxat Papæ in temporalibus potestate sententiam operosè confutat, eúmque isthoc nomine inter impios politicos aut hæreticos numerat, quin & cap. 5. anathema ipsi denuntiare non dubitat, approbante Cardinali, cui librum illum inscripsit, ipsóque Pontifice, cui palpum istum obtrusit. Imò quod mirere, inter Jesuitas ipsos non desunt, qui publicis scriptis hac in re Bellarmino, aliisque Theologis se oppositurerint. Sic enim Azorius Instit. Moral. p. 11. lib. iv. cap. 19. scribit: Concludimus veram esse Canonici Juris interpretum sententiam, Romanum Pontificem habere utramque potestatem spiritualem & temporalem &c. Mihi non placet modus loquendi, quo utuntur Victoria, Sotus, (Bellarminus) quia insinuare videntur, penes Papam solum unam esse potestatem spiritualem, non temporalem. In jure enim Canonico absolutè & simpliciter dicitur, Papam utrumque gladium habere, spiritualem & temporalem, jure quidem & habitu, quamvis usu & actu non nisi in certis quibusdam casibus.
units.tr: XLV. Therefore the Papist theologians are not more chaste, but somewhat more cautious, in extending the Pope's power in temporal matters; indeed, if we weigh the matter, they are more cruel than the canonists. For while they try to deceive the Christian world with such a trick, they in fact make the weapon of temporal power in the Pope far more terrible by tipping it with a spiritual point. By smearing over the distinction between direct and indirect power, like an unsuitable plaster [ὀφ φαρμάκῳ], they do not soften the harsher opinion of the canonists so much as make the matter itself more bitter. They assert that the lordship of the whole world belongs to the Pope, as a mystical Emperor, who under the pretext of spiritual things seizes the reins of the whole world. Nor do other theologians delight in such a disguise; rather, calling a boat a boat, they claim the direct lordship of the Pope not only in fact but in name too. Alexander Correrius, in On the Power of the Pope, book 5, shows that the greatest theologians among the Pontiffs think otherwise, and he laboriously refutes the opinion of Bellarmine and the theologians who agree with him, that the Pope has only indirect power in temporal matters. On this account he numbers Bellarmine among the impious politicians or heretics, and in chapter 5 he does not hesitate to pronounce an anathema against him, with the approval of the Cardinal to whom he dedicated that book, and of the Pontiff himself, to whom he offered this flattery. Indeed, what is more surprising, there are not lacking among the Jesuits themselves those who have openly opposed Bellarmine and other theologians on this point in their published writings. For Azorius, in the Institutiones Morales, part 1, book 4, chapter 19, writes: We conclude that the opinion of the interpreters of canon law is true, that the Roman Pontiff has both the spiritual and the temporal power, etc. I do not like the manner of speaking used by Victoria, Sotus, (Bellarmine), because they seem to insinuate that the Pope has only one power, the spiritual, and not the temporal. For in canon law it is said absolutely and simply that the Pope has both swords, the spiritual and the temporal, by right and by habit, although in use and in act only in certain cases.

units.la: XLVI. Non potuit sanè evitare Bellarminus, quin pafsim sibi ipse larvam egregiè detraheret, & quo loco Papam, & Hierarchiam universam, quo Imperatores Reges & Principes habeat, palam faceret.
units.tr: XLVI. Bellarmine could not, to be sure, avoid tearing off his own mask in many places, and making plain in what place he puts the Pope and the whole hierarchy above emperors, kings and princes.

units.la: En enim νυειας δοξας , directam quas verbis ejus proponam nonnullas, veluti, Reges potius esse servos, quàm Dominos, de Laicis cap. 7. Reges non solùm Pontificibus, sed Episcopis etiam, Presbyteris & Diaconis obnoxios & subjectos esse, de Pont. R. lib. j. 7. Quòd Imperatorem non gravatè bibere oporteat non solum post Episcopum, sed etiam post Presbyterum, ibid. Quòd Regum auctoritas atque functio non immediatè ex Deo descendat, neque ex jure Divino, sed duntaxat ex jure gentium, ibid. & de Clero cap. 28. Quòd Pontifices multos quidem Imperatores deposuerint, nemo autem Imperator aliquando Pontificem: Imò verò quòd Episcopis, qui mancipia sunt Papæ, deponere liceat Principes, & eorum leges rescindere, de Pontif. lib. iij. 16. v. 8. Quòd Ecclesiastici homines tam longè supra Principes sunt, quàm anima supra corpus, de Laicis cap. 6. Quòd Reges deponi possint per subditos suos ob multas causas, de Pontif. lib. j. cap. 18. Pontifices nullo modo deponi posse, nemini enim mortalium permissum esse de iis judicare, de Pontif. lib. ij. 26. Obedientiam Papæ deberi propter conscientiam, de Pontif. lib. iv. 15. Obedientiam autem Regibus non alio respectu deberi, quàm propter ordinem politicum, de Cler. cap. 28. Quòd ipsi illi homines Ecclesiastici, qui & nati sunt, & degunt in Regnis Principum, non tamen sint eorum subditi, nec ab ipsis judicari possint, ipsis autem fas sit Principes suos judicare, ibid. Quòd obedientia, quam Clerici tribuunt Regibus, etiam in minimis meréque civilibus negotiis non sit à necessaria aliqua subjectione, sed tantum ex discretione, & propter observationem boni ordinis atque moris, ibid. Hi eximii & Hyperbolici honores sunt, quibus Pontificii Theologi Reges Principésque hujus seculi mactant; de quibus merito Rex Angliæ Jacobus Apolog. pro juram. fidelit. pag. 280. pronuntiat, non magis opponi Christum Beliali, aut lucem tenebris, aut Cœlum inferno, quàm Roberti Bellarmini de Regibus opinio Divinis oraculis adversetur. XLVII. Pari certè furore Baronius in vastissimo Annalium suorum opere, id unum sibi negotium datum putavit, ut non spiritualem duntaxat, sed temporalem etiam dominationem directam ita amplam Papis vindicet, ut per ejus doctrinam Imperatoribus, Regibus & Principibus nihil restet aliud, nisi SERVIRE, & ad jussa ejus humiliter capessenda, sputáque ipsa lingenda maturè se se componere. Axiomata doctrinæ ejus Principibus funestæ, & erga potentes obliquæ Doctissimus Casaubonus Proleg. ad Exercit. sequentia colligit: Sacerdos quilibet est major Rege, quia politicus Princeps sacerdotali est subjectus, in A. xxxiv. 293. lvii. 18. 32. ccxvi. Sacerdotes & Episcopi jus habent antiquandi leges Imperatorum contrariis legibus in A. cclvii. 15. cccxviii. 64. cccxxxvi. 18. ccclxxxvii. 11. 12. 13. cdi. 60. Præsidibus Provinciarum præsident Episcopi, qui jus habent sententias illorum rescindendi si ipsis libuerit, in A. cdxi. Papa solus potest dare Imperium: ad cujus consecutionem nihil refert esse filium Imperatoris nisi placeat Papæ, in A. dccc. 15. mliii. 14. mclix. 7. Imperator debet Romano Pontifici inservire, ut ejus authoritas sarta tectaque servetur in A. cdxlv. Præsides Provinciarum tenentur jussa Paparum exequi, non adscripto PLACET, sicut fit hodie, in A. cdxix. 8. Quæ, similésque regulæ profligatissimi commatis abundè, quid de distinctiunculis directè, indirectè, proprie, improprie similibúsque νεῷριτως sentiendum sit, comprobant.
units.tr: Behold, here are his false opinions [ψευδεῖς δόξας], which I shall set forth in his own words, some of them: that kings are rather servants than lords (On Laymen, chapter 7); that kings are not only subject and liable to the Pontiffs, but also to bishops, presbyters and deacons (On the Roman Pontiff, book 1, chapter 7); that an emperor ought not to drink unhesitatingly after a bishop, but also after a presbyter (ibid.); that the authority and function of kings do not descend immediately from God, nor from divine right, but only from the law of nations (ibid., and On the Clergy, chapter 28); that Pontiffs have indeed deposed many emperors, but no emperor has ever deposed a Pontiff (indeed, that it is lawful for princes to be deposed by bishops, who are the slaves of the Pope, and for their laws to be annulled) (On the Pontiff, book 3, chapters 16 and 5, and 8); that ecclesiastical men are as far above princes as the soul is above the body (On Laymen, chapter 6); that kings can be deposed by their subjects for many causes (On the Pontiff, book 1, chapter 18); that Pontiffs cannot in any way be deposed, since it is not permitted to any mortal to judge them (On the Pontiff, book 2, chapter 26); that obedience is owed to the Pope on account of conscience (On the Pontiff, book 4, chapter 15); that obedience is owed to kings for no other reason than the political order (On the Clergy, chapter 28); that the ecclesiastical men themselves, who are born and dwell in the realms of princes, are nevertheless not their subjects, nor can be judged by them, whereas it is lawful for them to judge their princes (ibid.); that the obedience which clergy render to kings, even in the smallest and purely civil affairs, is not a necessary subjection, but only a matter of discretion and for the sake of observing good order and custom (ibid.). These are the extravagant and hyperbolical honours with which the Papist theologians load the kings and princes of this age. Of these the King of England, James, in his Apology for the Oath of Allegiance, page 280, rightly pronounces that the opinion of Robert Bellarmine concerning kings is no more opposed to the divine oracles than Christ is opposed to Belial, light to darkness, or heaven to hell. XLVII. With equal fury Baronius, in the vast work of his Annals, thought that this one task had been given to him: to claim for the Popes, not only spiritual but also temporal, direct lordship so broadly that, by his teaching, nothing remains for emperors, kings and princes but to SERVE, and to hasten to submit humbly to his commands and lick his spittle. The most learned Casaubon, in the Prolegomena to the Exercitationes, gathers the following axioms of his doctrine, which are harmful to princes and oblique toward the powerful: every priest is greater than a king, because the political prince is subject to the priestly office (in A. 34, 293; 57, 18, 32; 216). Priests and bishops have the right to abrogate the laws of emperors by contrary laws (in A. 257, 15; 318, 64; 336, 18; 387, 11, 12, 13; 60). Bishops preside over the governors of provinces, and have the right to rescind their sentences if they please (in A. 411). The Pope alone can give the empire; for attaining it, it makes no difference to be the son of an emperor unless it pleases the Pope (in A. 800, 15; 1053, 14; 1059, 7). The emperor ought to serve the Roman Pontiff, so that his authority may be kept safe and sound (in A. 445). The governors of provinces are bound to carry out the orders of the Popes, not with the words placet appended, as is done today (in A. 419, 8). These rules, and others like them, of a most shameless kind, amply show what is to be thought of the little distinctions directly, indirectly, properly, improperly, and similar [νεῷριτως] ones.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Et quicquid tandem clari obscurive nominis athletæ illi in umbra de potestate temporali Papæ historicè digladientur, ipsi certè Pontifices summam & directam in temporalibus potestatem ad se pertinere, nulli omnino dubitant. Etenim primò libentissimis patientissimisque auribus à Canonistis, alinsque gnathonibus suis in tantum culmen suam extolli cathedram audiunt. Sic Leo X. in Concilio Lateranensi Sess. 8. concionantem Baltharem Detrionem audivit: Accu Leo Rex quadrupedum, tu alter Leo hominum, non alter Rex tantùm, sed Rex Regum, & orbis terrarum Monarcha effectus, alias oves quas habes, quæ non sunt de hoc ovili, ad tuum ovile reducere, alliceres, revocares. Accingere ergo gladio super femur tuum potentissimè. Nam & tu duos gladios habes, spiritualem & temporalem. Similia declamantes alios acquis, vacivisque auribus Pontifices excipiunt. Secundò indirectam duntaxat sibi potestatem tribuentibus indignantur palam. Eo nomine non parum Bellarmino Sixtus V. successuit. Cùm non nisi indirectam auctoritatem Papis deberi disputâsset Bellarminus (verba sunt G. Barclaii de potest. Papæ lib. j. 13.) satisfacere non potuit ambitioni imperiosissimi hominis Sixti V. qui se supremam in omnes Reges & Principes terræ, cunctosque populos gentes & nationes, non humana, sed divina institutione sibi traditam potestatem obtinere affirmabat in bulla contra Henricum III Francorum Regem. Itaque parum abfuit, quin omnia doctoris illius opera Pontificia censura aboleret, uti illius ordinis Patres, cujus tunc erat Bellarminus, serió Barclaio narrarunt. Sed & tertiò nullus unquam Papa Pontificali, publica, bullata censura notavit, vel notari jussit quenquam Canonistarum & Theologorum, qua concrepantibus buccis potestatem ejus temporalem, publicis etiam scriptis, in immensum ferè extulerunt, maximóque cum Pontificiorum etiam Regum, Principum, populorum scandalo defenderunt. Extat scandalorum ejusmodi scriptorum catalogus in Bibliotheca Pontificum per Ludovicum Jacobum, à S. Carolo Carmelitam Lib. ÿ. nec non in Bibliotheca Jesuitica Philippi Alegambe pag. 493-499. Eminent, inter eos Creswellus in Philopatri, Personius, Fizherbertus, Pozmanius, Comitolus, Cellarius, Sanderus, Adamus Tannerus in defensione Ecclesiasticæ libertatis contra causæ Venetæ patronos; Thomas Bazzius de Ecclesiastica Monarchia temporali, Cardinalis Tuschus, Eudæmon Johannis Apologia pro Garneto, nec non dissertatio contra Politicam Leidresseri, & epistolam Causaboni, & Epistola monitoria ad Barclajum, Alexander Carrerius juris consultus Patavinus, qui in tractatu de potestate Papæ A. 1599. edito, Papam non secus ac Christum ipsum, cujus vicarius sit, jure Divino & directè totius orbis etiam in temporalibus, dominum esse, probare contendit; Guilhelmus Singletonus Theologus Duacenus, qui peculiari nuper libello, Pontificem plenum jus in omnia bona etiam temporalia Christianorum habere, disputavit; ne quid de Suarezio, Mariano, Becano, Bellarmino, Santarello, qui à filiis natu maximis Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Regibus Galliarum, per filiam eorundem natu maximam, Academiam Parisiensem, Curiámque supremam gravia passi sunt, alii-sque supra etiam nominatis, dicam. Ubi tubas & faces illas publicarum seditionum, generis humani furias obelo suo vel levissimè notavit? Ubi & quando proclamavit, & protestatus est, additis diris ac clausuris Bullarum solennibus, nimium vel indebitum quid sibi tribui? Cuncta isthæc non in angulis obscuris mustitata, sed in medio Papatu, ipsáque Romana urbe vulgata à Papa, sacro Consistorio, sacris congregationibus Cardinalium, officiis Inquisitionis, Expurgatoribus, Censoribus librorum, Conciliis Provincialibus, Curiis Provincialibus, quorum teretes adeò in iis, Papatui adversari vel minimùm videntur, aures sunt, audiuntur, leguntur, facileque adeò stomacho concoquuntur.
units.tr: Whatever the contenders, obscure or famous, may dispute historically about the temporal power of the Pope, the Popes themselves certainly hold, and no one doubts, that supreme and direct power in temporal matters belongs to them. For, first, they listen with the most willing and patient ears while Canonists and their other flatterers exalt the papal chair to such a height. Thus Leo X, in the Lateran Council, Session 8, heard Balthasar Detrion preaching: Behold Leo, king of the quadrupeds, you another Leo of men, not merely another king but King of kings and made monarch of the world, to lead back and call to your fold the other sheep you have, which are not of this fold. Gird your sword upon your thigh most mightily. For you also have two swords, the spiritual and the temporal. The Popes receive others declaiming similar things with eager and empty ears. Second, they openly show indignation at those who grant them only an indirect power. On this account Sixtus V was not a little successor to Bellarmine. Since Bellarmine had argued that only an indirect authority is owed to the Popes (these are the words of G. Barclay, On the Power of the Pope, book 1, ch. 13) he could not satisfy the ambition of that most imperious man Sixtus V, who affirmed in his bull against Henry III, King of the French, that he held power over all kings and princes of the earth and over all peoples, nations and tribes, handed down to him not by human but by divine institution. And so it was a close thing that he did not, by papal censure, abolish all the works of that doctor, as the Fathers of that order, of which Bellarmine then was a member, reported seriously to Barclay. But also, third, no Pope ever, by a public, bulled censure, marked or ordered anyone of the Canonists and Theologians to be marked, who with loud voices and even in public writings have extolled his temporal power almost without limit and defended it with great scandal even to the Papist kings, princes and peoples. A catalogue of such scandalous writers exists in the Bibliotheca Pontificum of Louis James of St. Charles the Carmelite, book 5, and also in the Bibliotheca Jesuitica of Philip Alegambe, pp. 493-499. Among them stand out Creswell in the Philopater, Persons, Fitzherbert, Pozman, Comitolus, Cellarius, Sanders, Adam Tanner in his defence of ecclesiastical liberty against the patrons of the Venetian cause; Thomas Bozio on the temporal monarchy of the Church; Cardinal Tusco; Eudaemon-Joannes, Apology for Garnet, and also the dissertation against the Politics of Leiden's Ressler, and the letter of Casaubon, and the monitory letter to Barclay; Alexander Carrerius, Paduan jurist, who in his treatise On the Power of the Pope, published in 1599, strove to prove that the Pope, no less than Christ himself, whose vicar he is, is by divine law and directly lord of the whole world, even in temporal matters; William Singleton, Theologian of Douai, who in a recent special little book argued that the Pope has full right over all the temporal goods of Christians; not to mention Suarez, Mariana, Becanus, Bellarmine, Santarelli, who, at the hands of the eldest sons of the Roman Church, the kings of France, through their eldest daughter the University of Paris and the supreme Court, have suffered grave treatment, and the others even named above. Where did he, with his pointed stylus, ever mark with even the slightest censure those trumpets and torches of public sedition, the furies of the human race? Where and when did he proclaim and protest, with added curses and the solemn clauses of bulls, that something excessive or undue was being attributed to him? All these things were not muttered in dark corners but made known in the middle of Papacy, and in the Roman city itself, by the Pope, the sacred Consistory, the sacred congregations of Cardinals, the offices of the Inquisition, the Expurgators, the Censors of books, the Provincial Councils, the Provincial Courts, whose ears are so smooth that in them what seems even slightly opposed to Papacy is heard, read, and so easily digested by the stomach.

units.la: XLIX. Plus verò est, quòd Quartò Pontifices etiam rem definiunt, non tamen ita accuratè, ut liquidò cuivis constet, quam in sententiam abeant, Canonistarum an Theologorum; sed id tamen omnibus constet, se à politicis recedere. Neglectis enim distinctionibus istis directè, indirectè, absolutè, respectivè &c. id unum velut è Cathedræ suæ tripode, suum esse utrumque gladium, pronuntiant. Quomodo enim habeant, quid intereat, dum habeant? Neque ignorant, leve utrosque inter discrimen esse, & Theologos verbis potiùs amoliri voluisse invidiam,quàm re potentiam minuere. Siveenim indirectè, five respectivè dicant, tamen judicium totius rei penes Papam relinquunt. Ipse igitur sibi arbiter est, quando sua illa potestate utatur, & quousque eam extendat, definiturus etiam ex Cathedra quandocunquee re sua esse judicaverit, directam & absolutissimam quolibet respectu potestatem in temporalibus sibi competere. Neglecto proin discrimine hactenus simpliciter pronuntiant, suum esse utrumque gladium, spiritualem æquèac temporalem. Ita Gregorius X. Epistola ad Episcopum Græcorum,apud Matthæum Paris in Henrico III. Illud tantùm adjicimus, quòd utrumque gladium ad Romanum pertinere Pontificem ex Euangelica lectione tenemus. Nicolaus II. apud Gratianum dist. 22. cap. 1. sicè Dodonæa quercu sua pronuntiavit, Romanam Ecclesiam solus ille fundavit, & super petram fidei nascentis mox erexit, qui beato æternæ vitæ clavigero terreni, simul & Cœlestis imperii jura commisit. Innocentius III. in Epistola ad Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum disertis verbis profitetur, commissam esse Petro (ac proinde & Romano Papæ) non solùm universam Ecclesiam, sed etiam totum seculum gubernandum, mox petitis ex Euangelio testimoniis, ita ratiocinatus est: Cùm aquæ multæ sint populi multi, cengregetionesque aquarum sint maria, per hoc quòd Petrus super aquas maris incessit, super universos populose potestatem accepisse monstravit. Clarissimè omnium Bonifacius VIII. in Extravagante Unam Sanctam, de majoritare & obedientia sic rem expedit: In hac ejus potestate duos esse gladios, spiritualem videlicet & temporalem, Euangelicis dictis instruimur. Nam dicentibus Apostolis: Ecce gladii duo hic, in Ecclesia scilicet, cum Apostoli loquerentur, non respondit Dominus nimis esse, sed satis. Certè qui in potestate Petri temporalem gladium esse ne- gat, gat, male verbum attendit Domini proferentis, Converte gladium tuum in vaginam: Uterque ergo est in potestate Ecclesiæ, spiritualis scilicet gladius & materialis: Ibidinem Manichæismi accusat eos, qui pertendunt, non omnem terrenam potestatem spiritualí, sive pontificiæ jurisdictioni à Deo subjectam esse. Pius V. in Bulla fulminante in caput Elisabethæ Angliæ astruit, Papam à Christo constitutum esse Principem & Dominum in omnes nationes & Regna, ad evellendum, destruendum, dissipandum &c.
units.tr: XLIX. But there is more: fourth, the Popes also define the matter, yet not so carefully that it is clear to anyone whether they incline to the opinion of the Canonists or of the Theologians; still it is plain to all that they depart from the political writers. For, neglecting those distinctions, directly, indirectly, absolutely, relatively, etc., they proclaim, as if from the tripod of their chair, this one thing: that both swords are theirs. For how do they hold them, when what matters is that they hold them? Nor are they unaware that there is only a slight difference between the two, and that the Theologians preferred to remove the odium by words rather than to diminish the power in fact. For whether they say indirectly or relatively, they still leave the judgment of the whole matter in the Pope's hands. He is therefore his own judge as to when he should use that power and how far he should extend it, and he will define, even from the Chair, whenever he judges it to be his own affair, that he has a direct and most absolute power in temporal affairs in every respect. So, disregarding the distinction, they have hitherto pronounced simply that both swords, the spiritual and the temporal alike, are theirs. Thus Gregory X, in his letter to the Bishop of the Greeks, as quoted by Matthew Paris under Henry III: "We add only this, that we hold from the Gospel reading that both swords belong to the Roman Pontiff." Nicholas II, as quoted by Gratian, dist. 22, cap. 1, pronounced in the manner of his oak of Dodona: "The Roman Church was founded by him alone, who raised it at once upon the rock of the newborn faith, who committed to the blessed keeper of the keys of eternal life the rights of both the earthly and the heavenly kingdom." Innocent III, in his letter to the Patriarch of Constantinople, professes in plain words that not only the universal Church but also the whole world was committed to Peter (and therefore to the Roman Pope) to govern; then, having cited testimonies from the Gospel, he reasoned thus: "Since the waters are many peoples, and the gatherings of waters are seas, by the fact that Peter walked upon the waters of the sea he showed that he had received power over all peoples." Most clearly of all, Boniface VIII, in the Extravagant Unam Sanctam, on the Majority and Obedience, settles the matter thus: "We are taught by the words of the Gospel that there are two swords in this his power, namely the spiritual and the temporal. For when the Apostles said, 'Behold, here are two swords,' that is, in the Church, the Lord, speaking to the Apostles, did not reply that it was too many, but that it was enough. Certainly he who denies that the temporal sword is in the power of Peter has not rightly attended to the word of the Lord who said, 'Put up your sword into its sheath.' Both, therefore, are in the power of the Church, the spiritual sword and the material sword." In the same place he accuses of Manichaeism those who maintain that not all earthly power is subject to God through the spiritual or papal jurisdiction. Pius V, in his thundering bull against Elizabeth of England, asserts that the Pope has been appointed by Christ as prince and lord over all nations and kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, scatter, etc.

units.la: L. Neque tantùm ita Pontifices definiverunt, sed Quintò etiam absolutam in temporalibus potestatem re ipsa nunquam non exercuerunt, adeòque quod definiverunt, etiam re implere conati sunt. Sanè Bonifacius ille VIII. in publici jejunii celebratione, publica pompa ostentavit se primò Papam, secundò Imperatorem, teste Cranzio Saxoniæ lib. viij. 36. ubi sic ille: utriusque penes se unam gladii potestatem manere affirmabat: quod ipso apparatu in eo, qui, ut diximus, tum agebatur in urbe, jubilæo solenniter fertur ostentâsse. Primo quidem solenni die in Pontificalibus apparens populo, Apostolicam illis benedictionem impartitur. Postero autem die Imperiali habitu, infula nihilominus Cæsarea insignis gladium ante se nudatum jussit deferri, & sedens alta voce testatur: Ecce duo gladii hic. Ad Philippum IV. Francorum Regem in hæc verba idem scripsit: Deum time, & mandata ejus observa. Scire te volumus, quòd in spiritualibus & temporalibus nobis subes. Sed & Augustinus Triumphus de potest. Eccl. q. j. art. 7. testatur, Papam consecrari ut Sacerdotem, & coronari ut Regem, festúmque coronationis nuntiare omnibus Regibus.
units.tr: L. Nor have the Popes only defined it in this way; fifth, they have also never ceased in fact to exercise absolute power in temporal affairs, and so they have tried to carry out in practice what they defined. Indeed that Boniface VIII, at the celebration of a public fast, displayed with public pomp that he was first Pope and second Emperor, as Cranzius of Saxony testifies, book 8, ch. 36, where he writes thus: he affirmed that the one power of the sword rested in him on both sides; and it is reported that he showed this solemnly by that very display in the jubilee which, as we have said, was then being celebrated in the city. On the first solemn day, appearing before the people in his pontifical vestments, he gave them the apostolic blessing. But on the following day, in imperial dress, adorned nonetheless with the Caesarean mitre, he had a sword carried before him bared, and sitting, he testified in a loud voice: "Behold, here are two swords." To Philip IV, King of the French, he wrote to the same effect in these words: "Fear God and keep his commandments. We wish you to know that you are subject to us in spiritual and in temporal matters." And Augustine Triumphus, On the Ecclesiastical Power, question 1, article 7, testifies that the Pope is consecrated as a priest and crowned as a king, and that the feast of the coronation is announced to all kings.

units.la: LI. Quemadmodum ad potestatem supremam temporalem Pontifices machinationibus variis enisi sint, & ean-
units.tr: LI. As the popes, by various machinations, strove after supreme temporal power, and

units.la: dem impotenter & flagitiose adversus Imperatores Henricos, Fridericos, Ludovicum Bavarum, Albertum, aliósque plures, Reges quin etiam Franciæ, Angliæ, Siciliæ, Bohemiæ, Navarræ &c. exercuerint, historia Papatus irrefragabilibus documentis in apertam lucem protulit. Neque heic operam ludimus, contenti illud animadvertere, Romanos Pontifices supremam in temporalibus potestatem, in Imperatores Reges & Principes utique exercere, quoties eos legibus suis temporalem statum concernentibus constringunt: judicia in casu devolutionis, uti appellant, exercent: Regum controversias ad suum tribunal revocant: Orbem occupatum, in quo nulla antehac Ecclesia fuit, donant, & pro arbitratu suo inter Reges distribuunt: fœdera Regum & Principum Pontificiorum cum infidelibus & hæreticis à suo nutu ita pendere asserunt, ut pro arbitratu suo contrahi, & contracta jam servari vel violari possint: gladii temporalis adversus infideles & hæreticos stringendi & recondendi arbitrium à suo nutu suspendunt, adeóque bellandi jus Principibus Christianis Europæis adversus Saracenos & paganos quosque, hæreticos quin etiam, assignato victoribus omni eo, quod armis occupari potest, dant, partésque imperio suo injungunt, cujus rei exempla plura Rouffelius Hist. jurisd. Pontif. lib. vj. 5. narrat: in Regna vi injusta occupata jus promittunt, uti quidem Pius II. Mahumetem II. Turcarum Imperatorem Constantinopoli occupata ad fidem Christianam invitavit, propósito hoc præmio, quòd velit illum Græcorum & Orientis Imperatorem appellare, ut quod vi occupavit, & cum injuria teneret, jure posthac possideat; quódque illum velit constituere legitimum etiam Principem Syrorum, Lybicorum, Arabum & quarumvis aliarum extra Christi caulas gentium: Pacis cum iis, quos hæreticorum in censu habent, farciendæ & constituendæ arbitrium sibi deposcunt: Imperatores & Reges pro imperio jubent, additis vocabulis merè imperativis: Volumus, Constituimus, jubemus, quales crebrò in bullis eorum ad Reges Principésque directis occurrunt: tributa, collationes, decimas ex clero, vel aliunde indicunt, annatas exigunt, sibique Collationes præbendarum, & sacerdotiorum injungunt: jura Regalia prætextu inani juris Ecclesiastici infringunt: ubi beneficiarius supremum diem Romæ abiit, sibi jus nominandi, attribuendi, implendi sacerdotium vacuum, & quando inhabilibus personis, quas Curtisanos olim vocârunt, illud, cum patroni & collatoris damno conferendi asciscunt, attributione asservata Principibus, si per expressam bullam & diploma ante aliter cautum fuerit, quod diploma collati juris jurisdictionis Regalis actus est: privilegia indulgent, ne in qualibet causa rei & actores Romam citentur, sed coram judicibus aut commissariis à se delegatis, iis in locis, in quibus lis & causa coeperunt, disceptetur, quod privilegium in Concordato Francifcum I. inter & Leonem X. successorésque pacto inito, concessum à Papa, insigne documentum est Papalis Imperii, per Pragmaticam Sanctionem dimidia sui parte accisi, Regiæque servitutis catena paulò laxiori & circumductiori, licet cùm alibi forsan locorum, ut in Hispania, Polonia &c. pugnantes partes Romam se conferre cogantur, & olim causas seculares in prima instantia ad Romanum tribunal, ad conservatores cæterósque judices Papales pertractas esse, Germani in gravaminibus suis, puta IX. X. XI.&c. questi sint: Xenodochia, Cœnobia, Abbatias, Episcopatus instituunt, eósque in plures Episcopatus dividunt: Decanocapitula & conventus religiosos ab Episcopi jurisdictione, quod olim Imperialis & Regii juris erat, eximunt: inter casus privilegiatos & delicti communis ita distinguunt, ut illos Regii in Gallia ad suum tribunal, quasi per privilegium Papale, pertrahere possint, hi vero non nisi Pontificio tribunali subsint, quae divisio causarum insigne documentum est Papalis in Gallia Imperii, ut & partitio cujusvis causae in duas classes, quarum altera petitorium, altera possessorium vocatur, hoc ad Regem pertinens, illud ad Papam, cujus est, uti volunt, de omni peccato cognoscere & judicare, ut poene in omni lite & controversia, Papa divisum cum Rege imperium habeat: laicos reos licet, ad forum ecclesiasticorum trahunt, uti olim in Germania factitatum, ex Gravamine LVI. liquet: excommunicationis telum, non ob notoriam impietatem & haeresin, sed causas meri civiles, ad quaestum Papae & cleri utcunque comparatas, stringunt: res causasque matrimoniales, quae juris naturalis, civilis & Divini, non positivi, sed perpetui sunt, partem non postremam rerum mere civilium, fictitio Sacramenti & mysterii praetextu, ad forum suum pertrahunt; denique similia fere innumera, quae ex Gravaminibus centum Germanicae Nationis, aliisque Regum & Principum querelis, & documentis publicis, quin & seculorum plurium usu & experimentis colligi nullo negotio possent, designant.
units.tr: exercised it impotently and shamefully against the emperors Henry, Frederick, Louis of Bavaria, Albert and many others, and even against the kings of France, England, Sicily, Bohemia, Navarre, etc. The history of the Papacy has brought this to plain light by irrefutable evidence. Nor are we playing games here. We are content to note that the Roman pontiffs do exercise supreme power in temporal matters over emperors, kings and princes, whenever they bind them by laws concerning their temporal state. In what they call cases of devolution they exercise judgments. They summon the disputes of kings to their own tribunal. They grant the occupied world, in which no church had existed before, and distribute it among kings at their discretion. They assert that the treaties of Papist kings and princes with infidels and heretics depend so much on their nod that they may be contracted at will, and once contracted may be kept or violated. They hold in their power the decision whether the temporal sword is to be drawn or sheathed against infidels and heretics, and so grant to Christian princes of Europe the right to wage war against Saracens, pagans and even heretics, assigning to the victors everything that can be seized by arms, and they enjoin on the parties submission to their rule. Rouffelius, Hist. jurisd. Pontif. lib. vj. 5., relates several examples of this. They promise right over kingdoms seized by unjust force. Thus Pius II invited Mahomet II, emperor of the Turks, after the seizure of Constantinople, to the Christian faith, holding out this reward: that he be willing to call him Emperor of the Greeks and of the East, so that what he had seized by force and held wrongfully he might henceforth possess by right; and that he be willing to appoint him legitimate prince also of the Syrians, Libyans, Arabs and of whatever other nations lie outside the fold of Christ. They claim for themselves the power to settle and establish peace with those whom they count among heretics. They order emperors and kings by their authority, with purely imperative words: We will, we decree, we command, such as frequently occur in their bulls addressed to kings and princes. They impose tributes, contributions and tithes from the clergy or elsewhere, exact annates, and claim for themselves the collation of prebends and priesthoods. They break royal rights under the empty pretext of ecclesiastical law. When a beneficed man has departed to his last day at Rome, they claim for themselves the right to nominate, assign and fill the vacant priesthood, and when they confer it on unfit persons, whom they once called courtiers, to the loss of the patron and collator, they keep the assignment for the princes if it has been otherwise provided for by an express bull and diploma beforehand; that diploma is itself an act of the conferred right of royal jurisdiction. They grant privileges that persons be not cited to Rome in any cause, whether as defendants or plaintiffs, but be heard before judges or commissaries delegated by themselves, in the places where the suit and cause began. This privilege, granted by the Pope in the Concordat made between Francis I and Leo X and their successors, is a notable document of papal empire, cut in half by the Pragmatic Sanction, and a somewhat looser and more roundabout chain of royal servitude; although elsewhere, as in Spain, Poland etc., the opposing parties are compelled to betake themselves to Rome, and the Germans complained in their grievances, e.g. IX, X, XI etc., that formerly secular causes in first instance were tried before the Roman tribunal, before conservators and other papal judges. They found hospices, monasteries, abbeys and bishoprics, and divide them into many bishoprics. They exempt chapters of deans and religious convents from the jurisdiction of the bishop, which formerly was of imperial and royal right. They distinguish between privileged cases and cases of common crime in such a way that royal courts in France can draw the former to their own tribunal, as if by papal privilege, while the latter are subject only to the papal tribunal. This division of causes is a notable document of papal empire in France, as is the partition of any cause into two classes, one called petitory and the other possessory, the former belonging to the king, the latter to the Pope, who, as they wish, has the right to know and judge of every sin; so that, in almost every suit and controversy, the Pope has empire divided with the king. They draw lay defendants before the forum of the ecclesiastics, as was formerly practised in Germany, as is clear from Grievance LVI. They wield the weapon of excommunication not for notorious impiety and heresy but for purely civil causes, arranged in some way for the gain of the Pope and clergy. They draw matrimonial matters and causes, which belong to natural, civil and divine law, not positive law, but perpetual, and a not unimportant part of purely civil affairs, into their own forum under the fictitious pretext of sacrament and mystery. Finally, they point out almost countless similar things, which could without any trouble be gathered from the grievances of the hundred of the German nation, from other complaints of kings and princes, from public documents, and indeed from the practice and experience of many centuries.

units.la: LII. Neque vero Pontificii Jurisconsulti potestatem Cleri Romani in res mere civiles quondam usurpatam, & causas ejusmodi plures a foro Ecclesiastico ad civilia passim revocatas, dissimulant. Historiam Pontificiae jurisdictionis ex antiquo, medio, & novo usu nostro seculo Michael Rouffelius JCus Gallus concinnavit, cujus libro sexto paulo fusius Ecclesiasticam jurisdictionem contentiosam in laicos & res temporales edisserit. Et primitus quidem Episcopos judiciis etiam temporalibus, ob compertam eorum moderationem & prudentiam, praefectos, non propriam tamen & nativam jurisdictionem exercuisse, & arbitrarias potius quam coactivas sententias tulisse, quin & arbitrii limites egressos, ab Imperatoribus in ordinem redactos esse, capite primo ostendit. Media ætate, & procedente tempore eosdem, partim de criminibus non nullis, veluti idololatria, cædे Episcopi, & aliorum Clericorum, nec non excommunicatorum, adulteriis, raptu, incendiis, violatione Ecclesiarum, sacrilegiis, sortilegiis, hæresi, aliisque, de quibus Summorum Pontificum decreta prostant, notionem suscepisse: partim civiles causas plures, puta contractus ob usuras reddituales, pupillares, dotales, montium pietatis; ob jus jurandum; nec non actiones reales ob prædia Ecclesiastica; causas personarum & rerum, earum scilicet, quæ in terram sanctam peregrinabantur; testamenta, hæreditates, legata pia, bona intestatorum, causas nuptiales, & accidentes illis dotem, hæreditatem ex jure natalium; causas viduarum, pupillorum, miserabilium personarum; negligentiam judicis laici discere, adeoque tum in criminalibus, tum in civilibus causis -lem exercuisse, ita tamen ut successu temporis, in Gallia, Anglia, Hispania, alibique eadem causæ, tum criminales, tum civiles etiam à jurisdictione Ecclesiastica ad Civilem à Regibus & Principibus jura sua rectius edoctis, revocatæ sint, capite secundo, tertio, quarto & quinto fusè admodum enarrat. Demum capite septimo Summi Pontificis jurisdictionem temporalem in laicos ex causis criminalibus & civilibus edisserens, jurisdictionem tum à Gregorio M. in causis partim criminalibus, puta Simonia, incantatione, sacrilegio, maleficio, &c. partim civilibus, velut in causis realibus & possessoriis, viduarum & pauperum, testamentariis, hæreditate, successione, præscriptione quadragenaria: tum à Nicolao I. in causa repudii inter Lotharium & Theupergam, aliisque merè civilibus: tum à Johanne VIII. Comitem Bernhardum ad Romanam Synodum ob infidelitatis crimen ei à Ludovico Rege intentatum Romam, & Mironem ac Huncfridum multorum scelerum laicorum reos ad Synodum Lugdunensem citante: tum à Gregorio VII. mulierem adulterii ream Episcopi inquisitioni subjiciente, & incestus notionem ad se revocante, nec non Bohemiæ Ducem, aliósque ob res merè temporales Romam citante: tum ab Innocentio III. judicem se inter Philippum Galliæ, & Johannem Angliæ Reges constituente: tum ab Urbano V. Dionysium Castellæ Regem & Henricum fratrem in causa hæreditatis dijudicante, tum denique ab aliis pluribus exercitam perstringit.
units.tr: LII. Nor do the Papist jurisconsults conceal the power once usurped by the Roman clergy over purely civil matters, and the many causes of this kind that were everywhere recalled from the ecclesiastical forum to the civil courts. Michael Rouffelius, a French jurisconsult, has put together a history of papal jurisdiction from its ancient, medieval and modern practice in our century, and in his sixth book he sets out the ecclesiastical contentious jurisdiction over laymen and temporal affairs somewhat more fully. In the first chapter he shows that at first bishops, because of their proven moderation and prudence, exercised over temporal judgments the authority of prefects, not their own and native jurisdiction, and pronounced arbitrary rather than coercive sentences; and that when they went beyond the limits of arbitration they were brought back into line by the emperors. In the middle age, and as time went on, they took cognizance, partly of certain crimes, such as idolatry, the murder of a bishop or of other clergy, excommunicated persons, adultery, rape, arson, violation of churches, sacrilege, sorcery, heresy and others, concerning which the decrees of the supreme pontiffs survive; partly of many civil causes, such as contracts involving interest on income, guardianship, dowry, and pious lending-houses; oaths; real actions concerning ecclesiastical estates; causes of persons and things, namely of those who went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land; wills, inheritances, pious legacies, the goods of those who died intestate; matrimonial causes and those incidental to them, dowry, inheritance by right of birth; causes of widows, orphans and wretched persons; and the negligence of a lay judge. Thus they exercised jurisdiction both in criminal and in civil causes. Yet in course of time, in France, England, Spain and elsewhere, these same causes, both criminal and civil, were recalled from ecclesiastical to civil jurisdiction by kings and princes who had learned their own rights more correctly. He recounts this quite fully in the second, third, fourth and fifth chapters. Finally, in the seventh chapter, setting out the temporal jurisdiction of the Supreme Pontiff over laymen in criminal and civil causes, he describes how that jurisdiction was exercised: by Gregory the Great in criminal causes, such as simony, incantation, sacrilege, witchcraft, etc., and in civil causes, such as real and possessory actions, those of widows and the poor, testamentary matters, inheritance, succession, and prescription of forty years; by Nicholas I in the case of divorce between Lothair and Theutberga, and in other purely civil matters; by John VIII, who summoned Count Bernard to the Roman synod on a charge of infidelity brought against him by King Louis, and summoned Miro and Hunfrid, accused of many crimes by laymen, to the synod of Lyon; by Gregory VII, who subjected an adulteress to the inquisition of a bishop and recalled the cognizance of incest to himself, and also summoned the Duke of Bohemia and others to Rome over purely temporal matters; by Innocent III, who set himself up as judge between Philip, king of France, and John, king of England; and by Urban V, who adjudicated between Peter, king of Castile, and his brother Henry in a case of inheritance; and finally by others in many more instances.

units.la: LIII. Accedit potestas, quam sibi adversus Imperatorem, Reges & Principes immensam ferè arrogat, & quotiescunque satis ei vires suæ placent, ἀυτοκρατορικὰς exercet. Ac primùm quidem absolutam sibi in Imperatoribus usus est. Et & Regibus constituendis, ceronandisque potestatem vendicat. Sub Coronationis scilicet, quæ initio simplex tantùm benedictio fuit, prætextu de ipso Imperio pro arbitrio suo disponendi facultatem arripuit, & quos olim Dominos suos (ita planè constat ex diplomate cujus meminit Guicciardinus in fragmento, Imperante Carolo Domino nostro) haud gravatim appellavit, eorum planè captivam post Pseudopetri triumphales currus Majestatem traducere cœpit. Ita mutatis rerum vicibus illud accidit Poëtæ veteris: Ἀεὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἱερῶν χωρῶν πηγαί. Sursum versus sacrorum fluminum feruntur cursus. Constat satis, post divisionem Imperii Orientalis & Occidentalis ipsis etiam Imperatoribus ut plurimùm consentientibus, coronæ Imperatorum capiti imponendæ jus velut à S. Petro acceptum, Romanum Pontificem ad se traxisse. Initium factum à Carolo M. cui pro beneficiis pluribus hostimentum redditurus Leò III. coronam imposuit, acclamante populo: Carolo Augusto à Deo coronato, magno & pacifico Imperatori Romanorum vita & victoria. Qui ita coronatus exemplum posteris reliquit, ut eandem coronationem à Pontifice appeterent, Ludovico etiam filio, qui Pius postea dictus est, cùm in cunis adhuc vagiret, Romam adducto, ut ab Adriano Pontifice Regali diademate ornaretur, quò sic verba referam Aimonii, beatorum Petri & Pauli suffragiis consulere subditis, perduellionúmque si emerfissent, proterviam proterere possent. Patre defuncto denuo idem Rhemis à Stephano Papa coronatus est, & filius ejusdem Lotharius à Paschali I. nepos Ludovicus à Sergio, hujusque filius Carolus Calvus à Johanne VII. largitionibus prius corrupto, coronati sunt. Ab his primordiis eò Romani Pontificis profecta est authoritas, ut inter Imperii rivales is se pro Imperatore venditaret, qui à Pontifice coronam capesslivisset, qui & à Deo coronatus propterea dici solet, eòque perventum, ut Gregorius V. legem tulerit, ne Imperatorem dici fas esset electum, priusquam à Romano Pontifice consecratus esset, quod in constitutiones etiam suas Germani retulerunt, constantérque deinceps Pontifices usurparunt, ut nisi coronatum pro Imperatore habendum negaverint, nisi Papali intercedente privilegio, cujusmodi Carolus V. obtinuit.
units.tr: LIII. Moreover, the power he claims over the Emperor, kings and princes is almost boundless, and whenever his own strength pleases him, he exercises autocratic [ἀυτοκρατορικὰς] authority. And first, he has claimed absolute power over emperors. He also claims the right to appoint and crown kings. Under the pretext of coronation, which at first was only a simple blessing, he seized the power of disposing of the empire itself at his own discretion. Those whom he once readily called their lords (as is clear from the diploma mentioned by Guicciardini in the fragment, Imperante Carolo Domino nostro) he began to drag, as captives, behind his triumphal chariot. Thus, with the turning of fortune, what the old poet said came to pass: Always the springs of sacred streams flow much higher [Ἀεὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἱερῶν χωρῶν πηγαί]. Upstream the courses of sacred rivers run. It is quite well established that, after the division of the Eastern and Western Empires, with the emperors themselves mostly consenting, the Roman Pontiff drew to himself the right of placing the imperial crown on the emperor's head, a right he took as if received from St Peter. The beginning was made by Charlemagne, to whom Leo III, about to repay many favours with gratitude, placed the crown, while the people acclaimed: To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, the great and peaceful Emperor of the Romans, life and victory. Having been crowned in this way, he left a precedent for his successors, so that they too sought the same coronation from the Pontiff. His son Louis, who was later called the Pious, was brought to Rome while still crying in his cradle, so that he might be adorned with the royal diadem by Pope Adrian. To quote Aimoin's words, this was to secure the prayers of the blessed Peter and Paul for his subjects, so that if rebels should arise they might crush their arrogance. After his father's death, the same man was crowned again at Rheims by Pope Stephen; and his son Lothar was crowned by Paschal I, his grandson Louis by Sergius, and Louis's son Charles the Bald by John VII, who had first been corrupted by bribes. From these beginnings the authority of the Roman Pontiff advanced to such a point that, among the rivals for the empire, whoever had obtained the crown from the Pope passed himself off as emperor; and such a man is commonly called crowned by God for that reason. It came to the point that Gregory V passed a law that no one elected might rightly be called emperor before he had been consecrated by the Roman Pontiff. The Germans also wrote this into their own constitutions, and the Popes steadily claimed it thereafter, so that they denied that anyone was to be regarded as emperor unless he was crowned, except by Papal privilege, of the kind Charles V obtained.

units.la: LIV. Quo verò animo Papæ Imperatoribus coronam sive præsentibus, usque ad Rodolphum I. sive posthac absentibus, & Romæ limina calcare renuentibus, per legatos dederint, quo eandem Imperatores admiserint, non tantùm ex corona à Gregorio VII. Rodulpho Suevo transmissa, atque tali carmine inscripta,
units.tr: LIV. In what spirit the Popes handed over the crown to emperors through legates, whether the emperors were present, as far as Rudolf I, or absent and refused to tread the threshold of Rome afterwards, and by what consent the emperors admitted it, is shown not only by the crown sent by Gregory VII to Rudolf of Swabia, inscribed with this verse,

units.la: Petra dedit Petro, Petrus diadema Rodolpho; quasi scilicet & Christus potestatem constituendi & coronandi Imperatoris S. Petro eximiam fecerit, atque quod Papa hic facit, authoritate & Christi & S. Petri faciat,
units.tr: The rock gave to Peter, and Peter gave the diadem to Rudolf; as if, forsooth, Christ had granted to St Peter the outstanding power of appointing and crowning an emperor, and as if what the Pope does here, he does by the authority of both Christ and St Peter,

units.la: Divino proin & Apostolico jure fretus Imperatores conſtituat & coronet: ſed etiam ex acri contentione, quæ Fri‐ dericum I. Barbarossam inter & Adrianum IV. occasione neglectæ à Friderico Londoniensis Episcopi in ditione ejus spolitati injuriæ exarsit, abundè colligitur. Adrianus e‐nim Sigonio de Regno Italiæ lib. xÿ. narrante, missis ad Fridericum Cardinalibus, Rolando & Bernhardo, qui de neglecta injuria cum eodem expostularent, inter alia Friderico per literas exprobravit, quàm honorificè eum olim Romæ acceperit, atque ei beneficium hoc dederit, ut coronæ Imperialis insigne ei contulerit. Quibus lectis literis Imperator & Principes mirum in modum offensi, veritique fuerunt, ne id Papa significaret, quod quidam etiam dictitabant, Reges Germaniæ Imperium Pontifi‐ cum Romanorum beneficio obtinere (siquidem idem etiam paulò ante Innocentius II. in coronatione Lotharii pictura Lateranensi, ac versibus decantatis scilicet illis Rex venit ante fores, juransque prius urbis honores: Post homo fit Papæ, sumit quo dante coronam.
units.tr: relying therefore on divine and apostolic right to appoint and crown emperors; but it is also amply shown by the bitter dispute that flared up between Frederick I Barbarossa and Adrian IV, over an injury to the property of the Bishop of London in Frederick's territory, which Frederick had neglected. For Adrian, as Sigonius relates in De regno Italiae, book 19, sent the cardinals Roland and Bernard to Frederick to complain of the neglected injury. Among other things, he reproached Frederick in a letter for how honourably he had once received him at Rome, and for having conferred on him this benefit, that he had bestowed on him the insignia of the imperial crown. When these letters were read, the emperor and the princes were marvellously offended, and they feared that the Pope meant what some were also saying openly: that the kings of Germany held the empire by the benefice of the Roman pontiffs. (Indeed, Innocent II had expressed the same, quite unambiguously, a little earlier, in the painting at the Lateran for Lothar's coronation, and in the verses sung there: The king comes before the gates, first swearing to the honours of the city; afterwards he becomes the Pope's man, and takes the crown at his giving.)

units.la: haud ambiguè expresserit,) dolorem non continerunt, atque Imperium haudquaquam Pontificis beneficium esse, dixerunt. Sciscitatus Rolandus, cujus ergo tandem erit, si Pontificis non erit? adeò Othonem Comitem Palati‐ num astantem ira incendit, ut stricto eum gladio appeti‐ erit, mortémque ei intentaverit. Sed prohibuit Impera‐ rator, & Legatis Romam properè redire jussis, legatio‐ nem Pontificis, dimissis per omnem Germaniam literis, significavit, adjiciens, se solùm Deo & Principibus Im‐ perium acceptum referre, proinde eos orare, ne tanti Im‐ perii Majestatem, à majoribus eorum ingenti cum nominis gloria partam imminui sua negligentia paterentur. Pon‐ tifex reversis Legatis ad Episcopos Germaniæ scripsit, ut Imperatorem ad officium redigerent. Cùm verò Adrianus non eandem in Germaniæ Episcopis contra Fridericum, quæ contra Henricum fuerat, alacritatem persentisceret, eorundem consilio morem gesturus nonnihil vela sinuavit, & Imperatorem mitiori legatione demulcere statuit. Duobus igitur prudentioribus, & majoris consilii legatis missis, scripsit, nihil causæ fuisse cur prioribus ejus literis Cæsar commoveretur. Licet enim hoc, inquit, Beneficii nomen apud alios in alia significatione sumatur, tamen accipiendum fuit in eam, in quam nos accepimus, & quam à prima institutione videtur habere. Est enim ex (bono) & (facto) junctum, dicitúrque non feudum, sed bonum factum &c. nos autem ut ipse optimè intelligere potes bene adeò atque honorificè Imperialis dignitatis insigne capiti tuo imposuimus, ut bonum factum possit ab omnibus judicari.
units.tr: They could not contain their grief, and said that the empire was by no means a benefice of the Pope. When Roland asked, Whose then will it be, if it is not the Pope's? Otto, Count Palatine, who was standing by, was so inflamed with anger that he drew his sword, made for him and threatened him with death. But the emperor prevented it, and ordered the legates to return to Rome at once. He sent letters throughout Germany announcing the Pope's embassy, adding that he referred the empire he had received solely to God and the princes, and so he asked them to pray that they would not allow the majesty of so great an empire, won by their ancestors with great glory, to be diminished through their neglect. When the legates returned, the Pope wrote to the bishops of Germany that they should bring the emperor back to his duty. But since Adrian did not perceive the same eagerness among the German bishops against Frederick as there had been against Henry, he decided, following their counsel, to lower his sails somewhat and to soothe the emperor with a milder embassy. So he sent two wiser legates of greater judgement, and wrote that there was no reason why Caesar should be moved by his earlier letters. For although this word benefice, he said, is taken by others in another sense, nevertheless it had to be understood in the sense in which we took it, and which it seems to have from its first institution. For it is joined from (bonum) and (factum), and is called not a feudum but a bonum factum, etc. We, however, as you yourself can best understand, have placed the insignia of imperial dignity on your head so well and so honourably that it can be judged a good deed by all.

units.la: Atque etiam illa in aliam significationem detorta sunt: CONTULIMUS TIBI INSIGNE IMPERIALIS CORONÆ, quia hoc verbo (contulimus) nihil aliud intelleximus, quàm impositimus. Postularat verò Cæsar ut deleretur pictura, scriptura revocaretur. Cæterum in ista Papali scripturæ aliquantulum etiam à legatis emollitæ mitigatione acquiescere vel invitus debuit. Et quàm bona fide ita scripturam Papa mitigaverit, vel ipso Baronio fidejussore cognoscamus licet. Hadrianus, ita ille ad A. 1155. n. 6. scribit, prudentissimus, ut furentem conciliaret Imperatorem, ex commonitione Apostolica, dans locum irae, exemplo pariter Apostolico, cedens ad tempus, ita vocem Beneficium, est interpretatus, ut concitatam discordiam sopiret magis quàm augeret: non autem scriò, sed ad breve tempus ista subsistere potuerunt. Neque post mitigatam ita Scripturam Papa cessavit cum Cæsare litigare, & in ejusdem se possessionem intrudere. Neque unquam Adriano vivo inter eos convenit. Sed animosus ille Cardinalis Rolandus factus post Adriani mortem Pontifex, Alexandri nomine insignis, adeò Fridericum veteri sua Papalium excommunicationum machina, & rebellionibus exagitavit, ut post multa status & vitæ suæ discrimina cedere & veniam petere impulsus sit. Quo conditionibus interpositis, concessò, Rolando Venetiis occurrit, ibique ad pedum ejus osculum se inclinavit, eum à dextra recepit, & palafridum ascendenti strepam tenuit, uti Sigonius idem loquitur. Cætera historia Papatus pandit.
units.tr: Moreover, these words have also been twisted into another sense: WE HAVE CONFERRED ON YOU THE INSIGNIA OF THE IMPERIAL CROWN, because by this word (conferred) we understood nothing other than (placed). Caesar, however, demanded that the picture be erased and the writing recalled. In the end, however, he had to acquiesce, even unwillingly, in that Papal writing, somewhat softened by the mitigation the legates had secured. And how good faith the Pope had in so softening the writing we may learn even from Baronius, his own guarantor. Adrian, so he writes at the year 1155, n. 6, being most prudent, in order to placate the raging emperor, following an apostolic admonition, giving place to wrath, and likewise yielding for a time by apostolic example, interpreted the word Benefice in such a way as to quell the stirred-up discord rather than increase it. But these arrangements could not stand seriously, only for a short time. Nor, after the writing had been so softened, did the Pope cease to contend with Caesar and to thrust himself into possession of the same. Nor did Adrian ever come to an agreement with them while he lived. But that spirited cardinal Roland, made Pope after Adrian's death and known by the name Alexander, harassed Frederick so with his old machinery of Papal excommunications and rebellions that, after many dangers to his state and his life, he was driven to yield and to seek pardon. With conditions agreed, and the concession made, he met Roland at Venice, bowed down to kiss his foot, received him at his right hand, and held the stirrup for him as he mounted his palfrey, as Sigonius himself relates. The rest of the history of the Papacy unfolds.

units.la: LV. Palam verò væsanam ambitionem suam Ludovici Bavari Imperatoris jurati hostes Pontifices prodiderunt. Etenim Johannes xxiii. Aventino lib. vij. p. 760. teste, sic Bullam suam fulminantem in Ludovicum vibratam orditur: Posteaquam à decessoribus nostris res Romana à Græcis ad Romanos translata, Carolo Magno in fidem atque tutelam commissa est, summus ille honor Beneficium Pontificis Maximi esse solet. &c. Post Clemens VI. eidem formulam reconciliationis durissimam, & cum perpetua turpitudine conjunctam, præscripsit, nimirum, ut in solidum omnes errores & hæreses confiteatur: item resignet Imperium: nec resumat, nisi hoc fiat de gratia Papæ, & se ac filios suos, & bona & statum suum in manus & voluntatem Papæ ponat, & multa insolita faciat. Pudendam formulam cùm recepisset, sigillóque suo firmassset Imperator, Papa ei graviora, tanquam ex facili toleranti, imperans, petere non dubitavit, ut edicto perpetuo sanciat publicè, Imperium beneficium, hoc est seudum, esse Pontificis, nec ante quenquam Cæsarem esse aut vocari, quàm Papa author fieret, uti quidem Albertus Argentinensis in Chronico memorat. Hæc scilicet Helena illa est, quam nunquam non avidè Parides illi rasturiebant.
units.tr: LV. Openly, however, the sworn enemies of Emperor Louis of Bavaria revealed the Popes' frenzied ambition. For John XXII, as Aventinus testifies (book 7, p. 760), begins his thundering bull, hurled against Louis, thus: After our predecessors transferred the Roman state from the Greeks to the Romans, and entrusted it to the faith and protection of Charlemagne, that supreme honour is wont to be the benefice of the Supreme Pontiff. etc. Afterwards Clement VI prescribed to him a most harsh formula of reconciliation, joined with perpetual disgrace, namely: that he confess wholly all errors and heresies; likewise that he resign the empire, and not resume it unless this is done by the grace of the Pope; and that he place himself, his sons, his goods and his state in the hands and will of the Pope, and do many unusual things. When the emperor had received this shameful formula and confirmed it with his seal, the Pope, regarding him as easily tolerant and commanding him more severe things, did not hesitate to demand that he publicly sanction by a perpetual edict that the empire is a benefice, that is a fief, of the Pope, and that no one is or may be called Caesar before the Pope has approved him, as indeed Albert of Strasbourg records in his Chronicle. This, of course, is that Helen, whom those Parises never ceased to contend for greedily.

units.la: LVI. Recentior quippe Ferdinandi I. Imperatoris historia, eundem interiorem animi Papæ sensum pariter propalat. Eum Histor. Pap. Ss. clxxxi. Thuani, aliorúmque verbis retulimus. Carolo V. Imperio cedente, Electores communibus suffragiis Ferdinandum Imperatorem legerant, qui recens electus Martinum Germanum Romam ad Paulum IV. legatum expediit, tum cessionem Caroli, tum electionem suam Pontifici nuntiaturum. Ut verò Neronis potius quàm Petri successorem se Papa ostenderet, quemadmodum olim Tacito Annal. xv. 29. memorante, Tiridatem Parthorum Regem, oportuit apud effigiem Cæsaris insigne Regium ponere, nec nisi manu Neronis resumere: sic à Ferdinando ipse impudentissimè postulare ausus est, quandoquidem & cessio Caroli inconsulto Pontifice processerit, & electio Ferdinandi facta sit per Electores quosdam hæreticos, mitteret igitur Romam procuratorem, per quem prius acta poenitentia, cessioni fratris ab Electoribus approbatæ renuntiaret, rem omnem Pontificis arbitrio & gratiæ permitteret, qui electionem & inaugurationem quamvis rite non factam, ex plenitudine potestatis suæ confirmet. Carolum quippe apud neminem nisi Papam Cæsaream dignitatem ejerare, nec Ferdinandum eam citra suum, vicarii Christi, cui claves Cœlestis ac terreni Imperii creditæ sint consensum accipere potuisse. Ni jussa Ferdinandus fecerit, ratum sibi esse, alium pro lubitu Imperatorem constituere. Neque Philippi etiam Hispaniæ Regis precibus curatissimis moveri potuit, ut vel cessioni Caroli, vel electioni fratris album calculum adjiceret, claro indicio, eam constanter Pontificum animo infixam sententiam fuisse, quòd fasces suos Imperatores Pontificum arbitrio & gratiæ acceptos ferre in solidum teneantur.
units.tr: LVI. The more recent history of the Emperor Ferdinand I likewise reveals the same inner attitude of the Pope. We have related it in the words of Histor. Pap. Ss. clxxxi., of Thuanus, and of others. When Charles V resigned the Empire, the Electors had by common vote chosen Ferdinand as Emperor. Newly elected, Ferdinand sent Martin the German to Rome to Paul IV as envoy, to announce to the Pope both Charles's resignation and his own election. But so that the Pope might show himself the successor of Nero rather than of Peter, just as Tacitus (Annals xv. 29) tells that Tiridates, king of the Parthians, had to lay down the royal insignia before the statue of Caesar and take them up again only from Nero's hand, the Pope dared to demand of Ferdinand the most shameless thing. Since Charles's resignation had gone forward without the Pope's consent, and Ferdinand's election had been made by certain heretical Electors, Ferdinand should send a procurator to Rome. This man would first do penance, then renounce before the Pope his brother's resignation, which the Electors had approved, and would leave the whole matter to the Pope's judgment and grace. The Pope, from the fullness of his power, would then confirm the election and inauguration, though they had not been properly made. For Charles, he said, could receive the Caesarean dignity from no one but the Pope, and Ferdinand could not receive it without the consent of the Vicar of Christ, to whom the keys of heavenly and earthly empire had been entrusted. If Ferdinand did not comply, the Pope would consider it settled that he could appoint another Emperor at his pleasure. Nor could he be moved, even by the most earnest prayers of Philip, King of Spain, to add his white ballot either to Charles's resignation or to his brother's election. This is a clear sign that the Popes held firmly to the opinion that Emperors must take up their fasces wholly at the Pope's judgment and grace.

units.la: LVII. Sed & indicium animi Papalis haud postremum faciunt tria dogmata, quæ quibuslibet interdictis illi desensitant. Primum est, quòd authoritate & potestate Pontificia
units.tr: LVII. But three dogmas, which defend that feeling against any objections, are also no small indication of the papal mind. The first is that by papal authority and power the Empire was transferred from the Easterners to the Westerners, from the Greeks to the Franks.

units.la: Ddd tificia Imperium ab Orientalibus ad Occidentales, à Græcis ad Francos translatum sit. Hoc asserentem supra Johannem XXIII. adversus Ludovicum Bavarum vidimus. Atque amplius etiam liquet ex capite Per Venerabilem, de Electione & Electi potestate. Proin etiam laborem satis arduum insumpsit Bellarminus post reliqua controversiarum opera epusculo satis amplo, translationem hanc confirmandi, & ab objectionibus eam oppugnantium vindicandi. Interalia lib. j. cap. 6. etiam Romanorum Pontificum authoritate, facto & testimoniis eandem propugnat. Quidni igitur Papæ in electione Imperatoris potestas utramque paginam faciat, si ejus authoritate Imperium ipsum, quod illi pertendunt, constitutum est? Huc quoque facit, quod Adrianus III. lege lata sanxit, ut moriente Carolo Crasso sine liberis Imperium à Francis ad Italos
units.tr: tificia Imperium ab Orientalibus ad Occidentales, à Græcis ad Francos translatum sit. We have seen this asserted above by John XXIII against Ludwig of Bavaria. It is clearer still from the chapter Per Venerabilem, de Electione & Electi potestate. Hence Bellarmine, after his other controversial works, also took up the rather arduous labour of a fairly large little treatise confirming this transfer and defending it against the objections of those who oppose it. Among other things, in lib. j. cap. 6 he also supports it by the authority of the Roman Pontiffs, by deed and by testimonies. Why, then, should the Pope's power in the election of the Emperor not carry both pages, if the Empire itself, which they claim for themselves, was established by his authority? This also bears on the fact that Adrian III, by a law he enacted, decreed that if Charles the Fat died without heirs, the Empire should pass from the Franks to the Italians

units.la: quòd autbo ritate Papali Imperium ab Oriental ibus ad Occidentales translatum fit, Eleatorum Romani Imperii institutio Papam authorem beatum & vocatur Imperii administratio ad Papam redeat: transferretur, quæ licet successu caruerit, tumultibúsque noxiis ansam præbuerit, Papalis tamen ambitionis testis locuples est. Secundum est, quòd Electorum Imperatoris institutionem Pontifici referendam esse acceptam, Hieromonarchici strenuè asserunt. Quanquam sanctionem de Electoribus cui potissimùm Pontifici authori tribuant, ipsimet ancipites, & varias in partes distracti hærent. Gregorium V. authorem facit author libri de Regimine Principum, lib. iij. 19. nec non Augustinus Triumphus in Summ. de potest. Eccl. q. 35. art. 2. Gregorium X. Aventinus libr. v. Annal. Bajor. & Onuphrius lib. de comit. Imp. Denique Innocentium IV. in Synodo Lugdunensi legem illam rogâsse, Baronius ad Annum 996. num. 56. sciscit, Martini Poloni, qui sub Innocentio eo vixit, authoritate fretus. Quanquam verò argumentis certis, quæ post alios M. Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. libr. vj. cap. ÿ. s. 31. 32. &c. attulit, constat, nulli Pontificum dictorum, neque alii etiam authori constitutionem illam tribui posse, ipsa tamen authoritatis hujus usurpatio abundè probat, Pontificem eo animo esse, ut sibi de Imperatoris electione disponendi jus & arbitrium deberi putet. Quò etiam pertinet, quòd discordantibus in electione suffragiis, sui juris Papa arbitratus est, Electores & Electos ad causam Romæ dicendam vocare, & quem liberet, confirmare. Qua authoritate usos Gregorium VII. inter Henricum IV. & Rodolphum; Innocentium II. inter Conradum & Lotharium; Urbanum IV. inter Richardum & Alphonsum, legimus. Tertium est, quòd vacantis Imperii administrationem ad se pertinere Pontifices palam asseruerunt. Atque id jam ætate Petri Damiani circa A. MLV. florentis, receptum erat. Is enim Christum inducit Victorem II. Papam ὑγχεοτον sic alloquentem: Ego te quasi Patrem Imperatoris constitui. Imò sublato Rege de medio totius Romani Imperii vacantis tibi jura commisi. Proin etiam Innocentius III. cap. 10. de foro compet. licere ajebat Vercellensibus laicis ad sedem Apostolicam appellare super rebus, quæ forum seculare contingunt, eo maximè tempore, quo vacante Imperio ad judicem secularem recurrere integrum non esset. Exemplum inprimis illustre est Clemens V. qui Robertum Siciliæ Regem ab Henrico VII. Majestatis damnatum, defuncto Imperatore absolvit, tam (inquit) ex superioritate, quam ad Imperium non est dubium nos habere quam ex potestate, in qua vacante Imperio succedimus Imperatori, uti in Clement. Pastoral. de sent. & re judic. in Clement. habetur. Qui Clementi successit Johannes XXII. Genuenses à vicecomitibus Mediolanensibus oppugnatos in suam tutelam suscepit. Objicientibus eos esse arbitrii Cæsarei, non Pontificii respondit: Nullo dum certo Cæsare (nam Ludovicum respuebat) arbitrium rerum etiam profanarum penes se Sacro sanctæ potestatis jure esse. Quin & lege lata promulgavit, in persona sona Petri ad Summum Pontificem terreni simul & cœlestis Imperii vacantis jurisdictionem, regimen & dispositionem devolutam esse, prohibens insuper, ne quisquam jurisdictionis, etiamsi Patriarchalis aut Regalis effet, vicariatum, licet sibi ab Imperatore concessum, Imperio vacante, retineret, neve retinenti obediretur, nisi consensus & confirmatio summi Pontificis accessisset, quæ lex Extravag. unic. ne sede vacante, scripta reperitur.
units.tr: by papal authority the Empire was transferred from the Easterners to the Westerners. The institution of the electors of the Roman Empire makes the Pope its blessed author, and the administration of the Empire returns to the Pope. It would be transferred. Although this lacked success and gave occasion for harmful tumults, it is nonetheless ample witness to papal ambition. The second is that the Hierocratic writers vigorously assert that the institution of the electors of the Emperor must be credited to the Pope. Yet they themselves hesitate in doubt, pulled in different directions, as to which Pope they should chiefly name as author of the decree on the Electors. The author of the book De Regimine Principum, lib. iij. 19 makes Gregory V the author, as does Augustinus Triumphus in Summ. de potest. Eccl. q. 35 art. 2. Aventinus, libr. v. Annal. Bajor., and Onuphrius, lib. de comit. Imp., name Gregory X. Finally, Baronius, ad Annum 996, num. 56, knows that Innocent IV proposed that law at the Synod of Lyons, relying on the authority of Martin of Poland, who lived under that Innocent. Yet although it is established by certain arguments, which after others M. Antonius de Dominis brought forward in de Rep. Eccl. libr. vj. cap. ÿ. s. 31, 32 &c., that this constitution cannot be ascribed to any of the Popes named, nor to any other author, the very usurpation of this authority amply proves that the Pope is so disposed that he thinks the right and power of arranging the Emperor's election is owed to himself. To this also belongs the fact that when the votes in an election were divided, the Pope judged it within his own right to summon the Electors and the Elected to plead their case at Rome, and to confirm whomever he pleased. We read that Gregory VII used this authority between Henry IV and Rudolf, Innocent II between Conrad and Lothair, and Urban IV between Richard and Alphonso. The third is that the Popes have openly asserted that the administration of a vacant Empire pertains to them. This was already accepted in the age of Peter Damian, who flourished around 1055. For he introduces Christ speaking thus to Victor II, the Pope: I have appointed you as, so to speak, the Father of the Emperor. Indeed, with the king removed from the midst of the whole Roman Empire, I have committed to you the rights of the vacant Empire. Hence Innocent III also said, in cap. 10, de foro compet., that lay Vercellese may appeal to the Apostolic See concerning matters that touch the secular courts, especially at a time when, the Empire being vacant, it was not open to them to resort to a secular judge. A most notable example is Clement V, who, when Henry VII had been condemned for treason, absolved Robert, King of Sicily, after the Emperor's death, saying: as much from the superiority, as to the Empire, there is no doubt that we hold, than from the power by which, the Empire being vacant, we succeed the Emperor, as is found in Clement. Pastoral. de sent. & re judic. in Clement. He was succeeded by John XXII, who took the Genoese, who were attacked by the Visconti of Milan, under his protection. When they objected that the matter belonged to the judgment of the Caesar and not of the Pope, he replied: No certain Caesar being yet in place (for he rejected Ludwig), the judgment of even profane affairs lies with him by the right of sacred power.
