Indeed he even promulgated a law by which, in the person of Peter, the jurisdiction, government and disposition of the vacant heavenly and earthly Empire were devolved upon the Supreme Pontiff, forbidding moreover that anyone, even if of patriarchal or royal rank, should retain a vicariate of jurisdiction granted him by the Emperor while the Empire was vacant, and that anyone retaining it should not be obeyed unless the consent and confirmation of the Supreme Pontiff had been added. This law is found written in Extravag. unic. ne sede vacante.

units.la: LVIII. Præterea non sine Sacramento quodam Impe- ratores à Pontificibus coronam capessivisse, constat.
units.tr: LVIII. Moreover, it is established that emperors received the crown from the Popes not without a certain sacrament.

units.la: Quippe coronanti juramento se obstringere sic satis mature consueverunt. Lotharius enim, juxta versus in palatio Lateranensi scriptos: venit ante fores, jurans prius urbis honores, &c.
units.tr: For they had quite early become accustomed to bind themselves by oath to the one crowning them. Thus Lothair, according to the verses written in the Lateran palace: he came before the doors, swearing first to the honours of the city, etc.

units.la: Ante Lotharium quoque Carolus Calvus à Johanne VIII. coronatus est, sanctissimo prius juramento devinctus, quòd adversus inimicos Ecclesiæ, perpetuò Pontifici adfuturus sit. Hinc, ita Sigonius, titulus Imperatoris Augusti posthac sincerum Pontificis beneficium esse, annisque Imperii à Pontificia coronatione repeti coeperunt. In decretis quoque Dist. 36. can. Tibi domino, Juramentum Othonis M. Johanni XII. Pontifici præstitum ejusmodi legere est: Tibi Domino Johanni Papæ, ego Rex Otho promittere & jurare facio per Patrem & Filium, & Spiritum S. & per lignum hoc vivificæ crucis, & per has reliquias S. quòd si permittente Domino Romam veneto, Sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam, & te rectorem ipsius exaltabo secundum posse meum, m nunquam vitam aut membra, & ipsum honorem quem habes, mea voluntate, aut meo consilio, aut meo consensu, aut mea exhortatione per des, & in Romana urbe nullum placitum aut ordinationem faciam de omnibus, quæ ad te, aut ad Romanos pertinent sine tuo consilio: & & quidquid de terra S. Petri ad nostram potestatem per‐ venerit, tibi reddam; & cuicunque Italicum regnum commisero, jurare faciam illum, ut adjutor tibi sit ad defendendam terram S. Petri, secundum suum posse. Sic me Deus adjuvet, & hæc S. Euangelia. Genuina sit ea juramenti Orthonis formula, nec ne dubitatum equidem est: sed de eo quicquid fiat, extat Sacr. Cerem. S. R. E. lib. j. Tit. 5. p. 23. ejusmodi juramenti formula: Ego Rex Romanorum futurus Imperator promitto & juro me de cætero Protectorem & Procuratorem fore Summi Pontificis, in omnibus necessitatibus & utilitatibus suis, custodiendo & conservando possessiones, honores, jura &c. Quin & Gregorius VII. illud Pontificiæ tyrannidis monstrum, non tantum misso ad Guilhelmum I. Angliæ Regem Huberto, exegerat, ut sibi & successoribus suis fidelitatem fateret, ipso Baronio Annal. Tom. xj. ad A. 1079. num. 25. teste, sed etiam formam juramenti ab Imperatore præstandi ejusmodi lib. ix. registri post epist. 3. expressit: Ego ab hac hora & deinceps fidelis ero per rectam fidem B. Petro Apostolo ejusque vicario Papæ Gregorio & quodcunque ipse præceperit suis videlicet verbis, per veram obedientiam, sicut oportet Christianum, observabo: de ordinatione vero ecclesiarum, & de terris vel censu, quæ Constantinus Imperator vel Carolus S. Petro dederunt, & de omnibus Ecclesiis vel prædiis, quæ Apostolicæ sedi ab aliquibus viris vel mulieribus aliquo tempore sunt oblata, vel concessa, & in mea sunt vel fuerint potestate, ita conveniam cum Papa, ut periculum sacrilegii, & perditionem animæ meæ non incurram: & Deo Sanctoque Petro adjuvante Christo dignum honorem & utilitatem impendam. Sic Otho electus contra Philippum A. MCCI. sic Fridericus II. & MCCXIII. sic Rodolphus I. A. MCCLXXIX. MCCLXXIX. juravit. Sic ab Iunocentio III. Johannes Anglia Rex coactus juravit: Ego Johannes Rex Angliae fidelis ero Ecclesiae Romanae, ac Domino meo Innocentio Papae tertio; uti apud Knigthon de Eventibus Angliae lib. ij. p. 2420. legere est. Ab Henrico VII. juramentum fidelitatis exigere ausus est per legatos Clemens V. Avinionetum residens. Cumque id fortiter recusasset, praeterexens scilicet, Aventino narrante, contra morem Majorum, & libertatem religionis Christianae, ut Princeps Principum, orbisque terrarum Dominus Servo Servorum Sacramentum diceret; ratus quin etiam, quod res est, juramentum fidelitatis proprie ad feuda & vasallos pertinere, denique aegre adduci potuisset, ut juramentum a fidelitatis juramento diversum longe praestaret ejusmodi: Ego Henricus Romanorum Rex, annuente Domino futurus Imperator promitto, spondeo & polliceor, atque juro coram Deo, & B. Petro, me de caetero protectorem, procuratorem & defensorem fore Summi Pontificis, & hujus S. Romanae Ecclesiae, in omnibus necessitatibus & utilitatibus suis, custodiendo & conservando possessiones & honores ejus, quantum Divino suffultus adjutorio fuero secundum scire & posse meum, recta & pura fide; sic me Deus adjuvet, & Sancta haec Dei Euangelia; Clemens idem delusi hiantis corvi instar, & exulceratus totus, constitutionem edidit, qua sanxit, posthac omnino Pontifici ab Imperatore coronando juramentum fidelitatis praestandum esse. Tametsi igitur juramentum ab Imperatore coronando Pontifici praestitum, ex Imperatoris quidem sententia, non sit proprie fidelitatis, obsequii, seu hominii & vasallagii juramentum, & prout conceptis verbis Otho III. aliique, & superiori etiam seculo Carolus V. jurarunt, solum de Papa non laedendo, ejusque personam ac S. Christi Ecclesia protegenda, promissionem contineat, excepta forte promissione subjectionis debitæ in spiritualibus qualem etiam Rex Romanorum in Germania Archiepiscopo Moguntino verba præeunte, jurare solet: ex juramento tamen à Gregorio VII. præscripto, Constitutione, Clementis, aliorumque Pontificum præsumtione, Theologorum quin etiam Pontificiorum contentione acri abundè liquet, ita juramentum ab Imperatore coronando Papam exigere, ut juramentum subjectionis, fidelitatis & vasallagii animo complectatur, neque aliud planè intendat.
units.tr: Before Lothair, Charles the Bald was also crowned by John VIII, having first been bound by the most sacred oath that he would always stand by the Pope against the enemies of the Church. Hence, as Sigonius says, the title of Augustus became a sheer benefice of the Pope, and the years of the Empire began to be counted from the papal coronation. Also in the decrees, Dist. 36. can. Tibi domino, one may read the oath of Otho the Great sworn to Pope John XII in this form: To you, Lord John, Pope, I, King Otho, promise and cause to be sworn, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these holy relics, that if, with the Lord permitting, I come to Rome, I will exalt the holy Roman Church and you, its ruler, according to my power; I will never, by my will, counsel, consent or urging, bring about the loss of your life or limbs or of the honour you hold; in the city of Rome I will make no decree or ordinance concerning all matters that pertain to you or to the Romans without your counsel; and whatever comes into our power from the land of St Peter I will restore to you; and to whomever I commit the kingdom of Italy I will cause him to swear that he will help you defend the land of St Peter according to his power. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels. Whether this formula of Otho's oath is genuine or not is indeed doubted; but whatever the case, the Sacred Ceremonies of the Holy Roman Church, book 1, title 5, p. 23, contains a formula of this kind: I, who am to be Emperor and King of the Romans, promise and swear that henceforth I will be the protector and procurator of the Supreme Pontiff in all his needs and advantages, guarding and preserving his possessions, honours, rights, etc. Indeed Gregory VII, that monster of papal tyranny, not only, as Baronius testifies, Annal. Tom. xj. ad A. 1079. num. 25., required Hubert, sent to William I, King of England, to profess fealty to himself and his successors, but also drew up the form of oath to be taken by the emperor in lib. ix. registri post epist. 3.: From this hour onward I will be faithful to Blessed Peter the Apostle and to his vicar, Pope Gregory, and I will observe whatever he commands, by his own word, with true obedience, as becomes a Christian. Concerning the ordering of churches, and the lands or revenues which Constantine the Emperor or Charles gave to St Peter, and all churches or estates which have at any time been offered or granted to the Apostolic See by any men or women, and which are or shall be in my power, I will so agree with the Pope that I incur no danger of sacrilege or loss of my soul; and with God and St Peter helping, Christ, I will render due honour and service. In this form Otho, when elected against Philippus, in 1201, swore; so did Frederick II in 1213, and Rudolf I in 1279; 1279. In the same way John, King of England, was compelled by Innocent III to swear: I, John, King of England, will be faithful to the Roman Church and to my lord Innocent the Third, Pope; as one may read in Knighton, de Eventibus Angliae lib. ij. p. 2420. Clement V, residing at Avignon, dared to demand an oath of fealty from Henry VII through legates. When he stoutly refused, since Clement, as Aventinus reports, was offended that contrary to the custom of our ancestors and the liberty of the Christian religion, the Prince of princes and Lord of the world should be called Servant of the Servants, and since he thought, as is indeed the case, that an oath of fealty properly pertains to fiefs and vassals, and was at last barely brought to accept an oath of a different kind, he took this: I, Henry, King of the Romans, by God's permission to be Emperor, promise, pledge and swear before God and Blessed Peter that henceforth I will be protector, procurator and defender of the Supreme Pontiff and of this holy Roman Church in all its needs and advantages, guarding and preserving its possessions and honours, as far as I am supported by Divine aid, according to my knowledge and power, with a right and sincere faith; so may God help me, and these holy Gospels of God. Clement, like a raven duped and wholly enraged, issued a constitution by which he decreed that henceforth an oath of fealty must absolutely be given to the Pope by the emperor who is to be crowned. Therefore, although the oath which the emperor to be crowned makes to the Pope is, in the emperor's view, not strictly an oath of fealty, obedience, or homage and vassalage, and, as Otho III and others, and in the last century Charles V, swore in set words, contains only a promise not to harm the Pope and to protect his person and the Church of Christ, perhaps excepting the promise of due subjection in spiritual matters, which the King of the Romans in Germany is accustomed to swear, the words being spoken first by the Archbishop of Mainz; yet from the oath prescribed by Gregory VII, the constitution of Clement, and the assumption of other Popes, and indeed from the bitter contention of the Papists' own theologians, it is abundantly clear that the Pope demands an oath from the emperor to be crowned in such a way that it embraces the spirit of subjection, fealty and vassalage, and intends nothing else at all.

units.la: LIX. De Imperatoris coronatione, confirmatione, juramento, quibus eum sui juris & beneficii, hominem faciere Pontifices contendunt, hactenus. De Regibus similia plura dici possent: Constat equidem, Reges Galliæ primos ferè à Papa coronari accepisse, Clodoveo Romam mittente coronam auream, quæ Regnum dicta est. Unde Pipinum Stephanus II. alios Reges Pontifices alii, sacrarunt. Idemque in Coronatione Regum, quod in Imperatoris coronatione, à Papa attentatum satis constat.
units.tr: LIX. Concerning the coronation, confirmation and oath of the emperor, by which the Popes contend that they make him subject to their right and benefice, a man of their own, so far. Similar things could be said about kings. It is indeed established that the kings of France were almost first to receive the crown from the Pope, Clovis having been sent a golden crown from Rome, which was called the Kingdom. Hence Stephen II anointed Pepin, and other Popes consecrated other kings. And it is quite clear that in the coronation of kings the same encroachment was attempted by the Pope as in the coronation of the emperor.

units.la: Cum enim Philippus I. coronandus esset Legati Papæ diserte asseruerunt, quòd sine Papæ nutu coronari Rex neutiquam posset; Hormisdæ Papæ, Remigio Rhemensi consecrandi Regis potestarem concedentis, & Victorem confirmantis, authoritatem allegantes, uti quidem Johannes Filius, & ex eò Vignierus Bibliotheca historica par. II, ad A. 1060. fusè commemorant. Jactatur inde à Pontificiis partibus ejusdem D. Remigii testamentum, quo Episcopis fas sit Regem impium & tyrannum non officii duntaxat monere, sed diræ ejusmodi sententiâ percellere: Fiant ejus dies pauci, & principatum ejus accipiat alter. Si fidem merentur, quæ Baronius ad A. 859. narrat, sic Carolus Calvus in Concilio Tulensi oravit: Se, qui electus esset cum voluntate & consensu Episcoporum ac cæterorum
units.tr: For when Philip I was to be crowned, the legates of the Pope plainly asserted that a king could by no means be crowned without the Pope's nod, appealing to the authority of Pope Hormisdas, who granted to Remigius of Reims the power of consecrating a king, and of Victor, who confirmed it; as indeed John Filius, and after him Vignier in his Bibliotheca historica, part II, ad A. 1060, relate at length. From this the Papists' party boasts of the testament of the same St Remigius, by which bishops may rightly admonish an impious and tyrannical king not only as a matter of duty, but may also strike him with a curse of this kind: Let his days be few, and let another take his principality. If the reports which Baronius gives ad A. 859 deserve credit, then Charles the Bald, at the Council of Toul, pleaded thus: that he, who had been elected with the will and consent of the bishops and the other faithful of the kingdom, and then acclaimed king and consecrated, anointed with chrism, and raised up on the throne of the kingdom, ought not to be cast down from the lofty station of the realm by anyone without a hearing and a judgment.

units.la: {a} Regnum etiam constitutionem & coronationem ad Pontificem traxerunt, ut coronandum sibi subjicerent. rorum Regni fidelium acclamatione, deinde in Regem consecratus, chrismate perunctus, & in Regni solio sublimatus, non debuisse de Regni sublimitate à quoquam projici, sine audientia & judicio Episcoporum, quorum ministerio in Regem esset consecratus, & qui throni sunt dicti, & per quos Deus sua decernit judicia: Quorum, inquit, paternis correptionibus, & castigatoriis judiciis me subdere sum paratus. Tentasse quin etiam in Henrici IV. Coronatione in arcano Papam, an vellet coronam ad pedes Pontificis deponere, ac signo isthoc Regnum Franciæ in manus ejus consignare, atque tentationi illi acriter procuratores Regios restitisse, Thuanus Annal. lib. CXIII. narrat. Majora etiam in Reges alios Pontifices ausi sunt. Hungariæ Rex D. Stephanus, Hungaria circa A. CMLXXXIV. ad fidem Christi conversa, ad Benedictum Papam Anastasium Episcopum Calacensem misit, cum his verbis, quæ Bonifacius recensét: Ut quando omnis potestas à Deo est, & maxima cæpta sine ope Divina confirmari nequeunt, Regalia insignia cum Pontificia benedictione piis precibus ab eo consequeretur. Unde Hungariæ Regnum sibi beneficiarium redditam esse, Pontifices pertendunt; Et Gregorius VII. lib. ij. Ep. 13.63.70. iv. 25. admoneri nuper electum Regem diserte jussit, ut per legatos suos obedientiam & reverentiam suam erga sedem Apostolicam exhibeat, increpans non parum Solomonem Regem, quod à Rege Teutonicorum suum Regnum in beneficium suscepisset, comminans etiam, non passurum se diutius eum regnare, nisi correctio errore Apostolicæ, non Regiæ Majestatis beneficium id recognoscut. Hinc adeo etiam Bonifacium VIII. Hungaris ipsdem invitis Catolum Regem obtrusisse, Bonifinius idem Decad. ij. lib. ix. narrat. Commemorare pluribus possem, Gregorium VII. Regna Russiæ, Dalmatiæ, Hispaniæ, Arogoniæ juri S. Petri mancipasse: Portugalliam eodem jure censere Pontifices, ex quo tempore Alphonsus Henriquius Rex à suis ob partam adversus Mauros victoriam proclamatus est, atque eam proclamationem Papa, tributo impositio, ratam habuit: Navarræ Regnum obnoxium censeri Papæ, ex quo Eunicus Arista à Pontifice unctus & coronatus meruit, ut primus Regis titulo donaretur, & post eum reliqui omnes, ut Vasæus in Catalogo Regum Navarræ refert: Polonis Regium titulum Papam impertitum esse & abstulisse diu, quòd à Pontifice sacrari se non paterentur, non ausi diu titulum sine nutu & consensu Papæ recipere, uti Cromerus lib. iv. ad A. 1080. & lib. v. fuse recensent: Venetos Ducis titulum à Deodato Pontifice acceptum referre P. Justiniano lib. vj. de rebus Venetis, teste: Bohemis Regis nomen & titulum Innocentium III. indulsisse: Armeniæ Regnum Honorium III. Johanni Hierosolymitano Regi confirmasse: Norwegiæ Principi Hacconi Regium titulum Innocentii IV. Legatos in Norwegiam misisse contulisse. Hetruriæ Ducem Cosmum Ducem Magnum Pium V. creasse fretum, uti Thuanus lib. xliv. ad A. 1569. scribit, exemplis Alexandri III. Innocentii III. & Honorii III. qui Portugalliæ, Walachiæ, Bulgariæ, & Hiberniæ Reges olim creassent: Angliæ & Hiberniæ Regna tributaria Papæ facta esse sub Johanne Rege inprimis, qui Innocentio III. Regna illa pro satisfactione peccatorum suorum subjecit, stipulatus censum annuum mille librarum, famosa non formosa subjectione, uti Matthæus Paris loquitur, unde Paulus IV. Elisabethæ Angliæ Reginæ interdixit Regno, eò quòd se insciò & inconsulto illud occupasset: Scotiam juris & beneficii Papalis censeri penitus; Bonifacio VIII. interdicente quondam Edvardo Anglorum Regi, ne Scotos bello vexaret amplius, eò quòd Regnum illud in Pontificis R. fidem & authoritatem ab ipsis Scotis Divino proin & Apostolico jure fretus Imperatores constituat & coronet: sed etiam ex acri contentione, quæ Fridericum I. Barbarossam inter & Adrianum IV. occasione neglectæ à Friderico Londoniensis Episcopi in ditione ejus spolitati injuriæ exarsit, abundè colligitur. Adrianus enim Sigonio de Regno Italiæ lib. xij. narrante, misit ad Fridericum Cardinalibus, Rolando & Bernhardo, qui de neglecta injuria cum eodem expostularent, inter alia Friderico per literas exprobravit, quàm honorificè eum olim Romæ acceperit, atque ei beneficium hoc dederit, ut coronæ Imperialis insigne ei contulerit. Quibus lectis literis Imperator & Principes mirum in modum offensi, veritíque fuerunt, ne id Papa significaret, quod quidam etiam dictitabant, Reges Germaniæ Imperium Pontificum Romanorum beneficio obtinere (siquidem idem etiam paulò ante Innocentius II. in coronatione Lotharii pictura Lateranensi, ac versibus decantatis scilicet illis
units.tr: The Pontiffs also drew the kingdom's constitution and coronation to themselves, so that they might make the one to be crowned subject to them. By the acclamation of the faithful of the realm, then consecrated as king, anointed with chrism and raised to the throne of the kingdom, he ought not to be cast down from the height of the kingdom by anyone without a hearing and judgment of the bishops, by whose ministry he had been consecrated king, and who are called thrones, and through whom God decrees his judgments. To their paternal corrections and chastising judgments, he said, I am ready to submit myself. Thuanus, Annal. lib. CXIII., relates that at the coronation of Henry IV they even tried, in secret, to ask the Pope whether he would lay the crown at the Pontiff's feet and by that sign deliver the kingdom of France into his hands, and that the royal procurators strongly resisted that attempt. They have dared still greater things against other kings. King Stephen of Hungary, when Hungary was converted to the faith of Christ about A. 1084, sent Anastasius, bishop of Calocsa, to Pope Benedict, with these words, which Boniface recounts: Since all power is from God, and the greatest undertakings cannot be confirmed without divine help, that he might obtain the royal insignia from him with the pontifical blessing, through pious prayers. Hence the Pontiffs contend that the kingdom of Hungary was rendered to them as a benefice. And Gregory VII, lib. ii. Ep. 13, 63, 70; iv. 25, plainly ordered the newly elected king to be admonished to show his obedience and reverence towards the Apostolic See through his legates, rebuking King Solomon not a little because he had received his kingdom as a benefice from the King of the Germans, and threatening that he would not suffer him to reign any longer, unless he acknowledged that benefit as coming from the Apostolic, not the royal, majesty. Hence Boniface VIII, Bonfinius relates in the same place, Decad. ii. lib. ix., forced King Charles upon the Hungarians against their will. I could mention many more: Gregory VII handed over the kingdoms of Russia, Dalmatia, Spain, Aragon to the right of St Peter; the Pontiffs judge Portugal subject to the same right, from the time when Alphonsus Henriques, the king, was proclaimed by his people after the victory won over the Moors, and the Pope, by imposing a tribute, ratified that proclamation; Navarre is judged subject to the Pope, since Eunicus Arista, anointed and crowned by the Pontiff, earned the right to be first given the royal title, and all the rest after him, as Vasaeus relates in his Catalogue of the Kings of Navarre; Poland was granted the royal title by the Pope, and for a long time he withheld it, since they would not allow themselves to be consecrated by the Pontiff, and did not dare for long to take the title without the Pope's nod and consent, as Cromer relates at length, lib. iv. ad A. 1080, and lib. v.; the ducal title of the Venetians is said, on the testimony of P. Justinian, lib. vi. de rebus Venetis, to have been received from the Pope Deodatus; Innocent III granted the name and title of king to Bohemia; Honorius III confirmed the kingdom of Armenia to John, king of Jerusalem; Innocent IV conferred the royal title on Prince Haakon of Norway and sent legates into Norway; Pius V, trusting the examples of Alexander III, Innocent III and Honorius III, who had earlier made kings of Portugal, Wallachia, Bulgaria and Ireland, created Cosimo Grand Duke of Etruria, as Thuanus writes, lib. xliv., at A. 1569; the kingdoms of England and Ireland were made tributary to the Papacy, especially under King John, who subjected those kingdoms to Innocent III in satisfaction for his sins, stipulating an annual census of a thousand pounds, a infamous, not a beautiful, subjection, as Matthew Paris puts it; whence Paul IV forbade Queen Elizabeth of England the realm, because she had seized it without his knowledge and consent. Scotland is judged wholly subject to the right and benefice of the Papacy: Boniface VIII forbade the former King Edward of the English to harass the Scots with war any longer, because that kingdom was held of the Pontiff's faith and authority, and by divine and apostolic right he appoints and crowns emperors. But the bitter quarrel which flared up between Frederick I Barbarossa and Adrian IV, over the injury done to the Bishop of London, whose property was plundered in Frederick's domain, and which Frederick neglected, also makes this abundantly clear. For Adrian, as Sigonius, de Regno Italiae, lib. xii., relates, sent the cardinals Roland and Bernard to Frederick, to complain about the neglected injury, and among other things he reproached Frederick in a letter for how honourably he had once received him at Rome and given him this benefice, that he had conferred on him the insignia of the imperial crown. The Reges Germaniae hold the Empire by the benefice of the Roman Pontiffs (since the same Innocent II had also, a little earlier, expressed this unambiguously in the painting at the Lateran at the coronation of Lothair, and in the verses sung there, namely these

units.la: Rex venit ante fores, jurans prius urbis honores:
units.tr: The king comes before the gates, first swearing the honours of the city:

units.la: Post homo fit Papæ, sumit quo dante coronam.
units.tr: Afterwards he becomes the Pope's man, and takes the crown at his giving.

units.la: haud ambiguè expresserit,) dolorem non continerunt, atque Imperium haudquaquam Pontificis beneficium esse, dixerunt. Scisçitatus Rolandus, cujus ergo tandem erit, si Pontificis non erit? adeò Othonem Comitem Palatinum astantem ira incendit, ut stricto eum gladio appeterit, mortémque ei intentaverit. Sed prohibuit Imperator, & Legatis Romam properè redire jussis, legationem Pontificis, dimissis per omnem Germaniam literis, significavit, adjiciens, se solùm Deo & Principibus Imperium acceptum referre, proinde eos orare, ne tanti Imperii Majestatem, à majoribus eorum ingenti cum nominis gloria partam imminui sua negligentia paterentur. Pontifex reversis Legatis ad Episcopos Germaniæ scripsit, ut Imperatorem ad officium redigerent. Cùm verò Adrianus non eandem in Germaniæ Episcopis contra Fridericum, quæ contra Henricum fuerat, alacritatem perspentisceret, eorundem consilio morem gesturus nonnihil vela sinuavit, & Imperatorem mitiori legatione demulcere statuit. Duobus igitur prudentioribus, & majoris consilii legatis missis, scripsit, nihil causæ fuisse cur prioribus ejus literis Cæsar commoveretur. Licet enim hoc, inquit, Beneficii nomen apud alios in alia significatione sumatur, tamen accipiendum fuit in eam, in quam nos accepimus, & quam à prima institutione videtur habere. Est enim ex (bono) & (facto) junctum, dicitúrque non feudum, sed bonum factum &c. nos autem ut ipse optimè intelligere potes bene adeò atque honorificè Imperialis dignitatis insigne capiti tuo imposuimus, ut bonum factum possit ab omnibus judicari. Atque etiam illa in aliam significationem detorta sunt: CONTULIMUS TIBI INSIGNE IMPERIALIS CORONÆ, quia hoc verbo (contulimus) nihil aliud intelleximus, quàm imposuimus. Postularat verò Cæsar ut deleretur pittura, scriptura revocaretur. Cæterùm in ista Papali scripturæ aliquantulum etiam à legatis emollitæ mitigatione acquiescere vel invitus debuit. Et quàm bona fide ita scripturam Papa mitigaverit, vel ipso Baronio fidejussore cognoscamus licet. Hadrianus, ita ille ad A. 1155. n. 6. scribit, prudentissimus, ut furentem conciliaret Imperatorem, ex commonitione Apostolica, dans locum irae, exemplo pariter Apostolico, cedens ad tempus, ita vocem Beneficium, est interpretatus, ut concitatam discordiam sopiret magis quàm augeret: non autem scriò, sed ad breve tempus ista subsistere potuerunt. Neque post mitigatam ita Scripturam Papa cessavit cum Cæsare litigare, & in ejusdem se possessionem intrudere. Neque unquam Adriano vivo inter eos convenit. Sed animosus ille Cardinalis Rolandus factus post Adriani mortem Pontifex, Alexandri nomine insignis, adeò Fridericum veteri sua Papalium excommunicationum machina, & rebellionibus exagitavit, ut post multa statūs & vitæ suæ discrimina cedere & veniam petere impulsus sit. Quo conditionibus interpositis, concesso, Rolando Venetiis occurrit, ibique ad pedum ejus osculum se inclinavit, eum à dextra recepit, & palafridum ascendenti strepam tenuit, uti Sigonius idem loquitur. Cætera historia Papatus pandit.
units.tr: haud ambiguè expresserit,) they could not contain their grief, and said that the Empire was by no means a benefice of the Pontiff. Roland was asked: then whose will it be, if it is not the Pontiff's? At this, Otto, the Count Palatine standing by, was so inflamed with anger that he drew his sword, lunged at him, and threatened his life. But the Emperor forbade it, ordered the legates to hurry back to Rome, and by letters sent through all Germany he made known the Pontiff's embassy, adding that he held the Empire received from God and the princes alone, and so he begged them not to suffer the majesty of so great an Empire, won by their ancestors with great glory to their name, to be diminished through their negligence. The Pope, when the legates returned, wrote to the bishops of Germany that they should bring the Emperor back to his duty. But when Adrian perceived that the bishops of Germany were not as eager against Frederick as they had been against Henry, he, to comply with their advice, lowered his sails somewhat and resolved to soothe the Emperor with a milder embassy. So, sending two wiser legates of greater judgment, he wrote that there was no cause for the Emperor to be moved by his earlier letters. For although this word benefice is taken by others in another sense, nevertheless it ought to be understood in that sense in which we have taken it, and which it seems to have from its first institution. For it is joined from (bonum) and (factum), and is called not a fief but a good deed, etc. But we, as you yourself can best understand, have placed the insignia of the imperial dignity upon your head so well and so honourably that it may be judged a good deed by all. And even those words were twisted to another meaning: WE HAVE CONFERRED ON YOU THE INSIGNIA OF THE IMPERIAL CROWN, because by this word (conferred) we understood nothing other than (placed). But the Caesar demanded that the painting be erased and the inscription recalled. Yet in regard to that papal writing, somewhat softened by the mitigation of the legates, he had to acquiesce, even unwillingly. And how much good faith the Pope showed in thus softening the writing, we may learn even from Baronius as guarantor. Adrian, so he writes, at the year 1155, n. 6, being most prudent, in order to win over the raging Emperor, following Apostolic admonition, giving place to wrath, and likewise following an Apostolic example, yielding for a time, interpreted the word Benefice in such a way as to calm the stirred-up discord rather than increase it; but these measures could hold only for a short time, not in earnest. Nor, after the writing had been softened in this way, did the Pope cease to contend with the Caesar and to thrust himself into possession of the same. Nor did they ever agree between them while Adrian lived. But that spirited cardinal Roland, made Pope after Adrian's death and distinguished by the name Alexander, so harassed Frederick with his old machinery of Papal excommunications and rebellions that after many perils to his state and life he was driven to yield and beg pardon. When conditions had been agreed and the pardon granted, he met Roland at Venice, bowed down to kiss his feet, received him on his right, and held the stirrup for him as he mounted his palfrey, as Sigonius himself says. The rest of the history of the Papacy unfolds it.

units.la: LV. Palam verò væsanam ambitionem suam Ludovici Bavari Imperatoris jurati hostes Pontifices prodiderunt. Etenim Johannes xxiii. Aventino lib. vi. p. 760. teste, sic Bullam suam fulminantem in Ludovicum vibratam orditur: Posteaquam à decessoribus nostris res Romana à Græcis ad Romanos translata, Carolo Magno in fidem atque tutelam commissa est, summus ille honor Beneficium Pontificis Maximi esse solet. &c. Post Clemens VI. eidem formulam reconciliationis durissimam, & cum perpetua turpitudine conjunctam, præscripsit, nimirum, ut in solidum omnes errores & hæreses confiteatur: item resignet Imperium: nec resumat, nisi hoc fiat de gratia Papæ, & se ac filios suos, & bona & statum suum in manus & voluntatem Papæ ponat, & multa insolita faciat. Pudendam formulam cùm recepisset, sigillóque suo firmasset Imperator, Papa ei graviora, tanquam ex facili toleranti, imperans, petere non dubitavit, ut edicto perpetuo sanciat publicè, Imperium beneficium, hoc est seudum, esse Pontificis, nec ante quenquam Cæsarem esse aut vocari, quàm Papa author fieret, uti quidem Albertus Argentinensis in Chronico memorat. Hæc scilicet Helena illa est, quam nunquam non avidè Parides illi rasturiebant.
units.tr: LV. Indeed, the Popes who were sworn enemies of the Emperor Ludwig of Bavaria openly revealed their mad ambition. For John XXIII, as Aventinus testifies (book 6, p. 760), opens his thundering bull hurled against Ludwig in these words: After the Roman affair was transferred by our predecessors from the Greeks to the Romans, and entrusted to Charlemagne for faith and protection, that highest honour is usually a benefice of the Supreme Pontiff. &c. Afterwards Clement VI prescribed for him a most harsh formula of reconciliation, joined with lasting disgrace, namely: that he confess all errors and heresies in full; likewise that he resign the Empire, and not resume it unless this is done by the grace of the Pope; and that he place himself, his sons, his goods and his state in the hands and will of the Pope, and do many unusual things. When the Emperor had accepted this shameful formula and confirmed it with his seal, the Pope, commanding harsher terms as from one who could easily be made to tolerate them, did not hesitate to demand that he publicly sanction by a perpetual edict that the Empire is a benefice, that is a fief, of the Pontiff, and that no one is Caesar or is called so before the Pope has approved him, as Albert of Strasbourg indeed records in his Chronicle. This, to be sure, is that Helen whom the Paris-like suitors of the Papacy never ceased eagerly to court.

units.la: LVI. Recentior quippe Ferdinandi I. Imperatoris historia, eundem interiorem animi Papæ sensum pariter propalat. Eum Histor. Pap. Ss. CLXXXI. Thuani, aliorúmque verbis retulimus. Carolo V. Imperio cedente, Electores communibus suffragiis Ferdinandum Imperatorem legerant, qui recens electus Martinum Germanum Romam ad Paulum IV. legatum expediit, tum cessionem Caroli, tum electionem suam Pontifici nuntiaturum. Ut verò Neronis potius quàm Petri successorem se Papa ostenderet; quemadmodum olim Tacito Annal. xv. 29. memorante, Tiridatem Parthorum Regem, oportuit apud effigiem Cæsaris insigne Regium ponere, nec nisi manu Neronis resumere: sic à Ferdinando ipse impudentissimè postulare ausus est, quandoquidem & cessio Caroli inconsulto Pontifice processerit, & electio Ferdinandi facta sit per Electores quosdam hæreticos, mitteret igitur Romam procuratorem, per quem prius acta poenitentia, cessioni fratris ab Electoribus approbatæ renuntiaret, rem omnem Pontificis arbitrio & gratiæ permitteret, qui electionem & inaugurationem quamvis ritè non factam, ex plenitudine potestatis suæ confirmet. Carolum quippe apud neminem nisi Papam Cæsaream dignitatem ejerare, nec Ferdinandum eam citra suum, vicarii Christi, cui claves Cœlestis ac terreni Imperii creditæ sint consensum accipere potuisse. Ni jussa Ferdinandus fecerit, ratum sibi esse, alium pro lubitu Imperatorem constituere. Neque Philippi etiam Hispaniæ Regis precibus curatissimis moveri potuit, ut vel cessioni Caroli, vel electioni fratris album calculum adjiceret, claro indicio, eam constanter Pontificum animo infixam sententiam fuisse, quòd fasces suos Imperatores Pontificum arbitrio & gratiæ acceptos ferre in solidum teneantur.
units.tr: LVI. The more recent history of the Emperor Ferdinand I likewise reveals the same inner mind of the Pope. We have related it in the words of Thuanus and others, Histor. Pap. Ss. CLXXXI. When Charles V ceded the Empire, the Electors by common vote had chosen Ferdinand as Emperor. Newly elected, Ferdinand sent Martin the German to Rome to Paul IV as legate, to announce to the Pope both Charles's cession and his own election. But the Pope wished to show himself the successor of Nero rather than of Peter. As Tacitus once related (Annals xv. 29), Tiridates, king of the Parthians, had to lay down the royal insignia before the statue of Caesar, and could take it up again only from Nero's hand. In the same way the Pope dared to demand most shamelessly of Ferdinand that, since Charles's cession had gone forward without the Pope's consent, and Ferdinand's election had been made by certain heretical Electors, he should send a procurator to Rome. Through this man he would first perform penance, then renounce the cession approved by the Electors, and leave the whole matter to the Pope's judgment and grace. The Pope would then confirm the election and inauguration from the fullness of his power, even though they had not been lawfully made. For Charles could receive the Caesarean dignity from no one but the Pope, and Ferdinand could not receive it without the consent of the Vicar of Christ, to whom the keys of the heavenly and earthly empire had been entrusted. If Ferdinand did not obey, he would be told that the Pope would appoint another Emperor at his pleasure. Nor could Ferdinand be moved by the most earnest prayers of Philip, King of Spain, to add his white ballot either to Charles's cession or to his brother's election. This is clear evidence that the Popes' firm conviction was that Emperors, who receive their fasces, are bound to hold them wholly by the Pope's judgment and grace.

units.la: LVII. Sed & indicium animi Papalis haud postremum faciunt tria dogmata, quæ quibuslibet interdictis illi defensitant. Primum est, quòd authoritate & potestate Pontificia
units.tr: LVII. But three doctrines, which they defend against all objections, also provide no small indication of the papal mind. The first is that by the authority and power of the Pope

units.la: Ddd tificia Imperium ab Orientalibus ad Occidentales, à Græcis ad Francos translatum sit. Hoc asserentem supra Johannem XXIII. adversus Ludovicum Bavarum vidimus. Atque amplius etiam liquet ex capite Per Venerabilem, de Electione & Electi potestate. Proin etiam laborem satis arduum insumpsit Bellarminus post reliqua controversiarum opera opusculo satis amplo, translationem hanc confirmandi, & ab objectionibus eam oppugnantium vindicandi. Inter alia lib. j. cap. 6. etiam Romanorum Pontuficum authoritate, facto & testimoniis eandem propugnat. Quodni igitur Papæ in electione Imperatoris potestas utramque paginam faciat, si ejus authoritate Imperium ipsum, quod illi pertendunt, constitutum est? Huc quoque facit, quod Adrianus III. lege lata sanxit, ut moriente Carolo Crasso sine liberis Imperium à Francis ad Italos transferretur, quæ licet successu caruerit, tumultibusque noxiis ansam præbuerit, Papalis tamen ambitionis testis locuples est. Secundum est, quòd Electorum Imperatoris institutionem Pontifici referendam esse acceptam, Hieromonarchici strenuè asserunt. Quanquam sanctionem de Electoribus cui potissimùm Pontifici authori tribuant, ipsimet ancipites, & varias in partes distracti hærent. Gregorium V. authorem facit author libri de Regimine Principum, lib. iij. 19. nec non Augustinus Triumphus in Summ. de potest. Eccl. q. 35. art. 2. Gregorium X. Aventinus libr. v. Annal. Bajor. & Onuphrius lib. de comit. Imp. Denique Innocentium IV. in Synodo Lugdunensi legem illam rogâsse, Baronius ad Annum 996. num. 56. scripsit, Martini Poloni, qui sub Innocentio eo vixit, authoritate fretus. Quanquam verò argumentis certis, quæ post alios M. Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. libr. vj. cap. ÿ. ß. 31. 32. &c. attulit, constat, nulli Pontificum dictorum, neque alii etiam authori constitutionem illam tribui posse, ipsa tamen authoritatis hujus usurpatio abundè probat, Pontificem eo animo esse, ut sibi de Imperatoris electione disponendi jus & arbitrium deberi putet. Quò etiam pertinet, quòd discordantibus in electione suffragiis, sui juris Papa arbitratus est, Electores & Electos ad causam Romæ dicendam vocare, & quem liberet, confirmare. Qua authoritate usos Gregorium VII. inter Henricum IV. & Rodolphum; Innocentium II. inter Conradum & Lotharium; Urbanum IV. inter Richardum & Alphonsum, legimus. Tertium est, quòd vacantis Imperii administrationem ad se pertinere Pontifices palam asseruerunt. Atque id jam ætate Petri Damiani circa A. MLV. florentis, receptum erat. Is enim Christum inducit Victorem II. Papam σύγχρονον sic alloquentem: Ego te quasi Patrem Imperatoris constitui. Imò sublato Rege de medio totius Romani Imperii vacantis tibi jura commisi. Proin etiam Innocentius III. cap. 10. de foro compet. licere ajebat Vercellensibus laicis ad sedem Apostolicam appellare super rebus, quæ forum seculare contingunt, eo maximè tempore, quo vacante Imperio ad judicem secularem recurrere integrum non esset. Exemplum inprimis illustre est Clemens V. qui Robertum Siciliæ Regem ab Henrico VII. Majestatis damnatum, defuncto Imperatore absolvit, tam (inquit) ex superioritate, quam ad Imperium non est dubium nos habere quam ex potestate, in qua vacante Imperio succedimus Imperatori, uti in Clement. Pastoral. de sent. & re judic. in Clement. habetur. Qui Clementi successit Johannes XXII. Genuenses à vicecomitibus Mediolanensibus oppugnatos in suam tutelam suscepit. Objicientibus eos esse arbitrii Cæsarei, non Pontificii respondit: Nullo dum certo Cæsare (nam Ludovicum respuebat) arbitrium rerum etiam profanarum penes se Sacro sanctæ potestatis jure esse. Quin & lege lata promulgavit, in persona sona Petri ad Summum Pontificem terreni simul & cœlestis Imperii vacantis jurisdictionem, regimen & dispositionem devolutam esse, prohibens insuper, ne quisquam jurisdictionis, etiamsi Patriarchalis aut Regalis esset, vicariatum, licet sibi ab Imperatore concessum, Imperio vacante, retineret, neve retinenti obedires-tur, nisi consensus & confirmatio summi Pontificis accessisset, quæ lex Extravag. unic. ne sede vacante, scripta reperitur.
units.tr: the Empire was transferred from the Easterners to the Westerners, from the Greeks to the Franks. We saw this asserted above by John XXIII against Ludwig of Bavaria. It is made even clearer in the chapter Per Venerabilem, de Electione & Electi potestate. Therefore Bellarmine also, after his other controversial works, undertook the fairly arduous labour of a rather lengthy little work confirming this transfer and defending it against the objections of its opponents. Among other things, in lib. j. cap. 6 he defends it by the authority, deeds and testimonies of the Roman Pontiffs. Would not the Pope's power in the election of the Emperor then make both sides of the page, if the Empire itself, which they claim for him, was established by his authority? This also bears on the point that Adrian III, by a law he passed, ordained that on the death of Charles the Fat, who left no children, the Empire should be transferred from the Franks to the Italians. Although this had no success and gave occasion to harmful disturbances, it is nonetheless ample witness to papal ambition. The second is that the institution of the Electors of the Emperor is to be referred to the Pope, as the Hierarchical Monarchists strenuously assert. Yet the writers themselves waver, and are pulled in various directions, over which Pope they should especially credit with this ordinance. The author of the book On the Government of Princes, lib. iij. 19, makes Gregory V its author, as does Augustine Triumphus, in Summ. de potest. Eccl. q. 35, art. 2. Aventinus, libr. v. Annal. Bajor., and Onuphrius, lib. de comit. Imp., name Gregory X. Finally, Baronius, ad Annum 996, num. 56, wrote that Innocent IV passed that law at the Synod of Lyons, relying on the authority of Martin of Poland, who lived under that Innocent. Yet, although it is established by certain arguments, which after others Marcantonio de Dominis brought forward in de Rep. Eccl. libr. vj. cap. ÿ. ß. 31, 32, etc., that this constitution cannot be attributed to any of the Popes named, nor to any other author, the very usurpation of this authority amply proves that the Pope is so minded that he thinks the right and power of disposing of the election of the Emperor are owed to him. To this also belongs the fact that, when the votes in an election disagreed, the Pope judged it his own right to summon the Electors and the Elected to plead their case at Rome, and to confirm whomever he pleased. We read that Gregory VII used this authority between Henry IV and Rudolf, Innocent II between Conrad and Lothair, and Urban IV between Richard and Alfonso. The third is that the Popes have openly asserted that the administration of the vacant Empire pertains to them. This was already accepted in the time of Peter Damian, who flourished around the year 1055. For he introduces Christ addressing Victor II, the contemporary Pope, thus: I have appointed you as a father to the Emperor. Indeed, with the King removed from the midst, I have committed to you the rights of the whole Roman Empire while it is vacant. Therefore Innocent III also said, in cap. 10. de foro compet., that lay people of Vercelli might appeal to the Apostolic See concerning matters which belong to the secular courts, especially at a time when, the Empire being vacant, it was not open to them to resort to a secular judge. A particularly striking example is Clement V, who, after the death of the Emperor, absolved Robert, King of Sicily, whom Henry VII had condemned for treason. Both by (he says) superiority, and by the power in which we succeed the Emperor when the Empire is vacant, there is no doubt that we have the right to the Empire, as is found in Clement. Pastoral. de sent. & re judic. in Clement. He was succeeded by John XXII, who took the Genoese under his protection when they were attacked by the Visconti of Milan. When they objected that the matter lay within the Emperor's judgment, not the Pope's, he replied: While no Emperor is certainly in place (for he rejected Ludwig), the judgment even of profane affairs rests with me by the right of sacred power. He even promulgated a law stating that in the person of Peter, the jurisdiction, government and disposition of the vacant heavenly and earthly empire had devolved upon the Supreme Pontiff. It further forbade anyone, even of Patriarchal or Royal jurisdiction, to retain, while the Empire was vacant, a vicariate granted to him by the Emperor, and forbade obedience to anyone retaining it, unless the consent and confirmation of the Supreme Pontiff had been added. This law is found written in Extravag. unic. ne sede vacante.

units.la: LVIII. Præterea non sine Sacramento quodam Imperatores à Pontificibus coronam capessivisse, constat. Quippe coronanti juramento se obstringere sic satis mature consueverunt. Lotharius enim, juxta versus in palatio Lateranensi scriptos.
units.tr: LVIII. Moreover, it is established that the Emperors received the crown from the Popes not without a certain sacrament, for they were accustomed quite early to bind themselves by oath at the coronation. For Lothair, according to the verses written in the Lateran palace:

units.la: venit ante fores, juráns prius urbis honores, &c. Ante Lotharium quoque Carolus Calvus à Johanne VIII. coronatus est, sanctissimo prius juramento devinctus, quòd adversus inimicos Ecclesiæ, perpetuò Pontifici adfuturus sit. Hinc, ita Sigonius, titulus Imperatoris Augusti posthac sincerum Pontificis beneficium esse, annique Imperii à Pontificia coronatione repeti cœperunt. In decretis quoque Dist. 36. can. Tibi domino, Juramentum Othonis M. Johanni XII. Pontifici præstitum ejusmodi legere est: Tibi Domino Johanni Papæ, ego Rex Otho promittere & jurare facio per Patrem & Filium, & Spiritum S. & per lignum hoc vivificæ crucis, & per has reliquias S. quòd si permittente Domino Romam veneto, Sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam, & te rectorem ipsius exaltaho secundùm posse meum, m nunquam vitam aut membra, & ipsum honorem, quem habes, mea voluntate, aut meo consilio, aut meo consensu, aut mea exhortatione perdes, & in Romana urbe nullum placitum aut ordinationem faciam de omnibus, quæ ad te, aut ad Romanos pertinent sine tuo consilio: &.
units.tr: venit ante fores, juráns prius urbis honores, &c. Before Lothair, Charles the Bald was also crowned by John VIII, having first been bound by a most solemn oath that he would always be present to the Pontiff against the enemies of the Church. Hence, as Sigonius says, the title of Augustus Emperor thereafter became a pure benefice of the Pontiff, and the years of the Empire began to be reckoned from the papal coronation. Also in the decretals, Dist. 36, can. Tibi domino, one may read the following form of the oath that Otho the Great swore to Pope John XII: To you, Lord John the Pope, I, King Otho, promise and swear, and cause to be sworn, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these holy relics, that if, with the Lord permitting, I shall come to Rome, I will exalt the Holy Roman Church and you, its ruler, according to my power, and I will never by my will, counsel, consent or exhortation cause you to lose life or limb or that honour which you hold; and in the city of Rome I will make no decree or ordinance concerning all those matters which pertain to you or to the Romans without your counsel: and so on.

units.la: denique ex juramento, quo Imperatores sibi Papa devinxit. & quidquid de terra S. Petri ad nostram potestatem per‐ venerit, tibi reddam; & cuicunque Italicum regnum commisero, jurare faciam illum, ut adjutor tibi sit ad defendendam terram S. Petri, secundum suum posse. Sic me Deus adjuvet, & hæc S. Evangelia. Genuina sit ea juramenti Othonis formula, nec ne dubitatum equidem est: sed de eo quicquid fiat, extat Sac. Cerem. S. R. E. lib. j. Tit. 5. p. 23. ejusmodi juramenti formula: Ego Rex Romanorum futurus Imperator promitto & juro me de cætero Protectorem & Procuratorem fore Summi Pontificis, & in omnibus necessitatibus & utilitatibus suis, custodiendo & conservando possessiones, honores, jura &c. Quin & Gregorius VII. illud Pontificiæ tyrannidis monstrum, non tantum misso ad Guilhelmum I. Angliæ Regem Huberto, exegerat, ut sibi & successoribus suis fidelitatem faceret, ipso Baronio Annal. Tom. xj. ad A. 1079. num. 25. teste; sed etiam formam juramenti ab Imperatore præstandi ejusmodi lib. ix. registri post epist. 3. expressit: Ego ab hac hora & deinceps fidelis ero per rectam fidem B. Petro Apostolo ejusque vicario Papæ Gregorio & quodcunque ipse præceperit suis videlicet verbis, per veram obedientiam, sicut oportet Christianum, observabo: de ordinatione verò ecclesiarum, & de terris vel censu, quæ Constantinus Imperator, vel Carolus S. Petro dederunt, & de omnibus Ecclesiis, vel prædiis, quæ Apostolicæ sedi ab aliquibus viris vel mulieribus aliquo tempore sunt oblata, vel concessa, & in mea sunt vel fuerint potestate, ita conveniam cum Papa, ut periculum sacrilegii, & perditionem animæ meæ non incurram: & Deo Sanctoque Petro adjuvante Christo dignum honorem & utilitatem impendam. Sic Otho electus contra Philippum A. MCCI. sic Fridericus II. & MCCXIII. sic Rodolphus I. A. MCCLXXXIX. MCCLXXIX. juravit. Sic ab Innocentio III. Johannes Angliæ Rex coactus juravit: Ego Johannes Rex Angliæ fidelis ero Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ac Domino meo Innocentio Papæ tertio; uti apud Knigthon de Eventibus Angliæ lib. y. p. 2420. legere est. Ab Henrico VII. juramentum fidelitatis exigere ausus est per legatos Clemens V. Avinioné tum residens. Cumque id fortiter recusâsset, præt exens scilicet, Aventino narrante, contra morem Majorum, & libertatem religionis Christianæ, ut Princeps Principum, orbisque terrarum Dominus Servo Servorum Sacramentum diceret; ratus quin etiam, quod res est, juramentum fidelitatis proprie ad feuda & vasallos pertinere, denique ægrè adduci potuisset, ut juramentum à fidelitatis juramento diversum longè præstaret ejusmodi: Ego Henricus Romanorum Rex, annuente Domino futurus Imperator promitto, spondeo & polliceor, atque juro coram Deo, & B. Petro, me de cetero protectorem, procuratorem & defensorem fore Summi Pontificis, & hujus S. Romanæ Ecclesiæ, in omnibus necessitatibus & utilitatibus suis, custodiendo & conservando possessiones & honores ejus, quantum Divino suffultus adjutorio fuero secundum scire & posse meum, recta & pura fide; sic me Deus adjuvet, & Sancta hæc Dei Euangelia; Clemens idem delusi hiantis corvi instar, & exulceratus totus, constitutionem edidit, quâ sanxit, posthac omnino Pontifici ab Imperatore coronando juramentum fidelitatis præstandum esse. Tametsi igitur juramentum ab Imperatore coronando Pontifici præstitum, ex Imperatoris quidem sententia, non sit proprie fidelitatis, obsequii, seu hominii & vasallagii juramentum, & prout conceptis verbis Otho III. aliique, & superiori etiam sæculo Carolus V. jurârunt, solum de Papa non lædendo, ejusque persona ac S. Christi Ecclesia protegenda, promissionem contineat, excepta forte promissione subjectionis debitæ in spiritualibus qualem etiam Rex Romanorum in Germania Archiepiscopo Moguntino verba præeunte, jurare solet: ex juramento tamen à Gregorio VII. præscripto, Constitutione, Clementis, aliorumque Pontificum præsumtione, Theologorum quin etiam Pontificiorum contentione acri abundæ liquet, ita juramentum ab Imperatore coronando Papam exigere, ut juramentum subjectionis, fidelitatis & vasallagii animo complectatur, neque aliud planè intendat.
units.tr: Finally, from the oath by which the Pope bound the Emperors to himself: And whatever comes into our power from the land of St Peter, I will restore to you; and to whomever I commit the kingdom of Italy, I will cause him to swear that he will be a helper to you in defending the land of St Peter, according to his power. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels. Whether this formula of Otho's oath is genuine or not has indeed been doubted; but whatever be the case about that, there is extant in the Sacred Ceremonies of the Holy Roman Church, book 1, title 5, p. 23, a formula of oath of this kind: I, who am to be Emperor and King of the Romans, promise and swear that henceforth I will be Protector and Procurator of the Supreme Pontiff, and in all his necessities and advantages I will guard and preserve his possessions, honours, rights, etc. Indeed Gregory VII, that monster of papal tyranny, did not only, by sending Hubert to William I, King of England, demand that he should swear fealty to him and his successors, as Baronius witnesses in his Annals, vol. 11, at the year 1079, no. 25; he also set out the form of oath to be taken by the Emperor in this manner, in book 9 of the Register, after letter 3: From this hour onward I will be faithful to Blessed Peter the Apostle and to his vicar, Pope Gregory, and I will observe whatever he commands, in his own words, with true obedience, as becomes a Christian. As for the ordering of churches, and the lands or revenues which Constantine the Emperor or Charles gave to St Peter, and all the churches or estates which at any time have been offered or granted to the Apostolic See by any men or women, and which are or shall be in my power, I will so come to terms with the Pope that I may not incur the danger of sacrilege and the perdition of my soul; and, with God and St Peter helping, through Christ, I will render due honour and service. In this way Otho, elected against Philip, swore in 1201; in this way Frederick II swore in 1213; in this way Rudolf I swore in 1279 and 1289. In this way John, King of England, was compelled by Innocent III to swear: I, John, King of England, will be faithful to the Roman Church and to my lord Pope Innocent the Third; as one may read in Knighton, On the Events of England, book 5, p. 2420. Clement V, then residing at Avignon, dared to demand an oath of fealty from Henry VII through legates. When he had stoutly refused it, the Pope, on the pretext, as Aventinus relates, contrary to the custom of the ancestors and the liberty of the Christian religion, that the Prince of princes and Lord of the world should say the Servant of Servants to the sacrament; and thinking (as is the case) that an oath of fealty properly belongs to fiefs and vassals, and finally being barely brought to it, he at last obtained an oath of this kind, differing from the oath of fealty: I, Henry, King of the Romans, by the Lord's permission future Emperor, promise, pledge and vow, and swear before God and Blessed Peter, that henceforth I will be protector, procurator and defender of the Supreme Pontiff and of this Holy Roman Church, in all its necessities and advantages, guarding and preserving its possessions and honours, as far as I shall be supported by Divine help, according to my knowledge and power, in a right and pure faith; so may God help me, and these holy Gospels of God. The same Clement, like a gaping crow that has been cheated, and utterly galled, issued a constitution by which he decreed that henceforth an oath of fealty was to be wholly rendered to the Pope by the Emperor to be crowned. Although, therefore, the oath sworn to the Pope by the Emperor to be crowned is, in the Emperor's view, not properly an oath of fealty, obedience, or homage and vassalage, and, as Otho III and others, and in the last century Charles V, swore in plain words, contains only a promise not to harm the Pope and to protect his person and the Church of Christ, perhaps excepting the promise of due subjection in spiritual matters, which the King of the Romans in Germany is accustomed to swear, the words being spoken first by the Archbishop of Mainz; nevertheless, from the oath prescribed by Gregory VII, from the constitution of Clement, and from the presumption of other popes, and indeed from the keen and abundant contention of the theologians even of the Papists, it is clear that the oath exacted by the Pope from the Emperor to be crowned is so framed as to embrace the intention of subjection, fealty and vassalage, and plainly intends nothing else.

units.la: LIX. De Imperatoris coronatione, confirmatione, jur- amento, quibus eum sui juris & beneficii, hominem face- re Pontifices contendunt, hactenus.
units.tr: LIX. On the coronation and confirmation of the Emperor, and on the oath by which the Popes contend they make him their subject and their dependent, up to this point.

units.la: De Regibus similia plura dici possent. Constat equidem, Reges Galliæ primos fere à Papa coronam accepisse, Clodoveo Romam mittente coronam aureain, quæ Regnum dicta est. Unde Pipinum Stephanus II. aliosque Reges Pontifices alii, sacrarunt. Idemque in Coronatione Regum, quod in Imperatoris coronatione, à Papa attentatum satis constat. Cum enim Philippus I. coronandus esset Legati Papæ diserte asseruerunt, quòd sine Papæ nutu coronari Rex neutiquam posset; Hormisdæ Papæ, Remigio Rhemensi consecrandi Regis potestatem concedentis, & Victorem confirmantis, authoritatem allegantes, uti quidem Johannes Tilius, & ex eo Vignerius Bibliotheca historiæ par. II. ad A. 1060. fuse commemorant. Jactatur inde à Pontificiis partibus ejusdem D. Remigii testamentum, quo Episcopis fas sit Regem impium & tyrannum non officii duntaxat monere, sed dira ejusmodi sententia percellere: Fiant ejus dies pauci, & principatum ejus accipiat alter. Si fidem merentur, quæ Baronius ad A. 859. narrat, sic Carolus Calvus in Concilio Tulensi oravit: Se, qui electus esset cum voluntate & consensu Episcoporum ac cæterorum rorum
units.tr: Much the same could be said of kings. It is certain that the kings of France almost all first received their crown from the Pope, since Clovis was sent a golden crown from Rome, which was called the Regnum. Hence Stephen II anointed Pepin, and other popes consecrated other kings. What the Pope is known to have attempted at the coronation of an emperor, he also attempted at the coronation of kings. When Philip I was to be crowned, the papal legates plainly declared that a king could in no way be crowned without the Pope's nod. They appealed to the authority of Pope Hormisdas, who granted Remigius of Reims the power to consecrate a king, and of Victor, who confirmed it. Johannes Tilius, and after him Vignerius, Bibliotheca historiae part II, at the year 1060, recall this at length. From this the papal party boasts of the testament of the same St Remigius, by which it is lawful for bishops to warn an impious and tyrannical king not only as a matter of duty, but also to strike him with a dire sentence of this kind: Let his days be few, and let another take his office. If what Baronius relates at the year 859 deserves belief, Charles the Bald spoke thus at the Council of Toul: that he, who had been elected with the will and consent of the bishops and the others, [...] of the rest.

units.la: Regum etiam constitutionem & coronationem ad se Pontifices traxerunt, ut eorundem subjicerent sibi. Portugalliam eodem jure censere Pontifices, ex quo tempore Alphonsus Henriquius Rex à suis ob partam adversus Mauros victoriam proclamatus est, atque eam proclamationem Papa, tributo impositio, ratam habuit: Navarre Regnum obnoxium censeri Papæ, ex quo Eunicus Arista à Pontifice unctus & coronatus meruit, ut primus Regis titulo donaretur, & post eum reliqui omnes, ut Vasæus in Catalogo Regum Navarræ refert: Polonis Regium titulum Papam impertitum esse & abstulisse diu, quòd à Pontifice sacrari se non paterentur, non ausi diu titulum sine nutu & consensu Papæ recipere, uti Cromerus lib. iv. ad A. 1080. & lib. v. fusè recensetur: Venetos Ducis titulum à Deodato Pontifice acceptum referre P. Justiniano lib. vi. de rebus Venetis, teste: Bohemis Regis nomen & titulum Innocentium III. indulsisse: Armeniæ Regnum Honorium III. Johanni Hierofolymitano Regi confirmasse: Norwegiæ Principi Hacconi Regium titulum Innocentii IV. Legatos in Norwegiam missos contulisse. Hetruriæ Ducem Cosmum Ducem Magnum Pium V. creasse fretum, uti Thuanus lib. xliv. ad A. 1569. scribit, exemplis Alexandri III. Innocentii III. & Honorii III. qui Portugalliæ, Walachiæ, Bulgariæ, & Hiberniæ Reges olim creassent: Angliæ & Hiberniæ Regna tributaria Papæ facta esse sub Johanne Rege inprimis, qui Innocentio III. Regna illa pro satisfactione peccatorum suorum subjecit, stipulatus censum annuum mille librarum, famosa non formosa subjectione, uti Matthæus Paris loquitur, unde Paulus IV. Elisabethæ Angliæ Reginæ interdixit Regno, eò quòd se insscio & inconsulto illud occupasset: Scotiam juris & beneficii Papalis censeri penitus; Bonifacio VIII. interdicente quondam Eduardo Anglorum Regi, ne Scotos bello vexaret amplius, eò quòd Regnum illud in Pontificis R. fidem & authoritatem ab ipsis Scotis adhuc pollebant. Neque adeò sine causa quondam Maximilianus Imperator, cùm cœlebs adhuc esset, consilia agitâsse fertur, quibus abjurato Imperio ad Papatum promoveretur, seriò cum animo suo reputans, excelsiorem augustioremque longè Papam, quàm Imperatorem esse; imò translatis jam in Papam Imperatoris juribus, ac præcipuè eminente illo Regios conferendi titulos privilegio, verum genuinúmque Imperatorem Papam esse, neque aliud quàm ludicrum quoddam schema ei, qui Romanorum Imperator audit, relinqui.
units.tr: The Popes have also drawn the making and crowning of kings to themselves, so that they might make them subject to themselves. The Popes hold that Portugal falls under the same right, since the time when King Alphonso Henriques was proclaimed by his people after a victory won against the Moors, and the Pope approved that proclamation by imposing a tribute. Navarre is held to be a kingdom subject to the Pope, since Eunicus Arista, anointed and crowned by a pontiff, earned that the title of king be given to him first and afterwards to all the rest, as Vasaeus reports in his Catalogue of the Kings of Navarre. The Poles were long denied the royal title, which the Pope had bestowed and then taken away, because they would not allow themselves to be consecrated by the pontiff; they did not dare to receive the title for a long time without the Pope's nod and consent, as Cromer is fully recounted in book IV at the year 1080 and book V. The Venetians, as P. Justinianus witnesses in book VI of De rebus Venetis, received the title of Duke from Pope Deodatus. Innocent III granted the name and title of king to the Bohemians. Honorius III confirmed the kingdom of Armenia for John, king of Jerusalem. Innocent IV conferred the royal title on Haakon, prince of Norway, through legates sent into Norway. Pius V, as Thuanus writes in book XLIV at the year 1569, created Cosimo, Duke of Etruria, Grand Duke, relying on the precedents of Alexander III, Innocent III and Honorius III, who had long before created kings of Portugal, Wallachia, Bulgaria and Ireland. The kingdoms of England and Ireland were made tributary to the Pope, above all under King John, who subjected those kingdoms to Innocent III as satisfaction for his sins, stipulating an annual tax of a thousand pounds, a shameful, not a handsome, submission, as Matthew Paris puts it. Hence Paul IV forbade Queen Elizabeth of England to reign, because she had seized the kingdom without his knowledge and consent. Scotland is held to belong entirely to the papal right and benefice; Boniface VIII forbade Edward, the former king of the English, to harass the Scots in war any longer, because that kingdom was still under the Pope's faith and authority, as the Scots themselves acknowledged. Nor is it without reason that the Emperor Maximilian, while he was still unmarried, is said to have planned to abjure the empire and be promoted to the papacy, seriously reflecting in his own mind that the Pope was far loftier and more august than the Emperor. Indeed, with the rights of the Emperor already transferred to the Pope, and especially with that outstanding privilege of conferring royal titles, the Pope is the true and genuine Emperor, and nothing is left to him who is called Emperor of the Romans but a kind of ludicrous shadow.

units.la: LXI. Qua verò Papa in constituendis Imperatore & Regibus, eadem in abdicandis iisdem, & excelso folio suo deturbandis potestate utitur: Solis ad instar, qui quos vapores in celsum aera evehit, eosdem mox discussos præcipitésque in terram sternit, principióque suo ignobili restituit. Res sanè ad cognoscendam penitus Papæ temporalem, eamque ferè infinitam potestatem consideratione perquam digna. Celsus Moncinus, vir doctus & Canonicus Regularis Ord. Aug. de Juribus Princip. lib. iij. 3. pag. 76. sic eam in rem scribit: Conspicuum est omnibus, à Summo Pontifice deponi, privarique Imperatores, idque non tantùm ratione eorum, quæ ad fidem spectant, verùm etiam eorum, quæ ad mores & jus civile spectant. Abrahamus Bzovius de Pont. Rom. c. 46. pag. 621. aliquantò plenius: Papa summam habet potestatem etiam in Reges & Principes Christianos, qui eos corrigat, ossicio amoveat, & in loco eorum alios constituat. Papa potest Regem propter hæresin, schisma, crimen intolerabile in populo, negligentiam aut socordiam, si juramento dato non satisfecerit, aut Ecclesiam opprimeret, Dignitate Regia exuere. Hæc ut probet Bzovius, triginta, plurésve Reges, Principésque à Pontifice damnatos, sedibúsque suis dejectos enumerat, & veritatem eam ab innumeris Anglicanis exceptiones solidissimè elisit. Potissima ad deprimendos ita Imperatores & Reges, quos πεpιδαπλέας suæ meditamentis obstare credidit, machina fuit excommunicationis fulmen, telum acerrimum, quod ille parùm putans tanquam spiritualem censuram adversus Principes adhibere, ad civilem pœnam detorsit, non modo iis communione fidelium interdicens, sed eos etiam omni potestate sua & in subditos authoritate abdicans, eósque ut ab Ecclesia, ita ab Imperio dimovens. Statim enim à displosis anathematum fulminibus bellorum civilium tempestates Imperatorum Principumque capitibus ingruebant: non secus ac tonitruorum murmura subintercipit lapidosæ grandinis imber. Ut non immeritò vir Summus, Franciscus Petrarcha, de hac Pontificum arte minimè sancta questus lib. Epist. sine titulo Ep. ÿ. in hæc verba proruperit: Ecclesiasticus iste Dionysius turbat omnia miscetque de industria non aliam ob causam, nisi ut circulatorum more, vel perplexo loco, vel confuso vulnere licentiùs fallat, & fraus propria sub umbraculo Reipublicæ delitescat. Et ille quidem pro qualitate propositi, artibus utitur non novis. Nam & in fruticoso gaudet auceps, piscator in turbido, fur in tenebris. Scilicet compositis rebus nulla spes, omne in turbido consilium.
units.tr: LXI. The power the Pope uses in appointing emperors and kings, he uses in the same way in deposing them and thrusting them down from their lofty throne. He is like the sun, which lifts up vapours into the high air and then, once they have been dispersed, throws them headlong to the earth and restores them to their base beginning. Certainly the matter deserves close consideration for understanding the Pope's temporal and almost boundless power. Celsus Moncinus, a learned man and canon regular of the Order of St Augustine, writes on this point in De iuribus principum, book III, chapter 3, page 76: It is plain to all that emperors are deposed and deprived by the Supreme Pontiff, and this not only on account of matters pertaining to the faith, but also on account of matters pertaining to morals and civil law. Abraham Bzovius, De Pontifice Romano, chapter 46, page 621, puts it somewhat more fully: The Pope has supreme power even over Christian kings and princes, to correct them, to remove them from office, and to set others in their place. The Pope may strip a king of royal dignity on account of heresy, schism, an intolerable crime against the people, negligence or sloth, if he has not fulfilled the oath he gave, or if he oppresses the Church. To prove this, Bzovius lists thirty or more kings and princes condemned by the Pope and cast from their thrones, and he very solidly refutes the countless objections of the English to this truth. The chief engine for thus crushing emperors and kings, whom he believed stood in the way of his designs, was the thunderbolt of excommunication, the most cruel weapon. He, thinking it too little to use it as a spiritual censure against princes, turned it to civil punishment, not only forbidding them communion with the faithful, but also stripping them of all their power and authority over their subjects, and removing them from the Church and from the Empire alike. For straight away, from the bursting thunderbolts of anathemas, the storms of civil wars broke upon the heads of emperors and princes, just as the rumble of thunder is followed by a shower of hail. Hence the eminent man Francis Petrarch, complaining with good reason of this not very holy art of the Popes, burst out in his letters, letter five without title, in these words: That ecclesiastical Dionysius deliberately throws everything into confusion and disorder for no other reason than, like the charlatans, to deceive more freely in a tangled place or with a confused wound, and to hide his own fraud under the shadow of the commonwealth. He, according to the nature of his purpose, uses arts that are not new. For the fowler delights in the bushes, the fisherman in troubled water, the thief in darkness. Clearly, when affairs are settled, there is no hope for him; his whole plan lies in disorder.

units.la: LXII. Initium inauspicati & dirissimi moris factum est ab Imperatoribus Orientis, quorum Romæ authoritas nescere coepit, adolescente authoritate Pontificum, quos Romani militésque protexerant. Hos scilicet excommunicationis fulmine percussos ab Ecclesiæ limine arcere, verbo, tanquam iconomachos, re, ut iis oppressis ipsi crescerent; subditos fidei vinculo, quo Principibus suis obstricti erant, nefariè solvere, solutos eorum obsequio abducere, suo devincire, nefariè ausi sunt. Parum erat, quòd Philippici Imperatoris Græci nomen in sacris Liturgiis ratore Ludovico, apud Aventinum Lib. vij. & Matthæum Paris in Henrico III. jactavit) hoc est, Imperium Alemannicum, contrivit, facile ipsi fuit serpentes & Reguli, id est, Reges Principesque cæteros conculcare, quorum plures fulminibus suis adflatos in eas redegit angustias, ut emolliendo tanto furori, vel se vasallos ejus renunciare, vel certè Romano fastui libidinique Regna sua prostituere, coronas tributis, annuo censu capita subditorum onerare necesse habuerint: cùm alia victima Romanas aras placare, atque se se dirarum adamantinis catenis exsolvere non possent. Nota lippis atque tonsoribus sunt exempla Roberti Galliæ Regis, A. CMXCVIII. à Gregorio V. quòd commatri suæ nupsisset, excommunicati, tanto cum terrore, ut statim cuncti ejus latus deseruerint, clientibus duobus solis ad obsequium victus residuis; & uxor fulmine isthoc perculsa, monstrum marito perperit: Johannis Angliæ Regis, cui Innocentius III. Regnum abrogavit, translato eo ad Philippum Augustum Galliæ Regem promissa ei peccatorum remissione, si aliena invaderet: Philippi Pulchri, Galliæ Regis, cui Regnum ademit, Alberto Imperatori oblatum: Petri Arrgoniæ Regis, cujus exauthorati subditos à juramento fidelitatis Martinus IV. absolvit: Ludovici XII. Galliæ Regis cui Julius II. Regnum adjudicavit, Galliam universam interdicto subjiciens: Johannis Albretani, Navarræ Regis, cui ab eodem Julio Regnum ademptum & Ferdinando Castiliæ Regi addictum est: Henrici III. Galliæ Regis, quem Sixtus V. diris devovit, datis novem annorum indulgentiis omnibus Gallis, qui adversus ipsum arma caperent, unde Rex fidem subditorum, atque mox etiam vitam amisit: Henrici IV. Navarræ Regis, quem diro fulmine percussum idem Sixtus inhabilem declaravit ad succedendum in Galliæ Regnum: Elisabethæ, Angliæ Reginæ, adversus quam pane doloris & aqua mæroris pœnitentiam retrudendi, omni humanitatis solatio destituti, Regna, Ducatus, seuda, dominia & bona hujusmodi publicentur, & publicata sint, efficiantúrque juris & proprietatis eorum, qui illa primò occuparint, si in sinceritate fidei, & unitate Sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, ac sub nostro & Successorum Pontificum Romanorum canonicè intrantium obedientia fuerint. Quæ à Pontificibus verè Babylonis Monarchis ita definita, & juxta definitiones effectum sæpissimè data sunt, ea, ceu dogma Catholicum, ejus promachi, inprimis Azorius Institit. Moral. p. 11. lib. iv. cap. 20. Sanderus de Vis. Monarch. lib. 4. Bellarminus de Rom. Pontif. lib. v. 7. aliique rationibus suadere & propugnare acerrimè conantur.
units.tr: LXII. The beginning of this ill-omened and most dreadful custom was made by the Emperors of the East, whose authority at Rome began to lapse, while the authority of the Popes, whom the Romans and the soldiers had protected, was growing. Those popes, struck by the thunderbolt of excommunication, they barred from the threshold of the Church, in word as heretics, in deed so that they themselves might grow as these were crushed. They dared impiously to dissolve the bond of faith by which the subjects were bound to their princes, and, having loosed them from their obedience, to bind them to themselves. It was not enough that Philippicus, the Greek Emperor, had his name cast out of the sacred liturgies (Aventinus, book VII, and Matthew Paris, under Henry III, report that this was done at the urging of Ludovicus), that is, the German Empire, was crushed. It was easy for them to trample on the serpents and petty kings, that is, the other kings and princes. Several of these, struck by their thunderbolts, they drove into such straits that, to soften such fury, they were obliged either to renounce their vassalage to him or certainly to prostitute their kingdoms to Roman pride and lust, to burden their crowns with tributes, and their subjects' heads with an annual tax, since they could not appease the Roman altars with any other victim or free themselves from the adamantine chains of the curses. Examples are well known to the blear-eyed and to barbers: that of Robert, King of France, excommunicated in 998 by Gregory V because he had married his godmother, with such terror that all at once his courtiers deserted his side, leaving only two attendants to serve him at table; and his wife, struck by this thunderbolt, bore her husband a monster. That of John, King of England, whose kingdom Innocent III annulled, the kingdom being transferred to Philip Augustus, King of France, with forgiveness of sins promised to him if he invaded the lands of another. That of Philip the Fair, King of France, from whom Boniface VIII took the kingdom and offered it to the Emperor Albert. That of Peter, King of Aragon, whose subjects, deprived of their king, Martin IV absolved from their oath of fidelity. That of Louis XII, King of France, to whom Julius II adjudged the kingdom, subjecting all of France to an interdict. That of John of Albret, King of Navarre, from whom the same Julius took the kingdom and made it over to Ferdinand, King of Castile. That of Henry III, King of France, whom Sixtus V cursed, granting nine years of indulgences to all the French who took up arms against him; whereby the king lost the loyalty of his subjects and soon his life as well. That of Henry IV, King of Navarre, whom the same Sixtus, struck by a dire thunderbolt, declared unfit to succeed to the kingdom of France. That of Elizabeth, Queen of England, against whom he decreed that penance be imposed upon her with bread of sorrow and water of woe, that, deprived of every solace of humanity, her kingdoms, duchies, fiefs, lordships and goods of this kind be confiscated, and have been confiscated, and become the property and possession of those who first seize them, if they are in sincerity of faith and in unity of the Holy Roman Church, and under our obedience and that of the Roman Pontiffs canonically entering in succession. What the Popes, truly the monarchs of Babylon, have thus defined, and have very often given effect to in accordance with their definitions, its champions, above all Azorius, Institutiones morales, part I, book IV, chapter 20; Sanderus, De visibili monarchia, book IV; Bellarmine, De Romano Pontifice, book V, chapter 7, and others, strive most fiercely to persuade and defend by arguments, as if it were Catholic dogma.

units.la: LXV. Quin eò crudelitatis adversùs Imperatorum, Regum & Principum vitam ac fortunas progressi iidem sunt, ut palam sustineant judicio excommunicationis de iis semel à Papa pronuntiato, adversùs eos licere, quæcunque in excommunicatos privatos licent, ita ut iis, siquidem abdicati à Papa vi Regnum retineant, ceu tyrannis & invasoribus vis inferri, conjuratio adversus eos concipi, & impetus in sacras eorum personas fieri impunè, & citra ullum parricidii crimen, possit. Licet enim Bellarminus, quem tragici hujus ψηφισματος, admissi & bona fide recepti licet, puduit, in sua ad Archipresbyterum Blakwellum Epistola scribere non dubitaverit, inauditum semper fuisse ab Ecclesiæ incunabulis in hanc usque diem, quòd unquam quispiam Papa jusserit, ut ullus Princeps, quamvis hæreticus, quamvis Ethnicus, quamvis persecutor occideretur, vel quod ullus Pontifex R. rem factam approbárit; plenissimam tamen historia Papatus s. ccxiv. fidem fecit, inter hæreses novissimas Jesuitarum, qui Papæ ocelli, & parricidialium Magistrorum portenta sunt, haud postremam, neque à quoquam Pontifice unquam vel damnatam vel improbatam hanc esse, Regem vel Principem quemvis in haeresin prolapsum, etiam ante explorat am Romani Pontificis voluntatem, dummodo subditia comitia habere prohibiti, Jesuitarum vel Theologorum similium consilio ad id usi fuerint, occidere, non fas duntaxat, sed etiam pium, laudabile & meritorium esse. Quem verò praeterea fugit, Innocentium IV. postquam excommunicationis fulmen in Fridericum Imperatorem evibravit, Apulienfem quempiam mercede conductum induxisse, ut venenum ei miseceret; ac postquam venenum discussum vim suam amisit, ab eodem pretio corruptum filium nothum Manfredum denuò venenum ei, ex quo interiit, propinasse. Sixtum etiam quintum declamasse in laudes fraterculi, qui Henricum III.
