Galliae Regem, quamvis Pontificiis sacris devotissimum, peremit, addito isthoc epiphonemate; Verus fraterculus simulatum fraterculum interfecit! atque parum abfuisse, quin cucullatus ille parricida in catalogum Sanctorum referretur. Quid verò multis? Annon Concilium Constantiense, cujus alias umbrā parricidale suum dogma Jesuitae tegere conantur, Seff. xv. eam demum Regum tyrannorum caedem damnat, quae fiat non expectata sententia aut mandato judicis? Unde clarissimum est, opinari eos, Judicem, cujus sententiam, aut mandatum expectare oporteat dari. Ridiculum enim planè esset, de expectanda judicis sententia mentionem facere, si nullus esset judex, cujus sententia expectari deberet. Et judicem Papam pridem constituerunt. Annon qui Regem & Principem vult Regno & Imperio omni moveri, eundem occidi vult? Spoliat nempe eum ea authoritate & potestate, quae ejus vitam tuetur, & sacram facit. Is quoque, ad quem Regnum Papa transtulerit, nihil non aget, ut de medio eum, cujus locum invasit, tollat. Rara quippe Regum exempla sunt, qui fuerint suo Imperio superstites. Perpaucos invenies, quos ruina tanta molliter deposuerit. Nec dubium est, quin Rex Papali fulmine afflatus, cujus subditos Papa à fide jurata liberavit, & ad rebellionem instigavit, arma infesta in rebelles moturus, vitámque discriminibus belli ad tuendam dignitatem suam expositurus sit. In quibus certaminibus, si Rex occumbat, fatebuntur omnes, Papam mortis ejus causam esse. Planè qui Regem spoliari, & præsidiis suis omnibus exui jubet, eundem si bello se defenderit, occidere etiam jubet.
units.tr: LXV. Indeed they have gone so far in cruelty against the lives and fortunes of emperors, kings and princes that they openly maintain that, by the judgment of excommunication once pronounced against such rulers by the Pope, whatever is permitted against private excommunicated persons is permitted against them. So those who, though deposed by the Pope, keep their kingdom by force may be attacked as tyrants and usurpers, a conspiracy may be formed against them, and attacks may be made on their sacred persons with impunity and without any guilt of parricide. Bellarmine, ashamed of this tragic decree, which has been admitted and received in good faith, nevertheless did not hesitate to write in his letter to the archpriest Blackwell: it has never been heard, from the cradle of the Church down to this day, that any Pope ever ordered any prince, however heretical, however pagan, however much a persecutor, to be killed, or that any Pope approved a deed so done. Yet the very full history of the Papacy, p. 214, makes it clear that among the newest heresies of the Jesuits, who are the eyes of the Pope and the monsters of parricidal teachers, this is not the least: that a king or any prince who has fallen into heresy, even before the will of the Roman Pontiff has been ascertained, may be killed, provided he was forbidden to hold assemblies of his subjects, by those who did so on the advice of Jesuits or similar theologians; and that this is not merely lawful but pious, praiseworthy and meritorious. No Pope has ever condemned or disapproved this. Who does not know that Innocent IV, after hurling the thunderbolt of excommunication at Emperor Frederick, brought in a certain Apulian hired for money to poison him; and when the poison was discovered and lost its force, his bastard son Manfred, bribed by the same money, gave him poison again, of which he died? Sixtus V too praised the little friar who killed Henry III, King of France, though most devoted to Papal rites, adding this exclamation: The true little friar has killed the pretended little friar! And it was barely short of that hooded parricide being entered in the catalogue of saints. What more need be said? Does not the Council of Constance, under whose shadow the Jesuits try to hide their parricidal doctrine, in Session 15 condemn that slaughter of tyrant kings which is done without awaiting the sentence or mandate of a judge? Hence it is very clear that they think there is a judge whose sentence or mandate must be awaited. For it would be utterly ridiculous to speak of awaiting the judge's sentence if there were no judge whose sentence ought to be awaited. And they have long since appointed the Pope as that judge. Does not he who wants a king or prince stripped of kingdom and empire want him killed? For he strips him of that authority and power which guards his life and makes it sacred. The one to whom the Pope has transferred the kingdom will also do everything to remove from the way the one whose place he has seized. Indeed there are few examples of kings who survived their own overthrow; you will find very few whom such a ruin has let down gently. Nor is there any doubt that a king struck by the Papal thunderbolt, whose subjects the Pope has released from their sworn fidelity and incited to rebellion, will take up arms against the rebels and expose his life to the perils of war in defence of his dignity. In these struggles, if the king falls, everyone will admit that the Pope is the cause of his death. Clearly, he who orders a king to be stripped and deprived of all his defences also orders him to be killed if he defends himself in war.

units.la: LXVI. Causas porrò abdicandorum ita, & præsentissimo vitæ periculo exponendorum à Papa Regum Principumque Cardinalis Perronius in oratione post cædem nesariam Henrici IV. Lutetiæ in consessu tertii ordinis VIII. Cal. Febr. A. MDCXV. habita, ad hæresin, apostasiam & persecutionem restrinxit.
units.tr: LXVI. Cardinal Perron, in his speech delivered at Paris after the accursed murder of Henry IV, in the assembly of the Third Estate, on 8 February A. MDCXV, restricted the causes for which the Pope deposes kings and exposes them to mortal danger to heresy, apostasy and persecution.

units.la: Cui non immeritò sic Sapientissimus Angliæ Rex Jacobus pro jure Regio contra Card. Perron. respondit: Debuerat Cardinalis ille à Pontifice literas attulisse, queis testaretur Pontifex, se cæterarum causarum gratiam facere, & sola hæresi jam contentum esse, ob quam Reges posthac abdicaturus sit: nec se illa in causa judicem fore, an Rex sit hæreticus, quia si id faceret, judicem simul ageret & actorem, & forte hæresin appellaret, quæ nulla esset: nimirum, ut se Regni Dominum constituat, aut alteri dominium transcribat, qui eo nomine semper ipsi futurus esset obnoxius. Ita ferox ille Bonifacius VIII. insignita impudentia hæreticos pronuntiat, quicunque Ecclesiastica beneficia à Rege conferri posse affirmet: ubi errorem Pontificis observa non facti, sed juris. Simile planè scelus erat, cujus prætextu Henrico IV. irati Pontifices filium adversus Patrem armârunt; cujus quoque exanimum corpus sepulchri honore prohibuerunt; quanquam miser de rebus Theologicis nullam unquam moverat quæstionem. Refert Aventinus lib. iÿ. hist. Bojorum, Virgilium Juvanensem Episcopum declaratum hæreticum, quòd antipodas negaret &c. Sanè longiùs multò & latiùs quàm ad solam hæresios causam fui Imperii limites producunt Pontifices, qui ob imminuta Monarcharum jura & libertates Cleri violatas Reges regnandi jure exuunt, uti ex privilegio, aut potiùs privilegio Abbatiæ S. Medardi Suessionum, quod assutum, & calci operum Gregorii M. ipsíque Gregorio illi suppositum: ob ingenii tarditatem Childericum Regno privârunt: ob beneficiorum & præbendarum collationes Johannem Angliæ, & Philippum Pulchrum Reges Galliæ Regno exuerunt: ob causas matrimoniales Philippum, qui repudiata Berta duxit Bertiadam, Comitis Andegavensis uxorem, sacrorum communione & Imperio moverunt. Neque sanè dici potest, quæ hæresis illa fuerit, ob quam Henrici, Friderici, Petrus Aragonum Rex, Ludovicus XII. Henricus III. alii plures Væjovis hujus fulmine ambusti sunt? Scilicet Cardinalis ille versipellis speciosissimum colorem arripuit, ratus sibi cum hominibus rerum gestarum rudibus, & negotii hujusce imperitis, rem esse. Hæresis, ingenii tarditas, matrimonialis causa, alia ejusmodi meri prætextus sunt. Germana causa est dedignatio parendi Papæ, qui Rex Regum, dominus dominorum ferre Imperatores, Reges & Principes absolutæ Monarchiæ & παμβασιλεια suæ quacunque ratione obsistentes non potest. Promptum illi est affingere Imperatori vel Regi crimen hæreseos, apostasiæ, tyrannidis, ingenii tarditatem, aliaque ejusmodi, speciem magnam apud imperitos præ se ferentia, ut potestate sua υπερεχόντ & παμβασιλικῆ usus, Regnum ejus involet, & alium Imperatorem Regémve Sedi Romanæ obnoxium, & dicto Papali audientem magis, creet. Jam diu est, quòd fraus detecta à cordatis pellucet, atque si non castiùs, saltem cautiùs Babylonius ille mango mercari occœpit. Et levato velo Johannes Semeca, qui Glossam in Gratianum conscripsit. Gloss. ad Can. Si Papa 6. Dist. 40. verb. à fide devium, quærenti, quo pacto possit Imperator deponi, respondit: Pro quolibet peccato potest Imperator deponi, si sit incorrigibilis, neque pro quolibet peccato tantùm, sed si tantæ potestati sit inutilis. Ergò pro omni peccato, & quandóque pro nullo deponi possunt.
units.tr: To him the most wise King James of England not undeservedly replied in For the Royal Right against Cardinal Perron: That cardinal ought to have brought letters from the Pope attesting that the Pope grants immunity in other causes and is content with heresy alone, on account of which he will henceforth depose kings. Nor would the Pope himself be judge in that case whether the king is a heretic, for if he did so he would be judge and party at once, and perhaps would call heresy what was no heresy: namely, so that he may make himself lord of the kingdom, or transfer lordship to another, who would always afterwards be bound to him on that account. So that fierce Boniface VIII, with remarkable impudence, pronounces heretics whoever affirms that ecclesiastical benefices can be conferred by a king: where you observe the Pope's error, which is one of law, not of fact. A similar crime was the pretext by which the angry Popes armed the son against the father, Henry IV; they also denied his lifeless body the honour of burial, though the wretch had never raised any question on theological matters. Aventinus, in book iv of the History of the Boii, reports that Virgil, bishop of Salzburg, was declared a heretic because he denied the antipodes, etc. Certainly the Popes extend the limits of empire far beyond the sole cause of heresy. On account of diminished rights of monarchs and violated liberties of the clergy they strip kings of the right to reign, as from the privilege, or rather the forged privilege, of the abbey of St Medard at Soissons, which was tacked onto the end of the works of Gregory the Great and falsely ascribed to Gregory himself. On account of slowness of mind they deprived Childeric of his kingdom; on account of the conferring of benefices and prebends they stripped John of England and Philip the Fair, kings of France, of their realms; on account of matrimonial causes they removed from the sacraments and from empire Philip, who, having repudiated Bertha, took Bertrada, the wife of the Count of Anjou. Nor can it be said what heresy it was on account of which Henry, Frederick, Peter, King of Aragon, Louis XII, Henry III and many others were scorched by the thunderbolt of this Vejovis. Clearly that slippery cardinal seized on a very specious colour, thinking the matter was one for men ignorant of the facts and inexperienced in such business. Heresy, slowness of mind, matrimonial cause and other such things are mere pretexts. The real cause is disdain for obeying the Pope, who, as King of kings and Lord of lords, cannot tolerate emperors, kings and princes who in any way resist his absolute monarchy and his all-kingship [παμβασιλεία]. It is easy for him to impute to an emperor or king the crime of heresy, apostasy, tyranny, slowness of mind and such like, which carry great weight in the eyes of the unskilled; so that, using his power as supreme [ὑπερέχων] and all-kingly [παμβασιλικῆ], he may seize their kingdom and set up another emperor or king, subject to the Roman See and more ready to obey the Papal word. For some time now the fraud has been detected by the wise and shines through; and if the Babylonian trader in wares has not begun to trade more honestly, at least he has begun to trade more cautiously. And when the veil was lifted, John Semeca, who wrote the Gloss on Gratian, answered one who asked in what way an emperor could be deposed: For any sin an emperor can be deposed, if he is incorrigible; and not for any sin only, but if he is useless for so great a power. Therefore they can be deposed for every sin, and sometimes for no sin at all.

units.la: LXVII. Superest potestas, quam Papa in Clerum, haud postremam, sive numerum, sive dignitatem spectemus, Regni Pontificii partem, quam nexu & mancipio totam sibi obnoxiam habet, quoad temporalia etiam, sibi pridem asseruit, & hodieque usurpat. Jam pridem enim est, quòd Pontificius Clerus se simul ac bona sua Reipublicæ subtraxit, & uti dicebat Appius ille Claudius ad tribunum, peculiarem patriam, peculiarem Rempublicam sibi constituit. Pertendunt nempe & summa contentione defendunt Clerici, se non esse subditos Regibus, negántque Clericos & Monachos vel posse conveniri coram judice civili, vel capite plecti ob crimen sententia Prætoris, quamdiu sunt Clerici; vel obnoxios se esse legibus Regni, aut capitationi & vectigalibus, vel cogi se ad Symbolos in in sumptus belli conferendos posse. Denique Regum Principúmque potestate, & imperio soluti emancipatíque, totos se in Papæ, Babylonii sui Regis, fidem clientelámque dediderunt, dicentes cum improbis illis Psal. xii. 5. מי ארן לנו Quis nobis præter illum dominus? & cum vite illa vacua Israëlis Hos. x. 3. אין מלך לנו Nullus nobis (præter illum) Rex est. Rex quid nobis faceret? Bonifacius VIII. in cap. quanquam de censibus sic eam rem definivit: Jure Divino & humano Clerici, & eorum bona libera sunt à potestate seculari. Concilium quo.que Constantiense Seff. xxxj. assa voce pronuntiavit, laicos in Clericos nullam habere jurisdictionem nec potestatem. Concilium Lateranense sub Leone X. celebratum Seff. ix. Cùm inquit, tam à jure Divino quàm humano, laicis nulla potestas in ecclesiasticas personas attributa sit, innovamus omnes & singulas constitutiones &c. Denique Concilium Tridentinum Seff.xxv.20. Ecclesiæ & personarum Ecclesiasticarum immunitatem Dei ordinatione, & sanctionibus canonicis institutam esse, sciscit. Unde porrò Clericos in rebellione contra Principes seculares læsæ Majestatis crimen admittere posse negant, quam sententiam communem esse, Card. Alex. in cap. Inprimis S. de pers. cal. 5. non obest opin. 2. q. 3. Somez in S. rursus n.24. Insist. de actionibus, aliique testantur.
units.tr: LXVII. There remains the power which the Pope has long claimed for himself over the clergy, no small part of his Papal realm whether we look at its number or its dignity, and which he holds wholly bound to himself by tie and ownership, even as to temporal matters, and which he still usurps today. For it has long been the case that the Papist clergy, as soon as they withdrew their goods from the commonwealth, set up for themselves, as Appius Claudius said to the tribune, a private fatherland, a private commonwealth. Indeed the clergy maintain and defend with the greatest vigour that they are not subjects of kings, and deny that clerics and monks can be summoned before a civil judge, or executed for a crime by the sentence of a praetor, as long as they are clerics; or that they are bound by the laws of the realm, or by poll-tax and taxes, or that they can be compelled to contribute to the costs of war. Finally, freed and released from the power and command of kings and princes, they have wholly surrendered themselves to the faith and clientage of the Pope, their Babylonian king, saying with those wicked men, Psal. xii. 5, [מי אדון לנו] Who is lord over us? and with that empty vine of Israel, Hos. x. 3, [אין מלך לנו] We have no king (besides him). What would a king do for us? Boniface VIII, in the chapter Quanquam de censibus, defined the matter thus: By divine and human law clerics and their goods are free from secular power. The Council of Constance, Session 31, also pronounced with one voice: laymen have no jurisdiction or power over clerics. The Lateran Council celebrated under Leo X, Session 9, says: Since by divine as well as human law no power over ecclesiastical persons has been granted to laymen, we renew all and singular constitutions, etc. Finally the Council of Trent, Session 25, decrees that the immunity of the Church and of ecclesiastical persons was established by the ordinance of God and canonical sanctions. Whence they further deny that clerics can commit the crime of treason against secular princes by rebellion; which opinion is common, as Cardinal Alexander attests in cap. Inprimis S. de pers. cal. 5. non obest opin. 2. q. 3., Somez in S. rursus n.24. Insist. de actionibus, and others.

units.la: LXVIII. De hac Clericorum exemtione latè admodùm Suarez, & Bellarminus cum primis disputant. Et Suarez, quidem in defensione fidei Catholicæ adversùs Anglicanæ sectæ errores libro quarto toto, itaque rem istam expedit, ut sustineat comprobare pluribus. Clericos omnes jure Divino & humano à potestate Principum Secularium esse exemptos, non solùm in spiritalibus & ecclesiasticis causis, cap. 2. sed etiam in rebus & causis temporalibus. cap. 3. Summum Pontificem omni jure Divino & humano ab omni jurisdictione secularium Principum esse exemptum, cap. 4. adeò ut non possit se humano judicio subjicere, cap. 7. Clericos omnes sub Pontifice existentes, à jurisdictione temporali Principum Divino jure esse exemptos, cap. 8. in causis civilibus, cap. 14. in causis criminalibus, cap. 15. Privilegium illud fori includere exemptionem à legibus civilibus, cap. 16. à tributis & oneribus, cap. 17. tam personalibus cap. 22. quàm realibus, cap. 25. Non dissimulat tamen idem Suarez cap. 8. multos Doctores Catholicos in alia omnia ire, statuentes scilicet, immunitatem Clerinon de jure Divino, sed humano esse. Bellarmini sanæ verò de immunitate Cleri disputationis propositionibus quibusdam innexæ, quæ libro de Clericis lib. 1. cap. 28. extat, summa huc redit: In causis ecclesiasticis, quarum cognitio non à legibus, sed ab Euangelio & canonibus Ecclesiæ pendet, liberos esse Clericos jure Divino à Secularium Principum potestate, (quasi scilicet causæ ecclesiasticæ à Magistratu civili, ad Ecclesiæ ordinem conservandam & stabiliendam, non etiam cognosci possint; vel in ejusmodi causis, quarum cognitio ab Euangelio pendet, clerici jure Divino à Secularium Principum potestate magis liberi sint, quàm alii Christiani quivis:) Non esse exemptos Clericos ab obligatione directiva legum civilium, quæ actiones humanas in commerciis temporalibus dirigunt, & sacris canonibus, vel officio Clericali non repugnant: exemptos tamen esse ab earundem legum obligatione coactiva, nisi eædem leges ab Ecclesia approbatæ fuerint,(qualis verò, Bellarmine est obligatio directiva, distincta à coactiva, seu potestate cogendi in superiore, & necessitate parendi in inferiore?) non posse Clericos à judice Seculari judicari, sileges civiles non servent, (quod cum legibus & Exemplis V. T. cum præcepto Apostoli Rom. xiii. 1. cum ipso denique jure naturali, quo partes omnes Reip. judicio totius sujiciuntur, è diametro pugnat:) Bona Ecclesiasticorum, tam Ecclesiastica quam secularia libera esse, ac merito esse debere à tributis Principum Secularium. (id verò licet in tenuibus ministrorum alimentis, & scholastica suppellectile, probatæ æquitatis sit; in Regalibus tamen Episcoporum & Monasteriorum opibus ac latifundiis cum iniquitate summa conjunctum est, cùm ita quoad communes sumptus ferendos, bona illa, præstantissima sint quasi extincta, & uti loqui amant, in manu mortua:) Exceptionem Clericorum in rebus politicis, tum quoad personas, tum quoad bona introducta esse jure pariter humano & divino positivo, non quòd id expressè in S. literis præceptum, sed quia id ab exemplis vel testimoniis Veteris vel Novi Testamenti per similitudinem quandam deduci posset: denique exemtionem eandem pertinere ad il-lum gradum præceptorum naturalium, quæ deducuntur quidem ex principio juris naturæ, sed per consequentiam, non absolutè necessariam, nec omnino evidentem, & ideo egere humana constitutione, adeoque ad jus gentium recte referri. (quasi scilicet vel de jure Divino sit, quod factum aliquando in quopiam scriptura testatur, vel ad jus naturale referri possit, quod consequentia absolutè necessaria & evidenti destituitur, ne dicam propositiones hasce posteriores Bellarmini à gregalibus Covarruvia, Medina, aliis pridem jugulatas, & obelo confossas esse) Hactenus Bellarmini etiam νομικὸν ἀξίωμα Exemtionem Cleri à juramento fidelitatis & Suprematus Principi temporali præstando, à tributis eidem pendendis denique à supplicüis, quæ civiles Magistratus à sceleratissimis expetere possit, palam doceri, & pro dogmate in Papatu certissimo haberi, idem qui supra Celeb. Barlovius Pap. Regiæ Pot. Everf. pag. 101--125. irrefragabilibus testimoniis probatum dedit.
units.tr: LXVIII. Suarez and Bellarmine both argue at great length for this exemption of the clergy. Suarez, in the fourth book of his whole Defence of the Catholic Faith against the Errors of the Anglican Sect, undertakes to prove by many arguments that all clergy are exempt by divine and human law from the power of secular princes, not only in spiritual and ecclesiastical matters, (ch. 2) but also in temporal affairs and causes. (ch. 3) He holds that the Supreme Pontiff is exempt by all divine and human law from every jurisdiction of secular princes, (ch. 4) so that he cannot subject himself to human judgment. (ch. 7) He holds that all clergy under the Pontiff are exempt by divine law from the temporal jurisdiction of princes: (ch. 8) in civil causes (ch. 14) and in criminal causes (ch. 15); that the privilege of forum includes exemption from civil laws (ch. 16) and from taxes and burdens, (ch. 17) both personal (ch. 22) and real (ch. 25). Yet Suarez does not conceal, at ch. 8, that many Catholic teachers go in all other directions, holding that the immunity of the clergy is not of divine right but of human right. The main point of Bellarmine's sound propositions on the immunity of the clergy, which appears in his book On Clerics, book 1, ch. 28, comes to this: In ecclesiastical causes, whose cognizance depends not on the laws but on the Gospel and the canons of the Church, clergy are free by divine right from the power of secular princes (as if ecclesiastical causes could not be taken up by the civil magistrate for preserving and establishing the order of the Church; or as if clergy, in causes whose cognizance depends on the Gospel, were by divine right more free from the power of secular princes than any other Christians whatever). Clergy are not exempt from the directive obligation of civil laws, which direct human actions in temporal dealings, and which do not conflict with the sacred canons or the clerical office; they are, however, exempt from the coercive obligation of those same laws, unless the laws have been approved by the Church (what sort of obligation is directive, Bellarmine, distinct from coercive, that is, from the power of a superior to compel and the necessity of an inferior to obey?). Clergy cannot be judged by a secular judge if the civil laws are not observed (which flatly contradicts the laws and examples of the Old Testament, the precept of the Apostle in Rom. 13.1, and indeed natural law itself, by which all parts of the commonwealth are subject to the judgment of the whole). The goods of the clergy, both ecclesiastical and secular, are free and rightly ought to be free from the taxes of secular princes. (This indeed may be a just thing for the meagre maintenance of ministers and for school furnishings; but in the royal wealth and vast estates of bishops and monasteries it is joined with the greatest iniquity, since in this way those excellent goods, as far as bearing common expenses goes, are virtually extinct, and, as they like to say, in mortmain.) The exemption of clergy in political matters, both as to persons and as to goods, was introduced by both human and positive divine law, not because this is expressly commanded in Holy Scripture, but because it could be drawn by similarity from examples or testimonies of the Old or New Testament; finally, the same exemption belongs to that class of natural precepts which are indeed derived from a principle of natural law, but by a consequence that is not absolutely necessary nor wholly evident, and therefore need human institution, and so are rightly referred to the law of nations. (as if what a fact in some passage of Scripture attests were of divine right, or as if what lacks an absolutely necessary and evident consequence could be referred to natural law; not to mention that these latter propositions of Bellarmine have long since been throttled by his fellows Covarruvias and Medina and others and pierced with the obelus.) Thus far Bellarmine's legal axiom [νομικὸν ἀξίωμα], that the exemption of the clergy from the oath of fidelity and supremacy to a temporal prince, from the taxes payable to him, and finally from the supplications which civil magistrates may demand of the most wicked persons, is openly taught and held as a most certain dogma in Papacy; the same Barlow, cited above, has shown this with irrefutable testimonies in Papal Usurpation over the Royal Power, pp. 101–125.

units.la: LXIX. Plenaria hac exemtione cleri haud scio quidquam ne sit vel magis adversum sive juri Divino, omnem animam potestati eminenti, quæ utique, ceu gladium gestans, & tributa imponens, secularis intelligitur, subjicienti; sive exemplis V. & N. T. ipsiúsque adeò Christi & Apostolorum, sive Imperatorum Christianorum genuino Papatu antiquorum, nominatim Valentiniani senioris, Theodosii utriusque, Martiani, Justiniani, Heraclii, Caroli M. Ludovici Pii, aliorum, quorum innumeras leges, quibus ecclesiam illi rexerunt, M. Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccles. lib. vi. 6. recensfet, praxi: vel Reipublicæ magis perniciosum. Nihil enim, uti quondam Imperator Antoninus apud Capitolinum in Pio, dixit, est sordidius, imò crudelius, quàm si Rempublicam ÿ arrodant, vel potius erodant, qui nihil in eam suo labore conferunt: Si, quod ferendum esse leges negant, onus subire recusent, qui lucrum amplectuntur: si lac comedant, & lana operiantur, & quod crassum est occidant, atque adeò florem bonorum Reipublicæ depascant, qui nescio quàm bene gregem Domini pascunt, certè cupiditatibus utplurimum suis unicè lenocinantur: nisi forte soli Cardinali Galeato (quod de eo Scaliger Exercit. ccxi. 2. scribit) arma, equos, canes, odores, scorta pro bibliotheca fuisse, quis existimet. Imò quæ major pestis est, quàm in medio sinu habere, non tantum contra quos, si te injuria affecerint, mutire non ausis; sed etiam, qui alienæ potestati fidem dederint, hoc est, qui teneantur ad nutum alterius contra te arma sumere, nec ut maximè velint, abnuente externa potestate, quicquam pro salute tua facere queant? Tales verò Clerici sunt, qui ad nutum Capitolini Imperatoris sui, contra ipsam, in qua degunt, Rempublicam insurgere non verentur. Ejus enim unius summum agnoscunt Imperium, ipsi soli tenentur fidelitatis juramento obstricti, ejus forum agnoscunt unicè. Quòd si ergo Pontisex classicum eccinerit, tot quælibet Respublica contra se experietur hostium exercitus, quod in sinu suo cœnobia Monachorum, conventus Sacerdotum, Collegia Canonicorum habet. Peregrini sunt, qui in Republica versantur, cui non sunt subjecti, à quibus maximè timendnm esse, Philosophus Polit. v. 3. monet. Unde nomen hostis, quod olim peregrinum significavit, in odium abiit. Proin Clerici, qui in Republica degentes, non Reipublicæ, sed alieno Imperio parent, non alio quàm peregrinorum loco haberi possunt, nec minus ab iis timendum, imò eo magis gis etiam, quò arctius suo superiori, Pontifici Romano, potenti adeò Domino obstringuntur, & quò penitiùs in Reipublicæ arcana penetrare valent.
units.tr: LXIX. Nothing is more wholly opposed to this full exemption of the clergy, either to divine law, which subjects every soul to the higher power (which, bearing the sword and imposing taxes, is certainly understood as secular), or to the examples of the Old and New Testaments, and of Christ himself and the Apostles, or to the genuine practice of the Christian emperors of old, which Marcus Antonius de Dominis, in On the Ecclesiastical Commonwealth, book 6, ch. 6, enumerates by name: Valentinian the Elder, both Theodosiuses, Martian, Justinian, Heraclius, Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and others, whose countless laws by which they governed the Church he recounts. Nor is anything more harmful to the commonwealth. For, as the emperor Antoninus once said in Capitolinus, in the life of Pius, nothing is more sordid, indeed more cruel, than when those who contribute nothing to the commonwealth by their labour gnaw at it, or rather eat it away; if they refuse to bear the burden which they deny should be borne by law, those who embrace the profit; if they eat the milk and cover themselves with the wool, and slaughter what is fat, and thus devour the flower of the goods of the commonwealth, those who I know not how well feed the flock of the Lord, surely for the most part serve only their own desires. Unless perhaps, as Scaliger writes of Cardinal Galeatus (Exercitationes 211.2), weapons, horses, dogs, perfumes, and whores were for him in place of a library, who would think so? Indeed, what greater plague is there than to keep in your very bosom those who, if they should do you wrong, would not dare to murmur against you, but who have pledged faith to another power, that is, who are bound to take up arms against you at another's nod, and who, even if they most wish to, cannot do anything for your safety while the foreign power forbids it? Such are the clergy, who do not hesitate to rise up at the nod of their Capitoline emperor against the very commonwealth in which they live. For they acknowledge his one supreme rule alone; they alone are bound by the oath of fidelity to him; they acknowledge his court alone. If then the Pontiff should sound the trumpet, any commonwealth whatever will experience the armies of enemies that it has in its bosom in the monasteries of monks, the assemblies of priests, and the colleges of canons. Those are strangers who live in a commonwealth to which they are not subject, and the Philosopher (Politics 5.3) warns that it is from these above all that one must fear. Hence the word hostis (enemy), which once meant a stranger, has come into odium. Therefore clergy who, while living in the commonwealth, obey not the commonwealth but a foreign empire, can be regarded in no other light than as foreigners; and they are to be feared no less, indeed all the more, the more tightly they are bound to their superior, the Roman Pontiff, a mighty lord, and the more deeply they are able to penetrate into the secrets of the commonwealth.

units.la: LXX. Si quando jurisdictionem in Clericorum personas & bona Supremæ potestates civiles exercent, uti à Venetis, Gallis, aliis, pro jure eorum strenuè factitatum, atque ejus rei vestigia non pauca, tum quoad criminales, tum quoad civiles Ecclesiasticorum causas, apud Rousseau lium Histor. Jurisdict. Pontific. lib. iv. cap. 3. 4. nec non Scriptores illos, qui incunte hoc seculo pro Venetis adversos. Pontificios fortissimè pugnarunt (quorum argumenta Thuanus Annal. lib. 137. repetit) legere est: vicissim Clerici Ecclesiæ libertates pupillam oculi sui, cujus quæsitissimus sensus est, lacessi, violari, clamitant. Ita libertas Ecclesiæ, illa scilicet ἐλευθερία τῆς ἀπολύτως, non jam liberationem à maledictione legis, Imperio Sathanæ; sed prærogativas temporales, & privilegia, per quæ Clerici jugum civilis potestatis excusserunt, iis sonat. Veluti si à Clero decimæ exiguntur, facinerosi Sacerdotes & Monachi à civili potestate poenis civilibus afficiantur, vectigalia bonis patrimonialibus Episcoporum imponantur, & si quid hujusmodi aliud. Sanè famosa illa de Cœna Domini Bulla, de qua fusius Historiæ Papatus Ss. CCXL disseruimus, quotannis die illa Jovis, quæ proximè diem Paschatis antecedit, non hæreticos duntaxat cujuscunque sectæ, & fautores eorundem, sed eos etiam, qui libertatem Ecclesiasticam perturbant, etiamsi, ita Papa solennia insaniens pronuntiat, Imperiali, Regali, Ducali, vel alia quacunque dignitate præfulgeant, solenni excommunicatione implicat. Ibi inter alios etiam diris dirissimè devoventur, qui à Clero decimas, taleas, præstantias, & alia onera, absque Romani Pontificis speciali & expressa licentia exigunt, nec non qui admittunt appellationes à gravamine, quas Galli vocant appellationes ab abu-su, per quas qui conqueruntur se injustè opprimi in foro Episcopali, ad judicia Secularia provocant. Excommunicatione decima quarta etiam diserte nominantur Parlamenta, Cancellarii & Consiliarii, qui ad se trahunt, causas spirituales, id est, quæ sunt Clericalis aut Episcopalis cognitionis, quamvis agatur de pecuniis & damnis civilibus. In Gallia bona patrimonialia Episcoporum Regi pendunt vectigal. Quod crimen Toletus Instruct. Sacerd. lib. j. 29. 2. pertendit decimo capite hujus excommunicationis comprehendi, sic loquens, Imponentes collectas super bonis patrimonialibus Ecclesiasticorum, excommunicati sunt. Tanta Regum patientia est, qui à Papa quotannis diro, maximè solenni & atroci anathemate percussi licet. Impense tamen adeò eum colunt, ac ne quidem ut clausulæ Bullæ istius, directè eos ferientes expunguntur, postulant.
units.tr: LXX. If at any time the supreme civil powers exercise jurisdiction over the persons and goods of the clergy, as the Venetians, the French and others have vigorously done in defence of their right, and of which there are not a few traces, both in criminal and in civil causes of ecclesiastics, one may read this in Rousseau, History of Papal Jurisdiction, book 4, chs. 3–4, and also in those writers who at the beginning of this century fought most strongly for the Venetians against the Papists (whose arguments Thuanus repeats in Annals, book 137). In turn the clergy cry out that the liberties of the Church, the apple of their eye, whose most sensitive nerve is their concern, are being assailed and violated. Thus the liberty of the Church, that is, the freedom [ἐλευθερία τῆς ἀπολύτως] which means not deliverance from the curse of the law or from the empire of Satan, but temporal prerogatives and privileges by which the clergy have shaken off the yoke of civil power, is what the phrase means to them. For example: if tithes are demanded from the clergy, if wicked priests and monks are punished with civil penalties by the civil power, if taxes are imposed on the patrimonial goods of bishops, and whatever else of this kind. Certainly that infamous Bull In Coena Domini, of which we have discussed more fully in the History of the Papacy, Ss. 240, is each year, on that Thursday which falls immediately before Easter, involved in solemn excommunication against not only heretics of any sect and their supporters, but also those who disturb ecclesiastical liberty, even if, as the Pope pronounces in his solemn madness, they shine with imperial, royal, ducal or any other dignity. There, among others, are most dreadfully cursed those who exact from the clergy tithes, tallages, dues, and other burdens, without special and express licence of the Roman Pontiff, and also those who admit appeals from a grievance, which the French call appeals from abuse, by which those who complain that they are unjustly oppressed in the episcopal court appeal to secular courts. In the fourteenth excommunication the Parlements, Chancellors and Councillors are expressly named, who draw to themselves spiritual causes, that is, those which belong to clerical or episcopal cognizance, even though the matter concerns money and civil damages. In France the patrimonial goods of bishops pay a tax to the King. Toletus (Instruction of Priests, book 1, 29.2) extends this crime to the tenth head of this excommunication, speaking thus: Those who impose levies on the patrimonial goods of ecclesiastics are excommunicate. Such is the patience of kings, who are struck each year by the Pope with a dire, most solemn and savage anathema. Yet they worship him so devotedly that they do not even ask that the clauses of that Bull which strike them directly be struck out.

units.la: LXXI. Eat nunc Academiæ Parisiensis Cancellarius
units.tr: LXXI. Let the Chancellor of the University of Paris now go forth

units.la: illustris famæ, Johannes Gerson, & miseratus fortem Imperatorum & Principum ob temporalia excommunicatorum, Pontifici suo inculcet denuo, abnunciétque excommunicationem non ob temporalia, quamvis spiritualibus annexa, sed ob merè spiritualia stringendam esse, quia (ita lib. de vita spirit. anime coroll. y. propos. 5. & de Eccles. potest. consider. 4. loquitur ille) excommunicatio est baculus purè spiritualis, propterea que non assumendus ad protectionem rerum temporalium, quoniam res temporales non debent conservari vel repeti cum majori detrimento eorum, à quibus repetuntur, quàm sit utilitas proveniens apud repetentes. Sed excommunicatio, inquit, majus damnum infert, quàm sit utilitas ulla temporalis. Ergo non est inferenda pro re temporali. Neque videtur æquum, ut Ecclesia in sceleribus vindicandis atrocior sit justitia seculari, cui sufficit in corpora sævire. Et si non pro quolibet contumacia infligitur mors apud Principes Seculares, quæ est ista Ecclesiasticæ libertatis mansuetudo, ut passim pro similibus aut minoribus culpis spiritualem mortem inferat? Hæc ille, surdis scilicet fabulam cantans.
units.tr: Let John Gerson, of illustrious fame, who pitied the unfortunate emperors and princes excommunicated over temporal matters, press upon his Pontiff once more and declare that excommunication is to be imposed not on account of temporal matters, though these are linked to spiritual ones, but on account of purely spiritual matters. For (so he speaks in the book on the life of the spirit, corollary y, proposition 5, and in On the Power of the Church, consideration 4) excommunication is a purely spiritual staff, and therefore it is not to be taken up for the protection of temporal things, since temporal things ought not to be preserved or recovered at a greater cost to those from whom they are recovered than the advantage that accrues to those recovering them. But excommunication, he says, inflicts greater harm than any temporal advantage. Therefore it is not to be inflicted for the sake of a temporal thing. Nor does it seem fair that the Church should be fiercer than secular justice in punishing crimes, since secular justice is content to rage against bodies. And if secular princes do not inflict death for every act of contumacy, what is this gentleness of ecclesiastical liberty, that it inflicts spiritual death everywhere for similar or even lesser faults? So he; singing a tale, of course, to the deaf.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Si quadruplicem Papæ, quam in rebus merè temporalibus is exercet, potestatem excussimus. Primam & Secundam, in patrimonium scilicet Petri, & Reges ac Principes feudi nexu sibi devinctos, qua Principem temporalem & Ecclesiasticum simul: Tertiam in Imperatores, Reges, Principes Christianos quosvis; Quartam in Clerum, seu homines, uti vocant, Ecclesiæ, qua Principem Spiritualem & Ecclesiasticum usurpare eum, Pontificiæ potestatis hyperaspistæ decernunt. Cæterum vocabulorum spiritualis & Ecclesiastici tectorio incrustari Pontificis Imperium merè terrenum, & temporalem in Christianos quosvis nomen & sacra ejus professos potestatem, nemo sanus inficias amplius iverit. Omnis enim jurisdictio, quæ non est potestas verbi Divini prædicati, & cordibus hominum per Spiritum S. & Ministerium Euangelicum applicati, mera est chimæra, vana, futilis & jurisdictio non re, sed nomine tenus talis, nisi quatenus cum potestate civili & terrena coincidit. Quæ sola probatio abundè fidem facit, Papæ in Reges & nationes, ac magnam etiam partem in Clerum ipsum, Imperium esse merè terrenum, temporale, Civile & politicum, quale in omni societate hominum exercetur. Neque magis Ecclesiastica jurisdictio propriè dicta, & à civili distincta jurisdictio est, quàm Medica, Juridica, mercatoria, fabrilis. Aliæ quidem sunt leges Ecclesiasticæ à civilibus, rituales à politicis, despoticæ à militaribus, matrimoniales ab illis, quæ fabris & mercatoribus finguntur. Robur tamen & sanctionem ab una eademque potestate civili summa & architectonica, cujus solius est jubere, cogere & punire, accipiunt. Ipsa lex Divina, ipsemet adeò Decalogus legum civilium formam à summa potestate civili accipit. Quantò magis leges Ecclesiasticæ, censuræ & constitutiones Pastorum? An diceres anus quispiam potest, in societate civili Decalogum, inter fulgura & tonitrua olim sancitum, robur, vim & sanctionem Summi Magistratus civilis exigere: Papæ verò solius sanctiones peculiari prærogativa vim legum habere, ut citra sanctionem potestatis Civilis jubere & punire possint? Cúmque Deus Christo per ministerium Euangelii omnem potestatem secularem, omnem animam, agenda & dicenda omnia subjecerit, neque adeò Christi Minister & Pastor Euangelicus aliquis in credendis & faciendis judicio utatur vel imperativo vel coactivo, sed suasorio, hortatorio & declarativo duntaxat: & tam latè pateat Pastoris Euangelici cognitio, quàm ipsa jurisprudentia, imò tantò latiùs, quantò officiorum quàm juris regula latiùs patet: ex adverso etiam Deus in terris omnem personam, omnes lites, dicenda, agenda omnia, de quacunque re aut negotio, in quocunque loco, tempore & cœtu hominum quoad judicium præcipiens, cogens & puniens, cognitioni & Imperio summi Magistratus, non utique Ecclesiastici (cujus in sacro codice, nulla uspiam mentio extat) sed civilis & politici, subjecerit, manifestum est, Papam, quatenus Imperium in Reges & populos extra territorium suum exercet, eatenus Imperium merè terrenum, jurisdictionémque civilem & politicam exercere, nec nisi ad fucum faciendum, illud vocabulis Ecclesiastici & Spirituális, ne imperium ejus terrenum dispalescat, obducere.
units.tr: If we have shaken off the fourfold power which the Pope exercises in purely temporal matters: the first and the second, namely over the patrimony of Peter and over the kings and princes bound to him by the bond of feudal tenure, by which he is claimed to be at once a temporal and an ecclesiastical prince; the third over emperors, kings, and any Christian princes whatever; the fourth over the clergy, or, as they call them, the men of the Church, by which they decide that he usurps the role of a spiritual and ecclesiastical prince, and so they act as the champions of papal power. But that the Pope's empire, which is purely earthly, and his power over all Christians and those who profess his sacred name, should be daubed over with the plaster of the words spiritual and ecclesiastical, no sane person will any longer deny. For every jurisdiction that is not the power of the divine Word preached, and applied to men's hearts through the Holy Spirit and the evangelical ministry, is a mere chimera, empty, futile, and a jurisdiction in name only and not in reality, except insofar as it coincides with civil and earthly power. This single proof amply establishes that the Pope's rule over kings and nations, and also to a large extent over the clergy themselves, is purely earthly, temporal, civil and political, of the kind that is exercised in every human society. Ecclesiastical jurisdiction, properly so called, and distinct from the civil, is no more a separate jurisdiction than medical, juridical, mercantile or craftsmen's jurisdiction is. There are indeed ecclesiastical laws distinct from civil ones, ritual laws distinct from political ones, disciplinary laws distinct from military ones, matrimonial laws distinct from those invented by craftsmen and merchants. Yet they all receive their force and sanction from one and the same civil power, the supreme and architectonic one, whose sole office is to command, compel and punish. The divine law itself, and indeed the Decalogue, receives the form of civil laws from the supreme civil power. How much more so ecclesiastical laws, censures and the constitutions of ministers! Could anyone say, as an old woman might, that in civil society the Decalogue, once enacted amid lightnings and thunder, demands the force, power and sanction of the supreme civil magistrate, while the Pope's decrees alone, by a peculiar prerogative, have the force of laws, so that they can command and punish without the sanction of civil power? And since God has subjected to Christ, through the ministry of the Gospel, every secular power, every soul, and all things to be done and said, and since no evangelical minister of Christ uses in matters of belief and action a command or compulsion, but only persuasion, exhortation and declaration; and since the knowledge of the evangelical minister extends as widely as jurisprudence itself, indeed more widely, to the same degree that the rule of duties extends more widely than the rule of law; and conversely, since God on earth has subjected every person, all lawsuits, all things to be said and done, concerning whatever matter or business, in whatever place, time and assembly of men, as far as judgment goes, commanding, compelling and punishing, to the cognizance and empire of the supreme magistrate, and of him not as ecclesiastical (of which no mention anywhere appears in the sacred code) but as civil and political, it is plain that the Pope, insofar as he exercises empire over kings and peoples outside his own territory, exercises a purely earthly empire and civil and political jurisdiction, and that he cloaks it with the words ecclesiastical and spiritual only to make a show, lest his earthly empire be exposed.

units.la: LXXIIII. Ex iis quæ hactenus dicta sunt, meridiano clarius jubare emicat, Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ
units.tr: LXXIIII. From what has been said so far, it shines forth clearer than midday light that the hierarchy, or clergy of the Roman Church,

units.la: Romanæ dominantem, in Principe suo Papa, supremam sibi in spiritualibus potestatem arrogare, ejusque prætextu & titulo summum, atque illud merè terrenum & temporale in Reges & populos terræ Imperium gerere ; adeóque, quod inde ἀναγκαῖως consequitur, Ecclesiasticæ & spiritualis potestatis titulo Regnum in Reges & populos terræ terrenum obtinere, & ceu Reginam super aquis, hoc est, populis, gentibus, linguis multis, ipsaque Bestia sedere, denique cæteris paribus Babylonem Magnam esse, quod præsens demonstrationis nostræ caput erat.
units.tr: which rules in the Roman Church, claims for itself, in its prince the Pope, supreme power in spiritual matters, and under the pretext and title of this power holds a supreme empire over kings and peoples of the earth, and that empire is purely earthly and temporal; and therefore, as necessarily follows, under the title of ecclesiastical and spiritual power it obtains an earthly kingdom over the kings and peoples of the earth, and sits, as a queen above the waters, that is, over peoples, nations and many tongues, and upon the beast itself [ἀναγκαῖως]; and, other things being equal, that it is therefore Babylon the Great, which was the chief point of our demonstration.

units.la: LXXIV. Judicem insuper appello ipsum Innocentium IV. ex quo nullo negotio Papam, ceu Babylonium Regem & Monarcham ἀνδρικώτατον sistere licet.
units.tr: LXXIV. I call Innocent IV himself as a further witness, from whom one may without any difficulty present the Pope as the Babylonian king and most manly [ἀνδρικώτατον] monarch.

units.la: Is nempe Epistola ad Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum scripta diserris verbis professus, Petro, proin etiam Romano Pontifici, non solum universam Ecclesiam, sed totum etiam Seculum gubernandum commissum esse, id approbare conatus est Scripturæ testimoniis, inter alia sic ratiocinatus: Cum aquæ multæ sint populi multi (id verò ipsi ex Apoc. xvii. 15. ubi de Babylone sermo est, constiterat) congregationésque aquarum sint maria; per hoc, quòd Petrus super aquas maris incessit, super universos populos se potestatem accepisse, monstravit. Quid ni eodem argumento personatum Petrum, Papam scilicet, & Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem, Babylonem magnam esse concludere fas sit? Cùm enim aquæ multæ sint populi multi (Apoc. xvii. 15.) & Babylon Magna non tam incedat, quàm, quod plus est, sedeat super aquis multis (Apoc. xvii. 1.) hoc est, imperitet populis, turbis, gentibus & linguis multis (cap. xvii. 15.) Papam etiam Romanum, & Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem, non ambulantem duntaxat, sed sedentem etiam super aquis multis, adeóque, uti Innocentius fatidico spiritu suo declaravit, super universos populos
units.tr: For in his letter written to the Patriarch of Constantinople he openly professed that the whole Church, and indeed the whole secular world, had been committed to Peter, and therefore to the Roman Pontiff, to be governed. He tried to confirm this by the testimonies of Scripture, reasoning among other things as follows: Since the many waters are many peoples (he had established this from Rev. 17:15, where the discussion concerns Babylon), and the gatherings of the waters are the seas; by this, that Peter walked upon the waters of the sea, he showed that he had received power over all peoples. Why, then, may one not conclude by the same argument that the Papacy and the clergy of the Roman Church, who play Peter's part, are the Great Babylon? For since the many waters are many peoples (Rev. 17:15), and the Great Babylon does not merely walk but, what is more, sits upon many waters (Rev. 17:1), that is, rules over peoples, crowds, nations and many tongues (Rev. 17:15), then the Roman Pontiff and the clergy of the Roman Church, who not only walk but also sit upon many waters and, as Innocent declared by his prophetic spirit, rule over all peoples, must be the Great Babylon.

units.la: Innocentii IV. ipsius consensu amplius firmatur. lospotestatem sortitum, Babylonem Magnam esse, invicta argumentatione consequitur. ὁ᾽ πρ ἱσλʼε ἀδὸξαυ.
units.tr: It is further confirmed by the very consent of Innocent IV, and from this invincible argument it follows that one who has obtained such power is the Great Babylon. [obscura]

units.la: DISSERTATIO NONA.
units.tr: DISSERTATION NINE.

units.la: QUA
units.tr: IN WHICH

units.la: Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem Babylonem Magnam esse probatur Quartò, quia Babylonis M. habitus externus prætumidus ei quadrat.
units.tr: It is proved, fourthly, that the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, is the Great Babylon, because the outward habit of the Great Babylon, excessively proud, suits it.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Argumentum quartum ab habitu Mulieris exteriori petitum Syllogismo innectitur, cujus propositio probatur.
units.tr: I. The fourth argument, drawn from the outward habit of the Woman, is set out in a syllogism, the major premise of which is proved.

units.la: II. Assumptio demonstrata per partes. Mulier geminua, altera casta, Sponsa Christi; altera Meretrix distinguitur.
units.tr: II. The minor premise is demonstrated part by part. The Woman is distinguished as twofold: one chaste, the Bride of Christ; the other a Harlot.

units.la: III. Hierarchia Romana, Mulier Meretrix est, Sponsæ Christi inimica.
units.tr: III. The Roman hierarchy is the Harlot Woman, hostile to the Bride of Christ.

units.la: IV. Idipsum muliebris ejus & lasciviens animus, dominantis licet Viris, ostendit.
units.tr: IV. Her womanish and wanton spirit, though she rules over men, shows this same thing.

units.la: V. Mulieris Sponsæ Christi exterior habitus.
units.tr: V. The outward habit of the Woman, the Bride of Christ.

units.la: VI. Oppositus eidem Mulieris Babylonicæ exterior habitus, purpura, coccus, aurum, pretiosus lapis, Margaritæ.
units.tr: VI. The outward habit of the Babylonian Woman, opposed to this: purple, scarlet, gold, precious stone, pearls.

units.la: VII. Cuncta hæc ad literam in Hierarchia Romana reperire est. Persica ejus religio, & Sybariticus luxus.
units.tr: VII. All these things are to be found literally in the Roman hierarchy. Its Persian religion and Sybaritic luxury.

units.la: VIII. Ex Platina Authore Oneris Ecclesiæ, & Bernhardo in genere descriptus.
units.tr: VIII. Described in general from the author Platina, On the Burden of the Church, and from Bernard.

units.la: IX. Papa purpura & cocco delectatur.
units.tr: IX. The Pope delights in purple and scarlet.

units.la: X. Ejus Corona triplex auro gemmisque præfulget.
units.tr: X. His triple crown shines with gold and gems.

units.la: XI. Crux eidem præferri solita auro gemmisque constat. Neque placet Hierarchicis cultus Dei nisi aureus & gemmatus.
units.tr: XI. The cross customarily carried before him is made of gold and gems. Nor do the hierarchs approve of any worship of God that is not golden and gemmed.

units.la: XII. Secus quàm S. Petro.
units.tr: XII. Otherwise than with St Peter.

units.la: XIII. Cardinalium Senatus ruber. Galerus & biretum eorundem rubrum, atque hujus necessitas. De vestitu rubri iis præscripti ratione ariolationes.
units.tr: XIII. The senate of cardinals is red. The galero and biretta of the same are red, and the necessity of this. Conjectures concerning the red clothing prescribed for them.

units.la: XIV. Habitus Mulieris mystico sensu expositus eidem quadrat.
units.tr: XIV. The habit of the Woman, explained in a mystical sense, suits her.

units.la: XV. Mulieris exterior habitus habet, quod externa specie purpuram, coccum, aurum &c. referat.
units.tr: XV. The outward habit of the Woman has the feature that by its outward appearance it recalls purple, scarlet, gold, and so on.

units.la: XVI. Purpuræ & cocci speciem habuit pretiosus sanguis Christi, quem Hierarchici ubique præferunt, & cujus merito hominem justificari, mereri, satisfacere, legem Dei implere prætendunt.
units.tr: XVI. The precious blood of Christ had the appearance of purple and scarlet; the hierarchs put it forward everywhere, and claim by its merit that man is justified, merits, makes satisfaction, and fulfils the law of God.

units.la: XVII. Auri speciem habent dona Spiritus S. Verbum Dei, doctrinæ eximiæ & salutares. Hæc sibi, ceu peculium suum, Hierarchia vendicat.
units.tr: XVII. The gifts of the Holy Spirit, the Word of God, and excellent and salutary doctrines have the appearance of gold. The hierarchy claims these for itself as its own private property.

units.la: XVIII. Lapis pretiosus, quo inaurata Mulier est, Petram, super quam ædificata est Ecclesia, quam Petrum Hierarchici faciunt, significare potest.
units.tr: XVIII. The precious stone with which the Woman is gilded can signify the Rock upon which the Church is built, which the hierarchs make to be Peter.

units.la: XIX. S. Petri existimatione & authoritate suam Hierarchici suffulciunt.
units.tr: XIX. The hierarchs support their own authority by the reputation and authority of St Peter.

units.la: XX. Cum margaritis fideles eximios S. Scriptura comparat.
units.tr: XX. Holy Scripture compares outstanding believers to pearls.

units.la: XXI. Talibus Mulier gloriatur; gloriantur Hierarchici, ci, apud quos in cultu Dei & fide Sancti, Apostoli, Martyres, Patres utramque paginam faciunt.
units.tr: XXI. The Woman glories in such things; the hierarchs glory, among whom, in the worship of God and in the faith, the Saints, Apostles, Martyrs and Fathers make up both pages (of Scripture and tradition).

units.la: XXII. XXIII. De Patrum inprimis consensu eorundem fraudulenta gloriatio.
units.tr: XXII. XXIII. On the fraudulent boasting of the consent of the Fathers above all.

units.la: XXIV. Ad exteriorem Muliebris habitum Aureum quoque poculum refertur. Philtri rationem habere probatur.
units.tr: XXIV. The golden cup also belongs to the outward habit of the Woman. It is proved that it has the character of a love potion.

units.la: XXV. Poculum ejusmodi Circæum, intus scortatione & abominatione plenum in manu habere, & propinare populis Hierarchicos, asseritur.
units.tr: XXV. It is asserted that the hierarchs hold in their hand and offer to the peoples a cup of this kind, Circean, full within of fornication and abomination.

units.la: I. Ad Babylonis Magnæ characterem Quartum, habitum scilicet ejus exteriorem, immani fastu turgidum, ut progrediamur, demonstrationem suscepta mus novo argumento, quod numero Quartum est, hic molimur:
units.tr: I. Having undertaken to demonstrate the fourth mark of the Great Babylon, namely her outward habit, swollen with monstrous pride, let us proceed to set out here, with a new argument, which is the fourth, the following:

units.la: Ille cœtus Babylon Magna est, qui, cæteris paribus, similis est Mulieri, amicta purpura & coccino, inaurata auro ac lapide pretioso, gestanti in manu poculum aureum, plenum abominationibus & impuritate scortationis.
units.tr: That assembly is the Great Babylon which, other things being equal, is like a Woman clothed in purple and scarlet, gilded with gold and precious stone, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurity of fornication.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans, cæteris paribus, similis est Mulieri, amicta purpura & coccino, inaurata auro ac lapide pretioso, gestanti in manu peculum aureum, plenum abominationibus & impuritate scortationes.
units.tr: But the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, other things being equal, is like a Woman clothed in purple and scarlet, gilded with gold and precious stone, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurity of fornications.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the hierarchy, or the clergy of the Roman Church, is the Great Babylon.

units.la: Propositio extra contentionis aleam ab ipso Dei Angelo ponitur Apoc. xvii. 4. ubi sic habitum exteriorem Babylonis Magnæ definit: Καὶ ἡ γυνὴ, ἡ περιβεβλημένη πορφύρα & κοκκίνῳ, καὶ κεχρυσωμένη χρυσῷ & λίθῳ τιμίῳ, ἔχουσα ποτήριον χρυσοῦν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτῆς, γέμον βδελυγμάτων καὶ ἀκαθαρσιῶν πορνείας αὐτῆς. Et Mulier erat induĉta purpura & cocco & inaurata auro & lapide pretioso, & marcharitis, habens poculum aureum in manu sua plenum abominationibus, & impuritate fcortationis ejus. Mulierem dici Babylonem non proprie, sed similitudine quadam, sani omnes concedunt. Sed & sensum indefinitum verborum illorum Differt. iij. 28. 29. 30. reddidimus. Cætera autem paria partim prosecuti jam sumus, partim deinceps prosequemur. Assumptionem nunc quoque probatam demus.
units.tr: The major premise is laid down beyond the dispute of the die by the Angel of God himself, Apoc. xvii. 4, where he defines the outward habit of the Great Babylon thus: "And the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stone and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations and the impurities of her fornication" [Καὶ ἡ γυνὴ, ἡ περιβεβλημένη πορφύρα καὶ κοκκίνῳ, καὶ κεχρυσωμένη χρυσῷ καὶ λίθῳ τιμίῳ, ἔχουσα ποτήριον χρυσοῦν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτῆς, γέμον βδελυγμάτων καὶ ἀκαθαρσιῶν πορνείας αὐτῆς]. That the Woman is called Babylon, not properly but by a certain likeness, all sound men concede. But we have also rendered the indefinite sense of those words in Dissertation iii, 28, 29, 30. Of the other like features, we have partly already pursued them, and partly will pursue them hereafter. Let us now also give the proof of the minor premise.

units.la: II. Babylon Magna vocatur τυνη Mulier, sequioris sexus homo. Cujus appellationis rationem Differt. iij. 8. reddere occupavimus. Etiam Ecclesia, Sponsa Christi, vocatur τυνη Mulier Apoc. xii. 1. &c. cujus ibidem habitus & fata describuntur. Hæc casta, Deo unicè dilecta, quæ peperit Filium pascentem gentes virga ferrea, quo ad Deum & thronum ejus rapto, illa aufugit in desertum, & à Dracone ex Cœlo in terram deturbato immanem persecutionem passa est. Illa Meretrix propudiosissima (solent autem etiam scorta simpliciter מזנות Mulieres nuncupari; veluti Jos. ii. 1. 4. 8. Prov. vii. 10. xxxi. 3.) venefica sceleratissima (solent enim etiam mulieres præ viris veneficia exercere, adeo ut lex Divina Exod. xxii. 18. non adversus Virum, sed מכשפה Mulierem veneficam supplicium dictaverit, significans sexus ejus ad veneficia propensionem) Draconis thronum occupans, cum Regibus hujus mundi incesta consuetudine coalescens, & eosdem, ut & incolas terræ vino scortationis inebrians, adversus priorem illam Mulierem, & Filium ejusdem ad Cœlestum thronum raptum, infesta signa fert, eámque crudelissimè persequens modis omnibus opprimere conatur.
units.tr: II. The Great Babylon is called a Woman [γυνή], a human being of the weaker sex. We have undertaken to give the reason for this appellation in Dissertation iii, 8. The Church also, the Bride of Christ, is called a Woman [γυνή], Apoc. xii. 1, etc., where her habit and fortunes are described. This woman is chaste, uniquely beloved of God, who bore a Son ruling the nations with an iron rod; when he was caught up to God and his throne, she fled into the wilderness, and, cast down from heaven to earth by the Dragon, she suffered a monstrous persecution. That other woman is the most shameless harlot (for even common prostitutes are usually called women [זנות] by Scripture, as in Josh. ii. 1, 4, 8; Prov. vii. 10; xxxi. 3), the most wicked sorceress (for women more than men are wont to practise witchcraft, so much so that the divine law, Exod. xxii. 18, has prescribed punishment not against the man but against the woman sorceress [מכשפה], signifying the propensity of that sex toward witchcraft). She, occupying the throne of the Dragon, joined in incestuous fellowship with the kings of this world, and, making drunk with the wine of fornication both them and the inhabitants of the earth, she bears hostile standards against the former Woman and against her Son, caught up to the heavenly throne, and, raging against her most cruelly, she tries to crush her by every means.

units.la: III. Hierarchiæ Romanæ ceu Lupæ Babyloniæ & scortationem cum Regibus & incolis terræ; & hostilitatem ac certamina cum Ecclesia, Muliere casta, Sponsa Christi, & Filio Dei in cœlesti throno ad dextram Patris sedente perpetua, & impietatem Magicam multifariam, procedens tractatio nostra apertam in lucem proferet.
units.tr: III. Our treatment, proceeding, will bring into the open the Roman hierarchy as the wolf of Babylon, with its fornication with the kings and the inhabitants of the earth; and its hostility and contests with the Church, the chaste Woman, the Bride of Christ, and with the Son of God, who sits perpetually at the right hand of the Father on the heavenly throne; and its magical impiety in many forms.

units.la: IV. Fallor, an Babylonem mysticam Spiritus Dei Mulieris appellatione insigniens, insinuare haud obscurè etiam voluit, non tam virilem & masculam ei virtutem, quàm muliebrem, lascivientemque animum inesse, & per viros sibi subjectos latè dominari. Id verò quemadmodum Hierarchiæ Romanæ congruat, nemo non videt. Neque enim gladium ipsa gestat, vel ipsa immediatè vim expedit, vel, exceptis ferocioribus nonnullis, qui Amazonas referunt, exercitus ductat, sed, sexus infirmioris instar, firmioris robore cuncta subigit, & humilitatis ac nescio cujus mysterii prætextu rerum omnium potitur. Olim quidem genius Imperatorius, sub cujus alis juvencula hæc Meretricula delitescebat, prævalescens viriliter adhuc dominabatur, cùm Imperatores sibi Imperii habenas ab Episcopis plus quàm civilia meditantibus, extorqueri nondum paterentur. Sed ea tandem rerum conversio secuta est, qua marcescente Imperii vigore illi Robusti, de quibus Daniel loquitur, succumbere cœperunt, & contra Pontificum & Sacrificulorum per invalescentem superstitionem potestas vehementer amplificata, insania, & specie quadam virilia transmittendo, & clientibus suis, Imperatori, Regibus, Principibus subactis, relinquendo, vim Imperii omnem rapuit; retinuit, & per subjectos sibi viros expediit. Sed hæc οὐδὲν. Quanquam Spiritum S. non innuisse id, quod planissimè sic evenit, verisimile neutiquam est.
units.tr: IV. Am I mistaken, or did the Spirit of God, in designating the mystical Babylon by the name of Woman, wish also to hint not obscurely that she has not so much a manly and masculine virtue as a womanish and wanton spirit, and that she holds wide dominion through the men subject to her? How this fits the Roman hierarchy, nobody fails to see. For she does not herself bear the sword, nor does she herself directly wield force, nor, except for some fiercer ones who resemble Amazons, does she lead armies; but, like the weaker sex, she subdues everything by the strength of the stronger, and under the pretext of humility and I know not what mystery she has gained possession of all things. Formerly indeed the imperial genius, under whose wings this little young harlot lay hidden, still ruled manfully while prevailing, at a time when the emperors did not yet allow the reins of empire to be wrested from them by bishops meditating more than civil power. But at length there followed that change of affairs by which, as the vigour of the empire withered, those "strong ones" of whom Daniel speaks began to yield; and, as the power of the Pontiffs and sacrificing priests was greatly enlarged through the spreading superstition, they seized all the force of empire, and retained it, and wielded it through the men subject to them, transferring it with a certain appearance of manliness and leaving the emperor, the kings and the princes subdued and enslaved to their clients. But these things are nothing [οὐδὲν]. Yet it is in no way probable that the Holy Spirit did not intend what has happened in exactly this way.

units.la: V. Mulieri Dei, castissimæ & Sanctissimæ Christi Sponsæ, suum Spiritus Dei habitum circumposuit. Nam induc itur illa [illegible, ~12 letters], [illegible, ~12 letters], [illegible, ~10 letters] in cujus pedibus Luna, & in cujus capite co- amicta sole, sub cujus pedibus Luna, & in cujus capite corona est duodecim stellarum, Apoc. xii. 1. Nihil equidem attinet hic cum insulsis quibusdam Monachis de B. Virgine Maria cogitare, vel ex hoc ipso habitu ejusdem imaginem sculpere. Hoc ego cum reliquis fabulosis commentis ad authores suos remitto. Sanctæ potiùs & Deo dileCtissimæ Sponsæ, Ecclesiæ, quæ Mulier dicitur ob infirmitatem in hoc mundo, perinde uti S. Petrus 1. Ep. cap. iii.7. Mulieres infirmiora vasa vocat, habitus describitur. Magnificè enim amicta Sole, luce verbi Divini, Euangelii cumprimis in Prophetarum & Apostolorum scriptis undiquaque fulgentis; sub pedibus veluti calcans Lunam, tenebras illas, quæ ante Christum mundo incubuerunt, denique coronata duodecim stellis, Sanctis Prophetis, Patriarchis duodecim tribuum, totidémque Apostolis, universfis in uno fundamento Christo suavissimè confentientibus, inducitur.
units.tr: V. The Spirit of God has clothed the Woman of God, most chaste and most holy Bride of Christ, with his own habit. For she is introduced "clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars" (Apoc. xii. 1). Certainly it is of no concern here to think with certain silly monks about the Blessed Virgin Mary, or to carve her image from this very habit. I refer this, with the other fabulous inventions, to their own authors. Rather, the habit of the holy and most beloved Bride of God, the Church, who is called a Woman because of her weakness in this world, just as St Peter, 1 Ep. iii. 7, calls women "the weaker vessels", is described. For she is introduced magnificently clothed with the Sun, the light of the divine Word, the Gospel shining everywhere especially in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles; treading under her feet, as it were, the Moon, those shadows which lay upon the world before Christ; and finally crowned with twelve stars, the holy Prophets, the twelve patriarchs of the tribes, and as many Apostles, all agreeing most sweetly in one foundation, Christ.

units.la: VI. Babylonicæ Mulieris diversus longè habitus, ab Angelo Dei depingitur, talis videlicet, qualis hujusmodi meritorium propudium non vulgare, sed Regium (nam Meretrix Regina, qualis quondam Cleopatra, vel potiùs Iezabel fuit, inducitur) decet, quod Christo Regi Regum, & Domino dominantium fidem fregit, crucique ejus valedicens, quæstum in mundo facere occœpit. Solent enim meretrices vel maximè confidere externo cultui, cui impendunt, quicquid habent rerum & temporis. Propterea Apoc. xviii. 14. quæcunque luxus instrumenta sunt, ὀπώρα τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ψυχῆς fructus desiderii animæ Babylonis appellantur. Nihil igitur habitus hic cœleste habet: Solaris puritatis & splendoris nihil: non calcat Lunam: non radiant cœlestibus sideribus capita. Terrestria omnia deperit, purpuram, coccum, aurum, pretiosos lapides, magaritas, aliáque ejusmodi oculiferia maximis in deliciis habet.
units.tr: VI. The Babylonian woman is depicted by the angel of God in a very different dress, one suited not to an ordinary harlot but to a royal one (for she is presented as a queen-harlot, like Cleopatra of old, or rather like Jezebel), since she has broken faith with Christ, the King of kings and Lord of lords, and, bidding farewell to his cross, has begun to trade in the world. Harlots especially rely on the outward display to which they devote whatever wealth and time they have. For this reason, at Rev. 18:14, all the instruments of luxury are called the fruit of the desire of the soul [ὀπώρα τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ψυχῆς] of Babylon. This dress therefore has nothing heavenly about it: nothing of solar purity and brilliance. She does not tread on the moon, and her head does not shine with heavenly stars. She wears only earthly things: purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones, pearls, and other such dazzling things, which she holds in the greatest delight.

units.la: VII. Si
units.tr: VII. If

units.la: VII. Si ad literam habitus hic explicetur, cuncta hæc sibi ceu eximia Hierarchia Romana vindicat. Omnia purapura, cocco, auro, lapidibus pretiosis margaritis nitent. Quicquid Orienti & Occidenti spoliorum eripitur, Meretrici huic fucandæ & officinæ ejus exornandæ impenditur. Quem enim latet Persica religio luxúsque Sybariticus Pontificum, totiúsque cleri & cultus Romani, qui in eorum palatiis, obeliscis, angiportis, arcubus triumphalibus, statuis, thermis, basilicis, templis, tholis, cippis, altaribus, idolis, stolis, infulis, galeris, dalmaticis, habitúque universo conspicuus est. Cuncta nitent purpura, cocco, auro, lapidibus pretiosis, margaritis; atque eo nitore se incolis terræ insinuant; sicut Daniel cap. xi. 38. 39. prædixit, Antichristum Deum suum מעוזים fortitudinum, auro, argento, lapidibus pretiosis & desiderabilibus veneraturum esse. Sed de cleri, Papæ & Cardinalium inprimis habitu nonnulla dicentes, fidem oraculo faciamus.
units.tr: VII. If this dress is explained literally, the Roman hierarchy claims all these things for itself as its own splendid possessions. Everything glitters with purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones and pearls. Whatever is snatched from East and West as plunder is spent on dyeing this harlot and adorning her workshop. Who does not know the Persian pomp and the Sybaritic luxury of the Pontiffs, and of the whole clergy and Roman worship, which is conspicuous in their palaces, obelisks, alleys, triumphal arches, statues, baths, basilicas, temples, domes, pillars, altars, idols, stoles, mitres, galeros, dalmatics, and the whole of their dress? Everything shines with purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones and pearls, and by that glitter they insinuate themselves to the inhabitants of the earth, just as Daniel foretold at 11:38-39, that the Antichrist would honour his god of fortresses [מעוזים], with gold, silver, precious stones and costly things. But, saying something first of the dress of the clergy, of the Pope and especially of the Cardinals, let us make the oracle our witness.

units.la: VIII. In universum sic Platina in Gregorio IV. quiritatur: In omnem luxum & libidinem sese effundit Ecclesiasticus ordo. Coccinatos & trabeatos nunc inspiceres, non homines; quod leve fortasse videretur, sed equos & jumenta: precedente, dum incedunt, magno adolescentum, & altero Presbyterorum agmine subsequente; non in asinis, ut Christus noştri dogmatis author, & bene vivendi unicum in terris exemplar: sed etiam in equis præferocibus & phaleratis: ac si ex hoste devicto triumphum ducerent. De argenteis vasis, & egregia eorum supellectile, déque cibariis non attinet dicere: cùm & Siciliæ dapes, & Attalica ornamenta, & vasa Corinthia, si hæc inspicias, nullius pretii dici possint. Author Oneris Ecclesiæ cap. 19. Quid quòd Papa incedit inauratus, gemmatus, vario ornatu decoratus, militefstipatus, equo albo vectus, aut à Ministris in altum portatus? Hæc sunt magis dæmonum quàm
units.tr: VIII. In general, Platina complains thus about Gregory IV: The ecclesiastical order pours itself out into every luxury and lust. You would see scarlet-clad and purple-robed men, not men but, as might perhaps seem a light matter, horses and beasts of burden: a great column of young men going before, and another of priests following, as they go; not on asses, as Christ, the author of our doctrine and the sole pattern of right living on earth, went, but even on very fierce and caparisoned horses, as if leading a triumph over a defeated enemy. There is no need to speak of their silver vessels and their splendid household goods, or of their food, since, if you look at them, the feasts of Sicily, the Attalic ornaments and the Corinthian vessels could be called of no worth at all. The author of Onus Ecclesiae, chapter 19: What of the fact that the Pope goes about gilded, jewelled, decked with various ornaments, attended by soldiers, carried on a white horse, or lifted high by his ministers? These are rather the pastures of demons than

units.la: Ex Platina Autore Oneris Ecclesiæ. Bernardo in gestis de scriptis. quàm ovium pascua. Ubi non est pastus ovium, sed pastus ovium, ibi non Petro, sed Constantino succeditur. Bernhardus de Consid. lib. v. cap. 2. sic Papam alloquitur: Inter hæc tu Pastor procedis deauratus, tam multa circumdatus varietate. Oves quid capiunt? Si auderem dicere: Dæmonum magis, quàm ovium pascua hæc.
units.tr: From Platina, the author of Onus Ecclesiae; from Bernard, in the Gesta, on the writings: than the pastures of sheep. Where there is not the feeding of sheep, but the feeding of sheep, there Constantine, not Peter, is the successor. Bernard, in De consideratione, book 5, chapter 2, addresses the Pope thus: Among these things you, a shepherd, go forward gilded, surrounded by so much variety. What do the sheep gain? If I dared to say it: these are rather the pastures of demons than of sheep.

units.la: IX. De Papæ, Principis Babylonii Supremi habitu multa equidem ad rem dici possent. Defungar paucis Rubrum ei colorem, purpureum & coccineum in deliciis esse, nemo nescit, atque à Marcello Episcopo Corcyrensi Cerem. Sacr. lib. iij. sect. 5. cap. 5. sic confirmatur: Ruber color præcipuè ad Papam pertinet. Idem Lib. Ceremon. iij. lit. 3. f. 4. p. 127. testis est, in nocte Nativitatis Domini Nostri Jesu Christi uti solere Pontificem cappa purpurea, pellibus armillinis duplicata, quam primus Bonifacius ix. invenerit. Addit, duobus Papam uti coloribus, albo & rubro, utroque in pluviali &c. In aliis vestibus non sacris supra rochetum, rubro tantùm; infra rochetum, toga alba, & caligis rubris. Baronius ad A. 324. n. 79. Privilegia Gentilium Sacerdotum, qui purpuram induebant, Christianis Sacerdotibus tributa esse asserit. Fictitia Constantini M. Donatio supponit, Sedem Romanam gloriosius exaltandam, quàm Sedem Imperatoris: atque adeò omnia ei concedit, quibus ad maximam pompam Imperatores uti solent. Inter alia sic pronuntiat: Beato Silvestro & omnibus ejus Successoribus tradimus palatium Imperii nostri Lateranense: deinde diadema, videlicet coronam capitis nostri, chlamydem purpuream, atque tunicam coccineam, & omnia Imperialia indumenta. Paschali II. authori acceptum alii referunt, quòd Papa electus coccinea chlamyde statim ornatur, atque sic in Papali dignitate confirmatur. Sed & Pius II. Perusiam ingressus est, equo vectus candidissimo, duodecim eodem candore præcedentibus stratis purpura, sine sessore, frœnis aureis: Magistratibus purpuream umbellam auro intextam præferentibus, sub qua ipse candida sindone, stola aurea, & purpureo superbus galero vehebatur, Wolphio Memor. Lett. Tom. ÿ. p. 457. narrante. Simon Majolus Dier. Canic. Tom. ÿ. p. 42. ex variis authoribus refert, aliis Diis alios colores placere; inferis atros, Cœlestibus purpureos, quibusdam, velut Cereri, albos. Papa igitur Cœlesti choro semetipsum adscribens, propterea, juxta Lancellotum Templ. Jud. lib. ÿ. 1. pag. 540. purpureis vestibus delectatur. En mulierem purpura coccóque indutam!
units.tr: IX. Many things could indeed be said about the dress of the Pope, the supreme prince of Babylon. I shall deal with it briefly. That red, purple and scarlet are his delight, no one is unaware; and Marcellus, bishop of Corfu, confirms this in Ceremonies, book 3, section 5, chapter 5: Red colour belongs especially to the Pope. The same author, in Liber Ceremoniarum, book 3, title 3, folio 4, page 127, is a witness that on the night of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ the Pontiff is accustomed to wear a purple cope, doubled with ermine furs, which Boniface IX first devised. He adds that the Pope uses two colours, white and red, both in the cope, etc. In other, non-sacred vestments, above the rochet only red; below the rochet a white toga and red hose. Baronius, at the year 324, no. 79, asserts that the privileges of the pagan priests, who used to put on purple, were granted to Christian priests. The fictitious Donation of Constantine the Great supposes that the Roman See is to be exalted more gloriously than the seat of the Emperor, and therefore grants it everything with which the Emperors are accustomed to use for the greatest pomp. Among other things it pronounces thus: To Blessed Sylvester and to all his successors we hand over the Lateran palace of our empire; then the diadem, that is, the crown of our head, the purple cloak, and the scarlet tunic, and all the imperial garments. Others refer to Paschal II as the author of the custom that a Pope, once elected, is at once adorned with a scarlet cope, and thus confirmed in the papal dignity. But Pius II also, entering Perugia, rode on a most white horse, with twelve attendants in the same white, their trappings purple, without a rider, with golden bridles; the magistrates carried a purple canopy embroidered with gold, under which he himself was borne, proud in a white linen cloth, a golden stole and a purple galero, as Wolphius relates in Memorabilia, volume 5, page 457. Simon Majolus, in Dierum Canicularium, volume 5, page 42, reports from various authors that different colours please different gods: black for the infernal ones, purple for the heavenly ones, and white for some, such as Ceres. The Pope, therefore, by ascribing himself to the heavenly choir, for this reason, according to Lancellotti in Templum Iudaicum, book 5, part 1, page 540, delights in purple garments. Behold the woman clothed in purple and scarlet!

units.la: X!.
