Inter insignia Papæ Corona triplex, quæ Tiara, Regnum, Cidaris, utpote speciem referens pilei summi Sacerdotis apud Hebræos, & juxta Dianam Chamaurus (obcurissima voce) alias appellatur, eminet; hieroglyphicum scilicet Papalis Majestatis, ad Cœlestia, terrena & inferna pertinentis, uti Reinaudus apud Dianam de Adorat. Papæ pag. ÿ. loquitur. De ejus origine sententiæ variant. Antonius Mazaronius lib. de tribus Pontif. coronis, Pafchalius Coron. lib. xix. 14. Sigebertus A. 550. alii authores sunt, Clodoveum diadema aureum unionibus & gemmis insigne, quod Regnum dicebatur, ab Anastasio Imperatore acceptum Ecclesiæ offerendum Romam misisse. Hanc Pontifices primùm mitræ suæ junxisse ferunt. Alterum addidisse Bonifacium VIII. qui dare regna & auferre pro arbitrio animi conabatur. uti Platina loquitur; post Extravagantem Unam Sanctam publicatam, communis est opinio. Quamobrem etiam Pontifex iste, ejusque Successores aliquot cum duplici corona in statuis ac imaginibus Romæ Avinionéque conspiciuntur. Benedictus XII. tertiam addidisse dicitur. Unde triregni appellatio orta est. Quamvis antiquius hoc gestamen fuisse, Jacobus Cardinalis Papiensis Comment. de rebus Pauli lib. ÿ. autumat. Sed de origine ejus quicquid fiat, auro pretiosifque unionibus intertextam esse, satis constat. In Paralipomenis enim Urspergensis, Amedeo Sabaudiæ Duce electo Basileæ in Pontificem, vocatoque Felici V. Ludovicus Cardinalis Hostiensis infulam Pontificalem imposuit, æstimatam aureis triginta millibus. Idque etiam Æneas Sylvius in Epistola ad Johannem de Segovia, quæ in fascic. rer. expet. sol. 25. 26. reperitur, confirmat. Clemens V. is, qui Sedem Roma Avinionem transtulit, cùm Lugduni coronaretur, in tumultu, equo deturbatus extiara carbunculum amisit pretii aureorum sex millium, Platina in ejus vita teste. Qui idem Pauli II. describendo luxui vix putavit stylum suum sufficere. Fuere, inquit, qui dicerent, eum, dum in publicum prodiret, faciem sibi fucis concinnare. De apparatu Pontificis non est cur ambigas, majores ab hoc uno superatos Regno præsertim, sive mitram velis appellare, in quam multas opes contulit, coemptis undique ac magnis pretiis, adamantibus, Saphiris, smaragdis, chrysolithis, jaspidibus, unionibus, & quicquid gemmarum in pretio est, quibus ornatus, tanquam alter Aaron, in publicum forma humana augustiore prodibat. Inspici tum ab omnibus volebat & admirari. Et in Hadriano I. eundem Paulum adeò his muliebribus delinimentis delectatum esse scribit, undique conquisitis magno pretio gemmis, & exhausto pœne Ecclesiæ Romanæ ærario, ut quotiescunque in publicum prodiret, Cybele quædam Phrygia ac turrita, non mitrata videretur. En mulierem inauratam auro, lapide pretioso & margaritis.
units.tr: X. Among the insignia of the Pope stands out the triple crown, which is called Tiara, Regnum, Cidaris, since it represents the form of the high priest's cap among the Hebrews, and, according to Diana, is also called Chamaurus (a most obscure word). It is the hieroglyph of papal majesty, pertaining to heavenly, earthly and infernal things, as Reinaudus speaks in Diana, On the Adoration of the Pope, page 5. Opinions differ about its origin. Antonius Mazaronius, in De tribus Pontificum coronis, Paschalius, Corona, book 19, chapter 14, and Sigebert, at the year 550, and other authors say that Clovis, having received from the emperor Anastasius a golden diadem remarkable for pearls and gems, which was called the Regnum, sent it to Rome to be offered to the Church. The Pontiffs are said first to have joined it to their mitre. A second crown was added, according to the common opinion, by Boniface VIII, who attempted to give and take away kingdoms at the will of his mind, as Platina says, after the Extravagant Unam Sanctam was published. For this reason, too, this Pontiff and several of his successors are seen with a double crown in statues and images at Rome and Avignon. Benedict XII is said to have added a third. Whence the name triregnum arose. Although Jacob Cardinal of Pavia, in Commentaries on the deeds of Paul, book 5, thinks this ornament is older. But whatever be the origin of it, it is quite certain that it was interwoven with gold and costly pearls. For in the Paralipomena of Urspergensis, when Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, was elected Pope at Basel and called Felix V, Cardinal Ludovico of Ostia placed the pontifical mitre on him, valued at thirty thousand gold pieces. Aeneas Sylvius also confirms this in his letter to John of Segovia, which is found in Fascicle of rare and desired things, pages 25-26. Clement V, who transferred the See from Rome to Avignon, when he was crowned at Lyons, was thrown from his horse in the tumult and lost a carbuncle from his tiara, worth six thousand gold pieces, as Platina testifies in his life. The same writer, describing the luxury of Paul II, thought his pen scarcely sufficient. There were, he says, those who said that he, when he came out in public, arranged his face with cosmetics. There is no reason for you to doubt the splendour of the Pontiff: he was surpassed by greater men, especially by the king, or if you wish to call it a mitre, into which he poured great wealth, buying up on all sides at great prices adamants, sapphires, emeralds, chrysolites, jaspers, pearls, and whatever gems are prized, with which adorned, like another Aaron, he came out in public with a human form more majestic. He wanted to be looked at and admired by all then. And concerning Hadrian I he writes that the same Paul was so delighted with these womanly enticements, having gathered gems on all sides at great price and having almost emptied the treasury of the Roman Church, that whenever he came out in public he seemed not mitred but like some turreted Phrygian Cybele. Behold the woman gilded with gold, precious stone and pearls.

units.la: XI. Nihil dicam de Cruce illa, quæ ante Pontificem à Subdiacono fertur, quámque Leo IV. ex auro gemmisque ornatam fieri jussit, dum nullum, inquit Platina, genus ornamenti relinqueret, quod ad dignitatem Salvatoris non. Nam ita jam pridem persuasum Pontificibus Pontificiisque, non bene honorari Deum, si non omnia scateant gemmis, si non omnia sint aurea.
units.tr: XI. I say nothing of that cross which is carried before the Pontiff by a subdeacon, and which Leo IV ordered to be adorned with gold and jewels, since, says Platina, he would leave no kind of ornament that was not befitting the dignity of the Saviour. For the Pontiffs and the Papists had long been persuaded that God is not honoured well unless everything glitters with gems and everything is gold.

units.la: XII. Non sic profecto Petrus, quia (sic Eugenium Papam Bernhardus jam olim pulsavit) nescitur processisse aliquando vel gemmis ornatus, vel sericis: non tectus auro, non vestitus equo albo, nec stipatus milite, nec circumstrepentibus septus ministris. Absque tamen his credidit satis posse impleri salutare mandatum: Si amas me, pasce oves meas.
units.tr: XII. Surely Peter did not do so. As Bernard once rebuked Pope Eugenius, it is not recorded that he ever went forth adorned with jewels or silks, not covered with gold, not dressed on a white horse, not attended by soldiers, nor surrounded by noisy ministers. Yet without these things he believed the saving command could be fulfilled: If you love me, feed my sheep.

units.la: - XIII. Papæ Senatus Edomiticus, Cardinales, toti purpura & coccino præfulgent. Ornamenta eorum sunt, galerus ruber, ab Innocentio IV. iis vindicatus: birretum rubrum, tam iis necessarium, ut si absens creatus intra annum cum ornamento hoc ad Curiam se non contulerit, dignitate sua excidat. Sic decernente Sixto IV. in Bulla A. 1586. die 3. Decembris edita. In conclavi Papam electuri vestibus croceis uti omnes Gregorius XV. Bulla A. 1621. 16. Nov. vulgata jussit. Et vestem purpuream Bonifacius VIII. vel, ut alii volunt, Paulus II. communem omnibus fecit. De ratione vero rubri coloris, galeri & vestis Cardinalibus præscripti diversimodè ariolantur. Johannes Baptista de Rubeis Ration. Div. offic. cap. 53. rationem hanc reddit, quòd Cardinales ad effusionem usque sanguinis ad defensionem Papæ & Ecclesiæ parati esse debeant. Alii rationem à dignitate & splendore eorum arcessunt. Alii alia conjectant. Rem acu tetigit, quisquis sic cecinit, vates: Semiviros quicunque Patres radiant & Galero Conspicis, & rubræ syrmata longa togæ: Crede mihi, nullo saturatas murice vestes, Divite nec coccopallia tincta vides. Sed quæ rubra vides Sanctorum cæde virorum, Et mersa insonti tota cruore madent; Aut memor iflorum, quæ celet, crimina, vestisPro dominis justo tacta pudore madet.
units.tr: - XIII. The Popes' Edomite senate, the Cardinals, shine out entirely in purple and scarlet. Their insignia are the red hat, which Innocent IV assigned to them; and the red biretta, which is so necessary to them that if one created while absent does not come to the Curia within a year with this insignia, he forfeits his dignity. So decreed Sixtus IV in the bull issued on 3 December 1586. Gregory XV, in the bull published on 16 November 1621, ordered that all who would elect a Pope in the conclave use saffron robes. Boniface VIII, or as others hold, Paul II, made the purple robe common to all. Concerning the reason for the red colour, of the hat and of the robe prescribed for Cardinals, people guess in various ways. John Baptist de Rubeis, Ration. Div. offic. cap. 53., gives this reason: that Cardinals ought to be ready to shed their blood, even to the last drop, in defence of the Pope and the Church. Others derive the reason from their dignity and splendour. Others conjecture other things. That poet hit the mark who sang thus: You see that the half-men, the Fathers, who shine with the Galero, and the long trains of the red toga: believe me, you see no robes soaked with the murex dye, nor coccopalls dyed by the wealthy. But what you see red is the slaughter of holy men, and all is soaked and drenched in innocent blood; or, mindful of the crimes that they conceal, the robe stained by the lords' guilt is soaked in a just shame.

units.la: Σοφὸς planè! Neque minùs argutè, imò planè ex sententia vaticinii nostri, Huldricus Zwinglius nostras dixisse fertur, non frustrà Cardinales rubros galeros, & purpureas vestes gestare. Sive enim ventilentur, nil eos nisi rubentes nummos, aureos & coronatos reddere; sive premantur, nil nisi rubentem sanguinem innocentum ex iisdem stillare.
units.tr: Wise indeed! Just as shrewdly, and indeed exactly in line with our prophecy, Huldrych Zwingli is said to have remarked that the Cardinals do not wear red hats and purple robes in vain. For whether they are shaken, they yield nothing but red money, gold and crowns; and whether they are squeezed, they yield nothing but the red blood of the innocent.

units.la: XIV. Quis ergo non videt, habitum exteriorem Babylonis Magnæ, si ad literam ille explicetur, Romanæ Hierarchiæ congruere exactissimè? Quòd si mystico sensu, quem Differt. iij. 29. explanavimus, idem explicetur, nulli certè magis, quàm Hierarchiæ eidem quadrare, comperietur facilè.
units.tr: XIV. Who then does not see that the outward dress of Great Babylon, if it is explained literally, fits the Roman hierarchy most exactly? And if the same is explained in the mystical sense, which we set out in Dissertation iii. 29, it will easily be found to fit that same hierarchy more than any other.

units.la: XV. Etenim Mulier purpura & cocco πεποικιλμένη indúcta, auro lapide pretioso & margaritis κεχρυσωμένη inaurata cùm dicitur; sic satis aperte insinuatur habere aliquid, quod speciem externam purpuræ, sanguinis, auri, lapidum pretiosorum, margaritarum exhibeat, & inquo unicè se proferat jactétque. Nam & induentes se externa indumentorum specie ostentare, & non raro alia omnia mentiri solent: & quæ inaurata sunt, auro extus fulgente, & lapidibus pretiosis foris exsplendescentibus, alia omnia intus tegere & abstrudere possunt. Inauratis enim instrumentis fucus subesse solet, ut foris aurum esse videatur, quod intus vix cuprum est. Mulieris hypocrisis apertè notatur, quæ cum inanibus larvis fuco & fallaciis, omnique ἐπιφυΐα τῆς κλάσης apparet.
units.tr: XV. For when the Woman is said to be clothed [indúcta] in purple and scarlet, [πεποικιλμένη], and gilded [inaurata] with gold, precious stone and pearls [κεχρυσωμένη], it is quite plainly hinted that she has something which displays the outward appearance of purple, blood, gold, precious stones and pearls, and in which alone she shows herself off and boasts. For those who dress up are wont to show off the outward appearance of their garments, and very often to deceive in every other respect; and things that are gilded, shining outwardly with gold and glittering on the outside with precious stones, can conceal and hide everything else within. For a pretence usually lies beneath gilded objects, so that what is gold on the outside is scarcely copper within. The hypocrisy of the Woman is plainly marked, who appears with empty masks, deceit and trickery, and with every outward show [ἐπιφυΐα τῆς κλάσης].

units.la: XVI. Purpuræ & cocci speciem habuit pretiosus sanguis Christi. Quis iste, qui venit de Edom, rubras vestes habens de Bozra? Quare rubrum est indumentum tuum, & vestimentum tuum est sicut calcantis in torculari? Efai.
units.tr: XVI. The precious blood of Christ had the appearance of purple and scarlet. Who is this that comes from Edom, with red garments from Bozrah? Why is your apparel red, and your garments like his who treads in the winepress? Isaiah.

units.la: LXIII. 1. 2. Peccata scilicet כשנים coccinea, & כתולע purpurea (Esai. 1. 18) coccineum & purpuratum sanguinem Christi, quo expiarentur, flagitárunt. Christum ergo, qui ἐν αἵματι in sanguine venit, 1. Joh. v. 6. eúmque pro Ecclesia effudit, isthæc Mulier profiteri & jactare debuit, sed specie potiús externa, quàm vi ulla pietatis; tegens externa isthac specie, quicquid impietatis est. Planè sic Hierarchia Romana Christum, ejus sanguinem pro peccatis hominum effusum ubique præfert. Ante omnium oculos Christum cruore madentem statuit. Sanguinis ejus merito nos justificari, regenerari, Sanctificari imò & mereri, satisfacere Deo pro pœnis temporalibus, legem Dei perfectè implere, liberi arbitrii nostri viribus salutem consequi, inter ζωὴν & δόξαν suas pridem retulit. Putares amore Christi crucifixi exarsisse totos. Sed profectò nonnisi purpurea & coccinea hæc Mulieris vestimenta sunt, sub quibus doctrinam merito sanguinis Christi prorsus inimicam, scortationem spiritualem, & omne genus turpitudinis occultari, infra manifestum faciemus.
units.tr: Isaiah 63:1, 2. Namely, sins [as scarlet, כשנים], and [as crimson, כתולע] (Isa. 1:18), demanded the scarlet and crimson blood of Christ, by which they were to be atoned. Therefore this Woman ought to profess and boast of Christ, who came in blood [ἐν αἵματι in sanguine], 1 John 5:6, and who poured out his blood for the Church; but she does so in an outward show rather than in any power of godliness, covering with that outward show whatever impiety there is. Just so the Roman hierarchy everywhere puts forward Christ and his blood shed for the sins of men. It sets Christ, drenched in blood, before the eyes of all. That by the merit of his blood we are justified, regenerated and sanctified, and even merit and make satisfaction to God for temporal punishments, fully fulfil the law of God, and by the strength of our free will attain salvation, it has long reckoned among its life and glory [ζωὴν & δόξαν]. You would think they were all on fire with love of the crucified Christ. But these are truly only the purple and scarlet garments of the Woman, under which, as we shall show below, a doctrine utterly hostile to the merit of Christ's blood, spiritual fornication, and every kind of wickedness are hidden.

units.la: XVII. Solent divina auri nomine insigniri. Ita pretiosissimæ Spiritus S. gratiæ Zach. iv. 12. eloquia Dei purissima. Psal. xix. 10. 11. doctrinæ maximè salutares & utiles.
units.tr: XVII. Divine things are wont to be marked by the name of gold. Thus the most precious graces of the Holy Spirit, the purest words of God, Zech. iv. 12; Ps. xix. 10, 11, are the most wholesome and useful doctrines.

units.la: 1. Cor. iii. 12. זהב χρυσὸς auri nomine veniunt. Tali auro inaurata procedit mulier: procedit Hierarchia Romana. Nihil enim magis quàm perpetuam Spiritus S. assistentiam jactat, eámque ceu peculium quoddam, à quo plebem procul removet, sibi vendicat. Illa spiritualis sola cluet: populus ceu animalis, neque aliter quàm derivato & veluti mutuò à Papa capite accepto Spiritu insignis, deprimitur. Verbum Dei à sua scilicet authoritate suspensum, & sensu suo animatum fœcundatúmque, ceu sibi proprium, allegat, & ejusdem testimonio omnem, quam usurpat, potestatem & authoritatem confirmare nititur.
units.tr: 1 Cor. iii. 12: they come under the name of gold [זהב; χρυσὸς]. The Woman goes forth adorned with this gold; the Roman hierarchy goes forth. For nothing does it boast of more than the perpetual help of the Holy Spirit, and it claims that help for itself as a kind of private possession, from which it keeps the common people far away. It alone is called spiritual; the people, as natural, are held down, marked by no Spirit except one received on loan, as it were, from the Pope, the head. It cites the Word of God, suspended from its own authority and given life and fruitfulness by its own sense, as if it were its own property, and strives to confirm by that witness all the power and authority it claims for itself.

units.la: Denique doctrinas quasdam ἐξωρίστως[?] & principales, cujusmodi sunt dogmata de S. Triade, Christo Salvatore & capite Ecclesiæ, remissione peccatorum, extremo judicio, aliáque ejusmodi frequenter in ore habet. Tali scilicet auro interiora sua, puta Spiritum mundi & Antichristi, dominationem merè temporalem, Suprematum Papæ, cultum creaturarum, ambitionis, avaritiæ, luxuriæ acres assectus, aliáque κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης[?] inaurare solet.
units.tr: Finally, it frequently has on its lips certain doctrines [ἐξωρίστως?] that are chief, such as the teachings about the Holy Trinity, Christ the Saviour and Head of the Church, the forgiveness of sins, the last judgment, and others of that kind. Under such gold it is wont to gild its inner things, namely the spirit of the world and of Antichrist, a purely temporal dominion, the supremacy of the Pope, the worship of creatures, and the keen desires of ambition, avarice and lust, and other hidden things of shame [κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης?].

units.la: XVIII. Forte λίθος τίμιος[?] Lapis pretiosus, quo se Mulier inaurâsse dicitur, significat Petram, super quam ædificata est Ecclesia, Matth. xvi. 18. Hunc pretiosum Lapidem, hanc Petram Hierarchia Romana, ceu palladium quoddam, sine fine & modo jactat, Petri ei omnia alligant; Eam Petrum esse, ejúsque Successores, Romanos Pontifices; atque his, ceu Ostiariis datas esse claves Regni Cœlorum, acerrimè contendit. Observárunt enim pridem Ecclesiæ Romanæ Antistites, hoc de Petro, Ecclesiæ Petra, seu Lapide pretioso, & de claudendi aperiendique potestate soli Petro commissa, dogma ad Imperii sui fines propagandos, & ad subjugandas terras omnes, per quidem commodum & opportunum esse. Quamobrem opinionem eam artificiosius alere, & infinitis technarum copiis, sub speciosò ubique Petri, ceu Lapidis illius pretiosi nomine, sustentare, curæ cordíque unicè habuit.
units.tr: XVIII. Perhaps the precious stone [λίθος τίμιος?], the precious Stone [Lapis pretiosus], with which the Woman is said to be gilded, signifies the Rock upon which the Church is built, Matt. xvi. 18. This precious Stone, this Rock, the Roman hierarchy boasts of without end or measure, as if it were a kind of palladium; it attaches everything to Peter. It contends most fiercely that he is that Rock, and that his successors, the Roman Pontiffs, are given the keys of the kingdom of heaven as its doorkeepers. For the bishops of the Roman Church long ago observed that this doctrine concerning Peter, the rock of the Church or precious Stone, and concerning the power of binding and loosing committed to Peter alone, is a convenient and useful means for extending their empire and subjecting all lands. Therefore they took special care, and cared for nothing more, to nourish that opinion more cunningly and to sustain it by endless crafts, always under the specious name of Peter, as of that precious Stone.

units.la: XIX. Etenim S. Petri exiʃtimatione & authoritate subnixi Hierarchici C. sic omnes Dist. 19. pronuntiârunt, Omnes sanctiones Apostolicæ Sedis accipiendas esse, tanquam ipsius Divina voce Petri firmatas. Docuerunt, suam Ecclesiam ab omni errore intactam permanere, gratia & auxilio Petri, uti Agatho Pontifex Epist. 6. Synod. Const. act. 4. loquitur. Decreverunt C. in memor. Dist. 19. licet vix ferendum ab illa Sancta sede imponatur jugum, tamen ferendum esse in memoriam B. Petri. Releverunt dolia sua, & in Donatione Constantini C. Constantinus dist. 96. exprompserunt: Concessisse eum illis coronam suam ex auro purissimo, & gemmis pretiosis; qua uterentur pro honore B. Petri. Illud quoque affinxerunt, Constantinum tenuisse frenum equi Papæ, pro reverentia B. Petri stratoris officium illi exhibentem. Imperatorem impulerunt, tanquam vasallum Pontificis, ut B. Petri eques esset, & conceptis verbis Petro juraret, se, quicquid de terra S. Petri ad suam potestatem pervenerit, Papæ sanctitati redditurum, & adjutorem Papæ sanctitatis futurum, ad defendendam terram S. Petri, secundum suum posse, uti S. Cerem. Eccl. Rom. lib. 1. sect. 10. legere est.
units.tr: XIX. Indeed, relying on the esteem and authority of St Peter, the hierarchs pronounced, C. sic omnes Dist. 19., that all the decrees of the Apostolic See are to be accepted as if confirmed by the very voice of Peter himself. They taught that their Church remains untouched by every error, by the grace and help of Peter, as Pope Agatho speaks in Epistle 6 to the Sixth Council of Constantinople, act 4. They decreed in C. in memor., Dist. 19, that although a yoke is imposed by that Holy See which can scarcely be borne, nevertheless it must be borne in memory of the blessed Peter. They opened their casks and drew out of the Donation of Constantine, C. Constantinus dist. 96., that he granted them his crown of purest gold and precious stones, to be used for the honour of the blessed Peter. They added also that Constantine held the bridle of the Pope's horse, performing for him the office of groom out of reverence for the blessed Peter. They drove the Emperor, as the vassal of the Pontiff, to be the horseman of the blessed Peter, and in express words swore to Peter that whatever of the land of St Peter came into his power he would return to the holiness of the Pope, and would be a helper of the holiness of the Pope in defending the land of St Peter according to his power, as may be read in S. Cerem. Eccl. Rom. lib. 1. sect. 10.

units.la: Archiepiscopis C. quoniam quidam, Dist. 100. & S. Cerem. Eccl. R. lib. 1. sect. 10. impositerunt, ut sentiant, suam potestatem nullam esse, nisi primum Pontifex mittat pallium de corpore B. Petri sumptum, in quo est plenitudo Pontificalis officii. Solenni Sacramento C. Ego N. Episc. Extra de jure jurando, Episcopos astrinxerunt, ut promittant obedientiam suam, & fidem S. Petro, Romanæ Ecclesiæ, & Domino suo Papæ. Imò ab Episcopis ad eos, qui dignitates recipiunt, devenerunt, quos eodem sacramento premunt, uti apud Felinum Comm. in cap. Ego N. Episcop. de jurejur. legere est. Et, quod cætera omnia facile vincat, ubi formula jurisjurandi in Jure Canonico descripta, obligat hoc pacto, ut defendant regulas S. Patrum, Papa Gregorius ix. apud Matthæum Paris in Henrico iij. & Gregorius xiii. in Bulla ad Mauritium Episcopum Imelacensem, jam olim hodieque in illorum locum subdiderunt, Regalia S. Petri. Hæc igitur Lapidis illius pretiosi, S. Petri, quem Petram illi nuncupant, ostentatio si non in maximis, tamen in maximè artificiosis præstigiis hactenus fuit spiritualium illarum fraudum, unde tot bonis hactenus Papa affluxit, & ad tantum Ecclesia Romana fastigium enixa est. Accedit, quòd, sicut Hortensius, Cicerone teste, Eloquentiam summis laudibus extulit, ut cum ea in Cœlum ipse ascenderet: sic Hieronymus, chici B. Petrum summis & Divinis elogiis mactare s ut una cum eo beatiores se ipsos reddant.
units.tr: The Archbishops, C. quoniam quidam, Dist. 100. and S. Cerem. Eccl. R. lib. 1. sect. 10., have been required to hold that their power is nothing unless the Pontiff first sends the pallium taken from the body of St Peter, in which is the fullness of the pontifical office. By a solemn sacrament C. Ego N. Episc. Extra de jure jurando, they have bound bishops to promise their obedience and faith to St Peter, to the Roman Church, and to their lord the Pope. Indeed, from bishops this practice has passed to those who receive dignities, and they are bound by the same oath, as may be read in Felinus, Comm. in cap. Ego N. Episcop. de jurejur. And, what easily outdoes all the rest, the form of oath described in canon law binds them in this way, that they defend the rules of the Holy Fathers. Pope Gregory IX, in Matthew Paris in Henrico iij., and Gregory XIII, in his bull to Maurice, Bishop of Imelac, have long since, and still today, substituted in their place the regalia of St Peter. This display, then, of that precious stone, St Peter, whom they call Petra, has until now been, if not among the greatest, at least among the most skilful tricks of those spiritual frauds, by which the Pope has been enriched with so many goods and the Roman Church has brought forth such a pinnacle of eminence. Add to this that, just as Hortensius, as Cicero testifies, raised eloquence to the highest praise so that he himself might ascend to heaven with it, so Jerome, in praising St Peter with the highest and most divine eulogies, makes himself the more blessed along with him.

units.la: XX. Non lapide tantùm pretioso, sed gemmis pretiosis, margaritis inaurata Mulier inducitur. F zelo fidei, pietatis, sanctitatis, cognitionis, patr eminentes Scriptura cum gemmis, seu nobilioribus la bus comparare suevit. Pertinet huc locus Zachar. Salvabit illos Jehova Deus ipsorum illo die, ut oves lum suum, quia אבני נזר lapides coronæ insigniter em super terra ipsius. Ubi lapides coronæ, seu coro gemmæ videlicet, notant homines fideles, quorun lucet coram hominibus. Qui etiam Ezech. xxviii. 14 cantur אבני אש lapides ignis, carbunculi, lapides quia in iis est charitas & lux.
units.tr: XX. The woman is shown gilded not only with a precious stone but with precious gems, pearls. Scripture was accustomed to compare those eminent in zeal for the faith, piety, holiness and knowledge to gems or to nobler stones. The passage of Zechariah belongs here: Jehovah their God will save them on that day, as the flock of his people, for [אבני נזר] stones of a crown shall be lifted up like a banner over his land. There stones of a crown, that is, crown jewels, denote faithful men, who shine before men. Those also are called in Ezekiel 28:14 [אבני אש] stones of fire, carbuncles, stones, because in them is love and light.

units.la: XXI. Talibus margaritis Hierarchia inaurata ir magnificè. Suos enim jactat fideles & Sanctos omnes triarchas, Prophetas, justos, Apostolos, Martyres tres, Doctores. His illa sideribus micat, his gemm diat. Hos sestis, statuis, imaginibus, votis honorat rum veneratio in externo ejus cultu utramque pa facit. Horum exuvias auro & argento obductas p lam ostentat, & venerantibus eas magnifica quæqu mittit.
units.tr: XXI. With such pearls the gilded hierarchy adorns itself magnificently. For it boasts of all its faithful and saints: patriarchs, prophets, the just, apostles, three martyrs, teachers. With these it gleams like stars and is bright with these gems. It honours them with feasts, statues, images and vows, and by its external worship it makes both parties. It openly displays their relics overlaid with gold and silver, and sends out for those who venerate them whatever magnificent things it has.

units.la: XXII. Conciliorum & S. Patrum imprimis in prol & stabiliendis fidei articulis authoritatem quantivis f re simulat. Consensum enim Ecclesiæ suæ cum Conc S. Patribus Ecclesiæ veteris inter rotas Ecclesiæ p retulit. Damasi illud: In Spiritum S. blasphemat cunque Patrum Canones Violat, injus Canonicum q. 1. c. 5. relatum, decantant passim. Crassè adm Glossator Decreti Can. Noli meis, dist. 9. docet, Augustini, & aliorum Patrum scripta olim quidem non suisse authentica, hodie autem juberi omnia teneri usque ad ultimum jota. Margo annotat: Scripta S. Patrum sunt ad unguem observanda. Sed & Patrum consensum normam esse doctrinæ, thesis erat Jesuitarum in Colloquio Ratisbonensi. Hinc adeò Tridentina etiam Synodus Sess. iv. cavet severè, ne quis in rebus fidei & morum S. Scripturam contra unanimem Patrum consensum interpretari audeat.
units.tr: XXII. Especially in proposing and establishing the articles of faith, it pretends that the authority of the councils and the Holy Fathers is of whatever weight. For it sets forth the consent of its Church with the councils and the Holy Fathers of the ancient Church among the wheels of the Church. The saying of Damasus, He who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit and violates the canons of the Fathers, cited in canon law, q. 1, c. 5, they sing everywhere. The gloss on the Decretum, Can. Noli meis, dist. 9., teaches crudely that the writings of Augustine and other Fathers were once indeed not regarded as authentic, but today everything is commanded to be held to the last iota. The margin notes: The writings of the Holy Fathers are to be observed to the nail. But also the consent of the Fathers is the norm of doctrine was a thesis of the Jesuits at the Colloquy of Regensburg. Hence the Synod of Trent also, Sess. iv., sternly forbids that anyone in matters of faith and morals dare to interpret Holy Scripture against the unanimous consent of the Fathers.

units.la: XXIII. Hæc & alia ejusmodi in speciem fancita sunt, ut liquidò appareat, Mulierem margaritis talibus inauratam quidem, hoc est, extus obductam & splendidè exornatam esse, at subesse margaritis, perinde ut auro, sucum. Nam cùm S. Patres habeantur merito pro gemmis pretiosissimis, quatenus per eos fides in mundo prædicata, & hæresis debellata est; & causam habemus exïstimandi, eos, si attendissent, aut sequentia tempora ipsis animus præsagivisset, suos lapsus correcturos fuisse: inprimis cùm illi non aliam regulam tradiderunt, nisi verbum Dei: Hierarchici contra ex Patribus collegerunt non gemmas, sed carbones quosdam, errores scilicet eorum & παρεφθαρμένα, nec non dicta quædam incautiùs, vel ἀναμφιβολίαν, quibus freti sibi & doctrinis suis authoritatem conciliarent; quasi Patres propterea ipsorum socii censendi essent. De cætero illos interpolare, lancinare, expurgare, perversum in sensum detorquere, subinde aperte sugillare, denique unius hominis, Papæ libidini subjicere, religio iis nulla planè est. Sensum enim Scripturæ ajunt examinandum Patrum trutina; Patres veritatis; veritatem populi; populum Conciliorum; Concilia Papæ. Hos scilicet saltatorios orbes versant; in his illi circulis tripudiare amant. Quid quòd hac ratione offundunt tenebras oculis, & sibi parant maximam fallendi opportunitatem, dum volunt causam dici coram judicibus ignotis, & qui à populo Christiano non leguntur; quippe quem linguæ peregrinitas, & operum immensa moles, & vita aliis curis intenta Patrum scripta attingere, nedum universa rufpari non patiuntur.
units.tr: XXIII. These and other things of this kind have been enacted in outward show, so that it may clearly appear that the woman is indeed gilded with such pearls, that is, covered on the outside and splendidly adorned, but that beneath the pearls, just as beneath the gold, there is filth. For although the Holy Fathers are rightly held to be most precious gems, inasmuch as through them the faith was preached in the world and heresy was overcome; and we have reason to think that, had they foreseen it, or had their minds anticipated the later times, they would have corrected their lapses: especially since they handed down no other rule than the Word of God. The hierarchs, on the contrary, have gathered from the Fathers not gems but certain coals, namely their errors and corrupted things, and some sayings spoken too carelessly, or without ambiguity, by which they, relying on themselves, win authority for their own doctrines, as if the Fathers were therefore to be counted as their companions. Otherwise, to interpolate them, mangle them, expurgate them, twist them into a perverse sense, now and then openly sneer at them, and finally subject them to the lust of one man, the Pope: they have no scruple at all about these things. For they say that the sense of Scripture is to be weighed in the balance of the Fathers; the Fathers in the balance of truth; truth in the balance of the people; the people in the balance of the councils; the councils in the balance of the Pope. Clearly they whirl around these dancing circles; in these circles they love to cavort. What more? By this method they cast darkness over the eyes and prepare for themselves the greatest opportunity of deceiving, while they want the case to be heard before judges who are unknown and whom the Christian people do not read; for the strangeness of the language, the immense bulk of the works, and a life given over to other cares do not allow the people even to touch the writings of the Fathers, let alone to look through them all.

units.la: XXIV. Adhabitum exteriorem Mulieris supra etiam Aureum poculum, quod habet in manu sua, plenum abominationibus, & impuritate scortationis suæ, retulimus. Poculum quoddam Circæum, philtrum, ad impuros amores pelliciens, quo Meretrices prostituti pudoris uti solent, indigetari, dubium non est. Res enim ipsa loquitur. Philtrum quippe est potio amatoria, virus amatorium, compositio ex rebus variis, veluti bufonum cineribus, cerebro hominum patibulis suspensorum, carminibus & execrandis verbis, ad amorem extorquendum ab eo, qui biberit. Tale poculum illud Aureum est, utpote tum hærens in Manu Mulieris & Meretricis, & veneficæ, quæ ἐν τῇ φαρμακίᾳ αὐτῆς per veneficium suum ac incantationem Nationes terræ seduxit: tum intus plenum οἴνου τῆς θυμοῦ τῆς πορνείας; vino iræ vel veneficii scortationis, Apoc. xiv. 8. xvii. 2. xviii. 3. quibus verbis philtri periphrasis continetur. Nam & Hebræa vox חמה & Græca θυμός non tantùm iram, excandescentiam, sed etiam veneficium significat, uti planissimè constat ex Deut. xxxii. 33. ubi חמה חנינים venenum Draconum à lxx. Interpretibus θυμὸς δρακόντων redditur. Sic plane etiam Cornelius à Lapide, Alcasar, alii interpretantur, & Grotius pluribus explicat.
units.tr: XXIV. We have also above referred the outward dress of the woman, the golden cup that she holds in her hand, full of abominations and the impurity of her fornication. There is no doubt that this is a certain Circean cup, a philtre, enticing to impure loves, the kind that prostitutes with shameless faces are accustomed to use. The thing itself speaks. A philtre is indeed a love potion, a love poison, a compound of various things, such as ashes of toads, brains of men hanged on gibbets, charms and accursed words, for extorting love from whoever drinks it. That golden cup is such, since it is held in the hand of a Woman, a Harlot and a sorceress, who [ἐν τῇ φαρμακίᾳ αὐτῆς] by her sorcery and incantation has seduced the nations of the earth; and inside it is full of [οἴνου τῆς θυμοῦ τῆς πορνείας] the wine of the wrath or poison of her fornication, Rev. 14:8, 17:2, 18:3, words in which the periphrasis of the philtre is contained. For both the Hebrew word [חמה] and the Greek [θυμός] signify not only wrath and fury but also poison, as is quite clear from Deut. 32:33, where [חמה חנינים] the venom of dragons is rendered by the Seventy [θυμὸς δρακόντων]. So also Cornelius a Lapide and Alcasar, and others, interpret it plainly, and Grotius explains it at greater length.

units.la: XXV. Poculum isthoc Circæum ex auro conflatum, externa specie purissima, pretiosissima, nitidissima quæque ostentat, quibus interiora sua commendare nititur. Sic planè Hierarchia corticem verborum Dei, Apostolicas traditiones, quibus vel malè detortis vel effictis authoritatem sibi conciliat; cenfenfum, multitudinem, antiquitatem, perpetuam successionem, Cathedram S. Petri; aliáque ejusmodi præ fe fert. Papa ipse aureos sibi titulos, quibus mundo vinum fcortationis suæ propinaret, assumpsit, cujufmodi sunt, Pater Patrum, Pastor Pastorum, Pater Sanctissimus, Beatissimus, Christi vicarius, Caput Ecclesiæ, Petri successor, Sponsus, fundamentum Ecclesiæ, Princeps Sacerdotum, Episcopus Apostolicus, universalis Vice-Deus &c. Sed verò quod crama intus aureum hoc poculum abscondit, & amaliis suis propinat? Nil nisi οἶνον τῆς θυμῶς τῆς πορνείας; vinum veneficii fcortationis & abominationis, venenum præsentissimum, dogmata impia, blasphema, veneficia, flagitia, apostasiam à vero Deo, à Regno Dei, à justitia Dei; idololatriam, amorem mundi & eorum, quæ in mundo sunt; fiduciam in falsa justitia, adorationem creaturarum, ipsam denique carnalem impuritatem & scortationem, quæ singula abominationis & scortationis nomine in sacris veniunt. Verbo, Circæum ifthoc poculum veneficiis & fascinationibus suis homines in bestias, metamorphosi omnium tristissima, commutavit. Id verò quemadmodum Hierarchici præstiterint, Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ universa facies comprobat, & ex iis, quæ deinceps dicturi sumus, magis etiam colliquescet.
units.tr: XXV. This Circean cup, fashioned of gold, displays on the outside whatever is purest, most precious and most shining, by which it strives to commend what lies within. Just so the hierarchy puts forward the husk of the words of God, the apostolic traditions, by which it wins authority for itself, whether they are badly twisted or made up; the consent, the multitude, the antiquity, the perpetual succession, the Chair of St Peter, and other things of this kind. The Pope himself has assumed for himself golden titles, with which he pours out the wine of his fornication to the world, such as: Father of Fathers, Pastor of Pastors, Most Holy Father, Most Blessed, Vicar of Christ, Head of the Church, Successor of Peter, Bridegroom, Foundation of the Church, Prince of Priests, Apostolic Bishop, Universal Vice-God, etc. But what poison does this golden cup hide within, and pour out to its lovers? Nothing but [οἶνον τῆς θυμῶς τῆς πορνείας] the wine of the wrath of her fornication, the wine of poison, fornication and abomination, the most present poison: impious, blasphemous dogmas, poisonings, shameful crimes, apostasy from the true God, from the Kingdom of God, from the justice of God; idolatry, love of the world and of those things that are in the world; trust in a false righteousness, the worship of creatures, and finally carnal impurity itself and fornication, all of which come under the names of abomination and fornication in the sacred books. In a word, this Circean cup has changed men into beasts by its poisonings and enchantments, the most wretched of all metamorphoses. How the hierarchs have accomplished this the whole face of the Papal Church proves, and it will melt away even more from what we are about to say.

units.la: MYSTERIUM DISSERTATIONIS DECIMÆ, QUA Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem Babylonem Magnam esse probatur Quintò, quia ejus Caput, Papa, se, ceu Numen Divinita- tis particeps, religiosè coli patitur;
units.tr: THE MYSTERY OF THE TENTH DISSERTATION, IN WHICH IT IS PROVED THAT THE HIERARCHY, OR THE CLERGY OF THE ROMAN CHURCH WHICH RULES, IS THE GREAT BABYLON. Fifthly, because its Head, the Pope, suffers himself to be religiously worshipped as a Numen partaking of the Divinity;

units.la: SECTIO PRIOR. QUA Papam Romanum, Hierarchiæ Caput, Divinita- tem affectare, tum ex nomine Dei, tum ex octo Divinis attributis, quæ sibi vindicat, demonstratur. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: FIRST SECTION. IN WHICH IT IS DEMONSTRATED THAT THE ROMAN POPE, HEAD OF THE HIERARCHY, AFFECTS DIVINITY, BOTH FROM THE NAME OF GOD AND FROM THE EIGHT DIVINE ATTRIBUTES WHICH HE CLAIMS FOR HIMSELF. SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Argumentum Quintum ab affectata à Papa Divinitate & religioso cultu petitum, & Syllogismo inclusum præponitur; ejusdemque propositio probatur.
units.tr: I. The fifth argument, drawn from the divinity affected by the Pope and from religious worship, is set forth enclosed in a syllogism, and its major premise is proved.

units.la: II. Assumptionis demonstratio de capite Hierarchiæ Papa ipsam Hierarchiam ferit.
units.tr: II. The demonstration of the assumption, that the head of the Hierarchy, the Pope, strikes the Hierarchy itself.

units.la: III. Numen particeps Divinitatis, seu Deum esse, tria significat, habere æternitatem &c. peccatori de ratione justitiæ & vitæ testari, & per testimonium illud fidem obligare; denique facto ipso salvare.
units.tr: III. A Numen partaking of the Divinity, that is, a God, signifies three things: to have eternity &c., to bear witness to the sinner concerning the reason of justice and life, and by that testimony to bind the faith ; finally, by the very fact, to save. Note: the italic marking is as in the source; see the correction below.

units.la: IV. Deum etiam se facit, quisquis aliquid eorum, quæ ad fœdus Dei, justitiam, vitam, salutem spectant, attrectat; non is solus, qui æternum Numen esse & haberi præsumit. Optati Milevitani eam in rem locus insignis. Aliud est vocis sonus, aliud res.
units.tr: IV. He also makes himself God, whoever handles anything of those things which concern the covenant of God, justice, life, and salvation; it is not only he who presumes that he is, and is held to be, the eternal Numen. Optatus of Milevis has a notable passage to this purpose. The sound of a word is one thing, the reality another.

units.la: V. Et tamen Papam etiam quoad vocis sonum syllabasque nomen Dei, Numinis sumpsisse vel admisisse, ex Conciliis Florentino & Lateranensi, Papæ Gregorii II. & Pauli V. testimoniis; Glossa Juris Canonici, libro Ceremoniarum,
units.tr: V. And yet that the Pope has also taken or admitted the name of God, the Numen, even as to the sound of the word and its syllables, is shown from the Councils of Florence and the Lateran, and from the testimonies of Popes Gregory II and Paul V; the Gloss of the Canon Law, the Book of Ceremonies,

units.la: VI. Cardinalibus Avinionensibus, Gualando, Aug. Steucho, Baronio & Bellarmino probatur.
units.tr: VI. It is proved from the Cardinals of Avignon, Gualandus, Augustinus Steuchus, Baronius and Bellarmine.

units.la: VII. Objectio Bellarmini, petita ex verbis, Vos Dii estis, diluitur.
units.tr: VII. The objection of Bellarmine, drawn from the words "You are gods", is refuted.

units.la: VIII. Si tamen Dei nomine nunquam Papa venisset, at fecisse eum ac passum esse, quæ vocis ejus defectum suppleant, probatur tum ex Glossatore Decreti, Consilio à Cardinalibus Pauló IV. exhibito,
units.tr: VIII. But even if the Pope had never been called by the name of God, it is proved that he has done and suffered things which make up for the lack of that name, both from the Gloss on the Decretum and from the Consilium presented by the Cardinals to Paul IV,

units.la: IX. tum maximè ex attributis Divinis orto, quæ Papa sibi vindicat.
units.tr: IX. and especially from the Divine attributes which the Pope claims for himself.

units.la: X. Cujusmodi sunt 1. Quod se facit objectum & regulam fidei, quale solus Deus & ejus verbum est.
units.tr: X. Such are: 1. That he makes himself the object and rule of faith, which only God and his Word are.

units.la: XI. Walenburgiorum de objecto & regula fidei sententia.
units.tr: XI. The opinion of the Walenburgii on the object and rule of faith.

units.la: XII. Propositio articulorum fidei distinguitur.
units.tr: XII. The proposition of the articles of faith is distinguished.

units.la: XIII. XIV. Propositio authentica, & cum authoritate, quam sibi Papa asserit, solius Dei est.
units.tr: XIII. XIV. The authentic proposition, and the authority which the Pope asserts for himself, belongs to God alone.

units.la: XV. 11. Quod leges innumeras religiosas fert, iisque conscientias fidelium obligari pertendit, quod solius Dei esse, ex Jacobi IV. 12. probatur.
units.tr: XV. 11. That he lays down countless religious laws and contends that the consciences of the faithful are bound by them, which is shown to belong to God alone from James 4:12.

units.la: XVI. Petulans detorsio loci illius rejecta.
units.tr: XVI. The wanton twisting of that passage is rejected.

units.la: XVII. Concilii Tridentini de Papæ potestate legislativa definitio.
units.tr: XVII. The definition of the Council of Trent concerning the legislative power of the Pope.

units.la: XVIII. Papa innumeris legibus suis Ecclesiam oppressit, & omnibusferè creaturis, actionibus humanis &c. peccati labem aspersit.
units.tr: XVIII. The Pope has oppressed the Church with his innumerable laws, and has sprinkled the stain of sin on almost all creatures, human actions, &c.

units.la: XIX. Jugulum ei ex Col. ÿ. 18-22. petitum.
units.tr: XIX. His throat is seized, from Col. 2:18-22.

units.la: XX. iii. Quòd media justificationis proprio motu, & aliunde non accepta tradit, quod solius Dei esse probatur.
units.tr: XX. iii. That he hands down the means of justification by his own motion, and not received from elsewhere, which is proved to belong to God alone.

units.la: XXI. Tridentini Concilii de modo & mediis justificationis definitiones proponuntur,
units.tr: XXI. The definitions of the Council of Trent on the mode and means of justification are set forth,

units.la: XXII. & justificationem sic definitam non esse eam, quam Deus in verbo suo revelavit, ostenditur.
units.tr: XXII. and it is shown that justification so defined is not that which God revealed in his Word.

units.la: XXIII. XXIV. Neque baptismi pœnitentiæ opus operatum satisfactiones, absolutio Sacerdotis, indulgentiæ, merita media justificationis in verbo Dei revelantur, quinimò cum merito Christi pugnant.
units.tr: XXIII. XXIV. Neither the sacrament of baptism, nor the work wrought by repentance, nor satisfactions, nor the absolution of the priest, nor indulgences, nor merits, are revealed in the Word of God as means of justification; indeed they fight against the merit of Christ.

units.la: XXV. Missæ sacrificium inprimis sacrificium Christi, justificationis causam unicam, evertit.
units.tr: XXV. The sacrifice of the Mass, above all, overthrows the sacrifice of Christ, the sole cause of justification.

units.la: XXVI. Antithesis veri Dei, & Papæ, novelli Numinis, justificationis modum & media dictantis.
units.tr: XXVI. The antithesis of the true God and of the Pope, a new Numen, dictating the mode and means of justification.

units.la: XXVII. iv. Quòd potestatem clavium berilem, & in peccatis remittendis judicialem, quæ solius Dei est, affectat.
units.tr: XXVII. iv. That he claims for himself the lordly power of the keys, and the judicial power in remitting sins, which belongs to God alone.

units.la: XXVIII. Clavium potestas ministerialis explicatur.
units.tr: XXVIII. The ministerial power of the keys is explained.

units.la: XXIX. XXX. Papa Claviger magnus sibi soli potestatem clavium vindicat.
units.tr: XXIX. XXX. The Pope, the Great Key-bearer, claims for himself alone the power of the keys.

units.la: XXXI. Claves insigne Papæ sunt.
units.tr: XXXI. The keys are the Pope's emblem.

units.la: XXXII. Petro claves in pictura appropriantur.
units.tr: XXXII. The keys are assigned to Peter in pictures.

units.la: XXXIII. De eodem solo clavigero fabula vetus, à Rege Angliæ Os Wi recepta, à Baronio laudata,
units.tr: XXXIII. Concerning the same sole key-bearer there is an old fable, adopted by the King of England, Oswy, and praised by Baronius,

units.la: XXXIV. & ab Ecclesia Pontificia Iudiosè nutrita.
units.tr: XXXIV. and nourished zealously by the Papal Church.

units.la: XXXV. De subjecto potestatis clavium Scholæ Papalis doctores licet disceptent, soli tamen Petro, ut ordinario, & cum jure successionis à Christo collatas esse, consentiunt.
units.tr: XXXV. Although the teachers of the Papal school dispute about the subject of the power of the keys, they all agree that it was conferred by Christ on Peter alone, as ordinary, and with the right of succession.

units.la: XXXVI. Papam solum sibi clavium potestatem, & quidem herilem ac dominantem afferere, probatur.
units.tr: XXXVI. It is proved that the Pope alone asserts the power of the keys for himself, and indeed a lordly and domineering power.

units.la: XXXVII. Idem claves in enses, lanceas, sceptra, coronas convertit,
units.tr: XXXVII. He also turns the keys into swords, lances, sceptres and crowns,

units.la: XXXVIII. XXXIX. & claves abyssi, in purgatorium & infernum sibi vindicat.
units.tr: XXXVIII. XXXIX. and claims for himself the keys of the abyss, for purgatory and hell.

units.la: XL. In usu clavium se à quoquam judicari posse, quod solius Dei est, Papa negat.
units.tr: XL. In the use of the keys the Pope denies that he can be judged by anyone, which belongs to God alone.

units.la: XLI. Judicialem in remittendis peccatis potestatem, quæ solius Dei est, sibi Papa vendicat.
units.tr: XLI. The Pope claims for himself the judicial power in remitting sins, which belongs to God alone.

units.la: XLII. Claviger Papa non Regni Cœlorum, sed abyssi claves habere, ab Angelo Apoc. ix. 1. pronuntiatur.
units.tr: XLII. The Pope as key-bearer is declared by the Angel in Apoc. 9:1 to hold not the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven but of the abyss.

units.la: XLIII. v. Quòd se Caput, Fundamentum, Petram Ecclesiæ, quæ solus Christus est, mentitur.
units.tr: XLIII. v. That he falsely claims to be the Head, the Foundation, the Rock of the Church, which is Christ alone.

units.la: XLIV. Papam non æquo jure aut gradu cum Christo caput esse Ecclesiæ, verbis profitentur, at dicis causa tantùm.
units.tr: XLIV. In words they profess that the Pope is head of the Church, but not with the same right or rank as Christ; they say so merely for form's sake.

units.la: XLV. Capitis primarii & Secundarii distinctionem nil hic obstare, quò minùs Papa Deum se faciat, probatur.
units.tr: XLV. The distinction between primary and secondary head is shown not to hinder, in this matter, the Pope from making himself God.

units.la: XLVI. Fundamenti primarii & secundarii monstrosa distinctio.
units.tr: XLVI. The monstrous distinction between primary and secondary foundation.

units.la: XLVII. Caput & fundamentum principale Papam habere velle, ejusdem tituli, & Scripturæ locorum, quæ de solo Christo intelligenda sunt, detorsio ad se,
units.tr: XLVII. That the Pope wishes to have the principal Head and Foundation, of the same title, and the twisting to himself of passages of Scripture which are to be understood of Christ alone,

units.la: XLVIII. nec non vis vocabulorum, Caput, Pontifex Summus &c. arguunt.
units.tr: XLVIII. and also the force of the words, Head, Supreme Pontiff, &c., argue this.

units.la: XLIX. vi. Quòd potestatem transferendi Regna, & imperitandi omnibus Regibus, Divinam sibi asserit.
units.tr: XLIX. vi. That he claims for himself the divine power of transferring kingdoms and of commanding all kings.

units.la: L. A se coronatos Reges à Deo coronatos pronuntiat, & sacrilegio huic ludibria addit. LI. vii. Quòd dispensandi contra legem Divinam juramenta & vota potestatem sibi tribuit. LII. Jus dispensandi contra legem Dei Papæ vindicatum à Petro de Monte, Gobelino Persona, Glossatore juris Canonici, Innocentio III. Vasquez, Caranza. LIII. Actu jus illud frequenter usurpat. LIV. Et in Constantiensi ac Tridentino Concilio, non sine putida detorsione verborum Apostoli, impudenter, cum primis exercuit. LV. Andradii & Melchioris Cani, LVI. nec non Bellarmini ἀπὸ φάρμακα discutiuntur. LVII. Bellarminus idem Papam de peccato non peccatum facere posse profitetur. LVIII. Dispensatio Papalis circa gradus matrimonii jure Divino prohibitos, LIX. circa juramenta, fidelitatis inprimis, LX. & votorum. LXI. Insolentia Bullarum, per quas dispensat. LXII. viii. Quòd in apotheosi Sanctos & Divos pro lubitu creat, quod solius Dei est. LXIII. Theopoëtice hæc Chrysopoëtices pars est. LXIV. Canonizationis Papalis modus. LXV. Inscriptionem in librum vitæ, & apertionem Codicis septem sigillis clausi sibi nefariè vindicat, LXVI. atque sic, quòd Deus sit demonstrat.
units.tr: L. He pronounces the kings crowned by himself to have been crowned by God, and adds mockery to this sacrilege. LI. vii. That he grants himself the power to dispense with oaths and vows contrary to the Divine law. LII. The right of dispensing against the law of God is claimed for the Pope by Peter de Monte, Gobelinus Persona, the Glossator of canon law, Innocent III, Vasquez and Caranza. LIII. He frequently uses that right in practice. LIV. And in the Council of Constance and in the Council of Trent he exercised it impudently, above all with a foul twisting of the words of the Apostle. LV. The arguments of Andradius and Melchior Cano, LVI. and also of Bellarmine, [ἀπὸ φάρμακα], are discussed. LVII. Bellarmine in turn professes that the Pope can make what is sin not to be sin. LVIII. The papal dispensation concerning the degrees of marriage prohibited by divine law, LIX. concerning oaths, of fidelity above all, LX. and of vows. LXI. The insolence of the Bulls by which he dispenses. LXII. viii. That in the apotheosis he creates Saints and Divine beings at his pleasure, which belongs to God alone. LXIII. This theopoetics is part of chrysopoetics. LXIV. The manner of papal canonization. LXV. He impiously claims for himself the inscription in the book of life, and the opening of the codex sealed with seven seals, LXVI. and thus demonstrates that he is God.

units.la: I. [A] rcem demonstrationis institutæ ingressuri, argumentum nunc palmarium, quod numero Quintum est, Syllogismo sequenti constrictum, proponimus:
units.tr: I. Now about to enter upon the demonstration we have undertaken, we set forth our chief argument, which is the fifth in number, bound in the following syllogism:

units.la: Ille cœtus Babylon Magna est, qui cæteris paribus, se in capite suo ceu Numen, Divinitatis particeps, à subjecto sibi populo religiosè colipatitur.
units.tr: That assembly is the Great Babylon which, other things being equal, suffers itself to be religiously worshipped by its subject people, as a Numen partaking of the Divinity, in its head.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans, ceteris paribus, se in capite suo, ceu Numen Divinitatis particeps, à subjecto sibi populo religiosè colì patitur.
units.tr: But the Hierarchy, or the Clergy of the Roman Church which rules, other things being equal, suffers itself to be religiously worshipped by its subject people, as a Numen partaking of the Divinity, in its head.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the Hierarchy, or the Clergy of the Roman Church which rules, is the Great Babylon.

units.la: Propositionem jam supra Differt. iij. 8-13. extra contentionis aleam posuimus. Ostendimus enim, Babylonis Magnæ, ceu Matris Scortationum terræ, & Borboritici propudii, scortationem non in eo duntaxat, quod ad cultum Divinum creaturarum, & scortationem corporalem seducit, sed in eo præcipuè, quòd se ipsam pro Numine Divinitatis participe venditans, ad cultum venerationémque sui Reges & incolas terræ invitat, iisque procumbens satietatem cupiditatum, deliciarum, bonorum omnium, temporalis & æternæ salutis, promittit. Planè sicut eadem Babylon Mystica Esai. xiv. 13. 14. in corde suo dicens inducitur: Cœlum conscendam, super stellas Dei exaltabo solium meum, & sedebo in monte congregationis, in lateribus Aquilonis. Ascendam supra altitudines nubis. אעלה לעלין Assimilabor Altissimo. Et sicut Filius perditionis 2. Thess. 11. 4. se efferre dicitur ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον θεὸν ἢ σέβασμα, super omnem, qui Deus aut Numen dicitur, adeò ut in Templo Dei tanquam Deus sedeat, ἀποδεικνύοντα ἑαυτὸν, ὅτι ἐστὶ θεός, demonstrans se, quòd sit Deus.
units.tr: We have already placed the proposition beyond the dispute above, in Differ. iii, 8-13. For we showed that the fornication of Babylon the Great, mother of harlots and of the earth, and of the Borboritic filth, consists not only in this, that she seduces to the worship of creatures and to bodily fornication, but chiefly in this, that by offering herself as a participant in the Divinity she invites the kings and inhabitants of the earth to her worship and reverence, and, prostrating herself before them, promises the satisfaction of desires, delights, all goods, and temporal and eternal salvation. Just as that same Mystical Babylon is introduced in Isaiah 14:13-14, saying in her heart: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, and I will sit on the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds. [אעלה לעלין] I will make myself like the Most High. And just as the Son of perdition, in 2 Thess. 2:4, is said to exalt himself above every one who is called God or worshipped [ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον θεὸν ἢ σέβασμα], so that he sits in the Temple of God as God, showing himself [ἀποδεικνύοντα ἑαυτὸν] that he is God [ὅτι ἐστὶ θεός].

units.la: II. Omnis ergo nunc cardo in eo vertitur, ut Assumptio liquidò probata in aperta luce statuatur. Procedet autem probatio nostra de Capite Hierarchiæ, Pontifice Romano, Præterquam enim quòd, quicquid capitis, partis potioris est, illud totius est, insuper etiam Hierarchiæ omnis vis & potestas dominans juxtu Hieromonarchicos in capite ejusdem Papa residet. Sicut contra omnis virtus & potestas Ecclesiæ, ceu corporis Christi, in Christo capite continetur. Quæstio enim illa, An Consilium, Hierarchiæ totius confluxus sit supra Papam, an Papa supra Concilium; Hieromonarchicos inter & Hierarchicos acribus studiis hactenus disceptata, nec dum definita est. Posterius autem à plerisque, imò verè Pontificiis omnibus, receptum cum sit; nos ubi Papam Hierarchiæ caput sibi, ceu Numini Divinitatis participi, religiosum cultum vendicare demonstraverimus, abundè partibus nostris defunctos, æqui rerum æstimatores judicabunt omnes.
units.tr: II. The whole question therefore turns on this: that the Assumption be proved clearly and set in the open light. Our proof will proceed concerning the head of the hierarchy, the Roman Pontiff. For apart from the fact that whatever belongs to the head is the most important part of the body, all the power and authority of the hierarchy that dominates, according to the Hieromonarchists, resides in the Pope as its head. Conversely, all the strength and power of the Church, as the body of Christ, is contained in Christ the head. The question, whether the full assembly of the hierarchy is above the Pope, or the Pope above the Council, has been hotly disputed between the Hieromonarchists and the Hierarchists, and it has not yet been settled. But since the latter view has been accepted by most, indeed by all true Papists, all fair judges of the matter will agree that we have fully discharged our side once we have shown that the Pope, as head of the hierarchy, claims for himself religious worship as one who shares in the divine majesty.

units.la: III. Numen Divinitatis particeps, seu Deum esse, tria significat. Primò habere æternitatem & immensitatem, esse omnium rerum causam, habere sufficientiam ad justificandum & sanctificandum peccatorem. Secundò testari peccatori de ratione justitiæ & vitæ, & per testimonium illud obligare fidem, adeóque se proponere ad fiduciam in se collocandam ad salutem. Ita habere aliquem pro Deo, est in aliquem credere, fiduciam in eo collocare, ei, ut legislatori, & per testimonium habenti, se subjicere, uti ex Deut. xxvi. 17. 18. Psal. xxxiii. 12. Zachar. xiii. 9. &c. liquet. Eum ergo ad quem nostra ὁμολογία fides, obedientia cum gloriatione & spe justitiæ, salutis, fertur, recipimus in Deum. Tertiò facto ipso salvare, tum merito, tum efficacia. Quò pertinent promissiones Genes. xvii. 8. Levit. xxvi. 12. Jerem. xi. 4. xxxi. 33. Hinc adeò Salvator ex illo elogio, Deus Abrahami, post mortem Abrahami audito conficit primò vitam Abrahami; deinde resurrectionem Matth. xxii. 32. Luc. xx. 38.
units.tr: III. To be a sharer in the divine majesty, or to be God, signifies three things. First, to have eternity and immensity, to be the cause of all things, and to have sufficiency to justify and sanctify the sinner. Second, to bear witness to the sinner concerning the rule of righteousness and life, and through that testimony to bind faith, and so to set oneself forth as the one in whom trust is to be placed for salvation. Thus to have someone as God is to believe in him, to place trust in him, and to submit to him as lawgiver and as one who holds the testimony, as is clear from Deut. 26:17–18, Ps. 33:12, Zech. 13:9, etc. We therefore receive as God the one to whom our confession, faith, obedience, with boasting and hope of righteousness and salvation, is directed. Third, to save by the very deed, both by merit and by efficacy. To this pertain the promises of Gen. 17:8, Lev. 26:12, Jer. 11:4, 31:33. Hence the Saviour, from that expression the God of Abraham, heard after Abraham's death, infers first the life of Abraham, and then the resurrection: Matt. 22:32, Luke 20:38.

units.la: IV. Cæterùm non ille duntaxat se Deum, Numen Divinitatis particeps facit, qui præsumit esse & haberi æternus Deus, causa rerum, author & largitor vitæ æternæ per efficaciam; sed etiam, qui quicquam eorum, quæ ad fœdus Dei, fidem, justitiam & vitam spectant, attrectat. Neque proin opus est, ut quisquis se, ceu Deum, religiosè coli patitur, se profiteatur æternum Deum, causam rerum omnium. Nam & ille se ἀπαιτ demonstrat, quòd Deus sit (2. Thess. II:4.) qui aliquid eorum, quæ soli Deo competunt, sibi arrogat. Ita Optatus Milevitanus lib. iij. Donati Carthaginensis temeritatem exagitans, sic ei insultat merito: Hoc modo exaltatum est cor ejus, ut sibi jam non homo, sed Deus videretur. Et paucis interjectis: Ad quem Deus sequitur, dicens, Dixistis. Ego sum Deus. Ideo quamvis non sit usus hac voce, tamen aut fecit, aut passus est, quod defectum hujus vocis impleret. Extulit cor suum, ut nullum hominem sibi comparandum arbitraretur: & de tumore mentis suæ altior sibi visus est esse: quia quicquid est supra homines, jam quasi Deus est. Deinde cum Episcopi Deo debeant famulari, tantum sibi de Episcopis exigit, ut eum non minori metu omnes venerarentur, quàm Deum. Hoc est, quòd sibi Deus visus est. Rursus: Dum Episcopus inter suos Coëpiscopos non fuit, nec homo inter homines esse voluit, constat, quòd extulit cor suum, & Deus sibi fuisse videbatur. Distinctæ ergo jam sunt quæstiones de vocabulorum sono, & de re per ea vocabula significata; potestque adeò, qui se non totidem Syllabis dicat esse Deum, tamen ita se gerere, quasi sit Deus.
units.tr: IV. Moreover, it is not only he who presumes to be and to be held as the eternal God, the cause of things, the author and giver of eternal life through efficacy, who makes himself God and a sharer in the divine majesty; but also he who lays hold of anything that pertains to the covenant of God, faith, righteousness, and life. Nor is it therefore necessary that whoever allows himself to be religiously worshipped as God should profess himself to be the eternal God, the cause of all things. For he too shows himself that he is God (2 Thess. 2:4) who arrogates to himself any of those things that belong to God alone. So Optatus of Milevis, in book 3, censuring the rashness of Donatus of Carthage, rightly insults him thus: In this way his heart was so lifted up that he seemed to himself no longer a man but God. And after a few words interposed: To him God is said to answer, "You have said, I am God." Therefore, although he did not use this word, nevertheless he either did or suffered something that fulfilled the lack of this word. He lifted up his heart so that he judged no man comparable to himself, and from the swelling of his mind he seemed to himself to be higher; because whatever is above men is already as it were God. Then, since bishops ought to serve God, he exacted so much from the bishops that all venerated him with no less fear than God. This is how he seemed to himself to be God. Again: While he was not a bishop among his fellow bishops, nor wished to be a man among men, it is evident that he lifted up his heart, and seemed to himself to be God. Thus the questions concerning the sound of the words are now distinct from the matter signified by those words; and so one who does not say in so many syllables that he is God may nevertheless so conduct himself as if he were God.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Sed possumus tamen præoccupare reliqua, & de ipsis syllabis ante omnia quæstionem intentare. Nam Dei nomen non semel Papa admisit. Testari possunt Concilia, Bullæ Papales, Inscriptiones publicæ, Jus Canonicum, libri Ceremoniarum, aliaque similia. Lubet ἀνέφ ἀνίαζων. In Concilio Florentino Johannes Abbas Ægyptius sic Eugenium IV. uti Acta Concilii p. iii. pag. 551. referunt, salutavit: Nil aliud quàm tremor apprehendere potest me hominem. Pulvis sum & cinis coram te Deo in terris verba faciens. Es namque Deus in terris, & Gregorii II.
units.tr: But we can nevertheless anticipate the rest, and before all else raise the question about the syllables themselves. For the Pope has more than once admitted the name of God. Councils, papal bulls, public inscriptions, the Canon Law, the books of ceremonies, and other similar things can bear witness to this. It pleases me [...]. At the Council of Florence, John, abbot of Egypt, greeted Eugenius IV in this way, as the Acts of the Council, part 3, page 551, report: Nothing but trembling can seize me, a man, speaking before you, God, as dust and ashes on earth. For you are God on earth, and of Gregory II.

units.la: L II
units.tr: L II

units.la: Christus & vicarius ejus. Tu Princeps Regum &c. Adeò grata fuit Papæ confessio, ut propterea cum eo unionem Jacobitarum nomine flagitatam promptè inivit. In Concilio Lateranensi Sess. 4. & 9. Julius II. insigniente Marcello, audiit alter in terris Deus: & Clericus Cameræ Apostolicæ Antonius Puccius Leoni Papæ tribuit Divinæ Majestatis conspectum, cujus rutilanti fulgore imbecilles oculi caligent. Acta Concilii hujus ab eodem Leone X. approbata sunt. Gregorius II. Epistola ad Leonem Isaurum: Denuntias te imaginem Petri eversurum, quam omnia Occidentis Regna velut Deum terrestrem habent, persuasum scilicet habens, in persona Papæ vivere Petrum. Quomodo etiam Papa Petri nomine in Concilio Rhemensi A. 1131. venit. Aræ cuipiam Romæ, si rectè memini, inscripta hæc verba sunt: Paulo V. ViceDeo, Pontificiæ omnipotentiæ Vindici acerrimo. Ubi licet Vice-Deus quiddam Deo minus sonet; non tamen sine summa Divini Numinis contumelia. Papæ Omnipotentia tribuitur. Prætereo libens elogium Filii Dei, quod Innocentius X. adhuc Cardinalis Pamphilii nomine insignis, sed jamjam Papa creandus, à Johanne Baptista Calumsyrito, homine Italo-Græco, sibi tributum æquo animo admisit, in Historia Papatus ff. 255. à nobis narratum. Sic autem Pamphilius ille cum Filio Dei ibi blasphemè comparatur, ut Filio Dei præferatur non uno modo. In jure Canonico Gloss. ad Cap. Cum Inter. 4. verbo Declaramus, de verb. Signif. in Extravag. Joh. xxiii. glossema extat, quod parùm timidè rem gerit. In eo enim sic habetur: Dominus Deus noster Papa. Ubi haud indignum notatu est, quòd cùm Thomas Manriquius, Sacri Palatii Magister, Censur. in Gloss. Jur. Can. Cal. A. 1572. pag. 13. 14. &c. Glossam hanc omittendam putaverit, Gregorius tamen XIII. aliter censuit, eámque cum pluribus. ribus id genus aliis Bulla Romæ A. 1580. 1. Jul. data, & Juri Canonico Romæ & Parisiis edito præfixa, comprobavit. Adhuc enim in eo Juris Corpore glossema superest. Licet autem Congregatio Indicis, atque Inquisitores in Indicibus Expurgatoriis has similésque sententias, Abraham fide justus: Christus credentibus salus: Justitia nostra Christus: Omnes sumus peccatores &c. expurgare nulli dubitaverint; execrandum tamen illud glossema in ultimis, emendatissimisque Juris Canonici editionibus intactum prætermiserunt. In postremis equidem exemplaribus ad marginem apponitur: Hæc verba sano modo sunt accipienda; hoc est, secundum Johannem Andream, qui Glossæ author fuerat, ita intelligenda sunt, ut Papæ Suprematum longè maximum efficiant. Prolata enim sunt, inquit, ad ostendendum amplissimam esse Pontificis Romani potestatem. Alibi Dist.96. Cane satis sic Nicolaus I. ad Michaelem Imperatorem Constantinopolitanum scribens inducitur: Satis evidenter ostenditur, à seculari potestate nec ligari prorsus, nec solvi posse Pontificem, quem constat à Pio Principe Constantino Deum esse appellatum, cùm nec posse Deum ab hominibus judicari manifestum sit. Placuisse verò idem Successoribus, argumento est, quòd hæc Nicolai verba in Decretum Gratianeum admiserunt omnes, expunxit aut emendavit nemo; etsi in rejiciendis iis, quæ vel leviter Papali honori derogant, nulli operæ harpyæ istæ pepercerint. Denique & in libro Ceremoniarum primo, Sect. 7. Cap. 6. Sedes Pontificis Sedes Dei appellatur.
units.tr: Christ and his vicar. You, Prince of kings, etc. So welcome was this confession to the Pope that he readily entered into union with the Jacobites, which had been demanded in his name. In the Lateran Council, sessions 4 and 9, Julius II, with Marcellus presenting, heard himself called another God on earth; and Antonius Puccius, a clerk of the Apostolic Chamber, ascribed to Pope Leo the sight of the divine majesty, by whose shining brightness weak eyes are dazzled. The Acts of this Council were approved by the same Leo X. Gregory II, in his letter to Leo the Isaurian: You announce that you will overthrow the image of Peter, which all the kingdoms of the West hold as an earthly God, plainly supposing that Peter lives in the person of the Pope. So too the Pope came to the Council of Rheims in 1131 in Peter's name. On some altar at Rome, if I remember rightly, these words are inscribed: To Paul V, Vice-God, most fierce avenger of papal omnipotence. Here, although Vice-God sounds something less than God, it is nonetheless not without the greatest insult to the divine majesty. Omnipotence is ascribed to the Pope. I gladly pass over the title Son of God, which Innocent X, while still a cardinal under the name of Pamphili, but about to be created Pope, accepted with equanimity when it was ascribed to him by John Baptist Calumsyrito, an Italo-Greek, as we have related in the History of the Papacy, p. 255. Pamphili himself is there so blasphemously compared with the Son of God that he is set above the Son of God in more ways than one. In the Canon Law, Gloss on chapter Cum inter, 4, under the word Declaramus, On the meaning of words, in the Extravagants of John XXII, there is a gloss which deals with the matter rather timidly. For in it stands: Our Lord God the Pope. Here it is worth noting that when Thomas Manrique, Master of the Sacred Palace, in his Censure of the Gloss of the Canon Law, Calends of 1572, pages 13, 14, etc., thought this gloss should be omitted, Gregory XIII nevertheless judged otherwise, and approved it, together with several other things of this kind, by a bull issued at Rome on 1 July 1580 and prefixed to the Canon Law edited at Rome and Paris. For the gloss still survives in that body of law. Although the Congregation of the Index and the Inquisitors have not hesitated to expurgate in the Expurgatory Indexes such sayings as Abraham justified by faith, Christ is salvation to believers, Christ is our righteousness, We are all sinners, etc., they nevertheless left that detestable gloss untouched in the latest and most carefully corrected editions of the Canon Law. In the most recent copies, indeed, a marginal note is added: These words are to be understood in a sound sense; that is, according to John Andreas, who was the author of the Gloss, they are to be understood so as to make the Supremacy of the Pope by far the greatest. For they were put forward, he says, to show that the power of the Roman Pontiff is most ample. Elsewhere, in Dist. 96, Cane satis, Nicholas I is introduced writing thus to Michael, the Emperor of Constantinople: It is sufficiently evident that the Pontiff cannot be bound or loosed at all by secular power, since it is agreed that he was called God by the pious prince Constantine, when it is plain that God cannot be judged by men. That the same view pleased his successors is shown by the fact that all have admitted these words of Nicholas into the Gratian Decree, and no one has expunged or emended them; although those harpies have spared no effort in rejecting whatever even slightly detracts from papal honour. Finally, in the first book of the Ceremonies, Sect. 7, Chap. 6, the seat of the Pontiff is called the Seat of God.

units.la: VI. Ex privatis Pontificiorum scriptis longè plura excerpi possunt. Excerpam pauca. Cardinales Avinionenses sic ad Regem Galliæ, Frossardo Tomo iv. Cap. 10. teste, scripserunt: Sicut unicus est in Cœlis Deus, sic nullo jure potest aut debet non esse unicus in terris Deus. Lælius Zx.
units.tr: VI. Far more can be picked out of the private writings of the Papists than I can cite here, so I will excerpt a few. The Cardinals of Avignon, according to Froissart Tome iv, chap. 10, wrote thus to the King of France: Just as God is one in heaven, so by no right can, or ought, God not to be one on earth. Lælius Zx.

units.la: Lælius Zx. probatur.
units.tr: Lælius Zx. confirmed.

units.la: Zœchius de Rep. Eccl. cap. de statu Papæ, art. 28. de Papa sic ampullatur: Est & dicitur Christi vicarius, & quasi Deus in terris, & quod ipse facit, non humanus Princeps, sed Deus facere videtur. Erasmus Annot. in N.T. 1. Tim. 11. testis est, suo tempore disputatum esse, Utrum Papa simplex homo sit, an quasi Deus participet utramque naturam cum Christo. Adoardus Gualandus, Episcopus Cæsenas de Morali & Civili fac. lib.xiv.3. sic Papam exornat: A Papa, inquit, tanquam à Capite in universum Ecclesiæ corpus, hoc est, in omnem Christianam Remp. Spiritus influunt Cœlestium gratiarum sensum fructúmque præstantes, & efficacem motum ad sempiternam Beatitudinem. Merito igitur sanctissimus & Beatissimus appellatur, & ab omnibus Christianam religionem profitentibus, quasi quidam Deus adoratur & colitur. Augustinus Steuchus, Papæ Bibliothecarius, postquam de Donat. Const. pag. 141. fabulam de Constantino, Papam Deum appellante, allegâssetl, hæc subjungit: Audis Summum Pontificem à Constantino Deum appellatum, & habitum pro Deo? Hoc videlicet factum est, cùm eum præclaro illo edicto decoravit, adoravit uti Deum, uti Christi & Petri successorem: Divinos honores ei, quoad ejus potuit, contulit, velut vivam Christi imaginem veneratus esset. Baronius, & ex eodem Spondanus Annot. pag. 1058. tradunt, ad pedes Alexandri III. accessisse Saracenorum industrium Principem, & deosculatum pedes ejus flexisse coram eo genua, & inclinato capite tanquam sanctum & pium Christianorum Deum ipsum Pontificem adorasse. Subjungitur approbatio facti his verbis: In his autem, quæ dicta sunt de Principe Mahometanorum, videas Dei opera, dum non solum Christiani Reges, sed & Saraceni assurgunt, & legatione honorifica venerantur Romanum Pontificem, cùm illum impium Romanorum Imperator dire persequeretur. Bellarminum his omnibus addere libet. Is in Responsione ad Gerson-em, quæ habetur inter acta & scripta varia Controversiæ inter Paulum v. & Venetos ,pag. 468.469. sic scribit: Teneant pusilli & simplices, Papam quendam Deum esse, & potestatem omnem habere in Cælo & terris. Deo plus placet eorum infirmitas & simplicitas, quàm firmitudo eorum, qui sibi prudentes videri volunt. Exiguum quid est, Papam pro Deo in terris haberi, cùm de omnibus Principibus in Psalmo dicatur: Ego dixi, Dii estis. Nec inconveniens est dicere Papam potestatem omnem habere in Cælo & in terra.
units.tr: Zoechius, On the State of the Church, chap. on the state of the Pope, art. 28, puffs up the Pope thus: He is and is called Christ's vicar, and as it were God on earth, and what he does, it is not a human prince but God who seems to do it. Erasmus, Annotations on the New Testament, 1 Tim. 11, is a witness that in his own time it was disputed whether the Pope is a plain man, or whether, as if God, he shares both natures with Christ. Adoardus Gualandus, Bishop of Cesena, On Moral and Civil Matters, bk. xiv, 3, adorns the Pope thus: From the Pope, he says, as from the head into the whole body of the Church, that is, into every Christian commonwealth, the Spirits flow, bringing a sense and fruit of heavenly graces and an effective motion toward eternal blessedness. Rightly, therefore, is he called most holy and most blessed, and by all who profess the Christian religion he is worshipped and honoured as a certain God. Augustinus Steuchus, librarian to the Pope, after citing On the Donation of Constantine, p. 141, the story of Constantine calling the Pope God, adds these words: Do you hear that the Supreme Pontiff was called God by Constantine and held to be God? This was clearly done when he honoured him with that famous edict; he worshipped him as God, as the successor of Christ and of Peter. He conferred on him divine honours, as far as he could, as if he were venerating a living image of Christ. Baronius, and from the same source Spondanus, Annotations, p. 1058, report that a shrewd Saracen prince came to the feet of Alexander III, kissed his feet, bent his knees before him and, with his head bowed, worshipped the Pontiff himself as the holy and pious God of the Christians. The approval of the deed is added in these words: In what is said about the Prince of the Mahometans, you may see the works of God, since not only Christian kings but also Saracens rise and honour the Roman Pontiff with a splendid embassy, when the impious Emperor of the Romans was cruelly persecuting him. It is pleasing to add Bellarmine to all these. In his Response to Gerson, which is found among the acts and various writings of the controversy between Paul V and the Venetians, pp. 468–469, he writes thus: Let the little and simple ones hold that a certain Pope is God and has all power in heaven and on earth. Their weakness and simplicity please God more than the firmness of those who wish to seem prudent to themselves. It is a small thing to regard the Pope as God on earth, since in the Psalm it is said of all princes: I have said, you are gods. Nor is it inappropriate to say that the Pope has all power in heaven and on earth.

units.la: VII. Imbellis tamen prorsus est illa Bellarmini ex verbis Psalmi lxxxii. 6. Ego dixi, Dii estis; petita ratio. Præterquam enim quòd hoc non de potestate ecclesiastica, sed de civili dictum est, quodque propterea nemo unus Imperator vel Rex pius se Deum vel Numen appellari sustinuit: quòd sermo Dei ad Papam, quo rector mundi constitueretur, factus nullus est: vident etiam omnes, alia mente Papis huncce titulum tribui. Nam confortes illi nullos admittunt, & soli inter homines ecclesiasticos Deus, quasi Deus &c. insigniri amant. Alioquin cùm disertum sit, Dii estis, si nullo id sibi alio jure vendicaret Papa, deberent quicunque in Ecclesiastica sunt dignitate, Dii in terris dici. Atqui Cardinales Avinionenses apud Froffardum Unicum in terris Deum nuncupant. Stapletonus quoque in dedicatoria Operis de Principiis, Gregorium xiii. plane supremum in terris Numen salutat.
