Observandum insuper, vocabulum יהוה Jehova in V.T. Deo Summo peculiare esse: & nomen אלהים aliis quoque tribui. At Novum Testamentum splendidius vocabulum, quo Summum Numen designet, non habet, quam illud DEUS, quod nulli proin tribuitur nisi Deo æterno, & Diabolo
units.tr: VII. Yet Bellarmine's argument drawn from the words of Psalm 82:6, "I have said, Ye are gods," is utterly feeble. Apart from the fact that this was said of civil power, not ecclesiastical power, and that for this reason no single pious Emperor or King ever ventured to be called God or a deity; and apart from the fact that no word of God was addressed to the Pope appointing him ruler of the world, everyone also sees that this title is given to the Pope with a different intent. For those companions admit no partners, and they love to be marked out alone among churchmen as God, as it were God, and so on. Otherwise, since it is plain that Ye are gods, if the Pope claimed this on no other right, all who hold ecclesiastical office should be called gods on earth. Yet the Avignon Cardinals, in Froissart, name him the only God on earth. Stapleton too, in the dedication of his work On the Principles, greets Gregory XIII as plainly the supreme deity on earth. Furthermore, observe that the word יהוה Jehovah in the Old Testament is peculiar to the Supreme God, while the name אלהים is given to others as well. But the New Testament has no more distinguished word to designate the Supreme Deity than DEUS, which is therefore given to no one except the eternal God and to the Devil,

units.la: 2.Cor.iv.3. quia apud impios locum veri Dei invasit. Novissimis Seculis accessit Papa tertius, qui Deus appellaretur, quo nomine nec Archangelum, nec Angelum ullum dignatur.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4:3, because among the impious he has usurped the place of the true God. In the latest ages a third Pope has been added, who is called God, a name he does not deign to grant to any archangel or angel.

units.la: VIII. Sed misso illo plus quàm Luciferianæ ambitionis titulo, de re ipsa dicamus. Esto enim, Papa vel Deus nunquam ab aliis dictus fuerit; vel axioma isthoc à gnathonibus sibi tributum, uti sanè debebat, dispuerit: Si tamen aut fecit, aut passus est, quod abundè ejus vocis defectum suppleat, ut verba Optati Milevitani repetam; jam, eodem judice, rem ipsam suam fecit, &, quòd Deus sit, declaravit manifeste. Quorsum autem, quæso, hæc referimus, quæ Glossator Decreti, Titulo de Trans- latione Episcopi, capite Quanta persona, undique tantà diligentia conquisivit? Nam cùm Innocentius III. dixitset, Romanum Pontificem non puri hominis, sed veri Dei vicem gerere in terris; Glossator citatis tum ex Decretis, tum ex Decretalibus locis, hinc sequi asserit, habere Papam cœleste arbitrium, naturam rerum immutare, substantialia unius rei applicando alii; de nullo posse facere aliquid; sententiam, quæ nulla est, posse facere aliquam; in his quæ vult, esse ei pro ratione voluntatem; nec esse, qui ei dicat, Cur ita facis? ipsum posse supra jus dispensare; de injustitia posse facere justitiam, corrigendo jura & mutando, plenitudinem obtinere potestatis. Quomodo etiam delecti Cardinales in consilio Paulo iv. exhibito, notant, extitisse Doctores, qui dicerent, voluntatem Pontificis, qualiscunque ea fuerit, esse regulam, qua ejus operationes & actiones dirigantur; unde procul dubio efficiatur, ut quicquid libet, id etiam liceat. Paulus II. Platina teste, Ita, inquiebat, ad judices nos revocas, ac si nescires, omnia jura in scrinio pectoris nostri collocata esse. Sic stat sententia, loco cedunt omnes, eant quò volunt, nisi eos moror: Pontifex sum, mihique licet pro arbitrio animi mei aliorum facta & rescindere, & approbare. Quis Divina ifthæc omnia esse, adeoque Divinitatem sibi arrogare, quisquis ea sibi vendicat; inficiari ausit?
units.tr: VIII. But, setting aside that title, more than Luciferian in its ambition, let us speak of the matter itself. Grant that the Pope has never been called God by others, or that he has rejected this maxim attributed to him by flatterers, as he certainly ought to have done. Yet if he has either done or suffered something which abundantly makes up for the lack of that word, to borrow the words of Optatus of Milevis, then by that same judge he has made the thing itself his own, and has plainly declared that he is God. But why, I ask, do we cite these things, which the Glossator of the Decretum, under the title On the Translation of a Bishop, at the chapter Quanta persona, has searched out with such diligence from every quarter? For when Innocent III had said that the Roman Pontiff bears the place not of a mere man but of the true God on earth, the Glossator, citing passages both from the Decretum and from the Decretals, argues that it follows that the Pope has heavenly authority; that he can change the nature of things, applying the substantial qualities of one thing to another; that he can make something out of nothing; that he can make a sentence which is nothing into something; that in those matters which he wills, his will is his reason; that there is no one who may say to him, Why do you act so? that he himself can dispense above the law; that he can make justice out of injustice by correcting and changing laws; and that he holds the fullness of power. In the same way, the chosen Cardinals, in the counsel presented to Paul IV, note that there were teachers who said that the will of the Pontiff, whatever it may be, is the rule by which his operations and actions are directed; from which it follows beyond doubt that whatever he pleases is also lawful. Paul II, according to Platina's testimony, said: "So you call us back to the judges, as if you did not know that all laws are stored in the casket of our breast. Thus the sentence stands; everyone gives way; let them go where they will, unless I detain them. I am the Pontiff, and it is lawful for me, at the discretion of my own mind, both to annul and to approve the acts of others." Who would dare to deny that all these things are divine, and that whoever claims them for himself arrogates divinity to himself?

units.la: IX. Sed posset horum perversè adeò dictorum culpa vel Glossatoris parasiti lenociniis, vel relationi cuipiam malæ fidei transcribi. Age ergo, rem ipsam demus authorem, & certissimis argumentorum notionibus decernamus. Is ergo Divinitatem sibi reapse arrogat, qui eam sibi authoritatem tribuit, quæ non nisi enti æterno, perfectissimo, sapientissimo, potentissimo competit. Data enim definitione non potest negari definitum. Hoc autem facit Papa. Nam, qua solus Deus authoritate pollet, in se credi postulat: leges fert, quibus per se conscientia soli Deo obnoxia obligetur: tradit media justificationis proprio motu, & aliunde non accepta: affectat potestatem clavium herilem & in peccatis remittendis judicialem: vult videri caput, fundamentum, petra Ecclesiæ: potestatem sibi transferendi regna & Regibus imperitandi vindicat: dispensandi contra legem Dei, & à juramentis ac votis legitimis absolvendi licentiam sibi sumit: Sanctos Divos pro lubitu creat: denique se adorari, adeóque religiosè coli patitur. Quæ omnia Divina, uti S. literæ & sana ratio dictant, ἀνχήμαΐα, cùm Papa sibi tribuat, adeóque Divinorum attributorum spoliis sese exornet; quid aliud se quam idolum, imò Matrem fcortationum & Babylonium Regem prodit? Juvabit singula paulò uberius exponere.
units.tr: IX. But the fault might be laid, perhaps, either on the wicked flattery of the parasite Glossator, or on some report written in bad faith. Come then, let us grant the matter itself its author, and let us decide it by the most certain notions of arguments. He, then, arrogates Divinity to himself in fact who attributes to himself that authority which belongs only to a being that is eternal, most perfect, most wise and most powerful. For once the definition is given, the thing defined cannot be denied. Now the Pope does this. For he demands to be believed in himself, in the power that only God has alone: he issues laws by which consciences, subject to God alone, are bound of their own accord; he hands on the means of justification by his own motion, not received from elsewhere; he claims the power of the keys, both lordly and judicial in remitting sins; he wishes to be seen as the head, foundation and rock of the Church; he claims for himself the power to transfer kingdoms and to rule over kings; he takes to himself the licence to dispense against the law of God and to absolve from lawful oaths and vows; he creates saints at his pleasure; and finally he allows himself to be adored, and so to be worshipped with religious honour. Since the Pope claims for himself all these things, which, as Holy Scripture and sound reason declare, are divine, and ἀνχήμαΐα [unlawful usurpations/ things to be grasped at], and thus adorns himself with the spoils of the divine attributes, what else does he reveal himself to be but an idol, indeed the Mother of harlotries and the Babylonian King? It will help to set out each point a little more fully.

units.la: X. Primò solum Deum esse ἀψὸμεον fidei objectum, adeóque in solum eum credendum esse, tum S. Scriptura Exod. xx. 3. Jerem. xvii. 5. Joh. xiv. 1. alibique passim testatur: tum recta ratio docet. Is enim fidei nostræ objectum est, qui prima veritas est, qui alio teste non indiget, quippe verax adeò & fidelis, ut de salute hominum teftanti fides sine exceptione debeatur, qualis solus Deus est. Papam verò fidei humanæ objectum sic constitui, ut in ipsum credere homines teneantur, liquet, tum quia sibi de Divinitate Scripturæ authenticè testificandi authoritatem arrogat, & uti quondam de Ethnicis Tertullianus Apol. c.5. dixit,de humano arbitratu Divinitatem pensitat; adeò ut vetet Scripturam pro Dei verbo accipi, eidémque fidem adhiberi nisi propter dictum suum, non ullo alio Divino vel majore testimonio nixum, sed incertis quibusdam duntaxat testificantis dictis suffultum: tum quia verbum quoddam non scriptum, sed traditum obtrudit, cujus Divinitas nullis certis & indubitabilibus notis, sed solius Papæ dicto, velut authentico nititur: tum quia Scripturæ, cujus obscuritatem, imperfectionem, impotentiam ad demonstrandam Divinitatem suam, palam causatur, sensum eum duntaxat fidelibus suis dictat, qui à sua voluntate & nutu pendeat, neque ampliori demonstratione ex verbo Divino scripto ipso indigeat, atque sic Scripturam subjicit τῇ ἰδίᾳ Ϡπλνσι, ἐχ ἰδίῳ Ϡελήματι propriæ dissolutioni, & propriæ voluntati, libidini & motui proprio; atque per ministros suos sensum ejusdem ad stabilimentum potentiæ & authoritatis suæ detorqueri, & pravis glossis corrumpi non tantùm patitur, sed etiam curat: tum quia canonicam librorum Sacrorum authoritatem sic ab arbitrio suo suspendit, ut canonicos censeri non eos, quorum Divinitatem certis notis & traditionis evidentia compertam & exploratam omni conscientiæ reddere possit, sed eos demum, quos modò velit ipse, non alia majore ratione, quàm nutu isthoc proprio, fretus jubeat: tum quia non patitur legi Scripturam, & versionibus ac explanationibus vernaculis populo illustrari, ut eò magis sibi & dicto suo obnoxios audientésque reddat: tum quia versionem Latinam authenticam esse, ex eadémque fontes examinari jubet, atque sic arbiter haberi vult Divinitatis: tum denique quia definitionibus suis sive in Concilio, sive extra illud conclusos articulos fidei conscientiam fidelium obligantes effici, qui ante definitiones ejusmodi licet clarè etiam in ipsis Scripturis comprehensi, tales neutiquam fuerint, adeóque liberæ hominum in utramque partem disputantium opinioni subjecti fuerint, pertendit.
units.tr: X. First, that God alone is the object of faith, and that we must believe in him alone, is attested by Holy Scripture (Exod. 20:3; Jer. 17:5; John 14:1, and passim elsewhere) and is taught by right reason. For he is the object of our faith who is the first truth, who needs no other witness, being so true and faithful that faith is owed without exception to one who testifies about the salvation of men, as God alone is. That the Pope is set up as the object of human faith, so that men are bound to believe in him, is plain: first, because he claims for himself the authority of authentically attesting the divinity of Scripture, and, as Tertullian once said of the heathen, weighs divinity by human judgement. So he forbids Scripture to be received as the word of God, or given faith, except on his own saying, which rests on no other divine or greater testimony but is supported only by certain uncertain sayings of the witness. Second, because he thrusts upon us an unwritten word, which is handed down rather than written, whose divinity rests on no certain and indubitable marks but on the Pope's word alone, as if it were authentic. Third, because he openly alleges the obscurity and imperfection of Scripture and its inability to demonstrate its own divinity, and dictates to the faithful only that sense which depends on his will and nod, and so has no need of further demonstration from the written word of God itself. Thus he subjects Scripture to its own dissolution, and to its own will [τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει, οὐκ ἐξ ἰδίου θελήματος], to his own lust and impulse; and he not only allows but takes care that its sense be twisted through his ministers to establish his power and authority, and corrupted by wicked glosses. Fourth, because he so suspends the canonical authority of the Holy Books at his own pleasure that those are deemed canonical not which he can prove to every conscience to be divine by certain marks and the evident testimony of tradition, but only those which he now wishes, relying on nothing greater than his own nod. Fifth, because he does not allow Scripture to be read, and the people to be enlightened by vernacular versions and explanations, so that he may make them more bound to himself and to his word and more obedient to him. Sixth, because he declares the Latin version to be authentic and orders that the sources be examined by it, and so wishes to be regarded as the judge of divinity. Last, because he holds that articles of faith, concluded by his definitions either in a Council or outside it, are made to bind the conscience of the faithful, although before such definitions they were by no means such, even if they were clearly contained in Scripture itself, and so were subject to the free opinion of men disputing on either side.

units.la: XI. Cuncta feré hæc pertinent ad eam controversiam quæ cum Pontificiis nobis intercedit de regula fidei, ejusdemque analysi, seu resolutione ultima, de qua jam supra Dißl. vÿ. 12-18. egimus; nec non de necessitate propositionis Ecclesiæ, ut illi loqui amant, hoc est, Papæ. Nam Papam non equidem facere verbum Dei, sensum ejusdem, vel articulum fidei, sed tantùm proponere; ac proin fidei objectum non Papam proponentem, sed verbum Dei à Papa propositum constitui, asserunt. Ut enim quis fide Divina assentiatur verbo Dei, quatuor requirunt, ut verbum Dei, sive objectum, quod creditur, sit Divinitus revelatum: ut illud objectum nobis sufficienter proponatur: ut veritas, quæ credenda proponitur, sit evidenter credibilis: denique gratiam Spiritus S. Sic ut probetur articulus fidei, tria exigere solent, Verbum Dei: ut sit qui proponat verbum Dei: ut de fidelitate proponentis sufficienter constet. Distinguunt etiam objectum fidei formale & materiale. Illud ajunt esse Deum, tanquam veritatem primam revelantem: hoc articulos fidei, uti ab Ecclesia, hoc est, Papa proponuntur. Sic passim Walenburgii aliique.
units.tr: XI. Almost all of these points belong to that controversy which we have with the Papists concerning the rule of faith and its analysis, or ultimate resolution, which we have already treated above (Diss. V, 12–18); and likewise concerning the necessity of the proposal of the Church, as they love to put it, that is, of the Pope. For they assert that the Pope does not indeed make the word of God, or its sense, or an article of faith, but only proposes it; and therefore that the object of faith is not the Pope proposing, but the word of God proposed by the Pope. For they require four things if anyone is to assent to the word of God with divine faith: that the word of God, or the object which is believed, be divinely revealed; that this object be sufficiently proposed to us; that the truth which is proposed to be believed be evidently credible; and, last, the grace of the Holy Spirit. Again, to prove an article of faith they usually require three things: the word of God; that there be someone who proposes the word of God; and that the faithfulness of the one proposing be sufficiently established. They also distinguish the formal and material object of faith. They say the former is God, as the first truth revealing; the latter are the articles of faith as they are proposed by the Church, that is, by the Pope. So Walenburgius and others, passim.

units.la: XII. Sed hæc mera sιτυαν, affecta simulatio mendaciloquorum, adeóque fucus Babylonis Magnæ meretricius est. Dolum enim Sophistæ in voce proponendi simplicioribus struunt. Aliud enim est proponere cum authoritate, ita ut ea propositio sit definitio, hoc, quod traditur, esse verbum Dei; & propter eam definitionem, tanquam credendi causam, absque ulla demonstratione, sola definientis & proponentis authoritate obligetur fides, & sine ea non obligetur. Aliud est proponere in significatu modestiore, hoc est, narrare ea, quæ Deus dixit, & non pati ea negligi, aut oblivioni mandari; eáque dicta esse à Deo, idoneis evidentibúsque argumentis astruere & demonstrare. Posterius non solì Papæ, sed omnibus in universum fidelibus Ecclesiæ Ministris Pastoribus & doctoribus, imò toti Ecclesiæ, pro suo cuique captu, incumbit. Quo officio mediante Divina revelatio semel ad homines facta per omnia mundi climata sic propagatur, ut etiam ii, qui non audiverunt, aut viderunt, participes fiant Divinæ revelationis, persuasi per ea, quæ constantissimè narrantur, & quæ conscientia ipsorum in verbo propósito vera, justa, Deóque decentia deprehendit, & quæ secundum verbi prædictiones in se, & extra se experitur, non ab hominibus ficta, sed à Deo facta esse. Ejusmodi propositio, humanæ modestiæ conveniens, apud eos, qui primi non viderunt vel audiverunt, ordinariè ad fidem intervenit, ut effectus revelationis Divinæ causam suam demonstrans, quia nisi talis revelatio primitùs revera facta esset, & Deus dixisset, authenticéque propósuisset, præcones, dictum à Deo evangelizantes, nulli extitissent.
units.tr: XII. But these are mere pretence, the feigned pretence of liars [ψευδολογία], and so the harlot's paint of Babylon the Great. For the Sophists lay their trick in the word to propose for simpler folk. For it is one thing to propose with authority, so that the proposal is a definition that what is handed down is the word of God; and on account of that definition, as the ground of belief, faith is bound without any demonstration, by the sole authority of the one defining and proposing, and without it is not bound. It is another thing to propose in a more modest sense, that is, to relate what God has said, not to allow it to be neglected or forgotten, and to establish and demonstrate by fitting and evident arguments that these things were said by God. The latter falls not only to the Pope, but to all the ministers, pastors and teachers of the Church in general, and indeed to the whole Church, each according to his capacity. By means of this office the divine revelation once made to men is so propagated through all the climes of the world that even those who did not hear or see it become partakers of the divine revelation, persuaded by what is most constantly related, and what their conscience finds true, just and fitting to God in the proposed word, and what they experience, in accordance with the predictions of the word, both in themselves and outside themselves, to have been made not by men's fiction but by God. Such a proposal, suited to human modesty, ordinarily brings faith to those who did not first see or hear, as an effect demonstrating the cause of the divine revelation; for unless such a revelation had really been made first, and God had spoken and authentically proposed it, there would be no heralds proclaiming the word given by God.

units.la: XIII. Dispar longè ratio est proponentis cum authoritate, atque ea propositione, ceu definitione sola, absque ulla demonstratione, quòd verbum à Deo editum sit, fidem obligantis. Hoc verò solius Dei est, qui solus cum authoritate, & sine demonstratione, ceu primus testis omni exceptione major, & prima veritas, fidem obligare poteßt. Nam si verbum Dei mihi revelatum est, sive primitùs, sive quòd ego, qui primitùs non vidi & audivi, tamen Θεοπνεύστος (2 Tim. iii. 14.) fide plenè mihi facta certior redditus sum (uterque enim habet revelationem, & qui primus audivit ac vidit, & qui cognovit ac rescivit inter ultimos) non est necessarius utique alius fidei dictator & author. Imò talem fidei auctorem ac Dictatorem introducere, est Divinæ vocis τὸ πρὸν ἐ ἀληθὲς mor, & veritatis fulgur, & Divinæ Majestatis authoritatem, & vim conscientiæ, Divino juri & Divinæ sapientiæ attestantis, negare; denique id quod Dei est, in hominem transferre, adeóque ex homine, qui natura mendax est, Deum facere.
units.tr: XIII. The reason for a proposer with authority, binding faith by that proposal alone, as a definition, without any demonstration that the word was put forth by God, is very different. This belongs only to God, who alone, with authority and without demonstration, as the first witness, greater than any exception, and the first truth, can bind faith. For if the word of God has been revealed to me, whether first, or because I, who did not first see and hear, have nevertheless been made fully certain by faith that it is God-breathed [Θεόπνευστος] (2 Tim. 3:14)—for both have the revelation, both he who first heard and saw and he who knew and learned it among the last—then surely there is no need of another dictator and author of faith. Indeed, to introduce such an author and dictator of faith is to deny the divine voice the first true thing [τὸ πρῶτον ἀληθές], and the flash of truth, and the authority of the divine Majesty, and the power of conscience bearing witness to divine right and divine wisdom; in short, it is to transfer to man what belongs to God, and so, out of a man who is by nature a liar, to make a God.

units.la: XIV. Talem propositionem authenticam nusquam Scriptura nobis commendavit.
units.tr: XIV. Scripture has nowhere commended to us any such authoritative proposition.

units.la: Piè potiùs considerandum, quid de propagatione Evangelii nobis Pf. lxviii. 12. prænuntiatum sit. Verba Psaltis habent : ארני יהן אמר המבשרות צבא רב Dominus dabat dictum. Evangelizantes exercitus magnus. Reges exercituum fugiebant. En loquentem Deum, turmas narrantium visa & audita, eásque magis magisque increbrescentes passim; hoc est, prædicationem Euangelii per Christi discipulos narrantes visa & audita, cum fide mendi; hinc certamina, hinc exercitus collectos contra Ecclesiam, & exercituum cum Regibus ingeminatam fugam. Nulla hic propositio authentica, dictatoria, præter אמר ארני dictum Domini, cui non propositio authentica unius hominis, sed ministerialis euangelizatio exercituum inservit. Atque sic Christus Θεοπνεύστος ἐν κόσμῳ creditus est in mundo 1. Tim. iii. 16. Eodem modo creditur à nobis & Christus, & verbum illud, in quo, uti ipsó experimento cognoscimus, sic prædicatio ipsius & fides prædicta est. Papam verò, Proponentem scilicet authenticè, ceu Novellum Numen, Babyloniis relinquimus.
units.tr: Rather, let us piously consider what Psalm 68:12 foretold about the spread of the Gospel. The Psalmist's words are: The Lord gave the word; those who bear good tidings are a great host; the kings of the armies fled [ארני יהן אמר המבשרות צבא רב]. Here is God speaking, and crowds of people telling what they have seen and heard, and spreading it more and more everywhere. That is, the preaching of the Gospel is carried by Christ's disciples, who tell what they have seen and heard, with faith and not with lies. Hence come the conflicts, hence the armies gathered against the Church, and the repeated flight of the armies and their kings. Here there is no authoritative, dictatorial proposition apart from the word of the Lord [אמר ארני], and to that word no authoritative proposition of a single man is joined, but only the ministerial evangelizing of the armies. And so Christ was believed on in the world [Θεοπνεύστος ἐν κόσμῳ], as 1 Tim. 3:16 says. In the same way Christ is believed by us, and so is that word, by which, as we know from experience itself, both his preaching and faith are carried. As for the Pope, who would put himself forward authoritatively as proposer, like a new deity, we leave him to the Babylonians.

units.la: XV. Secundò Deum fegerit Papa, cùm leges innume- ras
units.tr: XV. Secondly, the Pope makes himself God, since he issues countless laws

units.la: 11. Quod legis innu-
units.tr: 11. Because he issues countless

units.la: ras religiosas fert, iisque conscientias fidelium oblicontendit. Etenim ὁ νομοθέτης unicus Legislator, I
units.tr: religious laws, and binds the consciences of the faithful to them. For the Lawgiver is one, the sole Legislator [ὁ νομοθέτης], as James 4:12 says.

units.la: est, qui solus potest servare & perdere; Jac. iv. 12. igitur nemo, praeter solum Deum, potest servare & pere totum hominem: ita nemo conscientiis hominum leejusmodi imponere potest, qua observata homo salvviolata perdatur, à solo Deo si discesseris. Possunt quin societate civili homines communicata à Deo potimperare aliis, & legibus proprie dictis eosdem obstrre; non tamen sic, ut in religione & spiritualibus conftiis hominum, soli Deo obnoxiis Rom. ii. 14. 15. dnari, eaque legibus nusquam à Deo revelatis obstrivaleant. Hoc enim πεπληρωμα est illius Unius LegislatDei, quod tam non hominibus unquam communicquàm non potestatem creandi, vel aeternum salvandidendique. Alias leges humanae aequales Divinis, &Deo homo foret. Et sanè Leges ac judicia Ecclesicumprimis, longè inferiora sunt conscientia hominis.Apostolo I. Cor. iv. 3. 4. Mihi minimum est, ut à judicer, vel ab ulla humana die. Cùmque leges eccsticae de adiaphoris merè externae sint, conscientiaeinterna tota est, dominari nequeunt. Denique sic Letorem unicum, Deum, esse, S. Jacobus pronuntiainde nemini fas esse judicare alterum, concludat. Mste igitur legislationem & judicium in conscientias hobus abrogat, & uni solique Deo vindicat.
units.tr: is he who alone can save and destroy (Jas. 4:12). Therefore no one but God alone can save or destroy the whole man. So no one can impose upon men's consciences laws of such a kind that a man is saved if they are kept and lost if they are violated, unless he has departed from God alone. Indeed, in civil society men may command others with authority communicated to them by God, and bind them by laws properly so called. Yet not so as to rule in religion and in the spiritual matters of men's consciences, which are subject to God alone (Rom. 2:14, 15), and to bind them by laws nowhere revealed by God. For this is the fullness of that one God, the Lawgiver, which has never been communicated to men, any more than the power of creating, or of saving and condemning eternally. Otherwise human laws would be equal to divine laws, and man would be God. Indeed the laws and judgments of the Church, above all, are far inferior to the conscience of man: It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you, or by any human day (1 Cor. 4:3, 4). And since ecclesiastical laws concerning things indifferent are merely external, while the conscience is wholly inward, they cannot rule it. Finally, St James, pronouncing that there is one Lawgiver and Judge, concludes that it is not right for anyone to judge another. He therefore takes away legislation and judgment over consciences from men and claims them for God alone.

units.la: XVI. Locum difertissimum S. Jacobi putido & lanti cavillo Walenburgii Controv. 8. num. 8. elucquasi mens ei fuerit distinguere Legislatores, quorum solus salvare & perdere possit; reliqui nequeant. Sident Scripturas depravare, ne Papae Babylonica intas subolere possit. Atqui S. Jacobus contra ex eo, nemo potest servare & perdere nisi unus, unitatem Letoris clarissimè probat. Nam quid ad rem, quam tractabat, pertineret, si non est unus absolutè Legislator, dicere, unum esse Legislatorem talem, qui possit salvare & perdere?
units.tr: XVI. The most eloquent passage of St James is met with a foul and shabby quibble from Walenburg, Controv. 8, num. 8, as if his meaning were to distinguish between lawgivers, of whom only one can save and destroy while the others cannot. He is eager to distort the Scriptures, lest the Babylonian bane of the Pope should be scented. Yet St James, on the contrary, argues from the fact that no one can save and destroy except one, and so very clearly proves the unity of the Lawgiver. For what would it matter to the point he was treating if there were not one Lawgiver absolutely, but only one such lawgiver who can save and destroy?

units.la: XVII. De Papa, legibus religiosis latis conscientiis hominum dominante res manifesta est.
units.tr: XVII. Concerning the Pope, who rules the consciences of men by religious laws, the matter is plain.

units.la: Concilii enim Tridentini Patres Seff. vÿ. can. 8. illam Lutheri propositionem baptizatos liberos esse ab omnibus humanis præceptis, religiosis videlicet, & ccu parte necessaria cultus Divini conscientiam per se obligantibus, anathemate notârunt. Nos quidem Baptismum authoritatem, vel reverentiam Ecclesiastici Ministerii abolere, quasi videlicet baptizati Ecclesiam non audire, cùm monendi sunt; vel ei, qui in nomine Dei monentur aut corripiuntur, non obedire teneantur, haud statuimus. Neque etiam negamus, debere baptizatos omnibus & singulis fidelibus, nedum Ecclesiæ reverentiam, obedientiam & subjectionem, ut pareant admonitionibus in nomine Dei factis, & ordinem externum actionum toti coetui communi consensu non contra verbum Dei injunctarum, constitutum non turbent, & congregationem non relinquant; & talem denique, quæ ex Ecclesiastico præcepto, non Divino, cultui, ut pars quædam, adjungatur, sed præceptorum Dei executioni unicè inserviat. Sed aliud est, quod Tridentinum anathema intendit; esse videlicet in Ecclesia, capite cumprimis ejus, Papa, potestatem quandam ἀυτο-κεφάλευ & ιερωθικῶ, ἀρχῶ & βασιλείαν, Principatum & Regnum quoddam, propter quod Ecclesiæ, Papæ inprimis, qui Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ caput, cor & stomachus est, liceat leges Divinis æquipollentes, utpote à Spiritu S. perpetim Papæ assistente æquè immediatè profectas, & quidem plerunque de rebus carnalibus & terrenis, quas mysteriis Papa, alter scilicet אל מסר־חר Deus mysteriorum Esai. XLV. 15. impraegnare posset, condere: subditis verò necessum sit propter conscientiam, & in judicio Dei obedire. Quam potestatem ἐξουσίαν & ἀντικείμενον ad omnes actiones, corpora & bona baptizatorum, ipsorum etiam Summorum Regum & Principum saltem indirectè, quatenus ad Spiritualem finem referuntur, (quasi non omnis actio ad finem Spiritualem referenda sit. unde sive directè, sive indirectè dicas, perinde est) extendunt. Hic, si usquam, Papa venit in nomine suo ἀνθρώπου ἀνομίας, demonstrans se ipsum, quòd Deus sit.
units.tr: For the Fathers of the Council of Trent, Sess. 7, can. 8, condemned with an anathema Luther's proposition that baptized persons are free from all human precepts, that is, religious precepts which bind the conscience of themselves to the necessary part of divine worship. We indeed do not hold that baptism abolishes the authority or the reverence due to the ecclesiastical ministry, as if the baptized need not hear the Church when they are admonished, or need not obey those who are admonished or rebuked in God's name. Nor do we deny that the baptized, and indeed all the faithful, owe reverence, obedience and submission to the Church, so that they obey admonitions made in God's name, do not disturb the external order of actions established by the common consent of the whole assembly, provided it is not contrary to the word of God, and do not abandon the congregation; and finally that they add to worship, as a part of it, whatever is enjoined by ecclesiastical precept, not divine, and yet serves solely the carrying out of God's precepts. But the Tridentine anathema means something else: that there is in the Church, and above all in its head, the Pope, a certain autocephalous and hierarchical [αὐτοκεφάλευ, ἱερωθικῶ] authority, principate and kingdom [ἀρχῶ, βασιλείαν], by virtue of which the Church, and the Pope above all, who is the head, heart and stomach of the Papist Church, may enact laws equal to divine laws, as though proceeding immediately from the Holy Spirit who is always present with the Pope, and indeed mostly about carnal and earthly matters, which the Pope, that is, the God of mysteries [אל מסר־חר] Deus mysteriorum, Isa. 45:15, could make pregnant with mysteries; and subjects must obey them for the sake of conscience and before the judgment of God. They extend this power [ἐξουσίαν] and authority [ἀντικείμενον] over all the actions, bodies and goods of the baptized, and even of the highest kings and princes, at least indirectly, insofar as they are referred to a spiritual end (as if every action were not to be referred to a spiritual end; so whether you say directly or indirectly makes no difference). Here, if anywhere, the Pope comes in his own name, the man of lawlessness [ἀνθρώπου ἀνομίας], showing himself that he is God.

units.la: XVIII. In rem praesentem ut descendamus, annon Papa innumeris legibus, Decretis & Decretalibus Ecclesiam oppressit; actiones humanas infinitas sua natura liberas, saltem non malas, voluntate sua malas, peccaminosas esse jussit; omnibus propemodum creaturis peccati labem aspersit, ut jam nefas sit vesci butyro, ovis, caseis, lacticiniis, carnibus &c. quod jubente & permittente Deo fas erat; tempora & dies peccatorum nova labe polluit, sic ut certis & fixis nutu ejus temporibus, sub mortalis peccati reatu, prohibeantur homines usu ciborum, quos Deus condidit, ut à fidelibus & coelestis veritatis peritis cum gratiarum actione sumantur; loca & vasa plurima aurea, argentea, lapidea, lignea puta altaria, calicem, patinam, corporale, aliàque ejusmodi sic sanctificavit, ut sine gravi peccato à plebe ne contrectari quidem possint; thorum, quem almus Dei Spiritus apud omnes, juxta leges videlicet in verbo ejus praescriptas, honestum & impollutum esse jussit, ipse inhonestum & pollutum apud eos, quibus Deus in verbo suo liquidò matrimonium permisit, esse voluit, jussit: ipsos capitis mentique capillos immundos declaravit, tonsuram rasuramque lege lata, & sub peccato, sanciendo; omnem hominum plebejorum vitam, actionésque impuras declaravit, solúmque clerum & Hierarchiam suam sacerrimam, puram, spiritualem sanctámque declaravit; vestimenta Monachorum & Sacerdotum peculiaria sic consecravit, ut non ex præscripto ea gestantes grandem peccati reatum contraherent; denique ex pluribus aliis non peccatis peccata fecit, adeoque se supra Deum Deorum nefariè extulit? Nam Deus quidem per Mosen leges varias tulit, iisque actiones hominum liberas sic constrinxit, ut transgressores se peccatorum reos efficerent. Ita scilicet Supremo Numini, & Domino dominorum licuit. At hæc Dei, Supremi Numinis, simia non tantùm æmulum ejus se gerit, sed imperiis etiam suis & onerosis & numerosis Deum unicum Legislatorem multis parasangis antecellit, leges cultúmque ejus mirificè obscurat, contaminat, abrogat, peccata in immensum multiplicat, denique nihil non pro Numine Supremo & infinito, novus Deaster vel potiùs purpurata hæc Meretrix facit.
units.tr: XVIII. To come to the matter at hand: has not the Pope oppressed the Church with countless laws, decrees and decretals? Has he not ordered that innumerable human actions, free by their nature and at least not evil, be made sinful by his will? Has he not spattered almost all creatures with the stain of sin, so that it is now a crime to eat butter, eggs, cheese, milk products, meats and so on, which by God's command and permission was lawful? Has he not polluted times and days with a new stain, so that at fixed seasons, by his nod, under the guilt of mortal sin, men are forbidden the use of the foods God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful who know heavenly truth? Has he not sanctified many places and vessels of gold, silver, stone and wood, such as altars, the chalice, the paten, the corporal and the like, so that without grave sin the common people may not even touch them? He ordered the marriage bed to be honourable and undefiled among all, according to the laws prescribed in God's word, yet he himself wished and ordered it to be dishonourable and defiled among those to whom God in his word has plainly permitted marriage. He declared the hair of head and mind unclean, enacting by law, under pain of sin, the tonsure and shaving. He declared the whole life and actions of the common people impure, and declared only his clergy and hierarchy most holy, pure, spiritual and sacred. He so consecrated the distinctive vestments of monks and priests that those who wear them without his prescription would incur great guilt of sin. And finally, from many other things that are not sins, has he not made sins, and so wickedly exalted himself above God, the God of gods? For God indeed gave various laws through Moses, and by them bound men's free actions so that transgressors became guilty of sins. That, of course, was permitted to the Supreme Deity and the Lord of lords. But this ape of God, the Supreme Deity, not only acts as his rival, but with his burdensome and numerous commands far surpasses the one God, the sole Lawgiver, by many parasangs. He obscures, pollutes and abrogates his laws and worship in marvellous ways, multiplies sins beyond measure, and in a word, does everything in place of the Supreme and infinite Deity, as this new little god, or rather this purple-clad harlot, does.

units.la: XIX. Jugulum novo huic Deastro rectà petit S. Paulus Col. II. 18 – 22. sic scribens: Nemo vos καταβραβευέτω seducat (jure vestro privet, brabeo defraudet) volens (ex proprio motu) in humilitate & religione (cultu) Angelorum, quæ non vidit, ambulans, frustra inflatus sensu carnis suæ, καὶ οὐ κρατῶν τὴν κεφαλὴν, & non tenens caput &c. Si ergo mortui estis cum Christo ab elementis hujus mundi, quid adhuc tanquam viventes in mundo δογματίζεσθε decretis oneramini (cujusmodi sunt) μὴ ἅψῃ, μηδὲ γεύσῃ, μηδὲ θίγῃς. Ne tetigeris, ne gustaveris, neque contrectaveris. Dogmata, decreta Papæ, prohibentis quibusdam tangere uxores, nubere, vesci certis cibis, &c. adeóque ex indifferentibus facientis necessaria, ligantis, solventis, quod illis valet, jubere, vetare, liberum facere &c. denique Caput non tenentis, hoc est, à vero Capite, Christo, deficientis, & se ipsum Ecclesiæ suæ Caput, adeoque DEUM, Legislatorem unicum venditantis, ab Apostolo perstringi, clarissimè liquet. Nam quod de Judæorum festis & reliquis umbris, non de Papæ decretis S. Paulum ibi agere regerunt, dilutum est. Manifestè enim ab umbris ad totum genus præceptorum humanorum progreditur, & illa futurorum præscius exempla ponit, quæ naturam præceptorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ exprimunt, qualia sunt πανψευδοζωίη, ἀφυδία σώματος, θρησκεία ἀγγέλων, μὴ ἁψῆς &c.
units.tr: XIX. St Paul strikes this new little god directly, Col. 2:18–22, writing thus: Let no one defraud you of your prize [καταβραβευέτω] (deprive you of your right, cheat you of your reward), by choosing of his own accord humility and religion (worship) of angels, which he has not seen, walking in vain, puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding the head [καὶ οὐ κρατῶν τὴν κεφαλήν]. If therefore you have died with Christ from the elements of this world, why, as though still living in the world, are you burdened with decrees [δογματίζεσθε] of this kind: Touch not [μὴ ἅψῃ], taste not, handle not. That the decrees and dogmas of the Pope, who forbids some to marry, to touch wives, to eat certain foods, and so on, and who thereby makes necessary what is indifferent, binds and looses as he pleases, commands, forbids, and grants liberty as it suits him, and finally does not hold the head, that is, falls away from the true Head, Christ, and sets himself up as the Head of his own Church, and so as the sole Legislator, that is, as God, is clearly what the Apostle censures here. The reply that St Paul is speaking there of the Jewish feasts and other shadows, not of the Pope's decrees, has been refuted. For he plainly moves from the shadows to the whole class of human precepts, and, foreseeing the future, sets down examples that express the nature of the precepts of the Church of Rome, such as pansuperstition [πανψευδοζωίη], bodily asceticism [ἀφυδία σώματος], worship of angels [θρησκεία ἀγγέλων], Touch not [μὴ ἅψῃ], and so on.

units.la: XX. Tertiò Divinitatem Papa affectat, cùm media justificationis proprio motu, & aliunde non accepta tradit. Modum & media justificationis, & reconciliationis peccatoris cum Deo à solius Dei voluntate, Ἀδεκία libertate & revelatione ubique S. Scriptura arcessit. Nam Θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν Deus solus justificat, hoc est, & justificationis rationem omnem revelat, & secundum eam justificat, Rom. viii. 33. Et meritum Christi, offerentis se ipsum ἀνθ' ἡμῶν ὑπὲρ πάντων redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, verum justificationis medium est μαρτύριον testimonium Dei, & quidem καιροῖς ἰδίοις, propriis suis temporibus manifestatum dispensatúmque, 1. Tim. ii. 6. Cujus testimonii ibidem v. 7. S. Paulus se præconem, Apostolum, doctorem gentium in fide & veritate constitutum ait. Solus Deus notificavit nobis mysterium voluntatis suæ secundum beneplacitum suum, quod proposuit in Christo, Eph. ii. 9, 10. Media quoque illa justificationis nostræ non alia, quàm Christi meritum, ejusque vera fide acceptati donationem passim, inprimis Rom. iii. 24. &c. v. 14. &c. Gal. ii. 16. definit. Qui igitur media justificationis à Deo non constituta, non revelata, motu proprio, & ex animi tantùm sui sententia constituit, is haud obscurè Divinitatem sibi arrogat, se Numen, Deum quendam novitium demonstrat.
units.tr: XX. Thirdly, the Pope claims divinity when he hands down the means of justification of his own accord, not received from elsewhere. Scripture everywhere derives the manner and means of justification, and of the reconciliation of the sinner with God, from the will of God alone, from his freedom and his revelation. For God who justifies [Θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν], God alone justifies, that is, he both reveals the whole reason of justification and justifies according to it, Rom. 8:33. And the merit of Christ, who offered himself for us all [ἀνθ' ἡμῶν ὑπὲρ πάντων] as the price of redemption for all, is the true means of justification, the testimony [μαρτύριον] of God, manifested and dispensed at its own proper times [καιροῖς ἰδίοις], 1 Tim. 2:6. Of this testimony, in the same place, v. 7, St Paul says that he was appointed herald, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. God alone has made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in Christ, Eph. 2:9, 10. Likewise, the means of our justification are nothing other than the merit of Christ and the gift of it received by true faith, as is set out everywhere, especially Rom. 3:24 etc., Rom. 3:14 etc., Gal. 2:16. Therefore whoever establishes means of justification that God has not established or revealed, of his own motion and merely from the opinion of his own mind, plainly arrogates divinity to himself, and shows himself to be a deity, some new god.

units.la: XXI. Atqui id Papa, in Concilio suo Tridentino Seff. vj. διγμαλίζων definiens justificationis media manifeste fecit. Nam explosis, imò dirissimo anathemati subjectis veris justificationis mediis, justitia puta & merito Christi per gratiam Dei peccatori imputato, & fide justificante apprehensio; nova illa, nusquam revelata, ex animi sui libidine depromta justificationis media definivit, districtius pro Divina sua authoritate inhibens, ne audeat quisquam aliter credere aut docere, quàm decreto suo statuit & declaravit: uti patrati ejus Patres præfantur.
units.tr: XXI. Yet the Pope did exactly this in his Council of Trent, Session 6, when he defined dogmatically [δογματίζων] the means of justification. For, having rejected, indeed having subjected to the most dreadful anathema, the true means of justification, namely the righteousness and merit of Christ imputed to the sinner by the grace of God, and the apprehension of justifying faith, he defined those new means of justification, never revealed and drawn from the lust of his own mind, forbidding under strict penalty, by his divine authority, anyone to dare to believe or teach otherwise than as he has decreed and declared, as the Fathers who drew it up announce in their preface.

units.la: Suppositá autem, uti ex Sessione illa liquet, cap. 1. natura & legis ad justificandos homines imbecillitate, sed non impotentia (nam in justificandis liberum arbitrium viribus licet attenuatum & inclinatum, minimè tamen extinctum scisciunt) nec non cap. 5. &c. necessitate & modo præparationis ad illam, quem in eo collocant, quòd justificandi disponantur ad justitiam, dum excitati Divina gratia & adjuti, fidem ex auditu concipientes liberè moventur ad Deum, credentes vera esse, quæ Divinitus revelata & promissa sunt, atque illud inprimis, à Deo justificari impium per gratiam ejus, quæ est in Christo Jesu; & tamen peccatores se esse intelligentes, à Divinæ justitiæ timore, ad considerandam Dei misericordiam se convertendo, in spem eriguntur, fidentes Deum sibi propter Christum propitium fore; illumque diligere incipiunt, ac propterea moventur adversus peccata per odium & detestationem; denique proponunt suscipere baptismum, inchoare novam vitam, & servare Divina mandata, demum cap. 7. justificationem, quæ dispositionem hanc consequatur, definiunt, quòd non sit sola peccatorum remissio, sed & Sanctificatio, & renovatio interioris hominis per voluntariam susceptionem gratiæ & donorum, unde homo ex injusto fit justus, & ex inimico amicus
units.tr: But, as is clear from that session, chapter 1, assuming the weakness, though not the impotence, of nature and of the law in justifying men (for they hold that free will, though weakened and inclined, is by no means extinguished in justifying), and also chapter 5 etc., the necessity and manner of preparation for it, which they place in this: that men are disposed to justice when, stirred and aided by divine grace and receiving faith from hearing, they are freely moved towards God, believing true what has been divinely revealed and promised, and especially that the ungodly is justified by God through his grace, which is in Christ Jesus; and yet, understanding themselves to be sinners, they turn from the fear of divine justice to consider the mercy of God, and are raised to hope, trusting that God will be propitious to them for Christ's sake; and they begin to love him, and are therefore moved against sins by hatred and detestation; finally they resolve to receive baptism, to begin a new life, and to keep the divine commandments. Lastly, in chapter 7, they define that justification, which follows this disposition, is not merely the remission of sins but also sanctification and renewal of the inner man through the voluntary reception of grace and gifts, whereby a man becomes just from unjust, and a friend from an enemy,

units.la: Nnn amicus, ut sit hæres secundùm spem vitæ æternæ. [?] fas deinceps justificationis recensens, efficientem facit misericordem Deum, qui gratuitò abluit & sanctificat Meritoriam dilectissimum ejus unigenitum, Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, qui sanctissima passione in ligno crucis nobis justificationem meruit, & pro nobis Deo Patri satisfecit; Instrumentalem Sacramentum Baptismi; Formalem justitiam Dei, non qua ipse justus est, sed qua nos justos facit, qua ab eo donati renovamur Spiritu mentis nostræ, & non modò reputamur, sed verè justi sumus & sumus; justitiam in nobis recipientes, unusquisque secundum mensuram Spiritus. Lapsos porrò semel acceptam justificationis gratiam cap. 14. rursus justificari asserunt, cùm excitante Deo, per Sacramentum pœnitentiæ, merito Christi amissam gratiam recuperare procuraverint. Justificationis sic explicatæ fructum & meritum bonorum operum cap. 16. statuunt. Cùm enim dicunt, ille ipse Christus Jesus, tanquam caput in membra, & tanquam vitis in palmites, in ipsos justificatos continuo influat virtutem, quæ virtus bona eorum opera semper antecedit, comitatur & subsequitur, sine qua nullo pacto Deo grata & meritoria esse possent, nihil justificatis amplius deesse credendum est, quò minùs plenè quidem operibus, quæ in Deo facta sunt, Divino pro hujus vitæ statu satisfecisse, & vitam æternam promeruisse censeantur. Paucis, media justificationis... [illegible, ~3 letters] spositiones varias libera & cooperante voluntate adrem justitiam inhærentem, Sacramentorum Baptismi & Pœnitentiæ adeóque satisfactionis & absolutionis etiam operatum, indulgentias &c. definiunt, eidem meritum succenturiant; denique ne Christum & gratiam plane ejecisse videantur, virtutem se præparandi, justitiæ inhærentis perficiendi, merendi, satisfaciendi. à gratia & merito Christi, tanquam causa, eandem in hac mine operante, arcessunt. Sic Tridentini, imò Papa potius, in quem Conciliorum Pontificiorum omnis authoritas resolvitur.
units.tr: a friend, so that he becomes an heir according to the hope of eternal life. [?] Then, listing the causes of justification, they make the efficient cause God, merciful, who freely washes and sanctifies; the meritorious cause his most beloved only-begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ, who by his most holy passion on the wood of the cross merited justification for us and satisfied God the Father for us; the instrumental cause the sacrament of baptism; the formal cause the justice of God, not that by which he himself is just, but that by which he makes us just, by which we are renewed in the spirit of our mind after being gifted by him, and are not merely reckoned but truly are just; receiving justice in ourselves, each according to the measure of the Spirit. Further, in chapter 14 they assert that those who have fallen away after receiving the grace of justification are justified again, when, with God stirring them, they have procured through the sacrament of repentance to recover the grace lost through the merit of Christ. In chapter 16 they lay down the fruit and merit of good works, for they say: Since that same Christ Jesus, as the head into the members and as the vine into the branches, constantly flows virtue into the justified themselves, a virtue which always goes before, accompanies, and follows their good works, without which they could in no way be pleasing or meritorious to God, it must be believed that the justified lack nothing, so that they may be considered to have fully satisfied divine law, for the state of this life, by the works done in God, and to have merited eternal life. In short, the justification means [illegible] they define with various pronouncements, by free and cooperating will, that inherent justice, the operation of the sacraments of baptism and penance, and thus also satisfaction and absolution, indulgences, and so on, add merit to it; finally, lest they seem to have cast out Christ and grace altogether, they derive from the grace and merit of Christ, as the cause, the power of preparing themselves, of perfecting inherent justice, of meriting and of satisfying, which work in this life. Thus the Tridentines, or rather the Pope, to whom the whole authority of the Papal councils is reduced.

units.la: XXII. Sed justificatio hæc, quocunque colore pingatur non est profecto justificatio à vero Deo tradita, & à S. Paulo descripta; Nam dispositiones fidei, spei, dilectionis, obsignationis per Sacramentum Baptismi, libera voluntate admissas non recipit is, quem S.Paulus Rom. iv. ꝯ. à Deo justificari ἀσεβῆ impium, adeóque nondum credentem, sperantem, diligentem testatur. Neque S. Paulus ubi justificationem describit, usquam mentionem facit ullius justitiæ inhærentis, ac charitatis habitualis, quam novelli illius Deastri Apostoli justificationis causam formalem esse defendunt. Quid enim in Christi meritum dici posset injuriosius, quid in Dei gratiam contumeliosius? At Christi, & solius quidem, mentionem facit S. Paulus, quem dicit propitiationem factum esse pro peccatis nostris: fidei mentionem facit, qua propitiationem illam amplectimur & quidem χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus ullis: imputationis mentionem facit, per quam justitia Christi fit nostra. Sicut enim Christus, qui peccatum non novit, factus est peccatum pro nobis: ita nos, qui justitiam non novimus, facti sumus justitia Dei in ipso, 2. Cor. v. 21. Nondum dulcissimam illam ἀντάλλαγμα, optatissimam permutationem, ut quemadmodum Christo peccata nostra imputata fuerunt, ita nobis justitia ejus imputetur, novi illi novæ justificationis Architecti percipiunt. Hic aliquid aliud qui supponunt, quo justificemur, hi fundamentum nostræ cum Deo reconciliationis penitus evertunt.
units.tr: XXII. But this justification, however it is coloured, is certainly not the justification delivered by the true God and described by St Paul. For he does not admit the dispositions of faith, hope, love, and sealing through the sacrament of baptism, admitted by free will, to be the things by which he whom St Paul in Rom. 4:5 testifies to be justified by God is ungodly [ἀσεβῆ], and so as yet not believing, hoping, or loving. Nor does St Paul, where he describes justification, make any mention anywhere of inherent righteousness or habitual charity, which the advocates of that new little god's justification defend as its formal cause. For what could be said that is more insulting to the merit of Christ, what more contemptuous of the grace of God? But St Paul makes mention of Christ, and of him alone, whom he says was made the propitiation for our sins; he makes mention of faith, by which we embrace that propitiation, and indeed without any works [χωρὶς ἔργων]; he makes mention of imputation, by which the righteousness of Christ becomes ours. For as Christ, who knew no sin, was made sin for us, so we, who knew no righteousness, were made the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. 5:21. The new architects of this new justification do not yet grasp that most sweet exchange, that most desirable interchange, by which, as our sins were imputed to Christ, so his righteousness is imputed to us. Those who suppose anything else by which we are justified utterly overturn the foundation of our reconciliation with God.

units.la: XXIII. Accedunt Baptismi, Pœnitentiæ, quam Sa- cramentalem vocant, opus operatum, satisfactiones, ab- solutio Sacerdotalis, indulgentiæ, merita hominis, nu-s- piam
units.tr: XXIII. To these are added Baptism, penance (which they call sacramental), the work wrought (opus operatum), satisfactions, priestly absolution, indulgences, and the merits of man,

units.la: spiam in verbo Dei revelata, vel ut media, vel ut fructus justificationis; imò & ἀντίχαφα plané, uti alibi ostendimus; & Christi satisfactioni & merito undiquaque contrarium summato iniquissima. Adeò ut, dum umbris & quisquiliis his miseri Mortales inhiant, non possint non, Canis Æsopici instar, satisfactionis & meriti Christi nucleum perdere. Nam quòd omnem Poenitentiæ, operis operati, satisfactionum, meritorum virtutem à merito & satisfactione Christi, ceu conditione causæ formalis justificationis, hoc est, justitiæ inhærentis, ut ea nobis donetur, sive communicetur, vel etiam causa suspendunt; in eò meretricium potiùs & Babylonicum fucum produnt, coccei & purpuræ externa specie contumeliam in meritum Christi vetantes, & plumis Christi diras hasce aves suas, quæ ex cantu suo dignoscuntur, exornantes. Requiritur enim ad justificationem peccatoris δικαίωμα opus & justitia secundum legem perfectam, quæ nisi donata & imputata peccatori absolvere à peccatis, eorumque poena, & jus vitæ adjudicare nequit. Non meruit autem Christus, ut ejusmodi δικαίωμα in nobis & insita justitia nostra hæreat: neque etiam ejusmodi δικαίωμα plané in nobis hæret. Si ergo meritum ipsum & justitia Christi peccatori non imputatur, ita ut ipse pro peccatis mortuus, legi faciendo & patiendo satisfecisse censeatur (2. Cor. v. 15.) nihil pro nobis Christus egit, frustra mortuus est, sub ira fumus, peccata nostra expiata nulla sunt, meritum ejus omne expirat. Tantum abest, ut meritum Christi causa esse justitiæ inhærentis, poenitentiæ, satisfactionum &c. eásque ad virtutem justificandi provehere possit.
units.tr: nowhere revealed in the Word of God, either as means or as fruits of justification. Indeed they are plainly downright contraries [ἀντίχαφα], as we have shown elsewhere, and most unjustly altogether opposed to the satisfaction and merit of Christ. So it is that, while wretched mortals gape after these shadows and trifles, they cannot help losing, like Aesop's dog, the kernel of Christ's satisfaction and merit. For in making the whole power of penance, of the work wrought, of satisfactions and of merits depend on the merit and satisfaction of Christ, as the condition of the formal cause of justification, that is, of inherent righteousness, so that it may be given or communicated to us, or even making it a cause, they betray a harlot's and Babylonian deceit. By the outward show of scarlet and purple they forbid insult to Christ's merit, and they adorn their dire birds, which are known by their song, with Christ's feathers. For the justification of a sinner requires a δικαίωμα, work and righteousness [δικαίωμα] according to the perfect law, which, unless it is given to and imputed to the sinner, cannot absolve him from sins and their punishment, nor adjudge him the right to life. Christ did not merit that such a δικαίωμα should cling to us as our own implanted righteousness; nor indeed does any such δικαίωμα cling to us at all. If, then, the merit and righteousness of Christ is not imputed to the sinner, so that he is reckoned, as one who died for sins, to have satisfied the law by doing and suffering (2 Cor. 5:15), then Christ has done nothing for us, he died in vain, he is smoke under wrath, our sins are expiated by nothing, and all his merit expires. So far is the merit of Christ from being able to be the cause of inherent righteousness, of penance, of satisfactions and so on, or to raise these to the power of justifying.

units.la: XXIV. Non justitiam profecto, poenitentiam, satis- factiones nostras, non Sacramenta, ut ex opere operato ju- stificent, sed peccata nostra sanguine suo tinxit Christus.
units.tr: XXIV. Surely Christ did not dye our righteousness, our penance, our satisfactions, or the sacraments with his blood, so that they might justify by the work wrought; he dyed our sins with it.

units.la: Aliàs non solus ipse Servator noster esset, sed in tanti operis societatem hominem ipsum servandum ascivisset, & hac ratione servandi Servatores fierent. En atrocem in Christum Servatorem injuriam! Pro pœnis temporalibus ipsi fideles, & pro fidelibus Monachi satisfacere dicuntur. Si Christum immeritò exclusum conquerimur, ad tincturam suam confugiunt, quòd Christi meritum & sanguis satisfactiones suas tinxerit. Atqui Christus purgationem peccatorum di' ἑαυτοῦ per semet ipsum fecit, Hebr. 1. 3. Quid ergo commentitia illa tinctura opus est? An ut plebecula paulatim in amore Christi languescat, & in Sanctos majori feratur desiderio, utpote depulsores pœnarum temporalium, quarum metus & depulsio longè præsentior & gratior est homini carnali, quàm metus & depulsio pœnarum infernalium. Et quanta, proh Deum immortalem! hæc perversitas est, cùm justitiæ Christi imputationem exhibeant, optent tamen sibi imputari Opera supererogationis Sanctorum suorum per indulgentias.
units.tr: Otherwise our Saviour himself would not be the only one, but would have taken man himself into partnership in so great a work, and in this way there would be saviours who save. Behold the atrocious injury done to Christ the Saviour! For temporal punishments the faithful themselves, and for the faithful the monks, are said to make satisfaction. If we complain that Christ has been unjustly shut out, they take refuge in their tincture, that Christ's merit and blood have dyed their satisfactions. Yet Christ made the purging of sins by himself [δι' ἑαυτοῦ] (Heb. 1:3). What need then is there of that fictitious tincture? Is it so that the common people may gradually grow cold in the love of Christ and be carried with greater desire toward the saints, as deliverers from temporal punishments, the fear and removal of which are far more present and welcome to carnal man than the fear and removal of infernal punishments? And how great, O immortal God, is this perversity, that while they profess the imputation of Christ's righteousness, they nevertheless wish the works of supererogation of their own saints to be imputed to them through indulgences!

units.la: XXV. Quid verò meritum crucis Christi à justificatione peccatoris excludi querimur, cùm illud in dramate suo Missatico, Regni Pontificii nervo, & Ecclesiæ Papalis palladio, prorsus aboleverint? Nam sacrificium Christi cruentum in incruentum, corpus Christi in machinam fabricariam, propitiationem pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum per Sanguinem Christi in propitiationem pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum per oblatam spumam panis, Pontificem & Sacerdotem unicum Christum in Pontificem nescio quem Italum, & Sacerdotem impurum, Creatoris sui Creatorem, converterunt pridem. Missam enim esse Sacrificium reale propitiatorium proprie dictum pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum, Concilium Tridentinum sonorè canit, & contrarium tradentibus anathema dicit. Sic profecto Missa non subordinatur Sacrificio Christi, tanquam ejus ἀνάμνησις commemoratio, sed ei, tanquam Missæ sacrificium in pri-mis sacrificium Christi, justificationis causam unicam, evertit. quam sacrificium æquè propitiatorium, in quo fiducia collocanda sit, opponitur. Quid multa? Missa aut est ipsum sacrificium Christi, aut non est. Si ipsum est, Christus quotidie innumeris in locis moritur, quod blasphemum est; & jam Sacrificium Christi non illud est, quod ante Sessionem Christi ad dextram ab ipsomet in cruce semel peractum est; sed quod post Sessionem Christi ad dextram à Sacerdote Creatoris sui Creatore, nomine Christi se sistente quotidie innumeris super altaribus peragitur. Sin ipsum non est, sed ejus applicatio tantum, sacrificium proprie dictum non est, nec eo peccata vivorum & mortuorum expiantur.
units.tr: XXV. Why do we complain that the merit of Christ's cross is excluded from the justification of the sinner, when they have utterly abolished it in their Mass-drama, the sinew of the Papal kingdom and the palladium of the Papal Church? For they long ago turned the bloody sacrifice of Christ into an unbloody one, the body of Christ into a baker's machine, the propitiation for the sins of the living and the dead through the blood of Christ into a propitiation for the sins of the living and the dead through the offered foam of bread, and Christ, the sole High Priest and Priest, into I know not what Italian pontiff and impure priest, the Creator of his own Creator. For the Council of Trent sings loudly that the Mass is a real propitiatory sacrifice, properly so called, for the sins of the living and the dead, and it pronounces anathema on those who teach otherwise. Thus the Mass is certainly not subordinated to the sacrifice of Christ as its commemoration [ἀνάμνησις]; rather, as the sacrifice of the Mass, which is above all the sacrifice of Christ, it overthrows the sole cause of justification, and is set against a sacrifice equally propitiatory, in which trust must be placed. What more need be said? Either the Mass is the very sacrifice of Christ, or it is not. If it is, Christ dies daily in countless places, which is blasphemous; and now the sacrifice of Christ is not that which was once accomplished on the cross, once for all, before Christ sat down at the right hand of God; it is that which, after Christ sat at the right hand, is performed daily in countless places upon the altars by a priest, the Creator of his own Creator, presenting himself in the name of Christ. But if it is not the sacrifice itself, but only its application, then it is not a sacrifice properly so called, and by it the sins of the living and the dead are not expiated.

units.la: XXVI. Jam ergo in conspectu omnium est novellum Numen, Papa dictator Supremus novæ rationis, novorumque mediorum, quibus peccator coram tribunali Dei justificatur. Gratiæ Dei ille liberum hominum arbitrium, utcunque à gratia adjutum: Sacrificio sanguinis Christi in cruce semel peracto Sacrificium incruentum quoddam, à Sacerdotibus suis non Christi, sed suo nomine quotidie innumeris super altaribus offerendum: merito & justitiæ Christi peccatori, ut legi Divinæ agendo patiendoque satisfecisse ex justitiæ Divinæ tenore censeatur, donandæ, imputandæ diro à se anathemate percussæ, justitiam inhærentem propriam, satisfactiones, absolutionem Sacerdotis, opus operatum Sacramentorum, indulgentias, merito sanguinis Christi, in Missam scilicet conversa, veluti dibapho, cocco, purpura quadam leviter tincta omnia, fidei salvificæ, cujus pax illa conscientiæ, quæ omnem intellectum superat, verum est, eique soli, diro itidem anathemate percussæ, leves præviaque justificationi dispositiones quasdam, & inter eas fidem quandam generalem, quòd Christus passus, mortuus ac sepultus sit, qualem etiam Diabolus omnesque reprobi habent; nec non heterogenea applicationis media, satisfactiones inprimis propriας; denique fructibus justificationis, operibus resipiscentia dignis, operum merita proprie dicta, substituit. Sic venit in nomine suo, demonstrans se ipsum, quòd Deus sit.
units.tr: XXVI. Now, therefore, in the sight of all there stands a new deity: the Pope, the supreme dictator of a new scheme and of new means by which the sinner is justified before the tribunal of God. In place of the grace of God he has put the free will of man, however much it is aided by grace; in place of the sacrifice of Christ's blood, once accomplished on the cross, he has put a certain unbloody sacrifice, to be offered daily by his priests in countless places upon the altars, not in the name of Christ but in their own name; in place of the merit and righteousness of Christ, which are to be given and imputed to the sinner, so that he may be reckoned, by the tenor of divine righteousness, to have satisfied the divine law by doing and suffering, he has put his own inherent righteousness, satisfactions, the absolution of the priest, the work wrought of the sacraments, and indulgences, all of them slightly tinted, as it were with double-dyed cloth (δίβαφος), scarlet and some purple, with the merit of Christ's blood, converted into the Mass; in place of saving faith, whose peace of conscience surpasses all understanding, and which alone is true, he has put (under the same dire anathema, to it alone) certain slight dispositions preparatory to justification, and among them a certain general faith that Christ suffered, died and was buried, such as the devil and all the reprobate also have; likewise heterogeneous means of application, above all satisfactions of his own; and finally, in place of the fruits of justification, works worthy of repentance, he has substituted the merits of works, properly so called. Thus he has come in his own name, showing himself to be God.

units.la: XXVII. Quartò Divinam sibi authoritatem Papa vendicat, cùm potestatem clavium herilem, & in peccatis remittendis judicialem affectat. Potestas clavium principalis & herilis in eo consistit, quòd, qui iis instructus est, potestatem habet plenam aperiendi Cœlum & claudendi, cui voluerit; adeóque media etiam cœlestis consequendæ gloriæ, remissionem imprimis peccatorum, dispensandi pro lubitu. Quæ potestas cùm liberimam Αὐτοκρατορίαν, omnipotentiam, animarum & conscientiarum regimen, facultatem adducendi ad Ecclesiam per illuminationem, & excludendi per indurationem, docendi, leges ferendi, ut quisquis in Christum credit, & verba ejus tenet, sit filius Dei; qui non tenet, Diaboli; judicandi vivos & mortuos; denique potentiam ad subjiciendum sibi omnia, & removenda obstacula fidei ac propagationis Ecclesiæ includat, soli unique Deo eximia est. Unde Apoc. iii. 7. Angelus Philadelphiensi Ecclesiæ scribens illum, qui habet clavim Davidis, quo aperiente nemo claudit, & claudente nemo aperit, vocat ὁ ἅγιος, ὁ ἀληθινὸς Illum Sanctum, & illum Veracem; hoc est, immaculatum, secretum ab omni impuritate & vilitate, facientem fideliter ea, quæ promisit; verbo, Christum. Cui, claves eas manifeste appropriat, dicens, ὁ ἔχων, Qui habet, quod valet, Qui solus habet; & opponens eundem aliis claudentibus & aperientibus, ὁ κλείων, ὁ ἀνοίγων. Nemo aperit, nemo claudit; denique vocans κλεῖδα Δαβίδ clavem Davidis, hoc est, Clavem Regiam, qualem David typum Christi gerens habuit; & Davidi, omnibusque fidem Davidis habentibus promissam. Quomodo idem Christus tum Apoc. i. 18. de se loquitur: ἐγὼ εἰμὶ ὁ ζῶν, καὶ ἐγενόμην νεκρός, καὶ ἰδοὺ ζῶν εἰμι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. Habeo claves inferni & mortis, quia morte sua potestatem mortis extinxit, omnémque Diaboli potentiam superavit, ut nec infernus corpus nostrum detinere, nec Sathanæ Regnum sibi datos retinere, nec portæ inferorum Ecclesiam vincere valeant: tum Apoc. xx. 1. dicitur de Cœlo descendens habere κλεῖδα τῆς ἀβύσσου clavem Abyssi, potestatem educendi ex morte & inferno, & rursus εἰς τὴν γέενναν conjiciendi in gehennam.
units.tr: XXVII. Fourthly, the Pope claims for himself divine authority when he aspires to the lordly power of the keys, and judicial power in remitting sins. The principal and lordly power of the keys consists in this: whoever is entrusted with them has full power to open heaven and to shut it to whomever he will; and thus, too, to dispense at pleasure the means of attaining heavenly glory, above all the remission of sins. This power, since it includes the most free autocracy [Αὐτοκρατορίαν], omnipotence, the government of souls and consciences, the faculty of bringing men into the Church by illumination and of excluding them by hardening, of teaching and of making laws, so that whoever believes in Christ and holds his words is a son of God, and whoever does not hold them is a son of the devil; of judging the living and the dead; and finally the power to subject all things to himself and to remove the obstacles to the faith and the propagation of the Church, belongs exclusively and uniquely to God. Hence Rev. 3:7, where the angel writing to the church at Philadelphia describes him who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens, calling him the holy one, the true one [ὁ ἅγιος, ὁ ἀληθινὸς], that is, the immaculate one, free from all impurity and baseness, who faithfully does what he has promised; in a word, Christ. To him he expressly assigns those keys, saying the one who has [ὁ ἔχων], that is, who has in the sense of who alone has; and he sets the same one against the others who shut and open, the one who shuts, the one who opens [ὁ κλείων, ὁ ἀνοίγων]: no one opens, no one shuts. Finally, he calls it the key of David [κλεῖδα Δαβίδ], that is, the royal key, such as David had as a type bearing Christ, and which was promised to David and to all who have the faith of David. In the same way Christ himself speaks of himself in Rev. 1:18: I am the living one, and I was dead, and behold I am alive for evermore [ἐγὼ εἰμὶ ὁ ζῶν, καὶ ἐγενόμην νεκρός, καὶ ἰδοὺ ζῶν εἰμι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας]. I have the keys of hell and of death, because by his death he extinguished the power of death and overcame all the power of the devil, so that neither hell can hold our body, nor can Satan keep those given to him, nor the gates of hell prevail against the Church. Again, Rev. 20:1 says that the one descending from heaven has the key of the abyss [κλεῖδα τῆς ἀβύσσου], the power of leading out from death and hell, and again into gehenna [εἰς τὴν γέενναν] of casting into gehenna.

units.la: XXVIII. Alia longè ratio est clavium Regni Cœlorum, quæ S. Petro, & in ejus persona Ministris Ecclesiæ, ut οἰκονόμοις curatoribus & œconomis, non ut heris & Dominis Matth. xvi. 19. datæ sunt. Notant enim verbum Euangelii à S. Petro & Ministris Christi prædicandum, quo scilicet vocantur homines ad Regnum Cœlorum, puta gratiæ & gloriæ, quodque potens est per gratiam Dei ad dandum hominibus aditum, sive ad ducendum eos in Regnum Cœlorum. Explicantur ab ipso Christo statim per potestatem ligandi & solvendi, atque hæc per potestatem remittendi & retinendi peccata Joh. xx. 23. quæ tum in prædicatione remissionis peccatorum in nomine Christi, tum in consolatione & applicatione remissionis ad singulos, rata in Cœlis utraque non simpliciter, sed si Spiritus S. docens per verbum iis utriusque author fuerit; adeòque si claves non erraverint, ligatióque vel solutio legitima fuerit, consistit. Planum est, nec S. Petro quicquam hic concessum esse, quod concessum non fuerit omnibus Apostolis & Ecclesiæ Ministris, tum nihil hic διακονικὸν herile, potestatem Dominicam nullam vel S. Petro, vel cuiquam alii à Christo communicatam esse; sed merè ministerialem & œconomicam. Ita cùm in Republica Quæstor instituitur, qui publicam pecuniam tractet, clavis illi traditur ærarii: & Pater familiâs, cùm promum condum instituit, cellæ penuariæ clavim ei tradit. Ubi clavis traditio ministerii symbolum in accipiente, herilis imperii in tradente est.
units.tr: XXVIII. The keys of the Kingdom of Heaven are quite another matter. They were given to St Peter, and in his person to the ministers of the Church, as stewards [οἰκονόμοις] and managers, not as masters and lords (Matt. 16:19). For they signify the word of the Gospel, to be preached by St Peter and Christ's ministers, by which men are called to the Kingdom of Heaven, namely of grace and of glory, and which is powerful, through the grace of God, to open the way to men, or to lead them into the Kingdom of Heaven. Christ himself at once explains them as the power of binding and loosing, and this as the power of forgiving and retaining sins (John 20:23). Both of these, the proclamation of the forgiveness of sins in the name of Christ and the consolation and application of forgiveness to individuals, are ratified in heaven, not simply, but only if the Holy Spirit, teaching through the word, is the author of both. So they hold good provided the keys do not err and the binding or loosing is lawful. It is plain that nothing is granted here to St Peter that was not granted to all the apostles and ministers of the Church. Nor is there anything here of a servile [διακονικὸν] or lordly kind: no lordly power was communicated by Christ to St Peter or to anyone else, but a purely ministerial and economic one. So when a quaestor is appointed in a commonwealth to handle public money, the key of the treasury is handed to him; and when a householder appoints a steward of the pantry, he gives him the key of the storeroom. In such cases the handing over of the key is a sign of ministry in the recipient, and of lordly authority in the giver.

units.la: XXIX. Quid nunc de magno illo Clavigero, Papa, dicemus? Uni solique ubi claves vindicat: claves vindicat herilès, dominicas: claves in enses, lanceas, sceptra & coronas conflavit, atque earum obtentu sibi plenam in maxima Regna, denique in animas & corpora potestatem non pretio ullo, sed vi rapuit; adeóque sic Supremum aliquod Numen se mundo venditavit.
units.tr: XXIX. What shall we now say of that great Keeper of the Keys, the Pope? He claims the keys for himself alone, and claims them as a master and lord. He has fashioned the keys into swords, lances, sceptres and crowns, and under cover of these he has seized for himself, not by any purchase but by force, full power over the greatest kingdoms and finally over souls and bodies. In this way he has presented himself to the world as some supreme deity.

units.la: XXX. Uni solique sibi vindicat claves, personatus scilicet successor S. Petri, cui soli clavium jus & potestatem Supremam à Christo assertam pertendit. Hinc adeò inter insignia Papæ sunt Claves, jurisdictionis Papalis symbolum: sicut tiaram dignitatis symbolum possidet. Et quod mireris, cùm claves aliàs sint ministræ crucis, ἀδωλον hoc claves dextra, crucem sinistra gerit. Ea carnis scilicet est indoles. Claves potius quærit, quàm crucem. Ne dicam crucem in calceis suis purpureis auream eum gestare, atque sic impuris pedibus suis calcare.
units.tr: XXX. He claims the keys for himself alone, as the personal successor of St Peter, to whom he asserts that the right and supreme power of the keys was given by Christ alone. Hence among the Pope's insignia are the Keys, the symbol of papal jurisdiction, just as he holds the tiara as the symbol of his dignity. And what you may marvel at is this: though keys are otherwise the instruments of the cross, he carries the keys in his right hand and the cross in his left. The disposition of the flesh, of course, is like this: he seeks the keys rather than the cross. I say nothing of his wearing a golden cross on his purple shoes, and so trampling it under his unclean feet. The cross is not a sincere [ἄδολον] symbol for him.

units.la: XXXI. Quo tempore insignia hæc usurpare cœperit, difficile conjectu equidem est. Jam A.C. 726. Gregorius Papa Claves venerandi sepulchri cum aliis muneribus suis per legatos suos, inusitato antea more, Carolo Martello obtulisse in Apend. ad Gregorium Turonensem Cap. 110. dicitur, illius scilicet patrocinium ambiens. Eandem ob causam Leonem III. claves aureas cum vexillo Romanæ urbis Carolo M. Martelli nepoti transmisisse, Aimo lib. iv. 89. & Sigonius lib. iv. de Regno Italiæ scribit, addens ex Annonio rogatum simul à Leone Carolum, ut aliquem ex Optimatibus suis Romam mitteret, qui populum Romanum in fide & subjectione per Sacramenta firmaret. Patriarcham quoque Hierofolymitanum eidem Imperatori claves sancti sepulchri misisse in signum benedictionis, refert Baronius ad A. C. 719. Sed de usu clavium antiquitate quicquid fiat, citius sibi Hercules aliquis clavam, quam Papa & insigne ipsum clavium, & potestatem eo insigni significatam extorqueri sibi, aliisque vel tradi, vel communicari utcumque patietur. Solus ergo eas sibi vindicat, sicut clavim Davidis sibi soli Christus.
units.tr: XXXI. It is indeed hard to guess when he began to usurp these insignia. Already in the year 726 it is said that Pope Gregory, by his legates and in a manner unusual before that time, offered Charles Martel the keys of the venerable sepulchre along with other gifts, seeking his protection (in the Appendix to Gregory of Tours, chapter 110). For the same reason, Aimo (book 4, 89) writes that Leo III sent golden keys together with the banner of the city of Rome to Charles the Great, grandson of Martel; and Sigonius (book 4, On the Kingdom of Italy) adds, drawing on Annonius, that Leo also asked Charles to send some of his nobles to Rome, who should confirm the Roman people in faith and submission by the sacraments. Baronius, at the year 719, reports that the Patriarch of Jerusalem also sent the same emperor the keys of the holy sepulchre as a sign of blessing. But whatever the antiquity of the use of the keys, the Pope will sooner allow some Hercules to wrest his club from him than allow the insignia of the keys themselves, and the power signified by that insignia, to be taken from him, or to be handed over or shared in any way with others.
