He alone therefore claims them for himself, just as Christ alone claims the key of David.

units.la: XXXII. Jam olim quippe in picturarum quodam volumine, quod inscribitur, Non recedet volumen legis hujus ab ore tuo, Romæ A. 1577. excuso, res illa ante oculos simplicium vivis quasi coloribus pigmentisque exornata est. Depingitur in eo Christus, non quasi promitteret Petro, claves ei se daturum; sed quasi illo articulo temporis eas illi in manus traderet; & illi soli, non ceteris Apostolis traderet, adscriptis simul Christi verbis, & paraphrasi elegantula, à Poëta nescio quo, sic expolitis: Pastorum princeps esto, tibi jus datur uni, Claudere cælestes, & referare fores.
units.tr: XXXII. Indeed, long ago, in a certain picture-book entitled This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, printed at Rome in 1577, that matter was set before the eyes of simple folk, adorned with lively colours and paints. In it Christ is depicted, not as promising Peter that he would give him the keys, but as handing them into his hands at that moment, and handing them to him alone, not to the other apostles. Christ's words are added, together with a rather elegant paraphrase, polished thus by some poet or other: Be the prince of shepherds; the right is given to you alone, to shut the heavenly gates and to open them.

units.la: Petro autem & Papæ sors eadem tributa pridem est.
units.tr: Long ago, too, the same lot was assigned to Peter and to the Pope.

units.la: XXXIII. Anxiè profectò illam de Petro & Papa Clavigero & Janitore Cœli persuasionem apud plebeculam sic Pontificum gnathones nutriverunt, ut suo jam tempore Beda Hist. Eccl. Angl. lib. iij. 25. de Rege Osvi lepidum quid narraverit. Cùm enim orta de Paschalis celebratione Controversia Synodus convocaretur, & pars altera se Orientis Ecclesias sequi diceret, quæ ritum suum à Johanne Euangelista, dilecto Christi discipulo acceperant; altera, se Ecclesiam Romanam sequi, quæ suum à Petro acceperat, cui Christus claves dedit Regni Cœlorum; Regem litem tum composuisse, & secundum Ecclesiam Romanam judicasse. Nam ego inquiebat, vobis dico, quia hic est Ostiarius ille, cui ego contradicere nolo, sed in quantum novi vel valeo, hujus cupio in omnibus obedire statutis, ne forte me adveniente ad fores Regni Cœlorum, non sit qui referet, averso illo, qui claves tenere probatur. Atque hanc crassam de clavibus & Ostiario Regis illius cogitationem, ipsi etiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ eatenus adversantem, quòd per Regnum Cœlorum Ecclesiam militantem, ut visibilem Monarchiam probet, intelligit; non tantùm Synodus probavit; sed etiam Stapletonus in Anglicano Beda suo, his verbis, Nota Regis conclusionem, aliíque cantárunt; imò Baronius sic laudavit, ut diceret, scita sententia clausam disputationem. Persuasos quippe assidentes, veluti evidenti demonstratione, rem deductam certis principiis, ad quæ vult provocandos omnes à veritate devios; quibus & illud Propheticum sit inclamandum: ad petram, de qua scissi estis: quod perabsurdè ita ⟨Greek⟩ Ad Petrum, à quo divisi estis.
units.tr: XXXIII. Certainly the Pontiffs' flatterers have so anxiously nourished among the common people that persuasion about Peter and the Pope as Keeper and Doorkeeper of heaven, that already in Bede's time something amusing was related about King Oswiu (Ecclesiastical History of the English, book 3, chapter 25). When a controversy had arisen about the celebration of Easter and a synod was convened, one party said that it followed the churches of the East, which had received their rite from John the Evangelist, the beloved disciple of Christ; the other said that it followed the Roman Church, which had received its rite from Peter, to whom Christ gave the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven. The king then settled the dispute and judged in favour of the Roman Church. "For I," he said, "tell you that this is the doorkeeper to whom I do not wish to be opposed; but as far as I know and am able, I desire to obey his decrees in all things, lest perhaps, when I come to the gates of the Kingdom of Heaven, there should be no one to open them, since he who is held to have the keys has turned away." This crude notion of the keys and of the King's doorkeeper was not only approved by the synod, but was also sung by Stapleton in his English Bede, with the words "Mark the king's conclusion", and others as well. Baronius even praised it so highly that he said "a neatly worded opinion has closed the debate". Indeed, they seem to persuade themselves that the matter is drawn out, as by evident demonstration, from certain principles, to which they wish all who have strayed from the truth to be summoned. To them should be shouted that prophetic saying: to the rock from which you were hewn; which is absurdly turned into to Peter, from whom you have been divided.

units.la: XXXIV. Animadverterunt nempe, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Antistites, insulsam & crassam istam de solo Petro Claviger & Ostiario Cœli opinionem, ad Imperii sui fines propagandos & subjugandas terras omnes perquam commodam & opportunam esse.
units.tr: XXXIV. Clearly the bishops of the Roman Church noticed that this foolish and crude opinion, that Peter alone is the Keeper and Doorkeeper of heaven, was very convenient and opportune for extending the boundaries of their empire and subjecting all lands.

units.la: Nam in Papæ offensionem si quando homines incurrerent, in Petri offensionem se incurrisse persuasi sunt. De Petro autem acceperunt, Janitorem illum Cœlorum esse. Erant verò de eo anxii, ne omnes Janitor, præter Papæ, successoris sui amicos, ab ingressu Cœli propulsaret. Ut igitur æterna vita fruerentur, Papam colebant, observabant, & præmiis sibi conciliabant, ne si ille modò frontem contraheret, apud Petrum favore & gratia omni illi exciderent. Quare, utcunque exigua ista de Petro habeantur, in otiosis vulgarium sermonum generibus, non exiguum certè attulerunt emolumentum Petri Romani Curiæ, nec mediocres opes in ærarium ejus invexerunt: denique Papæ Divinæ Majestati augendæ non parùm inserviverunt.
units.tr: For if men at any time incurred the displeasure of the Pope, they were persuaded that they had incurred the displeasure of Peter. They had received from Peter that he was the doorkeeper of heaven. They were anxious indeed lest the doorkeeper should exclude everyone from entry into heaven except the friends of his successor the Pope. So, in order to enjoy eternal life, they courted, obeyed and won over the Pope with rewards, lest, if he merely frowned, they should lose all favour and grace with Peter. Therefore, however slight these notions about Peter may be thought, among the idle kinds of common talk, they have certainly brought no small profit to the Roman Curia of Peter, have carried no mean wealth into its treasury, and finally have served not a little to increase the Divine Majesty of the Pope.

units.la: XXXV. Haud equidem nos latet, Cadmæos fratres in sua umbra acriter satis disputare, an soli Petro, an reliquis etiam Apostolis à Christo claves traditæ sint? Sunt enim qui verba, Tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum, à sequentibus, & quicquid ligaveris in terra &c. sic dividelant, ut priora illa latiùs patentia, & omnem omnino potestatem complexa, ad solum Petrum; posteriora, utpote per particulam Et divisa, particulares quosdam clavium actus, quales sunt non in universum aperire & claudere; sed ligare & solvere; comprehendentia, ad Apostolos etiam reliquos referenda sint.
units.tr: XXXV. It is not hidden from us that the Cadmean brothers, in their own shade, dispute fiercely enough whether the keys were given by Christ to Peter alone or also to the rest of the apostles. For there are some who so divide the words I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven from what follows, whatever you bind on earth, etc., that the former, which extend more widely and embrace all power whatever, are referred to Peter alone, while the latter, being divided off by the particle and, which comprise certain particular acts of the keys, such as binding and loosing rather than opening and shutting in general, are to be referred also to the other apostles.

units.la: Quam observationem à Cajetano mutuati sunt Monarchici, Maldonatus, Stapletonus, Baronius, qui vanissimum illud commentum Anno 34. num. 205. recitat. Verùm, sic Bellarminus de Rom. Pont. lib. j. cap. 12. reclamat, hæc doctrina subtilior est, quàm verior. Inauditum est enim in Ecclesia alias esse claves, quàm ordinis & jurisdictionis, & planus verborum illorum, Tibi dabo claves Regni Cœlorum, sensus iste est, ut primò promiatur authoritas seu potestas designata per claves, deinde & actiones, seu officium explicetur per illa vocabula, solvere & ligare. Atque hoc ipsum Sanctius in Esai. cap. 22. observat. Proin claves Petro promissas, fatetur idem Bellarminus etiam reliquis Apostolis exhibitas esse; & quidem clavem jurisdictionis his verbis: Sicut me misit Pater; clavem verò Ordinis subsequentibus, Quorum remiseritis peccata, &c. Ne tamen Papæ Majestas detrimentum aliquod inde patiatur, Petro ut Ordinario, & cum jure successionis: reliquis Apostolis ut subdelegatis, mediante, & sine jure successionis claves collatas pertendit. Utrique ergo, diversa licet via, scopum feriunt, & nunc Papæ soli jus clavium competere, ὁμοψήφως Pontificii veri omnes severè pertendunt. Eos enim, qui cum Gersone aliisque Papam coactivæ Concilii sententiæ subjiciunt, & claves præcipuè & originaliter Ecclesiæ datas esse afferunt, Pontificii veri, ceu minùs bonos Catholicos, plorare, & res suas sibi habere hodie jubent.
units.tr: The Monarchists, Maldonatus, Stapleton and Baronius, borrowed this interpretation from Cajetan. Baronius recites that very absurd invention at year 34, no. 205. But, Bellarmine objects in De Romano Pontifice, book 1, chapter 12, this doctrine is more subtle than true. For it is unheard of in the Church that there are keys other than those of order and jurisdiction, and the plain sense of those words, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, is this: first the authority or power signified by the keys is promised, and then the actions or office are explained by the words to loose and to bind. Sanchez also observes this on Isaiah chapter 22. Accordingly, Bellarmine himself admits that the keys promised to Peter were also given to the other Apostles: the key of jurisdiction by the words As the Father has sent me, and the key of order by the following words, Whose sins you forgive, and so on. Yet, so that the majesty of the Pope may suffer no loss from this, he maintains that the keys were conferred on Peter as the ordinary, with the right of succession, but on the other Apostles as delegates, through an intermediary and without the right of succession. Both, then, though by different routes, aim at the same goal, and all true Papists insist with one voice (homopsephōs [ὁμοψήφως]) that the right to the keys belongs to the Pope alone. For those who, with Gerson and others, subject the Pope to the coercive sentence of a Council, and who assert that the keys were given chiefly and originally to the Church, the true Papists, as if they were less good Catholics, bid to lament and to mind their own business today.

units.la: XXXVI. Cùm ergo Papæ soli claves Hiero-Monarchici vindicent, præcipuam quandam, & minimè vulgarem potestatem clavium insigni adumbratam; verbo, herilem, dominantem, Divinam ei vindicare eosdem, mirum non est. Nos, ita Bellarminus de Rom. Pontif. lib. I. 15. scribit, & Catholici omnes per claves Petro datas, intelligimus summam potestatem in omnem Ecclesiam. Baronius clavium traditionem supremum dominium significare astruit. Tirinus in Matth. xvj. 19. per claves intelligit ait summam & absolutam potestatem regendi, quia hoc fine claves urbium solent Regibus tradi. Summa autem & absoluta in omnem Ecclesiam potestas, supremum dominium, Regia authoritas non humana certè, sed divina est, teste Christo, Matth. xxviii. 18. & S. Paulo 1. Cor. iii. 21. 22. 23. Et ne Divinam sic Papæ Majestatem tribui dubites, vetant iidem Cardinales, qui supremum isthoc Papæ in Ecclesiam imperium probaturi, comparant cum potestate Papæ potestatem clavis Davidis, quam ipse Sanctus ille & verax, Christus Apoc. iii. 7. sibi asserit: quam Divinam esse, supra probavimus, & res ipsa certè loquitur. Quomodo etiam apud Othonem Frisingensem lib. j. de vita Friderici cap. 57. Cardinalis de Sede Romana loquitur: Hæc est sola, quæ claudit, & nemo aperit; aperit, & nemo claudit. Planè uti de Solo illo Sancto & vera Angelus loquebatur. Ut jam Papa non Vicarius Christi, sed alter Dominus & Deus, pari vel majori jure cum Christo imperans, censeri debeat. Quam horrendam blasphemiam si audisset Petrus, vestem lacerans prae detestatione impietatis atrocissimae, dixisset procul dubio cum Paulo: Ego, & caeteri Apostoli praedicamus unum Dominum Jesum Christum: nos autem servos vestros per Jesum. 2. Cor. iv. 5.
units.tr: XXXVI. Since, then, the Hiero-Monarchists claim the keys for the Pope alone, a certain outstanding and by no means common power of the keys, shadowed forth by a remarkable sign, it is no wonder that they ascribe to him, in a word, a lordly, domineering and divine power. We, Bellarmine writes in De Romano Pontifice, book 1, chapter 15, and all Catholics understand by the keys given to Peter the supreme power over the whole Church. Baronius asserts that the handing over of the keys signifies supreme dominion. Tirinus, on Matthew 16:19, understands by the keys, he says, a supreme and absolute power of ruling, because keys of cities are customarily handed over to kings for this purpose. Now a supreme and absolute power over the whole Church, a supreme dominion, a royal authority, is not human but divine, as Christ testifies in Matthew 28:18 and Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:21-23. And lest you doubt that such divine majesty is ascribed to the Pope, the same Cardinals forbid it: wishing to prove this supreme empire of the Pope over the Church, they compare with the Pope's power the power of the key of David, which that holy and true one, Christ himself, claims for himself in Revelation 3:7; we have proved above that this power is divine, and the thing itself certainly speaks so. Likewise, in Otto of Freising, book 1, On the Life of Frederick, chapter 57, a Cardinal of the Roman See speaks thus: This is the only one who shuts, and no one opens; she opens, and no one shuts. Clearly the Angel was speaking of that One alone, holy and true. So now the Pope ought to be judged not the Vicar of Christ but another Lord and God, ruling with equal or greater right than Christ. If Peter had heard this horrible blasphemy, he would undoubtedly have rent his garments in detestation of such an atrocious impiety, and said with Paul: We and the other Apostles preach one Lord Jesus Christ; and we are your servants through Jesus. 2 Corinthians 4:5.

units.la: XXXVII. Denique claves Papa in enses, lanceas, sceptra, coronas conflando, ex iisdem potestatem non Re- gni duntaxat Coelorum, sed etiam terrarum, confecit.
units.tr: XXXVII. Finally, by fusing the keys into swords, lances, sceptres and crowns, the Pope has made from the same keys a power not only over the Kingdom of Heaven but also over the kingdoms of the earth.

units.la: Nam clavium potestate munitus sibi in totum mundum potestatem mere & directe temporalem, uti supra fidem pluribus argumentis fecimus, vindicat. Facit huc, quod olim Hildebrandini, referente Mornaeo Myst. Iniq. p. 238. jactare non dubitarunt, Clavi Romanae Reges non minus quam caeteros esse subjectos; utpote aequae oves Papae, in spiritualibus & temporalibus. Cum tamen, uti annotavit Ferus, tam signanter dictum sit, Tibi dabo claves Regni Coelorum, non Regni terrarum. Quod Feri testimonium ita Sixtum Senensem perturbavit, ut Biblioth. lib. vj. Annot. 72. ad testes fide dignos, scilicet, consugiat, qui pro certo asseverent, hunc ejus locum ab haereticis corruptum esse. Quod quidem facere nihil attinebat, cum etiam tacente Fero, res ipsa non tam id loquatur, quam clamet. Neque mirum profecto, Regni terrarum claves rapturivisse, qui Regni Coelorum claves rapturivit. Nam qui Coeli dominus est, multo magis terrae dominus est, in qua Sedem & thronum suum Regium potius, quam in Coelo habet. Hinc adeo ab adulatoribus DEUS in terris, Numen terrestre, quod in terris id est pollétque, quod Deus in Coelis, Visibilis Deus, qui quaevis faciat non tanquam homo, sed tanquam Deus &c. frequenter insignitur. Canonistarum flosculos ejusmodi plures apud Wolphium Lect. Memorab. Tom. I. pag. 992. legere est.
units.tr: For, armed with the power of the keys, he claims for himself over the whole world a purely and directly temporal power, as we have shown above by many arguments from the faith. To this belongs what the Hildebrandines once did not hesitate to boast, as Mornay reports in Mystery of Iniquity, p. 238: that the Kings of Rome are no less subject than the rest, as sheep equally subject to the Pope, in spiritual and temporal matters. Yet, as Ferus observed, it was said so pointedly, I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, not of the kingdom of the earth. This testimony of Ferus so disturbed Sixtus of Siena that, in his Bibliotheca, book 6, annotation 72, he has recourse to trustworthy witnesses, that is, to men who assert for certain that this passage of his was corrupted by heretics. There was in fact no need to do this, since even without Ferus the thing itself speaks, indeed cries out, not so much to be read as to be heard. Nor is it surprising that the one who seized the keys of the kingdom of heaven also seized the keys of the kingdom of the earth. For he who is lord of heaven is much more the lord of the earth, in which he holds his seat and royal throne rather than in heaven. Hence, too, he is frequently honoured by flatterers with titles such as God on earth, an earthly Divinity, a visible God, who does whatever he does not as a man but as God, and so on. Many flowers of this sort from the canonists can be read in Wolf, Lectiones memorabiles, vol. 1, p. 992.

units.la: XXXVIII. Christum abyssi quoque clavim habere, supra astruximus.
units.tr: XXXVIII. We have already shown above that Christ also holds the key of the abyss.

units.la: XXXVIII. Christum abyssi quoque clavim habere, supra astruximus. Suas quoque claveis Papa in abyssum, Purgatorium (ens illud fictum) & infernum, uti quidem Regum longæ manus sunt, protendit. Movet Augustinus Triumphus Anconitanus Summ. de Potest. Eccl. quæst. 29. art. 4. quæstionem: Utrum Papa possit dare indulgentiam iis, qui sunt in Purgatorio. Affirmat ille: & sententiam illam fide tenendam esse, Toletus Instruct. Sacerdot. lib. vj. 26. asseverat. In eo tamen, an id Papa faciat per modum jurisdictionis, an per modum suffragii, applicando satisfactiones aliorum in pretium, non plane calculi concordes sunt. Prius idem Augustinus Triumphus, Medina, alii statuunt, eò quòd purgatoriani viatores adhuc sint, & ad forum Papæ pertineant. Posterius Toletus, aliíque plures, qui animas illas sudantes ad forum Papæ pertinere inficiantur. Sed quo modo clavibus suis fores exeuntibus aperiat, parùm refert: aperiat modò! Huc pertinet disceptatio: An Papa per communicationem indulgentiæ possit totum Purgatorium expoliare? Triumphus idem secundum absolutam potentiam suam posse, affirmat. Quis ergo Clavigerum hunc Purgatorii dominum & Deastrum esse, dubitaverit?
units.tr: XXXVIII. We have already shown above that Christ also holds the key of the abyss. The Pope likewise stretches out his own keys over the abyss, Purgatory (that fictitious entity) and hell, just as kings have long hands. Augustinus Triumphus of Ancona raises the question in Summ. de Potest. Eccl. quæst. 29. art. 4.: Whether the Pope can grant an indulgence to those who are in Purgatory. He affirms it, and Toletus, in Instruct. Sacerdot. lib. vj. 26, asserts that this opinion must be held as a matter of faith. Yet they are not fully agreed on whether the Pope does this by way of jurisdiction or by way of suffrage, applying the satisfactions of others as payment. Augustinus Triumphus, Medina and others hold the former view, because the souls in Purgatory are still wayfarers and belong to the Pope's court. Toletus and many others, who deny that those sweating souls belong to the Pope's court, hold the latter. But it matters little how he opens the doors to those leaving with his keys; let him only open them! To this belongs the disputed question: Can the Pope, by communicating an indulgence, strip Purgatory bare altogether? The same Triumphus affirms that by his absolute power he can. Who, then, could doubt that this keeper of the key is the lord of Purgatory and a little god?

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: XXXIX. Sed non Purgatorii duntaxat, verùm Inferni etiam claves habet. Nam Regni Cœlorum & referandi, & claudendi, adeóque ad inferos præcipitandi æqua ipsi potestas est. Præterea etiam non parùm in liberandis damnatis pollet. Cùm enim damnatorum pœna fit partim damni, partim vermis conscientiæ, partim sensus, recepta Pontificiorum sententia est, indulgentias Papales damnatis ad imminutionem pœnæ sensus proficere. Imò & damni, & vermis, & sensus pœnam aliquando Papam non tantùm minuere, sed penitus averruncare, adeóque clavibus suis exitum ex inferno patefacere, non desunt, qui pronuntient assa voce. Quomodo apud Rodolphum de Diceto in Abbreviationibus Chronicorum, inter Scriptores Anglos antiquos relatum, pag. 461. Daemones inducuntur plangentes, quòd de suis manibus animae sic eripiantur. Stella etiam, aliíque longo ordine à Gerhardo de Inferno Ss. 63. recitati, Trajanum, hominem gentilem, Gregorii precibus ex inferno liberatum tradidere. Denique quanta cum authoritate Pluto hic dominium suum apud inferos exerceat, vel hinc etiam liquet, quòd Angelis ipsis praecipit, quid mortuis facere, quò eos, in Coelum, an in infernum avehere debeant. Sanè Clemens VI. in Bulla Jubilaei sic bullat: Et nihilominus prorsus mandamus Angelis Paradisi, quatenus animam à purgatorio penitus absolutam in Paradisi gloriam introducant. Item: Nolumus quòd poena inferni sibi aliquatenus infligatur. Ad quae verba sic olim Johannes Hufsus, Wolphio Lect. Memorab. Tom. I. pag. 751. citante commentatus est: Idolum illud Meretricium Romae Clemens VI. Papa nimis potestatem suam laxaverat, mandans in sua Bulla Angelis Paradisi, quòd animam peregrinantis Romam pro indulgentiis, & decedentis à purgatorio absolutam ad gaudia perpetua introducant. Ipse enim volebat, quòd ad mandata ejus genua Angelorum Coelestium flecterentur. Et cùm adjecit: Nolumus quòd poena inferni sibi aliqua infligatur: & sic ibi imperavit, quòd potestas vel genu inferorum ad mandatum ejus flecteretur.
units.tr: XXXIX. But he holds the keys not only of Purgatory but also of hell. For he has equal power to open and to shut the Kingdom of Heaven, and so to cast men down into the underworld. Moreover, he has no small influence in freeing the damned. For since the punishment of the damned consists partly of loss, partly of the worm of conscience, and partly of sense, it is the accepted opinion of the Papists that papal indulgences benefit the damned by lessening the punishment of sense. Indeed, there are not lacking those who declare openly that the Pope sometimes not only lessens but utterly removes the punishment of loss, of the worm and of sense, and so opens by his keys the way out of hell. So in Rodolphus de Diceto, in Abbreviationibus Chronicorum, reported among the old English writers, p. 461, the demons are introduced lamenting that souls are snatched so from their hands. Also Stella and others, recited in a long list by Gerhard, de Inferno Ss. 63, handed down that Trajan, a pagan man, was freed from hell by the prayers of Gregory. Finally, how great the authority with which this Pluto exercises his lordship among the dead is clear even from this: he commands the angels themselves what to do with the dead, whether they should carry them to heaven or to hell. Certainly Clement VI, in his Bull of Jubilee, thus decrees: And nevertheless we absolutely command the Angels of Paradise to lead the soul, fully absolved from Purgatory, into the glory of Paradise. Likewise: We will not that the punishment of hell be inflicted on it in any way. On these words John Hus once commented thus, citing Wolphius, Lect. Memorab. Tom. I. p. 751: Pope Clement VI, that Roman harlot idol, had relaxed his power too far, commanding in his Bull the Angels of Paradise to lead into eternal joys the soul of one who travels to Rome for indulgences and, having died, is absolved from Purgatory. For he wanted the knees of the heavenly Angels to bend at his commands. And when he added: We will not that any punishment of hell be inflicted on it, he thus gave orders there that the power and the knee of the underworld should bend at his command.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Nè verò ad dignoscendum isthoc idolum desiderari quicquam possit, Papolatrae, Papam, quocunque demum modo clavibus suis in aperiendo, claudendóve Coelo, Purgatorio, gehenna utatur, judicio cujusquam Mortalium subjacere negant. Est enim, sic Baronius in Actis Controversiae inter Paulum V. & Venetos pag. 39. baccha-
units.tr: Lest anything should be lacking for recognising this idol, the Papolaters deny that the Pope, however he uses his keys to open or shut heaven, purgatory or hell, is subject to the judgement of any mortal. For thus Baronius writes in the Acts of the controversy between Paul V and the Venetians, p. 39:

units.la: { } bacchatur, monstrum atque portentum Luciferi, velle judicare judicia Pontificis, Christi vicarii. Et pag. 43. sic Venetam Rempublicam ille alloquitur: Unde tanta vobis authoritas, ut judicetis (NB) JUDICEM UNIVERSORUM, quem nullum hactenus Concilium legitimè congregatum ausum est judicare. In Jure Canonico Dist. 40. C. Si Papa haec aprime huc spectantia, leguntur: Si Papa suæ & fraternæ salutis negligens deprehenditur, inutilis & remissus in operibus suis, & insuper à bono taciturnus, quòd magis officit sibi & omnibus, nihilominus innumerabiles populos catervatim secum ducit, primò mancipio gehennæ, cum ipso plagis multis in æternum vapulaturos, hujus culpas isthic redarguere præsumit Mortalium nullus: quia cunctos ipse judicaturus à nemine est judicandus. Cùm igitur Deus solus sit judex Ecclesiæ, à nemine Mortalium judicandus & judicium Ecclesiæ legitimum, juxta Dei verbum susceptum sit judicium ipsius Dei; Papa idem sibi arrogans, & Ecclesiæ judicium, ceu suo inferius, despectans, Divinitatem utique affectat, & idolum se constituit.
units.tr: raves, a monster and portent of Lucifer, to wish to judge the judgements of the Pontiff, Christ's vicar. And on p. 43 he thus addresses the Venetian Republic: Whence such authority to you, that you judge (note this) THE JUDGE OF ALL, whom no lawfully assembled council has hitherto dared to judge. In the Canon Law, Dist. 40, c. Si Papa, the following passages, most pertinent here, are read: If the Pope is found negligent of his own and his brothers' salvation, useless and slack in his works, and moreover silent about good things, which harms himself and all the more, and nonetheless leads countless peoples in droves with him, to be first handed over to the servant of hell, there to be scourged with many blows for ever, no mortal presumes to rebuke his faults there, because he who is to judge all is to be judged by no one. Since therefore God alone is the judge of the Church, to be judged by no mortal, and the judgement of the Church is lawful only according to the word of God, which is received as the judgement of God himself, the Pope, arrogating the same to himself and looking down on the judgement of the Church as beneath him, indeed aspires to divinity and makes himself an idol.

units.la: XLI. Accedit his omnibus judicialis illius processus, quo in remittendis vel retinendis hominum peccatis, clavium earundem obtentu, utitur, potestas. Nam remittendi peccata potestatem judicialem soli Deo competere, adeóque creaturis planè incommunicabilem esse, liquet clarissimè, tum quia solus Deus judex est Genes. xviii. 24. Psal. xcvii. 19. Hebr. xii. 23. Jac. iv. 26. tum quia peccata remittere propriè, Dei proprietatis essentialis est, Elai. xliii. 15. Mich. vii. 18. Matth. vi. 12. ix. 2. 5. 6. tum quia quisquis peccata propriè remittit, oportet sit & Καρδιογνώστης, qui peccata animi; quæ sub sensum non cadunt, cognoscat; & animarum conscientiæque dominus, qui poenas iis convenientes dictare & irrogare possit. Papa autem sive immediatè, sive in delegatis à se Sacerdotibus, judicialem & prætoriam peccata remittendi potestatem sibi tam severè vendicat, ut Concilii Tridentini Patres Seß. xiv. can. 9. anathema dirum intonuerint iis, qui dixerint, absolutionem Sacramentalem Sacerdotis non esse actum judicialem, sed nudum ministerium pronuntiandi & declarandi, remissa esse peccata confitenti, &c. De qua potestate verè Divina à Papa sibi arrogata, cum plura in Anatome & Funere Concilii Tridentini dixerimus, hæc ea repetere supersedemus. Satis esto inde cognoscere, quòd Papa Divinam jurisdictionem involaverit.
units.tr: XLI. To all these is added that judicial process by which, in remitting or retaining men's sins, he uses power under cover of the same keys. For that the judicial power of remitting sins belongs to God alone, and is therefore wholly incommunicable to creatures, is most clearly evident: first, because God alone is judge (Gen. 18:24; Ps. 97:19; Heb. 12:23; Jas. 4:26); second, because to remit sins properly is a property of God's essential nature (Isa. 43:15; Mic. 7:18; Matt. 6:12; 9:2, 5, 6); third, because whoever properly remits sins must also be a searcher of hearts [Καρδιογνώστης], who knows the sins of the mind that do not fall under the senses, and the lord of souls and consciences, who can prescribe and impose penalties fitting to them. But the Pope, whether immediately or through priests delegated by himself, so severely claims for himself the judicial and praetorian power of remitting sins that the Fathers of the Council of Trent, Sess. 14, can. 9, thundered a dread anathema against those who say that the sacramental absolution of the priest is not a judicial act, but a bare ministry of pronouncing and declaring that sins are forgiven to the one confessing, etc. Concerning this truly divine power, which the Pope has arrogated to himself, since we have said much on it in the Anatomy and Funeral of the Council of Trent, we will forgo repeating these things. It is enough to recognise from this that the Pope has usurped divine jurisdiction.

units.la: XLII. Sed de Clavigero hocce novello Numine abundè satis, ubi hoc unum adjecero, non obscurè illud ab Angelo quinto buccinante Apoc. ix. 1. sugillari. Vidit enim Angelus ille buccinans stellam, quæ ex Cœlo in terram ceciderat, cui data fuerit ἡ κλεὶς τοῦ φρέατος τῆς ἀβύσσου, clavis putei abyssi. Quæ cùm data sit stellæ ex Cœlo cadenti, alia longè est haud dubiè à clavi illa abyssi, quam Apoc. xx. 1. Christo datam esse, supra observavimus. Nam Christus quidem Abyssum clavi sua aperiens Sathanam coërcuisse dicitur: hæc verò stella in terras protrubata, aperiens puteum abyssi fumum inde, ut fumum fornacis magnæ, & ex fumo illo locustas in terram elicuit. Stella ex Cœlo cadens notabilem quendam Ecclesiæ doctorem, Episcopum, qui tanquam in Cœlo sedens loquebatur, authoritate, quam sibi arrogaverat, privatum notare potest. Talis profectò Papa est, quem Ecclesiæ Reformatio magna apud populos complures authoritate privavit, & ex Cœlo suo in terram extorrem provolvit. Restitare tamen ille, & clavium Regni Cœlorum sibi traditarum prætextu apud suos authoritatem retinere, & apud eos, qui Majestatem ejus dedignantur, asserere. Angelus concedit ipsi clavem, sed per insignem ωυκηεισμὸν clavem putei abyssi vocat, quia omni hac clavium potestate & exercitio homines sibi addictos non in Cœlum adducit, sed inferno, tanquam alter Deus hujus Seculi, mancipat, & fumum insuper falsarum doctrinarum, atque inde etiam pullulantes locustas ex inferno protrusit.
units.tr: XLII. But enough about this key-bearer, the new divinity, when I have added only this: that it is not obscurely censured by the fifth angel sounding the trumpet (Rev. 9:1). For that trumpeting angel saw a star which had fallen from heaven to earth, to which was given the key of the well of the abyss [ἡ κλεὶς τοῦ φρέατος τῆς ἀβύσσου]. Since this key was given to the star fallen from heaven, it is without doubt different from that key of the abyss which, as we observed above, was given to Christ (Rev. 20:1). For Christ, opening the abyss with his key, is said to have restrained Satan; but this star, thrust down to the earth, opened the well of the abyss, and from that smoke, like the smoke of a great furnace, drew locusts out upon the earth. The star falling from heaven can denote a notable teacher of the Church, a bishop, who spoke as though sitting in heaven, and who has been deprived of the authority he had arrogated to himself. Such indeed is the Pope, whom the great Reformation deprived of authority among many peoples, and rolled from his heaven into the earth as an exile. Yet he resists, and under the pretext of the keys of the kingdom of heaven entrusted to him, he tries to retain authority among his own and to assert it among those who disdain his majesty. The angel grants him the key, but with a pointed reproach [ὀνειδισμόν] he calls it the key of the well of the abyss, because by all this power and exercise of the keys he does not lead the men devoted to him up to heaven, but hands them over to hell, as another god of this age, and besides he has belched forth the smoke of false doctrines and the locusts sprung from it out of hell.

units.la: XLIII. Quintò Divinam sibi Majestatem Papa vendicat, cùm se caput, Fundamentum, Petram Ecclesiæ mentitur. Nam caput, Fundamentum, Petram Ecclesiæ esse, est πλειότητα solius Christi. Is enim est ἡ κεφαλὴ ἕ σῶμα caput illud corporis Ecclesiæ Ephef. 1.22.Col.1.18.11.19. ubi cum articulo ὁ definitè notatur is, qui est caput Ecclesiæ. Tum in Christo solo reperiuntur proprietates capitis, quales sunt, conjungi cum Ecclesia ἀχωρίστως & ἀδιαιρέτως, diligere Ecclesiam, συμπαθῆζει, pro ea fieri sacrificium, repræsentare corpus, ἐπιχορηγῶν suppeditare ei omnem vim & facultatem vivificam, nec non augmentum, ut crescat & educetur Ecclesia εἰς τὴν πλήρωμα ἕ Θεῶ, esse lucem corporis Ecclesiæ, & Doctorem unicum. Quæ capitis Ecclesiæ hieroglyphica soli Christo Ephef. 1. 22. 23.
units.tr: XLIII. Fifthly, the Pope claims for himself the divine majesty when he falsely calls himself the head, foundation and rock of the Church. For to be the head, foundation and rock of the Church belongs to Christ alone, the fullness [πληρότητα] of God. He is that head of the body [ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ σώματος] of the Church (Eph. 1.22; Col. 1.18; 1.19), where the article ho [ὁ] marks out definitely who is the head of the Church. Moreover, the properties of the head are found in Christ alone: to be joined to the Church inseparably [ἀχωρίστως] and indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως], to love the Church, to suffer with it [συμπάσχει], to offer himself as a sacrifice for it, to represent the body, to supply [ἐπιχορηγῶν] it with all life-giving power and ability, and also to give the growth by which the Church is brought up to the fullness of God [εἰς τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ]; to be the light of the body of the Church and its one Teacher. These hieroglyphics of the head of the Church are ascribed to Christ alone (Eph. 1.22, 23).

units.la: 1. Cor. viii. 6. 1. Tim. ii. 8. 1. Cor. xv. 45. 47. Joh. i. 4. 46. Matth. xxiii. 8. 10. &c. tribuntur. Sed & πέτρα fundamentum Ecclesiæ solus Christus Esai. xxviii. 16. 1. Cor. iii. 2. neque alius quisquam usquam designatur. Denique Petram esse Ecclesiæ, ex usu Scripturæ notat, salvandos, rupis ad instar, verbo sponsionis ferre, & in Spiritualem domum extruere. Unde צור rupes, quod idem est cum πέτρα petra, non alius usquam, quàm Deus, Christus insignitur.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 8.6; 1 Tim. 2.8; 1 Cor. 15.45, 47; John 1.4, 46; Matt. 23.8, 10, etc. Likewise the rock [πέτρα], the foundation of the Church, is Christ alone (Isa. 28.16; 1 Cor. 3.2), and no one else anywhere is designated so. Finally, that the rock is of the Church, Scripture usage shows: it signifies bearing up those to be saved, as a rock does, by the word of promise, and building them into a spiritual house. Hence tzur [צור], rock, which is the same as petra [πέτρα], is nowhere else assigned except to God and Christ.

units.la: XLIV. Papam porro se ferre Caput, fundamentum, Petram Ecclesiæ totius militantis, probatione equidem nulla indiget. Hoc enim est, quod ejus hyperaspistæ mordicus propugnant, & quibusvis interdictis defensitant. Hoc in dubium revocare, vel negare, scelus habetur piacularīlaribus flammis expiandum. Atque licet verbis profiteantur, Papam non æquo aut jure aut gradu cum Christo Ecclesiæ caput, fundamentum, Petram constitui, tamen sic amplificant postea, ut facilè appareat, dicis tantùm causa Christum præferri. Nam tum Papam sic summum faciunt, ut nulli prorsus potestati, quæcunque illa tandem sit, Civilis aut Ecclesiastica, obnoxium esse velint, etiam tum, cùm officio suo non fungitur: tum sic exempto ab omni potestate omnes reliqui absque exceptione ulla non in Ecclesiasticis tantum, sed in temporalibus etiam negotiis subjiciuntur, ipsamque adeòque Conciliorum authoritatem Sedis Apostolicæ authoritati subesse contendunt: tum Papæ sententiam definitivam esse ejusmodi volunt, ut contra ne hiscere quidem cuiquam liceat; perinde ac si ipsa Divina voce Petri firmata esset, uti Gratianus, Dist. 19. loquitur. Facit huc Concilii Florentini de potestate Papæ definitio, quam Differt. viij. sect. iij. thes. 28. posuimus: tum summam potestatem legislativam & judicialem, extensam etiam ad subjectionem omnis creaturæ, Papæ asserunt, uti hac ipsa dissertatione nec non supra loc. cit. sect. 30. &c. ostendimus: tum denique potestati huic mirè velificans dogma infallibilitatis Papæ in quæstionibus juris & facti, hodie inprimis præstruunt, uti ibidem sect. 34. 35. &c. latè deduximus.
units.tr: XLIV. Moreover, that the Pope bears himself as the head, foundation and rock of the whole militant Church needs no proof. For this is what his hyperaspists stubbornly defend and maintain by every kind of prohibition. To call this into doubt, or to deny it, is regarded as a crime to be expiated by the flames of the pyre. And although they profess in words that the Pope is not constituted head, foundation and rock of the Church with Christ on equal terms or equal right, yet afterwards they so magnify him that it readily appears Christ is put first only for form's sake. For then they make the Pope so supreme that they will have him subject to no power whatever, civil or ecclesiastical, even when he does not discharge his office; then, with him so freed from all power, they contend that all the rest, without exception, are subject to him not only in ecclesiastical but also in temporal affairs, and that the authority of the Councils itself is subordinate to the authority of the Apostolic See; then they want the Pope's sentence to be such that no one may so much as murmur against it, just as though it were confirmed by the very divine voice of Peter, as Gratian speaks (Dist. 19). The definition of the Council of Florence on the power of the Pope bears on this, which we set out in Dissertation 8, sect. 3, thes. 28; then they assert for the Pope a supreme legislative and judicial power, extended even to the subjection of every creature, as we have shown in this same dissertation and above in the cited place, sect. 30 etc.; and finally, to back this power they chiefly now put forward the dogma of the Pope's infallibility in questions of law and fact, which we have set out at length in the same place, sect. 34, 35 etc.

units.la: XLV. Neque Capitis & fundamenti primarii & secun- darii, imperialis & ministerialis distinctio quicquam m- utetur.
units.tr: XLV. Nor will the distinction between primary and secondary, imperial and ministerial, head and foundation change anything.

units.la: Præterquam enim quòd Bonifacius VIII. Cap. Unam Sanctam, Papaliter & Bullariter definivit, Christum, & Vicarium Christi Petrum, & Petri successorem Papam unum tantum esse omnes caput Ecclesiæ; etiam Scriptura unius solius Capitis & fundamenti, Christi, meminit. Proprie etenim caput illud est, quod ordine, dignitate, imperio & influxu cæteris membris præest. Vel igitur Papa propriè Caput Ecclesiæ non est ; vel tale est, quale Christus est. Ec quæ verò illi Capiti imperiali & ministeriali officia deputant ? Stapletonus quidem Princip. Doctr. lib. vj. 16. sic officia partitur, ut imperiale à se, tanquam fonte, vitam in cæteras corporis partes diffundat: ministeriale corporis externa munia imperio & potestate sua dirigat & administret. Atqui imperio & potestate sua sive interna, sive externa corporis munia dirigere, præcipua seu principalis est capitis functio, illo unico gna capite, quod vitæ, sensus, & motus potestatem omnem Spiritu suo corpori impartitur. Cùmque imperium hoc exercere sit prærogativa Regia, & Regis Regum propria, qui eam totam, vel partem ejus cuiquam subditorum, qui διὰ ὑρῶν διακονίας ad opus ministerum (Ephes. iv. 12.) constituti sunt, tribuit, is læsæ Majestatis Christi reum se reddit. Caput igitur esse, & ministrum esse, ἀντὶ sunt. Unde Papam suum Ecclesiæ caput non aliter Pontificii constituere potuerunt, quàm infinitam, meram, & reapse directam in temporalibus & spiritualibus potestatem ei arrogando, eúmque Regem Regum, & Dominum dominorum faciendo. Cujus videlicet actus proprios faciunt, adorari instar Numinis, oscula pedum à summis Monarchis excipere, Scripturæ Divinitatem suo arbitrio subjicere, fidem non probatam ex Dei verbo, non exploratam à fidelibus, conscientiis obtrudere, Concilia à suo nutu suspendere, contra leges Divinas dispensare, spiritualium prætextu Regnum merè terrenum in Imperatores, Reges, Principes mundi exigere, atque illud maximo cum splendore in mundo proferre. Hi Capitis hujus ministerialis actus ἐχαίρουσι, merè Divini utique sunt.
units.tr: For, apart from the fact that Boniface VIII, in the chapter Unam Sanctam, defined in papal and bullish style that Christ and his Vicar Peter, and Peter's successor the Pope, are one head of the Church, Scripture also speaks of one only head and foundation, Christ. For that is properly the head which in order, dignity, command and influence presides over the other members. Therefore either the Pope is not properly the head of the Church, or he is such a head as Christ is. But what offices do they assign to that head as imperial and ministerial? Stapleton indeed, in Principiorum Doctrinae book 6, chapter 16, divides the offices so that the imperial head, as a fount, pours life from itself into the other parts of the body, while the ministerial head directs and administers the external duties of the body by its command and power. But to direct the duties of the body, whether internal or external, by its command and power, is the chief or principal function of the head, that one head which imparts all power of life, sense and motion to the body by its Spirit. And since to exercise this command is the royal prerogative, proper to the King of kings, who grants it whole, or a part of it, to any of his subjects who are appointed for the work of ministry [εἰς ἔργον διακονίας] (Eph. 4.12), he makes himself guilty of injured majesty toward Christ. So to be head and to be minister are contradictory [ἀντικείμενα]. Hence the Papists could not make their Pope the head of the Church in any other way than by arrogating to him infinite, sheer and in fact direct power over temporal and spiritual things, and by making him King of kings and Lord of lords. Of course they make it his proper acts to be worshipped like a deity, to receive kisses on the feet from the highest monarchs, to subject the divinity of Scripture to his own judgment, to force on consciences a faith not proved from the Word of God and not tested by the faithful, to suspend Councils at his nod, to dispense against the divine laws, to extract under the pretext of spiritual matters a merely earthly kingdom from emperors, kings and princes of the world, and to display it in the world with the greatest splendour. These acts of this ministerial head are, beyond doubt, purely divine.

units.la: XLVI. Fundamenti inprimis Ecclesiæ primarii & secundarii distinctio monstrosa cui non videatur merito ?
units.tr: XLVI. Is not the monstrous distinction between a primary and a secondary foundation of the Church one that deserves to be rejected?

units.la: Etenim fundamentum quodvis ædificio suo adæquatum sit
units.tr: For any foundation must be adequate to the building it supports.

units.la: Fundamentum primarii & secundarii distinctio monstrosa fit oportet. Vel igitur secundarium illud fundamentum adæquatum est, vel non. Si adæquatum, unicum est, nec primarii vel secundarii nomine venire potest. Si inadæquatum, ne quidem fundamentum est. Sed quid multis? S. Paulus 1 Cor. iii. 11. disertis verbis dicit: Θεμέλιον ἄλλον οὐδεὶς δύναται θεῖναι παρὰ τὸ κείμενον, ὅς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστός. Fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest, præter illud, quod positum est; quod est Jesus Christus. Est autem prosecto fundamentum secundarium, vicarium non tantum ἕτερον alterum (quod ipsum etiam poni nefas erat, quia nullum aliud ponendum est παρὰ præter id, quod politum est ab Apostolis) sed etiam ἄλλο aliud, quippe numero diversum, & quidem peregrinum, propriæ domus, propriæ Ecclesiæ, ab Ecclesia Christi diverfiffimæ fundamentum, neutiquam ejusmodi, quale est Lapis ille in Sione fundatus, probatus, angularis, fundatiffimè fundatus. Efai. xxviii. 16. Neque quisquam Ecclesiæ fundamentum qualecunque proprie esse potest, nisi per meritum sanguinis, super quo, ceu fundamento unico, Ecclefia ædificari potuit. Qui igitur proprie fundamentum Ecclesiæ haberi vult, qualecunque illud, DEUM, Chriftum fe faciat plane necesse est.
units.tr: The distinction between a primary and a secondary foundation must be monstrous. Either that secondary foundation is adequate, or it is not. If it is adequate, it is the only foundation, and it cannot be called primary or secondary. If it is inadequate, it is not even a foundation. But why say more? St Paul says plainly, 1 Cor. iii. 11: Another foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ [Θεμέλιον γὰρ ἄλλον οὐδεὶς δύναται θεῖναι παρὰ τὸν κείμενον, ὅς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός]. Yet a secondary foundation is surely a vicarious one, not merely another [ἕτερον] (which itself could not be laid, since nothing else may be laid beside what the Apostles laid down), but something else [ἄλλο], numerically distinct and indeed foreign: a foundation of a private house, of a private church, utterly different from the Church of Christ, and in no way like that stone laid in Zion, tried, a precious corner stone, most surely founded, Isa. xxviii. 16. Nor can anyone properly be the foundation of the Church, of whatever kind, except through the merit of the blood on which, as the single foundation, the Church could be built. Therefore whoever wishes to be regarded as the proper foundation of the Church, whatever it is, must plainly make himself God and Christ.

units.la: XLVII. Atque id eo magis etiam liquet, quòd is ipse, qui fe Caput, fundamentum Ecclesiæ, quicunque sensus prætexatur, haberi vult, & Christi ipsius nomen usurpat (quomodo tum Bernhardus de Confid. lib. ij. 9. Eugenium unctione Christum appellat; tum Gregorius VII. in secunda bulla excommunicationis Henrici Imp. eos, qui sibi restiterunt, convenisse adversus Dominum & Christum ejus, qualis Pfal. ii. 2. Jesus Christus, unctorum omnium caput intelligitur, scribit.) & verba illa Esaiæ cap. xxviii. 16. Ecce pono in Sione pro fundamento lapidem, lapidem probatum, angularem &c. quæ & S. Paulus
units.tr: XLVII. This becomes even clearer from the fact that the man who wishes to be regarded as the Head and foundation of the Church, whatever meaning he pretends, also usurps the very name of Christ. So Bernard, in De Consideratione book ii, calls Eugenius Christ by anointing; and Gregory VII, in his second bull of excommunication of the Emperor Henry, writes that those who resisted him had gathered together against the Lord and his Christ, which in Ps. ii. 2 is understood of Jesus Christ, the Head of all the anointed. He also allows himself to be given the words of Isaiah xxviii. 16: Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, etc., which St

units.la: lus Ius Rom. ix. 33. & S. Petrus 1 Ep. 11. 7. de solo Christo interpretatur, sibi tribui patitur; (quomodo Bellarminum Præfat. in 3. Controv. Gen. lib. j. De Papa vaticinium illud blasphemè explicantem Papa tulit) & se Sponsum Ecclesiæ, quod nomen Scriptura soli Christo Πανθεῶπῳ tribuit, haberi vult; (uti non solùm Augustinus Triumphus de Pot. Eccles. q. 19. art. 1. ex professo, Papam esse Sponsum Ecclesiæ disputat; sed etiam Innocentius III. Serm. 3. in Confid. Pontificis sic arguit: Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est. Annon ego sponsus sum; & quilibet vestrûm amicus sponsi? Utique sponsus, quia habeo nobilem, divitem, & sublimem, decoram, castam, gratiosam, sacro-Sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam; quæ, disponente Deo, cunctorum fidelium mater & magistra est; & Leo X. in Bulla Concordatorum cum Francisco I. Nuper, inquiebat, siquidem, ut Ecclesia Sponsa nostra in sancta unione conservaretur) &, quod Christus sibi soli tribuit, omnem sibi in Cœlo & terra potestatem datam gloriatur; (uti tum Puccius & Stephanus Patracensis Concil. Later. Sess. 9. & 10. Julio Papæ datam esse blasphemat; tum Cerem. lib. tit. 7. Pontifici, summo in terris Christi Vicario potestatem summam datam esse statuit, juxta illud: Data est mihi omnis potestas &c.) & se Leonem de tribu Juda dici permittit (uti permisit Leo X. se in Concilio Lateranensi Sess. 6. à Simone Begnio dici) & se Agnum Dei tollentem peccata mundi proclamari haud iniquè fert (uti à Panormitanis se proclamari Martinus IV. teste Jovio in Philippo III. passus est) ut alia ejusmodi pessimi comatis omittam. Quid jam quæso Christo relinquit? Adeò nihil tam certè manifesteque de eo Spiritus S. prædixit, quod non iste sibi scelerate vel assumat, vel attribui patiatur. Tale ergo Caput Ecclesiæ, tale fundamentum Ecclesiæ haberi postulat, quale le fuit Christus ; verbo Caput, fundamentum planè Di-vinum.
units.tr: Paul (Rom. ix. 33) and St Peter (1 Pet. ii. 7) interpret of Christ alone. He likewise has himself taken to be the Bridegroom of the Church, a name which Scripture gives to Christ alone. (So Augustinus Triumphus, in his De potestate ecclesiastica, question 19, article 1, openly argues that the Pope is the Bridegroom of the Church; and Innocent III, in his third sermon on the consecration of the Pope, reasons thus: He who has a bride is a bridegroom. Am I not a bridegroom, and is not each of you a friend of the bridegroom? Surely I am a bridegroom, because I have a noble, rich, exalted, comely, chaste, gracious, most holy Roman Church, which, by God's arrangement, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful; and Leo X, in the bull on the concordat with Francis I, said: Lately, indeed, so that the Church, our Bride, might be kept in holy union.) He also boasts that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him, which Christ claimed for himself alone. (So Puccio and Stephen of Patras at the Lateran Council, sessions 9 and 10, blasphemously declare that all power was given to Pope Julius; and the Ceremonial, book... title 7, declares that the supreme power on earth was given to the Pope, the highest Vicar of Christ, according to the words: All power is given unto me, etc.) He permits himself to be called the Lion of the tribe of Judah (as Leo X allowed himself to be so called by Simone Begnio in the Lateran Council, session 6), and he bears it without complaint when he is proclaimed the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world (as Martin IV suffered himself to be so proclaimed by the people of Panormus, according to Jovius in his life of Philip III), not to mention many other such impious claims. What, I ask, is left to Christ? So certainly and so plainly did the Holy Spirit foretell nothing about him that this man does not wickedly take to himself or allow to be ascribed to himself. Such a Head of the Church, such a foundation of the Church, he demands to be regarded as, as Christ was: in name the Head and foundation, but in reality wholly divine.

units.la: XLVIII. Hinc adeò, ceu Caput & Oecumenicus Pontifex summus universali Ecclesiæ Christi dominatur basilicè: ne caput ministeriale somnies. Vocabulorum enim illorum, Caput, Pontifex Summus &c. vim modò attende, non dissimulatam ab Hierarchicis. Bonifacius VIII. Extravag. Unam Sanctam &c. Subesse, inquit, Romano Pontifici, omni humanæ creaturæ declaramus esse de necessitate salutis. Inde scilicet sunt consectaria ; Papa est immediatus Prælatus, & judex omnium fidelium, ut in toto orbe terrarum facere possit, quicquid inferiores Prælati facere possunt. Sic Johannes de Turre cremata in Summa de Ecclesia lib. v. 65. & 80. Romanus, ait, Pontifex jurisdictionis authoritate ac potestate superior ac major existit tota Ecclesia universali. Glossator Gratiani C. 9. quæst. 3. cap. Nemo; Concilium Papam judicare posse negat. Unde, inquit, si totus mundus sententiaret in aliquo negotio contra Papam, videtur, quòd sententia Papæ standum esset. Idque ex vi verborum ejus Canonis eruitur, in quo sic legere est : Neque ab Augusto, neque ab omni clero, neque à Regibus, neque à populo judex judicabitur. Negat ergo præfractè, se à quoquam judicari posse; imò se regulam fidei constituit, uti supra ostendimus, & Caranza Proleg. in Summam Concil. Controv. 3. omni posita fronte, & claris verbis pronuntiat. Denique Episcopos omnes titulorum illorum vi, ad ministrorum & vasallorum suorum subsellia redegit; &, quod indignius est, Episcopos, Archiepiscopos, quorum summa dignitas erat præfici Ecclesiæ, ad eam contumeliam projecit, ut magno honori ducant, si officiarii Papæ domestici, veluti Cancellarii, datarii, Quæstores, prætores, Presbyteri, Diaconi urbis Romæ quandoque creentur.
units.tr: XLVIII. Hence, as Head and supreme Pontiff of the whole world, he rules the universal Church of Christ in a kingly fashion; so do not dream of a merely ministerial head. Consider carefully the force of those titles, Head, supreme Pontiff, etc., which the hierarchs do not hide. Boniface VIII, in the Extravagant Unam sanctam, says: We declare, state, and define that it is necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff. From this, of course, follow the corollaries: The Pope is the immediate prelate and judge of all the faithful, so that he can do throughout the whole world whatever inferior prelates can do. So John of Torquemada, in his Summa de Ecclesia, book v, chapters 65 and 80: The Roman Pontiff, by the authority and power of jurisdiction, is and stands higher and greater than the whole universal Church. The gloss on Gratian (C. 9, q. 3, c. Nemo) denies that a council can judge the Pope: Hence, it says, if the whole world should pass sentence against the Pope in some matter, it seems that the Pope's sentence should stand. This is drawn from the force of the words of that canon, in which we read: The judge shall be judged by no one: not by the Emperor, not by all the clergy, not by kings, not by the people. So he flatly denies that he can be judged by anyone; indeed he sets himself up as the rule of faith, as we have shown above, and Caranza, in the prolegomena to his Summa of the Councils, 3, states it openly and in plain words. Finally, by virtue of those titles he has reduced all the bishops to the rank of his ministers and vassals; and, what is more shameful, he has so cast down bishops and archbishops, whose highest dignity was to preside over the Church, into such dishonour that they count it a great honour if they are sometimes created officials of the Pope's household, such as chancellors, datary, questors, praetors, elders, or deacons of the city of Rome.

units.la: nec non vis vocabulorum, Caput, Pontifex Summus &c. argumenti. tur. Quæ cùm ita sint, jubare meridiano clarius emicat, Papam titulis illis Capitis, fundamenti Ecclesiæ &c. se Christo æquare; Ecclesiæ universali, ceu Numen quoddam, præferre, denique demonstrare, quòd Deus sit.
units.tr: Since these things are so, it shines clearer than the midday sun that the Pope, by those titles of Head, foundation of the Church, etc., makes himself equal to Christ; sets himself above the universal Church as a kind of divinity; and, in short, shows that he is God.

units.la: XLIX. Sextò Divinitatem Papa affectat, cùm sibi potestatem transferendi Regna, & Regibus ipsis imperitandi eximiam facit. Quin hoc Divinæ Majestatis סמא quoddam sit, nemo sanus revocare in dubium potest. Nam הוא Ipse, Deus; non alius quisquam מהעדה transfert Reges, & constituit Reges, מלכין ומהקים מלכין Dan. II. 21. Non igitur consilius hominum, & eorum prudentia, aut brachio existunt, aut confervantur, aut tolluntur, sed nutu solius Dei. Qui aliquando erigit potentes in mundo, ad parvum tempus, donec destinata sua per eos fecerit. Concinit æterna Dei Sapientia, Filius Dei Prov. viii. 15. sic clamans: בי מלכים ימלכו Per me Reges regnant, & Principes justitiam decernunt. Et S. Paulus Rom. xiii. 1. ἐ γὰρ ἐστιν ἐξουσία εἰ μὴ ἀπὸ Θεοῦ, Non enim est potestas nisi à Deo. Quæ autem sunt potestates, à Deo ordinatæ sunt. Neque aliam certè ob causam Deus Regis Regum & Domini dominantium nomine venit. Supra quoque Differt. viij. sect. ij. th. 6. fusè comprobavimus, Secularis potestatis radicem esse immediatam institutionem Dei, & delegationem quorundam cæteris dominantium. Denique dominium transferre non potest, nisi qui dominium habet. Qui ergo omne dominium, omnia Regna transferre potest, is omne dominium habet. Solus autem Deus omne dominium habet.
units.tr: XLIX. Sixth, the Pope aspires to divinity when he claims for himself the power of transferring kingdoms and of ruling over kings themselves. That this is a certain token of the divine majesty [סמא], no sane man can call in doubt. For He himself [הוא] is God; no other person removes and sets up kings [מעדה מלכין ומהקים מלכין], Dan. ii. 21. Therefore the counsels, prudence, and arm of men do not bring kingdoms into being, preserve them, or destroy them, but only the will of God, who sometimes raises up the mighty of the world for a short time until he has accomplished his purposes through them. The eternal Wisdom of God, the Son of God, agrees, speaking thus in Prov. viii. 15: By me kings reign [בי מלכים ימלכו], and princes decree justice. And St Paul, Rom. xiii. 1: For there is no power but of God; the powers that be are ordained of God [οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ἐξουσία εἰ μὴ ἀπὸ θεοῦ]. Nor surely for any other reason is God called by the name King of kings and Lord of lords. We have also shown at length above (Diff. viii, sect. ii, th. 6) that the root of secular power is the immediate institution of God and the delegation of certain rulers over others. Finally, no one can transfer dominion unless he himself has dominion. Therefore he who can transfer all dominion and all kingdoms has all dominion. But God alone has all dominion.

units.la: L. Hanc potestatem sibi eximiam fecisse Papam illum orbis arbitrum, & Regem Regum, ac Dominum dominantium, cujus tribunal idem est cum tribunali Dei, uti Isidorus Musconius, Vicarius Generalis Archiepiscopi Bononiensis, & se niennensis de Majest. Eccles. Milit. lib. j. c. 7. loquitur; ejusdem, quam modò citavimus Dissertationis octavæ Sessione tertia integra, inprimis thesi 53-66. clarissimè demonstravimus. Et indignaretur Papa haud dubiè, si de eminentissimo & verè Divino hoc jure controversiam ipsi facere cuiquam liberet. Atque illud cumprimis memorabile est, quòd Papa à se coronatos à Deo coronatos appellat; quódque diadema à se datum à Petra Christo, & Petro datum interpretatur, juxta Hildebrandinum illud:
units.tr: L. This is the extraordinary power that the Pope, that arbiter of the world, has claimed for himself. Isidorus Musconius, Vicar General of the Archbishop of Bologna, and of Nienna, speaks of him as King of kings and Lord of lords, whose tribunal is the same as the tribunal of God (de Majest. Eccles. Milit. lib. j. c. 7.). We demonstrated this clearly in the whole third session of the eighth Dissertation, which I have just cited, especially in theses 53 to 66. The Pope would certainly be indignant if anyone chose to dispute with him this most lofty right, which is truly divine. Especially worth remembering is that the Pope calls those whom he has crowned crowned by God, and that he interprets the diadem given by him as given by Christ the Rock and by Peter, in line with that saying of Hildebrand:

units.la: Petra dedit Petro, Petrus diadema Rodolpho.
units.tr: The Rock gave to Peter; Peter gave the diadem to Rudolf.

units.la: Unicum addo, impietati huic & Divini honoris sacrilegio non erubuisse Pontifices subinde ludibria & contumelias addere. Nota est coronatio Henrici V. Imperatoris à Cœlestino Papa peracta; quam sic Henricus de Knygthon de Event. Angliæ lib. ij. cap. 13. describit: Secundo die consecrationis suæ coronavit Henricum V. Friderici Filium in Imperatorem sub hac forma. Inprimis recepto ab eodem Henrico juramento ante gradus Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quòd Ecclesiam Dei defenderet, ejus jura conservaret, rectam justitiam teneret, patrimonium Petri, si quod oblatum fuerit, pro posse revocaret. Contra Dominus Papa in cathedra sedens, coronamque Imperialem pedibus tenens inclinato capiti Imperiali demisit, quam statim cum pedibus in terram excussit, designans per hoc, quòd ipse Papa habet potestatem (NB) CREARE Imperatorem, si meruerit; & dejiciendi, si demeruerit. Cardinales verò adstantes coronam sic excussam capiti reposuerunt. Similem contumeliam Henrico IV. Galliarum Regi absenti coronato à Papa illatam, in Historia Papatus narravimus. Cùm ergo Papa & jus constituendi & dejiciendi Divinum Imperatores ac Reges omnes sibi vindicet, & jus illud exercuerit jam olim, uti loco citato fidem liberaliter fecimus, pro libitu; quis non hic novellum
units.tr: I add one thing: the Popes have not been ashamed, in this impiety and sacrilege against divine honour, to add mockery and insult from time to time. The coronation of the Emperor Henry V, performed by Pope Calixtus, is well known. Henry of Knighton describes it thus (de Event. Angliae lib. ij. cap. 13): On the second day of his consecration he crowned Henry V, son of Frederick, as Emperor, in the following form. First, after an oath had been taken by the same Henry before the steps of the Roman Church, that he would defend the Church of God, preserve its rights, maintain true justice, and recover, as far as he was able, the patrimony of Peter, if any had been alienated, the Lord Pope, sitting in his chair and holding the imperial crown at his feet, lowered it onto the bowed imperial head; then at once he struck it off with his feet onto the ground, signifying by this that the Pope himself has the power (NB) to CREATE an Emperor, if he deserves it, and to depose him if he has deserved otherwise. The cardinals standing by then replaced the crown, so struck off, on the head. We have related in the History of the Papacy a similar insult offered by the Pope to Henry IV, King of France, who was crowned in his absence. Since therefore the Pope claims for himself the divine right to appoint and depose all emperors and kings, and has long since exercised that right at his pleasure, as we have freely shown in the passage cited, who does not here see him flattering the new Babylonian god, the King of kings and Lord of lords?

Quod ipsum etiam idem, qui supra Henricus V. Imp. Aventino Annal. Bojor. lib. vj. teste, Papæ sic exprobrat: Genitore oppresso adversus me conspirat, neque modum ambitioni ponit, nisi alios omnes dignitate & honore expoliat, atque tandem PRO DEO SE ADORARI exigat.

(partly illegible)] Henry V, the same emperor who appears above, also reproaches the Pope in these words, according to Aventinus (Annal. Bojor. lib. vj.): He conspires against me, having oppressed his father, and sets no limit to his ambition, unless he strips all others of dignity and honour, and at last demands that he himself be adored as God.

units.la: LI. Septimò licentia Papalis dispensandi contra legem Divinam, juramenta & vota legitima Divinitatis affectatæ reum Papam liquidò reddit. Cùm dispensatio sit relaxatio quædam & solutio ab obedientia in lege præscripta in certo casu, manifestum utique est, non alii dispensandi contra legem Divinam, potestatem competere, quàm ei, qui legis author est, vel parem cum authore legis potestatem habet. Ejusdem enim est figere & refigere, obligare & solvere. Quod humanæ etiam leges demonstrant, à quarum obligatione vel in universum, vel in certo casu, relaxare, nisi qui easdem rogavit, potest nemo. Obligatio quippe ad legis obsequium, vel ab eadem obligatione solutio ab eo solo pendet, qui lege superior est. Recte igitur Zechius de statu Pontif. art. 2. scribit: Dispensare in lege potest, qui eam tulit, vel qui est supra id jus. Qui igitur contra legem Divinam dispensat, vel ipse Deus est, legis Divinæ author; vel parem cum Deo potestatem, adeòque Divinam habeat oportet. Par ratio dispensandi contra juramenta & vota legitima. In utrisque enim Deo aliquid promittitur, vel eodem teste asseritur. Solus autem Deus liberam hic adstringendi, vel relaxandi facultatem haberet, si qua omnino ejusmodi facultas locum habere posset: de quo hic non disputamus.
units.tr: LI. Seventhly, the Papal licence to dispense against the divine law, oaths and lawful vows, clearly proves the Pope guilty of claiming divinity. Since a dispensation is a certain relaxing and release from obedience to what the law prescribes in a particular case, it is plainly the case that no one has the power to dispense against the divine law except the one who is the author of the law, or who has power equal to the author's. For it belongs to the same person to fix and unfix, to bind and to loose. Human laws also show this: no one can relax their obligation, either generally or in a particular case, unless he is the one who enacted them. Indeed, release from the obligation to obey a law, or from the obligation itself, depends on him alone who is superior to the law. Zechius therefore rightly writes (de statu Pontif. art. 2.): He can dispense from the law who enacted it, or who is above that right. Whoever therefore dispenses against the divine law must either be God himself, the author of the divine law, or must have power equal to God's, and so must possess something divine. The same reasoning applies to dispensing against oaths and lawful vows. For in each case something is promised to God, or, as the same witness puts it, asserted before him. Only God would have the free power to bind or to loosen here, if any such power could exist at all. But we do not dispute that here.

units.la: LII. Papam porrò sibi dispensandi enormem illam licentiam sumere, in propatulo sanè est. Petrus de Monte in Monarchia disertissimè: Papa tollit jus Divinum, dispen-
units.tr: LII. Moreover, that the Pope assumes this enormous licence to dispense for himself is certainly obvious. Peter of Monte says most plainly in the Monarchia: The Pope removes the divine law by dispensing

units.la: {a} Qqq 2 pensando contra Euangelium. Papa dispensat contra universalem statum Ecclesiae. Dispensat contra vetus Testamentum. Dispensat contra multa capitula quatuor Euangeliorum. Gobelinus Persona Cosmodromii aetate 6. cap. 87. Bonifacius non solum contra Apostolum, sed etiam contra Euangelium dispensavit. Nam Ladislao Regi Siciliae, seu Neapolis indulsit, quod ipse abdicata a se uxore legitima, tam multis annis cum eo commorante, aliam superinduxit uxorem. Glossa super Decretal. 31. Tit. 8. c. propositum crude satis: Papa dispensat Vetus Testamentum, Apostolos & Euangelia. Ipse Innocentius III. Cap. Propositum, de Concess. Praebend. sibi aperte tribuit, quod secundum plenitudinem potestatis de jure supra jus dispensare possit. Expresse etiam Vasquez Tomo III. Disput. 226. num. 6. Licet, inquit, concederemus hoc fuisse Apostolicum praeceptum, nihilominus Ecclesia & Summus Pontifex potuerunt illud justis de causis abrogare. Neque enim major fuit potestas Apostolorum, quam Ecclesiae & Pontificis in ferendis praeceptis. Denique Caranza Controv. 2. Ecclesia, inquit, visa est aliquando facere contra Scripturas, aliquando praeter Scripturas. Ergo ipsa est regula eorum, quae traduntur in Scripturis. Et mox: Ergo credimus Ecclesiae contra formam Scripturarum. LIII. Quid vero multis? Res ipsa non loquitur, sed clamat. Plurima illa idololatriae, quae in Papatu obtinet, genera: mandatorum humanorum pro Divinis inculcatio: Calicis Eucharistici laicis surrepti nefas: Cultus Dei in Ecclesia lingua peregrina peragi solitus: Angelorum & Sanctorum cultus: Matrimonii & cibórum quorundam prohibitio, denique universa illa dogmata, quae praeter, contra & supra verbum Divinum Papa invexit & definivit, quid aliud, quam luculenta, Papalis contra jus Divinum dispensationis testimonia sunt?
units.tr: {a} Qqq 2 against the Gospel. The Pope dispenses against the universal state of the Church. He dispenses against the Old Testament. He dispenses against many chapters of the four Gospels. Gobelinus Persona (Cosmodromium, aetas 6, cap. 87): Boniface dispensed not only against the Apostle, but also against the Gospel. For he granted to Ladislaus, King of Sicily, or of Naples, that he might cast off his lawful wife, who had lived with him for so many years, and take another wife in her place. The gloss on Decretal 31, Title 8, chapter Propositum, puts it rather crudely: The Pope dispenses with the Old Testament, the Apostles and the Gospels. Innocent III himself, in chapter Propositum, de Concess. Praebend., openly ascribes to himself that by the fullness of power he can by right dispense above the law. Vasquez also says so expressly (Tomo III, Disput. 226, num. 6): Even if we grant that this was an apostolic precept, nevertheless the Church and the Supreme Pontiff could abrogate it for just causes. For the power of the Apostles was no greater than the power of the Church and the Pontiff in enacting precepts. Finally, Carranza (Controv. 2) says: The Church has sometimes seemed to act against the Scriptures, and sometimes beyond them. Therefore it is itself the rule of those things which are handed down in the Scriptures. And soon after: Therefore we believe the Church against the form of the Scriptures. LIII. But why say more? The thing itself does not speak; it cries aloud. Are not all those many kinds of idolatry that prevail in Popery, the inculcation of human commands in place of divine ones, the sin of withholding the eucharistic cup from the laity, the worship of God in the Church usually carried out in a foreign tongue, the worship of angels and saints, the prohibition of marriage and of certain foods, and, finally, all those doctrines which the Pope has introduced and defined beyond, against and above the Word of God, clear evidence of a Papal dispensation against the divine law?

units.la: LIV. Concilia inprimis Constantiense & Tridentinum
units.tr: LIV. The Councils of Constance and Trent in particular

units.la: illam dispensandi contra jus Divinum potestatem Ecclesiæ, hoc est, Papæ in solidum asserunt. In Constantiensi enim Seff. viij. c. 13. Patres præfati de institutione Christi, & de expresso mandato bibendi ex calice, ad omnes sine discrimine fideles directo, subjiciunt, Hoc (NB) non obstante prohiberi à se Laicis calicem. Unde Non-Obstantiense Concilium festivè Lutherus insignivit. In Concilio vero Tridentino Seff. xxj. cap. 7. habetur decretum, cujus titulus est: Ecclesiæ potestas circa dispensationem Sacramenti Eucharistiæ. Verba decreti, quo Calice Eucharistico plebs defraudatur, sic sonant: Præterea declarat Synodus, hanc potestatem perpetuò in Ecclesia fuisse, ut in Sacramentorum dispensatione, salva eorum substantia (scilicet ablato calice, materiæ Sacramenti parte essentiali, mansit substantia Sacramenti) ea statueret, vel mutaret, quæ suscipientium utilitati, vel ipsorum Sacramentorum veneratiōni expedire judicaret. Id autem Apostolus non obscurè visus est innuisse, cùm ait: Sic nos existimet homo, ut ministros Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Audi egregiam rationem. Paulus dicit: Sumus dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Mysteria sunt Sacramenta: & dispensare est jus relaxare. Ergò quæ Christus in dispensatione & usu Eucharistiæ instituit, Ecclesia potest abrogare. In tanta luce Thais illa Babylonica perfrictæ frontis ludere vocabulis non erubuit. Et qua conscientia hanc causam agat, omnes perpendant. Mysteria enim S. Paulo notant revelationem totius doctrinæ Euangelicæ, & Apostolos vocat illorum Mysteriorum οἰκονόμους dispensatores; hanc ipsam innuens antithesin, quòd non sint domini horum mysteriorum, qui potestatem habeant mutandi & abrogandi: sed quòd tantùm sint œconomi, in quibus hæc fidelitas requiritur, ut juxta institutionem & præceptum domini sui ea dispensent, quæ iis commissa sunt. In hac significatione vetus Interpres vocabulo dispensationis usus est. Illa verò vocis æquivocatio commoda visa fuit piis scilicet Patribus illis, qua Papam ubique Papaliter dispensare, ipsámque Cœnam mutilare posse, astruerent. Crimine ab uno disce omnes.
units.tr: They assert that the Church, that is, the Pope, has absolute power to dispense against divine law. In the Council of Constance, session 8, chapter 13, the aforesaid Fathers, although Christ instituted the Supper and expressly commanded that all the faithful without distinction drink from the cup, decreed that the laity be denied the cup notwithstanding this (NB). Hence Luther wittily named it the Non-Obstante Council. In the Council of Trent, session 21, chapter 7, there is a decree with the title: The power of the Church concerning the dispensing of the Sacrament of the Eucharist. The words of the decree by which the people are deprived of the Eucharistic cup run thus: Furthermore, the Synod declares that this power has always existed in the Church, so that in the dispensing of the sacraments, their substance remaining intact (namely, with the cup removed, the essential part of the matter of the sacrament, the substance of the sacrament still remains), it might ordain or change whatever it judged expedient for the benefit of those who receive them or for the veneration of the sacraments themselves. The Apostle seems to have hinted at this not obscurely when he said: Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and dispensers of the mysteries of God. Hear the excellent argument! Paul says: We are dispensers of the mysteries of God. Mysteries are sacraments, and to dispense is to have the right to relax. Therefore whatever Christ instituted concerning the dispensing and use of the Eucharist, the Church can abrogate. In so clear a light, that Babylonian harlot with brazen forehead was not ashamed to play with words. Let everyone weigh with what conscience they conduct this cause. For in St Paul the word mysteries denotes the revelation of the whole Gospel doctrine, and he calls the Apostles the stewards [οἰκονόμους] of those mysteries, thereby implying the contrast that they are not the lords of these mysteries, who have the power of changing and abrogating them, but only stewards, in whom this faithfulness is required, that they dispense, according to the institution and command of their Lord, the things committed to them. In this sense the old translator used the word dispensatio. But that ambiguity of the word seemed convenient to those pious Fathers, namely, to assert that the Pope may everywhere dispense in a papal manner and may mutilate the Supper itself. Learn all from one crime.

units.la: LV. Operæ pretium fuerit, ὡςΦὰ illa Φάρμακα, quæ Papalibus dispensationibus parasiti nonnulli obduxere, paucis discutere. Et Andradius quidem Defens. Fid. Trid. sol. 166. negat, eos errâsse, qui dicunt, Romanos Pontifices posse nonnunquam in legibus dispensare à Paulo, primisque quatuor Conciliis, ad Ecclesiam exornandam, morésque componendos, pro temporum necessitate edictis. Quo vero argumento? Quia, inquit, leges ejusmodi non fuerunt Christi voce rogatæ, sed hominum authoritate & prudentia latæ, qui illius (Papæ) ditioni subsunt, qui rerum summa potitur & universæ Ecclesiæ gubernacula tractat. Cum Andradio conspirans Melchior Canus cap. 18. duas constituit præceptorum Apostolicorum classes, quorum alia acceperint à Christo gentibus evulganda, alia non quidem à Christo acceperint, sed post Christum in Cœlos assumptum ipsi populis tradiderint, quæ tamen ipsa quoque Christi præcepta dicantur, quia Dei spiritu peculiariter suggerente edita fuerunt. Priora illa remitti posse negat, à posterioribus utpote propriè humanis & Ecclesiasticis liberare posse Pontificem suos subditos vel ex parte, vel omnino posse, asserit. Sed pudenda hæc esse κεπροφήτα, non tantùm Scripturarum authoritas uniformiter Divina, sed etiam ipsa praxis Papalium dispensationum loquitur. Nam v. 9. Copula Sacerdotalis nec legali, nec Euan-
units.tr: LV. It will be worth while briefly to examine those as-it-were remedies [ὡς φάρμακα], with which certain parasites have smeared the papal dispensations. Andradius, in his Defence of the Council of Trent, page 166, denies that those are wrong who say that the Roman Pontiffs can sometimes dispense from laws, which Paul and the first four Councils issued for adorning the Church and regulating morals, as the needs of the times required. But by what argument? Because, he says, laws of this kind were not enacted at the bidding of Christ, but were issued by the authority and prudence of men who are subject to his (the Pope's) dominion, who holds the supreme power and governs the helm of the whole Church. Agreeing with Andradius, Melchior Cano, chapter 18, sets up two classes of apostolic precepts: one class they received from Christ to be published among the nations, the other they did not receive from Christ, but after Christ was taken up into heaven they handed on to the peoples themselves, yet these too are called precepts of Christ, because they were issued under the special inspiration of the Spirit of God. He denies that the former can be remitted, but asserts that the Pope can release his subjects from the latter, which are properly human and ecclesiastical, either in part or wholly. But that these are shameful false prophecies [κεπροφήτα] is shown not only by the authority of the Scriptures, which speaks uniformly as divine, but also by the very practice of papal dispensations. For at verse 9, A priestly union is forbidden neither by legal, nor by

In Concilio etiam Constantiensi & Tridentino contra institutionem & exemplum ipsius Christi sub poena excommunicationis, & trino anathemate munitur novitia consuetudo communicandi populo Sacramentum sub una specie. Bellarminus quoque de Rom. Pontif. lib. v. 5. explicans potestatem clavium, Pontifici asserit dispensationem in lege, votis, juramentis, & similibus obligationibus; quæ ad ecclesiasticas constitutiones nullo schemate referri possunt, sed absolutè juris Divini sunt. Gospel, nor by apostolic authority (indeed any of them may be exchanged for any other), yet it is forbidden by ecclesiastical law, are the words of Gratian's Decree, part 2, case 26, question 2, canon Sors non est.
