Also in the Councils of Constance and Trent, against the institution and example of Christ himself, under penalty of excommunication and fortified by a threefold anathema, the novel custom of giving the people the sacrament under one kind is upheld. Bellarmine too, in his book On the Roman Pontiff, book 5, chapter 5, explaining the power of the keys, asserts that the Pope has the power to dispense from law, from vows, from oaths, and from similar obligations; which can in no way be referred to ecclesiastical constitutions, but belong absolutely to divine law. I say nothing of the countless dispensations against the Word of God mentioned above, and of the fact that that sly distinction neither at the outset [μηδὲ κατ' ἐναρ] came to mind for the authors cited in thesis 50.

units.la: LVI. Frustra ergo etiam Bellarminus de R. Pontif. lib. v. 5. hac protestatione utitur:
units.tr: LVI. Therefore Bellarmine too uses this protestation in vain:

units.la: Docemus nos uno ore Christi doctrinam & cultus non posse mutari. Idem tamen sibi discors lib. iv. de Antich. cap. 14. asserit, Papam posse dispensare in praeceptis positivis Apostolorum. Non tamen hoc esse contra Apostolum, sed juxta Apostolum, quia Apostolica potestas, qua Apostolus pro tempore aliquid in Ecclesia statuit, futura erat in successoribus, quod possent illi ipsi eadem moderari vel mutare, prout Ecclesiae expediret. Atqui Papam dispensâsse frequenter in iis, quæ sunt non juris Apostolici positivi, (quanquam & hæc, utpote à spiritu Dei profecta humana authoritate, indispensabilia sunt) sed quæ simpliciter juris Divini & perpetui sunt, satis jam constat. Est igitur distinctio hæc Φαντασία ουσίν. Quid quæso tam Divinum, tam Euangelicum est, quàm fidem servare publicè & privatim? Ecce autem perpetua est ista nundinatio Pontificis, qui simul atque
units.tr: We teach with one voice that the doctrine and worship of Christ cannot be changed. Yet he, inconsistent with himself, in book 4 of On the Antichrist, chapter 14, asserts that the Pope can dispense from the positive precepts of the Apostles. This is not against the Apostle, however, but in accordance with the Apostle, because the apostolic power by which the Apostle at the time ordained something in the Church was to pass to his successors, so that they might themselves moderate or change those same things as the Church found expedient. Yet it is already quite clear that the Pope has often dispensed in matters that are not of positive apostolic law (although these too, since they proceed from the Spirit of God, are indispensable by human authority), but which are simply of divine and perpetual law. This distinction, therefore, is an empty fancy [Φαντασία ουσίν]. What, I ask, is so divine and so evangelical as to keep the faith publicly and privately? Behold, however, this is a perpetual bargaining of the Pope, who, as soon as

units.la: Lot. 9 sit oportet. Vel igitur secundarium illud fundamentum adæquatum est, vel non. Si adæquatum, unicum est, nec primarii vel secundarii nomine venire potest. Si inadæquatum, ne quidem fundamentum est. Sed quid multis? S. Paulus 1 Cor. iii. 11. disertis verbis dicit: Θεμέλιον ἄλλον οὐδεὶς δύναται θεῖναι παρὰ τὸ κείμενον, ὅς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστός. Fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest, præter illud, quod positum est; quod est Jesus Christus. Est autem prosecto fundamentum secundarium, vicarium non tantùm ἑτερον alterum (quod ipsum etiam poni nefas erat, quia nullum aliud ponendum est παρὰ præter id, quod positum est ab Apostolis) sed etiam ἄλλο aliud, quippe numero diversum, & quidem peregrinum, propriæ domus, propriæ Ecclesiæ, ab Ecclesia Christi diversissimæ fundamentum, neutiquam ejusmodi, quale est Lapis ille in Sione fundatus, probatus, angularis, fundatissimè fundatus. Esai. xxviii. 16. Neque quisquam Ecclesiæ fundamentum qualecunque proprië esse potest, nisi per meritum sanguinis, super quo, ceu fundamento unico, Ecclesia ædificari potuit. Qui igitur proprië fundamentum Ecclesiæ haberi vult, qualecunque illud, DEUM, Christum se faciat planè necesse est.
units.tr: Lot. 9 must be. Either then that secondary foundation is adequate, or it is not. If adequate, it is unique, and cannot come under the name of primary or secondary. If inadequate, it is not even a foundation. But why say more? St Paul, 1 Cor. 3:11, says in plain words: Θεμέλιον ἄλλον οὐδεὶς δύναται θεῖναι παρὰ τὸ κείμενον, ὅς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστός [No one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ]. No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. Surely, however, there is a secondary and vicarious foundation, not only another [ἕτερον] (which it would itself be wrong to lay, because nothing else is to be laid beside [παρὰ] what has been laid by the Apostles), but a different [ἄλλο] one, indeed numerically distinct and, moreover, foreign, the foundation of a proper house, of a proper Church, utterly different from the Church of Christ, by no means of the kind that is that stone laid in Zion, tried, a corner stone, most surely founded. Isa. 28:16. Nor can anyone properly be the foundation of the Church, of whatever kind, except through the merit of the blood on which, as the one foundation, the Church could be built. Therefore whoever wishes to be regarded as the proper foundation of the Church, of whatever kind it be, must necessarily make himself God, Christ.

units.la: XLVII. Atque id eò magis etiam liquet, quòd is ipse, qui se Caput, fundamentum Ecclesiæ, quicunque sensus prætexatur, haberi vult, & Christi ipsius nomen usurpat (quomodo tum Bernhardus de Confid. lib. ij. 9. Eugenium unctione Christum appellat; tum Gregorius VII. in secunda bulla excommunicationis Henrici Imp. eos, qui sibi restiterunt, convenisse adversus Dominum & Christum ejus, qualis Psal. ii. 2. Jesus Christus, unctorum omnium caput intelligitur, scribit.) & verba illa Esaiæ cap. xxviii. 16. Ecce pono in Sione pro fundamento lapidem, lapidem probatum, angularem &c. quæ & S. Paulus Ius Rom. ix. 33. & S. Petrus 1 Ep. ii. 7. de solo Christo interpretatur, sibi tribui patitur; (quomodo Bellarminum Præfat. in 3. Controv. Gen. lib. j. De Papa vaticinium illud blasphemè explicantem Papa tulit) & se Sponsum Ecclesiæ, quod nomen Scriptura soli Christo Ϛαυθρωπῳ tribuit, haberi vult; (uti non solùm Augustinus Triumphus de Pot. Eccles. q. 19. art. 1. ex professo, Papam esse Sponsum Ecclesiæ disputat; sed etiam Innocentius III. Serm. 3. in Consid. Pontificis sic arguit: Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est. Annon ego sponsus sum; & quilibet vestrum amicus sponsi? Utique sponsus, quia habeo nobilem, divitem, & sublimem, decoram, castam, gratiosam, sacro-Sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam; quæ, disponente Deo, cunctorum fidelium mater & magistra est; & Leo X. in Bulla Concordatorum cum Francisco I. Nuper, inquiebat, siquidem, ut Ecclesia Sponsa nostra in sancta unione conservaretur) &, quod Christus sibi soli tribuit, omnem sibi in Cœlo & terra potestatem datam gloriatur; (uti tum Puccius & Stephanus Patracensis Concil. Later. Seff. 9. & 10. Julio Papæ datam esse blasphemat; tum Cerem. lib. tit. 7. Pontifici, summo in terris Christi Vicario potestatem summam datam esse statuit, juxta illud: Data est mihi omnis potestas &c.) & se Leonem de tribu Juda dici permittit (uti permisit Leo X. se in Concilio Lateranensi Seff. 6. à Simone Begnio dici) & se Agnum Dei tollentem peccata mundi proclamari haud iniquè fert (uti à Panormitanis se proclamari Martinus IV. teste Jovio in Philippo III. passus est) ut alia ejusmodi pessimi comatis omittam. Quid jam quæso Christo relinquit? Adeò nihil tam certè manifesteque de eo Spiritus S. prædixit, quod non ipse sibi sceleratè vel assumat, vel attribui patiatur. Tale ergo Caput Ecclesiæ, tale fundamentum Ecclesiæ haberi postulat, quale le fuit Christus ; verbo Caput, fundamentum planè Di- vinum.
units.tr: XLVII. This becomes all the clearer because he who wishes to be held the Head and Foundation of the Church, whatever sense he may pretend, and usurps the very name of Christ (thus Bernard, in On Consideration, book 2, chapter 9, calls Eugenius Christ by anointing; and Gregory VII, in the second bull of excommunication against the Emperor Henry, writes that those who opposed him had gathered against the Lord and his Christ, which Psalm 2:2 understands of Jesus Christ, the head of all the anointed), and who allows the words of Isaiah 28:16, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a corner stone, etc., which both St Paul, Romans 9:33, and St Peter, 1 Pet. 2:7, interpret of Christ alone, to be applied to himself (as Bellarmine, in the preface to the third controversy of book 1, when he blasphemously explained that prophecy about the Pope, accepted it for the Pope), and who wishes to be regarded as the Spouse of the Church, a name that Scripture gives to Christ alone (not only did Augustinus Triumphus, On the Power of the Church, question 19, article 1, expressly argue that the Pope is the Spouse of the Church; but also Innocent III, Sermon 3 on the Consideration of the Pontiff, argues thus: He who has a bride is a bridegroom. Am I not the bridegroom, and is not each of you a friend of the bridegroom? Certainly the bridegroom, because I have a noble, rich, exalted, comely, chaste, gracious, most holy Roman Church, which, by God's disposition, is the mother and teacher of all the faithful; and Leo X, in the bull of the concordats with Francis I: Recently, he said, indeed, so that the Church, our Spouse, might be preserved in holy union); and he boasts that all power in heaven and earth has been given to himself, which Christ claimed for himself alone (thus Puccius and Stephen of Patras blasphemously declare at the Lateran Council, sessions 9 and 10, that the supreme power was given to Julius the Pope; and the Ceremonial, book 1, title 7, states that supreme power was given to the Pope, the supreme Vicar of Christ on earth, according to that saying: All power has been given to me, etc.); and he allows himself to be called the Lion of the tribe of Judah (as Leo X allowed himself to be so called by Simon Begnius in the Lateran Council, session 6); and he bears with no great unfairness being proclaimed the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (as Martin IV, according to Jovius in Philip III, allowed himself to be proclaimed by the people of Panormus), to omit other such wicked trifles. What, I ask, is left to Christ now? So nothing so certainly and plainly did the Holy Spirit foretell of him that he does not wickedly assume it for himself or allow it to be attributed to himself. Therefore he demands to be held as the Head of the Church and the Foundation of the Church of such a kind as Christ was; in word the Head, the Foundation, truly divine.

units.la: XLVIII. Hinc adeò, ceu Caput & Oecumenicus Pontifex summus universali Ecclesiæ Christi dominatur basilicè: ne caput ministeriale somnies. Vocabulorum enim illorum, Caput, Pontifex Summus &c. vim modò attende, non dissimulatam ab Hierarchicis. Bonifacius VIII. Extravag. Unam Sanctam &c. Subesse, inquit, Romano Pontifici, omni humanæ creaturæ declaramus esse de necessitate salutis. Inde scilicet sunt consectaria; Papa est immediatus Prælatus, & judex omnium fidelium, ut in toto orbe terrarum facere possit, quicquid inferiores Prælati facere possunt. Sic Johannes de Turre cremata in Summa de Ecclesia lib. v. 65. & 80. Romanus, ait, Pontifex jurisdictionis authoritate ac potestate superior ac major existit tota Ecclesia universali. Glossator Gratiani C. 9. quæst. 3. cap. Nemo; Concilium Papam judicare posse negat. Unde, inquit, si totus mundus sententiaret in aliquo negotio contra Papam, videtur, quòd sententia Papæ standum esset. Idque ex vi verborum ejus Canonis eruitur, in quo sic legere est: Neque ab Augusto, neque ab omni clero, neque à Regibus, neque à populo judex judicabitur. Negat ergo præfractè, se à quoquam judicari posse; imò se regulam fidei constituit, uti supra ostendimus, & Caranza Proleg. in Summam Concil. Controv. 3. omni posita fronte, & claris verbis pronuntiat. Denique Episcopos omnes titulorum illorum vi, ad ministrorum & vasallorum suorum subsellia redegit; &, quod indignius est, Episcopos, Archiepiscopos, quorum summa dignitas erat præfici Ecclesiæ, ad eam contumeliam projecit, ut magno honori ducant, si officiarii Papæ domestici, veluti Cancellarii, datarii, Quæstores, prætores, Presbyteri, Diaconi urbis Romæ quandoque creentur.
units.tr: XLVIII. Hence, as Head and Supreme Oecumenical Pontiff, he lords it over the universal Church of Christ in a kingly manner. Do not dream of a merely ministerial headship. Attend to the force of those words, Head, Supreme Pontiff, etc., a force the Hierarchists do not conceal. Boniface VIII, in the Extravagantes, Unam Sanctam, says: We declare that it is necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff. From this, of course, follow the consequences: The Pope is the immediate prelate and judge of all the faithful, so that he can do throughout the whole world whatever inferior prelates can do. So John de Turrecremata, in his Summa de Ecclesia, book 5, at 65 and 80: The Roman Pontiff, by the authority and power of jurisdiction, exists as superior to and greater than the whole universal Church. The gloss on Gratian, C. 9, q. 3, cap. Nemo, denies that a council can judge the Pope: Hence, it says, if the whole world should pass sentence against the Pope in some matter, it seems that the sentence of the Pope should stand. This is drawn from the force of the words of that canon, which reads thus: The judge shall not be judged by Augustus, nor by the whole clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people. He therefore flatly denies that he can be judged by anyone. Indeed he sets himself up as the rule of faith, as we showed above, and Carranza, in the Prolegomena to his Summa of Controversies of the Councils, 3, pronounces it with brazen forehead and in plain words. Finally, by virtue of those titles he has reduced all bishops to the benches of his ministers and vassals. What is more shameful, he has cast bishops and archbishops, whose highest dignity was to preside over the Church, into such an insult that they count it a great honour if, at times, they are created household officials of the Pope, such as chancellors, dataries, questors, praetors, presbyters and deacons of the city of Rome.

units.la: nec non vis vocabulorum, Caput, Pontifex Summus &c. argumenti. tur. Quæ cùm ita sint, jubare meridiano clariùs emicat, Papam titulis illis Capitis, fundamenti Ecclesiæ &c. se Christo æquare; Ecclesiæ universali, ceu Numen quoddam, præferre, denique demonstrare, quòd Deus sit.
units.tr: Nor is the force of the words Head, Supreme Pontiff, etc. without argument. Since these things are so, it shines out more clearly than the midday sun that the Pope, by those titles of Head, foundation of the Church, and so on, equates himself with Christ; that he sets himself above the universal Church as a certain divinity; and, finally, that he shows himself to be God.

units.la: XLIX. Sextò Divinitatem Papa affectat, cùm sibi potestatem transferendi Regna, & Regibus ipsis imperitandi eximiam facit. Quin hoc Divinæ Majestatis ξικ̃ηε quoddam sit, nemo sanus revocare in dubium poterit. Nam Ipse Deus, non alius quisquam transfert Reges, & constituit Reges, Dan. II. 21. Non igitur consilius hominum, & eorum prudentia, aut brachio existunt, aut confervantur, aut tolluntur, sed nutu solius Dei. Qui aliquando erigit potentes in mundo, ad parvum tempus, donec destinata sua per eos fecerit. Concinit æterna Dei Sapientia, Filius Dei Prov. VIII. 15. sic clamans: Per me Reges regnant, & Principes justitiam decernunt. Et S. Paulus Rom. XIII. 1. Non enim est potestas nisi à Deo. Quæ autem sunt potestates, à Deo ordinatæ sunt. Neque aliam certè ob causam Deus Regis Regum & Domini dominantium nomine venit. Supra quoque Differt. viij. sect. iij. th. 6. fusè comprobavimus, Secularis potestatis radicem esse immediatam institutionem Dei, & delegationem quorundam cæteris dominantium. Denique dominium transferre non potest, nisi qui dominium habet. Qui ergo omne dominium, omnia Regna transferre potest, is omne dominium habet. Solus autem Deus omne dominium habet.
units.tr: XLIX. Sixthly, the Pope aspires to divinity when he claims for himself the outstanding power of transferring kingdoms and of ruling kings themselves. That this is a certain property of divine majesty no sane person can call into doubt. For God himself, and no one else, transfers kings and sets up kings (Dan. II. 21). Kings therefore do not stand, are preserved, or are removed by the counsel and prudence or the arm of men, but by the nod of God alone, who sometimes raises up the mighty in the world for a short time, until he has accomplished his purposes through them. The eternal Wisdom of God, the Son of God, agrees, crying out (Prov. VIII. 15): By me kings reign, and princes decree justice. And St Paul (Rom. XIII. 1): For there is no power but of God; the powers that be are ordained of God. Certainly God came under the name King of kings and Lord of lords for no other reason. Above, in Dissertation 8, section 3, thesis 6, we also showed at length that the root of secular power is the immediate institution of God, and the delegation of certain rulers over others. Finally, no one can transfer dominion unless he has dominion. Whoever, therefore, can transfer all dominion and all kingdoms has all dominion. But God alone has all dominion.

units.la: L. Hanc potestatem sibi eximiam fecisse Papam illum orbis arbitrum, & Regem Regum ac Dominum dominantium, cujus tribunal idem est cum tribunali Dei, uti Isidorus Musconius, Vicarius Generalis Archiepiscopi Bononiensis, & sc. mensis de Majest. Eccles. Milit. lib. j. c. 7. loquitur; ejusdem, quam modò citavimus Dissertationis octavæ Sessione tertia integra, inprimis thesi 53-66. clarissimè demonstravimus. Et indignaretur Papa haud dubiè, si de eminentissimo & verè Divino hoc jure controversiam ipsi facere cuiquam liberet. Atque illud cumprimis memorabile est, quòd Papa à se coronatos à Deo coronatos appellat; quódque diadema à se datum à Petra Christo, & Petro datum interpretatur, juxta Hildebrandinum illud: Petra dedit Petro, Petrus diadema Rodolpho.
units.tr: L. This power the Pope, that arbiter of the world, has made outstanding for himself, King of kings and Lord of lords, whose tribunal is the same as God's tribunal. So Isidorus Musconius, Vicar General of the Archbishop of Bologna, speaks in his book de Majestate Ecclesiae Militantis, book 1, chapter 7. We have demonstrated this most clearly in the whole third session of the eighth Dissertation, cited just now, especially in theses 53 to 66. And the Pope would doubtless be indignant if anyone were to care to raise a controversy against him about this most eminent and truly divine right. Especially memorable is the fact that the Pope calls those whom he has crowned "crowned by God", and that he interprets the diadem given by himself as given by Christ, the Rock, and by Peter, according to that saying of Hildebrand: The Rock gave to Peter, Peter the diadem to Rudolph.

units.la: Unicum addo, impietati huic & Divini honoris sacrilegio non erubuisse Pontifices subinde ludibria & contumelias addere. Nota est coronatio Henrici V. Imperatoris à Coelestino Papa peracta; quam sic Henricus de Knygthon de Event. Angliæ lib. ÿ. cap. 13. describit: Secundo die consecrationis suæ coronavit Henricum V. Friderici Filium in Imperatorem sub hac forma. Inprimis recepto ab eodem Henrico juramento ante gradus Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quòd Ecclesiam Dei defenderet, ejus jura conservaret, rectam justitiam teneret, patrimonium Petri, si quod oblatum fuerit, pro posse revocaret. Contra Dominus Papa in cathedra sedens, coronamque Imperialem pedibus tenens inclinato capiti Imperiali demisit, quam statim cum pedibus in terram excussit, designans per hoc, quòd ipse Papa habet potestatem (NB) CREARE Imperatorem, si meruerit; & deiiciendi, si demeruerit. Cardinales verò adstantes coronam sic excussam capiti reposuerunt. Similem contumeliam Henrico IV. Galliarum Regi absenti coronato à Papa illatam, in Historia Papatus narravimus. Cùm ergo Papa & jus constituendi & dejiciendi Divinum Imperatores ac Reges omnes sibi vindicet, & jus illud exercuerit jam olim, uti loco citato fidem liberaliter fecimus, pro libitu; quis non hic novellum Deum Babylonium, Regem regum, & Dominum dominantium palpat? Quod ipsum etiam idem, qui supra Henricus V. Imp. Aventino Annal. Bojor. lib. vj. teste, Papæ sic exprobrat: Genitore oppresso adversus me conspirat, neque modum ambitioni ponit, nisi alios omnes dignitate & honore expoliet, atque tandem PRO DEO SE ADORARI exigat.
units.tr: I add one thing: the Pontiffs did not blush to add mockery and insult to this impiety and sacrilege against divine honour. The coronation of the Emperor Henry V, performed by Pope Coelestine, is well known. Henry Knighton, de Eventibus Angliae, book 5, chapter 13, describes it thus: On the second day after his consecration, he crowned Henry V, son of Frederick, as Emperor, in this form. First, an oath was taken from the same Henry before the steps of the Roman Church, that he would defend the Church of God, preserve its rights, maintain true justice, and, so far as he could, recover the patrimony of Peter, if any of it had been alienated. Then the Lord Pope, sitting in his chair and holding the Imperial crown at his feet, lowered it onto the bowed Imperial head, but immediately knocked it off with his feet onto the ground, signifying by this that the Pope himself has the power (NB) TO CREATE an Emperor, if he has deserved it, and to depose him, if he has ill-deserved. The Cardinals standing by then replaced the crown, thus knocked off, on his head. A similar insult, inflicted by the Pope on Henry IV, King of the French, who was crowned while absent, I related in the History of the Papacy. Since the Pope claims for himself the divine right to establish and depose emperors and all kings, and has long since exercised that right at his pleasure, as I have freely attested in the place cited, who does not here see the new Babylonian God, King of kings and Lord of lords, being flattered? The same Henry V, mentioned above, also reproaches the Pope with this, as Aventinus testifies in Annales Boiorum, book 6: He conspires against me while my father is oppressed, nor does he set any limit to his ambition unless he strips all others of dignity and honour, and at last demands that he be WORSHIPPED AS GOD.

units.la: LI. Septimò licentia Papalis dispensandi contra legem Divinam, juramenta & vota legitima Divinitatis affectatæ reum Papam liquidò reddit. Cùm dispensatio sit relaxatio quædam & solutio ab obedientia in lege præscripta in certo casu, manifestum utique est, non alii dispensandi contra legem Divinam, potestatem competere, quàm ei, qui legis author est, vel parem cum authore legis potestatem habet. Ejusdem enim est figere & refigere, obligare & solvere. Quod humanæ etiam leges demonstrant, à quarum obligatione vel in universum, vel in certo casu, relaxare, nisi qui easdem rogavit, potest nemo. Obligatio quippe ad legis obsequium, vel ab eadem obligatione solutio ab eo solo pendet, qui lege superior est. Rectè igitur Zechius de statu Pontif. art. 2. scribit: Dispensare in lege potest, qui eam tulit, vel qui est supra id jus. Qui igitur contra legem Divinam dispensat, vel ipse Deus est, legis Divinæ author; vel parem cum Deo potestatem, adeòque Divinam habeat oportet. Par ratio dispensandi contra juramenta & vota legitima. In utrisque enim Deo aliquid promittitur, vel eodem teste asseritur. Solus autem Deus liberam hic adstringendi, vel relaxandi facultatem haberet, si qua omnino ejusmodi facultas locum habere posset: de quo hic non disputamus.
units.tr: LI. Seventhly, the Papal licence of dispensing against divine law, oaths and lawful vows clearly makes the Pope guilty of claiming divinity. Since a dispensation is a certain relaxation and release from obedience to a law prescribed in a certain case, it is plain that the power of dispensing against divine law belongs to no one but him who is the author of the law, or who has power equal to the author of the law. For it belongs to the same one to fix and unfix, to oblige and release. Human laws also show this: no one can relax the obligation of a law, either altogether or in a certain case, except the one who has asked for it. For the obligation to obey a law, or release from that obligation, depends on him alone who is superior to the law. Rightly, therefore, Zechius writes (de statu Pontif., art. 2): 'He can dispense in a law who has enacted it, or who is above that right.' Whoever, therefore, dispenses against divine law must either be God himself, the author of divine law, or must have power equal to God's, and so must have divine power. The same reasoning applies to dispensing against oaths and lawful vows, for in both something is promised to God, or affirmed with God as witness. Only God would have the free power of binding or releasing here, if any such power could exist at all, which we do not dispute here.

units.la: LII. Papam porrò sibi dispensandi enormem illam licentiam sumere, in propatulo sanè est. Petrus de Monte in Monarchia disertissimè: Papa tollit jus Divinum, dispenpensando contra Euangelium. Papa dispensat contra universalem statum Ecclesiæ. Dispensat contra vetus Testamentum. Dispensat contra multa capitula quatuor Euangeliorum. Gobelinus Persona Cosmodromii ætate 6. cap. 87. Bonifacius non solum contra Apostolum, sed etiam contra Euangelium dispensavit. Nam Ladislao Regi Siciliæ, seu Neapolis indulsit, quòd ipse abdicata à se uxore legitima, tam multis annis cum eo commorante, aliam superinduxit uxorem. Glossa super Decretal. 3 1. Tit. 8. c. propositi crudè satis: Papa dispensat Vetus Testamentum, Apostolos & Euangelia. Ipse Innocentius III. Cap. Propositi, de Concess. Præbend. sibi apertè tribuit, quòd secundum plenitudinem potestatis de jure supra jus dispensare possit. Expressè etiam Vasquez Tomo III. Disput. 226. num. 6. Licet, inquit, concederemus hoc suisse Apostolicum præceptum, nihilominus Ecclesia & Summus Pontifex potuerunt illud justis de causis abrogare. Neque enim major fuit potestas Apostolorum, quàm Ecclesiæ & Pontificis in ferendis præceptis. Denique Carranza Controv. 2. Ecclesia, inquit, visa est aliquando facere contra Scripturas, aliquando præter Scripturas. Ergo ipsa est regula eorum, quæ traduntur in Scripturis. Et mox: Ergo credimus Ecclesiæ contra formam Scripturarum.
units.tr: LII. Moreover, that the Pope takes to himself this enormous licence of dispensing is plain enough. Peter de Monte, in Monarchia, says very clearly: The Pope takes away divine law by dispensing against the Gospel. The Pope dispenses against the universal state of the Church. He dispenses against the Old Testament. He dispenses against many chapters of the four Gospels. Gobelinus Persona, Cosmodromium, age 6, chapter 87: Boniface not only dispensed against the Apostle, but even against the Gospel. For he granted to Ladislaus, King of Sicily, or of Naples, that, having put away his lawful wife, with whom he had lived for so many years, he might take another wife. The gloss on the Decretals, book 3, title 1, chapter Propositi, says quite crudely: The Pope dispenses against the Old Testament, the Apostles and the Gospels. Innocent III himself, in chapter Propositi, de Concessione Praebendae, openly ascribes to himself that by the fullness of power he can dispense by right above right. Vasquez also expressly, in Tome III, Disputation 226, number 6: 'Even if we grant that this was an apostolic precept, nevertheless the Church and the supreme Pontiff could abrogate it for just causes. For the power of the Apostles was no greater than the power of the Church and the Pontiff in enacting precepts.' Finally, Carranza, Controversy 2: 'The Church, he says, has sometimes seemed to act against the Scriptures, and sometimes beyond them. Therefore it is itself the rule of those things which are handed down in the Scriptures.' And soon after: 'Therefore we believe the Church even against the form of the Scriptures.'

units.la: LIII. Quid verò multis? Res ipsa non loquitur, sed clamat. Plurima illa idololatriæ, quæ in Papatu obtinet, genera: mandatorum humanorum pro Divinis inculcatio: Calicis Eucharistici laicis surrepti nefas: Cultus Dei in Ecclesia lingua peregrina peragi solitus: Angelorum & Sanctorum cultus: Matrimonii & ciborum quorundam prohibitio, denique universa illa dogmata, quæ præter, contra & supra verbum Divinum Papa invexit & definivit, quid aliud, quàm luculenta, PapaPapalis contra jus Divinum dispensationis testimonia sunt?
units.tr: LIII. But why say more? The thing itself does not speak; it shouts. Consider the many kinds of idolatry that prevail in the Papacy: the insistence on human commands as if they were divine; the sacrilege of withholding the chalice of the Eucharist from the laity; the worship of God in the Church carried on in a foreign tongue; the worship of angels and saints; the prohibition of marriage and of certain foods; and, in short, all those doctrines which the Pope has introduced and defined beyond, against, and above the Divine Word. What are these, if not clear proofs of a papal dispensation contrary to divine law?

units.la: LIV. Concilia inprimis Constantiense & Tridentinum illam dispensandi contra jus Divinum potestatem Ecclesiæ, hoc est, Papæ in solidum asserunt. In Constantiensi enim Seff. viij. c. 13. Patres præfati de institutione Christi, & de expresso mandato bibendi ex calice, ad omnes sine discrimine fideles directo, subjiciunt, Hoc (NB) non obstante prohiberi à se Laicis calicem. Unde Non-Obstantiense Concilium festive Lutherus insignivit. In Concilio vero Tridentino Seff. xxj. cap. 7. habetur decretum, cujus titulus est: Ecclesiæ potestas circa dispensationem Sacramenti Eucharistiæ. Verba decreti, quo Calice Eucharistico plebs defraudatur, sic sonant: Præterea declarat Synodus, hanc potestatem perpetuò in Ecclesia fuisse, ut in Sacramentorum dispensatione, salva eorum substantia (scilicet ablato calice, materiæ Sacramenti parte essentiali, mansit substantia Sacramenti) ea statueret, vel mutaret, quæ suscipientium utilitati, vel ipsorum Sacramentorum veneratione expedire judicaret. Id autem Apostolus non obscure visus est innuisse, cùm ait: Sic nos existimet homo, ut ministros Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Audi egregiam rationem. Paulus dicit: Sumus dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Mysteria sunt Sacramenta: & dispensare est jus relaxare. Ergo, quæ Christus in dispensatione & usu Eucharistiæ instituit, Ecclesia potest abrogare. In tanta luce Thais illa Babylonica perfrictæ frontis ludere vocabulis non erubuit. Et qua conscientia hanc causam agat, omnes perpendant. Mysteria enim S. Paulo notant revelationem totius doctrinæ Euangelicæ; & Apostolos vocat illorum Mysteriorum οἰκονόμους dispensatores; hanc ipsam innuens antithesin, quòd non sint domini horum mysteriorum, qui potestatem habeant mutandi & abrogandi: sed quòd tantùm sint œconomi, in quibus hæc fidelitas requiritur, ut juxta institutionem & præceptum domini sui ea dispensent, quæ iis commissa sunt. In hac significatione vetus Interpres vocabulo dispensationis usus est. Illa verò vocis æquivocatio commoda visa fuit piis scilicet Patribus illis, qui Papam ubique Papaliter dispensare, ipsámque Coenam mutilare posse, astruerent. Crimine ab uno disce omnes.
units.tr: LIV. The Councils, above all those of Constance and Trent, assert that the Church, that is, the Pope, has full power to dispense against divine law. In the Council of Constance, Sess. 8, c. 13. the aforesaid Fathers set against the institution of Christ and his express command to drink from the cup, which is addressed to all the faithful without distinction, the words this (NB) notwithstanding, and by that clause they forbade the laity the cup. Hence Luther wittily named it the Non-Obstante Council. In the Council of Trent, Sess. 21, c. 7. there is a decree whose title reads: The power of the Church concerning the dispensation of the Sacrament of the Eucharist. The words of the decree by which the people are defrauded of the Eucharistic cup run thus: Furthermore, the Synod declares that this power has always existed in the Church, so that in the dispensation of the Sacraments, their substance being preserved (namely, with the cup removed, the essential part of the matter of the Sacrament, the substance of the Sacrament nevertheless remains), it might ordain or change those things which it judged expedient for the benefit of the recipients or for the veneration of the Sacraments themselves. The Apostle seems not obscurely to have hinted at this when he said: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Hear the excellent reasoning! Paul says: "We are stewards of the mysteries of God." Mysteries are Sacraments, and to dispense is to relax a law. Therefore, whatever Christ instituted concerning the dispensation and use of the Eucharist, the Church can abrogate. In so clear a light that Babylonian Thaïs, with brazen forehead, did not blush to play with words. Let everyone weigh with what conscience she conducts this cause. For in St. Paul "mysteries" denote the revelation of the whole Evangelical doctrine, and he calls the Apostles stewards [οἰκονόμους] of those mysteries. He is thereby pointing to the contrast that they are not the lords of these mysteries, who have power to change and abrogate them, but only stewards, in whom this faithfulness is required: that they dispense, according to the institution and command of their Lord, the things committed to them. The old translator used the word dispensation in this sense. That ambiguity of the word seemed convenient to those pious Fathers, namely, who maintained that the Pope could dispense in every way as a Pope and mutilate the Supper itself. Learn all from one crime.

units.la: LV. Operæ pretium fuerit, œφα illa Φαςμακα, quæ Papalibus dispensationibus parasiti nonnulli obduxere, paucis discutere. Et Andradius quidem Defenf. Fid. Trid. sol. 166. negat, eos errâsse, qui dicunt, Romanos Pontifices posse nonnunquam in legibus dispensare à Paulo, primisque quatuor Conciliis, ad Ecclesiam exornandam, morésque componendos, pro temporum necessitate edictis. Quo vero argumento? Quia, inquit, leges ejusmodi non fuerunt Christi voce rogatæ, sed hominum authoritate & prudentia latæ, qui illius (Papæ) ditioni subsunt, qui rerum summa potitur & universæ Ecclesiæ gubernacula tractat. Cum Andradio conspirans Melchior Canus cap. 18. duas constituit præceptorum Apostolicorum classes, quorum alia acceperint à Christo gentibus evulganda; alia non quidem à Christo acceperint; sed post Christum in Cœlos assumptum ipsi populis tradiderint, quæ tamen ipsa quoque Christi præcepta dicantur, quia Dei spiritu peculiariter suggerente edita fuerunt. Priora illa remitti posse negat, à posterioribus utpote propriè humanis & Ecclesiasticis liberare posse Pontificem suos subditos vel ex parte, vel omnino posse, asserit. Sed pudenda hæc esse κενοφωνίας, non tantùm Scripturarum authoritas uniformiter Divina, sed etiam ipsa praxis Papalium dispensationum loquitur. Nam v. 9. Copula Sacerdotalis nec legali, nec EuanEuangelica, nec Apostolica authoritate prohibetur (imò quavis illarum permittitur) Ecclesiastica tamen lege interdicitur, verba sunt Decreti Gratiani parte 2. C. 26. q. 2. Can. Sors non est. In Concilio etiam Constantiensi & Tridentino contra institutionem & exemplum ipsius Christi sub poena excommunicationis, & trino anathemate munitur novitia consuetudo communicandi populo Sacramentum sub una specie. Bellarminus quoque de Rom. Pontif. lib. v. 5. explicans potestatem clavium, Pontifici asserit dispensationem in lege, votis, juramentis, & similibus obligationibus; quæ ad ecclesiasticas constitutiones nullo schemate referri possunt, sed absolutè juris Divini sunt. Taceo dispensationes contra verbum Dei innumeras supra indigitatas, quòdque authoribus thesi L. allegatis subdola distinctio isthæc μηδὲ κατ' ἔτος in mentem venit.
units.tr: LV. It will be worth our while to examine briefly those charms [φάρμακα] which some parasites have thrown over papal dispensations. Andradius, in his Defence of the Tridentine Faith, p. 166, denies that they are mistaken who say that the Roman Pontiffs can sometimes dispense from laws which Paul and the first four Councils issued for adorning the Church and regulating morals, as the needs of the times required. And on what argument? Because, he says, such laws were not enacted by the voice of Christ, but were promulgated by the authority and prudence of men who are subject to his (the Pope's) power, who holds the highest place in affairs and directs the governance of the whole Church. Agreeing with Andradius, Melchior Cano, ch. 18, establishes two classes of Apostolic precepts: one class they received from Christ to be published among the nations; the other they did not receive from Christ, but after Christ had been taken up into heaven they delivered to the peoples themselves, and yet these too are called precepts of Christ, because they were issued under the special prompting of the Spirit of God. Cano denies that the former can be remitted, but asserts that the Pope can free his subjects wholly or in part from the latter, since these are properly human and ecclesiastical. But these are shameful empty words [κενοφωνίας], for not only does the authority of the Scriptures speak uniformly of a divine law, but the very practice of papal dispensations speaks too. For in the Decree of Gratian, part 2, C. 26, q. 2, canon Sors non est, the words are: Sacerdotal marriage is forbidden by neither the Law, nor the Gospel, nor Apostolic authority (indeed, it is permitted by each of these), yet it is forbidden by ecclesiastical law. Also in the Councils of Constance and Trent, against the institution and example of Christ himself, the novel custom of giving the people the Sacrament under one kind is fortified under penalty of excommunication and a threefold anathema. Bellarmine too, On the Roman Pontiff, book 5, ch. 5, explaining the power of the keys, asserts that the Pontiff has dispensing power in law, vows, oaths, and similar obligations, which in no way can be referred to ecclesiastical constitutions, but are absolutely of divine law. I pass over the innumerable dispensations against the Word of God already pointed out, and the fact that the sly distinction not even once a year [μηδὲ κατ' ἔτος] comes to mind as in the authors cited in thesis L.

units.la: LVI. Frustra ergo etiam Bellarminus de R. Pontif. lib. v. 5. hac protestatione utitur: Docemus nos uno ore Christi doctrinam & cultus non posse mutari. Idem tamen sibi discors lib. iij. de Antich. cap. 14. asserit, Papam posse dispensare in præceptis positivis Apostolorum. Non tamen hoc esse contra Apostolum, sed juxta Apostolum, quia Apostolica potestas, qua Apostolus pro tempore aliquid in Ecclesia statuit, futura erat in successoribus, qua possent illi ipsi eadem moderari vel mutare, prout Ecclesiæ expediret. Atqui Papam dispensâsse frequenter in iis, quæ sunt non juris Apostolici positivi, (quanquam & hæc, utpote à spiritu Dei profecta humana authoritate, indispensabilia sunt) sed quæ simpliciter juris Divini & perpetui sunt, satis jam constat. Est igitur distinctio hæc ἀπαγγεία σωτῆρ. Quid quæso tam Divinum, tam Euangelicum est, quàm fidem servare publicè & privatim? Ecce autem perpetua est ista nundinatio Pontificis, qui simul atque
units.tr: LVI. Bellarminus therefore also uses this protestation in vain, in de Romano Pontifice book 5, chapter 5: "We teach with one voice that the doctrine and worship of Christ cannot be changed." Yet in the same book, chapter 14, of De Antichristo, he is inconsistent with himself and asserts that the Pope can dispense from the positive precepts of the Apostles. He adds that this is not against the Apostle but in accordance with the Apostle, because the apostolic power by which the Apostle at the time established something in the Church would pass to successors, who could moderate or change those same things as the good of the Church required. But it is already sufficiently clear that the Pope has frequently dispensed in matters that are not of positive apostolic law (although these, as proceeding from the Spirit of God, are not to be dispensed with by human authority), but are simply of divine and perpetual law. This distinction, then, is a [ἀπαγγεία σωτῆρ] piece of sophistry. What, I ask, is so divine and so evangelical as to keep faith both in public and in private? Yet behold, this is the constant bargaining of the Pontiff, who, as soon as a snake has fallen into his impluvium, or a mouse has gnawed at his sacred vestments, absolves the people from their faith, cities and kingdoms alike, and from his Vatican sounds the fatal trumpet of war. For some centuries now he has offered public guarantees of public perfidy, God condemning it and men paying the penalties of that furious conflagration.

units.la: lib. 5 atque per implavium anguis inciderit, aut sorex sacris sius occeritaverit; à fide absolvit populareis, civitates, regna, & de suo Vaticano canit fatale bellicum, inde ab aliquot annorum centuriis, perfidiæque publicæ publica auctoramenta præbet, Deo damnante, hominibusque luentibus furialis illius incendii poenas.
units.tr: lib. 5 and, as soon as a snake has fallen through the impluvium or a shrew has gnawed at his sacred things, he absolves the people from their allegiance, cities and kingdoms alike, and from his Vatican sounds the fatal trumpet of war. For some centuries now he has offered public pledges of public perfidy, God condemning it and men paying the penalties of that furious fire.

units.la: LVII.
units.tr: LVII.

units.la: Sed magis versutiam suam idem Bellarminus libello de excusatione Barclaii cap. 31. hac prosopopœia Dialogistica prodit: (Populus) Christus cum claves Regni Cœlestis Petro tradidit, non dedit ei potestatem faciendi de peccato non peccatum? (Pontifex) Nescis quid loquaris, siquidem in bono sensu dedit Christus Petro potestatem faciendi de peccato non peccatum. (En mox ἀπὸν Φαῦμαυτον.) Verum est tamen, Claves Petri ad id se non extendere, ut possit Summus Pontifex declarare non esse peccatum, quod est peccatum, aut esse peccatum, quod non est peccatum. Id enim esse docere malum bonum, & bonum malum, quod longissimè abest, & semper abfuit, & aberit à doctrina illius, qui Ecclesiæ præest, quæ est columna & firmamentum veritatis. Hactenus ille. Quem si audimus, bonus ille sensus, quo Christus dedit potestatem Petro faciendi de peccato non peccatum, & de non peccato peccatum, non patitur quidem, ut Pontifex declaret, peccatum esse non peccatum, in sensu composito: sed non repugnat, ut idem declaret in sensu divisio, id est, suppositá mutatione doctrinæ & præcepti per potestatem Papæ datam; qua jam non est amplius peccatum, quod modo erat peccatum. Cautum scilicet est Ecclesiæ datis Petro clavibus, ne Papæ lingua præcurrens mentem & voluntatem mutandi doctrinam virtutum & vitiorum, mentiatur. Non mentitur autem, nec fallit aut fallitur Pontifex, si usus potestatis Apostolicæ exercitio, ad veteris præcepti antiquationem, pronuntiet jam peccatum esse, quod olim Apostoli pronuntiárunt non esse peccatum, vel contra. Hæc est bella Judicis visibilis Ecclesiastici infallibilitas, quòd scilicet Pontifex in doctrinæ Apostolicæ de peccati ἀθετήσει seu antiquatione, nunquam dicto factum prævertat; de facto autem sit ὁ ἀνομος, Exlex ille 2 Thess. II. 1.
units.tr: But Bellarmine reveals his cunning more openly in his book On the Excuse of Barclay, chapter 31, in this dialogue speech. (People) When Christ gave the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven to Peter, did he not give him the power of making a non-sin out of sin? (Pope) You do not know what you are saying, since Christ did indeed give Peter the power of making a non-sin out of sin, in a good sense. (Behold at once a marvel beyond belief [ἄπιστον θαῦμα].) It is true, however, that the keys of Peter do not extend so far that the Supreme Pontiff can declare what is sin not to be sin, or what is not sin to be sin. For that would be to teach that evil is good and good is evil, which is far removed from, and always has been and always will be far from, the teaching of him who presides over the Church, which is the pillar and foundation of truth. So far he. If we listen to him, that good sense in which Christ gave Peter the power of making a non-sin out of sin, and a sin out of a non-sin, does not indeed allow the Pope to declare, in the compound sense, that sin is not sin. But it does not rule out that the same man may declare it in the divided sense, that is, on the supposition that doctrine and precept have been changed by the power given to the Pope, so that what was sin is now no longer sin. Clearly the keys given to Peter were meant to guard the Church against the Pope's tongue running ahead of his mind and will in changing the doctrine of virtues and vices, and so lying. But the Pope does not lie, nor deceive, nor is he deceived, if by exercising his apostolic power to abolish an old precept he now pronounces that a thing is sin which the apostles once pronounced not to be sin, or the reverse. This is the fine infallibility of the visible ecclesiastical judge: that the Pope, in the matter of the abrogation or annulment of apostolic doctrine concerning sin, never anticipates the deed by his word; but in fact he becomes the lawless one [ὁ ἄνομος], that Man of Lawlessness, 2 Thess. II. 1.

units.la: LVIII. Dispensationum Papalium haud extrema pars est, qua sibi arrogat Papa potestatem dispensandi in lege Divina gradus quosdam consanguinitatis & affinitatis in matrimonio contrahendo prohibente; adeóque quoad leges eas gratiam faciendi obsequii, & liberandi à necessitate parendi Deo.
units.tr: LVIII. Not the least part of the Papal dispensations is the one by which the Pope claims for himself the power to dispense, in marrying, with those degrees of consanguinity and affinity which the divine law forbids; and so, as far as those laws go, to grant the favour of disobedience and to free men from the necessity of obeying God.

units.la: Fucum quidem denuo moliuntur ejus parasiti distinguentes inter gradus prohibitos jure Divino naturali, & jure Divino positivo; atque in his, non in illis Papam dispensare posse, asserentes. Sed fucus ille pellucet nimiùm. Cùm enim ex Levit. xviii. 6. &c. abundè constet, prohibitiones illas ejusdem ferè generis omnes esse, & ob transgressionem legum illarum ipsos gentiles Cananæos, qui juri Divino positivo haud suberant, abominationi & poenæ subjici, distinctionis illius vanitas ultrò cognoscitur. Præterea leges Divinæ positivæ Christo adveniente non abrogatæ, Divinæ & inviolabiles manent, neque quidquam in eas juris esse Mortalium ulli potest. Ipsa Papæ dispensatio, quæ juris relaxatio est, lege in suo vigore permanente, arguit, leges illas obligare. Unde ergo obligandi illa potestas, quam leges eæ habent, est, nisi à Deo, authore legum? Quoties igitur dispensat in iis, in legis Divinæ observatione dispensat. Et si quod jus Papa dispensandi haberet, discrimen naturalium & positivarum legum non ab arbitrio Papæ suspendi, sed certis notis prius cognosci ab omnibus deberet. Aliàs pro lubitu primò decernere, hunc vel illum gradum esse juris positivi: & post in eodem dispensare posset; atque sic distinctio Ctio illa ludicra tota foret. Nunc autem de discrimine illo nihil Papistæ constitutum habent. Nam circa gradum primum consanguinitatis in linea transversa æquali, hoc est, circa matrimonia fratrum & sororum nondum inter eos convenit. Sunt enim, qui ea non àjure Divino naturali, sed positivo arcessunt; veluti Thomas Aquinas in 4. dist. 4. q. 1. art. 3. & in Summa par. 3. q. 54. art. 3. Bonaventura eadem dist. par. 2. q. 2. Richardus ibid. quæst. 2. Scotus quæst. unica, Durandus eadem Dist. quæst. 1. Alensis 2. par. q. 169. m. 4. Cajetanus 22. q. 154. art. 9. Roffensis tract. de matrimonio Regis Angliæ Henrici VIII. Victoria Relect. de matrim. par. 2. Ex principio ergo, quo Papæ potestatem dispensandi in omnibus gradibus, qui jure naturæ non sunt prohibiti, afferunt, juxta hanc capitum Scholæ sententiam, nuptias fratrum & sororum permittere, adeóque dispensare in Lege Divina eosdem prohibente poterit. Quomodo Angelus de Clavasio in Summa sol. 307. refert, D. Archiepiscopum Florentinum in Summa dicere, se audivisse à fide dignis, quod Papa Martinus V. habita consultatione cum multis doctissimis Viris in Sacra Theologia & jure Canonico, dispensávit cum quodam, qui acceperat GERMANAM suam in uxorem, propter multa mala & scandala, quæ evenissent, si eam dimisisset, & quæ evitari non poterant, nisi sic dispensaretur. Alios aliter sentire, & nuptias ejusmodi jure naturæ consistere non posse, probabilius censere, haud equidem ignoro. Sed de eo quicquid sit, saltem illud inde constat, quòd discrimen illud legum incertum apud Pontificios sit, adeóque totum illud quicquid est, à nutu & arbitrio Papæ pendere. Denique dispensandi authoritas est vel absoluta ipsiusmet Legislatoris; vel à superiore inferiori delegata. Qualem ergo Papa sibi arrogat? Si delegatam, cedo tabulas! Si absolutam, legis illius illius se facit conditorem, vel & conditore, & lege superiorem, adeóque Deum.
units.tr: His parasites again try to paint over this fraud, distinguishing between the degrees forbidden by divine natural law and those forbidden by divine positive law, and asserting that the Pope can dispense in the second kind but not in the first. But that veil is far too transparent. For since Leviticus 18:6 and following make it abundantly clear that those prohibitions are almost all of the same kind, and that the Canaanites themselves, who were not subject to divine positive law, were subjected to abomination and punishment for breaking those laws, the emptiness of the distinction is plain at once. Moreover, divine positive laws were not abrogated by the coming of Christ; they remain divine and inviolable, and no mortal can have any right over them. The Pope's own dispensation, which is a relaxation of law while the law remains in force, proves that those laws still bind. Where, then, does the binding power that those laws have come from, if not from God, the author of the laws? So whenever the Pope dispenses in them, he dispenses in the observance of God's law. And even if the Pope had any right of dispensing, the distinction between natural and positive laws ought not to depend on the Pope's judgment, but ought to be recognised by everyone beforehand by certain marks. Otherwise he could first decree at his pleasure that this or that degree belongs to positive law, and afterwards dispense in the same degree; and so the distinction would be wholly a mockery. As it is, however, the Papists have no settled view about that distinction. For concerning the first degree of consanguinity in the equal collateral line, that is, concerning marriages of brothers and sisters, they have not yet agreed. For some derive them not from divine natural law but from positive law, as Thomas Aquinas does in 4 Sentences, dist. 4, q. 1, art. 3, and in the Summa, part 3, q. 54, art. 3; Bonaventure in the same distinction, part 2, q. 2; Richard, ibid., q. 2; Scotus, unica quaestio; Durand, in the same distinction, q. 1; Alensis, part 2, q. 169, m. 4; Cajetan, 22, q. 154, art. 9; Rochester, in his treatise on the marriage of King Henry VIII of England; Victoria, Relectio de matrimonio, part 2. So, from the principle by which they assert the Pope's power to dispense in all degrees not forbidden by the law of nature, they hold, according to this opinion of the leading schoolmen, that he may permit the marriage of brothers and sisters, and so dispense in a divine law that forbids it. Angelus de Clavasio, in his Summa, s. v. 307, relates how the Archbishop of Florence says in his Summa that he had heard from trustworthy men that Pope Martin V, after consulting many very learned men in sacred theology and canon law, dispensed with a man who had taken his own sister [GERMANA] as his wife, because of the many evils and scandals that would have followed if he had put her away, and which could not be avoided unless he were so dispensed. I am not unaware that others think differently, and judge it more probable that such marriages cannot stand under natural law. But whatever the truth of that, at least this much is clear from it: that the distinction between laws is uncertain among the Papists, and so whatever it amounts to depends on the nod and judgment of the Pope. Finally, the authority to dispense is either absolute, belonging to the Lawgiver himself, or delegated by a superior to an inferior. Which of these, then, does the Pope claim for himself? If it is delegated, show me the documents! If it is absolute, he makes himself the author of that law, or both its author and above the law, and therefore God.

units.la: LIX. Jam & à legitimo juramento Papa dispensandi potestatem rapuit. Non veretur enim Regum ac Principum subditos à juramento fidelitatis, quo illis tenebantur, absolvere. Quin excommunicationem eorum, aut haereseos declarationem à Papa factam, hanc à juramento fidelitatis relaxationem ipso facto operari, Casuistæ pronuntiant. Quomodo in excommunicati poenam relaxari juramentum illi factum, post alios Toletus Instit. Sacerd. lib. iv. 23. docet, citatis etiam ex jure Canonico xv. q. 6. cap. Nos Sanctorum; & cap. Juratos. Quoties ergo Papis furoris sui oestro percitis libuit, Principes ob haeresin, vel aliam causam, veram vel fictam, excommunicare, eadem opera subditos à fidelitatis juramento absolverunt. Exempla obvia sunt in Germania, Gallia, quæ Papæ emissariis contranitentibus, in Comitiis Parisiensibus A. 1615. impetrare non potuit, ut articulus ille tertii ordinis, quo statuebatur, Regem ita independentem esse, ut nulla sit potestas in terris spiritualis vel temporalis, quæ jus aliquod in Regnum Gallia habeat, possitque vel Reges spoliare, vel eorum subditos à juramento fidelitatis absolvere, admitteretur; Anglia cumprimis, cujus juramentum fidelitatis, ex sontica necessitate à Rege Jacobo & Parlamento, à conspiratione pulveraria horribili recens liberato, præscriptum, duobus Brevibus sic Paulus V. oppugnavit, ut illud suscipi interdixerit, & susceptum irritum declaraverit, atque ab ejus observantia pura & perfecta voluntate, uti verba sonant, relaxaverit. Dispensationis similis à juramento exempla Pontificum Clementis VII. Antipapæ, Eugenii V. aliorumque referentem detestantémque Rousselium, Jurisconsultum Pontisicium Histor. Jurisd. Pontif. lib. j. cap. 6. videre est. Quin juxta doctrinam Toleti ejusdem Institut. Sacerd. lib. 121. 23. 2. quilibet sacrificulus seu confessarius, ex delegata scilicet potestate Papæ, absolvere à peccatis contra juramenta patratis, & accedente privilegio, juramenti facti obligationem auferre potest. Accedit doctrina peculiaris Jesuitarum in libro Theol. Mor. tract. 1. Ex. 3. cap. 5. quæ statuit, etiam perjurum dispensari posse, sive perjurium publicum sit, sive occultum.
units.tr: LIX. Moreover, the Pope has also seized the power of dispensing from a lawful oath. For he does not hesitate to absolve the subjects of kings and princes from the oath of allegiance by which they were bound to them. Indeed, the casuists declare that when the Pope declares them excommunicated, or declares them heretics, this relaxation of the oath of allegiance takes effect by that very fact. How an oath made to a man is relaxed as the penalty of excommunication, Toletus, after others, teaches in Institutes of the Priests, book 4, chapter 23, citing also from canon law 15, q. 6, cap. Nos Sanctorum, and cap. Juratos. Whenever, therefore, the Popes, stung by the gadfly of their own rage, have wished to excommunicate princes for heresy or some other cause, true or invented, they have at the same stroke absolved their subjects from the oath of allegiance. Examples are plentiful in Germany and France, where the Pope's agents strove in vain at the Paris Estates of 1615 to have that article of the Third Estate admitted, by which it was laid down that the King is so independent that no spiritual or temporal power on earth has any right over the kingdom of France, and can either depose the kings or absolve their subjects from the oath of allegiance. Especially in England, whose oath of allegiance, prescribed by King James and Parliament out of necessity, lately freed from the dreadful gunpowder conspiracy, Paul V attacked with two briefs, forbidding it to be taken, declaring it void once taken, and releasing men from keeping it by his pure and perfect will, as the words sound. Examples of a similar dispensation from an oath can be seen in Rousselius, a papal jurist, who recounts and condemns them in his History of the Papal Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 6, citing Popes Clement VII (the antipope), Eugene V and others. Indeed, according to the teaching of the same Toletus in Institutes of the Priests, book 1 (?), 23, 2, any little priest or confessor, by the power delegated to him by the Pope, can absolve from sins committed against oaths, and, with a special privilege added, can remove the obligation of an oath already sworn. To this is added the peculiar doctrine of the Jesuits in their Moral Theology, tract. 1, ex. 3, cap. 5, which lays down that even a perjurer can be dispensed, whether the perjury is public or secret.

units.la: LX. Superest Papalis dispensatio votorum: quorum obligatio non à politivo utique, sed a naturali jure pendet. Disertus hic est Ægidius Coninx Disput. 33. dub. 3. concl. 2. ubi sic ille: In votis potest Papa remittere nomine Dei obligationem abstinendi matrimonio: uti patet ex praxi, & communi doctorum consensu. Jure naturali obligare votum solenne castitatis, satis constans Pontificiorum sententia est. Quò spectat illud Bellarmini de Matrim. lib. 1. 21. Multi, inquientis, iique gravissimi Theologi, S. Thomas, Bonaventura, Albertus, Richardus, Durandus, Dominicus à Soto in IV. Sent. Dist. 38. contendunt, votum solenne jure Divino & naturali dirimere matrimonium. Imò cujuslibet voti obligationem esse juris naturalis, Fernandus de Moure Theol. Mor. par. 1. cap. 6. Sect. 9. asserit. Dispensare autem Papam posse in voto solenni castitatis, etsi sint qui negent, tamen alii melius concedunt, inquit Emmanuel Sà in Aphorismis ad vocem Votum n. 3. citantúrque in hanc sententiam Hervæus, Richardus, Durandus, Scotus alii. Certè, sic Azorius lib. xÿ. 7. scribit, Casimirus I. Poloniæ Rex D. Benedicti Monachus professus, concedente summo Pontifice, uxorem duxit.
units.tr: LX. There remains the papal dispensation from vows, whose obligation depends not on positive law but on natural law. Ægidius Coninx is explicit on this in Disput. 33, dub. 3, concl. 2, where he says: In vows the Pope can remove, in God's name, the obligation to abstain from marriage, as is clear from practice and from the common agreement of the learned. That a solemn vow of chastity binds by natural law is quite a settled opinion among the Papists. To this belongs Bellarmine's statement in de Matrim. lib. 1, cap. 21: Many, he says, and those the most weighty theologians, Thomas, Bonaventure, Albert, Richard, Durand, Dominic à Soto on Sent. IV, dist. 38, contend that a solemn vow dissolves marriage by divine and natural law. Indeed Fernandus de Moure, Theol. Mor. part 1, cap. 6, sect. 9, asserts that the obligation of any vow whatever belongs to natural law. That the Pope can dispense in a solemn vow of chastity, although some deny it, others however concede it more readily, says Emmanuel Sà in his Aphorisms under the word Votum, n. 3, and Hervæus, Richard, Durand, Scotus and others are cited in support of this view. Certainly, so Azorius writes, lib. xÿ. 7, Casimir I, King of Poland, a professed monk of St Benedict, took a wife with the consent of the supreme Pontiff.

units.la: LXI. Ne verò Papa sic dispensando non scriò, & summa cum authoritate agere videatur, inflare solet buccas, bullis suis inferens grandia hæc vocabula, In virtute SanIta obedientiæ: Aut has: sub indignatione Petri & Pauli. Aut istas: Motu proprio, & ex certa scientia; &c, Non obstantibus quibuscunque Constitutionibus Apostolicis &c. Quis ergo sic Papam, non obstantibus quibusvis Apostolicis, imò ne Divinis quidem Christi constitutionibus, omníque adeò jure naturali & Divino, Papaliter adeò dispensantem se ipsum demonstrare, quòd Deus sit, imò Deo vero major, in dubium amplius revocaverit? Nisi forte qui sic demonstrat, quòd Deus sit; palam facit, quòd sit אבדון Abaddon, seu אבר רין perdens jus omne, & ᾿Απολλύων, sive ᾿Απολλύων, diffulvens, dispensans, atque relaxans jus & fas omne Divinum & humanum.
units.tr: LXI. But lest the Pope, in dispensing thus, should seem to act carelessly and without great authority, he is accustomed to puff himself up, inserting in his bulls these grand phrases: In virtue of holy obedience; or these: under the indignation of Peter and Paul; or those: of our own motion and from certain knowledge, etc.; notwithstanding any Apostolic constitutions whatever, etc. Who, then, having seen the Pope dispensing thus, notwithstanding any Apostolic constitutions, indeed notwithstanding even the divine constitutions of Christ, and so notwithstanding all natural and divine law, would any longer call in doubt that he shows himself to be God, indeed greater than the true God? Unless perhaps the one who shows him to be God makes it plain that he is אבד דין [Abaddon], that is, one who destroys all law, and ᾿Απολλύων, that is, ᾿Απολλύων, one who undoes, dispenses with and relaxes all divine and human law and right.

units.la: LXII. Octavò denique Divinitatem Papa affectat in decantata sua apotheosi, qua Sanctos & Divos pro libitu creat. Etenim qui vel ἀπαθέωσις Deificat (qua voce Herodianus utitur) seu Divos & quidem adorandos facit, Deus ipse sit oportet, cùm hominem sibi Deos facere posse, neget Spiritus S. Jerem. xvi. 20. vel Sanctos, eósque adorandos declarat, Deus omniscius sit necesse est, cùm nemo hominum noverit, quid (adeóque quæ sanctitas,) sit in homine; sed solus Spiritus Dei, 1 Cor. ii. 10. vel Cœli ipsius mansiones pro libitu suo metatur, & disponit, Cœli Dominus, & Dominus ex Cœlo sit oportet. Et quomodo qui Deus ipse non est, & Divina virtute destituitur, creaturam in Creatorem adorandum, certarum solennitatum interventu, transfubstantiare potis erit?
units.tr: LXII. Finally, eighthly, the Pope claims divinity in his much-vaunted apotheosis, by which he creates saints and gods at his pleasure. For whoever deifies [ἀπαθέωσις] (the word Herodian uses), or makes gods, and indeed gods to be worshipped, must himself be God, since the Holy Spirit denies that man can make gods for himself (Jer. xvi. 20). Or whoever declares men saints and to be worshipped must be omniscient, since no man knows what sanctity is in a man, but only the Spirit of God (1 Cor. ii. 10). Or whoever measures out and arranges the mansions of heaven itself at his pleasure must be the Lord of heaven, and must be the Lord from heaven. And how can one who is not God himself, and is destitute of divine power, be able to transubstantiate a creature into a Creator to be worshipped, by the intervention of certain solemnities?

units.la: LXIII. Artem Chrysopoeticam tradunt Chymici. At Theopoeticen Pontificii, apud quos certum habetur, posse Papam Deificare, canonizare, Divos, Sanctos adorandos declarare: tametsi forte Theopoetice illa artis Chrysopoeticæ Papalis haud extrema pars est. Si enim S. Paulus & S. Petrus nondum Cœlo potirentur, neque ceu Sancti & Divi illud ingressi essent, hodie nisi per scalam auream ingredi illud neutiquam illis contingeret. Adeò ut hic redeat merito Demetrii istius ἀργυροκόπου apud Ephesinos ad Mechanicos suos Oratio: Viri, scitis, ex hoc quaestu nostras esse copias, Act. xix. 25.
units.tr: LXIII. The chemists teach the art of making gold. But the Papists, among whom it is held as certain that the Pope can deify, canonise, and declare gods and saints to be worshipped, teach a theopoetics; though perhaps that divine art is not the least part of the papal art of gold-making. For if St Paul and St Peter had not yet taken possession of heaven, and had not entered it as saints and gods, they could not today enter it except by a golden ladder. So the speech of that silversmith Demetrius among the Ephesians to his craftsmen returns deservedly to mind: Men, you know that our wealth comes from this trade (Acts xix. 25).

units.la: LIV. Sed de hoc quicquid sit, certè Divos, Sanctos, Beatos Papa, & quidem, uti hodie recepta fides est, solus creat. Et de Papali isthac apotheoseos arte ridicula & portentosa multa nobis Malvesius, Galesinus, Rocchus, & caeteri ex eadem cavea sycophantae prodidere. Sed succum omnem exprimens Bellarminus, tres theses posuit;
units.tr: LIV. But whatever be the case here, the Pope certainly, and indeed, as the accepted faith holds today, he alone, creates gods, saints and blessed ones. Malvezzi, Galesini, Rocchus, and the other sycophants from the same cage have brought forward much that is ridiculous and monstrous about this papal art of apotheosis. But Bellarmine, squeezing out all the juice, laid down three theses:

units.la: Ecclesiam rectè canonizare Sanctos; Monopolium hoc ad solum hodie Papam pertinere; & in munere hoc obeundo ipsius Sanctitatem non errare. Canonizationis hujus drama ob oculos ponit liber primus Ceremoniarum Sacrarum, sect. 6. & amplissimè Polyhistor Hospinianus de Orig. Fest. apud. Christ. cap. 6. Videre ibi est praeviam intercessionem amicorum, examen miraculorum, in modo agendi pompam, solennitatem, septem canonizati honores eximios, puta, quòd jam obtinet non Beati duntaxat, sed Sancti nomen: quòd non privatim, sed publicè invocatur: quòd Templa & aras in ipsius memoriam Deo dicantur: quòd Sacrificia & Officia in ejus honorem publicè Deo offeruntur: quòd Festum ei, in Calendario rubricatis literis distinguendum decernitur: quòd imagines ejus in signum gloriae certo lumine decorantur: quòd denique reliquiae ejus pretiosis theciis includuntur, & publicè honorantur. Sic quaestuosissimo hoc Deificandi artificio crebrò non tantum procudunt & protrudunt nova Sanctorum officia, novas Missas, novas horas, novos hortulos Marianos, novos flores, novos myrrhae & thuris fasciculos; sed etiam novos Deastros Coelites, & novos Coelos accumulant, dum Coelos interim novos, & terram novam à S. Petro praedicatos, in quibus habitat justitia, negligunt.
units.tr: The Church rightly canonises saints; this monopoly belongs today to the Pope alone; and in discharging this office his holiness does not err. The first book of the Ceremoniæ Sacræ, sect. 6, sets before our eyes the drama of this canonisation, and so does the most learned Hospinian in de Orig. Fest. apud Christ., cap. 6, at great length. There one may see the preliminary intercession of friends, the examination of miracles, the pomp and solemnity in the manner of proceeding, and the seven remarkable honours of the canonised: namely, that he now holds the name not merely of Blessed but of Saint; that he is invoked publicly, not privately; that temples and altars are dedicated to God in his memory; that sacrifices and offices are publicly offered to God in his honour; that a feast is ordained for him, to be marked in the calendar in red letters; that his images are adorned with a certain light as a sign of glory; and finally that his relics are enclosed in precious caskets and publicly honoured. Thus by this most profitable art of deifying they constantly hammer out and thrust forth not only new offices of saints, new masses, new hours, new little Marian gardens, new flowers, new bundles of myrrh and incense, but also new celestial little gods, and they heap up new heavens, while meanwhile they neglect the new heavens and the new earth proclaimed by St Peter, in which righteousness dwells.

units.la: LXV. Mandatis Papæ deificantis refragari, vel Divinam solenniter adeò creatorum à Papa Divorum sanctitatem in dubium revocare, crimen ingens & hæresis habetur. Petrus Coronus Jesuita Institt. lib. j. 26. miratur, quosdam esse, qui audeant convellere fidem canonizationum, quos ait eousque processisse audaciæ, ut audeant falsi accusare librum vitæ, & opponere se manifestationi prædestinationis, & codicem consignatum septem sigillis mendacii insimulare. Jam ergo Papa canonizans inscribit libro vitæ, æternam prædestinationem manifestat, & codicem septies obsignatum resignat: quod soli Christo Apoc. v. 6. tribuitur. Antequam ergo Papa sanctos canonizaret, nullus erat liber vitæ. Nisi forte statuendum est, librum vitæ, qui penes Deum ab æterno fuerat, his novissimis temporibus in Papæ scrinia translatum esse. Frustra quinetiam expectaretur Agnus Dei, qui solus potest obsignare librum obsignatum septem sigillis, cùm Papa eum aperiat, quoties vult, eíque nova subinde nomina inserat, Protonotariorum suorum ad hanc rem, ut & cætera hujus generis, opera utens.
units.tr: LXV. To resist the decrees of the deifying Pope, or to call in question the divine holiness of those whom the Pope has solemnly canonised, is held a great crime and heresy. Peter Coronus, the Jesuit, in Institt. lib. 1, 26, marvels that there are some who dare to overthrow faith in canonisations; he says they have gone so far in audacity as to dare to accuse the book of life of falsehood, to set themselves against the revelation of predestination, and to charge the sealed codex, sealed with seven seals, with lies. So then the canonising Pope enrolls men in the book of life, reveals eternal predestination, and unseals the codex sealed seven times, which is attributed to Christ alone (Rev. v. 6). Before the Pope canonised saints, therefore, there was no book of life. Unless perhaps we must hold that the book of life, which had been with God from eternity, was in these latest times transferred into the Pope's cabinets. And the Lamb of God, who alone can open the book sealed with seven seals, would be waited for in vain, since the Pope opens it whenever he wishes and from time to time inserts new names, using his protonotaries for this business, as also for other things of this kind.

units.la: LXVI. Cùm olim Thasii Deum Agesilaum redderent, non insipidè homo nasutus retulit, si Deos faciendi potestatem habeant Thasii, priùs se ipsos Deos facerent, quàm deificarent alios. Addere poterat, nisi Deos Agesilaum Deum reddere non potuisse. Sic planè est, uti supra probavimus. Deum nisi Deus facere, sanctitatem Cœlo, nedum tantis, qui canonizato tribuuntur, honoribus, dignam infallibiliter declarare, nisi Deus non potest. Cùm igitur id fecerit, & facere non desinat Papa, eo ipso etiam, quòd Deus sit, demonstrat, & cùm hoc, tum reliquis, quæ hactenus prosecuti sumus nominibus, Numen illud Babylonicum, seu potiùs Meretricem Babylonicam, quam Reges & incolæ terræ incestis amoribus suis deperierunt, & depereunt, seesse, clarissimè prodit. ὅτι ρἰδ δᾶξα.
units.tr: LXVI. When once the Thasians made Agesilaus a god, a witty man remarked, not foolishly, that if the Thasians had the power of making gods, they should first make themselves gods before deifying others. He could have added that unless they were gods they could not make Agesilaus a god. It is just so, as we have shown above. To make God, unless one is God, and to declare infallibly that someone's sanctity is worthy of heaven, let alone of such honours as are given to the canonised, is something that only God can do. Since, then, the Pope has done this and does not cease to do it, by this very fact he shows that he is God; and by this, as well as by the other names we have followed up so far, he most clearly reveals that that Babylonian divinity, or rather the Babylonian Harlot, with whom the kings and inhabitants of the earth have committed fornication with their incestuous loves, is himself: [ὅτι ἡ δόξα] because the glory.

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS DECIMÆ SECTIO POSTERIOR.
units.tr: DISSERTATION TEN, SECOND SECTION.

units.la: QUA Papam Romanum, Hierarchiæ Caput, sibi cultum Divinum religiosum vindicare, astruitur.
units.tr: In which it is maintained that the Roman Pope, head of the Hierarchy, claims religious divine worship for himself.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Quisquis Deus est, vel Divinitatem affectat, se religioso & Divino cultu affici vult jubetque. II. Papam à suis adorari, & praxis, & scriptores, vocem adorandi, adorationis usurpantes, arguunt. III. Ant. Mazaronii, Dianæ, Stevani de adoratione Papæ libri publicè prostant. IV. Adoratur Papa recens electus à Cardinalibus in Sacrario Conclavis, & Basilica Petri, altari impositus. V. Adoratur idem in coronatione. Cardinalis Columnæ claves ei tradentis adoratio solennis. VI. Adoratur etiam in Missa. VII. In Jubilæo. VIII. In Processionibus solennibus. IX. Christolatria & Papolatria, seu deportatio & gestatio Christi & Papæ comparatur. X. Stevani argumentum ex Esai. xlix. 22. pro gestatione Papæ. Papæ petitum discutitur. Eandem Diana ex pompa Regis apum derivat.
units.tr: I. Whoever is God, or aspires to divinity, wills and commands that he be honoured with religious and divine worship. II. That the Pope is adored by his own people, both in practice and in the writings of those who use the words "adore" and "adoration", is shown. III. The books of Antonio Mazzarone, Diana and Stevanus on the adoration of the Pope are published openly. IV. The newly elected Pope is adored by the Cardinals in the sacristy of the Conclave and in the Basilica of Peter, when he is placed upon the altar. V. He is adored at his coronation; the solemn adoration of Cardinal Colonna, who hands him the keys. VI. He is adored also in the Mass. VII. In the Jubilee. VIII. In solemn processions. IX. Christolatry and Papolatry are compared: the carrying of Christ and the carrying of the Pope. X. Stevanus's argument from Isaiah 49:22 for the carrying of the Pope is examined. Diana derives the same custom from the procession of the king of the bees.

units.la: XI. Adoratio Papæ in Conciliabulis, coronatione Imperatoris, canonizatione, &c.
units.tr: XI. The adoration of the Pope at the conciliabula, at the coronation of the Emperor, at canonization, etc.

units.la: XII. Adorationis ceremoniæ multiplices enumerantur; velut apertio capitis, etiam cùm nominatur tantùm; ipso interim caput aperiente nemini;
units.tr: XII. The ceremonies of adoration are listed in many forms: for example, the uncovering of the head even when his name is only mentioned, while he himself uncovers his head for no one;

units.la: XIII. incurvatio tum capitis, quoties nomen ejus nominatur, perinde ac cùm nominatur nomen Jesu; nec non capitis unà cum superiori parte corporis usque ad genua; genuum, & totius corporis:
units.tr: XIII. the bowing of the head whenever his name is mentioned, just as when the name of Jesus is mentioned; likewise the bowing of the head together with the upper part of the body down to the knees; of the knees, and of the whole body;

units.la: XIV. incensatio, nudipedalia, tunsio pectoris, servilia ministeria Magnatum,
units.tr: XIV. the incensing, the going barefoot, the beating of the breast, the servile services of the great men;

units.la: XV. osculum oris, pectoris, humeri, manuum, brachiorum, genuum, inprimis pedum ejus.
units.tr: XV. the kissing of the mouth, of the breast, of the shoulder, of the hands, of the arms, of the knees, and above all of the feet.

units.la: XVI. Pedum oscula Papa & solus, & ut jure debita, & ab omnibus, maximis etiam, & post mortem exigit.
units.tr: XVI. The Pope alone demands kisses of the feet, both as a right due to him and from all, even the greatest, and even after death.

units.la: XVII. Marcelli, Dianæ, Antonini Flor. de eo testimonia.
units.tr: XVII. The testimonies of Marcellus, Diana and Antoninus of Florence concerning this.

units.la: XVIII. Deorigine ritus illius Stevani, Cæs. Bullengeri, Dianæ, Lorini ariolatio.
units.tr: XVIII. On the origin of that rite: the divination of Stevanus, Caesar Bullinger, Diana and Lorinus.

units.la: XIX. Primus Cajus Caligula osculapedum excepit, à Seneca increpitus graviter. Lorini exceptio elisa.
units.tr: XIX. Gaius Caligula was the first to receive the kissing of the feet, and was severely rebuked by Seneca. Lorinus's exception is refuted.

units.la: XX. Caligula & Papa, osculapedum admittentes, comparantur.
units.tr: XX. Caligula and the Pope, who admit the kissing of the feet, are compared.

units.la: XXI. Caligulam Maximinus Junior & Diocletianus oscula eadem sibi figi præscripserunt: à qua superbia Trajanus, & Principes optimi quique abhorruerunt. Græcorum Imperatorum recentiorum fastus similis notatur.
units.tr: XXI. Maximinus Junior and Diocletian ordered that the same kisses be imprinted on their feet: Trajan and all the best princes shrank from that arrogance. The pride of the more recent Greek emperors is similarly noted.

units.la: XXII. Papæ, successorem S. Petri, & humilem se jactantis superbia exaggeratur; & à Cuspiniano etiam exagitatur.
units.tr: XXII. The pride of the Pope, who boasts of being the successor of St Peter and humble, is magnified; and it is also attacked by Cuspinian.

units.la: XXIII. Nihil eum exempla quaedam veterum juvant; & S. Petri ac Mardochei exempla potius damnant.
units.tr: XXIII. Certain examples of the ancients do not help him at all; and the examples of St Peter and Mordecai rather condemn him.

units.la: XXIV. Augustinus Christianos pedibus aliorum subjici vetat.
units.tr: XXIV. Augustine forbids Christians to be made subject to the feet of others.

units.la: XXV. Olim quidem Pontifices Imperatorum praeceptis se subjecerunt, & genubus advolverunt.
units.tr: XXV. Formerly the Pontiffs did submit themselves to the commands of the Emperors and threw themselves at their knees.

units.la: XXVI. At metamorphosi horrenda deinceps Pontifices maximos Imperatores & Reges, lege lata, ad osculapedum adegerunt:
units.tr: XXVI. But afterwards, by a dreadful metamorphosis, the supreme Pontiffs, by a law they passed, compelled Emperors and Kings to kiss their feet.

units.la: XXVII. tam rigidi exactores juris sui, ut in coronatione Imperatoris absentes protestati fuerint, ne quicquam ei derogetur.
units.tr: XXVII. They were such rigid enforcers of their own right that at the coronation of the Emperor, those who were absent protested that nothing be derogated from it.

units.la: XXVIII. Exceptio quod osculaa pedibus Papae fixa in honorem Christi redundent, examinatur. Legatus nemo Regis sui, nec Papae Legatus Papae honores impune delibat.
units.tr: XXVIII. The objection that kisses fixed to the feet of the Pope redound to the honour of Christ is examined. No legate of a King, nor legate of the Pope, touches the honours of the Pope with impunity.

units.la: XXIX. Papa ab eo qui Christi personam gerit in sexta Dominica Quadragesimae in Palmis, ipsoque adeo Christo oscula pedum excipit.
units.tr: XXIX. On the sixth Sunday of Lent, on Palm Sunday, the Pope receives kisses of the feet from him who bears the person of Christ, and indeed from Christ himself.

units.la: XXX. Et crucem auream calceamentis suis intextam, osculandam praebens, Christum conculcat.
units.tr: XXX. And by offering a golden cross woven into his shoes to be kissed, he tramples Christ underfoot.

units.la: XXXI. Diame exceptio, quod crucem in sandaliis Papae adorantes non tam Papae pedes osculentur, quam crucem Christi adorent, expenditur.
