units.tr: XXXI. Diana's objection, that those who adore the cross on the Pope's sandals are not so much kissing the Pope's feet as adoring the cross of Christ, is weighed.

units.la: XXXII. Impietatem illam male Stevanus ex Psal. lxxviij. 24. incrustare conatur.
units.tr: XXXII. Stevanus tries badly to cover over that impiety with Psalm 78:24.

units.la: XXXIII. Idem Stevanus, Bullengerus, Diana Scriptura loca, quae de adoratione Dei & Christi aperte sonant, ad oscula pedibus Papae infigenda maligne detorquent.
units.tr: XXXIII. The same Stevanus, Bullinger and Diana maliciously twist the passages of Scripture which speak plainly of the adoration of God and of Christ, so as to fit the kissing of the Pope's feet.

units.la: XXXIV. Adoratio Papae non est civilis; & si civilis etiam foret, pridem in idololatriam, qualis Politica est, degenerasset.
units.tr: XXXIV. The adoration of the Pope is not civil; and even if it were civil, it would long since have degenerated into idolatry of the kind that is political.

units.la: XXXV. Cultus civilis & religiosus distinguitur.
units.tr: XXXV. Civil and religious worship are distinguished.

units.la: XXXVI. Religiosum cultum eundem Divinum esse, probatur.
units.tr: XXXVI. It is proved that religious worship is the same as divine worship.

units.la: XXXVII. Adoratio Papæ civilis & humana major;
units.tr: XXXVII. The adoration of the Pope is civil and greater than human;

units.la: XXXVIII. adeóque cultus religiosus & Divinus est: quod oßo argumentis demonstratur. 1. Quia adorationis nomine venit: quod in N.T. religiosum semper & Divinum cultum notat.
units.tr: XXXVIII. and therefore it is religious and divine worship: which is demonstrated by eight arguments. 1. Because it is called by the name of adoration, which in the New Testament always denotes religious and divine worship.

units.la: XXXIX. Dianæ exceptio, quòd adorationis nomen commune sit, ventilatur.
units.tr: XXXIX. Diana's objection, that the name of adoration is common, is discussed.

units.la: XL. II. Quia defertur ei persona, quæ Divinitatem affectat.
units.tr: XL. II. Because it is paid to a person who aspires to divinity.

units.la: XLI. Exceptioni, quòd Papæ cultum à cultu Dei Papicolæ distinguant, neque Papam pro æterno Numine habeant, occurritur.
units.tr: XLI. The objection that the Papists distinguish the worship of the Pope from the worship of God, and do not regard the Pope as an eternal Deity, is met.

units.la: XLII. Adorandum esse Papam, ut Deum, non semel Papolatris excidit.
units.tr: XLII. That the Pope is to be adored as God has more than once slipped from the lips of the Papolatrists.

units.la: XLIII. III. Quia Papa adoratur, ut Pro-Deus, ProChristus, Ecclesiæ Monarcha, religionis vertex.
units.tr: XLIII. III. Because the Pope is adored as a stand-in God, a stand-in Christ, the monarch of the Church, the summit of religion.

units.la: XLIV. Neque honor Papæ habitus in honorem Christi vergit: & sic illum Pro-Deum, Pro-Christum suum adorant, ut ejus adoratio à Christi, quà is Deus est, adoratione nihil distet, & in Missa major Papæ, quàm Christo honor habetur.
units.tr: XLIV. Nor is the honour paid to the Pope directed toward the honour of Christ: and so they adore him as their stand-in God and stand-in Christ, so that his adoration differs in no way from the adoration of Christ insofar as he is God; and in the Mass greater honour is paid to the Pope than to Christ.

units.la: XLV. IV. Quia Papicolæ ab adorato Papa maxima quæque & Divina sibi beneficia promittunt.
units.tr: XLV. IV. Because the Papolatrists expect from the adored Pope all the greatest and divine benefits.

units.la: XLVI. V. Quia adorationis Papalis ceremoniæ religiosum & Divinum ejusdem cultum arguunt: inprimis tunsio cordis,
units.tr: XLVI. V. Because the ceremonies of Papal adoration prove his religious and divine worship: above all the beating of the breast,

units.la: XLVII. incensatio;
units.tr: XLVII. the incensing;

units.la: XLVIII. & Papæ in altari sedentis adoratio.
units.tr: XLVIII. and the adoration of the Pope seated on the altar.

units.la: XLIX. VI. Quia Papæ cultus haud inferior eo, quem Papicolæ Angelis, Deiparæ, Sanctis, cruci, Eucharistiæ, stiæ , imaginibus Christi , ossibus Sanctorum deferunt ; & quem olim arcæ fœderis delatum dicitant ,
units.tr: XLIX. VI. Because the worship of the Pope is no less than that which the Papolatrists pay to Angels, the Mother of God, the Saints, the cross, the Eucharist, images of Christ, and the bones of the Saints; and which they say was once paid to the Ark of the Covenant;

units.la: L. adeóque religiosus & Divinus est.
units.tr: L. and therefore it is religious and divine.

units.la: LI. vii. Quia ex hypothesi Papicolarum cultus duliæ , hyperduliæ & latriæ religiosus , adeóque etiam Divinus est.
units.tr: LI. VII. Because, on the hypothesis of the Papists, the worship of dulia, hyperdulia and latria is religious, and therefore also divine.

units.la: LII. Atqui adorationem Papæ ad duliam Diana , Baldellus , Mazaronius: ad hyperduliam Rainaudus, Florentini Legati ; ad duliam simul & latriam Caramuel, referunt.
units.tr: LII. But Diana, Baldellus and Mazzarone refer the adoration of the Pope to dulia; Rainaldus and the Florentine Legates to hyperdulia; Caramuel to dulia and latria at once.

units.la: LIII. viii. Quia adorationem Papæ religiosam & Divinum cultum esse , questi sunt Imperatores Fridericus II. & Ludovicus Bavarus , nec non Gerson ; asserunt . Alcasar, Gordonus Huntlæus, Petrus à Cordua, Hieronymus Balbus, Polydor. Vergilius, Stenchus, &c.
units.tr: LIII. VIII. Because the Emperors Frederick II and Louis of Bavaria, and also Gerson, complained that the adoration of the Pope is religious and divine worship; Alcazar, Gordon of Huntly, Peter of Cordova, Hieronymus Balbus, Polydore Vergil, Stenchus, etc. assert it.

units.la: LIV. Argumenti conclusio.
units.tr: LIV. Conclusion of the argument.

units.la: I. Divinitatem Papam , Tarpejum illud Numen , affectare , tum ex nomine DEUS, quod sibi tribuit , & tribui patitur ; tum quia vel fecit vel passus est , quæ nominis illius defectum suppleant: tum ex octo attributis Divinis, quorum se spoliis exornavit , hactenus ostendimus. Superest attributum Divinum haud postremum , cultus religiosus Divinus , quo se affici vult patiturque, affectatæ Divinitatis locupletissimus testis. Et sanè quisquis se Deum facit eo modo , quo se facere Papam superiori diatriba demonstravimus, is religiosè se coli, & Divino cultu assici, non potest non velle, jubere. Qui Deus est, is pro Deo religiosè colendus, adorandus est. Omne Σέβασμα Numen venerabile, Σεβαστὸν [?] & Σεβαστικὸν [?], actu venerandum, religiosè colendum, adorandum est.
units.tr: I. That the Pope aspires to divinity, that Tarpeian Deity, is shown thus far: both from the name GOD, which he claims for himself and allows to be claimed; and because he has done or suffered things which make up for the lack of that name; and from the eight Divine attributes, with whose spoils he has adorned himself. There remains a Divine attribute, by no means the least, religious divine worship, with which he wishes and allows himself to be honoured: the richest witness of an aspired divinity. And truly, whoever makes himself God in the manner in which we have shown in the preceding discourse that the Pope makes himself so, cannot but want and command that he be worshipped religiously and honoured with divine worship. He who is God must be worshipped and adored religiously as God. Every object of worship [sebasma], a venerable Deity, and [sebaston?] and [sebastikon?], must actually be venerated, worshipped religiously and adored.

units.la: II. Papam adorari à suis, inficiari nisi extremè impudens ausit nemo. Non tantum enim praxis id clamat; sed etiam scriptores vocem adorandi, adorationis frequentissime hic usurpant. Blondus Instauratae Romae lib. iij. sic scribit: Dictatorem nunc perpetuum, non Cæsaris, sed Piscatoris Petri successorem, & Imperatoris prædicti vicarium, Pontificem summum Principes orbis adorant & colunt. Jovius Histor. lib. v. Carolus (VIII. Galliæ Rex) ad ea respondit, se priusquam Galliæ fines exiret, voto pro salute & felicitate suscepto, decrevisse Romana Templa invisere, &c. ipsumque Pontificem, qui pietatis religionisque fastigium obtineret, adorare. Idem lib. xxxvij. de Imperatore Carolo V. Ille piè inflexo genu, pronus exosculato pede Pontificem adoravit. Antoninus par. iij. tit. 22. c. 5. ff. 4. negat minorem Papæ, quàm Angelis honorem deberi: Unde, inquit, Papa recipit à fidelibus adorationes, prostrationes & oscula pedum, quod non permisit Angelus à Johanne Evangelista sibi fieri. Idem Histor. par. iij. tit. 23. cap. 17. Orationem Florentinorum Legatorum, quorum Princeps erat Archiepiscopus, recitat, in qua hæc diserté habentur: Beatitudinem Tuam ipsa Civitas præcelsa &c. per nos Oratores veneratur: de tui magnifica exaltatione gratulatur plurimùm, & Sanctitatem hyperdulię adorat, &c. Notum celebre illud Mantuani vatis:
units.tr: II. That the Pope is adored by his own people no one would deny, unless he were most shamelessly impudent. For not only does practice proclaim it, but writers also very frequently use the words adore and adoration here. Blondus, in Rome Restored, book 3, writes thus: The Princes of the world now adore and worship the perpetual Dictator, not the successor of Caesar but of the fisherman Peter, and the vicar of the aforesaid Emperor, the supreme Pontiff. Jovius, Histories, book 5: Charles VIII, King of France, replied to these things that before he left the borders of France, having undertaken a vow for safety and prosperity, he had decided to visit the Roman temples, etc., and to adore the Pontiff himself, who held the summit of piety and religion. The same, book 37, concerning the Emperor Charles V: He, with knee piously bent, prostrate, having kissed the foot, adored the Pontiff. Antoninus, part 3, title 22, chapter 5, section 4, denies that less honour is owed to the Pope than to the Angels: Hence, he says, the Pope receives from the faithful adorations, prostrations and kisses of the feet, which the Angel did not permit John the Evangelist to do to him. The same, History, part 3, title 23, chapter 17, recites the oration of the Florentine Legates, whose leader was the Archbishop, in which these things are expressly stated: Your Beatitude is venerated by us, the orators, by this most lofty City, etc.; it greatly rejoices at your magnificent exaltation, and adores Your Holiness with hyperdulia, etc. The well-known, famous line of the Mantuan bard:

units.la: Ense potens gemino, cujus vestigia adorant
units.tr: Mighty with his twin-edged sword, whose footsteps adore

units.la: Cæsar, & aurato vestiti murice Reges.
units.tr: Caesar, and kings clothed in purple dyed with gold.

units.la: Apud Georgium Dounamum Diatribe de Antichristo lib. iv. 10. ex Capistrano hæc habentur verba: Omnes Christi milites sacris pedibus Summi Pontificis incurvantur, & flexis poplitibus etiam Reges & Imperatores adoratione debita prosequantur. In Concilio Lateranensi Sess. 5. & 10. Papa, ceu Deo simillimus, ab omnibus populis adorandus pronuntiatur.
units.tr: In Georgius Dounamus's Diatribe de Antichristo, book 4, 10, these words are cited from Capistrano: All the soldiers of Christ bow down at the sacred feet of the Supreme Pontiff, and with bended knees even kings and emperors pay him the adoration that is due. In the Lateran Council, Sessions 5 and 10, the Pope, as most like God, is declared to be adored by all peoples.

units.la: III. Quid verò multis? De adoratione Papæ Antoninus Mazaronius tractatum integrum de Adoratione & osculo pedum Pontificis edidit; & post eum similiter Antoninus Diana Panormitanus, Clericus Regularis, nomen inter laxiores Casuistas percelebre, Episcoporum sub Innocentio X. Examinator, tractatum integrum scripsit, undecimæ Resolutionum Moralium parti subjunctum, cui titulus est: De adoratione, qua Summus Pontifex à Catholicis veneratur. Tractatum, nobilem scilicet, claudit his verbis: Et hæc dicta sufficiant circa præsentem tractatum, quæ omnia sanctissimo Domino humiliter corrigenda submitto; præmissa prius adoratione Pontificia. Ideò procumbens & pronus in terra ejus pedes deosculando, in detestationem omnium hæreticorum, ingenti animi submissione ipsum venerabundus adoro. Macte, macte animo, Flamen, seu potius Scortator Babylonie! Sed & ante utrumque Josephus Stevanus Valentinus, Doctor Theologus de Osculatione pedum Romani Pontificis librum Gregorio XIII. inscriptum, & Coloniæ A. 1580. impressum, edidit, in quo vetustissimam esse adorationem tam manuum, quàm pedum, præfatus, Papæ adorationem adversus hæreticos (sic ipse lepus pulpamentum quæsitans) pluribus comprobare & vindicare conatur.
units.tr: III. But why say more? Antoninus Mazaronius published a complete treatise on the adoration and kissing of the Pope's feet. After him, Antoninus Diana of Palermo, a Regular Clerk, famous among the more lax casuists and an Examiner of Bishops under Innocent X, wrote a whole treatise, appended to the eleventh part of his Moral Resolutions, entitled On the adoration with which the Supreme Pontiff is venerated by Catholics. He closes this noble treatise with these words: Let these things said suffice concerning the present treatise; I humbly submit all of them to correction by the most holy Lord, having first set out the Papal adoration. Therefore, lying prostrate and face down on the ground, kissing his feet, in detestation of all heretics, with great submissiveness of spirit I adore him with reverence. Well done, well done, O Flamen, or rather harlot of Babylon! But before both of these, Josephus Stevanus Valentinus, Doctor of Theology, published a book On the kissing of the feet of the Roman Pontiff, dedicated to Gregory XIII and printed at Cologne in 1580. In it, having stated that the adoration of both hands and feet is very ancient, he tries to prove and defend the adoration of the Pope against heretics with many arguments (like a hare hunting for a dish of meat).

units.la: IV. Adoratio Papæ celeberrima omnium illa est, qua recens electus à Cardinalibus ille adorari consuevit. Nam altari primò in Conclavis Sacrario, post in Templo D. Petri insidens à Cardinalibus cernuis adorari solet. Adorationem hanc Marcellus Ceremon. lib. j. tit. 1. p.8. his verbis exponit: His peractis ducitur electus in Sacrarium, & à Diaconis Cardinalibus exuitur vestimentis communibus, quæ ex antiqua consuetudine cedunt Clericis ceremoniarum, induiturque Papali habitu. Paulò post: Demum Domini Cardinales depositis croceis, & parvis caputiis suas cappas resumunt, imponunt novo Pontifici pluviale rubeum pretiosum, & mitram auro & gemmis ornatam, illúmque sedere faciunt supra altare, cui Cardinales omnes reverentiam exhibent, per ordinem pedes, manus & os deosculantes. Post de descensu Novi electi ad Ecclesiam S. Petri hæc habet: Pontifex novus præcedente cruce & Cardinalibus ad Ecclesiam S. Petri descendit, & prostratus ante altare sine mitra aliquandiu orat, agitque gratias Deo, & Beatis Apostolis. Tum surgens à Cardinalibus super altare ad sedendum constituitur cum mitra, & prior Episcoporum genuflexus incipit: Te Deum laudamus; quem hymnum cantores persequuntur. Interim Cardinales iterum pedes Electi, manus & os deosculantur, servato ordine, quod & alii, qui adsunt, Prælati & nobiles faciunt. Hæc illa solennis maximè Pontificis in altari, quod soli Deo sacrum habetur, residentis adoratio est; cujus exempla moderna conclavia Pontificum, velut Innocentii X. Alexandri VII. &c. luculenta produnt.
units.tr: IV. The most celebrated of all the Pope's adorations is the one with which he is customarily adored by the newly elected, when the Cardinals pay it. For first, when he sits at the altar in the sacristy of the Conclave, and afterwards in the Temple of St Peter, he is usually adored by the kneeling Cardinals. Marcellus explains this adoration in his Ceremonies, book 1, title 1, p. 8, in these words: When these things are done, the elect is led into the sacristy, and the Deacon Cardinals strip him of his ordinary clothes, which by ancient custom go to the clerks of the ceremonies, and he is dressed in the Papal habit. A little later: Finally, the lord Cardinals, having put aside their saffron and small hoods, resume their capes, place on the new Pontiff a precious red cope and a mitre adorned with gold and gems, and make him sit upon the altar, to which all the Cardinals show reverence, kissing his feet, hands and mouth, in order. Afterwards, concerning the descent of the new elect to the Church of St Peter, he says: The new Pontiff, preceded by the cross and the Cardinals, descends to the Church of St Peter, and, prostrate before the altar without a mitre, prays for a while, and gives thanks to God and the blessed Apostles. Then, rising, he is set by the Cardinals upon the altar to sit, with the mitre on, and the first of the Bishops, kneeling, begins: "We praise you, O God"; which hymn the singers follow. Meanwhile the Cardinals again kiss the feet, hands and mouth of the Elect, in order, which the other present prelates and nobles also do. This is that solemn adoration of the Pope seated on the altar, which is held to be sacred to God alone; and the recent conclaves of Popes, such as those of Innocent X and Alexander VII, clearly show examples of it.

units.la: V. Sed & solennis admodum est adoratio Papæ in coronatione ejusdem, quam fusè admodum idem Marcellus Cerem. lib. j. tit. 2. pag. 12. describit. Tum enim ad manus & pedum oscula devotissima Cardinales, Prælatos, Canonicos &c. inter triumphalia signa humiliter adorantes admittit. Extat apud Banckium Romæ Triumph. pag. 383. formula adorationis, qua Archipresbyter Cardinalis Columna, unà cum toto Basilicæ Lateranensis Clero, post oscula pedibus ter infixa, Innocentium X. traditis duabus clavibus, una aurea, argentea altera, conceptis his verbis adoravit: Sanctissime & Beatissime Pater, Caput Ecclesiæ, Rector orbis: Quem Suprema illa Majestas, suum in Terris Vicarium, æterni gaudii dispensatorem, & libertatis Christianæ Restitutorem ac Vindicem, sin-
units.tr: V. But there is also a very solemn adoration of the Pope at his coronation, which the same Marcellus describes at length in his Ceremonies, book 1, title 2, p. 12. For then he admits the Cardinals, Prelates, Canons and others to kiss his hands and feet most devoutly, while they humbly adore him among the triumphal emblems. There is preserved in Banckius, Roman Triumph, p. 383, the formula of adoration with which the Archpriest Cardinal Colonna, together with the whole clergy of the Lateran Basilica, adored Innocent X, after kissing his feet three times, when the two keys, one gold and one silver, had been handed over. The words were: Most holy and most blessed Father, Head of the Church, Ruler of the world: whom that supreme Majesty, by his singular and divine providence, chose as his Vicar on earth, dispenser of eternal joy, and restorer and defender of Christian liberty,

units.la: Adoratur idem in coronatione. Cardinalis Columna clavet ci tradentis adoratio solennis. singulari sua & Divina providentia elegit, nobisque suis famulis, totoque Mundo stitit; Cui claves Regni Caelorum sunt commissae; cui potestas in terris ligandi & solvendi est concessa; Quem Angeli in Caelis reverentur, portae inferorum timent, totusque mundus adorat. Nos quoque Te solum nostrum Patronum, summum Caput & Episcopum ac Spiritualem Patrem, unicè veneramur, colimus & adoramus, & nos omniaque nostra paterna, & PLUS QUAM DIVINAE Tuae dispositioni ac curae reverenter submittimus, ac summè commendamus. Claves enim ligandi & solvendi, quas Christus ipse S. Petro tradidit, ejusque omnibus successoribus reliquit, tuae Sanctitati submisse offerimus in nomine Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Amen.
units.tr: The same is adored at the coronation. The solemn adoration of Cardinal Colonna as he hands over the keys. and has set over us, his servants, and over the whole world; to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven are committed; to whom power to bind and loose on earth is granted; whom the angels in heaven revere, the gates of hell fear, and the whole world adores. We too reverently worship, honour and adore you alone as our Patron, highest Head and Bishop and Spiritual Father, and we humbly submit and most earnestly commend ourselves and all that is ours to your fatherly disposition and care, which is more than divine. For we humbly offer to your Holiness the keys of binding and loosing, which Christ himself gave to St Peter and left to all his successors, in the name of God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

units.la: VI. Longum esset narrare, quemadmodum in Missa adorari Papa solenniter Missae sacra faciens soleat. Marcellus idem Cerem. lib. 3. p. 69. &c. fuse admodum ceremoniam edisserit; neque recensendo tot Cardinalium, Praelatorum, laicorum, ipsius etiam Regis & Imperatoris, si forte praesto illi essent, aquam porrigentium ad lotionem manuum, reverentias, oscula manibus, chirothecis, pectori, genubus, pedibus ejus fixa, genuflexiones &c. sibi satisfacere potest. Ibi pag. 70. Subdiaconus altari & Papae reverentiam exhibens nullo discrimine; Diaconus incensum ministrans, & Pontificem incensans, Christus absque ullo Sanctitatis epitheto simpliciter Domini; Papa vero Sanctissimi Domini, Sanctissimi Patris, Sanctitatis nomine insignis, pomposior longè Papae, quàm ipsius Panacei Numinis adoratio, aliaque ejusmodi, Jovehoc Capitolino digna leguntur. Neque absque causa Pontifici a nostris hoc exprobratum est, quòd Papa, secus ac reliqui sacrificuli, sedens Missam celebrat, neque adeò Christo assurgendum, vel praesenti ei corpore tenus, uti credere jubet, reverentiam exhibendam putat. Námque, teste Marcello pag. 79. facta Deo oblatione, in ara non perstitit, sed eminentem conscendit sedem sicque sedens peculiari ritu communicat, & absoluta communione surgens descendit à sede eminente ad altare. Cujus rei causam non allegoricam, sed historicam se audivisse, sed silentio premendam putare Innocentius III. de Missa. Missæ cap. 7. & 9. scribit. Forte vel turpe ac pudendum quicquam fuit, tenebris quàm luce dignius; vel affectata Divinitas Tarpejo Numini, ut in omni semper Missa Christo, pari, vel inseriori etiam assurgat, non permisit. Unde in precibus quoque suis, narrante eodem Marcello lib. II. pag. 72. aliquando tecto, aliquando semideteEto capite preces Deo fundit.
units.tr: VI. It would be long to relate how the Pope is customarily adored solemnly while celebrating Mass. Marcellus, in the same work, book 3, p. 69, etc., sets out the ceremony at great length; nor can I satisfy myself by listing the many reverences, kisses on his hands, gloves, breast, knees and feet, and genuflections, all made by so many Cardinals, Prelates, laymen, and even the King or Emperor himself, if he happened to be present, who offer water for the washing of his hands. There, p. 70, the Subdeacon shows reverence to the altar and to the Pope without any distinction; the Deacon, who serves the incense and censes the Pontiff, addresses Christ simply as Lord, without any title of holiness; but the Pope is distinguished by the titles Most Holy Lord, Most Holy Father, Holiness. Such adoration of the Pope far surpasses the adoration of the very Panacean deity, and similar things are read that would be worthy of Capitoline Jove. Nor without cause has this been thrown in the Pope's face by our people, that the Pope, unlike the other little priests, celebrates Mass sitting, and thinks no reverence is due to Christ by rising, or as he orders us to believe, to his body present there. For, as Marcellus attests at p. 79, after the offering is made to God, he does not stay at the altar, but mounts a raised seat, and sitting there communicates in a peculiar rite, and when communion is finished he rises and descends from the raised seat to the altar. Innocent III, in De Missa, Mass, chapters 7 and 9, writes that he had heard the reason for this, not allegorical but historical, yet thinks it should be passed over in silence. Perhaps there was something base and shameful, more fit for darkness than light; or perhaps the pretended divinity of the Tarpeian deity did not allow him to rise for Christ, who is equal or even inferior, at any Mass. Hence, in his prayers too, as the same Marcellus relates, book 2, p. 72, he sometimes pours out his prayers to God with his head covered, sometimes with his head half-uncovered.

units.la: VII. Jam & in Jubilæo illo, uti cum Chamiero nostro loquamur, Papismi corculo & deliciis, peccantium asylo, purgatorii scilicet mærore, & Diabolorum terriculamento, Papam magnificè se proferentem, adorari humiliter, cujus animum mirari subeat? Vis præsens Numen contemplari? Finge tibi Papam, terrestrem illum Deum, in Jubilæo, circumstantibus suis creaturis, præeunte illo suo furfuraceo Numine, crucibus ac reliquiis, quasi de Deo ipso sub his simulachris triumphantem, augusto illo suo habitu & triplici tiara, in aurea sella sublimem transvectum; dein aureo malleo Paradisi valvas (sic enim portam Basilicæ Petri nuncupant) aperientem, Missam intus eodem, quo supra diximus, modo celebrantem; & mox potentissimorum Regum ac Principum Legatos, quosdam etiam præsentes, sublimem illum re ipsa, ut alterum Deum, adorantes, circumstantem turbam ab eo vitam æternam expectantem ac petentem, denique ad pedum suorum osculum miseros ac cæcos homines vix admittentem!
units.tr: VII. Now, in that Jubilee, to speak with our Chamier, the darling and delight of Popery, the refuge of sinners, namely by the grief of purgatory and the terror of devils, who could wonder at the Pope proudly displaying himself and being humbly adored? Would you see the present deity? Imagine to yourself the Pope, that earthly god, at the Jubilee, surrounded by his creatures, preceded by that chaff-flavoured deity of his, with crosses and relics, triumphing as if over God himself under these images, carried aloft in his august dress and triple tiara on a golden chair; then opening the gates of Paradise (for so they call the door of St Peter's Basilica) with a golden mallet; celebrating Mass inside in the same manner as we have described above; and soon after, the envoys of the most powerful kings and princes, some of them present too, adoring him as if he were another god, while the crowd standing around asks and begs him for eternal life, and at last hardly admitting wretched and blind men to kiss his feet!

units.la: VIII. De Processionibus solennibus & Pontificalibus
units.tr: VIII. On Solemn and Pontifical Processions

units.la: Papæ quid dicam? In iis Papa, dominus omnium, infidens humeris suorum belphonierorum sublimis portatur, & corporibus hominum, ceu vehiculo nobilissimo, vehitur. Præsertim Pontificem, sic Diana de Ador. P. p. 10: loquitur, reverenter adoramus, cùm in quibusdam diebus solennioribus procedit ad Capellam, gestatus super humeros cum tiara in capite, &c. Exemplum ejusmodi Resol. 8. p. 6. recenset: Cùm quidam Concivis meus ex nostra religione, Vir satis pius, trina vice vidisset Summum Pontificem super humeros gestari cum tiara in capite, tanta devotione & reverentia erga illum affectus fuit, ut cœperit iteratis vicibus pectus suum obtundere. Tunc dubitavit, an ex conditto sic adorare Pontificem esset licitum, & in rigore ac speculative loquendo, adhæsit sententiæ affirmativæ. Quinimo portandi ifthoc officio ipse Imperator, aut Reges, si qui præsentes essent, defungi tenerentur. Sic enim Marcellus Cerem. lib. j. tit. 2. p. 17. scribit: Cùm Papa per scalam, quàm superius diximus, ascendit equum, major Princeps, qui præsens adest, etiamsi Rex esset aut Imperator, Stapham equi Papalis tenet, & deinde ducit equum per frænum aliquantulum. Si verò Pontifex non equo, sed sella veheretur, quatuor majores Principes, etiamsi inter eos Imperator, aut Princeps maximus adesset, in honorem Salvatoris Jesu Christi sellam ipsam cum Pontifice HUMERIS SUIS PORTARE aliquantulum debent. Licetenim hodie Reges, terrentibus vestigiis, uti Rodolphus I. Imperator dicebat, Romæ non amplius visantur; leges tamen has conditas esse eo tempore constat, quo Imperatores Germani Roma potiebantur, & Romam coronandi proficiscebantur. Exemplum Papæ Martini V. Sigismundi Imperatoris humeris in Concilio Constantiensi gestati, ipse Stevanus de Osculat. Pedum Papæ pag. 89. prodi-dit. dit. Interim hodie ab Imperatoris & Regum Legatis servilia isthæc munera quandoque obeuntur.
units.tr: What shall I say of the Pope? In these processions the Pope, lord of all, is carried high, seated on the shoulders of his bearers, and is borne along on human bodies as on the most noble of vehicles. Especially the Pontiff, thus Diana in his book on adoration, p. 10: speaks, we reverently adore, when on certain more solemn days he proceeds to the chapel, carried on the shoulders with the tiara on his head, and so on. Resolution 8, p. 6, recounts an example of this kind: When a certain fellow citizen of mine from our religion, a man quite pious, had seen the Supreme Pontiff carried on the shoulders with the tiara on his head three times, he was so moved by devotion and reverence towards him that he began to beat his breast again and again. Then he doubted whether it was lawful to adore the Pontiff in this way by agreement, and, speaking strictly and in theory, he adhered to the affirmative opinion. Indeed, the Emperor himself, or the kings if any were present, were bound to perform this office of bearing him. For Marcellus Ceremonies, book 1, title 2, p. 17, writes: When the Pope mounts a horse by the ladder which we mentioned above, the greater prince who is present, even if he were a king or emperor, holds the stirrup of the papal horse and then leads the horse a little way by the bridle. But if the Pontiff is carried not on a horse but in a chair, four greater princes, even if the Emperor or the chief prince were among them, ought to carry the chair itself with the Pontiff on their shoulders for a little while, in honour of our Saviour Jesus Christ. For although today kings, as Emperor Rudolf I used to say, are no longer seen walking on foot at Rome, it is nonetheless certain that these laws were established at the time when the German emperors held Rome and set out for Rome to be crowned. Stevanus On Kissing the Pope's Feet, p. 89, records the example of Pope Martin V, carried on the shoulders of the Emperor Sigismund at the Council of Constance. Meanwhile, today these servile duties are sometimes performed by the legates of emperors and kings.

units.la: IX. Libet hic Papolatriam cum Christolatria contendere. Nam Papa quidem procedens sublimis, humeris Principum innixus, vehitur. An sic etiam hostia, quam creatum per transubstantiationem Christum esse tuentur illi? Audi Marcellum eundem Cerem. lib. j. pag. 16. ubi sic ille: Post eos ducitur per familiarem Sacristæ rubro etiam indutum, & baculum in sinistra habentem equus albus, mansuetus, portans Sacramentum, habens ad collum tintinnabulum bene tinniens, & supra portatur baldachinum cum insignibus Papæ. En, equus, cui insidet Papa, ducitur manu Imperatoris aut Regis. At equus, quo vehitur juxta eos Christus, ducitur manu famuli sacristæ, qui servus servuli est. Si Papa sella vehitur, bajulant sellam Imperator, Rex, Principes. Christus vero bestiæ, neque equi duntaxat, verum quandoque etiam mulæ, uti Theodoricus de Nyem Nem. Union. Tract. 6. cap. 43. testis est, dorso imponitur. Cardinalis quoque Perronius de Eucharist. lib. iv. 19. scribit, Papæ extra urbem procedenti, vel peregre agenti, nunquam deesse crucem & Eucharistiam, quæ ante eum præferuntur, ad sacri scilicet illius capitis custodiam præsidialem & patrocinalem, non autem ministerialem: uti solerter ille distinguit.
units.tr: IX. Here I should like to set Pope-worship against Christ-worship. For the Pope, when he processes on high, is carried, leaning on the shoulders of princes. Is the host, which they maintain is Christ created by transubstantiation, carried in the same way? Hear Marcellus again, Ceremonies, book 1, p. 16, where he says this: After them is led, by a servant of the sacristan dressed in red and holding a staff in his left hand, a white horse, gentle, bearing the Sacrament, having a bell well tinkling at its neck, and above it is carried a canopy with the Pope's insignia. Behold, the horse on which the Pope sits is led by the hand of the Emperor or the King. But the horse on which Christ is carried beside them is led by the hand of a servant of the sacristan, who is a servant's servant. If the Pope is carried in a chair, the Emperor, the King and the princes carry the chair. But Christ is placed on beasts, not only horses but sometimes also mules, as Theodoric of Niem, On the Union of the Council of Constance, Tract. 6, chap. 43, bears witness. Cardinal Perronius also, On the Eucharist, book 4, 19, writes that when the Pope goes out of the city or travels abroad, the cross and the Eucharist are never lacking, carried before him, plainly as a guard and protection for that sacred head, not as a servant's office: as that shrewd man distinguishes.

units.la: X. Celebrem hanc gestationem Papæ Esai. XLIX. 22. verbis his: Et afferent filios tuos in ulnis, & filias super humeros portabunt, prædictam esse, Stevanus, Diana, aliique pertendunt. Mirum certè, Papam sic non ferri in ulnis, sed super humeros Principum. Hoc enim de filiis, in quorum censu haberi vult, prædictum est. Et quæ tum filiæ portantur humeris? Papissa enim Johanna una filia fuit. De filiabus Papissis aliis nihil constat. Et frustra Re-giginas Romæ humeris Principum gestari speres. Ipsi in Papatu doctores non inepti, Lyranus, Hector Pintus, Sanctius &c. de vocatione gentium ad Ecclesiam, filios filiásque suas promtè adducturarum, agi non diffitentur: & textus ipse, à fidiculis malorum illorum Interpretum Papolatriæ quovis modo velificantium liberatus loquitur. Rectiùs longè Papolatræ gestationi huic Papæ loca Amos. v. 26. Act. vii. 43. ubi gestasse quidam tabernaculum Molochi, & sidus Dei Remphan dicuntur, accommodassent; vel certè, quod Diana, sorex suo indicio sese prodens, Resol. 10. p. 11. scribere non erubuit, Majestatem illam Pontificis in magnis festivitatibus sese proferentis, graphicè depictam ostentassent in versibus illis Virgilii Georg. lib. iv. quibus pompam Regis apum sic ille describit: — Illum admirantur, & omnes Circumstant fremitu denso, stipantque frequentes, Et sæpe attollunt humeris.
units.tr: X. Diana, Stevanus and others maintain that this famous carrying of the Pope was foretold in Isaiah 49:22 in these words: And they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders. Surely it is strange that the Pope is not carried in arms but on the shoulders of princes, when this was foretold of the sons, whom he wishes to be counted among. And which daughters are carried on shoulders? Pope Joan was one daughter. Nothing is known of other papal daughters. And in vain would you hope that queens are carried at Rome on the shoulders of princes. The Papists' own teachers, not foolish men, Lyranus, Hector Pintus, Sanctius and others, do not deny that the text is about the calling of the nations to the Church, who will readily bring their sons and daughters; and the text itself, freed from the ropes of those bad interpreters who sail in every way for Pope-worship, speaks of this. Far more fittingly would the Pope-worshippers have applied to this carrying of the Pope the passages Amos 5:26 and Acts 7:43, where some are said to have carried the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan; or certainly the images which Diana, betraying himself as a mouse by his own sign, did not blush to write of in Resolution 10, p. 11, vividly depicting that majesty of the Pontiff appearing at great festivals, in those lines of Virgil Georgics, book 4, in which he describes thus the procession of the king of the bees: They all marvel at him and crowd around him in a dense hum, and often they lift him on their shoulders.

units.la: XI. Omitto Papæ adorationem in Conciliabulis suis (quomodo in Concilio Florentino Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus ab Angario Papam προσκυνεῖν adorare frustra equidem jussus est; & Burgundici Legati, nullo exhibito Imperatori Orientali reverentiæ signo, approximantes Papæ προσκυνῶ ἐ ἡαπάσμι μόνης τὸ πίδα adorárunt, & osculati sunt omnes pedem ejus, manum, genámque, narrante fusiùs Silvestro Sguropulo Histor. Flor. pag. 92. 176.) in coronatione Imperatoris, in receptione Imperatoris Romam profecti, canonizatione, creatione Cardinalium, Legati Apostolici de latere; Benedictionibus variis; Festis; Epistolis ad eum datis &c. Quæ, aliáque eò pertinentia, ex Marcello, aliisque studiosius ὁ μαχαίρης Cl. Myllerus suis de Adoratione Papæ diatribis excerpsit.
units.tr: XI. I pass over the adoration of the Pope in his own conciliabula (as at the Council of Florence, where the Patriarch of Constantinople was ordered in vain to adore the Pope [προσκυνεῖν]; and the Burgundian legates, without showing any sign of reverence to the Eastern Emperor, approaching the Pope, worshipped him [προσκυνῶ ... τὸ πίδα], and all kissed his foot, his hand and his cheek, as Silvester Sguropulus relates more fully in History of Florence, pp. 92, 176), at the coronation of an emperor, at the reception of an emperor who has come to Rome, at canonization, at the creation of cardinals, in the case of legates a latere, in various blessings, at feasts, in letters addressed to him, and so on. These things, and others pertaining to this, the distinguished Myllerus has more diligently gathered from Marcellus and others in his treatises On the Adoration of the Pope.

units.la: XII. Variæ equidem Papolatriæ partes & ceremoniæ commemorari possunt.
units.tr: XII. Indeed, various parts and ceremonies of Papolatry may be mentioned.

units.la: Omitto libens ejus vestitum, coronationem, positionem super altare, portationem, de quibus, idololatriæ crimine haud vacantibus, jam egimus. Omitti etiam poterat apertio capitis, vulgaris ceremonia ritus, nisi Marcellus Cerem. lib. iij. p. 113. negaret, Papam cuiquam Mortalium reverentiam facere, assurgendo manifeste, aut caput detegendo; nisi forte Imperatori vel Regibus; privatim scilicet, & cum in Pontificalibus non sedet, caput aliquantulum inclinando, non ex officio, sed laudabili humanitate; more scilicet, uti Baronius ad A.C. 324. n. 79. nos docet; Sacerdotum Gentilium, nunquam pileum, insigne Flaminum, deponentium; & contra idem Marcellus Cerem. lib. iij. pag. 129. asseveraret, Oratorem, quoties inter orandum Pontificem nominat, caput detegere; addente Diana Resol. 9. p. 70. rite & licite per apertionem capitis & inclinationem nomen Papæ adorari; imò nomen ipsum, non personam duntaxat eo nomine significatam, æquè ac nomen Christi & Deiparæ, apertione capitis & quidem ex præcepto religionis, adorandum esse.
units.tr: I gladly pass over his vestments, his coronation, his being placed upon the altar, and his being carried, which we have already discussed, since they are not free of the crime of idolatry. The uncovering of the head, a common ritual ceremony, could also be passed over, were it not that Marcellus (Cerem. lib. iii. p. 113) denies that the Pope shows reverence to any mortal by openly rising or uncovering his head, except perhaps to the Emperor or to kings; and then only privately, and when he is not seated in pontifical dress, by slightly inclining his head, not from duty but from laudable courtesy, in the manner, namely, which Baronius (ad A.C. 324, n. 79) tells us was practised by the Gentile priests, who never laid aside the pileus, the insignia of the Flamens. On the other hand, the same Marcellus (Cerem. lib. iii. p. 129) affirms that the orator, whenever he names the Pontiff while praying, uncovers his head. Diana (Resol. 9. p. 70) adds that the name of the Pope is rightly and lawfully adored by uncovering the head and bowing; indeed the name itself, not merely the person signified by that name, is to be adored, just as the name of Christ and of the Mother of God is, by uncovering the head, and indeed by a precept of religion.

units.la: XIII. Sed & adoratur Papa incurvatione tum capitis, quoties vel nomen ejus nominatur; adeóque sicut nomen Jesu per adorationem latriæ, inclinando caput adoratur, ita Sanctorum, Summique adeò Pontificis nomen cultu dulia adorari per inclinationem capitis debet, uti Diana Resol. 9. p. 6. nos edocet: tum capitis una cum superiori parte corporis, ad genua usque; qualis, nisi fallor, est profunda inclinatio Cardinalium, qua bis coram Papa incurvari solent: tum genuum, quæ γονυκλισία genuflexio dici solet; atque duobus coram Papa perinde ac coram Deo, genubus flexis peragi debet, Suarezio de Virt. & Stat. relig. Tr. lib. j. cap. 2. afferente, neque semel duntaxat, sed ter, inprimis quando in altari & Missa adoratur, tum denique totius corporis: quomodo, Marcello Cerem. p.68. teste, etiam Imperator à Pontifice excipiendus; in terram pronus, Pontificis pedes deosculatur. Quod inprimis Fridericum Barbarossam Alexandro III. collum ejus nefariè & Papaliter calcanti fecisse, historiarum monumenta, & ipsius Papæ pigmenta prodidere.
units.tr: XIII. But the Pope is also adored by bowing the head whenever his name is spoken; and so, as the name of Jesus is adored with latria by bowing the head, so the name of the saints, and of the supreme Pontiff too, ought to be adored with dulia by bowing the head, as Diana (Resol. 9. p. 6) informs us. The bow is made with the head together with the upper part of the body, down to the knees; this, unless I am mistaken, is the profound bow which Cardinals are accustomed to make twice before the Pope. It is also made by bending the knees, which is commonly called genuflection [γονυκλισία]; and this must be performed before the Pope with both knees bent, just as before God, Suarez (de Virt. & Stat. Relig. Tr. lib. i. cap. 2) asserting that it is to be done not once only but three times, especially when he is adored at the altar and during Mass. Finally, there is adoration of the whole body: in this way, as Marcellus (Cerem. p. 68) bears witness, even the Emperor, when received by the Pope, lies prone on the ground and kisses the Pope's feet. The records of histories, and the Pope's own publications, have handed down that Frederick Barbarossa did this especially to Alexander III, when Alexander impiously and haughtily trampled on his neck.

units.la: XIV. Sunt & aliæ adorationis ceremoniæ nonnullæ; veluti quòd Papolatræ Pontifici in solio & altari sedenti incensum faciunt: quòd nudipedes quandoque Papæ limina salutant; cujus rei exemplum Henricus IV. Imperator præbet: quòd tunsione pectoris eum adorari posse, Diana Resol. 8. pag. 6, 7. eo argumento tuetur, quia ἀποθανάτια illa signum sit agnoscentis ac deprecantis peccata, eorumque remissionem, quam Pontifex inprimis impertiatur, suppliciter orantis: quòd Papa pedem à limine suo movente, missificante, comestante, equitante, Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus servilia quandoque munera injungantur: qualia & Marcellus in Sacris suis Ceremoniarum libris definit, & historiarum scriptores posteris nosccenda reliquerunt. Sed missis his, cùm utramque ferè Papolatriæ paginam osculā sacra, Tarpejo Numini fixa, faciant, de iis paulò uberiùs agendum suerit.
units.tr: XIV. There are also some other ceremonies of adoration: for example, that the Papolaters burn incense to the Pope when he is seated on his throne and at the altar; that they sometimes greet the threshold of the Pope barefoot, of which Henry IV, the Emperor, gives an example; that he may be adored by beating the breast, which Diana (Resol. 8. pp. 6, 7) defends on the ground that that apothanatia [ἀποθανάτια] is a sign of one acknowledging and deprecating sins, and of seeking their remission, which the Pope especially grants to one who prays suppliantly; that when the Pope moves his foot from his threshold, sends forth messages, eats, or rides, servile services are sometimes enjoined on Emperors, Kings and Princes. Marcellus defines such things in his sacred books of ceremonies, and writers of histories have left them to be known by posterity. But setting these aside, since they perform almost each page of Papolatry with sacred kisses fixed upon the Tarpeian deity, I must treat of these somewhat more fully.

units.la: XV. Septem ferè modis Pontificem oscula admittere, nimirum ad os, ad pectus, ad humerum, ad manus, ad brachia, ad genua & ad pedes Durandus Mimatensis Rat. Div. offic. lib. iv. par. 3. Rubr. 5. notat. Osculum ad os complecti etiam potest osculum faciei, quod Imperato percepto Sacramento, Subdiaconus communicante Papa, nec non subinde Cardinales faciei Papæ figunt, & fixit quondam Guicciardino Histor. lib. 3. teste, Carolus VIII. Galliæ Rex Alexandro VI. postquam pedes ejus deosculatus est; nec non genæ à Legatis Burgundicis Eugenio V. narrat. narrante Sguropulo in Concilii Florentini historia, fixum: Ad oris verò osculum strictè dictum Papa Imperatorem, Reges, Cardinales, Legatos à Latere, Electores, sed non nisi prævia osculatione pedum, admittit. Pectoris oscula Cardinales; Humerorum Pontificis juxta cum mensa altaris, Primicerium in principio, Diaconum in medio, & Sacerdotem in fine Missæ, cui Papa præsens est: Manuum (quarum osculum proprie adorationem significare, apud Dianam Resol. 10 p. 7. Raphael de Torre & Thomas asferunt) & quandoque etiam chirothecarum & auriphrygii Imperatorem, Augustam, Legatum Apostolicum de Latere, Electores & Principes primores, Legatos ad Papam, denique omnes illos, qui Papæ aliquid tradunt, vel ab eodem aliquid accipiunt, quia, uti Strevanus pag. 37. loquitur, sicut dat propria, sic nunquam recipit aliena; gratitudinem sic testificaturos utrosque: Brachiorum eosdem ferè: Genuum Cardinales in Canonizatione, Episcopos Prælatos in Missa majori, Papa ipso celebrante, & Coronatione Papæ, admittit. Singula hæc ex libris Ceremoniarum Sacrarum eruere, & exemplis confirmare, adeoque camalinam hanc movere nihil attinet.
units.tr: XV. Durandus of Mende (Rat. Div. offic. lib. iv. par. 3, Rubr. 5) notes that the Pope admits kisses in about seven ways, namely to the mouth, to the breast, to the shoulder, to the hands, to the arms, to the knees and to the feet. The kiss to the mouth may also embrace the kiss of the face, which the Emperor, after receiving the Sacrament, and the subdeacon, when the Pope communicates, and afterwards at times the Cardinals, plant upon the Pope's face. Charles VIII, King of France, once fixed it on Alexander VI after he had kissed his feet, as Guicciardini (Histor. lib. 3) relates; and the cheek was fixed on Eugenius IV by the Burgundian envoys, as Sguropulus relates in his history of the Council of Florence. The kiss of the mouth, strictly so called, the Pope grants to the Emperor, the Kings, the Cardinals, the Legates a latere and the Electors, but only after the kissing of the feet has gone before. The Cardinals receive kisses on the breast; the Pope's shoulders are kissed by the Primicerius at the beginning of Mass, by the Deacon in the middle, and by the Priest at the end, when the Pope is present. The hands (whose kiss, Raphael de Torre and Thomas assert, properly signifies adoration, as Diana reports, Resol. 10, p. 7), and sometimes even the gloves and the gold-embroidered cuffs, are kissed by the Emperor, the Empress, the Legate a latere, the Electors and chief Princes, the envoys to the Pope, and finally all those who hand something to the Pope or receive something from him; for, as Strevanus says (p. 37), just as he gives his own things, so he never receives what belongs to others, and both parties thus attest their gratitude. The arms are kissed by nearly the same people. The knees are admitted to be kissed by the Cardinals at a canonization, by the Bishops and Prelates at the high Mass, with the Pope himself celebrating, and at the Coronation of the Pope. To draw out each of these from the books of sacred ceremonies and confirm them with examples, and so stir up that old Camarina, is unnecessary.

units.la: XVI. Papolitriæ potiùs caput proram & puppim Oscu- lapedum, seu calceamentorum Papæ, perstringere juva- bit.
units.tr: XVI. It will be useful to touch rather on the head, prow and stern of the Papal Osculapedum, that is, of the kissing of the Pope's slippers.

units.la: Nam, ut paucis multa dicam Papa solus post triplicem adgeniculationem non tantum admittit ut libera, sed etiam exigit ut debita oscula pedum, seu potiùs crepidarum, cruce phrygionis opere intexta insignitarum; neque ab idiotis duntaxat, qui raro aut nunquam ad osculationis illum honorem admittuntur; sed ab ipsis Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus aliisque, quos honore scilicet tanto dignatur; neque denique qui mos inprimis barbarus & brutus est, vivus duntaxat, sed etiam mortuus oscula excipit. quomodo Sixti V. corpus in Sacello Gregoriano ita repositum fuisse scribitur, ut pedes extra cancellos ferreos prominerent, ut à populo spectatum veniente osculaillis figi possent.
units.tr: To say much in few words: the Pope alone, after three genuflections, not only accepts kisses of his feet, or rather of his sandals, embroidered with a cross in Phrygian work, but demands them as his due. He does not do this only with laymen, who are rarely or never admitted to that honour of kissing, but also with the emperors, kings, princes and others whom he deigns to honour in this way. Finally, this custom, which is especially barbarous and brutish, is not confined to the living but extends to the dead. It is written that the body of Sixtus V was laid in the Gregorian chapel in such a way that his feet projected beyond the iron grating, so that they could be kissed by people coming to view him.

units.la: XVII. Marcellus equidem Cerem. S. lib. iy. sect. 1. p. 113. illud ante omnia, ceu maximè compertum, supponit, Papam nemini Mortalium reverentiam facere, assurgendo manifestè, aut caput inclinando, seu detegendo; Romanorum verò Imperatori, postquam illum sedentem ad osculum pedis & manus suscepit, aliquantulum assurgere ad oris osculum; mutuo charitatis amplexu eum recipientem; atque idem eum facere aliquando magnis Regibus. Quomodo autem clientes ejus Maxumi, Medioxumi, Infimi ad illud osculum, & quibus præviis ceremoniis veniant, sic porro exponit idem: Omnes Mortales & præsertim Christi fideles, cujuscunque sint dignitatis & præeminentiæ, cùm primùm in conspectum Pontificis adveniunt, distantibus spatiis ter debent ante illum genu flectere, & in honorem Salvatoris nostri Jusu Christi, cujus vices gerit in terris, ejus pedes osculari. Atque id Papam sibi, tanquam eximium quid vindicare, Stevanus de Osculi ped. Papæ pag. 97. ex dictatibus Hildebrandinis confirmat; quorum nonus est, Quòd SOLIUS Papæ pedes omnes Principes deosculentur. Diana Resol. 4. p. 4. monet, in aliis Ecclesiis sufficere promptitudinem ad oscula pedum, modò manibus oscula figantur: sed Papæ Romano semper ritum genu flectendi, & pedes osculandi inviolabiliter à Christi fidelibus observari. Antonius quinetiam strenuus Papæ parasitus, propter oscula hæc pedum Papam Angelis ipsis superiorem arguit: Nam, ita Sum. par. 3. tit. 22. cap. 5. sect. 4. loquitur, Papa recipit à fidelibus adorationes, prostrationes, & oscula pedum, quod non permisit Angelus à Johanne Euangelista sibi fieri. Pari scilicet ratione à facto ad jus procedendo, convicturus, & Nebucadnezaris statuam, & Antichristum ipsum Angelis superiores esse.
units.tr: XVII. Marcellus, in his Ceremonies, book 4, section 1, p. 113, first of all lays down this as something above all else most clearly established, that the Pope shows reverence to no mortal by rising visibly, or by bowing or uncovering his head; but that to the Roman emperor, when he has received him seated for the kiss of foot and hand, he rises a little to give the kiss of the mouth, receiving him in a mutual embrace of charity; and that he does the same at times for great kings. How his clients, the greatest, middling and lowest, come to that kiss, and with what preliminary ceremonies, the same author sets out thus: All mortals, and especially the faithful of Christ, of whatever rank and eminence they may be, as soon as they come into the presence of the Pontiff, must kneel before him three times at a distance, and in honour of our Saviour Jesus Christ, whose vicar he is on earth, kiss his feet. And Stevanus, in his work on the kissing of the Pope's feet, p. 97, confirms from the Hildebrandine dictates that the Pope claims this as a special privilege for himself. The ninth of these reads: That ONLY the Pope's feet are to be kissed by all princes. Diana, Resolution 4, p. 4, advises that in other churches readiness to kiss the feet is enough, provided the kisses are also given with the hands; but for the Roman Pope the rite of kneeling and kissing the feet is to be observed inviolably by the faithful of Christ. Antonius too, that zealous parasite of the Pope, argues from these kisses of the feet that the Pope is superior even to the angels. For he says, in Summa, part 3, title 22, chapter 5, section 4: The Pope receives from the faithful adorations, prostrations and kisses of the feet, which the angel did not allow John the Evangelist to do to him. By the same method, proceeding from fact to right, he would prove that both Nebuchadnezzar's statue and Antichrist himself are superior to angels.

units.la: XVIII. De origine moris hujus variè Pontificii ipsi ario-
units.tr: XVIII. Papists themselves give various accounts of the origin of this custom.

units.la: lantur. Non desunt tamen, qui æmulatione gentilium, Divorum suorum pedes aut manus osculantium, introdu-ctam divinent. Laudat hic Stevanus loc. cit. pag. 12. 13. morem Romanorum, Statuas osculo manuum venerantium, allegatis hisce Lucretii lib. j.
units.tr: Nevertheless there are some who guess that it was introduced in imitation of the Gentiles, who kissed the feet or hands of their deified men. Here Stevanus, loc. cit., p. 12, 13, praises the custom of the Romans who venerated statues by kissing their hands, citing these lines of Lucretius, book 1:

units.la: Signa manus dextras ostendunt attenuari,
units.tr: The right hands show themselves worn thin,

units.la: Sæpe salutantum tactu, propterque meantum &c.
units.tr: Often by the touch of those greeting, and by those passing by, etc.

units.la: Ex Prudentio idem subjungit, vetustam in apotheosi confuetudinem fuisse Divorum & Divarum pedes lambere; plantis Herculis advolvi: genua incurvare Dianæ. Apertè satis Cæsar Bullengerus adv. Cafaub. Diatr. 10. p. 29. Mos, inquit, ex eo fortean ortus, quòd prisca superstitio Deorum pedes aut manus osculabatur, cùmque Sanctos illos Viros Petrum, Clementem, Cletum, Numinis pæne loco haberent, eorum manus pedésque adorárunt. A Regibus Persarum, & Imperatoribus Romanorum alii morem derivant. Sic enim Diana Resol. 5. p. 4. 5. scribit: Cum Regibus Persarum nemo loqui poterat, nisi prostratus in terram vestigia pedum Regiorum exosculartetur, teste Xenophonte lib. 8. & Plutarcho in Alcibiade. Hic etiam mos fuit apud Romanos. De Cajo, Othone, Caligula, Nerone, Adriano, Antonino probat Lorinus in Act. c. 10. 24.
units.tr: From Prudentius the same author adds that in the ancient custom of deification it was usual to lick the feet of gods and goddesses, to fall at the soles of Hercules, to bend the knees to Diana. Caesar Bullinger has said quite plainly, against Casaubon, Diatribe 10, p. 29: The custom, he says, perhaps arose from this, that ancient superstition kissed the feet or hands of the gods, and since they held those holy men Peter, Clement and Cletus almost in the place of divinity, they worshipped their hands and feet. Others derive the custom from the kings of Persia and the emperors of Rome. For Diana, Resolution 5, p. 4, 5, writes: No one could speak with the kings of Persia unless, prostrated on the ground, he kissed the footprints of the royal feet, as Xenophon testifies in book 8 and Plutarch in the Life of Alcibiades. This custom was also among the Romans. Lorinus, in Acts chapters 10 and 24, proves it of Gaius, Otho, Caligula, Nero, Hadrian and Antoninus.

units.la: XIX. Ita est, Diana & Lorine. Ritus hic vilißimi ofculi, quem turpem & plusquam servilem Lipsius vester Elect. lib. ÿ. 6. appellat, natus est, eodem Lipsio judice, sub Cajo Caligula, imò à Cajo, qui, uti Dio ait, ἰφίλ{ ἀλλ- ... Παντίσσιμος ... Pancissimos osculatus est, plerisque autem Senatorum, vel manum, vel pedem adorandum dedit. Planè sicut Vester ille neminem osculatur, & omnium, etiam
units.tr: XIX. Yes indeed, Diana and Lorinus. This rite of the most vile kiss, which your Lipsius calls base and more than servile, Elect., book 1, chapter 6, arose, according to Lipsius' own judgement, under Gaius Caligula, indeed from Gaius, who, as Dio says, kissed everyone and gave most of the senators either his hand or his foot to adore. Just as that man of yours kisses no one, and begs servile and most vile kisses from all, even from emperors and kings.

units.la: Greek sentence in the text line: ἰφίλ{ἀλλ-ήσης, τῆς ἢ πλείσης ἐ τ' ... (Greek; not reliably legible). etiam Imperatorum & Regum oscula servilia & vilissima ambit. Sed audite Senecam hominem paganum, Caligulam, & in eo vestrum illud idolum, quod se servum servorum profitetur, sic de Benefic. lib. y. 12. detestantem: Cajus Cæsar dedit vitam Pompejo Penno, si dat, qui non aufert. Deinde absoluto & agenti gratias porrexit osculandum sinistrum pedem: (hæc verba etiam Stevanus cap.j. adducit, subdolè tacens sequentia, quibus profligatissimi Imperatoris tyrannidem execratus est, ne redivivum in Papa Caligulam agnoscamus) Qui excusant & negant (sic enim Seneca pergit) id insolentiæ causa factum, ajunt, socculum auratum, imò aureum, margaritis distinctum, ostendere eum voluisse. Ita prorsus: quid hic contumeliosum est, si vir consularis aurum & margaritas osculatus est, & alioqui nullam partem in corpore ejus electurus, quam puriùs oscularetur? Homo natus in hoc, ut mores liberæ civitatis Persica servitute mutaret, parum judicavit, si Senator senex, summis usus honoribus in conspectu Principum, supplex sibi eo more jacuisset, quo victi hostes victoribus jacuere: invenit aliquid infra genua, quo libertatem detruderet. Non hoc est Rempublicam calcare, & quidem dicet aliquis (non potest ad rem pertinere) sinistro pede. Parùm enim fœdè, furiosèque insolens fuerat, qui de capite consularis viri soccatus audiebat, nisi in os Senatoris injecisset Imperator pigros (Scaliger, à Gronovio Not. ad h. I. defensus epigros, clavos ligneos soccis suppactos legit) suos. O superbia magnæ fortunæ! O stultissimum malum! Occurrit Lorinus, Lojolæ pullus, Senecam non damnare morem absolutè, sed in aliquo casu, ob superbiam Principis. Egregiè sanè. Nam quod superbiam in Imperatore domino, id jam humilitatem in Pontifice Piscatoris successore, & Servorum servo redolet:
units.tr: Yet hear Seneca, a pagan, speaking of Caligula, and in him that idol of yours which professes itself the servant of servants, condemning it in these words, On Benefits, book 5, chapter 12: Gaius Caesar gave life to Pompeius Pennus, if one can call it giving when he does not take it away. Then, when the man had been released and was giving thanks, he held out his left foot for kissing. (Stevanus also cites these words in chapter 1, craftily leaving out what follows, in which he cursed the tyranny of that most abandoned emperor, lest we recognise a revived Caligula in the Pope.) Those who excuse it and deny that it was done out of arrogance, say that he wanted to show a gold slipper, indeed a golden one, studded with pearls. Quite so: what is insulting here, if a man of consular rank kissed gold and pearls, and was going to choose no other part of his body to kiss more purely? A man born to change the customs of a free state into Persian servitude thought it too little if an elderly senator, who had held the highest offices, in the sight of princes, should lie prostrate before him in the manner in which conquered enemies lay before their conquerors. He found something lower than the knees on which to trample liberty. This is not treading on the Republic, and someone will say (it cannot pertain to the matter) with the left foot. For it would have been too little foul and frenzied arrogance, to hear of a consular man's head being shod, unless the emperor had thrust his pigri (Scaliger, defended by Gronovius in his note on this passage, reads epigros, wooden nails fastened to the shoes) into the senator's mouth. O the pride of great fortune! O most foolish evil! Lorinus, Loyola's little chick, objects that Seneca does not condemn the custom absolutely, but in one instance, on account of the prince's arrogance. Admirably indeed. For what smells of arrogance in an emperor and master, that now smells of humility in the Pope, the successor of the Fisherman and the servant of servants:

units.la: XX. Sed
units.tr: XX. But

units.la: XX. Sed compara, si vis, Lorine, invicem Caligulam & Papam. Caligula semel osculandum pedem suum porrexit. Si enim ordinarium id fuisset, cur factum excusare studuissent nonnulli, quod commune fuisset? Papa id facit diebus singulis. Caligula osculandum pedem obtulit homini supplici, & cui vitam condonaverat: cui pro supplicio erat osculum. Papa offert non supplicibus, sed solpitatoribus, iis, quibus se & fortunas suas omneis debet, Imperatoribus. Auro & margaritis Caligula pedem suum ornavit. Papa pedem suum aurea crepida, & aurea cruce insignit. Caligula mores liberæ civitatis mutavit in luxum Persicum, quia, uti Lipsius notat, Persas Regibus suis manus pedésque osculatos, & humi stratos serviliter adoraße, constat. Papa mutavit mores liberorum Regnorum & Rerum publicarum; neque solùm hominem Senatorem ad pedes suos abjecit, eòsque ori ejus injecit; sed id ab Imperatoribus, Regibus exigit, quotiescunque potest. Et tamen, si Lorinum audimus, pedum admissa osculā in Caligula nil nisi insolentiam, in Papa extremam modestiam spirant. Macte virtute, incomparabiles parasitastri!
units.tr: XX. But compare, if you like, Lorinus, Caligula and the Pope with each other. Caligula once offered his foot to be kissed. For if that had been a regular practice, why did some men take pains to excuse the act on the ground that it was common? The Pope does it every day. Caligula offered his foot to a suppliant, a man to whom he had granted his life, for whom the kiss was a punishment. The Pope offers it not to suppliants but to petitioners, to those to whom he owes himself and all his fortunes, the emperors. Caligula decorated his foot with gold and pearls. The Pope adorns his foot with a golden slipper and a golden cross. Caligula changed the customs of a free state into Persian luxury, because, as Lipsius observes, it is established that the Persians kissed their kings' hands and feet and worshipped them in servile fashion, lying prostrate on the ground. The Pope has changed the customs of free kingdoms and commonwealths; not only does he cast senators down at his feet and thrust their mouths upon them, but he also demands this from emperors and kings whenever he can. And yet, if we listen to Lorinus, the admission of kisses to the feet breathes nothing but insolence in Caligula, but extreme modesty in the Pope. Well done, incomparable little parasites!

units.la: XXI. Semel forte Caligula osculum pedis sinistri à Senatore, ceu supplicium pro noxa poposcit. Sed Maximinus Junior, Capitolino narrante, in salutationibus superbissimus erat, & manum porrigebat, & genu sibi osculari patiebatur, nonnunquam etiam pedes: quod Maximinum seniorem passum nunquam esse, notavit idem, dicere scilicet solitum: Dii prohibeant, ut quisquam ingenuorum pedibus meis oscula figat. Excepit Diocletianus, de quo hæc Pomponius Lætus Comp. Hist. Rom. habet: Diocletianus edicto sanxit, ut omnes sine generis discrimine prostrati, pedes exoscularentur, quibus etiam veneracionem quandam adhibuit, exornans calceamenta au-
units.tr: XXI. Once, by chance, Caligula demanded a kiss on his left foot from a senator, as a punishment for some offence. But Maximinus the Younger, as Capitolinus relates, was most arrogant in his greetings, and offered his hand, and allowed his knee to be kissed, and sometimes even his feet; the same writer notes that the elder Maximinus never permitted this, and that he used to say: God forbid that any freeborn man should press kisses on my feet. Diocletian followed, of whom Pomponius Laetus in his Compendium of Roman History writes this: Diocletian by edict decreed that all persons, without distinction of rank, should prostrate themselves and kiss his feet; to these he also gave a certain reverence, adorning the shoes with gold, jewels and pearls.

units.la: Note: the marginal notes are set in very small type and several words are partly illegible; they are transcribed as far as legible. ro, gemmis, margaritis. Eundem ornatum commiscuit vestibus. Trajanum contra Plinius in Panegyrico sic laudat: Non tu civium amplexus ad pedes tuos deprimis, nec osculum manu reddis. Ex eo tempore osculi pedum vel exacti vel infixi exempla apud Romanos quidem nulla legere est. Ast apud Graecos recentiores, teste Curopalote de Offic. Palat. Constantinop. p. 145. usu invaluit, ut Imperatoris dextrum pedem, manum & genam Principes oscularentur, parato in triclinio throno, simul atque ille ex Ecclesia exibat. Quinto etiam die hebdomadis, cui Ἀναλαμψις renovationis nomen, Patriarcham una cum Summis Sacerdotibus Archimandritis, & Antistitibus mutatis vestibus convenisse Imperatorem, stantem in throno suo; accedentem osculatum esse Imperatorem ad os; & similiter ab Imperatore Δεσπότην, Dominum designatum, qui ei proximus esse deberet, osculatum esse Imperatoris pedem; addit.
units.tr: Note: the marginal notes are set in very small type and several words are partly illegible; they are transcribed as far as legible. ...gold, jewels, pearls. He mixed the same ornament into his garments. Pliny, on the other hand, praises Trajan in his Panegyric thus: You do not press the embraces of citizens down to your feet, nor do you offer your hand for a kiss. From that time one can read of no examples among the Romans of kisses of the feet, either demanded or imposed. But among the later Greeks, as Curopalates testifies in On the Offices of the Palace of Constantinople, p. 145, it became the custom that the princes kissed the emperor's right foot, his hand and his cheek, a throne being prepared in the dining hall as soon as he came out of the church. He adds that on the fifth day of the week, which bore the name of renewal [Ἀναλαμψις], the patriarch came together with the chief priests, archimandrites and bishops, clad in changed vestments; the emperor, standing on his throne, was approached and kissed on the mouth; and likewise the one designated by the emperor as Despot [Δεσπότην], that is, Lord, who ought to be next to him, kissed the emperor's foot.

units.la: XXII. Sic ergo Papae gnathones morem a monstro impuro, Cajo Caligula, coeptum, a non bonis Imperatoribus, Maximino & Diocletiano usurpatum, a bonis, qualis Trajanus erat, recusatum; Lipsio judice turpem, plusquam servilem, superbum & inhumanum, laudant & defendunt in eo, qui se successorem jactat Petri, cui, aeque atque aliis Apostolis, a Christo dictum est: Reges gentium dominantur eis, & qui potestatem habent in eas, benefici vocantur. Vos autem non sic. Sed qui maximus est inter Vos, sit sicut minimus est; & qui Princeps est, sicut qui ministrat. Luc. xxii. 25. qui a Magistro suo sic edoctus conservos suos jussit pascere gregem Dei, non ut dominantes cleris, sed ut qui sint exemplaria gregis. 1 Pet. v. 2, 3. Malunt tamen illi expressis Caligulae & Diocletiani vestigiis insistere, quam Petri, cujus aliis spoliis superbiunt. Quos Cuspinianus etiam, Maximiliano Imp. a consiliis, immeritò à Stevano de osculat. ped. p. 6. traductus, uti mendacia ejus perstringens Cl. Rivetus Jesf. Vap. cap. 28. ostendit, agens de Diocletiano, sic exagitavit: Divinos sibi (Diocletianus) usurpavit honores, veluti in eo esset Cœlestis Majestas, voluit adorari more Regum Persarum, pedésque exosculandos omnibus sine discrimine gentis exhibuit, idque edicto sanxit; quemadmodum hodie nostri sancti Pontifices faciunt, Caligulam imitatus, qui calceamenta auro gemmis & margaritis exornavit.
units.tr: XXII. So then the Pope's flatterers praise and defend the custom begun by the impure monster Gaius Caligula, usurped by the wicked emperors Maximinus and Diocletian, and rejected by the good ones, such as Trajan, which Lipsius judged vile, more than servile, proud and inhuman, in the case of the man who boasts that he is the successor of Peter, to whom, just as to the other apostles, Christ said: The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. But you are not so. Rather, let the greatest among you be as the least, and let the one who is leader be as the one who serves. Luke 22:25. Taught thus by his Master, he was ordered to feed the flock of God, not as lording it over the clergy, but as becoming examples to the flock. 1 Pet. 5:2, 3. Yet they prefer to tread in the footsteps of Caligula and Diocletian, which are plainly marked, rather than in Peter's, whose other spoils they boast of. Cuspinian, who was counsellor to the emperor Maximilian and was undeservedly quoted by Steven in On the Kissing of Feet, p. 6, and whose lies were exposed by the distinguished Rivet in Jesuitical Vapours, chapter 28, in discussing Diocletian, censured him thus: Diocletian (he says) claimed divine honours for himself, as though heavenly majesty resided in him; he wished to be worshipped after the manner of the Persian kings, and he offered his feet to be kissed by all people without distinction of race, and decreed this by edict; just as our holy Pontiffs do today, imitating Caligula, who adorned his shoes with gold, jewels and pearls.

units.la: XXIII. Quòd si quondam osculà quorundam pedibus fixa sunt (exempla autem mulierum peccatricis, & mulierum Christum resurgentem sic osculantium huc referri neutiquam possunt) ex voluntate, affectione, humilitate, devotione pia & libera sine apparatu, pompa & præscriptis ritibus figentium; nihil hoc Ausonium hunc Jovem juvat, qui oscula exigit, & solus exigit, & à summis, quandoque etiam additis ludibriis, exigit.
units.tr: XXIII. But if at some time kisses were fixed on the feet of certain persons (the examples of the sinful woman and of the women who kissed the risen Christ in this way cannot be brought in here at all), they were given from the free will, affection, humility and pious devotion of those who gave them, without display, pomp or prescribed rites. This does nothing to help this Jupiter of Ausonius, who demands kisses, and demands them alone, and demands them from the highest, sometimes even adding mockery.

units.la: Certè S. Petrus, quem primum & maximum Papam illi faciunt, adorationem liberam Cornelii Centurionis, pedibus ejus se advolventis, nec dum tamen eos osculantis; neque ignari, quòd Petrus Deus non esset, neutiquam admisit, argumento eo usus, quòd & ipse homo sit, Act. x. 25. 26. Ne quidem Angelus se à S. Johanne pedibus ejus accidente adorari passus est, Apoc. xix. 10. Unde majorem esse Papam Angelo Antonium supra egregiè arguentem vidimus. Sed & ἀξιομνημόνευτα sunt Mardochai in Apocryphis, quæ Adversariis nostris Canonica habentur, ad Estheram additionibus cap. xiii. 12, 13, 34. verba ad Deum ipsum: Σὺ πάντα γινώσκεις, σὺ οἶδας, κύριε, ὅτι οὐκ ἐν ὕβρει, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν ὑπερηφανίᾳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν Φιλοδοξίᾳ ἐποίησα τοῦτο τὸ μὴ προσκυνῆσαι τὸν ὑπερήφανον Αμαν, ὅτι ἐδώκαν Φιλεῖν πῖλμαςι ἐπὶ ἀντ᾽ ἔσωσα. Ἰνα μὴ δῶ δόξαν ἀνθρώπῳ ὑπερέχοντι δόξης Θεοῦ, ἡ ὁ προσκυνῆσαι ἐδίνα, πλὼ σε κύει, ἡ ὁ πίνειν αὐτῷ ἐν ὑπο- φαίᾳ. Cuncta nosti & scis, quia non pro superbia, & contumelia & aliqua gloriae cupiditate, fecerim hoc ut non adorarem Aman superbissimum (libenter enim pro salute Israël etiam vestigia pedum ejus deosculari paratus essem) Sed timui ne honorem Dei mei transferrem ad hominem, & ne quenquam adorarem excepto Deo meo.
units.tr: Certainly St Peter, whom they make the first and greatest Pope, when Cornelius the centurion threw himself at his feet in free adoration, and had not yet kissed them, did not allow it at all, knowing that Peter was not God, and he used this argument: because he himself is a man, Acts 10:25, 26. Not even an angel allowed himself to be worshipped by St John when he fell at his feet, Rev. 19:10. Hence we have seen Antonius above arguing very well that the Pope is greater than the angel. But also worthy of remembrance are the words of Mordecai in the Apocrypha, which our adversaries hold to be canonical, in the additions to Esther, chapter 13, verses 12, 13, 14, addressed to God himself: You know all things, you know, Lord, that I did this not in insolence, nor in pride, nor in love of glory, that I did not worship the proud Haman; for I would gladly have kissed the soles of his feet for the salvation of Israel. But I feared lest I should transfer the honour of my God to a man, and lest I should worship anyone except my God. [Σὺ πάντα οἶδας, κύριε, ὅτι οὐχ ὕβρεως οὐδὲ ὑπερηφανίας οὐδὲ φιλοδοξίας ἐποίησα τοῦτο τὸ μὴ προσκυνῆσαι τὸν ὑπερήφανον Αμαν.]

units.la: XXIV. S. Augustinus quin etiam magnam in eo superbiam agnoscit, qui pedibus suis Christianos velit subjicere. Explicans enim verba illa Psalmi xlvii. 4. subjecit populos nobis, & gentes sub pedibus nostris inter alia, Mirum, inquit, si Apostoli tam superbè loquerentur, & gauderent, gentes esse positas sub pedibus suis: id est, Christianos sub pedibus Apostolorum. Etenim gaudent nos esse sub pedibus illius, qui mortuus est pro nobis. Nam sub pedibus Pauli currebant, qui volebant esse Pauli, & dicebat eis: Num quid Paulus pro vobis crucifixus est? Quid ergo hic? Quid accepturi sumus? Subjecit plebes nobis, & gentes sub pedibus nostris. Omnes pertinentes ad haereditatem Christi in omnibus gentibus sunt, & omnes non pertinentes ad haereditatem Christi in omnibus gentibus sunt. En sensum Augustini, cui Christiani sic visi sunt subjecti pedibus solius Christi, ut schismatis, seu divisionis à Christo reos peragat, quotquot pedibus suis Christianos subjicere, adeòque sibi, non Christo mancipare conantur.
units.tr: XXIV. St Augustine even recognises great pride in the man who wishes to bring Christians under his feet. For explaining those words of Psalm 47:3, He subdued the peoples under us, and the nations under our feet, among other things he says: It would be strange if the apostles spoke and rejoiced so proudly that the nations were placed under their feet; that is, Christians under the feet of the apostles. For they rejoice that we are under the feet of him who died for us. For men ran under the feet of Paul, who wished to be Paul's, and he said to them: Was Paul crucified for you? What then is this? What are we going to receive? He has subdued the peoples under us and the nations under our feet. All who belong to the inheritance of Christ are among all nations, and all who do not belong to the inheritance of Christ are among all nations. Here is Augustine's meaning: he thought that Christians were so subject to the feet of Christ alone that he makes guilty of schism, that is of division from Christ, all who try to bring Christians under their own feet, and so to make them the property of themselves rather than of Christ.

units.la: XXV. Quid ergo Papae dicturus fuerat S. Pater, si ejus pedibus subjectos, imò pedes ejus plusquam serviliter osculantes, neque id liberè, sed lege lata inviolabili vidisset non promiscuè hos vel illos Christianos, plebejos, servos, sed cunctos, Tros Rutulisve suant, etiam Episcopos, Archiepiscopos, Cardinales, Reges, Imperatores? Qui si ad pedum osculA adacti sunt, magno jure ministri eorum Papae nates osculari tenerentur; uti de Rablaso illo Bellaii Praefulis sulis Papæ pedes osculantis famulo, post herum pedes Papæ deosculantem, Papæ approximare renuente cantavit nescio quis vates:
units.tr: XXV. What then would the holy Father have said of the Pope, if he had seen men subject to his feet, indeed kissing his feet more than servilely, and doing so not freely but under an inviolable law laid down, not only some Christians or others, common people or slaves, but all, Trojans or Rutulians alike, even bishops, archbishops, cardinals, kings and emperors? If these are driven to kiss the feet, then by right their ministers ought to be bound to kiss the Pope's buttocks; just as someone sang of that Rablasus, the servant of the Bishop of Bellai, who kissed the Pope's feet, and who, after his master had kissed the Pope's feet, refused to bring himself near the Pope:

units.la: Si Domino soleas porrexit ad oscula Pappas, Heu vereor servo porrigat ille nates.
units.tr: If the Pappas stretched out their feet for the Lord's soles to be kissed, I fear that the servant will then offer his buttocks.

units.la: Olim quidem Pontifices per multa Secula Imperatoribus se submisisse, clarissimè Rivetus Jesf. Vap. cap. 28. probavit. Octavo adhuc Seculo Papa Agatho ad Heraclium & Tiberium Augustos in sexta Synodo Constantinopol. Act. iv. Ep. j. scribens, promptam præceptis, jussioni eorum obedientiam, cum supplici cordis devotione, flexo mentis poplite &c. obstrinxerunt. Hadrianus quoque Papa sic A. 781. ad Constantinum & Irenem Synod. vy. Act. 2. scripsit: Pervestram JUSSIONEM exultatione sumus perfusi. Obsecrantes interim ex animi fervore vestram mansuetudinem obtestando, & veluti præsentes GENUBUS ADVOLUTI, & coram vestigia pedum volutando, ego cū fratribus meis coram Deo supplico, obtestor, adjuro.
units.tr: That popes once submitted themselves to emperors through many centuries, Rivetus has most clearly proved Jesf. Vap. cap. 28. Even in the eighth century, Pope Agatho, writing to the emperors Heraclius and Tiberius in the sixth Council of Constantinople Act. iv. Ep. j., said that they had bound themselves to prompt obedience to their precepts and commands, with a suppliant devotion of heart and with the knee of the mind bent, and so on. Pope Hadrian also wrote in the year 781 to Constantine and Irene Synod. vy. Act. 2. in this way: We have been filled with exultation through your COMMAND. Meanwhile, begging with fervour of spirit and imploring your mildness, and as though present, on OUR KNEES, and rolling ourselves before your feet, I with my brothers beseech, entreat and adjure before God.

units.la: XXVI. Quanta verò, Deum immortalem! deinceps rerum conversio secuta est? Quando videmus scilicet servos in equis, & Principes ambulantes super terram, quasi servos, Ecclef. x. 7. Quando, ut Blondi Rom. Instaur. lib. iy. verbis utar, Dictatorem (non olim, sed) nunc perpetuum, non Cæsaris sed Piscatoris Petri successorem, & Imperatoris (Christi) vicarium Pontificem Summum, Principes orbis & adorant & colunt. Quando, uti famosus ille Marcellus Cerem. S. lib. iy. tit. 1. pag. 113. sententias Papæ loquens scribit, Imperator, Reges, maximi Principes, & omnes alii in omnibus actibus pedem & manum Papæ osculantur. Exempla osculantium Imperatorum non pauca ipsi Papistæ decantant; veluti Justiniani II. Anastasius Bibliothecarius apud Baronium A. 710. n. 2. & Stevanus pag. 87. 88. Caroli M. idem Stevanus pag. 92.
units.tr: XXVI. But, immortal God, what a reversal of affairs followed after this? When do we see servants on horses, and princes walking on the earth as servants, Eccles. 10:7? When, to use the words of Blondus Rom. Instaur. lib. iv., do the princes of the world both worship and honour the Dictator, not formerly but now for life, the successor not of Caesar but of the fisherman Peter, and the Sovereign Pontiff, vicar of the Emperor (Christ)?
