When, as the notorious Marcellus Cerem. S. lib. iv. tit. 1. pag. 113., writing about the decrees of the Pope, records, the Emperor, kings, the greatest princes and all others kiss the foot and hand of the Pope in all their acts. The Papists themselves sing of not a few examples of emperors kissing: for instance, of Justinian II, as Anastasius the Librarian reports in Baronius A. 710. n. 2., and Stevanus pp. 87, 88. of Charlemagne, the same Stevanus p. 92.

units.la: Marginal notes in the right margin are small and partly illegible: "ut modo morbi horrenda", "Imperatores", "lege lata, ad osculandum". Diana Resol. 3. p. 3. Sigismundi Bulengerus adv. Casaub. pag. 30. Caroli V. Stevanus pag. 129. Regum & Principum exempla ab eodem Stevano, Diana & aliis jactata ad compendium pono. Jactata, dico. Nam de singulis fidem non fecerint; saltem quæ ex comitate delata sunt; quasi ex contractu jam deberi perperam illi censent. Sed quosdam serviliter oculatos, & oculantes, veluti Carolum V. & Carolum VIII. Regem Galliæ Romæ depictos, vel æri incisos, compertum est. Mirumne ergo cuiquam est, Imperatores & Reges Papolatras plures cruentis contra fideles consiliis innexos esse hactenus, cùm à pedibus Papæ nonnisi cruentum & pollutum os referre possint; uti non insciTE Budæus de Asse p. 436. dixit.
units.tr: Marginal notes in the right margin are small and partly illegible: "as if in a horrible disease", "Emperors", "a law passed, for kissing". Diana Resol. 3. p. 3. Sigismund Bullinger against Casaubon p. 30. Charles V, Stevanus p. 129. I set down briefly the examples of kings and princes bandied about by the same Stevanus, Diana and others. Bandied about, I say; for they have not established the truth of each one, at least of those that have been reported as a courtesy, which they wrongly think are already owed as if by contract. But it has been found that some emperors and kings, such as Charles V and Charles VIII, King of France, were depicted at Rome, or engraved in bronze, as servilely looking at and kissing the feet. Is it any wonder, then, that emperors and kings, who are Pope-worshippers, have so far been bound to many bloody counsels against the faithful, since from the feet of the Pope they can bring back nothing but a bloody and polluted mouth, as Budé, not unknowingly, said de Asse p. 436.

units.la: XXVII. Tam rigidi insuper Pontifices sunt adorationis & oculi hujus exactores, ut si quando in coronatione Imperatoris ob absentiam Papæ exigi nequiverunt, legati Pontificii solenniter protestati sint, nihil sic juri Papæ derogari.
units.tr: XXVII. Moreover, the Pontiffs are such strict exactors of this adoration and kissing that, when on some occasion at the coronation of an emperor, because of the Pope's absence, it could not be exacted, the papal legates solemnly protested that nothing had thereby been detracted from the Pope's right.

units.la: Quomodo in coronatione Caroli IV. voluit Innocentius Pontifex (verba refero ejusdem Marcelli pag. 65.) quòd Cardinales ad hoc delegati publicè protestarentur Domino Imperatori, quòd propter omissionem reverentiarum, obsequiorum & multarum ceremoniarum, quæ pertinent ad personam Romani Pontificis, non esset aliquo modo derogatum privilegiis & honorificentiæ Romanæ Sedis & successorum. Et de hac protestatione & consensu Imperatoris exigerent quadruplices literas, Regalibus & Imperialibus sigillis munitas: sicut factum. O horrendam metamorphosin! Tu, Domine Jesu, non habuisti, ubi reclinares caput tuum. Isti, vicarii tui scilicet, habeant ipsas Regum Imperatorumque cervices, quibus incumbant etiam pede, & premant nolentes pro authoritate officii! Veniet tempus, quando non catulus aliquis morsu (quomodo quondam pusillus catulus Comitis Angli Wiltonien-sis, fis, pedes Papæ protensos osculari dedignati, eosdem gemmis auróque radiantes lascivis dentibus morsúque, uti Britannicæ Antiquitates à Joffelino collectæ referunt, appetiit, indignante Papa, & ridentibus Anglis) sed Cœlestis Judex piacularibus flammis scelus ulciscetur.
units.tr: As at the coronation of Charles IV, Pope Innocent wished (I cite the words of the same Marcellus p. 65.) that the cardinals delegated for this purpose should publicly protest to the lord Emperor that, because of the omission of reverences, obsequies and many ceremonies which pertain to the person of the Roman Pontiff, nothing was in any way detracted from the privileges and honour of the Roman See and its successors. And they were to demand four letters of this protest and of the Emperor's consent, fortified with royal and imperial seals; and so it was done. O horrible transformation! You, Lord Jesus, had nowhere to lay your head. Those, namely your vicars, may have the very necks of kings and emperors, on which they may rest even their foot, and press them down against their will by the authority of their office! The time will come when not some puppy, as once the little puppy of the English Earl of Wilton, who disdained to kiss the outstretched feet of the Pope, and attacked them, shining with gems and gold, with playful teeth and bite (as the British Antiquities collected by Joscelyn relate), the Pope being indignant and the English laughing, but the heavenly Judge with expiatory flames will avenge the crime.

units.la: XXVIII. Sed id omne vergere in honorem ipsius Christi, cujus Papa in mundo vicarius sit, Papolatræ causantur. Quis verò unquam vicarius (quanquam Christi vices ne quidem Papa gerit) impunè delibavit honores soli Regi debitos? Etiamsi, sic ipse Navarrus Tom. j. com. in can. Humanæ aures, scribit, vicarius honorandus sit, tanquam vicem tenens & locum principalis Domini, tamen non eodem honore. Idque ex hoc ipso ritu osculationis pedum probat. Osculamur, inquit, pedes Papæ honoris gratia, non tamen facimus id ejus gratia etiam à latere, minùs ejus delegato. Si legatus, vicarius Pontificis, non eodem quo Pontifex honore affici debet, cùm uterque tamen homo sit: quomodo vicario Christi honor Christi, qui Deus & homo est, adeóque infinities major, competere potest? Sed duo insuper sunt, quæ nullam hic honoris Christi rationem haberi, apertè satis comprobant.
units.tr: XXVIII. But the Papists plead that all this tends to the honour of Christ himself, whose vicar the Pope is in the world. Yet what vicar (although the Pope does not even bear Christ's office) has ever gone unpunished for taking the honours due to the King alone? Even so, Navarrus himself writes in Tom. i. com. in can. Humanae aures, that the vicar is to be honoured as one holding the place and position of the principal Lord, yet not with the same honour. And he proves this from this very rite of kissing the feet. We kiss, he says, the feet of the Pope for the sake of honour, yet we do not do this for his sake even when he is at our side, much less for his delegate. If the legate, the vicar of the Pontiff, ought not to be honoured with the same honour as the Pontiff, although both are men: how can the honour of Christ, who is God and man, and therefore infinitely greater, be due to the vicar of Christ? But there are two further matters which clearly enough prove that no regard for the honour of Christ is had here.

units.la: XXIX. Prius est, quòd Papa in sexta Dominica Quadragesimæ in Palmis à persona illa, quæ Christum repræsentat, pedibus suis osculum infigi patitur. De eo sic Marcellus Cerem. S. lib. ÿ. pag. 89. scribit: Ibi tres dicturi passionum parantur amictu, qui Euangelistæ personam sustinet, albo, Judæus rubro, Christus nigro. Et circa finem tractus movent se à loco, ubi se induerant, & ille, qui Euangelistam aget, portat librum & præcedit; sequitur Judæus; deinde Christus. Faciunt reverentiam altari & Papæ, deinde
units.tr: XXIX. The first is that the Pope, on the sixth Sunday of Lent, on Palm Sunday, allows a kiss to be imprinted on his feet by the person who represents Christ. Of this Marcellus writes thus, Cerem. S. lib. v. p. 89.: "There three who are to speak of the passion are prepared, the one who sustains the person of the Evangelist in a white vestment, the Jew in red, Christ in black. And near the end of the procession they move from the place where they had dressed, and he who will act the Evangelist carries the book and goes before; the Jew follows; then Christ. They make reverence to the altar and to the Pope, then"

units.la: XXX de ascendunt ad osculum pedis Papæ, unus post alium, prout venerunt, &c. Viden Christum ipsum, seu eum, qui Christi personam gerit, æquè ac Euangelistam & Judæum, Papæ pedibus oscula figentem? In cujus ergo honorem Christus Papæ pedes osculatur?
units.tr: XXX. "they go up to kiss the foot of the Pope, one after another, in the order in which they came, etc." Do you see Christ himself, or he who bears Christ's person, just like the Evangelist and the Jew, fixing kisses on the feet of the Pope? In whose honour, then, does Christ kiss the feet of the Pope?

units.la: XXX. Posterius est, quòd Papa calceo, quem osculandum porrigit, intextam phrygionis opere habet crucem. Quæ non obscura professio est, crucem Christi à Papa non honorari, sed conculcari, ad pedes scilicet abjiciente id, quod in Ecclesia Romana cultu latriæ adoratur. Atque hic notabile etiam illud est, quòd Imperatores & Reges crucem in capite & diademate suo; at Papa in pedibus eam gestat. De quo more impio & profano, si quispiam alius est, sic apud Dianam Resol. j. p. 1. Papirius Massonus, scriptor Pontificius scribit: Qui mos an sit antiquissimus, nescio. Nondum enim omnia legi. Sed hoc scio, consuetudinem illam Cisalpinis populis minùs probari, quàm Italicæ genti, ad hujus generis obsequia & demissiones natæ. Nati sint ergo Itali ad hujus generis obsequia impia, & parùm ab Atheïsmo sejuncta. Nos Cisalpini ab iis toto pectore abhorremus, ne incidamus in pœnam eorum, qui Filium Dei conculcant, & sanguinem ejus profanum ducunt, Hebr. x. 29.
units.tr: XXX. The second is that the Pope has upon his shoe, which he offers to be kissed, a cross woven in gold thread. This is no obscure profession that the cross of Christ is not honoured by the Pope but trampled underfoot, since he casts down at his feet that which in the Roman Church is adored with the worship of latria. And here this is also notable, that emperors and kings wear the cross on their head and diadem, but the Pope wears it on his feet. Concerning this impious and profane custom, if any other man is to be heard, Papirius Masson, a Papist writer, says thus in Diana Resol. i. p. 1.: "Whether this custom is very ancient, I do not know, for I have not yet read everything. But this I know, that the custom is less approved among the peoples on this side of the Alps than among the Italian nation, which was born for such servile obeisances and prostrations. So let the Italians be born for such impious obsequies, which are scarcely separated from atheism. We of this side of the Alps abhor them with our whole heart, lest we fall into the punishment of those who trample underfoot the Son of God and count his blood profane, Heb. 10:29."

units.la: XXXI. Neque omnino insignitam impietatem illam purgavit Diana, qui Resol. 20. pag. 16. 17. obtendit, Papas crucem sandaliis seu calceamentis fixisse, ut Christi fideles coram genubus advoluti, & ad eorum prostrati pedes, deosculentur non tam eorum pedes, quàm Christi triumphale signum adorent; ipsíque Papæ à se honorem illum ad Christi Domini gloriam transferant, & tam suavi pedum præconio crucem Christi popopulo commendent. Veram Christi crucem, sive quam ipse pertulit, sive quam fidelibus imposuit, pro stultitia illi habent: præconium crucis ejus, ceu rem vilem & indignam aspernantur, ac posteriore loco amandant; denique cum Leone X. in sinu rident, quòd illæ de Christo & cruce ejus fabulæ, multùm sibi profuerint. Pictam verò fictámque crucem, quam Christus & fideles vicissim pro stultitia habent merito, loco corporis sordido intexunt, atque sic honori Christi egregiè scilicet illi velificantur. Decipimur specie recti, verba Polydori Vergilii, ex libro ejus quarto, cap. 13. Expurgatorum spongia expuncta sunt, & sæpe cum Caligula pedes protendimus, dum Christi humilitatem vel spernimus, vel fucato confervandæ Apostolica authoritatis titulo exornare laboramus. Quis amabo in Dominos redundabit honos, si Ministri illorum & Legati publica eorum instrumenta non manibus teneant, tracténtque, sed fœdis pedibus intexta & infixa propinent? Quin potiùs ore & pedibus illi ad Euangelizandum & veram Christi crucem ex puro Dei verbo prædicandam, non sordidis soccis vel calceamentis ad exponendum Judibrio impiorum hominum Christum uterentur? Sed & hac in re præivere illis non Christus, non Petrus, non ullus Apostolus, non ullus Imperator Christianus (cujus potiùs pedem, & in pede crucem, si decorum foret ibi eam pingere, Papa osculari deberet) sed Caligula, Diocletianus, Maximinus, calceamenta sua auro, gemmis, margaritis, velut osculantium illecebra quadam; perinde atque hi ofores veræ crucis, fiêta & aurea cruce exornantes; uti ex Seneca & Pomponio Lœto supra ostendimus.
units.tr: XXXI. Nor has Diana wholly purged that marked impiety, who in Resol. 20. pp. 16, 17. alleges that the Popes have fixed the cross on their sandals or shoes, so that the faithful of Christ, kneeling and prostrate at their feet, may kiss not so much their feet as adore the triumphal sign of Christ; and the Popes themselves transfer that honour from themselves to the glory of the Lord Christ, and by such a sweet proclamation of the feet commend the cross of Christ to the people. The true cross of Christ, whether the one he himself bore or the one he laid upon the faithful, they hold to be foolishness; the proclamation of his cross they scorn as a base and unworthy thing, and push it to the last place; finally, with Leo X they laugh in their sleeve, that those fables about Christ and his cross have served them very well. But the painted and feigned cross, which Christ and the faithful in turn rightly hold to be foolishness, they weave into a filthy part of the body, and thus they sail, forsooth, to the honour of Christ in a remarkable way. We are deceived by the appearance of the right, words of Polydore Vergil, from his fourth book, ch. 13. Things have been expunged by the sponge of the expurgators, and often we stretch out our feet as Caligula did, while we either scorn the humility of Christ or strive to adorn it with the counterfeit title of preserving apostolic authority. Tell me, whose honour will spill over upon the Lords, if their ministers and legates do not hold and handle their public instruments in their hands, but offer them woven and fixed upon foul feet? Would they not rather use their mouths and feet for evangelising and preaching the true cross of Christ from the pure Word of God, rather than for exposing Christ to the mockery of impious men in dirty socks or shoes? But in this matter they were preceded not by Christ, not by Peter, not by any Apostle, not by any Christian emperor (whose foot, and the cross on the foot, the Pope ought to kiss, if it were proper to paint the cross there), but by Caligula, Diocletian and Maximinus, who adorned their shoes with gold, gems and pearls, as a kind of lure to those kissing; just as those who forge the true cross decorate it with a feigned and golden cross; as we have shown above from Seneca and Pomponius Laetus.

units.la: XXXII. Haud felicior Stevanus de Ofcul当 pedum
units.tr: XXXII. No happier is Stevanus on the Kissing of Feet

units.la: cap. 3. Pontificem crucem pedibus impressisse nos edocet, cet, juxta illud Pfal. LXVIII. 24. Ut intingatur pes tuus in sanguine, lingua canum tuorum ex inimicis, ab Ipso: uti male Vulgatus Interpres Hebræa reddidit. Quid enim ex verbis, uti jacent, Papæ applicatis, aliud quàm Mulierem illam ebriam sanguine Sanctorum, & sanguine Martyrum Jesu, extundi rectius potest? Sed lepidè satis Stevanus: Tunc pedes sanguine tinguntur, cùm cruce Christi decorantur. Tunc linguæ canum imbuuntur sanguine, cùm hæretici, canum more, vestigia Summi Sacerdotis lingunt, & crucem sandaliis impressam osculantur. Mirumne ergo, repeto salem Budæi, dignum scilicet, quo carnis Stevani putredo perfricetur, Imperatores & Reges Papæ pedem osculantes, os inde cruentum referre, & ferro flammáque adversus eos, qui veram crucem fictæ piętæque præferunt, sævire? Sed ampliùs quid insani illius hominis verba portendunt; canes scilicet, hæreticos, inimicos Christi esse, qui vestigia Summi Sacerdotis lingunt, & crucem sandaliis impressam osculantur. Sunto sanè, & pace nostra sunto. Cæterùm verba Davidis obtorto collo ad stabilienda pedum Papæ osculæ Jesuita rapuit. Sic enim habent: Ut altè deprimas pedem tuum in sanguinem, linguam canum tuorum, ex Inimicis, ex illo. Sensus est, ita verberaturum Deum caput inimicorum suorum, verticem illum comatum (v. 22.) ut sanguis fluat ex inimicis ejus, tanta copia, ut pedem & linguam canum in eo demergere in proclivi futurum sit. Si Stevano innotesceret mysterium Capitis illius comati Inimici, non jam osculum pedum Papæ ex verbis illis invita Minerva elicere conaretur, sed potiùs impiæ illius osculationis pedum Papæ poenam justam subodoraretur facilè.
units.tr: In chapter 3 Stevanus teaches that the Pontiff pressed a cross with his feet, citing that saying of Psalm 68:24, That your foot may be dipped in blood, and the tongue of your dogs in your enemies, from him, as the Vulgate translator badly rendered the Hebrew. For what could more fitly be drawn from these words, as they stand, and applied to the Pope than that drunken woman of the blood of the saints and of the martyrs of Jesus? But Stevanus is witty enough: The feet are dipped in blood when they are adorned with the cross of Christ. The tongues of the dogs are steeped in blood when heretics, like dogs, lick the footsteps of the High Priest and kiss the cross impressed on his sandals. Is it any wonder, then, I ask, with Budaeus's salt, which is evidently fit to rub into the rotting flesh of Stevanus, that emperors and kings who kiss the Pope's foot come away with a bloodied mouth, and rage with sword and fire against those who put the true cross before a feigned and pious one? But what do the words of that mad man imply further? That dogs, that is heretics and enemies of Christ, are those who lick the footsteps of the High Priest and kiss the cross impressed on his sandals. Let them be so, and welcome to them. But the Jesuit has snatched David's words, twisted by the neck, to establish the kissing of the Pope's feet. For they read: That you may deeply press your foot into the blood, the tongue of your dogs from your enemies, from that one. The sense is that God will so strike the head of his enemies, that hairy crown (v. 22), that blood will flow from his enemies in such abundance that it will be easy to plunge foot and dog's tongue into it. If the mystery of that hairy-crowned enemy's head were known to Stevanus, he would not now try to extract from those words, against Minerva's will, a kissing of the Pope's feet; he would rather easily sniff out the just punishment for that impious kissing of the Pope's feet.

units.la: XXXIII. Neque illud prætereundum est, quòd idem Stevanus, Bullengerus, Diana, alii probare pedum Papæ osculandorum necessitatem conantur iis Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ de solo Deo disertè loquuntur. Ita enim verba Psal. lxxii. 11. Et incurvabunt se ei omnes Reges, omnes gentes servient ci; de Christo sine omni exceptione dicta, tum Romani, visis oculis, quæ Saracenorum Princeps & Comites Alexandro III. fixerunt, in eundem Papam; teste Baronio ad ann. 1162. n. 2, 3. tum Ant. Puccius in Concilio Lateranensi V. Sess. 9. in Papam Leonem X. deflexerunt. Et Stevanus pag. 55. verba Psal. xcix. 45. Tu stabilivisti rectitudinem. Judicium & justitiam fecisti in Jacob. Exaltate Jehovam Deum nostrum, & adorate scabellum pedum ejus: ad Papam traduxit eo argumento, quòd ipse justitiam maximè tueatur, & ad ipsum, tanquam supremum Christi Magistratum provocatio fiat. Sed verba Psalmis de exaltando Jehova, & adorando scabello pedum ejus aperte loquuntur. Sic jam Deo justitiæ authori & vindici unico, & Papæ, maximè scilicet justitiam tuenti, & supremo Christi Magistratui, unus idemque honos debebitur. Idem Stevanus pag. 29. verba Esai. lx. 14. Adorabunt ad plantas pedum tuorum omnes spernentes te; de Christo ἀνενδυάτως intelligenda, ad Papam referre non erubescit. Si Christi, inquit, pedibus osculla deferuntur, nonne & Ecclesiæ, quæ est caro de carne Christi? Taceo transubstantiationem Ecclesiæ in Papam. Saltem inde constat, Papæ & Christo unum cundemque honorem homines illos asserere; & quæ de Christo dicuntur, ad Papam rapere. Loca Esai. xlv. 23. & xlix. 7. de Christo clarè vaticinantia ad se abinsanis verpis trahi, Innocentius X. passus est, narrante Banckio Romæ Triumph. pag. 331. &c. Idem Stevanus nus pag. 23, 26. nec non Diana pag. 3. quæ Matth xxviii. 9. & Luc. xxiv. 52. de religiosa Christi adoratione, non de pedibus nudi hominis, osculo cultis, dicuntur, Papæ eadem eximia faciunt, & ex iis osculandos ejus pedes esse, conficere satagunt. Sed & ex osculo Christi pedibus à Muliere fixo Luc. vii. 38. Stevanus pag. 22, 23. necessitatem osculandorum pedum Papæ probare nititur. Poene oblitus eram, quòd Diana, Stevanus, Lorinus consentientes, verba illa Deuteron. xxxiii. 2, 3. In manu dextra illius ignea lex. Dilexit populos. Omnes Sancti in manu illius sunt, & qui appropinquant pedibus ejus, accipient de doctrina illius, à Mose de uno Jehova illo, qui venit in montem Sion, & illuxit è Paran &c. pronuntiata, non dubitant ad oscula Papalium pedum trahere. Cùm Romanus Pontifex, ita Stevanus cap. 10. scribit, omnes homines Christi authoritate perfunctus, Legem Dei ut Magister & (NB) Legislator edoceat, controversiasque omnes ut Judex dissolvat, status excellentia omnibus præsit; in fide & religione aberrantes fratres instituat, atque confirmet: meritò ad ejus pedes exosculandos accedimus, ut religionis & fidei disciplina imbuamur. Quod ex Deut. 33. liquidò constare arbitror &c. Quamobrem meritò ad Pontificis nostri pedes pervolvimur, non tam ut hoc humili pietatis voto ejus summam dignitatem atque excellentiam indicemus, quàm quòd etiam dum ejus pedibus obvolvimur, certissimis fidei & religionis institutis imbuamur. Non occurrerunt credo alii de pedum osculis, vel teverentia Deo & Christo Symbolo hoc deferenda textus; non immunes aliàs haud dubiè à fœdissima hac à Divino ad Papalem honorem detorsione futuri. Saltem hinc clarissimè constat, adorationem Papæ per osculà pedum, Divinum religiosum cultum, qualis uni soli quæ vero Deo debetur, à Papolatris haberi.
units.tr: XXXIII. Nor must it be passed over that the same Stevanus, Bullinger, Diana and others try to prove the necessity of kissing the Pope's feet by those testimonies of Scripture which speak plainly of God alone. For the words of Psalm 72:11, And all kings shall bow down before him, all nations shall serve him, spoken of Christ without any exception, were applied to the same Pope by the Romans, once they had seen the eyes which the Saracen Prince and the Counts fixed on Alexander III, as Baronius attests at the year 1162, n. 2, 3; and Antonius Puccius at the Fifth Lateran Council, session 9, turned them toward Pope Leo X. Stevanus, at page 55, also drew the words of Psalm 99:5 into the Pope's service, You have established righteousness; you have done judgement and justice in Jacob. Exalt Jehovah our God, and worship at his footstool, on the ground that he especially upholds justice, and an appeal is made to him as the supreme magistrate of Christ. But the words of the Psalm about exalting Jehovah and worshipping at his footstool speak plainly. So one and the same honour will be owed both to God, the sole author and avenger of justice, and to the Pope, who of course especially upholds justice and is the supreme magistrate of Christ. The same Stevanus, at page 29, without any hesitation applies the words of Isaiah 60:14, They shall bow down at the soles of your feet, all who despised you, which must be understood of Christ [ἀνενδυάτως], to the Pope. If kisses are offered to the feet of Christ, he says, are they not also due to the Church, which is flesh of Christ's flesh? I say nothing of the transubstantiation of the Church into the Pope. At least this shows clearly that those men assert one and the same honour for the Pope and for Christ, and snatch to the Pope what is said of Christ. Innocent X endured Isaiah 45:23 and 49:7, passages clearly prophesying of Christ, being dragged by the impious into his own service, as Banckius relates in Romae Triumphans, page 331, etc. The same Stevanus, at pages 23, 26, and Diana at page 3, do the same excellent work with Matthew 28:9 and Luke 24:52, which speak of the religious worship of Christ, not of kissing the feet of a naked man, and strive to conclude from them that the Pope's feet are to be kissed. But Stevanus, at pages 22, 23, also tries to prove the necessity of kissing the Pope's feet from the kissing of Christ's feet by the woman, Luke 7:38. Almost forgetting it: Diana, Stevanus and Lorinus, in agreement, do not hesitate to draw Deuteronomy 33:2, 3, In his right hand a fiery law. He loved the peoples. All the saints are in his hand, and those who draw near to his feet shall receive of his teaching, which Moses pronounced of that one Jehovah who came to Mount Sion and shone forth from Paran, toward the kissing of the Papal feet. Since the Roman Pontiff, Stevanus writes in chapter 10, is invested with the authority of Christ over all men, teaches the law of God as Master and (NB) Lawgiver, resolves all controversies as Judge, and presides over all by the excellence of his station, and instructs and confirms the brethren who go astray in faith and religion: we rightly approach to kiss his feet, that we may be imbued with the discipline of religion and faith. I think this is clear from Deut. 33, etc. Wherefore we rightly throw ourselves at the feet of our Pontiff, not so much to show by this humble vow of piety his supreme dignity and excellence, as that, while we cling to his feet, we may be imbued with the most certain precepts of faith and religion. I think no other texts about kissing feet or the reverence to be paid to God and Christ have occurred to them, though they would otherwise surely not be exempt from this most foul twisting of the divine honour to the Papal. At least from this it is most clearly established that the Papolaters regard the adoration of the Pope by kissing his feet as divine religious worship, the kind due to the one true God alone.

units.la: XXXIV. Atque id ipsum nunc certis & irrefragabilibus argumentis confirmandum restat; ne Divino & re- ligioso honore à se Numen isthoc coli, inficiari, adeó- que de injuria sibi facta, uti solent, quos Papolatriæ pudet, expostulationem facere sustineant. Quanquam enim ex iis, quæ hactenus diximus, inprimis nefario va-
units.tr: XXXIV. This very point now remains to be confirmed by certain and irrefutable arguments, lest those who are ashamed of Papolatry dare to deny that this Deity is worshipped by them with divine and religious honour, and so, as they usually do, lodge a complaint of injury done to them. For although from what we have said so far, above all the wicked...

units.la: XXXV. Cultus & honos omnis vel civilis seu humanus, vel religiosus seu Divinus est. Illum dilectionis & societatis, hunc servitutem Divinitati debitam, S. Augustinus contra Faust. Manich. lib. xx. 21: appellat. Cùm enim cultus & honos amoris quædam species sit; & amor omnis vel Dei vel proximi sit, non aliæ etiam honoris cultúsque species, quàm Divini & humani obtinere possunt. Accedit, quòd omnis cultus & honor recognitio quædam est excellentiæ personæ illius, quæ honoratur, ex affectu sic illam recognoscendi. Excelcellentia autem omnis vel finita, vel infinita est. Illa personæ finitæ, quales Angelus & homo sunt; hæc infinitæ, quæ Deus est. Illa proin cultu civili, humano, societatis, dilectionis: hæc religioso & Divino recognoscitur. Neque medium inter duo illa dari potest. Sic finitum inter & infinitum medium nihil interjacet.
units.tr: XXXV. Every honour and cultus is either civil or human, or religious or divine. Augustine, against Faustus the Manichean, book 20, chapter 21, calls the former the cultus of love and fellowship, and the latter the servitude owed to divinity. For since cultus and honour are a kind of love, and every love is either of God or of neighbour, there can be no kinds of honour and cultus other than divine and human. Moreover, every cultus and honour is a certain acknowledgement of the excellence of the person who is honoured, from the affection of acknowledging him so. But every excellence is either finite or infinite. The former belongs to finite persons, such as angels and men; the latter to the infinite, which is God. Therefore the former is acknowledged by civil, human cultus of fellowship and love; the latter by religious and divine. Nor can any middle ground be given between the two. Thus nothing lies between the finite and the infinite.

units.la: XXXVI. Tum omnis honos & cultus religiosus idem Divinus quoque est. Nam illi cultus religiosus debetur, in quem religio fertur. Fertur autem illa in solum Deum, ceu præcipua amoris Divini species. Unde Deus religionis objectum unicum & adeò adæquatum est, ut ad aliud illa objectum sine gravissima Dei injuria referri non possit. Huc enim spectat ille titulus Dei, quo passim ססק Zelotes, seu Zelotypus nuncupatur. Religio & veneratio (sic Lactantius Instit. Div. lib. j. 20. jam olim scripsit) nulla alia, nisi unius Dei tenenda est. Augustinus quoque de vera relig. cap. ult. apertè: Religet ergo nos religio uni omnipotenti Deo: quia inter mentem nostram, qua illum intelligimus Patrem & veritatem, hoc est, lucem interiorem, per quam illum intelligimus, nulla interposita est creatura. Ratio quoque, sub qua religio Deum respicit, est Divina illa excellentia, quæ in sufficientia & efficientia ejus elucet; adeóque non unum aliquod attributum, sed perfectio ex omnibus ejus attributis coalescens: quæ Exod. xxxiv. 6, 7. ab ipso Deo proclamatur. Omnis ergo cultus, qui vel ex natura & conditione sua, vel ex lege & consuetudine communi, vel ex mente & institutione deferentis, religiosum honorem alii defert, præterquam Deo vero, ille Deum novum ac falsum, catenus saltem, sibimet ipsi fingit. Et qui religiosum illum cultum Deo non defert, is profanus: qui alii quàm Deo defert, idololatra est, Act. x. 26. Apoc. xix. 10. & xx. 8.
units.tr: XXXVI. Then every honour and religious cultus is also divine. For religious cultus is owed to that in which religion terminates. But religion terminates in God alone, as the chief kind of divine love. Hence God is the sole and so adequate object of religion, that religion cannot be referred to any other object without the gravest injury to God. To this refers that title of God by which he is everywhere called Zelotes, or jealous. Religion and reverence (so Lactantius wrote long ago in Divine Institutes, book 1, chapter 20) must be held to no one but the one God. Augustine too plainly, On True Religion, last chapter: Let religion bind us to the one almighty God, since between our mind, by which we understand him as Father and truth, that is, the inner light by which we understand him, no creature is interposed. The ground also under which religion regards God is that divine excellence which shines forth in his sufficiency and efficiency, and so not any single attribute but the perfection coalescing from all his attributes, which is proclaimed by God himself in Exodus 34:6, 7. Therefore every cultus which, either by its nature and condition, or by law and common custom, or by the mind and institution of the one who offers it, gives religious honour to another than the true God, to that extent at least fashions for itself a new and false god. And whoever does not offer that religious cultus to God is profane; whoever offers it to anyone other than God is an idolater, Acts 10:26, Revelation 19:10 and 20:8.

units.la: XXXVII. Vel igitur omnis ille Pontificis cultus civilis, vel religiosus, adeóque Divinus est. Civilem esse, ex Papolatris largiuntur pauci: ii videlicet, qui nondum pudorem omnem decoxerunt, Politici nonnulli, qui se Papam, ut Principem politicum potentem, immensa illa ceremoniarum mole, adorare præferunt. Cùm verò is, qui tali adoratione civilem adorato honorem exhibet, eo ipso inferiorem se in civilibus profiteatur; Imperatores ergo, Reges & Principes, qui Papæ pedes osculantur, in civilibus & temporalibus se subesse Papæ profiteantur pariter, necessum est. Unde consequens est, Papam etiam in Civilibus & temporalibus directa & eminentissima potestate supra omnes alios pollere, adeóque esse Regem Regum, & Dominum dominantium: qui Babylonis, Magnæ illius Meretricis certissimus character est, Apoc. xvii. 18. Cúmque tantus honor civilis nullo jure Papæ competat, utpote ejus excellentia multis parasangis inferior, idololatriæ Politicæ labem eo ipso contrahit, adeóque in religiosum similémque illi, quem sibi Haman Nebucadnezar, Herodes haberi quondam jusserunt, degenerat.
units.tr: XXXVII. Either, then, all of that cult of the Pontiff is civil, or it is religious, and therefore divine. Few of the Papal worshippers concede that it is civil: those, namely, who have not yet cast off all shame, and some politicians, who prefer to adore the Pope as a powerful political prince, with that immense mass of ceremonies. But since whoever pays such adoration to the one adored thereby confesses himself inferior in civil matters, it is necessary that emperors, kings and princes who kiss the Pope's feet likewise profess themselves subject to the Pope in civil and temporal matters. Hence it follows that the Pope, in civil and temporal matters too, holds direct and supreme power over all others, and so is King of kings and Lord of lords. This is the most certain mark of Babylon, that great harlot (Rev. xvii. 18). And since such civil honour belongs to the Pope by no right, his excellence being many parasangs inferior, he thereby contracts the stain of political idolatry, and so degenerates into religious worship, similar to that which Haman, Nebuchadnezzar and Herod once ordered to be paid to themselves.

units.la: XXXVIII. Et sanè non civilem licitum, sed merè religiosum, uti veri Pontificii omnes testantur, adeóque Divinum honorem illum esse, jubare meridiano clarius est. Etenim primò honor ille Adorationis nomine venit. Nam libros de honore Papæ deferendo Mazaronins, Diana disertè de adoratione Papæ inscribunt: & in disputatione hac adorationis vox frequentissima est: & supra historicos induximus, qui adoratum Papam scripsere: & Romæ phrasis illa, Adorare Papam, in quotidiano usu est. Fatendum equidem, verbum הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה quod Græci προσκυνεῖν, Latini adorare reddunt; apud Hebræos pro-
units.tr: XXXVIII. And indeed, that this is not lawful civil honour but purely religious, as all true Papists attest, and so that this honour is divine, is clearer than midday sun. For, first, that honour goes by the name Adoration. Mazaronius and Diana plainly entitle their books on the honour to be paid to the Pope On the Adoration of the Pope; in this disputation the word adoration is very frequent; above we have cited historians who wrote of the adored Pope; and the Roman phrase to adore the Pope is in everyday use. I admit that the Hebrew word הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה [hishtachawah], which the Greeks render προσκυνεῖν [proskynein] and the Latins adorare, is among the Hebrews pro-

units.la: Y y y miscuum esse, & Deo juxta atque creaturis tribui. Sed primò tantum apud Orientales, ex quorum usu illa sunt, quæ in Scripturis legimus. Occidentales verò ceremoniarum harum fuère parciores, atque apud eos προσκύνησις adoratio non usitata fuit, nisi in Sacris: neque aut admissa, nisi ab iis, quibus tyrannidis insolentia mentem mutâsset; aut delata nisi ab iis, qui servilem in modum potentioribus adulari sueverunt. Quod verò ita in V. T. promiscuum erat, illud in N. T. Christianos inter cultui religiosò factum est eximium. Nunquam proin in N. T. legas aliter: & improbata προσκύνησις adoratio, cùm Petro, Angelo, quanquam neutri ut Deo, delata est. Neque apud veteres Theologos aliter legas, donec quidam posteriorum seculorum idololatria fascinari cœperunt. Quanquam hodie modestiores Pontificii à se adorari Sanctos, imagines negant: metuentes scilicet, ne sibi eos adorantibus impingatur merito, quòd Divinum iis honorem tribuant. Denique nunquam illi ferent, ut dicatur, Imperatorem, Reges, Principes adorari debere: quamvis civili & humano honore summo eos colendos esse constat. Cùm ergo Papam adorandum esse scisci unt, alium certè honorem, quàm civilem & humanum, adeóque ei immediatè oppositum religiosum & Divinum intelligant oportet.
units.tr: miscuous, and is attributed both to God and to creatures. But this was so only among the Orientals, from whose usage those things come that we read in the Scriptures. The Occidentals, however, were more sparing of these ceremonies, and among them προσκύνησις [proskynēsis], adoration, was in use only in sacred matters; nor was it admitted except by those whom the insolence of tyranny had changed in mind, nor was it paid except by those who were accustomed to flatter the more powerful in a servile manner. But what was common in the Old Testament became, in the New, a special part of religious worship among Christians. Therefore you will never read otherwise in the New Testament: adoration, προσκύνησις, when disapproved, was offered to Peter and to an angel, though neither as to God. Nor will you read otherwise among the ancient theologians, until some writers of later centuries began to be bewitched by idolatry. Even today the more moderate Papists deny that saints and images are adored by them, fearing, of course, that the charge would rightly be brought against them, that by adoring these they ascribe divine honour to them. Finally, they will never allow it to be said that the emperor, kings and princes ought to be adored, although it is agreed that they are to be honoured with the highest civil and human honour. Since, therefore, they decree that the Pope is to be adored, they must understand some other honour than civil and human, namely a religious and divine honour, which is immediately opposed to these.

units.la: XXXIX. Frustra ergo Diana Resol. 2. p. 2. nomen adorationis commune Deo, Angelis & hominibus facit, idque ea ratione, quòd in Deo & creaturis reperiatur excellentia adoratione digna. Si de honore & cultu sermo foret, id admitti posset. At de adoratione, juxta vim vocis, à Christo, Apostolis & omnibus Christianis veris in N. T. usurpatæ, admitti neutiquam potest. Nam quòd idem Diana illam προσκύνησιν adorationem allegat, quam à Christo Sathanas Matth. iv. 9. exigere ausus est, nec
units.tr: XXXIX. In vain, therefore, does Diana (Resol. 2. p. 2.) make adoration a name common to God, angels and men, and that for this reason: because excellence worthy of adoration is found in God and in creatures. If the discussion were of honour and cult, this might be admitted. But as to adoration, in the sense of the word used by Christ, the Apostles and all true Christians in the New Testament, it can by no means be admitted. For as to the fact that the same Diana cites that προσκύνησις [proskynēsis], adoration, which Satan dared to demand from Christ (Matth. iv. 9), nor

units.la: Diana exter-ptio, quòd adorationis nomen commune fit, vtnitur. nec non illam, quam Cornelius S. Petro Act. x. 25. detulit: profecto suo se mucrone sauciavit. Nam adorationem à Sathana exactam Christus repulit v. 10. eo argumento, quòd scriptum sit: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli servies. Pariter S. Petrus Cornelium adorantem v. 26. iussit surgere; eo argumento quòd etiam ipse homo sit. Annon hinc clarissime liquet, juxta stylum N. T. adorationem omnem uni soliquę Deo deferendam esse: & nullam homini ulli deferendam esse; adeoque adorationem Papæ delatam non aliam, quàm religiosam & Divinam esse posse.
units.tr: that which Cornelius offered to St Peter (Act. x. 25), he has certainly wounded himself with his own sword. For Christ repelled the adoration demanded by Satan (v. 10) on the ground that it is written: You shall adore the Lord your God, and serve him alone. Likewise St Peter, when Cornelius was adoring him, bade him rise (v. 26), on the ground that he too was a man. Does not this most clearly show that, according to the style of the New Testament, all adoration is to be paid to the one God alone, and none is to be paid to any man; and so the adoration paid to the Pope can be nothing other than religious and divine?

units.la: XL. Secundò religiosam & Divinam esse adorationem Papæ, multò magis res ipsa loquitur. Nam defertur ei personæ, quam sibi Divinitatem arrogare, ex titulis, & octo attributorum Divinorum, in quorum prædam Aquila hæc rapacissima involavit, complexione, superiori diatriba fecimus manifestum. Qualis excellentia putatur esse personæ, quæ colitur, talis cultus ipse est: quod fundamentum suæ disputationi Diana substravit. Atqui Papæ excellentia Divina putatur, non quasi æternum & infinitum Numen verbis afferatur, sed quia ea ei vendicantur, quæ soli&us Dei αὐτοκράτορα sunt. Cultus ergo, quo is colitur, merè religiosus & Divinus sit oportet. Quæ etiam haud dubiè causa est, quòd adorationem Papæ, uti jam jam vidimus, iisdem textibus probatum cunt, quibus Dei & Christi adoratio præcipitur.
units.tr: XL. Secondly, that the adoration of the Pope is religious and divine, the thing itself speaks far more loudly. For it is paid to a person who claims divinity for himself, as we have made plain in the previous discourse from his titles and from the combination of the eight divine attributes, into whose spoils this most rapacious eagle has swooped. Whatever the excellence of the person who is worshipped is thought to be, such is the cult itself; this is the foundation Diana laid for his argument. But the excellence of the Pope is held to be divine, not because an eternal and infinite Deity is named in words, but because those things are claimed for him which belong to God alone, that is, αὐτοκράτορα [autokratora], absolute authority. The cult by which he is worshipped, therefore, must be purely religious and divine. This is also doubtless the reason why the adoration of the Pope, as we have just seen, has been proved by the very texts by which the adoration of God and of Christ is prescribed.

units.la: XLI. Nihil ergo Papolatrarum causam juvat, quòd se Papam à Deo, adeoque cultum etiam Papæ à cultu Dei distinguere; neque Papam pro æterno Deo venerari, protestantur. Quomodo Costerus Enchirid. cap. 3. nobis maximo crimini vertit, quòd dicamus, Papistas Papam pro Deo, ac loco Numinis venerari. Similis enim hic verborum lusus est, quem etiam in quæstione de ado-raratione Sanctorum ludere solent; verborum, inquam, meræ præstigiæ, rei verò ipsius certa confusio. Quomodo si latro se absolvi vellet, quòd se profiteretur bonum virum; aut meretrix, quòd se adulteram dici non patererentur, imò castæ matronæ elogium adfectaret. Quasi vix delicet nunquam res vera sua nomina amisissent; vel injustitia illa, qua capitaliorem nullam esse Cicero affirmat, ut qui malus est, bonum se haberi velit, non crebrò obtineat. Sic omnino solent Papolatræ rem dissimulare, contenti externo verborum crepitu. Nam cùm reapse creaturis exhibeant cultum Divinum, tamen idololatriam negant, addentes modò summis labris, se Sanctos, imagines &c. non ut Deum venerari, neque pro Deo habere. Nos verò cordatiores non patimur nos hoc φναxισμὸ transversos abripi; sed missis inanibus, rei hærentes, ut in capite de Sanctis fœdam idololatriam, ita hic detestandam Papolatriam agnoscimus, traducimúsque meritò.
units.tr: XLI. Nothing, therefore, helps the cause of the Papolaters, that they distinguish the Pope from God, and so the cult of the Pope from the cult of God, and protest that they do not venerate the Pope as the eternal God. Thus Costerus (Enchirid. cap. 3.) turns it to our great discredit that we say the Papists venerate the Pope as God and in place of the Deity. For this is the same play on words which they are accustomed to play also in the question of the adoration of saints: a play, I say, of mere sleight of words, but of certain confusion in the thing itself. It would be as if a robber wished to be acquitted because he professed himself a good man, or a harlot because she would not be called an adulteress, but claimed the praise of a chaste matron. As if true things had never lost their names, or that injustice, which Cicero says is the greatest of capital crimes, namely that the bad man wishes to be thought good, did not often prevail. In exactly this way the Papolaters are accustomed to dissemble the matter, content with the outward rattle of words. For while in fact they offer divine cult to creatures, yet they deny idolatry, adding only with their lips that they do not venerate saints, images and so on as God, nor hold them to be God. We, however, being more discerning, do not allow ourselves to be turned aside by this babbling [φλυαρισμόν]. Setting aside empty words and clinging to the thing itself, as in the chapter on the saints we recognise the foul idolatry, so here we recognise the detestable Papal idolatry, and rightly charge it upon them.

units.la: XLII. Interim haud raro sorex suo se indicio prodit. Crebrò enim Papolatris, moderante sic Numine, ea verba excidunt, quibus adorandum esse Papam, ut Deum, affirmant. Etenim Romualdus, qui teste Baronio ad A. 1177. n. 40. præsens fuit, cùm Fridericus Imp. Alexandrum III. adorâsset, ib. n. 68. sic de Imperatore eodem scribit: Cùm ad Papam appropiâssset, tactus Divino Spiritu, Deum in Alexandro venerans &c. Pontificis pedes exosculatus est. Et eodem sensu Aug. Steuchus Papæ Bibliothecarius, in libro suo contra Vallam, disertè dixit, Fideles in Papa ipsum Filium Dei venerari, & suspicere ipsum non tam mortalem hominem, quàm in ipso Deum ipsum, qui eum sibi in terris suffecerit. Sic ergo in Papa adorant Deum, ac si Papa non homo mortalis, sed Deus ipse esset. Idem Steuchus de Donat. Constant. p. 141. hæc habet: Audis, summum Pontificem à Con-stianstantino Deum appellatum, & habitum pro Deo. Adoravit ut Deum, ut Christi & Dei successorem, Divinos ei honores, quoad ejus potuit, contulit, &c. Industrius ille Saracenorum Princeps Baronio ad A. 1162. n. 2, 3. Alexandrum III. tanquam Sanctum & pium Christianorum Deum adorâsse dicitur. Petrus à Cordua, Comes Capræ & & Hieronymus Balbus, Episcopus Gurcensis, Ferdinandi Arthiducis Austriæ Oratores, Papæ vicariam Christi personam, quam gerit in terris, ut Divinam & Cœlestem colendam esse, dixêre: non improbante Bzovio de Rom. Pontif. pag. 55. Archipresbyteri Cardinalis Columnæ verba, quibus Lateranensis Basilicæ Clerum Papam venerari, colere, adorare, & se omniáque sua paternæ & plufquam Divinæ ipsius dispositioni reverenter submittere, testatur, supra th. 25. recitavimus.
units.tr: XLII. Meanwhile the mouse often gives itself away by its own squeak. For, God so ordering it, the Papolaters often let slip those words by which they affirm that the Pope is to be adored as God. For Romualdus, who according to Baronius (at year 1177, n. 40) was present when the Emperor Frederick adored Alexander III (ibid., n. 68), writes thus of that same emperor: When he had approached the Pope, touched by the Divine Spirit, venerating God in Alexander, etc., he kissed the Pontiff's feet. And in the same sense Augustinus Steuchus, librarian to the Pope, plainly said in his book against Valla: The faithful venerate in the Pope the Son of God himself, and look up to him not so much as a mortal man, but as God himself in him, who has put him in his place on earth. So in the Pope they adore God, as if the Pope were not a mortal man but God himself. The same Steuchus, (On the Donation of Constantine, p. 141), has these words: You hear that the supreme Pontiff was called God by Constantine and held as God. He adored him as God, as the successor of Christ and of God, and conferred divine honours upon him as far as he could, etc. That industrious prince of the Saracens, according to Baronius (at year 1162, n. 2, 3), is said to have adored Alexander III as the holy and pious God of the Christians. Peter of Cordua, Count of Capra, and Jerome Balbus, Bishop of Gurk, envoys of Archduke Ferdinand of Austria, said that the vicarious person of Christ, whom he bears on earth, is to be worshipped as divine and heavenly; Bzovius did not disapprove (On the Roman Pontiffs, p. 55). Above, at th. 25, we have quoted the words of the archpriest Cardinal Colonna, by which he testifies that the clergy of the Lateran basilica venerate, cultivate and adore the Pope, and reverently submit themselves and all their possessions to his paternal and more than divine disposition.

units.la: XLIII. Tertiò adorandum esse Papam oi iξ ἐvaslías contendunt, quatenus is est Pro-Deus, Pro-Christus, Christi Vicarius, Ecclesiæ Monarcha Religionis vertex, uti ipsum Cardinalis Gabriel Palæottus de Consult. S. Constit. p. 2. q. 3. pag. 75. appellat. Adoratio illa cùm civilis & merè humana dici non possit, utpote qua non propter ullum civilem vel merè humanum respestum, sed propter solam religionem adoratores defunguntur, religiosa & Divina sit oportet. Nam mediam nullam dari supra ostendimus. Accedit, quòd Ecclesiæ caput & Monarcha, religionis vertex, nisi Divinitatis particeps nemo esse potest: uti superiori etiam diatriba demonstravimus: quòdque adoratio ea Papæ eo modo defertur, qui specialis ei est, & nulli alii, Imperatori etiam vel Regi, communicabilis. Qua re aperta idololatria committitur. Si enim coleretur Papa honore cum aliis communi, fortè præcaveri idololatria posset. Sed cùm honor ille sit singularis, & soli Papæ debitus, & ab omnibus, & Christi loco, jam dubium non est, quin civilis cultus non gradum duntaxat, sed speciem egrediatur, adeoque merè religiosus & Divinus evadat.
units.tr: XLIII. Thirdly, they contend that the Pope is to be adored [oi iξ ἐvaslías] inasmuch as he is Pro-God, Pro-Christ, Vicar of Christ, Monarch of the Church, head of religion, as Cardinal Gabriel Paleotti himself calls him (de Consult. S. Constit. p. 2, q. 3, p. 75). Since that adoration cannot be called civil and merely human, being paid not for any civil or merely human respect but for religion alone, it must be religious and divine. For we have shown above that there is no middle ground. Moreover, the head and monarch of the Church, the head of religion, can be no one except a sharer in divinity, as we also demonstrated in the earlier discourse. And that adoration is paid to the Pope in a manner peculiar to him and not transferable to anyone else, not even to an emperor or king. By this, idolatry is openly committed. For if the Pope were honoured with a honour shared with others, idolatry might perhaps be guarded against. But since that honour is singular, due to the Pope alone, and paid by all in Christ's place, there is now no doubt that the civil worship passes beyond a mere degree into a different kind, and so becomes purely religious and divine.

units.la: XLIV. Argumenti hujus nervum tria adstringunt. Primum est, quod supra jam probare occupavimus, honorem, quem sè Papæ, ut Vicario Christi deferre præ se ferunt, in honorem Christi neutiquam redundare. Terminatur ergo & quiescit in Papa. Cúmque religiosus & divinus sit, Divinus ergo & religiosus honor in Papa quiescit & terminatur. Secundum est, quòd sic Pro-Deum illum, Pro-Christum, Vicarium Christi, Monarcham Ecclesiæ se adorare profitentur, ut ejus adoratio à Christi, qua Deus est, adoratione nihil differet. Sic enim Augustinus de Ancona Summ. de Pot. Eccles. q. 9. art. j. pag. 63. hanc quæstionem movet: Utrum Papæ debeatur honor, qui debetur Christo, secundum quod Deus? Respondet inter alia: Videtur, quòd honor, qui debetur Christo, secundum quod Deus, debeatur Papæ, quia honor debetur potestati. Sed una est potestas Christi, secundum quod Deus est; & Papæ. Quod probatur, quia potestas Christi secundum quod Deus est, peccata remittere, juxta illud Marc. II. 7. Quis potest peccata dimittere, nisi solus Deus? Illud autem convenit Papæ, quia quodcunque ligat vel solvit super terram, est ligatum vel solutum in Cœlis: sicut dictum est Petro Matth. xvj. 19. Idem ergo honor debetur utrique. Sed & Stevanus de Oscul. Papæ cap. iij. p. 27. hoc ipsum insinuat: Quis, inquit, potest negare, Apostolos Christi pedes, & locum plantis signatum, osculis minimè contigisse? Quis inficiari, eodem pacto non adorandos esse Divinos maximosque Sacerdotes? Cùm Spiritus S. Templa sint, & uberrimi fontes gratiarum, quæ per eorum manus in nos omnes effunduntur. Johannes de Turrecremata Eccles. Hier. p. y. lib. 5. pag. 298. Osculo, inquit, submissis humi genibus dato, non tantùm benevolentiam significaficamus, sed etiam honorem devotionem & observantiam, qua adstricti sumus, & tenemur Pontificem Christi personam in Ecclesia sustinentem, ceu ipsius Ecclesiæ fundamentum & basin perpetua cum reverentia venerari, & SANCTISSIMUM VELUT NUMEN excolere. Denique Adamus Tannerus Lojolita Tom: iij. Disp. 5. q. 2. dub. 2. n. 60. eandem in rem sic disserit: Vicarius Christi duplici potest honore coli. Primò per simplicem mentis apprehensionem, agnoscendo quodammodo in illo Christum, cujus personam & munus sustinet. Et hoc modo eodem cultu, quo Christus & homo colitur, adorari posset: ita quidem, ut talis cultus proprie & per se ad Christum, per accidens verò solum & relative ad Vicarium tenderet. Secundò juxta propriam dignitatem Vicarii, à Christi dignitate, quam ut homo, & Supremus Ecclesiæ moderator habet, derivatam, honore quodam inferiori: quem ipsum tamen ad eum habitum pertinere censeo, quo Christus idem, ut homo colitur. Tertium est, quòd in Missa & solenni Papæ processione major Papæ quàm Christo ipsi honor habeatur, quod supra th. vj. & ix. fusiùs paulò expositum, non repetimus.
units.tr: XLIV. Three things form the sinew of this argument. First is what we have already undertaken to prove above: the honour which they claim is paid to the Pope as Vicar of Christ does not in any way redound to the honour of Christ. It therefore terminates and rests in the Pope. And since it is religious and divine, divine and religious honour rests and terminates in the Pope. Second is that they profess to adore that Pro-God, Pro-Christ, Vicar of Christ, Monarch of the Church in such a way that his adoration differs in nothing from the adoration of Christ, who is God. For so Augustinus de Ancona (Summa de Potestate Ecclesiastica q. 9, art. 1, p. 63) raises this question: Whether the honour owed to Christ as God is owed to the Pope. He answers, among other things: It seems that the honour owed to Christ as God is owed to the Pope, because honour is owed to power. But the power of Christ as God and the power of the Pope are one. This is proved because the power of Christ as God is to forgive sins, according to Mark 2:7, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" But this belongs also to the Pope, since whatever he binds or looses on earth is bound or loosed in heaven, as was said to Peter, Matthew 16:19. Therefore the same honour is owed to both. Stevanus too (de Osculo Papae cap. 3, p. 27) hints at this very thing: Who, he says, can deny that the feet of the apostles of Christ, and the place marked by their soles, were never touched with kisses? Who can deny that in the same way the divine and greatest priests are not to be adored? Since they are temples of the Holy Spirit and the most abundant fountains of graces, which are poured out upon us all through their hands. Johannes de Turrecremata (Eccles. Hier. p. y, lib. 5, p. 298) says: By a kiss given with knees bent to the ground, we signify not only goodwill but also the honour, devotion and observance by which we are bound, and obliged to venerate with perpetual reverence the Pontiff who sustains the person of Christ in the Church, as the foundation and base of the Church itself, and to worship him as a VERY HOLY DIVINITY. Finally, Adamus Tannerus the Jesuit (Tom. 3, Disp. 5, q. 2, dub. 2, n. 60) argues to the same effect: The Vicar of Christ can be honoured in two ways. First, by a simple apprehension of the mind, recognising in him in some way Christ, whose person and office he sustains. And in this way he could be adored with the same worship by which Christ as man is worshipped, in such a way that such worship would be directed properly and of itself to Christ, but only by accident and relatively to the Vicar. Second, according to the Vicar's own dignity, derived from the dignity of Christ which he possesses as man and Supreme Governor of the Church, with a certain inferior honour: which I judge nonetheless to belong to that kind of honour by which Christ himself as man is worshipped. Third is that in the Mass and in the Pope's solemn procession, a greater honour is paid to the Pope than to Christ himself, which we have set out somewhat more fully above in theses 6 and 9 and do not repeat here.

units.la: XLV. Quartò is cultus religiosus & Divinus utique est, quo ab eo, qui colitur, maxima quæque & verè Divina beneficia petuntur, & expectantur Divina enim munera à solo Deo & Patre Cœlesti expectari possunt. Talis adoratio Papæ est. Eo enim argumento, quòd Papa remissionem peccatorum impertiri valeat, etiam pectoris tunsione eum adorari posse, Diana Resol. 8. p. 6, 7. confirmat. Est enim, inquit, pectoris tunsio signum agnoscentis peccata, & eorum remissionem petentis. Ita Panormitani, Æmilio Veronensi de gestis Franc. Lib. vj. p. 384. teste, per Oratores suos ad pedes Martini IV. strati, velut pro ara hostidque Christum, Agnum Dei salu-
units.tr: XLV. Fourthly, that cult is surely religious and divine by which the greatest and truly divine benefits are sought and expected from the one who is worshipped; for divine gifts can be expected from God and the Heavenly Father alone. Such is the adoration of the Pope. For Diana (Resol. 8, p. 6, 7) confirms, on the argument that the Pope can impart forgiveness of sins, that he may be adored even with beating of the breast. For, he says, beating the breast is a sign of acknowledging sins and of seeking their forgiveness. Thus, as Aemilius of Verona (de gestis Franc. lib. 6, p. 384) attests, the envoys of the Panormitans prostrated themselves at the feet of Martin IV, as if before an altar and a victim, saluting Christ, the Lamb of God, salu-

units.la: iv. Quia Papicolæ adorato Papa maxima queque & Divina sibi beneficia promittuntur. salutantes, illa etiam ex altaris mysteriis verba supplices effabantur: Qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nostri. Iterum, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nostri. Tertium, Qui tollis peccata mundi, dona nobis pacem. Christophorus quoque Marcellus in Concilio Lateranensi Sess. 4. Orationc ad Julium II. habita, sic eum adoravit: Ad te supplex, tanquam ad verum Principem Protectorem, Petram & Sponsum accedo, quem oro, obsecro & obtestor, si quae corporis sunt, & temporanea jura respiciunt, armis curâsti, quae ad cujusque animam pertinent, non armis, sed sanctissimis legibus cura. Id namque longè facilius agere poteris, quam quae hactenus egisti. Cura, inquam, Pater Beatissime, ut Sponsae tuae forma decorque redeat, & pulchritudo. Cura, ut grex tibi commissus optimis ac spiritualibus alimentis alatur & vivat. Cura ut valetudo haec, quae totum terrarum orbem invasit, abscedat. Cura ut fluctuanti naviculae, in alto à diris agitatae ventis, salutis portus illuceat. Cura, ne fruges, cujus es cultor, prae nimia ariditate siccescat. Cura, ut ovile unum fiat, quod modò est in partes divisum. Cura denique, ut salutem, quam dedisti nobis, & vitam & spiritum non amittamus. Tu enim Pastor, tu Medicus, tu Gubernator, tu Cultor, tu denique alter Deus in terris. Quicquamne Divinius, majus à Papa, ceu Pastore, Gubernatore, Medico, Cultore, Deo, salutis Datore expeti poterat? Addatur formula precum, quas à Cardinale Columna, nomine Cleri Basilicae Lateranensis ad Innocentium X. fusas, supra thesi v. recitavimus: ubi inter alia: Nos te, solum nostrum Patronum, Summum Caput & Episcopum ac Spiritalem Patrem unicè veneramur, colimus & adoramus, & nos omniáque nostra paterne ET PLUS QUAM DIVINÆ Tuae dispositioni ac curae reverenter submittimus, ac unicè commendamus. Claves enim ligandi ac solvendi, quas Christus ipse S. Petro tradidit, ejúsque omnibus successoribus reliquit, Tuæ Sanctitati submisse offerimus in nomine Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Amen.
units.tr: iv. Because to Papists, when the Pope is adored, the greatest and divine benefits are promised, saluting, they also uttered in supplication those words taken from the mysteries of the altar: Who takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us. Again, Who takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us. Thirdly, Who takest away the sins of the world, grant us peace. Christophorus Marcellus too, in the Lateran Council, session 4, in his oration addressed to Julius II, adored him in this way: I come to you as a suppliant, as to the true Prince, Protector, Rock and Bridegroom, whom I beg, entreat and implore: if the things of the body and temporal rights are your concern, you have taken care of them with arms; let the things that pertain to each one's soul be cared for not with arms but with most holy laws. You will be able to do this far more easily than what you have done until now. Take care, I say, most blessed Father, that the form and beauty of your Bride may return. Take care that the flock committed to you may be nourished and live on the best and spiritual food. Take care that this sickness, which has invaded the whole world, may depart. Take care that for the little ship tossed on the deep by dire winds, the harbour of salvation may shine forth. Take care that the crops, of which you are the tiller, not dry up from excessive drought. Take care that the fold may be made one, which is now divided into parts. Take care, finally, that we do not lose the salvation, the life and the spirit, which you have given us. For you are the Shepherd, you the Physician, you the Governor, you the Tiller, you finally another God on earth. Could anything more divine be sought from the Pope, as from a Shepherd, Governor, Physician, Tiller, God, and Giver of salvation? Add the form of prayers which, poured out to Innocent X by Cardinal Colonna in the name of the clergy of the Lateran Basilica, we have quoted above in thesis 5, where among other things: We alone venerate, worship and adore you, our sole Patron, Supreme Head, Bishop and Spiritual Father, and we humbly submit ourselves and all that is ours to your paternal and more than divine disposition and care, and we commend ourselves to you alone. For the keys of binding and loosing, which Christ himself gave to St Peter and left to all his successors, we humbly offer to your Holiness, in the name of God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

units.la: XLVI. Quinto adorationis Papalis ceremoniæ Divinum & religiosum cultum manifeste arguunt. Ego paucas non- nullas attingam. Pectoris tunsio in nullius unquam hominis honorem adhibita est. Signum enim est compunctionis internæ cordis, qua peccata adversus Deum admissa homo agnoscit, dolet, detestatur, & sibi remitti cupit, Luc. xviii. 13. Act. ii. 37. Augustinus Enarrat. 2. in Psal. 31. & 146. Tu, inquit, dirige cor tuum, non potes? Tu frange, ille dirigat; quomodo tamen franges? quomodo tamen conteres? Confitendo, puniendo peccata tua. Quid aliud significat pectorum tunsio, nisi forte putamus, ossa nostra peccasse, aliquid cædimus & tundimus pectus? Sed significamus nos cor conterere, ut à Domino dirigatur. Diana Resol. 8. p. 6, 7. occasione motus civis sui, pectus bis tundentis, cum Papam tiara redimitum portari vidisset, dubitasse se ait, an ex condicto sic adorare Pontificem esset licitum? Addit: Et in rigore ac speculative loquendo adhæsi sententiæ affirmativæ. Raphaëlis de la Torre in eandem sententiam verba supra attuli.
units.tr: XLVI. Fifthly, the ceremonies of papal adoration plainly indicate divine and religious worship. I shall touch on a few. Beating the breast has never been employed in honour of any man. For it is a sign of inward contrition of heart, by which a man acknowledges, grieves over and detests the sins committed against God, and desires them to be forgiven (Luke 18:13; Acts 2:37). Augustine (Enarrat. 2 in Psal. 31 and 146): You say, direct your heart; can you not? You break it, let him direct it; but how will you break it? How will you crush it? By confessing and punishing your sins. What else does the beating of the breast signify, unless perhaps we think our bones have sinned, and strike and beat our chest? But we signify that we crush the heart, so that it may be directed by the Lord. Diana (Resol. 8, p. 6, 7), on the occasion of a fellow citizen who beat his breast twice when he saw the Pope carried, crowned with the tiara, says that he doubted whether it was lawful to adore the Pontiff in this way by prior agreement? He adds: And speaking strictly and speculatively, I adhered to the affirmative opinion. I have already cited Raphael de la Torre's words to the same effect above.

units.la: XLVII. Par ferè ratio est incensi, seu thurificationis. Cornelius à Lapide in Malach. j. 11. agnoscit, omnium gentium usu & ritu Deo thus adoleri. Idem in Daniel. y. 46. Thus, inquit, & suffitus nunquam à Principibus usurpata videntur, nisi cum insanientes adversus Numen Divinos honores affectárunt. Sanè etiam Israëlitis maximo datum vitio est, cùm serpenti æneo, typo Christi, thus adoleverunt, 2 Reg. xviii. 4. Atqui Papam incensari, & in solio sedentem cum mitra, & stantem à stante, ter ducente tractum thuribulum, cum aliqua distantia inter tractum & tractum, Marcellus Cerem. S. lib. iij. tit. 2. cap. 13. p. 120. scribit; & historiæ Conclavium, aliæque testantur.
units.tr: XLVII. Burning incense, or thurification, is much the same. Cornelius à Lapide, on Malachi 1:11, acknowledges that incense is offered to God by the custom and rite of all nations. On Daniel 6:46 he says: "Incense and fumigation never seem to have been used by princes except when, in their madness, they claimed divine honours against the Divine Majesty." Indeed, the Israelites were greatly blamed for burning incense to the bronze serpent, a type of Christ (2 Kings 18:4). Yet Marcellus writes (Caerem. S. lib. 3, tit. 2, cap. 13, p. 120) that the Pope is incensed while sitting on his throne with his mitre, and while standing before one who stands, the censer being swung three times, with some interval between each swing. The histories of the Conclaves and others bear witness to this.

units.la: XLVIII. Imprimis ceremonia illa, qua Papa recens electus in altari primò quidem Sacrarii Conclavis, post Templi D. Petri sedens vel cubans à Cardinalibus cernuis adoratur, religiosum & Divinum cultum apertissimè redolet. Ceremoniam ipsam ex Marcello Thesi iv. exposuimus: & de ea pariter historiæ Conclavium, & experientia unanimiter testantur. Solentque Itali illam adorationem per excellentiam l'adoratione appellare. Altaria porrò ad cultum foli Deo debitum pertinere, Bellarminus de Sanct. Beatitud. cap. 12. fatetur. Et constat planè, altaria ipsorum haberi ad sacrificia Deo offerenda, & Deum in iis adorandum. Cùm ergo Papam sic in altari consistentem adorant, quid aliud, quàm Deum, seu Idolum suum ibi adorant, ac religioso & Divino cultu prosequuntur? Mitto ceremonias reliquas, quas licet natura sua indifferentes ad utrumque Divinum & humanum cultum, illi tamen religionis testificandæ gratia omnes obeunt.
units.tr: XLVIII. First of all, that ceremony in which a newly elected Pope, first in the sacristy of the Conclave and afterwards in St Peter's Church, sits or reclines while the Cardinals kneel and adore him, plainly smells of religious and divine worship. We have set out the ceremony itself from Marcellus, Thesis 4, and the histories of the Conclaves and experience unanimously bear witness to it. The Italians commonly call that adoration, by excellence, "l'adoratione". Moreover, Bellarmine admits (de Sanct. Beatitud. cap. 12) that altars belong to the worship due to God alone. And it is plain that their altars are held to be for offering sacrifices to God, and for worshipping God upon them. Since, therefore, they adore the Pope standing thus at the altar, what else do they do than adore there their God, or Idol, and pay him religious and divine worship? I pass over the other ceremonies which, though in their own nature indifferent to both divine and human worship, they nevertheless all perform in order to attest their religion.

units.la: XLIX. Sextò Papæ cultus haud inferior illo est, quem Papicolæ Angelis, Deiparæ, Sanctis, Eucharistiæ, cruci, imaginibus Christi, Sanctorum reliquiis impertiuntur, & quem olim arcæ fœderis exhibitum illi pertendunt. Singula equidem probari pluribus possent. Nos defungemur paucis. De Angelis, supra thesi xvÿ. Antoninum Archiepiscopum Florentinum sic argutantem vidimus, quòd Papa Angelis major sit, quia ille adoretur, hi adorari se passi non sint. Augustinus de Ancona de Eccles. Pol. q. 9. art. 4. p. 65. instituta quæstione: An Papæ debeatur honos, qui debetur Angelis? sic inter alia respondet pariter: Apoc. ultimo scribitur, quòd Angelus, qui loquebatur cum Johanne, non permisit se adorari ab eo, dicens: Vide ne feceris; Conservus tuus sum, & fratrum tuorum. Sed Papa recipit à fidelibus Ecclesiæ adorationes, prostrationes & oscula pedum. Ergo major honor exhibetur Papæ, quàm Angelis. Papæ: Sic enim Indi quoque majorem Diabolo, quàm Angelis honorem exhibent. Deiparæ & Papæ cultum sic Raynaudus Monast. Pontif. Sub not. 3. fr. 1. comparat: Porrò spectata tam sublimi Pontificis dignitate, quæ est venerationis Pontifici debitæ fundamentum, addendum est, non qualemcunque cultum ei esse impendendum, sed supra communem ordinem cultus religiosi Sanctis tributi; ita ut cùm Sanctis exhibeatur cultus duliæ, spectata sola eorum sanctitate, Pontifici tamen debeatur cultus hyperduliæ. Nam ejus conjunctio cum Christo quoad fundamentum reverentiæ est longe altior, quicquid sit de Sanctitate personali. Sicut Beata virgo, quæ habet excellentiam specie diversam ab ea, quæ fundatur in gratia, nempe maternitatem, colitur adoratione superiore, quàm sit ea, quæ fundatur in sola sanctificante gratia, ut rectè statuit Suarez. 1,2,3. p. disp. 22. sect. 3. qui anceps est, an cultus ille sit religionis strictè sumta, à qua oritur Dei & Christi adoratio, an verò oriatur à speciali habitu, ob specialem Virginis dignitatem cultus prædicti fundatricem. Quod secundum circa B. Virginem mihi placet. Et ob paritatem rationis idem statuo in re præsenti circa cultum impensum Vicario Christi. Sanctorum & Papæ cultum sic Aug. de Ancona loc. cit. q. 9. art. 3. p. 65. comparat: Honorantur & adorantur Sancti & Sanctæ dulia: quo honore similiter honoratur Papa. Imò majorem Papæ quàm Sanctis cultum deberi, jam modò Raynaudum asserentem vidimus. Sed & Eucharistiæ ac crucis & Papæ cultum pari passu ambulare, Caramuel de Hierarch. Eccles. lib. 3. disp. 60. n. 580. insinuat. Instituta enim quæstione, An Papa etiam impius à fidelibus adorandus sit? illud crudè affirmat eo argumento, quòd etiam crux è Caini, aut Judæ, aut cujuscunque alius hominis damnati cineribus formata; & Eucharistia, quam hæreticus in stercora projecit, adoretur. Faciunt huc, quæ de adoratione Papæ in Missa Thesi vj. edisseruimus. Majorem quinetiam honorem Papæ, quàm imagini Christi deberi, Augustinus de Ancona loc.cit.p. 66. sic arguit: Videtur, quòd major honor debeatur Papæ, quàm imagini Christi, quia Papa est imago Dei naturalis, secundùm rationalem animam. Sed pictura Christi artificialis imago est. Major ergo honor debetur Papæ, quàm imagini Christi. Quidni autem, cùm Papam, velut vivam Christi imaginem à Constantino adoratum Steuchus de Donat.Const. M. p. 141. nos edocuerit? Idem, qui supra, Raphaël de la Torre in 2. 2. D. Thom. tom. 2. q. 84. art. 5. disp. 5. n. 26. oscula ossibus Sanctorum, & Pontificis pedibus infixa comparat, & utraque religiosæ adorationis species facit. Denique quid simílius est adoratione Papæ, & adoratione ea, qua adoratam olim arcam fœderis illi asserunt? Sicut enim olim à Levitis bajulabatur arca fœderis, atque sic bajulata, Papicolarum quidem sententia, adorabatur, ceu Jehova scilicet, uti Innocentius III. de Myst. Missæ lib. j. 15. docere vult: sic planè Papa in aurato solio sublimis, succollantibus Cardinalibus, ad eundem modum circumgestatur, & à Papolatris adoratur.
units.tr: XLIX. Sixthly, the worship of the Pope is no less than that which the Papists give to Angels, the Mother of God, the Saints, the Eucharist, the cross, images of Christ and relics of the Saints, and which they claim was once paid to the ark of the covenant. Each point could indeed be proved by many examples; we shall dispatch them briefly. Concerning Angels, above at Thesis 15, we saw Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, arguing thus: the Pope is greater than the Angels, because he is adored, whereas they did not allow themselves to be adored. Augustinus de Ancona (de Eccles. Pol. q. 9, art. 4, p. 65), raising the question "Is the honour owed to Angels owed also to the Pope?", answers among other things: "In the last chapter of Revelation it is written that the Angel who spoke with John did not allow himself to be adored by him, saying: 'See that you do not do it; I am your fellow servant and of your brethren.' But the Pope receives from the faithful of the Church adorations, prostrations and kisses of the feet. Therefore greater honour is shown to the Pope than to the Angels." Indeed, the Indians likewise show greater honour to the Devil than to the Angels. Raynaudus (Monast. Pontif., sub not. 3, fr. 1) compares the worship of the Mother of God with that of the Pope thus: "Moreover, considering the so sublime dignity of the Pontiff, which is the foundation of the veneration due to him, it must be added that he is to be given not just any worship, but worship above the common order of religious worship paid to the Saints. Thus, whereas the worship of dulia is given to the Saints, considering only their sanctity, the Pontiff is owed the worship of hyperdulia. For his conjunction with Christ, as the foundation of reverence, is far higher, whatever may be said of personal sanctity. Just as the Blessed Virgin, who has an excellence of a different kind from that founded on grace, namely her motherhood, is worshipped with a higher adoration than that founded on sanctifying grace alone, as Suarez rightly determines (1,2,3, disp. 22, sect. 3), who is uncertain whether that worship belongs to religion strictly taken, from which the adoration of God and Christ arises, or whether it arises from a special habit, the founder of that worship being the Virgin's special dignity. Of these, the second pleases me concerning the Blessed Virgin. And by the same reasoning I hold the same in the present matter, concerning the worship paid to the Vicar of Christ." Augustinus de Ancona (loc. cit., q. 9, art. 3, p. 65) compares the worship of the Saints with that of the Pope thus: "The Saints, men and women, are honoured and adored with dulia; with the same honour the Pope is honoured." Indeed, we have just seen Raynaudus asserting that greater worship is owed to the Pope than to the Saints. Caramuel (de Hierarch. Eccles. lib. 3, disp. 60, n. 580) also hints that the worship of the Eucharist and of the cross goes hand in hand with that of the Pope. For, raising the question "Must the Pope be adored by the faithful even if he is impious?", he flatly affirms it, on the ground that even a cross formed from the ashes of Cain, or of Judas, or of any other damned man, and the Eucharist which a heretic has cast into the dung, are adored. What we set out in Thesis 6 about the adoration of the Pope in the Mass bears on this. Augustinus de Ancona (loc. cit., p. 66) argues further that greater honour is owed to the Pope than to an image of Christ: "It seems that greater honour is owed to the Pope than to an image of Christ, because the Pope is the natural image of God according to his rational soul. But a painted picture of Christ is an artificial image. Therefore greater honour is owed to the Pope than to an image of Christ." And why not, since Steuchus (de Donat. Const. M., p. 141) has informed us that Constantine adored the Pope as "a living image of Christ"? The same Raphael de la Torre as above (in 2.2 D. Thom., tom. 2, q. 84, art. 5, disp. 5, n. 26) compares kisses pressed on the bones of the Saints with those pressed on the Pope's feet, and makes both kinds of religious adoration. Lastly, what is more like the adoration of the Pope than that adoration by which they claim the ark of the covenant was once adored? For just as the ark of the covenant was once carried by the Levites, and so carried was adored, in the opinion of the Papists, as Jehovah himself, as Innocent III (de Myst. Missae lib. 1, 15) wishes to teach, so plainly the Pope, raised high on his golden throne, is carried about in the same way, with Cardinals bearing him on their shoulders, and is adored by the Papolaters.

units.la: L. Angelorum porrò, Deiparæ, Sanctorum, Eucharistiæ, crucis, imaginum Christi, ossium Sanctorum cultum religiosum esse, & olim arcæ fœderis religiosum fuisse, ipsimet adversarii contendunt. Nos addimus, & religiosum & Divinum cultum esse, quem iis impendunt, tum quia religiosum à Divino separari non potest, supra probavimus: tum quia adoratio, invocatio, & omnis illæ cultus, quem objectis illis deferunt, Divinitatem quandam in adoratis, invocatis, cultis supponunt; uti quidem alibi demonstravimus. Prono planè hinc alveo fluit, etiam Papæ cultum, ut pote earum, quas diximus, rerum cultui vel parem, vel superiorem, religiosum planè & Divinum esse.
units.tr: L. Moreover, that the worship of Angels, the Mother of God, the Saints, the Eucharist, the cross, images of Christ and the bones of the Saints is religious, and that the worship of the ark of the covenant was once religious, the adversaries themselves contend. We add that the worship they pay to these is both religious and divine: religious, because religious worship cannot be separated from divine, as we have proved above; and divine, because adoration, invocation, and all that worship which they offer to these objects presupposes some divinity in the things adored, invoked and worshipped, as we have shown elsewhere. From this it flows plainly, as down a steep channel, that the worship of the Pope too, being equal or superior to the worship of those things we have mentioned, is plainly religious and divine.

units.la: LI. Septimò cultus duliæ, hyperduliæ, latriæ, à Pontificiis sic distinctus, religiosus haud dubiè, adeóque etiam Divinus est. Papæ verò adorationem Papicolæ alii ad duliæ, alii ad hyperduliæ, ad latriæ cultum alii referunt. Infra aliquem ex iis cultús generibus cum subsidere, vix quisquam ex illis affirmaverit. Quanquam discordes calculi sunt, adorarecio illa Papæ ad cultum duliæ, hyperduliæ, an latriæ referri debeat.
units.tr: LI. Seventhly, the worship of dulia, hyperdulia and latria, as the Papists distinguish them, is undoubtedly religious, and therefore also divine. But the Papists refer the adoration of the Pope, some to the worship of dulia, some to hyperdulia, and others to latria. Hardly anyone among them would affirm that it rests on any one of these kinds of worship. Although their opinions disagree as to whether the adoration of the Pope should be referred to dulia, hyperdulia or latria.
