units.la: LII. Sub quo adorationum harum genere adoratio Pontificis comprehendatur, quæstionem movet Diana Panormitanus Resol. 11. &c. pag. 8. &c. & variantes sententias recenset. Sunt ergo, qui ad duliam referant. Sic ipse Diana pag. 10. &c., quos sibi consentientes ibi allegat, Baldellus, & Mazaronius. Sunt, qui ad hyperduliam referant. Ita Raynaudus, cujus verba th. xlix. retulimus. Neque aliter Legati illi Florentini, quorum orationem Antoninus Florentinus recensuit loco & verbis, quæ thesi ÿ. jam expressimus. Denique Caramuel Hierarch. Eccles. lib. j. disp. 60. utramque & latriæ & duliæ adorationem Papæ competere pertendit. Potest enim, inquit, Papa considerari ut quod; potest ut quo. Et consideratur priori modo, quando ut persona: & posteriori modo, quando ut imago, umbra; quando ut ProChristus; quando ut Pro-Deus, hoc est, Christi Vicarius, Profectò Dulia cultum nemo Patri Optimo Maximo negare audebit, qui sciat in tabulis Divinis legem esse, quæ Parentes honorari præcipiat. Hic cultus debetur Pontifici considerato, ut quod. Quatenus enim homo est, est homo sacer, homo summus, & cæteris universis prælatus. At si consideretur, ut quo, ut Vicarius Christi, ut via ad terminum, ubi cessat erraudi periculum, Latriæ cultum requiret, eo sensu, quo cetere imagines Christi; cultum, inquam, qui non terminetur ad lapides, ad ligna, non ad carnem, aut sanguinem, sed ad Christum. Infra: Quia inter alias imagines Pro-Rex est Regis imago intelligibilis, cultu, quo cœ-terœ materiales Regis ex digniore motivo honorari debebit. Ergo idem dici debebit Pro-Christo. Quo enim sensu est intelligibilis imago Christi, eo debebit coli, sicut cœterœ imagines. Hactenus ille. Latriæ ergo cultum Papæ etiam vendicat; addens, terminari eum in Christo, cujus Papa visibilis imago sit. Cùm verò Christus eum in imagine tali cultum nec præceperit, nec acceptet; atque eum in honorem Christi neutiquam redundare supra probaverimus: terminabitur ergo & quiescet in Papa; atque sic cultus latriæ absolutus erit, quo Idolum hoc suum Papolatræ profequuntur. Faciunt huc illa Augustini de Ancona loc. cit. pag. 63.
units.tr: LII. Under which kind of these adorations the adoration of the Pontiff is comprised, Diana of Palermo raises the question (Resol. 11, etc., p. 8 etc.) and lists the differing opinions. Some therefore refer it to dulia: thus Diana himself (p. 10 etc.), citing as agreeing with him Baldellus and Mazaronius. Some refer it to hyperdulia: so Raynaudus, whose words we quoted in Thesis 49, and likewise those Florentine legates whose speech Antoninus of Florence recounted, in the place and words we have already set out in Thesis 5. Lastly, Caramuel (Hierarch. Eccles. lib. 1, disp. 60) contends that both latria and dulia adoration befit the Pope. For, he says, the Pope can be considered as quod (that which) and as quo (that by which). He is considered in the first way when as a person, and in the second way when as image, shadow; when as Pro-Christ; when as Pro-God, that is, Vicar of Christ. Surely no one who knows that the Divine tables contain a law commanding parents to be honoured will dare to deny dulia worship to the Most Good and Most Great Father. This worship is due to the Pontiff considered as quod: for insofar as he is a man, he is a holy man, a supreme man, and set above all others. But if he is considered as quo, as Vicar of Christ, as the way to the end, where the danger of error ceases, he will require latria worship, in the sense in which the other images of Christ [are worshipped]: worship, I say, which does not terminate on stones or wood, nor on flesh or blood, but on Christ. Further on: "For among other images the Pro-King is an intelligible image of the King, and is to be honoured with the same worship with which the other material images of the King are honoured, and for a more worthy motive. Therefore the same must be said of the Pro-Christ. For in whatever sense he is an intelligible image of Christ, in that sense he must be worshipped, like the other images." So far he. Thus he also claims latria worship for the Pope, adding that it terminates in Christ, of whom the Pope is the visible image. But since Christ has neither commanded nor accepted such worship of an image, and we have proved above that it in no way redounds to the honour of Christ, it will therefore terminate and rest in the Pope; and so the worship of latria will be complete, with which the Papolaters pursue this their Idol. The passages of Augustinus de Ancona (loc. cit., p. 63) bear on this.

units.la: Latria est servitus debita soli Deo. Latinè enim servitus, Græcè latria dicitur. Sed omnis servitus debetur Papæ. Ergo omnis honor, qui debetur Deo, debetur Papæ. Quid vobis, Papicolæ, videtur?
units.tr: Latria is the service owed to God alone. For in Latin it is called servitus, and in Greek latria. But all service is owed to the Pope. Therefore all honour that is owed to God is owed to the Pope. What do you think of this, you Pope-worshippers?

units.la: LIII. Octavò denique accedunt suffragia Adversariorum, quæ Papæ adorationem, religiosum Divinúmque cultum esse, ambigere non sinunt. Plura corraserunt alii. Nos pauca delibabimus. Fridericus II. Imperator fortissimus, qui Papæ Sinonias artes maximè compertas habuit, in suis ad Principes literis, ab Aventino lib. vÿ. recensitis, sic inter alia queritur: Pontifices Romani auêti divitiis & dignitate, æmuli sunt pertinacissimi omnium Regum atque Principum, neque parem ultra ferre possunt. Manibus pedibúsque noctes diésque id conantur, ut non tam me, quàm Sacrosancto Imperio Romano oppresso, facilè cœteris membris omnibus servitutem imponant. Affectant dominationem atque Divinitatem, nempe ut ab omnibus haud aliter, imò magis, quàm Deus timeantur. Concors ei Ludovicus Bavarus, Imperator omni laude major, Aventino eodem libro teste, in publico Edicto hæc de Johanne xxii. verba fecit: Se similem Altissimo facit (pla-
units.tr: LIII. Eighthly and finally, the testimonies of our adversaries add weight, and they do not let us doubt that the adoration of the Pope is religious and divine worship. Others have gathered many; we shall pluck only a few. The most valiant Emperor Frederick II, who had the clearest knowledge of the Pope's Simonian arts, complains in his letters to the princes, cited by Aventinus book 5, as follows, among other things: The Roman Pontiffs, swollen with riches and dignity, are the most stubborn rivals of all kings and princes, and can no longer bear an equal. Day and night they strive with hand and foot to put servitude on all the other members, and not so easily on me as on the holy Roman Empire, once it is crushed. They aim at lordship and divinity, so that they may be feared by all no differently, indeed more, than God. In agreement with him, Louis of Bavaria, an Emperor greater than all praise, in a public edict, as Aventinus in the same book attests, spoke these words about John XXII: He makes himself like the Most High (plain-

units.la: Quia adorationem Papæ religiosum et Divinum cultum esse... (planè, ùti de Babylone Esajas cap. xiv. 14. loquitur) sè adorari, quod Cœlitum quidam sibi à Johanne fieri prohibuit, pedes sibi ufculari more Diocletiani atque Alexandri, crudelissimorum tyrannorum, permittit. Cùm Christus manceps Divinitatis Dominus & Deus noster, pedes comitum suorum piscatorùmque laverit. Johannes Gerson Serm. j. de Angelis: Diabolus, inquit, tanto studio ab hominibus extorsit; & extorquere non cessat, ut adoraretur sicut Deus: imò ut extollatur super omne, quod dicitur Deus. Etiam homines utique Mortales, id est, ærumnis subditos hæc portentosa rabies invasit. Patuit in Nabuchodonosor, Cosdroë &c. Et verendum est, proh dolor, ne in Prælatos quosdam se hujusmodi insaniei virus infuderit: qui æquo animo tolerant se creatores, & eorum subditos suas creaturas ab eisdem appellari. Etenim quo nomine potiùs adorabitur Deus, quàm si Creator nuncuparetur; aut quæ differentia erit ad hominem, & ad Deum, si homo alterius creatura nominetur: & quo ampliùs indigueris. Hoc de se illi patiuntur facto, qui omnium se servos fatentur. Sed hos jam linquamus, qui bonis monitoribus obsurduerunt. Ludovicus ab Alcafar in carmine ad Johannem Apostolum, Commentario in Apocalypsin præfixo, de Paulo V.
units.tr: Because the adoration of the Pope is religious and divine worship... (plainly, as Isaiah in chapter 14 speaks of Babylon, verse 14) that he is adored, which one of the heavenly beings forbade John to do, and he allows his feet to be kissed in the manner of Diocletian and Alexander, the cruellest tyrants. Yet Christ, the chief Lord and our God of divinity, washed the feet of his companions and fishermen. John Gerson, Sermon 1 on the Angels: The devil, he says, has with such eagerness wrung from men, and does not cease to wring, that he should be adored as God; indeed that he should be exalted above everything that is called God. This monstrous madness has seized even mortal men, that is, those subject to miseries. It was plain in Nebuchadnezzar, Chosroes, etc. And we must fear, alas, lest he has poured the poison of this kind of madness into certain prelates, who bear with equanimity being called creators, and their subjects being called by them their creatures. For by what name would God be rather adored than if he were called Creator; or what difference will there be between man and God, if a man is named the creature of another; and the more you lack. These men suffer this to be done to themselves, who confess themselves the servants of all. But let us now leave these men, who have grown deaf to good advisers. Ludovicus ab Alcafar, in a poem to the Apostle John prefixed to his Commentary on the Apocalypse, concerning Paul V:

units.la: Quem Numinis instar Vera colit pietas
units.tr: Whom true piety worships as the likeness of the Deity

units.la: Jacobus Gordonus Huntlæus Epit. Controv. T. j. Controv. 2. c. 26. questus, criminari nostros, quòd Papa à suis adoretur, sic illum pag. 253. purgat: Si Deus in ea fuit voluntate, ut homines adorarent pedes Episcopi Philadelphiæ (quasi ante fidelium pedes, quod eorum, qui à fidelibus victi, iisque subjecti sunt, est adorare, quod de quibusdam ab Ecclesia victis Apoc. iii. 9. dicitur; sit pedes eorundem osculari, atque sic eosdem adorare) multò magis acceptum & gratum erit Deo, quòd Christiani homines pio affectu ad pedes supremi Episcopi totius Ecclesiæ, se prosternant, eíque osculi signo exhibeant adorationem non civilem duntaxat, sed etiam religiosam, nempe propter Deum, & Dei causa. Petrus à Cordua & Hieronymus Balbus, Gurcensis Episcopus, Ferdinandi Archiducis Austriæ Oratores, Bzovio in suo Romano Pontifice p. 55. laudante, sic loquuntur: Indubitatus Jesu Christi Vicarius, verus Petri successor, Christianorum Princeps, & universalis Dominus, vicaria Christi persona, quam gerit in terris, ut Divina & Cœlestis colenda est. Addenda sunt hisce suffragia Polydori Vergilii, Cuspiniani, Augustini Steuchi, Stevani, Antonini Florentini, Mazaronii, Baldelli, de la Torre, Raynaudi, Tanneri, Caramuelis, Dianæ, aliorum, quæ superius ἀπαρρήδην[?] expressa repetere nihil attinet.
units.tr: James Gordon of Huntly, in his Epitome of the Controversies, vol. 1, controversy 2, chapter 26, complaining that we accuse them because the Pope is adored by his own people, clears him as follows, page 253: If God was so minded that men should adore the feet of the Bishop of Philadelphia (as if before the feet of the faithful, which is to adore those who have been conquered by the faithful and are subject to them, as is said of certain people conquered by the Church in Revelation 3:9; that is, to kiss their feet and so adore them) it would be much more acceptable and pleasing to God that Christian men, with pious feeling, prostrate themselves at the feet of the supreme Bishop of the whole Church, and show him by the sign of a kiss an adoration not merely civil but also religious, namely on account of God and for God's sake. Peter of Cordova and Hieronymus Balbus, Bishop of Gurk, envoys of the Archduke Ferdinand of Austria, as Bzovius praises them in his Roman Pontiff, page 55, speak thus: The undoubted Vicar of Jesus Christ, the true successor of Peter, the Prince of Christians and universal Lord, in the vicarious person of Christ which he bears on earth, is to be worshipped as divine and heavenly. To these testimonies must be added those of Polydore Vergil, Cuspinian, Augustinus Steuchus, Stephanus, Antoninus of Florence, Mazarin, Baldelli, de la Torre, Raynaud, Tanner, Caramuel, Diana, and others; there is no need to repeat those already set out expressly [ἀπαρρήδην] above.

units.la: LIV. Sic ergo, Papam & Divinitatem, & cultum Divinum religiosum sibi vendicare, firmissimè comprobavimus, meritóque ei verbis Dei ipsius Zachar. xi. 17. sic acclamamus: הוי רעי האליל[?] Væ Tibi, Pastor Idolum, qui derelinquis gregem. Gladius erit super brachium tuum, & super oculum tuum. Dextrum brachium tuum arescendo arescet, & oculus tuus dexter caligando caligabit. Concludimus tandem Hierarchiam seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem, cæteris paribus, esse Babylonem Magnam, scortationum illam infamem & turpissimam Matrem: quod quintum demonstrationis nostræ caput erat.
units.tr: LIV. Thus we have most firmly proved that the Pope claims for himself both divinity and religious divine worship; and rightly we cry out to him in the very words of God, Zechariah 11:17: Woe to you, idol shepherd, who forsakes the flock. A sword shall be upon your arm and upon your eye. Your right arm shall utterly wither, and your right eye shall be utterly darkened. [הוי רעי האליל] Finally we conclude that the dominant hierarchy or clergy of the Roman Church, other things being equal, is Great Babylon, that infamous and most shameful mother of harlotries; and this was the fifth head of our demonstration.
